## [The Complete Works of St. Martin of León.]

[Col. 0009]

## The Printer to the Reader

The works of St. Martin, a priest and a canon under the Rule of St. Augustine in the royal monastery of León dedicated to St. Isidore, are now brought to light for the first time, nearly six centuries after their composition. Indeed, it has long been the desire of men who have rendered the Christian commonwealth excellent service that this work should be published. Above all, the canons regular who inhabited the monastery of St. Isidore especially wished the writings of their fellow-member and colleague Martin to be issued to the public. Yet they attempted the Martinian edition in vain: for a good undertaking, as they say, begun under ill-omened auspices, did not reach its desired conclusion.

But since we possessed a completed copy of these works, furnished with no insignificant annotations, prepared by command of the Most Excellent Lord Francisco Antonio, Archbishop of Toledo, and drawn from the fountainhead itself with the utmost fidelity and diligence possible, we firmly and without hesitation resolved that it should issue as soon as possible from our printing-house. Nor, in adopting such a resolution, were we guided by premature haste and our own judgment alone; rather, we awaited the counsel and opinion of men eminent for learning. After approving our wishes, they urged us, by encouragements in some cases and by weighty reasons in others, not to abandon the undertaking. The saying is addressed to one who is willing.

You have therefore, kindly reader, the works of St. Martin carefully printed by our press; through their constant reading you may draw forth most abundant fruits of virtue. Here the foundations of a purer ethics are laid; here the dignity of Christian philosophy, as though set in a place of safety, diffuses the rays of truth in every direction. Thus you will find nothing not measured by the standard of the Catholic religion, nothing that does not breathe moral holiness. Nor is this surprising: in composing his own books the author made use—to pass over others—of the teaching of Saints Gregory and Isidore, and also of the Master of the *Sentences* and the *Summa Theologica*; from their most fruitful field he selected all that was best with great discernment and prudence. If at times, however, you find certain passages mutilated, or certain matters dislodged from their proper places, we judge this should be attributed to the ignorance of copyists—unless our Martin appears to have excerpted not so much the words of those Doctors as their meaning. Be that as it may, we have found everything consistent with the intention of its own author; therefore we considered it a matter of conscience to alter nothing.

Yet Martin claimed for himself a fuller store of learning from the rich treasury of Holy Scripture, in searching out—or carefully expounding—whose inner recesses he is wholly occupied. He diligently explains the mysteries of both Laws; he brings the oracles of the prophets into the open; according to the allegorical sense, he discusses the events of the Jews as so many figures of our Lord Jesus Christ, and establishes and confirms, against Jewish objections, Christ’s divinity, foreshadowed of old by so many deeds of the Fathers of the Synagogue, using arguments drawn from every side. Since this is so, we trust that no small benefit will result from the publication of this book.

As for his manner of speaking, we do not hesitate to employ that saying of Cyprian: “In judicial proceedings, in an address from the rostrum, let abundant eloquence display itself with flowing ambition; when speech concerns the Lord God, the pure sincerity of the voice employs not the powers of eloquence for arguments of faith, but realities. [lacuna] Receive words that are not ornate but strong, not painted with polished speech for the attraction of a popular audience, but simple in unadorned truth for proclaiming the divine mercy.”

Moreover, those devoted to liberal studies know how greatly humane letters languished in Martin’s age; therefore I would not venture to compare him with the foremost Fathers of the Church in excellence of expression. This will not seem surprising to anyone who considers that obscure age, in which not the peace of learning but the movement and clash of arms occupied the regions, villages, and even the more populous cities of our Spain.

The present volume is completed in only four sermons. We give the last, entitled the second sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, divided into sections marked by the sign §. Before each section a summary is placed, briefly expressing its contents. Since this was lacking in some places, it has now been added for the reader’s benefit. Whoever wishes to know Martin’s deeds, studies, and finally the journeys he undertook for the sake of religion, may consult his *Life*, composed by Lucas of Tuy, a canon of the same order; we have arranged for it to be placed at the beginning of this work, where it may serve as a most complete prologue. Farewell, then, and judge our labor fairly and kindly.

[Col. 0009]

# Life of Saint Martin

Written by Lucas, deacon of León and afterward bishop of Tuy, while he was a canon regular of St. Augustine in the royal monastery of León called after St. Isidore; and taken from the work entitled *On the Miracles of St. Isidore*.

## Chapter I. How Blessed Isidore marvellously gave wisdom to Blessed Martin, a canon of his monastery, by means of a little book which he compelled him himself to devour.

[Col. 0009A]

At that time Martin, a priest of venerable life and a canon of that same monastery, whom I mentioned a little earlier above, was in his inward understanding of the Scriptures almost unlearned, [Col. 0010A] though he flourished conspicuously in works of virtue with the greatest wisdom. Although he was trained in ecclesiastical offices and, as has been said, did not grasp the inward meaning of Scripture—like one who had never attended the schools of grammarians—yet he possessed the strongest desire to understand the sacred Scriptures, and persisted in prayers and fasts, serving the Lord day and night in the spirit of truth (Luke 2).

> **Note: [Col. 0009A]** Thus the manuscript reads *inhierat* for *inerat* (“was in him”).

But while one night he was keeping vigil in prayer, the blessed Doctor Isidore appeared to him, carrying a very small book in his hands, and said: “Take this, my beloved, and eat it; and the Lord will give you knowledge of the sacred Scriptures, because you have been found faithful and just in his house (Matt. 25). I have also obtained from the Lord Jesus Christ that you shall receive whatever you ask of God (John 16); and you shall be a participant in the miracles which the Lord performs through me in this church. I am Isidore, patron of this place; and you shall endeavor to impart, to the glory of Christ’s name, the things which the Holy Spirit teaches you.”

But Martin, being of dovelike simplicity, was afraid to eat the book, lest perhaps such food should break his religious fast. Then the holy confessor, taking his chin, compelled him to swallow the book; and Martin was so wholly inflamed that it seemed to him as though he were iron glowing in a fire. When this had been done, [Col. 0011B] the saint who had been speaking with him disappeared.

From that day onward he flourished in such understanding of the holy Scriptures that, when discussing sacred questions with them, he surpassed all masters of theology. Nor could Jews and heretics withstand his wisdom and the Spirit who spoke through him (Acts 6). All marvelled at his teaching (Matt. 22), when, preaching among the wise, he set forth the word of God in eloquent Latin and well-chosen words. All who knew him were astonished that such knowledge of Scripture had been given when old age had already broken him down. The grace of healing was also given him (1 Cor. 12), and the prophetic spirit by which he subtly foresaw certain future things.

Moreover, he produced two volumes of immense size, called *Concordia* [“Harmony”], because in them the authorities of the New and Old Testaments are brought into harmony and the opinions of the holy Fathers are compiled. In these volumes obscurities of Holy Scripture are more clearly opened up, the Catholic faith is strengthened, Jewish unbelief is refuted, every heresy is separately assailed, and whatever pertains to upright conduct is demonstrated by testimonies of Scripture and sweetly commended with most gracious persuasiveness. Thus this Martin deserves to be numbered among the doctors of Christ’s Church. That his life, holiness, and miracles may become manifest to the faithful, let us pursue some account to the glory of Christ’s name and the praise of his confessor Isidore, taking the order of our narrative from its beginning.

## Chapter II. On the birth and lineage of Blessed Martin, canon of St. Isidore; on the names of his father and mother, and the meanings of those names.

This venerable doctor of Christ’s Church, Martin, was born of noble stock and begotten by Catholic parents, whose nobility of character adorned the nobility of their lineage with the flowers of virtues. By a divine foreshadowing, attested by the meaning of sacred names, he appears aptly to have been called Martin: a name interpreted in Greek as “witness,” or in Latin as “born for Mars.” [Col. 0011D] His parents were from the territory of León: his father was named John and his mother Eugenia. Those who deserved to bring forth the fruit of so great an offspring are fittingly considered to bear such names, because John is interpreted “the grace of God,” and Eugenia “good earth” or “fair countenance.”

The grace of God, from good earth, brought forth Martin—a truest witness, or one born for Mars. For God, maker of all and renewer of the faithful, enriched this most faithful servant of his with his grace in childhood; beyond all his contemporaries, he adorned his countenance—that is, his conscience and conduct—with a spirit of integrity and gentleness; he raised his mind to desire heavenly things; and in adolescence, making him prompt through the spirit of fortitude for Mars, that is, for a special contest, against the many-formed enemy the devil, against unlawful motions of the flesh, and against the varied misfortunes of the world, he fortified him beforehand. [Col. 0012A] In youth he enriched him with patience, obedience, and humility; in old age and advanced old age he illumined him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding; and at every age he strengthened this witness to truth and most valiant athlete, so that all may truly understand that divine grace brought forth this fruit of life from good earth for the salvation of many peoples.

## Chapter III. On the praiseworthy life of Blessed Martin from his childhood; and how, after the death of his wife, Martin’s father assumed the habit in the monastery of St. Marcellus.

> **Note: [Col. 0011D]** Supply: “conducted.”

When he was a little boy, his parents gave him to be educated in sacred letters. They lived their married life in holiness and honor; and they had bound themselves by a vow that, if either should pay the debt of all flesh while the other survived, the survivor would more freely preserve chastity and renounce the world. By frequent prayers they asked that their son might be heir not so much to their temporal possessions as to their holy manner of life. [Col. 0012B]

The boy was indeed taught outwardly by a master, but inwardly illumined by the Holy Spirit. He made no delay in learning, compared with his other companions, since divine grace was present as his teacher. When his mother entered upon the way of all flesh, his father, as if fleeing a storm, distributed the greater part of his goods to the poor and, together with all the rest that he possessed, gave himself to the church of St. Marcellus the martyr, situated in the city of León, to serve God under the Rule of Blessed Augustine. His son, however, because of his childhood years, remained in secular dress.

Nevertheless, all loved the boy because of his father’s religious devotion, and especially because in him shone forth an image of future deeds: unceasing cheerfulness, delightful gentleness, and prudence beyond his years. He rejected in himself whatever is childish in conduct; and, obedient to his elders on both sides through the spirit of counsel, he governed himself. Already in the tender age of his servant the Lord was working something praiseworthy [Col. 0012C] and wonderful: among the other clerics, strong in body and advanced in years, he was the first to rise in the night and in the daytime for the performance of the divine mysteries. Making himself helpful to all, vigilant in prayer, he disciplined his body with fasts. He often recalled the passion of the Lord Jesus; and, by forgiving those who sinned against him and sharing in the sufferings of others, he enjoyed the spirit of compassion.

## Chapter IV. How, after his father’s death and his promotion to the order of subdeacon, Blessed Martin vigorously disciplined himself through many holy pilgrimages in order to restrain the unlawful motions of the flesh.

Having therefore been thoroughly trained in psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, the Gregorian gradual, and the antiphonary, and sweetly praising God in ecclesiastical offices with a clear and resonant voice, when his boyhood years had passed he was ordained subdeacon through the good offices of the provost of the church, attaining that rank of ecclesiastical honor. By receiving the order he bound himself more closely as a debtor to God; and, lest the heat of the flesh, burning fiercely, should stain the order he had received, he strengthened his spirit for stricter disciplines to break the desires of the flesh. He compelled the flesh to serve the spirit and dashed with all his strength the onrushing wanton motions of the flesh against the rock which is Christ (1 Cor. 10).

When he perceived that, as commonly occurs near the end of adolescence, the motions of the flesh were violently rising against him, he considered that the proud impulses of slippery flesh are worn down by the exercise of holy pilgrimage, that the spirit is strengthened through the prayers and intercessions of the saints, and that pardon and God’s grace are obtained. When his father rested in the Lord through a precious death (Ps. 115), Martin endeavored to distribute to the poor everything he seemed to possess. Setting out as a pilgrim, [Col. 0013A] he visited the shrine of our Savior in the regions of Asturias and that of the blessed apostle James in Galicia. Then, seeking the help of the Mother of God and of the saints, he travelled eagerly through the other churches of the saints, especially where their most sacred bodies rested, imploring God’s mercy through the merits and prayers of the saints. Frequently pouring forth streams of tears, he washed away whatever sins or offenses he had committed.

## Chapter V. On Blessed Martin’s great abstinence while he was a pilgrim at Rome; and how he obtained favor in the eyes of the supreme pontiff and of those who guarded the church of St. Peter.

At last he came to the holy city of Rome, where, by the Lord’s bounty, he spent the holy season of Lent in ashes and haircloth, with restricted bread and scant water. Each week he observed two fasts of three days; [Col. 0013B] he took food only once on Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, and every day visited on foot each of the stations of the saints, in psalms and prayers. The Lord gave him favor in the eyes of the guardians of the church of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles; keeping vigil, chanting psalms, and praying before Peter’s sacred altar, he passed nearly the whole night without sleep.

When, therefore, the holy Lenten fast had ended and the radiant day of Easter, full of joy for all the faithful, had arrived, after receiving the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, he was granted the privilege of kissing the feet of the glorious Pope Urban and of receiving his blessing in a special manner beyond the other pilgrims who were present. This truly Catholic man repeatedly declared in every respect that he believed the present and inestimable reward of his labor would be his, if he deserved to touch the hem of the Vicar of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, the Roman Pontiff—and to receive his blessing and pardon from him, because [Col. 0013C] the Lord had bestowed upon him, above all prelates, full power to bind and loose and the dignity of a more excellent grace.

## Chapter VI. How Blessed Martin departed from Rome for various other holy pilgrimages; and, arriving at Constantinople, bought a beautiful chasuble to carry home.

Thus laden with such great labors—or rather, to speak more truly, greatly relieved by them—the man of God did not forget the purpose he had undertaken. He hastened for prayer to the shrine of St. Michael the Archangel on Mount Gargano and to the most holy body of Nicholas at Bari. From there, carried by a favorable voyage, he went to Jerusalem. Spending many days in the places of the holy Nativity and Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ in prayers and fasts (Luke 2), crucifying himself with his vices and desires (Gal. 5), he offered to the Lord sacrifices of a contrite and humbled heart [Col. 0013D] and often watered the holy places with the fountain of his tears.

After this, endowed with such humility and grace, he served the holy Jerusalem hospital for two years, so winning the hearts of all that he was most tenderly loved by everyone. Having happily accomplished all these things and visited the holy hermits who were in the mountains of Antioch, he proceeded to Constantinople. There he most devoutly venerated the relics of blessed apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins resting there, imploring the Lord’s mercy through the intercessions of the saints. The servant of God remained there for several days; and, among other items for sale, he saw a priestly chasuble of silk, which he bought from the merchants at a stated price, wishing to bring it as a gift to the church of St. Marcellus at León. For he perceived that the ardor of his exhausted body was now cooling within him and, as though secure concerning the battle against carnal temptations, rejoiced that, relying on divine help, he could obtain victory. He wished henceforth to serve the Lord in the land of his birth.

## Chapter VII. How Blessed Martin, while returning home, was captured in a certain city as though he had stolen the aforesaid chasuble.

[Col. 0014A]

As he returned, giving thanks to God for all the labors he had completed, he zealously visited the bodies of the saints: the blessed Dionysius, glorious martyr; Martin, bishop in Gaul; the most precious martyr Thomas in England; and St. Patrick in Ireland. He also wished to visit Saints Giles, Saturninus, and Anthony. Carrying the aforesaid priestly vestment with him, he was seized in the city of Viterbo by the city guards; they stubbornly accused him as though he had stolen the chasuble and placed him in prison.

But divine mercy, which does not abandon those who hope in it (Dan. 13), heard the man of God crying to it. While he prayed in prison, a certain woman infected with heretical error came to him [Col. 0014B] and began urgently to press him to agree with her, renounce the Catholic faith, and thereby obtain release from prison. But when the servant of God saw that she wished to plunge him into the precipice of error, stirred by bitter indignation he said to her: “Depart from me, wicked woman; for, if it were possible, I would rather die a thousand times than be defiled by the filth of your heresy.”

Angered by this, the woman struck him on the face and was immediately seized by a demon and more violently tormented. The citizens ran together and, investigating, marvelled greatly at what had happened. Some said that he was a saint; others that he was a great sorcerer; and there was division among them.

## Chapter VIII. How, while Blessed Martin was in prison, God’s angel assigned to guard him came to him and rescued him, commanding him to return to León.

While these things were taking place, the Lord sent his angel and rescued him from the hands of the wicked (Ps. [Col. 0014C] 30). For a certain man of handsome countenance and honorable dress came and began at the entrance of the city to inquire where such a pilgrim, a servant of God, might be, describing his appearance and former clothing. When he heard from those speaking that such a man was detained in prison, he came before the city judge and complained of those who had unjustly mistreated the man of God.

Seeing a man of such distinction, the judge rose for him and humbly asked what he knew of the pilgrim of whom he spoke in such a manner. He replied: “From childhood,” he said, “I have known him to live justly and devoutly, and I have known his father and mother to have lived in the fear of the Lord. Having distributed the greater part of all that he had to the poor for the purpose of pilgrimage, he went to Jerusalem. Afterward he also went to Constantinople for prayer, and there, in my presence, he bought the chasuble concerning which the question is being raised. I know that this man is holy and just.”

Then the judge, giving credence to so weighty a witness, hurried [Col. 0014D] to the prison. Finding a crowd disputing over the aforementioned woman tormented by the demon, and learning what had occurred, he fell on his knees before the servant of God Martin, begged pardon for so great a crime, brought him out of prison, and offered him money. In reparation for so great an offense, he begged him as insistently as possible to accept it. But the man of God forgave him and refused to take the money.

The aforesaid man then led him outside the city and said: “Return to the land of your birth; and, receiving the orders of deacon and priest in tranquility of mind and body, endeavor to offer to God an acceptable sacrifice in sacred vestments.” When Martin asked who he was that had mercifully shown him so great a favor, he said to him: “I am the angel of God assigned for your protection, and you have been granted by the Lord to have me as a helper in all that you do.” When he had said these things, his face shone like the sun (Matt. 17), and he vanished from the eyes of the beholder.

## Chapter IX. How Blessed Martin, immediately upon coming to León, received the orders of deacon and priest, assumed the habit of Blessed Augustine in the monastery of St. Marcellus, and lived there most honorably and praiseworthily.

[Col. 0015A]

The servant of the Lord Martin, filled with astonishment, became as though lifeless. At last recovering himself, with great weeping he gave thanks to God, who had deigned to protect him through his angel in all his tribulations and distresses. To fulfill the angel’s command, he hastened to return to León. When he arrived there, he was received by all with great joy, and by the hands of the reverend Father Manrique, bishop, he received first the order of deacon and then that of priest.

> **Note: [Col. 0015D]** Manrique was elected in the year 1181 and died on 14 February 1205.

He also assumed the religious habit according to the Rule of Blessed Augustine in the church of St. Marcellus the martyr. He withdrew into a small cell within the cloister, so that the more separated he was from [Col. 0015B] others, the more he might devote himself to contemplation and prayer; putting aside every secular disturbance, he might enjoy only divine service. While he was there, the clerics and guardians of the church daily experienced this marvel: though the church was locked, whenever they arose in the night to perform the office of Matins, they found him praying before the high altar.

## Chapter X. How the bishop of León removed the canons regular from the church of St. Marcellus and introduced secular clerics; how Blessed Martin transferred himself to the church of St. Isidore, afterward returned to St. Marcellus, and finally came to St. Isidore again at Isidore’s command.

It happened at that time that the aforesaid bishop removed the canons regular from that church. The man of God remained among the secular clerics who had recently been introduced, with only one of his own attendants, named Peter. But, considering it safer to dwell with more upright men, he transferred himself with that attendant to the monastery of St. Isidore the confessor, so that he might more securely lead the canonical life.

The brothers received him kindly; but because, for the sake of abstinence, he was unwilling to use wine or meat, certain persons took offense that he did not moderate the strictness of his rule like the other brothers and that it should become a scandal to others. He was compelled to return to the church of St. Marcellus, where he remained for several days. But the blessed confessor Isidore appeared to certain brothers of his monastery and said to them sternly: “Where have you driven the servant of God Martin? Let the prior and convent endeavor to call him back quickly with honor; unless they do so, let them know that they will incur the greatest dangers. For the brothers ought not to take offense, but rather rejoice together when they see a faithful companion soar to a stricter life.”

When these matters had been reported to the prior and convent, [Col. 0015D] they sent some of the elders of the house to ask him to deign to return to their monastery and there fulfill his will in every respect. But when the man of God would not consent, the abbot, named Facundus, who presided over the monastery, came to him barefoot with the elder brothers and begged him with tearful prayers to deign to return to their monastery. Overcome by their tears, since he overflowed with the bowels of compassion, he returned with them and withdrew into a more secluded part [Col. 0016A] of the monastery. There he built an altar in honor of the cross of our redemption,

> **Note: [Col. 0015D]** Because of the construction of this altar, and because of Martin’s great devotion toward the cross, a very old necrology calls him Martin of the Holy Cross. The time when Blessed Martin transferred himself to the monastery of St. Isidore cannot have preceded the year 1181, which, as we have said, was the year of Bishop Manrique’s election. Accordingly, Fr. Joseph Manzano erred greatly in the *Life of St. Isidore* when he assigned the year 1168; and Abbot Facundus was still alive in the latter case, contrary to the chronology of that same author, who places Facundus’s death in the aforesaid year 1168. But it will later become clear that Facundus was still living around the end of the year 1197.

where day and night he persisted in psalms, hymns, and prayers (Luke 2).

## Chapter XI. On the great austerity and abstinence of Blessed Martin’s life, and on his holy manner of life while he lived in the said monastery of St. Isidore.

His abstinence was so great that one could scarcely believe that anyone in our frail times could live while so afflicting his body. He never ate meat or fish; because of weakness of the stomach he rarely drank wine, and then so diluted that it could scarcely be distinguished from water either by taste or color. On chief feasts he sometimes ate in the community with the brothers, taking meat broth, eggs, and cheese. Except for a surplice, he wore no linen; instead, he was clothed against the flesh in the roughest haircloth. For a bed, he spread a little straw on the ground, upon which he sometimes refreshed his exhausted limbs with sleep after they had been wearied by the excessive labors of vigils. [Col. 0016B]

He made it his practice to visit the brothers in their sicknesses and especially to attend them at night, because then they were more heavily burdened by illness. He relieved them with services, comforted them with gentle words, invited them to confess their sins and receive the sacraments, commended to them everything belonging to holiness, and raised their minds to heavenly things. With his own hand he administered to all the sacrament of extreme unction, and divine power was perceptibly manifest in the sacrament, for the sick person immediately declared himself better. Whomever he observed in the community to be at discord, he recalled to concord with the greatest effort. Whatever he found disordered, he immediately strove to correct. He met all with cheerfulness and humility, as appeared fitting for each person, [Col. 0016C] and, full of grace, made himself welcome to all. Whoever came to him sad or troubled departed cheerful and glad through the graciousness of his consolation. The reputation of his integrity continually spread and increased for the better, and every day gave forth a sweeter fragrance.

## Chapter XII. How Blessed Martin, though old and infirm, began the great work of his books; how kings and magnates held him in the highest veneration; and how, during his lifetime, demons acknowledged his holiness.

As the works of virtue flourished in him each day with greater increase, and he was now worn out by venerable old age, and did not understand the Scriptures as he wished, as was written above, and had received from the Lord, through the blessed confessor Isidore, the understanding of the Scriptures which he desired, and wished to compose volumes of *Concordances*: since in writing he could not bear the weight of his hands and arms, [Col. 0016D] he had ropes fastened high up to a certain beam; passing them over his shoulders and arms, he was in a sense suspended and thus bore the weight of his weak body more lightly. Writing in wax tablets in this manner, he handed them over to scribes, who wrote down what he dictated or compiled, transferring it onto parchment. This too was very remarkable: he suffered intensely from a headache, yet did not in any way desist from so great a study.

He also began to shine forth in signs and miracles, which we judge must by no means be passed over altogether in silence, [Col. 0017A] although we omit many because of the reader’s weariness. When these miracles had been seen, King Alfonso held him in such reverence that he often visited the holy man and came before him with bent knees. His wife Queen Berengaria [Note: [Col. 0017D] Berengaria was already married to Alfonso, if we believe Enrique Flórez, vol. I of *Reginas católicas*, p. 352, on 17 December 1197. Therefore Martin began to write in this year, or a little earlier.] likewise humbly venerated the holiness of God’s servant. The bishops and barons of the kingdom also revered him with the deepest affection and submitted themselves most devoutly to his holy admonitions and commands. All regarded him as the master of confession for their sins; and all declared that, if they wished to conceal any sins or had consigned them to forgetfulness, the man of God brought them back to their memory.

Moreover, so that the Lord might clearly reveal in him the grace of miraculous powers and healings, and make him a partner in the miracles wrought through the blessed confessor Isidore, the possessed persons who lay before the altar of that most blessed confessor, seeking remedies for health—or rather the demons within them—cried out, saying: “Martin, servant of God, your prayers burn us. Henceforth we cannot remain here, [Col. 0017B] because Isidore has enlisted you as his ally against us.” And as they said this, those afflicted by the most severe suffering were healed. Therefore many who suffered from illnesses now came to him and obtained remedies of health.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Blessed Martin asked permission from his abbot to receive the alms necessary for completing and writing his works; how he revealed to him that blessed Isidore had given him wisdom through a little book which he compelled him to devour; and how he made the works already mentioned and, besides them, the church of the Most Holy Trinity.

But since it belongs to the substance of the Rule of blessed Augustine—under which, by God’s authorship, Martin the servant of Christ served the Lord—that regular canons should not merely possess nothing as their own, but should neither give nor receive anything without permission from their superiors: [Col. 0017C] the poor man of Christ, who possessed none of this world’s riches and could not compose the above-mentioned books without others’ assistance, being eager, through the grace he had received by God’s generous gift, to benefit not only those then living but also future generations, humbly entreated Abbot Facundus [Note: [Col. 0017D] See how Facundus was still governing the monastery about the end of 1197, as I said earlier.] to grant him permission to have scribes with whom he might produce books of holy compilation, and to receive alms mercifully bestowed upon him.

When the abbot heard this, he marvelled that the Holy Spirit had strengthened him so greatly that, though worn down by headache and old age, he strove to undertake a work of such labour. Yet, in the presence of certain senior brethren, he questioned him and, under the obligation of obedience, required him to tell how such great grace had come to him. In reply, the son of obedience related how the blessed confessor Isidore had appeared to him and had bestowed upon him understanding of the Scriptures in the manner noted above.

Then the abbot, giving thanks, [Col. 0017D] granted him permission to have copyists, to write whatever volumes he wished, and to receive alms from the faithful, by which he might accomplish whatever seemed best to him. Queen Berengaria, [Note: [Col. 0017D] Therefore, as has been said, Blessed Martin set himself to writing about the time of [Col. 0018D] Berengaria.] when she learned of the holy man’s wish, supplied adequate expenses. With these the holy man completed his volumes and built, within that same cloister, a church in honour of the Divine Trinity. Having gathered there relics of many saints, he caused it to be consecrated by the hands of the reverend Father John, bishop of Oviedo.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the lesser part of the ordinary portion which was given to Blessed Martin, as to the other canons, sufficed each day for his seven clerics, while a remainder of his portion always remained over.

[Col. 0018A]

He thus had with him seven clerics daily, to write out his volumes and perform the divine office. Since the custom of the monastery was that on certain stated days meat was eaten in the community, they gave the man of God his portion of meat, such as might suffice for one of the brethren, and which one man could consume completely at a single meal. This portion of meat was brought to the man of God; with his own hand he gave the greater part of it to two cats which he kept. He blessed the other portion with the sign of the cross and distributed it to his seven clerics, that they might eat it in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

He who satisfied five thousand men with five loaves and two fishes (Mark VI) increased that meat daily [Col. 0018B] so that on that day its eating satisfied the said clerics, and its remains lasted even until the following day. It happened, therefore, that some meat from a Thursday remained over. While the clerics were at their next meal, on the following Saturday, a certain boy named Alfonso—who is now honoured with the master’s title in the liberal arts and law, and who often came to eat with the said clerics—found and ate the meat left from Thursday.

But when the man of God came in and suddenly saw what was happening, thinking that his clerics were eating the meat, he said to them: “Why, wretches, do you Judaize? Perhaps you prepared it for us on Friday so that you might eat it on Saturday? Must there not be a distinction between Christians and Jews, between the children of God and the children of the devil?” Saying this, he expelled them from his fellowship.

The clerics, deeply distressed at what had occurred, informed certain brethren of what had happened to them. These came to the man of God and scarcely obtained [Col. 0018C] pardon for the clerics, on the condition that they first promised in his hands that henceforth, unless necessity compelled them, they would in no way eat meat on Saturday. But after some days had passed, when he had learned from the clerics the whole course of the matter, he was deeply grieved because this miracle had been disclosed through such an incident. Nevertheless, he commanded them not to stir up any further rumours concerning the affair.

## CHAPTER XV. How Blessed Martin cured the dean of León of quartan fever, while they were disputing together about Holy Scripture.

The dean of León, named Peter, a man highly learned and honourable, who, having been appointed archbishop, now energetically governs the Church of Santiago, [Note: [Col. 0018D] Enrique Flórez, vol. XXII of *España Sagrada*, p. 111, says that this Peter was already governing the Church of Compostela in 1208 and lived until 1224. If, therefore, this chronology is correct, Luke was writing this chapter in one of these sixteen years.] was at that time grievously afflicted by quartan fever. One morning he came to the man of God and conversed with him concerning the sacred Scriptures until [Col. 0018D] evening. But when he saw that he could not surpass God’s servant in any point by sophistical syllogisms, he began to raise objections against him.

To this the man of God said: “Stop, dean, stop; for falsehood seeks corners.” The feverish chill was now beginning to seize the dean. Prostrate at the feet of God’s servant, he said: “Servant of God, I beg you through our Lord Jesus, do not despise me. Eight months have now passed since I have been continually afflicted by quartan fever. Pray to the Lord for me, that through your prayers I may be restored to health.”

But the man of God, lest he be stained by the blemish [Col. 0019A] of vainglory, said to him: “This is not mine to do, for I am a sinful man” (Luke V).

As the dean persisted with tears, God’s servant, moved by compassion, said to him: “Let us both beseech God, that he may deign to grant you what you ask.” The dean prostrated himself in prayer before the altar of the Holy Cross; Martin came to a certain window from which he looked toward the altar of the blessed Isidore, where he customarily offered the incense of his prayers to the Lord. After praying for some time, he came to the dean and questioned him concerning the articles of faith, that he might give proof of his belief before God. When he confessed that he believed all things pertaining to the Catholic faith, the servant of the Lord said: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, by the prayers of the blessed confessor Isidore, may the Catholic faith which you confess be preserved in you; and be well.”

Immediately restored to health, he glorified God and his confessor Isidore; and thereafter he rendered himself obedient to the man of God Martin as though he had been one of his servants. That night he ate [Col. 0019B] Martin’s poor supper with him, as many bishops also repeatedly delighted to do. The said dean furthermore composed an outstanding homily in rhetorical colours, in which he gloriously celebrated Christ’s confessor Isidore with illustrious praise.

## CHAPTER XVI. How Blessed Martin cured a noblewoman of pain in her breast.

A certain noblewoman, grievously tormented by pain in her breast, came asking the man of God Martin to relieve her illness. When the man of God made the sign of the cross over her swollen breast, the swelling immediately subsided and she was made well. The woman’s name has escaped me; but two priests of the Lord who saw this reported it to me as testimony.

## CHAPTER XVII. How Blessed Martin cured his fellow canon of an acute toothache.

[Col. 0019C]

The venerable man García, abbot of the same monastery, testifies—he still survives, though because of great weakness he has relinquished the office of ruler. This man, I say, often testifies with tears that he himself was so afflicted by toothache that he could not even drink water, since it seemed to him that his teeth would immediately fall out from the excessive pain if he put even a little water into his mouth.

But coming to God’s servant Martin, he fell at his feet, saying: “Help me, lord Father, for six days have now passed in which I have neither eaten nor drunk.” Immediately moved by pity, Martin questioned him, as he was accustomed to do with all sick persons who came to him: “Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?” When he answered, “I believe,” he made the sign of the cross over his face and said to him: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 0019D] depart healed.” And he was immediately cured, so that for the rest of his life, although worn down by old age, he felt no toothache.

García was then a simple canon, and he immediately went to dine in the refectory with the other brethren. When the other brethren saw him eating and drinking cheerfully, though they had believed he would shortly die, and learned how he had been made well, they glorified God, who had deigned in his mercy to provide for them through his servant Martin.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How Blessed Martin freed a boy living in the monastery of Saint Isidore from quinsy.

When a noble boy named Munio, who was being brought up among the regular boys in that monastery, suffered from a quinsy abscess, and no remedy of physicians could aid him, he was brought to the man of God Martin by the aforesaid García, who was teaching him the rudiments of letters. [Col. 0020A] García fell with the said boy at Martin’s feet and tearfully begged that the grace of holy healing be granted to the boy. The man of God made the sign of the cross over the boy’s throat, and immediately the boy vomited up the abscess with blood. The said Munio still lives as a priest and canon, and together with many others is a witness to this miracle.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Blessed Martin delivered his goddaughter, a countess near death from the pains of childbirth, from death itself.

A most noble woman, Sancha, who reverenced the holy man with the deepest devotion, being pregnant and grievously oppressed by pains as childbirth approached, sent to the man of God, entreating him to deign to pour forth prayers to the Lord for her. [Col. 0020B] He graciously promised the messengers that he would grant what was requested.

But when night came and the servants stood around the bed of their almost dying mistress, she began to cry out: “Prepare seats, and receive the holy man of God, Martin.” Hearing this, all who stood around thought that she was speaking as though out of her senses. But she, perceiving that the others did not see what she was permitted to see, said to them: “All of you go out, and let only the women remain with me.”

After they had gone out, she descended from the bed and, falling down as though to pray, immediately gave birth safely to a male child; she herself was restored to health. Afterwards she declared that the holy man of God Martin had come to her, and that when she descended from her bed and worshipped him, the saint made the sign of the cross over her, departed, and she immediately gave birth.

The aforesaid Sancha was the wife of Count Froila, by whom she had borne this son. Bringing him to the man of God for baptism, [Col. 0020C] Ramiro, relying upon military power, [was] among the great men of the kingdom of León. *(The phrase is defective.)*

## CHAPTER XX. How, by the counsel and revelation of Blessed Martin, the city of León defended itself against the kings of Castile and Aragon, who were besieging it.

King Alfonso of Castile, with a great force of armies and with Peter, king of Aragon, as his ally, captured the Jewish castle which he had besieged, nearly one mile from the city of León. After this he began to attack the city of León with his armies. When the citizens saw the power of such great kings, they were greatly afraid. But they came to God’s servant Martin and begged him to assure them whether they could resist such armies.

He answered them: “Be steadfast; do not be afraid. Know certainly that this city will not [Col. 0020D] be taken by these kings, because the Lord protects it through the prayers of the blessed confessor Isidore. Know also that before long the king of Castile will receive news that the king of León is invading his kingdom with a great army; and, withdrawing from the siege of this city, he will prepare to meet him, but there will be no armed conflict between them.”

Exactly as the man of God predicted, so it wholly occurred; and the spirit of prophecy was manifested [perhaps *clare*, “clearly”] in him. Now, passing over many other miracles which almighty God deigned to work through him, let us come to his most sacred death.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Blessed Martin knew the day of his death long beforehand, and revealed it to his brethren, to their prior and the canons of Saint Isidore, and to others.

Therefore, while Martin the priest, doctor of Christ’s Church, flourished in these and other virtues and miracles, he began several days beforehand [Col. 0021A] to reveal to certain brethren the time, or day, of his death; and, by predicting the day of his death, made sad those who had been joyful in his most sweet presence.

A certain dependent of his, Pelagius, when word was brought to him that his father had died, asked the holy man’s permission to go to his family, to arrange matters concerning the property that had come to him from his father’s estate. The man of the Lord blessed him, saying: “Go, son, with God; and know that from now on you will not see me.” The dependent did not fully understand what had been said to him and departed. But others who stood by, understanding, were touched with grief in their hearts and mourned that the day of his death was near.

From that time, setting aside his study of reading, the man of God devoted himself day and night to prayers (Luke II), watched and prayed, that when the Lord came and knocked he might find him watchful in the hour of death (Luke XII). By every means possible he withdrew himself more than usual from human conversation, and with all attentiveness he eagerly adorned the bridal chamber of his soul, so that [Col. 0021B] he might worthily receive the Lord returning from the wedding.

On a certain Friday, followed by the eighth day of his most blessed departure, while the prior was in chapter with the brethren, God’s servant asked that all others who were absent be summoned. In chapter he delivered God’s word with such abundant exhortation that, in his eloquent and sweet preaching, he seemed already to stand in the company of angels. His words did not appear to be those of a man, because Christ truly spoke in his servant. He inserted certain remarks in the words of his preaching from which all clearly understood that he was assigning the eighth day then to come as the end of his departure.

## CHAPTER XXII. How Blessed Martin, before departing from this world, handed his prior the keys and everything which he administered by the prior’s permission, and asked to be blessed by him.

[Col. 0021C]

After this, he handed the prior the keys of the church of the Holy Trinity, which he himself had caused to be built in that cloister, and of a certain stone house in the monastery tower, where money entrusted by certain nobles was kept, lest when dying he should possess anything in his own name or in that of another poor man of Christ.

Then, with tears, he begged forgiveness from everyone if he had done or committed anything by which he had grieved any brother. He also begged, on bended knees, to be blessed by the prior. But the prior refused to bless him, because he wished to be blessed by one whom he believed to draw nearer to the Lord in holiness. Yet God’s servant persisted; they all forgave him with tears, and he obtained a blessing from his prior—that is, the provost.

Then, as the prior urgently begged and commanded under the obligation of obedience, Martin blessed him and the brethren, saying: “May the Lord bless you out of Zion, and may you always see the good things of Jerusalem” (Psalm 127). Having said this, he returned to the church of the Holy [Col. 0021D] Cross, all the brethren following him in tears, for they were exceedingly sorrowful at his death. All grieved that in the pilgrimage of this miserable life they were losing the consolation of so great a Father; for a vehement grief rightly constricted the inmost hearts of all the brethren.

## CHAPTER XXIII. How Blessed Martin, certain of his passage to glory, prepared himself for it with all his strength.

After these things had been done, while God’s servant endured the wretched approach of human mortality and awaited the most blessed prize of his labour, he was seized by a fever on the following Tuesday and, gradually losing bodily strength, fell ill. Nevertheless, every day, as he had been accustomed from the beginning of his priesthood, he celebrated Mass and, prostrate before the altar of the Holy Cross, gave himself to prayer. He also went to the window from which he looked upon [Col. 0022A] the altar of the blessed confessor Isidore and entrusted his departure to Isidore’s prayers.

Who could believe that a man would die so soon when he remained so watchful in strength of spirit? This was, indeed, some consolation to the brethren, who thought that the Lord, taking pity on them, had granted him a longer life. But as the sun was setting on the following Friday, Peter, keeper of the king’s towers—now a canon of the same monastery—came to him and found the man of God praying before the altar. Peter was Martin’s intimate friend and awaited his blessing.

Turning to him, the man of God blessed him and said: “Go, son, to the watch over the towers entrusted to you; and when you hear, tonight, the bells of this monastery first begin to ring, say the Lord’s Prayer and beseech the Lord for me.” Weeping, Peter said to him: “Is the hour of your departure at hand, Father and lord?” He replied: “Truly, son, it is at hand, and this night I shall leave the body.”

After Peter departed, [Col. 0022B] the man of God lay back on his poor little bed, which, at the brethren’s urging, he had raised on small linen-covered columns, according to the custom of the country, with *tantoris* (sic) straw and herbs, and he ordered the brethren to be summoned so that they might administer to him the sacrament of extreme unction.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the precious end and glorious departure of Blessed Martin, and the notable teaching which he left us concerning the sacrament of the most holy viaticum.

The brethren hastened together. Hearing that the hour of death was at hand, they came more to see his most sacred departure than to assist him with their prayers, since they hoped through him to obtain forgiveness of their own sins. They found him almost already struggling in his last moments. When they had administered to him the ministry of holy anointing, he took the cross, kissed it often, and placed it upon his breast. He fortified himself with the sign of the cross using his right hand, and held his left hand against the other side, where he saw the malignant spirit opposing him. [Col. 0022C]

He prayed silently and answered nothing, although the brethren repeatedly questioned him. Since he had celebrated Mass that day, it seemed to some brethren that the sacrament of the Lord’s Body ought not to be given to him after the anointing. When two canons, namely Peter and Ferdinand, who possessed knowledge of the Scriptures, saw this, they said to him with tears and most bitter sobbing: “Holy Father, leave us an example of truth. We beg you through Christ to whom you are going: do not depart from the body until you show us by your action what must be done concerning the sacrament of the altar.”

Then the holy man, as all present heard, drawing a sigh from his inmost heart with audible voice and returning to himself, said to the brethren: “Let the Body of Christ be brought quickly, for it is not fitting that a Christian should die without this most holy viaticum.” The said Ferdinand asked him whether he had seen anything on the left side. He replied: “I saw the enemy, but [Col. 0022D] he departed confounded.”

When the Body of Christ was brought, Martin descended from the bed, worshipped it humbly, and received it with the greatest devotion. Then, as all asked for a blessing, he blessed them in his customary words: “May the Lord bless you out of Zion, and may you always see the good things of Jerusalem” (Psalm 127). “I commend you to God, for I am going to God who calls me.” Having spoken these words, he surrendered his spirit to the Lord.

When his body was washed in the customary manner, it was found so radiant and bright that it seemed already to foreshadow its coming glorification. Nothing unseemly appeared in his private members, which seemed to attest the purity of a seven-year-old boy. On the following day, when it rang out through the city that God’s servant Martin had departed from the body, the city was filled with murmuring, and everyone mourned the loving Father. The people gathered, holding lighted candles in their hands, thronging more to Martin’s festival than to his funeral. [Col. 0023] Some wept because they had lost him for the present; others rejoiced, believing that they had a new patron [Col. 0024] in heaven. Standing at so great a crossroads, it was pious to weep for Martin and most pious to rejoice with Martin.

[Col. 0023]

## SOME EULOGIES OF BLESSED MARTIN, REGULAR CANON AND PRIEST, OF LEÓN IN SPAIN

[Col. 0023A] 1. John Bolland, for 11 February:

“León is a city of Spain, capital of the kingdom of the same name, commonly called Leon. Here is a distinguished abbey of regular canons, called Saint Isidore’s, because the translated relics of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, are there. Relics are also kept there of Blessed Martin the priest, who was a regular canon in the same monastery. Lucas of Tuy, a contemporary author, mentions him in this way in the preface to his *Chronicle of the World*: ‘What should be thought concerning the venerable Martin, priest of León, who obtained from the Lord through prayer so great a prerogative in the divine Scriptures that he may deservedly be compared in scriptural exposition with the holiest early doctors?’

“John Mariana also mentions him, Book II, chapter 16, when discussing events in the year 1188: ‘Martin the priest, illustrious in letters and life in these times, devoted himself at León to writing many books. Though untrained and unlettered, he suddenly became most learned, when Isidore, [Col. 0023B] in whose monastery he lived, offered him in a dream a book to eat. No part of those books has reached our hands; the canons of that church preserve, with great reverence, this splendid memorial of the event for posterity.’”

2. Ambrosio de Morales, *General Chronicle of Spain*, Book XII, chapter 21, testifies that he saw those books and that public honours were paid to Martin. Thus he writes:

“Three hundred years ago there lived in the monastery of Saint Isidore a canon named Martin, of very unpolished intellect but of great holiness of life, and because of this held in the highest veneration by the people. His soul was tormented because, however greatly he laboured, he could attain no knowledge of letters. One night Saint Isidore appeared to him in a dream, offered him a book, and commanded him to eat it. At once very extensive learning was infused into him. Thereafter he wrote several works in Latin, in words and style fairly polished. They are held by the canons, and I myself have read some of them. Throughout the city and province [Col. 0023C] he is held a saint; and although the Church has not yet decreed heavenly honours for him by solemn canonization, nevertheless a chapel has been erected in that monastery, bearing the title of Saint Martin, and his sacred body has been placed upon an altar, enclosed in an artfully carved and gilded shrine. The miracles of the same blessed man are painted on the altar panel. In the cloister of the monastery of Saint Mary of the Meadow at Salamanca, the same miracle is seen painted on an altar panel, with such artistry that a more elegant painting can scarcely be found in all Spain.” So Morales.

3. Athanasius de Lobera, a Cistercian monk, [Col. 0024A] in Part II of his *History of León, or On the Greatness of the City and Church of León*, chapter 32, calls Martin “a mirror of virtue, splendour of virginity, example of obedience, treasure of wisdom, rule of religious life, bulwark of faith, fragrance of holiness, honour of good morals.” He adds that his Life was written by Lucas, bishop of Tuy, a canon of the distinguished monastery of Saint Isidore at León, where Saint Martin himself was also a canon; that it exists in a book which the same author published concerning the translation of Saint Isidore; and that the book, printed from the press, is in circulation.

4. Thomas de Truxillo published the same Life in a somewhat shorter Latin form in volume II, part II of the *Treasury of Preachers*, where he says:

“His feast is celebrated in the city of León, and in the lessons read there in his office his Life is recounted as it has been described here by us; it is found in the ancient Breviary of that Church.”

There is also a Life of him written in Spanish by Juan Marieta, Book VI, chapter 5, *On the Saints of Spain*, [Col. 0024B] where he reports the same facts about the cult and office, chapel and title, relics and painted miracles. Alfonso de Villegas likewise wrote the same Life in Spanish, vol. I of the *Flower of the Saints*, fol. 406. Alfonso Venero mentions him honourably in the *Enchiridion of Times*.

5. Constantine Ghini includes him among the birthdays of holy canons on 11 February, in these words: “At León in Spain . . . . the heavenly birthday of Saint Martin, regular canon and priest.” Philip Ferrari, on the same day: “At León in Spain, Saint Martin, priest.” He also gives the same entry earlier, on 8 February. Yet in his Notes he admits that others record Martin’s heavenly birthday on 11 February. Lobera, through an error of the copyist, I think, says that he is honoured on 11 January; Villegas says 12 February; the others, 11 February. Gabriel Pennotto, Book II, chapter 31, no. 5, of the *History of Regular Canons*, says that he was abbot of the monastery of Saint Isidore, which those whom we have already cited [Col. 0024C] do not report.

[Note: [Col. 0023C]

Bolland and all whom he cites erred in assigning Saint Martin’s heavenly birthday to 11 January, as Lobera does, or to February, as the others do. Martin died on 12 January 1203, and his feast is celebrated by his canons on the 14th of the same month. The very ancient necrology kept by the aforesaid canons, and written before the middle of the thirteenth century, as we have examined at sufficient length, announces the saint’s death in these words:

“On the second Ides [12 January] [Col. 0024C] died Martin of the Holy Cross, of blessed memory, in the era 1241 [A.D. 1203].”

Nor was Martin abbot of the monastery of Saint Isidore, as Pennotto, Nicolás Antonio, and others supposed. Rather, he was merely a simple canon, wrongly confused by these authors with the abbots named Martin who governed the monastery in the saint’s lifetime. Of these, one died piously, as is clear from the above-mentioned necrology, on 31 August 1182; the other on 27 March 1209.]

Thomas de Truxillo, in the *Treasury of Preachers*, vol. II, 11 February:

“This glorious confessor and doctor of Christ, Martin, was indeed born of an illustrious family in the city of León. From his earliest age he devoted himself wholly to holy works, as befits a Christian man. His parents were called John and Eugenia. His life was such that he left to all an example of great holiness. He went to Rome to visit the relics of the holy apostles, received a blessing from Pope Urban, and then returned [Col. 0025A] to his homeland. Later he was ordained priest and assumed the habit of regular canons. Within a short time his fame flew abroad among all religious of the same profession, both as a perfect religious and as a holy priest.

“He had not, however, devoted himself to Holy Scripture, but was possessed by an incredible desire to know and learn it. Within the walls of his home he poured out prayers to the Lord to obtain such knowledge and, insofar as he could, strove to apply himself to that knowledge and study, although he had no teacher to instruct him and his intellect was not sufficiently suited to accomplish the task.

“But one night, while he was praying to the Lord for this thing, blessed Isidore appeared to him carrying a book in his hands and said: ‘Take this volume and eat it, and the Lord will give you knowledge of Holy Scripture.’ The holy man excused himself, saying that he was fasting and therefore could not [Col. 0025B] eat the book. Isidore then said to him: ‘The merit of your fasting will not therefore be taken away from you; for I announce these things to you on God’s behalf, and I am Isidore, patron of this place.’ Martin therefore took the volume and ate it.

“After Isidore departed, Martin, having eaten the book, was filled and set aflame with divine knowledge, so that he easily surpassed all the theologians of his age and no one could be compared with him. He held many disputations and contests with heretics, whom he very easily overcame. He also possessed the grace of healing the sick and the spirit of prophecy; he wrote two books called *Concordia*. At length the holy man, seized by fever, died, illustrious through many miracles, having previously foretold that his death would occur on 11 February.

“His feast is celebrated in the city of León; and in the lessons read there in his office, his Life is recounted as it has been described here by us [Col. 0025C] and as it is found in the ancient Breviaries of that Church.” [Note: [Col. 0025C] Today Martin’s feast is not celebrated in the diocese of León except in the monastery of Saint Isidore, and the office has nothing proper; everything is said from the Common of a Confessor who is not a bishop.]

Nicolás Antonio, vol. II of the *Ancient Spanish Library*, p. 19:

“Under Alfonso II (IX), king of León, and his father Ferdinand, there lived Martin the priest, outstanding for holiness and remarkable for learning not acquired but infused. During his life he was a canon of the Church of León, and now its protector in heaven; he was also abbot of the distinguished monastery of regular canons dedicated in that city to Saint Isidore of Seville. It is reported that, from being untrained and unlettered, he was suddenly made most learned by the same Isidore just mentioned, in the words of John Mariana [Note: [Col. 0025C] Book XI, chapter 26, at the end.], when the latter offered him in a dream a book to eat.

“Afterwards, intent upon fashioning sacred monuments of his learning for the benefit of posterity, he wished to be useful no less to his contemporaries by a rule of most holy life than to future generations by the composition of most learned works. In the possession of the canons of the aforementioned Church of Saint Isidore are preserved not only his sacred remains and an entire hand, still imitating the gesture of writing, but also several books, even now unpublished, written in the very ancient script of the age in which he lived. Namely:

A commentary on the Apocalypse, mentioned by Ludovicus Alcazar in his Prefatory Annotation 26, section 3, on this same book. [Col. 0026B] On the Epistles of the holy apostles James, Peter, and John. Sermons from Advent until the feast of the Trinity. And various individual works bearing these titles: That brethren should possess nothing of their own. On the prelates of the Church in relation to the care of their subjects. On obedience. On ecclesiastical discipline. How young men should flee idleness. How old men and young men ought to serve God. That monks and canons should not presume to frequent the king’s court. That monks and canons should not desire to know the secrets of princes. On the translation of Saint Isidore. On the Holy Spirit. On Saint John the Baptist. On the Ascension of the Lord; and many other sermons [Col. 0026C] for other feasts of the Church. All this is from Aegidius Gundisalvus Davila, in his *Theatre of the Church of León*. Alphonsus Venerus, author of the *Enchiridion*, adds a notable book, as he calls it, entitled:

*The Harmony of the Old and New Testaments.*  
[Note: [Col. 0026C] The Book of Harmony is the same as the treatise or sermons mentioned by Aegidius Gundisalvus Davila, except that it contains many more of them, as is evident in the edition which we publish.]

[Col. 0025]

EXTRACTS from original papers of the Royal Convent of Saint Isidore of León, concerning Saint Martin.

[Col. 0025D] On the thirteenth day of March in the year one thousand five hundred and thirteen, Don Rodrigo Fuertes, bishop of Matronia or Matroni [Note: [Col. 0025D] Canon Aller, in the book which he wrote concerning the affairs of this convent, says that Bishop Fuertes was legate of Spain. Bollandus [Col. 0026D] says that he does not know what bishopric Matroni is; nor have I been able to discover it.], at the request of the prior and canons of Saint Isidore, exhumed the bones of Saint Martin and transferred them to the place where they now are, enclosed in a gilded chest. Although, when the tomb was opened, the body was found to retain its form, nevertheless the flesh, skin, and sinews had all turned to dust; consequently the bones were easily separated. Only the right hand was [Col. 0026D] found sound and whole, with its skin, nails, and sinews; and its thumb, forefinger, and middle finger were arranged as they usually are when we write. The foregoing is established by an authentic instrument drawn up by Juan de Riba de Gil and Alvaro de Villagomez, notaries of this city of León, on the said day, month, and year. It is preserved in the archive of the aforesaid convent, and we have seen and read it for this extract.

On the twelfth day of January in the year one thousand five hundred [Col. 0027A] and seventy-six—on which day Saint Martin died, in the year one thousand two hundred and three—the saint’s right hand was taken from the chest mentioned above and placed separately in a silver-gilt case, where it now remains. This was done by Don Juan de Olivares, prior of Saint Isidore, while the abbacy stood vacant after the death of Don Gregorio de Miranda. For although Don Pedro Nuñez de Zuniga y Avellaneda had been elected two years earlier, he did not make profession until the fourth of March in the said year one thousand five hundred and seventy-six. This translation is attested by a pompous and puerile Latin account by one Santacruz de Villafañe y de Quiros, canon and secretary of the same convent, preserved in the archive and consulted by us. It says that the holy hand retained all its sinews, bones, joints, and ligaments, *quatuor duntaxat avulsis minoribus ungulis*—“only the four smaller nails having been torn away.”

There is an original deed made at Salamanca [Col. 0027B] on the twentieth of January, one thousand five hundred and thirty-four, before Cosme Gonzalez, public notary, between Bachelor Benavides, prior of Saint Isidore, acting for himself and for the convent, and Master Juan Fernandez Navarrete. It contains the following. Master Navarrete had agreed with Juan de Robles, vicar—now called rector—of the monastery of La Vega, that for forty ducats he would copy and publish the works of Saint Martin. The master apparently judged this too small a compensation for his labour and doubtless suspended it after he had received fourteen ducats and two reals. For the deed which we summarize states that, in order that the work might be completed, Prior Benavides, in the name [Col. 0028A] of the convent, was to give Navarrete fifty clear ducats in addition to what he had already received. In return, the master was to complete the copy by Saint John’s Day of that year and then, within a further year, see to its publication, as he had bound himself to do in the first deed with Juan de Robles; he was first to return the originals to the convent of Saint Isidore. If printing could not be completed by the appointed time, the copy also had to be brought to the same convent of Saint Isidore, and no transcript of the work was to remain in anyone’s possession, under a penalty of three hundred ducats to which Navarrete bound himself.

This, in substance, is what the deed says; and the provision concerning the return to Saint Isidore of Navarrete’s copy was fulfilled. It is preserved in the convent library together with the original from which it could have been copied, though with some variants. The edition was not carried through for want of funds, since considerable funds were needed for it. Prior Benavides [Col. 0028B] promised to make efforts to find them through the abbot, the convent, and as many other persons as he could; but he did not find them, and so the undertaking remained unfinished.

But although the publication of these works could not then be completed, and since that time—that is, since the years one thousand five hundred and thirty or forty—no one has undertaken it, now, through the great generosity of the Most Excellent Don Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, Archbishop of Toledo, etc., etc., this benefit is bestowed upon the public. His Excellency wishes to make the distinctive merit of this holy man, his fellow-countryman, etc., etc., better known.

[Col. 0027]

# BOOK OF THE SERMONS OF SAINT MARTIN OF LEÓN

## THE AUTHOR’S PREFACE BEGINS

Desiring, together with the poor widow, to put something from our poverty and slender means into the treasury of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0027B] From the Master of the *Sentences*, in the Preface.], we have presumed to climb steep heights and to undertake a work beyond our strength. Yet we place confidence for its completion and for the reward of our labour in the Samaritan—that is, in Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin—who, after giving two denarii for the healing of the half-dead man, promised to repay in full whatever should be spent beyond them. The love of him who makes this promise compels us—indeed, delights us—but the immensity of the labour terrifies us. The desire to finish urges us toward this work, but the weakness that may fail dissuades us. In this work I desire not only a devout reader but also a free corrector, especially where a profound question of truth is at issue.

It should be noted that this book is called the *Harmony of the Old and New Testaments*, because in it the Old and New Testaments harmonize with one another. So that what is sought may be found more easily, we have prefixed the headings by which the chapters of the individual sermons are distinguished.

Here the author sets out the chapters of the sermons.

## THE PROLOGUE TO THE BOOK OF SERMONS BEGINS

[Col. 0029]

[Col. 0029A] With God as author, dearest brethren, you ought gladly to hear continual divine reading; to receive what you have heard with a hungry and thirsty heart; to commit it more attentively to memory; and, so far as your strength permits, to fulfil it in action. “The diligent reader,” as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0029D] Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 8, from which much here is transferred.], “is readier to fulfil the good things which he reads than to learn what he does not know. For just as, by reading, we desire to know those things which we do not know, so we must fulfil by upright works the things which we have already learned. Why? Because divine reading has both reward and punishment: reward, if we fulfil it by living well; punishment, if [Note: [Col. 0029D] In Part III, ‘it.’] we despise it by living badly.” If we despise hearing or reading it [Note: [Col. 0029D] There: ‘are unwilling.’], we turn the divine Majesty’s hearing away from ourselves. Hence it is said: “He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law—[Col. 0029B] even his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. XXVIII). And blessed James says: “To one who knows what is good and does not do it [Note: [Col. 0029D] Another manuscript reads here: ‘to do.’], it is sin” (Jas. IV). Therefore it adds to the burden of a greater fault for anyone to know what he ought to follow, yet refuse to follow what he knows. Whoever departs from God’s commandments by living badly, whenever he recalls those same commandments through reading or hearing, blushes under inward rebuke from himself, because he neglects to fulfil in deed the good which he has learned. Hence the Psalmist prays, saying: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I consider all thy commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). As though he said: Grant me, Lord, to live so innocently in this present life that, when I consider thy law of commandments, I may not be ashamed [Col. 0029C] of my conduct. No one can understand the meaning of the holy Scriptures unless he has frequently devoted himself to reading [Note: [Col. 0030D] Isidore, there, chapter 9; see also the note of the very learned García de Loaysa on that passage.]. The more assiduous anyone is in sacred utterances, the richer an understanding he draws from them; just as the more the earth is cultivated, the more abundant fruit it produces.

Therefore, dearest brethren, love wisdom; and, as a certain wise man says: “She shall exalt you; you shall be glorified by her when you have embraced her” (Prov. IV). Set aside the cares of temporal life; desire the spiritual things of inward sweetness. For you can in no way fully know the wisdom of God unless you have first diligently withdrawn yourselves completely from the clamour of worldly things. Hence it is written: “Write wisdom in the time of leisure; and he who is lessened in activity shall receive [Col. 0029D] it” (Ecclus. XXXVIII). Therefore read the books of the holy Scriptures diligently; flee altogether the affairs of secular life. For divine Scripture is the table of spiritual life. As the body is refreshed by bodily [Col. 0030A] food, so the inward man—that is, the soul—is sustained by spiritual nourishment; and as the body dies without fleshly food, so the soul dies without the nourishment of evangelical instruction. Therefore devote yourselves without interruption to sacred reading, so that in it you may recognize what you ought to avoid and what you ought to do [Note: [Col. 0030D] Isidore, there, chapter 8.]. By prayers we are cleansed from sins; by reading we are instructed to do good. Great indeed is the benefit which arises for God’s servants from reading and meditation. By reading we learn what we do not know; by meditation we preserve what we have learned. Reading shows what we should avoid and what we should pursue. Thus David, rejoicing in the Lord, said: “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet and a light unto my paths” (Ps. CXVIII). The reading [Col. 0030B] of the holy Scriptures brings a twofold gift: it instructs the understanding of the mind, and it leads the person withdrawn from the vanities of the world to the love of God [Note: [Col. 0030D] Isidore, there.]. For often, stirred by its discourse, we are withdrawn from desire for human life; and, kindled with love of wisdom, we hold the vain hope of this mortality cheaper in proportion as eternal hope flourishes more abundantly.

Therefore always keep sacred reading before your eyes, so that, being watchful on every side, you may more easily avoid the deceits of the enemy. Thus the Bride—that is, holy Church—in the song of spiritual love, praising her bridegroom, namely Christ, says among other things: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting by most full rivers” (Cant. V) [Note: [Col. 0030D] Gregory, on this passage.]. The bridegroom’s eyes, that is, Christ’s, are ecclesiastical men, who live in simplicity and show others the straight way by word and example. They are said to be beside streams of water because they constantly occupy themselves in the refreshment of the holy Scriptures. They are washed with milk because through baptism they have been cleansed from sins by the grace of creative Wisdom, as though by a mother’s milk. What are the most full rivers beside which they sit, if not the profound and hidden things of sacred Scripture, which we gather and by which we are refreshed while we draw from them in reading or hearing? Doves customarily sit by streams for this purpose: that they may see in the water the shadow of a flying hawk, and, throwing themselves upon it, thus escape the claws of birds of prey. So holy [Col. 0030D] men foresee the deceits of demons in sacred Scripture; from the representation which they see, as from a shadow, they recognize the enemy. When they commit themselves wholly to the counsels of Scripture, so that they do nothing [Col. 0031A] except what they hear from its answer, they mock the enemy as though throwing themselves into water. These rivers are called most full because, whatever perplexities prompt the seeking of counsel in the Scriptures, there is found in full, without diminution, counsel concerning all things.

Read also, dearest brethren, among the other pages of the holy Scriptures, for your instruction, this book—not as though composed by me, but as though assembled from the flowers of the New and Old Testaments. I did not dictate it; rather, I compiled in it the sayings of the holy Fathers. For I suffered for a long time from an illness of the head; and because I was unable to undertake any other work, having found an opportunity, received permission from my lord abbot, and been preceded, followed, and accompanied by God’s grace, I gathered crumbs from beneath the table of the holy Fathers [Col. 0031B] for your benefit and instruction and for that of posterity. These crumbs I have presented to you in this little book, if not as I ought, at least as I could, since charity required it. Thus I see that, through God’s grace, what blessed Paul said of himself has been fulfilled in me: “When I am weak, then I am stronger” (II Cor. XII).

Therefore let your holiness have this book read before it and study it diligently, so that in it, as in a mirror, it may discover what in itself pleases or displeases the heavenly bridegroom, Jesus Christ. For, as we have said, it is adorned with flowers from the holy Scriptures and is authoritative through the sayings of venerable Fathers. In it, indeed, ecclesiastical doctors elucidate the figures and enigmas of the patriarchs, interpreting the law according to the rule of the true faith; the obscurity [Col. 0031C] of histories is made clear; the prophecies of prophets are explained; the proclamations of apostles and evangelists are expounded; the faith of the Catholic Church is strengthened; the perfidy of the Jews is rebuked; the superstition of pagans—[Col. 0032A] that is, the service of idols (Eph. V)—is destroyed; the perversity of heretics is uncovered and overthrown; the doctrine of philosophers is scorned; Christ is glorified; the devil is condemned; the presumption and craftiness of Antichrist are confounded; the general resurrection of all is proclaimed; the future judgment at the end of the world is foreshown; and it is affirmed that the Bride, that is, holy Church glorified, shall cleave to her bridegroom Jesus Christ forever and shall wholly enter with him into the kingdom of perpetual brightness and blessedness.
