Furthermore, most beloved, if you diligently strive to read this little book often; if you study it as a mirror; if you keep it continually at hand and recall what you have read to memory; there you shall find how you ought to live and teach others; [Col. 0032B] how to drive superfluous thoughts from the heart, tame the flesh, restrain the stomach from food, strengthen the spirit, and check the tongue from idle speech; how to avoid detractions, whisperings, and buffoonish words; how to turn away the eyes lest they see vanity, and hedge in the ears with the thorns of the fear of God lest they hear what is unlawful; how to devote fitting times to prayer, persist in reading, and give oneself to divine contemplation; how to avoid vices and pursue virtues with God’s help; how to love your neighbours in goodness as yourselves; and how to love God in all things—indeed, above all things.

This work began in the era 1223 (the year 1185).

I also entreat you, dearest brethren, to deign to pour out prayers for me, unworthy as I am, before the divine mercy, [Col. 0032C] so that, freed from the chains of sins, I may be able with you to attain the fellowship of God’s elect. Amen.

End of the prologue.

# FIRST SERMON: ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD

Jeremiah, instructed by the Holy Spirit and foreseeing Christ’s advent, shows how Christ came to us in his first advent through the Incarnation, as a gentle lamb; and how, in his second advent for judgment, he will come as a most mighty king. He also admonishes us how we ought to prepare ourselves for him, with contrition for sins.

[Col. 0031]

[Col. 0031D] The prophet Jeremiah, dearest brethren, descended from priestly stock. Before he was formed in the womb, he was known by the Lord, “who calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. IV); before he came forth from the womb he was sanctified; he was admonished to remain a virgin; and he was appointed to prophesy not only to the Jews but also to the nations. For he was truthful in prophecy, stern in exhorting the Jews to repentance, compassionate in mourning the people’s sins, acute in foreseeing future evils, patient and steadfast in enduring adversity, and gentle in his dealings with his fellow-countrymen.

[Col. 0032D] This man, then, of such great holiness, beholding the time of humanity’s restoration and, instructed by the Holy Spirit, foreseeing the advent of the Son of God, speaks as God proclaims to him for the consolation of humankind, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch; and a king shall reign, and he shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth. And this is the name by which they shall call him: The Lord our righteousness” (Jer. XXIII). The righteous Branch is the Word eternally coeternal with God the Father, but in time made flesh from the Virgin Mary, who descended from David’s root. He is fittingly called the righteous Branch, concerning whose righteousness the Prophet [Col. 0033A] says: “The Lord is righteous, and he has loved righteous deeds; his countenance has beheld equity” (Ps. X).

John the Evangelist also speaks of this king, his name, and his righteousness, saying in his Apocalypse: “I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it was called Faithful and True, and he judges and fights in righteousness. His name was called the Word of God; and he had written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Apoc. X) [Note: [Col. 0033D] See the commentaries of Saint Beatus on the Apocalypse, pp. 523–524.]. The white horse of which he speaks is Christ’s body, assumed from the virginal womb without sin. He who sat upon it is the Lord of majesty, namely the Word of God the Father. And he “was called Faithful and True,” for of him it is said: “God is faithful, in whom there is no iniquity” (Deut. XXXII). And he “judges [Col. 0033B] and fights in righteousness,” for it is written of him: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient” (Ps. VII). He fights in order to free us from our enemies; he is patient in enduring the things in which we have sinned against him. “He had written on his garment and on his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.” Christ’s garment is the body which he assumed. The thigh signifies the line of generation, for his person consists of divine as well as human substance. We therefore read that the name is written on garment and thigh because, in the mystery of Christ’s body, we recognize divinity and humanity. All, therefore, who are called sons of God through faith in Christ continually confess that he is King of kings and Lord of lords.

Thus this king “shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth” (Jer. XXIII), because in judgment he “will not regard the person of the poor, nor honour the countenance of the mighty” (Ecclus. XXXV). This king will not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor rebuke according to the hearing of his ears; but he will judge the poor in righteousness and rebuke with equity for the meek of the earth. Why? Because righteousness is the belt of his loins and faith the girdle of his reins. “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid” (Isa. XI). By the wolf we understand the rapacious; by the lamb, the innocent. The wolf dwells with the lamb when all rapacious and impious persons, converted from their perversity, come together with the innocent into the one Church of Christ. The wolf dwells with the lamb [Col. 0033D] when those who formerly used to seize prey from the Church are now changed to better ways and dwell together in Christ’s Church with the meek and humble. It follows: “And the leopard shall lie down with the kid.” Because the leopard has various colours upon itself, it signifies the deceitful and those imperfect in the faith of Christ. The kid, because it is a wanton animal, signifies sinners and those who gladly pursue vices. Therefore the leopard lies down with the kid because sinners and deceitful persons are mingled together in Christ’s Church.

Again he adds: “The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together, and a little child shall lead them” (ibid.). In the calf the priests of the Church are figured; in the lion [Col. 0034A] are signified worldly powers, namely kings and princes of the people. *Leo* in Greek means *rex*, “king,” in Latin; fittingly, of course, because as a king is more powerful than all peoples, so a lion is stronger than all beasts; and as all peoples fear a king, so that they do not dare to transgress his commands, so all beasts fear the lion, so that they do not dare in any way to cross the sign which he has made with his tail. The sheep signifies a humble, simple people devoted to God. It is therefore rightly said: “The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together,” because the rulers of the Church, the powers of the world, and all the throngs of believers together hear God’s commandments in the Church; and together receive its sacraments, namely baptism, penance, and Christ’s body. “And a little child [Col. 0034B] shall lead them.” That child will indeed lead—that is, govern—them, of whom the same [Note: [Col. 0034D] Manuscript: “the same.”] Isaiah says: “A little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX). He himself, who deigned to be born for us as a little child on earth, himself as the good shepherd leads his flock to pastures ever green.

“The lion, like the ox, shall eat straw; the infant at the breast shall delight himself over the hole of the asp; and shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk” (Isa. XI). By the lion, as was said above, kings and princes of the world are figured. There, therefore—that is, within holy Church—the lion eats straw like an ox when kings and princes of the people, like the rulers of the Church, receive the sacraments of the true faith. The lion feeds upon straw like an ox because, in holy Church, princes of the people have a common order with their subjects. It is also added: “The infant shall delight himself from the breast over the hole of the asp; and he who has been weaned shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk” (ibid.). This infant is the Lord Jesus Christ, whom the ever-Virgin Mary bore and nursed as an infant at her most sacred breasts. It is called an asp because it injects poison by its bite and kills. By the asp, then—that is, the poisonous serpent—are signified the Gentiles, who, when the apostles preached, uttered venomous, that is sacrilegious, words against Christ. But now the Gentiles, converted from the error of idols, gladly proclaim the glory of the little child Jesus Christ.

Therefore the infant, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, delights himself over the hole of the asp—that is, over the preaching of the Gentiles—provided that they most gladly praise him [Col. 0034D] whom before their conversion they used to blaspheme. It follows: “And he who has been weaned shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk” (ibid.) [Note: [Col. 0034D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII, chapter 4.]. *Basiliscus* in Greek is *regulus* in Latin, “little king.” *Regulus* is a diminutive name from *rex*, “king,” and is called a little king, as though it meant “small king.” It is a small serpent streaked with white spots, half a foot in length—that is, having half the measure of a foot. It is therefore interpreted as “little king” because, as the lion is king of all beasts, so the basilisk is king of all serpents. All other serpents flee from its presence because, as soon as it sees them, it kills them by sight and smell alone. Indeed, if it sees a person, it immediately [Col. 0035A] kills him. No bird flying passes its gaze unharmed; however far away it may be, burnt by its mouth and breath, it falls dead. Yet the basilisk is defeated by weasels, which people throw into the caverns where it lurks and lives.

In this passage the basilisk—that is, the little king—signifies the devil. The den of the basilisk is the hearts of unbelieving people, in which that twisting serpent, the devil, rested from the beginning of the world. Therefore into the basilisk’s den he who was weaned, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who as an infant was weaned, put his hand when he drew the devil captive from the hearts of unbelievers and condemned him bound in hell, lest he should harm upon his holy mountain, which is the Church. Thus the Psalmist, foreseeing the advent [Col. 0035B] of that same Jesus Christ, said to him: “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and shalt trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC).

All these names are fittingly applied to the devil. He is the most poisonous serpent, the asp, when he strikes secretly; he is the basilisk when he openly pours out poisons; he is the lion when he persecutes and seizes humankind; and he is the dragon when he impiously and insatiably devours the negligent. But all these things were cast down and destroyed beneath the feet of our Lord Jesus Christ at his advent.

Isaiah also says further that Christ was born according to the flesh from the seed of David: “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples, the nations shall entreat him, and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. XI). [Col. 0035C] The root of Jesse stands as a sign to the peoples because Christ, who descended from Jesse’s root, placed the sign of the cross upon their foreheads. “The nations shall entreat him”: we now see that this has all been fulfilled. His tomb is so glorious that, apart from the glory which we render to him because we have been redeemed through his death, the place itself, shining with miracles, draws the whole world to itself for the sake of his glory.

Again, with Isaiah’s prophetic mouth bearing witness, testimony is given concerning Moab at Christ’s birth: “I will place . . . . over . . . . . those who have fled from Moab, a lion, and over the remnant of the land” (Isa. XV). And again: “Send forth, Lord, the lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock [Col. 0035D] of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. XVI). For from this people of the Moabites came forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John I), and who rules throughout the whole circle of the earth. Ruth signifies the rock of the desert: bereft by the death of her husband, she bore Obed by Boaz; Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot King David; and Christ was born from David’s stock (Matt. I). By the mountain of the daughter of Zion he means either, in the historical sense, the city of Jerusalem itself; or, according to the tropological sense, the Church set upon a high place—that is, at the height of virtues.

Thus far, dearest brethren, we have recalled the prophecies concerning Christ’s first advent. [Col. 0036A] Now it is necessary that we say something concerning his second advent. In the first advent our Lord Jesus Christ came humble; in the second, indeed, he will come terrible. In the first advent he came “like a gentle lamb” (Jer. XI); in the second he will come “like a most mighty king” (Dan. XI). In the first advent he visited the world in great gentleness; in the second he will come to judge the world in great severity. In the first advent he went out from the Father and came into this world to sow his seed (Matt. XIII); in the second he will come to demand from us a hundredfold fruit of his seed (Luke VIII). In the first advent, like a man going abroad, he entrusted his goods to us, his servants (Matt. XXV); in the second he will come to require from us [Col. 0036B] doubled gain from his talents, to reward servants who work well for the profit they have brought, and to condemn servants sluggish and negligent in good work (ibid.).

What, then, dearest brethren, shall we say at his terrible advent, when we have received such great and innumerable goods from his hand, yet spend them unworthily? Or what excuse shall we be able to offer on the day of his strict examination, when from the talents received from him we not only bring back no profit, but, what is more serious, even hide them in the earth [Note: [Col. 0035D] Gregory, Homily 9 on the Gospels: “To hide a talent in the earth is to entangle one’s received ability in earthly actions; not to seek spiritual gain; never to raise the heart from earthly thoughts.”]? To hide talents in the earth is to entangle God’s gifts—sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—in earthly actions. Do we not hide the talent in the earth when we withdraw our eyes from reading sacred Scripture and fix them [Col. 0036C] upon things contrary to our souls? Do we not likewise hide the talent in the earth when we turn away our hearing so as not to hear God’s commandments, and gladly listen to shameful and harmful words? Or do we not conceal the talent in an underground cave when, despising common foods, we choose more delicate and more carefully prepared fare? We also bury the talent in the earth when we disdain the sweetness and delight of divine contemplation and delightfully seek the fragrances of passing things. We also hide the Lord’s money in the earth when our hands, which ought to work good things pleasing to God, are defiled by touching soft and pleasant things—and, more seriously, things unspeakable.

[Col. 0036D] What therefore shall we be able to answer on that day, when the Lord begins to settle accounts with us and requires doubled gain from the talents entrusted to us? (Matt. XVIII.) What shall we wretches say on that day, who at the first stage lost innocence, forfeited virginity, defiled chastity, never fully discharged the vows which we made to God, did not preserve our rule, stirred up quarrels and hatreds against our brethren, loved murmurings and scandals, delighted in idle and useless tales, desired carnal things, and neglected spiritual things? For if on that day the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall we unworthy people appear, who have lived so perversely and disorderly? [Col. 0037A] Or how can we be secure on that day, when we must even render an account of idle words? (Matt. XII.) Or how shall we be able to endure the face of so great a judge on that day, before whose presence fire shall go and a mighty tempest shall sweep round about him? (Ps. XLIX.)

Therefore, dearest brethren, before the day of judgment appears; before death overtakes us; before darkness envelops us; before Tartarus seizes us; before the dark whirlwind possesses us; before that most righteous and terrible judge comes, let us anticipate his face in confession, fasts, vigils, and prayers; and let us weep before him with all devotion (Ps. XCIV). Trembling, let us cry with the Prophet, saying: [Col. 0037B] “Enter not into judgment with thy servants, O Lord, for in thy sight no human being shall be justified by himself” (Ps. CXLII), unless through thee remission of all [Col. 0038A] sins is granted to them (Office for the Burial of the Dead).

Therefore, brethren and my lords, while we still live in the body (II Cor. V), let us wash sins and vices away with tears; let us amend the conduct of our life for the better; let us show true charity to our neighbours; let us strive to fulfil our vows to God without deceit; and let us raise our hearts with groaning to the Son of God himself, who redeemed us in his first advent and whom we await in the second as judge of all humankind. May he not permit us to perish with sinners in that terrible and most glorious advent of his, but may we deserve, with the elect, to hear that sweetest voice from his mouth: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV). May he deign to grant this, he who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

# SECOND SERMON: ON THE ADVENT OF THE LORD II

[Col. 0037]

In this sermon he sets forth how God resolved, through Christ’s advent, to free the human race from the yoke of bondage to the ancient enemy—an advent which he had foretold through the prophets—and how, although the Church might at one time have been barren, she is now fruitful, calling all nations to the worship of his divinity, to the confusion of the Jews; for God, born in the flesh through a Virgin, appeared to humankind in order to open the way of salvation to believers.

[Col. 0037C] I wish you to know, dearest brethren, that as God is by nature almighty, so He is by nature kind and merciful; supremely powerful and wise in His works, and abundant in mercy. He alone governs, rules, and sustains all things; and His mercies are over all His works (Ps. 144). Therefore God, kind and merciful, beholding the long servitude of the human race, by which it was cruelly oppressed by the ancient enemy, and resolving mercifully to deliver it, speaks through the prophet for its consolation, saying: “Strengthen the weary hands, and make firm the feeble knees. You who are fainthearted in mind, take courage [Note: [Col. 0037D] Another manuscript: “You who are fainthearted, recover strength.”]; for behold, God Himself comes for your captivity” (Isa. 35); that is, for the yoke of cruel slavery, the yoke of misery and unhappiness,

[Col. 0037D] by which the ancient enemy had subjected humanity to himself through the fault of the first man. [Note: [Col. 0037D] Another manuscript: “being about to remove it.”] For that author of all wickedness [Note: [Col. 0038D] Same manuscript: “originator.”] afflicted the human race so cruelly through the five ages of the world that neither offering, nor incense, nor sacrifice, nor holocaust of any patriarch or prophet could deliver it from the hand of hell. Hence Isaiah, making lament, says: “All our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruating woman” (Isa. 64). A certain wise man also, as though grieving over this most cruel yoke, says: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam [Col. 0038C] from the day of their birth until the day of their burial into the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40), that is, the earth.

Again, foreseeing the time of human restoration from this most harsh yoke, [Note: [Col. 0038D] Another manuscript: “the same.”] the prophet said in rejoicing: “The yoke shall rot away because of the oil” (Isa. 10). *Oleos* in Greek means “mercy” in Latin. Therefore, because of the oil—that is, the mercy—of our Redeemer, the yoke of our captivity rotted away; for He mercifully assumed our humanity, by which He overthrew the ancient enemy and broke apart the knotted cords of sins by which we were held bound. Jeremiah too foresaw that the human race would someday be freed from the rule of the ancient enemy and subjected to the service of God, when, at the Lord’s command, he proclaimed:

[Col. 0038D] “And it shall be in that day, says the Lord of hosts: I shall break his yoke from your neck, and tear apart his bonds; and strangers shall no longer rule over him. But he shall serve the Lord his God and David his king” (Jer. 30), that is, Christ. David, indeed, was already dead, but Christ was to be born from his stock. For David is interpreted “strong of hand,” because he was most valiant in battles (1 Sam. 17). He himself was also “the desired one” in his own lineage, prefiguring Him of whom the prophet sang: “The Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2): namely, the Son of God,

[Col. 0039A] who had been shown beforehand in spirit to the fathers of the Old Testament. David therefore fittingly signifies Christ in this place: Christ who, by the Father’s will, descended to a singular contest against the ancient enemy; having defeated him, He plundered his goods—that is, the hearts of men in which he had formerly dwelt—turning them to Himself; He bound him with fiery chains in the depths of hell; and He carried with Himself to heaven his prey, that is, the holy souls whom the enemy had held captive there.

Although God from the beginning of the world foretold the coming of His Son through the prophets, made it known by oracles, and confirmed it through most truthful witnesses, the Jewish people nevertheless neither receives their testimony nor gives faith to the words of the prophets. O unhappy Jews!

[Col. 0039B] How long will you remain unbelieving concerning Christ’s coming, you who call yourselves sons of Abraham? Did not the Son of God foreshadow His coming even to Abraham, from whose loins your race proceeded, while Abraham sat in the valley of Mamre at the entrance of his tent, when he saw three and worshipped one? “When he lifted up his eyes, three men appeared standing near him; and when he saw them . . . he worshipped . . . and said: ‘Lord, if I have found favor in your eyes . . . let your feet be washed, and rest beneath this tree . . .’ And Abraham went . . . to Sarah [Note: [Col. 0039D] The manuscript here and below reads: *Sarram*, *sarra*.], and commanded her . . . to make cakes baked under ashes . . . which he set before them with the calf which he had prepared, and likewise milk and butter; but he himself stood beside them beneath the tree. And when they had eaten, they said: ‘Where is Sarah your wife?’ But he said: ‘Behold, she is in the tent.’

[Col. 0039C] And He said to him: ‘Returning, I shall come to you at this time, and Sarah shall have a son.’ When she heard this, Sarah laughed” (Gen. 18).

[Note: [Col. 0039D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 14.] It should be noted that Abraham bears a threefold figure in himself. First, that of the Savior, when, leaving his kindred [Note: [Col. 0039D] “Kindred.” Thus St. Isidore; it better suits both the literal text and its allegory.], He came into this world; second, that of God the Father, when he sacrificed his only son; third, the figure present in this passage, that of the saints who welcomed Christ’s coming with joy. That tent of Abraham signifies Jerusalem itself, where prophets and apostles dwelt for temporal things; where, when the Lord first came, He was received by believers but was hung upon the wood by unbelievers.

In the three men who came to him, the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ was foretold; two angels accompanied Him, whom many understand as Moses and Elijah: the one, the giver of the ancient law, who by that same law indicated the Lord’s coming; the other, who is to come at the end of the world and announce Christ’s second coming, and preach His Gospel to Jews and Gentiles. Hence, when the Lord

[Col. 0039D] was transfigured on the mountain,

[Col. 0040A] those two—Moses and Elijah—were seen with Him by His apostles (Matt. 17). But Abraham’s seeing three and worshipping one shows the Lord and Savior, whose coming he desired to see, as the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8).

Then beyond doubt he beheld the mystery of the future sacrament, when he saw three and worshipped one. Thus he also washed their feet (John 13), to show the purification by washing which Christ would grant at the end to His faithful in baptism; for the feet signify the last things. He also prepares [Note: [Col. 0039D] Another manuscript: “for.”] a banquet, namely the fattened calf (Luke 15). This tender, fattened calf

[Col. 0040B] is the body of the Lord Jesus Christ, which in the Gospel is slain for sinners. In preparing this banquet, he also set butter and milk with the flesh of the calf. Our Apostle, declaring that milk held the figure of the ancient law, says to certain disciples still tender in faith: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, and indeed even now you are not able” (1 Cor. 3). For he had delivered the commandment of the law as milk drawn from the breasts of the two tablets, that is, the testimony of faith; for their infancy of understanding was not yet able to receive the solid and robust food of evangelical teaching.

Butter, however, is the exceedingly rich and fatty testimony of the Gospels, which is given to the faithful as the oil of the calf for a sign. Abraham accordingly set

[Col. 0040C] the calf to be eaten with butter and milk (Gen. 18), because neither the body of the Lord, which is the calf, can exist without the milk of the law, nor the milk of the law without butter—that is, without the testimony of the Gospel. The three measures from which Sarah made cakes baked under ashes (ibid.) signify the image of Noah’s three sons, from whom the whole human race was born: believing in the divine Trinity, they were to be mingled with the water of baptism through the Church, of which Sarah was the image, and gathered together into the one bread of Christ’s body. These are the three measures which, according to the Lord’s words, we know the woman in the Gospel to have leavened (Matt. 13). But since the Lord’s saying recalled the *satum*, that is, a measure of grain, charity compels me to write more fully for your love’s sake

[Col. 0040D] concerning measures of grain, wine, and oil.

A measure is so called properly because grain and wheat—that is, dry and liquid goods—are measured by it, such as modii, urns, and amphorae. The smallest part among measures is the spoon (*cochlear*), which is half a drachma in weight, amounting to nine *siliquae*; tripled, it makes a *concula*. A *concula* is filled by one and a half drachmas. The weight of a *cyathus* is ten drachmas.

[Col. 0041A] An *acetabulum* is a fourth part of an *hemina*, weighing twelve drachmas. A *cotyla* is an *hemina*, containing six *cyathi*. An *hemina* weighs one pound, and when doubled produces a sextarius. A sextarius is two pounds; taken twice, it is called a *bilibris*. Taken four times, it is called by the Greek name *conix*. Multiplied five times, it makes a *quinare*, or *gomor*; add a sixth and it makes the royal measure. For a *congius* measures six sextarii, from which they also gave the sextarius its name. For they call a measure of liquids a *metrum*, whence it is called a *metreta*. It is also called an urn, an amphora, and the other such names of measures; nevertheless, it received its name from the perfection of the number ten. *Metrum* applies to every measure: for *metrum* is called “measure” in Latin. A *modius* is so called

[Col. 0041B] because it is made complete according to its own mode. It is a measure of forty-four pounds, or twenty-two sextarii. A *satum* is a kind of measure according to the custom of the province of Palestine, holding one and a half modii; its name is drawn from the Hebrew language. There is also another *satum*, a measure capable of holding twenty-two sextarii, like a modius. A *bath* is a measure holding fifty sextarii. An urn is a measure which some call a quartary. A *cadus* is a Greek amphora containing three urns. A *gomor* weighs a load of fifteen modii. A *corus* is filled by thirty modii. For this reason, most beloved, we have described these measures to you, so that when you find them in the sacred Scriptures, you may more readily know their character, quantity, and weight.

[Col. 0041C] What follows.

[Note: [Col. 0041D] Isidore, as above, *Questions on Genesis*.] The breads which Abraham set before them are said to have been unleavened, because the unity of believers ought to be without the ferment of perverse teaching. They were baked under ashes so that, being cooked by the heat of the Holy Spirit through repentance for former sins, the faithful people might become acceptable to God like a pleasing food. Their sitting beneath the tree was a sign of the Lord’s Passion, of which Moses and Elijah themselves are preachers and prophets. But God’s promise of a son to barren Sarah—“I shall come,” He says, “about this time” (Gen. 18)—does not refer to times, but to the character of His coming, when the faithful people were to be born through the promised Son.

[Col. 0041D] For Sarah bore the person of the holy Church, to whom the Lord says through the prophet: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not give birth; for many are the children of the forsaken woman, more than of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54; Gal. 4). This barrenness was the Gentile world, which bore no children to God because it had neither law nor prophets; but now it begets more than the Synagogue, which thinks itself to have God as husband. Or it is the Church which was forsaken among the Jews, because, when the Lord came, it did not bear children to Him—so that we may refer these things to the Church gathered both from Jews and Gentiles, which remained barren.

[Col. 0042A] At that time the Synagogue appeared to have a husband and was fruitful in children; but the holy Church remained until Christ’s coming as though unfruitful and deprived of a husband. At the coming of our Redeemer, indeed, the Synagogue was weakened, and the holy Church was made fruitful in children; because through unbelief and hardness of heart the Synagogue was separated from her husband, namely Jesus Christ, while the holy Church was most graciously received by Him. Nor does she cease to bear children for Him from an incorrupt womb, because she perseveres a virgin and chaste in faith. Hence: “The barren has borne very many, and she who had many children has become weak” (1 Sam. 2). “The barren has borne very many,” namely the holy Church; “and she who had many children has become weak,” namely the Synagogue. To her Isaiah the prophet again says:

[Col. 0042B] “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare” (Isa. 54). As though he said: Enlarge the place of your tent not only in Judaea but throughout the whole world; stretch out the crimson skins, namely the martyrs, and the hyacinth-colored skins; do not spare—that is, the preachers who contemplate heavenly things and protect the Church. “Make your cords long,” he says, by keeping the divine commandments; “and strengthen your pegs” (ibid.), namely reason and understanding, by which the commandments stand firm. Again he adds: “You shall break forth to the right and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations” (ibid.). As though he said: O barren Church, you shall break forth to the right by doing good, and to the left by avoiding evil; and your seed shall inherit the nations, namely the holy apostles, of whom it is said:

[Col. 0042C] “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed” (Isa. 1), namely that of the holy Gospel; and it has inhabited the cities—that is, the nations or churches formerly abandoned by God (Isa. 54)—through Christ’s grace. He continues again: “Do not fear disgrace, for you shall not be put to shame as before; nor shall you blush, for you shall not be ashamed. For you shall forget the disgrace of your youth,” namely at the building of the tower of Babylon; “and you shall remember no more the reproach of your widowhood,” being joined to your husband through faith; “for He who made you shall rule over you” (ibid.), not the idols which she unlawfully worshipped in sacrifices to her own condemnation.

When the Babylonian tower—that is, Babel—was being built,

[Col. 0042D] the Gentile world, which God had betrothed to Himself in Noah and his sons, was forsaken by the Lord as a woman committing fornication in her youth, until the time of the Incarnation; the Jewish people was chosen, and therefore the former was a widow and the latter married. Hence: “The Lord’s portion is His people; Jacob is the cord of His inheritance” (Deut. 32). Therefore Zechariah says: “I took two staffs: one I called Beauty,” namely the Gentiles in Noah and his sons; “the other, Cord” (Zech. 11), namely the Jews, whom the Lord chose for Himself amid the confusion of languages, that is, in the family of Heber, from whom the Hebrew peoples—that is, the Jewish people—are named. Therefore it says there: “And I cut off from my tending the staff called Beauty, and took up that which

[Col. 0043A] is called Cord” (Zech. 11). Again Isaiah speaks for the Church’s consolation: “The Lord of hosts is His name, and your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel,” sanctifying the faithful by the blood of the Passion. “He shall be called the God of all the earth,” not of Judaea only; for “the Lord has called you as a woman forsaken,” namely by God, “and grieved in spirit,” that is, repentant with all her heart [Note: [Col. 0043D] Another manuscript: “through repentance.”] (Isa. 54)—you, namely, who had turned away from Him. The woman forsaken, therefore, was the Gentile world, which first committed fornication with idols and withdrew from the Lord; afterward, mercifully called by Him, it approached Him devoutly, repenting of former sins.

This may also be referred to the sinful soul, cast off by God not from hatred but by divine dispensation, so that, pressed beneath the weight of evils, it may return

[Col. 0043B] to its former husband; and, having lost its substance—that is, its virtues—it may not despair of the father’s mercy, who mercifully gives ring, robe, and kiss to the returning son.

Thus far, beloved, we have spoken of the barrenness and fruitfulness of the holy Church. It is now necessary to return to the history of Abraham, from which we had wandered rather far. As Scripture says, Sarah laughed when the Lord promised her a son. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Isidore, as above.] Yet her laughter must be regarded not as doubt but as prophecy. This laughter has a double meaning: either because Christ would become an object of laughter to unbelievers, or because He would deride all His enemies at His judgment. Thus he who was born from Sarah is himself called “laughter,” because the Son of God is a stumbling block to Jews,

[Col. 0043C] but foolishness to Gentiles (1 Cor. 1). For Isaac is interpreted from the Hebrew language into Latin as “laughter,” because Sarah laughed when he was promised to her by the Lord. Again, this same Isaac is promised a son who would become a great nation: “And in him,” He says, “all the nations of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen. 22). By these words two things were promised to him historically: the Jewish nation according to the flesh and all nations according to faith. Beyond doubt, in his seed—that is, in Christ—all nations of the earth are blessed, all those who before the ages were predestined in Him by God the Father to eternal life.

Therefore let the Jews be silent, let heretics be ashamed, let blasphemers be struck dumb, who, persevering in their malice even to this day,

[Col. 0043D] deny that the Son of God came in the flesh for the salvation of the world. But how can they believe us when we preach the truth of Christ’s Incarnation, when they disdain to hear their patriarchs and prophets foretelling His coming? Moses the lawgiver signified this most wretched blindness of the Jews when he descended from the mountain with veiled face and related the Lord’s words to the elders. [Note: [Col. 0044D] The same author, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 33.] The fact that Moses’ face, on his descent, was again seen glorified but nevertheless was covered with a veil signified that the same law is covered with a mystical veil, concealed and hidden from unbelievers.

[Col. 0044A] The speech of the law has a secret glory of knowledge among the saints; the law also has the horns of the two Testaments, with which it advances armed against doctrines of falsehood. For when Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts; and plainly, while reading the Scripture of the prophets, they understand the mystical senses of the commandments carnally through excessive dullness of heart, the entire face of Moses is covered by a certain veil, so that they cannot understand or endure the glory of the speaking law. But unless they are converted to God, the veil will not be removed from their hearts; and the killing letter will die, while the life-giving Spirit will be raised up. For God is spirit (2 Cor. 3), and the law is spiritual (Rom. 7). Hence David also prayed in the Psalm:

[Col. 0044B] “Unveil my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118).

Therefore the Lord, as has already been said above, who by the Father’s will decreed to help the human race in danger, showed beforehand to that very people from whose seed He was to be born figures in many forms and utterly certain signs of this His coming. Did Joshua son of Nun, leader of the people Israel, not prefigure the coming of that Son of God into this world when he sent two men to spy out the city of Jericho? [Note: [Col. 0044D] The same author, *Questions on Joshua*, ch. 2.] This Joshua sends two scouts into the city of Jericho, and they found lodging with Rahab, that is, a prostitute. That Joshua, leader of the people, signified in deed and showed by his name the Lord Jesus Christ who was to come.

[Col. 0044C] The city of Jericho signifies this world, to which the Lord Jesus Christ directed the two Testaments in order to examine human conduct. For in order more fully to prove in this world the faith of believers or the obstinacy of rebels, He sent, as it were, two scouts before the coming of His judgment: namely the law and the Gospel. Rahab, however, holds in her actions the type of the Church, gathered from foreign and alien peoples, which formerly lived in the desires of the flesh and committed fornication with idols (Judg. 8). Of such persons the Lord says: “Tax collectors and prostitutes go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21), such as Matthew and Mary, namely by devoutly receiving the preaching and, according to John’s preaching,

[Col. 0044D] producing fruits worthy of repentance.

Thus the Church alone received these two scouts of the Lord—the two Testaments—into herself and faithfully preserved them. She took the utmost care not to betray them, preferring herself to be endangered, provided that she might save them unharmed and safe. That woman, Rahab, knew that the city would fall; but the holy Church firmly believes and does not doubt that the world will fall. For her own salvation and that of all her people, the holy Church made a covenant with the scouts, that is, with the Lord’s Testaments; and in her house—that is, in herself—she reverently and faithfully placed scarlet, the sign of Christ’s Passion and blood.

[Col. 0045A] Whoever is found outside this holy Church will by no means escape the ruin and conflagration of the world. Here, then, the faith of the Catholic Church is confirmed, since not only is Christ foretold as to be born in the Old Testament, but even His glorious name (Deut. 28), namely Jesus, is preached most plainly. Jesus is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “Savior.” Of Him we know that the prophet said: “They shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and He shall send them a Savior and defender, who will deliver them” (Isa. 19). “Because of the oppressor,” he says, that is, the ancient enemy; “and He shall send them a Savior and defender,” namely the Son of God and of man, who will save and deliver them from the hand of that same most cruel enemy,

[Col. 0045B] or plunderer. Beyond doubt the Lord Jesus Christ, at His coming, defeated the captor of the human race, bound him with fiery bonds, and called all nations to the worship of His divinity. Foreseeing this in spirit, the prophet David says: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. 21). Again he adds: “And all the families of the nations shall worship before Him” (ibid.); and again: “Sing to the Lord a new song, for He has done wonders. The Lord has made known His salvation; before the nations He has revealed His righteousness” (Ps. 97). He explains how this multitude or diversity of nations is united in the worship of God: “When,” he says, “the peoples gather together as one, and kings to serve the Lord” (Ps. 101). As one, certainly—

[Col. 0045C] that is, as one flock—so that those who, through the rite of diverse images, were called many kingdoms and peoples may, by coming together in one faith, be called one people of God and one kingdom. This gathering of the people from the nations is the Church itself, to which the prophetic voice says in the Psalms: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; and forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty” (Ps. 44). The prophet calls the Gentile people to forget its own people, that is, the assembly of unbelievers, and the house of its father, namely Babylon, which is the wife and house of the devil, so that it may wish to be joined to Christ in the marriage of faith. To these peoples Isaiah cries, saying: “Gather yourselves, come, and draw near together, you who have been saved from the nations;

[Col. 0045D] for those who worship the image they have carved and pray to a god who does not save have no knowledge” (Isa. 45). Who are these saved from among the nations, except those among them who believed in Jesus Christ, the Son of God? But when he says, “Draw near together and gather yourselves,” he shows that the nations ought to glory in a single communion of faith. Again he says: “Turn to me and be saved, all ends of the earth, because I am God and there is no other besides me. I have sworn by myself; a word of righteousness shall go forth from my mouth and shall not return: every knee shall bend to me, every tongue shall swear in the Lord” (ibid.).

We now behold this fulfilled, when the Church of God is extended throughout all the ends of the earth and the faith of believers increases. By this prophecy let the Jews be ashamed,

[Col. 0046A] who claim God exclusively for themselves, when they hear, “Every tongue shall swear in the Lord”—not only now the people of the Hebrews, but also the entire multitude of nations. Isaiah, the same prophet, further foretold with noble and urbane elegance, speaking of the Church’s praises: “I have created the fruit of the lips: peace to him who is far off and to him who is near” (Isa. 57). The Apostle explains this when he says of the Church coming from circumcision and uncircumcision: “He preached peace to those who were far off and peace to those who were near” (Eph. 2). Likewise Hosea: “And it shall be in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. 1).

Without doubt, all whom the Son of God redeemed from the hand of the enemy and released from the bonds of original sin by holy baptism and the stream of His most precious blood,

[Col. 0046B] He adopted as sons for Himself. Hence John the Evangelist says among other things: “As many as received Him, He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in His name” (John 1). There, then—that is, in the holy Church—they are called children of God; because those who were formerly rejected and estranged from God by worshipping idols are now called and are children of God, not by nature but by grace, worshipping the one true God in three persons. This is in Zephaniah: “Then I shall give the peoples a chosen speech, that they may call upon the name of the Lord and serve Him with one shoulder” (Zeph. 3). And after this: “Men shall worship Him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2). In this passage the calling of the nations is also prophesied, since a place of prayer is shown to exist everywhere; no longer one place of prayer in which the carnal people

[Col. 0046C] must worship God, but a place of prayer throughout the whole world, when he says: “Men shall worship Him from their own place.”

Isaiah the prophet also foretells that all nations will gather to receive instruction in faith, thus: “And it shall be in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and He will teach us His ways, and we shall walk in His paths. For from Zion the law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’” (Isa. 2). These are the last days, in which faith in the Savior shone forth. The mountain prepared above the summit

[Col. 0046D] of the mountains is Christ, because He is the head of the apostles and prophets. The house of the Lord is Christ’s Church, established upon Him, to which the diversity of nations gathers in faith and harmony. The law went forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, whether because it was to come among the nations after the Jews had been abandoned for unbelief, or because, being among that same people, Jesus said to His disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). Likewise Zechariah the prophet says thus concerning the Church of the gathered nations: “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion; for behold, I shall come and dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations shall be joined to the Lord on that day, and they shall be my people, and I shall dwell in your midst;

[Col. 0047A] and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you” (Zech. 2).

The Son of God, seeing that the day of His coming was drawing near and wishing to alleviate the affliction of the holy Church, speaks through the prophet Zechariah for her consolation, saying: “Praise and rejoice, daughter Zion,” and so forth. It is as though He said: Since I see you bound by the chains of sins, I come from the Father’s bosom into this world in order to redeem you; I do not shrink from dwelling among human beings, that I may rescue you from such great evils and bring you into the fellowship of the citizens above. Therefore praise with the depths of your heart; praise with a voice of rejoicing, when you know that God dwells in your midst. Again He says: “And many nations shall be joined to the Lord on that day,” in accordance with that which the Psalmist says in the person of the Father: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance,” etc. (Ps. 2).

[Col. 0047B] It follows: “And they shall be my people,” namely my own peculiar people; “and I shall dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts has sent me to you.” Hence it is said: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Who, therefore, is this Lord sent by the God of hosts, except our Lord Jesus Christ, whom God the Father sent to deliver the human race from the harshest yoke of misery to which the ancient enemy had subjected it? Again the prophet Isaiah speaks of Christ’s greatness and glory thus: “The spreading of His wings shall fill the breadth of your land, Emmanuel”

[Col. 0047C] (Isa. 8). It is as though he said: His beginning or dominion shall extend so far, filling the breadth of your land, namely Judaea, that His greatness will exceed all your boundaries. *Emmanuel* means in Latin from Hebrew, “God with us,” because God, born through a Virgin, appeared to humankind in the flesh in order to open to the faithful the way of salvation, by which they might reach heaven and be joined to the angelic hosts.

Therefore, convicted at last by so many testimonies, let the Jews and the rivals of the converted Gentiles be ashamed, acknowledge, and hear the Lord proclaiming in Deuteronomy: “The nations shall be at the head, but the unbelieving people at the tail” (Deut. 28). It is clear that the Jews were always rebellious and unbelieving against God’s commandments from the day on which He powerfully and mercifully brought them out of the land of Egypt.

[Col. 0047D] Thus far, dearest brethren, to confirm and strengthen the foundation of our faith, we have recalled the prophecies concerning the Lord’s first coming. Now it is again necessary, for your instruction, to set forth certain matters concerning His second coming from the sacred books of the New and Old Testaments.

Just as, therefore, we rejoice in the Lord’s first coming, in which we were redeemed from the enemy’s power, so we must be watchful concerning his second, lest he come suddenly, like a thief in the night (1 Thess. 5), and find us—as God forbid—sleeping in our sins. That Christ the Judge is expected to come from heaven, and that the Father has given him all judgment (John 5), was foretold through Ezekiel as follows: “Thus says the Lord God: Remove the turban; take off the crown. Is not this she which raised up the lowly and humbled the exalted? Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity—I will make it so; and this has not come to pass until he comes whose is the judgment, and I will give it to him” (Ezek. 21).

“Remove the turban; take off the crown.” The turban belongs to the priest, the crown to the king. It is as though God said to King Zedekiah through the prophet in these words: “Remove the turban; take off the crown, because through your sins the priesthood, kingdom, and glory of the Jews have perished.” “Is not this she which raised up the lowly and humbled the exalted?” As though he said: This crown, this turban, or this person raised up the lowly and humbled the exalted without cause; for she acted in nothing according to judgment, but, like the king of Babylon, humbled whom she wished and raised whom she wished. “Iniquity, iniquity, iniquity—I will make it so”: because, speaking for that one’s condemnation, he set down “iniquity” not once, not twice, but a third time, signifying perpetuity.

Symmachus aptly says: neither the one nor the other—namely, priesthood or kingdom—remained; both ceased. Hence those who were kings afterwards, down to Christ, were also priests; among them Hyrcanus the high priest placed a diadem upon his own head (2 Macc. 3). In vain did he wish to claim both offices for himself, since kingship after Zedekiah was due not to him but to him—to Christ—for whom it had been reserved by God the Father before the ages. Of these unworthy men Malachi says: “You priests defile my name” (Mal. 1). And shortly afterwards: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not receive sacrifices from your hands” (ibid.). And again: “In every place a pure offering is hallowed and offered to my name” (ibid.). This occurs at the coming of Christ, when he came, “desired by all nations” (Hag. 2), sent from the highest height.

It follows: “And this has not come to pass until he comes whose is the judgment, and I will give it to him” (Ezek. 21). He speaks of Christ, whose is the judgment, because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). He also adds: “And I will give it to him.” The Father gave Christ the kingdom, the priesthood, and the whole Church gathered from the Gentiles. Hence it is said: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). And again: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71). And the patriarch Jacob says: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49).

Thus Isaiah says: “The Lord stands to judge, and stands to judge the peoples” (Isa. 3). As though he said: The Lord no longer sits as though angry, because he is ready to render to each according to his works (Matt. 16); or, he does not yet sit in order to judge at present, but stands, observing and distinguishing the works of all, as though still reserving a place and time for repentance. But at last the Lord will come for the judgment of the final assize with the elders of his people—that is, with the patriarchs and prophets. Hence Solomon’s words: “When he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31), followed by: “and with its princes” (Isa. 3). He calls the holy apostles princes of the people; concerning their election the Psalmist said: “You shall make them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44).

Again he says: “The Lord shall go forth as a mighty man, and like a man of war he shall stir up zeal” (Isa. 42). As though he said: The Lord, who in his first coming seemed weak, will in the second go forth as mighty, and, like a man of war against his enemies—namely the Jews—will stir up zeal for vengeance. And again: “He shall cry aloud and shout; he shall prevail against his enemies” (ibid.). Hence the saying: “They provoked me with that which was not God . . . and I will provoke them with that which is not a people, and with a foolish nation I will anger them” (Deut. 32). In another sense, he will cry against the Jews, saying: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8).

Again he adds: “I have kept silence; I have always been silent; I have been patient. Like a woman in labour I will speak; I will lay waste and swallow up together” (Isa. 42). “I have always been silent,” he says, overlooking your conduct; “I have been patient,” awaiting your repentance. “Like a woman in labour I will speak; I will lay waste and swallow up together.” As though it were said: Like a woman in labour I will speak—that is, I will bring the offspring of my counsel into the light; as a woman brings forth a child, so I will bring forth my concealed grief and reveal what I have conceived. I will scatter your plans and swallow you up together—that is, utterly destroy you.

[Note: These words are from Isidore, *Against the Jews*, book I, chapter 61, except that our author does not follow the holy doctor in the faulty reading, “like a woman in labour I will speak”; see there the very learned Juan de Mariana’s appended note.]

This pertains to the second coming, in which he will go forth not humble, to be judged, but mighty, to judge; nor will he keep silence, as he did in the first coming, or be patient, as he was in the passion of the flesh. Rather, judging terribly, he will utter his voice. Hence it is said: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power; give glory to God over Israel; his magnificence and his power are in the clouds” (Ps. 67).

This is also taught by the Psalmist’s testimony, when he says in the psalm: “God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not keep silence” (Ps. 49). Certainly, because if in the first coming of his humiliation he was judged and kept silence, in the second, when he comes openly to judge, he will not keep silence, but will cry aloud, so as to render to each according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5). It follows: “A fire shall go before him” (Ps. 49).

[Note: This reading agrees only with Augustine’s reading; all the other Vulgate texts in this place rather support another reading.]

For he will consume the works of sinners as wood, straw, and hay; and, as gold, silver, and precious stones, he will test the deeds of the righteous (1 Cor. 3), who will say: “We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65). “A fire shall blaze in his presence”: namely, material fire, or the fire of an evil conscience, will torment the impious when they behold those judging—Christ, namely, and the holy apostles. “And a mighty tempest shall move round about him” (Ps. 49): namely, the angels who separate, who on that day will separate the good from the evil.

[Col. 0050A] In this place “tempest” is not wind, but God’s power, by which his threshing-floor is winnowed through his sentence. That judgment is called a tempest because it will come unexpectedly and swiftly sweep the impious away to hell. “A mighty tempest shall be round about him,” because the righteous will sit with him to judge: first he will summon all together, but then he will summon in order to distinguish them. Therefore, in the presence of so great a Judge, the chaff—that is, impious human beings who in this life despised Christ’s commandments—will fear that it is about to burn.

It follows: “He will call heaven from above, and the earth, to discern his people” (ibid.). “He will call heaven from above”: that is, those who are coming; or he himself, coming from above from the Father to judgment, will call heaven—that is, all the perfect, who will judge with him and sit above. He will also call the earth, that is, sinners, that they may hear the terrible sentence of judgment pronounced by him.

In the first coming the Son of God called the peoples joined together from the rising of the sun to its setting; now, however, heaven distinguishes earth with him—that is, sinners—when by a subtle examination he investigates their sins. Again he says: “Gather to him his saints, who order his covenant above sacrifices” (ibid.). The prophet, seeing future things as though present, exhorts the angels and admonishes those gathering them, saying: “Gather to him his saints.” As though he said: O angels who reap, gather his saints from the four winds of heaven: those who order his covenant above sacrifices, that is, who think upon the Lord’s promises above those things which they perform, which are sacrifices to the God of heaven.

Alternatively: those who rank the New Testament above the Old; or those who say: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8); or those who, after labour, expect the denarius; or those who value works of charity more highly than animal sacrifices.

The reaping angels will carry some in their hands and some in their bosoms on the day of judgment: contemplatives in their bosoms, active persons in their hands, as being saved, as it were, through good will and action. Of the evil it is said: “He who reaps shall not fill his hand with it, nor he who gathers sheaves his bosom” (Ps. 128). It follows: “And the heavens shall declare his righteousness to the people that shall be born” (Ps. 49).

[Note: The words “to the people that shall be born” do not belong to Psalm 49, which this author expounds; they have been transferred here from Psalm 21:32.]

As though he said: The Son of God will come openly on the last day and will judge; and the heavens—that is, the teachers and holy apostles—will proclaim this righteousness of his to the whole world, because God is Judge (Ecclus. 35), who is not deceived in distinguishing, but is altogether most just in separating good from evil (Matt. 13), rendering to each according to his works (Matt. 16).

The Son of God himself has already announced this righteousness to us: some will be placed on the right hand and others on the left (Matt. 25). Then there will be no chaff mingled with grain, because God is a righteous judge who knows how to separate wheat from tares on his threshing-floor (Matt. 13). Hence Isaiah also says: “The Lord shall make the glory of his voice heard, and shall show the terror of his arm in the threatening of wrath and the flame of devouring fire; he shall strike with whirlwind and hailstone” (Isa. 30). For the arm of God is Christ, who will come to judgment in flame and in the terror of the tempest.

Concerning this judgment the same prophet again says: “Rise up as in days of old, in the generations of the ages. Was it not you who struck the proud one, who wounded the dragon?” (Isa. 51). Here Christ’s second coming is proclaimed: that he may rise in judgment for the separation of good and evil by that power by which he rose in the generations of the ages—that is, in the beginning—when he struck the proud one, namely the devil, separating him from the fellowship of the angels.

The Son of God will also rise in his second coming as in the days of eternity, when he struck the proud one, in order that “with the spirit of his mouth he may slay the impious one” (Isa. 11), namely Antichrist. The patriarch Jacob foresaw his coming in the Spirit and prophetically foreshowed him in words when, speaking figuratively to his son Gad, he said: “Gad, girded, shall fight before him; and he himself shall be girded behind.”

[Note: The text has “Gad,” Gen. 49:19; Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 31.]

This girded Gad represents the person of the Lord, who in the first coming of his humility comes prepared to fight before Antichrist’s coming, girded with the sword of his mouth about his thigh most mightily (Ps. 44). With it he divided enemies; with it he separated son from father, daughter from mother, and daughter-in-law from mother-in-law (Matt. 10). Hence he himself said in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (ibid.).

But when he says, “he himself shall be girded behind,” the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ in the heavenly kingdom is shown, in which he will be seen by all the elect. For when Antichrist comes near the end of the world, Christ will again meet him from behind—that is, advancing after his footprints—and by a swift coming will slay him with the sword of his mouth (Isa. 11). Hence Gad is aptly interpreted “raider” (*latrunculus*), because, coming later—that is, behind the feet—like a raider he will leap forth in a rapid and unexpected coming against Antichrist’s open assault, in order suddenly to destroy him. Hence the Lord said in the Gospel, when the disciples questioned him: “As lightning comes out of the east and appears even to the west, so shall the coming of the Son of Man be” (Matt. 24).

Christ, therefore, is written [Note: Another manuscript reads: “is said.”] to fight against Antichrist both before and behind, as has already been briefly set forth above. Before him, indeed, in the concealment of humility; behind him, by a swift and unexpected coming, in order suddenly to slay him with the spirit of his mouth, as the prophet foretells in these words: “With the spirit of his lips he shall slay the impious one” (Isa. 11).

Moses also clearly shows that this prophecy of the patriarch pertains especially to Christ; for he himself says concerning him: “Blessed be he in the breadth of Gad; he rested like a lion, and seized the arm and the crown of the head, and saw his own dominion” (Deut. 33).

Let the faithless nation of the Jews now acknowledge, then, who rested like a lion except Christ in his tomb; who broke the crown of the head and the arm of the mighty except our Redeemer, who humbled the head and arm of the lofty; who saw his own dominion except he to whom principalities, honour, and dominion were handed over by God the Father through infinite ages of ages.

[Note: Isidore, *Against the Jews*, book I, chapter 61.]

Concerning his judgment the prophet Micah speaks thus, as though with great terror: “Hear, O mountains, the judgment of the Lord, and you strong foundations of the earth; for the Lord has a judgment with his people, and he has disputed with Israel, saying: My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I troubled you? Answer me” (Mic. 6). For many maintain that the future judgment will take place where the Lord suffered, Isaiah saying: “The Lord God of hosts shall make a consummation and a cutting short in the midst of the whole earth” (Isa. 10). What could this consummation and cutting short be except that of the future judgment?

But where the middle of the earth is, David’s reliable testimony concerning the Passion shows when he says: “God our king before the ages worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73). It is as though he said: Our King—that is, he who assumed our nature—worked salvation before the ages, understood as predestined by God the Father, in the midst of the earth. For our salvation is nothing other than the redemption of our Lord, Saviour, and Judge, which arose in the midst of the earth.

It is as though holy David spoke in the person of the Jews: “God our king before the ages”—as though we doubted that Christ was to come—“God, however, our king, existing before the ages, worked salvation in the midst of the earth”: namely, firm faith in himself in the midst of the Gentiles, who until now have been like uncultivated land, while we were like heaven. But now the Gentiles are heaven and we are earth: they keep watch because they have received salvation, believing that Christ has come; we snore because we still doubt that he has come into this world.

The books of the Hebrews contain all these things: they read everything but do not understand, because all things are sealed to them, as the prophet testifies: “The words of this book shall be like the words of a sealed book: if someone gives it to a man who cannot read and says, ‘Read,’ he answers, ‘I cannot read’; and again, if it is given to another who can read and he is told, ‘Read,’ he answers, ‘I cannot, for the book is sealed’” (Isa. 29). These are the seals of the Old Testament, which the Son and Heir has sealed, enlightening the eyes of our heart. Hence it is written: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8). Why? So that neither the Jew nor the heretic who is not Christ’s disciple may understand it. For, in order to understand Christ, we have the Law as guide and the prophets as witnesses. From them we have declared his divinity, name, nation, lineage, country, birth, mighty works, healings, arrests, palms, scourges, spitting, suspension, the drinking of gall and vinegar, death, lance, burial, descent into hell, incorruption of the body, resurrection of the flesh, ascent into heaven, judgment, and kingdom.

John the Evangelist also, who truthfully bears witness concerning Christ in all the things he saw, says of his coming: “Behold, the Son of God and of man shall come in the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him” (Rev. 1). He first came hidden in the assumed man; after a little while he will come openly in majesty and glory to judge.

[Note: This expression is used by the more eminent Fathers of the Church, such as Augustine, Ambrose, Hilary, and Jerome, and by all our Spanish councils in the fourth and sixth Councils of Toledo, canon 1. Nevertheless, later theologians, following St Thomas, *Summa theologiae*, III, question 4, article 3, reply to the first objection, maintain that this expression should not be extended as though it were proper, but should be piously explained: we say “the assumed man” because his nature was assumed, and because the assumption was terminated in this: that the Son of God should be man. See the Benedictines’ annotation on chapter 24 of book II of St Augustine’s *On Genesis against the Manichees*, vol. I.]

John in the Apocalypse gives the clearest testimony to Christ: that he will come in the same flesh in which he suffered and was buried, to judge the world. *Apocalypse* is Greek and is translated into Latin as *revelatio* (“revelation”). Therefore, in the second coming the Son of God will come terrible in divine power, not as before, contemptible in humility. Yet, as testimony to the true man whom he assumed from the substance of his virgin mother, he will make himself visible not only to the righteous but also to the impious. Hence it is now said: “Every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him; and all tribes of the earth shall mourn over him. Even so. Amen” (ibid.).

[Note: Another manuscript adds: “he adds,” ibid.]

Thus *Amen* means “faithfully, truly.” Similar is what Zechariah says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced; and they shall mourn for him as for an only son, and grieve over him as one grieves at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. 12). For they will grieve that they crucified him when they see him judging and reigning in the majesty of his Father and of himself. That the Son of God will come in clouds to judgment in great majesty and power, he himself testifies in the Gospel when he says: “Then they shall see the Son of Man”—that is, of the Virgin—“coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (Matt. 24).

They will see in great power and majesty him whom they despised in humility and whose words they refused to hear.

[Note: Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 27.]

On that day the reprobate will see Christ’s humanity, in which he is to judge; but they will not see his divinity, lest they rejoice. For to those to whom divinity is shown, joy is certainly displayed. According to the differing character of consciences, Christ will appear gentle in judgment to the elect and terrible to the reprobate. For whatever conscience each person brings there, such a Judge will he have; so that Christ remains in his own tranquillity, but appears terrible only to those whom conscience accuses of evil.

[Col. 0054A] The Lord already signified this when he led the Israelite people by night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, having become the guide of their journey.

[Note: Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 13.]

This preceding cloud is Christ; likewise also the pillar, because he is upright and, for our weakness, shining and firm: as it were shining by night for believers and not shining by day for unbelievers. Hence the saying: “That those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9). This pillar of fire also foreshadowed the second coming of the Son of God from heaven, in which he will appear as fire—that is, terrible—to the unjust, and as cloud—that is, gentle—to the just.

At the judgment he will appear visible as in the terror of night, because then there will be great tribulation in the world; like fire he will burn the reprobate and shine upon the righteous. Yet among these matters, dearest brothers, it should be noted that judgment has not yet appeared, but judgment has nevertheless already taken place. Whoever lives wickedly, unless he reforms his life through lawful repentance, will perish in the future judgment. But whoever lives well will not perish in the future examination; rather, immediately upon leaving the body his soul will be in refreshment and will have fellowship with God’s elect forever.

Hence Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11). As though he said more openly: If in this present life we judged ourselves by doing good, pursuing virtues, and despising vices, we would certainly not be judged in the future—that is, we would not be condemned with the impious. Whoever lives wickedly hates the light and loves darkness. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “This is the judgment: that light has come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light” (John 3).

Judgment—that is, eternal condemnation—is nothing other than not knowing and not believing in the Son of God, just as blessedness and life are nothing other than knowing and believing in the Son of God. Hence it is said: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true and only God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). Why is the one who does not believe judged, except because light has come into the world, which arouses and admonishes human beings to know their evils, in which all are involved and by which they act contrary to God? But some hate and drive away the admonishing light, lest the evils they love be reproved; others, admonished by the light, accuse their own evils—which is to do truth—and are thus illuminated, so that they may do good and avoid evil.

Their works, he says, were evil: that is, impiety, unbelief, hatred of the eternal light, and unwillingness to look upon it, but willingness to remain in the darkness of sins. For everyone who does evil—that is, whose intention is evil and to whom evil is pleasing—hates the light, namely Christ, “who enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1), and who also enlightens “the hidden things of darkness” (1 Cor. 4); “and does not come to the light,” that is, to Christ, lest his works—the evil things which he does and loves—be reproved. But whoever does truth—that is, the good works that God commands—comes to the light, so that he may distinguish light from darkness and love the light, “that his works may be made manifest, because they are done in God” (John 3).

Without doubt, that person does truth and comes to the light whose own evils displease him and who accuses what he has done: he does not forgive himself and does not spare himself. He comes to the light and begins to act with God—that is, with the light—when he accuses his evils; for the beginning of good is the accusation of evil. Thus his works—namely, that he accuses himself as God accuses him—may be made manifest, because they are done in God, that is, in the light. For unless the light shone upon him, he would not displease himself.

Therefore, beloved, if we seek to have Christ the Judge, in great power and majesty, favourable to us, let us flee darkness—that is, wicked works—and love the light, namely those things pleasing to God.

[Note: All this is woven together from the Gloss and the Master of the Sentences, book IV, distinction 48, § *Putant quidam*.]

Concerning the place of judgment, however, I have read differing views in different authors. Some say that he will judge the world in the place where he himself chose to be judged for the salvation of the whole world, as the prophet Joel testifies: “Let all nations arise and come down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit to judge all the nations round about” (Joel 3). Some understand the exposition of this chapter childishly: namely, that the Lord will come down for judgment into the valley that lies on the side of the Mount of Olives. This is frivolous, because he will sit not on the earth but in the expanse of this air opposite the place of the Mount of Olives, whence he ascended into heaven. And, as John Chrysostom says, “the angels will bear before him the sign of the holy cross when he comes down to judge the human race.” Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Then the sign of the Son of Man shall appear in heaven” (Matt. 24), etc.

*Jehoshaphat* is interpreted “judgment of the Lord.” Therefore all the impious will be gathered into the valley of Jehoshaphat—that is, into the Lord’s judgment; but the righteous will not descend into the valley of judgment—that is, condemnation—but will be raised in the clouds to meet Christ, carrying lamps of good works in their hands.

When the Lord comes to judgment in strength and great power, the sun and moon are said to be darkened (ibid.), not because they are deprived of their own light, but because a greater brightness arrives. The powers of heaven—that is, the angels—are also said to be moved (ibid.), not through fear of condemnation or any disturbance of terror, but through a certain astonishment at the things they shall see, namely, the devil cast into the lake of fire. Hence Job says: “The pillars of heaven shall tremble at his coming” (Job 26).

Before the day of judgment, however, the sun and moon will suffer eclipse, as Joel testifies: “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2). The day of judgment is called great because God will do great and terrible things on it. But when heaven has become new and earth new, then the moon’s light will be like the sun’s light, as Isaiah testifies: “And the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, that is, like the light of seven days” (Isa. 30).

[Note: Perhaps this should be added here: “And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun”; for the cited words of the text do not accord with the matters stated above, but with those said afterwards. Yet the author follows the Master closely in the cited passage.]

For as much as the light shone in the first creation during the seven days before the first man’s sin, so much will it shine after the judgment. The light of the sun, moon, and other stars was diminished through the first man’s sin; but at last it will receive the reward of its labour, because it will shine sevenfold. Then there will be no alternation of day and night, but continuous day alone will remain. Hence Zechariah says: “There shall be one day known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and at evening time there shall be light” (Zech. 14), because there will then be no variation of day and night such as exists now, but continuous light and day.

Yet Isaiah seems to say that the sun and moon will then not shine for the assembly of saints, speaking thus: “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you by night; but the Lord shall be to you an everlasting light” (Isa. 60). But by these words he does not deny that the sun and moon will then shine; rather, he signifies that, for those who will be in eternal blessedness, the use of their light will be of no service. For, as Jerome says on the same passage, the office of heaven and earth, sun and moon, will cease for us, and the Lord himself will be light to his own forever.

This passage of Isaiah may also be understood in the same way, as some say, because the sun and moon will then not rise and set as they do now. Hence Isidore, the doctor of Spain, expounding Isaiah’s words as it were, says: “After the judgment the sun will receive the reward of its labour. Hence the prophet: ‘The sun shall shine sevenfold’ (Isa. 30); and it shall not come to its setting, nor the moon, but they shall stand in the order in which they were created, lest the impious, set beneath the earth in torments, enjoy their light. Hence Habakkuk: ‘The sun and moon stood in their order’” (Hab. 3). Behold, he plainly says that the sun and moon will then shine, but will remain fixed. There too he signifies that hell is beneath the earth.

[Note: These statements, as we have said, are taken from the Master, who attributes such an exposition to Isidore. But since it is not found among his genuine works, the Master fashioned it from chapter 5 of the book *On the Order of Creatures*, whether that work is Isidore’s offspring may rightly be doubted.
