Yet there alone is read this statement: “When . . . the saints, as the reward of their labour, . . . have shone like the sun of righteousness . . . then to this bodily sun itself, as the reward of its ministry, . . . a brightness sevenfold in splendour shall be restored.”]

[Note: Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 27.]

Christ knows the day of judgment, but in the Gospel he did not wish to state it or have the disciples know it. For when the same Lord says through the prophet, “The day of vengeance is in my heart” (Isa. 62), he indicates that he does not fail to know it, but does not wish to judge. “Judgment begins from the house of God,” as it is written (1 Pet. 4): when the elect—that is, God’s house—are judged here through scourges, while the impious are to be judged there for condemnation. Hence it follows: “But if first from us, what shall be the end of those who have not believed?” (ibid.).

Before the strict examination of the Judge, not even the righteousness of the righteous is secure, unless that very righteousness by which each righteous person is righteous, through God’s justifying him, is also justified by divine mercy. Otherwise, before God even that righteousness is sin. Hence Job says: “He consumes the innocent and the impious alike” (Job 3). For the innocent is consumed by God when his very innocence, more carefully examined and compared with divine innocence, is found to avail nothing unless a person is also justified in merciful compassion. The impious person is likewise consumed by God when he is searched by the subtlety of the divine examination and, his impiety having been exposed, is condemned by judgment. Innocent and impious alike are consumed by the end of the flesh, not by the penalty of damnation. Learned and unlearned alike die, but by the death of the flesh, not by the penalty of damnation. All go to one place when righteous and impious alike return to earth in bodily death; but their recompense will differ, as Solomon says: “What advantage has the wise man over the fool . . . except that he goes there where life is?” (Eccles. 6). Therefore all alike return to earth; for they do not alike go where life is.

[Col. 0057C] The impious person is punished by a double sentence: either here he is struck with blindness according to his deserts, so that he may not see the truth, or at the end he is condemned so that he may pay the penalties due. Divine judgment is twofold: one by which human beings are judged here, and another in the future, for which reason they are judged here, lest they be judged there. Therefore, for some, temporal punishment contributes to purification; but for others, condemnation begins here, and everlasting perdition is expected there.

There are two classes, or orders, of people in judgment: the elect and the reprobate; yet these are divided into four. One order is that of the perfect, who judge with the Lord. Another is less perfect and is judged. Yet both will reign with Christ. Likewise, the order of the reprobate is divided in two: those who are evil within the Church are to be judged and condemned; but those found outside the Church are not to be judged, but only condemned.

The first order, then, of those who are judged and perish is opposed to the order of the good who are judged and reign. The second order, of those who are not judged and perish, is opposed to the order of the perfect, in which are those who are not judged and reign. The third order, of those who are judged and reign, is contrary to the order of those who are judged and perish. The fourth order, of those who are not judged and reign, is opposed to the contrary order in which are those who are not judged and perish.

The punishment of the damned in Gehenna is double: sorrow burns their mind and flame their body. This is a just requital, so that those who devised in their minds the evil which they performed in deed may be punished both in soul and body. We read that the fire of Gehenna has light in one respect and lacks it in another: it has light for condemnation, so that the impious may see what makes them grieve; and it lacks light for consolation, lest they see what would make them rejoice. A fitting comparison is made with the furnace of the three children as an example of Gehenna’s fire: for just as that fire did not burn to punish the three children, but did burn to consume the bonds of their fetters (Dan. 3), so the fire of Gehenna will shine for the wretched to increase their punishments, that they may see what makes them grieve; and it will not shine for consolation, lest they see what would make them rejoice.

There is a great distinction between the misery of this life and that of future wretchedness. There, indeed, are both misery because of the torment of pains and darkness because of the absence of light. In this life, one of these—misery—exists, but the other does not; in hell, however, both exist. As bundles of wood for burning are gathered from similar pieces, so on the day of judgment persons guilty of similar faults will be joined to their like, so that punishment may bind together, as in a bundle, those whom conduct made alike in evil. As every saint will be glorified in the future judgment according to the measure of virtues, so every impious person will be condemned according to the measure of crimes. Nor will order be absent from the future punishment of condemnation; rather, punishment will be differentiated according to the quality of crimes, as the prophet confirms: “To you, Lord, belongs mercy, because you will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61).

The punishment of the dead is also increased by the sufferings of those dear to them, as the Gospel narrative declares concerning the rich man among the dead. Thus, too, for the increase of Judas’s punishment the Psalm says: “Let his children be shaken and driven away, and let them beg” (Ps. 108). The wicked are to be punished more severely in judgment by anguish of mind, because they will see that the righteous have obtained the blessedness of glory. The devil must be cast down before the sight of all, when, in the presence of all the good angels [Col. 0058D] and human beings, he is to be sent with those who belong to his party into eternal fire. Of him the Lord speaks to blessed Job, saying: “When he is raised up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified” (Job 41).

[Note: [Col. 0057D] Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXXIV, no. 12.] Sacred Scripture sometimes so intermingles past and future time that at times it uses the future [Note: [Col. 0057D] Editions: “the future.”] for the past, and at other times changes [Note: [Col. 0058D] Ibid.: “uses the past.”] the past for the future. Therefore, in this passage, when it is said, “When he is raised up,” namely Leviathan, “the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified,” those who were terrified [Note: [Col. 0058D] Ibid.: more correctly, “the past.”] are described under the form of future time. Nor do we lose the sense of correct understanding if we believe that, when Leviathan [Col. 0059A] fell from the height of blessedness, the elect angels also feared at his ruin: so that, when the fall of pride cast this one [Note: [Col. 0059D] Editions correctly read “him.”] out from their number, that very fear might establish the others more firmly in standing. Hence it is added: “And, terrified, they will be purified.” For the terrified angels were, as it were, purified because, when he fell together with the rejected legions [Note: [Col. 0059D] Editions: “departed.”], only those remained in the heavenly places [Note: [Col. 0059D] Ibid., after “heavenly places,” adds “seats.”] who would live blessedly for ever.

Thus this fall [Note: [Col. 0059D] Ibid.: “downfall.”] both frightened and purified them. It frightened them lest they should despise their Creator through pride; it purified them because, when the rejected fell away [Note: [Col. 0060D] Ibid.: “departed.”], it came about that the elect remained in heaven in the grace of their Creator. But because Sacred Scripture often designates the preachers of the Church by the name [Col. 0059B] of angels, since they proclaim the glory of the heavenly homeland, we may also understand “angels” here as holy preachers. If, therefore, what is said—“When he is raised up the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified”—is referred to future time [Note: [Col. 0060D] Editions somewhat differently: “when the strict Judge comes, the end of this Leviathan,” etc. Thereafter Gregory’s passage is excerpted piecemeal.], the final condemnation of this Leviathan is signified. For when the strict Judge, namely Christ, comes for judgment, he will cast him into the lake of fire before the eyes of all. He will be cast down with such weight of terror that even the strength of the angels—that is, of the holy preachers who are still to be found alive in their bodies—will be disturbed. “And, terrified,” he says, “they will be purified,” because, if any venial faults remain in them, these will be burned out by fear. Therefore the devil is called Leviathan, that is, a serpent of the waters, in the sacred writings, because he moves about with shifting cunning in the sea of this world.

[Col. 0059C] Let us consider, therefore, beloved brethren, how greatly the conscience of wicked people will then be shaken, when even the life of the righteous is troubled by such fear. What will those do who hate the coming of the Judge, if even those who love him dread the terror of so great a judgment? [Note: [Col. 0060D] Here Isidore begins again, as above.] Many may perish on the day of judgment who now appear to be elect and holy. Hence the prophet says: “The Lord called for judgment by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and it will consume part of the house” (Amos 7). A part of the house will indeed be devoured, because hell will swallow even those who now glory in the heavenly commandments. Of them the Lord also says: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, cast out demons, [Col. 0059D] and perform many mighty works?’ Then I will confess to them: ‘Because I never knew them, depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are’” (Matt. 7).

Meanwhile, brethren, it is fitting that we call to mind blessed Paul, teacher of the Churches, and diligently hear what he says in exhortation for our benefit: “Knowing that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. For now our salvation is nearer than when we believed” (Rom. 13). The term “sleep” is sometimes used in a good and sometimes in an evil sense [Col. 0060A]. In a good sense it is used where the Holy Spirit speaks through Solomon in the Song of Songs concerning the bride, namely the soul or the holy Church: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the stags of the field, do not rouse or awaken the beloved until she herself desires it” (Song 2). And again: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song 5). But in this passage it is used in an evil sense, where Paul urges us to rise from sleep. For if sleep did not sometimes signify sin, Paul would by no means elsewhere say to his disciples: “Awake, you righteous, and do not sin” (1 Cor. 15). Hence he exhorts his hearer, saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5). Solomon also rebukes the sinner, [Col. 0060B] saying: “How long, sluggard, will you sleep?” (Prov. 6). Therefore each person ought to be aroused to the watchfulness of righteousness all the more diligently as he sees himself more heavily burdened by the sleep of vices. Let it therefore be said: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep.” As though he said: Knowing this time of grace, by which we have been established in the root of love for God and neighbour: it is the hour—that is, the opportunity—for doing good, but a brief one; sleep is ignorance or negligence. “For now our salvation,” namely eternal salvation, “is nearer,” that is, more deserved through good works than when we merely believed in Christ, that is, when we had not yet done any good works. As though he said: Since we have believed and have done good works, it is more shameful if we do not rise. Or otherwise: our [Col. 0060C] eternal salvation is nearer, that is, nearer to death. One who works well is near to eternal life, because baptism has availed for pardon, but a good life for the crown.

It follows: “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near.” The night of ignorance and unbelief has passed—that is, it was, but is no longer; its memory warns you to beware. The day of eternal blessedness has drawn near, since sins have been forgiven and the way of righteousness has been shown. Or night is the old human being, who passed away in baptism; but day is the sun of righteousness, namely the Son of God, who descended from the Father’s bosom in order to enlighten us. By his light the faithful learned the truth, so that they might know what ought to be done or rejected. “Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness,” for the reasons stated above: those works which came from the darkness of ignorance, or which [Col. 0060D] love darkness and lead to everlasting darkness. It follows: “And let us put on, as an adornment, the armour of light,” that is, the virtues which faith requires; “and let us walk honourably as in the day,” namely, having received virtues, so that we may exercise ourselves in their practice, as befits believers in the day of faith. “Not in revelry and drunkenness,” that is, in luxurious banquets; “not in beds and indecencies,” namely in the sloth of sleeping and in luxury, which is apt to arise from excessive food and drink among those who live badly and follow the desires of the flesh. “Not in [Col. 0061A] strife,” he says, “and jealousy,” as some are accustomed to prefer themselves to one another, and as inferiors seek to envy superiors—an envy which proceeds from strife. “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13), that is, the pattern of Christ, so that, clothed with him, you may not be compelled to serve the flesh but the spirit.

It is necessary, therefore, beloved brethren, that in accordance with the Apostle’s counsel we rise from the sleep of vices and open the eyes of the mind for watchfulness, that is, for good works; lest, weighed down by the torpor of idleness and deprived of the fruit of good works, we arrive empty at the Lord’s threshing floor—God forbid. For the Son of God knows the wheat in his threshing floor, and he also knows the chaff. By wheat we understand those strong in faith and zealous in God’s service; by chaff, those weak in faith [Col. 0061B] and empty and barren of the fruit of good works. Therefore, those who hasten to the Lord’s threshing floor not laden with good works but empty are to be reckoned not as wheat but as chaff. But those who proceed to the Lord’s threshing floor, that is, to judgment, filled with the fruit of good works, will not be reckoned as chaff but as wheat; and they will be gathered into the barn, that is, into the heavenly kingdom. Hence John the Baptist said, when he preached to the crowds who were coming to him concerning Christ’s power: “He will cleanse you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (John 1), that is, by the cleansing of sanctification and the testing of tribulation. “He will cleanse you by fire,” namely unquenchable fire, because it will neither be extinguished nor extinguish those whom it torments, but will punish them eternally. It follows: “Whose winnowing fan is in [Col. 0061C] his hand,” namely the discernment of righteous examination; because the Father has given judgment to the Son, “and he will cleanse his threshing floor,” that is, the present Church at the end of this world, “and gather his wheat into his barn” (Matt. 3), namely those immovable in the hope of eternal goods, who now follow him with a perfect heart.

The Son of God cleanses his threshing floor when, either in the present life, the perverse are cast out of the Church on account of manifest sins, or after death they are condemned. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness: pride, envy, slander, and hatred; and let us put on the armour of light: charity, patience, humility, and sobriety. Armed with these on the right and on the left, we may overcome the attacks of the ancient [Col. 0061D] enemy and escape the wrath of the most just Judge.

With the utmost [Note: [Col. 0061D] These passages which the author takes from the book *On Wholesome Teachings* give us occasion to observe that this book is a work of Paulinus of Aquileia, as will be clear to anyone from the latest edition of his works, and especially from the Appendix to Augustine, vol. [Col. 0062D] VI, where learned revisers restored the book to Paulinus; yet our author, like many others, will frequently cite it hereafter under Augustine’s name.] zeal and the greatest vigilance we must take care that on the day of judgment we do not hear from Christ what sinners will hear, namely: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). For Gehenna is truly prepared for the devil, and not for human beings, if they renounce the devil’s works. But those who imitate him in wicked deeds will be tormented without end in the same fire. Woe to those for whom are prepared the pain of worms, [Col. 0062A] the burning of flames, tears of the eyes, thirst without quenching, weeping without consolation, gnashing of teeth, outer darkness without light, an unending punishment without cessation, where there is continual pain and groaning, where death is desired and not granted; where there is no honour for king or reverence for elder. There no master is above a servant, no one gives consolation to a neighbour, no daughter obedience to her mother, no son service to his father. There all indignation, stench, and bitterness, and every evil abound without end.

[Note: [Col. 0062D] Chapter 51.] Let us, dearest brethren, meditate upon these things without ceasing; let us hold them firmly in our minds; and let us beware of every sin, if we seek to escape wrath and to find the grace of Jesus Christ on the day of judgment. Therefore, while we have time, let us persist in good [Col. 0062B] works (Gal. 6), and with God’s help let us watch without ceasing, lest, suddenly overtaken by the day of death, we seek time for repentance and are unable to find it. We must sow while we are in this world; for in its own time—that is, after death, or on the day of judgment—we shall reap (ibid.) what we ought to possess in eternal life.

[Note: [Col. 0062D] Chapter 62.] Therefore now, I beg, let each one of us keep watch, lest on the day of judgment the devil find his own rags in him, that is, the filth of sins, and the person whom Christ wished to free by his grace begin to be held guilty for ever. Nor should those flatter themselves wickedly who, after receiving grace, refuse to amend their sin and return again to their former desires. On the day of judgment the Son of God will be present, namely the most equitable Judge, [Col. 0062C] who will show partiality toward no powerful person and will need no witnesses. All souls, namely the souls of all human beings, will stand by, so that each may give account according to what it did in the body, whether good or evil (2 Cor. 5). For then the adversary will also be at hand, namely the devil, the enemy of all good people; the words of our profession will be recited; and he will cast in our face whatever we have done—on what day we sinned, in what place, and what good work we ought then to have performed. And if we are found such in the sight of the most merciful Judge, that adversary will exult, declaring himself the stronger and pleading such a case before such a Judge. For then the devil will be able to say:

[Col. 0062D] “Most just Judge, judge this man to be mine because of guilt, for he was unwilling to be yours through grace. He is yours by nature and mine by misery. He is yours through your Passion, but mine through my persuasion. He was disobedient to you; he proved obedient to me. From you he received the robe of immortality; from me, this ragged tunic in which he is clothed. He lost your garment when he came here in mine. What business had unchastity, pride, luxury, greed, and the other vices with him? He forsook you and fled to me. [Col. 0063A] I see him accompanied by my sisters, that is, wicked actions. For because he disputed with pride, raged with anger, and did other evils, he stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. O most just Judge! Since righteousness and judgment are the foundation of your throne, therefore judge that he must go with me and be condemned with me. He chose to be mine, and I recognize as mine everything that he brought here. Because he desired what was mine, he ought to be punished with me; for the one whom you deigned to redeem at so great a price afterwards willingly chose to bind himself to me.” Alas, alas, dearest brethren! Will one who is found there in such a condition, so as justly to be assigned to the devil, be able to open his mouth?

[Note: [Col. 0063D] Chapter 63.] Let us therefore see what we are doing and how we may be freed from him while we still live. Let us see [Col. 0063B] and beware lest we have received the grace of God in vain [Note: [Col. 0064D] Another manuscript: “may receive.”] (2 Cor. 6). Rather, with an undivided heart and perfect faith, let us renounce and reject so ruinous an inheritance of the devil, lest we remain orphans and poor. Let the terrible judgment of the blessed Apostle Paul, terribly pronounced, be recited in our midst, so that it may make our hearts and bodies tremble together. “For if we sin deliberately,” he says, “after receiving the knowledge of truth, no sacrifice for sins remains” (Heb. 10). As though he said more plainly: if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of truth, we must hold fast to charity and cease from evil; otherwise no sacrifice for sins remains, as under the old law it was given to the Jews repeatedly to offer [Col. 0063C] sacrifices for sin. For Christ is not to be sacrificed again for sins; what has once been done need not be done a second time. Rather, those who have the knowledge of him must remain in faith and truth.

Or otherwise: for those sinning deliberately—that is, for us if we remain in the will to sin—Christ, who is the sacrifice for sins, is of no benefit already in this present life; from which it is clear that neither in the future, after receiving the knowledge of truth—that is, although we have come to faith, on account of which some are secure as though they would never perish. It should be noted that he did not say, “for us being willing,” but “for us sinning deliberately”; for a *voluntarius* is one persistent in something, while one *volens* is so only for a time.

It follows: “But there remains a certain terrible expectation [Col. 0063D] of judgment, and a zeal of fire which will consume the adversaries” (ibid.). As though he said: In the future there remains, or abides, a certain terrible expectation of judgment, which already inwardly afflicts the mind in the present life, and a zeal of fire—that is, an assault—which will consume Christ’s adversaries. Unless, therefore, we remain in the faith and truth of Christ, judgment awaits us, unless we remove it by repentance. In saying that there is a terrible expectation of judgment, he excludes not repentance but a second baptism. He does not say that repentance or remission is no longer necessary, but sacrifice—that is, a second cross—because one is sufficient; he wishes us not to wait longer, but to repent without delay. “But there remains a certain terrible expectation [Col. 0064A] of judgment and a zeal of fire which will consume the adversaries,” Christ judging. Concerning his coming a certain wise man said: “I think that the time of Christ’s coming will be when there will be such a manifestation of his divinity that not only no righteous person, but not even any sinner, will fail to recognize Christ; when sinners too will know their sins in his sight, and the righteous will plainly see the paths of their righteousness, to what end they have led them. And this is what was said: ‘All nations will be gathered before him’” (Matt. 25).

The Son of God will not appear in one place when he comes in his glory and fail to appear in another, just as he himself wished to represent his coming by comparison with lightning when he said: “As [Col. 0064B] lightning goes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24). Therefore, as lightning going out from the east appears as far as the west because it fills everything, so when Christ comes in his glory, because he will be everywhere, all people everywhere will be in his sight; and thus they will be placed before the throne of his glory, that is, before his kingdom and the authority of his dominion. His throne may mean certain more perfect saints, of whom it is written: “For there thrones sat in judgment” (Ps. 121); or certain angelic powers, of whom it is said: “Whether thrones or dominions” (Col. 1). Therefore God the Word, the King of the ages, [Col. 0064C] who was made in the form of a human being, will sit upon such a throne of his glory, and all nations will be gathered before him (Matt. 25).

In the future, compassion for the condemned will not make the hearts of the righteous sorrowful, where the saints’ joy in the contemplation of God will be so great that no entrance will be granted to sorrow. Just as white appears more beautiful when compared with black, so too the rest of the saints will be more glorious when compared with the condemnation of the wicked; thus righteousness is set off by injustice, and virtue by vice. Therefore the glory of the saints increases while the wicked are condemned to their deserved punishment. After the resurrection, ascent into heaven in the flesh is promised to the saints, Christ saying to Peter: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17). For if we are members of the Head, and Christ is one in himself and in us, then certainly where he ascended, we too shall ascend.

Therefore, beloved brethren, we must not only flee with all our strength the evils due to the rejected, but also seek with the greatest zeal the goods which God has prepared for his elect; we must shed tears without ceasing in longing for them and, advancing with all our strength from virtue to virtue, sigh for the heavenly homeland. May the Son of God himself, who is the way, truth, and life (John 14), deign to lead us to it—he who lives and reigns as God with the same God the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## THIRD SERMON: ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

[Col. 0065]

Since Paul sowed Christ’s grace more than others, he is brought forward for the instruction of ourselves and of the whole Church: that God has not merely spoken to us in the Son, whose name surpasses that of the angels, but that this designation was predicted beforehand—the Son ineffably begotten from God the Father before the ages, although no one had known him before. For eternal Wisdom has a way in one respect and a place in another; Christ shone forth from the Father in such a manner that one must either believe him to be the Son of God or judge the prophets to be liars. Although he is called both Son and angel, no creature can be compared with him. The mystery of Gideon is aptly applied to Christ’s Nativity; Isaiah likewise is introduced concerning Christ’s two births and his attributes. God, unwilling that the human race should perish, drove out the darkness of ignorance, gradually leading it to knowledge of his divinity and opening the secrets of his will. Paul shows this under the figure of the son of any human person. John is introduced together with Isaiah concerning Christ’s eternity, bringing our faith to its conclusion along with the power and effects of faith; and, with this, that faith alone cannot save a person, just as good works cannot save without it. He adds what a true Christian must meditate upon before his eyes.

[Col. 0065A] Paul, who, caught up on high, ascended to the third heaven; who, plunged below, spent night and day in the depths of the sea—that is, was held in the open sea amid storms; who in the second year after the Lord’s Ascension was baptized and obtained the dignity of the apostolate; and who, labouring more than all, sowed the grace of the Word far more widely among the rest and filled out evangelical teaching by his preaching—thus speaks for the instruction of the whole Church:

“God, in many portions,” that is, by many utterances, “and in many ways,” namely with many kinds of expression, so as to make the certainty of a thing understood in so many ways more assured, “formerly spoke to the fathers by the prophets” (Heb. 1). That is, it was fitting that servants should be prophesied to through servants, so that he would not arise suddenly when he came but would be awaited in faith. “In many portions,” he says, that is, many times to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the rest, and frequently to the same persons; “and in many ways,” because sometimes through dreams, as to Daniel; sometimes by an open voice, as to Moses; sometimes by inward inspiration, as to David. In saying “speaking” and “spoke,” he uses the present for the past and the past for the present. He signifies that he speaks through the Son the same thing that he spoke through the prophets, except that in the prophets truth was hidden and still to be fulfilled, whereas in the Son it is revealed and fulfilled. But when he says, “formerly he spoke to us in the Son,” it is evidently in the same way as formerly; “to us,” the children of those fathers, lest it be thought that he spoke to us of persons other than those of whom he spoke to them—which might seem possible if he were speaking to another nation. It follows: “In these last days he has spoken [Col. 0065C] to us in the Son,” namely at the end of the times, because after this utterance no other utterance follows. But when he says, “In these days he has spoken to us in the Son,” it is as though he said: there still survive people who heard and saw. “He has spoken to us in the Son,” who is greater than the prophets, “whom he appointed heir of all things,” namely the unchangeable heir, that is, possessor of every creature. Thus he commends him according to both natures, divine and human. “Through whom he also made the ages,” [Col. 0066A] not only the eternal ages, which are less known, but also temporal ones. “Who, being the brightness of glory” (ibid.), according to the divine essence, is the same as the Father, light from light: for the Father is glory, and the Son is the same with him; and, having become human, he makes him known like a ray of the sun. Hence: “Father, I have manifested your name to human beings” (John 17), and the rest. The brightness of glory: the Son is coeternal with the Father, as brightness is coeval with the fire from which it comes and is of the same nature; so God from God is no less God than a human being from a human being. It follows: “And the image of his substance,” namely the full manifestation of the Father’s essence. Here he is otherwise distinct personally, as an image from the one whose image he is; yet equal, because not at all dissimilar. “Upholding all things,” he says, because as all things were created by him, so all things are preserved by him: he is no less great in governing than in creating. “By the word of his power,” that is, by command alone. He adds again, saying: “Having made purification of sins, he sits at the right hand of Majesty on high” (Heb. 1): namely, he mercifully cleanses us from sins, he who is such according to humanity; and, exalted to equality with the Father, rests and reigns—not where Adam fell, but exalted above all things in heaven. Again he says: “Having become so much better,” that is, more worthy, “than the angels,” clearly having become so according to humanity, “as he has inherited a more excellent name than they,” namely honour, when he rose and ascended into heaven.

While he was still mortal, he had a name surpassing [Col. 0066C] that of the angels, because angels ministered to him from the very hour of his conception, as we believe. But after he became immortal through the resurrection, it was more surpassing. And because this might be understood otherwise, he adds “than they.” Without doubt the Son of God inherited a name more excellent than the angels, before whom all creatures reverently bend the knee.

The designation of the name Jesus is first found foretold in a figure of our Lord Jesus Christ: for a certain son of Nun was surnamed Jesus by Moses [Col. 0067A] [Note: [Col. 0067D] Isidore, Book I *Against the Jews*, ch. 6.]. After Moses’s death this man became leader; by the Lord’s grant and command he obtained authority and divided by lot among the children of Israel the land of promised inheritance. What did this change of name signify except that, after Moses—that is, the Law—had died, and the commandment of the Law had ceased, the Lord Jesus Christ was to become our leader and lead us, sanctified through the streams of the Jordan—that is, through the grace of baptism—to the land of the heavenly promise, after all enemies of vices had been expelled and the attacks of evil angels put to flight? For the Father begot him, equal to himself, before the ages; and at the end of time he willed that he should take flesh from an incorrupt virgin for the salvation of the human race, in which flesh he endured death for our sins and rose on the third day.

[Col. 0067B] For the Son of God himself, as we have already said above, was ineffably begotten of God the Father, as we find written concerning him in the ancient books. Long before, the prophet Micah said of him in the person of the Father: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata, are small among the thousands of Judah; from you will go forth the ruler of Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5). As though he said more plainly: Bethlehem—that is, “house of bread”—which is called Ephrata, that is, “seeing the fury of Herod’s slaughter,” is compared with the cities of Judah in which there are so many thousands. It is a small village; nevertheless, from you will go forth the ruler of Israel, namely Christ, who, although according to the flesh he is David’s son, was born from God the Father before the ages. The Creator of times is not confined by time in a narrow space, but [Col. 0067C] “his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity,” because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

[Note: [Col. 0067D] The same, Book XV of the *Etymologies*, ch. 10.] Bethlehem of Judah was the city of David, which gave birth to the Creator of the world. It is said to have been founded by the Jebusites and was first called Ephrata. But when Jacob fed his flocks there, he gave that place the name Bethlehem by a certain prophecy of the future (Gen. 35); the name is interpreted “house of bread,” because of that bread which descended from heaven there. Concerning his eternity the prophet David says: “He will endure with the sun and before the moon, from generation to generation” (Ps. 71). As though it were said: “He will endure with the sun,” that is, without end. Hence: “Your throne, O God, is for age upon age” (Ps. 44). And lest we should think that he did not exist before time, he adds, saying, “and before the moon”: as though to say, he preceded all time. He explains how “before the moon” should be understood by adding “generations of generations,” so that this may be an exposition of the preceding statement; or thus: “he will endure with the sun,” that is, with paternal brightness or equality, and “he was before the moon,” that is, before the Church in true dignity, because he was conceived in human nature free from sin; or “before the moon,” because he preceded his Church by his eternity and will endure through generations of generations.

[Col. 0068A] Note that the Church is not unsuitably designated by the moon, because, as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Church has no light unless she is illuminated by the true Sun, namely the Lord. Again the Psalmist added and said: “His name endures before the sun,” that is, before every temporal ordering; “and in his name all tribes of the earth will be blessed,” because all will magnify him (Ps. 71). Hence it is said: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone works wonders through himself and through his own; and blessed be the name of his majesty,” that is, may knowledge of his divinity be multiplied among human beings. And this will indeed happen, because “the whole earth will be filled with his majesty”: let this multiplication take place in the former people and in the latter, that is, the Christian people (ibid.).

[Col. 0068B] The Word itself, Power, and Wisdom plainly shows that the Son was begotten from God the Father before the ages when, confirming his own birth, he says: “The deeps did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood in their heavy mass; before the hills I was brought forth; he had not yet made the earth, the rivers, and the poles of the world … and I was with him, arranging all things” (Prov. 8). [Note: [Col. 0067D] Isidore, Book I *Against the Jews*, ch. 2.] Thus by such authority it has been declared that the Son was begotten of the Father before all ages, when all things are known to have been created by the Father through him.

The question is again raised: how was he begotten, since neither Apostle learned, nor prophet discovered, nor angel knew, nor creature recognized the sacred mysteries of his birth? Isaiah testifies, saying: “Who shall declare his generation,” [Col. 0068C] namely that of Christ (Isa. 53)?—his divine generation, which no one comprehends by human reason. Therefore, if the prophet could not recount his birth, who will profess to know how the Son could be begotten by the Father? Hence it is said in the book of Job: “Where will you find the Wisdom of God the Father? For it is hidden from the eyes of all human beings and concealed from the birds of heaven” (Job 28), that is, unknown even to the angels themselves. Again elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0068D] The manuscript less correctly reads “there.”]: “To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed?” (Ecclus. 1)—namely, the origin of the Son of God. Therefore, what exceeds even the knowledge and understanding of angels, who among human beings can recount? “God the Father alone understands its way, and he himself knows its place” (ibid.).

[Col. 0068D] [Note: [Col. 0068D] From Gregory, *Morals*, Book X, no. 5.] But amid these matters, dearest brethren, one must know that Wisdom, coeternal with God, has a way in one respect and a place in another. If anyone understands “place,” however, let it not be understood locally, for God cannot be contained bodily; but, as has been said, the place is not local, because he is wholly everywhere. Therefore the place of Wisdom is the Father, and the place of the Father is Wisdom. Hence Wisdom herself testifies concerning herself in the Gospel, saying: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14). Therefore Wisdom has a way in one manner and a place in another. She has a way through the passage of humility; she has a place through the abiding state of her divinity. Thus, inasmuch as the Wisdom of God [Col. 0069A] is eternal, she does not pass; but she passes inasmuch as she appeared temporal for our sake. Therefore it is rightly said: “God understands its way, and he himself knows its place” (Job 28), because it is evidently the Father’s alone to know how he begot the Son, and the Son’s alone to know in what manner he was begotten by the Father. Indeed, the manner of begetting a son is questioned because a son is born only from two persons; for the frail condition of mortals has such an origin for this kind of generation. But Christ shone forth from the Father as brightness from light, as word from mouth, as wisdom from heart.

But the impious Jews, denying Christ the Son of God in wicked unbelief, hard of heart and unbelieving toward the ancient prophets, yet closed against us, prefer to be ignorant and deny rather than believe Christ’s coming. For him whom they acknowledge as to come, they refuse to acknowledge as already come. But they pretend not to understand these things because in their sacrilege they do not recognize that they have been fulfilled. Therefore, to overthrow their faithlessness, we have assembled certain testimonies from the Old Testament, by which we prove with the truest reasoning that Christ was begotten by the almighty Father.

[Note: [Col. 0069D] Isidore, Book I *Against the Jews*, ch. 1.] God the Father himself testifies to the same thing, the Psalmist saying: “With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendours of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109). “From the womb,” therefore, means from that inward and incomprehensible substance, or from that divine and immeasurable secret of the Father’s breast, by which the Father brings forth a good Word from his heart, as he himself says in [Col. 0069C] the Psalm: “My heart has poured forth a good word” (Ps. 44), etc. Again, in the same book the Father speaks to the Son: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2). This was not said to David or to any of the kings who followed him; for there is added: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (ibid.). This was granted neither to David nor to the Jewish people, but only to Christ, whose name is throughout all nations, whom the nations serve and kings obey, as Scripture speaks of him, saying: “All kings of the earth will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. 71).

Likewise Solomon—[Note: [Col. 0069D] It is uncertain whether the Holy Spirit uttered these words through Solomon or through Agur son of Jakeh.]—when he wished to know the name of the Father and the mystery of Christ’s birth according to the Godhead, [Col. 0069D] thunders these words in Proverbs: “Who has ascended into heaven and descended? [Note: [Col. 0069D] Supply here, as in another manuscript: “Who has held the wind [Col. 0070D] in his hands?”] Who has bound up the waters as though in a garment? Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name [Note: [Col. 0070D] Another manuscript: “to him.”], or what is the name of his Son?” (Prov. 30). If you do not know who this Son of God is, that impious king, looking on in Daniel, said: “Behold, I see four men, unbound, walking in the midst of the fire … and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. 3). We faithfully believe, and do not doubt at all, that he was the Lord and Savior. [Col. 0070A] But an objection is also raised from Daniel that this Son of God is called an angel.

The Son of God is truly called an angel, as the prophet speaks of him: “The ruler whom you seek shall come to his holy temple, and the angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. 3). It is as though God the Father were speaking through the Prophet to faithful peoples desiring Christ in these words: Behold, the Savior whom you await with all devotion, from whom you desire salvation, who is truly the Creator of all and the cause of salvation, shall come to his holy temple—that is, to his Church or to each individual believer. He is also the angel of the covenant, that is, of the great counsel: he judges justly and does not show partiality, because he discerns according not to a man’s face but to his heart. “Behold, I send my angel” (ibid.): understand this as spoken in the person of God the Father; and immediately the Lord of all, namely Christ, shall come to his holy temple, for whom John prepared the way in the hearts of believers. God could not previously walk in them because of their perversity and unbelief. “Behold, he comes,” says the Lord of hosts. It is as though he said: Behold, the angel of the covenant comes, who will judge justly, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5). Again, speaking of him in wonder, he says [Note: [Col. 0070D] Another manuscript reads: “follows.”]: “And who shall be able to think upon the day of his coming?” No human understanding could indeed conceive when the Son of God would come, or what he would be like. It follows: “And who shall stand to behold him?” Therefore, if, as is true, no one can conceive the day of his coming because of the power of his majesty, who with dim eyes could behold him in his majesty or splendor, he who is the true Sun of righteousness? “He,” he says, “is like a refining fire, and like the herb of fullers” (ibid.). The Lord is truly a fire, consuming wood, hay, and stubble (1 Cor. 3), that is, severely punishing grave sins. Yet for those also who commit small and light offenses he is the fuller’s herb, so that he may restore cleanness to those who have been washed and cleanse the filth of the daughters of Zion, that is, of souls. It follows: “He shall sit, refining and cleansing silver; and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and strain them as gold and silver” (Mal. 3). In this place, priestly rank is understood by the Levites. Therefore, if priests must be refined and purified, what is to be said of the rest, since judgment begins with the house of God? [Note: [Col. 0070D] More correctly, with the Gloss: *quidquid*, “whatever.”] Whatever, then, in gold—that is, in our understanding—and in silver—that is, in speech—is mixed with brass, tin, or lead, is smelted in God’s furnace, so that pure gold and silver may remain and not be darkened by any contamination. “And they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness” (ibid.), because, when the priests of the holy Church have been purified from every filth of vice, then their offerings will be acceptable to God.

[Col. 0071A] Therefore Christ, as we said above, is called the Son of God in that he is begotten of the Father (Acts 13); but in that he is frequently recorded as sent by the Father to announce matters to the patriarchs, he is called an angel. The Father himself also bears this testimony concerning him to the lawgiver [Note: [Col. 0071D] Another manuscript adds here: “Moses.”]: “Behold,” he says, “I send my angel, who shall go before you, guard you on the way, and bring you into the place which I have prepared. Therefore observe and hear his voice; do not think him to be despised, for he will not pardon you when you sin: my name is in him” (Exod. 23). Who, then, is this angel to whom God gave his authority and name? If it is said that he is some angelic power, it is impious either to believe or say this, because no creature can be likened to the Son of God. Hence the Psalmist says: “Who among the clouds shall be made equal to the Lord, or [Col. 0071B] who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88). By the clouds we understand the preachers of the holy Church, who water human minds with spiritual rains. Those too are called sons of God who are adopted as sons through God’s grace.

Therefore, although the preachers of the holy Church are illustrious in preaching and awesome in miracles, they cannot be like Jesus Christ, because they have received these powers of good working not from themselves but from him. Likewise, Jesus Christ could have no equal among the sons of God, because the saints are sons by grace, whereas he is Son by nature. Therefore what the Psalmist says is true: no one among the clouds shall be equal to Christ, nor can anyone among the sons of God be like him. He who is not his equal in nature [Col. 0071C] cannot be his equal in name or power. For he is the Son who, being frequently sent by the Father, visibly appeared to human beings in the Old and New Testaments. Therefore, because he is sent to announce to human beings the will of the Father and his own will, he is rightly called an angel.

But Isaiah, more openly affirming that the Son was begotten of God the Father, proclaims thus: “The voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies” (Isa. 66), namely to those Jews who did not believe in him, and who shed the blood of the holy prophets, apostles, and the Lord himself around the sanctuary (1 Macc. 1). Again he adds: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; and before her travail came, she gave birth to a male child” (Isa. 66). It is as though he said: Before Mary gave birth to Christ in time, God the Father begot for himself the coeternal Word. And before Mary’s childbirth came, God the Father begot without time the male child, that is, the mighty Son, through whom all things were made and subsist. The same prophet says: “Before the child knows how to call his father or his mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria shall be taken away before the king of the Assyrians” (Isa. 8). But when he says “before he knows,” this means before he makes known, by his divinity, that he has God as Father and, through assumption of flesh, the Virgin as mother. Or otherwise: before the child, according to his humanity, knows how to call [Col. 0072A] God his Father, or Joseph his reputed father, and Mary his mother, the strength of Damascus shall be taken away by Tiglath-pileser. It is as though he said: Before this child is yet born, he will deliver his people by invocation alone.

To this most wise and almighty child the same [Note: [Col. 0071D] The manuscripts read *isdem* (“the same”), rather than *idem*.] prophet speaks as though in congratulation: “You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the scepter of his exactor, as in the day of Midian” (Isa. 9). It is as though he said: You have overcome the yoke of his burden, that is, the dominion of the devil; the rod of his shoulder, namely his power; and the scepter, that is, the rule, of his exactor, namely the devil, as in the day of Midian. Christ has a yoke, but it is gentle; the devil also has a yoke, but it is an unbearable burden. Christ has sovereignty upon his shoulder, upon which [Col. 0072B] he bore the cross; and the devil has a rod upon his shoulder, by which he overcomes. “You have overcome his rod,” he says, “as in the day of Midian.” He calls the day of Midian that day on which the Midianites were easily and without bloodshed defeated by Gideon (Judg. 7), in which Christ’s victory is also shown figuratively. It follows: “You have overcome the scepter of his exactor,” namely of the devil himself, who daily exacts the coin of sin which he first entrusted to the first man and demands from his descendants with the interest of punishments. Why is this so? “Because every violent plunder with tumult, and every garment mixed with blood, shall be burned and become food for fire” (ibid.). It is as though he said: The human race, which the devil had plundered, the Lord will violently—that is, powerfully—take away from him, and will thrust the devil himself with tumult into hell. Hence it is said both of him and of his members: “Their memory has perished with a sound, but the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 9). And “the garment mixed with blood” means the devil, full of the blood of prophets and apostles because he was a murderer from the beginning (John 8), as the Lord testifies in the Gospel; or it means human beings, with whom the devil is clothed as with a garment, whose hands are full of blood: they shall be in burning and become food for eternal fire by the wrath of God’s fury. By all these testimonies the unbeliever must be compelled to choose one of two alternatives: either to believe that Christ is the Son of God, or—an impiety—to regard the prophets, who sang these things instructed by the Holy Spirit, as liars.

[Col. 0072D] Knowing these prophets and patriarchs to be most truthful heralds of the Lord and defenders of our faith, and firmly believing what, enlightened by the Holy Spirit, they foretold concerning Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and second coming, let us bring forth from their people Gideon—a very valiant man strengthened by God’s grace—in order to overthrow Jewish unbelief and strengthen our faith; and let us take for our help whatever we discover was done or said by him, at an angel’s prompting, as a type of Christ’s birth.

[Note: [Col. 0072D] Isidore, Questions on Judges, ch. 4.] Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery; and although he was brave and faithful, he nevertheless sought further proofs of the Lord’s future victory: that one night he might place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor, and dew might descend only upon it while dryness lay over all the earth; and, again, place the fleece in the same way, while dew came over all the earth and dryness lay in the fleece (Judg. 6). Someone may perhaps ask whether he seems unbelieving, since he had already been instructed by frequent signs. Far from it! He was not doubtful; rather, he foresaw future mysteries, which he, being prudent, examined with the utmost care, so that he might believe the mystery more fully when he understood the oracle. What then do the dew-wet fleece and dry threshing floor, and afterwards the dry fleece and dew-wet floor, signify, except that at first the one Hebrew nation possessed the mystery of grace while the whole world was empty? But when, at Christ’s birth and preaching, the whole world received the dew of heavenly grace, the Jewish nation dried up empty. Finally, when the whole world was parched by the unfruitful worship of Gentile superstition, then the dew of heavenly visitation was in the fleece. But after [Note: [Col. 0073D] Another manuscript: “when.”] [Col. 0073B] the sheep of the house of Israel, shown under the figure of the fleece, had perished, and those sheep denied the fountain of living water, namely Christ, the dew of faith dried up in Jewish hearts, and that divine rain poured its grace into the hearts of the Gentiles. Hence the whole world is now moistened with the dew of faith, while the Jews lack prophets and every spiritual gift. Nor is it surprising that those whom the Lord deprived of the abundance of prophetic rain should fall into the dryness of unbelief, since he himself terribly threatens this: “I will command the clouds from above not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5). That nation is signified by the name of fleece, either because it was to be stripped of the authority of teaching as a sheep is stripped of its wool, or because in its refusal to obey it withheld that same rain which it did not wish preached to itself—that is, it took care that it should not be revealed to the uncircumcised Gentiles.

The truthful prophet David also, foreseeing Christ’s coming in the Spirit, spoke thus of him: “He shall descend like rain upon the fleece” (Ps. 71). For when he says that Christ descends like rain upon fleece, he seems to agree with the aforesaid history of Gideon. The heralds of truth agree with one another and convict the sons of unbelief. “He shall descend,” he says, “like rain [Col. 0073D] upon the fleece.” Enlightened by the Holy Spirit, the Prophet describes how the Lord descended from the Father’s bosom into the womb of the Virgin Mother for our restoration. Just as rain descends upon fleece without noise and without sensation, and does not damage the fleece itself, so the Word of the Father descended into the Virgin’s womb without carnal sensation and without corruption of the Virgin, for his mother knew no man at all. “And like drops falling upon the earth” (ibid.), which do not burn the earth but make it germinate; so the Son of God, descending from heaven, did not consume the human race but abundantly watered it with heavenly teaching [Col. 0074A] and caused it to germinate in good works. Hence that saying: “The Son of God came not to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9).

The fleece, then, as we have already said, first watered, signifies the Jewish people drenched with the divine Word. For there the Lord chose to have the mother in whom he would take the form of a servant and appear to human beings; there he chose the disciples whom he would send out to preach, and to whom he said: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. 10), etc. But because that people, remaining in the hardness of its heart, did not receive the divine word, what was signified by the wet threshing floor and dry fleece came to pass. For through Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection, the divine word was taken away from the Jews and spread among [Col. 0074B] the peoples of the Gentiles; and thus the threshing floor was wet, because the dry hearts of the Gentiles were watered with the dew of the divine word. Thus the Son of God silently descended into the womb of the undefiled Virgin as rain upon fleece.

Why then, Jews, do you remain unbelieving and, setting aside every doubt, not believe Christ’s birth, now shown to you by such certain proofs? How long will you refuse faith to the words of the prophets, who spoke in the Lord’s name, and disdain to hear with deaf ear and blind mind the mysteries of Christ ministered to you through them? But since, to increase your condemnation, you refuse to believe the holy fathers, namely the patriarchs and prophets, at least believe God the Father, who speaks thus openly through Isaiah the prophet concerning that same Jesus Christ, his Son: “Behold,” he says, “my servant: I will uphold him … my soul has delighted in him” (Isa. 42). Whoever you are, unbeliever, when you hear the Son of God called servant according to his humanity, do not be scandalized by this. Hear blessed Isidore, the most truthful herald of truth [Note: [Col. 0074D] Book I of the Sentences, ch. 14]:

> “The Son of God’s perfect birth neither began to be nor ceased to be. Therefore, let it not be past, if it ceased; nor imperfect, if it is still occurring; but let it be eternal and perfect, so that eternity and perfection may be found in that birth. We therefore confess two births in Christ: one, namely, by which God the Father begot him from himself before all ages; the other, by which the Virgin Mary bore him at the end of time. Therefore Christ is said to be less than the Father from the Virgin’s womb, namely according to his human assumption, not according to his divinity. Christ is servant in the form of a servant, and not servant in the form of a servant. For in the form of a servant he is servant of the Lord; and in the form of a servant he is Lord of all. Christ in the form of a servant, because of the excellence of his conception, is Lord of all; for although he assumed flesh, yet the Virgin bore him not from the lustful contamination of flesh, but by the operation of the Holy Spirit alone and the overshadowing power of the Most High” (Luke 1).

> “The mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is by no means one person in humanity and another in divinity; rather, in both natures he is the same one. He was neither conceived as a mere human being nor born as a mere human being; nor did he afterwards receive merit in order to become God. Rather, God the Word, remaining in the unchangeable essence which is coeternal with the Father and Spirit, assumed flesh for human salvation, in which the impassible could suffer, the immortal could die, and he who is eternal before the ages could be killed in time.

> “The mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, although he is one from the Father and another from the Virgin, is not one thing from the Father and another from the Virgin; but he himself is eternal from the Father and temporal from the Mother; he himself who made is himself made; himself from the Father without a mother, himself from the mother without a father; himself the temple of the Creator, himself the Creator of the temple; himself the author of the work, [Col. 0075B] himself the work of the author. He remains one from both and in both natures: neither confused by the union of the natures nor doubled by their distinction.”

Let God the Father therefore say of him: “Behold my servant: I will uphold him; my soul has delighted in him.”

[Note: [Col. 0075D] The same author, from Book VII of the Etymologies, ch. 2.] “Nor is it surprising if the Son of God is represented by visible signs in our flesh, since he is known to have descended even to the sufferings and humiliations of our flesh. Although he is the Son coeternal with God the Father before the ages, when the fullness of time came (Gal. 4), he took the form of a servant for our salvation (Phil. 2) and became the son of man, that is, of the Virgin. Hence some things are said of him in the Scriptures according to the form of God, while others are said according to [Col. 0075C] the form of a servant. According to the form of God he says of himself: ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10). According to the form of a servant he says: ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 14). Human nature is so joined to the Son of God that one person is made from two substances.” Thus it is now said: “Behold my servant,” that is, the Son according to his humanity; “I will uphold him,” namely on the day of the Ascension; “my chosen one,” namely chosen from thousands for the redemption of the world. Truly, from the whole mass of the human race, the Son of God was chosen, whom God the Father deigned to send for our deliverance. It follows: “My soul has delighted in him.” This resembles what the Father’s voice sounded concerning the same Son of God when he received baptism in the Jordan: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Mark 1). Therefore it is rightly said: “My soul has delighted in him,” because he is the power of God and the wisdom of God. Thus Isaiah ought to be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist, since he foretold the mysteries of Christ to come so openly.

It should be noted that the apostles are called the worm Jacob, Israel, and the seed of Abraham, to whom later, as though to servants and human beings, it is said: “Do not fear, my servant Jacob,” or “worm Jacob” (Isa. 41), etc. But Christ is called not Jacob or Israel, but servant, because he is shown to have obeyed God the Father in the form of a servant. Hence: “Father, not my will, [Col. 0076A] but yours be done” (Luke 22). Again he adds: “I have given my Spirit upon him” (Isa. 42), namely at his conception, as the archangel foretold to Mary, ever virgin: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). This was also evident at his baptism, when the Spirit rested upon him in the form of a dove (Matt. 3). Again he says of him: “He brings forth judgment to the Gentiles” (Isa. 42). The Jews having been blinded by the fault of unbelief, the Son of God brought judgment to the Gentiles who believed, because through the apostles he commanded them to keep new precepts which they had not previously known. “He shall not cry,” he says, because, like a sheep, meek and gentle, he was to be led to slaughter (Isa. 53). “Nor shall he show partiality,” namely in judgment; “nor shall his voice be heard outside”—understand, outside [Col. 0076B] Judea. Although he was in the region of Tyre, Sidon, and Caesarea Philippi, he nevertheless did not enter them. Christ, then, is servant by his assumption [Note: [Col. 0076D] See the note on folio 23.] of humanity; because, coming first to the Jews, he was not received, he brought forth judgment, namely evangelical precepts, to the Gentiles. What judgment, except that the peoples of believers might be justified by faith? “His voice shall not be heard outside,” namely among heretics and Jews situated outside God’s Church. It follows: “He shall not break a bruised reed,” because he is merciful to sinners and will convert them to himself. “He shall not break a bruised reed,” namely the scribes and Pharisees, outwardly shining but inwardly empty: they did not worship idols, and therefore shone; but they did not have faith, and therefore were empty. Thus at his coming the Son of God did not crush them, [Col. 0076C] but mercifully called them to repentance. According to these interpreters, then, the bruised reed means the kingdom of the Jews, shaken because a foreigner, namely Herod, already held sovereignty. “He shall not quench smoking flax,” namely the priesthood now almost extinguished; for priests’ garments are made of linen. Again it says: “In truth he shall bring forth judgment,” because, fearing neither scribes nor Pharisees, he shall render to each according to his work on the day when he comes to judge the world (Matt. 16). “He shall not be sad or troubled,” because at all times he shall preserve an even expression. “Until I establish judgment in the earth,” that is, the future assize among people pursuing earthly things. Hence: “For judgment I came into this world” [Col. 0076D] (John 9). It follows: “And the islands shall await his law.”

Christ’s law is his Gospel, which at that time the islands—that is, the Gentile nations, assailed on every side by tribulations—were awaiting. Great tribulation indeed afflicted the islands, that is, the Gentile peoples, before Christ’s coming, when the blindness of ignorance held their minds and the ancient enemy possessed them through the worship of idols. But almighty God, merciful and compassionate, not wishing the human race to perish, drove away from its eyes the darkness of ignorance and gradually opened to it knowledge of himself: first through the patriarchs, then through the law and prophets, and afterwards through his most beloved Son [Col. 0077A] [Note: [Col. 0077D] Isidore, Sentences, Book I, ch. 14.]. Therefore the Son of God came into humanity by the Father’s will because he could not be known by human beings through himself. But where he provided for us, there he brought contempt upon himself, because proud humanity despised the weakness he assumed for our sake. For this reason he chose the weak and foolish things of the world, that he might confound the stronger and wiser things through which he was not known (1 Cor. 1). Just as a weak infant cannot take solid food unless it has first been eaten by the mother [perhaps: *esus*, “eaten”] and converted into the liquid of milk, so that what it could not take in food it may drink by sucking in milk through the flesh; so also, while we were weak for beholding the eternity of the Word, the Word itself was made flesh, so that, nourished through the flesh and made stronger, we might, by contemplating solid food—that is, the true [Col. 0077B] God everlasting with the Father—be satisfied like angels. Therefore, as a wise and loving father, cutting off the faults of his son from infancy, gradually shapes his conduct for the better through the stages of age, nourishes him, and advances him toward more perfect things; so almighty God, chastising the iniquities of the human race, forming its conduct, illuminating its darkness, gradually brought it to knowledge of his divinity and opened to it the secrets of his will.

Paul aptly, as a prudent and wise man, shows this under the image of a small child, the son of any human being, when he says: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in no respect from a slave, though he is lord of all” (Gal. 4), etc. It is as though he said: As long as the heir is a child, namely in age and knowledge, he differs in no respect from a slave—that is, [Col. 0077C] he has no authority—although he is, that is, although he will be, lord of all. But he is under guardians and stewards, who defend him against enemies, plead cases for him, and instruct his conduct, until the time fixed by his father—that is, the determined time—in which freedom over himself and what is his is given to him. For after he has become an adult, he has freedom over himself and what is his; otherwise he would rightly be disinherited.

The law was a pedagogue because it restrained by fear and compelled service to God’s commands. It was guardian and steward for the Jews, whom God appointed heirs, while they were children in knowledge of God and in strength to resist sin. During that time, evil people, terrified by legal penalties and prompted by promises, ruled neither themselves but their vices, nor what was theirs—that is, their inheritance—although they had been appointed its rulers by God. [Col. 0077D] The law served as their guardian, defending them against assaults of evil spirits and the persuasions of Gentiles who drew them toward idolatry, by warning, rebuking, and sometimes punishing them (2 Tim. 4); it preserved eternal goods for them when Christ freed many of them from hell. It also served as their steward because it pleaded their cause before God by making God favorable to them through sacrifices and expiations; and this continued until the appointed time, that is, until Christ’s coming, at which God ordained that they should become perfect and free and obtain their inheritance; otherwise they would be disinherited.

So also, when we were children, namely in knowledge of God and in strength, we were under the elements of this world, that is, under the law, which is the first instruction toward faith and righteousness. For the law promised not heavenly things but earthly things, or things transitory like the world. “We were serving,” he says, now frightened by threats, now captured by blandishments. By “elements” he means new moons—that is, lunar days—and the Sabbath, not because they hoped in the elements like pagans, but because they worshiped God through these observances [Note: [Col. 0077D] Isidore, Etymologies, Book VI, ch. 18.].

Among us *neomenia* means the Kalends; but among the Hebrews—because months are calculated according to the lunar course—and in Greek *mēnē* [printed *menie*] means “moon”; hence *neomenia*, that is, “new moon.” Under the legal institution, the Hebrews held the days of the Kalends themselves as solemn days, [Col. 0078B] concerning which it is said in the Psalter: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemn feast” (Ps. 80).

It follows: “But when the fullness of time came,” that is, after the preceding time had been completed; or because in him the gifts of the Holy Spirit are given in fullness. The Son of God knew when he ought to come, and also when to suffer and do the rest; for neither his hour nor ours is anything but his will. Yet the testimonies of so great a coming had first to be sent beforehand and proclaimed in a long succession of heralds. It follows: “God sent his Son,” visible to human beings, “made of a woman,” though in his divinity he was uncreated. Following Hebrew usage, he calls women females who are not corrupted. “Made,” he says, “under the law,” that is, under the burden of the law as under other penalties, not in order that he might be expiated by it, but in order that he might [Col. 0078C] free and redeem those who were under the law, oppressed and liable to punishment. “And that we might receive adoption as sons,” that is, the goods given by grace through which we are sons. As he shares our nature, so he adopts us into his own.

“Made under the law,” he says, in order that he might appear circumcised, as Abraham’s son, to whom he had been promised; in him the promise was fulfilled, and therefore the sign of circumcision now ceases (Rom. 4). For Abraham believed that he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed (Gen. 22); we believe that this has now happened, and do not doubt it at all.

Jesus Christ is truly Son of God and of man: promised from the beginning of the world to the fathers, namely the patriarchs [Col. 0078D] and prophets, but given to us by God the Father at the end of time. Concerning his eternity John the Evangelist says in his Apocalypse, when speaking of him to the seven Churches in Asia: “Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come” (Rev. 1). Grace is said to be freely given, not a wage paid, but pardon bestowed. “Grace to you,” he says, etc. [Note: [Col. 0077D] From this point up to the beginning of the excerpt taken, inclusive [the phrasing is uncertain], [Col. 0078D] you will find nearly the same material in the exposition of the Apocalypse by blessed Liebanus, published by Henry Flórez, p. 39 ff.] Just as Scripture shows his name in its title where it says, “John to the seven Churches which are in Asia,” so in the likeness of the words he made it most plainly evident that he is John when he said: “Who is, and who was, and who is to come.” Therefore let it be said [Col. 0079A]: “Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come.” God the Father gave to Christ, Christ to John, and John in particular to the seven Churches of which he had been appointed teacher.

By the seven Churches we understand the one Catholic—that is, universal—Church, full of the sevenfold Spirit. “Grace to you and peace,” that is, remission of sins and rest, “from him who is,” namely Christ, formerly corruptible [Note: [Col. 0079D] Perhaps “to the corruptible one,” but now glorified and immutable; for the nominative case seems incorrectly placed here, whereas it is fitting in the Gloss.], but now glorified and immutable; “and who was,” eternally, though born in time; “and who is to come,” such as he is, though he does not now appear such [Note: [Col. 0080D] Below it reads “to the world.”]. For in God, to be is always to be. Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3). And John the Apostle himself says in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1). When he says, “In the beginning was the Word,” he signifies that the Word transcends every beginning [Note: [Col. 0080D] Gregory, Morals, Book II, no. 20.]. He also shows that it has no beginning, because it was with God; that it receives no end, because the Word was God; that it remains always, because it was in the beginning with God; and he says that this same one will come, from whom he never departed. For he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Again he says: “I alone have encompassed the circuit of heaven” (Ecclus. 24). Again it is said of his Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wis. 1). Hence elsewhere he says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. [Col. 0079C] 66; Acts 7). And again it is written of him: “He measures heaven with his palm and encloses the earth in his fist” (Isa. 40). The throne, indeed, over which God presides shows him to remain within and without. By measuring heaven with his palm and enclosing earth in his fist, he is shown to be outside all the things he created on every side; for what is enclosed within is held from outside by that which encloses it. Thus by the throne over which he presides, he is shown to be within and above; by the fist with which he holds, he is indicated to be without and beneath. For he remains within all things, outside all things, above all things, and beneath all things: above by power, beneath by support, outside by magnitude, and inside by subtlety; ruling above, sustaining below, surrounding outside, penetrating within. He is not in one respect above, another beneath, or in one respect outside and another within; rather, one and the same whole is everywhere, presiding by sustaining and sustaining by presiding; penetrating by surrounding and surrounding by penetrating. Thus from where he presides above, there he sustains beneath; and from where he encompasses without, there he fills within. Without disturbance he rules above; without labor he sustains below; within, he penetrates without attenuation; without, he surrounds without extension. Therefore he is beneath and above without place; spacious without breadth; subtle without attenuation. How, then, is he said to come who, though by the bodily bulk is at the Father’s right hand [Col. 0080A], by the uncircumscribed substance through which he is with the Father is everywhere and, together with the Father and Holy Spirit, is absent from nowhere, according to all that has been said above? In what respect, then, is he said to come? Namely in that respect in which he took the form of a servant and emptied himself (Phil. 2). His emptying is to show himself visible as a man from the invisible character of his divinity. He rightly says, therefore: “Who is, and who was, and who is to come,” because he remains and was; because he made all things with the Father and did not take his beginning from the Virgin.

This, therefore, beloved, is our faith: that we believe the Son of God to have been begotten by God the Father before all ages, and at the end of time to have been born for our salvation from the Virgin Mother without male seed; tempted, that he might deliver us from temptations; suffering, that he might give us [Col. 0080B] an example of following his footsteps and suffering for love of him and the salvation of our brothers; crucified, that we might crucify our flesh with its vices and desires; given gall to drink, that he might banish from us the sweetness of the forbidden tree; pierced with a lance, that he might heal us by the wound of his body; dead upon the cross, that he might mercifully bear our sins; buried, that we may wholly die to flesh and the world and live to God in spirit; raised again, that, dead to sins, we may live to righteousness (1 Pet. 2) and, despising the things that are in the world, seek those which are above in heaven (Col. 3); glorified at the Father’s right hand, that he might open to us the gate of heavenly life and grant us forever the vision of himself and of the Father; having sent, for our instruction and consolation, the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself and the Father; and thence, at the end of the world, to come in order to render to each according to his works (Matt. 16).

This is the faith which the patriarchs before the Law foreshadowed in words and deeds. Under the Law the truth-speaking prophets foretold it. The holy apostles preached it throughout the whole world; and, affirming it to be true, they contended for it even to the shedding of their own blood. For it the whole host of martyrs surrendered their bodies to many torments and to innumerable kinds of martyrdom. For it not only men, but also women, tender virgins, and children shed their blood; and sword, chains, [Col. 0080D] fires, prisons could not overcome them, guarded as they were by the protection of the heavenly King. The heralds of truth—the holy confessors, that is—expounding the Old and New Testaments, striking human hearts like clouds with the thunderbolts of their preaching and watering them with the rain of heavenly doctrine, extended it most widely.
