Through this faith the holy apostles, and those who held their teaching in word and deed and followed the footsteps of their most religious manner of life, raised the dead, cleansed lepers, gave sight to the blind, restored hearing to the deaf, restored to the mute the function of speech, strengthened the steps of the lame, expelled demons from [Col. 0081A] possessed bodies, healed paralytics, restored the sick from various diseases to their former health, extinguished fire by divine power, crossed rivers with dry feet, checked the boldness of serpents and wild beasts, by prayer brought forth veins of water from the deep for the benefit of the faithful; according to the Lord’s promise, they moved a mountain from one place to another; they overcame enemies of peace, partly by resisting them and partly by enduring them; with God’s help they obtained every prosperity for the advancement of the holy Church and, as far as they were able, drove adversities away from it.

This faith nourishes virtues in the soul, drives vices away from it, produces peace and concord, dissolves disputes, brings enemies back to peace, grants perseverance [Col. 0081B] in good works; it hates evil, loves good, rejects carnal things, makes one cleave to spiritual things, despises the world’s prosperity, does not shrink from suffering adversity, holds transitory things cheap, desires eternal things. Hell shall not prevail against it; it directs the way even to heaven, makes a human being near to God, leads one into the company of angels, and, through doing good works, admits one to the vision of one’s Creator. It is altogether impossible for anyone to please God without faith (Heb. XI).

Yet, beloved, I do not wish you to be unaware that a human being cannot be saved by faith alone. For we know that the apostle James said the same thing: “As the body is dead without the soul, so faith is dead without works” (Jas. II). Shall we therefore be able to [Col. 0081C] be saved by faith alone, or merit eternal joys? Because we believe Jesus Christ to be the Son of God and of man, shall we be able to attain the rewards of eternal blessedness unless we join good works to faith? By no means. For thus we read that the Lord said in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII), etc. He does not say that the one who merely confesses in words that the Son of God came in the flesh (I John IV) enters the kingdom of heaven, but rather the one who is proved to fulfill the Father’s will by doing good.

Again, dearest brethren, I want you to know that a good work without faith cannot bring a person to heaven. However diligently anyone may devote himself to good works, [Col. 0081D] if true faith does not strengthen him, charity—which gathers and unites all the faithful—does not count him among the members of the Church. Thus an angel is sent by the Lord to Cornelius the centurion, who gave many alms but did not know the true God, namely the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, lest, as an unbeliever, he lose the fruit of his alms; and he is commanded to send a messenger to Peter, summon him to himself, and receive from him the teaching of the true faith (Acts IX). For if a good work sufficed for eternal salvation without faith, God would never have sent his angel to him to summon Simon, who would preach to him the mysteries of the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, Ascension, and also the coming of the Holy Spirit, and baptize him himself and all who heard the word of God in the name of the holy Trinity. Therefore, when God sent his angel to him, he mercifully delivered him from the error of unbelief and showed him how to perform his good works, not in the darkness of ignorance, but in the light of faith. [Col. 0082B] Therefore, as was said above, neither a good work without the light of faith nor faith without the practice of good works can bring a person to the heavenly kingdom. It is certain, therefore, that the one who, with right faith, performs the good that he is able to perform will attain eternal joys.

I therefore exhort you, dearest brethren, not as unbelievers but as those truly faithful to Christ: while you have the light, do not neglect to do good works (John XII). Let right faith dwell in the mind of every one of you, and righteousness in your conduct. Let purity be preserved in the heart, truth in the mouth, and discernment in action. Believe that the Son of God was ineffably begotten of God the Father before all ages, and, out of love for him, devote yourselves to good works. Do not doubt that he was also born, at the end of time, of the Virgin [Col. 0082C] Mother; and, to strengthen your faith in so great a mystery, persevere in conduct worthy of his service. Believe with the whole affection of your minds, and affirm publicly in devout proclamations, that the Holy Spirit is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, proceeds eternally from them, and that in him the remission of all sins is established.

Therefore, beloved, render thanksgivings to almighty God without ceasing, and do not consign such great and immeasurable benefits of God to forgetfulness. Raise the desires of your hearts without ceasing toward the heavenly homeland; behold with the eyes of a pure mind the very Son of God and man reigning at the Father’s right hand; and, so that after death you may reach him and behold his face eternally with [Col. 0082D] all the saints, pour out tears without omission, through the grant of him who with the same God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Fourth Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord II

[Col. 0083]

### § I

[Col. 0083A] Whereas the other evangelists set forth Christ’s temporal generation, this sermon indicates how John the Evangelist came to know the power of his divinity, through which all things were made, and handed down to us the means of knowing it. It expounds the Gospel of John, declaring in what way John the Evangelist tells us concerning Christ who he was before the Virgin’s giving birth, what he was like, when he was, what he was doing, where he came, how he came, and for what cause he came. For he descended in order to gain brothers for himself by their receiving him; and no one ought to doubt that he can become a son of God, since the Word was made flesh (John I). For by his birth he made an ointment for the eyes, by which, wiping the eyes of our hearts, we may be able to see him. Although the incarnate Word received grace, the cause of the Incarnation was voluntary: out of charity he made angel and human being. Sin, namely the disobedience of the first parent, impeded our justification. Therefore a human being ought to raise the mind’s gaze, [Col. 0083B] considering how much he owes his Creator, and to consider, when he is sick, in what manner he ought to know his Creator through the remedies of infirmity; for the Christian’s spiritual birth is not greatly unlike Christ’s birth. It explains the sanctification of the mother, so that the subtle heretic may be confuted; and that God became man in such a way as, by what he has in common with us, to reconcile, and by what is equal with the Father, to raise us up. It asks first: Why was the Son incarnate and not the Father or the Holy Spirit? And did he assume the whole nature with its properties? Second, did he assume the soul before the body? Was it conceived before it was assumed? And was the flesh, before it was conceived, bound by sin and thus assumed by the Word? Third, how was Levi tithed in Abraham, but not Christ? Fourth, why is the Incarnation attributed to the Holy Spirit? Fifth, since we confess that the Savior was born, why does the Apostle say that he was made? Sixth, since he is the Son [Col. 0083C] of God and of man, should he be said to have been begotten twice? Seventh, should Christ’s flesh and soul be adored with the same adoration as the Word? Eighth, is Christ, insofar as he is man, the adoptive Son of God? Finally, could Christ, according to his human nature, increase in wisdom and grace?

Blessed John, apostle and evangelist, who obtained the singular privilege of chastity, understood the divinity of the Son of God more deeply than the other evangelists and disclosed its mysteries more clearly for the instruction of the whole Church. It is not without reason that he is reported to have reclined at the supper upon the breast of the same Son of God and of the Virgin (John XXI); rather, by this he is taught figuratively to have drunk more abundantly than the others of the draught of heavenly wisdom from the most holy fountain of that same breast. Thus he is deservedly compared, in the figure of the four living creatures, to a flying eagle. For, as the Venerable Bede says, the eagle is accustomed to fly higher than all birds and, of all living creatures, fixes its gaze upon the rays of the sun more clearly.

The other evangelists, therefore, expound Christ’s temporal generation and his temporal deeds; but John, contemplating more sublimely in mind the power of his divinity, through which all things were made, came to know it [Col. 0084A] and handed it down to us in writing for our knowledge, saying: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), etc. The substantial Word is meant: that which remains within the man Christ himself; it is understood by reference to the sound of a voice, but is not itself the passing sound. Turn your mind, O human being, to that word which you have in your heart, as to a plan born in your mind, so that your mind may bring forth a plan, and the plan may be like the offspring of your mind, like the son of your heart. For first the heart generates a plan, so that you may build some structure. The plan has now been born, though the work has not yet been completed. You see what you are going to make, while another does not marvel unless you have made that work. People observe your building and marvel at the builder’s plan; they are astonished at what they see and love what they do not [Col. 0084B] see. But if a human plan is praised because of some building, do you wish to see what kind of plan the Lord Jesus Christ is—that is, the Word of God? Consider the fabric of the world; see what things were made through the Word, and then you will know what the Word is like. Nor was the fabric of the world alone made through the Word, but invisible things as well. Yet although mutable things were made through the Word, the Word itself is immutable. Thus the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I). It is the same thing; it always is in the same manner.

God the Father is called “the beginning,” because from him all things received their beginning in order to exist. For “word” has a twofold meaning: sometimes it indicates temporal movements, according to the analogy of other [Col. 0084C] verbs; sometimes it signifies the substance of the thing of which it is predicated, without any temporal movement, and therefore it is also called substantive. Such is the statement, “In the beginning was the Word.” It is as though he said: “The Son subsists in the Father.” For *was* is used not with reference to time, but to substance. Therefore let blessed John the Evangelist state more clearly concerning Christ before the Virgin’s birth who he was, what he was like, when he was, what he was doing, where he came, how he came, and for what cause he came.

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word.” The Son is called the Word because through him God the Father became known to the world, or because, by speaking him—that is, by begetting him—the Father created all things; for he is the Father’s utterance, Word, and speech. The Father is the beginning from whom are all things; [Col. 0084D] the Son is the beginning through whom are all things.

The other evangelists describe Christ as born in time; John, however, affirms that he was in the beginning, that is, in the Father, who was the beginning. He is neither bounded by time nor preceded by a beginning, because the Father was not before the Son. Therefore the Father is beginning, not from a beginning; but the Son is beginning, yet from [Col. 0085A] the beginning. Or: the Word was in the beginning of all creatures and times; for whatever creature had any beginning in order that it might exist, then existed through the Word of God, through whom all things were made. Altogether four times he places the substantive word *was*—“was, was, was, was”—so that you may understand that the Son, coeternal with God the Father, preceded all times. “Word” means either the sound emitted and heard from the mouth of one speaking, or the understanding itself, which, when uttered, produces a sound in the hearer’s heart through hearing. This voice—

> [Note: [Col. 0085] Thus the manuscripts; but perhaps: “when this voice is uttered, [we understand] God of the Father,” etc. Or rather it ought to be read: “By this utterance we understand God of the Father,” etc.]

—we understand “God of the Father” as a certain ineffable, immutable, inconceivable substance which does not pass away with the uttered sound. This Word is coeternal with God the Father and of the same essence. And lest anyone should doubt that the Son subsists in the Father, so that no difference may be believed to exist, he adds: “And the Word was with God.” It is as though he said: “The Son subsists in the Father in unity of essence and distinction of person.” The other evangelists say that the Son of God suddenly appeared among human beings; John says that he was always with God. “And the Word was with God,” that is, the Son with the Father. The others declare him a true man; John affirms that he himself is true God, saying, “And the Word was God,” that is, the Son himself was God. The others describe him as a man conversing among human beings in time; John, however, shows him abiding with God in the beginning, saying: “He was in the beginning with God.” He was so one with the Father while with the Father that his essence preceded every beginning of creatures. The others say how he performed miracles in [Col. 0085C] the world; this one testifies that all things were made through him, saying: “All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing”: namely, every visible and invisible creature; and without him nothing among subsisting creatures was made.

It is clear, therefore, that he through whom every creature was made, and without whom nothing was made, is not himself a creature—understand, among those things which subsist. For evil, sin, and an idol were not made through him, because they are nothing; they subsist in no nature of their own. Indeed, all things capable of weight, measure, and number were made through the Word: every form, every structure, every harmony of parts—God made all things and set them in their ranks. [Col. 0085D] And when anyone hears that mutable creation was made through the Son, he should not suppose his will to be mutable, as though he suddenly wished to make something which he had not made from eternity.

Again he adds, saying: “What was made, in him was life.” It is as though he said: What was made in time, whether living or without life, always lives and has lived in its spiritual maker. A craftsman making a chest first has the chest in his art, and then brings it forth by constructing it. The chest may rot, and another may again be made from that chest which is in the art. The chest in the work is not life; the chest in the art is life, because it lives in the craftsman’s soul, where such things exist before they are brought forth. [Col. 0086A] What is made passes away; what is in wisdom cannot pass away. And if anyone cannot grasp how all things made through the Word uniformly lived and live in their maker, let him nourish his heart from Christ made milk through the flesh, so that he may attain solid food—that is, the same Christ, true God, born of the Father before all ages.

It follows: “And the life was the light of men.” That life, that is, that wisdom of God through which all things were made, which in the nature of its divinity was unknown above all things, descended into the knowledge of angelic and human nature through assumption of a nature in which it could be seen. Therefore it is not cattle but human beings, made in God’s image, who are illumined by that life; for, being capable [Col. 0086B] of reason, if they are clean from vices, they can comprehend the knowledge of divine Wisdom. That life is the light of minds and above minds, and surpasses all minds. But the foolish, who because of sins are called darkness, think that light to be absent, as though it were not present; for “the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II). Therefore he adds, saying: “And the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” Just as a blind man has the sun present in the sunlight, but he himself is absent from the sun, so Christ plainly knows the hearts of ungodly people, although he is unknown by them; for through vices they have departed from the honor of the human condition. Compared to senseless beasts (Ps. XLVIII), they are deprived of the light of right will. Yet divine mercy made provision for them [Col. 0086C] so that they might reach that true light and become children of light, though they had been children of darkness; for he who appeared as a human being was hidden in the human being according to divinity. “There was a great man sent from God, whose name was John.” For what purpose? Namely, that he might bear witness to Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin. This man could rightly speak of God because he was sent by God. He was a man, not an angel, as heretics wish. Therefore, when God was about to be spoken of, a man was sent beforehand by God, so that through his testimony one greater than man might be proclaimed. “There was,” he says, “a man sent from God, whose name was John,” that is, “the grace of God,” or “one in whom is grace,” who first made known to the world through his testimony the grace of the New Testament, that is, Christ. Or John is interpreted “to whom it was given,” because by God’s grace it was granted to him not only to go before the King of kings, but also to baptize him.

This man, sent by God, came in the freedom of the will to bear witness, that he might bear witness to the light. John bore witness to Christ when he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). And again: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John III). John bore witness so that all might believe through him; for John himself was not God, but so that through him—that is, through his testimony—they might believe in the light [Col. 0087A] which they did not yet know how to see: Christ, who said of himself, “I am the light of the world” (John VIII). This great man was sent beforehand and bore testimony. We may marvel at him, but as at a mountain; yet a mountain is in darkness unless it is clothed with light. This mountain, however, was created in order to receive the rays first and announce the light to holy eyes. Hence it follows: “He was not the light, but was sent to bear witness to the light.” Why was this? Namely, that all might believe through him. The saints are called lights; but there is a great difference between the light which illuminates and the light which is illuminated. And concerning what light does John bear witness? Concerning that, of course, of which it is said: “There was the true light.” John too was a light, but not the true light, for unless he were illuminated, [Col. 0087B] he would be darkness. Christ, however, is the illuminating light, substantial light, which shines in all and approaches all things; he is corrupted by no stains and obscured by no darkness. John was not such a light, but was “a burning and shining lamp” (John V): burning in faith and love, shining in word and deed. But what was this light like, what did it do, and where was it? “There was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.” Not that all are enlightened, because many are in darkness; but whoever are enlightened are enlightened through this light. And if it enlightens every person coming into this world, then it also enlightened John himself, by whom it wished to be pointed out. It enlightens every person, whether by natural ability, as the philosophers of the Gentiles, or by spiritual wisdom, as persons who have knowledge of God. For as no one exists from himself, so no one is wise from himself. Human beings were created in great brightness, but by departing from God were darkened. Therefore all who are born into the world, all being dark, must approach this true light, which is Christ, and behold it; or, if they are not fit to see it, they must fix their gaze upon John, already enlightened, and come through him to Christ. The Evangelist next describes both his natures: the divine, by which he wholly remains always and everywhere, and the human, by which he was born in time and appeared confined in a place, saying: “He was in the world.” What then? If he came here, where was he? He was everywhere in his divinity; he came here in his flesh. He was in [Col. 0087D] the world in his humanity, which he had made in his divinity. Or otherwise: he subsisted “in the world,” that is, in the universal creation; for he is not external to what he makes, but, filling the world with the presence of his majesty, he makes what he makes. By his presence he contains and governs what he makes.

It follows: “And the world was made through him.” For the Creator of the universe does not dwell in the works of another, but in his own works, which he made. “And the world did not know him.” Every creature knew its Creator: the elements and the angels rendered testimony and service to Christ at his birth, death, and resurrection. But those clinging to the world and dwelling in the world in their hearts did not know him. Or a human being is called “the world,” because in the human being is a workshop in which the whole creation is gathered together. [Col. 0088A] The division of all creation is fivefold: it is either merely corporeal, as a stone; living, as plants; sentient, as cattle; rational, as a human being; or intellectual, as an angel. All these are assembled in a human being and constitute, as they say, the whole worldly adornment—that is, the human being. This world, that is, the human being, did not know its Creator, because darkness did not comprehend the light. And because he was in the world, yet the world did not know him, he came by assuming humanity into his own things, which were made through him; and his own—that is, human beings created by him—did not receive him. He came in order that he might at least thus be known; but even thus he was not known by humanity. Him whom they did not know as creating and reigning over all things in the power of divinity, [Col. 0088B] they refused to receive when he shone with miracles in the weakness of the flesh. Or “he came into his own,” that is, into the Jewish people, whom he had chosen above all nations; and his own peculiar people did not receive him. Was Christ therefore incarnate in vain? By no means. Hence he added: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.” O ineffable mercy! He was born the only-begotten from the Father, and he did not wish to remain alone; rather, he descended to gain brothers for himself, to whom he might distribute his Father’s kingdom. Born God from God, he did not wish merely to remain the Son of God; rather, he became Son of man in order to transform human beings into sons of God and make them co-heirs of his glory, so that what he had by nature they might have by grace.

[Col. 0088C] It follows: “As many as received him.” God does not show partiality; rather, “in every nation, he who fears him and does righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X). To those who receive him he gave power to become children of God; to those who do not receive him he gives time for receiving him. Human beings are his inheritance, God being their possessor, as it is said: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II). And he in turn is their inheritance, whence the Lord himself says: “I am their inheritance” (Ezek. XLIV). He possesses us as servants; we possess him as our salvation and as eternal light. The Evangelist next explains what it is to receive the Son of God, saying: “To those who believe in his name”: those who most firmly believe and receive him as true God and true man. Great is [Col. 0088D] the power of faith, by which God is received and the human being is made divine. Hence it is written: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Heb. II). He indicates in what order people can become children of God, and how far this generation differs from carnal generation, when he says: “Who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.” Natural philosophy teaches that, at the time of conception, two bloods—that is, those of male and female—are mingled. By the name “flesh” the female sex is denoted; by the name “man” the male sex is understood. Adam says of Eve: “Flesh of my flesh” (Gen. II). Therefore, since the carnal generation of each person takes its origin from the union of male and female, and the carnal desire of both is there fulfilled, spiritual generation, [Col. 0089A] which is ministered through the grace of the Holy Spirit, is distinct; for “what is born of flesh is flesh, but what is born of spirit is spirit” (John III).

But lest anyone doubt that he can become a son of God and co-heir of Christ: in order that human beings might be born of God, God was first born from them. If what is greater came first, who doubts that what is lesser can occur? If the Word was made flesh, if the Son of God was made man, what wonder if a human being who believes in the Son of God is to become a son of God? The Word descended into flesh so that flesh might ascend into the Word. Therefore do not marvel at so great a grace of the Lord; do not recoil in disbelief. Let Christ’s human generation assure you of your spiritual regeneration. “The Word [Col. 0089B] was made flesh”: the Son of God was made man and dwelt among human beings (Baruch III). By the name “flesh” the whole human nature is signified, namely flesh and soul, according to the saying: “All flesh,” that is, every human being, “shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III). As a human being consists of flesh and soul, so Christ consists of divinity, soul, and flesh.

> [Note: [Col. 0089D] These are the three substances of Christ, which our fathers defended at the Fifteenth Synod of Toledo with so remarkable a mass of testimonies from Scripture [Col. 0090D] and the Fathers.]

God, existing from eternity to eternity, true as he was, assumed in time into unity of person a human being whom he had not possessed. When we believe that an incorporeal soul is joined to a body, so that one human being results from these two, we can more readily believe that an incorporeal divine substance is joined to an incorporeal soul in unity of person, so that the Word was not changed into flesh [Col. 0089C] nor flesh confused into the Word, just as neither the body is changed into the soul nor the soul into the body.

Again he adds, saying: “And we saw his glory.” He indicates what has been conferred upon us by this birth. We were blind and could not see God; but by his birth he made an ointment for the eyes by which we might wipe the eyes of our hearts. Thus we saw his glory: when we beheld his humanity shining with miracles, we understood the divinity hidden within. Many saw Christ’s glory, but especially those who beheld his brightness when Christ was transfigured on the mountain; who saw him risen from the dead, entering among them while the doors were shut, and ascending into heaven; who plainly knew that such glory did not belong to any of the saints, but [Col. 0089D] to him alone who was the Father’s only-begotten in divinity. When he came, no one could see this glory unless healed by the humanity of the flesh. There was dust in the human eye, which had wounded it so that it could not see the light; an eye-salve is made from earth and put into the eye. The Word was made flesh, and we saw the light. Flesh had blinded the soul consenting to carnal affections; the Word made flesh heals you, O human being, extinguishes through flesh the vices of flesh, and through death kills death, so that you may now say: “We saw his glory.” To this glory the human gaze, healed through flesh, has been brought.

It follows: “Full of grace and truth.” The fullness [Col. 0090A] of grace refers to his humanity; the fullness of truth, to his divinity. For the incarnate Word, namely the Son of God and of the Virgin, received grace according to his humanity; by a singular gift, above others, it was granted to him that, from the time when he began to be conceived as man in the Virgin’s womb, he was also God. For as the Word received flesh, so that flesh itself received through the Word the power of divinity; and this is rightly called grace, since he becomes God through no preceding merits. Hence the glorious—indeed, most glorious—Virgin is called and believed to be Mother not only of a human being but also of God. He was full of truth, that is, of the very divinity of the Word, which singularly chose that man with whom it might become one person; for in him, as the Apostle says, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II). Or, “full of grace” according to the Old Testament, in which that is promised which is fulfilled in the New; or “full of grace,” that is, of the Holy Spirit himself, who is called the Spirit of grace because he distributes all spiritual gifts, whose sevenfold grace, as Isaiah testifies, filled Christ’s humanity: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. XI).

Meanwhile it should be noted, dearest brethren, that the principal reason why the Son of God became man was his will alone, by which he with the Father disposes all things from eternity; by which he “did all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. CXIII). For just as no necessity compels that will, so no impossibility delays it. But charity and grace caused him to deign to will this: for, just as he was full of charity, so he willed to be full, as was said above, of grace also. Out of charity he had made angel and human being, so that there might be beings whom he could love, by whom he could be loved, and who might enjoy blessedness with him. Therefore by the grace of that same charity he willed to become human, wherein he showed the fullness of his grace when he willed to reform through grace the human being who had proved ungrateful for grace and had disfigured in himself God’s own image. Of this fullness of grace, Blessed Augustine says in his book *On Seeing God*: “Although the Only-Begotten of God was Son by nature, he became the son of man by grace, that he might be [Col. 0090D] full of grace.” Hence above the Evangelist says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.” And through Gabriel the archangel it is said to the most blessed Virgin Mary: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with thee” (Luke I). And he added: “Thou hast found grace with the Lord” (ibid.). Hence the Apostle says: “The kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared; not from works of righteousness which we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus III). And again: “God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh on account of sin, that he might fulfill justification in us [Col. 0091A] who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. VIII). By these words the Apostle indicates that God sent the Son in order to condemn sin on account of sin and fulfill justification in us.

Therefore, beloved brethren, we judge it necessary to consider what that sin was, and how great it was, which impeded our justification and for whose condemnation the Son of God was sent—as though it could not be condemned by another.

It should be noted that this sin was the disobedience of the first human being. For his Creator had placed him under the safeguard of humility and the guardianship of subjection, so that he might know himself inferior to his Creator, lest, becoming proud through the great dignity which he had received, [Col. 0091B] he should follow Lucifer in his fall. Rather, he had been created for this purpose: that by persevering in the praise of God, through the merit of obedience he might ascend to the place from which that proud one had fallen. The command imposed upon him was indeed slight and small. He was not commanded to weary himself by doing something or exhaust himself by laboring, but only to abstain from the fruit of one tree. He could most easily have kept it, if he had willed. But, as Blessed Augustine says in the book *On Correction and Grace*, “he had received the ability to do what he wished, but did not have the will to do what he could; he was pressed by no necessity. Therefore, by his own choice he consented to the woman’s suggestion and subjected himself to the devil’s dominion.” But because, as the Apostle says, “where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. [Col. 0091C] V), the Son of God mercifully deigned to become human in order to redeem humanity from the hand of the enemy.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us raise the gaze of our minds to the greatness of divine compassion, and from the recollection of his benefits consider how much the rational human being owes to his Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0091D] Another manuscript reads “Creator”; Ivo of Chartres, Sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, in Hittorp, p. 439.]. First, when man did not exist, God wonderfully formed him from the earth; then, when he had been ruined by the serpent’s craft and the deception of the seduced woman, he restored him yet more wonderfully. In his forming, wondrous power appeared; in his restoring, the still more wondrous humility of the Almighty. In his first created state, man acted foolishly because he swelled with power [Note: [Col. 0092D] Printed edition: “feared power.”], did not love majesty, sought liberty, and fell into slavery. Though by obedience he could have been made divine, by seeking this from himself he deserved to be subjected to vanity.

Therefore the kindly Creator, unwilling that the one whom he had created should perish, appeared to servants in the form of a servant, so that by familiar conversation he might make his majesty known to them and stir them to love. Thus, as has already been said, he made clay from earth and spittle and opened the eyes of the man born blind (John 9), because the Wisdom of God, united in one person with our nature, restored within the human race—blinded from its first origin—the understanding by which it might know God and the love by which it might love him when known. Thus, already bound by many benefits, it might love above all things him whose many benefits it knew itself to have received [Col. 0092A]. In the benefit of the first creation the wisdom and power of the Creator shone forth; but in the benefit of reconciliation, by which he recalled to himself those who were hostile and ill-deserving, remitted punishments, and promised rewards, he clearly showed how greatly he loved what he had created. Thus he kindled in those whom he had first loved the fire of his own love.

For the sick man recognized his physician as deeply concerned for his salvation and highly skilled; he marveled at his wisdom and loved health. He recognized how precious was the antidote that his physician had prepared to cure so acute and inveterate a disease. Therefore he could not be ungrateful, having received so many benefits from the hand of his Redeemer. He recognized humility, for our physician lay down amid the weakness [Col. 0092B] of our flesh as though in the bed of the sick, that he might learn by experience what was necessary for healing his sick patients. The sick man also knew the wisdom of this physician, because, according to the principles of medicine, in some patients he bestowed health through like things, while in others he cured diseases through contraries.

Through like things: he who was born endured the sufferings of our mortality, that we might be healed from every capacity for suffering; he was crucified, lest we be subjected to eternal torments; he died temporally according to his humanity, lest we die eternally; he rose from the dead, that we might rise with him; he ascended, that through his sitting at the right hand of God the Father he might raise with himself the lowliness of his devoted flock. But if we consider by what contraries he cured contrary diseases [Col. 0092C], we see that through the form of a servant he restored our liberty; through his humility he cast down the pride of the ancient enemy; through his obedience he healed our disobedience. He taught all these things in word and proved them by example, so that we might fulfill in obedience what he set before us for imitation, and without hesitation hope for what he promised as our hope.

How great a price this physician paid for our redemption the blessed apostle Peter indicates when he says: “For you were redeemed, not with corruptible gold or silver, from your vain manner of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood of the spotless and undefiled Lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1). In agreement with him is Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, enlightened by the Sun of righteousness [Col. 0092D]. “You were bought,” he says, “at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6).

This spotless Lamb is not the one required in the ancient sacrifice, born from cattle without variation of blemish, but the true and innocent one born from the immaculate womb of the Virgin. He is not the one with whose blood doorposts were stained, but the one in whose faith the foreheads of the faithful are marked with the impress of the cross; not the one whose blood was poured out by priests’ hands, but the one who was prefigured as to be offered by himself, the true priest, for our salvation. For no sacrifice equally worthy and pure could be found to be offered for our cleansing [Col. 0093A], nor any priest equally worthy and pure by whom so worthy a sacrifice might be offered. For he himself says of himself: “No one takes my life from me; but I lay it down, and I take it up again” (John 10).

This Lamb without blemish and wrinkle joined to himself as bride the Virgin—that is, the holy Church—just as he had previously consecrated the Virgin as his mother. Hence the birth by which Christ was born in time is not unlike the birth by which a Christian is born spiritually. For as the virgin mother conceived Christ, bore him as a virgin, and remained a virgin after giving birth, so the holy mother Church, Christ’s bride, consecrated by the washing of water, the word of truth [Note: [Col. 0093D] The printed edition lacks: “of truth, and consecrated by the sanctification of the Holy Spirit.”], and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0094D] Perhaps *consecrated*, or “consecrating.”], daily gives birth to Christian peoples and remains a virgin in faith. In Mary, bodily integrity is commended; [Col. 0093B] in the holy Church, purity of faith.

Let us hear blessed Paul, the friend of the heavenly bridegroom, zealously loving the bride of the Corinthian Church with chaste love—not for himself but for the bridegroom—saying: “For I am jealous over you with the jealousy of God. For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). For the holy Church, pledged with the earnest of the Holy Spirit, is a virgin in integrity of faith and uprightness of conduct, to be led from hope to sight, so that there, in full joy and full love of the bridegroom, she may rejoice, preserving his pledge while scorning every seduction of the serpent.

Let us next hear how the Son of God sanctified the mother of his flesh, so that every Catholic may rejoice [Col. 0093C] and the subtle heretic be confuted. For he removed from her every defect of both original and actual fault; and, taking flesh from her flesh, transformed that same flesh into divine purity. Scripture says: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). Therefore, just as material fire converts into itself, while purifying, everything that it consumes, so the material substance of our flesh which the divine fire assumed he purified from every stain of sin.

For the first parent of the human race, because she received the poison of the serpent’s persuasion, fell under a twofold curse: namely, that with her husband she should incur death, and that she should conceive children with fleshly delight but bring them forth in pain. All Eve’s daughters succeeded as heirs to this curse and gave birth to all their children under the condemnation of necessary death [Col. 0093D]. This mother alone, who believed not the serpent’s hiss but the words of the announcing angel, deserved to hear a blessing that excluded both curses: “Blessed are you among women” (Luke 1), because you shall neither conceive through fleshly concupiscence nor bear your Son in pain; and “blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid.), namely God and man, Jesus Christ, who, born “not of the will of the flesh nor of the desire of man” (John 1), underwent temporal death not by necessity but by will, and freed us from eternal death.

In this birth, therefore, God and man was born [Col. 0094A], that human beings might be reborn as gods; in this birth God the Word enters the Virgin’s womb, that humanity might be exalted. God, the Son of God, as a strong helper for lifting up humankind, as it were put his shoulder beneath it. Between the immense dissimilarity of human nature and the immutable substance of divinity, he placed his own person as mediator, sharing in both natures: through what he has in common with us, reconciling us; through what he has equal with the Father, lifting us up. And, as though providing the outlines of flesh to bleary eyes able to see the sun only beneath a cloud, he poured forth the radiance of eternal light and illumined the darkness of our ignorance.

For wretched man, made in the image of God, “when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared [Col. 0094B] to irrational beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48 [49]). It is as if he said more plainly: Man, when he was in honor—that is, made in God’s image, not in body but in rational understanding—did not understand. It is as if he openly said: Man pursues vain things, and therefore God is not to be accused; rather, man is to blame, because, though he was in honor, made in God’s image, he did not understand his own dignity, namely that he surpasses beasts by understanding, not by strength. As though he said: He did not act intelligently, but, having lost reason, was compared to irrational beasts—not in some other respect, but in irrationality. And rightly so, because he became like them through his fault, not by nature.

For this reason the bread of angels became fodder for rational animals, that is, food [Col. 0094C] for the simple, so that the little child might suck milk from that source by which the angel is refreshed with strong food. Thus, raised to mature strength through the nourishment of milk, he may at last attain the inward and eternal taste of the divine majesty: that is, through the fact that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), he may contemplate with the angels the Word of the Lord, who was in the beginning with God—now through a mirror and in an enigma, but afterward openly at the end (1 Cor. 13); here as on the way, there as in the homeland. (Thus far Ivo.)

[Note: [Col. 0094D] Book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 1, § “Diligently.”] Here it must be carefully noted why the Son, rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit, was incarnate. The Son alone assumed humanity. Certainly the Wisdom of God did this by fitting order and lofty counsel, so that God, who had created the world in his wisdom according to the words, “You made all things in wisdom, O Lord” (Ps. 103 [104]), might restore the things in heaven and the things on earth [Col. 0094D].

This is the woman in the Gospel, namely the Wisdom of God, who lights a lamp and finds the tenth drachma which had been lost (Luke 15). Therefore the Wisdom of God the Father lit the earthen vessel of human weakness with the light of his divinity and restored lost man, marked with the king’s name and image. Hence the Son was sent, and not the Father, because it was more fitting that he who is from another should be sent than he who is from no one. The Son is from the Father; but the Father is from no one. Hence blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*: “The Father has no one from whom he is” [Col. 0095A]. Therefore, just as the Father begot and the Son was begotten, so fittingly the Father sent and the Son was sent. The Word of God is appropriately sent by him whose Word he is; he is sent by him from whom he was born. The Word which was begotten is sent; but the Father who sent is from no one. Therefore the Father was not sent, lest, if he were sent, he should be thought to be from another.

Thus first the Son, who is from the Father alone, was sent; then also the Holy Spirit, who is from the Father and the Son. But the Son alone was sent to be incarnate, not the Holy Spirit, any more than the Father. This occurred so that he who in divinity was the Son of God might in humanity become the son of man. The Father or the Holy Spirit did not clothe himself in flesh, lest one be Son in divinity and another in humanity, and lest the same person be both Father and Son [Col. 0095B], if God the Father were born of a human being.

Hence in ecclesiastical dogmas we read: the Father did not assume flesh, nor did the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone; so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might himself become the son of man in manhood, lest the name of Son pass to another who was not Son by eternal generation. Therefore the Son of God became the son of man: according to the truth of nature, Son of God from God; and according to the truth of nature, son of man from man. Thus the truth of the begotten one might possess the name of Son by birth in both generations, not by adoption or appellation, and one Son might be true God and true man. Therefore there are not two Christs or two sons, but God and man [Col. 0095C], one Son, whom we therefore call Only-begotten, remaining in two substances as the truth of his nature gave him: not with the natures confused or mixed, as the Timotheans maintain, but united in fellowship. You now have why the Son, and not the Father or the Holy Spirit, assumed flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0095D] Ibid., distinction 2.] And because in humanity the whole human nature had been corrupted by fault, he assumed the whole—that is, soul and flesh—that he might heal and sanctify the whole. That by the term “human nature” or “humanity” soul and flesh are meant is plainly taught by Jerome in his exposition of the Catholic faith: “Thus we confess one person of the Son in Christ, that we may say there are two perfect and complete substances,” namely divinity and humanity, which consists of [Col. 0095D] soul and body. Behold, he plainly shows that soul and body are meant by “humanity”; and the Son of God is understood to have assumed these two wherever he is said to have taken man, humanity, or human nature.

For God assumed the entire human nature—that is, soul and flesh—and their properties or accidents: not flesh without soul, nor soul without flesh [Note: [Col. 0095D] Mag.: “by reason.”], as the heretics wished, but flesh and soul also with their senses, apart from sin. Hence John Damascene says [Col. 0096A]: “The Word assumed everything that God planted in our nature: namely, body, intellectual soul, and their proper attributes.” For the whole one assumed the whole, that he might freely grant salvation to the whole of me. For what is not assumed is not healed.

“Therefore,” as John Damascene says, “the Son of God assumed flesh and soul—but flesh through the mediation of soul. For the Word of God is united to flesh through the medium of intellect. The divine essence,” he says, “is of such subtlety and simplicity that it is not fitting for it to be united directly to a body formed from the clay of the earth [Note: [Col. 0095D] Correctly: “is not fitting”; certainly not, “was not able.” For the divine essence could be united to a body through any essence whatsoever, however unfitting this might appear, as the Fathers generally and theologians acknowledge.], unless through the mediation of a rational essence.”

But that union is so inexplicable that even John, sanctified from the womb, confesses himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Jesus’ sandal (John 1), because he was not capable of investigating the mode of that union and explaining it to others [Col. 0096B]. “Therefore,” says blessed Augustine in *On the Christian Conflict*, “we must not listen to those who say that the Son of God did not assume a true man, nor was born of a woman, but displayed to observers a false flesh and an imitation image of a body.” They rush into this error because they fear what cannot occur: namely, that the truth and substance of God might be defiled by human flesh. Yet they proclaim that this visible sun scatters its rays through every kind of filth while keeping them clean and undefiled. If, therefore, visible clean things can touch visible unclean things and not be defiled by them, how much more can the immutable and invisible [Col. 0096C] truth, assuming the soul through the spirit and the body through the soul, assume the whole human being without contamination to itself and free him from all infirmities?

See: here he says that the Wisdom of God assumed the soul through the spirit and the body through the soul. For spirit, namely the higher part of the soul, approaches God through a greater likeness than the soul itself according to its lower part; and the soul more nearly than the body. Thus it is not unfitting to say that the soul was assumed through the spirit and the body through the soul.

But if it is asked whether the Word assumed flesh and soul at the same time; and whether he assumed soul before flesh or flesh before soul; and whether that flesh was first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and afterward [Col. 0096D] assumed: it is most truly and without any ambiguity said that from the moment God assumed humanity, he assumed the whole and united both soul and flesh to himself at once. Nor [Note: [Col. 0096D] The author: “this.”] was the flesh conceived first; rather, in its conception it was assumed, and in its assumption it was conceived.

Hence blessed Augustine says in his book *On Faith to Peter*: “Hold most firmly and do not doubt at all that Christ’s flesh was not conceived in the Virgin’s womb without divinity before it was assumed by the Word; rather, the Word, God himself, was conceived through the assumption of his flesh, [Col. 0097A] and the flesh itself was conceived through the incarnation of the Word.” The same author says in his book *On the Trinity*: “He would not be mediator between God and human beings unless he were the same God and the same man, one and true in both; the whole Trinity, whose will and operation are one, made that servant-form assumed by the Son alone.”

The flesh was not first assumed in the Virgin’s womb and divinity afterward came into the flesh; rather, as soon as the Word came into the womb, while the truth [Note: [Col. 0097D] The author: “virginity.”] of his proper nature remained intact, he became flesh and perfect man—that is, he was born in the truth of flesh and soul. On this also Gregory the teacher says in the *Moralia*: “At the angel’s announcement and the Spirit’s coming, immediately the Word was in the womb; immediately, within the womb, the Word became flesh.”

[Col. 0097B] [Note: [Col. 0097D] Ibid., distinction 3.] It is also asked concerning the flesh of the Word whether, before it was conceived, it was bound by sin; and whether it was assumed by the Word in such a condition. It may safely be said, and ought to be believed in accordance with the concordant testimony of the saints, that it had first been liable to sin, like the Virgin’s remaining flesh; but that by the working of the Holy Spirit it was cleansed so as to be united to the Word free from every original sin—punishment nevertheless remaining, not by necessity but by the will of the one assuming.

The Holy Spirit, coming beforehand into her, also entirely cleansed Mary from sin and freed her even from the fuel of sin: either by wholly removing that fuel itself, as some hold, or by so weakening and diminishing it that afterward no occasion for sinning could arise in her. He also prepared in the Virgin the power of giving birth [Col. 0097C] without a man’s seed. For the words of the Gospel teach this, where the angel, addressing the Virgin, says: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. And that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1). The sacred Virgin replied to him: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.).

Explaining this, John Damascene says: “After the assent [Note: [Col. 0097D] Mag.: “consent.” Book II, *On the Orthodox Faith*, chap. 2.] of the holy Virgin, the Holy Spirit came beforehand upon her, according to the word of the Lord which the angel spoke, cleansing her and preparing her to receive the divine Word, and at the same time preparing her to give birth. Then the Wisdom and Power of God Most High, existing in himself—that is, the Son of God, *homoousios* [ὁμοούσιος], that is, consubstantial with the Father—overshadowed her as divine seed [Col. 0097D], and joined to himself, from the most holy and most purified blood of that Virgin, flesh of our ancient mixture, animated by a rational and intellectual soul; not sowing it, but creating it through the Holy Spirit.”

From these things it is clear what we said above: namely, that the flesh of the Word was conceived and assumed at the same time, and that this same flesh—indeed, the whole Virgin—was purified from every stain of sin through the prior action of the Holy Spirit. To her was granted, in a new manner, the power of giving birth, so that without intercourse with a man and without lust in the conceiving woman, the conception of God and man might take place [Col. 0098A] in the Virgin’s womb [Note: [Col. 0098D] Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, chap. 2, among the works of Augustine, vol. III; now in the Appendix, vol. 6.]. For that flesh which God deigned to unite to himself from the Virgin was conceived without defect and born without sin. Yet do not suppose this flesh to be of heavenly, aerial, or any other nature, but of that nature which is the flesh of all human beings.

That the sacred Virgin thereafter remained free from every sin Augustine clearly shows in his book *On Nature and Grace*, saying: “With the exception of the holy Virgin Mary, concerning whom, for the honor of the Lord, I wish to raise absolutely no question when sins are being discussed [Note: [Col. 0098D] Augustine, *On Sins.*]. For from this we know that more grace was bestowed on her for overcoming sin in every respect, since she merited to conceive [Col. 0098B] and bear him who, as is certain, had no sin.”

With this Virgin excepted, if all holy men and women could be assembled and asked whether they had sin, what would they answer but what blessed John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1)? “But that Virgin,” says blessed Augustine in *On Faith to Peter*, “was anticipated and filled with singular grace, so that she might have as the fruit of her womb him who from the beginning had been Lord of the universe; so that what was born from the lineage of the first human being might derive from it only the origin of the race, and not of guilt.”

Although that flesh, whose singular excellence cannot be expressed in words, was liable to sin in Mary and in the others from whom its propagation was transmitted before it was united to the Word [Col. 0098C], it may not improperly seem that it was subject to sin in Abraham, whose whole flesh was subject to sin. Hence it is usually asked why Levi is said to have been tithed in Abraham but not Christ, although each was in Abraham’s loins according to material causation when Abraham was tithed—that is, when he paid tithes to Melchizedek.

For then the apostle says that Levi was tithed in Abraham as in a material cause (Heb. 7), because by that tithing, just as Abraham is shown to be inferior to Melchizedek, to whom he personally paid tithes, so too is the Levitical order, which was in Abraham according to seminal causation and descended from him through the concupiscence [Col. 0098D] of the flesh. Christ, however, was not tithed, because although he was there according to the flesh, he did not descend from there according to the common law, namely through fleshly lust; just as all sinned in Adam, but not Christ.

Hence blessed Augustine says *On Genesis*: “As those who were in Adam’s loins sinned when Adam sinned, so those who were in Abraham’s loins were tithed when Abraham gave tithes.” But this does not follow in Christ, although he was in Adam’s and Abraham’s loins, because he did not descend from them through fleshly concupiscence. Therefore, although Levi and Christ were both in Abraham’s loins according to the flesh when he was tithed [Col. 0099A], they were not both tithed because Christ was not there in the manner in which Levi was there. Levi was there according to that seminal causation by which he was to come into his mother through intercourse; Christ’s flesh was not there according to that causation, although the flesh of the most blessed ever-Virgin Mary was there according to it. Therefore he was tithed in Abraham who was in Abraham’s loins as he was in his own father’s loins—that is, who was born from father Abraham as Levi was born from his own father, namely through the law of the flesh and invisible concupiscence.

Accordingly, Christ is rightly said to have assumed the firstfruits of our mass [Col. 0099B], because he took not sinful flesh but “the likeness of sinful flesh.” For, as the Apostle says, “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8). The Word assumed flesh like sinful flesh in punishment, but not in guilt; and therefore not sinful flesh. Hence blessed Augustine says: “All other human flesh is flesh of sin; his flesh alone is not flesh of sin, because his mother conceived him not through concupiscence but through grace.”

Nevertheless, it has the likeness of sinful flesh through passibility and mortality, because he hungered, thirsted, and the like. Therefore, though it is the same flesh as ours, it was not made in the womb as ours is. It was sanctified in the womb [Col. 0099C] and born without sin; nor did he ever sin in it. Thus it is like ours in punishment, not in the quality of sin, because it had absolutely none of the defilement conceived from the motion of concupiscence, nor was it born from carnal pleasure. Therefore he came to an immaculate body, conceived apart from lustful concupiscence. It did not contain in itself the defect that is in others the cause of sin; nor did he sin in it. Therefore it is truly said that the flesh of the Word in Christ was not bound by sin.

The assertion made above—that the flesh of the Word was not conceived before it was assumed—seems to be opposed by what blessed Augustine says *On John*, where we read: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). [Note: [Col. 0099D] To be added from the Master: “Therefore the Jews said: ‘This temple was built in forty-six years, [Col. 0100D] and will you raise it in three days?’”] [Col. 0099D] “This number,” he says, “fits the perfection of the Lord’s body because, as physicians say, the form of a human body is completed in so many days.”

On the occasion of these words some have ventured to say that the form of the Lord’s body was perfected during that many days, after the manner of other bodies, and distinguished by the outlines of its members; and that immediately thereafter the Word united flesh and soul to himself. In this way, they say, that number fits the perfection of the Lord’s body. But there is another explanation of that saying, from which a sound understanding of the statement arises. Augustine did not say this so as to deny that, as soon as that flesh had been sanctified by the operation of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0100A] and separated from the rest, it was united with its soul to the Word of God, so that he might be perfect and true God and perfect and true man. Rather, he meant that the differentiation of the members of that Lordly body, at the very moment of conception and of the union of God and man, was so slight and small that it could scarcely be submitted to human sight; but during the days mentioned by Augustine it became complete and perceptible.

Therefore the Word of God the Father was incarnate, and is wholly in the Father, wholly in the Virgin, wholly uncircumscribed everywhere. He was in all things and above all things, and existed in the womb of the most holy Mother; but in her by the act of incarnation, everywhere else by the power of divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] Distinction 4.] Since, as has been treated above, the incarnation of the Word is truly an operation of the Father [Col. 0100B], the Son, and the Holy Spirit, it seems worthy of investigation why Scripture more often attributes this work to the Holy Spirit and recalls that Christ was conceived and born of him. The operation of the Incarnation is not more often attributed to the Holy Spirit because he alone performed it without the Father and Son, but because the Holy Spirit is the love and gift of the Father and Son; and through God’s ineffable love the Word of God became flesh, and through God’s immeasurable gift the Son of God united the form of a servant to himself.

Therefore, the frequent naming of the Holy Spirit does not exclude the Father or the Son from that work. Rather, when one is named, all three are understood, as often happens in other works. Hence blessed Augustine, raising this question, resolves it in the following manner in the *Enchiridion*: “Although the whole Trinity made that creature whom the Virgin conceived and bore, though it pertains to the person of the Son alone—for the works of the Trinity are inseparable—why was the Holy Spirit named in making it? Or, whenever one of the three is named in any work, are we to understand that the whole Trinity works? Truly it is so, and this can be taught by example.” You have heard the proposed question and its solution or exposition.

The question is how Christ is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit, although he is in no way the Son of the Holy Spirit. But we must not grant that whatever is born from a thing must immediately be called that thing’s son. Certainly, as blessed Augustine says [Col. 0100D], those born of water and the Holy Spirit would not properly be called sons of water; rather, they are called sons of God the Father and of the Church their mother. Thus Christ was born of the Holy Spirit, yet he is not the Son of the Holy Spirit.

Conversely, not all who are called someone’s sons are consequently said to have been born from that person, as with those who are adopted. People are also called sons of Gehenna, not because they were born from it but because they are prepared for it. Therefore, since something may be born from another, as stated, without being its son; and since, conversely, everyone called a son is not born from the one whose son he is called, this mode by which [Col. 0101A] Christ was born of Mary as a son and of the Holy Spirit not as a son makes known to us the grace of God. By it, with no preceding merits, at the very beginning of his human nature—when he began to exist—the man was joined to the Word of God in so great a unity of person that the Son of God was the same as the son of man, and the son of man the same as the Son of God. Thus, in the assumption of human nature, grace itself became in some manner natural to that man, through which he could admit no sin. This grace is signified through the Holy Spirit because he is God in such a proper sense as also to be God’s gift. Therefore, in saying that Christ’s birth is from the Holy Spirit, what else is shown, as blessed Augustine says, than the very grace through which man was joined and united in a wonderful and ineffable manner to the Word of God [Col. 0101B] and filled bodily with divine grace?

Christ may also be said, according to his humanity, to have been born of the Holy Spirit because, as blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*, the Spirit made him. For insofar as he is man, he too was made, as the Apostle says. Therefore he is said to have been conceived and born of the Holy Spirit, not because the Holy Spirit was seed for the Virgin. For, as blessed Jerome says in his exposition of the Catholic faith, the seed of the birth was not taken from the substance of the Holy Spirit; rather, through the grace of God and the operation of the Holy Spirit, that which was united to the Word was assumed from the Virgin’s flesh. In this sense the Gospel reads of Mary that she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0101C] (Matt. 1).

Indicating the reason for this statement, Saint Ambrose says in the second book *On the Holy Spirit* (chap. 5): “Whatever is from another is either from its substance or from its power. From substance: as the Son, who was begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. From power: as all things are from God. How, then, did Mary have in her womb from the Holy Spirit? If it was as from substance, then the Holy Spirit was changed into flesh and bones—which certainly is not true. But if the Virgin conceived as from his operation and power, who would deny that the Holy Spirit is the author of the Lord’s incarnation?”

But it may be asked: since we confess that the Savior was born [Col. 0101D], why does the Apostle say that he was made from the seed of David (Rom. 1), and elsewhere made from a woman, since being made is one thing and being born another? He meant something by this expression. Because the Lord’s flesh was not created from human seed in the Virgin’s womb, nor was his body produced in that way, but by the efficacy and power of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says “made,” not “born.” For it is one thing to generate by mingled seed and coagulated blood; another to produce, not by mixture, but by power. Human beings can indeed generate children, but cannot make them. See why the Apostle said “made,” not “born”: lest his birth, which was without a man’s seed, be thought like ours, which is accomplished by the mingling of seed [Col. 0102A].

Yet when the Apostle said “made,” he added “from the seed of David,” because, although no human seed intervened in the Virgin’s conception, nevertheless, as blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Trinity*: “Because Christ was formed from that flesh which is known to be from the seed of David, namely the Virgin’s flesh, he is rightly said to have been made.”

[Note: [Col. 0101D] Distinction 8, final.] It is also commonly asked whether Christ should be called twice begotten, as he is called Son of God and son of man. It may be said in response that Christ was twice born and possessed two natures. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*: “The Father begot from his own substance the Son, God equal and coeternal with himself. This same only-begotten God was also born a second time: once from the Father and once from the Mother. He was born from the Father as God the Word; he was born from the Mother as the Word made flesh. Therefore one and the same Son of God was born before the ages and born in time [Col. 0102B]; and both births belong to the one Son of God, namely the divine and the human.”

John Damascene also says of this: “We venerate two births of Christ: one from the Father before the ages, beyond cause, reason, time, and human nature; and another in the last times, for us, according to us, and above us. For us, because it was for our salvation; according to us, because he was born as man from a woman and after the time of conception, namely nine months; above us, because he was born not from seed but from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin, beyond the law of conception.” From these things it plainly appears that Christ has two births and was born twice [Col. 0102C].

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Distinction 9.] Furthermore, it must be investigated whether Christ’s flesh and soul ought to be adored with one and the same adoration as the Word—namely, that called *latria*. For if *latria*, understood as the service or worship owed to the Creator alone, is offered to Christ’s soul or flesh, then what is owed to the Creator alone is offered to a creature, since Christ’s soul or flesh is merely a creature; and this is reckoned idolatry. Therefore, some hold that Christ’s soul or flesh should not be adored with the adoration called *latria*, but with that called *dulia*, which they say has two kinds or modes.

[Col. 0102D] For there is one mode of *dulia* that may be offered to any creature whatsoever; and there is another that is to be offered to Christ’s humanity alone, and to no other creature, because Christ’s humanity is to be venerated and loved above every creature—not, however, so greatly that worship owed to the divinity should be offered to it. This worship consists in love, the offering of sacrifice, and reverence; in Latin it is called *pietas*, and in Greek *theosebia*, that is, worship of God, and *eusebia*, that is, good worship.

Others, however, maintain that Christ’s humanity is to be adored with one adoration together with the Word—not on its own account, but on account of him whose footstool it is and to whom it is united [Col. 0103A]. Nor is that humanity itself to be adored alone or nakedly, but together with the Word to whom it is joined; nor on its own account, but on account of that Word. Nor can one who does this be judged guilty, because he serves neither a creature alone nor the creature on its own account, but the Creator with his humanity and in his humanity. Hence John of Damascus says [Note: [Col. 0103D] Book III, *Orthodox Faith*, ch. 8.]:

> “The two natures of Christ differ in definition and manner, but are united according to hypostasis, that is, according to person. Therefore Christ is one: perfect God and perfect man. We adore him with the Father and the Holy Spirit in one adoration, together with his undefiled flesh; we do not say that the flesh is not to be adored. For it is adored in the one hypostasis, that is, person, of the Word—the hypostasis which was begotten—not offering veneration to a creature. For we do not adore it as naked flesh [Col. 0103B], but as united to the Godhead in one hypostasis, that is, in the person of God the Word, the two natures being brought back to one. I fear to touch the coal because of the fire joined to the wood. Therefore I adore both aspects of my Christ together because of the united Godhead: for I do not introduce a fourth person into the Trinity, but confess one person of the Word and of his flesh.”

By these words of John of Damascus it seems to be implied that Christ’s humanity is to be adored with one adoration together with the Word.

On this matter blessed Augustine also says, concerning the Lord’s sermon in which he says, “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14): “Here heretics say that the Son is not God by nature, but created. They must be answered thus: if the Son is not God by nature but a creature, [Col. 0103C] then he is not at all to be worshipped or adored as God, as the Apostle says: ‘They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator’ (Rom. 1). But in reply to this they say: Why do you adore his flesh, which you do not deny to be a creature, together with the divinity, and serve it no less than the divinity? I answer: I adore the Lord’s flesh—indeed, the complete humanity in Christ—because it was assumed by the divinity and united to the Godhead, so that I confess not one person and another, but one and the same Son of God, God and man. Finally, if you separate the man from God, I shall never believe in him or serve him. Suppose that someone found a royal purple garment or diadem lying on the ground: would he attempt to adore it? [Col. 0103D] But when the king has put it on, a person incurs the danger of death if he disdains to adore it together with the king. So also, if anyone disdains to adore in Christ the Lord not humanity alone or nakedly, but humanity with divinity united to it—that is, the one true Son of God and true man—he shall die eternally.”

By these words blessed Augustine plainly teaches that Christ’s humanity is to be adored together with the Word. Again, on the Psalm where it is said, “Adore his footstool, for it is holy” (Ps. 98), Augustine says:

> “It must be understood that in Christ there is earth, that is, flesh, which is adored without impiety. For he took earth from earth, because flesh is from earth [Col. 0104A]; and he took flesh from Mary’s flesh. This flesh, assumed by the Word of God, is adored by us without impiety, because no one eats his flesh unless he first adores; but one who adores does not look to the earth, but rather to him whose footstool it is, for whose sake he adores.”

By these authorities the resolution of the foregoing question is explained.

[Note: [Col. 0104D] Distinction 10, § “But if.”] But if it is asked whether Christ, insofar as he is man, is an adoptive Son, or so in some other manner, we reply that Christ is in no way an adoptive son, but only a natural Son; for he is Son by nature, not by the grace of adoption. He is not an adoptive son because he was not first something else and afterwards adopted as a son, as we are called adoptive sons: having been born children of wrath (Eph. 2), we were made children of God by grace [Col. 0104B]. Christ, however, was never not a Son; and therefore he is not an adoptive Son, since he is called the Son of the Virgin not by adoption but by union. For he is called the Son of the Virgin because in the Virgin he assumed manhood into the unity of his person; and this was by grace, not by nature.

Hence blessed Augustine says on John: “That the Only-begotten is equal to the Father belongs not to grace but to nature. But that man was assumed into the unity of the person of the Only-begotten belongs to grace, not to nature. Therefore Christ is the Son neither of God nor of man by adoption, but naturally Son of God, and naturally and by grace Son of man.”

That he is naturally the Son of man, Augustine shows in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “He, namely God, became naturally the Son of man, who is naturally the only-begotten Son of God the Father.” That he is not an adoptive Son and yet is Son by grace is proved by the testimonies that follow. Jerome says on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Of Christ Jesus it is written that he was always with the Father, and that the Father’s will never preceded him in order that he might exist. He indeed is Son by nature; we, however, by adoption. He was never not Son; we, before we existed, were predestined, and then received the Spirit of adoption when we believed in the Son of God.” Hilary likewise says in the third book *On the Trinity*: “When the Lord says in the Gospel, ‘Father, glorify your Son’ (John 17), he testified that he is Son not by the name alone, but also by proper possession. We are sons of God, but this Son is not such as we are. For he is true and proper Son by origin, not adoption; by reality, not appellation; by birth, not creation.” Augustine also says on John: “We are sons by grace, not by nature; but the Only-begotten is Son by nature, not grace. Is this also to be referred to the man in the Son himself? Certainly it is.” Ambrose likewise says in the first book *On the Trinity*: “Christ is Son not by adoption but by nature. We are called sons of God by adoption, whereas he is Son through the truth of his nature.” From these passages it is clearly shown that Christ is not Son by the grace of adoption.

[Col. 0105A] [Note: [Col. 0105D] Distinction 13.] After this, it is asked whether Christ, according to his human nature, could advance or did advance in wisdom and grace. “[Therefore the Wisdom of God, which is called the Only-begotten Son, having assumed manhood in the womb and from the womb of the Virgin, revealed the liberation of man.” [Note: [Col. 0105D] What we enclose in brackets may perhaps have been inserted here incorrectly, since it has no bearing on the question proposed. The words are also those of the Master, final section, [Col. 0106D] distinction 12.]]

Furthermore, it must be known that Christ as man received the fullness of grace from the moment of his conception: the Spirit was given to him without measure, and in him “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). Augustine says to Dardanus that it dwells in him in such a way that he is full of every grace; for it dwells differently in Christ from how it dwells in the saints. In the saints it dwells as sensation is present in the individual members of our body, though not as fully as in the head; for in the head [Col. 0105B] are sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, whereas in the other members there is touch alone. Thus in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells, because he is the head, in whom are all the senses; but in the saints there is, as it were, touch alone, for the Spirit was given to them by measure, since they received from his fullness. Yet they received from his fullness not according to essence but according to likeness, because they never received that same grace essentially, but only a similar grace.

Therefore that child was full of wisdom and grace from his very conception. Hence Jeremiah rightly says, “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass her man” (Jer. 31); because in the Virgin’s womb he existed as a perfect man, not only in respect of soul and flesh [Col. 0105C], but also in respect of wisdom and grace, with which he was full.

But this view seems opposed by what is read in the Gospel of Luke: “Jesus advanced in wisdom, age, and grace before God and men” (Luke 2). For if he advanced in wisdom and grace, he does not seem to have possessed from conception the fullness of grace without measure. To this one may properly reply that, as man, he received such great wisdom and fullness of grace that God could not confer more fully upon him. Yet he is truly said to have advanced in wisdom and grace, not in himself, but in others who advanced through his wisdom and grace, while, in accordance with the progress of his age, he made the gifts of wisdom and grace ever more manifest to them.
