Hence Gregory, the eminent teacher, says in a homily: “According to his human nature, Jesus advanced in wisdom, not because he himself became wiser with time, since from the first hour of his conception he remained full of the Spirit of wisdom, but because he gradually displayed to others in time the wisdom with which he was full. According to his human nature, he advanced in age, from infancy to youth; according to his human nature, he advanced in grace, not by receiving over time what he did not possess, but by revealing the gift of grace which he possessed, before God and men. For in proportion as [Col. 0106A], with advancing age, he disclosed to men the gifts of grace and wisdom inherent in him, he stirred them to the praise of God; and thus he advanced toward praise before God the Father and toward salvation before men. In the same Gospel that child is declared to be full of wisdom and grace” (Luke 2).

Thus he is said to have advanced in wisdom and grace as an ecclesiastical ruler is said to advance in the charge entrusted to him when, through his diligence, others advance.

§ II.---

He adduces testimonies of the Law and prophetic declarations against the perfidy of the Jews, who obstinately deny that Christ is the Son of God. First he introduces David speaking of Christ’s anointing; second, Isaiah the prophet, calling Christ God and Lord; third, the testimony of Genesis, where God the Father, begotten by none, begot from himself one Word, through whom he created all things from nothing; in that Word, whom God the Father did not make but eternally begot from his own substance, he said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), indicating in what manner man was made in God’s image—not according to the body, but according to the human mind. Fourth, he introduces David, who shows us that when God spoke once, he begot the one Word through whom he made all things, and whom the shepherds saw. And although he testifies that he heard two things, namely power and mercy, Christ became for us a true and complete man; and he discusses how the one and same God, the Son of God, was born before the ages and born in time; and finally he treats of both births of the Son of God.

I desire you to answer, O Jews, who, following the blindness of your fathers, obstinately deny the Son of God even to this day. For your salvation, therefore, I shall bring forward for you abundant and most true testimonies from the Law and the prophets, so that, when the unbelief of your hearts has been driven away and the truth of the catholic faith recognized, you may believe him—the Son of God and of the Virgin—to be one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and may faithfully adore with us him who reigns at the right hand of that same God his Father. Therefore, you who persist to the present day in denying that Christ is the Son of God, answer my questions.

If Christ is not God, to whom did David, king and prophet, say in the Psalm: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom” (Ps. 44)? [Col. 0106D] And again: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (ibid.)? Who then is this God anointed by God? [Note: [Col. 0106D] Isidore, book I, *Against the Jews*, ch. 3.] I do not wish you to hide yourselves in the silence of malice and wickedness; rather, if you can, answer briefly the testimony of so truthful a prophet. But because you cannot answer so evident an objection or contradict the words of the Psalmist, I shall, God granting it, explain to you how you ought to understand the foregoing.

[Note: [Col. 0106D] Isidore, book VII, *Etymologies*, ch. 2.] Who, then, is God anointed by God? Certainly he [Col. 0107A] is the one who speaks through Isaiah the prophet as follows: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to announce to the meek, to heal the broken-hearted, and to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those shut in” (Isa. 61). Thus Christ is shown by that very anointing when he is called anointed God. For when, O Jews, you hear of God anointed by God, you ought to understand Christ, the true Son of God and of the Virgin. For Christ is named from *chrisma*, that is, from anointing.

The Jews had been commanded to prepare sacred ointment, with which those summoned to priesthood or kingship might be anointed. And just as a purple garment is now for kings the insignia of royal dignity, so for them the anointing with sacred ointment conferred the name and authority of king; and from *chrisma*, which means anointing, they were called Christs. For *chrisma* is Greek and is interpreted in Latin as *unctio*, “anointing.” The spiritual reality likewise gave this name to the Lord Jesus Christ, because he was anointed by God the Father with the Holy Spirit, as is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “They were gathered together in this city against your holy Son, whom you anointed” (Acts 4)—not, of course, with visible oil, but with the gift of spiritual grace signified by visible ointment.

Therefore Jesus Christ, God and man, was anointed with a spiritual anointing and established above all the works of God the Father’s hands [Note: [Col. 0107D] “Works” is lacking.]. He indeed loved righteousness and hated iniquity, because the sceptre of his kingdom is a sceptre of uprightness. Therefore he is king and priest, anointed by God the Father with the Holy Spirit and power, and established above everything created [Col. 0107C]. Unless you, O Jews, faithfully adore this true king, whom God the Father crowned with glory and honor and beneath whose feet he subjected all things (Ps. 8), you shall without doubt perish eternally.

At the beginning of our disputation I warn you, O Jews, not to presume to contradict the utterly true proclamations of the Law and prophets, but willingly to lend the ears of your hearts. It is of no benefit to you—indeed, it is exceedingly dangerous—to oppose the testimonies of the Law and the prophets, because whoever resists truth contradicts God. But, aided by God’s help, I wish to conquer you with your own weapons, namely, the oracles of the Law and prophets; for an adversary is never conquered more effectively [Col. 0107D] than when he is overcome by his own darts. Hear, therefore, you rebellious and unbelieving people, the testimonies of the Law; hear the prophecies of the prophets; hear the words of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness concerning Jesus Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, that he is true God and true man.

God the Father testifies through Isaiah the prophet, under the person of Cyrus king of the Persians, that this Jesus Christ whom you deny, but whom we embrace with the arms of faith and love and with the highest devotion, is God and Lord. He says: “To my Christ, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, that I may subject nations before his face and turn the backs of kings, and may open doors before him, and gates shall not be shut. I will go before you and humble the glorious ones of the earth; I will shatter bronze gates and break iron bars. And I will give you hidden treasures and disclose the secrets of mysteries, that those from the rising of the sun and those from the west may know that I invoke your name, O Lord God of Israel” (Isa. 45).

In these verses Christ was prophesied under the person of King Cyrus. For God the Father subjected nations and kingdoms to Christ in faith; indeed, we do not read that there was anyone named Cyrus in the kingdom of Israel [Col. 0108B]. This prophecy is read before the Nativity of the Lord because it is believed to have been spoken of him. But if perhaps, O Jews, you believe it was prophesied about Cyrus king of the Persians, it would be absurd [Note: [Col. 0107D] It would be still more absurd and impious to understand the words of the following verses as concerning Christ the Lord: “I have made you like, and you did not know me . . . I girded you, and you did not know me” (Isa. 45). Therefore St. Jerome, on this passage, says that those who refer the earlier words of the chapter in their literal sense to Christ the Lord rather than to Cyrus are gravely mistaken. Nevertheless, some of the ancients, such as Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, in his letter against Migetius, read, with the very ancient Septuagint version, “to my Christ, my Lord,” as may frequently be seen in commentators on this passage. But À Lapide asserts that an error slipped into this version; and certainly the more recent version agrees with the Vulgate. See Juan de Mariana on chapter 3, book I of St. Isidore’s *Against the Jews*, from whom Martin translated these things.] and profane that an impious man devoted to idolatry should be called Christ, God, and Lord. Hence in the translation of the Seventy Interpreters one finds not “to my Christ, Cyrus,” but “to my Christ, my Lord”; and this is understood specifically in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Believe, therefore, O unhappy Jews, that this was said concerning Christ, not Cyrus king of the Persians. For Christ is God and Lord, and naturally one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. God the Father grasped his right hand [Col. 0108C] when he delivered him from the hands of his persecutors and raised him from the tomb on the third day. He subjected nations before his face and turned the backs of kings, because through the Gospel of his beloved Son he powerfully subjected to the yoke of true faith not only the common peoples who occupied a lower rank, but also their kings and princes. He opens doors before him, and the gates were not shut, because the closed door where the apostles were gathered did not obstruct the mass of Jesus’ body, within which divinity lay hidden (John 20); and when he ascended, the gates of heaven opened themselves to him of their own accord.

God the Father went before him, because long beforehand he foretold through prophets taught by the Holy Spirit that he would be born. He humbled the glorious ones of the earth before him, because at the coming of this same Lord Jesus Christ his Son he laid low, through evangelical preaching, the pride of the haughty, the glory of the rich, and the fierceness of tyrants; and rendered them devoted and humble before the sacraments of the Church [Col. 0108D]. He shattered bronze gates and broke iron bars because, when Christ descended there to free his elect [Col. 0109A], he destroyed the powers of the devil and the barriers of hell before him.

“And I will give you hidden treasures and disclose the secrets of mysteries.” It is as though God the Father spoke more plainly to his Son Jesus Christ according to the fact that he was to be born of the Virgin, saying: When the fullness of time has come and you have been conceived of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, I shall give you hidden treasures—that is, I shall pour into you all my wisdom and knowledge—and through you I shall then disclose to all nations the secret mysteries, that is, the Gospel sacraments, which are unknown to almost all mortals; so that you may know that I am the Lord who invokes—that is, causes to be invoked—your name throughout the whole world, so that at your name every knee may bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2).

[Col. 0109B] But perhaps, O Jews, if you say that these things still do not suffice for you, then in order utterly to refute your perfidy and the blindness of mind full of manifold error, and to confirm the truth of our faith, we shall bring forward abundant and fitting testimonies from the Law and prophets. Therefore, if with polluted mouths and faithless hearts you still dare shamelessly to say that Christ is not God and not the true Son of God, tell me: To whom did God speak in Genesis when he said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1)? And again: “God made man; in the image of God he created him” (ibid.)?

Let blessed bishop Fulgentius, distinguished in wisdom and holiness and most careful in expounding the teachings of Scripture [Col. 0109C], come forward and explain to you this prophecy, uttered by Moses and full of so great a mystery. Tell us, holy Fulgentius [Note: [Col. 0109D] A remarkable and noteworthy matter. Earlier our author often attributed to Augustine, along with certain older writers—though incorrectly, as is now established—St. Fulgentius’s book *On Faith to Peter*. But here he ascribes this passage to Fulgentius, although Peter Lombard, whom he appears closely to follow, in explaining this testimony from Genesis, [Col. 0110D] § “Let us set forth,” distinction 2, book I, writes that the author of the book is Augustine.], according to the wisdom given you by God, how we ought to understand what God said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.”

> “For when,” he says, “God used the singular number, ‘image,’ he showed that there is one nature in whose image man was to be made. But when he says, in the plural, ‘our,’ he shows that the God in whose image man was made is not one person. For if that one essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were one person, he would not say, ‘in our image,’ but ‘in my image’; nor would he have said, ‘Let us make,’ but ‘I shall make.’ But if three substances were to be understood or believed in those three persons [Col. 0109D], he would not say, ‘in our image,’ but ‘in our images’; for one image could not belong to three unequal natures.”

Therefore, O Jews, if you wish to attain knowledge of the true faith, it is necessary that you diligently open the ears of your hearts for understanding the words of the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0110D] *Sentences*, I, distinction 3.]. First, then, I wish you to know and learn in what manner man was made in God’s image. For the human body was not made in God’s image [Col. 0110A], but the human mind. And although the human mind is not of the same nature as God, the image of God—than whom nothing is better—must nevertheless be sought and found where our nature has nothing better, that is, in the mind. For the mind is God’s image precisely because it is capable of him, namely God, and can participate in him.

Let us therefore seek in it the Trinity that is God. Behold, the mind remembers itself, understands itself, and loves itself. If we perceive this, we perceive a trinity—not God himself, but God’s image. For here appears a certain trinity: memory, understanding, and love. As blessed Augustine says, these three are not three lives but one life; not three minds but one mind and one essence. For they are equal and mutually contain one another. Each is contained by each, and all by each. For I remember that I have memory, understanding, and will; and I understand that I understand, will, and remember. Behold: the human mind is an image, although an unequal one, of that supreme unity and Trinity of God, in which there is one essence and three persons.

But “mind” is here taken for the soul itself, in which that image of the Trinity exists. Strictly speaking, however, as blessed Augustine says, the mind is called not the soul itself but that which is most excellent in it. Whoever keenly considers the mind, divinely established by nature, sees both what great a thing it is and that within it the eternal and unchangeable nature may be remembered, perceived, and desired. Through memory it remembers God; through understanding it beholds him; through love [Col. 0110C] it embraces him. Certainly the mind finds the image of that supreme Trinity.

Nevertheless, let it beware of comparing this image, made by the same Trinity which is God, with that Trinity in such a way as to judge it altogether similar. Rather, even in whatever likeness it possesses, let it perceive a great unlikeness also. This may briefly be shown. One man, by means of those three powers, remembers, understands, and loves; yet he is neither memory nor understanding nor love, but possesses these three things. Thus one man possesses these three things, but he himself is not these three things. In the supreme simplicity of the nature which is God, however, although God is one, there are three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and these three are one God.

Therefore the Trinity itself is one thing [Note: [Col. 0110D] The sense is confused; it is more clearly restored from the Master: “Therefore the Trinity itself is one thing, and the image of the Trinity in another thing is another.”], and the image of the Trinity in another thing is another [Col. 0110D]. Because of this image, both the thing in which these three occur and the image itself are called an image—namely, man—just as both a panel and the painting upon it are called an image; but the panel is called an image on account of the painting that is on it. Thus, in this image of the Trinity, these three things are not one man, but belong to one man. In that supreme Trinity, of which this is an image, those three are not of one God, but are one God; and they are three persons, not one person [Col. 0111A]. For those three are not man, but belong to man or are in man. But can we say that the Trinity belongs to God in such a way that it is something of God and is not God himself? Far be it that we should believe this! Let us then say that in our mind there is an image of the Trinity, but a small and merely partial one, which bears such a likeness to the supreme Trinity that in the greater part it is unlike.

It must further be known that this trinity of the mind, as blessed Augustine says, is not God’s image merely because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, but because it can also remember, understand, and love him by whom it was made. Therefore the rational mind, considering these three things and the one essence in which they exist, stretches itself toward contemplation of the Creator and sees unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity. For it understands that God is one, essence one, principle one; and it sees that he is not without wisdom, and therefore understands that he possesses wisdom begotten from himself. And because he loves his wisdom, it also understands that there is there love, that is, the Holy Spirit.

Behold, O Jews, we have described to you what the image of God is: namely memory, understanding, and love; that the body of man was not made in God’s image but the soul; and what it is to have God’s image in oneself: namely, to remember, understand, and love one’s maker. Above, moreover, through the explanation of blessed Fulgentius, it has been sufficiently shown to you that God said in the first creation, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” because he is three in persons and one in essence.

Therefore God the Father, God begotten of none, begot from himself one Word through whom he created all things from nothing. For God the Word was born of the Father without beginning and coeternal in the same divinity by which the Father himself is naturally eternal. Therefore it was in that Word, whom God the Father did not make but eternally begot from his own substance, that he said, “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” To confirm so fitting a testimony, so sufficiently explained, and that you may doubt it no longer, O Jews, let us bring forward David the prophet and reverently hear what he has said to us concerning this eternal speech of God the Father by which he created all things from nothing.

He says: “God spoke once; these two things I heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, O Lord, belongs mercy; for you will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61). It seems contradictory that God should speak once and that I heard two things. What, moreover, is meant by what is read in the Apostle: “In many portions and in many ways, God formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets” (Heb. 1)? But God speaks among men in many ways; with himself, however, once, because he begot one Word through whom he made all things and in whom he ordered all things together.

I do not want you to consign to forgetfulness, O Jews, that this is my contention: almighty God is three in persons and one in essence; but you say that, just as God is one essence, so he is one person. Thus, when you say that the divine essence is only one person [Col. 0112A], you deny that God has a Son; and, as John the Evangelist says, “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either” (1 John 2). Know then with certainty that, if you deny the Son coeternal with God the Father, you can by no means have God the Father propitious to you. But if perhaps you do not believe me because you hate the Christian name, you ought at least to give credence to the teachings of the prophets. Listen diligently, therefore, and retain in memory what you hear for your instruction, so that, believing in one God in Trinity, you may attain his love.

Let David the prophet then speak for our instruction: “God spoke once.” Explaining this, blessed Augustine says: “God spoke once because he begot one Word through whom he made all things. The other two things heard by the Prophet are power and mercy, concerning which all the Scriptures speak, and for the sake of which the Law and prophets exist, and for the sake of which Christ himself was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world, as were also the holy apostles. Therefore let power be feared and mercy loved; let not power be despised because of mercy, nor mercy despaired of because of power.”

Therefore God the Father spoke once—that is, he eternally begot the Word in whom he made and ordered all things. This is that Word, O Jews, of whom your shepherds—or rather, to speak more truly, shepherds who became ours through faith—who were keeping the watches of the night over their flock, said to one another: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this Word which has happened, which the Lord has shown us” (Luke 2). I warn you, O Jews, to listen attentively to what those shepherds did, how they believed, and how they glorified God. “They came,” says the Evangelist, “in haste; and they found Mary and Joseph and the infant”—that same Word, coeternal with God the Father, made flesh in time for the deliverance of the human race. “And seeing, they learned concerning the word that had been spoken to them about this child.” But what did the shepherds do? “They returned, glorifying and praising God for all that they had heard and seen, as had been told them” (ibid.).

Therefore, O Jews, follow their footsteps with the steps of good works [Col. 0112D]. Following their example, embrace Christ, true God and true man, with the arms of true faith and love. In imitation of them, believe that Christ is naturally one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. With like devotion praise and glorify forever, in his works, him who is true God—three in persons and one in essence.

This Word, begotten of God the Father before all ages and made flesh in the Virgin’s womb, is not only ineffable; moreover, as Master Peter says on that verse of the Psalm, “God spoke once,” his name is ineffable. It was written on the gold plate of the high priest and was the Tetragrammaton, that is, the four-lettered name, whose letters are JOTH, HE, VAU, BETH, meaning “the beginning [Col. 0113A] of the passion of this life.” The name formed from these letters, as some hand down, is *ja, ja, je, je*, which is called ineffable; and because, whereas the other names of the Lord signify an ineffable reality, this name, according to the interpretations of its letters, designates a more ineffable reality. It is as though one said: He whose name this is, through the humility of his passion is the beginning of the life lost through Adam. And what is more wonderful than that, by suffering and dying, he freed us from death?

The name is called ineffable, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0113D] Book VII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 1.], not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot in any way be comprehended or delimited by human sense and understanding; and therefore, because nothing worthy can be said of it, it is ineffable. Thus the generation of the Word is ineffable, whose name too is ineffable.

[Col. 0113B] Yet this Prophet, apprehending something of this, says: “God has spoken once,” that is, he eternally begot the Word, in whom he disposed all things. This Prophet saw it, as Blessed Augustine says, lifted above all things, transcending the angels, and arriving at that clear region where the One begot the One. Among all these things he heard these two things on high, whither he had leapt. As though he said: “I do not say this from myself, but I heard it when caught up to the only-begotten Word of God the Father.” What things? Namely this: that power belongs to God—that is, to the only-begotten Son, God and man—who not only possesses power in himself, but also confers it upon others, because, as the Apostle says: “There is no power belonging to anyone except from the righteous God” (Rom. XIII). For God the Father established him over all the works of his hands. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII). [Col. 0113C] It follows: “And mercy is yours, O Lord; for you will render to each according to his works” (Ps. LXI). Therefore power and mercy belong to Christ, because God the Father committed all judgment to him. This power, then, is to be feared, because he can save the godly and condemn the ungodly. The devil has a certain power and often wishes to do harm, yet cannot: he pushes the leaning wall only so far as he receives power; for he who gives power to the tempter himself offers mercy to the tempted. For there is no power except from God; he himself is in all things and above all things. Do not ask why God gives the devil so much power, [Col. 0113D] without, on the other hand, giving power [Note: [Col. 0113D] Perhaps: “mercy.”]? God, who gives power, possesses equity. Therefore do not fear the enemy: he does only as much as he receives power to do.

Behold, you have heard, O Jews, that God spoke once: namely, that he eternally begot the Word from himself, through whom he created all things out of nothing. Through him God the Father sustains, governs, and rules all things; through him he redeemed the human race from eternal damnation [Note: [Col. 0114D] From Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2.]. But this same Son of God, though he is eternal and true God, and naturally one God with the Father according to his divinity—as he himself says, “I and the Father are one” (John X)—the same one [Col. 0114A] became for us true and complete man. He is true in this respect, that he has a true human nature; complete in this respect, that he assumed both human flesh and a rational soul. Yet the same only-begotten God was born a second time, once from a mother. For the Word was born God from the Father; the Word made flesh was born from the mother. Therefore one and the same God, the Son of God, was born before the ages and born within time; and both births belong to the one Son of God: the divine birth, according to which the Creator, God in the form of God, is coeternal with the Father; and the human birth, according to which, emptying himself and taking the form of a servant (Phil. II), he not only formed himself in the conception of his mother’s womb, when he became man, by that same assumption of a servant’s form, but also came forth from that same [Col. 0114B] mother’s womb—the same God made man; and the same God made man hung upon the cross; and the same God made man lay in the tomb; and the same God made man rose on the third day from the dead. But in the tomb the same God lay according to the flesh alone, and he descended into hell according to the soul alone. When that soul returned from hell to the flesh on the third day, he rose from the tomb according to that flesh in which he had lain in the tomb. On the fortieth day after the resurrection, the same God made man ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father (Col. III), and from there, at the end of the age, he will come to judge the living and the dead.

§ III.—

David, king and prophet, the instrument of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0114C] bears witness that Christ is true God and the Son of the Virgin: without beginning from God the Father, and in time from the Virgin Mother. From the testimony of Genesis, the Lord is shown to be from the Lord, namely the Son from the Father; from Zechariah, the Lord is sent to the nations for the glory of his divinity, though they despised the counsel—that is, his coming. Isaiah testifies that he is true God and true man at the end of times. The author further considers what the same prophet says of his six names and of the divinity by which he is coeternal with God the Father. David is introduced concerning Christ’s eternal and ineffable birth. From Isaiah he exhorts them, having abandoned Jewish superstition, devoutly to receive the catholic faith, since according to him seven women laid hold of him. By David’s testimony he adds the eternal birth by which Christ is eternal in himself. How beautifully he concludes why absolutely no tongue can either speak perfectly or say anything adequately [Col. 0114D] concerning this immeasurable generation. From the same prophet he introduces testimony concerning Christ’s temporal birth from the Christ-bearing Virgin.

Hear, therefore, O Jews, what I say; hear what I urge for your salvation. If you desire to be delivered from eternal damnation, you must faithfully believe that Christ was born without beginning from God the Father and in time from the Virgin Mother. If you deny him in this present life, you will by no means be able to escape eternal damnation. For, as was said above, he will judge the living and the dead and will condemn unbelievers. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I also will confess him before [Col. 0115A] my Father who is in heaven; and whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God” (Luke XII). Know therefore with certainty, O Jews, that unless you believe him in this present age to be one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, you will by no means be able to escape his judgment in the age to come. Unless you obtain his grace in this present life, you will not be able in any way to flee his wrath in the life to come. Or has unbelief perhaps not yet been wholly expelled from your hearts by the testimonies cited above? But if, hindered perhaps by the blindness of your fathers, you still doubt concerning Christ, that he is the true Son of God, we shall introduce other witnesses from among your own people to overcome your unbelief. Therefore, if you still need other witnesses, let David, king and [Col. 0115B] prophet of your people, who truly was an instrument of the Holy Spirit, come forward and bear witness to Christ that he is the true Son of God and of the Virgin.

“The Lord said to my Lord,” he says, “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. CIX). Tell us, therefore, O unhappy Jews, who is this Lord of David to whom the Lord said, “Sit at my right hand”? Without doubt, the Lord Father said to the Lord Son, who truly is with him one God and Lord, that he should sit at his right hand until he made his enemies the footstool of his feet. The Prophet speaks after our manner when he says, “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand,” namely in order that man may be instructed; for he did not utter this with his mouth, but spoke by the deed—that is, by generation. [Col. 0115C] As though the Prophet said more plainly: “The Lord said,” that is, God the Father eternally ordained, “to my Lord,” that is, to the Son who is Lord and one true God with God the Father. By repeating the same name in saying “Lord to Lord,” he distinguishes the persons and shows their one nature and power. Likewise, when he says, “to my Lord,” this is an indication of divinity. But when he says, “sit,” he notes two things: namely, that after the labor of the Passion he rests and reigns with the Father. As though he said: “Sit at my right hand,” that is, reign with me as my equal, so that by “right hand” may be understood the equality Christ has with the Father. “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet,” that is, until I make them subject to your divinity; by this complete subjection is indicated. This is done and accomplished daily [Col. 0115D] and gradually in those who are converted. “I will make,” he says, “your enemies, whether willing or unwilling, the footstool of your feet,” that is, subject to you by will or by necessity.

These things ought to suffice for you, O Jews, so that, abandoning the error of long-standing unbelief and receiving the truth of the Christian religion, you might enter the holy Church. But if you say that these things still do not suffice for you, and refuse to believe that the Son of God is one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, then, to refute your unbelief and to augment the truth of our faith, we shall introduce testimony after testimony from the books of the Old Testament.

[Col. 0116A] [Note: [Col. 0115D] Isidore, *Against the Jews*, Book I, ch. 3.] Tell us, unhappy Jews, who deny that there are three persons in the divine essence: what Lord rained fire from the Lord upon Sodom? For thus we read in Genesis: “And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord” (Gen. XIX). In this statement, O wretched Jews, made almost stony by the hardness of unbelief, do not doubt that Christ is the second person in the Trinity. For who is that Lord from the Lord except, without doubt, the Son from the Father, who was sent into this world by that same Father? By this testimony the divinity of the Son, which he naturally possesses from God the Father, is shown, and the distinction of the persons is clearly demonstrated. Again, if Christ is not Lord, tell us, O Jews, who is that Lord of hosts [Col. 0116B] who is sent by the Lord of hosts, as Zechariah himself says: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: For glory he sent me to the nations that plundered you; for whoever touches you touches the pupil of his eye. For behold, I raise my hand over them, and they shall be spoil to those who served them; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me” (Zech. II). Whose voice, then, is this, O Jews, except that of Jesus Christ, Savior of the world? When almighty God declares that he has been sent by almighty God, he undoubtedly shows himself to be the Son of God the Father. He was sent to the nations for the glory of the divinity which he had eternally with the Father, because he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death (Phil. II). And so that you may know, O Jews, that what is said is true, [Col. 0116C] the Son of God himself, for the consolation of his Church, which he was to redeem by his own blood, speaks thus in what follows: “Praise and rejoice, daughter of Zion; for behold, I am coming, and I shall dwell in your midst. And many nations shall be joined, namely by faith, to God on that day, and they shall be my people; and I shall dwell in your midst; and you shall know that the Lord of hosts sent me to you” (Zech. II). As though the Son of God, sent from God the Father, spoke more plainly for the consolation of his Church, saying: “Praise and rejoice, daughter of Zion,” that is, daughter of contemplation; “for behold, I am coming,” according to the saying, “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John XVI); “and I shall dwell in your midst,” says the Lord (Zech. II). Hence comes that saying: “After this he was seen on earth and conversed with men” (Baruch III). “And many nations shall be joined [Col. 0116D] through my Gospel to the Lord,” that is, to the Father, on that day; and then they shall be my special people, as they are also the Father’s, and I shall dwell in your midst. Hence we read in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). And from this you will know, O Church, that the Lord of hosts, that is, the Father, sent me, his Son, into this world to you.

You can in no way contradict, nor ought you to contradict, the testimonies given above, O Jews. Therefore you ought not to doubt, but readily to believe, that the Son of God and of the Virgin came long ago into this world for the redemption of the human race. [Col. 0117A] But you, O wretched and unhappy people, have always acted contentiously against the Lord; and therefore you have lost your holy place and your nation, and are dispersed throughout the whole world like murderers and reprobates. Hence the prophet David fittingly rebukes you in the Psalms, saying: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII), that is, you trembled at the loss of temporal possessions. For you feared to lose an earthly kingdom where there was no need to fear, and you did not fear to lose heaven where there was cause for fear. For you said: “If we let Christ go on thus, all will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John XI). Then, therefore, O wretched people, you “confounded the counsel of the poor man” (Ps. XIII), that is, you despised Christ’s humble coming; [Col. 0117B] and therefore you were delivered into captivity among all nations under heaven.

Christ’s coming is called “counsel” because he admonished those whom he called to place their hope not in this present world but in God alone. Hence Isaiah calls this same Son of God and of the Virgin “Counsellor,” saying: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. IX). Therefore you confounded—that is, refused to receive—the counsel according to the humanity of the poor, namely poor Christ, who had come to deliver you. Indeed, what is more unhappy, you rendered him evil for good when you fastened him to the cross without cause; and from that for which you ought to have shown him greater reverence [Col. 0117C] you despised him all the more. And what shall I say to you, O wicked and perverse generation? You will in no way be able to be numbered among the remnant of Israel that is to be saved unless through that same Son of God and of the Virgin whose counsel you confounded—that is, whom you despised in his humility. Without doubt, unless you confess him truly, render him true faith, and believe him to be one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, you will not at all be able to belong to the fellowship of his elect. Tell us, O unhappy people: “Who will give salvation to Israel out of Zion?” (Ps. XIII). You indeed confounded Christ’s counsel; nevertheless, God the Father will give salvation to Israel—that is, Christ, descended in the flesh from the stock of the Jews—because he will save the remnant [Col. 0117D] of Israel, namely the Jews who believe in him. For he himself will come in glory and majesty for judgment. He, therefore, will save his faithful in the future; he will turn back the captivity of his people at his second coming, when the devil, who had held his people captive, is cast into the depths of hell. Then Jacob will assuredly exult with the children of the Church, and Israel will rejoice in the Lord, having received Christ’s baptism in the name of the holy Trinity.

And that you may believe, O Jews, that what is said is true, and that “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts IV) except in this same Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, we prove it by the testimony of the prophet Isaiah, whom you cannot contradict at all. “There shall come from Zion,” he says, [Col. 0118A] “one who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob” (Isa. LIX). Do these things suffice for you, O Jews, or shall we introduce still more able witnesses from the Law and the Prophets to convict your unbelief and strengthen the truth of the catholic faith? For the sun will sooner set than our abundance of witnesses fail us. Therefore, if in your wicked conspiracy you still presume to say that Christ is not the true Son of God, let the prophet Isaiah, trained in civic eloquence, come forward; and let him, before you his fellow-countrymen who are listening, bear witness for us that Christ is true God before all ages and true man, born of the Virgin at the end of times.

“A little child,” he says, “has been born to us, and a son has been given to us” (ibid.). Tell us also, O prophet Isaiah, of his power, glory, and name: do you know anything through the revelation of the Holy Spirit? “And dominion,” he says, [Col. 0118B] “has been made upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” This little child, then, is Christ, who was born to us in order to redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works (Tit. II). A little child was born to us in time from the Virgin Mother; and a Son was given to us, ineffably begotten of God the Father before all ages. A little child was born to us in time, namely a true man from a woman. A Son was given to us, namely true God, begotten from God the Father before [Col. 0118C] all ages. God the Son was given to us by God the Father and by himself, namely to redeem us from the harshest dominion of the devil. A little child was born to us according to the flesh, who fought against the ancient enemy for our salvation; the Son of God was given to us by grace alone. Therefore Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, was born to us as a little child; yet according to his divinity he is great and exceedingly praiseworthy in the bosom of the Father [Note: [Col. 0117D] Isidore, *Sentences*, Book I, ch. 14.], because he could not be known by human beings through himself—that is, in his divine essence—and in the very act by which he provided for us he endured contempt, because proud man despised the weakness which he assumed for our sake. For this reason, as Paul says, God chose the weak and foolish things of the world, in order to confound the stronger and wiser things through which he was not known (I Cor. I). [Col. 0118D] Just as a weak infant cannot take strong food unless it is first eaten by the mother and changed into the juice of milk, so that what the infant could not use as food may be drunk by sucking it in milk through the flesh [Note: [Col. 0118D] Perhaps: “her”], so too, when we were weak in desiring the eternity of the Word, the Word itself became flesh, so that, nourished through the flesh and made stronger, we and the angels might be satisfied by contemplating solid food—that is, the Word of the Lord, eternal with the Father.

It follows: “And dominion was made upon his shoulder.” His dominion is said to be upon his shoulder because he carried the cross for himself upon his own shoulders, and because Pilate wrote the title of his kingdom upon his shoulders and [Col. 0119A] above his head. For thus he said, although he was a Gentile: “This is Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John X). Therefore his dominion upon his shoulders is the cross, on account of which God exalted him according to his humanity and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of things heavenly, earthly, and infernal (Phil. II). For when he was led to the Passion, he carried his cross, in which, according to his humanity, he obtained dominion over heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings.

You have now heard, O Jews, what testimony the prophet Isaiah, taught by the Holy Spirit, gave concerning Christ’s humanity and divinity, and concerning his dominion, by which God the Father, insofar as he was born of the Virgin, established him over all the works of his hands. [Col. 0119B] I urge you also carefully to hear what he says concerning his six names and the divinity by which he is coeternal with God the Father. “His name,” he says, “shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace.” As though he said more plainly: “His name shall be called Wonderful,” that is, God and man, which is unheard-of; “Counsellor,” namely the Angel of Great Counsel; “God,” that is, Creator of all things; “Mighty,” whom no one can resist; “Father of the age to come,” enduring without end; “Prince of Peace,” who made both one and reconciled us to God and the angels. It follows: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” As though he said: Through the preaching [Col. 0119C] of the apostles and their successors, his dominion—that is, the multitude of the faithful—will be multiplied within the holy Church; and there will be no end to the peace of his saints, although for a short time they are troubled in defense of the faith. “He shall sit upon David’s throne and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and justice.” As though he said: The people whom David ruled in his time by a temporal dominion, the Son of God and of the Virgin himself will transfer to an eternal kingdom and establish it so that it can sin no more; and over it he has reigned from now and for ever, that is, unto ages of ages.

Do so many witnesses concerning Christ—that he is the true Son of God and the true son of the Virgin—suffice for you, O Jews? Or do you also wish us to introduce others in order to drive every uncertainty from your hearts? Believe me, O unbelieving people, and do not doubt: compelled by charity, I willingly undertake this labor so that, God granting it, I may lead you by exhortation to the true faith. If, therefore, doubt still remains in your minds and you do not believe fully, and if you doubt whether Christ existed before the Virgin’s childbirth, let David, a faithful witness, come forward and explain to us, who desire to hear, what God the Father said in the Psalms concerning his eternal and ineffable birth.

“With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX). As though God the Father said more plainly to the Son, coeternal and coequal with himself: “You are my Son by nature, because the beginning is with me with you; I shall not say to you, ‘with me,’ lest you seem in some respect later than I. You and I are the one beginning of all things. This is not seen here, but it will be seen [Col. 0120A] in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints,” that is, in eternity, where divine power is beheld not by others but by the saints, when at the resurrection they shall shine like the angels of God. Or God the Father speaks thus: “You already rule, O Christ the Son, but on the day of your spiritual power—that is, in the future—the beginning will be with me with you. This is always so, but it is not seen; then, however, it will be seen,” as Blessed Augustine says, “when Christ, who was once seen in the form of a servant, will be seen by pure hearts in the form of God; from this sight the ungodly will be removed, lest he see the glory of God.” I say, “in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints,” namely when the saints [Col. 0120B] will shine resplendently like the sun in the kingdom of the Father (Matt. XIII). Then, as Blessed Augustine says, the beginning will be with him—and even now the beginning is, namely the Father with the Son—but then it will be seen how the beginning is with him, because then, being like him, they shall see him: namely, immortal and impassible persons shall see him as he is (I John III). Philip had seen him according to the form of a servant, and, rebuked because he did not recognize in the Son the Father whom he sought to see, when he said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us,” he heard: “He who sees me” (John XIV)—not merely the form of a servant, but sees me as I am to hidden minds and as I make myself to be seen by those who hope—“sees the Father also.” But one must believe in this way in order that he may then [Col. 0120C] be seen. Hence Philip is also told: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (ibid.). As though he said: Believe, so that you may deserve to see the Son with the Father and in the Father—the one whom you are not yet able to see—and how the Father is the beginning with him. This vision is eternal life. Hence the same Son of God and of the Virgin says to the Father in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII). It follows: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” As though God the Father addressed him, saying: “From the womb,” that is, from my hidden and secret substance, “I ineffably begot you, and this before the morning star,” that is, before all times. The morning star, which announces day to the world, a preeminent star, as Blessed Augustine says, is put here for all the stars and heavenly bodies, [Col. 0120D] as a part for the whole; through these heavenly bodies times are understood, because they were set for signs and times, as is read in Genesis: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day from night; and let them be for signs, and times, and days, and years, that they may shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth” (Gen. I).

Behold, you have heard, O Jews, that our Lord Jesus Christ was ineffably born before all times from the eternal essence of God the Father, and that he is coeternal and coequal with God the Father. For he is eternal and without beginning of birth, because through him God the Father created all things out of nothing. Again and again I urge you, O Jews, once unbelief has been rooted out from your hearts, carefully to hear also [Col. 0121A] what Isaiah says to you about his temporal birth, by which he was born without sin from the Virgin.

“On that day,” he says, “the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth exalted, and rejoicing for those of Israel who shall have been saved” (Isa. IV). By these words the Prophet foretells your conversion, so that, abandoning the superstition of the Jewish people, you may receive the catholic faith with a devout mind. As though he said more plainly: “On that day,” that is, after the fullness of time has come, “the remnant of Israel shall be saved” (Rom. IX). Why? Because the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory. And the fruit of the earth—namely the Son of God and of the Virgin—will be lifted above the hills, that is, above all saints [Col. 0121B] and all orders of angels and everything created, according to the saying of the Psalmist: “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Ps. VIII). And from him there shall be rejoicing for those who have been saved—that is, for those of Israel who have believed (Isa. IV). And then everyone who is left in Zion, that is, in the Church which contemplates God and enjoys the vision of peace, and who remains in Jerusalem—namely, by Christ’s Gospel the remnant of Israel will be converted to God and, abandoning their former error, will be cleansed from sins through baptism—shall be called holy, that is, Christian from Christ, everyone inscribed in life, that is, in the book of life in the heavenly Jerusalem.

Know, therefore, O Jews, that in no way, as I have often testified, will you be able to be saved with the remnant of Israel which is to be saved [Col. 0121C] or joined at all to the children of the Church, except through that same Son of God and of the Virgin, whom you have heard to be exalted in magnificence and glory—that is, crowned by God the Father and established over all the works of his hands. He is full of grace and truth (John I); in him are hidden all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge (Col. II). For among all men he alone is the perfect man, because he is not merely man but true man and true God. For he was conceived and born without sin, and conversed among human beings in the world (Baruch III), nor was deceit ever found in his mouth (Isa. LIII). Of him Solomon, praising the Church figuratively, says: “Her husband is noble in the gates when he sits,” namely [Col. 0121D] in judgment, “with the elders of the land” (Prov. XXXI), namely with the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and other teachers of the Church. We believe that the prophet Zechariah also said of this man: “BEHOLD THE MAN; HIS NAME IS THE BRANCH” (Zech. VI). Isaiah likewise speaks typologically of this man: “Seven women shall lay hold of one man on that day, saying: ‘We will eat our own bread’” (Isa. IV). As though he said more plainly: “Seven women,” that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. XI)—“shall lay hold of one man,” namely Christ, who alone appeared among men without sin, “on that day,” namely when the loftiness [Col. 0122A] of men—that is, nobility of birth—will be bowed down, because no one will be able to escape God’s wrath except through Christ.

For this reason the gifts of the Holy Spirit are called women in this passage: no one is begotten for God except through the Holy Spirit. And one woman is not named; instead, they are called women in the plural because the gifts of the Holy Spirit are many. Rightly, therefore, is it said: “Seven women,” that is, seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, “shall lay hold of one man,” namely Christ, “on that day,” that is, on the day of new grace, because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily (Col. II). Of him John the Baptist is told: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John I). These seven virtues mentioned above are the seven eyes, concerning which we read thus in Zechariah: “Upon one stone are seven eyes, and in one golden lampstand seven lamps and seven pouring vessels” (Zech. III). [Col. 0122B] It follows: “We shall eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments” (Isa. IV), which means that the Holy Spirit possesses all things equally with the Father and the Son and lacks nothing. “Only let your name be called upon us,” they say, as though the seven virtues of the Holy Spirit said to Christ: “Let those who desire to enjoy our indwelling be called Christians after you. Take away our reproach, lest, driven from human hearts by the stench of vices, we may often be compelled to change our dwelling.”

For this reason I return so often in speaking to you, O Jews, because I grieve exceedingly at your unhappiness. Yet I wish [Col. 0122C] to know from you whether, having laid aside the death-dealing obstinacy of unbelief, you believe Christ to be naturally one God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit; or perhaps, drunk with the poison of malice and wickedness, you still doubt his eternal birth. Beyond doubt, convicted by so many fitting witnesses and instructed by so many most true arguments, you ought by now to abandon the unbelief of your ancient error and receive true faith with devout mind. But if you seek testimony once more concerning his eternal birth, by which he is coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, let holy David come forward and say to you who doubt—and to us who firmly believe and desire to hear devoutly—what, under the person of this same Son of God, he uttered in the Psalms when taught by the Holy Spirit: “The Lord said [Col. 0122D] to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II). As though God the Father said more plainly to the Son coeternal and coequal with himself: “You are my Son by nature, truly and by ineffable consubstantial generation, because I, who am coeternal, have begotten you today,” that is, eternally. As though he said: “This generation is not new but eternal. ‘Today’ signifies the present, and that which is eternal always is.”

Meanwhile, I wish you to know, O Jews, that absolutely no tongue can speak perfectly of God or say anything adequately. For the divine essence exceeds every utterance, surpasses every sense, and overcomes every understanding, not only of human beings but even of angels. For what can a human being say worthily and adequately about God, when he does not fully know even himself? Therefore, when man strives to speak of God, who speaks of whom? A human being of God; a mortal of the immortal; a visible being of the invisible; a changeable being of the unchangeable; a work of its maker; a creature of the Creator; a thing made of its maker; a small thing of the immeasurable; a temporal being of the eternal; a lowly being of the Most High; one fashioned from mud of him who created all things out of nothing. And although it is truly so—that no one still mortal can say anything adequately about God—nevertheless, concerning Christ’s eternal birth, by which God the Father begot him before all times as coeternal and consubstantial with himself, we have offered you many and fully suitable testimonies from the Law and from your own people. Thus, having recognized the truth which Christ is, you ought to seek nothing further, resist no longer, and not oppose so evident [Col. 0123B] an assertion.

But if you seek testimony concerning his temporal birth, by which he was born from the Virgin and, according to his humanity, is less than God the Father, who willed him to be incarnate for us, let the prophet David come forward. Let him say again what, speaking to God the Father, he joyfully sang of him in the Psalms many ages beforehand, to augment more and more our faith and glory and to destroy your unbelief altogether: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and established him over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII). As though the Psalmist plainly addressed God the Father, saying: “For the redemption of the human race, you made him, [Col. 0123C] who is head of all the faithful, lower than the angels, because he was passible and mortal; but only a little lower, because in other respects he surpasses the angels, whom he commands. I say, O most holy Father, you made him a little lower; but afterward you crowned him with glory,” that is, with the splendor of a corruptible body, “and with honor,” so that he should be venerated by all. And he fittingly says, “you crowned,” because the circle of the world, which is like a crown, came to his faith. “And you established,” that is, made firm, “him over the works of your hands.” Since the angels are works of God’s hands and the only-begotten Son of God was established over them, it follows: “You subjected all things under his feet,” that is, beneath his dominion and power.

Meanwhile I urge you, O Jews, not to be sluggish but diligent and watchful in hearing testimonies [Col. 0123D] concerning Christ’s divinity and incarnation. You ought not merely willingly but most willingly to hear these testimonies, which, compelled by charity, I do not begrudge explaining to you. Certainly I shall be able to have great joy with you in the Lord when I see you inseparably joined to the children of the Church by the bond of faith and charity.

§ IV.—
After the admonition in which he urges that Christ, the Redeemer of the human race, possesses a natural and eternal divinity from God the Father, and a natural substance from the Virgin Mother, he shows from Daniel’s words that Christ has already come; indeed, he also reckons the time of his coming and its years. He summons [Col. 0124A] Christ’s killers to true repentance; finally David is introduced to demonstrate Christ’s true divinity and humanity, and likewise Nathan, promising David a righteous shoot. Isaiah is brought forward, with Jeremiah bearing witness, that he whom God the Father begot from himself assumed flesh from the immaculate Virgin; in that flesh God the Father established him as king above everything he himself created. And by Gabriel’s testimony our Lord Jesus Christ is declared to be the Son of the Most High, begotten before all ages and destined to reign for ever. He proceeds to discuss the humility of Mary, ever virgin, together with her question in response to the angelic greeting: for although she believed it could happen, she asks how it would happen. Explaining the heavenly messenger’s reply, he expounds Christ’s conception and the overshadowing of the most blessed Virgin.

Thus you have heard, O Jews, that the Virgin’s Son, according to [Col. 0124B] his humanity, was made a little lower than the angels; you have heard that God the Father crowned him with the glory of resurrection and ascent into heaven, and set him over all the works of his hands. That glory, namely, which the Son of God eternally possessed with God the Father, this same man, born of the Virgin, temporally received from God the Father. Believe, therefore, O Jews, that Christ, the Redeemer of the human race, has a natural and eternal divinity from God the Father, and a natural bodily substance from the Virgin Mother. “Thus the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, is not one person in humanity and another in deity, but is the same one in both natures: neither was he conceived as a mere man, nor [Col. 0124C] was he born as a mere man; nor afterwards, as Blessed Isidore says in the book of *Sentences* (ch. 13), did he receive the merit of becoming God.”

I urge you, O Jews, who even to the present time deny the Son of God, not to hear with a deaf ear but with attentive concern what is said concerning his divinity and humanity. God the Word, remaining in the unchangeable essence which is coeternal to him with the Father and the Holy Spirit, assumed flesh for human salvation, in which, as Blessed Isidore says, “the impassible might suffer, the immortal might die, and the eternal, before all ages, [Note: Above, the author reads: ‘and the eternal before the ages might temporally be killed.’] might be shown temporal. Therefore the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, as Blessed Isidore says, although one thing is from the Father and another from the mother, is nevertheless not one person from the Father and another from the Virgin; but the same one is eternal [Col. 0124D] from the Father and temporal from the mother; the same one who made is the same one who was made. The same one is from the Father in heaven without a mother, and from the mother on earth without a father; the same one is a temple to the Creator and creator of the temple; the same one is the maker of the work and the work of the maker; remaining one from both natures and in both natures, neither confused by the union of the natures nor doubled by their distinction.”

Are so many and such suitable testimonies from your Law and your people sufficient for you, O Jews, so that, embracing the faith, you may believe Jesus Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be one true God? Or does the hardness of ancient unbelief still occupy your mind [Col. 0125A]? But if perhaps you say that Christ, of whom all these prophetic predictions sang, has not yet come, but that you await his coming, I shall bring forward the prophet Daniel. He not only proclaims Christ’s future coming, as all the prophets do, but also plainly shows the time of his coming, counts the years, and openly declares his signs. Speak, holy Daniel, to us now faithful through God’s grace, and to Jews still doubtful; give testimony concerning Christ, lest, persisting in their wickedness, they perish with Antichrist, whom they expect to come as Christ near the end of the world. Speak, Daniel, man of desires, and say what was revealed to you by an angel in a vision concerning Christ’s coming; and by your utterly true prediction convict the Jews [Col. 0125B] who persist in their long-standing unbelief, just as you convicted the shameless elders who made false accusations against innocent Susanna and sought to hand her over to death (Dan. 13).

“Behold,” he says, “the man Gabriel . . . flying touched me at the time of the evening sacrifice” (Dan. 9). Angels are not men, but appear to human beings in the form of men, just as three men appeared to Abraham at the oak of Mamre—though they were certainly not men. Of them Scripture says: “He saw three and worshipped one.” Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: “Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8). *Angel* is rendered in Latin as *nuntius*, “messenger.” Therefore we believe that the man named Gabriel, flying and announcing future things to the prophet [Col. 0125C], was an angel. For Gabriel is rendered in our language as “strength” or “strong one of God.” Hence, at the time when the Lord was about to be born, to wage war upon the demons, and to triumph over the world, the angel Gabriel announced his birth to Mary. Rightly, therefore, is he called Gabriel—that is, “strength of God”—who is sent by the Lord to preach the time of Christ’s coming to the praying prophet who desires to know God’s secrets. For it is fitting that a strong angel should announce the coming of the mightiest Christ for the redemption of the human race: Christ who, at the beginning of creation, cast the devil out of heaven, who, when placed in human nature, fought and conquered him courageously and rightly, and finally hurled him into the depths of hell. Concerning him the Psalmist exultantly says: “The Lord is strong and mighty; the Lord is mighty in battle” (Ps. 23).

But now let us hear what the angel Gabriel says to Daniel. “O Daniel,” he says, “I have now gone forth to instruct you. Therefore attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks are shortened concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be consumed, sin may receive its end, iniquity may be abolished, everlasting righteousness may be brought in—that is, Christ—and vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Dan. 9). If those seventy weeks are reckoned from Daniel’s time, it is beyond doubt known that the Holy of Holies, who is Christ, came long ago [Col. 0126A]. For in sacred speech a week is defined as seven years, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall count seven weeks of years, that is, seven times seven, which together make forty-nine years” (Lev. 25). From the time of the prophet Daniel to Christ’s birth there are more than seventy weeks.

Therefore, O unhappy Jews, Christ has already been born, whom prophetic speech long ago foretold. Perhaps, O wretched ones, you refuse to believe that he came because you fastened him to the cross without cause. For he himself powerfully and mercifully freed you from Egyptian bondage; he caused you to cross the Red Sea with dry feet; by day a pillar of cloud and by night a pillar of fire showed you the unknown path through the wilderness; [Col. 0126B] through raining clouds he sufficiently fed you with manna, without the labor of your hands; he fought for you against your enemies; he gave you, as a possession, the land of promise flowing with milk and honey. Finally, when he himself was specially sent to you from heaven by God the Father—namely, so that he might call you back, who had long departed from the way of truth by serving idols, to the worship of the true God, whose natural Son he is and with whom, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, he is one true God—by preaching, illuminating the blind, raising the dead, and performing other miracles, you not only disdained to hear him, but, what is far more grievous and far more disastrous, handed him over to a most shameful death and offered gall and vinegar to his honeyed mouth. You acted very foolishly, therefore, since toward him whom you ought to have obeyed [Col. 0126C] in all things you proved not only rebellious, but even repaid immense benefits with reproaches and insults. Thus he complains of you through the Prophet, saying: “They repaid me evil for good, barrenness to my soul” (Ps. 34). And because you sought without cause to hand over to death the true life, which he himself is, you have consigned yourselves to eternal death: one kills oneself who endeavors to extinguish life.

Yet, although you have committed so grave a sacrilege, if you truly repent, if you confess him in truth, if you show him true faith, if you beseech him with your whole heart, even with tears flowing, you will beyond doubt be able to obtain full pardon from him. For he is merciful and kind, and ready to spare those who truly repent. He himself mercifully invites you to repentance, saying: “Turn to me and you shall be saved” (Isa. 45). Hence through the prophet Ezekiel he consoles not only you, but also all who hope in him, saying: “It is not my will that the wicked should die, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 18). Indeed, he can save those who hope in him because he is true God and true man. He is true God because he came forth from God the Father; true man because from David’s lineage he assumed a human body without sin. But if you still refuse to believe me, if you do not yet give faith to my warnings, if you do not assent to my just exhortations, [Col. 0127A] if through hatred of Christ’s name you disdain to hear me, if you intend to persist in your perfidy and in your confusion doubt that this same Jesus Christ our Lord is naturally the true Son of God, I urge you to hear with a receptive ear what the prophet David sang long beforehand about his divinity and humanity.

Speak, holy David; give testimony to Christ’s divinity, by which you may convert the unbelieving Jewish people to true faith. For he says: “Will Zion say: ‘Man and man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her’?” (Ps. 86). It is as though he said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you” (*ibid.*), that is, of that city; and this miracle also happened in it: namely, that a man was born in it, and that he who truly is [Col. 0127B] God Most High himself founded it. It should be noted, as Master Peter says, that carnal Zion is the Synagogue, and spiritual Zion is the holy Church. Thus a man was born in Zion, that is, in the Synagogue—namely, among the Jewish people—and in the city of Jerusalem, in suffering, that same man became most lowly; and that same one founded it, because he is its foundation, he who truly is the Most High God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit.

What do you say to this, O unhappy—indeed, most unhappy—Jews? What objection do you make? What answer do you give? Beyond doubt you have been defeated to such an extent that you ought no longer to resist or contradict so manifest a truth. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ was born ineffably from God the Father before all ages; he was born in Zion from the Virgin Mother. But from what, O holy David, can you prove all these things just stated? Namely from this: that the same Lord related them in the writings of peoples and rulers (*ibid.*), that is, in the Scriptures directed to faithful peoples and published by rulers—namely, Moses, the prophets, and the apostles. Tell us, then, O depraved and perverse people, wholly without rational judgment and without spiritual understanding: what could you hear more true, clearer, or more explicit concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity together? A perfect man was born in Zion, and the same one is the exalted Lord: man, because he was born human; exalted, because he was raised above all the choirs of angels at the right hand of God the Father, with whom, according to his divinity, [Col. 0127D] he is naturally one God; Lord, because every creature, some willingly and some unwillingly, is subject beneath his feet.

Because I see you, O Jews, freely—that is, with no one compelling you—hastening toward eternal destruction down the precipice of unbelief, grieving over your miseries, I therefore bring before you abundant and most true testimonies from the Law and Prophets, that I may correct you. This is not burdensome to me, compelled as I am by charity, but is very necessary for you. For your salvation I again urge you not to hear with a deaf but with an open ear what God the Father says through the prophet Nathan to David concerning Christ. “Go,” he says, “and tell David my servant: Thus says the Lord: When you have completed your days and go to your fathers, I shall raise up your seed [Col. 0128A] after you, who shall be your son, and I shall establish his kingdom for ever. He shall build me a house, and I shall establish his throne for eternity. I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; but I shall not remove my mercy from him, as from the one who was before you. And I shall establish him in my house and in my kingdom for ever; and his throne shall be most firm for ever” (1 Chron. 17).

Whoever thinks that all this was fulfilled in Solomon is mistaken. For how can what was said be understood of Solomon: “After you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up your seed after you, which shall be of your sons, and I shall establish his kingdom”? Is this believed to have been prophesied concerning Solomon? Not at all. For he began to reign while his father was alive. But here it is said: [Col. 0128B] “When your days have been completed and you sleep with your fathers, I shall raise up seed for you.” From this it is understood that another is promised, one foretold to be raised up not before David’s death but after it. Therefore Christ is the true King who is prophesied to be born from David’s seed according to the flesh. He also built a house for God the Father, namely the holy Church, which he mercifully redeemed from the bondage of the ancient enemy with the price of his most holy body and blood; and in it, through ministers conformed to himself, since he has been made priest for ever, he does not cease daily to offer to that same God the Father acceptable sacrifices for the salvation of the human race.

Therefore, lest you doubt that this is so, O Jews, I exhort you diligently to hear how plainly God the Father announces this very thing through the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous shoot; and a king shall reign and be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice upon the earth . . . and this is the name by which they shall call him: namely, the Lord our righteous one” (Jer. 23). This, then, is the shoot promised by God the Father to David when he sleeps with his fathers. Therefore the righteous shoot is the Word, ever coeternal with God the Father, but in time made flesh without sin from the Virgin Mary, who drew her origin from David’s seed.

Meanwhile I urge you, O Jews, to prepare yourselves with attentive concern to hear the most [Col. 0128D] true oracles of the prophets concerning Christ: that with God the Father and the Holy Spirit he is one true God. For Isaiah the prophet says—indeed, a man endowed with urbane elegance, holiness, truthfulness in speech, whom you cannot possibly contradict—“A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root. And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). This rod that came forth from Jesse’s root is the Virgin Mary, sprung from his root, who bore the flower, namely the Lord Savior. Hence in the Song of Spiritual Love he himself says concerning himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2). Christ fittingly calls himself a flower, because [Col. 0129A] while he uproots the thorns of sins, he adorns the mind of the bride—that is, the holy soul—with the beauty of his righteousness, and, when he applies heavenly desire to the nostrils of the heart, refreshes and restores the soul’s inward parts as it were with fragrance.

Again, O Jews, let us recall what Jeremiah above said in the Lord’s utterance, so that the Catholic faith may be strengthened in every respect and you who deny Christ even today may be shown defeated in all things. “A king,” he says, “shall reign and be wise” (Jer. 25). This king, according to the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist, has written on his garment and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19). Therefore he is not only king, but King of kings and Lord of lords. Hence he himself speaks in Solomon’s book of Proverbs, saying: “By me kings reign, and lawmakers decree what is just. By me princes rule, and the powerful decree justice” (Prov. 8). Beyond doubt, no one has ever acquired a kingdom without him; for just as God the Father created all things through him, so also through him he governs, sustains, and rules all things that are in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all the deeps. That he is truly King also inasmuch as he was born of the Virgin, he himself asserts in the psalm where he says: “But I was appointed King by him”—namely, by God the Father—“over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2), that is, over the holy Church, which he redeemed from the enemy’s hand by his most precious [Col. 0129C] blood, “proclaiming his command” (*ibid.*), that is, the holy Gospel. For he powerfully and mercifully rescued it from everlasting condemnation through his most merciful Passion and holy cross; through himself and his devoted ministers he rules it most diligently without interruption.

Meanwhile I urge you, O Jews, not to hear carelessly but wisely the authorities of the Old and New Testaments which we offer to confirm the Catholic faith and overcome your mad disputation. You ought gladly—indeed, most gladly—to hear the testimonies of the holy Churches which, you know, we bring forward in defense of the Catholic faith and for your correction. Let us again continue by explaining what God the Father said above through the prophet Jeremiah concerning Jesus Christ, the eternal King, so that we may truthfully show you, though you still doubt, that he is true God from the coeternal divine nature of this same God his Father, and true man from the bodily substance of the Virgin Mother. “A king shall reign and be wise” (Jer. 25). That “he shall reign” is said of future time must be understood according to his humanity. As has often already been said, he whom God the Father begot from himself before every creature, for the redemption of the human race temporally assumed our humanity without sin from the substance of the Virgin Mother; in that humanity God the Father established him as king above all that he created through him. Similar to this [Col. 0130A], O Jews, is what the angel Gabriel announced to Mary, ever virgin, about this same eternal King: “Hail, Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke 1). And he added: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with the Lord. Behold, you shall conceive in the womb and bear a Son, and you shall call his name Jesus” (*ibid.*). Jesus means “Savior” or “saving one”: “for he shall save his people” (Matt. 1), whether from circumcision or from uncircumcision, in one fold under one shepherd—namely, under himself, who is the true shepherd of all believers. It follows: “He shall be great and shall be called Son of the Most High” (Luke 1). It should be noted that John the Baptist was great before the Lord; but this one, namely the Son of God, is great as God and God’s Son. John [Col. 0130B] was great through the merit of abstinence, because he drank neither wine nor strong drink (*ibid.*); but this one is great in power, because he ate with sinners and cleansed them from sins.
