In contrast, the streams of holy Church’s teaching are both broad and open, because its sayings are abundant to those who find them and plain to those who seek them. Thus Blessed Job says (chapter 28): ‘God searched out the depths of rivers and brought hidden things into light,’ because, by infusing the spirit of understanding into the Church’s interpreters, he opened the ancient obscurities of the prophets. And holy Church now knows this through the Holy Spirit, whereas you, O Jews, are utterly unable to understand it through the letter.”

This is what Isaiah foretold to you: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand, nor shall you remain” (Isa. 7). As though he said more plainly: Unless you believe those things announced to you concerning Christ, you will not be able to understand the Scriptures spiritually, because the hardness of unbelief darkens the eyes of your mind. “Nor shall you remain,” he says, namely in faith and love of Christ.

Moses the lawgiver undoubtedly prefigured this blindness of yours, O unhappy Jews, when he covered his face while speaking to the Israelite people. By this he signified that you—who, as Moses himself testifies, always murmured against the Lord (Exod. 15), always provoked him to anger, and were always unbelieving toward his word—would know the words of the Law but would not at all see the brightness of that Law. Hence it is rightly said through Blessed Paul, your fellow-countryman, who was not left in your error but was mercifully chosen by the Lord: “To this very day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart” (2 Cor. 3), that is, over the heart of the Jews.

This faith, therefore, as was said above, almighty God made known from the beginning of the world through figures, declared through oracles, promised through what went before, and fulfilled through what followed: namely, that the Son of God was begotten from God the Father before all ages, and that the same God was made man from the Virgin Mother at the end of time. “For the Word was made flesh,” as the Evangelist says, “and dwelt among us” (John 1).

But if you still, O Jews, doubt his eternal generation; if doubt still remains in your minds; if you say that so many testimonies of the holy Fathers do not yet suffice for you: hear what blessed Job says, as though investigating that same Wisdom coeternal with God the Father: “Where is wisdom found, [Col. 0155D] and what is the place of understanding? Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly. The deep says, ‘It is not in me’; and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’ Refined gold is not given for it, nor is silver weighed in exchange for it” (Job 28).

Let blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0155D] In the place cited above, chap. 22.], whom God endowed with the gift of great wisdom and holiness, come forward and graciously expound for us verses of such depth:

> “It must first be noted,” he says, “that he proposed two things to himself and answered with two things. For to what he had said above, ‘But where is wisdom found, and what is the place of understanding?’ he replied in this verse: ‘The deep says, “It is not in me”; and the sea says, “It is not [Col. 0156A] with me.”’ But to what he had said, ‘Man does not know its price, nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly,’ he supplied the following verse, saying: ‘Refined gold shall not be given for it, nor silver weighed in exchange for it.’ Thus he answered both points, but by enlarging what he had raised, not by resolving it. For when he sought the place of wisdom, and then answered below, ‘The deep says, “It is not in me,”’ he indicated not where it was, but where it was not.  
>
> “Yet it is plain to all that this human wisdom can neither be held in a place nor bought with riches. But the holy man, full of mystical meanings, leads us on to understand other things: that we should seek not created Wisdom but creating Wisdom, which is Christ. For unless we search out in these words the hidden meanings of allegory, the things which follow are altogether [Col. 0156B] worthy of contempt if they are judged from the historical narrative alone. For shortly afterward he says:
>
> “‘Gold or glass shall not be equal to it.’ And since, as we know, glass is far cheaper than gold and unlike it, why, after naming gold—a precious metal, certainly—did he also say, for the immense praise of wisdom, that glass is not equal to it? Therefore the very difficulty of the letter compels us to attend carefully to the mystical sense of these words. What Wisdom, then, does the holy man contemplate, except that of which the apostle Paul says, ‘Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God’ (1 Cor. 1); and of which the Psalmist says, ‘You have made all things in wisdom’ (Ps. 103)? Man does not know the price of this Wisdom [Col. 0156C], because he finds nothing worthy to estimate it. Yet this price of wisdom is not said both to exist and to be unknown; rather, it is said to be unknown because it is absent—according to that manner of speaking by which one caught in straits, when he finds no remedy for help, commonly confesses that he does not know what to do.
>
> “‘To know no price for this Wisdom,’ therefore, is to find no merit of worthy work by which one may receive it. For we give a price in order that, in exchange for it, we may possess the thing we desire. But what did we give, that we might deserve to receive this Wisdom, which is Christ? For we have been redeemed by grace. Indeed, the only works we gave were those performed by living wickedly; if just recompense had been maintained, [Col. 0156D] not Christ but punishments would have been rendered to us. But man deserved one thing by justice and received another by grace. Paul testifies by what thorns of error he had been pressed before his mind received the seed of gratuitous truth: ‘I was formerly,’ he says, ‘a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent; but I obtained mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief’ (1 Tim. 1). Let him [Note: [Col. 0156D] Blessed Gregory: “testifies.”] also testify for what sort of persons Christ deigned to die: ‘While we were still sinners,’ he says, ‘at the appointed time Christ died for the ungodly’ (Rom. 5). Since, therefore, we were found ungodly when Wisdom came, what good work did we give by which we might deserve to receive that same Wisdom? [Col. 0157A] Man does not know the price of this Wisdom, because whoever is distinguished from brute [Note: [Col. 0157D] Manuscripts: “buried” (*obrutis*).] animals by rational understanding knows that he has not been saved by his own merits, and acknowledges that he gave no good work by which he might come to the end. For to give a price in order to receive wisdom is to attain to the knowledge of God through the recompense of one’s own action. He knew that this Wisdom, which is Christ, has no price, who said: ‘Who has first given to him, and shall be repaid?’ (Rom. 11). Hence it is again written: ‘By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, for it is God’s gift, not from works, lest anyone should boast’ (Eph. 2). Hence the same Apostle also speaks of himself, saying: ‘By the grace of God I am what I am’ (1 Cor. 15). From the breathing-in of that grace, indeed, [Col. 0157B] works of virtue are immediately produced in the heart, so that action may follow also from free choice, to which eternal recompense may answer after this life. He therefore at once added: ‘And his grace in me was not empty’ (ibid.).  
>
> “But there are some who rejoice that they are holy [Note: [Col. 0157D] Blessed Gregory: *salvos se*, “themselves saved.”] by their own strength and boast that they were redeemed by their preceding merits. Their assertion is certainly found contrary to themselves, because while they assert that they are innocent and redeemed, they thereby render void in themselves the very name of redemption. For everyone who is redeemed is undoubtedly freed from some captivity. From what, then, has such a person been redeemed, if he was not first captive under sin? It is plain, therefore, that whoever thinks these things is greatly foolish.” [Col. 0157C]

Therefore, O Jews, we do not know the price of this most perfect Wisdom, which is Christ, because we gave no good work by which we might come to faith; rather, we were saved by his grace alone. He did not descend to us because of our preceding merits, but redeemed us solely by his gratuitous goodness. “For heavenly grace,” as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0158D] In the place cited above.], “does not find man’s ruin in order that it may come; rather, after it has come, it acts.” God, coming to an unworthy mind, makes it worthy of himself by coming, and creates in it the merit which he rewards—he who found in it only that which he would punish.”

But let us hear what blessed Job further says concerning this Wisdom, which is Christ. “It is not found,” he says, [Col. 0157D] “in the land of those who live pleasantly.” What is designated here by the name “land,” except the human soul, of which the Psalmist says: “My soul is like waterless land before you” (Ps. 142)? Therefore this Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, cannot be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because whoever is still fed by the pleasures of this life is separated from understanding eternal Wisdom. Wisdom, which is God, cannot therefore be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because they are the more truly foolish insofar as, losing greater things, they delight in lesser things. Hence blessed Peter rebukes this same folly of the wicked, saying: “Regarding pleasures [Col. 0158A] as the delights of the day, defilements and stains” (2 Pet. 2).

It follows: “The deep says, ‘It is not in me.’” What does he call the deep here, except human hearts, which through their fall are fluid and through the darkness of duplicity are obscure? This deep confesses that this Wisdom is not in it, because the wicked mind, while desiring to be wise in a fleshly fashion, shows itself foolish in spiritual matters. For, as Paul testifies, “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3); the more anyone strives to appear wise outwardly, the more foolish he becomes inwardly. When a person hides malice in his heart while displaying flatteries with his mouth; when he obscures his thoughts by duplicity; when he avoids words of purity as though they were foolishness; [Col. 0158B] when he turns aside from the paths of simple innocence—the deep, as it were, refuses to possess the Wisdom of God the Father. And because minds devoted to this world are troubled by the cares and anxieties of the present life, and therefore cannot enjoy the tranquillity of that Wisdom, it is rightly added: “And the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’” For what is signified by the name of the sea except the bitter restlessness of worldly minds, which, while they attack one another in mutual hostilities, clash like opposing waves? The life of worldly people is rightly called a sea, because, agitated by the stormy motions of its actions, it is separated from the repose and stability of inward Wisdom. Thus it is fittingly said of that Wisdom, which is Christ: “The deep says, [Col. 0158C] ‘It is not in me’; and the sea says, ‘It is not with me.’” As though it were said more plainly: The disturbed minds of worldly people themselves proclaim that they are far separated from true Wisdom by the fact that they are not at rest.

But because this Wisdom of God, abiding with the Father before the ages, was to be incarnate at the end of the ages, so that, in redeeming the human race, it might send not holy angels and not righteous men, but might itself come in the manifestation of visible presence, it is rightly added:

“Shall refined gold be given for it?” What is designated by refined gold except holy angels? They are rightly called both gold and refined gold: gold, because they shine with the brightness of righteousness; refined gold, because they have never had any contagion of sin. [Col. 0158D] Righteous human beings, however, so long as they live mortally in this corruptible flesh, may indeed be gold, but cannot at all be refined gold: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind full of many thoughts” (Wis. 9). For though they shine in this life with great brightness of righteousness, they are nevertheless by no means wholly free from the filth of sins. Angels, therefore, are rightly called refined gold, because, remaining in the innocence in which they were created, they both shine with the brightness of righteousness and are stained by no filth of sin. But because no angel [Col. 0159A] was to be sent to redeem the human race in place of this eternal Wisdom, which is Christ—lest anyone should place hope in the angels themselves, whom we have learned frequently appeared in assistance of human beings—it was said: “Refined gold shall not be given for it.” As though it were plainly said: The Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, will manifest itself, in order that the human race may be redeemed from sin. No angel will be sent in its place, because creation must be freed through the Creator. Hence in the Gospel Jesus Christ himself, God and man, says: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8). Concerning this same Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, it is further fittingly added:

“Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.” Since divine utterances are often signified by silver, [Col. 0159B] the writers of those utterances may also be understood under the name of silver; their lives shone among crowds of men with the light of virtues. But because the law could point out sins, not remove them, none of the ancient Fathers—not even Moses the lawgiver—became the redeemer of the human race. Therefore silver is not weighed in exchange for this Wisdom, which is Christ, because, though they could become holy by God’s grace, in comparison with the only-begotten Son of God—through whom God the Father created all things from nothing and rescued the whole world from the power of the devil—they are judged to possess no merit. Had they not known themselves to be servants of this Wisdom, which is God, they could not have been holy at all. Because it was certain that, with the passage of time, the ailments of the declining age [Col. 0159C] would increase, it was arranged that the eternal Wisdom of God should itself come at the end of the ages to this great sufferer of extreme infirmity—that is, to the human race lying sick throughout the whole world. After first sending sinners, as it were, certain visitors, the Physician’s power came afterward all the greater as the patient’s disease had grown more severe. Therefore, because no one is sent in its place to save us, it is rightly said: “Nor shall silver be weighed in exchange for it.” As though he said more plainly: However greatly the life of righteous preachers may flourish in the light of holiness, it does not replace for us, by its own presence, the coming of heavenly Wisdom.

[Col. 0159D] Again he adds concerning this same Wisdom of God the Father: “It shall not be compared with the dyed colors of India.” What is understood by India, which produces a dark-skinned people, except this world, in which human life is made dark through sin? The dyed colors of India are the wise persons of this world, who, although ugly through unbelief and often through their conduct, are darkened before human eyes by a coating of assumed respectability. But Wisdom, coeternal with God the Father, which is Christ, is not compared with the dyed colors of India, because whoever truly understands it recognizes how far it differs from those persons whom the world has esteemed wise. The very words of its commandments differ greatly from the wise people of this world. For the teaching of this Wisdom, [Col. 0160A] which is Christ, is beautiful in its proclamation and manifest in pure truth. It does not outwardly pretend through deceit to be one thing while inwardly preserving another; nor does it seek to appear beautiful in its sayings through rhetorical brilliance, but through integrity of truth. Thus in its commandments God’s Wisdom is not compared with the dyed colors of India, because, having none of the painted ornaments of eloquence, it pleases like a garment without dye.

It follows: “Nor is it compared with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.” Sardonyx bears the likeness of red earth, whereas sapphire has an airy appearance. Thus human beings may be signified in sardonyx by red earth, while angels may be signified in sapphire by the heavenly appearance. [Col. 0160B] For since the sardonyx stone has the appearance of red earth, it not unreasonably signifies man; for Adam, the first created, is called “red earth” in the Latin language. What then is meant by the statement that this Wisdom is not compared with sardonyx or sapphire, except that he who is the power of God and the Wisdom of God—the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2)—surpasses all things by such greatness that neither the first men on earth, namely patriarchs and prophets, nor angels in heaven, may be compared with him? Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “Who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88).

But by the sardonyx stone the Fathers [Col. 0160C] of the Old Testament may be represented, and by sapphire the preachers of the New Testament. For those Fathers of the Old Testament, though they maintained a great life of righteousness, nevertheless served bodily propagation. Since it is clear that they performed certain earthly acts, they are not improperly signified by sardonyx, which, as we said above, bears the appearance of red earth. But by sapphire, which is of heavenly color, we fittingly understand the preachers of the New Testament, who, setting aside desires for bodily propagation, pursued heavenly things alone. Of them the prophet Isaiah says: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). As though he said plainly: We walk upon the earth, still entangled in marriages and expending the works of flesh on propagating offspring; [Col. 0160D] but these do not walk upon the earth; rather, they fly like clouds, because, desiring heavenly things, they touch none of earthly desires. Therefore let blessed Job say: God’s Wisdom is not compared with sardonyx or sapphire. As though he plainly indicated: No one among ancient Fathers or new is equal to him who is seen as man among men, because he possesses from deity that whereby, in humanity, he has no one like himself. Hence it is further added: “Gold or glass shall not be equal to it.”

We know that gold shines with a brilliance superior to all other metals. The nature of glass is such that what is seen from without shines through with pure transparency within. In another metal, whatever is contained inwardly is hidden; but in glass, whatever liquid it contains within is displayed outwardly as it is, and, so to speak, every liquid enclosed in a glass vessel lies open. [Col. 0161A] What else, then, do we understand in gold and glass except that heavenly country, that fellowship of blessed citizens, whose hearts both shine with brightness and are transparent to one another in purity? John beheld it in the Apocalypse, when he said: “The structure of its wall was of jasper stone; but the city itself was pure gold, like clear glass” (Rev. 21). Because all the saints will shine there with the brightness of highest blessedness, gold is mentioned in its structure. And because their brightness is mutually open to one another in their hearts, and when the face of each is observed the conscience too is penetrated, this gold itself is said to be like clear glass. [Col. 0161B] For there the bodily substance of the limbs does not hide the mind of one person from another’s eyes, but the spirit will lie open; the very harmony of the body will lie open to bodily eyes. Thus each person will then be visible to another as he cannot now be visible even to himself. But now, while we are in this life, because our hearts cannot be seen from one person into another, they are enclosed not in glass vessels but in earthen vessels. That city, therefore, which mutually reveals each person’s heart to all, is called gold like clear glass, so that it may be signified as bright in gold and transparent in glass.

But although all the saints there shine with such brightness and gleam through with such transparency, they cannot be equal to that Wisdom, from whose image they possess all that they are. Therefore, in praise of this eternal Wisdom, which is Christ, he rightly says: “Gold or glass shall not be equal to it.” [Col. 0161C] For all the saints attain those joys in order that they may be like God, as it is written: “When he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Yet it is written: “Lord, who is like you?” (Mic. 7). And again: “Who shall be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88). In what sense, then, are they like, and in what sense not like, except that they will be like this Wisdom in image, yet not like it in equality? For in beholding God’s eternity, they become eternal; and, while receiving the gift of his vision, they imitate through participation in blessedness what [Col. 0161D] they see. They are therefore like him because they are blessed; yet they are not like the Creator, because they are creatures. Thus they possess a certain likeness to God because they have no end; yet they do not possess equality with the uncircumscribed Son of God, because they are circumscribed. Therefore it is rightly said in praise of this eternal Wisdom: “Gold or glass shall not be equal to it,” because, however greatly the saints shine in brightness or transparency, it is one thing [Note: [Col. 0161] More aptly in St Gregory: “It is one thing for men to be wise in God, and another for the man to be the Wisdom of God.”] for human beings to be wise in God and another for the man—namely Christ—to be the Wisdom of God the Father. Blessed Job truly recognized this Wisdom, since he did not presume to compare any of the saints to the mediator [Col. 0162A] between God and men.

Hence it is added: “Lofty and eminent vessels of gold shall not be exchanged for it.” Elijah was indeed a lofty vessel of gold; Jeremiah was a lofty vessel of gold; the earlier Fathers were lofty and eminent vessels of gold. But this Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, appeared in the flesh in order to redeem us from perpetual damnation and draw us away from fleshly conduct. Whoever did not truly recognize it as the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, thought him one of the prophets; whereas the eyes of the elect held him by faith to be God when they saw a man. Hence he says to the holy disciples: “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” When they immediately replied, “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets,” they are [Col. 0162B] at once questioned concerning their own opinion: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter, answering in the voice of the whole Church, says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). Since, therefore, according to Paul’s declaration, we know Christ as the power of God and the Wisdom of God, Peter refused to exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this Wisdom, because he understood of it nothing other than what it was. John, as stated, was a great vessel of gold, and Elijah or Jeremiah was a great vessel of gold; but whoever believed the Lord himself to be any one of them exchanged a lofty and eminent vessel of gold for Wisdom. [Col. 0162C] The Church, however, does not exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this Wisdom, which is Christ, because it believes Christ the Son of God to be not one of the prophets but the one Lord of the prophets. Seeing the Wisdom of God the Father itself come to it, the Church would not fix itself upon those golden vessels, but strove to pass over to it in most certain faith. Therefore let blessed Job say of the eternal Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ: “Lofty and eminent vessels of gold shall not be exchanged for it,” because all the elect venerate the life of the saints for its sublimity, yet do not accept them in error. For those whom they know to be merely human they do not at all compare with God-man, that is, Christ.

Hence it is further added: [Col. 0162D] “They shall not be mentioned”—that is, the aforesaid lofty and eminent vessels of gold—“in comparison with it.” All the elect of the heavenly country are indeed holy and righteous, but by participation in that Wisdom which is Christ, not by comparison with it. What, indeed, are human beings in comparison with God? Wisdom is called light, and the servants of Wisdom are commonly called light; but Wisdom is illuminating light, whereas the servants of Wisdom are illuminated light. Hence it is written: “There was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world” (John 1). But to these it is rightly said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5). Wisdom is righteousness [Col. 0163A]; and the servants of this Wisdom, which is Christ, are also called righteousness. But Wisdom is righteousness that justifies; they are righteousness that has been justified. Of Wisdom itself, which is God, it is said: “That he may be just and the justifier” (Rom. 3); but those who are servants of this Wisdom say, “that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5). Thus illuminating light must be revered differently from illuminated light; justifying righteousness differently from justified righteousness.

Wisdom both is and is wise; it does not have one thing as its being and another as its wisdom. But servants of Wisdom can indeed be wise, yet do not have being identical with wisdom: for they can exist and not be wise. Yet the Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, has essence and has life, but what it has, [Col. 0163B] it itself is. Therefore it lives unchangeably, because it lives not through an accidental gift but essentially. It alone, then, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, truly is; compared with whose essence our own being is non-being. If we are joined to this Wisdom, which is Christ, we are, live, and are wise (Acts 17). If we are compared with it, we neither are wise nor live nor exist at all. Hence all the saints, the more they advance in the vision of God, the more they behold inwardly the divine nature, and the more subtly they recognize themselves to be nothing. Therefore, in order that we may be something in comparison with that supreme essence, let us recognize of ourselves that we are almost nothing. Thus it is well said that lofty and eminent vessels of gold “shall not be mentioned in comparison with it,” namely with Wisdom, [Col. 0163C] because although through participation in that Wisdom, which is Christ, they are something, they are not worth mentioning by comparison with it.

But because this Wisdom is secretly infused into human hearts, as is also said of the Holy Spirit, “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3), it is suitably added: “For Wisdom is drawn from hidden places” (Job 28).

Wisdom is drawn from hidden places because, being invisible, it is found only invisibly. It is rightly called “drawn,” because, as we draw breath so that the body may live, so the Spirit of Wisdom is drawn from within so that the soul may endure unto life. Hence Wisdom itself says through the Psalmist: “I opened my mouth [Col. 0163D] and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118). This Wisdom of God the Father, having assumed human flesh with a rational soul, appeared from hidden places; and in visible manifestation this world, which could not see its Creator, recognized as invisible God him whom it beheld as visible man. The Gentile world, formerly proud in its turning away, was converted from the darkness of its unbelief; faith grew through signs and wonders; and as faith spread, the eminence of the holy Church shone forth in the veneration of all. When open adversaries were lacking, it began to be tested by its own members. Consequently, some arose within this holy Church who said that the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, was a mere created man, but deified by grace; [Col. 0164A] and they attributed to him only as much holiness as they recognized in the other saints, his servants. Blessed Job, inspired by the spirit of prophecy, rebukes them by the determination of his saying:

“The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it.” What do we understand by Ethiopia except the present world, which by blackness of color signifies a sinful people through the ugliness of their merits? At times, however, by the name Ethiopia the Gentile world is especially signified, formerly black with the sins of unbelief. Hence the prophet David, seeing that the Lord would come to redeem Judaea, but that the Gentile world would first believe and Judaea follow afterward, said: “Ethiopia shall hasten her hands to God” (Ps. 67); that is, before Judaea believes, the Gentile world, black with sins, offers itself to almighty God to be saved. [Col. 0164B] Topaz is a precious stone; and because in Greek **πᾶν** (*pan*) means “all,” it is called *topazion*, as though *topatus*, because it shines in every color. But when the Gentile world, converted to God, believed, many from it were so enriched by the gift of the Holy Spirit that they shine, as it were, in many virtues just as in many colors. Yet lest anyone be exalted by virtues received, blessed Job rightly says: “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it.” As though it were said more plainly: No saint, however full of virtues, though gathered out of this blackness of the world, can be equal to the Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, of whom the angel Gabriel said to Mary, ever-virgin and his mother: “The holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke [Col. 0164C] 1). We indeed, although made holy by God’s grace, are not born holy, because the very condition of corruptible nature binds us so that each of us says with the Prophet: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50). But he alone was truly born holy, who, in order to overcome the very condition of corruptible nature, was not conceived through the union of carnal intercourse.

Again, O Jews, compelled by love, I return to speak with you, wishing to know whether, now that you have laid aside the death-dealing treachery of unbelief, you believe that Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is naturally one God; or whether, still darkened by the blindness of ancestral error [Col. 0164D], you doubt his divinity coeternal with God the Father. If you deny that he is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, you are deprived of eternal blessedness and happiness. Since, then, persevering still in your wickedness, you say that he is not the natural Son of God the Father but an adoptive son by grace, like the other saints, you also depart from God the Father. For according to the testimony of John the Evangelist: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father either” (1 John 2). Thus, by your impious conspiracy in denying that Christ is true God, you make yourselves strangers to God, who is truly one in essence and three in persons. O wicked and perverse nation! Why do you not understand that you dishonor God the Father when you deny that his natural Son—begotten from his own [Col. 0165A] essence before all ages—is God, and maintain that he is not Creator but creature, as other holy men are? Why do you not consider, O unhappy Jews, that you inflict great injury on God the Father when you believe that Jesus Christ, the Son whom he begot equal to himself, is not true God but a mere man?

You also say that the same Redeemer of the human race, our Lord Jesus Christ, was not conceived by the Holy Spirit but begotten from Joseph’s seed. The stench of your blasphemies, O unhappy—indeed, most unhappy—Jews, defiles not only the ears of those hearing them but even pollutes the air itself. These most wicked words of yours are full of falsehood and lies. This most lying speech disagrees with the holy prophets [Col. 0165B] and insults almighty God. Your false assertion is shown to be discordant with the sayings of the holy Fathers and altogether contrary to the divine dispensation. Blessed Job undoubtedly destroys this objection of yours, which is truly contrary to the law and prophets, in the aforesaid saying when he declares: “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it.” As though he said more plainly: No human being, however full of virtues, since he has been begotten from male seed, can be equal to Jesus Christ, who was conceived by the Holy Spirit, born sinless from a virgin womb, and lived in the world without sin. In your objection, therefore, he asserts that you have lied, when he says that the topaz of Ethiopia cannot [Col. 0165C] be equal to Christ. O unhappy people! You neither understand nor attend to the fact that it is one thing for people born from carnal intercourse to receive the grace of adoption, and another for the one Lord Jesus Christ, uniquely by the power of divinity, to have come forth as God from the very moment of conception; nor can the glory of the Only-begotten, possessed by nature, be equal to the glory of others received by grace.

For the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, is not—as you, O unhappy Jews, falsely say—one person in humanity and another in divinity; nor, conceived and born as a mere man, did he afterward receive divinity through merit. Rather, when the angel announced and the Holy Spirit came, immediately the Word was in the womb; immediately within the womb the Word became flesh; and, while the unchangeable essence coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit remained, he assumed human nature within the virgin’s womb.

[Col. 0165D] For this reason, O foolish and malicious Jews, we wish briefly to repeat the aforesaid words of blessed Job: that, abandoning the treachery of unbelief, we may make you certain concerning Christ’s divinity; or, if you still choose to persist with obstinate mind in your wickedness, that we may prove you to have lied throughout your dispute. This holy man therefore says, in the aforesaid statement, concerning Wisdom coeternal with God the Father, which is Christ: “Refined gold shall not be given for it.” By refined gold, as has been said, angels are signified. Let it therefore be said more plainly: The Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, will itself be manifested, in order that the human race may be redeemed from original sin. No angel [Col. 0166A] will be sent from heaven in its place, because creation must be freed through the Creator. It is therefore plainly shown, O Jews, enemies of righteousness, that because the human race is freed not through a creature, which is an angel, but through Christ, who is Creator, Christ is not a creature but Creator.

And to show that blessed Job regarded the ancient Fathers who interpreted the divine word—namely Moses, Joshua, David, Solomon, and the other teachers of the Old Testament—as inferior to Christ, he added: “Silver shall not be weighed in exchange for it.” For by silver, as has been said, the teachers of the old law are understood. Since the law could point out sins but could not heal them, none of the teachers [Col. 0166B] of the ancient law became redeemer of the human race. Attend here, O Jews, to the fact that Jesus Christ is not, as you say, a mere man, but is true man and true God, who could redeem the human race from the power of darkness. Blessed Job therefore shows quite plainly that your objection is false, when he says that no human being, however holy, can be equal to Jesus Christ, Redeemer of all.

And to show that the wisdom of this world’s philosophers lies far beneath this Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, he continued: “Nor shall it be compared with the dyed colors of India.” By India, as was said above—India which produces a dark people—this world is understood, in which human life is made dark through sin. But the wise people of this age, that is, pagan [Col. 0166C] philosophers, were like dyed colors, because, although they appeared outwardly clothed with the color of honorability, through unbelief and wicked conduct they were black and dark. For “the wisdom of this world is hostile to God” (Jas. 4). But the Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, is not compared with dyed colors, because whoever truly knows this eternal Wisdom recognizes how far it differs from the philosophers of this world. Therefore, with every ambiguity removed, acknowledge, O Jews, that true Wisdom, which is Christ, is above all human beings; for no person, however holy or however wise, can in any way be equal to him.

Again blessed Job, wisely perceiving that the eternal Wisdom, which is Christ, surpasses in holiness and power all the saints on earth [Col. 0166D] and the heavenly powers in heaven, adds, saying: “It shall not be compared with the most precious sardonyx stone or sapphire.” As though he said more plainly: This Wisdom of God the Father is not comparable to sardonyx or sapphire, because he who is the power of God and the wisdom of God—namely, the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2)—so surpasses all things in greatness that neither holy men on earth, namely patriarchs and prophets, nor angels in heaven can be compared with him. It is therefore evident, O unhappy Jews, that this Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, is not created, as you blasphemously say, but creative; neither earthly creation nor even heavenly creation can be made equal to it. And in order to show that, even in that heavenly city [Col. 0167A] Jerusalem, no one can attain equality with the Only-Begotten of God and of the Virgin, the holy man added: “Gold or glass shall not be equal to it.” As though he said more plainly: Although all the saints in that supreme and heavenly city shine with such brilliance and gleam with such transparency, they can by no means be made equal to that Wisdom, that is, Christ, from whose image they possess all that they are.

Take heed, therefore, O Jews, enemies of truth: Christ, in whom are all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God the Father (Col. 2), and to whom none of the saints can be made equal in power and greatness, is not temporal, as you say, but eternal. For he is the Wisdom coeternal with God the Father, through whom all things were made—a fact which you can neither wholly deny nor ought to deny. Blessed Job indeed recognized this Wisdom with subtle discernment, as a devout man full of mystical utterances, since he did not dare to compare any saint with that same Jesus Christ. He further says of him: “High and eminent vessels of gold shall not be exchanged for it.” As though he said: The holy Church does not exchange lofty and eminent vessels of gold for this Wisdom, which is Christ, because it unhesitatingly affirms that Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, is not one of the prophets but the Lord of the prophets. All the elect, as has been said, venerate the lives of the holy Fathers because of the sublimity of their virtues; yet they do not receive them in a way that leads to error. Why? Because, although they know them to be mere human beings and outstanding in virtues, they do not at all compare them with God made man—that is, Christ, the Son of God and [Col. 0167C] of the Virgin. Observe here, O Jews, that this Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, to whom the teachers of the Old Testament can by no means be made equal, is not temporal, as you falsely say, but eternal; not human, but divine, through whom all things were made from nothing.

Nor could any of those who, from the Gentiles, have been converted in the New Testament to faith in the holy Trinity be made equal to that same Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ. The holy man adds: “The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it.” As though he said more plainly: No saint, however full of virtues, gathered out of the blackness of Gentile life, can be equal to the Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ. [Col. 0167D] As though he clearly intimated: Those who come from the blackness of sin—that is, from Gentile life—to conversion cannot be equal to God made man, that is, Christ, however much they may appear to shine with many-hued virtues. Of them it is aptly added: “Nor shall the purest dyeings be compared with it.” The “purest dyeings” are those who are truly humble and truly holy, who know that they do not possess the beauty of virtues from themselves, but hold it through the gift of grace that comes upon them. For, as blessed Gregory says, they would not be dyed if they possessed holiness naturally. Yet they are purest dyeings because they humbly preserve within themselves the grace of virtues that has come upon them [Col. 0168A] and that they have received. Hence the Bridegroom’s voice says of the holy Church: “Who is this that comes up whitened?” (Song 8). Since the holy Church does not naturally possess heavenly life, but, when the Holy Spirit comes upon it, is adorned with the beauty of spiritual gifts, it is called not white but “whitened.”

It should be noted that above, when he said, “It shall not be compared with the dyed colours of India,” he did not call those colours pure. But here, in order to distinguish the dyeing of true virtues from that cosmetic colouring of the philosophers, he adds “purest dyeings.” For those are rightly called the purest dyeings who were formerly foul through evil deeds but, when the Holy Spirit comes upon them, are clothed in the brightness of grace, so that they appear far other than they had been. Thus our descent into water itself is called baptism, that is, dyeing. We are dyed, because we who had formerly been unbeautiful through the ugliness of vices, once faith is received, are made beautiful through the grace and adornment of virtues. Therefore, although the purest dyeings—the children of the Church coming from the Gentiles—are set alongside it, that is, are filled with spiritual grace and cleansed of sins by sacred baptism, yet because they do not possess these things at all from themselves, they cannot be made coequal with the eternal Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ.

You have heard, O Jews, from blessed Job’s teaching, that neither any angel in heaven, nor any patriarch before the Law, nor any prophet or teacher under the Law, nor anyone in the New Testament—however holy or [Col. 0168C] however full of virtues—could be purified to the Wisdom coeternal with God the Father, which is Christ [the Latin reads purificari, perhaps for “be made equal”]. Thus, by the most truthful testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, we prove sufficiently clearly that you lied in your objection when you say that Christ was not the true Son of God, but, like any other saint, was adopted by grace and enriched with virtues by God. It is plainly given to understand, O Jews, enemies of truth, that if Christ, as you say, were a mere man, he would not surpass by his own power either holy human beings on earth or angelic powers in heaven, as blessed Job says. But because he is not a mere man but the true Son of God, no human being on earth, however holy, nor angel in heaven can be made equal to him. [Col. 0168D] Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is not adoptive, but is naturally one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing. The testimonies of the Law affirm this same thing; the prophecies of the prophets bear witness to it; the truth of the holy Scriptures declares it; the holy teachers of the Old and New Testaments affirm it; and the holy Church preaches it. Christ, therefore, is the Wisdom of God the Father, through whom all things were made.

[Note: [Col. 0167] An alternative manuscript begins another sermon here; but the order of our text is more fitting.]

I urge you, O Jews, that we should hear together what blessed Job also says about this Wisdom, which is Christ. For he says in the form of a question: “Whence then shall wisdom come, and what is the place of understanding?” [Col. 0169A] “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things.” We must consider most carefully that the holy man asks whence wisdom shall come. As blessed Gregory says, it comes from him from whom it has its origin. But because it is born from the invisible and coeternal Father, its way is hidden. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). The place of its understanding is the human mind, which this Wisdom of God makes holy when it fills it. Therefore, because he from whom it proceeds is invisible, and because it is uncertain to us in whose mind it rests when understood, it is rightly said: “Whence then shall wisdom come, or what is the place of understanding?” But it is very remarkable that he immediately adds: “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things.” For if Wisdom, which is Christ, were hidden from the eyes of all living beings, surely none of the saints would have seen it.

But behold, I hear John agreeing with this statement, saying: “No one has ever seen God” (1 John 4). Yet when I look upon the Fathers of the Old Testament, I discover, on the testimony of sacred history itself, that many of them saw God. Jacob saw the Lord, for he says: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32). Moses saw the Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend” (Exod. 33). Job too saw the Lord, saying: “By the hearing of the ear I heard thee, but now my eye sees thee” (Job 42). Isaiah saw the Lord, saying: “In the year in which King Uzziah died, [Col. 0169C] I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6). Micaiah also saw the Lord, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him at his right hand and at his left” (3 Kings 22).

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that so many Fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while it is nevertheless said of this Wisdom, which is God, namely Christ, “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things,” and John says, “No one has ever seen God”? Is it not this, which is plainly given to understand: so long as we live here in mortality, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the very appearance of his nature? The soul, inspired by the grace of the Holy Spirit, sees God through certain [Col. 0169D] figures, but does not attain to the very power of his essence. Thus Jacob, who testifies that he saw God, saw him only in an angel. Thus Moses, who spoke with God face to face as a man speaks with his friend, says to him in the very words of his speech: “If I have found grace in thy sight, show me thyself plainly, that I may see thee” (Exod. 33). Certainly, if the one with whom he spoke was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” not “Show thyself.” But if the one with whom he spoke face to face [Col. 0170A] was God, why did he ask to see the one whom he saw? From this request it is inferred that he thirsted to behold, in the brightness of his uncircumscribed nature, the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images; so that the divine essence might be present to the eyes of his mind in such a way that, for the vision of eternity, no created temporal image should intervene.

Therefore the Fathers of the Old Testament saw the Lord, yet according to John’s saying, “No one has ever seen God”; and according to blessed Job’s statement, “Wisdom, which is God, is hidden from the eyes of all living things.” For those abiding in this mortal flesh could see him in the Old Testament through certain circumscribed images, and in the New through the humanity he assumed; but they could not see him through [Col. 0170B] the uncircumscribed light of eternity. But if, while still living in this corruptible flesh, some persons who nevertheless grow in immeasurable strength can see the eternal brightness of God by a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with blessed Job’s statement, “It is hidden from the eyes of all living things.” For whoever sees Wisdom, which is God, dies utterly to this life, so as no longer to be held by its love. No one sees it who still lives carnally, because no one can embrace God and the world at once. For whoever sees God dies in that very respect in which, either by the intention of the heart or by [Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscripts read, less correctly, “by affection.”] the effect of action, he separates himself with his whole mind from the pleasures of this life. Hence it is said also to the same Moses: “For no man shall see me [Col. 0170C] and live” (ibid.). As though it were said plainly: No one ever sees God [Note: [Col. 0169D] St Gregory: “spiritually.”] in a special manner and yet lives carnally in the world.

Hence too the Apostle Paul, who, as he himself testifies, had so far known the invisible things of God only in part, declared that he was wholly dead to this world: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). As we said at considerable length [Note: [Col. 0169D] Gregory the Great very properly referred himself to what he had said in *Morals*, book 5, chapter 3, on these words of Paul; but since our Martin had nowhere previously explained them, he did not very properly transplant the thought of the most blessed pontiff here so closely.] above, it was not enough for him to say, “I have been crucified to the world,” unless he also first said, “The world has been crucified to me,” so that he might testify not only that he was dead to the world, but that the world too was dead to him, in order that neither he might seek the world nor the world now seek him. For if perhaps two people are in one place, one living and the other [Col. 0170D] dead, although the dead person does not see the living one, the living person nevertheless sees the dead one. But the preacher of God, to show that through the abasement by which he had cast himself down in humility he had become such that neither he saw the world nor the world saw him, not only said that he was crucified to the world—so that, when he sought the world’s glory, he did not see it, as one dead—but also asserted that the world had been crucified to him. He had so humbled himself that the world itself was, as it were, dead to him and could no longer see one who had become somewhat lowly and despised.

[Col. 0171A] It should indeed be known that there were some who said that God, even in that realm of blessedness, is beheld in his brightness but by no means seen in his nature. Such persons were deceived by an insufficient subtlety of inquiry. For in that simple and unchangeable essence, brightness is not one thing and nature another; rather, his very nature is his brightness, and his brightness is his nature. Since this Wisdom of God the Father, which is Christ, will show himself in the future to those who love him, he promises in himself: “He who loves me shall be loved by my Father; and I will love him and will manifest myself to him” (John 14). As though he said plainly: You who now behold me in your own nature still have to see me in my own nature in the life to come. Hence he says again: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they [Col. 0171B] shall see God” (Matt. 5). Paul likewise says: “Now we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13).

But because it is said of God through the foremost preacher of the Church, “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1), there are some who suppose that not even angels see God. Yet we know that Truth himself said: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 18). Does Truth, then, declare one thing and the preacher of truth another? No: when each statement is compared, it is recognized that they are in no disagreement. Angels both see God and desire to see him; they behold him and thirst to behold him. For if, as blessed Gregory says, angels desire to see him without enjoying the fulfilment of their desire, desire without fruition entails anxiety, and anxiety entails punishment. But blessed angels are far removed from every punishment of anxiety, since punishment and blessedness can never coexist. Again, when we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God because the Psalmist says, “I shall be satisfied when thy glory is manifested” (Ps. 16), we must consider that satiety is normally followed by distaste. Therefore, in order that both statements may rightly agree, let Truth say that they always see, and let the eminent preacher, namely the Apostle Peter, say that they always desire to see. So that no anxiety may exist in desire, those who desire are satisfied; and so that no distaste may exist in satisfaction, [Col. 0171D] those who are satisfied desire. Thus they desire without labour, because satisfaction accompanies their desire; and they are satisfied without distaste, because that satisfaction itself is ever kindled from desire.

Such too shall we be when we come to the fountain of life itself. Both thirst and satisfaction will be delightfully impressed upon us together. But necessity will be far from thirst, and distaste far from satisfaction; for we shall be satisfied while thirsting, and thirst while satisfied. Therefore we shall see God, and he himself will be the reward of our labour, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice when his light is approached. But when we say that his light is approached, Paul’s saying stands in the mind’s way: “Who inhabits inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen, nor indeed can see” (1 Tim. 6). Yet again I hear the Psalmist say: [Col. 0172A] “Approach God, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). How then are we enlightened by approaching, if we do not see the very light by which we can be enlightened? But if, by approaching him, we see the light by which we are enlightened, how is it said to be inaccessible?

In this matter we must consider that he called it inaccessible, but inaccessible to a human being who thinks in a human way. Sacred Scripture commonly denotes all followers of the flesh by the name “human beings.” Hence the same Apostle says to certain people in discord: “For whereas there is among you jealousy and contention, are you not carnal, and do you not walk according to man?” (1 Cor. 3). A little later he adds: “Are you not human beings?” (ibid.). Likewise elsewhere he brought forward the testimony: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, the things which [Col. 0172B] God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). And having said that this was hidden from human beings, he immediately added: “But God has revealed it to us through his Spirit” (ibid.), distinguishing himself by his calling from human beings, since, caught up above humanity, he now thought divine thoughts. In the same way here, after calling God’s light inaccessible, he added, to show for whom it was so: “Whom no human being has seen, nor indeed can see” (1 Tim. 6).

In his customary fashion, by calling them “human beings” he means all who think human thoughts, because those who think divine thoughts are above humanity. Therefore, as blessed Gregory says, we shall see God if we deserve through heavenly conduct to be above human beings. Yet we shall not see him as he sees himself. For [Col. 0172C] the Creator sees himself in a manner far different from that in which the creature sees its Creator. With respect to God’s immensity, a certain limit is fixed upon our contemplation, because we are bounded by the very weight of being creatures. Thus we do not behold God as he beholds himself, just as we do not rest in God as he rests in himself. Our vision or rest will be in some way like his vision or rest, but it will not be equal to it. Lest we shine for ourselves, the wing of contemplation will lift us up, and we shall be raised from ourselves to behold him. Carried away by the attention of the heart and the sweetness of contemplation, we shall in some manner go out from ourselves into him in eternal blessedness. Even this going of ours is less than resting; yet to go thus into God is to rest perfectly. Thus it is perfect rest because God is beheld; nevertheless our rest is not to be equated with his rest, because God’s rest does not pass from himself into another in order to rest. There is therefore a rest, so to speak, both like and unlike: our rest imitates what God’s rest is. For in order that we may be blessed and eternal, we imitate the eternal one, namely the eternal God, who is true eternity; and for us, eternity is a great imitation of eternity. Nor are we deprived of the one whom we can imitate, because in seeing we participate, and in participating we imitate.

This vision is now begun in faith, but will then be perfected in sight, when we shall drink the Wisdom coeternal with God the Father, which is Christ [Col. 0173A]—whom we now drink from the mouths of preachers, as from flowing streams—at his very fountain, that is, in the Father, from whom he is always born. Hence blessed Isidore, our patron, says in the first book of the *Sentences*: “The perfect birth of the Son of God neither began to be nor ceased.” Therefore the Son is always born from God the Father, and yet his birth is eternal and perfect. This Wisdom of God the Father speaks thus through Solomon: “God was begetting me before all hills” (Prov. 8).

Meanwhile I urge you, for your salvation, O Jews, not to consign the words of blessed Job expounded to you thus far to careless forgetfulness, but diligently commit them to memory. Giving faith to his words, set aside every doubt and believe Christ, whom he testifies [Col. 0173B] to be the natural Wisdom of God the Father, to be true God. For blessed Job himself testifies above, though a Gentile, that neither a human being on earth nor an angel in heaven can be made equal to Christ, who is truly the wisdom and power of God the Father. Therefore cease, O wicked and perverse nation, from calling Christ a mere man or a creature, when you have learned from so many testimonies of the Law and the Prophets that he is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Without doubt, if he were a creature, he would not surpass holy people on earth or angelic dignities in heaven. But because he is not a creature, as you blasphemously say, but the true Creator of all things, he surpasses by his own power and authority not only holy human beings but even the principalities and powers [Col. 0173C] of the heavenly orders. Thus blessed Job plainly convicts you, O unhappy Jews, in your assertion, when he says that no creature can be made equal to Jesus Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin. Consider, therefore, O Jews, enemies of truth, that, as has often been said, if he were a creature, he would not surpass by his own power all rational creatures, both heavenly and earthly. We know that blessed John the Baptist said of him: “He who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3). What remains, then, except that, casting away the error of unbelief, you should believe the Son of God and of the Virgin to be the divine Wisdom through whom God the Father created all things from nothing?

[Col. 0173D] But so that you may believe more certainly and hold more firmly that God the Father created all things from nothing through that Wisdom, which is Christ, I urge you to listen diligently to what David, most glorious among the prophets, says to God the Father in the Psalm: “How magnified are thy works, O Lord! Thou hast made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103). Therefore, setting aside every doubt, O foolish and malicious Jews, you ought to give faith to the words of this holy prophet. At the Lord’s command, he was anointed with oil; he played with lions as with lambs, and did the like with bears. He also killed the giant and removed reproach from Israel (1 Kings 17); and, moreover, he raised up with all his strength the horn of your people, O Jews. He crushed your enemies on every side and uprooted your adversaries. With all his heart [Col. 0174A] he praised the Lord; he set singers before the altar and gladly supplied sweet melodies for their sounds. In celebrations he gave great splendour and adorned the seasons until the end of his life; and he established that they should praise the holy name of the Lord and that posterity should magnify his holiness.

Hear gladly, then, the words of this prophet of such holiness and authority, so that, putting away all unbelief and embracing faith in Christ, you may be able to attain fellowship with the children of the Church. The greater the benefits you received from almighty God through this holy prophet and king, the more devoutly you ought to receive his most true testimonies concerning the Wisdom coeternal with God the Father, which is Christ. Hear him patiently, therefore, so that, pierced by his testimony, you may most certainly believe Christ to be true God. Speak, holy David; speak to God the Father those things which, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, you learned about his coeternal Wisdom, which is Christ. “How magnified,” he says, “are thy works, O Lord! Thou hast made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with thy possession” (Ps. 103). As though he said more plainly: O almighty God the Father, behold, thou hast made all things in thy Wisdom, that is, in Christ; and because they are many, the earth is filled with thy possession, namely thy creation. For through his Wisdom, that is, through Christ, as has been said, God the Father created whatever exists in heaven, on earth, and in the sea.

But what is said here is better understood mystically of the new creation which Christ stripped off from the old [Col. 0174C] man, because he filled the world, that is, the Church: “A grain of wheat falling into the earth bore much fruit” (John 12). For formerly the Son of God and of the Virgin was alone until he should pass over. Hence he says of himself in the Psalm: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140). But when he passed from this world through his passion, he found the lost drachma and restored the wandering sheep to the flock. Therefore God the Father made all these things in his Wisdom, that is, in Christ: he filled the earth with his possession, that is, he enlarged the holy Church with faithful peoples. Believe firmly, therefore, O Jews, that Christ is the true Wisdom of God the Father, through whom all things were made. Believe that he has a natural substance of flesh from the Virgin Mother [Col. 0174D] and a natural divinity from God the Father. Believe without doubt that he is true man and true God, to whom God the Father has given all judgment (John 5). Worship him as one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and fear without ceasing his coming as the dreadful Judge.

Hear, O foolish and malicious Jews, what I say; hear what I speak; listen to what I urge. If, by faithful belief in this present life, you do not have him propitious, you will by no means escape him angry in the age to come. If you refuse to confess before human beings that he is true God, beyond doubt you will perish with the unbelievers at his coming. Know for certain that if you choose to remain in your unbelief, [Col. 0175A] you will in no way escape his judicial sentence. Take heed, O wretched and pitiable Jews, lest through your unbelief you incur eternal condemnation. It has now been sufficiently shown to you by the testimonies of the sacred Law and the most true authorities of the prophets that Christ is not a creature but the Creator; not a mere man but true God and true man, who with God the Father governs all things, contains all things, and encompasses all things. Recognize, therefore, that you are convicted in your most false objections, and do not any longer be willing to doubt Christ’s divinity, by which he is equal to God the Father.

§ VII.—

By Isaiah’s testimony he has convicted the Jews concerning the Incarnation of the Son of God and Christ’s dwelling among them in [Col. 0175B] our corruptible nature, though under no compulsion of necessity. David’s testimony is introduced; and, so that Christian faith may be strengthened by the testimony not merely of two or three but of many witnesses, Isaiah is adduced not only once but repeatedly; some saw him with the eyes of the heart, others with bodily eyes. Baruch’s assertion is introduced for the same purpose: that they may believe that he assumed human flesh and dwelt among human beings.

Meanwhile, I should like to know whether, having now laid aside unbelief, you believe that Christ is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, or whether, still persisting in your wickedness, you entertain some doubt concerning him. This is both your reply and your objection. For you say that it appears incredible to you that the Son, coeternal with God the Father, assumed human nature, [Col. 0175C] grew as a human being through intervals of time and stages of age, and dwelt among human beings. To this we respond in turn: if you still do not believe that he assumed from the Virgin Mother, for the redemption of humankind, a true, natural, and perfect human being; if it seems incredible to you that the Word of God the Father, clothed in flesh, dwelt among human beings; if you say that a human being cannot be joined to the Son coeternal with God the Father; if you deny that Christ was true God and true man—then hear the testimonies of the Law, hear the proclamations of the prophets, hear the sayings of those who prophesy, hear the oracles of the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore hear what the Son of God himself—who was to be born of the Virgin Mother and to show humankind his bodily presence—says through the prophet Isaiah: “Therefore my people shall know my name in that day, because I myself who was speaking, behold, am present” (Isa. 52).

As though the Son of God said more plainly: Because you, O Jews, by living wickedly have transgressed my commands and violated my covenant, my name is therefore blasphemed through you among the Gentiles and in your synagogues. Because you have provoked me to anger, therefore my people shall know my name in that day—namely, the day of the Incarnation, the day of new grace, the day of the New Testament. My faithful Christian people shall know my name, that is, Christ, so that Christians are called after me, Christ. And what else shall they know? Namely this: that I myself, who formerly spoke through the prophets, behold, am present through myself.

What do you say to this, O foolish Jews? What do you answer to this? Without doubt you are defeated when you say that Christ did not assume a human body and deny that he dwelt among human beings. Through the prophet he openly says that he is present to his people; yet you say that he did not assume human flesh or appear to human beings in it. Thus he powerfully convicts you in your assertion when he plainly says, “Behold, I am present.” But you, O unhappy—indeed, O utterly senseless—Jews, who are you to contradict the mouth of the Lord? From the beginning of the world, through the oracles of the prophets, he foretold that he would be born of an incorrupt Virgin and redeem humankind; and, for the instruction of his Church, as he had foretold, he manifested himself to human beings in that same flesh which he had assumed without sin from the Virgin. [Col. 0176B] Know with certainty, therefore, O unhappy Jews, that unless in this present life you depart from this folly of blasphemy and cruelty, you will without doubt perish eternally.

Accordingly, you plainly recognize, O wretched men, and cannot at all deny, that when the Son of God says that he is present, he showed humankind his own presence—not only divine, but also human, which he assumed from the sinless Virgin. And so that the catholic faith may be strengthened in every respect and your false assertion utterly refuted, let us hear together what the prophet Isaiah further says of him: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and proclaiming peace, saying to Zion, ‘Your God shall reign’” [Col. 0176C] (ibid.).

As though he said more plainly: How beautiful—that is, how free from the dust of sin—are the feet of Christ upon the mountains, that is, upon the apostles and upon all the saints eminent in virtues: Christ, I say, announcing and proclaiming to the faithful people, namely the Christian people, eternal peace with God and his angels, to those near and those far off. “For he is our peace,” as the Apostle says, “who made both one” (Eph. 2), namely Christ. It continues: “announcing good,” that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit and the holy Gospel; “proclaiming salvation,” namely the redemption of souls and eternal blessedness; “saying, O Zion,” that is, holy Church, “your God shall reign,” once the devil has been conquered; and sin shall not reign, but shall die.

By the testimony of the prophet Isaiah it has been shown plainly enough to you, O Jews [Col. 0176D], that Jesus Christ, God and man, lived among human beings (Baruch 3), though he “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Yet you, as though still doubting about this matter, ask us, saying: “Why did he whom God the Father, before all ages, begot from himself as a Son equal to himself, as you say, choose to descend from the bosom of that same Father and, as you maintain, assume a human body from an incorrupt Virgin, and to live among human beings as a man? What necessity lay upon him, that he should put on the form of a servant?”

In reply we say that no necessity falls upon God, who by his will alone does whatever he wishes (Ps. 113). For his will is omnipotence. Therefore, solely by his freely bestowed goodness, he descended from the bosom of God the Father and truly received from the undefiled Virgin, without male intercourse and without sin, a human body subject to mortality [Col. 0177A], in order fittingly and mercifully to redeem the human race through the cross. Through himself and his apostles he preached sufficiently to it, and showed the most straight path—that is, himself—by which it might ascend to heaven.

Thus the Son of God, born of a woman, lived among human beings (Baruch 3), not by necessity but mercifully for human salvation. But if you still doubt, O Jews, concerning his Incarnation, let King David and prophet, from whose seed Christ himself proceeded according to the flesh, come forward and testify how he entered this world. For he, rejoicing and exulting exceedingly [Col. 0177B], and speaking of the future as though it had already passed, says thus in the Psalm to that same Son of God and of the Virgin: “They saw your goings, O God, the goings of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary” (Ps. 67).

As though he said more plainly: “They saw your goings, O God,” namely those by which you came from the bosom of God the Father into the womb of the most holy Virgin. This grace was undoubtedly hidden in the Old Testament, but now is manifest in the New, when the Son of God and of the Virgin is proclaimed among the nations. Tell us, holy David, faithful and true witness: whose goings into this world did human beings see? “The goings,” he says, “of my God,” in creation, namely of the Word through whom God the Father created all things from nothing; “of my King,” in governance, through whom kings reign; “who is God in the sanctuary,” that is, in a human body [Col. 0177C] taken from the Virgin without male seed.

Thus the prophet David plainly testifies in the aforesaid verse that the Son of God came down from heaven into this world, assumed a human body, and was seen by human beings. For he could not at all have been seen in his divine essence unless he had possessed a human body. Since, therefore, O Jews, you cannot possibly contradict prophets of such authority, you must acknowledge yourselves defeated in your assertion.

But if you say that the aforementioned testimonies do not suffice to expel from your hearts the doubt that the Son of God assumed flesh and lived among human beings (Baruch 3), let us bring forward the prophet Isaiah, so that the Christian faith may be strengthened by the testimony not only of two or three but of many witnesses [Col. 0177D], and that we may show you defeated in every respect. Speak, Isaiah, of Christ: how did he appear clothed in flesh among human beings, so that your fellow-countrymen the Jews, who deny the Incarnation of this same Son of God and of the Virgin, may be convicted and pierced by your most truthful testimony; may they cast aside the deadly obstinacy of their unbelief, believe that he is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and faithfully worship him.

“The Lord,” he says, “prepared his holy arm in the sight of all nations; and all the ends of the earth saw the salvation of God” (Isa. 52).

As though he said more plainly: The Lord, namely God the Father, prepared his holy arm—that is, caused his Son to be incarnate [Col. 0178A]—and caused him to be proclaimed everywhere by apostolic preaching before the eyes, namely the hearts, of all nations. And all the ends of the earth—that is, every quarter of the world—saw with the eyes of the heart the salvation of our God, namely the Son of God and of the Virgin.

It should be noted that some saw Christ at his coming with bodily eyes, while others saw him with the eyes of the heart. The holy apostles and evangelists and the rest who were present with him saw him with bodily eyes. But we, who are descended from the stock of the nations after his ascension, embrace him with the arms of true faith and love, and unceasingly contemplate with spiritual eyes the one true God together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Hence, in the Gospel, the Lord said to the apostle Thomas, once his doubt had been removed and he had believed [Col. 0178B]: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen me and have believed” (John 20).

But if, O Jews, impeded by deadly obstinacy, you still do not give credence to the foregoing statements, hear how clearly Isaiah the prophet also shows in what follows that the Son of God, for the redemption of the world, assumed flesh without sin from a virgin womb, suffered and died in it, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of that same Father.

It follows: “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be exceedingly high.” Therefore, lest you doubt who said above, “I who spoke, behold I am present,” and that this same one is the arm of the Lord, he added these things about him more plainly. It is as though God the Father openly said of the same Jesus Christ [Col. 0178C], his Son, whom he determined to incarnate and whom he willed to live among human beings for human salvation (Baruch 3): “Behold my servant, obedient to me according to his humanity unto death, in whom truly are my Word and my wisdom: he shall understand my will in all things; he shall be exalted through the preaching of the apostles unto heaven; and he shall be lifted up, because ‘the Word became flesh’ (John 1), above all heavens; and he shall be exceedingly high, at my right hand.”

It follows: “As many were astonished at him, so shall his appearance be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men.” As though he said more plainly: As many were astonished at him, admiring his miracles before the Passion, so his appearance among men shall be without glory [Col. 0178D], namely in the Passion, because for the salvation of humankind he was by his own voluntary will spat upon, scourged, and crucified; and his form—that is, his appearance—was without honor among the children of men.

Indeed, as the Psalmist says: “He was beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44); but in the Passion he was seen to have neither form nor comeliness (Isa. 53). Thus it is made sufficiently plain, O senseless Jews, that the Son of God mercifully assumed our humanity, in which nevertheless he chose to live among human beings without fault. Set doubt aside and know that, unless the Son of God had assumed a human body from the Virgin, no human being could have endured his appearance. And unless he were true God, he could in no way have lived without sin among sinners.

Therefore that Son of God [Col. 0179A], who formerly foretold through the prophets that he would come, when the fullness of time came said through himself: “Behold, I am present.” Thus, by a clear argument, the Son of God convicts you Jews in your opposition: he who once promised through the prophets that he would come, in the time of grace presented himself before human eyes, clothed in flesh from the substance of his Virgin mother, as he had promised.

And so that you may certainly know and no longer doubt at all that he appeared as a man not only to Jews but also to gentiles, hear what Isaiah the prophet again adds concerning him (chapter 52): “Those to whom nothing had been told of him saw; and those who had not heard considered.”

In this passage, O Jews, enemies of righteousness, your hardness and unbelief are rebuked [Col. 0179B], for you saw this same Son of God and of the Virgin living among you and working innumerable miracles, yet refused to believe in him. The simplicity of the gentiles, by contrast with your unbelief, is praised: they had heard almost nothing concerning him through the prophets, yet, upon hearing the voice of the Gospels, faithfully believed in him.

It is as though Isaiah said more plainly: The nations to whom nothing concerning him had been related through the prophets saw him with the heart; and those who did not hear him preaching in the flesh contemplated him by faith. Thus the Son of God was born of God the Father before all ages and, in time, of his Virgin mother without carnal union; and, clothed in human flesh, he lived among human beings (Baruch 3). You ought not, therefore, O Jews, to contradict this truth so clear, to which you see so many and such fitting witnesses agree. For it is foolish not to grant belief to the sayings of the Law and the prophets, and, by resisting the Truth, which is Christ, to consign yourselves to eternal flames.

But if you still deny that the Son of God appeared clothed in flesh among human beings, let the prophet Isaiah come forward again, in order to overcome your false opposition and strengthen the catholic faith in every respect; let him testify concerning Christ’s Incarnation and how he lived among human beings (ibid.).

“For Zion,” he says, “I shall not be silent; and for Jerusalem I shall not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like splendor, and her savior is kindled like a lamp” [Col. 0179D] (Isa. 62).

As though he said more plainly: For Zion—that is, for the kings and princes of the Jews—even if they forbid me to speak, I shall not cease from prayers until the Son of God comes. Hence the saying: “Would that you would tear open the heavens and come down” (Isa. 64).
