And for Jerusalem, namely for the priests and scribes, even if they threaten death, I shall not rest from sighing and prayer until her righteous one—namely Christ—goes forth from the womb of the Virgin. From him is all righteousness; indeed, he is the splendor of God the Father and the Sun of righteousness. And Jesus, her Savior—namely the Savior of the Church—shall be kindled as a lamp in the hearts of believers.

[Note: [Col. 0179D] “Lamp,” says Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 20, chapter 10, is so called because it appears to show the motion of something licking. But our Martin, ever devoted [Col. 0180D] to the *Gloss*, expressed the origin of the word more correctly, since it is established that the word is Greek.]

*Lampas* is Greek; *flamma* (“flame”) is Latin [Col. 0180A]. Hence it is said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). Filled with this fire, the apostles spoke in various languages (Acts 2).

It follows: “And the nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your glorious one.” As though he said plainly: The nations shall see, by faith also and in mind, your righteous one—namely Christ, O primitive Church—and all believing kings your glorious one, that same Son of God and of the Virgin. “And a new name shall be called for you, which the mouth of the Lord named.” It is as though he said: When the Son of God is seen on earth clothed in flesh, then a new name shall be called for you, O Church: namely, your children shall be called Christians, a name which the mouth of the Lord named. In the Old Testament you were called the Synagogue; but at the coming of Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, you shall be called the Church [Col. 0180B].

Convicted by so many utterly true testimonies, O Jews, and overcome by so many arguments, you should now, laying aside all doubt, receive the right faith which is in Christ Jesus and believe most certainly that he is true God, true man, and that he lived among human beings (Baruch 3). But if, persevering in your wickedness, you still say that you have not been defeated in your opposition, let Baruch, secretary of the prophet Jeremiah, come forward and convict you by his faithful testimony that you have uttered falsehood.

“This is our God,” he says, “and no other shall be reckoned in comparison with him” (ibid.). Truly Jesus Christ, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God, besides whom no other shall be reckoned. Hence he himself says in the Gospel [Col. 0180C]: “I and the Father are one” (John 10).

It follows: “He discovered all knowledge and the way of prudence and instruction, and gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. After these things he was seen on earth and lived among human beings.” What could you wish to hear more openly, more clearly, or more brilliantly, O Jews, concerning Christ’s Incarnation and his life among human beings? It is clearer than light that you have been defeated in your assertion. The foregoing authority says that God, after these things—that is, after the carnal ordinances of the old Law, namely in the time of grace—was seen on earth and lived among human beings. But you, full of deceit and fraud, deny that he assumed human flesh and lived among human beings [Col. 0180D]. O unhappy people, who are you to contradict divine goodness and dispensation? You are deprived of the light of truth, since you refuse, for your salvation, to receive the testimonies of the Law, the oracles of the prophets, and the proclamations of the evangelists that bear witness to Christ.

§ VIII.—

Baruch [Note: Rather, Habakkuk.] shows by his assertions that God would assume human nature for the redemption of the human race, and in what way he would be known in the midst of two living creatures; and from his sayings he demonstrates that the person who has been unbelieving toward the divine dispensation does not possess a right intention. Since faith in Christ is eternal life, Hosea truly declares Christ to be the Son [Col. 0181A] of Man, who became for us the latter and early rain, and whose coming was prepared like dawn.

Since [Note: Another manuscript: “If.”] therefore you still doubt the Incarnation of the Son of God, let us bring the prophet Habakkuk into the midst, so that we may prove that you are defeated in all things—indeed, that throughout your dispute you have spoken falsely. Speak, prophet Habakkuk; speak concerning Christ’s Incarnation what has been revealed to you through the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

“Lord,” he says, “I heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. 3). As though he said: Lord, I heard this report of you, namely that you, true God, would assume human nature for the redemption of the world; and I was afraid because such a work is exceedingly wonderful. “Lord, make your work live in the midst of the years” [Col. 0181B].

As though he said more plainly: Lord, in the midst of the years—that is, in the fullness of time—bring to life that aforementioned wonderful work of yours, namely that you will redeem the world through an assumed man. “You shall make it known in the midst of the years.” As though he said: When the time of fulfillment comes, you shall show to be true what you promised concerning Christ’s Incarnation. It is as though the prophet more earnestly beseeched God the Father, saying: I pray, Lord, fulfill what you promised; namely, when the time is ended, give us the Christ whom you promised. Let not your work perish fruitlessly, but bring it to life—that is, fulfill it—in its own time.

This may also be understood concerning Christ’s resurrection: that he who died for us may rise from the dead. Let us hear together, O Jews, what this holy prophet, instructed by the Holy Spirit, says to Christ who would come for the redemption of the world [Col. 0181C].

“In the midst,” he says, “of two living creatures you shall be known.” As though he said more plainly: Lord, I heard your word in the Scriptures with the inner ear, and contemplated your works, so that from created things I might understand that you are the Creator of all; and through these I was astonished, lost the faculty of ordinary human understanding, was transformed into holy madness, or was troubled by wonder, and immediately burst forth into your praises, saying: “In the midst of two living creatures you shall be known.”

[Note: [Col. 0181D] These words, so closely rendered, are found in no version, so far as we can tell, except that used by the Mozarabic Breviary [Col. 0182D] at Lauds for the third Sunday of Advent, and retained by the Roman Church in the prophetic Tract at the Mass of Good Friday.]

“When the years draw near, you shall be made known; when the time comes, you shall be revealed”: namely, in the midst of two cherubim, who look toward one another and have the oracle between them; or of two seraphim, one of whom cries out to the other the mystery of the Trinity, one of whom was sent and cleansed the prophet’s lips; or between the two Testaments; or in the midst of Moses and Elijah; or between the two thieves hanging on either side; or between the two peoples, namely Jews and gentiles, surrounding him on either side [Col. 0181D].

Therefore, O Jews, you cannot possibly deny that the Son of God descended from the bosom of the Father, assumed flesh without sin from an incorrupt Virgin, and lived among human beings (Baruch 3), since this holy prophet plainly foretold that he would come and be known by human beings in the midst of two living creatures. But if you still say these things are not enough for you, O Jews [Col. 0182A], I urge you to listen more attentively to what this same prophet says concerning Christ’s coming.

“I will stand upon my watch and plant my step upon the fortification; and I will see what shall be said to me, and what I shall answer to the one who rebukes me” (Hab. 2). As though he said more plainly: “I will stand upon my watch,” that is, I will guard my heart with all diligence; “and plant my step,” namely the steadfastness of my mind, “upon the fortification,” that is, upon Christ; and I will contemplate, in order to see what is said to me. Thus I shall see what God the Father answers me concerning the Incarnation of his Son, and what I in turn ought to answer him who rebukes me, namely God the Father himself.

It follows: “And the Lord answered me and said: Write the vision and explain it upon tablets, so that whoever reads it may run through it.” As though he said: Write the vision—that is, the revelation—and explain [Col. 0182B] it upon tablets, that is, upon the spaciousness of faithful hearts, so that it may not be obscured by any perplexing turns of enigmas, and that whoever reads may run through it with understanding and without hindrance. Why? Because “the vision is still far off; and it shall appear at the end and shall not lie. If it delays, wait for it, because it will surely come and shall not be late.”

As though he said: Because the vision is still distant, at the time appointed by God the Son of God, clothed in flesh, shall appear at the end and shall not lie. Namely, when the end of the Law comes, then he also shall come, and the vision shall be declared true by the fulfillment of the event. But if it delays, O Jewish people, wait for it; that is, if Christ who is promised to you seems slow in coming because of your desire to see the vision, nevertheless do not despair: wait patiently. For behold, I promise you that he shall surely come and shall not be late in relation to himself, although he may seem to you to delay [Col. 0182C].

You plainly understand, O Jews, and cannot at all deny, that this prophecy concerns Christ’s coming. Therefore God the Father fulfilled what he promised: he sent his Son, for the redemption of the human race, in the likeness of sinful flesh at the end—that is, at the appointed time (Rom. 8). “He shall appear at the end,” he says—that is, at the end of the Law and the prophets; for “the Law and the prophets prophesied until John” (Luke 16). Hence the Apostle says: “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

Therefore believe, O Jews [Col. 0182D], and doubt no longer, that Christ has already come for the redemption of the world and, if I may so say, lived among human beings clothed in flesh without sin. But if you remain in your unbelief, you will surely make yourselves guilty before God and before the testimonies of the Law and the oracles of the prophets.

Habakkuk the prophet testifies to this next, saying: “Behold, the unbeliever’s soul shall not be right within himself” (Hab. 2). Indeed, one who is unbelieving toward the divine dispensation will have a soul—that is, an intention—that is right neither toward God nor within himself. Whoever does not believe that God’s promise will be fulfilled does not have right faith in the heart [Col. 0183A]. How can one possess a right intention of mind who refuses to grant credence either to the testimonies of the Law or to the oracles of the prophets? How then do you, O wretched and unhappy Jews, call yourselves worshipers of almighty God, when you contradict not only the sayings of the Law and prophets but even his mouth, namely Jesus Christ, who truly is the mouth of God the Father?

Since, therefore, you resist God’s dispensation and his eternal counsel, you do not possess within yourselves a right soul, namely right faith in the heart. Thus the Son of God appeared clothed in flesh, as was said, at the end of the Law and the prophets, and did not lie. Rather, just as he promised that he would come, he came without any ambiguity. And he will come again at the end of temporal things, with thousands of saints, to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire [Col. 0183B].

Therefore, if you believe without doubt, O senseless Jews, that the Son of God and of the Virgin, as stated above, has already come for the redemption of the world and will come again to judge the world, you shall always live in the same Jesus Christ, who is eternal life. But if you persevere in the treachery of unbelief, you shall undoubtedly perish eternally.

Moreover, I want you to know, O Jews, that the faith which is in Christ is eternal life. But whoever does not believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God the Father, as blessed John the Baptist says, does not have life, but the wrath of God shall remain upon him (John 3). That faith is eternal life is testified by the Lord, who subsequently says through the prophet Habakkuk [Col. 0183C]: “But my righteous one lives by faith” (ibid.). As though he said: For the righteous person who believes my promise, faith obtains this: that he may live eternally.

Therefore, if you wish, O Jews, to live on earth and in heaven, believe that Jesus Christ, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God, and that for the liberation of the human race he assumed true flesh from his Virgin mother through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Hosea the prophet also plainly testifies that he would come for the redemption of the world and illumine it, saying: “His coming is prepared like dawn, and he shall come to us like the early and latter rain upon the earth” (Hos. 6).

Dawn is the beginning of light, when darkness is driven away. Thus Christ’s coming was like dawn [Col. 0183D], because, descending from the bosom of the Father and assuming human nature from the incorrupt Virgin, he drove away the darkness of errors, and the light of spiritual teaching shone upon the whole world. Therefore Christ is truly called the Son of Man, because he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb not from a carnal father but from the Holy Spirit. He is therefore called Son of Man, that is, Son of the Virgin. As the darkness of night is driven away at the rising of dawn, so, when Christ came forth from the bridal chamber of the incorrupt womb, the darkness of sins was blotted out and the hearts of the faithful were enlightened by the light of truth.

It follows: “And he shall come to us like the early and latter rain upon the earth.” In the literal sense, early rain makes the sown seeds take root, whereas latter rain brings the fruit to maturity. Hence the saying: “I will give you rains in their seasons” [Col. 0184A] (Lev. 26). Mystically, early rain is when we know in part, and latter rain when that which is perfect has come. Spiritually, Christ is early rain to us when he inspires faith, and latter rain when, after good works, he leads us to the granaries.

Again, if you please, O Jews, let us consider briefly the aforementioned statement of the prophet Hosea, in order that we may prove from this prophet’s own words that you have spoken falsely in your assertion, and show by clear reasoning that Jesus Christ—whom in your blind minds you deny to be God—is true God and true man.

“His coming,” he says, “is prepared like dawn.” Whose coming? Tell us, whose? Do you wish to hear whose? It is his who is in the heights [Col. 0184B] without a mother, and on earth without a carnal father; his who in heaven, according to divinity, is in the bosom of God the Father, and according to the assumption of humanity is in the bosom of his Virgin mother; his who in heaven refreshes the holy angels from himself by sight, and on earth feeds faithful human beings by faith; his who mercifully descended from the bosom of almighty God the Father and assumed our nature without sin from his Virgin mother; because, clothed in it, he conquered the devil and through the cross snatched the human race from everlasting condemnation.

“His coming is prepared like dawn,” he says, namely the coming of Jesus Christ, God and man, because by his coming he illumined the whole world with the rays of Gospel preaching and drove away the darkness of sins [Col. 0184C].

§ IX.—

Micah, instructed by the Holy Spirit, did not deny Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, but knew beforehand that he would come—the one whom God the Father established over the works of his hands. For that reason he was exalted above the heavens, because he was obedient. From Genesis he brings forward a figure: God sent him, made flesh through the womb of the inviolate Virgin, to overthrow the ancient enemy; and thus, by prophecies and testimonies of the Law, he convicts the Jews as false witnesses concerning the Incarnation of the Word. He introduces Micah, in whom, although Christ’s goings forth are from God the Father from the days of eternity, he nevertheless took the natural substance of flesh from his incorrupt mother. Zechariah, together with David, testifies that he came humble and gentle, was received by the Jews, gave the nations everlasting dominion, and left peace that would endure forever; his dominion extends from sea to sea. God the Father, testifying through Malachi, declares that Christ, God and man, has now come to his holy Church—he whom not only the Jews sought but also the gentiles, to whom God bestowed gifts of prophecy [Col. 0184D].

That same Son of God and of the Virgin, O Jews, whom you deny, the prophet Micah did not deny; instructed by the Holy Spirit, he knew beforehand that he would come for the redemption and instruction of the human race, when he publicly proclaimed concerning him: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared upon the summit of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it, and many nations shall hasten and say: ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he shall teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths. For from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem’” (Mic. 4).

Tell us, O Jews, who is this mountain of the house of the Lord, which is said to be prepared upon the summit of the mountains in the last days [Col. 0185A] and exalted above the hills? He is undoubtedly the one whom God the Father begot from himself before all ages, through whom he also created all things from nothing, whom he willed to be born of his Virgin mother for the salvation of the world, and whom he established over all the works of his hands.

It is as though the prophet Micah said more plainly concerning him: “In the last days,” that is, at the end of the ages, namely in the time of grace, that is, at the eleventh hour, the mountain of the house of the Lord—namely the Son of God and of the Virgin—shall be prepared, that is, raised up, not only among the mountains but even upon the summit of the mountains, above the patriarchs and prophets who prophesied concerning him; and exalted above the hills, namely above the apostles and evangelists. Because in the form of a servant he was obedient to God the Father unto [Col. 0185B] death, therefore he was exalted and was given the name above every name (Phil. 2).

For, as has been said, he came at the eleventh hour to hire laborers for his vineyard (Matt. 20). Hence it is added: “Peoples shall flow to him”; namely, great multitudes of Jews shall gather to him as rivers flow. And many nations, from every nation under heaven (Acts 2), shall hasten to believe in him and, encouraging one another toward the banner of the cross, shall say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” For believers indeed require an ascent if anyone is to be able to reach Christ. Hence David’s saying: “They shall go from strength to strength, and the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83).

“And to the house of the God [Col. 0185C] of Jacob,” that is, to the Church of this same Savior of the world; “and he shall teach us of his ways, and we shall walk in his paths.” Namely, through the preaching of the apostles we shall believe without doubt that this same Son of God and of the Virgin, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God. It is as though he said more plainly: Therefore we shall go up to that mountain of God—that is, to Christ—so that he may teach us through angels, that is, through bishops and the other teachers who preside over his Church, and through the holy Scriptures ordained by him.

Thus we shall go up to the mountain of the Lord, that is, to Christ, and to the house of the God of Jacob, namely to his holy Church through baptism and confession, because from Zion, namely from the holy Church, the spiritual law and the word of the Lord—that is, the word of preaching—shall go forth from Jerusalem to the nations [Col. 0185D].

It follows: “And he shall judge among many peoples and rebuke strong nations even unto a distance.” As though he said: Because God the Father “gave all judgment to the Son” (John 5), therefore he, the Son of God and man, shall judge among many peoples, those worthy of salvation and those who shall be unworthy; and he shall rebuke strong nations even unto a distance—that is, he shall catch the wise of this world in their craftiness and know the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain (Ps. 93).

Therefore Christ, as has been said, O Jews, is the mountain of the house of the Lord—that is, the head of the whole Church—prepared upon the summit of the mountains, that is, exalted above the patriarchs [Col. 0186A] and prophets, apostles and evangelists, and the other teachers of the Church. To him peoples flow through faith, and, as you see, many nations hasten. God the Father, as has been said, begot him from himself before all ages; and the undefiled Virgin, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, conceived him without carnal desire and gave birth to him, clothed in flesh from her own substance and without sin.

Believe without doubt, O Jews, that through him God the Father created all things from nothing; and that, in order to overthrow the ancient enemy, he sent him, made flesh through the womb of the inviolate Virgin.

Without doubt this was spiritually prefigured in Genesis, where it is written: “God made heaven and earth, every shrub of the field, and every herb of the land. For the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was no man to till the ground” (Gen. 2). [Col. 0186B] As if it said openly: Before man sinned, he had not yet granted, through the clouds of the Scriptures, the rain of doctrine to water the soul; nor, on account of man, who is earth, had our same Lord Jesus Christ yet assumed the cloud of our flesh, through which he now pours forth most abundantly the rain of the holy Gospel.

It follows: “And there was no man to till the ground.” Appropriately, indeed, in this passage the earth is understood as the ever-virgin Mary. Therefore there was no man to till the ground, because no man had intercourse with that most glorious Virgin, from whom Christ was born. For he is the stone “cut out of the mountain without hands” [Col. 0186C] (Dan. 2), that is, without sexual union and human seed; from the virginal earth, as from the mountain of human nature, he was cut out in the substance of flesh.

Again it is said: “But a spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth.” The earth, as we have said, is most fittingly understood as the most blessed Virgin Mary, the Lord’s mother, of whom it is thus written in the Psalm:

> [Note: [Col. 0185] “Rightly” is read differently in another manuscript, “in Isaiah”; for this sentence belongs to that prophet, ch. 45:8.]

“Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior.” The Holy Spirit watered this earth; in the Gospel he is signified by the name of a spring and water. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and live; rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). And again: “Whoever drinks the water which I shall give him shall become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life” (John 4).

“Therefore the Lord God formed man from the mud of the earth” [Col. 0186D]; that is, Christ was made, as the Apostle says, “from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1), as though from the mud of the earth. “And he breathed into his face the breath of life,” that is, by the infusion of the Holy Spirit, who fashioned the man Christ. “And man became a living soul,” so that he who was perfect God might also be believed to be perfect man.

See how the Law and the Prophets agree with each other; see how clearly they show you, O Jews, to be false witnesses. The Law and the Prophets proclaim Christ to be true God and true man, and plainly demonstrate that you, who deny Christ, have been defeated in your assertion. The Old and New Testaments agree in maintaining that Christ [Col. 0187A] was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world, and they convict you, who say that he did not come and did not assume a human body, of having lied in every respect in your objection.

Hear also, O Jews, enemies of truth, how openly God the Father convicts you in your false argument. Bearing testimony through the prophet Micah to the same Jesus Christ, his Son, he says:

“And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are little among the thousands of Judah: from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5).

Here God the Father plainly determines both the place of Christ’s birth and that he is true God and true man. As if God the Father said more openly: [Col. 0187B] “You, Bethlehem Ephrathah—that is, house of bread, in which the bread of life is to be born—are little among the thousands of Judah; yet from you shall go forth the ruler of Israel. Although he is David’s son according to the flesh, yet he was born from me before all ages; and the Creator of times is not bound by time, but his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity.” Hence it is written in the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

It follows: “Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor shall give birth; but the remnant of his brethren shall be converted to the children of Israel.” As if it said: The Lord shall give up the Temple, Jerusalem, and the Jews; that is, he shall allow the rulers of the Jews to reign until the time when the Virgin gives birth to Christ. At his birth, when the Jews are blinded, the remnant of Israel shall be converted [Col. 0187C] to faith in the Holy Trinity.

What do you observe in these things, O Jews? What do you say? What do you answer to these things? By the testimony just cited, God the Father most openly destroys your false objection. He says that Christ did not begin in time, as you falsely maintain, but declares that his going forth was from the beginning, from the days of eternity. You ought without doubt to believe, and not doubt at all, that Christ’s going forth is from the same eternal Father, to whom he is the coeternal Son.

For in saying that he will be ruler in Israel, he shows you, who deny him to be the true King, to be false witnesses. Likewise, in indicating the place of his birth, [Col. 0187D] he plainly shows that he assumed the true substance of flesh from his Virgin mother. Therefore, since his going forth is from God the Father from the days of eternity, and he received from his Virgin mother the natural substance of flesh, he is not a mere man, as you blasphemously say, but true God and true man—a fact which you cannot possibly deny.

But if you still do not give credence to the testimonies above, and still doubt his divinity and humanity, I urge you patiently to hear how clearly the prophet Zechariah proclaims him to be true God and true man, and how humbly he was to come for the redemption of the human race.

“Exult greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem” (Zech. 9). The holy prophet Zechariah, foreknowing that the Son of God and of the Virgin was to come [Col. 0188A] to set humankind free, rejoicing and exulting exceedingly, exhorts Zion—that is, Jerusalem, that is, the holy Church—to spiritual joy and gladness, saying: “Exult greatly, daughter of Zion; shout for joy, daughter of Jerusalem.” Why? “For behold, your King shall come to you, righteous and a savior; he is poor and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass.”

As if he said more plainly: “Behold, your King shall come to you, righteous and a savior”—that is, Jesus, promised by the prophecies of all the prophets—“he is poor,” though he was rich, “and riding upon an ass,” that is, upon the people of the circumcision, oppressed under the yoke of the Law; “and upon a colt, the foal of an ass,” that is, upon the Gentile people, governed by no law and plunged headlong into idolatry, but now, by the Lord’s seating upon it, taking upright steps.

This was without doubt fulfilled when the Jews went out to meet Christ with palm branches, crying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest” (Matt. 21). In Hebrew, *Hosanna* is said to God; as St. Isidore says in Book VI of the *Etymologies* (ch. 19), it is translated into Latin as “save,” with “your people” or “the whole world” understood.

It follows: “And he shall scatter the chariot also from Ephraim, and the horse from Jerusalem.” Ephraim is interpreted “fruitfulness” or “increase,” and signifies the multitude of heretics, of whom the Psalmist says: “The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back in the day of battle” (Ps. 77). But their horse—that is, their deceitful confidence—shall be scattered [Col. 0188C] from Jerusalem, that is, from the Church, at Christ’s coming; and they themselves shall be called to repentance by the Church’s ministers, who ceaselessly cry with the Prophet: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31).

Again God the Father adds through the prophet Zechariah: “The bow of war shall be scattered”; that is, the bow of heretics at Christ’s coming, so that fiery darts may not be shot from it—that is, arguments of falsehood and deception to strike the hearts of the Church’s children. It follows: “And he shall speak peace to the nations, and his power shall be from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth.” This assuredly ought not to be explained away or diminished by allegory, but must be believed to have been truly fulfilled, [Col. 0188D] in accordance with what God the Father promises his same most beloved Son Jesus Christ through the Psalmist: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Ps. 2).

Therefore, in foreshadowing the coming of his Son Jesus Christ, God the Father plainly shows how meekly he will come, how he will preach, and how great his power will be. “He shall speak peace to the nations,” he says. This the Son of God and of the Virgin himself fulfilled when he said to his disciples in the Gospel: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you” (John 14)—understand, not only to the Jews but also to the Gentiles. That at Christ’s coming there was peace throughout the whole world is also attested by the Psalmist, who says: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and abundance of peace” (Ps. 71).

[Col. 0189A] As if he said openly: “In his days righteousness shall arise,” that is, the faith which justifies each person; “and abundance of peace,” because at his coming peace shall extend not merely to friends but also to enemies. Thus he himself says in the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5).

This abundance of peace shall endure until the moon is removed, that is, until the Church, having conquered death, is assumed into immortality. Or, according to another translation, until the moon is exalted, that is, until the holy Church, through the grace of the resurrection, reigns eternally with him who preceded her in the glory of the resurrection.

[Col. 0189B] Therefore, O Jews, you ought greatly to exult and rejoice, because Jesus Christ, God and man, came to you humble and meek, as the prophet Zechariah foretold. You ought to rejoice most greatly because he came humbly for your salvation and that of the whole world; but because you refused to receive him with proud minds, you ought to weep most bitterly. Because he came especially to you, you ought to rejoice in him with the utmost devotion; but because you not only refused to receive him, but even delivered him over to a most shameful death, you ought to do penance before him with tears.

Therefore, O Jews, you cannot deny that he has already come for the redemption of the world, since, as he hastened toward Jerusalem riding upon an ass, you offered him palm branches and spiritual [Col. 0189C] praises from the magnificent glory, blessed him, and testified that he came in the name of God the Father. Yet I do not want you to be unaware that you did this not willingly or by your own choice, but prompted by divine inspiration.

Meanwhile, O Jews, let us question the prophet Zechariah again, and let him tell us how Christ came, why he came, and what he did in his coming. Therefore, O prophet Zechariah, do not shrink from repeating the judgment stated above, so that by your most truthful testimony the unbelief of the Jews may be convicted and the Catholic faith may be strengthened more and more in every respect. Tell us, then, how Christ came. “Humble,” he says, “and meek.” And why did he come? Namely, to draw us away from the worship of idols [Col. 0189D] and to cleanse for himself an acceptable people, zealous for good works (Tit. 2). And what did he do in his coming? He preached peace to the nations: that they might not render evil for evil, and might willingly spare those who sinned against them. Tell us also what else he did. “He ruled from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71).

It is plainly made clear, O Jews, that unless he were true God, he could by no means have power from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth. And unless he were true man, he could in no way live among human beings as a human being. Therefore you must confess yourselves defeated in your own assertion, since you deny that the Son of God lived among human beings in the substance of our flesh [Col. 0190A] (Bar. 3). Do not be ashamed humbly to confess that you have lied in your dispute, so that by humble confession you may escape his wrath and obtain mercy.

That the same Son of God and of the Virgin, who is truly King of heaven and earth, rules over all nations and all things under heaven, the Psalmist attests. Taught by the Holy Spirit, foreseeing him—or rather, certainly knowing that he would be born of the Virgin—he rejoices greatly in his praises and says: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the world.” As if he said: He shall rule from the eastern sea to the western sea, beginning from the River Jordan and extending to the ends of the world.

[Col. 0190B] Note, O Jews, that the Prophet plainly declares that Christ wished to manifest his power from the place where he also began to choose his disciples: namely, from the River Jordan, where, when the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord after his baptism, a voice sounded from heaven, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). Thus his teaching begins there, and the authority of his heavenly mastership spreads to the ends of the earth, when the Gospel of the kingdom is preached throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations.

Or otherwise: The Son of God and of the Virgin shall rule from the sea—understand, the sea of the Jews—to the sea of the Gentiles. Note that although the Jews received knowledge of the Law, they can nevertheless be called a sea, because, longing after earthly things, [Col. 0190C] they are troubled by the storms of the age as though by the waves of the sea. The Gentile people, on the other hand, because it received no knowledge of the Lord, is fittingly denoted by the name of sea. Thus the saying means: “He shall rule from sea to sea,” beginning from the River Jordan, that is, from those who descend from pride to humility, or who anathematize themselves, and reaching to the ends of the earth—that is, to those who, making their own earth round, make themselves boundaries for others by their example, as far as they extend.

Therefore, O Jews, you ought without doubt to believe that Jesus Christ has true divinity from God the Father and humanity from the Virgin mother, he who has power from sea to sea and from the river to the ends of the earth—that is, over all nations. [Col. 0190D] For if he were not true God, he would not have dominion from sea to sea. But because he was naturally begotten of God the Father before all ages, he is Lord of angels and Prince of the kings of the earth. Before that all-powerful King Ethiopians shall fall down—that is, those formerly most blackened in sins or evil habits shall humble themselves—and his enemies shall lick the earth (Ps. 71), namely, by venerating him. Or “his enemies,” that is, heretics, shall lick the earth before him: they shall delight in earthly things, arrogating to themselves the authority of earthly things, so as thereby to confirm in others what they have acquired by perversely interpreting the Scriptures.

Believe, therefore, O Jews, and do not doubt at all, [Col. 0191A] that Jesus Christ is true man and true God, sent by God the Father for the redemption of the human race. But if you say that you do not yet believe perfectly, and feel in your minds some scruple of doubt concerning his divinity, I urge you patiently to hear what testimony God the Father bears concerning his coming through the prophet Malachi. Thus God the Father says to his same beloved Son, whom he sent for the redemption of this world: “Behold, I shall send my angel, who shall prepare the way before my face” (Mal. 3).

As if God the Father openly said to his Son Jesus Christ, who was to come for the redemption of the world: “Behold, I shall send my angel, namely John the Baptist, who shall prepare your way before you.” If a priest is questioned about the Law, he should teach the ignorant and convict those who resist; otherwise he vainly boasts that he possesses a dignity whose function he does not perform. Therefore the prophet Malachi says: “The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they shall seek the Law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2). Since *angelus* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as *nuntius*, “messenger,” one who fittingly announces God’s will to the peoples is called an angel.

Accordingly, in this passage we understand John the Baptist under the name angel, concerning whom we read that the Lord said in the Gospel: “This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my angel” (Matt. 11), etc. God the Father therefore rightly called John [Col. 0191C] the Baptist an angel, in bearing testimony through the prophet Malachi to Jesus Christ, his coeternal Son; for John himself, with free voice, announced to the crowds flocking to him the coming of this same Son of God and of the Virgin, pointed with his finger to him as present, diligently preached that they should prepare a way for the same Lord Jesus Christ, and commanded them by admonition to make his paths straight.

Again, foreshadowing for his faithful people that this same beloved Son was soon to come, God the Father accordingly adds: “And immediately the ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple” (Mal. 3). As if he said: “Immediately the ruler whom you seek shall come to his holy temple,” that is, to the holy Church or to each one of the faithful: namely Jesus Christ, ruler of heaven [Col. 0191D] and earth, who is the Creator of all things; “whom you seek,” that is, whom you desire, if you have been predestined for eternal life. Of him it is said: “Behold, the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2); and “the Angel of the covenant,” namely Jesus Christ, God and man, of great counsel, “whom you desire.” For what purpose will he come? Namely, in order not to show partiality, and to judge justly.

John the Baptist prepared a way in the hearts of believers for this Angel of such great authority—Jesus Christ, founder of the Old and New Testaments—in hearts in which Jesus Christ, true God and true man, could not dwell with God the Father and the Holy Spirit because of their unbelief. Therefore the Angel of the covenant came: namely Jesus Christ, God and man, creator and ordainer of both Testaments, to his holy temple, [Col. 0192A] that is, to the holy Church, which he adopted in the womb of his Virgin mother as his bride, redeemed with his most precious blood on the cross, and washed from sins in baptism. Therefore, as God the Father attests, as soon as the fullness of time came, the Angel of the covenant—that is, Jesus Christ, lawgiver and judge—came mercifully to his holy temple, namely, to his holy Church [Col. 0192B].

Thus, in saying that the Angel of the covenant would come immediately, he completely convicts you, O Jews, who obstinately deny that he came, of being false witnesses. Therefore Jesus Christ, God and man, came to his holy Church as God the Father promised, and through his apostles made his coming known to the whole world. “For the sound of the apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18).

What do you say to this? What objection do you raise, O Jews? You surely recognize plainly that, as God the Father testifies through the prophet Malachi, the Angel of the covenant—Jesus Christ, God and man—has now come to his holy temple, that is, to his Church; and, as has been said, immediately made his coming known to the whole world through his most truthful disciples. How long, then, O Jews, will you remain unbelieving and deny that the Son of God descended from the bosom of the Father and mercifully and humbly assumed true flesh from the incorrupt Virgin for the redemption of the human race? You ought already to have given credence to the testimony of God the Father stated above, and firmly believed that he came long ago and lived among human beings without sin.

God the Father says: “Immediately the ruler whom you seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire, shall come to his holy temple.” This passage makes it plain that not only the Jews [Col. 0192D] sought Christ’s coming, since they knew from the Law and the Prophets that his advent would take place, but also the Gentiles, to whom God granted gifts of prophecy and showed what he would do in the last days, desired his coming for the redemption of the world—as did Job,

> [Note: [Col. 0191D]
>
> It seems fitting to adduce their testimonies concerning Christ’s coming. Job, ch. 19:25: “I know … that my Redeemer lives.” Since he did not say “my Creator” but “my Redeemer,” Gregory the Great explains that he openly announces him who, after creating all things, … appeared incarnate among us.
>
> Balaam’s testimony is that celebrated prophecy [Col. 0192D] read in Numbers, ch. 24:17: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel,” etc. Nebuchadnezzar’s testimony appears to be this: “Behold … I see four men loosed … and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. 3:92); on this, the highly learned commentators Pererius and Calmet should be consulted.
>
> Virgil, says the same Calmet, derived from the Sibylline poems what he sings concerning the Messiah’s birth in Eclogue 4. For those verses could scarcely be diverted to another meaning:
>
> > “Now comes the last age of the Cumaean prophecy;
> >
> > A great order of the ages is born anew.
> >
> > Now the Virgin returns; Saturn’s reign returns.
> >
> > Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven,” etc.
>
> Mention of Christ the Lord in poems circulated under the name of the Sibyls is extremely frequent, as will be evident to anyone who reads their books. But on this subject one should consult those who have treated the question expressly, especially Baronius in the *Apparatus to the Annals*, nos. 18 through 26.]

Balaam, Nebuchadnezzar, Virgil, the Sibyl, and many others.

§ X.—

The obstinate perfidy of the Jews is convicted by John’s testimony, and faith in Christ is strengthened: from him we received grace for grace. Although the announcement was made through Moses, the fulfillment of salvation through Christ affirms that he would come into Israel not as a mere man but as true God. Although John is declared to surpass all the sons of women in dignity, he is incomparably surpassed by Christ, whom he declares true God and Redeemer of the world. Further, in response to the Levites’ and priests’ questioning, John declares that, though he was considered Elijah, he is neither Elijah nor the Prophet, although he preceded Christ’s coming in Elijah’s spirit and power, because he is the voice crying in the wilderness. Finally, the figure of Christ’s baptism in the Jordan is added.

At the sight of Christ John calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world; indeed, for this reason he is more than a prophet, though his baptism did not take away sins. He further introduces Matthew explaining why Jesus comes to John for baptism, together with John’s response, the opening of heaven, and the appearance of the dove; and how those renewed by sacred baptism ought to be filled with the dove’s qualities. He did not entrust the power of baptism alike to good and evil ministers, though he could have done so; but he rightly entrusted the ministry, which, if John’s baptism is repeated, Christ’s is not.

Then he indicates that Christ is truly the Son of God, and finally Joseph as his most faithful foster-father. For likewise, by Luke’s testimony, he shows that the Holy Spirit descended like a dove and that the Father was pleased in the Son; for the same purpose he introduces Mark, together with the figure from Genesis. The four rivers of paradise signify the four holy Gospels flowing abundantly through the world; likewise Ezekiel’s four animals signify Christ’s four heralds and witnesses. John’s words are recapitulated; the mystery of the Trinity is shown in Christ’s baptism. From these sayings he refutes the errors of certain heretics, because, although Christ could have redeemed the world while remaining in his majesty with God the Father [Col. 0193C] and the Holy Spirit, he nevertheless chose to assume flesh from a woman.

Let that same angel, namely blessed John the Baptist, whom God the Father sent before the face of his same most beloved Son to prepare his way, also come forward and bear testimony concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity. Speak, holy John; speak what you know of Christ, so that by your testimony the obstinate perfidy of the Jews may be convicted and faith in Christ Jesus himself strengthened: “He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was before me” (John 1).

As if he said: “He who is to come after me has been made before me,” that is, has been set above me even in humanity. Why? Because he was before me in the eternity of his divinity. It follows: “And from his fullness we all [Col. 0193D] received grace for grace; because the Law was given through Moses, grace and truth [Col. 0194A] were made through Jesus Christ.”

As if he said: Because the Spirit was given to Christ without measure, we have all therefore received from his fullness the Spirit according to the measure of his gift (John 3; Eph. 4). For in him are all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2). We also received from him grace for grace: not only the grace given entirely without merit,

> [Note: [Col. 0193D] “We are said to be justified gratuitously,” says the Council of Trent, “because none of those things which precede justification … merits the grace of justification”; but by faith, because faith is the beginning, foundation, and root of all human salvation and justification. Session 6, ch. 8. Unless hope and charity are added to faith, it neither unites one perfectly with Christ nor makes one a living member of his body. For this reason it is most truly said that faith without works is dead and idle (Jas. 2), and that in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any force, but faith which works through charity. Ibid., ch. 7.]

such as faith, which works through love (Gal. 5), by which the righteous person lives (Gal. 3); but also, in exchange for this grace, another grace, namely eternal blessedness, which is called the reward of righteousness.

> [Note: [Col. 0194D] “To those who do good works … eternal life is to be proposed, both as a grace mercifully promised through Christ Jesus to the children of God and as a reward faithfully rendered, in virtue of God’s own promise, to their good works and merits … So great is the Lord’s goodness toward human beings that he wills their merits to be those things which are his own gifts.” Ibid., ch. 16.]

And it is called grace because it is merit arising from grace. Why? Because the Law, which the Israelite people received from the same Son of God through Moses, was given through Moses; that Law did not perfectly cleanse people from sins [Col. 0194B] but rather disclosed their sins. Hence St. Paul says: “For through the Law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3). And again: “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound; but where transgression abounded, grace superabounded” (Rom. 5).

Therefore grace, which becomes salvation to human beings, and truth, which had long been promised, came through Jesus Christ. Through Moses the servant, then, the announcement was made; through Jesus Christ the Lord, salvation was fulfilled. This is grace and truth because it was promised long ago and is now supplied: namely, that God may be in a human being, filling that person with every virtue and, through that person, those subject to himself. For the highest grace and truth is knowledge of the most holy Trinity. Hence Jesus Christ himself, God and man, says to God the Father in the Gospel: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). This knowledge is not complete in this life, because no one while placed in the flesh can see God as he is.

Let us therefore recall, O Jews, the testimony of the blessed John the Baptist stated above, which he bore before the crowds to Jesus Christ, God and man, so that, by explaining it more subtly and understanding it more clearly, the Catholic faith may be strengthened and your long-standing unbelief completely refuted. For he said: “He who is to come after me has been made before me, because he was before me.” As if he said: “He who is to come after me,” namely the Son of God in the flesh, “has been made before me,” namely, has been set above me in dignity and power, because he was before me, [Col. 0194D] namely from eternity with God the Father.

Therefore, holy John, when you say that Christ is to come for the redemption of the world, you contradict the Jews, false witnesses who deny that he came. In maintaining that he was made before you—that is, set above you—you convict the deadly unbelief of the same Jews, who maintain that he is not the true Son of God but will be a mere man. For we know certainly, and do not doubt at all, that among all the children of women no one could surpass you in holiness or excel you in dignity. Great dignity was granted you when the Son of God and of the Virgin bowed himself to be baptized in your hands. Therefore he alone is in every way truly greater than you who was born of the Virgin mother.

Appropriately, he surpasses you in power [Col. 0195B] and dignity whom the undefiled Virgin conceived through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when you say that Christ is set above you, you convict the Jews as false witnesses, since they testify that he is not true God but a mere human being. For just as no one among those born of women surpassed you in holiness and righteousness, so neither would he have surpassed you if he were not true God. Thus, in saying that he is greater than you, you show the Jews’ objection to be futile and implicitly affirm him to be the true Son of God. Moreover, when you add that he was set above you because he was before you, you plainly show that he did not begin in time, as the Jews maintain, but is coeternal with God the Father. Thus, in preaching that he is to come after you, you plainly condemn the error of the Jews’ unbelief [Col. 0195C] which denies that he is the Redeemer of the world.

As you see, O Jews, your lying claim is refuted by the testimony of blessed John stated above, and the Catholic faith is strengthened in believers’ hearts. Therefore believe without doubt that the Son of God descended from the bosom of his same Father into the womb of the undefiled Virgin Mary and assumed flesh from her without sin; that he mounted the cross for the redemption of the world; that, hanging upon that same cross, he gave up his soul when he wished and as he wished; that, leaving his body in the tomb, he descended in his soul to hell; that, after despoiling it and drawing up with himself to the heights those of his own who were held there, he returned in that same soul to his body [Col. 0195D] and raised it from the tomb on the third day; that after his resurrection he appeared to his disciples through forty days with many proofs, speaking to them concerning the heavenly kingdom; and that on the fortieth day, while his disciples watched, he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father (Acts 1). From there he will come on the last day, with great power and glory, to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire. For that most just Judge, according to the diversity of merits, will hand the wicked over to eternal torments, but will lead the righteous with himself into eternal joys.

For this reason, O Jews, I have briefly set out for you these articles of true faith: so that, with the hardness of unbelief driven from your hearts, you may believe Jesus Christ to be one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0196A] and may hasten to be numbered and joined with the children of the Church through him. Without doubt, this is the faith which Jesus Christ himself, God and man, commanded his disciples to preserve; which the patriarchs and prophets held; which the holy apostles and evangelists preached throughout the whole world; for which holy martyrs gave their bodies to diverse torments; and for which not only men but women also, not only boys under age but tender virgins also, struggled even to the shedding of blood. This faith cast out demons, raised the dead, healed the sick, overcame visible and invisible enemies, worked innumerable miracles, and daily works them through servants belonging to it in the name of the Holy Trinity.

At last I should like to know, O Jews, whether, now that you have laid aside [Col. 0196B] the treachery of unbelief, you are willing to give credence to the most truthful testimonies of the Law and the Prophets and, with faithful mind and simple heart, believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man; or whether you still stubbornly wish to persist in the wickedness of unbelief? But since you feel the prick of doubt to be present in your minds, and say that you do not yet believe perfectly, let us again bring forward blessed John the Baptist, and hear together what answer he gave, when you questioned him as he stood beside the waters of the Jordan. Speak, holy John; bear witness to Christ. For this purpose God the Father sent you before His face: that you might baptize the peoples flocking to you, and bear public witness to Him. Let us therefore hear what answer you gave to the priests and Levites sent by the Jews, when they asked whether you were the Christ.

“I am not the Christ,” he says (John 1). As though he said: “I am not Christ, nor the Judge manifest in power.” And they asked him: “What then? Are you Elijah?” And he said: “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered: “No” (ibid.). As though he said: “I am neither Elijah nor the Prophet, because I have come not only to announce Christ beforehand, but also to point Him out.”

The Jews thought John to be the Christ foretold in the Law. Some thought him Elijah because of his extraordinary abstinence and chastity, his solitary life, his very severe rebuking of sinners, and his most stern warning of future vengeance. Others thought him one of the prophets because of the grace of prophecy. Since all then knew the name of Christ, and knew also that Elijah would precede Him, they supposed John to be Elijah, sent before His face. For Elijah is to precede Christ’s second coming, when God and man, Jesus Christ Himself, shall come with great power and majesty to judge the living and the dead, and the world by fire (Luke 21). John, however, figuratively—that is, in the spirit and power of Elijah—preceded the first coming of that same Son of God and of the Virgin, when He came to Jerusalem to suffer for the redemption of the world.

But now let us hear what the Jewish messengers say to blessed John: “Who are you, that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?” (John 1). As though they said more plainly: [Col. 0197A] “Make known clearly who you are, so that, on returning to those who sent us, we may report the truth concerning you.” John answered them, saying: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said” (ibid.). He did not say, “I am a man,” or “I am John,” or “the son of Zechariah”; nor did he consider in himself human substance or lineage, but is lifted above all these things. The Forerunner of the Word leaves behind all that is contained within the world; raised on high, he becomes the voice of the Word. He acknowledges in himself no substance except the abundance of grace which surpasses every creature. One who cleaves to God with a devout mind transcends all things, because in mind he reaches even Him who is above all things. Hence the Apostle says: “He who is joined to God is one spirit with Him” (1 Cor. 6).

As though he said more plainly: “I am the voice in which the Word sounds—that is, prophecy, manifestation, and the lamp of the present Word. I am,” he says, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” As though he said: “I am the voice of the incarnate Word crying in me in the wilderness, announcing consolation to the forsaken Judea.” But let us hear what He cries: “Make straight the way of the Lord,” namely, through faith and good works, by which the Lord enters human hearts, as Isaiah the prophet said.

It should be noted that the priests and Levites came to question John because they had heard him preach the common resurrection of all, which they too believed; hence they agreed with Christ in many matters, and likewise heard the apostle Paul in many matters. “And those who had been sent,” says the Evangelist, “were from the Pharisees.” The Pharisees had heard in the Law and the Prophets that Christ would come and baptize. They also knew that the Jordan bore the figure of baptism; and, since Elijah and Elisha had crossed it dry-shod, they did not doubt that baptism had been prefigured in Elijah and Elisha. Hence they now ask particularly whether he is Elijah, who prefigured baptism.

Again they questioned him and said to him: “Why then do you baptize, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?” (John 1). As though they said: “Why do you presume to baptize, if you are neither Christ nor Elijah, who have authority to baptize?” I urge you, O Jews, to hear attentively what blessed John answered the Jewish messengers. “I baptize in water,” he says; “but one stands in your midst whom you do not know.” As though he said plainly: “Let not what I do be imputed to boldness, because by my baptism I wash bodies but do not take away sins; so that, as I am forerunner by birth and preaching, so also I am by baptizing. But He who takes away sins stands among you.” As though he said: “He stands in your midst, that is, He appears bodily present to you; but you do not know Him because He came humble, and therefore I, the lamp, am kindled beforehand. He is the one who, as He is to come after me in birth, so also in preaching, yet was made before me; that is, it was determined before all ages that He should [Col. 0198A] come after me, because He is set above me. I am not worthy to loosen the strap of His sandal.”

He did not say, “I do not loosen it,” but “I am not worthy to loosen it.” For the one who loosens the strap of His sandal is one who has made Him known and has disclosed much concerning His divinity and humanity; but John said, “I am not worthy,” because he judged himself unworthy for this task. “These things were done in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.” As though he said: “These things occurred in Bethany, that is, in the house of obedience; he baptizes there in order to signify that obedience befits the baptized.” There are two Bethanies: one beyond the Jordan, and the other on this side of it, not far from Jerusalem, where Lazarus was raised. The Bethany beyond the Jordan signifies human nature under the natural law, before the streams of grace, which followed Christ’s Incarnation; it was created for this end, that under the law of nature it might obey God.

[Note: Col. 0197D. Alternatively, and perhaps more clearly, the Gloss: “Which grace was abundant; which nature,” etc.]

John baptizes there because he does not free from sin. He baptizes beyond the streams of divine gifts, which [Note: Col. 0198D. Thus the manuscript. But we think it should read: “Which had not, up to Christ, begun to descend into human nature,” etc.] had not yet begun in Christ to descend into human nature. But the Bethany on this side of the Jordan near Jerusalem signifies that same human nature obedient under the law of grace, which is near Jerusalem—that is, the vision of peace through charity. There Christ raises the dead because He frees from sin.

From the Evangelist’s narrative we have learned, O Jews, that when John the Baptist, in prophetic spirit, bore the testimonies mentioned above concerning Christ’s coming, he had not yet seen Christ. But when God and man, Jesus Christ Himself, came bodily to him, let us all hear together what blessed John said and answered to Him, and what testimony concerning Him he gave to the crowds. For the Evangelist says: “John saw Jesus coming to him, and said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold Him who takes away the sins of the world’” (ibid.). John saw Jesus coming to him not only by bodily steps, but also in the inward contemplation of his soul, because the Son of God and of the Virgin deigned to make Himself known to John according to both divinity and humanity. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God,” namely, the innocent Victim to be slain, prefigured in the Paschal lamb.

It should be noted that the Lamb of God provides three things to those who possess Him: the milk of simple teaching, by which little children are nourished; wool, that is, the garments of virtues; and the food of His most sacred body. “Behold Him who takes away the sins of the world.” The sins of the world are called original sins, common to the whole world, by which all human nature, created together and at once, transgressed the divine laws through disobedience in Paradise. Christ’s grace remits these original sins through baptism. Yet it should be known that this most gentle Lamb, the Son of God the Father, forgives not only original but also daily actual sins, as blessed John says in the Apocalypse: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in His blood” (Rev. 1)—namely, when He gave His blood for us on the cross, or when each one of us has been washed by the mystery of His most holy Passion and by baptism.

And not only then, but daily He takes away the sins of the world and washes us from our sins in His blood, when the memorial of that same most holy Passion is repeated upon the altar; when, as the Venerable Bede says on the passage, “Behold the Lamb of God, behold Him who takes away the sins of the world,” the creature of bread and wine is transformed, by the ineffable sanctification of the Spirit, into the sacrament of His flesh and blood.

Again, O John the Baptist, repeat what you above bore witness concerning Christ to the crowds standing by you, so that the Jews, convicted by your most truthful testimony, may not perish with the unbelievers [Col. 0199B] through the fault of their long unbelief, but may with the utmost devotion receive faith in Christ and baptism, in order that they may attain eternal joys with the children of the Church. “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold Him who takes away the sins of the world.” Why do you call Him a Lamb? Because of His innocence and gentleness. For as He was “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44), so He was innocent and gentle.

O blessed John the Baptist, tell us more plainly about Him, if you know anything, so that Catholic faith may be strengthened by your testimony and the mouth of the Jews, false witnesses, may be shut. “This is He,” he says, “of whom, when the Jews questioned me before they saw Him, I said above: ‘After me comes a man who was made before me, because He was prior to me’; and I did not know Him.” Here blessed John identifies the one of whom he said above: “One stands in your midst whom you do not know.” “And I,” he says, “did not know Him.” O holy John, why did you not know Him whose coming you proclaimed aloud? “I said that I did not know Him because, although I foretold His coming, I had not yet seen Him with the eyes of the body.” Why then, O blessed John, did you presume to baptize people in His name when you plainly did not know Him? “Undoubtedly I did not know Him—that is, I had not yet seen Him bodily. But for this reason I come baptizing in water, that God and man, Jesus Christ Himself, may be manifested in Israel. God the Father sent me beforehand before the face of that same most beloved Son of His, so that first I might proclaim His coming, and then openly point Him out as present.”

[Col. 0199D] You have plainly heard, O Jews, the testimony which blessed John the Baptist bore to Christ: how he foretold to the peoples who flocked to him that Christ would come, and openly showed Him to the crowds standing by as present. I do not want you to be unaware that John the Baptist is called a prophet because he foretold Christ’s coming; and that he is greater than a prophet because he showed Him to be present.

Therefore, O Jews, I urge you at this point to hear attentively what I say. Know for certain, and do not doubt at all, that because you refuse faithfully to receive the sayings of the Law and the oracles of the Prophets which bear witness that Christ is true God and true man, you expose yourselves to the danger of eternal condemnation. But if, hindered by the evil of unbelief, you will not give credence to the sayings of the other prophets, who truly declared Christ’s Incarnation, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven, you must certainly obey with all devotion the testimony of blessed John the Baptist, who is greater than a prophet. He foretold that the Son of God would come in the flesh; then, seeing Him bodily present among men and pointing to Him with his finger, he said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold He who takes away the sins of the world.”

O Jews, what truer thing do you wish to hear? John saw Him with his own eyes among men, walking in bodily fashion and speaking, and humbly coming to him in order to be baptized by him. If, therefore, as has been said, you will not believe the other prophets who foretold from afar [Col. 0200B] that Christ would come, you ought beyond doubt to believe blessed John the Baptist, who foretold His coming, showed Him present, and saw Him with his own eyes.

But if you say that the aforesaid testimonies of blessed John are still insufficient to drive unbelief from your hearts; if you still doubt concerning Christ whether He is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, let us bring forward blessed Matthew, apostle and evangelist, and hear carefully what he says to us concerning the same Son of God and of the Virgin. “Jesus,” he says, “came from Galilee to the Jordan, to John, to be baptized by him” (Matt. 3).

Who came to whom? God to man; the king to the soldier; the highest priest to the minister; the lord to the servant; the Creator to the creature; the great One to the little one; the sun to Lucifer; Christ to John, to be baptized by him.

When did He come? Namely, when John was baptizing and preaching; that is, when Christ Himself was already thirty years old, showing that no one ought to become a priest or preacher unless he is of mature age. Thus Joseph, at thirty, took up the kingdom of Egypt; David began to reign at that age; and Ezekiel began to preach. And why did Jesus come to John? For these reasons: to approve John’s baptism; to fulfil every righteousness and humility of the Law, as one who was man; and, by sanctifying the waters, to show through the dove the coming of the Holy Spirit. He came also not because He needed cleansing, but so that no one, however holy, might judge the grace of baptism superfluous.

Hear, O Jews; hear, rebels and unbelievers; hear what blessed John answered God and man, Jesus Christ, as He came to him, and how he received Him. Convicted by John’s most truthful testimony, believe Christ to be true God and true man, and receive His baptism with devout mind, so that you may no longer presume arrogantly to murmur against Him. “I ought,” John says, “to be baptized by You, O Christ, and do You come to me?” As though he said: “I ought to be baptized by You because God the Father begot You from Himself before all ages, whereas the corruption arising from the transgression of the first parent has befallen me. Through You God the Father created all things out of nothing; but I, begotten through carnal intercourse, am subject to guilt. You are true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit; but I, begotten of a fleshly father, am stained by sin. God the Father sent You for the redemption of the world; a natural union of man and woman begot me. An incorrupt Virgin, overshadowed by the power of the Most High, brought You forth; a woman made pregnant by a man bore me. I am an earthly man, who cannot possibly live without sin; but You are the Lamb of God, in whose mouth no falsehood was found. ‘My mother conceived me in sins’ (Ps. 50); the most holy Virgin Mary, unknown to man, bore You. Therefore You were born to redeem me; but I was born to be redeemed by You. It is thus more fitting that You, who take away the sins of the world, should baptize me than that I, who have sinned in many things, should baptize You.”

But Jesus answered and said to him: “Allow it for the present; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness.” As though the Son of God and of the Virgin said more plainly to John the Baptist with the highest affection of charity and humility: “All that you have mentioned thus far is indeed true; but for the present allow the spiritual ministry to be fulfilled, for whose fulfilment I came down from the bosom of the Father. Allow Me, therefore, to be baptized now, so that afterward you may, as you desire and say, be baptized by Me in the Spirit. For thus it is fitting that we give an example of fulfilling all righteousness, so that all may learn that no one is perfect or can be saved without the water of baptism.” Then blessed John allowed Him—that is, he consented to do what God and man, Jesus Christ, commanded. Having thus learned the order in which righteousness was to be fulfilled, he allowed Him, because true humility is one which obedience, its companion, does not abandon. What he had first humbly refused, he afterward devoutly performed.

Hear, O Jews, enemies of truth, who even today stubbornly deny Christ to be the Son of God; hear the testimony which Matthew the Evangelist again bore concerning Him, immediately after He had been baptized and had come up from the water. By this testimony the faith of Christians is strengthened in every respect, and your lying assertion is utterly refuted. “And when Jesus Christ had been baptized,” as Matthew the Evangelist relates, “He immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to Him, and He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon Him” (Matt. 3). “Having been baptized,” he says, “He immediately came up from the water,” and this was for the fulfilment of righteousness. It was not that the heavenly things were then first opened to Him, or that the Holy Spirit was then given to Him; rather, He showed us that, through baptism received, the way of heaven lies open and the Holy Spirit is given. The first Adam, deceived by the devil through the serpent, lost heaven; the second, glorified by the Holy Spirit through the dove, opened it. The water of baptism extinguished the flame, or flashing sword, which barred the way to Paradise for the first humans and their descendants.

[Col. 0202A] It should be noted that the Holy Spirit appeared over the Lord in a dove because He came to gather us through gentleness; but He appeared over the disciples in fire, because He came to inflame them against themselves for consuming the rust of sins. The Holy Spirit was fittingly seen in the likeness of a dove, which is simple and gentle, so that He might show both the simplicity of His nature and that He upon whom He descended was gentle and the author of mercy. Likewise, all renewed by sacred baptism ought to be filled with the seven virtues signified in the dove.

[Note: Col. 0201. All this is transferred here from the Gloss; but see John Grialius’s annotation on chapter 3 of book VI and book IX, chapter 7, of the *Etymologies* of St Isidore.]

For the dove is free from the malice of gall: in this we are forbidden anger. It harms no one with beak or claws: in this innocence is indicated. It does not attack even tiny birds or worms, on which other birds nourish themselves [Col. 0202B] and their young: in this robbery is forbidden. It feeds on pure grain: in this abstinence is indicated. It cherishes other birds’ young as its own: behold charity. It has a groan instead of song: behold compunction. It sits over waters so that, on seeing the hawk’s shadow beforehand, it may avoid the hawk and thus escape its claws: behold vigilance.

It should nevertheless be known that not only did God and man, Jesus Christ, see the Spirit of God the Father descending like a dove and coming upon Him; John the Baptist also saw Him, as John the Evangelist himself testifies in his Gospel, saying: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, this is He who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1). “And I,” he says, “did not know Him.” The Spirit is said in a special sense to remain in Christ, from whom He never departed through sin, in whom He always lived and worked wondrously.

On seeing the dove, John says that through it he learned what he had not known before. He knew indeed that Jesus was Lord, that He was the Lamb taking away sins, and that he ought to be baptized by Him; for he had confessed this. But he did not know that Christ would retain for Himself, and entrust to no one, the power of baptism, though He would entrust its ministry. Thereby the unity of the Church is maintained, even if there are as many baptisms as baptizers.

Accordingly blessed Augustine says in Book IV of the *Sentences*, distinction 5, that the power of the Lord’s baptism was not to pass from the Lord to any human being, although its ministry would indeed pass on; the power from the Lord to no one, but the ministry to good and bad alike. Let not the dove shrink from the ministry of evil men, but look to the Lord’s power. What harm does a bad minister do you where the Lord is good? “Neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3). If the minister is proud, he will be reckoned with the devil; nevertheless, Christ’s gift will not be defiled, because what flows through him is pure. Water passes through a stone channel into garden-beds; nothing grows in the stone channel, yet the garden bears very many fruits.

Therefore not [Col. 0203A] only the good but also the bad possess the ministry of baptizing; but neither possesses the power of baptism. Christ gave His servants the ministry of baptizing, but retained the power for Himself. Had He wished, He could have given that power to His servants, so that the baptism of the servant would have as great an efficacy as the baptism of the Lord. But He did not wish this, lest a servant place his hope in a servant. There is no difference in the Lord’s baptism whether administered through a good or a bad minister; nor is it repeated, because it is always the Lord’s. John’s baptism is repeated because it is not the Lord’s, but a man’s. Judas’s baptism, however, is not Judas’s but the Lord’s, and is therefore not repeated.

Thus, in order that unity and brotherly peace may be preserved without tearing apart among all the baptized, as in one dove that groans amid this world’s miseries and brings to the ark a branch that is outside if it bears fruit, the Spirit in whom they are baptized is shown by a dove. But so that, possessing unity and peace, they may burn within themselves against temptations and impending evils, the Holy Spirit was afterward given to the Apostles in fire and in tongues divided according to the diversity of nations (Acts 2), which are now united through faith in Christ. Formerly they were divided from one language among the swollen-up builders—that is, the proud and haughty—who zealously persisted, against God’s will, in building the tower of Babylon.

Meanwhile I urge you, O Jews, who say that Jesus Christ is not true God but a mere man, to listen more attentively to what Matthew the Evangelist next adds concerning Him. “Behold,” he says, “a voice from heaven saying: ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3). I do not want you, O Jews, to pass carelessly over this most truthful testimony of God the Father; rather, for the salvation of your souls, ponder it with the greatest vigilance of mind. You therefore who until today have obstinately refused to believe the most certain testimonies of the Law and the Prophets that testify concerning Jesus Christ that He is true God and true man must give full credence with the greatest devotion to so manifest and most truthful a testimony of God the Father, which you cannot contradict in any way.

By this most truthful testimony of God the Father Catholic faith is undoubtedly strengthened, and your false assertion, by which you deny Christ, is most openly condemned. As your unbelief [Col. 0203D] is refuted by this testimony, so the superstition of the pagans is also rendered futile, and the faith of Christians, as has been said, is confirmed in every way. This statement, mentioned above, by which God the Father calls Jesus Christ His beloved Son from heaven, is the strength and firmest foundation of the whole Church, and an unconquerable defence against all temptations and deceits of Jews, pagans, and heretics.

Therefore, in saying, “This is My beloved Son,” God the Father contradicts you, O Jews, false witnesses who deny Him to be true God. How are you not false witnesses, when you contradict the mouth of the Lord, who has never lied?
