God the Father says: “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”; you say that He is not the Son of God, but of Joseph the carpenter. All the faithful also know most certainly that Joseph was not His father but His most faithful guardian and the most certain witness of His most holy mother’s spotless virginity. We therefore prove that you lie in this dispute, when you say that He is not true God, while God the Father openly declares from heaven that He is His beloved Son. For He is eternal light from eternal light, true God from God the Father, and coeternal with that same God the Father.

Since, therefore, you do not believe the testimony of God the Father that Christ is the true Son of God, you provoke from heaven against yourselves the wrath of that same omnipotent God the Father. You hasten, then, not toward life but toward eternal death, since you do not believe such manifest testimony pronounced by the voice of God the Father. Or [Col. 0204B] do you not know, O rebels and unbelievers, that you cannot at all attain God the Father, who is truly the highest and true Good, unless you faithfully believe Jesus Christ to be one true God with that same Father and the Holy Spirit? For He is true life, and without Him no one can attain eternal life. Nor can anyone come to the Father except through Him (John 14), because He is the door of the sheep (John 10). For this reason the Son of God was incarnate: that through Himself He might introduce us to faith and, in the future, lead us to the vision of His most glorious countenance.

Hence He Himself says in the holy Gospel: “If anyone enters through Me, he shall be saved; and he shall enter and go out, and find pasture” (ibid.). He shall enter, namely, into faith on the day of baptism; and he shall go out into vision on the day of death or on the day of judgment. He shall find pasture in eternal fullness. Therefore the Psalmist says: “May the Lord guard your going in and your going out” (Ps. 120). For the Lord guards the entrance of each soul, by which it enters into faith, and also its departure, by which it leaves the body to contemplate the vision of the divine majesty: so that neither, in entering the Church, it may be tripped up by the errors of heretics, nor, departing from this temporal Church to the eternal one, may it be snatched away by enemies. Therefore, O Jews, believe faithfully in Him, so that through Him, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14), you may attain God the Father and rejoice without end in the fellowship of His elect.

[Col. 0204D] The testimonies already mentioned of the holy Evangelists, namely John and Matthew, suffice for you, O Jews, to drive every uncertainty from your hearts concerning this: that the Son of God, for the redemption of humankind, assumed true sinless flesh from a Virgin Mother, and dwelt among men (Baruch 3); that John the Baptist also baptized Him in the river Jordan while crowds looked on (Matt. 3); that the Holy Spirit descended upon Him after His baptism in the form of a dove, John the Baptist seeing it (ibid.); and that God the Father bore testimony to Him from heaven in a voice that He is His true and beloved Son, and that in Him He was pleased above all people (Matt. 17).

Do you still wish to hear other testimonies to overcome your unbelief and confirm the truth of Catholic faith? We have already brought forward two suitable witnesses to Christ from the New Testament, the Evangelists John and Matthew. But because your hearts of stone have not yet been pierced by their most truthful testimonies so as to receive the most true faith of the Holy Trinity, let us again bring forward a third suitable witness to Christ from the New Testament—holy Luke—“who [Note: Col. 0205D. The words marked are from the prayer of the Church in the Office of St Luke the Evangelist.] continually bore in his body the mortification of the cross for the honour of God and man, Jesus Christ Himself”; and let us hear together what he says to us concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity.

Speak, holy Luke; speak of the Son of God and of the Virgin what you know, so that, pierced to repentance by your most truthful testimony and devoted to receiving the true faith, the Jews may unquestionably believe that, for the salvation of the world, He was born of a Virgin Mother under King Herod, suffered under Pontius Pilate, rose from the tomb on the third day, and, now exalted at the Father’s right hand, may worship Him with us in the utmost devotion. Speak then, O holy Luke, what you know concerning Christ, so that, convicted by your testimony, the Jews may cast the falsehood of error from their hearts and believe beyond doubt that Jesus Christ is the true Son of God. “And it came to pass,” he says, “when all the people were being baptized, and Jesus also having been baptized and praying, that heaven was opened; and the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in bodily form [Col. 0205C] like a dove” (Luke 3).

It should be known that the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in bodily form like a dove because, in the nature of His divinity, He could not be seen by mortals. Since the Son of God Himself also took a human body without sin from the incorrupt Virgin, the Holy Spirit descended upon Him in the form of a dove and remains in Him forever. For according to Solomon, “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1). Therefore He descended and remained upon Him because He alone among men lived without sin. The Spirit is thus rightly said to remain in Christ, from whom it never withdrew through sin; for He Himself never sinned, and in Him that same Spirit lives eternally and always works wondrously with Him.

The Holy Spirit comes into the saints and sometimes departs from them because of sin. Yet He remains in them in one respect: namely, that they may always persist in good works, as God and man, Jesus Christ Himself, promised them. But in another respect He does not remain in them: namely, so that they do not always prophesy or always work miracles. Thus the Evangelist’s statement, “The Holy Spirit descended and remained upon Him” (John 1), is properly the sign by which Christ is recognized. At this point I urge you, O Jews, to hear attentively the voice of God the Father Almighty bearing witness from heaven to Jesus Christ His Son. And a voice came from heaven, saying: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.” God the Father praises not something alien but His own proper things in the Son. As though He said: “Whatever You have is Mine.” Or more plainly: “You are My beloved Son, consubstantial and coeternal; in You I was pleased with what displeased Me in Adam. In You I established My good pleasure—that is, through You I decreed before all ages to do what pleases Me.”

It is plainly made clear that John the Baptist is second to none among those born of women: the Son of God and of the Virgin gave Himself to be baptized by John’s hands; the Holy Spirit displayed Himself in the form of a dove for John to see; and in John’s hearing God the Father praised the Son from heaven. For when God the Father says, “You are My beloved Son,” He does not show to His Son [Col. 0206B] Jesus Christ something which Christ did not know; rather, He makes known to John and the others present what they did not know. Hence John the Baptist, who had previously proclaimed Him as the stronger man, now, instructed, openly proclaims Him as the Son of God.

O Jews, behold three suitable witnesses from the New Testament: the three Evangelists John, Matthew, and Luke. By their most truthful testimonies they proclaim Jesus Christ to be the true Son of God the Father and of the Virgin Mother, and openly show that you, in your assertion by which you deny Him, have lied.

You, O unhappy and wretched Jews, who are you that you do not believe so many utterly truthful and competent witnesses affirming that Christ is true [Col. 0206C] God and true man? Yet it is no wonder that you give no credence to the proclamations of prophets and evangelists, since you do not believe almighty God the Father, who most plainly testifies that Jesus Christ is his beloved Son. Therefore, since you say that the three aforementioned sufficiently competent witnesses of the New Testament do not yet suffice for you to embrace the true faith of Christ, let us introduce a fourth witness—praiseworthy and truthful in every respect—the evangelist Mark, both to confute your utterly false disputation and to strengthen Christian hearts ever more firmly in the Catholic faith. Let us hear together, with all attentiveness, whatever he says to us about Christ, or whatever testimony he long ago delivered in his Gospel concerning him. For he was of such holiness, religious devotion, learning, and continence of life that he compelled all followers of Christ to live according to his example.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] These are Jerome’s words in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, which the Roman Breviary recites in his office as the first reading of the second nocturn.]

Come then, holy Mark, and say what you know about Christ, so that, just as in the time when you still lived in the flesh you invited all the children of the Church to live well by your example, so now by your most truthful testimony you may convert Jews and pagans to the true faith of the holy Trinity. “Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee,” he says, “and was baptized by John in the Jordan. And immediately, coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened and the Holy Spirit descending like a dove [Col. 0207A] and remaining in him” (Mark 1).

After the Flood it was not a raven but a dove that brought a branch announcing peace restored (Gen. 8), mystically teaching that the anointing of the Holy Spirit is present only to those baptized in simplicity of heart. It follows: “And a voice came from heaven, saying: You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased.” Behold how plainly the witnesses of truth agree with one another; behold how unmistakably they declare, by their most truthful testimonies, that Jesus Christ is without doubt the true Son of God, and most openly condemn the Jews and pagans who deny him. Hence that saying: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16).

These four aforementioned competent witnesses of the New Testament—that is, the four evangelists—[Col. 0207B] establish the Catholic faith by their holy proclamations and utterly nullify your false assertion, O Jews, and that of the pagans. By their preaching the holy Church is strengthened, and your faithlessness is openly overthrown. They instruct the whole Church by evangelical teaching, and prove that you are false witnesses in your objection, you who deny that Christ is the Son of God.

I want you to know, O Jews, that through these four competent and most truthful heralds of the New Testament, the very Son of God and of the Virgin waters his whole Church with spiritual waters, uproots heretical perversity, and mightily overcomes your madness and that of the pagans. For Moses in the book of Genesis typologically prefigured Jesus Christ, God and man, [Col. 0207C] when he said:

[Note: [Col. 0207D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 3.]

“A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Gen. 2). And again: “A river went forth from Paradise, which watered all the trees of Paradise” (ibid.). The river going forth from Paradise therefore bears the image of Christ, who, flowing from the paternal fountain—that is, from God the Father—waters the whole Paradise, namely the whole thirsty Church, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the word of preaching, and the dew of holy baptism. Of him it is aptly said through the prophet: “The Lord our God is a glorious river, leaping forth into a thirsty land” (Isa. 44).

The four rivers of Paradise, flowing from Jesus Christ, the great river, are the four Gospels, pouring forth over the whole world. Through [Col. 0207D] the four aforementioned competent heralds of the New Testament, and through their successors, the hearts of believers are continually watered with a spiritual infusion. Tell us, O Jews, if you know, why we have brought forward this statement from the prophetic utterance of Moses, or why we have inserted it into the foregoing reading. Surely it was in order to make known to us how great is the authority of these four aforementioned witnesses of Christ—that is, the holy evangelists—who wrote the Gospels of this same Jesus Christ, God and man, and sowed them in the minds of their hearers throughout the world as spiritual wheat, like good farmers upon rational soil. Since these spiritual [Col. 0208A] seeds came especially from the hand of the Lord, they therefore yielded a hundredfold fruit in the hearts of those who heard them. Great, then, is the authority of those through whom the Son of God and the Virgin wished his works, which he performed in this world for the redemption of the world, to be written and commanded to be made known to all people throughout the earth.

Moreover, “their sound went out into all the earth, and their preaching resounded to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). Therefore, as we have said, O Jews, the holy evangelists possess great authority: to them Jesus Christ, God and man, granted that they should write the deeds of his coming—the most holy mysteries, namely, of his incarnation, birth, manifestation, baptism, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven—and openly [Col. 0208B] preach them to others.

The prophet Ezekiel likewise foresaw that these most truthful witnesses and competent heralds of Jesus Christ would be in the holy Church, when he spoke of them figuratively: “I saw four living creatures full of eyes before and behind. The first living creature was like a lion; the second living creature like a calf; the third living creature had a face like a man; and the fourth living creature was like a flying eagle” (Rev. 4). That these four winged living creatures signify the four holy evangelists is attested by the beginnings of each Gospel book. Since Mark began with a cry in the wilderness, he is rightly figured by the lion. Since Luke began with a sacrifice, he is fittingly denoted by the calf. Since Matthew began with human generation, [Col. 0208C] he is rightly understood through the man. Since John began with the divinity of the Word, he is worthily signified by the eagle, for he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1).

Therefore, as we have said, O Jews, great is the authority of these four heralds of the holy Gospel, whom Jesus Christ, God and man, himself willed to be prefigured before he was born of the Virgin for the salvation of the world. Whoever faithfully receives their most truthful testimonies concerning Christ and fulfils them in deed may without doubt be joined to the children of the Church. But whoever refuses to believe them shall without doubt perish eternally.

[Col. 0208D] I therefore urge you, O Jews, to hear their testimonies attentively and believe with your whole heart; for if you remain in unbelief, you will by no means be able to be saved. But now let us again hear what testimony they gave above concerning Christ, what they said, how—although separated from one another in different provinces—they agreed in their truthful declaration, and how, as though taught by the Holy Spirit with one mouth, they bore witness to the word of God: “When Jesus had been baptized, he immediately came up from the water; and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and coming upon him. And behold, a voice from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am [Col. 0209A] well pleased.”

I urge you, O Jews, who deny that Christ is the Son of God the Father, to listen more carefully to what is said. This voice, which came down from heaven and was heard by men—namely by John and by the crowds who had flocked to his baptism—is beyond doubt the voice of God the Father. But let us hear what this voice of God the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Without any ambiguity, he of whom God the Father himself says, “This is my beloved Son,” is the natural Son of God the Father. For in adding, “in whom I am well pleased,” he seems to show that he was displeased in all other people. Thus he himself speaks in Genesis in human fashion, saying: “I repent that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6). Thus, as it were, he was displeased with himself in the sinners whom he created, when he said that he regretted having created them. In our Lord Jesus Christ alone, the only-begotten, he was well pleased, because among all people he found him alone without sin.

Speak, holy John the Baptist; speak of Christ what you know, so that by your testimony the Catholic faith may be strengthened against the subtleties of heretics and Jewish faithlessness may be confuted. “He who sent me,” he says, “to baptize in water, told me: He upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining—this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1). Speak still more plainly, John, in a clear voice, whether you saw him, so that the Jews who deny him, convicted in their assertion, may with faithful minds believe that he is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and may devoutly receive his baptism. “I saw,” he says, “and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

I urge you more attentively, O Jews, to hear carefully what is said, lest, through the hindrance of the evil of obstinacy—God forbid!—you depart empty from this most sacred reading. “And,” says the evangelist, “a voice came from heaven, saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” John therefore saw the Spirit descending in the form of a dove and remaining upon Christ, now baptized; he also heard God the Father saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Consider, O Jews, enemies of truth, how great a grace was disclosed to believers in the baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ, when under such a sacrament the Trinity revealed itself to a man—[Col. 0209D] namely, John—for the strengthening and instruction of its whole Church. For the Father is heard in the voice; the Son is manifested in the man; the Holy Spirit appears in the form of a dove.

By what wonderful mystery did our Lord Jesus Christ, through the touch of his body and the passage of his glory, sanctify and illumine his creation for a moment? For he consecrated the waters in baptism; he consecrated the earth when he was placed in the tomb, and glorified it when he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father. But as the Spirit descends upon the Lord, let us see, O Jews, and carefully attend to what follows. “Behold,” says the evangelist, “a voice from heaven saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” Therefore, because the Son [Col. 0210A] of God is baptized as man, the Spirit of God descends in a dove, and God the Father is present in the voice, the mystery of baptism declares the holy and indivisible Trinity. And rightly so: he who was about to command the ministers of his sacraments, “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), first personally disclosed the whole Trinity in his own baptism.

In this voice of the Father also, as in the other mysteries of the Lord’s baptism, the fulfilment of all righteousness is declared. For the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, is made known to men by the Spirit descending upon him, so that through this people may learn that, through the grace of baptism and upon receiving the Holy Spirit, they can be transferred from being children of the devil to being children of God, as the Apostle teaches, speaking thus to believers: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

I want you to know, O Jews, that John the Baptist had previously said: “After me comes a man who was made before me” (John 1); now he bears witness that “this is the Son of God,” most plainly designating both human and divine natures in one and the same person. Let Manichaeus blush on hearing, “After me comes a man who was made before me,” he who said that Christ possessed not a real body from the Virgin Mother but a phantom body. Let the Valentinian heretics, so called from a certain Valentinus, follower of Plato, be silent: they asserted that Christ assumed no bodily substance from the Virgin, but passed through her as through a pipe. Let also the [Col. 0210C] Allogian heretics fall silent when they hear the voice of God the Father saying, “This is my beloved Son.” They are called Allogians as though “without the Word”; for *logos* in Greek means “word.” They do not believe in God the Word, rejecting the Gospel of John and the Apocalypse.

Let the Photinians, named from Photinus, bishop of Smyrna in Galatia, blush when they hear John the Baptist say: “I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (ibid.). For these Photinians assert that Christ was conceived from Mary through marital intercourse with Joseph; but they lie altogether, since he was conceived in the Virgin not from human seed but from the Holy Spirit. You likewise, O unhappy Jews, be silent, you who say that he was not true God but merely man, on hearing God the Father testify concerning him and say in a clear voice: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

“Let the meek hear and rejoice” (Ps. 33)—that is, the Christian peoples—because after John came a man stronger than John, who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. Why? Because this is the Son of God. Perhaps, O Jews, you ask us: Why, as you say, did the Son of God wish to assume flesh from a woman, when, abiding in his majesty with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, he could have redeemed the world? To this we answer: the Son of God mercifully became man because we had long ago departed from God through pride, so that he, through divinity, might correspond to the Father, and through humanity might correspond to us: through a humanity [Col. 0211A] like ours, he might fight for us against the enemy; through a divinity consubstantial with the Father, he might worthily restore us to the image and likeness of God, which we had lost by sinning. Through the death of our frailty he might destroy him who held the power of death; and through the impassible power of his divinity he might reconcile us to God the Father, with whom he abides eternally in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

I should like to know, O Jews, whether, having now cast off the faithlessness of your long-standing unbelief, you are willing with devout mind to believe the faith of the holy Trinity—one God in Trinity and threefold in unity—or whether you still intend to persist in the evil of your unbelief. Surely so great a number of witnesses, and such utterly truthful testimonies of the Law and the prophets, interpreted and expounded according to the rule of true faith, ought beyond doubt to suffice for you, so that you should never again doubt concerning Christ whether he is true God and true man, but should believe faithfully and firmly.

§ XI.—

**From the sayings of Genesis: the Word of God the Father incarnate for the salvation of human beings.** Just as no human being can be perfectly equated or made like God, so no one else could free the human race from eternal death. What was fulfilled historically in Adam is signified prophetically in Christ. The old Adam prefigured the new Adam; so too righteous and innocent Abel prefigured him in his righteous deeds and death, whose sacrifice is accepted. Cain is rejected; Cain recognizes his rejection; his curses apply to the Jewish people, whose type he bore. Slain by Lamech in the seventh generation, [Col. 0211C] the Jewish nation, marked with his sign, is received everywhere.

But if any scruple of doubt still remains in your minds as to whether he is not the true Son of God, let us hear what Moses says concerning him under the person of the first man, Adam. “The Lord God took man,” he says, “and placed him in the Paradise of delight, to work and keep it” (Gen. 2). These words, undoubtedly understood spiritually, signify the Word of God the Father, incarnate for the salvation of humankind, placed in the Church. God the Father therefore took the man—that is, the Word coeternal with himself, made flesh from the incorrupt Virgin—and placed him in Paradise, that is, in the Church: namely, he established him as the head of all believers. [Col. 0211D] Why? Namely, that he might work and keep it; that is, by the will of the Father he might build the Church from all nations, and that the saying might be fulfilled which Jesus Christ, God and man, himself spoke to God the Father in the Gospel: “Father, I kept them; those whom you gave me I guarded” (John 17).

God also said: “It is not good for man to be alone” (Gen. 2). Let the heretics who think that Christ was alone—that is, merely man and not also true God—be confuted. In this passage too, O Jews, your unbelief is reproved and convicted, you who deny that the Word of God the Father assumed human nature, when God the Father plainly says: “It is not good for man to be alone.” Truly, according to the judgment of almighty God, it would not be good for man to be alone; for, if he were alone, [Col. 0212A] he could neither overcome diabolical temptations, nor conquer the devil himself, the prince of all wickedness, nor return to the delights of Paradise, from which he had been cast out, nor recover the grace of God which he had lost through sinning.

Therefore, O God, make for him a helper, so that, helped by this aid, he may overcome sins and vices, love virtues, mightily conquer the strong and armed prince of this world (Luke 11), love you above all things and cling to you, ascend to heaven, and come to you. God therefore said: “Let us make for him a helper like himself.” In saying not in the singular but in the plural, “Let us make for him a helper,” almighty God showed that the divine essence has three persons, not one. God likewise made a helper for man when, by the Father’s will, God the Word descended into the womb of the undefiled Virgin and joined human nature to himself.

“Let us make,” he says, “for him a helper like himself.” Without doubt, in no respect can a human being be perfectly equated or likened to God; but it is said, “Let us make for him a helper like himself,” because God and man are one person and one Christ for the redemption of the world, chosen out of the whole mass of the children of men. Concerning his beauty, the holy Church rejoicing and exulting exceedingly in the Song of spiritual love says: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5). Concerning him also God the Father says through the prophet: “Behold my servant, my chosen one; my soul is well pleased in him” (Isa. 42). As though he said more plainly: “Behold my servant according to his humanity; [Col. 0212C] my chosen one, because I chose him to redeem the human race and acquire for me the holy Church; my soul is well pleased in him, because before all other people I found him uniquely without blemish.”

Let almighty God therefore say concerning the Incarnation of his only-begotten Word: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.” God the Father accordingly made a helper for man when he sent the Word, coeternal and consubstantial with himself, begotten of himself before all ages, and joined human nature to him in the womb of the Virgin; namely because in that assumed man he united the holy Church to God.

It follows: “Adam called all the living creatures, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the earth, by their names [Col. 0212D].” “The first man,” as the Apostle says, “is earthly, from the earth; the second is heavenly, from heaven” (1 Cor. 15), namely Christ. The second Adam—that is, Christ—therefore gave his names to all the living creatures, the birds of heaven, and the beasts of the earth, signifying the nations that would be saved in the Church and would receive through him the name which they previously did not possess, as he himself says through the prophet: “I shall call my servants by another name” (Isa. 65), namely, Christian.

But for Adam himself—that is, for the Son of God and the Virgin—no one like him was found, because however faithful and righteous anyone may be, no one can be made equal to him. To him the prophet David says in the Psalms: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there is none according to [Col. 0213A] your works” (Ps. 85). For no one could deliver the human race from eternal death except Christ, as the blessed apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “No one was found worthy, neither in heaven nor on earth nor beneath the earth, to open the book and loose its seals” (Rev. 5).

God also sent a sleep upon Adam; and when he had fallen asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled its place with flesh. And the Lord built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman. The first Adam sleeps, and a rib is drawn out of his side, from which a woman is formed; Christ suffers upon the cross, his side is pierced with a lance, and the sacraments flow forth, from which the holy Church is formed. King David and prophet foresaw this sleep in the Spirit, when, rejoicing in the person of this same Son of God and the Virgin, he said: “I slept and began to sleep; and I arose, because the Lord sustained me” (Ps. 3).

He adds again, saying: “And the Lord filled with flesh the place of the rib which he had taken from Adam’s side.” So also Christ gave his flesh upon the cross for the holy Church. “And the Lord built the rib which he had taken from Adam into a woman, and brought her to Adam, that he might see what he would call her.” And Adam—the second Adam, namely Christ—said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” because whether they are holy men, spiritual and strong in temptations, or less perfect persons, both are nevertheless one body of Christ and one Church. “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.” [Col. 0213C] All these things therefore happened as a figure of things that would be beneficial in the Church. “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Interpreting this, the Apostle says: “But I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5).

Therefore, what was fulfilled historically in Adam was signified prophetically in Christ, who proceeded ineffably from God the Father when he says: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16). He also left his mother, namely the Synagogue, which clung carnally to the Old Testament and was his mother from David’s seed according to the flesh; and he cleaved to his wife, that is, the holy Church, which he acquired with his own blood. And the two are in the peace of the New Testament, in one Spirit and in one flesh [Col. 0213D].

You have heard, O Jews, how clearly the old Adam prefigured in certain of his deeds the new Adam, namely Jesus Christ, God and man; and how, while he slept upon the cross, the holy mother Church proceeded from the wound in his most sacred side and, redeemed, grew through spiritual increase. Therefore do not doubt that he whom you to this day deny with proud and obstinate mind is true God and true man; and believe without doubt that he was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world.

This stubborn and, so to speak, adamantine faithlessness of your unbelief was prefigured in his evil deeds by hateful [Col. 0214A] Cain. Although he killed his innocent and righteous brother Abel, he nevertheless did not humbly repent that he had acted wickedly; rather, with an obstinate mind he despaired of God’s mercy, saying: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve forgiveness” (Gen. 4). Hear also, O rebellious and unbelieving ones, how plainly righteous and innocent Abel prefigured Christ and the whole Christian people redeemed by him, both in his righteous works and in his death. Hear therefore the history of Cain and Abel attentively, and grasp it in your minds not according to the letter but according to spiritual understanding, so that, having recognized the truth—which is Christ—you may not perish with the unbelievers but may, by right belief, attain eternal joys with the children of the Church. [Col. 0214B] Therefore understand attentively their history as expounded spiritually, so that in every respect the Catholic faith may be strengthened and your lying assertion shown altogether false.

[Note: [Col. 0213] All this is from Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 6; Aerialius’s annotations there should certainly be consulted.]

The birth of Adam’s two sons, as has been said, bore the figure of two peoples, namely Jews and pagans, who were to come from their stock at different times to the true faith. Abel was a shepherd of sheep, and Cain a farmer. But just as Cain’s offering from the fruits of the earth is rejected, while Abel’s sacrifice from sheep and their fat is received, so the faith of the New Testament, praising God from the grace of innocence, is preferred to the earthly works of the Old Testament. Why did God turn his eyes from Cain’s sacrifice? Namely, because he did not offer it out of [Col. 0214C] charity. And unless charity had been in Abel, God would never have accepted his sacrifice. For when both had offered sacrifice to God—Cain from the fruits of the earth and Abel from the offspring of the sheep—let no one suppose that God disregarded the fruits of the earth and loved the offspring of sheep. “Man sees the face; God sees the heart” (1 Sam. 16). God therefore did not attend to the hands of the offerer, but looked inwardly at the heart; and when he saw someone offering with charity, he regarded that person’s sacrifice; but when he recognized someone offering with envy, he turned his eyes from that person’s sacrifice.

Here the question is raised: How could Cain know that God had accepted his brother’s gifts and rejected his own? It must be said in reply that, in the sacrifices of the ancient [Col. 0214D] fathers which were acceptable to God, fire came down from heaven and immediately consumed them. Fire therefore descended upon Abel’s sacrifice and did not descend upon Cain’s gifts. For Cain, as stated above, bore the type of the greater people, namely the Jews; while Abel bore the figure of Christ and the Christian people.

Cain was very angry, and his countenance fell. Cain said to Abel his brother: “Let us go out into the field.” And when both were in the field, Cain rose up against his innocent brother Abel and killed him (Gen. 4). Thus Abel was killed in the field, Christ at the place of Calvary. Hear, O foolish Jews, [Col. 0215A] who often have the Law and the prophets in your hands and yet do not hold their spiritual meaning, but zealously seek a carnal sense—hear what God said to Cain, who bore the type of you all: “If you offer rightly and do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” As though almighty God said to you more plainly, O Jews: “If formerly you did some things rightly in the Law, nevertheless you are guilty of unbelief, because, when Christ came from the bosom of God the Father for the redemption of the world, you no longer distinguish the time of the New Testament from the time of the Old Testament.”

But if Cain had obeyed God saying, “Be quiet; its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it,” he would have ruled over sin, rather than sin ruling over him; being a slave of sin, he would not have killed his [Col. 0215B] innocent brother.

[Note: [Col. 0215D] This negative particle is superfluous. Isidore reads: “If it had not ruled over him, he would not have been a slave of sin, nor would he have killed his brother,” etc. But our Martin preferred to follow Augustine.]

Likewise the Jews, in whose figure these things were done, if they rested from their disturbance and recognized the time of salvation through grace and the remission of sins, would hear Jesus Christ saying: “I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Luke 5).

God questions Cain, not as one ignorant and needing to learn from him, but, knowing him as a judge knows the accused whom he is to punish, he says: “Where is Abel your brother?” He replied that he did not know and was not his keeper. Likewise you, lying Jews, are accustomed to answer us, when we question you about Christ by the voice of God—that is, of the holy Scriptures—that you do not know Christ. Cain’s lying answer is your false denial. You would in a manner be Christ’s keepers, O Jews, if you received the Christian faith with devout mind [Col. 0215C] and kept it by living well.

God also said to Cain: “What have you done? The voice of the blood of your brother Abel cries to me from the earth.” So too concerning you, O Jews, the very Son of God and the Virgin complains through the prophet Jeremiah, saying: “The house of Judah has dealt treacherously against me, says the Lord. They have denied me and said: He is not” (Jer. 5). Again he cries through Isaiah: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who do not believe and contradict me” (Isa. 65).

[Note: [Col. 0215D] The words we note are Augustine’s, *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 10. But why the author inserted them here we do not know. For since they allude to the old [Col. 0216D] rite according to which those receiving sacred Eucharistic communion answered “Amen” to the priest, they seem not very appropriately placed here—unless someone should say, though this cannot easily be proved, that this custom still prevailed in the twelfth century. Our Martin, however, closely translated Isidore.]

For Christ’s blood has a great voice upon the earth when, having been received faithfully and devoutly, all nations answer: “Amen.” Again God said to Cain: “You shall be cursed from the earth, which opened [Col. 0215D] its mouth and received the blood of your brother from your hand.” You too, O Jews, are cursed from the earth—that is, from the Church—which opened its mouth in confession of sins and received the blood of Christ, poured out for the remission of all sins, while you crucified him.

God also said to Cain: “When you cultivate the earth, it shall not yield its fruit to you.” As though God the Father said more plainly to you, O Jews: “When you have cultivated the earth by crucifying Christ—that is, when you have worked the salvation of the whole Church in the earth of his body—it nevertheless shall not give its fruits to you, that is, its power, but to faithful Christians.” You have not been justified by the power of Christ’s resurrection, “who died for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4). Without doubt, if you had faithfully believed in him, you could have obtained from him the fruit of that earth—namely, of his passion and resurrection—that is, the salvation of your souls. It follows:

“Wandering and fugitive,” he says, “you shall be upon the earth.” You too today, O Jews, are wandering and fugitive upon the earth—that is, scattered among all nations. You wander and are dispersed through the loss of an earthly and heavenly kingdom, because you denied Christ before Pilate when he judged that he should be released [Col. 0216B] (Acts III). Because you deny Christ, promised to you through the prophets and sent from heaven by God the Father for the redemption of the human race, what you feared has therefore happened to you: you have lost both place and nation. You are therefore unhappy, O Jews: fugitives from Jerusalem and scattered through every region under heaven. Or, as it is written in the Septuagint interpreters: “Groaning,” the Lord says to Cain, “and trembling you shall be upon the earth.” And now who does not see, who does not recognize, that this rebellious and stiff-necked people is dispersed throughout the whole world, wandering from good works and fugitive from the land of promise? Who does not see how it groans with sorrow at its lost kingdom, and trembles with fear of suspected death [Col. 0216C] among countless Christian and pagan peoples?

And Cain said to the Lord: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve to be forgiven. Behold, today you drive me from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face; and I shall be wandering and fugitive on the earth. Therefore everyone who finds me will kill me.” The Jewish people groans as a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth, fearing temporal death more than eternal death. For it does not think it grievous to have God angry with it, because it thinks not spiritually but carnally. In this, O Jews, enemies of righteousness, it is apparent that in the divine Scriptures you seek not a spiritual understanding but a carnal meaning: because you judge it more grievous that, having lost the land of promise, you grieve and groan as wanderers and fugitives amid earthly hardships, than that the land [Col. 0216D] of Christ’s body does not give you its fruits—namely, remission of sins and eternal reward. Cain grieved carnally for his guilt and the evils which he suffered in the present age, and not spiritually.

“Everyone who finds me,” Cain says, “will kill me.” But let us hear what the Lord answered him. “By no means,” he says, “shall this happen; but everyone who kills Cain shall be punished sevenfold”; or, as the Septuagint interpreters rendered it: “Everyone who kills Cain shall pay seven [Col. 0217A] punishments.” As if he said: You shall not die as you suppose, nor shall you receive death as a remedy; rather, you shall live to the seventh generation, and you shall always be so tormented by the terror of death that whoever kills you will free you from great suffering. This does not mean that the person who kills Cain will be subjected to seven punishments, but that he who kills Cain—who had rightly been left to punishment—will discharge the seven punishments which had pursued Cain for so long, when Cain himself is killed. As our elders think, Cain was killed by Lamech in the seventh generation.

Moreover, God placed a mark upon Cain, so that not everyone who found him might kill him. This is indeed very remarkable: all the nations which were subdued by the Romans passed over into the rites, sacred observances, and ceremonies of the Romans, receiving them to be observed and worshipped sacrilegiously. But the Jewish nation, whether under pagan kings or under Christians, has not lost the mark of the Law and circumcision by which it is distinguished from other nations and peoples. Rather, every emperor or king who finds them within his kingdom finds them with that very mark, and does not kill them.

Cain therefore went out from the face of the Lord and dwelt in the land of Naid, which is interpreted as “commotion,” or “unstable,” or “wavering,” and “of uncertain abode.” Hence the Psalmist entreats God, saying: “Do not [Note: [Col. 0217D] Isidore has: “Do not give my feet into movement,” apparently from Psalm 120, where Augustine consistently reads: “Do not give my foot to be moved.” The other part, “and let not the hand of the sinner move me,” is from Psalm 35, except that Isidore says “of sinners,” as do Ambrose and many others cited by Sabbatier [Col. 0218D], as does the Mozarabic Psalter in the new edition of the Breviary.] give my feet into commotion, and let not the hand of the sinner move me.” Therefore, just as Cain went out from the face of the Lord, so you also, O [Col. 0217C] Jews, who stubbornly resist the most true Truth—that is, deny the Son of God—go out from the face of God: that is, from the sweetness of God’s love and participation in his light. You dwell as fugitives in the land of commotion, that is, in the turmoil of this fluctuating age and of carnal desire, contrary to the delight of God—that is, contrary to Eden, which in Hebrew is interpreted as “delights” or “feasts,” where paradise is planted.

It has been shown to you clearly enough, O Jews, how plainly Cain prefigured the malice of your unbelief, and his innocent brother Abel foreshadowed Christ in his death. Cain, prompted by envy, killed his righteous brother Abel, as you heard above; and you, goaded by envy, fastened innocent Christ to the cross without cause. And because [Col. 0217D] you acted so proudly toward the giver of the Law himself and judge of all, you have therefore lost place and nation; and, as you see, you wander throughout the world, destitute of good works, and are scattered as fugitives from the land of promise. We plainly know, and do not doubt at all, that if you had known the Lord of glory himself, you would never have crucified him (1 Cor. II). But because you did this in ignorance, as did also your rulers (Acts III), if you turn to God with your whole heart and do fitting repentance before him for so great a sacrilege, you may obtain forgiveness from him. But if [Col. 0218A] you choose to persist in your unbelief, you will without doubt perish eternally.

Therefore believe that the Son of God and of the Virgin himself, whom you have hitherto denied, is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, so that through him—who is the way, the truth, and the life (John XIV)—you may be able to attain the joys of eternal life. Thus, as we have already often testified, Jesus Christ, God and man, was prefigured from the beginning of the world by the figures of the patriarchs, foretold by the testimonies of the Law, foreshown by the prophecies of the prophets, and openly displayed by the proclamations of the apostles and evangelists. For the Old and New Testament proclaims him to be true God and true man; to have been sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world; to have suffered for the sins of the human race [Col. 0218B]; to have risen on the third day; now to sit at the right hand of God the Father; and thence to come to judge the living and the dead. If you faithfully believe all these things which we have said beforehand, aided by his help you may attain ever-green pastures with his faithful sheep, whom he himself acquired for God the Father by his most precious blood.

## XII

Melchizedek prefigures Christ, true God and man, in deed and name. The most chaste union of Christ and the Church was prefigured in Sarah and Abraham; from it she bore spiritual children destined for the joys of eternal blessedness. David’s testimony is introduced, that they may believe him to be the Church’s most faithful bridegroom and true God, and may not, through their unbelief, be excluded from the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. The history of Hagar with [Col. 0218C] Ishmael is adduced, exhorting them to return to the holy Church, humble themselves under her hand, and finally merit, with Christ as their guide, to arrive at most delightful loveliness.

[Note: [Col. 0218D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 11.] But if you still doubt in any respect that he is true God and true man, listen carefully, I urge you, to how plainly Melchizedek, king and priest, prefigured him in deed and name. For sacred Scripture relates that Melchizedek himself, priest of God Most High, was begotten of unutterable parentage. The Apostle Paul, calling him “without father, without mother,” refers him figuratively to Christ (Heb. VII). For Jesus Christ, God and man, alone is begotten of the Father without a mother in respect of divinity, and of the mother without a father in respect of humanity.

[Col. 0218D] He is also the eternal priest, to whom David the prophet says in the Psalms: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). Christ is called an eternal priest according to the order of Melchizedek, namely because of the sacrament of the mystery which he commanded Christians—that is, his whole Church—to celebrate: that we should offer in sacrifice not animal victims according to Aaron, but the offering of bread and wine, that is, the sacrament of the body and blood of the same Lord Jesus Christ. And because [Note: [Col. 0218D] The sense becomes clearer if read: “For this reason the true great patriarch,” etc.] the great patriarch gave Melchizedek the priest tithes of all [Col. 0219A] his substance after receiving the blessing (Gen. XIV), he knew spiritually that the priesthood among the people of the nations would be better than the Levitical priesthood. He also knew that Israel would be born from himself and that it would come about that the priesthood of the Church, possessing uncircumcision, would bless, in Abraham’s circumcision, the priesthood of the Synagogue. For he who blesses is greater than he who is blessed (Heb. VII). Hence priests born from the seed of Abraham blessed their brothers—that is, the people Israel—and that people gave them tithes according to the commandment of the Law, truly as to their greater and more eminent persons.

The name itself, Melchizedek, is interpreted “king of peace and righteousness.” This fittingly refers to Christ, who, after his resurrection, ascended into heaven, sits [Col. 0219B] at the right hand of God the Father, and became high priest for ever. For he is king of peace because through him we are reconciled to God the Father. He is also king of righteousness because he came for this purpose: to separate the holy from the ungodly. He is likewise one priest and king, because for the redemption of all he offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father; he governs his people as true king in the present age, and in the future will judge justly.

More clearly than daylight, O Jews, it is established that Christ is the true Son of God the Father: him whom the patriarchs foreshadowed from the beginning of the world in figures and enigmas, whom the holy prophets foretold would come, and whom the apostles and evangelists openly proclaimed had already come and lived among them. By these authorities—namely, O Jews, the figures and enigmas of the patriarchs, [Col. 0219C] the testimonies of the Law, the prophecies of the prophets, and the most true proclamations of the apostles and evangelists—the faith of Christians is without doubt strengthened in every respect, and the faithless treachery of your unbelief, by which you deny Christ to be the true Son of God, is wholly convicted.

Therefore, as the authorities of the Old and New Testament truthfully bear witness to him, the Word, coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, descended mercifully from the bosom of that same Father for the redemption of the human race into the virginal bridal chamber—that is, into the Virgin’s womb. There he united to himself human nature, namely the holy Church, not phantasmatically, as heretics falsely say, but truly and mercifully. Later [Col. 0219D] he redeemed that same nature, according to that humanity, by his most precious blood; and, ascending after his Passion to God the Father, from whom he had come forth, he opened for it the entrance to the heavenly homeland, and placed that same human nature in himself at the right hand of God the Father. If you believe with devout mind in this union, by which the Son of God adopted the holy Church, without spot or wrinkle, as his bride (Eph. V), O Jews, you may be saved with the children of that same Church; but otherwise you cannot at all attain the salvation of your souls.

But so that you may not doubt that what we say is true, let us recall the history of the patriarch Abraham and his wife Sarah [Col. 0220A], and examine more attentively how clearly this most sacred and most chaste union of Christ and the Church was prefigured in them. After the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Abraham sojourned in Gerar. He said of Sarah his wife, “She is my sister,” fearing that he might die on account of her beauty (Gen. XX). Abraham therefore concealed [Note: [Col. 0219D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 16.] that Sarah was his wife and said that she was his sister, lest, after he had been killed, she should be possessed as a captive by strangers; for he was certain concerning God that he would not permit her to be violated, just as he had not permitted it formerly by Pharaoh in Egypt.

But Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent and took her. Then God came to Abimelech in a dream by night and said to him: “Behold, you shall die because of the woman whom you have taken, for she has a husband.” But Abimelech had not touched [Col. 0220B] her. And he said: “Lord, will you destroy even an ignorant and righteous nation? Did he not himself say to me, ‘She is my sister’? And she said, ‘He is my brother.’ In the simplicity of my heart and the cleanness of my hands I did this” (ibid.). Thus Abimelech, warned in sleep by the Lord as was said, did not defile her, but restored her untouched to her husband.

Yet who was figured then in that man, Abraham? And whose wife is she who, in this pilgrimage and among foreigners, is not allowed to be defiled, so as to remain for her husband without spot and without wrinkle? For the Church rightly lives in the glory of Jesus Christ, so that her beauty may be an honor to her husband, namely Jesus Christ himself, just as Abraham was honored among foreigners because of Sarah’s beauty. To her the heavenly Bridegroom himself says in the song of spiritual love: “You are altogether beautiful, my beloved, and there is no spot in you” (Song IV). Kings rightly offer gifts to the beauty of the Church—that is, to her dignity and holiness—as Abimelech offered to Sarah, marveling in her more at the splendor of her form than he could love; he could not violate her.

For the holy Church is secretly the wife of the Lord Jesus Christ. Secretly and hiddenly, the spiritual soul clings to the Word of God, so that the two may be one flesh; and the Apostle especially commends this as the sacrament of marriage in Christ and the Church (Eph. V). Therefore the earthly kingdom, namely that of this world, whose figure was borne by those kings who did not dare to defile Sarah, did not experience the Church, nor recognize that the Church herself was Christ’s spouse, except when it attempted to violate her. For it yielded to the divine testimony through the mystery of faith, because it was unable to corrupt or violate the faith of the holy Church. Thus, in later kings the earthly kingdom, corrected, honored Christ’s bride—the holy Church—with gifts, though in earlier kings it had not been able to subject her to its corruption.

Then Abimelech said to Abraham: “Why did you say that she was your sister?” Abraham replied: “She is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, but not of my mother, and therefore I took her as my wife” (Gen. XX). As if the Son of God said more plainly concerning the holy Church joined to himself: Therefore the holy Church is my sister, the daughter [Col. 0221A] of my Father, because God the Father, whose eternal Son I am, has adopted her through me as his daughter. Hence that saying of David: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). And John the Evangelist says in the Gospel: “He gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name, who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God” (John I).

“She is the daughter,” he says, “of my father and not of my mother; and therefore I took her as my wife.” As if he said openly: Truly, the holy Church is my sister, who through the grace of adoption and through the water of the sacred font is the daughter of God my almighty Father. And she is not the daughter of my carnal mother—that is, the Synagogue—which begets not spiritual children for God but carnal children for the world. Since therefore the holy [Col. 0221B] Church, my sister, has put off the old man with his deeds and faithfully believes me to be the true Son of God the Father, she is now no longer the daughter of the earthly father Adam, but of the spiritual Father, God. The first man, formed from earth, begot earthly children; the Son of God, coming from the Father’s bosom and uniting human nature to himself, made them heavenly.

Let Jesus Christ, God and man, then say of the holy Church, his sister: “She is my sister, the daughter of my Father and not the daughter of my mother; therefore I took her as my wife, because she begets not carnal children, as the Synagogue was accustomed to do, but spiritual children.” For the Word of God rightly calls the holy Church, made new through grace, the daughter of his Father and his sister, and not the daughter of his mother—that is, of the Synagogue, made old through transgression of the Law [Col. 0221C]—because the fact that the Son of God himself was willing to be incarnate for the redemption of the world must be ascribed not to the merits of human nature but to the gift of divine grace.

The same God and man, Jesus Christ, also summons this holy Church, through Solomon, to his affection and love, calling her not only “sister” but also “bride”: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have mingled my myrrh with my spices” (Song V). Therefore, when the Church is said to be Christ’s sister from the Father and not from the mother, this commends not a kinship of earthly generation, which will be abolished, but one of heavenly grace, which shall remain eternally. By that grace we shall no longer be a mortal race, having received power to be called and to be children of God (1 John III). For we received this grace not from the Synagogue, Christ’s mother according to the flesh, but from God the Father.

Christ teaches us to deny, rather than acknowledge, this earthly kinship in the present life, in which we all die, when he says to his disciples: “Call no one your father upon earth; for one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XXIII). The reason why it is concealed from foreigners whose wife the Church is, but not concealed whose sister she is, readily suggests itself: it is hidden and difficult to understand how the soul is joined or mingled with the Word of God—or, as may better and more plainly be said, since that Word is God and the soul is a creature. In this respect [Col. 0222A] Christ and the Church are called bridegroom and bride, or husband and wife. But that all the saints are Christ’s brothers by kinship, not earthly consanguinity but divine grace—that is, from the Father and not from the mother—is expressed more accessibly and heard more readily. For all the saints are brothers among themselves through that same grace.

Therefore, O Jews, you ought without hesitation to believe that the Son of God descended from heaven for the salvation of the world, united the holy Church to himself, and begot from her spiritual children destined for the joys of eternal blessedness. Strive earnestly to enter that same holy Church faithfully, so that, reborn in her spiritual womb from water and the Holy Spirit and cleansed from all sins, you may be numbered among the children of God [Col. 0222B] (John III). Thus he is the true Son of God and of the Virgin, O Jews: he who betrothed the holy Church to himself in most chaste embraces, from whom he daily begets new children and continually sends them to the heavenly homeland.

Of him the holy Church herself, the most chaste mother of all Christians, rejoicing in the Song of Spiritual Love, says: “My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices, that he may feed in the gardens and gather lilies” (Song VI). The Church’s beloved, namely Christ, goes down into his garden, to the bed of spices, because when he visits the Church, he comes in greater grace to those whom he knows, through holy works and examples of virtues, to send forth from themselves to their neighbors the fragrance of a good reputation. Christ, the Church’s bridegroom, feeds in the gardens [Col. 0222C] when he delights in the fruits of many souls. He gathers lilies when he cuts down from this life each of the perfect.

Therefore the holy Church, as has been said above, is united in her children to Jesus Christ, her bridegroom, by faith; is upheld by hope; and is bound together by love, so that she may love nothing outside Christ her bridegroom, and may hold him as inseparable from herself through faith and spiritual love. Therefore, O Jews, receive Christ’s baptism with devout mind in the name of the Holy Trinity within the bosom of that holy Church, so that with faithful Christians you may happily attain the reward of the heavenly homeland.

You ought therefore, O Jews, to believe without hesitation that Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of the holy Church, is the true Son [Col. 0222D] of God the Father and of the Virgin mother, and is naturally one God with that same Father and the Holy Spirit: containing, ruling, governing, ordering, and embracing all things. Before all ages God the Father ineffably begot him from himself. In the time of grace, the incorrupt Virgin, overshadowed by the power of that same Most High, her Father, conceived him from the Holy Spirit without sin and bore him without pain—indeed, with the greatest exultation and joy. After the triumph of his most victorious Passion and resurrection, God the Father established him as prince of all kings and exalted him at his right hand above everything created.

And lest you doubt, O Jews, that this is as we say—you who to this day with stubborn spirit deny that he is [Col. 0223A] true God—let faithful David, from whose seed according to the flesh he proceeded, come forward and set forth what God the Father foretold concerning him before he was born of the Virgin. Speak, holy David; speak concerning Christ what you learned through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, so that the Jews, enemies of truth, convicted by your most true testimony, may cast from their hearts the unbelief of deadly obstinacy and believe the Church’s most faithful bridegroom to be true God.

Speak, therefore, holy David: what did God the Father foretell concerning him? “I,” he says, “will make him my firstborn, exalted above the kings of the earth” (Ps. 88). As if God the Father said more plainly of that same only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ: “I will make”—that is, establish—him firstborn above the other human beings whom I have exalted in honor, and I will make [Col. 0223B] him exalted above the kings of the earth. This has now been wholly fulfilled in his resurrection and ascension. And because this power is not temporal but eternal, he adds: “I will keep my mercy for him for ever,” namely when perpetual power in heaven and on earth was given to him (Matt. XXVIII); “and my covenant [shall be] faithful to him,” because everything foretold concerning him through the prophets was wholly fulfilled in him. Or the covenant—that is, the promise of the eternal inheritance—is faithful to him, because he is the mediator, that is, the signer, guarantor, and witness, of that covenant.

It follows: “And I will establish his seed for ever and ever [Col. 0223C]”—that is, the Christian seed—“and his throne as the days of heaven.” The throne of earthly kings is like the days of earth, which pass away; but the days of heaven are always present, where the throne of that same Son of God and the Virgin is for eternity.

More clearly than daylight, O Jews, it is established that Jesus Christ is true God, whom God the Father established higher than all the kings of the earth. It is plainly established that, if he were not true God, God the Father would by no means have given him all power in heaven and on earth, nor exalted his throne, like the days of heaven—that is, eternally—above everything created. Thus, in calling him firstborn, God the Father plainly shows him to be not a creature, as you Jews blasphemously assert, but the Creator. And in establishing him higher than all the kings [Col. 0223D] of the earth, he plainly shows that he suffered for human salvation, rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and was exalted by him at his right hand.

Also, in adding that his seed shall remain eternally, he plainly shows that Christ’s evangelical teaching is sown by him throughout the whole world in the hearts of those who hear it; that the heavenly homeland is attained through the multiplied fruit of souls; and that it shall not be changed until the end of the world, as the traditions of the Pharisees have been changed. For in saying that he will establish his throne as the days of heaven, God the Father openly shows him to be true God and to have given him all judgment (John V).

Therefore, by the testimony stated above, O Jews, God the Father clearly demonstrates Jesus Christ his Son to be true God, and most plainly proves you, who deny him with a stubborn mind, to be false witnesses. I am greatly afraid, O Jews, and deeply dread that, because of the obstinacy of your unbelief, you may lose your dwelling in the heavenly homeland. Because you fastened Jesus Christ, God and man, to the cross without cause, you have therefore been expelled from the land of promise and scattered throughout the world without honor, subjected to insults and diverse injuries. I therefore fear that, just as you were expelled from Jerusalem because of his most sacred blood, which you demanded upon yourselves and upon your children and cruelly caused to be shed, so also [Col. 0224B] because of your unbelief you may be shut out from the inheritance of the heavenly homeland.

Without doubt, if you remain in this unbelief and refuse to obey my saving warnings, Hagar will be cast out with her son Ishmael (Gen. XXI)—that is, the Synagogue with all of you—from a share in Abraham’s seed, namely from the fellowship of the children of God, that is, Christians, and from the inheritance of the heavenly homeland. Nevertheless, if it pleases you, let the truthful history of that time be brought forward; and, spiritually expounded, let us all listen together more attentively to what it says for the instruction of us all.

[Note: [Col. 0223D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 17.] Abraham was already one hundred years old when Sarah his wife bore him a son, whom he called Isaac. When his mother saw him playing with Ishmael, [Col. 0224C] she said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (ibid.). We must now ask why Sarah had formerly wished her husband to receive a son by the slave-woman, or why she now commands that he be expelled from the house together with his mother. This, as we believe, she did not from jealousy but under the compulsion of prophetic mystery. For Hagar, as the Apostle says, bore in slavery the people of the Jews. But free Sarah bore the people called not according to the flesh but in the freedom with which Christ called it (Gal. IV).

This mystery therefore prefigured that the Jewish people, born into slavery to sins, would not remain for ever in Sarah’s house—that is, in the Church—nor be an heir or a companion to the worshippers of Christ, nor possess the kingdom of heavenly glory together with the noble son, that is, with the faithful people. When Abraham therefore cast Hagar out of his house, he took loaves and a skin of water, gave them to her, placed the child upon her shoulder, and dismissed her. Going out, Hagar wandered through the wilderness of Beersheba. And when she had cast her son, dying from thirst, beneath a tree, an angel of the Lord appeared to her, showed her a spring of water, and gave her son to drink (Gen. XXI).

What does this signify, O Jews—that, as Hagar went out, she placed the child upon her shoulders—except that you, foolish and wicked people, then burdened the neck of the Synagogue, your mother [Col. 0225A], when concerning Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, you irreverently cried out to Pilate: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII)? The loaves indicated that the old priesthood, just as it bore and offered the loaves of presentation, so also fed upon them. But the skin of water, which failed, signified your defective purification, O Jews, or your carnal teaching enclosed in dead skin—that is, in the flesh of the old man condemned by the sentence for transgression—which gives neither refreshment nor quenches thirst, but, lukewarm in heat, produces vomiting.

Hagar’s wandering in the wilderness with her son Ishmael signifies the unbelieving Synagogue with her son—that is, with the Jewish people, with all of you, O Jews—expelled from its own land and wandering over the whole world without [Col. 0225B] king, Law, priesthood, altar, or sacrifice, and wholly ignorant of the way which is Christ. That Hagar’s son began to die, afflicted by thirst, signified you Jews, enfeebled through transgression of the Law and unbelief of mind, possessing no spiritual purification. That she cast her son, dying from thirst, beneath a tree and, when the angel showed her, saw a spring, foreshadowed some among you, O Jews, who would one day obtain the refreshment of eternal salvation beneath the shadow of the wood of Christ’s cross.

That the boy cried weeping and the Lord heard him, and that, as the angel showed him, he thus saw a spring, prefigured those Jews who turn to Christ and, weeping for their past errors, are heard; and, once the eyes [Col. 0225C] of their hearts have been opened, see the spring of living water, that is, Christ the Son of God, who says: “Who [Note: [Col. 0225D] The order of these passages has been disturbed; it should be restored thus: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John VII.37). “Whoever drinks of the water which I shall give him . . . shall become in him a spring [Col. 0226D] of water leaping up into eternal life” (John IV.13).] believes in me, as Scripture says, shall become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.” And again: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” Hence Ishmael is interpreted “hearing.” The angel himself bore the figure of Elijah, through whom the Jewish people will believe near the end of the world, as the Lord says through the prophet Malachi: “Behold, I will send you Elijah, who shall turn the hearts of the fathers to the children” (Mal. IV), etc.

But the angel’s immediate summons to Hagar, saying, “Arise, take the boy, for I will make him into a great nation” (Gen. XXI), signifies either that the Jewish people itself would become numerous and widely propagated [Col. 0225D], or that those among them who would believe in Christ would attain the glory of the heavenly kingdom. Since Scripture first shows that the one speaking to Hagar was an angel and then calls him God, it must be believed that he was the Son of God, who always spoke through the Law and the prophets. He is called an angel because he announces the will of God the Father to humankind. Wherever throughout the whole course of the Old Testament an angel is said to have been sent, neither God the Father nor the Holy Spirit is to be understood. For nowhere do we read that God the Father was sent.

Of him we read that God the Father said to the Israelite people: “I [Note: [Col. 0226D] This sentence appears to be composed from several verses of Exodus 23—namely vv. 20, 21, 22, 23, and 27.] will send my angel before you, and I will kill every people into whose land you enter.” And again: “Observe and hear my voice, and I shall be an enemy to your enemies, and my angel shall go before you.”

Plainly it has been shown to you, O Jews, how clearly Ishmael with his mother Hagar prefigured the Jewish people and its mother the Synagogue, and how he was cast out with her from the share in the seed of Abraham and Sarah—that is, from fellowship with the sons of God and the holy Church. You therefore need no other interpreter on this matter; for, as you see with your own eyes, so it will happen to you as it was prefigured in them. Ishmael with his mother Hagar was cast out [Col. 0226B] from the house and inheritance of Abraham and Sarah; and you also, O Jews, have been cast out with your mother the Synagogue from communion in the Church’s sacraments and from the society of God’s elect.

But now let us hear what the angel said to Hagar. “What are you doing here, Hagar?” She answered: “I flee from the presence of Sarai my mistress” (Gen. XVI). Hagar fled from the presence of Sarai her mistress; and you also, O Jews, flee from the presence of the holy Church. For you withdraw far from the house of Abraham—that is, from the holy Church—when, in pride of mind, you refuse to receive Christ’s Gospel and the Church’s sacraments. Indeed, you depart far from the bosom of the holy Church in despising to receive with devout mind the catholic, that is, universal faith and the baptism of Christ.

I do not wish you to be unaware, O Jews, enemies of truth, that the holy Church sharply rebukes you for the hardness of your hearts’ unbelief precisely because she desires you to be joined to the ranks of God’s elect. Yet you not only refuse to receive her saving teaching, but—what is more damnable for you—by finding fault, blaspheming, and uttering utterly false words, you withdraw far from her presence together with your mother the Synagogue. But do not be unwilling, O Jews, to hear what the angel said to Sarah’s handmaid—that is, to your mother the Synagogue: “Return,” he says, “and humble yourself under the hand of Sarai your mistress.”

As though the angel himself, who truly bore the figure of Jesus Christ, God and man, were saying more plainly to your mother the Synagogue: “Return, O Jewish people, [Col. 0226D] truly without counsel and without spiritual prudence; at last return and humble yourself beneath the hand of your mistress—namely, the holy Church, bride of almighty Jesus Christ.” As though he said: “O Jewish people, humble yourself under the hand of the holy Church: faithfully receive the evangelical teaching with your ears; meditate upon it constantly in your heart; carry it out in holy works; fulfil it by living well; reject the observance of the carnal law; humbly and faithfully receive baptism within the bosom of that same holy Church, in the name of the holy Trinity, namely, of the Father [Col. 0227A] and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; confess to God and to the Church’s priests, with tears, the crimes and offences of your former life; humbly accept the penance imposed upon you by them; strive to fulfil it with the utmost devotion, so that through the same Son of God and of the Virgin, who is truly ‘the way, the truth, and the life’ (John XIV), you may attain the joys of eternal life, which you lost by denying that same God and man, Jesus Christ.”

“Return,” says the angel, “Hagar, to Sarai your mistress, and humble yourself under her hand.” As though he said more plainly: “O Jews, sons of the Synagogue, return to the holy Church, your mistress, which is truly your mistress through the merits of spiritual virtues and through purity of faith and devotion; humbly [Col. 0227B] submit yourselves to her governance. Be obedient to her in all things and receive her teaching with devout mind, so that, faithfully joined to the fellowship of her children, you may deserve, with Christ as your guide, to reach the pleasant—indeed, most pleasant—delight of Paradise.”

And so that you may know for certain, O Jews, enemies of truth, that unless you faithfully and humbly submit yourselves to the Church’s sacraments, you can by no means be saved, we urge you patiently to hear how the holy Church, through Solomon, admonishes your mother the Synagogue with all her children to withdraw from unbelief and to be converted as swiftly as possible to the catholic faith.

“Return, return, return, return, that we may look upon you” (Cant. VI). For *Sunamitis* is interpreted “captive woman.” [Col. 0227C] Your mother the Synagogue, O Jews, is called by the Church for this purpose: that she may come to her senses from the devil’s snares, by which she is held captive at his will, and return by faithfully believing in Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world. For the holy Church greatly pities your miseries and therefore unceasingly pours out prayers to God for you, that you may return to the catholic faith. She also deeply grieves for you because you are dispersed through the four quarters of the world, without altar, without sacrifice, without law, without king, and without shepherd—that is, without Christ, the supreme high priest.

Therefore let the Shulamite—that is, the Synagogue—come forth from the devil’s captivity with all her offspring, return to the holy mother Church, [Col. 0227D] and receive worthy penance for her former unbelief, so that she may not perish with unbelievers but may possess eternal life with the children of that same holy Church.

Therefore believe without hesitation, O Jews, that Jesus of Nazareth is true man and true God, whom God the Father sent into this world to redeem the human race. He, as has often been said, was begotten by God the Father from himself before all ages; the holy patriarchs foreshadowed him, to be born of a virgin, by figures and riddles; the prophets, taught by the Holy Spirit, foretold his coming; and the holy apostles and evangelists openly preached that he had already come.

[Col. 0228A]

§ XIII.—

The patriarch Noah prefigured Christ by his deeds. For just as neither Noah nor those with him could be saved from the danger of the flood except through the ark, so neither could the human race be saved except through baptism and the sacraments of the Passion. Indeed, Noah prefigures Christ suffering and crucified for humanity’s salvation, and mocked by Ham’s son. Shem and Japheth, covering their father’s nakedness, are blessed; Ham is cursed. Isaac’s sacrifice prefigures the Son of God and the Virgin suffering for the redemption of the human race. He admonishes the Jews that, just as an ass always needs a goad and straw, they should be stirred by fear of eternal damnation as by a goad, cast out sluggishness and asinine laziness, and receive faith through desire for eternal reward.

[Note: [Col. 0227D] Isidore, ibid., chap. 7.]

I therefore admonish you, O Jews, who in pride of mind deny that he has already come, diligently to hear how clearly the patriarch Noah prefigured the Son of God and the Virgin [Col. 0228B] in his deeds. For Noah is interpreted “rest.” The same Jesus Christ, God and man, says of himself: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

Noah alone is found righteous in that generation, and seven souls are entrusted to him in one ark; likewise Christ alone is found without sin in the whole human generation, and the seven Churches, because of the sevenfold illuminating Spirit, are granted by God the Father in one Church, lest they perish with this world. The wood and water by which Noah is delivered from danger of death signify Christ’s cross and baptism. Therefore, just as Noah and his household are saved through water and wood, so Christ’s household is delivered through baptism and the passion of the cross [Col. 0228C] from everlasting condemnation. Noah built the ark from incorruptible wood; Christ built the Church from human beings who shall live for ever. For that ark prefigured the holy Church, which floats amid the waves of this world—that is, amid dangers and afflictions.
