Moses was tending the sheep of Jethro, his kinsman, priest of Midian; and when he had driven the flock to the inner parts of the wilderness, he came to Horeb, the mountain of God. The Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush. Moses saw that the bush was burning and was not consumed (Exod. III). The Lord said to Moses: “I have seen [Col. 0254B] the affliction of my people. But come, I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may lead my people out of Egypt” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0254D] Isidore, ibid., ch. 7.] The Lord appeared, then, to Moses in a bush when sending him to a people whom he foreknew would be wicked; and there was a flame in the bush—that is, among thorns—yet the bush was not burned. The bush signified the thorns of the Jews’ sins. The flame in the bush, then, is the precepts of the Law in the Jewish people, because the Law was given to them as a flame. Thus the flame in the bush openly showed that, though the Law was given, the Jews’ sins were not consumed. As the bush was not burned under the fire, so the transgressions of the Jews were not perfectly corrected even under the Law. Since, then, the Law perfectly purified no one’s sins, it could not, as stated above, open the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0254C] to anyone, O Jews. I want you to know, O Jews, that those who were circumcised under the Law according to the Lord’s command could not enter the gate of the heavenly kingdom immediately after death. Rather, placed in blessed rest in Abraham’s bosom, they awaited with happy hope entrance into heavenly peace. They most certainly believed that Christ, who had given the Law, would come; and they longed with supreme desire for him to grant them the blessing—that is, permission to enter the heavenly kingdom and behold the God of gods, namely himself together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit in highest Zion (Ps. LXXXIII). But now, after the passion and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, all who receive with devout and faithful minds baptism in the name of the holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and [Col. 0254D] live soberly, justly, and piously (Titus II), when they depart this world arrive without doubt, by a blessed passage, at the heavenly homeland. For this very purpose the Son of God descended from the Father’s bosom: mercifully to redeem humankind through the cross and, first, to open the gate of the heavenly homeland to those obedient to him. The first Adam, by sinning, cast his posterity down with himself into hell; the second Adam, coming from the Father’s bosom, restored his elect to liberty and carried them with himself into heaven, where he himself first ascended. This is why I return so often to speaking with and admonishing you, O Jews: because I deeply grieve for [Col. 0255A] your misfortune. Carnal circumcision, therefore, as stated above, does not suffice for attaining eternal blessedness; nor does it admit observers of the Law to the vision of heavenly peace, but rather excludes them from it.

I do not wish you to be ignorant, O Jews, that all legal precepts were ended in Christ’s death. From that time circumcision, as has been said, lost its force, so that it thereafter did not benefit its observers but harmed them instead. For observance of the Law could be beneficial until the offering of the true sacrifice. If the legal precepts had ended before the Lord’s passion, he himself would not have eaten the old Passover with his disciples when that passion was imminent.

Now, therefore, O Jews, the Son of God long ago descended from the Father’s bosom; now for the redemption of the world he took sinless human nature from the Virgin; he mercifully endured the passion of his most sacred body, not unwillingly but by voluntary choice, for our redemption; he swallowed up and destroyed death; he powerfully conquered the prince of darkness and shattered the gates of hell; he drew out the saints who were held there; on the third day he truly rose from the dead; he brought into heaven with himself those whom he recalled from the lower regions to the heights; and he himself ascended to the right hand of God the Father.

What do you say to this, O Jews? What do you answer? Do you still doubt Christ’s coming and his divinity? Do you still not believe that he has already come and redeemed the world through the cross? Have you still not been confirmed in the catholic faith and perfected in Christ’s charity, though instructed by so many testimonies of the Law, taught by so many prophetic oracles, and admonished by so many proclamations of the evangelists? Know for certain that, with God’s grace going before me, accompanying me, and following after me, I shall grant you neither silence nor rest until I prove by the most true testimonies of the holy Scriptures, with manifest reasoning, that you who stubbornly deny that he has come or was true God are false witnesses.

What then do you say, O Jews? What do you answer, or what do you object? This is your answer. You say that Jesus of Nazareth, whom Pilate crucified at the request of your fathers, could by no means [Col. 0255D] rise from death. To this we answer in opposition that without doubt the Son of God descended from the Father’s bosom and took from the undefiled Virgin a sinless human body, in which, according to his humanity, he truly underwent passion and death and rose on the third day. Therefore, to prove that you have lied in your objection, let us introduce and expound spiritually the most true figure in the book of Exodus of Christ’s most merciful death and resurrection. Listen, therefore, most attentively to what the Lord said to Moses on Mount Horeb: “Go down into Egypt, that you may lead my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt.” Moses answered: “What sign [Col. 0256A] shall I show them, that they may believe that you have sent me?” (Exod. III). The Lord said to him: “Cast the rod which you hold in your hand upon the ground.” He cast it down, and it was changed into a serpent. Moses was afraid and fled. The Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” He took hold of it, and it again became a rod (Exod. IV). The rod signified Christ, to whom it is said through the Psalmist: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV). [Note: [Col. 0255D] Isidore, cited above, ch. 8.] The serpent likewise signified death. The serpent persuaded humankind to death; death, therefore, comes from the serpent. Thus the rod changed into a serpent is Christ changed into death. Yet Moses was afraid and fled. What did Moses’ fleeing from that serpent signify except what we read happened in the Gospel? Christ died, and all the disciples, leaving him, fled [Col. 0256B] (Matt. XXVI). But what was said again? “Take hold,” he says, “of its tail.” What is the tail except the posterior parts of the body? This signified what the Lord said elsewhere to Moses: “You shall see my back parts” (Exod. XXXIII). Christ was first made a serpent in death; but, when the tail was grasped, he became a rod, because he was killed and then, by rising, returned to what he had been. There, through the restoration of life, death having been consumed, nothing mortal any longer appeared in him, because “death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Thus the Son of God and of the Virgin died, according to that same human nature which he had assumed without sin, because of our crimes; and he rose for our justification. Therefore the aforesaid figure of the Old Testament plainly prefigures that God-and-man Jesus [Col. 0256C] Christ would suffer for human salvation and rise from death; and it openly proves you false witnesses in your objection, since you assert that he did not come, did not suffer, did not die, and did not rise on the third day.

O crooked and perverse nation, O foolish and senseless people, is this how you repay the Lord your Creator, who created you from nothing? O unbelieving nation, why do you deny him who chose your fathers—the patriarchs and prophets—as his special people, delivered them from the house of bondage, freed them from Egypt’s iron prison, fed them manna from the clouds for forty years in the wilderness, uprooted mighty kings and many nations before them, and settled them in the land of promise? Finally, in order to redeem humankind, he took flesh from their offspring, freely endured passion and death, rose on the third day, and, the same true God and true man, ascended to the right hand of God the Father. Why, then, O Jews, are you ungrateful for such great benefits from him? Almighty God had bestowed a great dignity upon your ancient fathers—the patriarchs and prophets—above all peoples under heaven, when he said of them: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV). But your fathers lost the privilege of so great an authority when they not only refused honorably to receive Jesus Christ, specially sent to them by God the Father, [Col. 0257A] but even delivered him to death without cause. You also, following your fathers’ blindness and denying that Christ has already come and was true God and true man, render yourselves not only unworthy of such great gifts of God but also liable to eternal condemnation. For this reason you lost the land of promise and were scattered throughout the world as reprobate and sacrilegious persons. Jacob the patriarch, filled with the spirit of prophecy, foresaw as future both this election of the patriarchs, prophets, and all those who lived justly and piously before Christ’s coming, and your shameful rejection, O Jews, after Christ’s passion, when he spoke with a kind of indignation to his firstborn son Reuben:

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my sorrow; first in gifts, greater in authority. You are poured out like water; do not increase, because you ascended your father’s bed and defiled his couch” (Gen. XLIX). Jacob the patriarch seems to have displayed in Reuben the person of the former people. For according to what was due to firstborn sons at that time, he was to receive the priesthood or kingship. [Note: [Col. 0257D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] It follows: “You are my strength.” Certainly because from that people the foundation of faith proceeded, and from it came the power of God, which is Christ. But in what way is the Jewish people itself “the beginning of sorrows,” [Col. 0257C] unless because it continually inflicted injury upon God the Father, turned its back and not its face toward him, and frequently provoked him to wrath? This people of the Jews is first in gifts, because to them were first entrusted the oracles of God (Rom. III), the giving of the Law, and the promise of the covenant was first made to them. It is greater in authority, certainly because of its great power and royal nobility, by which that people flourished in the times of David and Solomon. Again Jacob adds: “You are poured out like water,” namely by sinning against Christ. It is as though he said: You are poured out like water which is not contained in a vessel because of the force of its movement. He also added: “Do not increase any more.” The Jewish people deserved the curse that it should increase no further because it fastened Jesus [Col. 0257D] Christ to the cross without cause. Since that people has been scattered throughout the world, it has been greatly diminished and despised. But he shows why the Jewish people deserved to suffer such things when he immediately adds: “Because you ascended your father’s bed.” This was not said of the past, as you falsely claim, O Jews, because Reuben slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine (Gen. XXXV); rather, it must be understood of the future. For at the beginning of this prophecy the holy patriarch said to his sons: “Gather together, that I may declare to you what shall come to pass in the last days” (Gen. XLIX). Therefore what he foretold would happen must not be believed to refer to the past. [Col. 0258A] It must be understood to have been said concerning Christ’s passion. For Jacob already foresaw in the Spirit Christ’s passion and the most impious audacity of the Jewish people, who shamelessly approached the bed of God their Father and, as it were, defiled his couch when they suspended on the cross, wounded with iron, and stained with blood the most holy body of Jesus Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge and in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. II).

Therefore true enough is that saying, O Jews, which the book of Job declares: “Wisdom is commonly found among the aged” (Job XII). In the ancient patriarch Jacob, then, truth and wisdom were found, the spirit of prophecy teaching him inwardly. He knew with certainty that Christ would come and suffer for the salvation of the human [Col. 0258B] race; and, under the person of his firstborn Reuben, he cursed the Israelite people, his firstborn son, from whom he foresaw that Christ’s venerable, glorified, and adored passion would be celebrated in the last days. Touched inwardly by the grief of his heart and drawing deep sighs from his inmost breast, he said: “Do not increase any more.” Why, holy Jacob, do you curse with such severe and weighty punishment the Israelite people to be born from you? Why do you strike your offspring, whom you do not yet see with bodily eyes, with so cruel a sentence of cursing? Why is a people not yet born into the world already bound by the chain of a curse? Tell us, then, why that people deserved so grave a sentence of cursing, when it had as yet [Col. 0258C] done neither good nor evil in this world and had not transgressed the Law of God’s commandments. Why did you so emphatically forbid your firstborn son—the Israelite people—to increase any further, when you had not yet found it guilty of any actual sin?

[Col. 0258D] What answer, O Jews, did the righteous and holy patriarch Jacob give to these things? What testimony did he utter concerning you, who nailed Christ to the cross without cause? For what reason did he pronounce upon you a sentence of such weight? Let us all hear together. “For this reason,” he says, “I curse, under the person of my firstborn son Reuben, that Jewish people which shall descend from the seed of my loins: because I know beforehand that in the last days it will commit deeds of dreadful wickedness.” As though he said more openly: “For I know that after my death it will act wickedly and in many matters oppose the divine dispensation. For it will be stiff-necked and proud, rebellious and contentious against the Lord. Moreover, what will be more grievous and more condemnable, in the last days—that is, when the fullness of time has come—it will ascend the bed of God, its Father, namely the body of Jesus Christ, in whom it pleased God to dwell, and in whom God the Father himself was well pleased (Matt. XII); it will pierce it with nails and wound it with a lance. And,” he says, “you have defiled his bed.”

Here the most holy patriarch speaks of the future as though of the past. [Col. 0259A] As though he openly said to that same Jewish people which was to commit so great a sacrilege: “You will defile the bed of God your Father; that is, you will attempt to defile that same body of Jesus Christ, God and man, in which all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God rest (Col. II); you will pollute it with unclean spittle, outrage it with blasphemies, dishonour it with insults, shame it with reproaches, and repeatedly assail it with curses. For he will glorify God his Father; but you, foolish and senseless people, will dishonour him.” Therefore that dishonouring itself is understood as the defilement of the bed of God the Father—that is, of the most holy body of Jesus Christ. Since, then, taught inwardly by the prophetic Spirit, I foresaw that in the last days you would carry out the evils mentioned above, [Col. 0259B] I therefore cursed you so emphatically and forbade you to increase further.

What do you think, O Jews? What do you say, or what answer do you give to these things? Do you doubt that this most true sentence of so great a patriarch has already been fulfilled? Do you not plainly recognize that you are the source of that grief because you nailed Christ to the cross without cause? Why also, unhappy and miserable people, do you not understand that, from the day when you suspended on the cross the Son alike of God and of the Virgin, you have not increased, but on that account have been diminished more than all nations? Therefore, O Jews, believe without doubt that Christ has already come, since you plainly recognize that the evils with which the patriarch Jacob threatened you have overtaken you in your wickedness. [Col. 0259C] From the day when, as has been said, you dishonoured Jesus Christ, God and man, you have made no progress toward better things, but have always fallen into worse.

If, then, you wish to escape Jacob’s curse and attain the salvation of your souls, believe without doubt that Jesus Christ, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God. If you also desire to grow in his chaste fear and love in this present age and the age to come, do true repentance before him for the past treachery of unbelief, and receive his baptism with devout mind in the name of the supreme and undivided Trinity. You, therefore, who until now have been occupied with earthly and transitory affairs, must now, though late, be concerned for eternal salvation.

[Col. 0259D]

§ XVIII.—

He shows the way in which one must proceed through the wilderness with Moses, so that, rescued from Egyptian slavery, they may attain salvation. Moses prefigured by the rod the Word made flesh, who suffered for human salvation and rose again on the third day. The patriarch Jacob, when blessing his son Issachar, foresaw by the prophetic Spirit the Christian people faithfully serving God and attaining eternal rest. That God and man could be seized and bound, crucified and die, was prefigured when Moses commanded the Passover to be celebrated. He explains how the blood of the spotless lamb ought to be placed upon the lintels and both doorposts. He advises the Jews to strive to enter the holy Church, adorned with heavenly gifts, which the patriarch Jacob [Col. 0260A] prefigured when he addressed Zebulun, and which follows the footsteps of Christ its Redeemer. The wonderful pillar which went before the Israelite people prefigured Christ. He openly attacks, by the words of blessed John, the blindness of Jewish unbelief, which the pillar of cloud that overshadowed the camp by day prefigured.

We have long ago reproved you for your spiritual good because, when Abraham and Isaac of old proceeded to the place of sacrifice, you did not accompany them: that is, you did not believe that the Lord Jesus Christ truly suffered, died, and rose on the third day for the redemption of the world, but remained a long time with the ass—that is, you have persisted in the folly of your unbelief until the present day. At least now, going out of Egypt with Moses and all the children of Israel, proceed, according to the Lord’s command, [Col. 0260B] three days’ journey into the wilderness, that you may there sacrifice to God.

[Note: [Col. 0259D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 11.] I wish you to know, O Jews, that this way on which you must travel for three days is Christ, so that, departing from Egypt—that is, from the incitements of vices and the corrupt manner of carnal life—you may reach the place where you must offer sacrifice to God. This way, therefore, is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). On this way we and you alike must travel for three days. For whoever confesses in his heart that Jesus is the Son of God, and believes without any doubt that God raised him from the dead on the third day, and adorns this faith with good conduct, shall nevertheless be saved, [Col. 0260C] because he offers to God a sacrifice well pleasing to him.

Otherwise: “We shall go three days’ journey to sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Exod. III). We shall go, namely, by faith, hope, and charity to sacrifice to the Lord our God through contrition of heart, confession of the mouth, and satisfaction in deed. This is the way of three days, by which one reaches the place where sacrifice is offered and a sacrifice of praise rendered to God (Ps. CVI). Therefore, O Jews, walk faithfully by this most straight way—that is, through Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin—so that, rescued from Egyptian slavery, that is, freed from the dominion of the ancient enemy, you may by right belief attain the place of sacrifice, that is, the salvation of your souls.

But let us now see what Moses said among other things to Pharaoh. “We shall go,” he says, “three days’ journey [Col. 0260D] through the wilderness, and we shall sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians” (Exod. VIII). For the Egyptians disdain to eat sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate, the Israelites offer to God. For the simplicity of conscience which the citizens of Egypt—that is, the wise of this world—regard as folly, righteous people sacrifice to God and thereby strive to please God, because they regard as rejected and contemptible in this world what the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound [Note: [Col. 0259D] Rather, “wisdom” or “the wise,” as Isidore, whom Martin transcribes, and all the others read here [Col. 0260D]; for “the strong” corresponds to “the weak,” not to “the foolish,” whose opposite is “wisdom.”] the strong” (I Cor. I).

[Col. 0261A] I should like to know, O Jews, whether, now that deadly unbelief has been removed from your hearts, you believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man, or whether you still doubt his divinity, by which he is coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father. In answer you say that you cannot at all believe either that he was true God or that he has already come. To this we, on the contrary, reply that he was naturally begotten from God the Father before all ages, and that, in the time of grace, he assumed from the incorrupt Virgin the natural substance of flesh for the redemption of the world. Thus he has from God the Father the natural substance of divinity, and from the Virgin Mother the true nature of flesh.

And so that you may not doubt that what we say is true, listen carefully as we explain how the rod of Moses prefigured this same Jesus Christ, God and man, [Col. 0261B] as suffering for the salvation of humankind and rising again on the third day. [Note: [Col. 0261D] Isidore, in the place cited above, ch. 12.] Thus, as the history of that time relates, Moses, at the Lord’s command, threw down his rod in Pharaoh’s presence; it was changed into a dragon and devoured the rods of the magicians (Exod. VII), signifying that in the last days—that is, in the time of grace—the Word would become flesh and would destroy the serpent’s dreadful poisons, that is, the devil’s dominion. The rod signifies the Word of God the Father, that is, Christ: the Word, I say, upright, royal, full of power, distinguished by sovereignty. To him it is said through the Psalmist: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of thy kingdom” (Ps. XLIV).

The rod, therefore, became a serpent, because he who was the Son of God, born of God the Father before all ages, became the Son of Man—that is, [Col. 0261C] of the Virgin—born from the Virgin at the end of time. Exalted upon the cross like a serpent, he poured healing into human wounds. Hence the most merciful Redeemer of the human race himself says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John III). The rod of Moses, changed into a dragon, swallowed the rods of the magicians; and Christ became obedient to God the Father unto death, even death upon the cross (Phil. II), and through that death of the flesh consumed—that is, destroyed—the sting of death, as he himself testifies and strongly threatens through the prophet Hosea: “O death, I will be thy death; I will be thy bite, O hell” (Hos. XIII).

[Col. 0261D] Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, O Jews, is true God and true man. The holy patriarchs before the Law foreshadowed with the clearest figures and enigmas his coming for the redemption of the world; the prophets, instructed by the Holy Spirit, unanimously foretold that he was ineffably begotten of God the Father before all ages and would be born in time from the incorrupt Virgin, would suffer, and would rise on the third day; and the apostles and evangelists openly preached that he had already come and redeemed the world. Receive his baptism, therefore, O Jews, with devout mind, so that with faithful Christians [Col. 0262A] you may through him—without whom no one can be saved—attain the salvation of your souls.

For the Christian people believe him, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, to be one true God; they serve him faithfully; they have laid upon themselves with all devotion his easy yoke and light burden; and after him they run with the highest desire toward the heavenly homeland. The patriarch Jacob undoubtedly foresaw by the Spirit of prophecy that the Christian people would serve God faithfully, be obedient in all things, and receive eternal rest from that same omnipotent God, when, blessing his son Issachar, he said:

“Issachar is a strong ass lying down within the boundaries of the sea. [Note: [Col. 0261D] Here perhaps the word *inter* (“between”) has dropped out, which neither Isidore nor anyone else has, since it is certain that no tribe except Zebulun dwelt between the bounds of the sea.]. He saw that rest was good, and that the land was excellent; and he bent his shoulder to bear, and became a servant under tribute” [Col. 0262B] (Gen. XLIX). [Note: [Col. 0262D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.]

Issachar, as has been said, whose name is interpreted “reward,” refers to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord Jesus Christ purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is called a strong ass because the Gentile people was formerly like a brutish and lustful animal. But now it is truly strong, submitting its neck to the yoke of the Redeemer of the world and bearing the light burden of evangelical discipline. Dwelling by the bounds of the sea, it saw that rest was good and the land excellent. To lie down by the bounds of the sea is to rest while awaiting the end of the world, to seek nothing of those things now passing in the midst of the world, but to desire the last things. And the strong ass sees eternal rest to be excellent [Col. 0262C] when simple Gentile faith raises itself to the strength of good work precisely because it tends toward the homeland of eternal life. Hence it also sets its shoulder to bear, because, while it desires to reach the promised rest, it willingly bears all the Lord’s commandments. Thus it became a servant under tribute: that is, offering to its eternal King, Jesus Christ, the gifts of faith and the offerings of good works.

Why then, O Jews, do you stand idle all day? (Matt. XX). That is, why have you remained idle from good works from the time of Christ’s passion until the present? You do not keep the Law; you do not receive the Gospel; you are not Jews—that is, confessors of Christ—and you do not wish to be Christians. Since, then, you have remained so long a time in this world devoid of the fruit of good works, it is at last necessary that you submit yourselves with devout mind to the evangelical sacraments together with faithful Christians. [Col. 0262D] Therefore drive from your hearts the long-standing hardness of unbelief, and strive faithfully to enter the gate of the holy Church with its faithful peoples. Take upon yourselves, with the patriarch Issachar, the easy yoke and light burden of Jesus Christ (Matt. XI), so that you may obtain pardon for your unbelief and attain, by his working, the reward of the heavenly homeland.

What do you say to these things, O Jews? What do you oppose, or [Col. 0263A] what do you answer? We urge you to show us of what will or what faith you are. If you already believe Christ to be true God and true man, and to have suffered for the salvation of the whole world, you do rightly; but if you still doubt concerning him, make this known to us. This is your answer and objection: you say that, if Christ, as we have often testified, were true God and true man, he could by no means have been seized, bound, scourged, crucified, die, and be buried by human beings.

To this we reply contrariwise that Jesus Christ, God and man, according to his divinity, by which he was naturally born of God the Father before all ages, is incomprehensible, impassible, and immortal; but according to his humanity, which he assumed without sin from the Virgin for the redemption of the world, he could be seized, bound, scourged, crucified, and die. But God raised him from the dead (Rom. X). After his resurrection he openly appeared to his disciples in that same humanity in which he had suffered and died for the redemption of the world (Acts VII); and, to show that he was truly risen, he ate and drank before them and, as they watched, ascended into heaven (Acts I), and sits at the right hand of God the Father (Heb. XII). Thus he suffered according to the humanity which he assumed from the Virgin Mother, while remaining impassible and immortal in his divinity.

According to that same flesh in which, through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, he was conceived in the Virgin and born from her, he offered himself upon the altar of the cross to God the Father as a sweet savour; [Col. 0263C] he fittingly overcame the ancient enemy who had deceived the first man, despoiled hell, rose on the third day, and raised us with himself to eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0263D] *On Faith to Peter*, ch. 2, among the works of Augustine, vol. III, now in the Appendix to vol. VI. See the note at fol. 88.] “Thus,” as blessed Fulgentius, a wise man full of God, says, “the same God made man came forth humbly and mercifully from the same womb of his mother; the same God made man hung upon the cross; the same God made man lay in the tomb; and the same God made man, returning from the lower regions, rose on the third day. Yet the same God lay in the tomb according to the flesh alone, and descended into hell according to the soul alone.”

Therefore, O Jews, who deny that Christ is true God and true man and that he suffered for the redemption of the human race, so that we may prove you to be lying in your assertion, listen more attentively as we show how plainly God the Father prefigured him as destined to suffer and mercifully die for the redemption of humankind when, through Moses, he commanded the children of Israel in Egypt to celebrate the Passover.

For he says: “Let the whole multitude of the children of Israel sacrifice a lamb at evening; and they shall take of its blood and put it upon both doorposts and upon the lintels [Col. 0264A] of the houses in which they shall eat it” (Exod. XII). [Note: [Col. 0263D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 15.] Thus the Passover takes place in the killing of the lamb; Christ is killed for the salvation of many. The lamb is sacrificed in the evening; Christ suffered in the evening of the world. Of him Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and thus he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). It follows: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John XIX). So too we read concerning Christ in the Gospel: “When they came to Jesus and found him already dead, they did not break his legs; but one of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0263D] For the sense to be complete, verse 36 seems to be missing: “These things . . . happened that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of it.’” Isidore says more briefly: “The Lord’s bones are not broken on the cross, as the Evangelist testifies . . . .” “You shall not break a bone of it.”]

The doorposts of the Israelites are anointed with the lamb’s blood, lest the destroying angel dare bring destruction. Faithful peoples are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s passion for the protection of salvation, so that those alone may be delivered from ruin who are marked in heart and forehead by the blood of the Lord’s passion, and who also sing to God in such a work: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. IV). Therefore this feast of Passover itself is interpreted as “passing over,” because we must leave dark Egypt—that is, the present world, darkened by diverse errors and entangled in manifold sins—while passing in mind from worse things to better, that is, from carnal conduct to the joys of the heavenly homeland which are to be desired.

But what is said concerning the eating of that lamb—“No foreigner shall eat of it; and it shall be eaten in one house, nor shall any of its flesh be offered outside” (Exod. XLIX)—must be understood as written specifically concerning the sacrament of the body [Col. 0264C] of Christ, of which that lamb bore the figure. His body and blood are commanded to be eaten in one house—that is, in one Church—and not offered outside among the peoples, namely those of heretics, who wander outside the same unity of the Catholic Church.

What do you say to these things, O Jews, enemies of truth? Or what do you answer? You ought plainly to understand and, all doubt removed, believe that the lamb which, by the Lord’s command, as has been said, the whole multitude of the children of Israel sacrificed at evening, unquestionably bore the figure of Jesus Christ, God and man, by whose sacrifice God the Father redeemed the human race from demonic dominion. Through that figurative lamb, God the Father [Col. 0264D] liberated the children of Israel from Pharaoh’s most severe rule. But through Christ, who is truly the Lamb without blemish, he delivered the entire world from the power of the devil. “For all these things,” as the Apostle says, “happened to them in figure” (I Cor. X).

Thus the Israelite people was rescued from the iron prison of Egypt by the blood of that figurative lamb; but the Christian people was mercifully redeemed from the most cruel yoke of the devil by the blood of the uncontaminated and spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ. [Col. 0265A] Passover, then, as we have said, is interpreted as “passing over.” Rightly, therefore, each passing over—the legal and the evangelical—was consecrated by blood: the former by the blood of the paschal lamb, the latter by the blood of him of whom the Apostle says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V). The latter was consecrated by the blood of the Son of God and of the Virgin, shed upon the cross; the former by blood sprinkled in the form of a cross upon the middle doorpost and lintel.

Jesus Christ, therefore, is true God and true man, so evidently prefigured in the paschal lamb. The sacrifice of the lamb itself, O Jews, which foretold Christ’s suffering and death for the redemption of the human race, openly convicts you—who say that he neither came nor was true God—of being false witnesses. Hear then, rebellious and unbelieving people; hear what I say, listen to what I urge. If you nevertheless persist in the wickedness of your unbelief, you shall without doubt perish eternally. But if you believe without doubt that he is true God, that he has already redeemed the world by his own blood as was prefigured in the paschal lamb, and if you receive his baptism with devout mind, you may attain the joys of eternal life with the children of the holy Church, he himself helping and leading you.

If, then, you desire to attain the salvation of your souls, place the blood of Jesus Christ, the spotless Lamb, upon both doorposts: that is, faithfully drink it with the mouth of heart and body for the remission of your sins. You must also place his blood upon the lintels [Col. 0265C] of the houses, lest through any onset of temptations you fall from the state of true faith.

Perhaps you ask, O Jews, who allegorically are the two doorposts and what are the two lintels of the houses, upon which you must place the blood of Jesus Christ, the spotless and uncontaminated Lamb. Let us therefore ask blessed Gregory, the most subtle interpreter of the holy Scriptures, and carefully hear from him how the doorposts and lintels of houses should be understood. [Note: [Col. 0265D] Homily 22 on the Gospels.] “The blood,” he says, “of the most holy Lamb, Jesus Christ, is placed upon both doorposts when it is received not only with the mouth of the body but also with that of the heart. For the lamb’s blood is placed upon both doorposts when the sacrament of his passion is received with the mouth unto redemption and considered with attentive mind unto imitation. For one who receives the blood of his Redeemer in such a way that he does not yet wish to imitate his passion places the blood upon only one doorpost. The blood of Christ’s passion must also be placed upon the lintels of houses. For what do we understand spiritually by houses except our minds, in which we dwell by thought? The lintel of this house is intention itself, which stands over action. Therefore whoever directs the intention of his thought toward imitation of the Lord’s passion places the lamb’s blood upon the lintel of his house. Or certainly our houses are our bodies themselves, in which [Col. 0266A] we dwell as long as we live. And we place the lamb’s blood upon the lintel of the house because we bear the cross of his passion upon our forehead.”

Believe, therefore, O Jews, that he is true God and true man; receive baptism with devout mind; receive the blood of his passion with heart and mouth; mark your foreheads with the sign of the holy cross for the protection of your bodies and souls, so that the destroying angel who passes by may not presume to harm you. Strive in every way faithfully to enter the holy Church of Christ, O Jews, because there you will find a harbour of rest, a refuge of consolation, a medicine of salvation, teaching of truth, a fountain of purification, a standard of uprightness, a rule of true faith and piety, and a holy manner of life pleasing to God, which, if you attain it, will enable you to reach the reward of the heavenly homeland.

Without doubt the patriarch Jacob prefigured this holy mother Church, adorned with heavenly gifts and strongest against every temptation, “ordered as an army in array” (Song VI), when he said figuratively concerning his son Zebulun: “Zebulun shall dwell by the shore of the sea, and at the station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon” (Gen. XLIX). [Note: [Col. 0266D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] Zebulun, therefore, whose name is interpreted “dwelling of strength,” signifies the Church, most strong for enduring every suffering. It dwells by the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that it may be a refuge for believers and show the harbour of true faith to those in peril. With immovable and unshaken firmness, it looks down upon the shipwreck of Jews and heretics [Col. 0266C] and upon every storm brought against it. Although it is beaten by their waves, it itself breaks the waves and is not broken by them; it yields neither to any tempests of heresy nor, shaken by any wind of schism, falls.

Moreover, this holy virgin and mother Church reaches as far as Sidon—that is, as far as the Gentiles—because it began in the patriarchs and prophets and, advancing in faith and devotion, reached the peoples of the Gentiles. We also read in the Gospel that some of the apostles were taken from there and that the Lord frequently taught in those regions, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the [Col. 0266D] Gentiles: the people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX), namely Jesus Christ, God and man, and his splendid teaching.

Meanwhile, I wish you to know, O Jews, that the gate of this holy Church is the Catholic faith. No one can enter it unless he first firmly believes in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For without faith no one can be saved (Matt. XVI). Therefore strive as quickly as possible to enter the holy Church by faithful belief and right action, that you may deserve to enter the gate of the heavenly homeland with the children of that Church. For it follows in the footsteps of Jesus Christ its Redeemer; with devout faith and right action it imitates him as far as possible; and it tirelessly contemplates with spiritual eyes him who sits at the right hand of God the Father.

Therefore believe, O Jews, that this most glorious bridegroom of the holy Church is true God and true man; hasten to ascend through him, who is the most straight way to the dwelling of the heavenly homeland. He provides guidance to the peoples who faithfully flock to him; he enlightens those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke I). He goes before people so that they may will good things; he urges them to begin what is right; he helps them to complete it. He calls his faithful to good works and enlightens their eyes to contemplate himself.

[Col. 0267B] O Jews, hear what I say; hear what I speak for your admonition and salvation. That admirable and terrible pillar which went before the Israelite people travelling through the wilderness, in the form of a cloud by day and in the form of fire by night (Exod. XIII), most fittingly prefigured Jesus Christ, God and man, “who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I). Jesus Christ, God and man, is also rightly signified in the pillar, because he is upright and just, and the strongest helper of those who hope in him. Of him the Psalmist indeed says: “For the Lord our God is upright, and there is no iniquity in him” (Ps. XCI).

In appearing by day in the form of a cloud and by night in the form of fire, it prefigured Christ as gentle and mild toward the righteous, but terrible toward sinners and the unjust. Otherwise: by day we understand the life of the righteous; by night, the corrupt conduct of sinful people. The Jews, therefore, because they had knowledge of God, were as it were day. But the Gentiles, because they did not know God and served not God but idols, remained not in day but as it were in night. Thus the pillar of fire, which went before the people at night, prefigured the future light of faith among the Gentile people, by which they were to be enlightened through divine grace in the last times. To them the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. V).

But the pillar of cloud, O Jews, which overshadowed the tabernacle by day, prefigured the future blindness of your unbelief. [Col. 0267D] Concerning this blindness of your unbelief the Lord plainly says: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). As though Jesus Christ, God and man, said more plainly: “For judgment I came into this world: namely, so that those who do not see may, by just judgment, see—that is, so that the Gentiles, who worship and adore idols not through the wickedness of rebellion but through ignorance, and do not know me, who am the light of the world (Matt. V), may see that I was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world, may know me, and may believe without doubt that I am one true God with that same Father and the Holy Spirit. And those who see—that is, the Jews, who have always remained rebellious against my commands and often provoked me to anger, and now boast that they see in the carnal precepts of the Law but disdain to hear my preaching—may become blind, that through the demands of their sins they may lose that of which they are proudly swollen.” Concerning them the Lord himself also says: “Leave them alone; they are blind guides of the blind” (Matt. XV).

You have heard, O Jews, how clearly the pillar of fire which went before the Hebrew people at night prefigured the future light of true faith by which Christians were to be enlightened. You have heard also how plainly the pillar of cloud which overshadowed the tabernacle and camp by day prefigured the thickest darkness of your unbelief. For you so provoked and angered that same omnipotent God who had delivered you from Egyptian slavery, as has been said above, [Col. 0268B] that he seemed to say with a certain indignation that he would wipe you from the face of the earth, unless Moses and Aaron and others continually opposed him with prayers and entreaties. Therefore, faithless Jews, drive from your hearts the darkness of long-standing unbelief; hasten to enter the holy mother Church by right belief and good works, that you may not perish with unbelievers but attain heavenly blessedness with faithful peoples.

§ XIX.—

The patriarch Jacob, full of the prophetic Spirit, speaking of his son Dan, foresaw that Antichrist, the son of perdition, would be born for the condemnation of many; yet Jacob himself awaited Christ, sent for the redemption of the world. From the Old Testament he introduces a most evident figure of sacred baptism: as Paul testifies, the fathers of the Jews were baptized in Moses, in the cloud, and in the sea, as type and figure of Christ. Three kinds of baptism prefigure Christ’s baptism before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. Isaiah declared that Christ would overcome Antichrist, and Jacob, speaking figuratively of his son Gad, foresaw it; he proves by the testimony of Moses that this figure pertains to Christ.

Meanwhile, I should like to know, O Jews, of what faith or purpose you are. If you believe without doubt that Christ has already come and is true God and true man, you do rightly; but if you doubt his coming or divinity, make this known to us. In reply you say that you do not believe Christ has already come and lived among human beings (Baruch [Col. 0268D] III), but still await his future coming.

O rebellious and unbelieving people! O adversaries of all goodness! O enemies of all righteousness and truth! Though you have so often been convicted by the authorities of the Law, overcome by so many prophecies of the prophets, and reasonably and sufficiently taught by the most true and manifest proclamations of so many evangelists that Christ is true God and true man; that he lived among human beings; that he truly suffered, died, and was buried for the redemption of the human race; that he rose from the dead; and that on the fortieth day after his resurrection he ascended to God the Father from whom he had come forth—why do you still doubt that he has come or that he was true God, and await another with whom you may perish?

Do you not know, unhappy and miserable people, that he whom you await will not be a loving shepherd of souls but a most cruel ravager? Do you not know that he will come not to preserve souls and restore them to a better condition, but “to destroy, scatter, steal, and kill” (John X), and cast them with himself into the pit of perdition? All Scripture calls him the son of perdition because he draws many with himself into perdition. The patriarch Jacob, full of the prophetic Spirit, foresaw this son of perdition (John XVII), namely Antichrist, as to be born for the condemnation of many and to do many evils contrary to God’s will near the end of the world, when he spoke figuratively concerning his son Dan, saying:

“Dan shall judge his people, as also the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan become a serpent upon the road, a horned serpent upon the path, biting the horse’s hoofs so that its rider falls backward. I shall await thy salvation, O Lord” (Gen. XLIX).

I urge you, O Jews, to listen attentively to how you ought to understand the things foretold concerning that son of perdition—that is, Antichrist—whom you await as though he were a redeemer. For, as I have often testified to you, you must understand the sayings of the Old Testament not literally but spiritually. Thus let the patriarch Jacob, filled with the spirit of prophecy, declare under the person of his son Dan what sort of being Antichrist will be, and what he will do at the time of his coming. “Let Dan,” he says, “become a serpent upon the road, a horned serpent upon the path.” The teachers of the holy Church apply this prophecy, as has been said, to Antichrist.

[Note: Col. 0269D. Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.]

For they maintain that Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, because in this passage Dan is called both a serpent and a biter. Hence, not without reason, when the Israelite people received the land in the division of the encampment, Dan was the first to encamp to the north (Num. II), signifying him who had said in his heart: “I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I shall ascend above the height of the clouds, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Concerning him it is said through the prophet to Dan: “The snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. VIII).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*, a horned serpent. A *cerastes*—

[Note: Col. 0269D. These words are inserted from the cited passage of the *Etymologies*, whereas Isidore in the aforesaid chapter of the *Questions* says only: “For in Greek *cerasta* means horns; and this serpent is said to be horned,” as follows below.]

—is a serpent so called because it has horns on its head like those of a ram.

[Note: Col. 0270D. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII, ch. 4.]

For the Greeks call horns *cerasta*. This creature has four little horns, by the display of which it entices and draws birds, and kills animals. It covers its entire body with sand and gives no sign of itself except from the part by which it catches the birds or animals it has lured. It is more sinuous than other serpents, so that it seems to have no backbone. This serpent, then, is said to be armed—

[Note: Col. 0270D. Isidore: “horned.”]

—and by it the coming of Antichrist is fittingly indicated, because, against the life of the faithful, he will be armed not only with the pestilential bite of his preaching but also with the horns of power.

But let us hear what Jacob said: “Dan, a serpent upon the road, a horned serpent upon the path” [Col. 0270A]. Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Antichrist, then, will be a serpent upon the road, because, while he induces people to walk in the broad way of this present life, he will flatter them by seeming to spare them. But he will bite upon the road, because he will consume with the poison of his malice those to whom he grants the freedom of his error. He will also be a horned serpent upon the path, because he will oppress the faithful whom, in his time, he finds confining themselves to the narrow ways of the heavenly command—not only by the force of crafty persuasion but also by the terror of power—and, as though amid the distress of harshness after the benefits of a feigned sweetness, he exercises—

[Note: Col. 0270D. Better: “will exercise.”]

—the horns of power.

It follows: “Biting,” he says, “the horse’s hoofs, so that its rider falls backward.” In this place the horse signifies this world, which foams in the course of passing times through its own pride [Col. 0270B]. And because Antichrist will endeavor to seize the final things of the world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s hoofs. To bite the horse’s hoofs is to strike and shake the end of the age.

[Note: Col. 0270D. Isidore: “to touch.”]

“So that its rider falls backward.” The rider of the horse is anyone exalted in the dignities of this world. To fall upon one’s face is, after laying aside the pride of one’s mind, to recognize one’s sins in this life and bewail them in repentance. But to fall backward, where one cannot see, is for sinners suddenly to depart from this life and to be led to punishments of which they are unaware.

And because you, O senseless Jews, say that you await Antichrist in place of Christ, the patriarch Jacob fittingly speaks to God the Father, in the voice of the children of the Church, with the highest devotion, saying: “I shall await thy salvation, O Lord” [Col. 0270C]. It is as though he said: “Though, taught by the spirit of prophecy, I know beforehand that that very son of perdition, Antichrist, will come for the condemnation of many, I shall faithfully await not him but thy Salvation, O God the Father—that is, thy Son, whom thou wilt send for the redemption of the world.”

Therefore you too, O Jews, together with the patriarch Jacob, faithfully await him who, already under King Herod and under Pontius Pilate the governor, redeemed the world by his most precious blood. Believe without doubt that he has already redeemed the world; know that he will come to judge the living and the dead. For he is the Salvation of God, through whom God the Father redeemed the human race from the power of the devil. Of him the Psalmist sang in rejoicing: “Announce from day to day the Salvation of God” (Ps. XCV). The prophet also said of him: “Our salvation will come swiftly, and it will break the yoke of our captivity.” Christ, therefore, is the true salvation of those who are near, namely the faithful Jews—the apostles and evangelists—and salvation to those who are far off, that is, the Gentiles who believe him to be the one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, O Jews, faithfully believe that this Salvation of God—that is, Christ—has already come and redeemed the world [Col. 0271A]; await him with fear and spiritual love as he comes to judge the living and the dead; desire to see him reigning at the right hand of God the Father; hasten to come through him to God the Father by right belief and good works. But if you place the anchor of your hope in that son of perdition, Antichrist, whom you say that you await, you will certainly perish with him. Receive Christ’s baptism with devout minds, so that, cleansed alike from original and actual sins, you may be counted among the elect.

What do you say to these things, O Jews? What do you answer or object? This is at once your answer and your objection. You say that baptism, which is diligently and reverently administered within the Church by priests [Col. 0271B] and received with the utmost devotion by the faithful, is not observed by you but held to be nothing, because it was neither prefigured by God in the Law nor foreshadowed in the deeds of the patriarchs or prophets. You further say blasphemously that baptism washes the bodies of those baptized but does not cleanse the sins of their souls.

To this we answer you in return: baptism, which within the holy Church, Christ instituting and commanding, is bestowed upon faithful peoples in the name of the holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—was foreshown and truly pre-signified by figures and enigmas before the Law and under the Law. Nor is the water of sacred baptism useless and superfluous for those baptized, as you falsely claim; rather, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, it washes away bodily dirt and cleanses the stains of sin.

Therefore, to confirm the most true religion of Christians and to disprove your most false objection, O Jews, we shall bring forward from the Old Testament a most evident figure of sacred baptism. Let us therefore recall the sacred history of the Book of Exodus, and hear together what Moses did, by the Lord’s command, at the departure of the children of Israel.

Then the Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they may set out. But lift up thy rod and stretch out thy hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the children of Israel may walk through the midst of the dry sea.” And when Moses had stretched out his hand over the sea [Col. 0271D], the Lord removed it, a mighty burning wind blowing all night; and he turned it into dry land. The water was divided, and the children of Israel entered through the midst of the dry sea. The Egyptians pursuing them entered after them—all Pharaoh’s cavalry, his chariots, and his horsemen—through the midst of the sea (Exod. XIV).

When the Egyptians were pursuing them, therefore, as has been said, Moses struck the waters with the rod, and they were divided this way and that; and the children of Israel crossed through the midst of the Red Sea. What did this signify except baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood?

[Note: Col. 0271D. Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 19.]

The pursuing enemies, dying with the king behind them, are past sins, which are blotted out [Col. 0272A], and the devil, who is drowned in spiritual baptism. The pressing Egyptians do indeed pursue; sins press on as far as the water of sacred baptism. After the crossing of the Red Sea, moreover, the people of God sing a hymn, Pharaoh and the Egyptians having been submerged. Spiritually, after the faithful rise from the font with their sins extinguished, they utter a hymn in a voice of rejoicing, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV). Yet those say this better and more worthily who have timbrels in their hands like Mary (ibid.), that is, who crucify their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V), and mortify their members which are upon the earth (Col. III).

[Col. 0272B]

Meanwhile, I do not wish you to be ignorant, O Jews, that your fathers were baptized in Moses, in the cloud and in the sea, as a type and figure of Jesus Christ and of his baptism. Thus says blessed Paul, who before believing in Christ had been the disciple of your teacher Gamaliel (Acts XXII): “I do not wish you to be ignorant, brethren, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all crossed the sea, and all were baptized in the cloud and in the sea” (I Cor. X).

It is as though he said more plainly: “I do not wish you to be ignorant,” that is, I do not wish you not to know that all your fathers, both good and bad, were under the cloud, which protected them from the heat and from being seen by the Egyptians; and all crossed the Red Sea after the enemies had been drowned. Indeed, all were, so to speak, baptized in Moses [Col. 0272C], that is, with Moses himself as their leader, in the cloud and in the sea.

Likewise, all ate the same food as we do: they ate a different bodily food, certainly, but the same spiritual food, because they had manna while we have the bread of eternal life. They also all drank the same drink as we do: another in visible appearance, but the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the rock that followed them: literally, wherever they went. Or, they drank from the following rock, that is, from the rock signifying the power of Christ that was to follow. But we truly, and without any mere signification, drink with desire and are filled with the chalice of Christ’s passion.

Thus the sea had the form of baptismal water; the cloud, that of the Holy Spirit; the manna, that of the bread of life, that is, the body of Christ [Col. 0272D]; and the drink, that of the blood of the same Jesus Christ, which flowed from his side for the remission of sins and which all the faithful people drink most gladly as the remedy of their salvation. There, as the examples of the Fathers teach, the Egyptian is drowned and God’s people rise, renewed by the Holy Spirit.

John too baptized, as blessed Isidore says—

[Note: Col. 0272D. Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 25.]

—but not entirely in the Jewish manner: not with water alone, nor yet in the Spirit, but he added only this, that he baptized unto repentance. For thus Paul the apostle says in the Acts of the Apostles: “John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, saying that they should believe in him who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus” (Acts XIX).

Yet John was given baptism in water so that Christ, who was to baptize in water and the Holy Spirit, might be manifested to Israel by John’s baptism [Col. 0273A]: namely, when, by the descent of the Holy Spirit and the Father’s voice, the Son of God was openly shown to all those present who were granted to see. Perfect baptism therefore began with Jesus Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin. For he first baptized in the Holy Spirit, as John also says: “I indeed baptize in water; one stands in your midst whom you do not know” (John I). “He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III). This is the perfection of baptism. For it is God who baptizes, so that those who are baptized may become children of God.

There are three kinds of baptism, as blessed Isidore says in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. The first baptism [Col. 0273B] is that by which the stains of sins are washed away through the laver of regeneration. The second is that in which persons are baptized in their own blood through martyrdom; Christ too was baptized with this baptism, so that in this as in other things he might give a pattern to believers. Hence he said to his disciples, the sons of Zebedee:

[Note: Col. 0273D. Isidore says: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” Thus water, etc.]

“Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. XX). It is as though he said more plainly: “Can you be baptized with the baptism with which I am to be baptized?” Thus water and blood are the twofold figure of baptism: the one by which we are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit; the other by which we are consecrated by our own blood.

And the third baptism is that of tears, which is undergone more laboriously, like that of the one who every night waters his bed with tears [Col. 0273C] (Ps. VI), who imitates the conversion of King Manasseh (II Chron. XXXIII) and the humility of the Ninevites (Jonah III), through which they obtained mercy.

More clearly than daylight, O Jews, it has been shown to you how openly and evidently Christ’s baptism was prefigured before the Law, under the Law, and under grace. The sea, therefore, as was said above, bore the form of water; the cloud bore the type of the Holy Spirit. The crossing of the Red Sea thus openly prefigured Christ’s baptism. Why, then, O senseless Jews, do you refuse to be baptized with Christ’s baptism, when you read plainly that your fathers were baptized in the cloud and in the sea? Why do you persist longer in assailing the Church’s sacraments with perverted minds, though you plainly know that, by God’s ordering, they were pre-signified from the beginning of the world by the most true figures of the patriarchs and proclamations of the prophets [Col. 0273D]?

Why, then, O blind nation, estranged from the light of truth, which is Christ, do you refuse to receive the saving baptism by which your fathers were figuratively baptized in the crossing of the Red Sea? Therefore, because we find with complete certainty in many places in the Old Testament that Christ’s baptism was prefigured, we most openly prove that you—who deny that it was foreshown anywhere—have lied in your objection. Sound reasoning shows you in every respect to be false witnesses, sufficiently convicting you through the most true authorities of the New and Old Testaments [Col. 0274A].

If, therefore, O Jews, you gladly lend an ear to my most salutary counsels and assent to my most just advice, you will undoubtedly attain the fellowship of God’s elect. Most certainly believe that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and that he has already redeemed the world by his most precious blood; and firmly maintain that he will come again at the end of the world to judge the living and the dead.

But do not place your hope in Antichrist, because he will not come to redeem the human race happily, but to draw it unhappily after himself into eternal damnation. Nor will he come to save those who hope in him, but to cast them with himself into Gehenna. God and man Jesus Christ will slay that very son of perdition [Col. 0274B], Antichrist, with the breath of his mouth, and will powerfully destroy him by the manifestation of his coming (II Thess. II).

But if you, O Jews, do not wish to believe me, a Christian man, because of hatred for Christ’s name, you ought at least to give credence to the prophecy of Isaiah. For he was born of noble stock, endowed with urban refinement, eminent in holiness, and filled with the Holy Spirit. The greater his authority, therefore, the more willingly you ought to credit his prophecies. I urge you to listen carefully to what he says concerning Christ: “He shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall slay the wicked” (Isa. XI), namely Antichrist himself [Col. 0274C].

The Son of God and of the Virgin will vigorously overcome that inventor of all wickedness and cast him into the most hideous lake of fire and sulphur, there to be tortured without end. Jacob certainly foresaw that God and man Jesus Christ would come for the redemption of the world and would overcome the aforesaid enemy of the human race, Antichrist, the author of all iniquity, when, speaking figuratively of his son Gad, he said:

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him; and he himself shall be girded backward” (Gen. XLIX).

[Note: Col. 0274D. Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.]

This girded Gad signified the person of Jesus Christ, who in the first coming of his humility has already come forth to fight before the coming of Antichrist, girded with the sword of his word and most powerfully about the thigh (Ps. XLIV), by which he divided son from father, daughter from mother, and daughter-in-law from mother-in-law. Hence he himself said: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. X). And of this sword he said: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (ibid.).

But by saying, “He himself shall be girded backward,” the brightness of our same Lord Jesus Christ, in which he himself will come at his second advent, is shown. For when Antichrist comes, then God and man Jesus Christ, as though from behind—that is, advancing swiftly after his footprints—will slay him with the sword of his mouth.

Moreover, in that this Gad is interpreted “robber,” he signifies Christ, who at his second advent, after Antichrist, and as one coming later near the end of the world, will leap forth like a robber by a sudden and swift advance against Antichrist’s open attack.

[Note: Col. 0275D. Isidore omits the marked words and says instead, “that is, near the feet,” as Martin also does, fol. 21.]

This is what is openly written in the Gospel:

[Note: Col. 0275D. Isidore says: “Hence the evangelist cries aloud, saying: ‘For the day of the Lord will come in the night as a thief.’” Blessed Martin’s reading is found in the same words in Paul, at the passage noted in the margin; similar passages occur at II Pet. III.10; Apoc. III.3 and XVI.15. Martin, at the cited folio, presents another testimony from Matthew.]

“The day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night” (I Thess. V). Christ, therefore, is written to fight against Antichrist both before and behind: before him indeed in secret, that is, in the first coming of his humility; but behind, after the deceptive and crafty preaching of Antichrist himself.

And so that you may know certainly, O Jews, and not doubt at all, that this prophecy of the patriarch Jacob pertains specifically to Christ, I urge you to listen attentively to what Moses the lawgiver says concerning him.

“Blessed in the abundance of Gad: he rested like a lion, seized arm and head, and saw his own dominion” (Deut. XXXIII) [Col. 0275B]. Consider carefully, therefore, O Jews, and understand wisely: who rested like a lion except Christ in his tomb? Who seized—that is, humbled—the head and arm of the powerful, except our Redeemer, who humbled the pride of the lofty—namely, kings and emperors who worship idols as God—and of the aerial powers that desire to oppose souls tending toward eternal rest? Who also saw his own dominion except him of whom Daniel said in his vision, among other things: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven and came as far as the Ancient of Days”—that is, to God the Father, ascending into heaven—“and there was given to him kingdom and honor, and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him. His power is an eternal power which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII) [Col. 0275C].

“He saw his own dominion,” he says (Deut. XXXIII). Moses speaks of the future as though it were past. It is as though he said more plainly: God and man Jesus Christ sees his own dominion—that is, he possesses it omnipotently with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, governs it justly, and orders it with moderation. Isaiah also says of him: “Dominion has been placed upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX). Jesus Christ therefore has dominion upon his shoulder, O Jews, because God the Father truly set him over all the works of his hands [Col. 0275D].

Therefore believe without doubt that he is true God and true man; that he was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world; that he truly took flesh from his Virgin mother; that he mercifully underwent passion and death for our sins; that he rose from the dead for our justification, ascended into heaven, and will come again through fire to judge the living, the dead, and the world.

For he is the refuge of the miserable [Col. 0276A], the medicine of the sick, rest for the weary, the harbor of the shipwrecked, the food of travelers running their course, and the fullness of the blessed who rest in the heavenly homeland. The human pilgrim eats him, lest he grow weary on the present way; the angel eats him with a full mouth, rejoicing in him through eternal ages. He who gave himself to angels as the joy of eternal stability gave himself to human beings as the remedy of health. The body of our same Redeemer is a provision for the journey of salvation to all who faithfully receive it. Therefore he, the living bread—namely the Lord Jesus Christ—descended into this world, so that if anyone faithfully eats of him, that person may not die eternally (John VI).

[Col. 0276B]

§ XX.—

Melchizedek first displayed the rite of the sacrament of the most holy altar. From this he demonstrates that Christian sacraments are earlier. The distinction between baptism and the Eucharist, so named with excellence, is set forth. In the sacrament of the Eucharist, the human body born from the Virgin is given to human beings. It is prefigured in manna, though there is a great difference between the reception of the two. Christ’s body is rightly called provision for the journey; therefore the patriarch Jacob, blessing his son Asher, plainly prefigured Christ as the living bread who descended from heaven. Moses is at last introduced at God’s command striking the rock that brought forth water; it bore the figure of Christ, who is said to have been prophesied in the wilderness. Commands delivered by Christ to the disciples are appended. Again, in Jacob’s blessing of Joseph, the wondrous beauty of Christ is prefigured. Finally, although God is one, there are two Testaments, and both are called one; the New is prefigured through Moses in the saving wood that sweetened the bitter waters [Col. 0276C]. Eternal God, although he has granted whatever was appropriate to each time, is not thereby changeable.

In reply to these things, O Jews, you say that it seems incredible that the Son of God should descend from the bosom of his Father, receive a human body from an undefiled virgin, and give that same body to peoples obedient to himself for the remission of sins. You further say that you do not know how a body made from a woman can be received and eaten by human beings.

But although the Lord forbade giving what is holy to dogs and casting pearls before swine (Matt. VII), nevertheless, because we desire you to be within the bosom of the holy Church and to have true knowledge of the same God and man Jesus Christ, we shall briefly explain to you, by his gift, how the faithful people eat his most holy body for the remission of their sins, while God and man Jesus Christ himself nevertheless remains always whole and perfect at the right hand of God the Father [Col. 0276D]. Yet I do not wish you to be ignorant, O Jews, that no one ever has been, or ever will be, able to say anything perfectly concerning so great and profound a sacrament.

We believe that Melchizedek first displayed the rite of this sacrament when he offered bread and wine to Abraham as he returned from the slaughter of the four kings (Gen. XIV). From this it is understood that Christian sacraments are earlier than Jewish ones [Col. 0277A].

I urge you, O Jews, to listen diligently to what we have proposed; for if—God forbid!—you depart empty from this most sacred reading, you will be far from the salvation of your souls. Hence the Psalmist speaks to God, saying: “Salvation is far from sinners.” Why? Namely: “Because they have not sought thy justifications” (Ps. CXVIII).

If, therefore, O Jews, you wish happily to attain the salvation of your souls, seek by every means from the ministers of the Church the ordinances of God and man Jesus Christ—ordinances which he, before all ages, determined with God the Father and the Holy Spirit should be made; which he prefigured through patriarchs, foretold through prophets, firmly established through himself, commanded to be openly preached through the apostles to all nations under heaven [Col. 0277B], and ordered to be kept inviolate by the whole Church—and take the greatest care to fulfill them.

[Note: Col. 0277D. *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 8.]

I wish you to know, therefore, O Jews, that through Christ’s baptism we are cleansed from sins, and through the holy Eucharist—that is, through the most holy body of the same God and man Jesus Christ—we are strengthened and perfected in good works. Baptism therefore extinguishes the heat of vices, but the Eucharist spiritually refreshes the mind. Hence it is excellently called *eucharistia*, that is, “good grace,” because in this sacrament there is not only an increase of virtue and grace, but, as blessed Ambrose says in the book of *Sentences*: “He is wholly received spiritually, who is the fountain [Col. 0277C] and origin of all grace, whose figure came before when God rained manna upon the fathers in the wilderness, and they were fed with the daily food of heaven.”

Of this the Psalmist says: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII). But your fathers who then ate that bread died; whereas this living bread, namely God and man Jesus Christ, who descended from heaven, gives life to the world. That manna was from heaven; this is from above heaven. That manna, when kept until the next day, swarmed with worms; but this is free from all corruption, and whoever reverently tastes it shall not see death for ever. That was given to the ancients after the crossing of the Red Sea, where the Hebrews were freed when the Egyptians had been drowned. This heavenly manna, that is, the body of Christ [Col. 0277D], ought to be given only to those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit.

That bodily bread, O Jews, led your fathers through the wilderness to the land of promise. This heavenly food, that is, Christ’s body, carries the faithful, as they cross the wilderness of this age, up into heaven. Thus Christ’s body is rightly called provision for the journey, because, refreshing us on the way, it leads us as far as the homeland.

But so that you may understand more fully, O Jews, how the manna which God rained upon the ancient fathers in the wilderness prefigured the most sacred body of Christ, let us, if you please, recall the history of that time. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread; and you shall know that I am your God.” So it happened in the evening that quails came up and covered the camp; and in the morning dew lay around the camp. When it had covered the surface of the earth, there appeared in the wilderness something small, as though pounded with a pestle, resembling frost upon the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another: “*Manhu?*” This means, “What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them: “This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat. This is the word which the Lord commanded: Let each person gather from it as much as is sufficient to eat, namely a gomor for each head” (Exod. XVI) [Col. 0278A].

Meanwhile, it is necessary that blessed Isidore, our patron, should come forward—

[Note: Col. 0277D. Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, ch. 26. See fol. 10.]

—and graciously explain for us, who desire to know, the measures of grain established by sacred law. “The smallest part of measures,” he says, “is the spoonful (*coclear*), which is half a drachma and weighs nine siliquae; this number, tripled, makes a *conchula*. A *conchula* weighs one and a half drachmas. The weight of a *cyathus* is ten drachmas. An *acetabulum* is a fourth part of a hemina and weighs twelve drachmas. A *cotyla* is a hemina, containing six *cyathi*; it is called a *cotyla* because in Greek speech *cote* means a cutting. A hemina is formed when a sextarius is divided equally into two, and makes a *cotylata*. A hemina weighs one pound; doubled, it makes a sextarius. A sextarius is two pounds and, taken twice, is called a two-pound measure. Taken four times, it is called in Greek a *conix* [Col. 0278C]. Multiplied fivefold, it makes a *quinare* or *gomor*.”

Having briefly stated these things from blessed Isidore concerning measures of grain, let us hear what the Lord says to the children of Israel: “Let each person gather from the manna as much as is sufficient to eat, namely a gomor for each head, according to the number of your souls that dwell in the tents; so shall you gather.” And the children of Israel did so, gathering some more and some less. They measured it by the measure of a gomor; and the one who had gathered more had no excess, nor did the one who had prepared less find less; but each gathered according to what he was able to eat.

Moses said to them: “Let no one leave any of it until the morning.” They did not heed him, but some of them kept portions until morning; and it began to swarm with worms and rotted. But they gathered each one as much as was sufficient to eat; and when the sun grew hot, it melted (ibid.) [Col. 0278D].

It is said of manna that it hardened by fire and melted in the sun (Wis. XVI): that is, the divine word, by instilling terror of Gehenna into human beings, hardens in the hearts of those in whom it melts by promising the sweetness of eternal life. On the sixth day they gathered double food, that is, two gomors. And the house of Israel called its name *Man*; it was like white coriander seed, and its taste was like—

[Note: Col. 0278D. Here an adulterating hand is plainly recognized, by which the Pergamum manuscript was handled and perhaps unhappily corrected. Previously it read *similae* (“of fine flour”), in whose place the ignorant corrector put *similis* (“similar”), perhaps thinking the word an adjective and not recognizing that *similae* was the genitive of *simila*, “fine flour,” but instead treating it as the neuter ending of the adjective *similis*, which for that reason could not agree with the noun *gustus* (“taste”).]

—fine flour mixed with honey.
