As I have often testified, O Jews, the Old Testament [Col. 0279A] must be understood not literally but according to its mystical sense. Therefore I urge you to listen even more willingly to the spiritual exposition of what you have above willingly heard historically.

[Note: Col. 0280D. Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 23.]

Manna clearly signified Christ, who descended from heaven as the living bread, and who is rained upon the whole world through the cloud of the Gospel—not upon the Synagogue now murmuring and testing him, but upon the Church that believes and places its hope in him. This is the unfailing manna. This is the bread of heaven and the true food of angels. It is the Word of God, who incorruptibly feeds mortal beings; and so that humanity might eat him, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). Those who feed upon him live spiritually.

I do not wish you to forget, O Jews, that your fathers who ate manna in the wilderness [Col. 0279B] died and were buried in that same vast wilderness and did not enter the land of promise. If you too receive the old figure carnally and scorn to taste with the palate of soul and heart the truth that is Christ, you will by no means be able to reach the land of promise—that is, the heavenly homeland—but will die in your sins in the wilderness of the present age.

For God and man Jesus Christ himself, summoning you to eternal life, said: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness and died” (John VI). Again exhorting you to knowledge and true faith, he said: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (ibid.); and: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (ibid.). Therefore, if you seek to live for ever, faithfully receive the Son of God and of the Virgin with the mouth of mind and body.

[Note: [Col. 0280D] Isidore, ibid.] Not unfittingly, the heavenly utterances are also signified by the manna. Hence the interpretation of the name itself has this sense: manna is interpreted, “What is this?” For when we hear the law of God recited in the Church, we ask the teachers, saying, “What is this?” Now this manna was fine like coriander seed and pleasant to eat. What, then, is finer than the word of God, what more subtle, or what sweeter and more delightful than God’s utterances, which are above honey and the honeycomb? But what does it mean that on the sixth day a double portion was commanded to be gathered, sufficient also for the Sabbath? The sixth day, this in which we now live, is the sixth age of the world. Therefore, in this sixth age, he gathers a double supply of sustaining food who, in hope of eternal life, hears the word of God from teachers and fulfils it by good works. In this age he stores up a double portion who both lives well and, according to his ability, bestows mercy on others. What was stored after the Sabbath decayed. For good works done for eternal rest will endure in the world to come. But those who were faithless to the Lord’s command and, apart from the Sabbath requirement, kept manna after the Sabbath—the surplus that they stored—boiled with worms and rotted. [Col. 0280A] So too those who heap up treasure for the present life and from love of this world will boil in hell with worms that shall not die. The Lord threatens them terribly, saying: “Their worms shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI). These are the worms generated by greed and the blind desire for riches. Those also who possess wealth and, seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts against them will be tormented by these worms (I John III). But he too who sins after receiving the word of God finds that word of God made a worm to him, ever piercing his conscience and gnawing at the secrets of his breast. Yet by resemblance the worm is Christ himself, as he says: “I am a worm and no man” (Ps. XXI). As he is [Col. 0280B] to some for ruin and to others for resurrection (Luke II), so in manna he becomes sweetness of honey to believers but a worm to unbelievers.

Therefore that bodily bread, O Jews, as was said above, led the ancient people through the desert into the land of promise. This heavenly food, namely Christ, carries believers crossing the desert of this age up into heaven. It is rightly called food for the journey, because it refreshes us on the way through the present age and leads us to ever-green pastures. Therefore, as the Red Sea prefigured baptism, so manna displays the glorification of the Lord’s body. I want you to know, O Jews, that these two sacraments were then shown when blood and water flowed from Christ’s side [Col. 0280C] (John XIX), because he came to redeem from the devil and from sin those who believe in him, through the blood of redemption and the water of baptism, just as he freed the Israelites from the destroyer through the blood of the paschal lamb and from the Egyptians through the water of the sea. It has indeed been shown to you with sufficient reason, O Jews, enemies of truth, how manifestly that manna, ministered from heaven to the ancient fathers in the desert, prefigured Jesus Christ, the redeemer of the human race; how God and man himself gave himself to faithful peoples for food; and how perfectly he refreshes them from himself in the present life and in the life to come. He himself, as has been said, feeds those who hope in him by faith, lest they fail on their present journey; and he himself refreshes all the saints by sight [Col. 0280D] in the heavenly homeland. We therefore demonstrate most certainly that you lie in your objection—you who have dared to assert, to increase your condemnation, both that he was not prefigured throughout the whole sequence of the Old Testament and that his body cannot benefit the salvation of believers.

Jacob the patriarch clearly prefigured that very living bread which came down from heaven, namely Jesus Christ, when, blessing his son Asher, he said: “Asher’s bread is rich; he shall provide delights for kings” (Gen. XLIX). Therefore, O Jews, to strengthen our faith in every respect [Col. 0281A] and utterly to refute your most false assertion, I urge you diligently to hear the spiritually explained meaning of this saying of so great a patriarch. [Note: [Col. 0281D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] This Asher, whose name signifies riches, plainly prefigured Christ, true God and true man, whose height of wisdom and knowledge is incomprehensible; and yet, though he was rich, he chose to become poor for us. His bread became rich—that is, his flesh, which is the Holy of holies; whoever worthily eats it shall not die eternally. He also provides delights for kings: namely, for those who govern their own senses well, who also rule over their vices, chastise their bodies, and subject them to servitude.

At last, therefore, O Jews, lay aside the long-standing madness of unbelief, and believe most certainly that Christ is true God and true man, and that he was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world. For he is, as we have said above, the refreshment of believers, the satisfaction of the citizens above, and the unfailing source of every good. Through him all who rightly believe are cleansed from the filth of sins. By him, those progressing in good works are helped to progress ever more and more; from him, those now dwelling in heaven are satisfied without satiety. What do you say to these things, O Jews? What do you object, or what do you answer? For if you believe that Jesus Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God, you can without doubt attain [Col. 0281C] the salvation of your souls. But if you doubt either his divinity, by which he is equal and consubstantial with God the Father, or his humanity, which he assumed without sin from an incorrupt Virgin, by which he mounted the cross, defeated the ancient enemy, and redeemed humankind, you are tending not toward life but toward eternal death.

Now, therefore, I should like to know what will or what faith you hold. In answer to this, O Jews, you stubbornly say that Christ has not yet come, has not redeemed humankind by the blood of his passion, and has not washed it from sins by the water of baptism. We, on the contrary, answer you that from the beginning of the world the Son of God showed in advance, through the figures and enigmas of the patriarchs, that he would come, redeem humankind by his own blood, and wash it from sins by the wave of sacred baptism; he foretold this through the prophecies of the prophets; and, at the time appointed and fulfilled by God the Father, he accomplished it in person, clothed in flesh, and proclaimed through the apostles to the whole world that these things had already been fulfilled. Therefore, so that you may not doubt that what we say is true and may know with certainty that you are defeated in your most false assertion, we shall introduce an exceedingly illustrious figure of the Old Testament, which we urge you to hear attentively.

Thus the Lord said to Moses: “Go on before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel. Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go. [Col. 0282A] And I shall stand before you there upon the rock of Horeb; you shall strike the rock, and water shall come forth from it, so that the people may drink.” Therefore Moses struck the rock before the children of Israel, and waters came forth in great abundance, so that the people and their beasts drank (Exod. XVII). [Note: [Col. 0282D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 24.] Therefore, O Jews, lest you depart empty from this sacred reading, apply your ears diligently to what is said. The smitten rock that poured forth water undoubtedly bore the figure of Christ, from whose breast, opened upon the cross, all the sacraments of the holy Church flowed. To him the wood of the Passion came like a staff, so that grace of eternal salvation might flow out to those who believe in him. For the struck rock sent forth a fountain from itself; Christ struck upon the cross poured out for those desiring salvation the grace of the laver and the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle proves that this [Col. 0282B] rock bore the figure of Christ when he says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

Now, the thirsty people murmured against Moses for water, and for this reason God commands that the rock from which they should drink be shown to them. What did this signify except that, when the Christian people read the Old Testament, they murmur against Moses because the carnal precepts written according to the letter displease them? Moses, therefore, by God’s command, shows the Christian people the rock, which is Christ, and leads them to him so that they may drink from him and relieve their thirst. Moses himself, indeed, taught by the Holy Spirit, showed this rock—namely, the same God and man, Jesus Christ—to Jews and Gentiles desiring [Col. 0282C] to discover the truth, which is Christ, when in the wilderness he solemnly declared to the children of Israel: “The Lord your God shall raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, that is, from the tribe of Judah, like me; you shall hear him in all things whatsoever he shall speak to you” (Deut. XVIII). And he added: “Everyone who will not hear that prophet shall be exterminated from among his people” (Exod. XXX). Therefore, since from the beginning of the world God the Father showed beforehand, by most truthful figures and terrible signs, that his most beloved Son would be born and would suffer for the salvation of humankind, he openly convicts you, O Jews, who deny that Son of his, of lying in your assertion. Therefore, if you wish [Col. 0282D] to attain the salvation of your souls, according to the aforesaid counsel of Moses, hear the Son of God and of the Virgin in all that he commanded his disciples. If you do not faithfully hear him—that is, if you are not obedient to him in all things—you shall perish from the fellowship of the elect.

Perhaps, O Jews, questioning us, you say: “What are the commandments which Christ gave his disciples?” As he ascended to the Father, he commanded them among other things: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). And again: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who truly does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark XVI). Elsewhere [Col. 0283A] the heavenly Master himself, speaking with Nicodemus and fully teaching him the catholic faith, testified among other things: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John VIII). What more lucid, more open, or clearer do you wish to hear, O senseless Jews? Reason plainly teaches that unless you are reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, according to the command of this same God and man, Jesus Christ, you cannot enter the kingdom of God. For if you truly believe that Jesus Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God, and are baptized in the name of that same holy Trinity, you can attain the salvation of your souls. But if you refuse to believe, you shall utterly perish from the fellowship of God’s elect.

For this purpose God the Father raised up that prophet, namely Christ, from among your brothers: that you might hear him in all things, that is, be obedient to him in every respect. Therefore, if you do not hear him—that is, if you do not receive the baptism instituted by him and the other sacraments of ecclesiastical religion—you shall perish from the assembly of his saints, because you have made void the covenant which God the Father firmly established through him before all ages. But if you keep his commands, you shall be free from everlasting condemnation. Therefore, O Jews, believe that he is true God and true man; strive with all earnestness to keep his commands; believe without doubt that he was sent by God the Father [Col. 0283C] for the redemption of the world. The more your fathers sought to remove him from the face of the earth through the passion of the cross and death of the flesh, the more God the Father made him increase in the faith and knowledge of the Gentiles. The malice of the Jews delivered that grain of wheat to death, but God the Father, raising him, caused him to return to himself with the fruit of many souls. Jacob the patriarch, taught by the Holy Spirit, prefigured this God and man, Jesus Christ—rejected indeed by the Jews, chosen and honoured by God the Father, and received by the Gentiles with the highest reverence and honour—when he blessed his son Joseph and said (Gen. XLIX):

“Joseph is a growing son, a growing son.” [Note: [Col. 0283D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] This prophecy, after the Lord’s Passion, assumed the form of the Father’s voice, by which the Father addresses Christ as he returns [Note: [Col. 0283D] “Returning,” as in the edition; or “to the returning . . . Christ.”] to heaven after his victory: “Joseph is a growing son, a growing son,” namely among the Gentiles. For when he had left the people because of the unbelief of the Synagogue, he chose the holy Church from all nations, and multiplied and enlarged it throughout the whole world. David also foretells this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI). “A growing son,” he says, “and beautiful in appearance.” For Christ’s beauty surpasses every beauty, according to what is written of him in the Psalms: [Col. 0284A] “Fairer in form than the children of men; grace is poured out upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV).

It follows: “The daughters ran upon the wall.” As if he said more plainly: the nations of the Church that believed in Christ, set aflame by love for Christ’s beauty, run upon the firmness of faith as upon a wall, so that they may behold by contemplation him who is the true bridegroom of the Church, and may be united and cleave to him by the kiss of charity. Hear, O unhappy Jews, how clearly Jacob the patriarch foretold that Christ would suffer for the redemption of humankind, saying: “His brothers rebuked him.” He speaks of the future as though it had already passed. It is as though, speaking more openly of Christ under the person of his son Joseph, he said: Christ’s brothers rebuked him, namely the chief [Col. 0284B] priests with the scribes and Pharisees, when they wronged him without cause by false testimony and reproaches, saying: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a man, make yourself God” (John X). [Note: [Col. 0284D] St Leo, Epistle 28 [otherwise 24], or the First to Flavian, ch. 4, discusses most beautifully the properties of each of Christ’s two births and natures.]

For he was a true man, healing human infirmities by touching them with his own hands and, compassionately sharing their miseries, shedding tears. Existing as true God, he raised the dead and plainly saw human thoughts. He was true man, whom people could hear and see. True God lay hidden in the form of man, and holy angels ministered to him from his very conception. At one and the same time, according to his divinity, he governed the holy angels in heaven, while on [Col. 0284C] earth the same God, made man, preached the Gospel to the poor (Matt. XI). He who, with God the Father, disposed all things before all ages gave the ancient fathers carnal precepts, like milk to little children; he, at the appointed time, assuming human nature without sin, bestowed spiritual commandments upon all nations throughout the world, like solid food upon more perfect men. For he commanded the Hebrew people to observe the ceremonies of the Old Testament; he renewed through the womb of the sacred font the Gentiles who wandered far and wide throughout the whole world from good works and knew not the true God, and, summoning them to desire heavenly things, taught them through his apostles to live spiritually. Therefore, the Son of God and of the Virgin gave the Old Testament to the Hebrew people and commanded the children of the Church to keep the New with all earnestness, that they might live more perfectly and worthily.

What, then, do you say to these things, O Jews? What do you answer or object? This is your answer: you say that there is one God, who gave one testament to the ancient fathers. For just as there are not two gods, but one true God who created all things from nothing, so there are not two testaments, but one testament commanded to be kept by the children of Abraham. To this we answer, on the contrary, that there is without doubt one God in heaven and on earth, who created all things from nothing. For Father and Son [Col. 0285A] and Holy Spirit are one true God: one in essence and three in persons. He who of old gave figurative precepts to Abraham and his seed mercifully drew the Gentile people, in the last times, to knowledge of himself through his most beloved Son. He who commanded the ancient fathers to fulfil the legal ceremonies likewise, through his Son consubstantial and coeternal with himself, called the Gentiles in the time of grace to receive the sacraments of evangelical institution. Therefore the Almighty, who orders all things justly, placed the New Testament before the Old Testament and taught the children of the Church to live more perfectly. He did not, indeed, come to dissolve the law, but to fulfil it (Matt. V).

[Note: [Col. 0285D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, ch. 1.] I want you to know, O Jews, that the Old Testament is so called because, when the New came, its carnal precepts ceased. The excellent teacher Paul mentions this, saying: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V). Hence also the blessed evangelist John says: “Beloved, I write a new commandment to you, which is true in him,” that is, in Christ, “and in you, because the darkness”—that is, the shadowy and carnal precepts of the Old Testament—“has passed away, and the true light now shines” (I John II): namely, the New Testament, by which those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit are renewed in knowledge and in faith in the whole holy Trinity. The testament is called New because it renews in holy and spiritual conduct those who faithfully receive it and live according to it. [Col. 0285C] For, as blessed Isidore says, only people renewed from the oldness of the first man by grace and belonging to that New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven, learn it.

Therefore, as has been said, O Jews, God the Father set the New Testament through Jesus Christ above the Old Testament, because this God and man, Jesus Christ, came not to dissolve but to fulfil the law (Matt. V). Therefore, so that you may not doubt the truth of what we say, we urge you to hear attentively how clearly Almighty God prefigured through Moses that New Testament which you have rejected with proud minds.

Moses and all the children of Israel went out from the Red Sea and walked three days through the wilderness [Col. 0285D] without finding water. And they came to Marath [Note: [Col. 0285D] The text reads: Mara.], and they could not drink the waters of Marath because they were bitter. And the people murmured against Moses, saying: “What shall we drink?” But he cried to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood. When Moses cast it into the waters, they were immediately turned to sweetness (Exod. XV). You have heard, O Jews, the simple history of the book of Exodus; I urge you to hear it again in its spiritual exposition. I have often testified to you that the Old Testament must be understood not according to the letter but spiritually. Therefore, in the fact that the murmuring people came in thirst to bitter waters and yet could not quench their thirst because of the excessive bitterness, it is plainly understood that the Old Testament without faith in Christ could not suffice the ancient fathers for attaining the rewards of eternal blessedness. As we believe that he has now come and redeemed the world, so they believed that he was to come and would redeem humankind.

Therefore Moses, at the Lord’s command, cast wood into the bitter waters, and they became sweet. What, then, is denoted by the bitter waters except the killing letter? And what by the wood except the cross of Christ’s Passion? [Note: [Col. 0285D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 21.] Therefore we understand that the bitter waters bear the figure of the killing letter and of the law. If the confession of the cross is cast into them and the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion is joined to them, the water becomes marvellously sweet: [Col. 0286B] that is, the bitterness of the letter is changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding. Hence it is written: “The Lord established for the people a law and judgments, and tested him, whether he would fear him or not” (Exod. XV). Therefore observe in this place, O Jews, that the law was given to the ancient fathers as a test and proof, whether they would fear and love God. Hence Moses himself, the lawgiver, says to the children of Israel: “The Lord our God tests you, that he may know whether you love him” (Deut. XIII). For if a law had been given that could give life or introduce people to behold the face of Almighty God, righteousness would truly be from the law. But the Scripture of the law shut up all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers not from the justification of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ [Col. 0286C] (Gal. III). Blessed Paul likewise testifies: “By works of the law no flesh shall be justified in God’s sight” (Rom. III). The Lord himself also affirms through the prophet Isaiah: “My soul has hated your solemnities, new moons, and sabbaths” (Isa. I). And again: “I have not desired the blood of rams, bulls, and goats” (ibid.).

In another sense, the fact that waters of extreme bitterness, when they received the wood into themselves, became sweet [Note: [Col. 0286D] Isidore: “are sweetened.”] signified that the bitterness of the Gentiles would at some time be turned, through the wood of Christ’s cross, to sweet use. It should also be known, according to the foregoing sense, that the people were first led to salty and bitter waters; after the wood shown by the Lord had been cast into the waters and they had been refreshed by their sweetness, they were afterward led [Col. 0286D] to twelve springs. Israel was first led to the letter of the law, and while it remained in that letter it could not depart from hardness of heart and blindness of mind; that is, it had no spiritual understanding. [Note: [Col. 0286D] Isidore, ch. 22.] But when, through the wood of life, the water—that is, the letter—has been made sweet, and the law has begun to be understood spiritually, then, O Jews, one comes from the Old Testament to the New and comes to the twelve springs: that is, to the twelve apostles, whom sacred Scripture calls springs. There too the faithful seek the trees of seventy palms, because not only did the twelve apostles preach Christ’s faith, [Col. 0287A] but another seventy-two disciples also are said to have been sent to preach the word of God, through whom the world might know the palms of Christ’s victory. Indeed, these twelve springs watering the seventy palm trees prefigured apostolic grace, so that the Decalogue of the law might be fulfilled through the sevenfold gift of the Holy Spirit.

You have heard, O Jews, how clearly Almighty God set forth the Old Testament in advance through the bitter waters and prefigured the New Testament through the saving wood by which, in Moses’ mystery, he sweetened the bitterness of those same waters. Through the bitter waters he signified in advance the future severity of the law; through the sweetness of the healing wood he showed beforehand the benefit of Christ’s cross. Therefore, in the fact that Moses led [Col. 0287B] the people to bitter waters and, with the Lord at once commanding and cooperating, transformed their bitterness into sweetness by the touch of wood, he plainly showed beforehand that, when the illustrious teaching of Christ came, the carnal institutions of the law and the bitterness of the killing letter would be transformed and changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding. Therefore, when Christ suffered on the cross for the redemption of humankind, the Old Testament ceased in its carnal observance, because he spiritually fulfilled through the New Testament what was lacking to the law.

Meanwhile, I do not want you to be ignorant, O Jews, that Almighty God, who contains and governs all things, has apportioned with great ordering what suited each time: just as in the law he commanded marriage, but in the New Testament praised chastity and commanded that the other cheek be offered to one who strikes the cheek (Matt. V). The former he gave for the time to a rough and frail people, namely the Hebrew people; the latter to a more perfect people, namely the Christian people—commending to each, according to its time, what was fitting. Yet because of this change, as the great teacher Isidore says, [Note: [Col. 0287D] Book I, *Sentences*, ch. 20.] God should not be considered changeable, but should rather be proclaimed admirable; for, remaining unchangeable, he apportioned with great ordering what was useful for each time, as has been said. Under the Old Testament sins were of lesser guilt, because not truth itself but the shadow of truth was present in it. For in the New Testament, as blessed Isidore, our patron, says, [Col. 0287D] [Note: [Col. 0288D] Ibid.] we are commanded to abandon certain things openly through higher precepts which had served the shadows of truth among that people. There the union with many wives and retaliation for injury were permitted and did no harm. But in the New Testament, those who admit such things are condemned by severe judgment.

O Jews, hear what I say; hear what I urge; listen to what I commend to you for the salvation of your souls. You have heard that Almighty God commanded the ancient fathers to keep the Old Testament; you have also heard that the same Old Testament plainly prefigured the New Testament and was its shadow. Therefore he placed the New Testament above the Old Testament [Col. 0288A] when he abolished the carnal ceremonies of the law and commanded that the spiritual sacraments of the holy Gospel be firmly observed to the end of the world. Since, therefore, O Jews, charity compels me to desire that you be within the number of the elect, I accordingly give you this salutary counsel: reject the carnal precepts of the law and hasten diligently to observe the spiritual institutions of the New Testament. For if you live according to the carnal ceremonies of the Old Testament, you shall utterly perish; but if you strive to keep the most sacred commandments of the holy Gospel, you can belong to the lot of God’s elect. What, then, do you say to these things, O Jews? What do you answer or again object? You plainly recognize that we have reasonably overthrown all your superstitious assertions by the most truthful authorities of the holy Scriptures, and have moreover sufficiently and spiritually expounded to you the foundation of catholic faith, which is Christ.

## § XXI

He admonishes the Jews, who boast alike of receiving the law, hearing the voice, and the thunder, that—as in the vision of the smoking mountain—they ought to understand and fulfil these things not according to the letter but spiritually. The giving of the Holy Spirit and the ordering of the apostles are prefigured for them. He then sets forth the order of the Decalogue’s commandments, and how its first three commandments show knowledge and love of the Trinity, while the other seven on the second tablet show love of neighbour. He presents a fine allegorical exposition of the commandments: what they prohibit and why they were written on two tablets. Further, he adduces Augustine concerning the correspondence between the plagues of Egypt [Col. 0288C] and the commandments; explains in what sense “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (II Cor. III) must be understood; and shows in what manner the letter of the Gospel differs from the letter of the law, and likewise how the hardness of the Jews is prefigured by tablets of stone. From the statements of Exodus he prefigures that Christ, true God, assumed human flesh. He then adds the manifold reason why the eternal Father willed his only-begotten Son to undergo the Passion of the cross and permitted him to be scourged and bound; and why he endured the instrument of the cross rather than decapitation. How beautifully he raises the eyes of the heart to understand the length, breadth, and depth of the most holy cross. Then he teaches the Jews how they ought to believe the mystery of the most holy Trinity together with unity of essence, and prefigures it from the words of Exodus.

Therefore, if you wish to receive the catholic faith with ready mind and all doubt put aside, let us give thanks to Almighty [Col. 0288D] God, the giver of every good. But if you still doubt anything, or wish to raise any objection, make this known to us. This is your answer and objection together, O Jews. You say that, uniquely before all peoples beneath heaven, you received the law written by God’s finger and deserved to hear the voice of that same Almighty God speaking; that you saw voices, thunders, lightnings, the resounding blare of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain; and that therefore you wish to observe that law not spiritually but according to the letter as it sounds. To this we answer, on the contrary, that the law is good and holy if it is understood spiritually [Col. 0289A] and fulfilled lawfully. But after Christ’s Passion, anyone who observes it carnally cannot attain the salvation of his soul. It must therefore be understood mystically and fulfilled in deed according to its spiritual sense. I urge you, therefore, O rebellious and unbelieving people, to hear attentively how you ought to understand the law which you boast that you received written by God’s finger.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 28.] Therefore the children of Israel celebrated the Passover in Egypt, came to Mount Sinai, and on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb received the law written by God’s finger through Moses’ hand. Therefore, just as Moses’ law was given on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been performed, so on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passion—which that Passover prefigured—the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete promised by Christ, descended upon the apostles and those who were with them in the city of Jerusalem: that is, one hundred and twenty men, established in a number corresponding to Moses’ age. In a diversity of languages, and after the disciples had been scattered everywhere, the whole world was filled by evangelical preaching.

Again all the people there behold voices, lamps, a smoking mountain, thunders, lightnings, and the resounding blare of the trumpet. I urge you, O Jews, to hear carefully what these things signify spiritually. In the voices and thunders is understood the cry of the preaching of the apostles and the other disciples of Christ. In the lamps is signified the brightness of miracles. In the sound of the trumpet is the strong preaching of the saints. [Col. 0289C] All these things were fulfilled at the coming of the Holy Spirit, when all Christ’s disciples thundered forth in diversity of languages, commandments, miracles, and signs. Sinai is interpreted “bush,” signifying the Church in which the Lord speaks to Moses. The fact that the Lord descended in fire and smoke when about to give the law signified that by the brightness of his manifestation he illumines believers and darkens the eyes of unbelievers through the smoke of their own vices, according to what he himself says: “I came into this world so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX). The fact that he is said to be seen in darkness signified that the ungodly, who savour earthly things, did not know him when he descended—that is, when he was born in humility—because of the darkness of wickedness.

Therefore, as we have said, O Jews, if you wish to attain the salvation of your souls, strive to understand the Old Testament not according to the letter but spiritually. Believe firmly also that the Word, coeternal with God the Father, assumed flesh from the Virgin Mother for the salvation of humankind; chose disciples; underwent the cross in that same flesh; tasted death; rose from the dead on the third day; after forty days ascended into heaven in great glory while the disciples looked on and marvelled; on the fiftieth day after his resurrection sent to those same disciples the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and himself; [Col. 0290A] divinely taught them the various kinds of languages; and through them filled the whole world with evangelical teaching. Therefore the law given on the mountain, through which God gave a rough people knowledge of himself, signified the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, through whom he watered all nations with spiritual teaching. But now let us see together, O Jews, how Almighty God gave the law of which we speak to the ancient fathers, distributed it over two tablets, in what order he began to give it, and how it ought to be understood.

[Note: Col. 0289D, *Sentences* III, distinction 37.] The Decalogue contains ten commandments, distributed in such a way that the three on the first tablet concern God—namely, knowledge and love of the Trinity—while the seven on the second tablet [Col. 0290B] concern love of one’s neighbour. Let us therefore hear what the first commandment on the first tablet is. “You shall have no strange gods; nor shall you make for yourself a graven image, nor any likeness” (Exod. 20). Origen says that these are two commandments; but Augustine more fully explains that this is one and the same commandment as “You shall have no strange gods,” when it forbids the worship of a fabricated thing, namely an idol or the likeness of anything. It is as though almighty God were more plainly declaring how human beings ought to believe, saying: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” [Note: Col. 0290D, Isidore, cited above, ch. 29.] Surely this is so that, hearing this, we may worship one God the Father and not pour out our fornication among many invented gods.

At this point you object to us, O Jews, that just as almighty God is one simple essence, so he is one person. We, on the contrary, reply and unhesitatingly maintain that the divine essence is not one person but truly three persons. The essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one; but the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, and these three are one true God. Therefore, through this very objection by which you thought to defeat us, O Jews, we who have been divinely instructed desire to overcome you. Let almighty God therefore speak: the first commandment of the first tablet is, “The Lord your God is one God.” This concerns God the Father, in whom, as Master Peter says in the *Sentences*, are unity and authority. For in him the Son and the Holy Spirit [Col. 0290D] abide eternally.

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. 20). Literally, this means: “You shall not swear by the name of your God for nothing.” The second commandment therefore concerns the Son when it says, “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”; that is, do not judge Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to be a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity (Rom. 8). Rather, believe him equal to God the Father: God from God, the true Word with God the Father, through whom all things were made from nothing.

The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. 20). Literally, Sabbath observance is commanded here; allegorically, however, it means: remember to keep rest here from vices and to await it hereafter in the contemplation of God. The third commandment therefore concerns the Holy Spirit, by whose gift everlasting rest is promised us. For since the Holy Spirit is said to be sevenfold, the Lord sanctified the seventh day. On the other working days sanctification is not mentioned, except on the Sabbath, where it is said: “God rested from all his work” (Gen. 22 [an apparent erroneous citation]). Therefore this commandment concerns the Holy Spirit, both because of the name “sanctification” and because eternal rest belongs to the gift of the Holy Spirit.

For above it is said: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” And again: “For six days you shall labour and [Col. 0291B] do all your work. But the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it” (Exod. 20). [Note: Col. 0291D. See here the annotations of the most learned John Grialius on chapter 6 of the *Questions on Genesis*, and chapter 29 on Exodus, and those of John Mariana on chapter 15, book I, *Against the Jews*. He seems to us to have penetrated Isidore’s meaning better than Grialius did, Col. 0292D.] In the six working days the course of six thousand years is signified, while in the seventh the blessed rest of the heavenly kingdom is foreshadowed.

Attend to this point, O Jews: because you now observe the Sabbath carnally after Christ’s Passion, you do not reconcile God to yourselves, but rather offend him, as he solemnly and terribly declares through the prophet: “My soul hates your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isa. 1). What profit, then, O Jews, enemies of truth, is there in observing Sabbaths which God says that he hates? That Sabbath alone is sanctified, beneficial to those who observe it, and pleasing to God, in which, after the good works of this life, eternal rest will be granted us. Therefore, whatever good we do in the present age, if we do it for the rest of the age to come, we truly observe the Sabbath.

Plainly, O unhappy Jews who deny that the divine essence is three persons, the law itself—which is declared to have been written by God’s finger—convicts you of being false witnesses in your assertion, since it declares that the aforesaid three commandments of the first tablet severally concern the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For when it says, “The Lord your God is one God,” it openly shows the person of the Father, from whom all things are and in whom all things subsist. When it says, “You shall not take the name of God in vain,” it indicates the person of the Son of God, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing. And when it [Col. 0291D] adds, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day,” it foreshadows the person of the Holy Spirit, through whom eternal rest will be given to all the faithful—not because the Holy Spirit accomplishes this apart from the Father and the Son. [Note: Col. 0292D, Master, cited above.]

The Church has indeed received this gift: namely, that forgiveness of sins should take place in the Holy Spirit. Although the whole Trinity undoubtedly brings about this forgiveness, it is nevertheless said properly to belong to the Holy Spirit, because, as St Paul says, he is the Spirit of the adoption of sons (Rom. 8). For he is the love of the Father and the Son, and their bond or communion; and therefore [Col. 0292A] our justification and rest are often attributed to him. These, then, as we have said, are the three commandments of the first tablet which concern the most holy Trinity, who is truly one God. The first, concerning the worship of one God, pertains to the Father, in whom is unity or authority; the second to the Son, in whom is equality; the third to the Holy Spirit, in whom is the communion of both.

Most clearly, then, O Jews, the law given on Mount Sinai to the ancient fathers defeats you in your most false disputation, because it proclaims that almighty God, three in persons and one in essence, is to be worshipped. There are, therefore, three persons—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and not one; but the divinity of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, with equal [Col. 0292B] glory and coeternal majesty. I therefore testify to you, O Jews who deny that the divine essence is three persons, that if you remain in this evil of unbelief, you will perish from the number of the elect. Believe, then, that the holy and indivisible Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is one true God, governing all things, containing all things, embracing all things; he gave the law to the ancient fathers, and in the last times through that same beloved Son chose the holy Church from Jews and Gentiles, and handed down to it the Gospel commandments to be observed. Therefore, after Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, O Jews, do not observe the law carnally; rather, understand it spiritually [Col. 0292C] and strive to fulfil it in deed, so that, putting off the old man and putting on the new—Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin—you may deserve to be joined to the fellowship of Christians (Eph. 4).

But now let us hear what the law says concerning the remaining seven commandments of the second tablet. The first commandment of the second tablet is: “Honour your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the land”—namely, the land of the living. [Note: Col. 0292D. Isidore and the Master, cited above; for all these matters are transcribed from them.] Thus children are commanded in this precept to honour their parents: not to behave insultingly, but to render them the reverence due through the duty of filial devotion. For one who does not know how to give honour to parents—to whom will he offer reverence or dutiful service? Or how can one love strangers who hates his own?

The second commandment [Col. 0292D] of the second tablet is: “You shall not kill.” We have often told you already, O Jews, that the commandments of the law are to be read according to the letter but understood spiritually. “You shall not kill” is therefore said: literally, the act of homicide is forbidden; but according to spiritual understanding, even the will to kill. An addition is made to this commandment in the Gospel according to the letter, because the letter of the Gospel expressly states what the letter of the law did not state. The letter of the Gospel expresses the spiritual understanding—that which spiritual people possess and according to which they live spiritually. [Col. 0293A] The letter of the law expresses the carnal meaning—that which carnal people possess and according to which they live carnally—and to it an addition has been made.

The third commandment of the second tablet is: “You shall not commit adultery,” that is, you shall not unite yourself with anyone outside the covenant of marriage. The whole meaning is plainly understood. Under the name of adultery, therefore, every unlawful sexual union and every illegitimate use of those members must be understood to be forbidden. More particularly, however, the person who approaches another’s wife in addition to his own commits adultery.

The fourth commandment of the second tablet is: “You shall not steal,” in which sacrilege and every kind of robbery are forbidden. For he who forbade theft did not permit robbery; rather, under the name of theft he rightly intended every unlawful appropriation of another’s property to be understood. Moreover, it should be known that sacrilege [Col. 0293B] is committed in three ways: when either a sacred thing is taken from a sacred thing, a non-sacred thing from a sacred thing, or a sacred thing from a non-sacred thing. Sacred means whatever has been dedicated to divine worship, such as a church or church property. Usury is also forbidden here, as included under robbery.

Hence St Jerome says: “There is no difference between seeking usury, defrauding, or robbing. Lend to your brother and receive what you gave; seek nothing excessive, because excess is reckoned as usury.” And, as St Augustine says: “Usury exists when someone demands more in anything whatever than he had received.” Hence St Jerome again says: “Some think that usury exists only in money; but they should understand that excess is called usury—for example, if in winter we give ten bushels and at harvest receive fifteen.” If, however, a question is raised concerning the children of Israel, who, at the Lord’s command, asked the Egyptians for vessels of silver and gold and costly garments and carried them away—did they commit theft? We say that those who did this in order to obey the Lord’s command did not commit [Note: Col. 0293D. “Have committed.”] theft and did not sin at all. Hence St Augustine says: “The Israelites did not commit theft, but rendered a mystery [Note: Col. 0293D. ‘Service’—*ministerium*—apparently the intended reading.] to God who commanded it.” For God, who gave the law, commanded this.

Just as an officer of a judge kills without sin the man whom the law commands to be killed, but if he does this of his own accord he is a murderer, even if he kills one whom he knows is to be executed by the judge; so the Hebrews who deceived the Egyptians from greed rather than from the Lord’s command undoubtedly [Col. 0293D] sinned. But those who accomplished this simply, not from the malice of rapacity but solely by the Lord’s command, did not sin at all.

The fifth commandment of the second tablet is: “You shall not speak false witness against your neighbour,” in which the crime of lying and perjury is forbidden. A question is commonly raised, however: is every lie forbidden? Some say that only the lie which harms and does not benefit the person to whom it is told is forbidden. For such a lie is not against one’s neighbour.

[Note: Col. 0293D, Master, ibid., distinction 38.] Nevertheless, it should be known that there are three kinds of lies. There are lies spoken for someone’s safety or advantage, not from malice but from kindness, as the midwives lied (Exod. 1), and Rahab the prostitute (Josh. 2). There is another kind of lie uttered in jest, which does not deceive those who hear it; for the person to whom it is said knows that it is said for the sake of a joke. These two kinds of lies are not without fault, but not with grave fault. Hence, among other statements, Isidore, teacher of Spain, says: [Note: Col. 0293D, *Synonyms*, book II, “On Lying.”] “No lie is just.” And again: “Do not strive to lie, even in order to help.” It does not befit perfect men to lie, not even for someone’s temporal life, lest they destroy their own soul for another’s body. They may, however, sometimes conceal the truth: for example, if someone does not wish to betray a person to death, let him keep the truth silent; [Col. 0294B] but let him never speak falsehood. The third kind of lie is that which a person utters from malice and duplicity of heart.

The sixth commandment of the second tablet is: [Note: Col. 0294D, distinction 40.] “You shall not covet your neighbour’s house; nor shall you desire his wife.” Whoever covets his neighbour’s property makes his soul saleable, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Nothing is more wicked [Note: Col. 0294D. Manuscripts: *more heavenly*—an erroneous reading.] than to love money.” For such a person makes his soul saleable, because “in his lifetime he casts away his innermost parts” (Ecclus. 10). [Note: Col. 0294D, Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, ch. 41.] Many have such greed for others’ possessions that they do not shrink even from committing murders, like Ahab, who caused Naboth to be killed because he coveted one vineyard (2 Kings [Vulgate numbering], 21).

“And you shall not desire his wife,” it says. Whoever therefore covets another man’s wife acts contrary to the commandment of the law. Although he does not touch her bodily but desires her only by sight, he nevertheless already sins against God, who said: “You shall not desire your neighbour’s wife.” “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Whoever covets another’s wife should know certainly that God will judge—that is, condemn—fornicators and adulterers. But if you who desire shamelessly to approach another’s wife think that what we say is to be despised, I urge you to hear patiently what the Apostle Paul has terribly threatened against adulterers and fornicators: “Neither adulterers, nor fornicators, nor men who lie with males shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). O how brief is the hour of unlawful intercourse by which [Col. 0294D] eternal life is lost! What salvation, I ask, does it bring to the body, or what gain, that leads the soul to Tartarus? Whoever therefore lives chastely and piously will rejoice without end with God’s elect.

The seventh commandment of the second tablet is: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property”—namely, neither slave, nor maidservant, nor ox, nor ass, nor field, nor anything that belongs to him. Greed never knows satisfaction; it is always avaricious, and the more it acquires, the more it seeks. [Note: Col. 0294D, Isidore, ibid.] The greedy person is tortured not only by the desire to increase his wealth but is also distressed by fear of losing it. [Col. 0295A] Indeed, many powerful men, inflamed by the frenzy of greed, covet not only the movable property of their fellow citizens but even drive such fellow provincials as they can from their borders and do not permit them to live with them. To such people the prophet Isaiah rightly says: “Woe to you who join house to house and couple field to field, even to the boundary of the place! Shall you alone live in the midst of the earth?” (Isa. 5). When such people are removed from this world, hell is accustomed to receive them for their condemnation. The same prophet subsequently announces this, saying: “Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit; and its mighty, lofty, and glorious ones shall descend to it” (ibid.). Nor is it surprising if, when they die, they are assigned to the fires of hell, who while living did not extinguish the flame of their greed.

“As St Isidore says, those who seethe with the desire of their greed are burned by the blast of diabolical inspiration. For the devil inflamed Eve’s mind with pride so that she ate from the forbidden tree. He inflamed Cain’s mind with envy so that he killed his brother. He inflamed Solomon with the torches of lust so that through love of desire he worshipped idols. He inflamed King Ahab’s mind with greed so that he added murder to avarice. Thus by these inspirations the devil secretly corrupts human hearts with desires.” What, then, dearest brothers, shall we say amid these things? We are born poor into this life, and poor we shall depart from this life. If we believe that the goods of this world are perishable, [Col. 0295C] why do we love perishable things with such love? Everything, therefore, that cannot remain with us longer must be utterly despised by us.

God set forth the aforesaid ten commandments in few words, wrote them with his finger on tablets of stone, and through the hand of Moses gave them to the children of Israel for knowledge of himself and love of neighbour. In them he most plainly showed how believers ought to believe. [Note: Col. 0295D, Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 29.] The first commandment forbids the superstition of idols; the second, the error of foolish people who take God’s name in vain; the third extinguishes love of the world and commands cessation from unlawful deeds; the fourth opposes impiety; the fifth drives out fornication; the sixth forbids cruelty [Note: Col. 0295D. Manuscripts erroneously read *credulity*]; the seventh repels rapacity; the eighth turns away falsehood; the ninth excludes adultery; the tenth declares that another’s property is not to be coveted. Why was the law written upon two tablets, except either to signify the two testaments or because of those two commandments of the love of God and neighbour, on which the whole law and the prophets depend? (Matt. 22.) These matters are written on the individual tablets: on one, three commandments concerning love of God; on the other, seven concerning fellowship with one’s neighbour.

[Col. 0296A] Furthermore, I wish you to know, O Jews, that just as the Egyptians are struck by ten plagues, so the tablets by which God’s peoples are governed are inscribed with ten commandments. Let us hear what blessed Augustine, the most subtle interpreter of the holy Scriptures, says about the ten plagues of Egypt and the ten commandments of the law—how each plague is set in opposition to a commandment, as though a medicine to a wound. [Note: Col. 0295D. Sermon 95, *On Time*, now no. 21.]

“The first commandment,” he says, “concerns one God, as is written in the law: [Note: Col. 0295D. Augustine in both places: ‘You shall have no other gods besides me.’] ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God’ (Deut. 6). The first plague is water changed into blood (Exod. 7), opposed to the first commandment of the first tablet. Understand by water the one God from whom all things are, since all things are generated from it. For by God’s just judgment they drank blood from that river in which they had been accustomed to kill the Hebrew infants.

“The second commandment is: ‘You shall not take [Note: Col. 0296D. Augustine, sermon 8: *you will take*; sermon 95: *you shall take*.] the name of your God in vain.’ God’s name is truth, as he himself says: ‘I am the truth’ (John 14). The second plague, an abundance of frogs (Exod. 8), is opposed to this second commandment. By these are understood heretics and philosophers, lacking reason and retaining only vanity and clamour against truth; in the ignorance of unbelief, like frogs in mournful marshes, they have a chattering voice.

“The third commandment is: ‘Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.’ This sanctification is to be free for virtues and to abstain from vices. Hence: ‘Be still and see that I am God’ (Ps. 45). The plague of gnats [Col. 0296C] (Exod. 8) is opposed to this commandment: tiny flies born from the mud of the earth, flying disorderly, rushing into the eyes, allowing no one to rest as they depart and rush back, and, when driven away, return again. Such as these flies are, such are restless people, who refuse to observe the Sabbath—that is, to devote themselves to good works and persevere in reading and prayer (1 Tim. 4). Therefore keep the commandment; beware the plague.

“The fourth commandment is: ‘Honour your father and mother,’ which is indeed human. [Note: Col. 0296D. The words ‘which is indeed human’ are not Augustine’s.] The opposing plague is the dog-fly, called in Greek *cynomyia*, because it is dog-like not to acknowledge the parents who begot one or to show them kindnesses.

“The fifth commandment is: [Note: Col. 0296D. He reverses the order of the divine commandments.] ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ The fifth plague is death among livestock (Exod. 9). For everyone who either uses his own wife without restraint, apart from the desire for children, or—what is a most serious crime—lies in wait for another man’s wife, daughter, or slave-woman [Note: Col. 0296D. Supply from the same source: ‘lies in wait for.’], overcome by the desire of lust, will be like a beast, as though he had lost his humanity: not transformed in shape but made like a beast in likeness and understanding. He does not understand David when he says: ‘Do not become like horse and mule, in whom there is no understanding’ (Ps. 31). And again: ‘Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them’ (Ps. 48).

“The sixth commandment is: [Col. 0297A] ‘You shall not kill.’ The sixth plague is boils upon the body, with swollen and bursting blisters (Exod. 9)—that is, the burning of wounds from furnace ashes. For anger, pride, and envy burn. If we could [Note: Col. 0297D. Augustine, sermon 95: ‘O, if we could.’] see the souls of murderers, without doubt we would weep more than at the festering wounds of ulcers. [Note: Col. 0297D. The same source in both places: ‘the festering bodies of those covered in sores.’]

“The seventh commandment is: ‘You shall not steal.’ The seventh plague is hail upon the crops (ibid.). No one gains unjust profit without causing unjust loss: where there is profit, there is loss. Therefore those who steal outwardly for their own desire are, by God’s just judgment, inwardly pelted with hail.

“The eighth commandment is: ‘You shall not bear false witness.’ The eighth plague is locusts (Exod. 10), an animal harmful by its tooth. For what does the false witness desire except to harm by biting and consume by lying? Hence the Apostle [Col. 0297B] [Note: Col. 0297D. Our Vulgate reads: ‘But if you bite and devour one another, take heed lest you be consumed by one another.’] says: ‘Thus you bite and devour one another, lest you be consumed by one another’ (Gal. 5).

“The ninth commandment is: ‘You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife.’ The ninth plague is thick darkness (Exod. 10). For nothing so pains the heart of the sufferer as that his wife should be desired; and this is thick darkness to him. [Note: Col. 0297D. Augustine contains nothing like the words enclosed in parentheses, except only in sermon 8, ‘every man is readier for another’s woman.’ We do not doubt that the manuscript consulted by B. Martin lacked this eighth sermon, since he excerpted in summary from the other, sermon 95, everything he had said about the ten plagues and ten commandments. Yet the greater similarity in the readings *accipies* and *accipias*, and in the phrase ‘for another’s,’ while another reading than the one noted here was sought in vain in sermon 95; and the exclamatory reading, ‘O, if we could,’ which belongs to this sermon and not the other, may perhaps cause hesitation as to why this is asserted so confidently.] (Conversely, nothing is so pleasing to the man who abuses her.)

“The tenth commandment is: ‘You shall not covet your neighbour’s property.’ Opposed to this commandment is the tenth plague, namely the death of the firstborn (Exod. 12). Among the possessions human beings have, the firstborn is dearest. One rightly loses this who desires fraudulently to take away his neighbour’s property. For example: you wish or hope to become someone’s heir; you would wish him to die at once. If he has children, [Col. 0297C] you would wish them to be destroyed. Therefore you are rightly punished by the death of the firstborn. But it is grievous that through this hidden and unjust desire you may lose the firstborn of your heart, which is faith. All your good works are your spiritual children, but among them faith is the firstborn. Whoever secretly covets another’s property loses inward faith, the firstborn. For no one works well unless faith has gone before.”

Thus far, O Jews, we have first set out for you according to the letter the law distributed by the Lord into ten commandments and given through Moses to the ancient fathers; next we have expounded it allegorically for the benefit of your souls, so that after Christ’s Passion and Resurrection you may no longer wish to observe it Jewishly, but may keep it spiritually. Hold as certain and do not doubt at all that, after the institution of the New Testament, whoever observes the law ceremonially is no longer a doer of the law but a transgressor. Therefore, as was said above, O Jews, the law is to be understood not according to the letter but spiritually, and to be fulfilled in deed in accordance with the rule of Gospel teaching. [Col. 0298A] “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3).

At this point you reply, O Jews, that the letter of the law is holy and good, most worthily bestowed by almighty God for the governance of the people, and thus was given not to kill but to give life to souls. You also say that you wish to know what the killing letter is and how it kills. Let Paul, therefore, apostle of Christ, born from your people and educated at the feet of your noble Gamaliel (Acts 22), yet by divine mercy not left in your error, now graciously come forward and plainly show what the killing letter is. Tell your fellow tribesmen, holy Paul—those who are of Abraham’s seed, for whom you grieved in the Acts of the Apostles and to whom you bore witness that they had zeal for God, [Col. 0298B] but not according to knowledge—tell them what is the killing letter and what grace gives life.

[Note: Col. 0298D, *Sentences* III, distinction 40, chapter “But if.”] “The killing letter,” he says, “is the Decalogue of the law. Yet it is not called the killing letter because the law is evil, but because, while forbidding sin, it increases desire and adds transgression unless divine grace frees a person. This grace did not abound under the law as it now abounds in the Gospel. Therefore the law is good, and yet without grace it kills, because it commands what cannot be fulfilled without grace. Since grace was lacking, then, the letter was killing.

“The letter of the Gospel also differs from the letter of the law because their promises differ. There—that is, in the law—earthly things were promised; but in the Gospel heavenly things are promised. The sacraments of the law and of the Gospel also differ, because the former only signified things to come, while these unquestionably confer divine grace. Their commandments also differ, namely as regards ceremonial matters, not as regards moral matters. For in moral matters they are the same, but are set forth more fully in the Gospel.”

You have heard, O Jews, the ten strings of the psaltery—that is, the ten commandments of the law—spiritually harmonized with Gospel teachings and imposed on both sexes. The strings of the New and Old Testaments are to be struck by the hand of love, so that the beasts of vices may be destroyed and the emblems of virtues may be nourished in believers’ hearts. You must therefore believe without doubt, O faithless Jews, that the ten commandments of the law prefigured the New [Col. 0298D] Testament and, when spiritually understood and mystically expounded, agreed with it. Thus, by the truest proofs from the law and prophets, we demonstrate that you lie in your assertion that the New Testament was neither foreshadowed in the holy Scriptures nor instituted by God.

O [Col. 0299A] unhappy Jews, slow of heart to believe those things concerning Christ which the holy patriarchs prefigured, the prophets foretold, and the apostles have now shown with clearer light to have been fulfilled! Do you not know that almighty God foreshadowed this future hardness of your unbelief when he wrote the law not on wooden tablets or on paper but on tablets of stone? [Note: Col. 0299D, Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter omitted in the source.] The tablets of the law were therefore of stone because they signified beforehand your stony heart. Thus, by the hardness and insensibility of stones is understood the stupidity of your hardened mind, concerning which the Lord says to you through the prophet Ezekiel: “I will take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11).

At his coming Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the human race, took away the heart of stone from certain children of Israel—namely, the apostles, evangelists, and his other disciples—softened the hardness of their unbelief, and gave them a heart of flesh, that is, an understanding heart. This was so that they might firmly believe that he had come from God the Father, redeemed the world through the cross, risen from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sat down at the right hand of God the Father. A heart of stone is therefore used for the hardness of unbelief, while a heart of flesh here means spiritual understanding. It is as though he said more plainly: “I will take away from you the heart of stone,” that is, the insensibility of a hardened and unbelieving mind; “and I will give you a heart of flesh,” that is, a heart capable of understanding and of receiving spiritual teaching.

Hence the Apostle also says that Christ’s teaching is written not [Col. 0299C] on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts (2 Cor. 3), that is, hearts possessing rational understanding. For these are not fleshly tablets in the sense that they require us to think carnally; rather, since flesh feels in comparison with stone, which has no sensation, an understanding heart is signified by a fleshly heart.

Therefore, O Jews, now drive from your hearts the hardness of long-standing unbelief. Believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man, so that you may deserve to receive from him the light of true understanding. For God is able, as St John the Baptist says, “to raise up children of Abraham from these stones” (Matt. 3). After Christ’s Passion and Resurrection, it is not those who are Abraham’s children according to the flesh, but those who are Abraham’s children according to faith, who are reckoned as his seed. God is therefore able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones: that is, he has the power to convert your stony hearts into the softness of faith and love for him, so that, raised from the eternal death of unbelief, you may always live by right belief in him who is true life and may be numbered among the children—not, I say, of Abraham’s flesh, but of Abraham’s faith.

For if you hold Abraham’s faith, you are truly Abraham’s children. But if you are not children of Abraham by faith, you are strangers to the blessing of his seed. In his seed also, which is Christ, all nations shall be blessed (Gen. 12). If, therefore, you do not hold Abraham’s faith, you are children not of Abraham but of Ham, Noah’s son, who earned a curse. For Abraham [Col. 0300A] was the first worshipper of the holy Trinity, when he saw, as it were, three angels in the form of three men and worshipped one God. If, therefore, you call yourselves Abraham’s children and long to rest after this life in his bosom, hold firmly the faith of the holy Trinity, which you persistently deny to this day: believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God.

What do you say to these things, O Jews? What do you answer or object? Do you still doubt that Christ is true God and true man? Do you intend to persist in the perfidy of unbelief? Yet I should like to know what faith you hold. This is at once your reply and your objection, O Jews. You say that you cannot in any way believe Christ to be one God [Col. 0300B], that he was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world, or that he was prefigured throughout the whole sequence of the Old Testament. You object falsely, you advance falsehood, O Jews, and you plainly lie in your assertion. From the beginning of the world Jesus Christ, God and man, was foreshown in the figures and enigmas of the patriarchs, most evidently foretold by the predictions of the prophets, and finally manifested by the proclamations of his holy apostles and openly shown to all nations under heaven.

God the Father therefore without doubt sent into this world, through the womb of the undefiled Virgin Mary, his most beloved Son, everywhere coequal and coeternal with him, and reconciled the human race to himself through him. For this purpose, indeed, Jesus Christ himself, God and man, offered himself upon the cross to God the Father as an odour of sweetness: that he might redeem the human race—that is, the holy Church—from the dominion of the ancient enemy and gain a kingdom for the same God the Father. Through him the holy Church offers acceptable offerings to God the Father; through him God the Father mercifully grants pardon to those who piously cry to him and truly repent. For he is the mediator of God and men, the man Jesus Christ, who for the redemption of the world received from the Virgin Mother a true body without sin; by it, as has been said, he reconciled the human race to God the Father.

Therefore, to demonstrate most plainly that you lie in your objection, O Jews, let us draw from the history of the book of Exodus how God the Father foreshadowed him as about to come into this [Col. 0300D] world and assume human flesh for the salvation of humankind.

For when God had said to the children of Israel, “You shall not make for yourselves gods of gold or gods of silver,” he immediately added: “You shall make me an altar of earth, and upon it you shall offer your holocausts and your peace-offerings” (Exod. 20). [Note: [Col. 0300D] Isidore, ibid., ch. 32.]

To make God an altar of earth is for the ancient people faithfully to await the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, mediator between God and man, and through him to offer sacrifices of devotion to God the Father. We also, the children of the holy Church, then make God an altar of earth when, strengthened by faith in the Incarnation of that same mediator between God and man, [Col. 0301A] Jesus Christ, we offer through him the gift offered to God the Father. Therefore, if, as has been said, we establish our feet firmly in faith in the Lord’s Incarnation, we spiritually sacrifice offerings acceptable to God the Father through Jesus Christ.

Let us hear again what God Almighty says to the children of Israel—indeed, to all the children of the holy Church: “But if you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of cut stones; for if you lift your tool upon them, they shall be defiled” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0301D] Isidore, ch. 33.] The cut stones are those who divide the unity of peace and divide themselves from brotherly charity through hatred and schisms. Christ does not admit such persons into his body, of which the construction of that altar cast a shadow as a figure. But the uncut stones from which the altar is commanded to be built [Col. 0301B] are those established in unity of faith and conduct. To them the blessed apostle Peter says: “Like living stones, be built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer” [Note: [Col. 0301D] Another manuscript: “offering.”] “spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 2). Nor has iron been applied to these, because they are uncorrupted and have not received the fiery darts of the evil one—that is, of the ancient enemy. Such persons make one altar through unity of faith and harmony of charity.

Recognize, therefore, O Jews, that you have lied in your assertion, you who say that Jesus Christ, God and man, is neither the true Son of God nor prefigured in the Old Testament. Without doubt, therefore, God the Father, as he promised through the mouth of the holy prophets from the beginning of the age, [Col. 0301C] sent his beloved Son for the redemption of the world; through his Passion and cross he redeemed the holy Church from the enemy’s dominion; and after the Resurrection he crowned him with glory and honor, exalted him at his right hand, and set him over all the works of his hands.

At this point, raising a question, O Jews, you say to us: “Why did God the Father wish Jesus Christ his Son to undergo the Passion of the cross, when he could redeem the entire world by a word alone?” We answer: God Almighty therefore wished Jesus Christ his Son to redeem the human race through the cross because we, who had been wounded in Adam through the tree of concupiscence [Note: [Col. 0301D] Perhaps: “through desire for the tree.”], might be healed [Col. 0301D] through the mystery of the wood of the cross from the wounds inflicted on us by the serpent’s bite.

We therefore owe innumerable thanksgivings to that same God and man Jesus Christ, who by the will of God the Father deigned to redeem us with the blood of his own Passion and, like an innocent Lamb, to take away through the cross, death having been conquered, the sins of the whole world. You say, O Jews, that God could never be seized by men, nailed to a cross, or die for men. But we, greatly grieving over your misery and unbelief and wishing you to know the rule of the Catholic faith, answer you briefly as follows. [Col. 0302A] God indeed cannot be seized or die, as you say, because he is incomprehensible and immortal. But Jesus Christ is true God and true man: according to his humanity he could be seized and die, while according to his divinity he remains incomprehensible and immortal with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Hence Isidore, teacher of the Spains, says in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 30:

> “It was not the substance of Christ’s divinity that endured the injury of the cross, but only the assumed nature of humanity. Christ’s body sustained the Passion; his divinity, however, had no share in the injury.”

Still doubting Christ’s divinity, O Jews, you raise this objection to us, saying: “If [Col. 0302B] Christ is one true God with God the Father and, as you Christians assert, can do with him whatever he wills, why did he permit himself to be seized by men, bound, scourged, crucified, wounded, to die, and to be buried?” In response we say that the Son of God and the Virgin, though he truly can do all things with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless humbly subjected himself to the Passion and piously willed to die for the redemption of the human race for three reasons. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Isidore, ibid.]

The first reason was that Christ might be given as redemption for the guilt of the world [Note: [Col. 0302D] “as redemption for the guilt of the world.”], and that the ancient enemy might be caught as if by the hook of the cross: namely, so that he might vomit forth those whom he had swallowed and lose the prey he held—not conquered by power [Col. 0302C] but by justice, not by domination but by reason.

The second reason was to provide a rule of life for those who would follow. For he ascended the cross in order to give us an example of Passion and Resurrection: of Passion, to strengthen patience; of Resurrection, to awaken hope in those who believe in him. That is, he showed us two lives in the flesh: one laborious in the present age, the other blessed in the age to come—the laborious life which we must endure, and the blessed life for which we must hope.

The third reason for undertaking the cross was that the proud and puffed-up wisdom of this age might fall humbled through the preaching of the cross, considered foolish. [Note: [Col. 0302D] Supplied from Isidore: “might fall humbled.”] Thus, as blessed Paul says, it might be manifest how much wiser than human beings is that which is God’s foolishness, and how much stronger than all human strength is that which is God’s weakness [Col. 0302D] (1 Cor. 1).

It has been plainly shown to you, O Jews, for what reasons Jesus Christ, God and man, in order to free the human race from the devil’s dominion, mercifully willed to subject himself to the Passion and to ascend the cross, though he could redeem it by the mere nod of his will. For he suffered not unwillingly but voluntarily; nor as though overcome in power by the Jews, but freely, because mercy overcame him.

At this point, O Jews, enemies of truth, as though scorning the saving Passion of Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, and despising the triumph of his most glorious [Col. 0303A] cross, you ask us: “Why did your Christ choose rather to die on a cross than by decapitation or by any other death? Why, too, do you show such reverence to his cross, or what gain do you think you will obtain from it?” Although you ask us these things, O Jews, not with right intention but with a perverse mind, nevertheless hear attentively what, God granting, we answer for the benefit of the faithful.

Christ therefore chose to undergo the torment of the cross in order to give believers in him instruction in enduring adversities and an example of patience. For this reason, too, all the Christian people show great reverence to his most holy cross: because upon it hung the one who truly is the salvation of the world. Hence the prophet [Col. 0303B] says: “Our salvation will come swiftly, and it will break the yoke of our captivity.” We therefore rightly show great reverence to that life-giving cross, because upon it we humbly adore Jesus Christ, God and man, and with all devotion venerate the cross itself in Christ.

Compelled by charity, I therefore urge you, O Jews, to raise the eyes of your heart in pure devotion, so as to understand the breadth, length, height, and depth of the most holy cross. [Note: [Col. 0303D] Isidore, as above.] Whoever wishes perfectly to understand the things that concern Christ must indeed have the eyes of the heart cleansed from the filth of vices.

The breadth of the cross is the transverse beam upon which the hands of the suspended one are extended. Its length is from the breadth downward to the earth. Its height is from the breadth upward [Col. 0303C] to the head. Its depth is that part hidden when fixed in the earth. I do not wish you to be unaware, O Jews, that the entire life of the saints is portrayed by this sign of the holy cross. It is as though each person were told: “Take up your cross” (Matt. 16). For [Note: [Col. 0303D] Perhaps: “then.”] when the flesh is afflicted, when our members that are upon the earth are put to death (Col. 3)—namely fornication, impurity, lust, and so forth—and when the outward person is being destroyed while the inward is renewed day by day through the Passion of the cross (2 Cor. 4): these are good works indeed, yet still laborious works, whose reward is rest. Hence the Apostle says: “Rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12), so that, thinking of future rest, we may do good works with cheerfulness and labor.

[Col. 0303D] The breadth of the cross in its transverse beam, where the hands are fastened, signifies this cheerfulness. For by the hands work is understood; by breadth, the charity of the worker, because sorrow produces not breadth but narrowness.
