This signifies faith in the holy Trinity, from which the entire Church hangs and by which it is sustained. In the fact that curtains of one measure were stretched twenty-eight cubits in length and four in width, the law of the holy Gospel is signified.

[Col. 0329A] For the number seven customarily signifies the Law because of the many sevenfold mysteries which are joined to the four Gospels. Four times seven makes the number twenty-eight [Note: [Col. 0329D] Isidore, as cited above, ch. 53.]. Ten curtains are therefore made in order to make the complete number of perfection and signify the Decalogue of the Law. Yet these curtains are connected to one another by fifty golden rings, because all believers are joined by the gift of the Holy Spirit in the bond of faith and charity; they are spiritually united to Jesus Christ, who is the head of the whole Church (Eph. 5), and through him, who is the straightest way, are daily raised to the heavenly homeland.

If you, O Jews, enemies of truth, attentively consider the aforementioned testimony of Exodus spiritually expounded [Col. 0329B], you plainly recognize that you yourselves have lied in your objection—you who deny that Jesus Christ is true God and refuse to receive the New Testament. For while it proclaims the concord of the Old and New Testaments and figuratively shows that all believers are joined by the bond of faith and charity to Jesus Christ their head and may through him reach the vision of the splendor of God the Father, it indisputably proves you false witnesses, since you assert that he is not the Savior of those who hope in him. But I urge you, O Jews, enemies of truth, who say that Christ cannot forgive the sins of those who hope in him, patiently to hear what the goat-hair veils, of which we made mention above, signify spiritually in the holy Church [Col. 0329C] [Note: [Col. 0329D] Idem, ch. 54.].

For eleven veils are commanded by the Lord to be made. Sin is also represented in goat hair, because of the goats to be placed at the left hand of Jesus Christ when he judges (Matt. 25). Therefore, since those who possess perfection of the Law by the gift of the Holy Spirit were signified above in the ten curtains, sinners in the Church—that is, transgressors of the Law—are in turn understood in the number eleven of goat-hair coverings, because it exceeds the number ten [Note: [Col. 0329D] “Number.”]. Yet those goat-hair veils too were joined by fifty loops, namely because of the sign of repentance and hope of remission through true confession of sins. Therefore, as was said, the goat-hair veils suspended by loops in the construction of the tabernacle prefigured the future repentance of sinful people [Col. 0329D] in the holy Church.

[Note: [Col. 0329D] Isidore, book 2, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 17.] Job first provided an example for penitents when, after his scourges, he undertook lamentations of repentance even in ashes and goat hair, still reproaching himself, saying: “Therefore I reproach myself and do penance in dust and ashes” (Job 42). After him David gave us instruction in repentance when, having fallen through a grave fault and having heard his sin from the prophet [Col. 0330A], he immediately repented and healed his fault by the confession of repentance (2 Kings 10). Thus the Ninevites, at Jonah’s preaching, repented in ashes and goat hair and, God being favorable to them, escaped the danger alike of body and soul (Jonah 3). They displeased themselves for what they had become by sinning; and, for what they became by repenting and reforming their lives, they pleased God. Many others also in the Old Testament offered true repentance to God and deserved to obtain mercy from him.

“But repentance,” as says blessed Isidore, our patron, “is the medicine of a wound, the hope of salvation through which sinners are saved and through which God is moved to mercy. It is not measured by time but is accomplished by the depth of mourning and tears [Col. 0330B]. For repentance takes its name from punishment, by which the soul is tortured and the flesh is mortified from vices and fleshly desires. Those who perform lawful repentance accordingly let their hair and beard grow, in order to show the abundance of crimes by which the sinner’s head is burdened. Hence it is written: ‘Each person is bound by the cords of his own sins’ (Prov. 5). For if a man lets his hair grow, it is a disgrace to him (1 Cor. 11). Penitents take upon themselves this very disgrace according to the merit of their sins.

Why are penitents laid prostrate in goat hair? Clearly because goat hair is the remembrance of sins, owing to the goats, as we said above, who will be at the left hand of God and man Jesus Christ on the day of judgment [Col. 0330C] (Matt. 25). Since goat hair is woven from the hairs of goats, sinners are signified by goat hair. Therefore, casting themselves down [Note: [Col. 0330D] “Casting themselves down” (*consternentes*).], they lie prostrate in goat hair, as though saying: ‘My sin is always before me’ (Ps. 50). They are also sprinkled with ashes, that they may remember that they are ash and dust, or because they have become dust—that is, lowly persons [Note: [Col. 0330D] Editions: *impii*, “the ungodly.”]. Hence those transgressors, namely the first human beings, who departed from God by sinning and offended their Creator by their evil deeds, returned to the dust from which they had been taken and made. Penitents therefore rightly mourn sins in goat hair and ashes, because goat hair displays the harshness and piercing of sins, whereas ashes display the dust of the dead. Therefore we rightly perform repentance in both, so that in the piercing of goat hair [Col. 0330D] we may recognize the vices which we committed through fault, and in the dust of ashes weigh the sentence of death to which we came by sinning.

The catholic Church faithfully binds the remedy of repentance to be practiced in hope of pardon; and after the one sacrament of baptism—which it carefully forbids to be repeated, as commended by singular tradition—it supplies the aid of a healing remedy. All ought to recognize that they need its remedies for the daily excesses of human frailty [Col. 0331A], without which we cannot live in this life; with the dignity of ecclesiastical orders preserved, so that confession is made by priests and Levites to God alone as witness, but by the rest solemnly before God and before the altar, with a priest present. Thus fruitful confession here covers what rash desire or neglect marked by ignorance has brought upon a person. For as we believe that in baptism all iniquities are remitted, or that no sin is imputed to anyone through martyrdom, so in the fruitful compunction of repentance we confess that all sins are wiped away. For tears of repentance, as Isidore, teacher of the Spaniards, says, are reckoned before God in place of baptism. Hence, however great or grievous sins may be, one must not despair of God’s mercy concerning them.

But in the work of repentance, [Col. 0331B] as was said above, the measure of time is not so much to be considered as the measure of sorrow. For God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart (ibid.). Nevertheless, as great as was the intention of a mind recklessly bent upon evil in sinning, so great must be the devotion of mourning. There is a twofold groaning of repentance: when we lament either what we did badly or what we did not do but ought to have done. One truly performs repentance who neither neglects to repent of and bewail past deeds nor commits again deeds requiring repentance. But whoever pours out tears without ceasing and nevertheless does not cease to sin has lamentation but does not have cleansing from sins. If anyone is converted to repentance through God’s grace, he should not be disturbed if, after amendment, abandoned vices again strike at his heart, provided they cannot harm his good manner of life; for such thoughts are not for condemnation but for testing. Nor are they an occasion for entering danger, but rather for increasing virtue.

For even if someone ceases to be evil through repentance near the end of life, he ought not despair because he is at the last limit of life; for God does not consider what we were before, but what we shall be near life’s end. God justifies or condemns each person according to that person’s end, as it is written: ‘He judges the ends of the earth’ (1 Kings 2); and elsewhere: ‘He himself considers the end of all things’ (Job 28). Therefore we do not doubt that a person is justified near the end through the compunction [Col. 0331D] of repentance. But because this rarely happens, one must fear that, while conversion is postponed to the end, unexpected death may come first before repentance brings aid. For this reason, although conversion at life’s end is good, conversion made long before the end is better, so that one may pass more securely from this life.”

[Note: [Col. 0329D] From here to “moved to mercy” are words of Sermon 41, *To the Brothers in the Desert*, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VI [Col. 0330D], except that where this text reads *provocatur* (“is moved”), that text reads *inclinatur* (“is inclined”). Let others judge whether Isidore, or the author of that sermon, copied Isidore.]

Therefore, O Jews, as was said, the goat-hair veils suspended in the tabernacle of the covenant prefigured the repentance of converts in the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0331D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 54.]. These goat-hair coverings, as I wrote much earlier, by which the tabernacle was covered at the Lord’s command so that it might endure rains, winds, and storms, may be understood as the coarse minds [Col. 0332A] of certain persons who, by the hidden judgment of God, are sometimes set over others in the Church, though they are harsh. Hence he fittingly added afterward ram skins, so that by rams he might signify the leaders and superiors of the Churches. And because such men do not fear to serve secular concerns, they must also bear the winds of temptation and this world’s adversities, so that those who shine spiritually within the holy Church as fine linen, hyacinth, and purple may securely shine inwardly, while their superiors and rulers labor outside against the storms and tempests of the age.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, O lying—indeed, most lying—Jews, is true God and true man. Through true repentance he forgives sins to those who believe in him [Col. 0332B], causes them to adhere to himself indivisibly by the cords of true faith and loops of perfect charity, and through himself admits them into the heavenly kingdom to behold the splendor of his almighty God the Father. Therefore, since the authorities of the Old Testament agree spiritually in Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, they indisputably prove you false witnesses, you who wholly disagree with truth and assert that he cannot forgive sins to those who hope in him, unite them spiritually, or lead them to the heavenly homeland.

Here consequently you say, O Jews, that no one can forgive sins except God alone. To this we, on the contrary, reply that truly and without any ambiguity God alone forgives sins; and by his most just judgment he imputes sins to whom he wills and absolves whom he wills from sins. For almighty God truly releases the penitent person from the guilt of punishment, and he releases him when he inwardly enlightens the mind by inspiring true contrition of heart. [Note: [Col. 0331D] *Sentences*, IV, distinction 18, § “But it is asked.”] For no one is truly compuncted concerning sin, having a contrite and humbled heart, except in charity. Whoever has charity is worthy of eternal life. But no one is at the same time worthy of life and death. Therefore he is no longer then bound by the debt of eternal death. He has ceased to be a child of wrath from the time when he began to love God and neighbour and to repent. From that point, therefore, he has been released from the wrath which does not remain upon one who believes in Christ, but upon one who does not believe. [Note: [Col. 0332D] The Master does not have what we enclose in brackets.] [For thus the blessed Evangelist John says: “He who believes in the Son of God has eternal life; but he who does not believe does not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3).] Therefore he is not afterwards, through the priest to whom he confesses his sins, liberated from eternal wrath, from which he has already been liberated by the Lord from the time when he said: “I will confess [the evils that I have done].” Thus God alone inwardly cleanses a person from the stain of sin and releases him from the debt of eternal punishment, he who says through the prophet: “I alone blot out the iniquities and sins of the people” (Isa. 43). For just as God reserved to himself the power of baptism, so also that of penance; and therefore, just as by his grace he inwardly enlightens the soul, so at the same time he remits the debt of eternal death.

[Col. 0333A] For he himself, by himself, then covers the sins of penitents when he does not reserve them for punishment—that is, when he remits the debt of punishment. That he himself covers them Augustine plainly indicates in expounding that passage of Psalm 31: “Whose sins are covered,” that is, concealed and abolished. For if God has covered sins, he has not wished to take notice of them; if he has not wished to take notice of them, he has not wished to punish them, but has wished to forgive. Thus he says that sins are covered by God, not because God does not see them, but because he does not punish them eternally. For God’s seeing sins is his imputing them for punishment; but his turning his face away from sins is his not reserving them for punishment. Those whose sins God forgives, he covers, so that they may not be revealed in judgment.

Therefore we may rightly say and believe [Col. 0333B] that God alone forgives sins, and yet that he has granted the Church the power of binding and loosing; but he himself looses or binds in one manner, and the Church in another. For he alone, by himself, forgives sin, because he both cleanses the soul from its inward stain and absolves it from the debt of eternal death. He has not granted this to priests, though he has given them the power of binding and loosing—that is, of showing persons to be bound or loosed. Hence the Lord first restored the leper to health by himself, and then sent him to the priests, that he might be shown cleansed by their judgment (Matt. 8). So too he presented Lazarus, already restored to life, to the disciples to be loosed (John 11), because although someone may be loosed before God, he is nevertheless not loosed in the sight of the Church [Col. 0333C] except through the judgment of a priest. Therefore, in loosing or retaining sins, the evangelical priest acts and judges as did formerly the legal priest in the case of those defiled by leprosy (Lev. 13), which signified sin.

Hence blessed Jerome says on Matthew, where the Lord says to Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matt. 16): “Some,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0333D] The Master wished to soften the sharpness of the most holy doctor by substituting *some* for *bishops and priests*, as Jerome wrote, and by omitting the adverb *rightly*.] “who do not understand this passage rightly, take something from the arrogance of the Pharisees, so that they think they can condemn the innocent or absolve the guilty, whereas before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of those accused that is considered. In Leviticus lepers are commanded to show themselves to the priests (Lev. 14); the priests [Col. 0333D] do not make them leprous or clean, but distinguish who are clean and who unclean; so too [Note: [Col. 0333D] The Master reads somewhat differently: “Thus here also it is plainly shown that God does not always follow the judgment of the Church, which through misinformation . . . judges; but God always judges according to truth. And in forgiving . . . sins evangelical priests have that legal right . . . which formerly,” etc.] now the priests of the Gospel.” For it is plainly shown that God does not [Note: [Col. 0334D] Supply: *always*.] follow the judgment of the Church, which sometimes judges through misinformation and ignorance. But God always judges according to truth in forgiving [Col. 0334A] or retaining sins. Evangelical priests now have, as Master Peter says in the *Sentences*, the same right and office that legal priests formerly had under the Law in treating lepers. Thus they forgive or retain sins when they judge and declare them forgiven or retained by God. For priests place the name of the Lord upon the children of Israel, but he himself blesses, as is read in the book of Numbers, chapter 6. Blessed Jerome noted this manner of binding and loosing above.

Here another manner of binding and loosing is also shown. Priests bind [Note: [Col. 0334D] § “They bind.”] when they impose penitential satisfaction upon those making confession. They loose when they remit some part of it, or admit those purified through it to communion in the sacraments. [Col. 0334B] In this sense priests too are said to forgive or retain sins. Hence blessed Augustine says: [Note: [Col. 0334D] These are not Augustine’s words but the Master’s. The authority of the blessed bishop is the one which the Master himself cites, namely: “Those whose sins priests forgive, God forgives,” etc. Yet the book *On True and False Penance*, where these words occur, is a spurious work attributed to Augustine, as the Benedictines demonstrate in the Appendix, vol. VI.] “Priests exercise the work of justice upon sinners when they bind them by a just penalty; the work of mercy when they relax some part of it or reconcile them to communion in the sacraments.”

Although in your other objections, O faithless Jews, against Christ and against his bride, that is, against the holy Church, you are accustomed to utter many lying blasphemies, here you have advanced a truth when you said that no one except God alone can forgive sins. Christ, therefore, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God, who mercifully forgives sins to those who faithfully believe in him and perfectly [Col. 0334C] repent of the evils they have committed; who grants them spiritual gifts of virtues so that they may persevere in good works; and who unceasingly raises them up to merit the reward of the heavenly homeland. He who offered himself upon the altar of the cross to God the Father for the redemption of humankind, he himself truly forgives sins to those who trust in him.

You, O Jews, enemies of truth, who until now, with obstinate minds, refuse to give credence to the authorities of the Old Testament which furnish the truest testimonies that Christ is true God and true man: I urge you at least diligently to hear what the doctors of the holy Church say of him. Instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, the doctors of the Church expound spiritually the teachings of the New and Old Testaments; and therefore they utter unquestionably true statements concerning the mysteries of Christ and [Col. 0334D] the Church, by which they raise the minds of their hearers to desire heavenly things. Let us therefore bring forward blessed Peter, O faithless Jews—the unyielding pillar and most valiant defender of the true faith—and carefully hear from him whether Jesus Christ, God and man, can forgive sins to those who faithfully [Col. 0335A] believe in him.

“Men and brethren,” he says, “and fathers: the Lord commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead. To him all the prophets bear witness, that all who believe in him receive forgiveness of sins through his name” (Acts 10). Since, therefore, he is without any doubt judge of the living and the dead, it is plainly evident that in him forgiveness of all sins is established for faithful peoples. So that you may not doubt that what is said concerning him, the mediator of God and humankind, is true, I urge you patiently to hear what the aforesaid apostle again adds while reproving your fathers concerning Christ’s passion: “The God of [Col. 0335B] our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted this one at his right hand as Prince and Saviour, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins” (Acts 5). Therefore, in that blessed Peter calls Christ Prince and Saviour, declares that he was exalted at the right hand of God the Father, and affirms that repentance and forgiveness of sins are given through him to Israel—that is, to all who rightly believe in him—he plainly convicts and confounds, all ambiguity removed, you who deny that he can forgive sins.

Let Paul also, the apostle, founder and organizer of Christ’s Church, come forward, O faithless Jews, and offer us testimony concerning Christ. For he himself says in [Col. 0335C] the Acts of the Apostles [Note: [Col. 0335D] Rather, in First Corinthians 3:10.]: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation, besides which no one can lay another, which is Christ Jesus.” Therefore let him, as a wise and discerning man fully instructed in the pages of the Old and New Testaments, graciously come forward and testify to us concerning Christ: whether he is the true Son of God, and whether he can truly forgive sins to those who hope in him. Then, once the faithlessness of deadly obstinacy has been driven from your hearts, you may be able with us unquestionably to believe that he is one God by nature with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, and devoutly receive his baptism. Speak, Saint Paul, to us who now perfectly believe by God’s grace, and to the Jews who still doubt; speak concerning Christ’s divinity [Col. 0335D] and power, what was revealed to you through the Holy Spirit (Eph. 3). For you affirm that you are yourself debtor to Jews and Greeks, Gentiles and barbarians, wise and foolish. Speak, then, of Christ, so that the Jews, convicted by your most true testimony, may abandon the error of unbelief and turn to the true faith of the holy Trinity: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

“Let us give thanks,” he says, “to God the Father, who has made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints in light; who has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption through his blood, in the forgiveness of sins: who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature” (Col. 1).

[Col. 0336A] I urge you, O Jews, not carelessly to pass over this authority of such manifest truth, hindered by the blindness of malice or wickedness, but to lay it up more attentively in your hearts for the salvation of your souls. Let us therefore carefully consider the apostle’s foregoing testimony and examine more subtly how it should be understood. In that the Apostle urges us to give thanks to God the Father because he made us worthy to share in the inheritance of the saints, rescued us from the power of darkness, and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, it is certainly clear, O Jews, enemies of truth, that Christ is not a mere man, as you falsely blaspheme, but is true man and true Son of God.

But in what the Apostle subsequently says of him—“in [Col. 0336B] whom we have redemption through his blood, in the forgiveness of sins”—he openly shows that Christ offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for the redemption of the world, and washed his people from sins in his own blood. For our redemption is, after the power of the devil has been destroyed, the capacity for freedom. I urge you, O Jews, patiently to hear what the apostle Paul further adds concerning him: “Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.” It is as though he said more plainly: Great benefits have rightly come to us through the Son of God and of the Virgin, who is the image of God—that is, fully like God the Father—“invisible,” that is, incomprehensible, “the firstborn of every creature,” namely eternal and the only-begotten before every creature.

The image of a king is one thing [Col. 0336C] on a coin and another in a son. We are the coin, made in the image of God; Christ is the Son, the image in every respect like God the Father. Hence Master Peter Lombard says on this verse in the Epistles: “Christ is the image of God the Father because he is from him and differs from him in nothing.” Again he says: “No image of God ought to be worshipped except that which is what he is; nor should it be worshipped instead of him, but with him.”

It is plainly evident, O rebellious and unbelieving Jews, that Jesus Christ, God and man, inasmuch as he is God, was naturally begotten of God the Father before all ages; and that in time he assumed sinless flesh from the undefiled Virgin; that according to that flesh he offered himself [Col. 0336D] to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for the redemption of the world; that he mercifully shed his own blood for the forgiveness of our sins; and that he possessed the fullest power to forgive sins even inasmuch as he is man. For the power which the same Son of God had eternally from God the Father, he who was born in time as man from the Virgin received. Thus, when they brought him a paralytic lying on a bed to be healed, and the scribes murmured against him and envied him, he said: “That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins”; then he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Matt. 9). Therefore, O unhappy Jews, as the doctors of the Old and New Testaments proclaim Jesus Christ [Col. 0337A] true God and true man and affirm that he has the fullest power to forgive sins, they prove beyond doubt that you are false witnesses in your most lying assertions.

But if you still doubt the divinity of Jesus Christ, God and man; if you still do not believe that he can forgive sins to those who hope in him; if you deny that he was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world: let us bring forward blessed John the Evangelist and unquestionably believe whatever he tells us concerning Christ. For this most holy Evangelist bore true testimony to Christ in all the things that he saw. Speak then, Saint John, of Christ what you know, so that the Jews who deny that he was [Col. 0337B] sent by God the Father for the salvation of humankind and can forgive sins to those who hope in him, may be convicted by your authority, believe him to be true God, and devoutly receive the catholic faith: “In this is charity,” he says, “not as though we had loved God, but because he first loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4). O holy John, in affirming that God the Father loved us and sent his Son as the propitiation for our sins, you rightly contradict the Jews, false witnesses, who stubbornly deny that he is the Son of God and suffered according to his humanity for our sins; indeed, in their objection you powerfully convict them.

[Col. 0337C] Let blessed Ambrose also, held in great reverence in Christ’s Church, come forward to strengthen the catholic faith and wholly confound your faithlessness, O Jews; and let him declare before all whether Christ has power to forgive sins to those who hope in him. “He alone,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0337D] *Sentences*, distinction 18, § “But it is asked.”] “forgives sins who alone died for our sins.” Let blessed Augustine also, the strongest hammer of heretics, pagans, and Jews, graciously come forward and bear witness to Christ, to refute your faithlessness, O Jews, enemies of truth, and to strengthen the catholic faith more and more. “No one,” he says, “takes away sins except Christ alone, who is the Lamb of God the Father taking away [Col. 0337D] the sins of the world” (John 1).

Yet it must be known that the Son does nothing without the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the works of the holy Trinity are indivisible. Let us hear, moreover, what blessed Augustine adds concerning Christ’s power: “Christ takes away sins both by forgiving what has been done, and by helping so that they may not be done again, and by leading to eternal life, where they cannot be done at all.” See how the heralds of truth agree with one another, O Jews hard and slow of heart to believe! See by what clear reasoning they prove that you have lied in all your assertions! Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is true God, begotten of God the Father before all [Col. 0338A] ages; and he is also true man, born in time from the incorrupt Virgin, having true power to forgive sins to those who hope in him.

§ XXIV.—

How the veil concealing the inner part of the tabernacle prefigured the Jews’ long-lasting blindness; and how it also signifies the present Church, although ignorance of the truth to be known was less imputed to it. He exhorts the Jews willingly to hear the doctors of the holy Church and to fulfil their precepts by good works. He presents a most beautiful measure for the Church’s prelates in preaching, and prefigures it from the sayings of Exodus. He adds how great a rigor tempered by mercy ought to be present in a confessor, and the history of Moses. In good rulers there should be joined the authority of governing and the kindness of consolation; and how close likewise is the union of mercy with discipline [Col. 0338B], and whether those who oppose God’s wrath set themselves against the onset of divine destruction. He asks: since no one can resist God’s wrath, how do the words of the Lord testify that many have opposed the indignation of the heavenly judgment? He answers from the sayings of blessed Gregory. Furthermore, he enumerates the diverse kinds of faithful persons within the holy Church and prefigures them in the variety of the tabernacle’s works. He summons the Jews to receive the Christian name from Christ and to believe that he was sent for the redemption of the world and anointed with spiritual anointing; he washes his own from sins and seals them with the chrism of sanctification. He prefigures holy chrism, together with prayers and virtuous works.

If, therefore, you desire through him to attain eternal life with his elect, firmly believe that he is one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit; devoutly receive his baptism, [Col. 0338C] and hold firmly that he will come to judge the living and the dead. But if you persist in the faithlessness of your unbelief, you will without doubt perish eternally. What do you say to these things, O Jews? What objection do you raise, or what answer do you give? I would like to know whether, now that the faithlessness of unbelief has been cast aside, you believe Christ to be true God, or whether you still doubt his divinity in order to increase your condemnation. In answer to this you say that you neither wish to believe Jesus Christ to be true God nor receive his baptism, but desire to end your life in Judaism, as did all your fathers. O perverse and faithless nation! O nation indeed corrupt and without spiritual prudence! Do you still intend to persist in the wickedness of your unbelief? O [Col. 0338D] blind nation, alienated from the light of truth which is Christ! Would it not be much better for you to be saved with the faithful than to perish with the unbelieving? You will without doubt perish eternally unless you believe Jesus Christ to be one true God with God the Father and the Holy Spirit.

That long-lasting blindness of your unbelief, O wretched and pitiable Jews, was undoubtedly prefigured figuratively by the veil which concealed the inner part of the tabernacle so that it might not be seen by all. [Note: [Col. 0338D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 55, near the end.] For what the Law and Prophets sang at the prompting of the Holy Spirit was hidden and could not be openly understood while the veil intervened. Therefore those obscure and covered things which they uttered concerning Christ and the Church, the New Testament, and the future judgment generated this deadly obstinacy in your hearts. For when there was no one to interpret spiritually the Scriptures of the Old Testament, ignorance of the truth that ought to be known was less imputed to you. But after Christ came and, at the time of his Passion, tore that veil from top to bottom (Mark 15), all those things that had been hidden were revealed through his Passion to confirm our faith, as the Apostle says: “God has revealed them to us through his Spirit; for the Holy Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2).

Now therefore, O unhappy Jews, Jesus [Col. 0339B] Christ, God and man, has delivered the world from the power of the devil by his most precious blood; he has torn from top to bottom the veil hung between the holy place and the holy of holies (Mark 15), that is, he has taught the spiritual understanding of the obscure sayings of the Law and Prophets. He has regenerated us, who through the disobedience of the first man were born unto death, to eternal life through the grace of the Holy Spirit and the water of sacred baptism. To those who believe in him he has graciously opened the gate of the heavenly homeland—which was not granted to the ancient fathers—and daily admits them to behold the glory of his Father. Thus, O wretched and pitiable Jews, you now have no excuse for your unbelief, seeing that the precepts of the Law and sayings of the Prophets, once set forth obscurely, are now openly understood in [Col. 0339C] the holy Church and spiritually fulfilled. You therefore tend not toward life but toward eternal death, because you do not understand the Old Testament spiritually and refuse to receive the New.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] Isidore, as above, at the beginning.] The same veil, which was hung in the middle of the tabernacle between the holy place and the holy of holies so that the inner part should not be seen by all, can indeed signify that the people of the Church cannot now see by direct sight the heavenly and eternal goods promised to them. Thus the Apostle also says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; but then,” namely in the age to come or after the resurrection, “face to face” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore, as long as [Col. 0339D] we are in the tabernacle, that is, in the present Church, we see the truth which is Christ as through a mirror, as though positioned in the sanctuary and not yet having come to the holy of holies. For the holy things may be those who are able to have a holy manner of life in the present age. But the holy of holies are those places into which entry is made only once: heaven, where are the propitiatory, the ark, and the cherubim—that is, Jesus Christ, God and man—together with all the heavenly orders of blessed spirits and [Col. 0340A] the souls of the righteous, where God himself appears to the pure in heart.

Yet in this manner of life, namely in the present life, we do not stand without the help of the Holy Spirit. For from the one fountain of the Holy Spirit we have seven lamps that enlighten the people of the Church: that is, the sevenfold grace of the Lord sent throughout the whole world, which illuminates the peoples of the Church with the radiance of the Holy Spirit in a diversity of charismatic splendours.

Therefore, as we have said above, O faithless Jews, you now have no excuse for your ignorance, because Jesus Christ, mediator of God and humankind, who is true God and true man, came into this world sent by God the Father; through his Passion and most holy cross he has redeemed humankind; [Col. 0340B] he has explained the obscure and mystical precepts of the Mosaic Law and taught that they were spiritually fulfilled in himself; and what the Law lacked he supplied through himself. Therefore, O senseless Jews, compelled by charity I urge you in this place diligently to hear what I say: believe Jesus Christ—whom you have often blasphemed and to whom you have inflicted many injuries—to be true God and true man. Make true repentance before him for past sins; humbly submit yourselves to the ministers of the holy Church; devoutly receive through their hands Christ’s baptism in the name of the holy Trinity, so that, cleansed from sins through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, you may deserve to be joined to the children of the Church. Willingly hear the doctors of the holy Church, and whatever [Col. 0340C] they command you, fulfil with good works in a devout spirit.

For the prelates of the holy Church exhort the good to remain in God’s service; they rebuke the wicked so that they may depart as quickly as possible from their wickedness. To the more perfect they proclaim loftier precepts; to the uneducated and simpler, lesser and simpler ones. They refresh the stronger with solid food, but nourish little children with milk. Hence the Apostle says to certain disciples still somewhat deficient in perfection: “You have become such as need milk, not solid food” (Heb. 5). And again: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3). Isidore, teacher of Spain, also advises every prelate of the Church, as it were: [Note: [Col. 0339D] Divine Isidore, book II of the *Synonyms*, chapter “On Teaching,” says without qualification: “When . . . you teach . . . speak so that you may be understood; neither displease the simple by your speaking nor offend the prudent . . . The diversity of persons must be considered . . . proclaim what is open to all, what is hidden to few.” Thus what the holy bishop teaches all persons in whatever doctrine, blessed Martin proposes for the prelates of the Church to follow in the exposition of Scripture.] “Proclaim the hidden things of the divine Scriptures [Col. 0340D] to few and more perfect persons, but the open things to all.” And again: “Teach in such a way as neither to displease the simpler nor to offend the prudent.”

The Lord undoubtedly prefigured this measure, or discretion, of teachers that would exist in the holy Church when, among other things, he said figuratively to Moses: “You shall make dishes and bowls, censers and cups, in which drink-offerings are to be offered” (Exod. 25). Let us ask blessed Gregory, a man especially cautious in expounding the meanings of the holy Scriptures, and diligently hear from him [Col. 0341A] what the aforesaid vessels of the tabernacle signify. We ask you, O Saint Gregory, to stand among us and graciously expound for us the allegorical meanings of the vessels mentioned above.

“What,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0341D] What Saint Gregory said on Job 29:22, “And my utterance fell like drops upon them”—namely, that in this falling of the utterance nothing other than the measure of preaching is understood—our author has interpreted as referring to bowls and cups.] “is understood by bowls and cups except the measure of preaching? For the grace of exhortation ought to be given to each person according to the capacity of his understanding. The one who teaches must carefully take heed not to strive to preach more than can be received by the hearer. He must also descend by restraining himself to the weakness of his hearers, lest, while he speaks lofty things to little hearers which will consequently not profit them, he take more care to display himself than to benefit his hearers. But at the Lord’s command not only bowls are prepared for the table of the tabernacle, but cups also. For what is signified by bowls except extended preaching, and what by a cup except a brief and slight discourse about God? Thus at the Lord’s table both bowls and cups [Col. 0341B] are prepared, because in the teaching of sacred discourse not only great and hidden things that intoxicate must be presented, but also small and subtle things that, as it were, provide knowledge through an open taste.” [Note: [Col. 0342D] The same, Homily 6 on the Gospels.] “What then is signified, as has been said, by bowls except abundant teaching, and what by cups except small and narrow knowledge? For one person, full of the teaching of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers and, by what he says, surely offers a bowl. Another cannot express fully what he understands; yet because he somehow proclaims it, he surely offers a taste through a cup.

[Col. 0341C] “Meanwhile it should be noted that a cup has a broad belly but a very narrow mouth. A bowl, however, has an open and large mouth. Thus those are rightly signified by cups who cannot perfectly bring forth for the instruction of their neighbours what they understand from the holy Scriptures. Bowls, however, signify those who, full of spiritual knowledge, water the hearts of their hearers more abundantly by preaching.” Therefore, in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the holy Church—those who are represented by cups, if they cannot administer bowls through the wisdom of doctrine, should nevertheless not cease, insofar as the bounty of divinity enables them, to give their neighbours cups of good speech.

You have heard, O Jews, how much discretion good rulers of the Church exercise in preaching [Col. 0341D] and what a measure of teaching they offer to the peoples subject to them. Hear also with what diligence they rebuke those who sin. For good rulers of the holy Church maintain rigor in the examination of justice and mercy in the determination of sentence. With them, compassion accompanies the testing of justice, and indulgence tempers the censure of discernment. [Note: [Col. 0342D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 46.] The doctors of the holy Church sometimes strike their subjects with harsh rebukes, [Col. 0342A] yet do not withdraw from charity toward those whom they correct.

Moses, leader of the people of Israel, most rightly maintained this discernment when, descending from Mount Sinai, he saw the people of Israel playing before the idol; and, breaking at the foot of the mountain the two tablets written by the finger of God which he carried in his hands, he said to the sons of Levi, as if moved by anger: “Let every man put his sword upon his thigh” (Exod. 32). And he added: “Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbour” (ibid.). Let blessed Gregory, the most faithful defender of the catholic faith, therefore come forward and, as a wise and discerning man, carefully expound Moses’ aforesaid judgment for our edification—indeed, for that of the whole Church.

“To put the sword,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0342D] *Pastoral Rule*, part III, chapter 26.] “upon the thigh is to set the effort of preaching before the pleasures of the flesh, so that when someone strives to preach holy things, he must take care to overcome temptations. To go from gate to gate is, in rebuking, to range from vice to vice, through which guilt enters the mind. But to pass through the midst of the camp is to live within the holy Church with such impartiality that one who rebukes the faults of sinners ought not to incline himself toward anyone’s favour. Hence it is rightly added: ‘Let a man kill his brother, friend, and neighbour.’ He kills brother, friend, and neighbour who, when he finds things requiring punishment, spares not even those whom he loves by kinship from the sword of rebuke. [Col. 0342C] Therefore, if that person is called God’s who is stirred by zeal for divine love to strike at vices, then he surely denies that he is God’s who, as far as he is able, refuses to rebuke the life of the carnal.”

Since we have heard from blessed Gregory the spiritually expounded severity of Moses toward the children of Israel, it is necessary that we survey the same history somewhat more fully for the edification of the holy Church. Therefore the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Go, descend, because your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt has sinned. They have quickly departed from the way which you showed them; they have made for themselves a molten calf and worshipped it, and, sacrificing victims to it, have said: ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’” And again the Lord said to Moses: “Let me alone, [Col. 0342D] that my wrath may grow hot against them and I may destroy them; and I will make you into a great nation” (ibid.).

Let the rulers of the Church read this history carefully, and listen more attentively to what wise Gregory says in expounding it [Note: [Col. 0342D] *Moralia*, Book XX, chapter 8, and *Paterius on Exodus*, chapter 53.]. “The history just recounted can greatly edify the reader if he considers how, in good rulers, the authority of governing is joined with the kindness of consoling. For discipline is greatly deficient without mercy, and mercy without discipline, if either [Col. 0343A] is maintained without the other. Thus rulers ought to possess, toward their subjects, both mercy that gives counsel justly and discipline that rages piously. For it is pleasing to behold mercy joined with severity in Moses’ breast. Let us therefore see one who loves piously and rages sternly. Certainly, when the Israelite people had contracted before God’s eyes an offence almost beyond pardon, so that its ruler heard, ‘Go down, thy people has sinned grievously; it has provoked God against itself to anger,’ as though the divine voice said to him more plainly: ‘The people that has fallen into such sin is now no longer mine; but let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against it and destroy it, and I will make thee into a great nation.’ Yet Moses, once and again opposing himself to the onset of God’s anger on behalf of the people over whom he ruled, said: [Col. 0343B] ‘Either forgive them this offence; or, if thou dost not, blot me out of thy book which thou hast written.’ Let us consider, then, with what tenderness he loved that same people, for whose life he asked to be blotted from the book of life. Yet let us consider with what zeal for righteousness this man, who was bound to that people by so great a love, was inflamed against their offences. For as soon as, by his first petition, he obtained pardon for their guilt, that they might not be destroyed, he came to that same people and said: ‘Let every man put his sword upon his thigh; go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbour.’ And on that day there fell about [Note: [Col. 0343D] The edition reads ‘twenty-three,’ with the Vulgate. See here the Benedictines’ note.] three thousand men. Behold Moses, who sought the lives of men even at the cost of his own death, extinguished the lives of a few with the sword. Within he burned with the fire of love; without he was inflamed [Col. 0343C] with zeal for severity. His compassion was so great that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord for them; his severity so great that he himself struck with the sword of judgment those whom he had feared might be struck by God. Thus he loved those whom he governed, that for their sake he did not spare even himself; and yet he so pursued in punishment those whom he loved that he overthrew them even though the Lord had spared them. Mighty advocate in both respects; marvellous mediator in both respects. By prayers he pleaded the people’s cause before God; by swords he pleaded God’s cause before the people. Loving inwardly, he resisted the divine wrath by supplication; raging outwardly, he consumed guilt by striking it. By the death of a few displayed, he came more swiftly to the aid of all; and for this reason almighty God more quickly heard His faithful servant acting for the people, because He saw what Moses himself would do on behalf of [Col. 0343D] God concerning the people. Thus, in governing the people, Moses blended both things: namely, that discipline might not be lacking to mercy, nor mercy to discipline.”

Therefore, as we said above, O devout rulers of the Catholic Church, you will be able to profit greatly if, in the government entrusted to you, you imitate Moses, leader of the Israelite people. Let both the authority of governing and the kindness of consoling be joined in you. Let there be toward subjects mercy that gives counsel justly, and discipline that rages piously.

But now let us hear what almighty God, who is truly mighty in His works and merciful [Col. 0344A] and compassionate toward His servants, said to His servant Moses: “Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them and destroy them.” “All saints,” says blessed Gregory in his Commentary on Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0343D] Rather, in *Moralia*, Book IX, chapter 9, and *Paterius on [Col. 0344D] Exodus*, chapter 54.], “who withstand the wrath of God receive it from God Himself that they may set themselves against the onset of His chastisement; and, so to speak, they are raised up with Him against Him. The divine power itself sets them in opposition to itself, because when they outwardly oppose the wrath of One raging against them, inwardly the grace of that same angry One cherishes them; and inwardly it lifts up those who serve it, while outwardly it tolerates them as though they were adversaries. Therefore God bears the contradiction of those who entreat Him, though He Himself inspires it; and what He commands to be done by Himself is, as it were, imposed upon Him as willing. Thus He says to Moses, ‘Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them,’ and the rest. What then is it to say to His servant, ‘Let me alone,’ except to grant him boldness in entreating? As though it were said to him more plainly: ‘Consider how much you prevail with me, and know that you will obtain whatever you pray for on behalf of the people.’

“But although these things are so, the reader’s mind is greatly moved by what is said in opposition through blessed Job: ‘God, whom no one can resist’ [Note: [Col. 0344D] The same Gregory, ibid.]. It is very remarkable that no one is said to be able to resist the wrath of God, whereas the divine utterances testify that many have withstood the indignation of heavenly judgment. Did not Moses withstand God’s wrath, when, praying for the sinful people, he restrained the very onset of heavenly punishment by offering his own death, saying: ‘Forgive them this offence; otherwise blot me from the book which thou hast written’? Did not Aaron withstand God’s wrath when he took the censer [Col. 0344C] and stood between the living and the dead (Num. XVI), and tempered the fire of judgment with the smoke of incense? Did not Phinehas withstand God’s wrath when, slaughtering those who committed fornication with foreigners in the very act of intercourse, he offered his zeal to divine indignation and appeased wrath with the sword? (Num. XXV.) Did not David withstand God’s wrath when he offered to God a sacrifice of propitiation while the angel was smiting the people (II Kings XXIV), and thereby obtained it even before the appointed time? Did not Elijah withstand God’s wrath when, after the earth had long been dry, he recalled by prayer the rains withdrawn from heaven? (III Kings XVIII.) How then is it said that no one can resist divine wrath, when examples testify that many often did resist it?

“But if we consider closely both blessed Job’s words and their deeds, we shall recognize as true [Col. 0344D] both that no one resisted divine wrath (Job IX), and that many often resisted it. For many saints resisted the Lord’s wrath, as the foregoing account of each truly taught. Yet God’s wrath cannot be resisted when His indignation, so to speak, is stirred from the very marrow. Once it has been stirred, human opposition does not restrain it. Nor does any person’s prayer usefully oppose it when God once, in anger, ordains something from His depths. Thus Moses, who wiped away before God by his prayers the guilt of the whole people and, offering himself as a barrier, appeased the force of divine anger, nevertheless, when he came to the rock of Horeb (Exod. XVII) and distrusted concerning the giving of water (Num. XX), could not enter the land of promise while God was angry. He was often afflicted on this account, often disturbed by longing; but he could never avert from himself the anger decreed in vengeance—he who, when the Lord willed it, had removed it from the people. Thus David, because [Note: [Col. 0345D] ‘Who.’] after the people had been struck down he later restrained the angel’s sword by prayer (II Kings XXIV), had first fled from his son, weeping and wailing, with bare feet; and until he had fully received the punishment for the crime he had committed (ibid.), he could not by himself calm God’s wrath. Thus Elijah, that he might feel something small of divine judgment as a man, he who opened the heavens by his word fled through the desert in terror before [Col. 0345B] a woman’s indignation (III Kings XIX); and he who had appeased God’s wrath for others by intercession was himself weakened into fear on his own behalf. Therefore God’s wrath can be resisted when He who is angry Himself gives aid; and it cannot at all be resisted when He rouses Himself to exact vengeance and God Himself does not inspire the prayer offered to Him.”

Since blessed Gregory has expounded these matters for our instruction, it is necessary, O Jews, that we return again to what we earlier passed over concerning the salvation and exhortation of your souls. This then was our aforesaid exhortation and admonition: that, abandoning at last the long-standing perfidy of your unbelief, you humbly submit yourselves to the teachers of the Church, faithfully receive Christ’s baptism through their ministry, and hasten to be joined with the sons of the holy Church in the utmost devotion and joy. For there—that is, within the holy Church—strong men perform strong and great deeds in God’s service; there too the utmost and smallest acts of the weak and feeble find a place for the use of Christian religion when accompanied by right faith. There the virtues of strong men are set before all the faithful as an example; there the good works of lesser persons, although imperfect, are mercifully tolerated by the rulers of that same holy Church. For there—that is, within the holy Church—some are stronger than others in God’s service, some humbler than others, some wiser than others, some holier than others, and some more perfect than others. Almighty God prefigured that these differences among the faithful would exist within the holy Church [Col. 0345D] when, among other things, He spoke typologically to Moses concerning the offerings of the children of Israel:

“Speak,” He said, “to the children of Israel, that they may take up first-fruits for me; from every man who offers willingly, you shall receive them. Thus men together with women, with minds most willing and devout, provided first-fruits to the Lord for making the work of the tabernacle of testimony, and whatever was necessary for its service and for the holy vestments. They offered bracelets and earrings, rings and ornaments for the right hand. Every vessel of gold was set apart as an offering to the Lord. Whoever had blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, reddened rams’ skins, and blue skins, offered metals of gold, silver, and bronze to the Lord. The chiefs, however, offered onyx stones and gems for the ephod and breastpiece, spices and oil for preparing the lamps, and for making the ointment and compounding the incense of sweetest fragrance” (Exod. XXV; Exod. XXXV).

Here I admonish you, O Jews hard and slow of heart to believe, to attend carefully to what the aforesaid ornaments of the tabernacle of the covenant prefigured in the holy Church, so that you may strive no longer to observe the Old Testament carnally but to understand it spiritually, and may hasten with devout minds to receive, together with all the Church’s children, the saving sacraments of the New Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0345] Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXX, chapter 6, and Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 56.] By the offerings of this former tabernacle [Col. 0346B] are signified the gifts of merits with which the holy Church is adorned. In adorning the tabernacle, men together with women offer gifts, because, in carrying out the worship of the holy Church, both the exalted deeds of the strong and the least works of the weak are counted. The faith of the holy Church is compared to gold, and the word of preaching to silver. That men together with women provided what was necessary for constructing the tabernacle signified that within the holy Church the virtues of the strong, expressed by men, and the small good works of the weak, signified by women, are not despised by God, the most just Judge, but are mercifully received for the work of holy edification. The contribution itself, moreover, is not made from compulsion but from free will, because faith is voluntary.

For by bracelets, which bind the arms, are shown the deeds of rulers who labour vigorously. By earrings, however, the obedience of subjects is expressed. By rings is shown the seal of hidden mysteries. Thus teachers of the Church conceal certain deep and secret matters, as though under a seal, from persons of lesser understanding, lest God’s sacraments be entrusted to the unworthy. For the prelates of the Church often seal up what they perceive cannot be grasped by their hearers. Hence the Psalmist says: “I have hidden thy words in my heart, that I may not sin against thee” (Ps. CXVIII). Further, by ornaments of the right hand are signified good works, which are called the right hand. A vessel of gold set apart as an offering to the Lord is understood as the knowledge of divinity; it is separated from the love of lower things in proportion as it is raised up to love only what is eternal. Blue signifies hope for heavenly goods. What does purple signify except bloodshed and the endurance of sufferings undertaken for love of the everlasting kingdom? And what does twice-dyed scarlet signify except charity, by the perfection of which each person is dyed twice, because he is adorned by love of God and neighbour? By fine linen we understand those unstained in flesh and incorrupt in mind, preserving the most splendid whiteness of holiness before God and before men. For fine linen is a very white plant. What, moreover, is signified by goats’ hair, from which the harshness of haircloth is woven, except the hard [Col. 0347A] affliction of penitents?

Thus some exercise a strong mystery by bracelets and rings; others display devout obedience and right action by earrings and ornaments of the right hand; others hold a brilliant and more subtle knowledge of God through the vessel of gold set apart; others, by blue, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope for and love the heavenly things of which they have heard, and believe that they will attain by God’s grace what they do not yet know through more subtle understanding; others offer incorrupt flesh through fine linen; others bitterly mourn through goats’ hair what they willingly lost. Behold: from such a great diversity of works one tabernacle is completed, just as one globe of earth is formed from diverse dust, watered by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Further, by the incorruptible setim wood are understood all saints incorrupt in mind and body, not perishing in the world but abiding eternally. The precious stones are likewise apostles, martyrs, confessors, and all saints, whom the blessed apostle Peter, calling them living stones, says: “You also, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (I Pet. II). All these things, therefore, are offered in God’s tabernacle, so that no one may despair of salvation.

Because I grieve exceedingly for your unhappiness, O Jews who are enemies of truth, I return so often in speaking to you. Gloriously, then, as you read, the Lord’s tabernacle was adorned with the offerings of the children of Israel; but the holy Church, [Col. 0347C] of which that tabernacle itself bore the figure, is adorned far more gloriously by the spiritual endeavours of faithful Christians. The children of Israel offered material gifts to adorn the Lord’s tabernacle; but the children of the holy Church do not cease to offer within that same Church gifts of merits to the praise and glory of almighty God. Believe without doubt, O Jews, that as far as heaven is from earth, so far do the virtues of holy conduct and the ecclesiastical sacraments—which the faithful continually offer through Christ to God the Father according to the rule of Gospel instruction, and by which the holy Church is adorned and propagated—differ from the offerings of the Hebrews with which Moses built the tabernacle. For those were earthly; these heavenly. Those were carnal; these spiritual. Those were transitory; these are, nevertheless, everlasting. And, to speak briefly, that tabernacle which Moses, at the Lord’s command, built and carefully adorned from the offerings of the children of Israel, Jeremiah the prophet hid in a certain cave lest it be plundered by the Chaldeans (II Macc. II); but the holy Church God and man Jesus Christ daily conveys through Himself to eternal blessedness. That tabernacle, therefore, bore the type of the holy Church and consequently did not long endure with its carnal ceremonies; but the holy Church, redeemed by Christ’s blood, will reign without end in the heavenly homeland with Jesus Christ, her bridegroom.

[Col. 0348A] Therefore strive with all diligence, O Jews, to enter faithfully that holy Church, mother of all the faithful. Receive with devout minds Christ’s baptism through the hand of the holy ministers of that same holy Church, so that with faithful Christians you may deserve to be sharers in eternal blessedness. Without doubt it will be well with you here and eternally if by faith and work you are called Christians from Christ; for as Jews are named from Judah, so Christians are named from Christ. Christ, indeed, is called from *chrism*—that is, “anointed” [Note: [Col. 0347D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VII, chapter 2.]. For the Jews had been commanded to prepare a sacred ointment, with which those called to priesthood or kingship might be anointed. And as the purple garment is now the badge of royal dignity for kings, so for them the anointing with sacred ointment conferred the royal name and authority; and from *chrism*, which is anointing, they were called Christs. For *chrisma* is Greek, and in Latin is called *unctio*, “anointing.” This anointing, spiritually accomplished, also supplied the name to our Lord Jesus Christ, because He was anointed by God the Father with the Holy Spirit, as it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “For they have gathered together in this city against thy holy Son whom thou hast anointed” (Acts IV)—not, of course, with visible oil, but with the gift of spiritual grace, signified by visible ointment.

Concerning this the blessed apostle Peter, chief of the apostles, also says: “Men, brethren, you know what word has gone through all Judaea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism preached by John: Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and power; he went about [Col. 0348C] doing good and healing all oppressed by the devil, because God was with him” (Acts X). That God and man Jesus Christ Himself was anointed by God the Father with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, He openly declares through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to announce to the meek” (Isa. LXI), and the rest. Thus the Son of God and of the Virgin was anointed with a spiritual anointing, as the Psalmist testifies when, speaking to Him, he says: “God, thy God, has anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy companions” (Ps. XLIV). As though King and Prophet David, rejoicing and exulting exceedingly for Jesus Christ, whom he foresaw would come in the Spirit, said more plainly: “God the Father has anointed thee with spiritual anointing, and this above thy companions—that is, above thy sharers, namely, above all those who share with thee in human nature.” And because he says that Christ was anointed above all, he shows that the anointing of faithful Christians is great, so that we may understand the anointing of that same God and man Jesus Christ to be wondrous and spiritual, since He was anointed by God the Father above them all.

You ought therefore to believe without doubt, O Jews, that Jesus Christ was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world and was anointed by Him in our humanity with a spiritual anointing. He Himself washes the people believing in Him from sins in the water of sacred baptism, [Col. 0349A] seals them with the chrism of sanctification, and confirms and sanctifies them by the invisible anointing of the Holy Spirit. Blessed John the Baptist testifies to this, saying: “There comes after me one mightier than I, whose sandal-strap I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke III). This holy chrism, with which Christians are anointed for remission of sins and confirmation in the Catholic faith, was prefigured by the oil of sanctification with which Moses, at the Lord’s command, anointed the tabernacle and all its vessels on the day it was set up [Note: [Col. 0349D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 57.]. The ointment with which Moses anointed the tabernacle therefore prefigured the holy chrism by which the faithful people is joined together in the holy Church, in which divinity dwells as in a tabernacle.

This ointment may indeed also be understood as the virtues of the saints, or as the fragrance of righteousness spread far and wide, of which the Apostle says: “But thanks be to God, who triumphs us”—that is, makes us triumph—“in Christ Jesus, and makes manifest upon us and through us in every place the fragrance of his righteousness” (II Cor. II) [Note: [Col. 0349D] Another manuscript reads *notitiae* (“knowledge”), and shortly afterward reads only *upon us in every place*. Isidore reads *righteousness*, as does our text; but afterward only *through us in every place*.].

Since, then, Christ’s baptism was so plainly prefigured in the crossing of the Red Sea, and holy chrism in the anointing of the tabernacle, you ought, putting aside every doubt, to offer yourselves to the Church’s priests to be baptized. For unless you are reborn of water and the Holy Spirit within the holy Church in the name of the Holy Trinity, you will utterly perish apart from the company of the saints (John III). Therefore receive the Catholic faith with devout minds; humbly ask to be baptized by the ministers of the holy Church; make satisfaction to God by fasts and prayers for your former unbelief; with tears, sighs, and deep groaning of heart seek pardon for your sins; adorn faith with good works; flee vices with all earnestness; love virtues; maintain charity, humility, and true patience in your conduct, so that, cleansed from the stains of sin and strengthened by virtues, you may reach the joys of eternal blessedness with the children of the holy Church.

God almighty also showed beforehand that the fragrance of prayers and the virtues of good works, which the children of the holy Church now perform by divine grace, should be offered to Him by the faithful within the holy Church, when among other things He commanded Moses figuratively, [Col. 0349D] saying: “Take for thyself spices: stacte, onycha, sweet-smelling galbanum, and the clearest frankincense; all shall be of equal weight. And thou shalt make incense composed by the work of a perfumer, carefully mixed and pure” (Exod. XXX). “We make incense,” says blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0350D] *Moralia*, Book I, chapter 19, and *Paterius on Exodus*, chapter 51.], “compounded from spices when, upon the altar of good work, we are fragrant with a multiplicity of virtues. It is mixed and pure because, in proportion as virtue is joined to virtue, the incense of good work is offered more sincerely. And there is aptly added: ‘When thou hast beaten all these into the finest powder, [Col. 0350A] thou shalt put some of it before the tabernacle of testimony.’ We beat spices into the finest powder when we pound our good works in the mortar of the heart by hidden examination, and reconsider whether they are truly good. Thus to reduce spices to powder is to grind virtues by reflection and bring them back to the subtlety of hidden scrutiny.

“And it should be noted that it is said of this same powder: ‘Thou shalt put some of it before the tabernacle of testimony,’ because then our good works truly please in the sight of the Judge, when the mind grinds them more subtly by reconsidering them and, as it were, renders powder from spices. Therefore, lest the good done be coarse and hard, lest, if the hand does not crush it by this close reconsideration, it fail to scatter a fragrance from subtle things.”

[Col. 0350B] [Note: [Col. 0350D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 58.] This same incense, composed from the aforesaid four most fragrant kinds of spices ground into the greatest fineness—namely stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense—may also typologically signify the form of the faithful’s prayers. John testifies in the Apocalypse, saying: “When the Lamb had opened the book, the four living creatures and the twenty-four elders, each having harps and golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints, sweetly fragrant to God, fell before the Lamb” (Apoc. V). Although these four colours also seem to signify the nature and species of the four elements, so that frankincense, which is translucent [Note: [Col. 0350D] Supplied: “is.”], is compared with air; stacte with waters; galbanum and onycha with earth and fire; so that through this there may be here an incense pleasing to God: the prayer of praise offered by every creature that is in heaven [Col. 0350C] and beneath heaven, on earth and in the waters.

Therefore flee sins and vices with all earnestness, O Jews; love virtues; believe with complete certainty that Jesus Christ is true God and true man; and receive His baptism with devout minds through the ministers of the holy Church, so that it may not befall you to perish with unbelievers, but that with the faithful Christian people you may attain the salvation of your souls. What then do you say, O Jews? What do you answer to these things, or what objection do you raise?

§ XXV.—

From the statements of the Book of Exodus he announces that Christ would come for the redemption of the world and would wash His faithful people from sins in His own blood. Jeremiah likewise, drawing sighs from his inmost breast, says that the Jews bear their fathers’ iniquities. Finally, he asks in what manner a son bears the iniquity of his fathers. He adds in what manner God visits the iniquities of parents upon their children, why little children are possessed by demons, and why punishment extends to the third and fourth generation. From David’s words he declares Christ to be true God. Moreover, Aaron’s garments prefigure Christ, the Virgin’s Son, His Church, and the virtues of priests. Further, although Leviticus commands sacrifices to be offered from different kinds of animals, these are wholly insufficient for the redemption of humankind; they bore only the figure of Christ, in whose sacrifice remission of sins must be effected; and by the different kinds was figured that a true Christian must offer different things. By Ambrose’s words, neither the burnt offerings of the Old Testament nor the sacrifice of a mere man was a sufficient offering for human redemption: Christ alone was true and sufficient also to erase the handwriting of the decree, according to Paul’s judgment. By Christ’s death the entrance to the kingdom was opened. He asks and at the same time resolves whether the Redeemer of humankind freed humanity from the devil and sin by His blood, and whether the devil found anything harmful in Christ such that he caused Him to be crucified by his ministers. He adds that Christ became a mortal man for the devil’s defeat; and why God willed to rescue the world not by an angel, a new man, a prophet, or a patriarch, but through His only-begotten Son—whose victory was prefigured by sacrifices of fire consuming offerings into a sweet fragrance, and whose Passion was prefigured by Abel.

I should like to know what disposition or faith you have: whether, that is, you now believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man, or whether you still doubt something concerning His divinity. This is both your answer and your objection. For you say that you cannot in any way believe Jesus Christ to be true God, nor that He truly redeemed the world, nor that He washed from sins in His blood the people believing in Him. You further say that throughout the whole sequence of the Old Testament He was never prefigured as one who would redeem the world in His blood. But we, answering you in return, say that He is without doubt true God and true man, and that from the beginning of the world it was prefigured by figures and enigmas, in the books of the Old Testament and in many places, that He would redeem the world. Therefore, that we may openly prove you liars in your objection, as we have already proved many times above, let us bring forward the testimony of the Book of Exodus. For it says:

“Moses built an altar at the foot of Mount Sinai and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel. He sent young men from among the children of Israel, and they offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of calves to the Lord. Moses then took half of the blood and put it into bowls; the remaining part he poured upon the altar. Taking the book of the covenant, he read it in the hearing of the people. They said: ‘All that the Lord has commanded we will do, and we will be obedient.’ Then he sprinkled the blood he had taken upon the people and said: ‘This is the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words’” [Col. 0351D] [Note: [Col. 0351D] Isidore, codex, chapter 58.] (Exod. XXIV).

That blood, therefore, by which Moses sprinkles and purifies the people, the tabernacle, and everything that was in it, saying, “This blood is the blood of the testament,” is plainly shown to proclaim the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. By it the hearts of all believers are cleansed; by it the faith of the holy Church is sealed and propagated; by it all the people—that is, the entire work of the tabernacle, namely the assembly of the whole Church—is sanctified, as the Lord says to His disciples: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI), [Col. 0352A] namely, to fulfil the truth that had been shown to Moses in the Paschal lamb.

It should be noted that, in building an altar at the foot of the mountain and offering a burnt offering to God upon it, Moses bore the figure of God and man Jesus Christ. For God and man Jesus Christ, as it were, built an altar to God the Father at the foot of the mountain when, descending from the bosom of that same His Father, He assumed from the undefiled Virgin a human body without sin. On this altar He offered peace offerings, because, offering Himself as a sweet fragrance for the redemption of the world, He reconciled humankind to God the Father. Moses also purified the people, the tabernacle, and everything in it with the blood of the Old Testament; but Christ daily cleanses the holy Church [Col. 0352B] and all her children from sins by the blood of His own Passion, and continually refreshes them lest they fail on this way of pilgrimage. He called this blood the blood of the New Testament.

What could you hear more openly, more luminously, or more clearly concerning Christ, O Jews, enemies of truth? As you see, the Book of Exodus certainly announces that He would come for the redemption of the world and would wash His faithful people from sins in His own blood; and it openly shows you to be false witnesses in your opposition, you who say that He was neither prefigured nor able to redeem the world. The Old Testament foretold by figures, enigmas, and the utterances of the prophets that He is true God and true man; and it openly convicts you, who stubbornly deny Him, of having lied in your assertions. For the obstinacy that hardened the hearts of your fathers unto unbelief has also blinded the eyes of your minds, so that you cannot see the light of the eternal sun, which is Christ. Your fathers crucified Christ without cause, and you endure their sins through the long servitude of this world. They crucified through envy Christ, who was promised to them in the Law and specially sent by God the Father for their salvation; and you endure throughout this world’s long exiles the most grievous crimes committed by them.

Seeing this in the Spirit, and grieving deeply for your unhappiness, the prophet Jeremiah, speaking of the future as though of something already past, drew sighs from the depths of his breast and said: “Our fathers sinned, and are no more; and we have borne their iniquities” (Lam. V). Why, O unbelieving and perverse Jews, do you bear your fathers’ iniquities, except because you imitate their unbelief and malice? Although they crucified Christ, Redeemer of the world, without cause, nevertheless, if you faithfully believe in Him, receive His baptism with devout minds, and confess Him in truth, you will by no means perish because of your fathers’ iniquities. But if you imitate their wicked acts, you will bear both the sins of your own unbelief and their iniquities [Col. 0353A], as Moses testifies when he humbly invokes the Lord, saying:

“Lord, Master, God merciful and gracious, patient, of great compassion, and true, who keepest mercy unto thousands; who takest away iniquity, wickedness, and sins; and no one is innocent before thee by himself; who renderest the iniquities of fathers to children and grandchildren unto the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XXXIV).

Yet the Lord says through Ezekiel: “What is this that you turn into a proverb among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying: ‘Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be used as a proverb in Israel. As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. XVIII). What, then, is meant by what is now said through Moses: “Who renderest the iniquities of fathers to children and grandchildren unto the third and fourth generation”? (Exod. XXXIV.)

“But in each statement a different sense is found, and the hearer’s mind is instructed to seek with discernment the path of distinction. For, as St. Gregory says, we derive original sin from our parents; and unless we are absolved through the grace of baptism, we bear our parents’ sins, because we are, that is, still one with them. [Note: [Col. 0353D] Moralium, Book XV, ch. 31; and Paterius on Exodus, ch. 60.] God therefore repays the iniquity of the fathers in the children when, on account of the parent’s fault, the offspring’s soul is defiled by original sin. And again, he does not repay the parents’ iniquity in the children, because, when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer bear our parents’ faults, but those which we ourselves have committed. [Col. 0353C]

“Yet this can also be understood otherwise.
