Whoever imitates the iniquity of a wicked parent is held guilty through that parent’s offence; but whoever does not imitate the parent’s iniquity is in no way burdened by that parent’s offence. Hence it comes about that the wicked son of a wicked father pays not only for what he himself has added, but also for that father’s sins, when he does not fear to add his own further wickedness to the ways [Note: [Col. 0354D] The printed text has *vitiis*, ‘vices’.] of his father—ways by which he knows that the Lord is angered. It is altogether just that one who, under a strict Judge, does not fear to imitate the ways of a wicked parent should be compelled even in this present life to pay the penalties of that wicked parent’s sins. [Col. 0353D] Thus it is said there: ‘As the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine’; and again: ‘The soul that sins shall itself die’; for sometimes sons are destroyed in the flesh because of their father’s sin.”

Why, indeed, are little children so often seized by demons? Let St. Gregory, held in great reverence in Christ’s Church, come forward and graciously resolve the question already set before us. [Note: [Col. 0354D] In the same place.] “Why,” he says, “are little children sometimes afflicted by demons, unless because the son’s flesh is punished for the father’s penalty? The wicked father is struck in himself and despises to feel the force of the blow. Often he is struck in his children, so that he may burn more sharply; and the bodily pain of the children [Col. 0354A] is returned upon the father, so that the wicked mind of the father may be punished through his children’s penalty. But when not little children, but sons already more advanced in age, are stricken because of their parents’ fault, what else is indicated except that they pay the penalties of those whose deeds they have followed? Thus it is rightly said: ‘Unto the third and fourth generation.’ For, since children can see the life of their parents which they imitate as far as the third and fourth generation, vengeance extends to those who have seen what they might wickedly follow.”

Therefore do not imitate the depravity of your unbelieving fathers, but be imitators of God and of the man Jesus Christ, and walk in his love; for love is the fulfilment of the law (Rom. XIII), just as he himself loved us all and gave himself for us, [Col. 0354B] an offering and sacrifice to God the Father for a sweet-smelling savour (Eph. V). For if, as has been said, you follow the unbelief and iniquities of your fathers, you will without doubt perish with them. But if you believe that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and receive his baptism with devout mind, you can, through him who is the true priest, offer to God the Father sacrifices of godly conduct and attain the salvation of your souls.

In answer to these things, you say, O Jews, that you cannot possibly believe Jesus Christ to be true God and to have received priestly dignity from God the Father; nor are you willing through him to offer spiritual sacrifices [Col. 0354C] of good conduct, because, you say, you have never been able to find that his future priesthood was prefigured throughout the whole Old Testament. You further say that this is why we call him king and priest: because we love him greatly and believe him to be true God.

But we, O Jews, answer you to the contrary: Jesus Christ is true God, ineffably begotten of God the Father before all things; and true man, born in time of the incorrupt Virgin. He is also the true king, whom God the Father established over all the works of his hands, as he himself testifies, saying of himself through the Psalmist: “But I have been established king by him over his holy mount Sion” [Col. 0354D] (Ps. II), that is, over the holy Church. Again the Psalmist speaks to God the Father concerning him, saying: “Thou hast crowned him with glory and honour, and hast established him over the works of thy hands” (Ps. VIII). God the Father likewise appointed him supreme priest, through whom he reconciled the human race to himself. To him David the prophet speaks in the Psalms: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

Therefore, to strengthen in every respect the truth of our faith and wholly refute the treachery of your unbelief, O Jews, let us bring forward the history of the book of Exodus and listen carefully to it all together. Let us examine more attentively how Aaron the priest, clothed in sacred vestments, prefigured [Col. 0355A] the Son of God and of the Virgin himself, and his Church.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “You shall make a holy garment for your brother, for glory and beauty: namely, a breastpiece and ephod, a tunic and close-fitting linen garment, a turban, a girdle” (Exod. XXVIII), etc. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Isidore, Questions on Exodus, ch. 59.] Aaron the priest, therefore, as has been said, signified Christ, to whom it is said: “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). The priestly garment prefigured the holy Church, which is truly Christ’s garment. Of it the Apostle says: “Therefore Christ suffered, that he might present to himself a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle” (Eph. V). For all [Col. 0355B] the faithful are Christ’s garments, as Isaiah testifies, saying to that same God and man Jesus Christ: “With all these thou shalt be clothed as with an ornament” (Isa. XLIX).

The four colours—blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen—from which his garment is woven are the various kinds of merits that shine within the holy Church, in Christ’s body, which is the assembly of the faithful. But we understand that linen garment, that is, the priestly linen tunic, as Christ’s Incarnation, [Note: [Col. 0356D] “Flesh.”] which is from the earth and is signified in the feet; for flax springs from the earth. By his turban upon his head and the golden plate we understand the splendour of divinity, so that one and the same person is adorned with the linen garment according to his humanity, but with the turban according to his deity. Those breeches with which Aaron the priest was clothed [Col. 0355C] prefigured the chastity and bodily integrity of Christ. The girdle with which the priestly breast was bound prefigured the choirs of saints and their concord.

This whole garment was blue; for blue shines with the colour of the air. This signifies that the whole Church should set its mind on things above and rise wholly toward love of ecclesiastical religion. The pomegranates placed at the lower edge declare the unity of that same Church. For just as many seeds within a pomegranate are protected by one outer rind, so the unity of faith covers the innumerable peoples of the holy Church, while diversity of merits contains them within. The bells sounding among the pomegranates [Col. 0355D] signify the prophets and holy teachers placed in the midst of the Church, whose tongue, sounding with the teaching of knowledge, strikes both sides of the bell: that is, the parts of the Law and the Gospel. These bells are placed at the garment’s extremity so that, discoursing about the end of the world and the life to come, they may never be silent.

The ephod, that is, the pallium, denotes the Saviour’s power and kingship, as Isaiah says of him: “Government has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. IX). The two onyx stones placed on the ephod, on the right and the left, signified the two peoples: namely, the Gentile people on the right and the Jewish people on the left. They bore [Col. 0356A] the engraved names of the twelve patriarchs, in order to imitate the example of life of the holy apostles. Others have called these same two stones the two Testaments, or letter and spirit, in which all the mysteries of the Law and the Gospel are most fully contained: on the right, the spirit which gives life to believers; on the left, the letter which kills transgressors.

The breastpiece placed upon the priest’s breast and marked out by four rows of stones represented the Gospel word, which in its fourfold order set forth for us the truth of faith and the doctrine of the most holy Trinity. The apostolic message corresponds to it in the gems, both in power and in number. This breastpiece is double, because the knowledge of evangelical doctrine is open and hidden, [Col. 0356B] plain and mystical.

Likewise, our priest Jesus Christ is not inappropriately signified in his members, and especially in the bishop who abides among the saints and offers victims for the people, consecrating with his sacred mouth the flesh of the spotless Lamb. First, the breastpiece of judgment impressed upon Aaron’s breast by binding bands signifies that fleeting thoughts must never possess the priestly heart, but reason alone must bind it. It is also carefully joined to this breastpiece that the names of the twelve patriarchs be inscribed upon it. The priest must always bear the holy fathers thus inscribed upon his breast, never ceasing to imitate their examples.

The priest is rightly bound on both shoulders by the covering of the ephod: namely, so that, against adversity [Col. 0356C] and prosperity, he may always be fortified by the ornaments of virtues. For the command that the ephod be made of gold and blue, purple and twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, shows with what diversity of virtues the priest ought to flourish. In the priest’s garment gold shines when understanding gleams with wisdom. Blue, shining with an airy colour, is joined to it, so that in everything he undertakes he may rise toward the love of heavenly things. Royal purple is mixed with it, so that he may repress the suggestions of demons as if by royal power. Twice-dyed scarlet is likewise joined to the ephod, so that all good works of virtue may be shown before the eyes of the inward Judge to proceed from charity. This charity, because [Col. 0356D] it depends upon love of God and neighbour, shines as though from a twofold joining. Twisted fine linen is joined to the twice-dyed scarlet. For fine linen arises from the earth with a bright appearance, and thereby the radiant beauty of purity and bodily chastity is signified. It is woven, indeed, into the beauty of the ephod because chastity is brought to the perfect brightness of purity when the body is afflicted through abstinence. The priest is also girded with a belt, by which the incitements of the loins and movements of lust are restrained.

When the priest enters the tabernacle, he is surrounded by bells upon his tunic, so that he may possess the voice of preaching [Col. 0357A] and not offend the judgment of the heavenly Inspector by silence. Pomegranates are also joined to the bells, so that the unity of faith may be indicated through the priest’s teaching. The priest’s daily entrance into the first part of the tabernacle to immolate victims commands us to be daily diligent: never to depart from this place where God’s people are nourished and spiritually refreshed by heavenly utterances, but daily to offer to God the spiritual sacrifice of confession and praise—that is, the humility of our souls and tears of a contrite heart, which are true sacrifices. Hence it is written: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L), etc.

But the high priest’s entrance once a year, leaving the people behind, into the Holy of Holies, [Col. 0357B] where the mercy-seat was, signified our Lord Jesus Christ, the supreme high priest. While in the flesh, he was with the people throughout the whole year: that year of which he himself said, “He sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of propitiation” (Isa. LXI). Therefore this our true high priest entered the Holy of Holies once in this year, that is, on the day of propitiation: when the dispensation of our redemption was complete, he penetrated the heavens, entering to God the Father who sent him, in order to make him propitious toward the human race and, according to his humanity, to intercede for all who believe in him.

Thus St. Paul, speaking to the Hebrews, says: “Jesus, [Col. 0357C] because he remains for ever, has an everlasting priesthood. Therefore he can save for ever those who approach God through himself, ever living to intercede for us” (Heb. VII). St. John the Evangelist likewise says: “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the propitiation for our sins” (I John II).

It has been shown quite clearly, O Jews, that Jesus Christ was prefigured in Aaron’s priesthood and was appointed by God the Father, according to his humanity, supreme high priest of the holy Church. Through him God the Father created all things from nothing and redeemed the human race from the devil’s power. After the triumph of his most victorious passion and resurrection, he [Col. 0357D] crowned him with highest glory and honour and exalted him at his right hand. Therefore, since the book of Exodus shows that he was prefigured, it openly convicts you, who stubbornly deny him, of having lied in your objection.

He is indeed the most merciful Redeemer of humankind, the true mediator between God and human beings, the mightiest conqueror of the ancient enemy, and the all-powerful preserver of those who hope in him. Descending from the bosom of God the Father, he took the substance of our flesh from an incorrupt Virgin, and for the redemption of humankind mercifully offered himself upon the altar of the cross to God [Col. 0358A] the Father as an acceptable sacrifice of sweet savour.

At this point, in answer to us, you object, O Jews, that God never commanded a human being to be offered for the people’s sin, but ordered calves, rams, and goats to be sacrificed for the cleansing of offences. To this we answer in reply: those fleshly sacrifices of the Old Testament were not sufficient to free the human race from the guilt of transgression. This alone—the spotless victim, God and man Jesus Christ—could do so, once offering himself to God the Father for the redemption of humankind; because he was conceived in a Virgin without male intercourse, born without any defilement, and lived among human beings without sin (Baruch III); and because he gave his blood on the cross not for his own sins but for the sins [Col. 0358B] of the whole world. Those fleshly sacrifices of the old dispensation, as has been said, could not redeem humankind; they only bore the figure of this most true and fully sufficient sacrifice, our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0357D] Isidore, Questions on Leviticus, ch. 1.] Let us therefore, if you please, bring forward the history of the book of Leviticus and carefully consider the different sacrifices, whose types bore the image of Christ’s passion. For after Jesus Christ himself, God and man, was offered to God the Father for the world’s redemption, all those sacrifices ceased which had gone before as a type or shadow of that Redeemer, prefiguring the sacrifice which this one true priest offered [Col. 0358C] as a sweet savour—that is, himself. Previously, it was necessary to celebrate in animal victims the promissory figures of that sacrifice, for the future cleansing by flesh and blood through which remission of sins would come about through this one victim.

For the mediator between God and human beings was offered in a calf because of the power of the cross; in a lamb because of innocence; in a ram because of princely authority; in a goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, “that he might condemn sin in the flesh through sin” (Rom. VIII); and in a turtledove and dove because of God, since the mediator between God and human beings was to exist in the union of two substances. Moreover, the sprinkling of fine flour clearly showed the holy mother of all believers, the Church, gathered by the water [Col. 0358D] of baptism, which is Christ’s body.

Morally, we offer God a calf when we conquer the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we overcome irrational and foolish impulses by reason; a kid when we avoid wantonness; a dove when we preserve simplicity of mind; a turtledove when we maintain bodily chastity; unleavened loaves when we walk not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (I Cor. V).

Therefore the aforesaid sacrifices of the Old Testament, O Jews, were not sufficient, as has been said, to redeem humankind; but they prefigured him who was to offer himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for the salvation of the whole world. [Col. 0359A] [Note: [Col. 0359D] *Sentences*, distinction 18: “To what end, therefore …”.] By his most merciful death, cross, and resurrection, he obtained for us unworthy sinners access to Paradise, redemption from sin, and freedom from punishment and from the devil. Through his death and glorious resurrection we attained redemption and adoption as children of glory (Rom. VIII). For by dying he became the sacrifice sufficient for our deliverance—what all the burnt offerings of the Old Testament could by no means accomplish.

I exhort you, O Jewish enemies of truth, to listen carefully to the dispensation of our restoration, so that, pierced to repentance for the treachery of your former unbelief, [Col. 0359B] you may believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man and the most merciful Redeemer of humankind. Let us therefore bring forward blessed Ambrose, the unconquerable assailant of Jews, pagans, and heretics, and gladly hear whatever he tells us concerning the articles of our redemption.

“God,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0359D] *Sentences*, same passage.] “had decreed in mystery, because of the first human being’s sin, that a human being should not be admitted into Paradise—that is, should not be admitted to the contemplation of God—unless in the one man Christ, who is true God and true man, there should be such humility as could suffice for all who belong to him; just as in the first human being there was such pride as harmed all who belong to him. But among human beings no one was found [Col. 0359C] able to fulfil this except the Lion of the tribe of Judah, who opened the book and loosed its seals by fulfilling in himself all righteousness (Rev. V), that is, the most perfect humility, than which none can be greater. For other human beings were debtors, and each person’s own virtue and humility scarcely sufficed for himself. Therefore none of them could offer a sacrifice sufficient for our reconciliation.

“But Christ was a sufficient and perfect sacrifice, for he was humbled far more by tasting the bitterness of death than Adam had been proud in enjoying the harmful delight of eating the forbidden tree. If, therefore, Adam’s pride was once a ruin, casting him out of Paradise and closing the gate to others, much more could Christ’s humility, by which he tasted death, open the entrance of the heavenly kingdom to all who are his, the decree of God having been fulfilled, and erase the bond of the decree. For, as St. Ambrose says in *Sentences*, Book III: Our sin was so great that we could not be saved unless Jesus Christ, for us who were debtors to death, should die piously and humbly; but in this way he made us worthy of the covenant and of the promised inheritance. [Col. 0359D] This is not to be understood as though he could not have saved us in another way than through his death, but that access to the heavenly kingdom could not be opened for us, nor salvation accomplished, through another sacrifice, except through the death of the Only-begotten; whose humility and patience were, as has been said, so great that by his merit the entrance of the kingdom was open to those who believe in him.” [Col. 0360A]

I exhort you, O Jews, to listen carefully and store more attentively in your minds the things reported by the holy teachers of the Old and New Testaments concerning the benefits bestowed on us by God the Father through Jesus Christ. Great gifts were granted to us in the death of Jesus Christ, the mediator of God and human beings: namely, that we might be allowed to return to our homeland, just as in former times those who had fled to a city of refuge were safely allowed to return to their own possessions upon the death of the high priest (Num. XXXV). Behold, O Jews hard and slow of heart to believe, it has been shown to some extent how access to the kingdom has been prepared for us through Christ’s death. [Col. 0360B]

At this point, raising a question, you ask us because you desire to know how humankind could be redeemed, through the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, from the devil, from sin, and from sin’s punishment. But we, greatly grieved at the stubbornness of your unbelief and desiring the salvation of your souls, answer such questions for you. Through his most merciful passion and most glorious resurrection, as has been said, Jesus Christ delivered his faithful from the devil, sin, and punishment, and opened for them the entrance of the heavenly kingdom.

And so that you, O unbelieving and subversive Jews, may not in any way doubt that what we say is true, let us bring forward your fellow-countryman St. Paul, educated at the feet of your noble Gamaliel [Col. 0360C] but not left in your error, and carefully hear from him the truth concerning your question already stated. “Do you not know,” he says, “that to whom you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey: whether of sin unto death, or of obedience unto righteousness? But thanks be to God that you were servants of sin; but having been freed from sin, you have become servants of righteousness” (Rom. VI). To make us still more certain of our redemption, he adds again: “While we were still sinners, he died for us. Much more, therefore, now justified in his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him” (Rom. V). [Note: [Col. 0359D] *Sentences*, distinction 19: “Now therefore …”.] Therefore, in that we have been justified through his blood—that is, freed from sins—we have been delivered [Col. 0360D] from the devil, who held us bound in the chains of sins.

Perhaps you ask, O Jews, how we were freed from sin and the devil through Christ’s death. But if you say or wish to know this, know that, as the Apostle Paul says, through his death God’s love is commended to us (*ibid.*): that is, the supreme and praiseworthy love of God toward us is made manifest in this, that he gave his Son over to death for us sinners. [Note: [Col. 0360D] *Sentences*, Book III, same passage.] When so great a pledge of love toward us has been displayed, we too are moved and inflamed to love God, who did such great things for us; [Col. 0361A] and through this we are justified—that is, being freed from sins, we are made righteous. Thus Christ’s death justifies us when through it Christ’s love is stirred up in our hearts.

We are also said to be justified through Christ’s death in another way: because by faith in his death we are cleansed from sins. Hence the Apostle says: “The righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ for everyone who believes” (Rom. III). And again: “Whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood” (*ibid.*), that is, through faith in his passion; just as formerly those who looked upon the bronze serpent raised upon the wood were healed from serpent bites (Num. XXI). Therefore, if with the gaze of right faith we look upon him who hung upon the wood for us, we are immediately freed from the devil’s bonds—that is, from sins—and so delivered from the devil that after this life he finds in us nothing to punish.

By his death Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0361D] This nominative is superfluous.] extinguished, by one most true sacrifice, whatever sins there were by which the devil formerly held us liable to undergo punishments, so that in this life he may not prevail against us by tempting. Although after Christ’s death he tempts us in the ways in which he tempted before, nevertheless, as St. Augustine says, he cannot conquer us as he conquered before. For Peter, who before Christ’s death, frightened by the voice of a servant girl, denied him (Matt. XXVI), after his death did not yield when brought before kings and governors (Acts V). Why? Because the Stronger One—that is, Christ—came into the house of the strong man—that is, our hearts, where the devil dwelt—and bound the strong man (Matt. XII); [Col. 0361C] namely, he restrained him from the seduction of the faithful, so that the temptation still permitted to him might not be followed by seduction.

Therefore, O Jews, in Christ’s blood—who paid what he did not seize—we have been redeemed from sin and, through this, from the devil. For, as St. Augustine, the most faithful defender of the Catholic faith, says, the invisible hostile powers are conquered in him where the invisible desires hostile to us are conquered. For when blood was shed without guilt, all the bonds—that is, debts—of sins were cancelled, by which believers in him had formerly been held as debtors by the devil. Concerning this blood, the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, on the day before he suffered, said to his disciples—indeed, to all then present and to all of future time who would faithfully believe in him: “My blood, which is truly [Col. 0361D] of the new and eternal covenant, shall be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. XXVI). Therefore, through his blood the Redeemer of humankind freed us from sin and the devil. Through his most beloved Son, in whom the ruler of this world—that is, the devil—found nothing of his own, God the Father mercifully redeemed us.

You ask, O Jews, whether the devil found anything in Christ, since through his ministers he fixed him so cruelly to the cross. In answer we say that the devil found nothing in Christ that made him liable to die; but Christ chose to die according to the Father’s will. He had no cause of death in sin, but tasted death for obedience [Col. 0362A] and righteousness, by which he redeemed us from the devil’s servitude. For we had fallen under the ruler of this age, who deceived Adam and made him his servant, and began to possess us as though we were his household slaves; but the Redeemer came, and the deceiver was defeated.

I exhort you, O Jews, to listen carefully and store more attentively in your minds what our Redeemer Jesus Christ did to our captor, the captor of humankind. He stretched out for him a mousetrap, namely, his cross, and placed in it as bait his blood. But he, who was indeed a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth (John VIII), cruelly shed Christ’s blood through the ministers subject to his malice, and by that blood withdrew from us who were debtors. [Col. 0362B] For Christ gave his blood for us and allowed himself to be killed by Pilate and the other satellites of the devil, in order to blot out our sins and redeem us from the power of that same ancient enemy. That by which the devil held humankind captive was therefore destroyed by the Redeemer’s blood. For he held us bound only by the chains of our sins. These were the captive’s chains.

Therefore the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, came and bound the strong man with the chains of his passion; he entered his house, that is, the hearts in which the devil himself dwelt; and he snatched away his vessels, namely ourselves, whom the devil had filled with his bitterness. God and man Jesus Christ, rescuing those vessels from him and making us his own, [Col. 0362C] emptied our minds of bitterness and filled them with the sweetness of his love, redeeming us from sins through his death and granting us adoption as sons. [Note: [Col. 0362D] *Sentences*, Book III, same passage, § “He became.”] Thus he became a mortal human being in order, by dying, to conquer the devil. For if he who conquered the devil were not human, it would seem that the human being who voluntarily subjected himself to the devil had been taken from him not justly but violently. But if a human being conquered him, the devil plainly lost the human being by right; and for a human being to conquer, God had to be in him—that is, God had to be human—so that he might make the human being free from sins.

Perhaps you ask, O Jews, saying: Since almighty God had many means available for redeeming humankind, why did he choose for his only-begotten Son to take flesh from an incorrupt Virgin, conquer the ancient [Col. 0362D] enemy through him, and snatch the world from that enemy’s dominion? Why did God the Father, as you Christians assert, send his most beloved Son, coeternal with himself, from heaven to redeem the first human being through the cross, rather than deliver him from the devil’s slavery through an angel or archangel?

We answer to the contrary: if God had sent an angel for humanity’s redemption, then a human being would be the angel’s servant. Moreover, an angel was incapable by his nature of redeeming a human being. If he became human, he would have still less power. Perhaps you also ask, O Jews: Why did God not create another human being from the earth [Col. 0363A] and send him in place of the lost one? We answer to the contrary: if God had created a new human being and sent him for the redemption of humankind, redemption would not pertain to Adam’s race; for the one who made satisfaction to God for it had to belong to its own race.

If you further ask, O faithless Jews, why God did not send a patriarch or prophet for the redemption of the world, we answer: because patriarchs and prophets were conceived and born in sins, and therefore could not redeem humankind. If a human being alone existed, or if an angel assumed human nature, neither could redeem the world; rather, either could readily sin, since both angel and human being are known to have fallen from the contemplation of God. For the human being had to be restored [Col. 0363B] in such a manner as to be equal to the angels.

Therefore the Son of God assumed from the Virgin mother a passible human being without sin, in whom he might taste death and thereby open heaven to us, and free us from the devil’s slavery—that is, from sin. Since, therefore, an angel ought not to redeem a human being, and a human being could not by himself make satisfaction to God, the Son of God, through whom all things were made, assumed humanity so that redemption too might occur through him. He became one person in two natures; and in the nature in which [Note: [Col. 0363D] “In which.”] he was God, he conquered the devil, just as the devil had conquered the human being, opened heaven to all the predestined, and made them equal to the angels—things which God alone could do. In the nature in which he was human, however, through the injury he endured—that is, when he underwent an undeserved death—he freed the world from [Col. 0363C] sin, which a human being alone had to do.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, O Jews, is true God and true man. By his most precious blood he redeemed the world, conquered the devil, opened heaven to those who believe in him, and daily admits them through himself to behold the glory of his Father. As an all-powerful king, he conquered the devil and snatched humankind from his tyranny; as a true priest, compelled by love, he offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross for our sins as a sweet-smelling savour. That most victorious king and most merciful priest, Christ, and his works were prefigured by the fire which, in the Old Testament, consumed upon the sacred altars the sacrifices offered to God [Col. 0363D] as a sweet savour (Lev. VI).

[Note: [Col. 0363D] Isidore, Questions on Leviticus, ch. 2.] Therefore the fire consuming the sacrifice on the altar signified Christ’s victory swallowing up death. Among the Jewish people themselves, the legal sacrifices were duly celebrated in their appointed time; their kingdom and priesthood were a prophecy of the coming King and Priest, namely Christ, who would rule and preserve his faithful among all nations, introduce them into the kingdom of heaven, and bring them into the sanctuary of the angels for eternal life. Thus the sacrifices of the Hebrews, duly celebrated according to the law, as has been said, prefigured Christ—the true king and true priest—who would come in the fullness of time. [Col. 0364A] But the Gentiles sacrificed not to God but to demons. Of them the Apostle says: “The things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice not to God but to demons” (I Cor. X).

I do not wish you, O rebellious and unbelieving Jews, to be ignorant that the sacrifice of blood is an ancient and prophetic matter, testifying from the beginning of humankind to the future passion of Jesus Christ, mediator of God and human beings. For Abel is found in the sacred Scriptures to have been the first to offer it (Gen. IV). Therefore all the sacred Scripture of the Old Testament proclaims Christ to be the true Son of God the Father and the true son of a human mother, and to have come for the redemption of the world; and it most clearly proves you, who deny him with obstinate mind, to be false witnesses.

[Col. 0364B]

§ XXVI.—

The many matters which the history of Genesis relates concerning Isaac’s betrothal to Rebecca are recognized and explained as laden with mysteries; and in them especially the spiritual union of Christ with the Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles. The spiritual generation of that same Church, and the teaching by which she nourishes her children, are shown in the earth bringing forth grass and the tree producing fruit. Repentance is necessary, not superstitious; it was instituted by Christ, and without it no one can obtain forgiveness. The threefold kind of conversion and its qualities, according to Isidore. Repentance must be performed in this life, since after death no place remains for correction. Rational discernment, signified by the salt customarily used in sacrifices, is necessary for the Jews, so that they may prefer the New Testament to the Old. God is to be served not with sadness, but with devotion and gladness.

Believe, therefore, that he is true God and true man, and was sent by God the Father from heaven to unite to himself the holy Church.  
[Note: Another manuscript begins differently, namely: “For I warn you, O Jews, to believe that Christ is true God and true man . . . . . . .” [Col. 0363D; 0364D].]

In reply you say, O foolish Jews, slow of heart to believe, that you are unwilling to believe either that Christ is true God, or that Christ’s Church was instituted or foreshadowed by God, or that the people of that Church can in any way be saved. You further assert, in opposition, that you wish to receive the Old Testament alone; but you falsely maintain that the New Testament and everything Christians do therein are to be regarded as nothing. To these objections of yours, O Jews, we answer as follows. If you understand the Old Testament spiritually, as you ought, you can find in it that Christ was sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world, united the holy Church to himself, enriched her nobly—indeed most nobly—with heavenly gifts, and adopted her as his bride. He also bestowed upon her such a privilege that no one can be saved except within her.  
[Col. 0364C–D; Note: “within,” another reading.]

Therefore, wholly to refute your false assertion and increasingly to confirm the religion of the Catholic Church, which you regard as nothing, let the history in the book of Genesis be brought forward; and, having expounded it spiritually, let us carefully consider how it prefigured Christ as about to come for the redemption of the world and to unite the holy Church to himself.

Abraham therefore said to his servant, the steward of his household: “Put your hand under my thigh, that I may bind you by oath through the Lord of heaven and earth, that you will not take a wife for my son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell; but that you will go to my land and to my kindred, and from there take a wife for my son Isaac” (Gen. 24).  
[Note: Patherius, on Genesis, ch. 53; Col. 0365D.]

It is worthwhile to recall certain matters from the history of Abraham and Isaac, so that in them we may more clearly set forth something to be understood allegorically. Abraham calls the servant and commands him to put his hand under his thigh. And, as the ancient translation has it, he ordered the servant to swear “through the Lord God of heaven”; then he commands him not to take a wife for his son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, but to go to his own kindred and bring back a wife from there.  
[Note: “God,” as in Patherius; the manuscripts wrongly put *Domini* (“of the Lord”) in place of *Deum* (“God”). No translation reads “Lord of Lord”; all read “Lord God,” except the version previously cited by the author, which read only “Lord of heaven and earth.” Col. 0365D; 0366D.]

The servant accordingly put his hand under Abraham’s thigh, as he had been commanded, and swore to him. He took from all his master’s goods and went into Mesopotamia. There, standing beside a spring, he proposed this in prayer: that the maiden to whom he should say, “Lower your jar that I may drink,” and who should answer, “Drink; indeed I shall also give water to your camels,” should be the wife of his master Isaac.

Immediately Rebecca came out. To the servant asking for water she replied, “Drink, my lord”; quickly lowering the jar upon her arm, she gave him drink. She also drew and supplied water for the camels. Abraham’s servant immediately gave her golden earrings weighing two shekels and bracelets weighing ten shekels. When questioned by the servant, she told him her lineage, and reported that in her father’s house there was ample room to stay and a great abundance of straw and hay.

Rebecca had a brother named Laban. He hurried out; seeing his sister’s earrings and bracelets, he invited the servant inside, gave him straw and hay, supplied water to wash the feet of the camels and of the men who had come with him, and set bread before them. But the servant sent by Abraham refused to eat unless he first obtained the marriage arrangement for his master’s son. As soon as he obtained what he sought, he brought out vessels of gold and silver and garments, increased Rebecca’s gifts, and presented gifts to her brothers and mother.

Rebecca and her maidens mounted camels and followed Abraham’s servant, who promptly returned to Abraham his master. At that time Isaac was walking along the road leading to the well called “of the Living and Seeing One.” He dwelt in the southern country and had gone out to meditate in the field as day was already declining. But as soon as Rebecca saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel and asked the servant who that man was coming through the field. He replied, “He is my lord.” She quickly took her veil and covered herself. Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother, took her as his wife, and loved her so greatly that he moderated the grief which had come to him from his mother’s death (ibid.).  
[Col. 0365A–0366A.]

Let blessed Gregory, the unbending pillar of the Catholic faith, graciously approach and expound spiritually for us the aforesaid history from the book of Genesis.  
[Note: “Patherius, in the place cited,” rather than Gregory; “Genesis,” rather than “Exodus.” Col. 0366D.]

“What,” he says, “does it mean that Abraham commands the servant to put his hand under his thigh and swear through the Lord of heaven, unless that the flesh of him was to descend through that member—the one who was Abraham’s son according to humanity, and God the Father’s Son according to divinity?”

I urge you, O Jews, diligently to hear the things blessed Gregory expounds spiritually and to store them more attentively in your minds; so that, once the long-standing treachery of unbelief has been expelled, you may unquestionably believe that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, was sent by God the Father from heaven for the redemption of humankind, and spiritually united to himself the holy Church gathered from Jews and Gentiles.

For the aforesaid history in Genesis, which seems to recount the bodily deeds of the holy patriarchs Abraham and Isaac, and of wise Rebecca, when spiritually interpreted is fittingly understood of Christ and his Church. “All these things,” says the Apostle, “happened to them as figures” (1 Cor. 10). Let us therefore hear what Abraham said to his servant.

“Put your hand,” he says, “under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven.” This means more plainly: Touch my Son Christ, who according to humanity is to be born from my offspring in order to unite the holy Church to himself; and swear by that same God of mine, who possesses true divinity with God the Father and will assume natural humanity from his virgin mother. Thus the servant is commanded to place his hand not upon but beneath the thigh, because from that thigh he was to descend who, though indeed man, would come above all human beings. It was surely fitting that he should put his hand beneath the thigh, because no flesh has ever existed above that flesh which the Only-begotten of God the Father united to himself for our redemption.  
[Col. 0366B–C.]

What also does it mean that Abraham forbids a wife to be taken for his beloved son Isaac from the daughters of the Canaanites, except that no reprobate souls are joined to him of whom it is written: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3)? But the servant is commanded to take a wife from Abraham’s kindred because the holy Church of the elect alone was to be united to the Only-begotten Son of God the Father—the Church whom that Only-begotten One already knew through predestination and foreknowledge.

Who, then, is this servant sent to bring back a wife, except the order of prophets and apostles and of all teachers? When they speak the word of preaching to good minds, they become agents in joining each individual soul to the Only-begotten Son of God. As he went, he took with him from all his master’s goods, because, in what the Church’s teachers say concerning the Lord, they display in themselves the riches of virtues. Thus they draw peoples to follow God more swiftly, insofar as they show their hearers in themselves the things they proclaim.

The servant stood beside the spring and, on the basis of his predetermined criterion, proposed which maiden should be chosen; because holy preachers consider the streams of sacred speech and from them gather what words of their preaching they should entrust to which hearers, and from whom they may take confident assurance. The servant asked for drink because a good preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer. But wise Rebecca supplied drink because the holy Church of the elect satisfies the desire of her preachers from the virtues of her faith. For when she confessed the God whom she had heard, she offered her preacher the water of refreshment and cooled his mind.

It should be noted that prudent Rebecca lowered the jar from her shoulder to her arms, because that confession is pleasing to God and to the Church’s teacher which proceeds from good work. Thus the holy Church certainly supplied water spiritually, because she did not remain barren in what she believed. For she immediately made it her concern to preach what she had heard; and by teaching she produced many preachers from herself. Water in the jar is knowledge of preaching held in due measure, because the holy Church strives “not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Rom. 12). Therefore, the jar of water in the arms is the doctrine of preaching in action.

Rebecca supplied drink not only to the servant’s companions but also to the camels, because the holy Church preaches the word of life not only to the wise but also to the foolish, according to Paul’s saying: “I am debtor both to the wise and to the unwise” (Rom. 1). Or, certainly, water is also given to beasts when care is ordered as to how the flesh is to be maintained: it should not be indulged at its own desire, yet should not be denied in necessities, as it is written: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). He who forbids such provision in desires undoubtedly permits it in necessities, according to what is again said: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. 5).  
[Col. 0366D–0367D.]

The servant gave Rebecca earrings and bracelets because every preacher adorns the hearing of the holy Church through obedience, and her hands through the merit of good works. The earrings weigh two shekels, but the bracelets ten shekels, because the first virtue, obedience, is found in charity; and charity is distinguished in two commandments: that God and neighbour be loved. Right action is fulfilled by completion of the Decalogue, so that, once good deeds begin to be done, no evil deeds are any longer committed.

Rebecca provided an ample place to stay in her father’s house because the holy Church showed that she already knew the natural law from the former people, and received the words of preaching into the spacious bosom of charity. For the teachers’ place of lodging is spacious when breadth of goodness rests in the hearer’s heart. Hence Paul, I think, says to certain people: “Beware. We have wronged no one; we have corrupted no one. You are not restricted in us, but you are restricted in your own affections” (2 Cor. 7; 6). This means more plainly: Make a spacious place in your minds to receive doctrine; but remain narrow in entertaining fleshly thoughts.  
[Note: Another manuscript: “Receive us. We have wronged no one,” etc., as commonly read. But the reading *you are restricted* is the author’s own, and a ludicrous hand corrected it in our manuscript to the commoner *be restricted*, in both places, to conform it to another exemplar. Col. 0367D; 0368D.]

She also reported that she had an abundance of straw and hay because, on hearing the word of life, the holy Church rendered earthly support to her preachers. Blessed Paul, regarding such support as almost nothing, said: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9).

Laban was Rebecca’s brother. Hurriedly coming out and seeing his sister’s earrings and bracelets, he invited the servant inside, because there are fleshly persons connected with the faithful who, when they behold gifts of spiritual virtues, become in admiration, as it were, guests. Though not as far as deeds, they nevertheless admit the word of preaching into their souls as far as receiving faith. Since they often see good persons shining with miracles, they do not refuse to believe what they hear about eternity, although they do not follow the conduct of the elect in the holy Church and remain in fleshly practice.

Laban offered straw, water, hay, and bread; but the servant sent by Abraham refused to accept them unless he first obtained his master’s marriage arrangement. For there are indeed many ready to support their preachers from temporal means; but holy preachers will not receive temporal things unless they first obtain eternal things. If they find no fruit in souls, they disdain bodily recompense. They do not wash their feet with water, because no consolation relieves their longing born of labour.

But once the servant obtained his master’s marriage arrangement, he brought out vessels of gold and silver and garments, which he gave Rebecca, because the teachers of the holy Church bestow as many adornments as they teach gifts of virtues. She who had earlier received earrings and bracelets now received vessels of gold and silver and garments, because the holy Church, which first received obedience and action through faith, subsequently grows strong in spiritual gifts; filled with the spirit and grace of prophecy, she becomes rich as her gifts are enlarged.

The servant also presented gifts to her mother and brothers because, from the time when the Church came to faith, the Gentile world has prospered in temporal glory after her conversion, as we now see: Christians everywhere suffer affliction, while Gentiles glory in earthly power. Rebecca’s brothers also receive gifts because those who retain the faith verbally in the Church but live carnally, not following their profession in conduct, are customarily honoured kindly by the faithful because they appear to be believers. Thus mother and brothers receive gifts, yet remain strangers to the portion of the inheritance; because both unbelievers and carnal persons who are enclosed within a profession of faith do not come to the inheritance of the eternal portion, though they obtain temporarily the glory of heavenly generosity.  
[Col. 0368A–0369A.]

Rebecca followed the man with her maidens because the holy Church has with her as companions souls of lesser merit. Though such persons do not, in certain respects, possess contemplation on the throne through ascent of mind, they are Rebecca’s maidens, as it were: they follow in conduct but do not ascend at all to the throne of contemplation. The servant likewise had some companions, because among the holy prophets there were some who lived well but did not have the spirit of prophecy; and with the blessed apostles there were persons who maintained an upright life in conduct yet did not sow words of preaching among the peoples.

The servant returns swiftly to his master because, when holy preachers gain the lives of their hearers through preaching, they immediately give thanks to him from whose gift they have received this result. They attribute nothing in that work to themselves, but to its Author.  
[Col. 0369B.]

“At that time Isaac was walking back and forth along the way that leads to the well called ‘of the Living and Seeing One.’” Who is the Living and Seeing One but the almighty Lord, of whom it is written: “I live for ever, says the Lord” (Deut. 32)? And that he himself sees all things is again said: “All things are naked and laid open to his eyes” (Heb. 4). The well of the Living and Seeing One is the depth of sacred Scripture, which almighty God gave us for the watering of the mind.

What is the road leading to the well of the Living and Seeing One, except the humility of the passion of the Only-begotten Son of God? Through it, that which the streams of sacred Scripture had formerly spoken secretly was opened to us. Unless the Only-begotten of God the Father had been incarnate, tempted, seized, struck with blows, smeared with spittle, crucified, and dead, the depth of the well—that is, of Scripture—would not lie open to us. What, then, did the humility of his passion become for the faithful except the key of opening, through which we find the well of God’s mysteries, so that we may drink the water of knowledge from its depth?

Sacred Scripture speaks of his incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension. Since we know that these things happened, we now understand what we have heard. They could indeed previously be read, but because they had not yet happened, they could not be understood. Hence it is said through John: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered, to open the book and loose its seals” (Rev. 5). He opened the book and loosed its seals who, by being born, dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven, revealed to us the hidden meanings of sacred Scripture.  
[Col. 0369C–0370A.]

It should be noted that the text does not say, “he walked along the way leading to the well,” but “he walked back and forth.” One walks back and forth when, going and returning, one treads the road on which one walks. In the humility of his passion the Lord walked back and forth, because he endured now verbal insults from the Jews, now false testimony against himself, now slaps, now spittle, now a crown of thorns, now the cross. Thus to have walked back and forth in the humility of the passion is to have endured repeatedly, in different ways, so many adversities and reproaches.  
[Col. 0370A.]

But when Rebecca came, Isaac dwelt in the southern land because the Only-begotten Lord and our Redeemer, when the Church came to him, dwelt in the minds of those born from Judaea whom not the chill of torpor but the fervour of charity possessed. From that people came the prophetess Anna, and from it came Simeon, who received the Lord into his arms.

“Isaac,” it says, “had gone out to meditate in the field.” The Lord himself explains that the field is understood as the world, saying: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13). The Son of God went out in that he deigned to appear visibly, as it was said of him through the prophet: “You went out for the salvation of your people, to save your anointed ones” (Hab. 3).

Strong young men customarily practise the use of arms. Isaac therefore went out to meditate in the field because our Redeemer, giving a pattern of humility to those who follow him, showed in himself examples of patience through the exercise of his long-suffering and passion. The practice of arms, as blessed Gregory says, is frequent endurance of sufferings.  
[Note: Patherius, in the place cited, rather than blessed Gregory. Col. 0369D.]

For he who endured the blows of hands, the spear, and the cross allowed his passion to be repeatedly inflicted upon him even to death. We take up the weapons of suffering because through them we are freed from the adversary, as the Lord himself says: “By your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21). Therefore Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and men, goes out into the field to practise, as the day is already declining, because he undertook the exercises of suffering near the end of the world. Thus he speaks through the Psalmist in an expression of his crucifixion: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140).  
[Col. 0370B–D.]

What does it mean that Rebecca is brought to Isaac on a camel’s back, except that Rebecca, as we have said, signifies the Church, and the camel she rode signifies the Gentile people, twisted in conduct and laden with the worship of idols? Those who found gods for themselves to worship, as it were, caused the burden they had to carry to grow upon their own backs.
[Note: Gregory, *Morals*, book 1, ch. 6, and book 35, ch. 11. Col. 0369.]

Rebecca therefore comes to Isaac carried upon a camel’s back because the Church hurrying to Christ from the Gentile world is found amid the twisted and vicious habits of her former life. When she saw Isaac, she dismounted from the camel, because the more subtly the holy Church recognizes her Redeemer, the more humbly she abandons the pursuits of fleshly life and resists in herself the crookedness of vice. When Isaac was seen, Rebecca dismounted from the camel, because, having known the Lord, the Gentile world abandoned its former life and sought the lowliness of humility instead of the height of pride.  
[Note: The manuscripts corruptly read *una* (“one”) for *ima* (“lowest things”). Col. 0371A, D.]

What does it mean that Isaac saw Rebecca sitting on the camel, except that the Church coming from the Gentiles knew that her Redeemer had come into this world while she still relied upon vices and adhered not yet to spiritual but to animal impulses?  
[Note: Another manuscript reads *inhaerent* (“adhering”) rather than *inhaereret* (“she adhered”). Col. 0371D.]

Nor should it trouble us that the servant also came with camels bearing his master’s riches; for the holy preachers themselves, although they now excel in understanding and in life, both in comprehending and expressing higher things, still feel in themselves the conflicts of the flesh. “They see another law in their members, resisting the law of their mind and leading them captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7). They carry riches on camels because, lest the greatness of revelations exalt them, a thorn of their flesh is given them (2 Cor. 12). “We have this treasure,” says the Apostle, “in earthen vessels, that the surpassing power may be of God and not of ourselves” (2 Cor. 4). Those who speak heavenly things through the flesh yet still feel the conflict of temptation carry riches on the crooked backs of camels.  
[Col. 0371A–B.]

When Rebecca sees Isaac, she learns from the servant, whom she asks, who that man is; because each day the holy Church understands, from the sayings of the prophets and apostles, what she ought to believe concerning her Redeemer. She immediately covered herself with her veil because, the more subtly she penetrates the mysteries of her Saviour, the more deeply she is ashamed of her previous life. Since she acted perversely, she is ashamed; she took care to cover herself with a veil because, having seen her lord, she blushed at the weakness of her conduct. She who had formerly been freely borne upon the camel, after dismounting is covered in modest shame.

Therefore the apostolic voice says to that Church turned from its former pride, as it were to Rebecca dismounting from the camel and drawing a veil over herself: “What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6).  
[Note: Another manuscript reads *quasi* (“as if”). Col. 0371D.]

Isaac brought her into the tent of his mother and took her as his wife because, in place of the Synagogue from which the Lord was born according to the flesh, he loves the holy Church and joins her to himself in love and contemplation. She who was first of a great kindred—that is, known through predestination—afterwards, now joined in continual love, becomes his wife. He loved her so greatly that he moderated the grief which had come to him from his mother’s death, because through the gain of the holy Church our Redeemer wiped away the sadness that might have arisen from the loss of the Synagogue. When Rebecca is joined to Isaac, grief at his mother’s death is moderated, because when the holy Church coming from the Gentile world is brought as far as the bed of contemplation, Judaea is counted as nothing, as blessed Gregory says in his *Morals* on this passage.  
[Note: Patherius, in the place cited. Col. 0371D–0372A.]

If we take care to interpret the names themselves, Isaac means “laughter,” while Rebecca means “patience.” Laughter, says blessed Gregory, comes from joy, but patience from tribulation.  
[Note: Patherius, in the place cited. Col. 0372D.]

Although the holy Church is already raised up in contemplation of heavenly joy, she nevertheless still has something sorrowful to endure from the weight of mortal flesh. Isaac and Rebecca are joined—that is, laughter and patience are mingled—because in the holy Church there takes place what the Apostle commands among other things: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12). Thus prosperity gladdens her in contemplation, while adversities from tribulation still trouble her.  
[Col. 0372A–B.]

Therefore, O lying and treacherous Jews, our Lord Jesus Christ is true God and true man, who descended from heaven in order to redeem humankind and unite the holy Church to himself. In asserting that sacred Scripture prefigured him in the clearest figures and enigmas of the New and Old Testaments, it plainly shows that you lie in your objections, since you stubbornly deny that he came for the redemption of the world, united the holy Church to himself, or can save those who believe in him.

Thus the holy Church has truly been redeemed by Jesus Christ her bridegroom and joined to her own head; she indeed instructs believing peoples through spiritual teaching, refreshes them with the bread of the heavenly word, and gathers them in the unity of true faith.  
[Col. 0372B–C.]

Moses undoubtedly prefigured these virtues of the holy Church typologically when, speaking among other things about the works of the six days, he said: “The earth brought forth green grass bearing seed according to its kind, and a tree producing fruit, each having seed according to its own species” (Gen. 1). Let us hear what blessed Gregory says on this passage.  
[Note: Patherius, on Genesis, ch. 4. Col. 0372D.]

“This which history attests was truly done in such a way as to signify something truly to be done. By the earth the Church is signified, which refreshes us with the nourishment of the word and guards us with the shelter of her protection. She feeds us by speaking and protects us by helping, so that she not only brings forth the grass of refreshment, but also provides the tree of protection with the fruit of good work.  
[Col. 0372C–D.]

“A tree also produces seed according to its kind when our mind draws consideration from itself toward another and produces the shoot of right action. Hence a certain wise man said: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another’ (Tob. 4). Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them’ (Matt. 7). This means more plainly: Look to one another in your hope, and recognize from yourselves what you ought to offer to others.”  
[Note: The same author, ch. 5. Col. 0372D–0373A.]

Therefore, O Jews, our Lord Jesus Christ is true God, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing; and he is true man, through whom he redeemed humankind from the dominion of the ancient enemy. He himself purchased the holy Church at the great price of his blood; he himself espoused her to himself; he himself continually begets spiritual children from her; he himself daily raises her by sacred instruction to attain the prize of eternal blessedness.

I urge you therefore, O wretched and pitiable Jews, willingly to give faith to the authorities of the Old and New Testaments, which most truly establish that Christ is true God and true man. Humbly perform penance for your former unbelief and blasphemies, by which you dishonoured him many times—not only while he still lived among people on earth, but even now when he reigns at the right hand of God the Father—so that you may deserve to be rescued from eternal condemnation and numbered among his elect.  
[Col. 0373A–B.]

At this point, as though making an accusation, O Jews, and still resisting belief, you answer us thus: “Why is repentance necessary for us, and what benefit is there in it? We consider it superstitious and useless, and therefore do not at all believe that forgiveness of sins can be obtained through it. For we trust that we are saved not through the repentance of ecclesiastical religion, but through the commandments of the law, as our fathers were.”  
[Col. 0373B–C.]

In reply, O Jews, we answer you contrariwise that repentance is not, as you falsely say, superstitious or useless, but fruitful and pleasing to God for those who keep it with their whole heart. For Christ, who truly has been appointed high priest by God the Father, instituted it for the forgiveness of sins, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). He instituted it, therefore, and through it grants remission of all sins to those who faithfully believe in him.

However sinful and ungodly anyone may be, if that person turns to God with the whole heart and produces fruits worthy of repentance, he or she can obtain from Christ—who unquestionably takes away the sins of the world—full pardon for offences. For we shall obtain pardon not by living pleasantly in fleshly desires, but by humbly repenting and bitterly mourning past sins. Thus Jesus Christ, himself God and man, says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).  
[Col. 0373C–D.]

Meanwhile, I wish you to know, O Jews, that conversion to God has a threefold form.  
[Note: Isidore, *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 8. Col. 0373D.]

The first is that of beginning, with sweetness; the second, of the middle stage, with labour; the third, of perfection, with rest. Yet, as blessed Isidore says in the second book of the *Sentences*, some begin with sweetness, others with the bitterness of temptations. Every convert must therefore first begin with weeping for sins and then pass to desire for heavenly things. The vices we have committed must first be cleansed by tears; then, with the eye of the mind purified, we may contemplate what we seek. For when the darkness of sin has first been washed away from us by weeping, heavenly things may be freely seen with the purified eyes of the heart. One must first turn to God with fear, so that fleshly enticements may be overcome by fear of future punishments; then, once fear has been cast aside, one must pass to love of eternal life.  
[Col. 0374A.]

The Lord undoubtedly signified this severity of repentance as future in the holy Church when he prohibited honey from being offered in every sacrifice, saying: “Every offering presented to the Lord shall be made without leaven; neither any leaven nor honey shall be burned in sacrifice to the Lord. You shall offer them only as firstfruits and gifts; but they shall not be placed upon the altar as an odour of sweetness” (Lev. 2).  
[Note: Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 3. Col. 0373D–0374B.]

Thus, honey not being offered in sacrifice indicates that nothing pleasurable, nothing sweet of this world, and nothing without some biting element of truth pleases God. Hence the Passover is eaten not with honey—that is, with fleshly delights—but with wild lettuces (Exod. 12), that is, with contrition of heart. We rightly celebrate the Passover with wild lettuces when we believe that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and that he unquestionably suffered for the redemption of the world; and when, repenting of our sins before him, we are pierced with tears, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe from the stomach of the mind the love of a perverse life.  
[Col. 0374B–C.]

“Compunction of heart,” says blessed Isidore, “is humility of mind arising with tears from the remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. That is the more perfect affection of compunction for converts which repels from itself every affection of fleshly desires and fixes its purpose, with the entire effort of the mind, in contemplation of God. We read that compunction is twofold; consequently the soul of every elect person is moved toward God either when it considers the evils of its own deeds or when it sighs for the desires of eternal life.”  
[Note: Isidore, *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 12. Col. 0373D–0374C.]

“There are four kinds of affections,” says blessed Isidore, “by which the mind of the just is pierced with salutary weariness: remembrance of past crimes; recollection of future punishments; consideration of one’s pilgrimage in the remoteness of this life; and desire for the heavenly homeland, so that one may be able to reach it as swiftly as possible. Whoever is pierced by the memory of sins into lamentation should then know that he is visited by God’s presence, when he inwardly blushes because he remembers having sinned and already punishes himself by his own judgment through repentance. For Peter then wept when Christ looked upon him (Luke 22). Hence the Psalmist says: ‘He looked, and the earth was moved and trembled’ (Ps. 76)—namely, the hearts of sinful people.

“The steps of God in the inward human heart occur when good desires arise and evils are trampled down. Therefore, when these things happen in the human heart, one should know that God is then present to the human heart through grace. Hence a person ought to apply himself more earnestly to compunction when he senses God working inwardly. What the just person’s mind is seized by through true compunction, and how it returns weakened from the greatness of the light it has tasted, can be known by one who has already tasted something of it. There are some who become accusers of themselves not from true compunction of heart, but only represent themselves as sinners in order to find a place of holiness through the constructed humility of confession.”  
[Col. 0374D–0375A; Notes: “There are,” for “There are four”; Isidore, ibid.]

Therefore, as has been said above, O Jews, enemies of truth, God prohibited honey from being offered to him in sacrifice in the Old Testament because he determined to grant pardon not to those living pleasurably amid the desires of their enticing flesh, but to those bitterly repenting from remembrance of their offences.  
[Note: Isidore, ibid., ch. 13. Col. 0375D.]

The bitterness of repentance also makes the mind examine its deeds more closely and recall in tears the gifts of God which it despised in sinning. I therefore urge you, O Jews, in no way to doubt God’s mercy. If you approach him with whole-hearted, humble repentance for your past unbelief, you can obtain full forgiveness from him. For he himself says through the prophet to you—indeed, to all people: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved” (Isa. 45). This means more plainly: If you wish to attain the salvation of your souls, depart from evil, believe faithfully in me, adorn faith with good works, fear me also in the things you do rightly, and love me above all things.  
[Col. 0375B–C.]

I want you to know, O Jews uncircumcised and untamed in heart, that the freedom to repent extends only through this life; after death there is no opportunity for amendment. [Note: [Col. 0376D] Isidore, ibid.] Hence the Lord says: “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work” (John 9). Therefore the prophet says: “Give glory to the Lord your God before darkness comes” (Jer. 13), that is, before eternal death overtakes you: while you are in this life, glorify God through repentance. Thus King Hezekiah also says: “O Lord, hell will not confess you, nor will death praise you; those who go down into the pit will not await your truth” (Isa. 38). As though he said more plainly: O Lord, hell—that is, the reprobate once damned—will not confess you in praise; nor will death—that is, the devil—praise you. Those who descend into the pit will not await your truth: namely, those wholly damned in the pit of hell will not await your truth, that is, the deliverance wrought by your Son, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). As though he said openly: Those now damned without end will neither repent in hell nor render praises to God.

And so that you may know certainly, O Jews, that it is not those in hell, but those who truly repent in the present age and those who now happily abide in the heavenly kingdom, who praise God, I urge you patiently to hear what King Hezekiah subsequently says to God: “The living, the living, shall confess you, as I do this day; the father shall make known your truth to the children” (Isa. 38). As though he said: The living—the one now under your protection and, in the future, in eternal rest—shall confess you in praise, just as I today, delivered from enemies and from the temptations of the flesh, give you thanks. As a good father, he shall make your truth known to his obedient children, namely the worship of true religion, so that your mercy may be proclaimed to posterity.

[Col. 0376B] The Psalmist also testifies that truly no one in hell confesses God, saying: “O Lord, there is no one in death who remembers you; but in hell who shall confess you?” (Ps. 6). As though he said more plainly: “Save me, O Lord, for the sake of your mercy” (ibid.); for unless, by inwardly inspiring me, you bring about compunction of heart and humble confession of sins, I shall not remember you, because I shall be in death—that is, in sin—and no one remaining in sin and distrusting your mercy remembers you. By this analogy sin is called death, because, just as death separates the soul from this transitory life, so sin separates it from eternal life. As though he said: O Lord, unless you save me and heal me from the wounds of sins, I shall not confess you, because I shall be placed in hell.

[Col. 0376C] Hell is the depth of vices; and everyone who persists in sin and despises God’s goodness despairs. Therefore he who despises your goodness, O Lord, will not confess you, because he despairs. This is said by analogy with the sick: while they are ill, they can be cured by physicians; but after death they have no need of bodily medicines. So too, one who hopes can be healed; but after he has despaired, no medicine can be applied to him. Otherwise: since someone who is in death will not remember you, much less will one who is in hell confess you.

Therefore, while permission to live in this present life is still granted to you, O faithless Jews, perform true repentance for the treachery of your former unbelief; firmly preserve true faith in heart and deed; wash away with tears the stains of your past life; change your conduct as quickly as possible according to the rule of ecclesiastical religion; so that, before eternal death overtakes you, you may believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man, and through him may attain eternal life—which he himself is, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, before perpetual death snatches you away because of your unbelief and impenitent heart, O crooked and perverse nation; before eternal destruction seizes you; [Col. 0377A] before the day of judgment arrives; before the dark tempest possesses you; before darkness envelops you; before hell swallows you; before eternal fire devours you—I urge you, drawing deep sighs from the inmost heart, uttering the bitterest groans of a sinner, pouring forth abundant tears, and lamenting greatly, to say to God with the Psalmist: “Do not turn your face from me, and I shall become like those who descend into the pit” (Ps. 142).

As though he said: Do not turn away your face—that is, do not take your mercy from me—for if you take it away, I shall be like those descending into the pit, namely into the depth of sin, in which people despise and confession perishes. Hence a certain wise man says: “When the wicked man comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). [Col. 0377B] “For he,” as Master Peter says upon this verse, “descends into the depth of sin who also loses confession, or who proposes to himself freedom to sin, or hope of pardon, with the reins of iniquity let loose. Such a person does not hear the Lord saying: ‘Return to me, and I will return to you’” (Zech. 1).

Therefore, as has been said, while repentance is still being performed in this present age, O Jews, enemies of truth, the mercy of God comes to help; but in the future repentance will no longer be joined to a person, and instead an account of deeds will be rendered. [Note: [Col. 0377D] Isidore, ibid.] For this reason the wicked often become worse, as Blessed Isidore says: they receive, through God’s patience, time for amendment, but use the delay of life not for repentance but arrogate to themselves boldness in sinning. He goes from bad to worse [Col. 0377C] who uses the time granted him for repentance as freedom for evil action. Everyone ought to hasten to God in repentance while he can, lest, if he refuses while he can, when he finally wishes to do so he be altogether unable.

Accordingly the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55). And where can he be found except in the present life, in which he is near to all who call upon him? Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is near to those who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144). For then he will already be far off, when he says to the reprobate: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). For now he is not seen, yet he is near; then he will be seen, yet he will not be near, because he may be seen but cannot be found.

[Col. 0377D] Therefore, while you are still given time to live in the present life, O wretched and unhappy Jews; while permission is granted to turn to God; while time for repentance is bestowed; while the door of mercy is opened; while hope of pardon is promised: believe without doubt that Christ is true God and true man. Through the severity of true repentance, hasten to obtain pardon for the unjust treachery of your unbelief; offer yourselves with devout minds to be baptized by the ministers of the holy Church, so that, cleansed of the stains of sins and renewed in Christ by sacred baptism, you may deserve to be joined to the children of the holy Church.

[Col. 0378A] I do not want you to be ignorant, O Jews, that whatever you do without discernment will be a fault, whereas whatever you do with discernment will be a virtue. For a virtue without discernment occupies the place of vice. You indeed exercise true discernment if you prefer the New Testament, established spiritually and firmly by Jesus Christ, to the Old Testament, and if you believe without doubt that the Old Testament is to be observed not carnally but spiritually. You are not irrational like brute animals, but truly rational human beings, if you give unhesitating assent to the figures of the patriarchs, the prophecies of the prophets, and the proclamations of the apostles and evangelists, which were truly and spiritually delivered concerning Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

Therefore the Lord, speaking figuratively to Cain as he offered gifts without right intention, says: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Gen. 4). [Col. 0378B] As Blessed Gregory says, [Note: [Col. 0377D] *Patherius on Genesis*, ch. 31.] an offering is made rightly when something is done with right intention; but it is not rightly divided if that which is devoutly done is not also subtly discerned. To divide offerings rightly is to weigh all our good endeavours by careful discernment. Whoever neglects to do this sins even while offering rightly. For often, even when we act with good purpose, if we negligently fail cautiously to discern the end by which it is to be judged, we do not know its end; so that sometimes what is thought a cause of virtue is a guilt of sin. We therefore offer rightly when we perform a good work with good purpose; but we do not divide rightly if we set aside discernment in good works.

[Col. 0378C] Therefore, O foolish and malicious Jews, you ought reasonably to discern what you should choose, what reject, what and how you should believe, what you should do, and what you should avoid. [Note: [Col. 0378D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 4.] Beyond doubt, the Lord figuratively commanded that this discernment of true faith and of all good works—which is indeed the standard of holiness and righteousness—be employed with the utmost diligence in his worship, when in the Old Testament he commanded salt to be offered in every sacrifice (Lev. 2). Thus salt is commanded to be mixed into every sacrifice, so that everything we offer in Christ’s honour may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.

Therefore, O Jews, believe without doubt that Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is true God and true man; love him with fear and fear him with love. [Col. 0378D] Keep his spiritual commandments not from sadness or necessity, but with all devotion and joy. Persevere day and night with cheerful mind in his holy praises, so that, living according to the rule of ecclesiastical religion, you may be deemed worthy to be called by the Christian name. That we ought to serve God not in sadness but in spiritual joy, the Psalmist openly teaches us, saying: “Make a joyful noise to the Lord, all the earth; serve the Lord in gladness” (Ps. 99).

“Jubilation,” that is, confession, as Master Peter says, “is twofold: one is confession of praise; the other, confession of sins. Confession of praise befits the perfect; confession of sins those beginning to serve God.
