[Col. 0379A] The Psalmist teaches us joyfully to praise God and to bewail our sins, because one must neither despair amid evils nor be elated in good things.

“Note that true jubilation is by voice and heart. Therefore let the heart understand inwardly and the voice jubilate outwardly. The sound of the heart is understanding. Jubilation is a sound of joy without words, which the very joy of the soul cannot express: when a man rejoicing in things that cannot be expressed in words bursts forth into a certain wordless cry of exultation, so that it appears that he rejoices in the very sound itself. This jubilation is made by the good in confession; it is not made by the evil in confession, when they rejoice so greatly in earthly things—for example, as reapers or vintagers delight in an abundance of fruits, rejoice in the fertility of the earth, sing, and among their songs insert certain wordless sounds in the modulation of an exulting mind. This jubilation is to be condemned. But the righteous rejoice, seeing with a pure heart who God is, and in what order and how wonderfully he made such great things; and therefore they sing in exultation. This is the exultation that is to be crowned.”

It follows: “Serve the Lord in gladness,” namely not from compulsion but from the love by which you have been set free through Christ. As though King David and prophet, counselling the Christian people, said more plainly: You who have been redeemed through Jesus Christ from your vain manner of life (1 Pet. 1), ought to serve the Lord not murmuring, as the Jews [Col. 0379C] murmured in the wilderness and perished by the destroyer (1 Cor. 10), but in gladness.

Hear also, O rebellious and unbelieving Jews, what is written concerning your fathers themselves in the book of Exodus. “They committed fornication in their inventions,” it says (Ps. 105), “and twenty-three thousand of them fell in one day” (Exod. 32). And again: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (ibid.). [Note: [Col. 0379D] Gregory, *Morals*, book 10, ch. 9, and *Patherius on Exodus*, ch. 52.] Eating and drinking impelled them to play; play drew them into idolatry. For when the fault of vanity is not cautiously restrained, the unwary mind is immediately devoured by iniquity. Solomon testifies: “He who does not despise small things will gradually fall” (Ecclus. 19). [Note: [Col. 0379D] Superfluous.] For when we neglect to beware of small things, imperceptibly deceived, we boldly commit greater ones also.

[Col. 0379D] Therefore, as we said above, O Jews, you ought not serve the Lord in sadness or anxiety of mind, but in gladness and exultation of spirit, offering him praise and thanksgiving with the utmost devotion for benefits bestowed. This service is not one of bitterness or indignation, but of happiness and freedom. For it ought to be pleasing to those redeemed that they are Christ’s servants. Therefore let love make you servants, O Jews; for if you truly receive the faith of Christ, truth itself—which is Christ—will make you free. Thus he says to his disciples, indeed generally to all who will believe in him: “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you shall truly be my disciples; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 15).

[Col. 0380A] God himself prefigured in the book of Leviticus that very spiritual joy, which is truly necessary and exceedingly pleasing to God for his servants, when he commanded oil to be offered to him in sacrifice (Lev. 2). [Note: [Col. 0380D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 5.] Thus the offering of oil in sacrifice signified that whatever we render for the worship of Christ and the honour of the saints, we should do wholly in spiritual cheerfulness; and, as the Apostle says, do nothing from sadness or necessity. For just as God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9), so also one who serves joyfully. Oil signifies cheerfulness, as it is written: “That he may make the face glad with oil, and bread strengthen the heart of man” (Ps. 103). What do you say, O Jews? What objection do you raise, or what answer do you make to these things?

§ XXVII.—

The Jews cannot excuse themselves from believing in Christ because the Christian faith confesses that he suffered, died, and was buried in a tomb, since he endured all these things not under compulsion but through voluntary obedience, and not according to the power of his divinity but according to the weakness of his flesh. Those who did these things also served the divine will; and from the very source from which they intended disgrace, glory and exaltation of Christ’s name came to him, as Gregory confirms by examples drawn from Holy Scripture. The Father delivered Christ out of love, Judas out of avarice, the Jews out of envy, and Christ delivered himself out of ineffable mercy. The Jews cannot understand this because they cling to the letter of the Law. He exhorts them to continual love of Christ, who is that fire always burning on the altar. He also answers them why, although the will of his Father is omnipotence, he nevertheless decreed to redeem the world through no one other than his Son, who was also prefigured in the four kinds of offering commanded in Leviticus.

I should like to know what will or purpose you hold: whether, having now put aside the treachery of your long-standing unbelief, you believe without doubt that Jesus Christ is true God and was sent from heaven by God the Father for the redemption of the world; or whether you still doubt in any respect concerning his divinity, coeternal with God the Father. This, O Jews, is your answer and objection. You say that you do not wish to believe Jesus Christ true God because, when your fathers accused him, the governor’s [Col. 0380D] soldiers were able to fasten him to the cross like another man, hand him over to death, and bury him in a tomb. You further add blasphemously that, if he were true God, he could by no means have been crucified, killed, and buried by men.

In response, we say conversely that Jesus Christ is indeed true God and man, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing and mercifully rescued the world from the devil’s power. That he was seized, bound, and fastened to the cross by the Jews, your fathers, and mercifully chose there to die not for his own guilt but for our offences, [Col. 0381A] he endured not from powerlessness but from the obedience which he rendered to God the Father. According to the weakness of the flesh assumed by him, he voluntarily underwent death for the redemption of humankind; but according to the divinity which he naturally has from God the Father, he lives forever. Insofar as he is man, he “drank from the torrent on the way” (Ps. 109), that is, he tasted death as if in passing; insofar as he is true God, he destroyed death.

He therefore did not suffer as though he could not be delivered from the hands of his persecutors, but, having power to lay down and take up his life, he chose of his own free will to die for his sheep. As the good shepherd he willingly gave his life for his sheep (John 10); as true God, on the third day he powerfully raised from the tomb his body, which he had assumed without sin from the Virgin. For it was a greater power and strength to rise from the tomb after death than to escape his persecutors’ hands before his passion. He who could raise his body from the tomb after death could certainly, before his passion, if he had wished, have escaped the plots of his persecutors so as not to be seized. He could therefore be seized, bound, crucified, and die according to his humanity; yet this was not because the Jewish people prevailed against him, but because he himself freely willed it in order to redeem the world. Thus the clearest and truest reasoning demonstrates that Christ suffered of his own free will for the redemption of humankind; and it proves that you, O Jews, who say that he underwent the passion unwillingly, have lied in your objection.

Hear, then, what I say, O unbelieving and perverting Jews, who do not enter the kingdom of heaven through right belief and who incessantly block, by wicked persuasions, the way of entry for others who might enter. Hear what I speak for your correction, compelled by love. The more zealously and earnestly you and your fathers ought to have received the faith and teaching of Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, the more you dishonoured him with insults and manifold injuries. And where you ought to have shown him greater reverence, there instead you tormented him and his disciples with reproaches, beatings, and diverse punishments, and attempted, if it were possible, to blot out his name [Col. 0381D] and memory from beneath heaven.

But you, O wretched and pitiable Jews—who are you, that you have attempted to oppose God’s eternal counsel? Who are you, O unhappy ones, that you presume with perverse mind and defiled mouth to deny the eternal benefit which God the Father decreed in his predestination to bestow upon humankind, and mercifully accomplished at the appointed time through his most beloved Son? Why, O wretched and pitiable Jews, do you stubbornly deny the redemption of humankind, which from the beginning of the world God made known through figures, disclosed through oracles, promised through things preceding, truly accomplished through Jesus Christ, his Son coeternal with himself, and has now openly displayed to the whole world through the preaching of the apostles and evangelists, as celebrated by that same Son of God and of the Virgin? Moreover, why do you blasphemously maintain that the very Son of God was a mere man?

Do you not know, O wretched ones, that the more stubbornly your fathers’ malice wished to erase Christ’s memory from the earth, the more his name and glory grew in the knowledge of the nations? While they obstinately resisted the divine dispensation, they undoubtedly served the divine will without knowing it.

But, O Jews, in order to make you more certain of these things which we say, let us bring forward the true history of Joseph. “Behold, the dreamer comes,” his brothers say; “come, let us kill him, and then it will appear what his dreams profit him” (Gen. 37). [Col. 0382B] Let us all hear together what Blessed Gregory says on this passage. [Note: [Col. 0381D] *Patherius on Genesis*, ch. 71.]

“Frequently, some persons puffed up with human wisdom, when they perceive that divine judgments oppose their desires, attempt to resist them by crafty schemes; and, in order to bend the force of the heavenly dispensation to their own wish, they persist in cunning thoughts and seek subtler plans. But by the very means through which they strive to change God’s will, they carry it out; and, while they endeavour to resist the counsel of almighty God, they serve it more fully. For often even that which frivolously resists God through human endeavour fittingly serves his dispensation, as it is written: ‘He takes the wise in their own craftiness’ (Job 5). He takes the wise in their craftiness [Col. 0382C] when human deeds then suitably serve his counsels precisely when they resist them. Hence it is also said through the Psalmist: ‘The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain’ (Ps. 93).

“We shall show this better if we bring forward a few examples from recorded events. Joseph, as stated above, had seen a dream: the sheaves of his brothers bowed down to his sheaf. He had seen a dream: the sun and moon, with eleven stars, worshipped him (Gen. 37). Because he related these dreams to his father and brothers, envy and fear of his future dominion immediately struck their hearts. When they saw him coming toward them, with malice raging they said: ‘Behold, the dreamer comes; come, let us kill him, and see what his dreams profit him.’ And, because they feared to be subjected to his rule, they put the dreamer into a pit and sold him to the passing Ishmaelites. Taken to Egypt, reduced to slavery, condemned on an accusation of lust, aided through the merit of chastity, and delivered by prophetic judgment, he was set over all Egypt. Through heavenly wisdom he prudently gathered grain and forestalled the danger of a future scarcity. When famine prevailed throughout the world, Jacob, concerned for provisions, sent his sons into Egypt. Not recognizing Joseph, set over the distribution of grain, they found him; and, in order to deserve to receive food, they were compelled to worship that same dispenser, Joseph, with their necks bowed to the ground.

“Let us therefore consider the sequence of this event; let us consider [Col. 0383A] how the divine power catches human thoughts in their very contrivance. Joseph had been sold so that he might not be worshipped; but then he was worshipped because he had been sold by his brothers. They boldly attempted to act craftily so that God’s counsel might be changed; but, by the divine judgment, in resisting they served that which they had attempted to evade. They attempted to fulfil God’s will by the very means through which they had attempted craftily to alter it. Thus, when the divine counsel is avoided, it is fulfilled; thus, when human wisdom resists, it is caught. The brothers feared that Joseph might rise above them; but their effort to avoid what had been divinely ordained caused it to happen. Human wisdom condemned itself: by the very intention through which it resisted God’s will, it became entangled in its service.

“Thus Saul, when he saw David, his subject, daily growing through success after success in valour, promised him his daughter in marriage and required from him one hundred Philistine foreskins as her dowry, so that, when the provoked soldier sought to exert himself beyond his strength, he might be handed over to his enemies’ swords and lose his life. As it is written: ‘The king has no need of a bride-price except one hundred Philistine foreskins, so that vengeance may be taken on the king’s enemies.’ Now Saul thought to hand David over into the hands of the Philistines (1 Sam. 18). But David, strengthened by the favour of the inward dispensation, declared that he would give a hundred and brought back two hundred. Thus, overcome by the evidence of this deed, [Col. 0383C] through the ordaining of heavenly Providence Saul was caught in the counsel of his own foolishness, because the very means by which he thought to extinguish the life of the rising soldier increased all the more the glory of his valour.

“But because even the elect sometimes endeavour craftily to devise something, let us bring forward another wise man, and demonstrate that mortal cunning is truly caught in the fold of the inward counsel. Jonah thought himself prudent when, sent to preach repentance to the Ninevites, he feared that Judaea would be abandoned in favour of the elect nations. He therefore refused to fulfil the office of preaching, sought a ship, and chose to flee to Tarshish. But at once a storm arose, and lots were cast so that it might be known by whose fault the seas were disturbed. Jonah was then found guilty, plunged into the depths of the sea, and swallowed by a devouring sea-creature; and the creature carrying him brought him to the place where he had scorned to go of his own accord (Jonah 1). Behold: the storm finds God’s fugitive, the lot binds him, the sea receives him, the creature encloses him; and because he refuses to obey the voice of his Creator, guilty as he is, he is carried in his own prison to the place to which he had been sent. At God’s command the man refused to minister prophecy; at God’s prompting the creature vomited out the prophet. Thus God bends human prudence, as stated above, to his own service, when he brings into the use of his will even that through which the human will opposes him.

[Col. 0384A] “Let us further examine, if you please, the wisdom of the Hebrews, so that we may see what it sought to prevent by forethought and what it provoked by preventing. Certainly, when a crowd of believers flocked to the miracles of our Redeemer, and priests and people, inflamed with the fires of envy, cried out that the world was going after him, [Note: [Col. 0383D] Supply: ‘were crying out’.] they attempted to end his power by death, in order to cut off from him the force of so great a concourse, saying: ‘It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish’ (John 11). But the death of our Redeemer availed for the binding together of his body, namely the Church, not for its division. Therefore he brought even this hostility, by which human cruelty burned against him, into the service and operation of his mercy.

“For he, righteous and merciful, disposing human acts, graciously grants some things and angrily permits others; and he so endures those things which he permits that he turns them to the use of his own counsel. Thus it happens in a wonderful way that what is done without God’s will is not contrary to God’s will, because, when evil deeds are turned to good use, those things which resist his counsel serve his counsel. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: ‘Great are the works of the Lord, sought out in all his wills’ (Ps. 110). His works are great in this way: through everything done by human beings, his will is accomplished. For something is often achieved by the very means through which it is thought to be repelled. Again he says: ‘All things whatsoever the Lord willed, he has done in heaven and on earth’ (Ps. 134). Solomon says: ‘There is no wisdom, no prudence, [Col. 0384C] no counsel against God’ (Prov. 22). It remains, therefore, that in all we do we should seek the force of the heavenly will. Once known, our action ought devoutly to serve it and follow it as the guide of its journey, lest, in proudly turning aside from it, one serve it unwillingly. The force of the heavenly counsel can by no means be avoided; but he controls it with great strength who restrains himself beneath its nods, and he lightens its burdens for himself who willingly bears them on the shoulder of a subject heart.”

Therefore, as stated above, O Jews, enemies of truth: the more diligently your fathers wished, by crucifying Christ, to resist God’s eternal counsel, the more perfectly they fulfilled it without knowing, while persisting in their malice. God the Father, because of the exceeding love with which he loved us, delivered up his Son so that through the passion and cross he might redeem us from the enemy’s power. Hence Blessed John the Evangelist says: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3). The Son of God also gave himself for us, to redeem us from all iniquity (Titus 2), so that we might receive adoption as sons (Gal. 4). Of him the Apostle says: “Christ gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour” (Eph. 5). But Judas Iscariot, full of deceit and malice and inflamed by the fires of avarice, delivered [Col. 0385A] him to the Jews. The Jews, blinded by the darkness of envy and hatred, delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor to be crucified.

But it should be noted that God the Father delivered his most beloved Son because of his great love; the Son himself, compelled by love and overcome by ineffable mercy, gave himself up in order to free us from the devil’s power and cleanse us from the filth of sins by the blood of his passion: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). Ineffable mercy also moved him to descend from the bosom of God the Father, unite human nature to himself, undergo the passion, ascend the cross not for his own sins but for the sins of humankind, lay down his most beloved and most holy soul, descend to the gates of hell, recall to ever-green pastures his own who were held captive there, rise on the third day from the tomb in that same flesh which he had assumed without sin from the Virgin, confirm his disciples in faith, sow through them the seeds of God’s word in rational soil—that is, in the hearts of all nations—and on the fortieth day after the resurrection ascend, crowned with glory and honour, to the Father from whom he had come forth.

A certain wise man, greatly marvelling and rejoicing exceedingly, says of him [Note: [Col. 0385D] From the hymn at Vespers for the Ascension]:

> What mercy conquered you,  
> That you should bear our crimes,  
> Suffering cruel death  
> To raise us from death?  
>
> Penetrating hell’s gates,  
> Redeeming your captives,  
> Victor in noble triumph,  
> Seated at the Father’s right hand.

Perfect love, therefore, impelled Christ; supreme mercy overcame him so that he might redeem us. Avarice deceived Judas’s heart so that he might betray the very Son of God and of the Virgin to the Jews; and the cloud of envy and malice blinded the eyes of the priests, scribes, and Pharisees, who delivered Christ to Pontius Pilate to be crucified. Therefore Christ did not, as you Jews falsely claim, come unwillingly to the passion in order to redeem the world; rather, of his own free will [Col. 0385D] he gave himself into the hands of the wicked.

Still persisting in the malice of your unbelief, O Jews, you answer us and say that whether Jesus Christ came willingly or unwillingly to his passion, you nevertheless maintain that he was by no means true God but a mere man. To this we answer in return that Jesus Christ is indeed true man and true God; but you do not believe him to be true God because the covering of Joseph’s cloak darkens the eyes of your mind. Therefore you will in no way be able spiritually to understand those things written concerning Christ in the Old Testament unless you endeavour, as stated, to remove Joseph’s cloak from the eyes of your heart by the hand of discernment.

Note that the patriarch Joseph, a man indeed innocent and righteous, bore in his deeds the figure of Jesus Christ, God and man. The adulterous woman, however, in whose hands he left his cloak when he fled outside, represented the Synagogue, which believes Christ to be not true God but merely man. Fittingly, indeed, the Synagogue in the Old Testament bore the figure of an adulterous woman: it did not keep faith with almighty God, but repeatedly committed fornication with foreign gods. Therefore, just as that adulterous woman wished Joseph to join himself to her in adulterous love, so the Synagogue wished to hold Christ fast in the adultery of its crime, so that he might deny that he was God; and to observe spiritually the traditions of the Pharisees [Col. 0386B] and Scribes rather than the commandments of the Law, though he himself was as her husband. But he, in no way yielding to the adultery of unlawful teaching, seized by the hand of the adulterous Synagogue through the garment of his body, stripped himself of the flesh and, free from death, ascended into heaven. Jesus Christ, God and man, kept the ten commandments of the Law spiritually; but the Synagogue, observing the Law carnally, cried out that he was a transgressor of the Law. The Son of God and of the Virgin expounded the Law and the Prophets spiritually; but the Synagogue said that he taught things contrary to the Law and the Prophets. What more need be said? [Note: [Col. 0386D] *Pather.*, as above, ch. 73.] Therefore, when the adulterous woman wished to misuse Joseph, Joseph fled outside, leaving his cloak behind; because, when the Synagogue [Col. 0386C], believing the Lord Jesus Christ to be merely man, wished to bind him as it were in an adulterous embrace, he left before its eyes only the covering of the letter, and showed himself openly to the Gentiles for the knowledge of the power of his divinity. Hence the apostle Paul says: “To this day a veil lies over the heart of the Jews” (2 Cor. 3). That adulterous woman retained the cloak with herself, because, after Christ suffered on the cross, rose from the dead on the third day, and was exalted at the right hand of God the Father, the adulterous woman—that is, the Synagogue—retained with herself its ignorance of the Law and the Prophets; for it strove to understand all the books of the Old Testament not spiritually, but only according to the letter. Therefore, because the Synagogue wished unlawfully to hold Christ [Col. 0386D]—that is, it tried to subject him to the carnal institutions of the Old Testament—it lost him naked, like a harlot: the one whom it held wrongly and believed to be not true God but merely man.

Hear what I say, O Jews; hear what I speak; listen to what, compelled by charity, I urge. If you desire to escape eternal damnation and attain the joys of eternal life, believe without hesitation that Jesus Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God. Receive the New Testament; strive to understand the sacred pages of the Old Testament not carnally but spiritually, and to fulfill them in deed. Thus, renewed by holy baptism and enlightened by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0387A], you may be faithfully joined to that same Jesus Christ, who is truly the head of all believers, and united to the company of his elect. For unless you firmly believe Christ to be true God and true man, you will in no way be able to drive the darkness of unbelief from your hearts.

Therefore believe that he is truly the Redeemer of the world; fear him as the most righteous Judge who will come at the end of the world; love him, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, in all things and above all things; and put your complete trust in your ability through him to attain the salvation of our souls. If you believe him to be true God and love him perfectly, I believe that you will willingly keep his commandments. Keep Christ’s love continually in your hearts [Col. 0387B], and, if you truly love him, show this by good works. May his love always burn in your hearts, and may the effect of that same love shine forth in your actions.

Beyond doubt, the Lord signified that this perfect observance of divine love must be effectually maintained when he spoke figuratively to Moses in Leviticus: “Fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it by placing wood upon the altar every morning, day by day; and, after the burnt offering has been laid upon it, he shall burn over it the fat of the peace offerings. This fire is perpetual; it shall never fail from the altar” (Lev. 6). “The altar of God is our heart,” says blessed Gregory [Note: [Col. 0387D] *Pather.*, on Leviticus, ch. 5], “upon which fire is commanded always to burn, because the flame of charity must continually and unceasingly [Col. 0387C] rise from it to the Lord. Each day the priest must lay wood upon it, lest it be extinguished. Every preacher of Christ is certainly called a member of the high priest, as the apostle Peter says to all the faithful: ‘But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood’ (1 Pet. 2). And as it is said in the Apocalypse to that same high priest: ‘You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God’ (Rev. 5), and so forth. Therefore the priest, feeding the fire on the altar, must lay wood upon it daily; that is, lest the flame of charity fail within him, every believer must not cease to gather in his heart both the examples of the Fathers who went before and the testimonies of Holy Scripture. For to provide, as it were, fuel for the fire is, in the exercise of charity, to minister to peoples either the examples of the Fathers [Col. 0387D] or the commandments of the Lord. Since our inward newness itself grows old every day through the course of this life, this fire must be fed with wood, so that, while it is diminished through the habit of our oldness, it may revive through the testimonies and examples of the Fathers. And it is well commanded that wood be gathered every day in the morning; or certainly because morning is the first part of the day, each of the faithful, setting aside thoughts of the present life, should make this his first concern: by what efforts he may kindle the zeal of charity which now seems, as it were, to be failing within him. For this fire upon the altar of the Lord—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is restored by diligently applied [Col. 0388A] examples of the Fathers and testimonies of the Lord. It is also well added there: ‘After the burnt offering has been laid upon it, he shall burn over it the fat of the peace offerings’ (Lev. 6). For whoever kindles within himself this fire of charity places burnt offerings upon himself; because he burns away every vice by which he had been living wrongly. When he considers the inward movements of his thoughts and slays his reprobate life with the sword of imitation, he places himself upon the altar of his own heart and burns himself with the fire of charity. The fat of the peace offering gives forth fragrance from this sacrifice, because the inward richness of the new life, making peace between us and God, renders to God from us a most sweet odour. But because this same charity remains unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is fittingly added there: ‘This fire is perpetual; it shall never fail [Col. 0388B] from the altar’ (ibid.). Truly this fire never fails from the altar, because even after this life the fervour of charity increases in their minds. For eternal contemplation brings it about that almighty God, the more he is seen, is loved the more abundantly.”

Therefore, O Jews, love with your whole heart Jesus Christ, God and man; receive his baptism with devout minds; hasten faithfully to enter his holy Church through him, so that you may deserve not to perish with unbelievers but to enjoy eternal joys with his elect. What do you say, O Jews? What do you answer, or what objection do you raise? Now surely, having laid aside the error of unbelief, you ought to believe with us without hesitation that Jesus Christ is true God and true man; that he redeemed the world by his precious blood; that he rose from the dead on the third day; that he ascended into heaven [Col. 0388C] as his disciples watched; and that he sits at the right hand of God the Father. Yet we wish to know of what will or faith you are, and what your answer is. This is your answer, O Jews: you say that you greatly wish to know by what necessity God the Father was compelled—he who does whatever he wills, whose will is omnipotence—to send his most beloved and coeternal Son, as we Christians affirm, from heaven, hand him over to the hands of the wicked, and will him to suffer, be crucified, and die, when by a word alone he can immediately accomplish whatever he wills in heaven and on earth (Ps. 134).

Wishing to answer this question of yours, O [Col. 0388D] Jews, we reply to you as follows: almighty God indeed does whatever he wills in heaven and on earth; and his will, as you say, is omnipotence. Yet through his Son—that is, through his Word, coeternal with himself, through whom he created all things from nothing and formed the first man, saying, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1)—through that same Word he willed to redeem the man whom he had made. For he decreed not to redeem him through an angel or an archangel, but through his Son coeternal with himself, through whom he created all things. [Note: [Col. 0388D] *Pather.*, on Genesis, ch. 7.] And although God the Father created all things through that same Son coeternal with himself, nevertheless in the very account of creation it is shown how greatly man is preferred above all animals and above earthly or heavenly things, though these are without sense. For God spoke all things, and they were made (Ps. 32). But when he decreed to make man, he first said—something that must be reverently considered—“Let us make man in our image and likeness.” For it is not written of man, as of the other things, “Let it be made,” and it was made; nor did the earth bring forth man as water produced flying creatures. Rather, before he was made, “Let us make” is said, so that, because a rational creature was being created, he might seem to have been made as though with deliberation. As though by careful work he is formed from the earth and, by the Creator’s breath, raised to the power of a living spirit [Col. 0389B], so that he might exist not through the utterance of a command but through the dignity of an operation, since he was being made in the image of the Creator. This, therefore, O Jews, was the reason, as stated above, why God the Father sent his only-begotten Son from heaven: namely, because he willed through him to redeem the man whom he had formed in his image and likeness.

Still persisting in your malice, O Jews, you object to us, saying that you can in no way believe Christ to be true God or assent to our admonitions unless we show him to have been clearly prefigured in the Old Testament. To this we answer you, O Jews, as follows: Jesus Christ, God and man, was indeed long before the time of the Law foreshadowed in the figures and enigmas [Col. 0389C] of the patriarchs; foretold by the oracles of the prophets; present among men at the time of his coming; and after his passion and cross, by the proclamations of the apostles and evangelists, was openly preached throughout the whole world as one who had already come and redeemed the world. Yet, to convict your unbelief completely and to strengthen the Catholic faith more and more, O Jews, enemies of truth, we urge you to listen carefully as we show how clearly he was prefigured in the four kinds of principal offerings.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 6.] At the beginning of the book of Leviticus four principal kinds of offerings are described, which appeared to be offered to the Lord as a sweet odour: first, [Col. 0389D] an unblemished calf from the herd; second, a lamb from the sheep; third, a turtledove and a dove; fourth, fine flour kneaded, unleavened, anointed with oil, baked in an oven. The remaining sacrifices, however, were offered on behalf of the people according to the nature of their cases. The first sacrifice, then—the calf from the herd—prefigured Christ descending from the lineage of the patriarchs. Beyond doubt, with the plough of his cross he subdued the earth of our body and enriched it with the crop of the seed of the Holy Spirit. This calf, namely Christ, is without sin, because he was conceived without a man’s embrace, born without defilement, and crucified without guilt. The calf is offered not in [Col. 0390A] the tabernacle, but at its door, because Christ was crucified outside the camp (Heb. 13). His blood is offered through the sons of Aaron the priest; this is understood of Annas and Caiaphas, who, having formed a council, shed Christ’s blood by the hands of soldiers.

The second victim is a lamb offered from the sheep, that is, Christ, who is represented in the lamb because of his innocence. This is the lamb who is led to sacrifice through Isaiah and pointed out to men by John. Of him the prophet Isaiah says: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent, and thus he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). John the Baptist also showed this most gentle lamb to men, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). [Col. 0390B] The lamb is rightly offered in sacrifice, so that the figure of Christ’s innocence and passion may be shown. A goat is also rightly offered, because through Christ’s death sin was destroyed and the devil, the author of sin, was defeated.

The third sacrifice is the turtledove and the dove. The turtledove signifies the supreme and perfect chastity of Christ’s body. The dove, however, is shown to bear the figure of the Holy Spirit, as the Lord says to blessed John the Baptist: “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And John says: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him” (ibid.), that is, upon Christ. Therefore the turtledove and dove—that is, Christ’s flesh joined to the Holy Spirit—are offered to God the Father through the mystery [Col. 0390C] of the passion as a sacrifice of sweet odour. Christ Jesus offers these three sacrifices according to his humanity.

The Church, however, offers the fourth sacrifice, of fine flour; [Note: [Col. 0390D] Supply here again: “fine flour.”] it signifies the figure of that same holy Catholic Church, which is gathered from harmonious members, like fine flour from the many grains of believers; renewed by the mill of the Law and Gospels in letter and spirit; united through the water of baptism; anointed with the oil of chrism; made firm by the fire of the Holy Spirit; and made a sacrifice pleasing to God through humility of spirit.

Thus Christ, O Jews, enemies of truth, was prefigured in the calf because of his passion; in the lamb because of his innocence; and in the turtledove and dove because of his [Col. 0390D] incomparable chastity and simplicity of life. His bride too, namely the holy Church, was prefigured in fine flour; she is joined to him by the bond of charity and, like limbs to a head, united by the cement of spiritual love. By these and similar most true figures of the Old Testament, therefore, O Jews, the Christian faith is strengthened and your false assertion is plainly disproved. Believe, then, that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and receive his baptism with devout minds, so that through right belief and good works you may attain the fellowship of his elect.

## § XXVIII.—

The Jews are the Synagogue of Satan and children of the devil, not of Abraham and the patriarchs, whom they do not imitate. They are exhorted to acknowledge their fault humbly and not follow Adam, who hid himself after he sinned. They are also exhorted to baptism and to wash away with tears the stain of past unbelief; diligently seeking true teaching from the apostles and evangelists, they should strive to advance through it, and offer spiritual sacrifices to God, as their fathers offered carnal ones. They are also exhorted to flee pride and self-exaltation, which cast down angels. Whoever through ignorance or negligence fails to fulfill a vow he has made will obtain pardon through true contrition of heart, since legal sacrifices are no longer pleasing to God. Christ was not separated from the Church by death, but rather united her to himself. As a sign of this, the Law commands that the sacrifice of a dove be offered in such a way that its head remains attached to its neck. Jews must beware lest the devil deceive them under an appearance of good.

[Col. 0391B] Still persisting in the malice of unbelief, O Jews, “to excuse excuses in sins” (Ps. 140), you again say in consequence that you are unwilling either to believe Christ to be true God or to receive the New Testament, but that you have determined to remain in Judaism, as all your fathers did. As though defending and excusing the fault of your unbelief, you boast that you are the fortunate descendants of patriarchs, prophets, and holy men; and you say that for this reason you do not wish to embrace another, new religion which they did not know.

In answer, O Jews, hard and slow of heart to believe, we say to you that each person is called the son of the one whose teaching he follows; just as the Lord says through the prophet that Israel has an Amorite father and a Hittite mother, not by birth but by imitation (Ezek. 16). So also, in a better sense, those who keep God’s commandments are called sons of God. Hence we too cry to God in prayer, not by nature but by imitation: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6). We know, therefore, that people are called someone’s sons not only by birth but also by imitation. For you, O Jews, are sons of Abraham according to the flesh, but according to your manner of life you are called sons of the devil. For Jesus Christ himself, God and man, when he saw your fathers to be incorrigible and perceived them persisting in their malice, said to them: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John 8). Thus they were sons of Abraham [Col. 0391D] because of their fleshly origin, but they were not sons of Abraham because of the vice of diabolical persuasion. They were of the father, the devil, because by imitating the devil they had become children of the devil. Let us all together hear, O Jews, what Jesus Christ also said of you among other things, speaking in the Apocalypse through his angel to his servant John for the consolation of his sevenfold Church.

“These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and your poverty, but you are rich; and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the Synagogue of Satan” (Rev. 2). As though he said: O my faithful ones, do not fail in tribulations, because I am the first alone [Col. 0392A], existing before all things and he through whom all things subsist; and the last, through whom all things shall be brought to completion. For you I suffered death, from which I rose; and you too must await and suffer it for me. I was dead for you, through whom you shall live, because I live. John describes Christ as one able to deliver from tribulations those who are troubled for his name.

I urge you, O Jews, patiently to hear what Jesus Christ himself, God and man, says for the consolation of his Church, so that, abandoning the folly of unbelief, you may believe with us without hesitation that he is true God. “I know,” he says, “your tribulation,” because “blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5); “and your poverty,” because “blessed are the poor in spirit” [Col. 0392B] (ibid.); “but you are rich” in the hope of reward; “and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews,” that is, confessing themselves to be such, “and are not,” because if they were children of Abraham, they would do the works of Abraham (John 8); “but are the Synagogue of Satan,” that is, the assembly of the adversary.

Hear, O faithless Jews, what I say; hear what I speak. Beyond doubt, O wretched ones, you are deceived in boasting that you are Abraham’s children while you do not do Abraham’s works or hold his faith. For you say in vain that you are children of the saints, since you do not preserve their faith by good conduct but merely pretend in words to preserve it. Therefore, in saying that you are children of the saints and for that reason refusing to receive the rule of the New Testament, which they did not know [Col. 0392C], you offer an excuse so as not to receive the norm of the Catholic faith and believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man. Your glorying in the nobility of Abraham’s lineage pertains to self-exaltation; but your determination to observe the Law not spiritually but carnally, as your fathers observed it, pertains to the excuse of unbelief.

I do not want you to be ignorant, O Jews, that when Adam in paradise ate the fruit of the forbidden tree through disobedience, he sinned gravely; but he sinned far more grievously when, in the audacity of his mind, he wished to excuse himself, saying: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave me from the tree, and I ate” (Gen. 3). “Sin is committed in the heart in four ways,” says blessed [Col. 0392D] Gregory [Note: [Col. 0391D] *Pather.*, on Genesis, ch. 22], “and is consummated in deed in four ways. In the heart, it is committed through suggestion, delight, consent, and the audacity of delight. Suggestion comes through the adversary; delight through the flesh; consent through the soul; the audacity of defense or excuse through self-exaltation. For the fault which ought to terrify the mind instead exalts it, and, though it raises it by casting it down, more grievously trips it up by raising it. Thus the ancient enemy broke the uprightness of that first man by these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve delighted; Adam consented; and, when questioned, he would not confess his fault because of audacity.

“What was done in the first parent [Col. 0393A] of our race is known to occur daily in the human race. The serpent suggested, because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evils to human hearts. Eve delighted, because the carnal senses immediately submit themselves to delight at the words of the serpent—that is, of the suggesting devil. Adam, set over the woman, gave his own assent to her, because when the flesh is drawn into delight, the weakened spirit also inclines away from its uprightness. And Adam, when questioned, would not confess his fault, because the spirit, in the very measure in which by sinning it is separated from truth, is hardened in the audacity of its ruin. Adam had fled in swelling pride, intending to hide himself, yet, when questioned, he showed how proudly he swelled in fear. For when the present punishment resulting from sin is feared and the lost face of God is not loved, the fear arises from pride, not [Col. 0393B] from humility. For one is proud who would not abandon sin if he were permitted not to be punished for it.

“Sin is also consummated in deed in the same four ways. First, the hidden fault is committed; afterward the guilt is openly displayed even before human eyes without shame; then it is led into habit; and finally it is nourished either by the seductions of false hope or by the obstinacy of miserable despair.”

At this point I urge you for your salvation, O Jews, humbly to recognize the most grave fault of your unbelief, and no longer presume to defend it through the exaltation of your heart. Instead, strive as quickly as possible to obtain from almighty God pardon for it through true repentance and contrition of heart, lest, suddenly overtaken [Col. 0393C] by the day of death, you perish with unbelievers for excusing or defending so deadly a sin.

The marks of true humility, as blessed Gregory says, are that each person should recognize his own iniquity and disclose what he has recognized in a verbal confession. On the contrary, it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling, to defend what has been committed by denying it, and to multiply what has been proved against one by defending it. We derive these increases of wickedness from that fall of the first man, from which we drew the very root of fault. For after he had touched the forbidden tree, he hid himself from the face of the Lord among the trees of paradise. In this hiding—since he could not be hidden from God—the effect of hiding is not described, but the intention is noted. When the Lord rebuked him [Col. 0393D] for having tasted the forbidden tree, he immediately answered: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion, she gave me from the tree, and I ate.” The woman herself, questioned in turn, answered: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid.). They had been questioned by the Lord so that they might erase by confession the sin which they had committed by transgression. Therefore that serpent, the persuader, who was not to be called back to pardon, was not questioned about his fault.

Thus man is asked where he is, so that he may look upon the fault he committed and recognize in confession how far he has departed from the face of his Creator. But both chose rather to apply to themselves the consolations of defense than the remedies of confession. And, while the man wished to excuse his sin through the woman and the woman through the serpent, they increased the fault [Col. 0394A] which they tried to protect: Adam indirectly implicating the Lord, as though he who made the woman were the author of their sin; Eve referring the fault to the Lord, who had placed the serpent in paradise. Since they had heard the words of the deceiving devil, “You shall be like gods,” and could not become like God in divinity, they sought, to complete the measure of their error, to make God like themselves in guilt. Thus, while they attempted to defend their guilt, they added to it, so that their fault, when examined, became more heinous than it had been when committed.

Therefore even now the branches of the human race draw bitterness from this same root. And when anyone is rebuked for his vice, under the shadow of defenses he hides himself as though under certain leaves of trees; and he wishes to flee the face [Col. 0394B] of his Creator into certain secret places of his excuse, because he does not wish what he does to be known. Yet in this concealment he does not hide himself from the Lord but hides the Lord from himself. For he acts so that he may not see the One who sees all things, not so that he himself may not be seen. On the contrary, for every sinner the beginning of illumination is now the humility of confession, by which a person refuses to spare himself when he is not ashamed to confess the evil he has done; and what he could excuse by defending it, he most swiftly ceases to defend by accusing himself.

Thus, when Lazarus was dead and weighed down by a great stone, it is not said to him, “Come to life,” but “Come forth” (John 11). By that resurrection, which took place in his body, is signified the way in which we are raised again in heart. To that dead man [Col. 0394C] it is said, “Come forth,” so that a person dead in sin and now buried under the weight of evil habit, because he lies concealed within his own conscience through wickedness, may come out from himself through confession. For the dead man is told, “Come forth,” in order that he may be called out from the excuse and concealment of sin to accuse himself with his own mouth. Thus the prophet David, coming back to life from the death of so great a crime, came forth, as it were, at the Lord’s voice when, rebuked by Nathan, he accused what he had done (2 Sam. 12).

Therefore, O Jews, hold to the example of this holy patriarch David; strive to imitate the devout confession of this king; hasten to make the humble repentance of this holy prophet for your past unbelief [Col. 0394D], so that you may not perish through the fault of unbelief but may attain with believing peoples the happiness of the heavenly homeland. Do not, then, continue to excuse the fault of your long-standing unbelief by exaltation of mind. Do not henceforth presume to defend the sin of most obstinate hardness by the swelling of your heart. Do not any longer wish to resort to the weapons of cunning disputation. Do not seek to hide yourselves under the covering of malice and wickedness. Almighty God hates the deeds of sinners and willingly receives the repentance of those who turn back. He reproves the life of the wicked and mercifully waits for them to come to their senses.

Beyond doubt, almighty God himself, merciful [Col. 0395A] and compassionate, signified this when, walking in paradise in the breeze after midday, he sought Adam after the fault of his transgression, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3). What must be observed here? [Note: [Col. 0395D] *Pather.*, ch. 21.] Did divine power not know to what hiding places Adam had fled after his fault—Adam whom it had formed from the clay of the earth only a little before? But because God saw him fallen into fault, now hidden under sin as though from the eyes of truth; because he does not approve the darkness of his error, he acts as though he does not know where the sinner is, and calls and seeks him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” In calling him, he gives a sign that he calls the elect back to repentance. In seeking him, however, he openly intimates that he regards sinners as though he does not know them, since they are justly to be condemned.

[Col. 0395B] Therefore, O Jews, repent humbly of your past unbelief, and do not flee to the hiding place of your defense. Now lay aside the weapons of your cunning disputation, humbly recognize the fault of unbelief, and hasten to wash it away with tears, so that through true repentance and contrition of heart you may receive remission of all sins. Diligently keep also Christ’s spiritual commandments; receive his baptism with devout minds; wash away without ceasing the stains of sins with tears, so that you may faithfully and worthily enter with us through the gate of the holy Church.

Beyond doubt, Moses also prefigured in the holy Church this observance of Christ’s commandments [Note: [Col. 0395D] Supply: “and remission.”] and the remission of sins necessary through the washing of tears, when at the Lord’s command he made in the tabernacle a bronze basin in which priests might wash, from the mirrors of women. Thus Moses made a bronze basin with its base from the mirrors of women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle (Exod. 38). Let blessed Gregory—a man indeed most useful and necessary in Christ’s Church—come forward and explain to us what the bronze basin made from the mirrors of women signifies. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Pather.*, on Exodus, ch. 62.] “Moses,” he says, “sets up a bronze basin in which priests must wash and enter the Holy of Holies, because the Law of God first commands us to be washed through compunction, so that our impurity may not be unworthy to enter the purity of God’s holy places. It aptly declares that the basin was made from the mirrors [Col. 0395D] of women who keep continual watch at the door of the tabernacle. The mirrors of women are the commandments of God, in which holy souls always look at themselves; and if they discover any stains of ugliness in themselves, they correct the vices of their thoughts and, as it were, arrange their countenances by the image returned to them. For while they diligently attend to the Lord’s commandments, they undoubtedly recognize in them both what pleases the heavenly bridegroom in themselves and what displeases him. While they remain in this life, they cannot enter the eternal tabernacle. Yet women keep watch at the door of the tabernacle [Col. 0396A], because holy souls, even while still burdened by the weakness of the flesh, nevertheless continually await with love the entrance into eternal entry.

“Thus Moses made a basin for the priests from the mirrors of women, because the Law of God provides the washing of compunction for our sins, through which holy souls have pleased the heavenly bridegroom. It offers us heavenly commandments to behold; if we attend diligently to them, we see the stains of our inward image. Seeing these stains, we are pierced with the pain of repentance; and when pierced, we are washed, as it were, in the basin made from the mirrors of women. Then we are truly pierced with compunction concerning ourselves when we earnestly consider the deeds of the Fathers who went before, so that, seeing their glory, our own life may become foul in our own eyes. Then we are truly pierced with compunction [Col. 0396B] when we diligently search the commandments of God, so that we may strive to advance by those very means through which we know those whom we revere have already advanced.”

Therefore repent, O Jews, that until now you have denied Christ; truly repent of the exceedingly grave fault of your unbelief, lest, remaining longer in the hardness of unbelief—God forbid—you should perish with your unbelieving fathers. Diligently seek from ecclesiastical men the commandments of Jesus Christ, God and man, and take care to fulfill them more earnestly in deed; for by these you know without hesitation that the fathers who went before—the apostles and evangelists, martyrs and confessors, and the other teachers of the holy Church—have advanced. [Col. 0396C] For if you keep without deceit the commandments of that same high priest, Jesus Christ, and follow with unoffending foot the footsteps of those same teachers of the holy Church, aided by their prayers you will be able to attain their fellowship. Therefore keep their deeds continually before your eyes, so that, recognizing their righteousness and holiness, you may gladly receive Christ’s baptism through their most sacred ministry and hasten to entrust yourselves with devout minds to their guidance; thus, renewed by the water of sacred baptism and the grace of the Holy Spirit, you may happily be united to their most holy company along with the other children of the Church. Repent, then, that until this day you have lived in the filth of your sins; that with an obstinate mind you have denied Christ; that with sacrilegious spirit and polluted [Col. 0396D] mouth you have blasphemed him; that you have irreverently disparaged the ministers of the holy Church; that with proud mind you have rejected the New Testament; and that you have repeatedly insulted with insolent words that same Jesus Christ, who firmly instituted it and commanded that it be kept and most diligently preserved by his holy Church. And while in the present age you are still granted time for living, change your life and conduct for the better; wash away the stains of sins with tears, so that, first renewed by sacred baptism and then exercised in good works, you may deserve to receive pardon for all offenses.

[Col. 0397A] Hear, O faithless Jews, what I say; hear what I speak; listen to the admonitions which I offer for your salvation. The sacrifices which your fathers offered carnally in the Old Testament, you, having first received the grace of baptism, should strive to offer spiritually in the New, for the expulsion of vices and the acquisition of virtues. They offered oxen and sheep; but place upon the altar of your heart the strictness of perfect religion and the innocence of devout conduct. They sacrificed calves and rams; offer instead the discernment of good works. They offered doves and turtledoves; sacrifice to God pure prayers and tears of true compunction. Therefore, as has been said above, O Jews, your fathers offered carnal sacrifices; but you must offer spiritual ones for the forgiveness of your sins.

[Col. 0397B] Meanwhile, let us hear in what order the Lord commanded a sacrifice to be immolated in Leviticus: “The man who offers a victim shall offer it at the entrance of the tabernacle, and shall place his hands upon the victim’s head; and the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer its blood, pouring it around the altar which is before the entrance of the tabernacle. And, its skin having been stripped off, they shall cut its limbs into pieces, lay fire upon the altar with a pile of wood first arranged, and place the severed members above it, namely the head and all that clings to the liver, the entrails and the feet having been washed with water” (Lev. 1).

“The skin of the victim,” says blessed Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0397D] *Patherius*, on Leviticus, chap. 1.], “we strip away when we remove from the eyes of our mind the outward surface of virtue; we cut its limbs into pieces when, making subtle distinctions, we consider its inward parts member by member. Yet amid these matters it must be known that we are sometimes afflicted by the prompting of an unlawful thought because, in certain actions of earthly life, although unlawful, we willingly occupy ourselves. And when even in the smallest things earthly action is touched by desire, as the strength of the ancient enemy increases against us, our mind is assailed by no small importunity of temptation. Hence the limbs of the victim, cut into pieces, together with the head and everything around the liver, are commanded to be burned by fire.

“To wash first the feet and entrails of the victim with water [Note: [Col. 0397D] Add here: ‘But first wash the feet and entrails of the victim with water.’] is for us to offer ourselves as a sacrifice to God, when we dedicate our life to divine worship. We place the limbs of the victim, cut into pieces, upon the fire when, distinguishing the works of our life by virtues, we sacrifice them. We burn the head and the things close to the liver when, in that faculty of our mind by which the whole body is governed, and in our hidden desires, we burn with the flame of divine love. Yet it is commanded that the feet and entrails of the victim be washed. For the earth is touched by the feet, while filth is carried in the entrails; because often we are already kindled by a longing for eternity, already with the whole disposition of devotion we yearn for the desire of our mortification. But because, through weakness, we still sometimes act in earthly ways, we endure in our heart certain unlawful things which we have already subdued. And when unclean temptation defiles [Col. 0398A] our thoughts, what else do the entrails of the victim carry but filth? Yet in order that they may be burned, they are washed; for tears must indeed wash away impure thoughts, which heavenly love burns in the action of sacrifice. And whatever the mind suffers, whether from an open conflict or from the memory of its former life, must be washed, so that it may burn the more sweetly in the sight of the eternal Inspector, inasmuch as, when it begins to stand before him, it places upon the altar of its prayer nothing earthly and nothing slippery.”

Therefore, O Jews, understand the Old Testament spiritually, and take care to offer faithfully to God the Father, through Jesus Christ, not carnal but spiritual sacrifices, so that you may obtain forgiveness for all your sins [Col. 0398B] and attain eternal blessedness with the children of the holy Church. Love virtues, then; flee vices; contend with all the effort of your mind against temptations both carnal and spiritual, so that you may not be conquered by them, but may courageously conquer them with God’s help. Moreover, conduct yourselves cautiously in all your actions: that pride may not raise you up, arrogance may not puff you up, ambition may not tear you apart through earthly pleasures, adversity may not disturb you, and the prosperity of this present life may not make you negligent in seeking eternal joys.

That a person ought to act cautiously and diligently in all his works is shown figuratively in Genesis, where we read: “The Lord God took man [Col. 0398C] and placed him in the paradise of delight, that he might work it and keep it” (Gen. 2). Let us hear what blessed Gregory says upon this passage. [Note: [Col. 0398D] *Patherius*, on Genesis, chap. 12.] “We must consider most carefully that good things cannot profit us if the evils which creep in are not guarded against. Everything that is done perishes if it is not diligently kept in humility. Hence it is well said also of our first parent: ‘The Lord placed him in the paradise of delight, that he might work it and keep it.’ He works who does the good which is commanded. But he does not keep what he has worked if that which is forbidden steals upon him. Therefore it is especially necessary always to do good things, and cautiously to guard ourselves in thought even against our good works. For if they lift up the mind, they are not good, since they plainly serve not the doer but self-exaltation.

[Col. 0398D] “In this matter we do not act improperly if we bring forward testimony from books which, though not canonical, were nevertheless published for the edification of the Church.” Thus it is read in the Book of Maccabees that Eleazar, striking an elephant in battle, brought it down, but himself fell beneath the one he killed (1 Macc. 6). Whom, then, did this Eleazar signify, whom his own victory crushed, except those who overcome their vices and, through pride, succumb beneath those very vices which they cast beneath themselves? For he dies as though beneath the enemy he overthrows who is exalted because of the fault he conquers.

Therefore, O Jews, hold the catholic faith with devout minds [Col. 0399A] and flee self-exaltation in good works, lest in the very matters in which you think you overcome vices, you perhaps fall beneath them. [Note: [Col. 0399D] Isidore, *Synonyms*, book II, “On Humility.”] For whoever is proudly lifted up shall be humbled in his own confusion; whoever is exalted shall be cast down; whoever is raised shall be overthrown; whoever is puffed up shall be dashed down. Why? Because the fall is heavier from a height, and the ruin greater from an eminence. For pride is the beginning of every sin (Ecclus. 10). Pride cast down angels; swelling dissolved kingdoms; self-exaltation brought down the lofty; arrogance humbled the high. Conversely, humility knows no fall; humility knows no stumbling; humility never incurs ruin; humility has never suffered a fall.

Therefore maintain deep humility in your conduct, as has been said, O Jews; flee pride; beware of self-exaltation; receive with devout minds faith in the holy Trinity—namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and humbly submit yourselves [Col. 0399B] to the sacraments of the Church, so that, freed from the slavery of sin and cleansed from the stains of your former life, you may attain the salvation of your souls. Vow to Jesus Christ, the supreme priest, an uncorrupted faith, a pure conscience, holy conduct, and a religious life, so that you may be judged worthy to enter the holy Church with the faithful peoples.

Perhaps you ask us, O Jews, saying: “After we have vowed our vow to God, if we break it in any respect, if through ignorance or negligence we do not fulfill it, if perhaps through human [Col. 0399C] frailty we transgress it, how shall we be able to make satisfaction to God?” We answer you thus: if through ignorance, negligence, or forgetfulness you abandon your vows, you may obtain pardon from almighty God through amendment of life, true contrition of heart, and humble penitence.

But let us all hear together what the Book of Leviticus says concerning one who has bound himself by an oath and afterward, through ignorance, negligence, or forgetfulness, has broken it: “The soul that has sworn and uttered with its lips that it would do something evil or good, and has confirmed this very thing by oath and word, but afterward, having forgotten, has recognized its offense, shall do penance for its sin and offer a ewe from the flock or [Col. 0399D] a she-goat; and the priest shall pray for her and for her sin. But if he cannot offer livestock, let him offer to the Lord two turtledoves or two young doves, one for sin and the other as a whole burnt offering” (Lev. 5). The Old Testament, O Jews, as I have declared, is to be understood not according to the letter but spiritually.

Let blessed Gregory, therefore—a wise man and very discerning in expounding the meanings of the holy Scriptures—[Note: [Col. 0399] *Morals*, book XXXII, chap. 4, and *Patherius*, on Leviticus, chap. 2.] come forward and show us spiritually the distinctions between the aforesaid sacrifices. “To utter an oath,” he says, “is to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service. For when we promise good works, we undertake to do good; but when we vow abstinence and the affliction [Col. 0400A] of our flesh, we swear to do ourselves present harm. Yet because no one in this life is so perfect that, however devoted to God he may be, he does not sin amid his devout vows, however numerous, a ewe or she-goat is commanded to be offered for sin. For what is signified by the ewe except the innocence of the active life, and what by the she-goat, which often feeds while hanging upon the highest and most remote crags, except the contemplative life?

“Whoever therefore sees that he has not fulfilled what he promised and purposed ought to equip himself more earnestly for the sacrifice of God, either with the innocence of good work or with the sublime pasture of contemplation. And it is rightly commanded that a ewe be offered from the flock, but not a she-goat from the flock, because the active life belongs to many, but the contemplative life to few. When we do those things which we see many doing and having done, we give, as it were, a ewe from the flock. But when the strength of the offerer does not suffice for a ewe or a she-goat, there is added as a remedy of penitence the offering of either two young doves or two turtledoves. We know that young doves and turtledoves have groaning for their song. What, then, is signified by the two young doves or turtledoves except the twofold groaning of our penitence? Thus, when we do not rise to offer good works, [Col. 0400B] we may weep for ourselves in two ways: because we have not done what is right and have done what is wrong. Hence one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin, the other as a whole burnt offering. For a whole burnt offering is called that which is wholly burned. We offer one turtledove for sin when we give groaning [Col. 0400C] for our fault. But from the other we make a whole burnt offering when, because we have neglected to do good, we burn ourselves utterly with the fire of sorrow.”

Therefore, O Jews, receive the catholic faith with devout minds; take care to understand the Old Testament spiritually; receive in every respect the sacraments of the New Testament; strive to offer to God the Father, through Jesus Christ the supreme priest, sacrifices of good works for the forgiveness of your sins. After the passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of Jesus Christ our Lord, sins are no longer to be purged by the blood of bulls, calves, he-goats, rams, or lambs, but by [Col. 0400D] tears, prayers, fasts, vigils, alms, and other good works. Without doubt, these legal sacrifices are now neither necessary nor pleasing to God in the New Testament. For if God had wished these carnal sacrifices to be offered to him in the New Testament, he would by no means have rejected them through the prophet Isaiah, saying to you: “What is the multitude of your victims to me, says the Lord? I am full of the burnt offering of rams and the fat of fatlings; the blood of calves and lambs and he-goats I have not desired. When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands? Do not,” he says, “continue to offer sacrifice in vain” (Isa. 1).

Therefore, in saying, “Do not [Col. 0401A] continue to offer sacrifice in vain,” the Lord plainly demonstrates that after the institution of the New Testament the carnal sacrifices of the Old Testament have been rejected by him and are useless to those who offer them. It is thus evident that the carnal ceremonies of the Old Testament came to an end at the advent of Jesus Christ, God and man; and that the sacraments of ecclesiastical religion, by which forgiveness of sins is granted and the heavenly kingdom opened to believers, had their beginning. If, then, you desire to obtain forgiveness for your offenses, take great care to offer not the blood of bulls or calves, nor the flesh of cattle, but worthy fruits of penitence: namely, tears of true compunction, alms given of free will, prayers of a contrite heart, and other works worthy of and pleasing to God.

[Col. 0401B] What do you say to this, O Jews? What do you object, or what answer do you give? Do you now believe that Jesus Christ is true God? Or are you still, darkened by the mist of malice and wickedness concerning his divinity, in some doubt? Yet I should like to know more certainly what faith or disposition you hold. If indeed, as we exceedingly desire, you now believe that Jesus Christ is the one God, we shall give thanks to God for your conversion. But if you intend still to persist in the malice of your unbelief, tell us this very thing. I have already declared above that we shall by no means dismiss you against your will until I have plainly shown, by the truest testimonies of the New and Old Testaments, that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and have most clearly proved you false witnesses who assert with obstinate [Col. 0401C] minds that he is not true God.

This is your answer, O Jews, and likewise your objection. You say that Jesus Christ was not of such virtue or power as to be able to redeem the holy Church from eternal damnation and raise it up to the heavenly homeland; indeed, you assert that he was separated from it by the death of the cross.

But in answer to this most false objection of yours, O Jews, we declare without hesitation that Jesus Christ is true God and true man; that in the womb of the undefiled Virgin Mary he joined the holy Church inseparably to himself; that through his cross and most merciful death he powerfully and mercifully [Col. 0401D] redeemed it from eternal damnation, washed it from sins by his own blood, consecrated it by holy baptism, and perfectly instructed it by the teaching of the Holy Spirit; that in himself, through himself, and after himself he led it to the blessedness of the heavenly homeland—that is, to the vision of the glory of his Father—and that he was made eternally the head of that same holy Church. And so that you may not doubt, O Jews, that what we have said is true, we wish immediately to prove it by the testimony of the Book of Leviticus. To strengthen our faith, therefore, and entirely convict the treachery of your unbelief, let us all hear together what the Book of Leviticus says: “If a whole burnt offering to the Lord is made from a [Col. 0402A] turtledove or a dove, which is commanded to be offered for sin, its head shall be twisted back toward the feathers, so that the head remains attached by the neck and is not wholly torn off” (Lev. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0401D] *Patherius*, on Leviticus, chap. 3.] What is signified, O Jews, in this offering of a turtledove or dove commanded to be offered for sin, and in the fact that after the victim’s death the head remains attached to the body, except the person of Jesus Christ our Redeemer? For the death of our Mediator, as blessed Gregory says, served to join him to his body—that is, the Church—not to separate him from it. For the Mediator of God and men, namely the head of us all and the victim of true cleansing, by the very means through which he suffered death for us clung more truly to us. Therefore, after severance, the turtledove’s head remains joined to its body, [Col. 0402B] because even intervening death did not divide Christ from the Church.

Moreover, the persecutors accomplished what they had wickedly planned. They inflicted death upon him in order to cut away from it the devotion of the faithful; but faith rather grew from the very source by which the cruelty of unbelievers thought to extinguish it. And while they supposed that by persecuting him they were cutting off his miracles, they were compelled unknowingly to spread those very miracles. [Note: [Col. 0401D] More correctly, “indeed,” as in *Patherius*.] Who then is our head, O Jewish enemies of truth, except Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the human race, concerning whom the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0401D] The editions adduce another Pauline testimony [Col. 0402D], Eph. 1:22: “He gave him as head over all the Church”; not, however, the passage presented by Martin.]: “All things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers, were created in him; all things were created through him and in him; and he is before all things, and all things subsist in him; and [Col. 0402C] he is the head of the body, the Church, who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he may hold primacy in all things” (Col. 1).

When your fathers persecuted him, they attempted to erase his name from the earth. And when they saw him crucified and buried, they believed that they had separated him from the love of all. But the turtledove’s head was cut, yet not separated from its body, because through what Christ suffered for us he joined all of us to himself more truly in that very death. Therefore the severed head of the turtledove remained attached to the body, because our Redeemer indeed suffered for us, but, contrary to your lies, O Jews, was not separated from us.

This history of the Book of Leviticus, thus spiritually expounded, [Col. 0402D] confirms beyond doubt in the catholic faith us who firmly believe Jesus Christ to be our head, and openly proves you, who obstinately assert that he was separated from the holy Church, to be advocates of falsehood. Therefore you, O Jewish enemies of truth, who with stubborn minds resist by unbelief such most evident assertions of the New and Old Testaments that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, have perhaps already been enticed by the suggestions of the ancient enemy. Perhaps he who deceived Eve with persuasive words, so that she might taste the fruit of the forbidden tree against God’s command, has entangled [Col. 0403A] your hearts with the arguments of his cunning, lest you believe Christ to be true God and true man. You must therefore diligently understand and avoid the snares of the ancient enemy, O Jews, lest, deceived by his most cunning suggestions, you perish through the malice of unbelief. [Note: [Col. 0403D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chap. 5.]

Thus you ought to be simple in innocence of life, yet with simplicity you must also be prudent. O Jewish people, wicked and perverse people, hold without doubt that if you do not mingle prudence with simplicity, you are, according to the prophet, “a deceived dove, without a heart” (Hos. 7). You are a dove because simple; but without a heart because you lack prudence. You ought to possess such discernment, O Jews, that, endowed with reason, you may distinguish between good and evil, between good [Col. 0403B] and better, between truth and falsehood, lest, deceived by the hidden suggestions of the devil under an appearance of good, you incur the danger of eternal damnation. And, to state it more plainly, this is the inquiry of Joshua, leader of the people of Israel: “Are you one of us, or of our adversaries?” (Josh. 5). It is as though he were saying more plainly: “Are you a virtue by which the soul is stirred to do good and is continually preserved in good work, or a vice by which, at the devil’s suggestion, it is deceived under an appearance of good and, once deceived, plunged into the depth of eternal death?” Hence the Lord says also to the prophet Jeremiah: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15).

I do not want you to be unaware, O Jews, that many are deceived by the devil and yet do not know that they have been deceived, as the testimony of the prophet Hosea declares: “Strangers have devoured his strength, and he did not know it” (Hos. 7). The strangers, therefore, signify malignant spirits, who gnaw away the virtues of the mind; but negligent hearts do not understand this. “Then the devil is conquered as though unarmed,” says our patron blessed Isidore in the book of *Sentences*, [Note: [Col. 0403D] Isidore, as above.] “when he tries to corrupt a person by manifest iniquity. But he advances armed when, under an appearance of holiness and virtue, he destroys what is holy; then the one deceived does not feel his losses, but pursues and loves as though they were virtues the things which are vices. In the eyes of carnal persons the devil is terrible, but in the eyes of the elect his terror is contemptible. [Col. 0403D] He is feared as a lion by unbelievers; he is despised as a worm by those strong in faith, and, once seen for a little while, is easily repelled. Whoever does not receive the devil’s suggestions does not at all fall into his snares. For he is easily repelled in the ensuing deed if his first enticements are rejected.

“The devil is slippery like a serpent,” says blessed Isidore in the book of *Sentences*, [Note: [Col. 0403D] As above.] “and if resistance is not made to its head—that is, to its first suggestion—it slips, without being perceived, wholly into the inward parts of the heart. The beginnings of diabolical temptations are weak; if they are not guarded against, but through use pass into habit, [Col. 0404A] they grow strong at the end, so that they are never overcome, or only with difficulty. Although throughout life the devil desires to trip a person, yet he desires all the more to deceive him at the end.”
