Hence in the beginning the Lord threatens the serpent, saying: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed” (Gen. 3). And he added: “She shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” (ibid.). “To crush the serpent’s head,” says blessed Gregory, [Note: [Col. 0403D] *Patherius*, on Genesis, chap. 25.] “is utterly to uproot, by the hand of careful reflection, the beginnings of diabolical suggestion from the entrance of the heart. Yet when the serpent is detected at the beginning, [Col. 0404B] it strives to strike the heel; for even if it does not strike the person’s intention with its first suggestion, it nevertheless desires with all its effort to deceive him at the end. But if once the heart is corrupted in its intention, the excess [Note: [Col. 0404D] ‘Middle course’ (*medietas*).] and end of the subsequent action are securely possessed by the crafty enemy, because he sees that the whole tree bears fruit for him whose root he has corrupted with his poisonous tooth.” [Note: [Col. 0404D] Isidore, as above.]

Therefore, because the devil desires to deceive a person not only in youth but also in old age, and not only in old age but even at the end, it is necessary that a person in this life, however just or holy he may be, never be secure; but that he always beware in humility and always fear anxiously lest he fall at the end.

Hear then what I say, O rebellious and faithless Jews; hear what I speak; listen diligently [Col. 0404C] to the counsels which I offer you with a right intention for the salvation of your souls. If the ancient enemy suggests to you that you should depart from the worship and love of God, give him no assent whatsoever. [Note: [Col. 0404D] Isidore, *Synonyms*, book II, near the end of section II.] Drive the devil’s first suggestion from your hearts, and you will be able more easily to cast away impending temptations from your minds. As soon as the scorpion appears, crush its head: that is, drive the beginning of its deadly suggestion from the entrance of your mind, and it will not break out into action. Tread upon the serpent’s head—that is, reject the beginning of wicked persuasion—so that you may innocently escape the stain of sin and believe without doubt that Jesus Christ is true God and true man.

Therefore take care, O Jews, to understand the Old Testament spiritually; receive the New with devout minds; strive eagerly to fulfill the precepts of evangelical instruction; despise the superstitious traditions of the Pharisees; observe the commandments of the Law not carnally but spiritually, that you may deserve to be reckoned worthy of the Christian name. Now, after the birth, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of Jesus Christ, not carnal offerings of the Old Testament nor the useless traditions of the Pharisees, but the spiritual sacrifices of the holy Church, through that same supreme priest Jesus Christ, are acceptable to God the Father. [Col. 0405A] Bringing to an end the ceremonies of the old Law which God the Father commanded the Hebrew people to observe for a time, at Christ’s coming he promulgated to the world through his Son Christ, that same new priest, new commandments; unless you receive these with devout minds and faithful devotion, O Jews, you cannot be saved.

§ XXIX.—

In Nadab and Abihu, who were slain by the Lord while offering strange fire, are signified those who disturb the Church by the traditions of the Pharisees and heretical doctrines. There follows, according to Isidore, a discussion of the various sects among the Jews and of the nature of heresies, which the Church overcomes by her wisdom just as she overcomes persecutions by patience. Since heretics separate themselves from her through voluntary choice, according to the etymology of their name, they shall [Col. 0405B] perish eternally by the example of those like themselves. Paul’s teaching is set forth concerning the philosophers of the Gentiles, who, not finding Christ, the Way, fell among the transgressing angels and turned the glory of God shining in creatures into vanity and the worship of idols; for this reason they cannot be excused or find salvation, since righteousness is only from faith in Jesus Christ. He answers Jews who ask: “Why do Christians, who receive the Old Testament, eat unclean animals?” Because Christ, in coming, disclosed the spiritual meaning hidden in those precepts, so that one is superstitious who, execrating God’s creation, abstains from certain foods. Concerning the usefulness of contemplation: that the higher part should govern the lower; and that we should act manfully in every work, lest, being lukewarm, we be despised by God. He also discusses the evils of pride, which, because it refuses to submit to God, suffers adversity from things beneath itself.

[Col. 0405C] Therefore, if you receive another doctrine, or live otherwise than Christ taught Christians to live, you shall utterly perish from the company of his elect. Do you not know, O wretched and pitiable Jews, that Nadab and Abihu, the priestly sons of Aaron, perished for this reason: because they offered strange fire upon the altar to the Lord? But so that we may know more fully how this came to pass, O Jews, let us, if you please, review at greater length the history of that time.

When the burnt offerings had been offered upon the altar as an odor of sweetness to the Lord, Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle of testimony; and, coming out, they blessed the people of Israel. And the glory of the Lord appeared to the whole multitude of the children of Israel; and behold, fire went out from the Lord and devoured the burnt offering and the fat which were upon the altar. When the crowds saw this, they praised [Col. 0405D] the Lord, falling upon their faces (Lev. 9). Then Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, seized their censers, placed fire and incense upon them, and offered strange fire before the Lord, which had not been commanded them. And fire went out from the Lord and devoured them, and they died before the Lord. Moses said to Aaron: “This is what the Lord spoke: ‘I shall be sanctified in those who approach me, and before the sight of all the people I shall be glorified.’” Hearing this, Aaron their father kept silence. Immediately they carried them out, as they lay, clothed in linen tunics, and cast them outside the camp (Lev. 10).

Nadab and Abihu, then, who offered the strange fire forbidden by the Lord, [Col. 0406A] signified those who, abandoning the teaching of Jesus Christ, God and man, scandalize the holy Church by the traditions of the Pharisees and the false doctrines of heretics. The Lord himself rebukes and reproves them in the Gospel, saying: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” (Matt. 15). And again: “In vain do they worship me, teaching the doctrines and commandments of men” (ibid.).

“Heresy, in Greek,” says blessed Isidore in the book of the *Etymologies*, [Note: [Col. 0405D] *Etymologies*, book VIII, chap. 3.] “is so called from *choice* (*hairesis*), because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him: as the Peripatetic, Academic, Epicurean, and Stoic philosophers did; or as others did who, devising a perverse doctrine, withdrew from the Church by their own decision. [Col. 0406B] Therefore heresy is so called by the Greek word, from the interpretation ‘choice,’ because each person chooses for himself, by his own decision, whatever he himself wishes either to establish or to receive. But we, O Jews, are permitted to introduce nothing on our own decision, nor may we choose what anyone has introduced by his own decision. Know for certain that we have as our authorities the apostles of Jesus Christ, who themselves chose nothing by their own decision to introduce, but faithfully delivered to the nations the teaching received from Christ; so that even if an angel from heaven should preach another Gospel, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1).

But what blessed Isidore says concerning the heresies of the Jews, who deny Christ, persecute his most faithful disciples, and blaspheme without interruption, [Col. 0406C] troubling the holy Church with various conflicts and barkings, I urge you, O Jews, to hear carefully; so that, recognizing the malice of your perversity and unbelief, you may believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man, and receive his baptism with devout minds for the forgiveness of your sins.

“Jews” is interpreted as “confessors,” because Leah, when she bore Judah, from whom the Jews take their name, gave praise to the Lord, saying: “Now for this I shall confess the Lord.” And for this reason he was called Judah (Gen. 29). Thus his name was derived from confession, which is thanksgiving. Jews, therefore, as has been said, are interpreted as confessors; but now they are not confessors, [Col. 0406D] but are the synagogue of Satan. Why? Because they do not praise God the Father but dishonor him, while they stubbornly deny and insolently blaspheme his most beloved Son, through whom God the Father created, rules, and governs all things. [Note: [Col. 0406D] Id., book VIII, chap. 3.]

“Hebrews” means “those who pass over”; by this name they are admonished to pass from worse things to better and leave their former errors. Pharisees and Sadducees are opposed to one another. For “Pharisees” is interpreted from Hebrew into Latin as “separated,” because they prefer the righteousness of traditions and observances, which they call *deuteroses* [secondary traditions]; hence they are called separated from the people, as though by righteousness. “Sadducees” is interpreted as [Col. 0407A] “the righteous.” For they claim for themselves what they are not: they deny the resurrection of bodies and declare that the soul perishes with the body. These receive only the five books of the Law and reject the prophetic oracles.

The Efnei [Note: [Col. 0407D] Essenes.] say that he is Christ who taught them every abstinence. The Marbonei [Note: [Col. 0407D] Marbothaeans.] say that he is Christ who taught them to keep sabbath in every matter. The Genistae [Note: [Col. 0407D] Genistae.] are so called because they boast that they are of the race of Abraham. For when the people of God came into Babylon, many, abandoning their wives, joined themselves to Babylonian women. But certain persons, content only with Israelite marriages, or born of such unions, when they had returned from Babylon separated themselves from all the people and assumed for themselves this boastful name, namely Genistae. The Meristae [Note: [Col. 0407D] Meristae.] [Col. 0407B] are so called because they divide the Scriptures, believing not all the prophets and saying that they prophesied by different spirits. The Samaritans are so called because they keep the Law alone, for they do not receive the prophets. Others are called Immerobaptists [Note: [Col. 0407D] Hemerobaptists.] because they wash their garments and bodies every day.

All these aforesaid are heresies of the Jews. These heretics—namely Pharisees, Sadducees, Efnei, Marbonei, Genistae, Meristae, Samaritans, and Immerobaptists—who, as was said above, place human traditions before God’s commandments and trouble the holy Church with various conflicts, were prefigured by Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, who offered upon the altar to the Lord the strange fire which had been forbidden. Truly, [Col. 0407C] those who disturb the holy Church through heresies and schisms offer to the Lord not permitted but forbidden fire. They do not nourish within the same holy Church, Christ’s bride, the Lord’s own fire, of which he himself says, “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and I desire that it burn” (Luke 12)—namely, charity, which works through love upon the altar, that is, in the holy Church. Rather, stirred by the fury of diabolical cruelty and intoxicated by the poison of that same malignant enemy, they bring strange fire into that holy Church and kindle persecutions and scandals within it.

I want you to know, O Jews, that the Church has a twofold beauty: one which she attains here by living well, and another by which she will be crowned in heaven through recompense. “The holy Church, on account of Christ, as blessed Isidore says [Note: Book I of the *Sentences*, ch. 16], undergoes two kinds of tribulations: those which she has suffered from pagans in her martyrs, and those which she endures from heretics through their various conflicts. Yet by God’s grace she overcomes both, partly by bearing them and partly by resisting them. As the holy Catholic Church patiently tolerates within herself those who live wickedly, so she repels from herself those who believe wrongly. The holy mother and virgin Church strives most earnestly against the stubbornness of pagans and heretics [Col. 0408A] by wisdom and patience; wisdom is exercised when she is tested by words, patience when she is tested by swords. Because of heretical perversity, as blessed Isidore says in the first book of the *Sentences* [Note: [Col. 0408D] As above], the holy Church has been enlarged through teachings; formerly it flourished only by faith [Note: [Col. 0408D] The edition reads better: ‘formerly she flourished only by simple faith.’ See the notes on this chapter by the very learned García de Loaysa]. Thus, on the occasion of heretics, teachers arose and increased in the holy Church. For the assertion of truth is then made clearer when any disagreement has appeared. I do not want you to be ignorant, O Jews, that the holy Church is called Catholic because she is spread universally throughout the whole world. For the conventicles of heretics are confined to certain parts of the world; but she is extended throughout the whole globe, as the Apostle Paul testifies when he says: ‘I give thanks to my God for all of you, because your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world’ (Rom. 1). Heresies, as Isidore, the doctor of Spain, says [Note: [Col. 0408D] As above], are found to operate either in some corner of the world or in one nation; but the Catholic Church, just as she extends through the whole world, is also built up by the fellowship of all nations.”

Perhaps you wish to know, O Jews, who heretics are, or for what reason, or through what cause, heresy comes about. Let us therefore bring forward blessed Isidore, the special patron of the city of León, and, if you please, attentively hear from him the solution of the foregoing questions. “Who are heretics,” he says, “but those who, having abandoned God’s Church, have chosen private associations for themselves? Concerning them, making as it were a complaint, the Lord says through the prophet: ‘My people have done two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water’ (Jer. 2). What is the cause for which heresy occurs? Plainly, the exercise of faith. But the means through which it occurs is the obscurity of the divine Scriptures, in which heretics, being in darkness, understand matters otherwise than they are. For, thinking wrongly, they do not acquire knowledge; indeed, they tend toward nothingness. Heretics learn their falsehoods with great zeal and struggle with intense labor lest they come to the unity of the Church. Of them it is fittingly said through the prophet: ‘They taught their tongues to speak lies, and labored to act wickedly’ [Col. 0408D] (Jer. 9). Then in turn heretics provoke one another when they draw each other into their own sects; yet they clash with one another in such a way that they contend against the Church with an equal spirit of error. Though divided from one another, they are united together in opposition to the Church.

“Yet it must be known that heretics cannot obtain pardon except through the holy Catholic Church, just as Job’s friends could not please God by themselves unless blessed Job had offered sacrifice for them [Col. 0409A] (Job 42). Moreover, I want you to know, O Jews, that the works which heretics perform, though they seem right to them, will nevertheless profit them nothing unless they first endeavor to amend their life according to the rule of the holy Church, as the Lord testifies through the prophet Jeremiah [Note: [Col. 0409D] In the printed editions one read ‘through Jeremiah,’ says the aforesaid García de Loaysa here; but I emended it to ‘Isaiah,’ with the agreement of all the manuscripts and of the truth. The passage is Isaiah 57:11–12. Therefore the most learned annotator did not see our manuscript, which retains ‘Jeremiah’; nor was there any need to correct the printed text from elsewhere. Among the ancients—even among the canonical writers themselves—it is customary to alter the order of the prophets, as everyone knows from the evangelists Matthew and Mark, [Col. 0410D] who cited Zechariah and Malachi under the names of Isaiah and Jeremiah: the former at ch. 27, v. 9, the latter at ch. 1, v. 2. On this matter see, among others, the most illustrious Toledo theologian Hieronymus de la Rua, *Controversiae theologicae*, part I, controversy 4, from the *Positiva*, and the preface in the newest edition of the Mozarabic Breviary, where you will read several examples from venerable manuscripts]: ‘Because you have forgotten me, my people, behold, I will declare your righteousness, and your works will not profit you.’ Although heretics fulfill the Law and the Prophets with their whole mind, because they are not Catholics, God is not in their assemblies, as the Lord himself testifies when he says: ‘Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, my soul is not toward this people. Cast them out from before my face, and they shall depart’ (Jer. 15). By Moses and Samuel understand the Law and the Prophets; although heretics strive to fulfill these in deed [Col. 0409B], nevertheless, because of the ungodliness of their error they are cast away from the face of God. The pagan and the heretic are separated from the assemblies of the righteous: the former because he was never with God’s people; the latter, namely the heretic, because he departed from God’s people. Each, departing from Christ, belongs to the devil’s body. Those who pass from idolatry to Judaism and from Judaism to heresy have, according to the prophet, gone forth from evil to evil (Jer. 9), and have not known the Lord, because they have passed from the error of unbelief into another error.

Hear what I say, O Jews; hear what I speak; listen to what I urge. Do not presume any longer to offer strange fire with Nadab and Abihu. Do not seek to introduce in addition the traditions of the Pharisees, Sadducees, Marboneans, and the other [Col. 0409C] heretics, lest perhaps it befall you—God forbid!—to perish with those same transgressors, Aaron’s sons. Without doubt, if you choose to hold the sect of the aforesaid heretics and to depart from Christ, you will perish with them eternally. But let us again recall what the foregoing history in the book of Leviticus says: ‘Immediately, entering in, the young men took them and cast them outside the camp’ (Lev. 10). So too you, O Jews, if you bring in strange fire—as has often been said—that is, if, abandoning the most illustrious teaching of Jesus Christ the supreme priest, you introduce the traditions of Pharisees or Sadducees, or wish to observe the superstitious sects of other heretics, you will unhappily be cast by the angels of that same Jesus Christ, God and man, outside the camp of faithful [Col. 0409D] Christians, and will perish forever.

And what shall I say to you, O Jews, of the foolish wisdom of the philosophers of the nations? The philosophers of the nations, because they did not seek God with their whole mind as they should have done, fell among the transgressing angels; and, as Isidore, doctor of Spain, says in the first book of the *Sentences* [Col. 0410A] [Note: [Col. 0410D] As above, ch. 17], the devil became for them a mediator unto death, just as Christ became for us a mediator unto life. The philosophers of the world teach many things concerning the measurement of times, the courses of the stars, and the movement of the elements; yet they received this only from God. Flying proudly, like birds through the air; plunging into the depths, like fish into the sea; and walking the earth like cattle, they described these things. Yet they refused to understand their Author with their whole mind. Why, then, are they unable to question brute animals? Clearly, because they do not know how to reason. Therefore pagan people are not unlike animals, since they do not consider such matters; loving these things more, they became vain even to the point of worshipping them. Therefore Christ is the straight way, O Jews; and if anyone does not walk in it, there is no way [Col. 0410B] for him to reach God the Father. The philosophers of the world undoubtedly knew God; but because the humility of Christ’s Incarnation and Passion displeased them, they passed into a trackless place and not into the way (Ps. 106). Thus, becoming vain, they changed the glory of God into falsehood; abandoning the straightness of the way, they fell into the winding paths of error.

Know for certain, O Jews, that the power of God is for salvation to everyone who believes. For the righteousness of God, as blessed Paul says, is revealed in it—that is, in the Gospel of Christ—from faith to faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous lives by faith’ (Rom. 1). It is as if he said more plainly: righteousness and salvation are from faith; and thus the righteous person lives in Christ, who is eternal life, not by the Law but by faith. The righteousness [Col. 0410C] of God, therefore, is that which freely justifies the ungodly through faith apart from works of the Law (Rom. 3). The preaching of the Gospel reveals it when it gives faith to a person, through which the one who believes that God is righteous and true in his promises is justified. Therefore, O Jews, you will by no means be able to be justified by works of the Law, as you suppose, unless you firmly believe that Jesus Christ, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God. Thus God’s righteousness is revealed from the faith of God who promises into the faith of the human being who believes. “From faith to faith,” that is, with respect to all the parts of faith: from the faith of the Old Testament, where one God is believed and is; into the faith of the New Testament, where Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are preached, believed, and are one God; from faith in the first advent into faith in the second; from faith in the first resurrection [Col. 0410D] into faith in the second; from faith in promise into faith in fulfillment; from the faith of preachers into the faith of peoples; from the faith of sowers into the faith of reapers. Therefore righteousness belongs to the one who passes from faith to faith, so that a Jew and anyone else may pass from faith in the Old Testament into faith in the New: from faith in words and hope into faith in realities and sight. Faith, therefore, is that by which things not seen are believed. There is also a faith, as Master Peter says on this passage, ‘the righteous lives by faith’ [Col. 0411A], when what will be is believed not by words but by present realities—when God shall give himself to be seen in the future. Therefore he says: from faith in words, by which we believe what we do not see, into faith in realities, by which we shall possess what we have believed.

Accordingly, the philosophers of the nations and the other pagans will by no means be able to excuse themselves for their unbelief and wicked way of life, since they changed the truth of God into falsehood, as the Apostle says: ‘Although they knew God, they changed the glory of God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man’ (Rom. 1), and so forth. Detesting their abominable conduct and considering their just condemnation, the Apostle subsequently says: ‘The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and unrighteousness of those people who hold the truth of God in unrighteousness, because what is known of God is manifest to them; for God has manifested it to them’ [Col. 0411B] (ibid.). Having commended the piety of faith, by which, being justified by God, we ought to be grateful, he adds the contrary in detestation: that the pagans, puffed up in themselves, fell into idolatry. For he says: ‘The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety,’ and so forth. Here the Apostle addresses pagans according to their former condition, who boast of a good nature and excuse their shameful deeds through ignorance. In opposition to them, blessed Paul says both that they once possessed knowledge of God and later lost it through fault, and that the good nature left to them by God was by themselves precipitated into every evil [Col. 0411C]. They could indeed have known God, but they take away his knowledge from themselves, preferring to remain in their wicked actions rather than in God’s works. It is as though the Apostle spoke more plainly for the correction of pagans and the warning of Christians, saying: ‘The wrath of God is revealed’—namely, the wrath to come from heaven at the judgment—‘against all impiety and unrighteousness of people,’ that is, against every kind of impiety and unrighteousness, arising from the fault of those who hold the truth—that is, the true knowledge of God—in unrighteousness, remaining in evil work when it freely presents itself. For what is known of God is manifest to them by the guidance of reason. It is as though he said: what of God can be known, they possess in themselves, as it were, the means by which they may know it according to natural reason [Col. 0411D]. Yet there are some things concerning God which cannot be known by nature, such as the mystery of our redemption. ‘God,’ he says, ‘has manifested it to them.’ By what means? Namely, through his work. It is as though he said: not only did natural reason benefit them, but God also helped daily, lest nature alone should seem sufficient.

Again he adds: ‘For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made.’ Here the Apostle more plainly shows what pagans could know concerning God even without the Law. He uses the plural, “the invisible things of God,” because God is known in many respects: namely, that he is eternal, omnipotent, immeasurable, and so forth. He also says that these invisible things, once understood, are evident, because through heaven and [Col. 0412A] earth and the other creatures, which they perceived to be immense and enduring, they beheld in mind their Creator as incomparable, immense, and eternal. It is as though he said openly: ‘The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world,’ that is, not only by angels but also by human beings from the constitution of the world onward, ‘are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made.’ Again, openly showing that the philosophers and pagans of the world are inexcusable, he says: ‘His everlasting power also and divinity, so that they are without excuse; because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened; for, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.’ It is as though he said more plainly: [Col. 0412B] his everlasting power, which governs all things—namely Jesus Christ—and divinity, that is, the Holy Spirit, namely the goodness of God the Father which fills all things, are also seen. Therefore they are inexcusable, because when they knew God by natural reason, they did not glorify him as God by worshipping him and living well, nor give thanks for the knowledge granted to them. Rather, they became vain in their thoughts and prayers, which they had from themselves and not from God—or rather, which they attributed to themselves. In this they were vain and false, thinking themselves to be something when they were nothing. Little by little, as the swelling of pride cast its shadow, their foolish heart—that is, their reason—was darkened even to folly. See how they became vain in speech or heart: ‘For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools’ [Col. 0412C], because they said that they were wise in the natures of things through themselves and not through God. Therefore they became foolish toward God, not only in understanding but also in deed. ‘And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed animals, and of serpents.’ It is as though he said: as far as they were concerned, they changed glory—that is, the worship due to the incorruptible God—into the likeness of an image, first of corruptible man, namely an image resembling him whose image it was; then of birds, then of four-footed animals, and finally of serpents. Here the Apostle condemns idols, in one of which they worshipped the earth, in another the sun, and the like. It was an ancient Roman custom to worship images of men [Col. 0412D], such as Romulus, Jupiter, and others, especially from Aeneas’ arrival in Italy. But images of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents began to be worshipped and venerated after Alexandria had been conquered by Caesar Augustus and subjected to Rome. Therefore, because the pagans changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to uncleanness, so that they might dishonor their bodies among themselves. “It is plain that God works in human hearts,” as blessed Augustine says, “to incline their wills wherever he wills: toward good by his mercy, or toward evil according to their deserts—by a judgment which is sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, but always just.” God therefore gave them over [Col. 0413A]—because nothing occurs without his permission—to the desires of their hearts, which had been left to them by God, and afterward to such practical uncleanness that they applied their bodies, naturally resisting, by a certain force, and made them more suited to vices. Thus he shows that they changed God’s glory in its several parts: namely, that they considered to be God what was not God, worshipped it, and served it. He then details the forms of uncleanness, because females burned in desire for females and males for males; in these he compares punishment to fault, so that, just as they sinned against nature, they might be punished in their nature. Hence he concludes, saying: ‘Receiving in themselves the due recompense of their error.’ Therefore because of idolatry, impiety, and the other evils which they foolishly committed, God gave them over—that is, permitted them, withdrawing [Col. 0413B] his grace from them—to go into the desires of their hearts, into uncleanness, so that, as far as they themselves and nature were concerned, they might dishonor their bodies, having this not from elsewhere but from themselves. Of them he subsequently says: ‘Who changed the truth of God into a lie; and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.’ It is as though he said: those who dishonor their bodies among themselves changed the truth of God, which above he called glory, into a lie; that is, they ascribed to an idol what is true of God. They worshipped it by diligently adorning it and served the creature rather, as if it were better, than serving the Creator alone, who is blessed—that is [Col. 0413C], exalted above all things—forever, that is, without end. Amen.

What do you observe in these things, O Jews? What do you say, or what do you think about what is said concerning the foolish wisdom of the pagans? ‘Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.’ Why? Because, as far as they were concerned, they changed the glory of almighty God, creator, ruler, and governor of all things on land and sea, into the likeness of the image of corruptible and most wretched man. Truly the pagans and their philosophers became fools beyond what can be said, since they changed the glory of the Creator of the world into the likeness of wicked people. Without doubt they became vain in their wicked thoughts, since they preferred images of dead people to the Maker of all and Ruler of all ages [Col. 0413D]. Truly, more than all other people, they had a heart darkened by the shadows of folly and malice, since, changing God’s truth into falsehood as far as they were concerned, they reverently offered to the images of ungodly people the honor due to the divine majesty. These people did not deserve to find God the Father because they did not humbly seek Christ, who is the most straight way, nor wisely receive him; rather, they proudly despised him in their holy works.

“Therefore each person’s first concern is to know what he seeks; the second is to obtain what he seeks. Imperfect wisdom also is, as blessed Isidore, our patron, says [Col. 0414A] [Note: [Col. 0413D] As above], to know where you are heading and not know the road by which you ought to go. For what profit is it if someone, at a time of famine, sees a region of abundance but does not know the road by which to travel there? Behold, everyone seeks his homeland; but if he has lost the road, he proceeds by wandering, not by making progress; and the more he walks, the farther he removes himself from what he seeks. Thus whoever abandons the royal road—that is, Christ—even if he sees abundance, sees it from afar, because, unless he is on the road—that is, through Christ—how can he approach it, that is, the heavenly homeland? But if, travelling through the desert, he encounters the lion—that is, the devil—let him reproach himself because he did not rightly believe in Christ when he became caught in the devil’s jaws.”

[Col. 0414B] Therefore, if—as is true—the righteous lives by faith, the peoples of the nations and their philosophers, who despise Christ on account of the weakness of our flesh which he mercifully assumed for the redemption of humankind, and refuse to believe him to be true God, cannot live by faith. For they neither profess with their mouths that they wish to hold that faith unto true salvation nor preserve it by upright conduct. Therefore, O Jews, I urge you with the greatest earnestness that, after the Incarnation, Nativity, Passion, and wondrous Ascension into heaven of Jesus Christ, God and man, you no longer set before yourselves the traditions of Pharisees and Sadducees as an example for living. Flee with all seriousness the false sect of heretics and the foolish wisdom of philosophers [Col. 0414C]. Receive Christ’s Baptism with devout mind; faithfully submit yourselves to the sacraments of ecclesiastical religion, so that by living justly and piously you may deserve to attain fellowship with God’s elect. Let no impulse of diabolical temptation move you from the state of true faith; let no suggestion of the ancient enemy turn you from knowledge of Christ; let no persuasion of perverse teaching cast you down from the uprightness of Catholic faith. Although wicked temptation strikes at the mind, nevertheless let the light of true faith never depart from your attention. Although a perverse suggestion attempts to turn the mind aside from the straightness of faith, nevertheless let the light of truth, which is Christ, always remain in the mind.

[Note: [Col. 0413] Gregory, *Morals*, book VIII, ch. 6, and the *Patericon*, on Genesis, ch. 3.] In this present life sin is by no means abandoned through the practice of righteousness in such a way that that righteousness remains unshaken. For although uprightness now drives fault out from the dwelling-place of the heart, yet the fault which is repelled stands at the doors of our thought and continually knocks to be admitted again. Moses indicated this spiritually when he narrated in bodily terms the successive moments of time, saying: ‘Light was made’; and shortly afterward he adds: ‘Evening came’ (Gen. 1). For the Creator of all, foreknowing human fault, then expressed in time what is now enacted in the mind. Light is said to be followed by evening, because the shadow of temptation surely follows the light of uprightness. But because the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, it is said that evening, not night, came [Col. 0415A]; for temptation often conceals the light of righteousness in the hearts of the upright, but does not wholly extinguish it.

Therefore, O Jews, I urge you to let the light of Christ’s faith and love remain continually in your hearts. Although punishment compels you, although tortures rage, although death threatens, although some worldly power stubbornly constrains you to depart from the uprightness of Catholic faith, nevertheless do not in any way give it your assent. For it is better to die well than to live badly. It is far better to subject the body to various torments for the truth of faith than to depart from faith in the holy Trinity.

What do you say, O Jews? What objections do you make, or what do you answer to these things? I would like to know what disposition or faith [Col. 0415B] you have. To this you answer us in the form of a question, saying: “Why, O Christians, who boast that you are in a special sense God’s servants above the other nations under heaven, do you receive the Old and New Testaments, give credence to the sayings of the prophets, and eat unclean animals which God prohibited in the Law? Why do you persistently urge us to receive the sacraments of ecclesiastical religion when you live blameworthily?” To this we answer in return that both the things granted in the Old Testament and those prohibited must, as we have often testified, be understood not carnally but spiritually. Therefore we believe that those gifts of the Lord which we receive with thanksgiving are by no means unclean [Col. 0415C], but clean. In the animals rejected as unclean, however, uncleanness itself is not meant, but wicked habits, by which people are made unclean. Therefore everything created by God is good, and none of those things received in the Lord’s name with thanksgiving is to be rejected.

[Note: [Col. 0415D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 9.] What then? In animals, as has been said, are understood human habits, actions, and wills, through which people themselves become clean or unclean. But now let us see how the Law distinguishes clean things from unclean. “Every animal,” it says, “which has a divided hoof and chews the cud, among cattle you shall eat” (Lev. 11). In saying this, it distinguished not cattle but human habits. Thus those people are clean who continually chew, as it were, the commandments of God as food with their mouths. They also divide the hoof, because, believing the two Testaments, namely the Law and the Gospels, they walk with a strong step in innocence, righteousness, and life. You wretched and pitiable Jews also chew the words of the Law, but you do not divide the hoof because you do not receive the two Testaments. Therefore you are altogether unclean, because you do not set the steps of faith in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Heretics, indeed, though they divide the hoof by believing in God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit and receiving the two Testaments [Col. 0416A], are nevertheless likewise unclean because they do not chew with their mouths the teaching of truth.

Again Scripture adds, saying: “Whatever among all things produced in the waters has fins and scales—what does not have them shall be abominable to you” (ibid.). Therefore, insofar as the rough scales of fish are accounted clean, bristling, hairy, firm, and weighty habits are approved. What does it mean that the Law says, “You shall not eat camel,” unless it condemns, by the example of that animal, a shapeless life twisted by crimes? When the Law forbids the pig for food, it surely rebukes a life that is filthy and muddy and delights in the foulness of vices. And when Scripture condemns the hare, it condemns men softened into women [Col. 0416B]. Who would make food from the body of a weasel? Yet in declaring that a weasel is not to be taken as food, it rebukes theft among people. Who would ever eat a lizard even if the Law had not prohibited it? Yet in forbidding it to be taken for food, it undoubtedly hates the unstable variety of a perverse life. Who could also eat a stellio, even if the Law had not strongly prohibited it? “The stellio,” as blessed Isidore says in the book of the *Etymologies* [Note: [Col. 0415D] Book XII, ch. 4], “is a kind of serpent, named from its color. Its back is painted over with spots lying like stars. Of it Ovid says:

> [lacuna] and it has a name suited to its color,  
> being starred over its body with varied spots.

[Col. 0416C] This creature is said to be so hostile to scorpions that its very appearance brings them fear and paralysis.” Therefore, when the Law says that the stellio is not to be taken for food, it figuratively shows that the blotches of a perverse life are to be detested and abhorred. Who would eat a hawk, kite, or eagle even if the Law had not forbidden these at all? Therefore, when it forbids the foregoing birds to be eaten, it figuratively hates all rapacious, violent, and criminally living persons. When it says that the owl is not to be eaten, it figuratively drives far from the fellowship of the faithful the enemies of true light and those who flee the light of truth. Who would ever eat a vulture even if the Law said it was edible? Yet in declaring that it is not to be taken for food [Col. 0416D], it figuratively detests those who seek gain from another’s death. Likewise, when it forbids the raven to be taken for food, it figuratively rejects the unclean desires of people. When the Law says that the *caladrius* [Note: [Col. 0415D] *Charadrius*] is not to be eaten, it rebukes the garrulous and unrestrained talkativeness of the tongue. [Note: [Col. 0415D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XII, ch. 7.] The *olor* is a bird which the Greeks call *cygnus* (“swan”). It is called *olor* because it is wholly white with feathers. It is called *cygnus* from singing, because it emits the sweetness of song in modulated notes. It sings sweetly because it has a long, curved neck [Col. 0417A]; and a voice forced out through a long and winding passage must produce varied modulations. They relate that in the Hyperborean [Note: [Col. 0417D] “Hiperborean,” i.e. Hyperborean] regions, when cithara-players sing, many *olores*, that is, swans, fly to them and sing exceedingly well in harmony. *Olores* is the Latin name, for in Greek they are called *cygni*. Sailors say that this bird gives them a favorable omen, as Aemilius says:

> The swan, a bird ever most joyful in auspices.  
> Sailors desire it, because it plunges itself into the waves.

Therefore, when the Law says that the swan is not to be eaten, it restrains the pride of the lifted neck. Who would ever eat a bat, even if the Law had not forbidden its being eaten? Yet in declaring that it is not to be eaten, it hates the darkness of the long-standing error of Jews and [Col. 0417B] heretics.

The Law therefore detests these and similar things in animals. They are not blameworthy in the animals themselves, because they were born this way; rather, they are figuratively sought out because they are contrary to nature, arising not from divine institution but from error. But there was once an ancient time, namely the time of the Law, when these figures or shadows had to be practiced or observed by the people, so that they were to abstain from foods which God’s ordinance had indeed commended in Noah’s time but the Law had prohibited. Meat indeed, and [Note: [Col. 0417D] You would look in vain for this concession of wine in the sacred books] wine, were granted for human use after the Flood (Gen. 9). For at the beginning of the world, namely in Adam’s time, nothing had been permitted except what is written: ‘I have given you every fruit-bearing tree and seed-bearing herb for food’ [Col. 0417C] (Gen. 1). Later, however, every animal was given to Noah and his sons for food, and permission for wine was then granted. Thus both those things which the Law permitted people to eat and those which it prohibited are to be understood not literally but spiritually, interpreted in accordance with moral conduct. For it did not speak openly, but obscurely. But after Christ came—who is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Rom. 10)—he opened all that was veiled in the Law, disclosed its obscurities, and clearly revealed all the sacraments which antiquity had woven for us: he himself, the eminent Master, heavenly Teacher, and establisher of disclosed truth. Under him the Apostle Paul now says: ‘All things are clean to the clean; but to those who are defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, but their minds and consciences are defiled’ [Col. 0417D] (Tit. 1).

Hear, O Jews, what I say; listen to what I urge upon you for the salvation of your souls. Whoever abstains from eating meat not by a vow of abstinence but by detesting God’s creation is himself rather to be detested, because he rejects God’s creation granted for human use. For nothing is regarded as defiled or unclean for Christ’s faithful. I do not want you, O Jews, to forget your foregoing objection. You said that we ought not to eat meats prohibited by God in the Law, although we call ourselves, above the other nations under heaven, God’s special [Col. 0418A] worshippers. Truly, as you assert, O Jews, we profess that we are faithful worshippers of the whole holy Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and we bless in his name the creation granted to us by him, and eat it with thanksgiving without hesitation. We clearly prove you to be superstitious in your objection. You are rather to be detested, because you reject as abominable a good creation made by the good God and granted to human beings for the use of life. But we, understanding spiritually the animals which the Law called clean or unclean, bless them in the Lord’s name and receive them with thanksgiving, doubting nothing.

Therefore, O Jews, believe Jesus Christ to be true God [Col. 0418B] and true man; for love of him despise earthly things, and desire to see with the eyes of your heart him reigning at the right hand of God the Father. You will by no means be able to behold in mind him who is exalted above every choir of angels and above everything created unless you endeavor to draw the attention of your heart inward from outward occupations. [Note: [Col. 0418D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XXX, ch. 12, and the *Patericon*, on Genesis, ch. 13.] Nor can we in any way attain the summit of divine contemplation unless we first cease from the occupations of outward life. Know for certain, O Jews, that we cannot perfectly examine ourselves, so as to know that in us one thing is rational and governs and another is animal and governed, unless, hastening to the secret of this silence—that is, contemplation [Col. 0418C]—we are enclosed from every outward disturbance.

Adam sleeping fittingly prefigured this silence of ours, from whose side woman immediately came forth. For whoever is drawn up to understand inward things closes his eyes to visible things; and then he distinguishes within himself both the things which ought to preside manfully and the weaker things which can be subject, so that one thing in him may be able to rule as a man, and another, as a woman, may be ruled.

Therefore let reason hold dominion in your minds, O Jews; let reason choose the virtues, restrain the unlawful impulses of the flesh, and distinguish between good and evil, between good and better. Let true reason, like a man in the heart, hold primacy over all thoughts, and let all the affections of the soul be obedient to it in all things. Let reason guard the virtues in the soul with the utmost diligence, and by the hand of authority manfully drive vices far away from it. Therefore receive the Catholic faith with devout mind, O Jews, and in it act manfully by doing good works. If you are soft and lax in God’s service, you deserve to be reckoned not by a masculine but by a feminine name. Thus the bridegroom, namely Christ, in the Song of spiritual love, says to the bride—that is, the soul devoted to divine contemplation—that she is not to be roused by certain persons occupied with the cares of worldly life: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and hinds of the fields, do not awaken or stir up the beloved until she herself wishes” (Song II). Carnal people within the holy Church sometimes importunately rouse the holy soul, intoxicated with Christ’s love and devoted to contemplation; they desire to entangle it in worldly business, because, seeing it withdraw from their concerns, they judge its life useless. Such persons, as we have said, are quite fittingly called not sons but daughters: because, while cultivating effeminate habits and losing masculine dignity, they are outwardly designated by a feminine name according to what they are held to be inwardly. They are forbidden, under the weight of this adjuration, to awaken the beloved soul: namely, lest they disturb with importunate solicitations the mind which prepares itself to be free for God and desires to cling solely to spiritual pursuits, and lest they cloud the eye of its heart with the darkness of earthly cares. Therefore, as we said, those who do not gird themselves manfully for God’s service, but are weak and lax, are called not sons but daughters.

Let, then, the lower part of reason in your mind, O Jews, stand for the woman; let the higher part of the same reason stand for the man, so that nothing may be done in that mind without its authority or counsel. For this higher part of reason is the man, who according to the Apostle is called the image and glory of God; and that lower part of reason is the woman, who according to the same Apostle is called the glory of the man (I Cor. XI). Between this man and this woman there is, as it were, a certain spiritual marriage and natural union. Therefore the higher part of reason, as we have said, ought like a man to preside and rule in the mind; the lower part, like a woman, ought to be subject and obedient. Hence, as the Apostle says, a man ought not to have a covering upon his head, but a woman ought to have one (ibid.). Let the woman, namely the lower part of reason, obey the man, namely the higher part of reason, in the human mind, and presume to do nothing without its authority. Let reason therefore be mistress in the human mind among handmaids—that is, among righteous thoughts—and queen among sisters, that is, among the corresponding virtues of the soul.

Therefore receive the Catholic faith with devout mind, O Jews, and fulfil the precepts of evangelical instruction not laxly, but manfully and faithfully. As has been said, those who are sluggish and lax in God’s service are called not sons but daughters. Moses undoubtedly foreshadowed this future courage in certain servants of God, and the future sluggishness and weakness of others within the holy Church, when, by the Lord’s command, he said to the children of Israel: “If a woman, having received seed, bears a male child, she shall be unclean seven days; but on the eighth day the infant shall be circumcised; she herself, after sixty days, shall be purified by offering sacrifices. But a woman who has borne a female shall be unclean for two weeks; she cannot be purified on the sixtieth day, but on the eightieth day she shall be clean” (Lev. XII).

[Note: [Col. 0419D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 10.]

There can be no doubt that in these commandments of the Lord certain mysteries of hidden meaning are contained. For the number sixty can signify the whole duration of this present life, because the world was completed in the work of six days. While we remain placed in the flesh, we cannot be wholly pure until the eighth day comes—that is, the age to come—in which, without doubt, the person who turns from evil and girds himself manfully for God’s service will be purified. For his mother, that is, the flesh, will immediately be made clean. In the resurrection he will receive flesh cleansed of vices. But the person who has never resisted sin, who has done nothing manful against the temptations of the flesh, but has remained lax in God’s service and effeminate in all his actions, will be unable, as we think, to be cleansed from his uncleanness either in this present week of the age or in the future one. For if the righteous person, diligent in God’s service, will scarcely—that is, with great labour and effort—be saved, where will the impious person, negligent in God’s service, lax, dissolute, and lukewarm, appear? (Prov. XI).

This aptly applies to what the Lord says in correction to the angel of Laodicea in the Apocalypse: “I know your works: you are neither cold nor hot; but because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Apoc. III). It is as if he said: I know—that is, your works are not hidden from me—namely, that you do not wish to be corrected from your wickedness; for you are neither cold, that is, wholly ignorant of the faith, nor hot, namely, you do not openly deny the faith you have received. Cold is the person who has neither knowledge of God nor works of charity. Hot is the person who, possessing knowledge of God, possesses the ardour of charity. It follows: “But because you are lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth.” We call lukewarm the person who has knowledge of God but lacks the ardour of charity, or who holds faith without works. It is as if he plainly said: But because you are lukewarm, that is, torpid, and neither cold nor hot, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth—that is, remove you from the fellowship of my saints.

Therefore receive the Catholic faith with devout mind, O Jews, and hold it not merely in word but in good works. In God’s service be not lukewarm but diligent, that among the companies of God’s elect you may deserve to be reckoned by the name not of daughters but of sons. Do you not know, miserable and unhappy Jews, that it is pride to refuse obedience to the divine dispensation and always, in all things, to oppose its most just will? How will you be able to be freed from sin or from sin’s punishment—you who, denying, blaspheming, and detesting, proudly disdain to believe, or even to hear, down to this present day, those things which from the beginning of the world God the Father made known concerning the Incarnation of his Son through figures, declared through the oracles of the prophets, and openly revealed to the whole world through the preaching of the apostles? How, so to speak, will you be able to rule yourselves when you are rebellious and opposed to God?

Know for certain, O Jews, that you will by no means be able to overcome vices and sins unless you are subject with your whole heart to almighty God. We recognize this from the fact that Adam, as soon as in sinning he proudly set himself against God, felt the lust of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XXVI, ch. 13, and *Paterius, on Genesis*, ch. 19.]

Therefore, whoever truly wishes to preserve the purity of chastity must always be humble before God in all things. Continence of the flesh must be preserved through the guarding of humility. For if the spirit is devoutly held down beneath God, the flesh is not illicitly raised up against the spirit. The spirit indeed has flesh entrusted to its dominion, provided that it recognizes the lawful claims of servitude owed to its Lord. But if, as said above, it proudly despises its Creator, it rightly finds warfare in the flesh subject to it. Thus that first disobedient person, Adam, as soon as he sinned by pride, covered [or: *covered over*] his private parts with leaves (Gen. III), because as soon as the human spirit offered insult to God, it immediately felt the insult of the flesh. And the one who refused to be subject to his Creator lost the right over the subject flesh which he governed, so that the disgrace of his disobedience might recoil upon himself, and, conquered, he might declare what he had lost when he was exalted.

I do not wish you to be ignorant, O Jews, that almost all evils have been transmitted as punishment through the sin of that first man to the whole human race.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] Supplement: “into.”]

“Accordingly,” as our patron Blessed Isidore says,

[Note: [Col. 0421D] *Sentences*, book I, ch. 9.]

“whatever evils are seen serve us partly by origin and partly by fault. Perverse people curse many things in creation: fire because it burns; iron because it kills; a beast because it bites. But, failing to consider their benefits, a person accuses in them what he ought rather to impute to himself, since these things became harmful through his sin, though before sin they had in part been subject to man himself. Thus the things that harm us are evil to us through our fault, not through their own nature. For light, although good, is harmful to diseased eyes; and then the defect belongs to the eyes, not to the light; and so with the rest. Therefore, when a person is scourged by the stings of creatures and the adversities of the elements, the punishment of sin requires that a human being who has proudly rebelled against God should suffer adverse things from what is beneath him. Hence it is also written in the Book of Wisdom: ‘The world of the earth will fight for him against the foolish’ (Wis. V).”

It is therefore deservedly on account of sins that things naturally favourable are changed for human beings into adversities.

[Note: [Col. 0422D] Printed edition: “adverse things.”]

Hence Solomon says: “Creation burns fiercely in punishment against the unjust, and is gentler in doing good to those who trust in God” (Wis. XVI). Therefore, as said above, flesh will not be subject to soul, nor vices to reason, if the mind is not subject to its Creator. But all things beneath us are rightly made subject to us when we are subject to him by whom they were made subject to us. For even the things which appear subject to one who is not subject to God are rather things to which that person is subject, because he subjects his own will to love for things which he thinks are subject to him.

Therefore, if you truly desire, O Jews, to overcome sins and vices, submit yourselves with faithful mind to the rule of Jesus Christ; receive his baptism with devout purpose; and thereafter presume to do nothing contrary to his will. Let the members of the body therefore be subject to the soul, vices to reason, and the human being to the Creator, so that, aided by his grace, having shaken the yoke of servitude from your necks and now cast off the reproach of unbelief by rightly believing, you may deserve to be joined to the fellowship of Christians.

§ XXX.—

The Church does not expel bodily lepers, but those who follow false doctrine. Those among them who deny the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as offending against the first principle of all things, have leprosy upon the head. He enumerates among these Valentinians, Marcionists, Photinians, Manicheans, Arians, and others; he reports and refutes their heresies from Isidore and the Master of the *Sentences*. He likewise refutes the Anthropomorphites, who attribute a body to God, and with great learning in Scripture explains the passages that seem to ascribe human form and bodily affections to God. In order to refute the Eutychians, he introduces Paul, Daniel, and Stephen, who saw Christ, according to his humanity, enter into the holy place—that is, heaven—and standing at the right hand of God the Father. Those, therefore, who follow heretical doctrine must be shown to the priests of the Church, so that they may be reconciled by them; for they are infected with leprosy rather than those whom diverse bodily infirmities waste away.

What do you say, O Jews, what do you answer, or what objection do you raise?

[Note: [Col. 0422D] Another manuscript begins: “I have, O Jews, a desire to know whether,” etc.]

Do you now believe Jesus Christ to be true God and true man, or do you still intend to remain in the malice of your unbelief? Do not delay to disclose to us what you are considering in your minds; with divine grace now inspiring us, you will find us prepared with an answer.

In answering us thus, O Jews, you raise this objection, saying: O Christians, you who receive the Old Testament spiritually, who read the five books of Moses, who believe that the prophets spoke under the inward teaching of the Holy Spirit, who affirm that the law was given by God through the hand of Moses on Mount Sinai—why do you permit lepers of your nation, and those having continual scab and scars upon their bodies, to live among you, and why do you not, according to the law, cast them outside the camp? In answer to this question of yours, O Jews, we first say what we have often declared: namely, that after Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, the law is to be understood not carnally but spiritually. Therefore, the lepers of whom you speak—whether of our nation or indeed of any foreign people—we do not permit to dwell with us within the holy Church; rather, with the greatest vigilance, we drive them far from us as enemies. Let us all therefore hear together, O Jews, what the Lord says to Moses concerning lepers.

The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “A man in whose flesh or skin there shall arise a differing colour, or a pustule, or something as though shining—that is, a plague of leprosy—shall be brought to Aaron the priest, or to one of his sons. When he sees the leprosy in the skin and the hairs changed to a white colour, it is a plague of leprosy, and by his judgment the man shall be separated from the camp” (Lev. XIII). I urge you, O Jews, diligently to hear and more attentively store up in your minds what this history, spiritually expounded, signifies.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 11.]

For leprosy signifies false doctrine. Thus lepers are not unreasonably understood as heretics, who, lacking the unity of true faith, introduce various doctrines of error and mingle true things with false, just as leprosy defiles human bodies by altering them in various and different places. We find that the lawgiver set down six kinds of this leprosy in a human being: first, that of the head and beard; second, that of baldness and receding baldness; third, that of flesh and skin; fourth, that of the skin of the body and a white scar with redness; fifth, that of an ulcer and scar; sixth, that of a burn.

I urge you, O Jews, diligently to hear what this aforesaid bodily leprosy, spiritually expounded, signifies. He bears leprosy upon his head who sins concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which is the head and principle of all creatures. Or he bears leprosy upon his head who sins against Christ, who is the head of man—indeed, who is head of the whole Church (I Cor. XI). You undoubtedly bear this leprosy upon your heads, O Jews, as you cannot wholly deny, since you deny that Jesus Christ is true God and true man—the one through whom God the Father redeemed you from Egyptian bondage and established you in the land of promise, and who moreover mercifully rescued the whole world from the devil’s power. Therefore, so long as you deny Christ, you will be smitten with the leprosy of unbelief, so that you cannot attain the fellowship of God’s elect. Valentinians, Marcionists, Photinians, Manicheans, Arians, Sabellians, Macedonians, Anthropomorphites, Priscillians,

[Note: [Col. 0423D] Priscillianists.]

Donatists, Nestorians, and Eutychians also bear leprosy on the scalp, because they defend the faithlessness of their error with open cunning.

Let us hear what Isidore, teacher of Spain, says in book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Etymologies* about the aforementioned heretics designated by leprosy.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] “Why the Valentinian heretics are so called. They hold concerning Christ that he assumed no bodily thing from the Virgin, but passed through her as through a pipe. They are refuted by this argument.” Thus the *Summa* of another manuscript.]

“The Valentinian heretics are called after a certain Valentinus, a follower of Plato, who introduced Aeons—that is, ages—into the origin of God the Creator; they also assert that Christ assumed no bodily thing from the Virgin, but passed through her as through a pipe.” This, however, is false, because the Son of God did not pass through the Virgin emptily, as through a pipe, but assumed from her the true substance of flesh, in which, being a true human being among human beings and without sin, he lived, and according to which he could be seized, bound, scourged, crucified, killed, buried, and rise from the tomb.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] *Sentences*, book III, distinction 1, “Diligently.”]

It must be known that neither God the Father nor the Holy Spirit assumed flesh, but the Son alone, so that he who was the Son of God in divinity might himself become the son of the Virgin in humanity, lest the name “Son” be transferred to another who was not Son by eternal generation. Therefore the Son of God became the Son of man: according to the truth of nature, Son of God from God; and according to the truth of nature, son of the Virgin from the virgin; so that the truth of the begotten one might possess the name of Son by birth in both nativities, not merely by appellation, and that one Son might be true God and true man.

[Note: [Col. 0424D] Distinction 3, “And because.”]

And because in humankind the whole human nature had been conceived in defect, he assumed the whole of it—that is, soul and flesh—in order to heal and sanctify the whole. Therefore the Son of God did not, as the Valentinian heretics assert, pass through the Virgin as through a pipe, assuming none of those things which belong to human nature; rather, he assumed the whole nature—soul and flesh and their properties or accidents—not flesh without soul, nor soul without reason, but flesh and soul also with their senses. Hence John of Damascus says: “The Word of God assumed everything which he planted in our nature, namely the body, the intellectual soul, and their idioms, that is, their properties. For the whole Word of God the Father assumed the whole human nature; for what is not assumed is not healed.” Let, therefore, the heretic Valentinus and all his disciples blush, who falsely say that the Son of God did not assume a true body from the Virgin Mother of God, but displayed an apparent flesh to those looking upon him.

“The Marcionists [or Marcionites]

[Note: [Col. 0424D] The Marcionist heretics, who assert one good and another just God, are refuted, because there is one principle of all creatures—although the three divine persons are only one principle.]

are heretics,” as Blessed Isidore says,

[Note: [Col. 0424D] *Etymologies*, as above.]

“named after Marcion, a Stoic philosopher. Following Cerdo’s doctrine, he maintained that one God was good and another just, as though there were two principles of creation and goodness.” This man too thought wrongly when he said that there are two gods. For there is one God in heaven and on earth, the principle of all creatures, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom all things subsist. For “principle” is said in a relation marking reference to certain things.

[Note: [Col. 0424D] *Sentences*, book I, distinction 29, “And besides.”]

Thus God the Father is a principle, the Son is a principle, and the Holy Spirit is a principle, but in different respects. For the Father is called a principle in relation to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the fourth book *On the Trinity*: “The Father is the principle of the whole Godhead, because he is from no one. For he has none from whom he is or from whom he proceeds; but from him the Son is begotten and the Holy Spirit proceeds. Therefore the Father is principle without principle; the Son, principle from principle, as light from light, brightness from brightness; the Holy Spirit, principle from both, that is, from Father and Son. This does not mean that the Father is prior to the Son or the Holy Spirit, but that with them he is the one principle of all creatures. These three are therefore called not three principles but one principle of all creatures, because in one and the same way they are the principle of all things.” Therefore the Apostle, understanding that this Trinity is the one principle of all things, says: “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI).

For when we hear that all things are from God, as Blessed Augustine says in the book *On the Nature of the Good*, we must certainly understand all natures—that is, all things that are natural. Sins are not from him, because they do not preserve nature but corrupt it, and they arise from the will of sinners. Therefore the Father with the Son and Holy Spirit is the one principle of all things that exist naturally. Truly the Son too is the principle of creatures: when the Jews asked who he was, he answered, saying: “I am the principle, who also speak to you” (John VIII). Therefore, when he said that he was principle, he wished to show that he was Creator of all creatures together with God the Father, because through him God the Father created all things from nothing. Thus the Son, like the Father, is principle of creation, because all things were made through him. But when we call the Father principle and the Son principle, we do not show two principles of all creatures, but one, because Father and Son together are one principle in relation to creation, just as they are one Creator. Nor can or should we deny that the Holy Spirit is rightly called principle, since we do not separate him from the designation or operation of Creator. Of him we read that Blessed Paul, having enumerated the gifts of the same Holy Spirit, said: “One and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as he wills” (I Cor. XII). Therefore, with Father and Son, the Holy Spirit is one principle in relation to creation, not two or three principles. Marcion therefore thought wrongly about God and departed far from the path of truth when he asserted that there were two gods or two principles of creatures, whereas the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God, one Creator, and one principle of all things. He should therefore not be heard or joined to the fellowship of believers, but should rather be driven far from the Church as a leper, since he did not acknowledge the one true God who contains, governs, and embraces all things, but, blinded by the darkness of error, asserted that there are two gods.

“The Photinian heretics,” as Isidore, teacher of Spain, says,

[Note: [Col. 0425D] The Photinians affirm that Christ was conceived from Mary through Joseph by marital intercourse.]

[Note: [Col. 0425D] As above.]

“are named after Photinus, bishop of Sirmium in Galatian Greece, who revived the heresy of the Ebionites and asserted that Christ was conceived from Mary through Joseph by marital intercourse.” This man too lied altogether in his assertion. Mary certainly conceived Jesus Christ from the Holy Spirit without a man’s embrace; she bore him without defilement, giving birth without pain or corruption. For she was a virgin before conception, a virgin in conception, a virgin in childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. She, the queen of heaven and earth, remained a virgin before the coming of her Son, a virgin at her Son’s birth, and a virgin after her Son was born.

[Note: [Col. 0426D] *Sentences*, book III, distinction 3, “It is asked.”]

When the Holy Spirit came upon her, he entirely cleansed her from sin and also freed her from the tinder of sin, either wholly emptying that tinder or weakening and diminishing it, so that thereafter no occasion for sinning could exist for her; and he prepared in her the power of begetting without a man’s seed. The words of the holy Gospel testify to this, where the angel, addressing the Virgin, says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; and that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I). To him the sacred Virgin humbly assents, saying: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). Hence John of Damascus says: “After the assent

[Note: [Col. 0426D] The Master: ‘consent.’]

of the most holy Virgin, the Holy Spirit came beforehand into her according to the Lord’s word which the angel spoke, cleansing her and preparing her to receive the power of the divine Word, and at the same time preparing her for generation. Then the wisdom and power of God Most High, existing in itself—the Son of God, *homoousios*, that is, consubstantial with the Father—overshadowed her as divine seed; and from the most holy and pure blood of the Virgin he united to himself flesh of our ancient mixture, animated by a rational and intellectual soul, not sowing it but creating it through the Holy Spirit.”

From these things it is clearly apparent what Blessed Augustine says in the book *On Faith to Peter*: namely, that the flesh of the Word was conceived and assumed at the same time, and that the same flesh—indeed the entire Virgin—was made chaste from every stain of sin by the Holy Spirit’s prior coming. To her was granted the power of bearing in a new manner, so that the conception of God-and-man Jesus Christ might be accomplished in the Virgin’s womb without intercourse with a man and without the lust of concupiscence. Therefore that flesh which the Son of God deigned to unite to himself from the Virgin was not conceived from marital intercourse, as the utterly false heretic Photinus asserted, but was assumed through the Holy Spirit—that is, through the operation of the Holy Spirit—without sin and born without defect. Yet do not suppose, most wicked heretic Photinus, that this flesh is of heavenly, airy, or any other nature, but that it is of the same nature as the flesh of all human beings. This heretic Photinus also, O Jews, as you see, bears leprosy upon his head, since he publicly blasphemes Christ and preaches perverse doctrines about him.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Isidore, as above.]

The Manichean heretics

[Note: [Col. 0427D] Why the Manicheans are so called. They affirm two substances, namely good and evil, and assert that souls flow forth from God as from a kind of fountain. It is shown how nothing is evil by nature, although through our improper use it sometimes becomes harmful. From Isidore’s statements: that the soul does not flow forth from God; of what nature it is; and when it is introduced into the body; and what the ancient philosophers thought concerning its introduction. Although it is changed only in its affections, in which respect it turns toward sin.]

arose from a certain Persian called Maneth.

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Manes.]

He introduced two natures and substances, namely good and evil, and asserted that souls flow forth from God as from a fountain. He too is rightly reckoned among heretics, because ecclesiastical writers prove that he advanced falsehoods in his assertion. For in saying that there are two substances or two natures, one evil and one good, he undoubtedly strayed far from the path of truth. God did not create evil; rather, all the things he made are not only good but very good.

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, ch. 9.]

Evil was not created by the devil either, but discovered; and therefore nothing is evil because “without God nothing was made.” But God never made evil. There was not anywhere or at any time an evil from which the devil might be made evil; but since evil is a vice, an angel who was good became evil by pride, and evil is therefore rightly said to have been discovered by him.

“There is no nature of evil,” says Blessed Isidore,

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Ibid.]

“because every nature is either unchangeable, as God is, or changeable, as a creature is. Evil, however, is no nature, because, when it enters a good nature, it makes it defective. When it departs, the nature remains, but the evil which was present is nowhere. From the fact that vice harms nature, it is recognized that vice is not nature, because nothing natural harms. When a good nature is condemned because of an evil will, that evil will itself bears witness to the goodness of nature, testifying that it is so good that God does not leave it unpunished for evil. Heretics believe that the mind was created by God and vice by the devil; hence they suppose there are two natures, good and evil. But vices are not natures; and though they truly arise from the devil, they are nevertheless not creatures. For what reason did God permit the condition of evil to arise, except that he might adorn the good of nature by contrary evils? This pattern is also found in words. The pattern is called *antitheton*”

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Greek: *antitethon*.]

“which in Latin is termed an opposite or counterposition. Fine expression results when contrary things are set forth immediately after favourable things. Thus evil is mingled in things so that the good of nature might stand out in comparison with evil.”

Therefore, as the heretic Maneth asserted,

[Note: [Col. 0428D] Manes.]

God did not create a good and an evil nature; rather, all things that he made are very good. Therefore nothing is evil by nature, since even those things in creation which seem punitive and harmful are good and beneficial if used well, but harmful if used badly.

But even if some perhaps judge this doubtful or false, surely no one is permitted to deny what is remarkable in serpents. For, as Blessed Bishop Fulgentius says in his sermon *On the Incarnation of Christ*, no one is ignorant that vipers are naturally venomous, since by their deadly bite they kill much more quickly than scorpions kill with their venomous sting. Yet, in order to show that it is not malice of nature but unsuitability that harms, we know that remedies against viper bites are made from viper flesh suitably mixed with other substances; and that help is beneficially given not only to those struck by scorpions but also to those bitten by vipers. Who here would not marvel at God’s wisdom? Who would not magnify his goodness and praise his providence? He does not restrain his mercies in anger: from the very source from which he caused dangers to arise for sinners, he ordained that aids should be supplied to those in danger, so that we might experience, through his goodness, benefits from those things whose inconveniences we feel on account of our iniquity. Who could adequately set forth in words the Creator’s praise, when he made one and the same viper so that it bears in itself both death and remedy, and, while alive, inflicts destruction, yet when dead restores health; both brings and repels life’s ruin; and the venom instilled by a serpent’s tooth is extinguished by the flesh of that same serpent? Thus the viper, which alive served human weakness and death, serves life and salvation when dead. Who, I ask, does these things except him to whom the Church sings, “Mercy and judgment”?

Who does not know how harmful the substance called *scammonia* is to healthy persons if taken alone, and how beneficial to sick persons if suitably mixed with other substances?
