Let me also speak of things often desired by everyone, and whose daily use is found necessary not only for health but even for human life itself: let us consider bread and wine, neither of which is suitable for one suffering from fever. For we see physicians forbid sick persons to drink wine and sometimes even to eat bread. But this occurs not because bread or wine are evil, but because they do not suit an invalid. For once they are received suitably, they are food, preserve strength, and sustain health. Yet immoderate consumption of them takes strength away even from the robust, compelling the healthy to become sick. Behold how great is the power of the Creator God’s order and the suitability of things, to which immoderation and unsuitability are opposed. When nature is harmed by these, it is not natural malice but an accidental infirmity that is found—a fact readily observed in nearly all creatures by anyone who considers goods created by the highest Good in such a way as to recognize in them their inexplicable and inexpressible Creator. Thus he himself is to be loved above all, since even in those things which we experience as punitive because of our iniquity, he is found merciful and just: he relieves the weak from the very source by which he crushes the obstinate. And because misery immediately followed humanity upon preceding pride, the merciful and just Lord applies relief for misery from the very source from which he imposes the burden of pride. Therefore no creature is evil, as was said above, since even the things in creatures that appear punitive and harmful are good and beneficial if used well, but harmful if used badly. Creation must therefore be evaluated thus: through our improper use, not through its own very good nature, it is sometimes made harmful.

Maneth the heretic also subsequently asserted, among other things, that souls flow forth from God as though from some fountain. Yet even in this assertion, as in the rest, he strayed far from the rule of truth when he declared that souls flow forth from God. For the soul is not a divine substance, but a noble creature of divine condescension. It has been granted to the soul by God to possess the gift of rational understanding, not a share in the divine essence. But let us hear what blessed Isidore says concerning it in the first book of the *Sentences*, chapter 12:

> “The soul is the life of the body; God is the life of the soul. And as the body is dead without the soul, so the soul is dead without God. The soul of a human being is not the human being; rather, the body, which was made from earth, is alone the human being. But when the soul dwells in the body, through its participation in the body it receives the name of ‘human.’ Thus the Apostle also says that not the flesh but the soul was made in God’s image. Therefore some wrongly believe the human soul to be bodily, although,” as blessed Isidore says, “it was made in God’s image in this respect: that, although it was not immutable as God is, it might nevertheless exist incorporeally, as God does. Souls are like angels: they have a beginning, but no end. For among things, some are temporal, some perpetual, and some everlasting. Temporal things are those which have beginning and ending; perpetual things, those which have a beginning but no end; everlasting things, those which have neither beginning nor end.”

Blessed Isidore says in the same first book of the *Sentences*:

> “The soul is not a part of the divine substance or nature, nor does it exist before it is joined to the body; rather, it is created when the body is created, into which it appears to be introduced or mingled.”

Therefore Maneth and his disciples the Manichaeans lied when they assert that the soul possesses a divine substance or nature. For God creates it from nothing when, through it, he gives life to the body in its mother’s womb.

> “The opinions of philosophers also say that the soul exists before it is joined to the body; but no evidence establishes this as true. For whether we existed previously, we ourselves do not know; nor has any truly wise person said that we do know. Therefore one should not inquire into that which is made more troubling by inquiry. Pagans and heretics attempt to dispute about the soul; but how can those who do not know the Creator in whose image it was made rightly think anything about it? Therefore they have said many things worthy of error. The soul is mutable,” as Isidore, master of the *Etymologies*, says [Note: [Col. 0429D] This doctor is supplied here from another manuscript.], “not locally, but temporally, in its affections. The body, however, is mutable both in place and in time, because it is changed in time and altered in place. What change of places is to the body, mutability of thoughts is to the soul. This variation of evil motion attached itself to the mind when the first human, withdrawing from the contemplation of eternal things, refused to remain in him from whom he wickedly withdrew; and, by a just condemnation, became unstable and flowed away amid the shifting seizure of things. The soul indeed possesses much splendor from its own nature, but it is darkened by its mingling with the flesh in which it is held enclosed. For from that side it is turned toward the weakness of sin, as Solomon testifies, saying: ‘The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things’ [Wisdom 9].”

We have set forth these matters from the authorities of the holy Fathers in order to refute the false assertion of the Manichaeans and strengthen the catholic faith. Now let us again listen carefully to what Isidore, doctor of Spain, says concerning the sect of the Arians.

[Col. 0430C] “The Arians [Note: [Col. 0429D] Since they do not acknowledge the Son as divine, the Arians assert different substances in the Trinity: one, namely, of the Father and another of the Son. Thus they maintain that Christ is not true God but a creature. Their claims are refuted by the sayings of the doctors.],” he says, “arose from Arius, a presbyter of Alexandria. Failing to acknowledge the Son as coeternal with God the Father, he asserted different substances in the Trinity, contrary to what Jesus Christ himself, God and man, says to God the Father: ‘I and the Father are one’ [John 10].” [Note: [Col. 0430D] *Etymologies*, as cited above.]

The Arians themselves are said to prove that the Father is of one substance and the Son of another, because the former is unbegotten and the latter begotten [Note: [Col. 0430D] *I Sentences*, distinction 9, “Now.”]. They must be answered thus: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet he who is the Son is not himself the Father, nor is he who is the Father himself the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit himself either the Father or the Son. For there is one essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in which the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. The Son is begotten of the Father; therefore the Father is one and the Son another. Yet the Father did not exist before the Son, nor before the Holy Spirit, for the three persons are coeternal with one another.

But against this Arius the heretic says, as Ambrose reports in the first book *On the Trinity*: “Everything that is born has a beginning; and therefore, because the Son is born, he has a beginning and began to exist.” Thus it was spoken from the mouth of heretics. For Arius himself, presbyter and heretic, is reported—as blessed Augustine recalls in the sixth book *On the Trinity*—to have said: “If he is Son, he was born; and if he was born, there was a time when the Son was not.”

Augustine the catholic replies against Arius the heretic:

> “Whoever says this does not understand that to be born of the eternal God is to be eternal, so that the Son may be coeternal with the Father, just as the radiance which is produced and diffused from fire is coeval with it, and would be coeternal if the fire were eternal.”

Likewise, in the same book, Saint Augustine objects against the same heretic Arius:

> “If the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, and God was never without power and wisdom, then the Son is coeternal with God the Father. The Apostle says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God [Col. 0431B]. Therefore either there was no time when the Son was not, or at some time God did not possess power and wisdom—which is madness to say. For it is certain that God has always possessed wisdom; therefore he has always possessed the Son.”

Blessed Ambrose likewise replied to this Arian question as follows: “I confess the Son to be from God the Father; I shudder at what remains of impiety.” [Note: [Col. 0431D] Better than the reading *fidem* in the edition.]

Again he adds:

> “It is written in the Old Testament—to name only one passage among many—‘Before me no other God was, and after me there shall not be’ [Isaiah 43]. Who says this: the Father or the Son? If the Son says, ‘Before me there was no other God,’ then if the Father says, ‘After me there shall not be,’ the former, namely the Son, has no predecessor, and the latter, namely the Father, has no successor. For the Father is known in the Son and the Son in the Father. When you say ‘Father,’ you designate his Son, because no one is father to himself. When you name the Son, you also confess the Father, because no one is son to himself. Thus neither can the Son exist without the Father nor the Father without the Son. Therefore the Father always exists, and the Son likewise always exists.”

[Note: [Col. 0431D] *III Sentences*, distinction 11, “It is customary.”] This was the perfidy of Arius the heretical presbyter, as is read: falsely asserting different substances in the Trinity, he said that Christ was not true God but a creature. But the wretch was foolish, as John the Evangelist testifies, saying of Christ’s divinity and eternity: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This [Col. 0431D] was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him” [John 1]—that is, every creature. He does not say “all things” except those that were made, that is, every creature. From this it clearly appears that he through whom all things were made was not himself made. And if he was not made, he is not a creature. But if he is not a creature, he is of the same substance as the Father. For every substance which is not God is a creature, and whatever is not a creature is God. But if the Son is not of the same substance as the Father, then he is a created substance. And if he is a created substance, not all things were made through him. But because he is truly not a created substance, he is of one substance with God the Father.

Therefore, that we may prove Arius the heretic—who asserted that Christ is a creature—to have lied in his own objection, let us take testimony from the words of the same Jesus Christ, God and man. For he said to his disciples: “Going into the whole world, preach the Gospel to every creature” [Mark 16]. Thus, in saying “every creature,” he omitted none. Let Arius the presbyter therefore be ashamed of his objection and repent of his presumption. For if, as he lies, Christ were a creature, he would command the Gospel to be preached to himself and would be subject to apostolic teaching. [Note: [Col. 0431D] A corrupt passage, to be corrected from the edition thus: “and he would be subject to futility, because, as the Apostle testifies, every creature is subject to futility.”] Therefore Christ is not a creature but the Creator, who, in saying [Note: [Col. 0431D] “To be instructed.”] “to every creature,” assigned a task to his disciples.

Therefore Arius, that unhappy presbyter, was lying and perfidious in his assertion; because he denied that Christ is true God, he burst open in the middle and all his entrails were spilled out [Acts 1], and he fell face-down prostrate. His foul mouth, polluted by those things through which he had denied Christ, received from the same Jesus Christ, God and man, a punishment worthy of his impiety. You Jews plainly recognize that Arius the presbyter, as stated above, bore in his head the leprosy of heretical perversity, since he publicly blasphemed Christ and asserted that he was not of the same substance as God the Father. Holy Church unquestionably rejects him and all the adversaries of the catholic faith named above, and drives them far away from herself as stained with the leprosy of heretical perversity.

“There was besides a certain heretic [Note: [Col. 0431D] The Sabellians affirm one person of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. By David’s testimony the person of the Son is shown to be other than that of the Father, although such generation surpasses every understanding. By other testimonies, the person of the Holy Spirit is shown to be other than that of the Father and the Son.] named Noctus [Note: [Col. 0432D] Noetus.],” as blessed Isidore says, “from whom the Noctian [Note: [Col. 0432D] Noetian.] heretics arose.” [Note: [Col. 0432D] *Etymologies*, as cited above.] The Sabellians too are said to have sprung from the same heretic Noctus [Note: [Col. 0432D] Noetus.]. Sabellius is reported to have been his disciple; from Sabellius’s name they became especially known, and hence were called Sabellians. “They assert that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one person.”

But the Sabellians plainly lied in their assertion that God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one person. Tell us, unhappy Sabellians, estranged from the light of truth: if God is one person, why did David the prophet, instructed by the Holy Spirit, say in the Psalm: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” [Psalm 109]? Tell us: who is this Lord who said to the Lord, “Sit at my right hand”? Without doubt one is he who said, “Sit at my right hand,” and another he to whom he said, “Sit.” If, therefore, as you cannot deny, one spoke to another, then assuredly the Father and the Son are two and not one—two in persons, I say, but one in essence. For God the Father placed his Son, Jesus Christ, God and man, at his right hand after the triumph of his most victorious passion and resurrection; and this is what it means to say, “Sit at my right hand.”

Observe, senseless Sabellians: if God were one person, he would by no means have said to himself, “Sit at my right hand.” But because the Father is one in person and the Son another, the Father said to the Son: “Sit at my right hand.” The Father is one in person and the Son another, but in essence the Father and the Son are one God.

But if, Sabellians, you refuse to give credence to the aforementioned authority and intend still to remain in your perfidy, I want you to answer what I shall ask. If God is one person, who is he to whom God said in the Psalm: “With you is sovereignty in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” [Psalm 109]? Did God speak to himself before the morning star—that is, before any creature was made—or could he beget himself? By no means. For it is impossible for anyone to beget himself. To whom, then, did he say, before making any bodily or spiritual creature, “I begot you”? Tell us, Sabellians, enemies of truth: to whom did God say, “I begot you”? But since, partly through malice and partly through ignorance, you cannot answer, I—preceded, accompanied, and followed by God’s grace—will unfold for you the spiritual meaning of this verse. Therefore I warn you, foolish and perfidious Sabellians, who assert that the divine essence is one person: listen carefully, and do not surrender what you hear to forgetfulness, but store it more attentively in your minds, so that, having cast off the various color of leprosy—that is, having driven away heretical perversity—you may be able, by the judgment of the priests, faithfully to enter the holy catholic Church.

Therefore God almighty and eternal, before the morning star—that is, before every creature—begot from the womb, that is, from his own innermost and natural essence, the Son coeternal and consubstantial with himself. What then does it mean for God the Father to say to the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with himself, “From the womb I begot you,” except openly to show angels and human beings that he begot from his own natural essence that same Son who is coeternal with him? Therefore, when in his eternity God the Father said to the Son, coeternal and coequal with himself, “I begot you,” he made manifest that he had begotten him naturally from himself.

Therefore recognize, foolish and hard-hearted Sabellians, that you lied in your assertion, since from most true and mutually concordant authorities you hear that the Son of God was naturally begotten from God the Father before all ages. At this point you Sabellians answer by questioning us: “If God has a Son, how, as you assert, did he beget him from himself?” We in turn ask you, heretics, how you think the Son was begotten by God the Father. Certainly it is impossible for us to know the secret of that generation [Note: [Col. 0433D] *I Sentences*, distinction 9, “But you ask.”]. Mind fails and speech is silent—not ours only but even that of angels. Such generation is above powers and angels, above cherubim and seraphim, and above every understanding, according to what is written: “The peace of Christ surpasses every understanding” [Philippians 4]. And if Christ’s peace surpasses every understanding, without doubt that generation surpasses every understanding. Therefore, senseless Sabellians, put your hand over your mouth, because it is not permitted to search out heavenly mysteries. It is permitted to know that he was born; it is not permitted to investigate how he was born. For that generation is ineffable, concerning which Isaiah says: “Who shall declare his generation?” [Isaiah 53].

The generation of the Son of God from the Father has neither beginning nor end. Our Savior himself is the Wisdom of God the Father; and Wisdom is the radiance of eternal light. Therefore believe without doubt, Sabellians, that God the Father naturally begot the Son from himself before all ages and created through him everything in heaven and on earth. For if God the Father had not naturally begotten Jesus Christ, according to his divinity, from himself before all ages, he would never have said aloud, after Christ’s baptism, in the hearing of John the Baptist and certain others: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” [Luke 3]. Truly, if he were not naturally his Son, he would never have testified before mortals that he was his Son. Again, if the same Jesus Christ, God and man, had not been naturally begotten from God the Father before all ages according to his divinity, he would never have said: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father” [John 6]. By these words Jesus Christ himself, God and man, taught that life is in him through the living Father. And in order to assure us that he is not from himself but from the Father, he said: “As the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” [John 5]. Thus the living Son is begotten by the living God the Father. We therefore confess the only-begotten Son of God the Father as born, but born before all ages.

[Col. 0434D] [Note: [Col. 0434D] *III Sentences*, distinction 8, “It is asked.”] God the Father therefore begot from his natural essence the Son, God coequal and coeternal with himself. This same only-begotten God was born a second time—once from the Father, once from the mother. For he was born from the Father as God the Word; he was born from his mother as the Word made flesh. Thus the one and same Son of God was born before the ages and born in time; and both births belong to the one Son of God, the one divine and the other human. John Damascene likewise says of this:

> “We venerate two births of Christ: one from God the Father before the ages, which is beyond cause, reason, time, and nature; and the other in the last times, for our sake, according to us, and above us. For our sake, because it was for our salvation; according to us, because he was born as a human being from a woman and after the period of conception, namely nine months; above us, because he was not born from the seed of a man.”

Therefore in all things, senseless Sabellians, as we have said, the Son is equal to the Father and is of one and the same substance. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit also, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is the third person in that same unity and Trinity [Note: [Col. 0435D] *I Sentences*, distinction 11, “Here it must be said.”]. That he proceeds from both is proved by many testimonies of the divine utterances. For the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” [Galatians 4]. Behold: here he is called the Spirit of the Son. And again: “But anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” [Romans 8]. The Son himself also says in the Gospel concerning the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” [John 15].

He is called the Spirit of the Father where it is read: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, you walk not in darkness but in light” [Romans 8]. Jesus Christ himself, God and man, also says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father himself speaks in you” [Matthew 10]. And elsewhere: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything that I have said to you” [John 14]. By these and many other authorities, Sabellians, it is plainly shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore recognize that you lied in your assertion, you who say that the divine essence is only one person. For in this also—that you publicly blaspheme almighty God, who truly is the head of all angels and all the faithful—you bear on your head the leprosy, that is, the stain of heretical perversity. Unless you cleanse it through humble repentance and by making worthy satisfaction through good works under the judgment of priests, and show the color of health, namely the right confession of the catholic faith, you will nevertheless perish from the company of the righteous.

The Macedonian heretics also [Note: [Col. 0435D] The Macedonian heretics denied that the Holy Spirit is God, while affirming that he is a creature. Authorities from the Old and New Testaments are set forth in opposition.] are so called, as blessed Isidore says, from Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople [Col. 0435D], who denied that the Holy Spirit is God. Macedonius and his disciples indeed thought perversely concerning God when they denied that the Holy Spirit, who is the third person in the divine essence, is God. Therefore, lest we appear to conceal the matter by silence and be judged more severely for our silence, let us bring forward testimonies from the holy Scriptures, showing that the Holy Spirit is truly God, in order to refute their false assertion and strengthen the faith of the catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0436D] *I Sentences*, distinction 2, “Let us set forth.”].

Therefore, that the truth of the divine unity and Trinity may be more openly shown and the perfidy of heretics more clearly overcome, let us present to them the authorities of the Old and New Testaments. Moses says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” [Deuteronomy 6]. Likewise: “I am the Lord your God” [Exodus 20]. He also shows together the plurality of persons and unity of nature in Genesis, saying: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” [Genesis 1]. For in saying “let us make” and “our,” he shows the plurality of persons; but in saying “image,” he demonstrates the unity of essence. For, as blessed Augustine says in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “If there were only one person in that nature of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it would not be said, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’ For when he says ‘in our image,’ he shows the one nature of essence in whose image man was to be made; but when he says ‘our,’ he shows that the same God is not one person but three.”

That greatest of prophets and kings, David, who sets his understanding above that of others, saying, “I have understood more than the elders” [Psalm 119], likewise showing together the unity and eternity of that divine nature, speaks in the person of almighty God himself: “Israel, if you would listen to me, there shall be no new God in you, nor shall you worship a foreign god” [Psalm 81]. One of these expressions, as blessed Ambrose says in the first book *On the Trinity*, signifies eternity; the other, the undifferentiated unity of substance [Note: [Col. 0436D] “Undifferentiated.”], so that we may not believe either that the Father is later or that the Son or Holy Spirit is of another divinity. For if the Son or Holy Spirit is later than the Father, he is new; and if he is not of one divinity, he is foreign. But because the Son is not later, he is not new; nor is he foreign, because he is born from the Father. Nor is the Holy Spirit new or foreign, because he proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son. Let Macedonius therefore, and all his disciples who deny that the Holy Spirit is God, beware lest for the blasphemy of so great a sacrilege they incur the danger of eternal condemnation. For anyone who speaks a word against the Holy Spirit incurs sacrilege and can obtain forgiveness neither in this age nor the future [Matthew 12], unless he believes without doubt that the Holy Spirit, together with God the Father and Son, is one true God.

[Col. 0436D] Moreover, Macedonians, that you may no longer doubt that the Holy Spirit is one true God with God the Father and Son, I urge you to listen carefully to the most true testimony which the prophet David gives concerning him: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” [Psalm 33]. What could you wish to hear more clearly or openly than that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the mouth of God the Father, is true God? It is as though he said: God the Father, through his Word coeternal with himself—that is, through his Son coequal with himself—established the heavens, that is, the apostles and their successors, namely the teachers of the holy Church, by Gospel preaching and works of power; and by the Spirit of his mouth, namely he who proceeds eternally from him, he strengthened them so that they might neither fear adversities nor dread the threats of the impious.

Therefore, Macedonians, you must believe without doubt that the Spirit of God’s mouth is not a creature but truly God, who truly is all the power of the heavens. For he himself and the Spirit of his mouth are not different things; rather, whatever is in him is God. For, as blessed Augustine says in the seventh book *On the Trinity*:

> “For him, to be great is not one thing and to be God another. Thus the power of God is God, the will of God is God, the beauty of God is God, and the eternity of God is God himself. So too the Spirit of God is God. For in God there is supreme simplicity, and therefore he himself is not one thing and that which is in him another.”

Therefore recognize, Macedonian heretics, that you have lied in your assertion, since even now you deny that the same Holy Spirit, coeternal with God the Father and Son, is God. Truly he is not a creature, as you lie, but is true God, proceeding naturally from God the Father and the Son. For, unlike a creature, he is not circumscribed; rather, like God, he is wholly everywhere, which belongs properly to divinity. Since every creature is confined within definite bounds of its nature, how, foolish heretics, are you not ashamed to call the Holy Spirit a creature, when he has no circumscribed or determinate power and is always in all things and everywhere? This is certainly proper to divinity and lordship. Therefore, because he is always naturally in God, he is also everywhere with him who says: “I fill heaven and earth” [Jeremiah 23].

Therefore, heretics, that you may not doubt that what we have said is true and may recognize yourselves as defeated in your assertion, I urge you to listen carefully to what the prophet says concerning that same Holy Spirit: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life” [Job 33]. The works of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are inseparable. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit can make and breathe life into a human being together with God the Father and Son, he must be believed to be Creator, not creature. The Holy Spirit is therefore Creator, just as are the Father and the Son; accordingly, he is not a creature but one God with the same Father and Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son, and the Father and Son are one because the Father has nothing that the Son does not have.

That the Holy Spirit is not a creature, as you heretics plainly lie, but God by nature, the book of Genesis shows where it says: “Darkness was upon the face of the deep, and the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” [Genesis 1]. In this it plainly appears that he was not a creature but God by nature: he could be borne over the waters and governed the already designated matter of the world. Rightly indeed did the Holy Spirit preside over the formless matter at the very beginning of the world, in order to form and order it and distinguish it into diverse shapes.

David, king and prophet, also shows that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and Son, is truly God and is present everywhere. Considering God’s omnipotence and understanding his own weakness, he says: “Lord, where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your face?” [Psalm 139]. Explaining this immediately afterward, he says: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” [ibid.]. David the prophet rightly perceived the power of the Holy Spirit when he said that he could not escape his presence. He believed him to be God, and therefore did not doubt that he was present everywhere. For unless he believed that the Spirit was truly one God with the God from whom he proceeds, he would never have said that he is everywhere present.

A similar passage is where the same patriarch David, considering the power of the same Holy Spirit proceeding from God, says elsewhere: “There is none who can hide from his heat” [Psalm 19]—that is, from the knowledge of that same Holy Spirit, who knows all things and searches not only human thoughts but even the depths of God. Therefore the Holy Spirit is not a creature but the Creator, who searches not merely human thoughts but also the depths of God [1 Corinthians 2]. It is also written in the book of Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” [Wisdom 1]. And again: “For the Holy Spirit is gracious, and he will free [Note: [Col. 0437D] All read: “and he will not free.”] the accursed person from his lips” [ibid.]. Truly the Holy Spirit is supremely gracious, because he is the coeternal love of the Father and Son, and in him forgiveness of sins is assured to all the faithful [Note: [Col. 0438D] *I Sentences*, distinction 10, “Now indeed that.”]. The Holy Spirit, therefore, is the affection or love of the Father and Son, by which the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father.

Blessed Augustine indicates that the Holy Spirit is truly God and equal to God the Father and Son, saying:

> “In all things the Son is equal to the Father and is of one and the same substance. Accordingly, the Holy Spirit also subsists in the same unity and equality, because he is the unity, holiness, and charity of both, by which each is joined to the other, by which the begotten is loved by the begetter and loves his begetter, both keeping the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” [Ephesians 4].

Therefore, Macedonians, that you may believe the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and Son to be true God and no longer doubt his divinity, I urge you willingly to hear what the book of Wisdom says concerning his greatness, which he shares with God the Father and Son: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” [Wisdom 1]. If, then, the Holy Spirit has filled the world by his own power and operation, he is undoubtedly not a creature, as you lie, but naturally one true God with the Father and Son from whom he proceeds. Moreover, because with God the Father and Son he contains and governs all things, he most plainly shows himself to be Creator with the same Father and Son. In saying that the same Holy Spirit has knowledge of speech, the book of Wisdom also plainly indicates that he is he of whom Jesus Christ, God and man, said to Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice; but you do not know whence he comes or where he goes” [John 3]. For by the will of the Father and Son, from whom he proceeds, he pours out gifts of graces upon whom he wills and makes whom he wills eloquent in spiritual matters.

See how the testimonies of truth agree that the Holy Spirit is true God; see how plainly they refute your false assertion, Macedonians, who deny that he is true God. The competent witnesses of the Old and New Testaments truly agree and wholly condemn your abominable sect. Let your lying perfidy, therefore, now defeated, fail; and let your minds believe without doubt that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God. Finally, I urge you humbly to show the priests of the holy Church the stains of foul leprosy—that is, the horrible blasphemies of heretical perversity—and under their judgment healthfully cast them off. Receive with devout minds, under their instruction, the color of true health—that is, the true teaching of the catholic Church—so that thereafter, withdrawing from wicked deeds and producing worthy fruits of repentance, you may be able to attain the joys of eternal blessedness with the children of the same holy Church. Amen.

Let us also hear what blessed Isidore says concerning the Anthropomorphite [Note: [Col. 0439D] The Anthropomorphites suppose that God has the human members written of in the divine books. Yet it is shown that these are to be understood spiritually in a wonderful way.] heretics. They are called Anthropomorphites because, in rustic simplicity, they suppose that God possesses the human members written of in the divine books. For Greek *anthropos* means “human being” in Latin. The Anthropomorphites therefore think that God has human members, unaware of the Lord’s saying when he sat by the well in Samaria and spoke with the Samaritan woman: “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” [John 4].

You therefore I address and entreat, O anthropomorphite heretics, that you no longer believe God to possess human limbs, as you have believed until now. Truly you are simple and unlearned, who believe that God has, like a human being, the outlines of bodily members. Indeed, the Son of God received from the Virgin Mother the members of our frailty and mortality, according to which he redeemed the world through the cross, died, rose again, and ascended to the right hand of God the Father, from whom he had come forth; nevertheless, the divine essence, insofar as it is God, must not be believed—as you suppose—to possess human members. Therefore one must not rush into so foolish a judgment [Col. 0440A] as to say that the divine essence has human members. [Note: [Col. 0440D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, ch. 5, and the author of the *Speculum*, ch. 12, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VI.]

Meanwhile, one must understand certain affections which Scripture transfers to God from human feeling, so that he may be believed immutable in himself, yet, according to the dispositions of circumstances, may be called mutable, in order that the modes of our speech and mutability may be more readily understood. Thus forms are transferred to God not according to essence but according to likeness, nor by a property of substance but according to the effects of causes. Hence God is believed never to have appeared visibly to human beings except by assuming the appearance of creatures. Certain foolish persons are mistaken when, reading that man was made in God’s image, they suppose God to be corporeal; whereas it is not the flesh, which is the body, but the soul, which is spirit, that has God’s image. Therefore, because he made man in his own image—that is, created the mind, not the flesh, in his likeness—we must not believe God to have bodily form. [Note: [Col. 0440D] Supplied from Isidore: “let us believe.”]

This is your answer, O anthropomorphite heretics, and also your objection: “What wrong do we do if we believe God to have human members, when we find this very thing written in many places of the holy Scriptures? Thus David the prophet, praying to God, says: ‘Make your face shine upon your servant’ (Ps. 118). Elsewhere likewise it is read: ‘Open your eyes and see our affliction’ (Dan. 9). And blessed Job: ‘Your hands, O Lord, made me [Col. 0440C] and fashioned me’ (Job 10). Hence almighty God himself says: ‘Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet’ (Isa. 66). What wrong, then, do we believe if we believe God to have human members, when we maintain this very point on the sure testimony of Scripture?”

To this, O heretics, we reply in opposition that you unquestionably think wrongly about God, since you believe him to have human members, whereas even the testimonies of the holy Scriptures which you bring forward concerning his members in your own defence ought to be understood not bodily, nor literally as they sound on the surface, but spiritually. Why? [Note: [Col. 0440D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, as above.] Because, plainly, forms of qualities are very often taken from human bodies and applied to God, [Col. 0440D] although they are not in God, since in his proper nature he is incorporeal and unbounded; and forms of things are described in him according to the effects of their causes. Thus, because he sees all things, he is called an eye; because he hears all things, he is called an ear; because he turns away, he is said to walk; because he waits, he is seen to stand. So likewise in all other similar cases, a likeness is drawn to God from human minds or bodies. Consider, therefore, O heretics, what body Truth has; and when you cannot find one, know that this is God.

[Col. 0441A] Hear, then, O simple and unlearned heretics, how you ought to understand the members of God which you read of in the holy Scriptures. [Note: [Col. 0441D] Isidore, there.] In the sacred Scriptures, God’s face is understood not as flesh but as divine knowledge, for the same reason that each person is recognized by a face when it is seen. Thus in prayer we say to God: “Show us, O Lord, your face.” [Note: [Col. 0441D] Here Isidore alludes to the prayer of the Gothic Breviary which was said on the second Sunday of Advent, in these words: “Come to deliver us; Lord God of hosts, turn us back; and show your face, and we shall be saved,” etc. But since by Martin’s age the Spanish rite had already been abolished and the Roman rite introduced—in which we find no similar prayer—the blessed author rather incautiously transferred Isidore so closely. Nor did the very learned García de Loaysa properly grasp the point of the matter in his note on this passage of the holy Father, when he added: “As these verses are now prefixed in ecclesiastical prayers: ‘Show us your face and grant us your Salvation.’” In [Col. 0442D] the Roman Breviary it is always said: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy, and grant us your Salvation.” He would have done better to mention the weekday prayers at Terce and None in Advent, Lent, etc., where before the prayer we preface: “Lord God of hosts, turn us back; and show your face, and we shall be saved.” If these prayers were already recited in Martin’s time, Isidore may have had them in view when he was copied.]

That is to say: “Give us your knowledge.” The mouth of God the Father is his Only-begotten Son. For just as, in place of words uttered through the tongue, we often speak of such-and-such a “tongue,” so God’s Word is also called a mouth, because words are customarily formed by the mouth. The Only-begotten of God the Father is called the Word because through him God the Father made or commanded all things. For mouth is rightly put for word, just as tongue is put for words and hand for [Col. 0441B] letters. [Note: [Col. 0442D] *On the Essence of Divinity*, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VIII.]

The tongue of God mystically signifies the Holy Spirit, through whom God the Father reveals his secret to prophets and holy persons. Hence: “My tongue is the pen of a scribe writing swiftly” (Ps. 44). Tongue stands for word, pen for writing: that is, he has put the cause for the effect. It is as though he said: “My word is not transitory, but is the pen of a scribe,” that is, comparable to written and enduring speech. I say, “of a scribe writing swiftly,” that is, writing without delay and comprehending many things. For there are certain scribes who comprise an entire discourse in one point or one line. In some manner the Word of the Father is compared with this swiftness, because nothing is swifter than to have said all things at once. Hence the saying: “God spoke once” (Ps. 61), [Col. 0441C] and so forth.

In the Scriptures, God’s lips are understood as the harmony of the Testament, of which it is said: “Wisdom is on his lips, and his mouth has not erred in judgment” (Prov. 16). [Note: [Col. 0442D] In *On the Essence [of Divinity]*, “divination,” as in the Vulgate.] Solomon also rightly says of his lips in the Song of Songs: “His lips are lilies, dripping first myrrh” (Song 5). [Note: [Col. 0442D] Gregory, on this passage.] For what are meant by the lips of God and of the man Jesus Christ except the preachers of the holy Church? When they preach the deaths of martyrs, they drip, as it were, myrrh for bodies that are to be mortified, as a seasoning of salvation. This myrrh is rightly called “first,” because no one is mortified as is the person who is brought to death by martyrdom for Christ. “First” is said not with reference to time but to dignity. What does it mean that we call the lips of God and of the Virgin’s Son lilies, except that those through whom he speaks must be pure and that through them a sweet fragrance is spread abroad? Among them was the apostle Paul, who said: [Col. 0442A] “We are a sweet fragrance to God in every place, among those who perish and among those who are saved” (2 Cor. 2).

The image of God the Father is his Only-begotten Son. For the image of God the Father is in one way in his Son, whom he begot not from elsewhere but from himself—that is, from his own substance, wholly like and equal to himself—and in another way in the human soul, which he did not beget from himself, that is, from his own substance, as certain heretics have supposed, but created from nothing. Likewise, the image of any king is one thing in his son, whom he begets from himself, like himself—that is, a human begets a human—and another in his ring or in wax, where his image is impressed, which is not what he himself is, as the son naturally is what the Father is. For substance or essence is called *usia* in Greek; *homo* is said to mean “one.” Both together, therefore, sound as “one substance”: this is called *homoousion*, meaning, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), that is, of the same substance as the Father. *Homoousion*: of like substance, because God is equal, such as is also his image. The invisible God has an invisible image.

The arms of God the Father are understood as his Son and the Holy Spirit, as God the Father himself testifies in Isaiah, saying: “My arms shall judge the peoples” (Isa. 51). The arm of God the Father, however, is understood in the singular as his Son, of whom Jeremiah speaks to him thus: “Lord God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm” (Jer. 32). Isaiah the prophet also, instructed by the Holy Spirit and understanding that the Son of God himself would come for the redemption [Col. 0442C] of the world, and considering his power, says: “Behold, the Lord will come in strength, and his arm shall rule” (Isa. 40). And again: “The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all nations” (Isa. 52). Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is rightly called the arm of God the Father, because all things are sustained by him.

The Son of God is also called the right hand of God the Father, because of the effecting of the whole work of creation, which was formed through him. Therefore the right hand of God is his Only-begotten, whence it is said in the person of the assumed man: “The right hand of the Lord has done mighty deeds; the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Ps. 117). In another sense, God’s right hand signifies the Father’s glory and eternity. Hence it is said from the person of [Col. 0442D] the Father to the Son: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). God’s right hand is also called all the elect creation in heaven and on earth, just as by his left hand is understood all reprobate creation, [Col. 0443A] that is, demons and all the ungodly, who are to be set on the left and will suffer eternal punishments. The Psalmist testifies that the right hand of almighty God ever aids elect creation and advances it to a better state, saying: “For it was not by their sword,” that is, by their own strength, “that the elect possessed or will possess the land of the living; and their arm,” that is, their strength, “will not save them from everlasting condemnation; but your right hand, and your arm, and the light of your countenance delivered them, because you were well pleased with them” (Ps. 43). The Israelite people, prefiguring the holy Church and praising God at the crossing of the Red Sea, also openly declared that the right hand of God the Father crushes and restrains the reprobate and drives them far from the fellowship of the elect, saying: “Your right hand, [Col. 0443B] O Lord, is magnified in strength; your right hand, O Lord, struck the enemy, and in the multitude of your glory you cast down my adversaries” (Exod. 15).

The hand of God the Father is understood as his Son, because all things were made through him. Hence Isaiah speaks in the person of God the Father: “My hand made all these things” (Isa. 66). Hence Moses says: “In the beginning,” that is, in the Son, “God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). And John the Evangelist: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). In another sense, God’s hand is understood as his power, as he himself says through Jeremiah: “As clay in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel” (Jer. 18). Doubtless David the prophet had this power of God in view when he said: “If I take up my wings at dawn and [Col. 0443C] dwell in the farthest parts of the sea, even there your hand will lead me, and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 138). Again, the hand of the Lord is understood as a scourge, concerning whose blow Zephaniah reads thus: “I will stretch out my hand over Judah and over the inhabitants of Israel, and I will destroy from this place the remnants of Baal” (Zeph. 1). Blessed Job also testifies that the Lord’s hand signifies a scourge, saying: “The hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 10).

The finger of God is understood as the Holy Spirit, by whom the law is said to have been written on two tablets of stone (Exod. 31). For he wrote who dictated what was to be written, namely the Holy Spirit. Of him God and man Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, [Col. 0443D] by what do your sons cast them out?” (Luke 11). [Note: [Col. 0443] This clause was attached less suitably to verse 20, though it belongs to verse 19: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebub …”] Another Evangelist, making this plain, says: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has indeed come upon you” (Matt. 12). For just as finger, hand, and arm are one with the body in nature, so the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed three persons but one essence of divinity. The fingers of God, in the plural, are understood as the holy prophets, through whom the Holy Spirit is set forth by his inspiration in the book of the Law and the Prophets. Of them it is figuratively said to almighty God: “I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8). Hence in Genesis it is mystically read: [Col. 0444A] “God made the firmament heaven” (Gen. 1), namely, holy Scripture. Therefore by “heavens” he mystically indicated all the books of the sacred Law and Prophets, and by “fingers,” as stated, the holy prophets.

The heart of God the Father mystically signifies the hidden mystery of his wisdom, from which he begot his Word, that is, his Son, without beginning, as he himself says: “My heart has poured forth a good Word” (Ps. 44), etc. God is said to have wings because, in the manner of a bird, he gathers and cherishes his elect beneath himself like chicks, and protects them from the snares of the devil and evil people. The Psalmist prays for this, saying: “O Lord, preserve me from those who resist your right hand, as the pupil of the eye. Protect me under the shadow of your wings from the face of the ungodly who have afflicted me” [Col. 0444B] (Ps. 16). God is said to have shoulders because he carries the weak members of the Church as though upon his shoulders, as is read in the Psalm: “He has overshadowed you with his shoulders, and beneath his feathers you will hope” (Ps. 90).

The womb of God is understood as the inner and hidden generation of his Son. Hence it is said to the Son from the person of the Father through the Psalmist: “In the splendours of the saints, from the womb before Lucifer I begot you” (Ps. 109). In another sense, the womb of God mystically signifies his incomprehensible judgments, which cannot be searched out. Rebuking blessed Job as though by a question, the Lord himself says: “Tell me, if you know: who is the father of the rain? Or who begot the drops of dew? From whose womb came the ice? And who begot frost from heaven?” (Job 38). [Col. 0444C] The Son of God is also called the Father’s power because he has in himself the whole power of the Father and governs, sustains, and rules every creature of heaven and earth.

He is also called wisdom because he reveals the mysteries of knowledge and the hidden things of wisdom. Yet although Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are wisdom, power, brightness, and light, the Son is nevertheless specifically named by these titles. He is also called splendour because he manifests the light, namely God the Father; and light because he opens the eyes of the heart for the contemplation of truth.

The “back parts” of the Son of God are understood as his Incarnation. Concerning this latter aspect, the Son of God himself said to Moses on Mount Sinai through an angel: [Col. 0444D] “You shall see my back parts; you shall not be able to see my face” (Exod. 33). We believe that this promise was fulfilled when the disciples saw God and man, Jesus Christ, transfigured on Mount Tabor, in the midst of Moses and Elijah (Matt. 17). Moses therefore saw Christ’s back parts: that is, he saw what was accomplished in the latter and final days.

The feet of God are the firmness of his power, because he is himself everywhere present and all things are subject to him. Hence he says through Isaiah: “Heaven is my throne, but earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). The feet of the Son of God are understood as his Incarnation, which is subject to divinity. For as his divinity is expressed by the head, so his humanity is expressed by the feet, as is figuratively read of him in Exodus: [Col. 0445A] “Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of the people saw the Lord God of Israel; and beneath his feet was something like sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24). As by the sapphire stone he wished figuratively to indicate heavenly creatures or holy angels, so by the clear sky he wished to indicate the holy Church gathered from elect human beings. Over these two creatures the man assumed by the Word and joined to him reigns with him forever. Of him the Psalmist, exulting and greatly rejoicing, speaks to God the Father: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and moreover [Col. 0445B] the beasts of the field” (Ps. 8). In another sense, the feet of Jesus Christ signify the holy apostles and other teachers of the Church, concerning whom it is written in Deuteronomy: “Those who draw near to his feet shall receive from his teaching” (Deut. 33).

The garment of the Son of God is sometimes figuratively understood in the divine books as his flesh, assumed by divinity. Of this garment of flesh Isaiah says: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosra?” (Isa. 63). And again: “Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those treading in the winepress?” (ibid.). Again, his garment is called the holy Church, joined to him through faith and love. Hence the Psalm is sung: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with majesty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength [Col. 0445C] and girded himself” (Ps. 92). In another Psalm the Prophet, exulting, says to the same God and man Jesus Christ: “You have put on confession and beauty; you are clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103).

Christ’s cloak is understood as the Church already mentioned. [Note: [Col. 0445D] This is from Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] Concerning it, Jacob, figuratively blessing his son Judah, says in Genesis: “He shall wash his robe in wine” (Gen. 49), that is, his flesh in the blood of his Passion, or the holy Church in that wine which is poured out for many for the remission of sins. It follows: “And his cloak in the blood of grapes.” Christ’s cloak is the Gentiles, whom he joined to his body in everlasting love, as the prophet says of him: “As I live, says the Lord, I shall clothe myself with men as with a garment” [Col. 0445D] (Isa. 49). Isaiah the prophet, seeing with spiritual eyes that God and man Jesus Christ would join the Gentiles to himself through the mystery of the Incarnation, rejoicingly says to the same Jesus Christ, bridegroom of the holy Church: [Note: [Col. 0445D] Ibid., according to the Vulgate.] “You shall put on all these as an ornament.” For the Son of God and of the Virgin washed these peoples of the holy Church in the blood of the grape—that is, he cleansed them of sins in the blood of his body—when, like a cluster, he hung upon the wood of the cross for the redemption of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0446D] *On the Essence [of Divinity].*] The Lord’s footwear mystically signifies his Incarnation, which he assumed from the mortality of the human race. Concerning it he says in the Psalm: “Into Idumea [Col. 0446A] I shall stretch out my footwear” (Ps. 107): that is, “To the people of the Gentiles I shall reveal my Incarnation, and thus foreigners will be subject to me.” What, then, is meant by Idumea but Gentilehood; and what by footwear but assumed mortality? Thus the Lord declares that he stretches out his footwear into Idumea, because, when he made himself known to the Gentiles through the flesh, divinity came to us, as it were, shod. For who does not know that shoes are made from dead animals? [Note: [Col. 0446D] “Are made.”] Therefore, coming in the flesh, the Lord appeared as though shod, he who in his divinity assumed the deadness of our corruption. Thus the Lord’s feet sometimes signify the stability of eternity, sometimes the humanity through which knowledge of divinity came to us, and sometimes holy preachers, of whom it is written: [Col. 0446B] “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace and proclaim good things” (Isa. 52).

The steps of God are understood as the coming of the Son of God into the world and his return to the Father. Of these the Prophet speaks thus in the Psalm to the same Son of God: “They saw your goings, O God—the goings of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary” (Ps. 67). From heaven he came into the Virgin’s womb; from the Virgin’s womb he was born and laid in a manger. But after accomplishing all for which he had been sent by the Father, he was hung upon the wood of the cross; taken down from the cross, he was buried in body and descended into the underworld in soul; on the third day, through the power of divinity, he raised his flesh from the tomb; and on the fortieth day after the day of resurrection, while the apostles looked on, he ascended into [Col. 0446C] heaven (Acts 1) and sits at the Father’s right hand in his glory. Amen. These are the steps of the Son of God: this his ascent and descent, which are frequently read of in the sacred Scriptures.

God’s ascent is spoken of when the Son carried back to heaven, as a captive, the flesh taken from us, as the Psalmist says of him: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Eph. 4). That is, he raised with himself to heaven, where it had never previously been, as a captive—that is, as something captured—the nature of the human race which was held captive in the world by the devil. “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive,” because he swallowed up our corruption by the power of his incorruption. “But he gave gifts to men,” [Col. 0446D] because, having sent the Holy Spirit from above, he granted to some a word of knowledge, to others a word of wisdom, to others the grace of healing, to others kinds of tongues, and to others interpretation of utterances (1 Cor. 12). Thus he gave gifts to people when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, he ordered their life in the world.

God is said to hide his face when, because of sins requiring it in certain people, he conceals his knowledge from them. We now see this fulfilled in the Jewish people, because by denying the Son of God they have lost the knowledge of God, so that they may be like the Gentiles who did not know God. Concerning them God and man Jesus Christ rightly complains through Jeremiah the prophet, [Col. 0447A] saying: “They denied me and said: ‘It is not he’” (Jer. 5). But let us hear what the Lord says of those who denied him: “I shall forsake my people and depart from them” (ibid.). To them also, because of sins requiring it, he says through Isaiah: “When you multiply prayer, I shall not hear; and when you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you” (Isa. 1). And elsewhere: “I shall hide my face from them and shall consider their latter end” (Deut. 32). Therefore, as stated above, God is said to hide his face from certain people because their sins require it: that is, not to give them knowledge of himself.

God is also said to show his face when, through the regard of his grace, he makes himself known by hidden inspiration in the hearts of those whom he wills, namely his holy and elect ones, and pours into them his love so that they may love him. David prays for this, saying: “Lord God of hosts, turn us back; and show your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79). [Col. 0447B] That is, more plainly: “Lord God of all the heavenly hosts, powerfully draw us back from carnal desires; mercifully turn us to your love; graciously show us your face, that is, knowledge of your majesty; and thus, with your help, we shall be able to be saved from the evils that threaten us.”

God is said to sit, not bodily after the human manner, but to preside in power over all creation. Hence the Psalmist says: “God will reign over [Col. 0447C] the nations; God sits upon his holy throne” (Ps. 46). He is also said to sit upon the cherubim, which is interpreted “a multitude” or “fulness of knowledge.” By it are signified holy angels or the minds of spiritual persons, in whom God invisibly sits and reigns. For he sits and reigns in those who are filled with the knowledge and love of God and neighbour. Hence Proverbs reads: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom.” Christ is the wisdom of God the Father, and he is said to sit in the souls of the saints.

God is also said to descend into the world when he performs in human creation something new which had not existed before. Thus, when the Lord wished to overthrow Sodom and Gomorrah because of the wickedness of their inhabitants, Genesis reads that he said [Col. 0447D]: “I shall descend and see whether they have carried out the outcry in deed” (Gen. 18). Thus also the Son of God the Father descended from heaven when he assumed true flesh from the Virgin for our redemption. Of this descent, that is, the Incarnation, it is written in the Psalm: “He bent the heavens and descended, and darkness was under his feet” (Ps. 17). He bent the heavens because before his coming he sent angels and prophets to proclaim his Incarnation to people. He chose and taught apostles and sent them throughout the whole world, to announce this Incarnation, now accomplished, to every nation under heaven. Darkness was under his feet because ungodly people, on account of their wickedness, could not recognize his Incarnation, nor indeed can they do so even today. In another sense: darkness is beneath his feet [Col. 0448A] because he is not seen by lower people with the brightness in which he rules among the higher.

God is said to stand when he patiently bears with us in our weakness, awaiting repentance and conversion. Of him the prophet Habakkuk says: “The devil shall go out before his feet; he stood and measured the earth” (Hab. 3). By the feet of the Son of God, as stated above, we rightly understand the humanity which he assumed from the Virgin, in which he mounted the cross for the redemption of humankind, overcame the devil, and redeemed humankind. We also understand his feet as the holy apostles, in whom he went throughout the world and preached to the Gentiles. Therefore it is rightly said: “The devil shall go out before his feet,” because when he himself had come in the flesh and the apostles were preaching the Gospel throughout the world, the devil was expelled from the hearts of believers. Hence we read that God and man Jesus Christ himself said: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12). It continues: “He stood,” it says, “and measured the earth.” [Col. 0448B] As though it said: God and the Virgin’s Son stood in his coming, rebuking the perversities of people, reproving their evils, preaching good things, and awaiting the elect’s conversion and true repentance; and he measured the earth because, although he preserves what is first, he nevertheless first weighs their strength in the work. For he commands no one to do the impossible, nor requires from anyone what he has not given, and does not reap what he has not sown. Therefore he stood in our humanity and measured the earth, because, considering each person’s mind, he happily rewards those who do good but justly condemns the ungodly.

Again, continuing, he says: “He looked and dissolved the nations, and the everlasting mountains were broken” (Hab. 3). [Col. 0448C] That is, in his coming the Son of God looked upon and dissolved the nations: he mercifully looked upon the Gentile people and, through his cross and resurrection, loosed them from the bonds of sins and delivered them from everlasting condemnation. In another sense: he looked upon the error of the Gentile people rendering service to idols and, by apostolic preaching, dissolved their sacrilegious conspiracy; and “the everlasting mountains were broken,” that is, the powerful—namely emperors and rulers of this world—were humbled at his coming and made subject to his dominion.

[Col. 0448D] God is also said to pass over when he withdraws from the hearts of certain persons in which he was previously believed to dwell, because unbelief or some sin has subsequently crept in, and passes to others: for example, from Esau to Jacob, from Eli to Samuel, from Saul to David, from Judas the traitor to Matthias, from the Jews to the Gentiles, and from heretics to Catholics. He customarily does this not locally or visibly, but invisibly and by hidden judgment.

God is also said to walk, not by passing from place to place, but his walking is his dwelling in the hearts of the saints, as it is written: “I shall dwell in them, and walk among them, and I shall be their God” (Lev. 26). Or certainly, God’s walking is his passing from place to place in [Col. 0449A] his holy preachers.

God’s speaking is his invisibly inspiring, without sound of voice or any noise, his will and right understanding secretly into the minds of saints, or revealing future things, as to the holy prophets. This speech of God, as some hold, is understood in three ways. First, through a subject creature, as he appeared to Moses in the fire of the bush (Exod. 3), or as to Abraham (Gen. 18), Jacob, and other saints to whom he deigned to appear in angels (Gen. 28). Second, in dreams, as to Jacob, Zechariah, one of the twelve prophets (Zech. 1), Joseph the husband of the ever-virgin Mary, and others to whom he wished to reveal his secret (Matt. 2). [Col. 0449B] Third, neither through a visible creature nor through an angel, but only by secret inspiration, touching their hearts and making them speak, as is written in the books of the Prophets, when the prophets themselves, suddenly inspired by the divine Spirit, cried out: “Thus says the Lord.”

God’s seeing is his approving good deeds, as in Genesis: “God saw all that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). “He saw,” that is, he showed to those who understand that they were good. Again, God’s seeing is choosing or delivering, as he himself says to Moses: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt, and I have descended to deliver them” (Exod. 3). Hence God and man Jesus Christ himself says to Nathanael in the Gospel: “Before Philip called you, [Col. 0449C] when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1), that is, “I chose you.” Hence it is also read there: “Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee, saw two brothers, Peter and Andrew” (Matt. 4), that is, he chose them. In another sense, God’s seeing is making those who do not see sharp-sighted so that they may see. Hence the Psalmist prays: “Lord, see whether there is a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Ps. 138). That is, more plainly: “Lord, make me see, that is, know, the ways of my iniquity, so that it may not happen that I descend by the way of error into perdition, but may always walk in you, who are the way of eternal salvation.” This manner of speech is likewise found in the book of Job. After saying much concerning that wisdom and the same Father [Col. 0449D] from whom it proceeds, he adds: “Then he saw it, declared it, searched it out, and prepared it” (Job 28). That is: God saw it, namely, he made human beings see it with the eyes of their heart; “and declared it,” that is, he made people declare it to one another; “and searched it out,” namely, he made them search it out; “and prepared it,” that is, he illumined human minds with the light of his brightness so that they might understand wisdom itself, and instructed them sufficiently so that they might preach these things to others.

God’s knowing is his making people know him, as he says to Abraham: “Now I have known that you fear God” (Gen. 22), etc. For he who knows all things before they happen does not come to know in time (Dan. 13). Such also is the saying [Col. 0450A] in the Law concerning the Israelite people: “That I may test them,” he says, “whether they keep my commandments or not” (Exod. 16). [Note: [Col. 0449] Deut. 8:2, or 13:3, as the Benedictines note; which does not please us.] Therefore he is said to know, that is, to make them know, so that those who were previously ignorant of what sort of persons they were might, by his questioning or testing, become known to themselves.

God’s not knowing is his rejecting the ungodly, as God and man Jesus Christ himself says to the foolish virgins in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you: I do not know you” (Matt. 25). So also at the judgment he will say to the reprobate: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know where you are from” (Luke 13). Hence he also says to the entire company of the elect: “You alone have I known among all nations” (Amos 3). God therefore knows both righteous and ungodly persons; nevertheless, he declares that he knows the righteous [Col. 0450B] and does not know the ungodly—that is, rejects them—as the Psalmist testifies: “Behold,” he says, “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy the memory of them from the earth” (Ps. 33).

God is said to be jealous when he wills to leave no sin unpunished. For he is supremely just, and therefore every injustice is abhorrent to him; he leaves it unpunished in no way. Thus God is said, in our manner of speaking, to be jealous or to grieve, not by his own nature. For there is no disturbance of these emotions in God, in whom there is supreme tranquility. Therefore one must not hastily judge that a disturbance of anger or jealousy can happen to God; rather, sacred reading has called “wrath” or “jealousy” the very equity of justice by which he punishes the guilty, [Col. 0450C] because what is justice in the judge is fury or indignation in the sufferer.

God is said to repent, yet not in the sense that he repents of his past works. For he who knows all things before they happen (Dan. XIII) cannot repent of acts already performed; rather, God’s repentance is to change what has been decreed and to transform into something else what had previously been begun otherwise. Thus we read that he said to Noah: “I repent that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. VI). For no repentance can occur in God, since he is immutable and incorruptible; but when he said, “I repent that I made man,” he signified that, because their sins demanded it, he willed by just judgment to destroy human beings [Col. 0450D] from the face of the earth. Likewise, wishing, because of sins requiring it, to transform into something else what had formerly been begun differently, he said to Samuel: “I repent that I have appointed Saul king over Israel” (I Kings XV). “But rise, take a horn of oil, and I shall send you to the house of Jesse; and you shall anoint David his son as king over Israel” (I Kings XVI).

People are often changed from good to evil because of sins requiring it, as we now see accomplished in the Jewish people: though they had been God’s people, because of their impiety they became the synagogue of Satan. From evil to good, on the other hand, they are changed as happened among the Gentile people, who formerly were not God’s people but now, through the grace of God and [Col. 0451A] of the man Jesus Christ, have become God’s people. In this same manner, by God’s hidden judgment, Judas fell from the rank of apostleship and was plunged into the abyss of hell, while the thief, after the crime of robbery, was transferred from the cross into paradise (Luke XXIII). Therefore we call “God’s repentance” this change from good to evil, God permitting it, or from evil to good, he himself effecting it, which occurs by God’s hidden and just judgment, through the severity of his justice or through his mercy. God’s not repenting is his in no way changing what has been decreed, as in this passage: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent,” that is, the Father saying to the Son: “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX). The Son is called priest of God the Father, not according to his divinity but according to his humanity, [Col. 0451B] in which he offered himself for us through passion and death as an acceptable sacrifice to God the Father, so that he himself was both priest and sacrifice.

God is said to forget when he does not have mercy upon certain wicked persons. This certainly does not happen through ignorance, which is not in God, but through his hidden and just judgment. Hence the Psalmist complains to God, saying: “Why have you forgotten me, and why do I go about sadly while my enemy afflicts me?” (Ps. XLI). As though he said more plainly: Why have you forgotten me, O Lord—that is, why do you permit me to be tempted beyond what I can bear and to fall so easily into the cesspool of vices? Why do I go about sadly, while the corruptible flesh in which I dwell, by desiring fleshly things and suggesting forbidden things, [Col. 0451C] provokes me to sin; while the ancient enemy, incessantly attacking me with diverse temptations, afflicts me and continually prevents me from rising out of the mire of vices to a better manner of life? Therefore I beseech you, O most gracious Father: before I am cast headlong into Gehenna for my sins, mercifully stretch out your right hand to me, the work of your hands, and make me attain everlasting blessedness with your elect.

God is said to harden certain wicked persons, as is written concerning Pharaoh—not because almighty God hardens their hearts by his own power, which it is impious to believe, but because, their sins requiring it, they do not expel from their hearts the hardness of heart by which they themselves nurture within themselves [Col. 0451D] every evil. Thus he is said, as it were, to have hardened those whom by just judgment he permits to be hardened.

God’s sleeping is when God and man, Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, deigned to die for us; his death was figuratively foretold by Jeremiah as a sweet sleep in these words: “I,” he says, “have risen as though from sleep; and I saw, and my sleep is sweet to me” (Jer. XXXI). God is also said to sleep in another sense when his faith does not keep watch amid the prosperities of this world and in the hearts of certain believers, but sleeps. Blessed Paul urges them to wakefulness, saying: “Keep watch; stand firm in the faith; act manfully and be strengthened” (I Cor. XVI). And: “Let all that is yours be done in charity” (ibid.). Again: “Awake, you righteous, from sleep”—namely, from the sleep of sin or from excessive concern for earthly things—“and do not sin” (I Cor. XV). And elsewhere: “Arise, you who sleep,” namely in sins, “and rise from the dead,” that is, from delight in and the habit of mortal sin, “and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V), that is, will shine upon you.

God and man, Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of holy Church, is also said to sleep when, now exalted at the right hand of God the Father, he rests, while his faithful, through love and desire for him, outwardly abandon earthly affairs and inwardly seek heavenly and spiritual pursuits. Hence the same bridegroom of holy Church says in the Song of spiritual love: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch” (Song V). [Note: [Col. 0451D] This is from Gregory, on this passage.] For the elect may fittingly be called the bridegroom’s heart: the more they flee the outward things that are in the world, the more secretly they know the bridegroom’s inward things. Thus Christ sleeps and his heart keeps watch; because, while he himself now glorified rests in the glory of God the Father, all who love him perfectly labor with all their might to attain him. Or certainly, God’s sleeping is his coming more slowly to the aid of those in tribulation. Hence the Psalmist, drawing long sighs from the depths of his breast, grieving and weeping bitterly, complains to God: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord? Rise up, and do not cast us off for ever” (Ps. XLIII). As though he said more plainly in the person of the afflicted: Rise up, O Lord, [Col. 0452C] who seem to have lain and slept for a long time; rise up to help us. And since we are now reckoned as sheep for slaughter, O Lord, why do you sleep so long and not defend us more quickly? Christ himself, God and man, aptly signified those who profess the faith of the holy Trinity merely in words but fix the eyes of their minds upon the love of temporal things, when he slept amid the waves of the sea (Matt. VIII). Rebuking them in the psalm, the Prophet says: “They slept their sleep, and all men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV).

God’s wakefulness is his immediately making himself manifest in the defense of the good and the punishment of the wicked, as he himself testifies when he says among other things to Jeremiah the prophet: [Col. 0452D] “What do you see, Jeremiah?” “I see,” he says, “a wakeful rod.” The Lord answered him: “You have seen well, for I shall watch over my word in order to perform it.” [Note: [Col. 0451D] Here the book *On the Essence* ends in certain manuscripts, according to the Benedictine note, and in those consulted by our author.] (Jer. I).

Hear therefore what I say, O Anthropomorphite heretics; hear what I speak; listen to what I admonish. Almighty God, in his divine essence, as has been stated above, is not to be understood as bodily, as you falsely maintain, but is firmly to be believed spiritual. Yet it is not surprising if the Son of God is represented by lowly signs, since he is known to have descended even to the abasements of our passions and flesh. He who [Col. 0453A] is the coeternal Son of God the Father before the ages, the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0453D] This word remains.], when the fullness of time came [Note: [Col. 0453D] Supply: “came.”], for our salvation took the form of a servant (Gal. IV) and became the son of man [Note: [Col. 0453D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, ch. 2.]. Accordingly, some things are said of him in Scripture according to the form of God, and some according to the form of a servant. Two examples are mentioned, so that each may be referred to its proper category. According to the form of God, he said of himself: “I and the Father are one” (John X); but according to the form of a servant: “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV). But certain people, understanding too little what is said for what reason [Note: [Col. 0453D] “For what reason.”], wish to transfer to the form of God those things said because of the form of a servant; and, conversely, they wish the names said so that the persons may be referred to one another [Col. 0453B] to be names of nature and substance. Thus they make an error in faith.

I want you to know, O Anthropomorphite heretics, that human nature was so joined to the Son of God that one person was made from two substances. Therefore the man alone suffered the cross, yet, because of the unity of person, God too is said to have suffered it. Hence blessed Paul says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II). “Therefore we confess that the Son of God was crucified,” as blessed Isidore says in the book of the *Etymologies*, “yet not by the power of divinity but by the weakness of humanity; not through the immutability of his own nature, but through his assumption of our flesh.”

Therefore recognize yourselves, O Anthropomorphite heretics, to have lied in your assertion, you who have presumed to maintain that the divine essence possesses human limbs.
