For he is not to be thought corporeal, but incorporeal. He is indeed immeasurable, uncircumscribed, and wholly present everywhere. I therefore admonish you in the affection of charity to reveal humbly to the Catholic priests of holy Church the varied and hideous stains of leprosy—that is, the condemnable blasphemies of heretical perversity—and to receive with devout mind, by their instruction, the color of health, that is, the sound doctrine of the Catholic faith, so that by believing rightly you may attain with the children of that same holy Church the eternal reward of the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0453D] Let us all hear together what blessed Isidore [Note: [Col. 0454D] In this place Priscillianist heretics are refuted. The Priscillianists, together with the Donatists, affirm that the Holy Spirit is lesser than the Son. The claim that Catholics ought to be rebaptized is likewise attacked. Definitions of sin against the Holy Spirit are set forth. Likewise, the second question asks whether the sacrament is valid if the words of baptism are pronounced corruptly; what is to be done concerning one whose baptism is doubtful; and whether the form of baptism is retained in jest.] says concerning the Priscillianist heretics. [Note: [Col. 0454D] *Etymologies*, book VIII, ch. 5.] “The Priscillianists,” he says, “are called after Priscillian, who in Spain compounded a mixed doctrine out of the error of the Gnostics and Manichaeans.”

The Donatists, as Isidore, teacher of the Spains, says, are named from a certain Donatus of Africa. Coming from Numidia, he deceived almost all Africa by his persuasion, maintaining that the Holy Spirit was less than the Son and rebaptizing Catholics. [Col. 0454A] [Note: [Col. 0454D] *Sentences*, I, distinction 10, chapter “Nunc post.”] Truly this man held erroneous views concerning the divine essence, since he taught that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son. For the Holy Spirit is the love or affection of Father and Son. Hence blessed Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “The Holy Spirit is neither the Father’s alone nor the Son’s alone, but belongs to both; and therefore he suggests to us the mutual charity by which the Father and the Son love one another. We discover where the Holy Spirit is called charity if we examine carefully the utterance of John the Evangelist.” [Note: [Col. 0454D] Chapter “Sed Dei verbum.”] For after saying, “Let us love one another, because charity is from God,” he added: “And everyone who loves has been born of God, because God [Col. 0454B] is charity” (I John IV). Here blessed John made clear that he had called that charity God which he said was from God. Therefore charity is from God.

Moreover, it must be known that the Father alone is God in such a way that he is not from God; therefore the love which is God in such a way as to be from God is not the Father himself, but either the Son or the Holy Spirit. Since, then, he had spoken of love and immediately wished to say something more plainly on this subject, he said: “By this we know that we abide in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit” (ibid.). Therefore the Holy Spirit, of whom he has given us, causes us to abide in God and God himself to abide in us. Thus the Holy Spirit himself is God who is charity. Therefore the Holy Spirit, God who proceeds from God, is signified where it is read: “God is charity, and charity [Col. 0454C] is from God.” Therefore the Holy Spirit is the charity of Father and Son, by which Father and Son love one another; and for that reason he is not less than the Father or the Son, but equal to Father and Son. For the Father or the Son is not greater than his own love or goodness, any more than he is greater than his own wisdom or power.

Hence blessed Augustine says in the second book *On the Trinity*, chapter 6: “Therefore it is nowhere written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is less, because no creature was assumed in which the Holy Spirit might appear, as the Son of Man was assumed, in whose form the person of the very Word of God might be manifested. He is called simple because whatever is in him is God. He is not one thing and that which is in him another. For the strength [Col. 0454D] of God is God; the wisdom of God is God; the love of God is God; the eternity of God is God.” Therefore, in this Trinity which is God, nothing is earlier or later, nothing greater or less; but the three persons are altogether coeternal and coequal with one another. Receive, then, O heretics, with devout mind this true faith, without which no one can be saved; preserve it with a pure heart; [Col. 0455A] hasten through it, as through an eastern gate, to enter the holy Catholic Church.

I do not want you to be ignorant, O Donatist heretics, that whoever sins against God the Father shall be forgiven, and whoever sins against his Son shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the same Father and Son, shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. XII). But what is it to sin against the Holy Spirit? It is, namely, to persist in sin with an obstinate mind, or wholly to despair of God’s goodness. [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Sentences*, II, distinction 43, chapter “Est praeterea.”] Obstinacy is the persistence in evil of a hardened mind, through which a person becomes unrepentant. Despair is that by which someone wholly distrusts God’s goodness, judging his own wickedness to exceed the greatness of divine goodness, like [Col. 0455B] Cain, who said: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. IV). Both are called sin against the Holy Spirit because, as we have said, the Holy Spirit is the love of Father and Son, and the goodness by which they love one another and us; it is so great that it has no end. Therefore, O Donatist heretics, having expelled deadly obstinacy from your minds, repent that you have been authors of such great blasphemy; and believe most certainly that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God, so that, humbly repenting before him and faithfully confessing him, you may obtain pardon from him. Take the greatest care that, in this most turbulent sea of iniquities, you do not by obstinacy of mind deprive yourselves of the harbor of forgiveness, into which, after the shipwreck of so grievous an error, [Col. 0455C] you may receive yourselves while tossed by the waves.

Moreover, it must be known that, as blessed Augustine says, that person sins against the Holy Spirit who commits sin and, through obstinacy of mind, is unwilling to repent or through repentance to amend the evil he has done. This sin alone, blessed Augustine says, cannot merit forgiveness. Therefore, if you, O Donatists, expel from your minds the false superstition of heretical perversity and worthily perform penance for the blasphemies uttered against the Holy Spirit, you can obtain pardon from the most merciful God. It is necessary, then, O Donatist heretics—you who call the Holy Spirit equal to Father and Son, yet less than the Son—to recognize that you have lied in your assertion, and to perform lawful penance, under the judgment of Catholic priests, for [Col. 0455D] such false and condemnable blasphemy, so that you may no longer presume, through wicked belief, to bring blasphemy against the divine essence.

I address also you, O Donatist heretics, who have added evils to evils and joined sins to sins: namely, you rebaptize persons baptized in the Catholic manner, contrary to the custom of ecclesiastical religion. What malice compelled you, what madness incited you, what malignity deceived you, what audacity moved you to presume to rebaptize those baptized according to the form of Jesus Christ, the supreme pontiff? I want you to know, O Donatist heretics, that whoever the baptizer may be, if the form handed down by Christ is preserved, he administers true baptism; and therefore one who receives that baptism ought not to be rebaptized. [Col. 0456A] [Note: [Col. 0455D] *Sentences*, IV, distinction 6, chapter “Nunc quibus.”] Hence the venerable Bede says in a certain homily: “Whether a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal person baptizes in confession of the holy Trinity, one who has been baptized may not validly be rebaptized by good Catholics, lest the confession or invocation of the holy Trinity appear to be annulled.”

Likewise blessed Augustine, the most powerful hammer of heretics, responding to Orosius’s questions, says: “Although there is one baptism—both that of heretics who baptize in the name of the Father and the Son and [Col. 0456B] the Holy Spirit, and that of the Catholic Church—nevertheless those baptized outside the Church receive baptism not for salvation but for destruction, possessing the form of the sacrament but denying its power” (II Tim. III). “Therefore the Church does not rebaptize them, because they have been baptized in the name of the most holy Trinity, and that itself is the form of baptism.” Likewise, in replying to Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0455D] Correctly thus, not as in the edition, “Mag. Maximianum.”], he says among other things: “To rebaptize a heretic who has received these signs of holiness is altogether a sin; but to rebaptize a Catholic is a most monstrous crime.” From these statements it is clearly understood that even those baptized by heretics, provided the character—that is, Christ’s form—has been preserved, are not to be rebaptized, but only reconciled through the laying on of hands, namely, in order that they may receive the Holy Spirit as a sign [Col. 0456C] of repudiation of heretics.

It is also customarily asked [Note: [Col. 0456D] Ibidem, chapter “Quaeri etiam.”] whether baptism is valid if a priest pronounces those words corruptly in baptism. Pope Zacharias wrote thus on this subject to Bishop Boniface: “Your messengers reported to me,” he says, “that there was a priest in that province who was wholly ignorant of the Latin language; and while baptizing, ignorant of Latin speech and mangling the language, he said: ‘I baptize you in the name of the *patria* [fatherland], and the *filia* [daughter], and the Holy Spirit *sancta* [feminine “holy”]’; and on this account you considered rebaptizing those whom he had baptized. But if he who baptized in this manner did so not by introducing error or heresy, but solely through ignorance of Roman speech, saying it while mangling the language, we cannot agree that those baptized by him should be baptized again.” [Col. 0456D]

Furthermore, [Note: [Col. 0456D] Chapter “Praeterea.”] it must be known that concerning those for whom there is no evidence among relatives, clerics, or neighbors to show that they have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be born again, lest they perish. In cases in which no act is shown, reason does not permit it to be regarded as repeated. Therefore that which is unknown to have been conferred seems to be conferred upon them, because there is no rash presumption where there is careful piety.

It is also customary to ask [Note: [Col. 0456D] Chapter “Solet.”] concerning one who, joking like [Col. 0457A] an actor, is nevertheless immersed with invocation of the Trinity, whether he has been baptized. Blessed Augustine did not determine this, saying: “If everything were done playfully, theatrically, and in jest, I would judge that it must be sought by prayer from divine judgment, through the miracle of some revelation, whether baptism so administered ought to be approved. Yet it seems to the learned that it was not baptism when some persons are immersed in a bath or river in the name of the Trinity, since it is not done with the intention of baptizing. For in this and in other sacraments, as the form must be preserved, so the intention of celebrating it must be present.” Therefore recognize yourselves, O Donatist heretics, to be most certainly defeated in your assertions, and subject yourselves with devout minds to ecclesiastical doctrines. Believe that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God, and do not rebaptize those baptized by churchmen according to Christ’s form. Hasten, by right belief and good works, to enter your Catholic mother Church, so that with her children you may attain the joys of eternal blessedness.

Let us hear what Isidore, teacher of the Spains, [Note: [Col. 0457D] *Etymologies*, book VIII, ch. 5.] says concerning the Nestorian [Note: [Col. 0457D] Nestorius preaches one Son of God and another son of the Virgin. His departure from the path of truth is demonstrated by the testimonies of the saints.] heretics. “The Nestorians,” he says, “are named after Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who maintained that the most blessed Virgin Mary was mother not of God but only of a human being, in order that he might make one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead. Nor did he believe that Christ, the Word of God the Father, was one incarnate being; rather, separately and distinctly, he preached one Son [Col. 0457C] of God and another son of man.”

But without doubt this Nestorius was foolish and strayed exceedingly far from the path of truth when he denied that the Son, coeternal with God the Father, assumed human nature—namely, flesh and soul—from the incorrupt Virgin. For it is certain and true beyond ambiguity that the person of the Son of God assumed human nature without sin, as is proved by the testimonies and established by the teachings of the saints. For most blessed Augustine says in the book *On Faith to Peter*: [Note: [Col. 0457D] *Sentences*, III, distinction 5, chapter “Praeterea.”] “When God the Only-Begotten was conceived, he received the truth of flesh from the Virgin; and when he was born, he preserved the integrity of virginity in his mother.” And shortly afterward: “The Son of God assumed human nature in the unity of his person; humbling himself through mercy, he filled the womb of the incorrupt Virgin, from whom he was to be born. Therefore, as Nestorius falsely maintained, there is not one person of the Son of God and another, separately, of the son of man; rather, truly and without any ambiguity, God and man are one Christ. For the Word of God the Father assumed not a person but human nature, that is, soul and flesh.”

For it is recorded [Col. 0458A] that the Council of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0457D] Editions of the *Master* vary here: some, indeed very ancient ones, attribute these words to the eighth Council of Toledo, others to the sixth Council of Toledo; but the latter must be followed, [Col. 0458D] for the words are canon 1 of the aforesaid sixth synod.] handed down the following: “The Word alone became flesh and dwelt among us; and although the whole Trinity effected the formation of the assumed man, because the operations of the Trinity are inseparable, the Son alone assumed the man into the singularity of his own person, that is, into that which is proper to the Son. (Therefore the incarnation of the Son of God must be believed to have been effected by the whole Trinity; nevertheless, the Son alone received the form of a servant [Note: [Col. 0458D] The words placed by us in parentheses are from the Eleventh Council of Toledo.].)”

Therefore Nestorius lied in his assertion, saying that Christ’s divine and human substance was not one person but two persons. The Son of God is not one person and the son of the Virgin another; rather, as rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ. Repent, therefore, O [Col. 0458B] Nestorians, of having thought unworthily of Christ until now and uttered falsehoods. Drive this lying and condemnable sect from your hearts as quickly as possible; humbly and devoutly subject yourselves to the most true doctrines of the Catholic Church, so that you may not perish with heretics but may attain, with the children of that same holy Church, the salvation of your souls. Reveal in confession of heart, with tears and contrition of heart, to the priests of the Catholic Church the abominable stains of leprosy—that is, the detestable blasphemies of heretical perversity—and receive through their counsel and teaching the color of health, namely, the rule for living well, so that with them you may be able to live happily both in the present age and in the age to come. Amen.

[Col. 0458C] Let us also hear what blessed Isidore says in the book of the *Etymologies* concerning the Eutychian [Note: [Col. 0458D] The Eutychian heretics asserted that, after the assumption of humanity, Christ did not subsist in two natures but that only the divine nature existed in him. They are refuted by the strongest authorities of Paul, Daniel, Stephen, John, and Ezekiel.] heretics. “The Eutychian heretics,” he says, “are called after Eutychius, abbot of Constantinople, who denied that Christ, after the assumption of humanity, subsisted in two natures, but maintained that only the divine nature existed in him.”

This abbot Eutychius also held erroneous views concerning Christ when he said that, having put off the humanity which he had put on without sin for the redemption of the world, Christ subsisted in divinity alone. But Paul, teacher and expounder of the Catholic faith, plainly refutes his false assertion. Concerning God and man, Jesus Christ himself, Paul says: “Christ, having appeared as high priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, [Col. 0458D] not made with hands, that is, not of this creation, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption” (Heb. IX).

Let us now see why this high priest of the good things to come, namely Christ, is called high priest, how he appears, and before whom. He is called priest because, for our salvation, he offered himself as an unblemished sacrifice to God the Father on the altar of the cross. Therefore he is priest [Col. 0459A] and sacrifice. He is called high priest because, receiving a human body from the incorrupt Virgin and, after the triumph of his most victorious passion and resurrection, ascending into heaven in the same flesh which he assumed without sin from his virgin Mother, he stands always before God the Father and intercedes for us. The Apostle also testifies to this afterward, saying: “For Jesus did not enter into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true, but into heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God for you” (ibid.). Why did Jesus not enter temples made with hands? Because the true priest had to enter not shadows but the true reality, that is, heaven.

Tell us, then, O Eutychian heretics: before whom does this eternal high priest, who entered heaven through his own blood, stand in heaven? Tell us before whom he stands. Do you wish to hear before whom? Before God the Father, namely, who sent him into this world for the redemption of the human race and willed him to assume flesh from the incorrupt Virgin. And how does he stand before that same Father, who begot him before all ages and decreed that he should be incarnate in time? Namely, in that humanity, now glorified, which he assumed from the Virgin, conceived by the Holy Spirit and without fault. In it the Son of God redeemed the world; in it he ascended into heaven; in it, now an eternal and immortal high priest, he stands before God the Father; in it he foretold that he would come to judge the living, the dead, and the world by fire. Therefore the Son of God and of the Virgin did not stand at the right hand of God the Father in divinity alone, as you, O Eutychian [Col. 0459C] heretics, plainly lie; rather, the true God, through the humanity which he assumed from the Virgin, stands before God the Father and intercedes for all predestined to eternal life. But, to overthrow your false sect more plainly and strengthen the truth of Catholic faith, let us bring forward the testimonies of the holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments.

Tell us, holy Daniel, what was revealed to you in vision concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity and his exaltation, so that by your most true testimony the Eutychian heretics, convicted of their false assertion, may receive the Catholic faith and truly believe with us that Jesus Christ, true God and true man, is in the glory of God the Father. “I looked,” he says, [Col. 0459D] “in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a Son of Man, and he came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him” (Dan. VII). For the prophet, taught by the Holy Spirit, foresaw that Christ would be born of the Virgin, redeem the world, ascend into heaven, and sit at the right hand of God the Father; and therefore he spoke of the future as though it were past. As though he said more plainly: “I looked in the vision of the night,” that is, being amid the clouds of ignorance of the present age; “and behold, with the clouds of heaven,” that is, with patriarchs and prophets watering human minds with spiritual rain, “the Son of Man came.” Namely, after the most noble triumph of passion and resurrection, he ascended into heaven in great glory, accompanied by angels, [Col. 0460A] and came even to the Ancient of Days, that is, to God the Father, to whom the Psalmist says among other things: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI). And the angels who accompanied this Son of Man presented him before him. It follows:

“And to him was given by that Ancient of Days, namely God the Father, kingdom and honor; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him.” And he added: “His power,” namely the power of that same Son of God and man, “is an eternal power which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII). By this testimony, O Eutychian heretics, the prophet Daniel plainly refutes your false assertion, by which you say that Christ, having put off the humanity which he received without sin from his Virgin mother, subsists in divinity alone; and he unquestionably strengthens the truth of Catholic faith. He strengthens in faith the minds of those who believe in Christ, and plainly condemns you who deny that Christ, from two substances, namely divine and human, is one person.

But, further to increase our faith and convict your unbelief, let us introduce other witnesses. Let us bring forward blessed Stephen the Levite, one of the seven deacons ordained by blessed Peter the apostle and stoned by the Jews for the faith of Christ; and let us all hear what he said to us concerning Christ. Tell us, holy Stephen, [Col. 0460C] Christ’s first martyr; tell us, as we listen, that testimony concerning Christ which, while the Jews stoned you for the truth of the faith, you gave as you looked toward heaven and beheld God’s glory. “Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts VII). As though he said more plainly: I see Jesus Christ, true God and true man, standing at the right hand of the power of God the Father and strengthening me, lest I be moved from the steadfastness of faith by the blows of those stoning me. Therefore, in saying that he saw the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power, blessed Stephen wholly refutes your false assertion, O Eutychian heretics. You deny that Christ remains for ever in the humanity which he assumed from the Virgin, but say that he stands before God the Father in divinity alone, which he eternally possesses from God the Father. Thus, by this most true authority of blessed Stephen, the unbelief of your heretical perversity is proved false, and the faith of Christians is strengthened in every respect.

But to confirm our faith and overcome your most lying unbelief, let us again introduce other witnesses, so that Catholic faith may be confirmed more and more and your most lying sect wholly refuted. Let us therefore bring forward blessed John the Evangelist and see whether Jesus Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father in the same flesh which, for the redemption of humankind, he received without fault from the undefiled Virgin, or whether, in divinity alone, [Col. 0461A] as you falsely claim, he stands before that same God the Father. [Note: [Col. 0461D] Supply: “let us see.”] Tell us, then, holy John, what you saw concerning Christ in the Spirit, so that the Eutychian heretics, convicted by your most true testimony, may be corrected from their perversity and the truth of Catholic faith be strengthened in every way. Tell us, then, what you saw: namely, that on the Lord’s day you were in the Spirit, heard a loud voice behind you, and turned your face in order to see the voice speaking with you. “I turned,” he says, “to see the voice that was speaking with me; and I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like a Son of Man, clothed in a long robe and girded at the breasts with a golden belt. His head and hair were white like white wool and like snow; his eyes were like [Col. 0461B] a flame of fire, and his feet were like bronze, as in a furnace of burning fire” (Rev. I). By this testimony of blessed John the Evangelist, O Eutychian heretics, your most lying assertion is unquestionably proved false, and the faith of holy Church is most certainly established. Nevertheless, let this vision of blessed John be brought again to mind, and let us carefully consider how it ought to be understood according to the mystical sense.

And turning, he says, I saw seven golden lampstands, that is, seven Churches aflame and enlightened by the wisdom of the divine Word. And in the midst of the seven golden lampstands, one like the Son of Man: that is, not as though he were now the Son of Man, but like the Son of Man, because he no longer dies and death shall have no more dominion over him [Col. 0461C] (Rom. VI). Or he was like the Son of Man because he appeared not with sin, but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. VIII). Clothed in a robe reaching to the feet—that is, in a priestly garment, namely human flesh, in which he offered himself and daily offers himself, presenting himself to God the Father. Or the garment reaching to the feet is the Church, with which God is clothed and which is ankle-length, because it is extended to the end of the world. And girded about the breasts, because he, the head of the whole Church, first showed in himself what he now requires from his own. “Girded,” he says, “with a golden belt,” that is, with the girdle of charity, because he ministers love to his saints. Hence he himself says of himself in the Gospel: “Passing by, he will minister to them” (Luke XII); that is, after the judgment he will prepare, namely appoint for them, eternal dwellings. But his head and hair were [Col. 0461D] white as white wool and as snow. As though he said: Christ’s head was white, in which are all things necessary for the governance of the Church; and his hair was white with the brightness of righteousness—namely, the saints, imitators of his innocence and simplicity, refined by disciplines and clinging to that head like white wool, that is, a garment against cold, namely against vices; and like white snow—namely, [whiter than] every creature—by which the brightness of immortality is signified. And his eyes were like a flame of fire, namely the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which belong both to Christ who possesses them and gives them to his faithful, and to the Church which receives them; they enlighten the faithful and make them burn in the love of God. [Col. 0462A] Or Christ’s eyes are the spiritual men in the Church. His feet were like bronze, as in a furnace of burning fire. As though he plainly said: His feet—that is, the last faithful, who are to be found near the end of the world, namely in the times of Antichrist—tested as though by many beatings through the greatness of their sufferings and diverse tribulations, will not retain the oldness of the old man, but will be changed through Christ into a better color, that is, into the newness of spiritual life; just as bronze, the more it is burned and beaten, is seen the more brightly. In another sense, the Lord’s feet sometimes signify the stability of eternity, sometimes his humanity, sometimes the preachers of the holy Church, of whom it is written: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace and [Col. 0462B] proclaim good things” (Isa. LII).

By this testimony of the blessed John the Evangelist, as we have said, the faith of the holy Church is greatly strengthened, the assertion of heretics is refuted, the perfidy of the Jews is overcome, and the superstition of the pagans is brought to nothing. But if you, Eutychian heretics, still do not believe that Jesus Christ stands in the humanity which he assumed from the Virgin without the contagion of sin; if you intend to persist in the malice of your perversity; if you are still unwilling to give credence to the aforesaid testimonies of the holy Fathers; if you resolve still to continue in the sect of your perversity: let us bring forward the prophet Ezekiel and diligently hear whatever he may tell us concerning the Son of God and man.

[Col. 0462C] Speak then, O prophet Ezekiel, you who deserved to serve God with a chaste body and a simple, pure heart. Speak concerning the Son of Man that which was revealed to you when you were among the captives by the river Chebar—namely, when the heavens were opened and you saw visions of God—so that the aforesaid heretics, overcome by your most faithful testimony, may depart from the wickedness of their perversity and faithfully believe that Jesus Christ, true God and true man, sits at the right hand of God the Father. “Above the firmament,” he says, “which was over their heads,” namely the living creatures, “was something like the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne; and upon the likeness of the throne, the likeness as it were of the appearance [Col. 0462D] of a man above” (Ezek. I). Let the blessed Gregory, eminent doctor of the Catholic Church, come forward and explain to us this verse of such profundity.

“What,” he says, “is signified by the throne but those angelic powers which excel even the angels themselves by the dignity of a higher rank? For although angels are called messengers, and angels often come to men to announce certain things, thrones are never read of as messengers sent for ministry, because the Creator of all, far more sublime than they, presides over them. Hence the apostle Paul, describing the orders of the heavenly hosts which he had seen when caught up to the third heaven, says: ‘Whether thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and [Col. 0463A] in him’ (Col. XI). He therefore placed thrones before the orders of the angels [Note: [Col. 0463D] Of the angels.], whom he recognized as set over them. The throne is aptly compared to a sapphire stone, because sapphire has an airy color. Thus the powers of heavenly spirits are signified by the sapphire stone, because these spirits, over whom God Almighty presides more highly, hold the dignity of a higher place in heaven. But above the throne was the likeness of a man, because above those powers also which precede the angels is the glory of our Redeemer.

“Therefore it should be noted what order is preserved: over the living creatures is the firmament, over the firmament the throne, and over the throne a man is described; because above holy human beings still living in this corruption [Col. 0463B] of the body are angels; above angels are the higher angelic powers nearest to God; and above the powers nearest to God is exalted the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, raised up at the right hand of God the Father.”

Therefore, in saying that the prophet Ezekiel saw the likeness of a man above thrones—that is, above principalities and powers—he was undoubtedly foreseeing in the Spirit the very Son of God and of the Virgin, who was to be born according to the flesh and sit at the right hand of God the Father. Since, then, the prophet declares that the likeness of a man sits above all angelic powers, he plainly contradicts you, Eutychian heretics, who say that he stands before God the Father not in the humanity which he received without sin from the undefiled Virgin, but in divinity alone. Recognize, therefore, that you have lied in your assertion, and believe that Jesus Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father not in divinity alone nor in humanity alone, but as true God and true man. For the Son of God assumed our humanity in the unity of his person, and by it he was undoubtedly to redeem us from the power of the ancient enemy. And because his humanity, as has been said, is never separated from the Son of God, he rules in heaven over all angels and on earth over all human beings. According to his properly human nature, the Son of God humbled himself, becoming obedient to God the Father unto death, even death on a cross. According to that nature God the Father also [Col. 0463D] exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of that God-and-man, Jesus Christ, every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that he, our Lord Jesus Christ, is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II). For the Son of God loved our nature so greatly that he not only freed it from the devil’s power, but also placed it in himself at the Father’s right hand above all good angels. The human nature which had been taken captive by the devil in the first man Adam now itself reigns above all angels in our Redeemer Jesus Christ.

By these aforesaid most true [Col. 0464A] authorities, O Eutychian heretics, you and your master Eutyches are undoubtedly defeated in your false assertion, whereby you say that Jesus Christ, God and man, stands before God the Father in divinity alone. Competent witnesses of the Old and New Testaments agree most plainly that Christ is true God and true man, and prove that you are teachers of heretical perversity. They affirm that Jesus Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father in the same humanity which he assumed without sin from the Virgin Mother; and they utterly overcome you, who stubbornly deny this, in your argument. It is therefore necessary for you to believe without doubt that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and humbly to do penance before God and before the prelates of the holy Church for the blasphemies you have uttered, so that, producing fruits worthy of repentance, you may obtain forgiveness of sins from that same Jesus Christ, the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. Show the leprosy of your heretical perversity to the priests of the Church in accordance with the command of that same God and man, Jesus Christ; and receive with devout mind, according to their judgment or instruction, the color of health—that is, the truth of the Catholic faith—so that by right belief, humble repentance, and worthy works you may recover the grace of that same Son of God and of the Virgin. Amen.

I do not wish you, O Jews, to forget your objection which you recently raised against us concerning lepers. For you said that we who read the Law instituted by God and believe the prophets sent by him ought not [Col. 0464C] to receive lepers or permit them to dwell with us, but ought, according to the Lord’s command, to drive them far from us. But we, understanding the Law not literally but spiritually, cast you, O Jews, who publicly blaspheme Christ, and all the aforesaid heretics, whom above we have most openly convicted by the most true testimonies of the holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, outside the camp—that is, outside the holy and devout communities of all believers—as men full of sores and struck with leprosy. Truly you, O Jews, and all heretics who blaspheme Christ, are to be condemned, not those whom various illnesses weaken. Therefore you and all the aforesaid heretics bear leprosy—that is, false teaching—upon your heads: you who publicly dishonor Jesus Christ, God and man, and not only do not conceal the blasphemies of your error, but, worse still, utter them aloud publicly and defend them with the full effort of your minds. Therefore you are especially to be called leprous and separated from the camps of the faithful—you whom heretical perversity defiles—rather than those whom an accidental sickness weakens and an under-the-skin discharge disfigures.

§ XXXI.

The Alogian heretics do not believe that the Word of God was begotten of God the Father before all ages. They reject John’s Gospel and Apocalypse. They are refuted by John’s Gospel.

Since, therefore, we have openly marked the false sects of the heretics—those, namely, who bear leprosy upon the head, that is, who openly defend heretical perversity—and, with God’s help, have manifestly overcome their cunning assertions by the most true arguments of the holy Scriptures, it remains again to consider who those are who bear leprosy in the beard. For as the beard is an ornament of a man, so the holy apostles and doctors provide an ornament to the body of Christ, that is, the Church. They therefore bear leprosy in the beard who think perversely of the apostles and other holy leaders of the Church, and pretend that they preached some falsehood—such as the Alogian heretics, who contradicted those same holy apostles in many matters.

“The heretics are called Alogians,” says blessed Isidore [Note: [Col. 0465D] *Etymologies*, Book VIII, ch. 5], “as though *without the Word*; for *logos* in Greek means ‘word.’ [Col. 0465B] They do not believe that the Word of God was begotten from God the Father before all ages, rejecting John’s Gospel and Apocalypse.” Rightly, indeed, are these Alogian heretics also said to bear something like leprosy in the beard: not believing in the Word of God the Father, through whom all things were made, and rejecting the sayings of the apostles, they endeavor to inflict the greatest ugliness upon the whole Church. But they will not succeed at all, for in their argument they plainly lie. The blessed John the Evangelist openly destroys their error at the beginning of his Gospel, when he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

It should be noted that the aforesaid Alogian heretics, who do not believe the Word coeternal with God the Father, do not accept this Gospel because in it John the Evangelist testifies that Christ, according to his divinity, was the Word in the beginning, was with God the Father, and was God. When that most blessed apostle and evangelist John was detained on the island of Patmos by Domitian’s command because of his unconquerable constancy in evangelizing, the Churches of Christ—which the blessed Paul, assisted by God’s grace, had planted, Apollos had watered, and the same blessed John the Evangelist had illuminated by preaching spiritual teaching—were disturbed by Alogius, Ebbius, and Cerinthus, heretics, and other false apostles in the error of heretical perversity. They said that Christ, according to his divinity, was not coeternal with God the Father, but had taken his beginning in time from the Virgin. [Col. 0465D] Therefore, after the emperor Domitian had already been killed by the Roman Senate, the blessed John, returning from the island of Patmos by the ordering of divine grace, was asked by the bishops of Asia to write a Gospel of truth against the aforesaid heretics and destroy their deadly, venomous heresy. Having proclaimed a three-day fast to the whole Church, he wrote the Gospel under the instruction of the Holy Spirit. Through it the crafty assertion of all heretics is destroyed; the whole Church is strengthened in the Catholic faith; the minds of believers are raised to desire heavenly things; the hearts of the elect are increasingly kindled in love of God and neighbor; all God’s devout people are further stirred to good works; and the holy people redeemed by Christ’s blood more devoutly strive after the better gifts [Col. 0466A].

Let us therefore again bring forward the aforesaid testimony of the blessed John the Evangelist, O heretics, and diligently hear what it tells us concerning Christ according to his divinity. “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Thus, by saying that it was in the beginning, he openly refutes you in your lying assertion, who deny this. By testifying also that it was with God the Father, he plainly demonstrates that Father and Son are not one person but two. Again, in declaring that it was God and was with God, he clearly overcomes you who deny [i.e., assert the contrary: “maintain”] that Christ [Col. 0466B] is not true God but merely a human being [Note: [Col. 0466D] “Rather, you assert this, or something similar.”]. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ has from God the Father the natural substance of divinity and from his Virgin Mother the true nature of flesh. He was born ineffably from God the Father before all ages; he was born in time from the incorrupt Virgin Mary.

To refute completely your false assertion and confirm the truth of our faith, let us produce the testimony of the book of the Apocalypse and carefully hear what it says concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity. Surely, if we give unquestioning faith to the words of the holy prophets, we ought to believe the holy angels sent by God for the ministry of our salvation. Let us all therefore hear what the angel says to the whole Church in the person of Jesus Christ, God and man: “These things says the first and the last, who was dead and lives: I know your tribulation and poverty” (Apoc. II). As though, more openly revealing his divinity and humanity for the consolation and strengthening of the faithful, and for the refutation of Jews, pagans, and heretics, he said: Do not fail, my faithful ones, amid the tribulations inflicted upon you by the ungodly because of hatred for my name. For I, being so great, am the first—namely, existing before all things and he through whom all things subsist—and the last, he through whom all things will be brought to completion; and I suffered death for you. I admonish you, O heretics, who stubbornly deny that Christ was eternally [Col. 0466D] in God the Father, to listen attentively to what is said. Therefore, because Christ is called through the angel the first—that is, existing before every creature—he must plainly be believed to be not a mere man, as you lie, but true God. And because the same angel subsequently declares him the last—that is, he through whom all things will be brought to completion—and dead and living, he is understood, and firmly believed by the whole Church, to be true God and true man. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is the first, begotten ineffably from God the Father before all ages; and he is the last, after whom is none, namely he in whom all things shall end. [Col. 0467A] He is also to come with power and majesty to judge the living and the dead. Recognize, therefore, O heretics, that you have lied in your assertion, and believe without doubt that Jesus Christ is true God and true man. For the authorities of the holy Scriptures proclaim him to be the true Son of God the Father and the true son of his human mother; and they prove you liars, who maintain that he took his beginning not from God the Father before all ages but in time from his mother. Thus, O heretics, you bear leprosy, as it were, in the beard, because you have rejected the words of the holy apostles and publicly blaspheme Jesus Christ, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing. Yet if with all your heart you withdraw from so damnable a sect, humbly repent before God for the blasphemies you have uttered, and receive through the ministers of the holy Church the rule of true faith, you may obtain pardon from the same almighty God, who is three in persons and one in essence. Amen.

§ XXXII.

The Severian heretics, who do not receive the Old Testament and deny the resurrection of the flesh, and do not drink wine, are refuted. The contrary is affirmed by Job’s declaration, the prefiguration in Exodus, and Paul’s testimony. At what age, in what condition, and in what state we shall rise. Likewise, in what manner Christ will descend with the voice of an archangel, with the sound of a trumpet, and at the hour of midnight. He again prefigures this from Ezekiel’s words; and Hosea proclaims in Christ’s resurrection the resurrection of all the faithful of the world; likewise does the narrative of the book of Numbers. Even though bones are reduced to dust, we shall nonetheless rise. He delivers a fine outcry against the Severians [Col. 0467C].

Those also bear leprosy in the body who disparage the holy Church: such as the Severian heretics, who do not receive the Old Testament and deny the resurrection of the flesh; the Heraclites, who condemn marriage and do not believe that little children possess the kingdoms of heaven; and the Cathari [Note: [Col. 0467D] *Cathari*.], who, glorying in their own merits, deny forgiveness of sins to penitents and condemn widows, if they remarry, as adulteresses. All these heretics of whom we have spoken, who publicly disparage the holy Church, which is Christ’s body, bear leprosy, as it were, in the body.

But now let us hear what the blessed Isidore says about the aforesaid heretics. “The Severians,” he says [Note: [Col. 0467D] *Etymologies*, as above], “are heretics [Col. 0467D] originating from the heretic Severus. They do not drink wine, they do not receive the Old Testament, and, among other damnable errors, deny the general resurrection of all human beings.” Rightly, then, are they cast out by ecclesiastical men from the gathering of the faithful as though leprous—that is, they are reckoned among heretics—since they deny the resurrection of the flesh and think themselves religious by a false estimate. Blessed Job openly convicts them of having lied in their false assertion when he declares that he will rise on the last day in his own flesh, saying: “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; [Col. 0468A] and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior” (Job XIX). For when he asserted without doubt that he would rise in the same flesh in which he lived and would see his Redeemer, he plainly overcame you in your most lying argument and entirely frustrated your damnable sect.

But to confirm also our faith, who firmly believe that the resurrection of the flesh will come, and to overcome your perfidy, let us bring forward the blessed apostle Paul and gladly hear whatever he tells us concerning the general resurrection of all human beings. “For this we say to you in the word of the Lord,” he says, “that we who are alive, who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not go before those who [Col. 0468B] have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven at the command, with the voice of an archangel and with God’s trumpet; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, shall together be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. IV). By these most true words of the blessed apostle Paul, O Severian heretics, the holy Church, mother of all the faithful, is more firmly strengthened in the Catholic faith, and your lying assertion is wholly brought to nothing and refuted. For he not only simply relates the general resurrection of all human beings, but plainly proclaims also the order in which it will be celebrated. Indeed, the Lord foreshadowed that future resurrection of all in the book of Exodus, when he spoke figuratively to Moses: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” He answered, “A rod.” “Cast it,” he says, “upon the ground.” And he cast it down, and it became a serpent. Moses was afraid and fled. The Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail.” And he took hold of it, and it became a rod (Exod. IV). [Note: [Col. 0467D] From Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 8, near [Col. 0468D] the end.] In the serpent’s tail the end of the age is understood, because the mortality of the human race rolls onward through the slippery course of time. Some come by being born, others go by dying, as it were through the serpent. Death is the path; but at the final end, as at the tail of the age, through the resurrection we shall return to the hand of God. Seized by that hand, we shall be restored to a better state; and, when hostile death has been destroyed, we shall rise as the rod of royal power in the right hand of God.

[Col. 0468D] By the aforesaid authorities, O heretics, the truth of the future resurrection is openly shown, and the falsity of your argument—you who deny it—is wholly refuted [Note: [Col. 0468D] “Is refuted.”]. It seems very useful and necessary to us, O Severian heretics, that the blessed Paul should come again into our midst and explain to us more plainly the order of the resurrection which he learned through the inward instruction of the Holy Spirit, as he stated above. Tell us, then, if you know, O holy Paul: shall we who are still alive in this age, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, rise first on the day of resurrection, or those who departed from this age from the beginning of the world? “We who are alive,” he says, “who remain at the coming of the Lord, shall not go before those who have fallen asleep before us.” Tell us also, holy apostle Paul, in what manner Jesus Christ, king of kings, lawgiver, and judge, will come to judgment. “The Lord himself,” he says, “will descend from heaven at the command, with the voice of an archangel and with God’s trumpet; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first.” Who are those dead in Christ? Namely, those who in the Old Testament believed without doubt that Christ would come, be born from the Virgin, redeem the world through the cross, rise from the dead, judge the living, the dead, and the world through fire, and save through himself; and those who in the New Testament truly upheld the Catholic faith in word and deed. [Col. 0469B] O holy apostle Paul! Since those dead in Christ will have risen, what then will become of us? “We,” he says, “who are still alive, who remain, shall together be caught up with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and thus shall we always be with the Lord.” O holy Paul, we also ask you to tell us at what age or measure we shall rise. “We shall all attain,” he says, “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV). [Note: [Col. 0469D] *Sentences*, IV, dist. 44, “They are accustomed” and “But this.”] Here the Apostle used “man,” not, however, to distinguish sex, but to signify the perfection of strength which we shall then possess; yet not all will have the same bodily stature. Hence blessed Augustine says: “The Apostle did not say ‘to the measure of Christ’s body or stature,’ but ‘of age,’ [Col. 0469C] because each person will receive his own measure: either that which he had in youth, even if he died old, or that which he would have had if he died earlier. But the age will be that which Christ reached, namely youth, around thirty years. For Christ’s age when he died and rose was thirty-two years and three months. The bodies of the righteous will therefore rise radiant as the sun, without any defect, all deformities which they had here having been cut away.”

Perhaps you ask, O heretics, what is that voice of the archangel and trumpet of God, with which, according to the Apostle, Jesus Christ, God and man, will descend from heaven, and at whose sound the dead will be raised from their tombs? [Col. 0469D] [Note: [Col. 0470D] The same, dist. 43, “The cause.”] If you wish to know these things, let Master Peter, a wise and discerning man, come forward and explain them to you. “The cause,” he says, “of the resurrection of the dead will be the voice of the trumpet, which all will hear at the coming of the Judge and by whose power the dead will be awakened and rise from their tombs. Thus the Prophet says concerning that same Son of God and of the Virgin: ‘He will give to his voice a voice of power’ (Ps. LXVII), that is, the effect of raising the dead. Hence John the Evangelist also says: ‘The hour comes in which all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God, and the good will come forth to the resurrection of life, but the evil to the resurrection of judgment’ (John V).”

[Col. 0470A] But you also ask, O Severian heretics, what and what sort of voice that is. Let us bring blessed Paul forward again and diligently hear from him what and what sort it is: “The Lord himself,” he says, “will descend from heaven with the voice of an archangel and with God’s trumpet.” The one whom the Apostle calls archangel is certainly understood to be Jesus Christ, judge of the living and the dead. The same voice is also called a trumpet because it will be manifest and final: after it there will be no other. This trumpet is also the cry, as wise Augustine says, of which the Gospel says: “At midnight a cry arose: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. II). Thus, what the Apostle calls the voice of an archangel and God’s trumpet is called in the Gospel the voice of the Son of God and a cry. The Lord Jesus Christ, God and man, indicates in the Gospel itself at what hour he will come for judgment, saying: “At midnight a cry arose: behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him.” Explaining this, blessed Augustine says: “Midnight is not stated for an hour of time, but because he will come when he is not expected. Therefore he will come at midnight, namely when it will be very dark—that is, hidden.” Hence it is said: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. V).

But let us hear what Master Anselm says concerning the last trumpet. “Just as when the Lord gave the Law on Mount Sinai the voice of a trumpet was heard, so angels appointed for this purpose, with bodies and trumpets made of air, will make God’s terrible judgment resound to the world with a trumpet blast—Christ, namely, acting through them. Hence: ‘For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise’ (1 Cor. XV). [Col. 0470C] Thus it is said of the reprobate through the Psalmist: ‘Their memory has perished with a sound’ (Ps. IX), namely with that of the last trumpet. At that voice both good and evil dead will rise in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet—that is, in as long as you can open your eye.”

What do you say to these things, O Severian heretics, who deny the general resurrection of all human beings? What do you object, or what do you answer? Do you now give unquestioning faith to the aforesaid authorities, which agree truthfully that the resurrection of all human beings is to come, or do you still doubt it? But because you do not yet fully believe that it will occur, let us bring forward other witnesses to overcome your perfidy and confirm faith in that resurrection. Let the blessed Job therefore come forward again and offer us testimony of the future resurrection. “I know,” he says, “that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth; and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God my Savior, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (Job XIX). Mark the words, O Severian heretics, and apply understanding of mind to so clear an authority. Let us therefore hear what the blessed Job says concerning our Redeemer, who truly suffered and rose for us, and by his resurrection plainly foreshadowed the future resurrection of us all. [Col. 0471A] “I know,” he says, “that my Redeemer lives.” [Note: [Col. 0471D] From Gregory, *Morals*, Book XIV, ch. 26.] Since he did not say “Creator” but “Redeemer,” he plainly announces him who, after creating all things, appeared incarnate among us in order to redeem us from the devil’s captivity and by his passion freed us from everlasting death. As though he said more plainly: All unbelievers know that he was scourged, mocked, struck with hands, crowned with thorns, smeared with spittle, crucified, dead, and buried; yet they did not believe that he was true God and lived after death. But I believe with assured faith that he lives after death; with a free voice I profess that this same Redeemer of mine lives, having risen from the dead—he who died in the hands of the ungodly. For he speaks of the future as though of the past. But what, O blessed Job, do you hope concerning the resurrection of your own flesh also through his resurrection? We beseech you, confess it in plain words, so that the Severian heretics, converted from their perversity by your testimony, may believe that they will rise, though to this day they deny the resurrection of the flesh. “On the last day,” he says, “I shall rise from the earth” [Note: [Col. 0471D] Ibid., ch. 27.]. Why? Because the resurrection which my Redeemer himself displayed in himself he will also accomplish in me without doubt. In this place—that is, in this great strength of faith—blessed Job represents the person of the whole Catholic Church. He therefore showed the resurrection in himself so that we might trust that we can rise. Hence he willed that death itself should last no more than three days, lest, if resurrection were delayed in him, it should altogether be despaired of in us. This is well said of him through the Prophet: “He shall drink from the torrent in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. C). For he deigned to drink, not at a dwelling-place but on the way, as it were from a certain stream of our passion: he willed to taste death only temporarily, that is, for three days. Therefore, by rising on the third day, he showed what follows in his body, that is, in the Church.

Perhaps, O Severian heretics, because you observe that the spirit is separated from the flesh, that flesh is turned into decay, that decay is reduced to dust, that dust is dissolved into the elements and is thereafter no longer seen by human eyes, you therefore despair that resurrection can occur. Moreover, when you look upon dry bones, you distrust that they can be clothed with flesh and again revive into life. But if you do not hold the faith of reason from obedience, you certainly ought to hold it from reason. You continually see small seeds of trees entrusted to the earth’s moisture, from which not long afterwards you see great trees rise and put forth leaves and fruit. What wonder, then, if, when he wills, he refashions into a human being the finest dust—even dust reduced to the elements beyond our sight—he who restores immense trees from the smallest seeds? Therefore, since you have been created rational by God, O heretics, you ought to derive hope for your resurrection from the very appearance and contemplation of things [Note: [Col. 0471D] “Appearance and contemplation.”].

[Col. 0472A] But now, O Severian heretics, I urge you to listen diligently to what blessed Job says. “I believe that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” Behold, O blessed Job, we have now heard from you the most true testimony of resurrection; yet we wish to hear again about the result of resurrection. We believe without doubt that we shall rise, but we still desire to know what we shall be like in that resurrection. We wish, indeed, to know whether we shall rise in some other, perhaps subtle or airy body, or in that body in which [Note: [Col. 0472D] “In which.”] we die. For resurrection cannot properly be called resurrection where that which dies does not rise again. Remove this doubt from us, then, O blessed Job; and if our flesh is truly to rise, clearly show it [Col. 0472B] for the strengthening of the Catholic faith.

It follows: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin.” When you say, blessed Job, that you will again be clothed with your skin, every doubt concerning the true resurrection is plainly removed from our minds. Therefore we can no longer doubt the hope of our resurrection, since you affirm that you will rise on the last day. Yet, that you may remove from us every ambiguity, we ask you to offer again some testimony concerning the condition of the true resurrection. “And in my flesh,” he says, “I shall see God my Saviour.” Nothing whatever remains, O Severian heretics, on account of which your minds ought any longer to doubt, when you plainly hear blessed Job declaring that on the last day he will rise, be clothed again with his own skin [Note: Col. 0472D: “be clothed”], and see God his Saviour in his own proper flesh [Col. 0472C]. But whether we shall rise in this same flesh in which we live, or in some other, we ask you, blessed Job, to show more certainly to us who desire to hear. Add, therefore, blessed Job, what you think, and remove from our hearts the scruple of doubt. It follows: “Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.” [Note: Col. 0472D: From Gregory, cited above, ch. 30.]

For if after the resurrection the body will not be tangible, as some suppose, then assuredly one person dies and another rises; and—what it is impious even to say or believe—it is as though I die and another rises. But blessed Job destroys this notion with his truthful utterance when he says: “Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.” In affirming without doubt that he himself, and not another in his place, will see God, he plainly demonstrates the condition of the true resurrection [Col. 0472D]. Likewise, when our Redeemer after his resurrection offered his bones and flesh to his doubting disciples to be touched, he displayed beforehand the reality of his flesh, already raised, and of our resurrection, still to come. “Handle and see,” he says, “for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24).

Here I admonish you, O Severian heretics, to give faith to the testimony of blessed Job; firmly believing that Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, had a tangible body after his resurrection [Col. 0473A], abandon the unbelief of heretical perversity and believe without any doubt in the universal resurrection yet to come for all human beings. For we confess that our flesh after the resurrection will be both the same and different: the same in nature, different in glory; the same in reality, different in power. It will therefore be subtle and incorruptible; it will be tangible, because it will not lose the substance of its true nature.

We ask you also, holy Job, to add with what hope you hold this confidence of resurrection, with what certainty you await it: “This hope of mine,” he says, “is laid up in my bosom.” We believe most certainly that we hold what we lay up in our bosom. Thus this holy man had hope laid up in his bosom [Col. 0473B], that is, in his heart; enlightened by the Holy Spirit, he uttered most true testimonies concerning the hope of the resurrection with such certainty.

But if, O heretics, persisting still in your condemnable unbelief, you refuse to credit these most true authorities of the New and Old Testaments—that all human beings will truly rise with their bodies—then listen more attentively, I urge you, to how plainly God Almighty himself, Creator of body and soul, foreshadowed through the prophet Ezekiel the resurrection of all the righteous.

“The hand of the Lord,” he says, “came upon me, and led me forth in the Spirit of the Lord; and he set me down in the midst of a field” [Col. 0473C] “which was full of bones. And he led me around among them in a circle. They were exceedingly numerous upon the face of the field and very dry; and he said to me: Son of man, do you think these bones can live? And I said: Lord God, you know.” As though he said: Lord God, who possess full knowledge of all future things, you know whether these bones can live again. And the Lord said to me: “Prophesy over these bones, and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord” (Ezek. 37).

It is remarkable that he speaks to dry bones, so that before they have sinews, flesh, skin, and a life-giving spirit, they may hear God’s word. “Thus says the Lord God to these bones: Behold, I shall send spirit into you, and you shall live; and I shall put sinews upon you, so that you may be joined together; and I shall cause flesh to grow upon you” [Col. 0473D], “and shall spread skin over you, and shall give you spirit, and you shall live, and know that I am the Lord. And I prophesied as he commanded me. And as I prophesied there was a sound, and behold, a shaking; and the bones came together, bone to bone, each to its own joint. And I saw, and behold, sinews and flesh came upon them; and skin was stretched over them above, but they had no spirit. And he said to me: Son of man, prophesy, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord God: Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain persons, that they may live again. And I prophesied as the Lord commanded me. And the spirit entered into them and they lived; and they stood upon their feet, an army exceedingly great. And he said to me: Son of man, these bones are the house of Israel.”

For Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God.” These bones, therefore, are the house of Israel: that is, the holy Church, which is truly the house of Christians who see God through faith and works [Col. 0474A].

But let us hear what the dead themselves say: “Our bones are dried up, our hope has perished”—that is, so far as we are concerned—“and we are cut off.” As though they said more plainly: Unless we rise through divine omnipotence, we can no longer rise by ourselves. “Therefore,” he says, “prophesy, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall open your tombs and bring you out from your graves, my people; and I shall lead you into your land, Israel; and you shall know that I am the Lord.”

Here it is asked: if tombs still have to be opened, how were the bones upon the face of the field? [Col. 0474B] Therefore, by saying that the tombs of the dead still had to be opened, he made known that he was speaking figuratively. It follows: “When I have opened your graves,” he says, “and brought you out of your tombs, my people, and have given my spirit within you, and you have lived, and I have caused you to rest upon your own soil, you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken and done it, says the Lord God.”

These things stated above should not be understood of the general resurrection, that is, of both the good and the wicked, but of the first resurrection in which the saints shall rise; of it it is said: “Blessed is he who has a part in the first resurrection, because over him the second death shall have no power” (Rev. 20). Hence blessed Paul says: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first” (1 Thess. 4). Therefore the resurrection of the saints will be one thing, and that of sinners another. For thus the Psalmist says: “The ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous” (Ps. 1).

But let us recall again what the Lord said above to the righteous who are in the tombs—that is, who place their confidence not in themselves but in him—so that faith in the resurrection may be strengthened more firmly in the hearts of all believers, and your false assertion, O Severian heretics, who deny it, may be more clearly overcome. For he said: “Behold, I shall open your tombs and bring you out from your graves, my people.” Similar is what God and man, Jesus Christ himself, says of himself in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when the dead who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good shall come forth” [Col. 0474D] “to the resurrection of life” (John 5). And again: “Those who hear the voice of the Son of God shall live” (ibid.).

“And I shall lead you,” he says, “into your land, Israel”: that is, into the land of the saints who live forever and see the face of God, concerning which the Son of God and of the Virgin himself says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5); and concerning which the Psalmist sang with rejoicing: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114). By these and similar most true authorities of the New and Old Testaments, O heretics, the Catholic faith is especially confirmed, and your unbelief altogether convicted.

Yet this vision mentioned above can also be understood of a temporal resurrection. For when any perverse persons live pleasurably and persistently in their crimes [Col. 0475A], and despair of being saved through God’s goodness, although they still live in their bodies, they are already dead to God in their souls. But when, illuminated by divine grace, they presume upon God’s mercy, mourn their past sins, and by mourning do not commit them again, and submit themselves with devout minds to the zeal of good works, beyond doubt they rise from everlasting death. For no one can mourn sins or receive hope of pardon in the heart unless God looks upon him. Thus we read in the Gospel: “The Lord turned and looked upon Peter” (Luke 22).

Accordingly, those who are dead in sins, weighed down by the burden of despair, lying prostrate in the breadth of the field—that is, in the habit of seeing evil—say within themselves: “Our bones are dried up, our hope has perished” [Col. 0475B], “and we are cut off.” As though they said: “Our bones are dried up”—that is, the strength for good works has failed within us; “our hope has perished,” namely, the hope of rising from sins; “and we are cut off” in our own estimation, that is, rejected from the company of God’s elect. But when the grace of divine goodness mercifully enlightens their minds, it immediately raises them from the death of despair and confidently lifts them up to obtain pardon for sins.

Therefore above, admonishing the prophet Ezekiel, the Lord says: “Prophesy, son of man, and say to the spirit: Thus says the Lord: Come from the four winds, O spirit, and breathe upon these slain persons, that they may live again. And I prophesied as the Lord commanded me, and the spirit entered into them, and they lived; and they stood” [Col. 0475C] “upon their feet.” God breathed into the face of the first human being the breath of life, and the human became a living soul (Gen. 2); he also breathes today into the hearts of whichever sinners he wills, raises them, and refashions them into a life-giving spirit.

What do you say to these things, O Severian heretics? What do you answer, or what do you object? Do you now believe in the general resurrection of all human beings to come on the last day, or do you still doubt it? But if you still do not believe that all human beings shall rise, if any scruple of doubt [Note: Col. 0475D: “Any … scruple.”] remains in your minds, if you do not yet believe the authorities mentioned above—that the human race shall truly rise and render an account of its own deeds before Christ’s judgment-seat [Col. 0475D]—then, to convict utterly your most false unbelief and to strengthen more and more the truth of the Catholic faith, let us again bring forward other suitable witnesses.

I urge you, therefore, to hear patiently how plainly the prophet Hosea, taught by the Holy Spirit, foretells the resurrection of all human beings at the end of the world through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, celebrated long ago. For he says in the person of the Gentiles, who first worshipped idols and afterward mutually urged one another toward faith in Christ: “Come, and let us return to the Lord; for he has seized us and will heal us; he will strike and cure us” (Hos. 6).

This prophecy most fittingly applies to the Gentiles, who, afflicted through the long slavery of the devil while worshipping idols, finally rise through faith from the darkness of unbelief when the light of truth dawns in Christ’s advent, and exhort others to good works. As though they said more plainly: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, from whom we had departed by sinning; for he has seized us,” namely, “when the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), “and he will heal us from the wounds of sins,” that is, cure us through repentance.

It follows: “He will make us alive after two days; on the third day he will raise us, and we shall live in his sight.” As though they said: Not only will he cure us, but he will also make us alive after the two days during which he lay in the tomb; and, rising from the dead on the third day, he will raise us with himself. Thus, healed of all sins through repentance [Col. 0476B], made alive through his Gospel in the knowledge of God the Father, and raised with the same Jesus Christ from the everlasting death of body and soul, we shall live in his sight both now and in the future; without him we lay dead. Taught by his instruction, we shall know what we ought to avoid and what we ought to follow; and we shall follow him either now by imitation or by ascending into heaven, that we may know the Lord face to face as he is (1 Cor. 13). Hence God and man, Jesus Christ himself, says to God the Father in the Gospel: “Father, this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

Perhaps you ask, O Severian heretics, who deny the general resurrection of all human beings [Col. 0476C], what are these three days in which the prophet asserts that through Christ’s resurrection we are healed, made alive, and raised from death. We answer you, therefore, that the first day is Christ’s humble advent; the second, when he will be seen by human beings coming in power and great majesty for judgment in glory [Note: Col. 0476D: “coming”]; the third, when, judgment completed, he will show his elect a fuller glory of his brightness.

Or, the first day is the first age of the world; the second came in Christ’s advent, in which we are made alive through faith, or already sit with Christ in the heavenly places through hope; the third is the day of resurrection, in which we shall rise through Christ, who was raised long ago. This blessed Paul testifies, saying: “From heaven, indeed, we await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform”—in the resurrection—“the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3) [Col. 0476D].

See how the witnesses of truth agree that all human beings are to rise; see how plainly they prove you, O Severian heretics, who deny the general resurrection, to have lied in your assertion. I want you, unhappy heretics, to answer my questions. For if, as you falsely say, we shall not rise from the dead, how do we possess Christ’s resurrection as the firstfruits? For the Apostle says of him: “Christ rose from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep; for since through a human being”—namely Adam—“came death, through a human being”—that is, Christ—“came the resurrection of the dead. And as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15) [Col. 0477A]. If therefore, as has been said, we do not rise from the sleep of death, how do we possess the Lord’s resurrection as the firstfruits?

See: the fathers of the Old and New Testaments agree in one spirit concerning the resurrection of the flesh. See how plainly they convict you of being defenders of falsehood. See: Truth itself first taught by word what it afterward demonstrated by deed concerning the resurrection of the flesh; and yet you miserable people still remain in doubt about it in your unbelief. You ought therefore to believe without doubt that Jesus Christ rose from the dead on the third day, and that on the last day, through his resurrection, all human beings will rise with their bodies [Col. 0477B].

For the Redeemer of humankind accepted death so that we might not fear to die. He showed resurrection in himself so that we might be confident that we can rise. Thus, when he rose on the third day, he showed what would follow in his body, that is, the Church. By his own example he displayed what he promised his faithful as their reward: so that, as his faithful recognized that he had risen, they might hope for the rewards of resurrection in themselves at the end of the world. See: through the death of the flesh we remain in the dust until the end of the world; but on the third day he blossomed forth from the dryness of death [Col. 0477C], and by that renewal of the flesh showed us the power of his divinity.

Therefore, to convict the hardness of your obstinate minds and to confirm the truth of the Catholic faith, let us set forth how plainly the history in the book of Numbers prefigures both the three-day resurrection of this same Redeemer of ours and the future general resurrection of all human beings. Thus the Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, and receive from them one rod for each of their kindreds, from all the leaders of the tribes, twelve rods; and write the name of each one upon his rod. The name of Aaron shall be upon the rod of Levi, and one rod shall represent all their families. You shall place them in the tabernacle of the covenant before the testimony, where I shall speak to you. The rod of him whom I choose” [Col. 0477D] “shall bud; and I shall put an end to the complaints of the children of Israel by which they murmur against you.”

Moses therefore spoke to the children of Israel, and all the leaders gave him rods according to their tribes; and there were twelve rods, apart from Aaron’s rod. When Moses had placed them before the Lord in the tabernacle of the testimony, on the following day he returned and found that Aaron’s rod, from the house of Levi, had budded; swelling buds had burst into flowers, which, spreading with leaves, had formed into almonds. Moses therefore brought all the rods out from the presence of the Lord to all the children of Israel; they saw, and each received his own rod. And the Lord said to Moses: “Return Aaron’s rod to the tabernacle of the testimony, that it may be kept there as a sign for the rebellious children of Israel” (Num. 17) [Col. 0478A].

It should be noted that the rods mentioned above were, by the Lord’s command, placed in the tabernacle of the covenant so that the priesthood of Aaron, who had arisen from the tribe of Levi and was proudly despised by Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, might through the miracle mentioned above be openly acknowledged by those present and those to come as approved and commended by the Lord. [Note: Col. 0477D: From Gregory, *Morals*, book XIV, ch. 28, and Paterius, on Numbers, ch. 12.]

Accordingly, since, as has been said, Aaron’s ministry was scorned with envy, lest his tribe should be thought worthy to offer burnt offerings, twelve rods corresponding to the twelve tribes were commanded to be placed in the tabernacle. And behold, the rod of Levi became green on the following day and showed what power Aaron’s office possessed. What else, indeed, is signified by this sign, except that all of us who lie in the death of the flesh until the end of the world remain, like the other rods, in dryness? But while all the rods remained dry, the rod of Levi returned to flower, because the body of the Lord Jesus Christ, our true priest, placed in the dryness of death, burst forth into the flower of true resurrection [Col. 0478B].

By this flower Aaron is rightly known to be a priest, because by this glory of resurrection our Redeemer—who arose from the tribe of Judah and Levi—is shown to be our intercessor with God the Father. See therefore: Aaron’s rod now flowers after its dryness, but the rods of the twelve tribes remain dry.
