For the body of the Lord indeed now lives after death, but our bodies are still deferred from resurrection glory until the end of the world [Col. 0478C]. Blessed Job, carefully considering this delay [Note: Col. 0478D: “delay”], says: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” We therefore have hope of our resurrection when we consider the glory of our head.

But perhaps, still remaining doubtful about the general resurrection, you raise such an objection against us, saying: [Note: Col. 0478D: From the same Gregory, ibid.] What wonder is it if Christ rose from the dead on the third day, since he was not a mere human being but true God and true man, and overcame by his divinity the death he suffered in his humanity? But we, who are mere human beings, can by no means rise from the dust at the end of the world. To this we answer you, O Severian heretics [Col. 0478D], that at the time of the resurrection of this same Lord Jesus Christ, not only did he who is true God and true man rise from death, but he also caused many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep to rise with him (Matt. 27), so that he might show us an example of resurrection in himself and strengthen us by the resurrection of others, who were like us in mere humanity. Thus, when a human being despaired of receiving in himself what God-man had shown in himself, he might presume that it could happen in himself because he knew it had happened in those whom he did not doubt to have been merely human beings.

Still persisting in the unbelief of your faithlessness, you object to us, saying: The spirit is dissolved from the flesh; the flesh is turned into decay; decay is reduced to dust; dust is dispersed among the elements, so that it can no longer be seen at all by human eyes. How can it rise on the last day? Or how can dry bones stripped of flesh and sinews be clothed again with flesh and grow green anew into life? [Col. 0479A]

We answer you that, if you do not hold faith in the resurrection through obedience, you certainly ought to hold it through reason. But let us bring blessed Gregory forward, and hear from him what answer should be given to your objection stated above. Therefore we earnestly ask you, holy Gregory, to teach us how we ought to answer the Severian heretics on these matters. “What else,” he says, [Note: Col. 0479D: Homily 20 on Ezekiel] “ought we to answer their aforementioned objection, except that they should first consider how they came into this world, and then they will discover how they shall rise?”

Therefore, I urge you, Severus the heretic, who deny the general resurrection of all human beings, carefully to hear what blessed Gregory says to you. “Certainly,” he says, “you heretic who doubt the resurrection, were once in your mother’s womb a foam of blood. There you were a little, liquid mass formed from your father’s seed and your mother’s blood. Tell, then, if you know, how that moisture of seed hardened in bones; how it remained liquid in marrow; how it was made firm in sinews; how it grew in flesh; how it was stretched out in skin [Col. 0479C]; how it was differentiated into hair and nails—so that hairs are softer than flesh, and nails are more tender than bones but harder than flesh. If, therefore, so many and such great things arise from one seed, are differentiated into kinds, and yet remain joined together in one form, what wonder is it if Almighty God can raise from dust at the resurrection the body which he was able so wonderfully to create? He is called Almighty because he does whatsoever he wills (Ps. 134); for his will is omnipotence. How then, O heretic, do you wish by human reason to comprehend how you will return from death to life, when you do not know how you came into this world? Grant, therefore, to the power of your Creator what you cannot comprehend concerning yourself.

“For certainly, because you were made from earth, and earth from nothing, you were created from nothing. Therefore, lest you despair of the resurrection of your flesh, consider wisely that it is less for God to restore what existed than to make what did not exist. If you cannot comprehend, O heretic, the effect of resurrection, consider how many things there are which you do not understand how they are, and yet do not doubt that they are. Tell, then, if you know, where the circuit of heaven, the foundations of earth, and the abyss of waters end, or upon what they are suspended.” Hence blessed Gregory says: “We know that what has been made from nothing hangs upon nothing.” Again he says: “But if there is something which is called nothing, then nothing is no longer nothing. But if it is nothing, the mass of the world hangs nowhere upon nothing, nor is there a place where that which was created to exist can be. How, then, is that which we know exists nowhere?” [Col. 0480A] But perhaps, O heretic, these matters are too numerous and difficult for you to understand.

“Return therefore to yourself, and carefully consider, if you can, how you were created. Certainly you were made of spirit and clay: the one invisible and the other visible; the one perceptible and the other imperceptible. How then could spirit and clay be mingled in you, and from different things a thing not different be made, so that spirit and clay were mixed in such great harmony that when the flesh is afflicted, the spirit languishes, and when the spirit is distressed, the flesh wastes away? But perhaps, O heretic [Col. 0480B], you are not yet able to examine even yourself. Consider, I ask, how the bush appeared to burn, and yet the fire did not touch it (Exod. 3); how the Red Sea was divided by a rod (Exod. 14); how the hardness of rock poured forth waters when struck with the rod (Exod. 17); how Aaron’s dry rod flowered (Num. 17); how the prophet Habakkuk, with the doors shut, was able to bring a meal to Daniel placed in the lions’ den (Dan. 14); how the Virgin Mary, coming from Aaron’s lineage, conceived without a man’s embrace, and how she remained a virgin in giving birth (Luke 1); how a man dead four days, raised at the command of God and man Jesus Christ, came out from the tomb with his hands and feet bound, and afterward the Lord commanded the disciples to loose him [Col. 0480C] (John 11); how this same Redeemer of ours, rising in true flesh and bones, entered in among the disciples when the doors were shut (John 20). See: you cannot investigate these matters, O heretic, and yet you believe that they are so. Why then do you doubt the glory of resurrection by disputing and examining it, when you believe so many mysteries without examination?”

But still doubting the resurrection, you Severian heretics again ask us, saying: A wolf eats a human being; a lion devours the wolf; the lion, dying, returns to dust. When that dust is raised, how can the human flesh be separated from the flesh of the wolf and lion? But to this we answer briefly: it is easy for God on the day of resurrection [Col. 0480D] to distinguish human flesh from the flesh of lion and wolf, since he was able to create human flesh from nothing. What wonder is it if Almighty God can, in that resurrection of the dead, separate human flesh from the flesh of beasts, so that one and the same dust does not rise insofar as it is the dust of wolf and lion, yet rises insofar as it is the dust of a human being?

What do you say to these things, O Severian heretics? What do you object or what do you answer? This is your answer, O heretics: you greatly wonder how the flesh of a human being eaten by beasts can rise from the earth’s dust. But we, in reply, say to you [Col. 0481A] that you ought not in any way to wonder or doubt God’s omnipotence, but firmly believe that he can do everything whatsoever he wills. For we know that the Psalmist said of him: “The Lord has done all things whatsoever he willed, in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. 134).

Therefore, that you may not doubt the truth of what we say, we wish to prove it from the history in Genesis. Thus the Lord said to Noah and his sons among other things after the flood: “I shall require the blood of your souls from the hand of every beast” (Gen. 9). When Almighty God said this, what else did he foreshadow than the future resurrection of all human beings? Blood is used here for human flesh, as though Almighty God showed more plainly the general resurrection of all human beings, saying: Although human flesh has been devoured by beasts, yet I, who do whatsoever I will, shall on the last day separate the dust of the human body from the dust of the beasts by which it was eaten, and shall raise it from death [Col. 0481B]. [Note: Col. 0481D: Gregory, in the same homily.]

Marvel, therefore, if you can, O heretics, at the height and breadth of heaven, the mass of the earth, the abyss of waters, and everything in the world, including the angels themselves, created by God from nothing. For, as we have already said, it is far less to make something from something than to have made all things from nothing. Do you not know, foolish heretics, that the elements themselves and the forms of things themselves proclaim to us an image of resurrection? The sun daily seems to die before our eyes and daily rises again. The moon also, as it waxes and wanes over thirty days and again receives its former light, seems to rise after death. The stars set for us in the morning and rise in the evening. In summer we see shrubs full of leaves and fruits; in winter they remain bare of leaves, flowers, and fruits, and as though dry; but when the spring sun returns and sap rises from the root, they are again clothed in their own beauty [Col. 0481C].

Why then, O Severian heretics, do you doubt the resurrection of human beings, when you frequently see it happen in trees? Look also upon the small seeds of huge trees, and consider diligently in them, if you can, the divine working. Tell, if you know: where within them are concealed such a mass of timber, such a diversity of branches [Col. 0481D], such a multitude and greenness of leaves, such beauty of varied flowers, such abundance, flavour, and scent of fruits? Do the seeds of trees have the scent or flavour which the trees afterward produce in their fruits? If, therefore, a tree can be produced from a seed that cannot be seen, why do you distrust that from the dust of human flesh a form that cannot be seen may be restored?

Hear, therefore, O Severian heretics, hear what blessed Gregory says for your correction and for the strengthening of the Catholic faith [Col. 0482A]. “Although,” he says, [Note: Col. 0481D: The same homily] “you heretic believe the things stated above, yet if you deny the resurrection, you believe all things without purpose; for in this spectacle of angels you seem indeed to run swiftly, but after you have completed the course of life, you oppose receiving the prize of eternal recompense. Hence it is said through Paul: ‘So run that you may obtain’ (1 Cor. 9). And again he says: ‘If in this life only we have hoped in Christ, we are more miserable than all human beings’ (1 Cor. 15).”

The mysteries of divine power which cannot be comprehended, therefore, must not be examined by human understanding, but venerated by faith. We must know that whatever can be comprehended by human reason can no longer be wonderful; but the sole reason in miracles is the power of the one who performs them [Col. 0482B].

Because I desire you, O Severian heretics, to be joined to the faithful people, I return so often in speaking with you and faithfully exhorting you to receive the Catholic faith. Therefore, conquered by so many authorities of the Old and New Testaments and overcome by so many testimonies of the holy Scriptures, now lay aside the unbelief of your obstinate minds. Believe faithfully and firmly that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God; that baptism was instituted by the same Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, for the remission of sins; and that all human beings shall rise with their bodies on the last day.

Furthermore, show the leprosy of heretical perversity to the true priests of the Catholic Church, and with devout mind receive, according to their judgment [Col. 0482C], the colour of health—that is, the teaching of ecclesiastical religion—so that with the children of that same holy Church you may be able to attain the joys of eternal blessedness. Amen.

§ XXXIII.—

The Hierachites, who receive only monks, reject marriage, and believe that little children do not possess the kingdom of heaven, are refuted. By God’s testimony marriages are shown to be lawful in both Testaments. The heretics of Tatian detest marriage; they are rejected by Christ’s testimony.

Let us all together hear what Isidore, teacher of Spain, says for our instruction concerning the Heraclite heretics, who have leprosy in their body—that is, who malign the holy Catholic Church, which is Christ’s body. “The Heraclites,” he says, [Note: Col. 0482D: “Hierachites,” from Hieracha.] [Note: Col. 0482D: *Etymologies*, book VIII, ch. 5.] “sprung from Heracleus their founder, receive only monks [Col. 0482D], reject marriages, and do not believe that little children possess the kingdom of heaven.”

Truly you also, O Heraclite heretics, stray far too greatly from the path of truth, since you presume to separate lawful marriages which God has joined, and doubt that little children, cleansed through baptism from original sin, can attain the heavenly kingdom. Thus, in rejecting marriage, you make yourselves heretics, inflict injury upon all ecclesiastical teachers, and indeed malign the whole Church. Therefore, in order utterly to destroy your heretical perversity and strengthen the truth of the Catholic Church [Col. 0483A], let us see when, where, and by whom marriage was first instituted.

[Note: Col. 0483D: *Four Books of Sentences*, Distinction 26.] Whereas the other sacraments began after sin and because of sin, the sacrament of marriage is read to have been instituted by the Lord even before sin, not only as a remedy but as an office. For the history of Genesis relates that, when sleep had been sent upon Adam, one of his ribs taken, and woman formed from it, the man, understanding in the Spirit for what purpose the woman had been made, said prophetically after his sleep: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2). And he added: “Therefore,” he says, “a man shall leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh” (ibid.).

[Col. 0483B] It should be noted that the institution of marriage is twofold: one institution, namely, was made before sin in Paradise for its proper office, so that the marriage-bed might be undefiled and marriage honourable (Heb. 13); through it they would conceive without ardour and give birth without pain. The other was made after sin, outside Paradise, as a remedy, in order to avoid unlawful impulse. The first institution was made so that nature might multiply; the second, so that nature might be preserved and vice restrained. For before sin God said to Adam and his wife: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 1); and after sin, when nearly all humankind had been destroyed by the Flood, he said the same thing to Noah and his sons. That marriage was instituted before sin for its proper office, but was granted after sin as a remedy, is attested by St Augustine, who says:

> “What is an office for the healthy is a remedy for the sick. For the weakness of incontinence, which is in flesh dead through sin, is received into the honourableness of marriage lest it fall into the ruin of shameful acts. Had the first human beings not sinned, they and their descendants would have come together without the incentive of flesh and the heat of lust. And just as some good work is rewardable, as St Augustine says, so their intercourse would have been good and rewardable. But because, through sin, the law of deadly concupiscence has adhered to our members, without which carnal intercourse does not take place, intercourse is blameworthy and evil unless it is excused by the goods of marriage.”

[Col. 0483D] Since, therefore, marriage is manifestly established by the Lord before sin for its proper office and after sin as a remedy, O Heraclite heretics, you who have rejected it by condemning it depart very far from the rule of the Catholic Church, and thereby incur upon yourselves the stain of heretical perversity. We wish to prove, by the testimony of God and of the man Jesus Christ, that marriage was instituted by the Lord before and after the Flood, and is not to be condemned or rejected, as you assert, but is good and honourable.

Thus the Son both of God and of the Virgin himself said to the Pharisees, when they asked whether a man might dismiss his wife for any cause: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19). By saying, “He who made them from the beginning made them male and female,” he introduces the authority of the Old Testament.

But it should be noted that he did not say, “male and females,” but “he made them male and female”: that is, to show that one marriage is lawful for secular persons, not several marriages at once. “For this reason,” he says, “a man shall leave his father and mother and shall cleave,” not to wives, but to his one wife; “and they shall be,” not three in carnal union, but “two in one flesh” [Col. 0484B]. “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh,” because carnal union makes them one. Therefore, what God joined from the beginning by making one flesh, let no human being separate by dissolving marital honour. Since, then, from the beginning of the world God instituted and praised marriage, and afterwards prohibited its separation by human beings through his most beloved Son, he has utterly refuted your superstitious and damnable sect, you who reject marriage in detestation.

There were, moreover, other heretics who detested marriage, called Tatianists. [Note: [Col. 0484D] *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 26: “There were.”] They utterly condemn marriage, treating it as equivalent to fornication and other corruptions, and admit into their own number neither man nor woman who uses marriage. [Col. 0484C] These too, who condemn the marriage instituted by God, denigrate the holy Church, which is Christ’s body; and therefore they bear, as it were, leprosy in the body. For the holy Church repels them from herself as lepers in proportion as she recognizes that they have departed further from the teaching of right living.

That marriage is a good thing, O heretics, is proved not only from the fact that the Lord is recorded to have instituted it between the first parents, but also from the fact that Christ attended the wedding at Cana of Galilee (John 2), and commended it by the miracle of turning water into wine. He himself later prohibited a man from dismissing his wife except for the cause of fornication (Matt. 19). The Apostle also says: “A virgin does not sin if she marries” (1 Cor. 7). Marriage, therefore, is plainly a good thing; otherwise it would not be a sacrament. For a sacrament is a sacred sign. The sacrament among married persons is so called because, just as the Church cannot be divided from Christ, neither can a wife be divided from her husband.

Since marriage, then, is a sacrament and a sacred sign of a sacred reality—namely, the union of Christ and the Church—as the Apostle says: “‘It is written,’ he says, ‘a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ But this,” he says, “is a great sacrament; and I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). For just as among married persons there is union through consent of minds and through mingling of bodies, so the Church is joined to Christ by will and nature: for it wills the same as he, and he assumed a form from human nature. Thus the bride is united to the bridegroom spiritually and bodily—that is, by charity and conformity of nature. The conjunction of these two unions is yet to come.

Hence the bride, that is, the holy Church, speaks figuratively in the Song of spiritual love to the same Jesus Christ, her heavenly bridegroom, saying: “Come, my beloved; let us go out into the field; let us remain in the villages. Let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the blossoms bear fruit, whether the pomegranates have flowered.” [Note: [Col. 0485D] Gregory on this passage.] For the field, according to Truth’s testimony, is this world. Therefore the bridegroom went out into the field with the bride [Col. 0485B] when the Word of God the Father, having assumed flesh in the chamber of the Virgin, was manifested to the world.

For the holy Church, in her children, is joined to Christ by faith, is upheld by hope, and is bound fast by charity. The bridegroom also remains in the villages with the bride when he visits the nations through faith and grants her to those who devoutly receive her. He rises early to the vineyards because, after his resurrection, seated in the glory of God the Father, he even now mercifully visits and powerfully defends the churches which he built by suffering and preaching. He sees whether the vine has flowered because he weighs every advance of the Church by strict examination. He sees whether the blossoms bear fruit because he carefully observes to what maturity the tender and imperfect grow. He also sees whether the pomegranates have flowered [Col. 0485C], because he beholds each of the perfect, and, as though recognizing the fruit of trees in their flowers, discerns what usefulness they possess for their neighbours. Of these it is fittingly added: “There I shall give you my breasts.” In the pomegranates the bride gives her breasts to the bridegroom, because in perfect persons there lives a twofold charity, by which, while they nourish the weak members in the Church, they as it were nurse Christ.

The consent of marriage, therefore, as has been said, signifies the spiritual union of Christ and the Church, which occurs through charity; while the union of the sexes signifies that union which occurs through conformity of nature.

Perhaps you ask, O Heraclite heretics, whether a woman who has not experienced carnal union belongs to marriage. But let St Augustine, the most powerful hammer of heretics, answer you on this point. For he says: “There is no doubt that a woman with whom there is shown to have been no union of sex does not belong to marriage.” Likewise Pope Leo: “Since the partnership of marriage was so instituted from the beginning that, apart from the mingling of the sexes, it has in itself no sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that a woman in whom there is shown to have been no nuptial mystery does not belong to marriage.” Likewise St Augustine: “Marriage is not complete without the mingling of the sexes.”

These foregoing statements, as Master Peter says in the *Sentences*, if anyone receives them according to the surface of the words, will be led into such error as to say that marriage cannot be contracted without carnal union, and that there was no marriage between the most blessed Virgin Mary and Joseph, or that it was not complete—which it is impious to think. For it was holier and more perfect insofar as it was freer from carnal activity. The foregoing statements, then, must be understood in this sense: not that a woman with whom there has been no mingling of the sexes does not belong to marriage, but that she does not belong to that marriage which possesses the explicit and complete figure of the union of Christ and the Church. For it signifies, as Master Peter says, that union of Christ and the Church which consists in charity, but not that which consists in conformity of nature. Thus that marriage also has a type of the union of Christ and the Church [Col. 0486B], but only of that union by which the Church is united to Christ through charity, not of that by which, through the assumption of flesh, the members are joined to the head. Yet that marriage is not therefore less holy, because, as St Augustine says in the book *On the Good of Marriage*, the holiness of the sacrament is of greater worth than the fruitfulness of the womb. Marriage is also a sign of the spiritual union and love of minds by which spouses ought to be joined to one another.

Marriage, therefore, O Heraclite heretics, was instituted by God from the beginning of the world; at the time of his coming it was praised and confirmed by Jesus Christ his Son; it was earnestly preached by the holy doctors of the Church and handed down to secular persons in great honour. Since, then, you reject it with proud minds [Col. 0486C] and consider it a great crime, you show yourselves alien from the fellowship of faithful Christians. It would indeed be fitting enough, and necessary for your salvation, that, receiving the goods of marriage with devout minds, you should faithfully submit yourselves to the venerable sacraments of the Catholic Church.

But in answer to this, O heretics, you ask us: “What are the goods of marriage?” If, then, you wish to know them, let St Augustine come forward and satisfy you concerning them. He says: [Note: [Col. 0485D] *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 31.] “The good of marriage is threefold: namely, fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. In fidelity it is considered that, after the marriage bond, one should not unite with another man or another woman; in offspring, that it should be lovingly received and religiously brought up; but in the sacrament [Col. 0486D], that marriage should not be separated, and that neither the dismissed man nor the dismissed woman should marry another, not even for the sake of offspring.”

Separation is twofold: bodily and sacramental. They may be separated bodily, namely on account of fornication or by mutual consent for the sake of religion, whether for a time or until the end. But sacramentally they cannot be separated while they live, if they are lawful persons. For the marriage bond remains between them even if, having departed from one another, they attach themselves to others. Hence St Augustine says in the book *On Marital Good*: [Note: [Col. 0485D] Rather, in book I of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, ch. 10, where these words occur; but in the Master: “the established rights of marriage remain . . .,” not, as in our author: “the united life of marriage remains . . . .”] “So greatly does the life of marriage once united remain between living persons that they are spouses to one another even when separated, rather than spouses with those others to whom they have attached themselves.” Likewise in the same work: “Among living persons there remains a certain marital bond which neither separation nor union with another can take away; just as an apostate soul, as though departing from Christ’s marriage, does not lose the sacrament of faith which it received in the washing of regeneration, even when faith has been lost. For it would be given back to one returning if one had lost it in departing. But the person who departs possesses it for the increase of punishment, not for the merit of reward.”

For fidelity is lacking where a husband unites with another woman or a wife with another man; nevertheless the bond of marriage remains. This good, namely fidelity, adheres to marriage in such a way that, if it is present, marriage is more highly commended; if it is absent, marriage is nevertheless not annihilated. A woman who is an adulteress is not thereby not a wife; indeed, if she were not a wife, she would not be an adulteress. When this happens, guilt is committed, but the sacrament is not nullified.

What do you think, O Heraclite heretics? What do you consider concerning the good of marriage, and what do you resolve to maintain about it? Do you now praise marriage with us and consider it good, knowing that it was instituted by God and seeing that it is enriched with so many gifts? Or, still persisting in your unbelief, do you reject it as usual with proud minds by condemning it? The honour of marriage, which God instituted in the first creation and which Paul, doctor of the Catholic Church, asserted to be without sin, you ought not to condemn [Col. 0487C], but willingly receive. For the blessed Apostle himself says: “If a virgin marries, she will not sin” (1 Cor. 7). We also believe that, if marital intercourse could not occur without sin, the Lord would not have commanded them after the Flood to join together, saying: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 9), when they could no longer have intercourse without the concupiscence of carnal union.

Intercourse necessary for procreation is blameless, and it alone is marital. But the person who goes beyond necessity obeys not reason but lust. Therefore marital honour is chastity, faithfulness in begetting and in rendering the carnal debt. This is the work of marriage which the Apostle defends from every sin, saying: “A virgin does not sin if she marries.”

[Col. 0487D] Perhaps, still persisting in your unbelief, O Heraclite heretics, you object to us in this fashion, saying: “How can marriage be good, when married people defile themselves every night by the pleasure of marital intercourse, and nevertheless constantly and irreverently enter the holy Church without washing their bodies?” You who say this, O heretics, I urge to listen attentively to Master Peter’s response in the book of the *Sentences*:

> “Those who come together not for the sake of offspring,” he says, “whose pleasure is not without sin, and scarcely anyone can now be found who avoids carnal embraces and does not sometimes come together apart from the intention of procreating offspring—whenever this occurs, they ought to abstain from entering the Church.”

[Note: [Col. 0487D] “Experiencing” (*experientes*).]

St Gregory also attests this, saying:

> “If anyone uses his own wife not carried away by desire for pleasure, but only for the sake of begetting children, that person is certainly to be left to his own judgment both concerning entering the Church and receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body; for he ought not be prohibited by us from receiving it, who, though placed in fire, does not know how to burn.”

But when, as Gregory says, not love of producing offspring but pleasure rules in the act of intercourse, spouses should have something in their intercourse to mourn; they should give alms and endeavour to restrain themselves from entering the Church. Then a man who, after intercourse with his wife, has washed with water may also receive holy communion. [Note: [Col. 0487D] The author confuses the sense of the sentence through the omission of another part: “Then . . . the man . . . may receive communion,” when he has been permitted to enter according to the Church’s established rule. The words that follow, “the custom of the Romans,” and so forth, have been displaced from their own location; they occur, namely, in the *Master* before “But perhaps,” and in the actual sentence of Gregory the Great transcribed there, as in Gregory himself. This should certainly be consulted.]

Nevertheless, the custom of the Romans, from ancient times, has always been, as St Gregory says, after intercourse with one’s own wife, also to seek the purification of bathing and to abstain for a little while from entering the church.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Distinction 32.] It should also be known that, although in all other matters the husband presides over the wife as the head over the body—for “the husband is the head of the wife” (1 Cor. 11)—yet in rendering the debt of the flesh they are equals. Therefore the Apostle commanded each to be subject to the other in this matter, saying: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband; for the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Cor. 7). For neither the wife has authority over her body to approach another husband, nor the husband authority over his body to approach another wife. To render the marital debt is no crime; but to demand it beyond the necessity of procreation is a venial fault; to commit fornication or adultery is a punishable crime.

That a husband cannot practise continence without his wife’s consent is proved by the following testimonies. St Augustine says in his exposition on the Psalms:

> “If the husband says, ‘I now wish to be continent,’ but the wife says, ‘I do not wish it,’ the husband cannot be continent. For what you wish, O man, she does not wish. Must she become a fornicator because of your continence? If she marries another while you are alive, she will be an adulteress. God does not wish such loss to be compensated by such gain. Render the debt; and if you do not demand it, render it. God will count it to you as perfect sanctification if you do not demand what is owed to you, but render what you owe to your wife.”

Likewise St Augustine, following the Apostle’s words, says to Ecdicia: [Note: [Col. 0488D] The sense is clear in this form: Likewise St Augustine to Ecdicia, or in Letter 262 [otherwise 199] to Ecdicia, says, following the Apostle’s words, “Even if your husband,” etc.]

> “Even if your husband wished to be continent, and you did not wish it, he would be compelled to render the debt to you; and God would [Col. 0489A] reckon continence to him if he yielded not to his own weakness but to yours, lest you fall into adultery.”

It should further be known that, although the debt must always be rendered to one who demands it, it is nevertheless not lawful to demand it on every day. Hence St Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old and New Testament*:

> “At one time a Christian may lawfully come together with his wife, and at another time he may not. For on days of processions and fasts it is sometimes not lawful to come together, because one must abstain even from lawful things in order that what is asked may be obtained more easily.”

Likewise:

> “Whenever either the days of the Nativity or other festivals arrive, one must abstain not only from the company of concubines but even from one’s own wives.”

Likewise Ambrose:

> “If a wife is taken for the purpose of begetting children, not much time seems to have been granted for that use itself, since feast days, days of processions, and the very rationale of conception and childbirth according to the law show that the use of the flesh ought to cease at these times.”

Perhaps you ask, O Heraclite [Note: [Col. 0489D] Hierachite.] heretics, whether, because we praise marriage, we place it above virginity. But in answer we say that “the bed of married persons is honourable and the bed undefiled,” as St Isidore says in the book *On the Kinds of Offices*, [Note: [Col. 0489D] Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 2.] “and it is not without fruit; and that which is praised in virginity comes from marriage, namely, every virgin is a daughter of marriage. Yet although this is so, we do not make marriage equal to the good of virginity, continence, or widowhood. Marriages are good in themselves [Col. 0489C]; but through the things surrounding them they are evil. For they are evil through what the Apostle says: ‘He who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and is divided. But he who is without a wife is concerned with the things of God, how he may please God’” (1 Cor. 7).

[Note: [Col. 0489D] This Pauline passage on praise of continence has been introduced less correctly here, since the discussion concerns what is evil in marriage. Another apostolic authority should be substituted, which Isidore also gives in the edition: [Col. 0490D] “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife,” as is likewise read in him in the passage from the *Sentences* cited immediately above.]

Hence St Isidore says in the second book of the *Sentences*, ch. 40:

> “Marriages and offices of authority are indeed good in themselves, but through the things surrounding them they become evil. Therefore, although offices of authority are good, they become evil through arrogance, through oppression of the poor, and through violation of justice. Thus marriages harm, and offices of authority harm, but through what is added to them, not through themselves: as on a straight road thorns grow beside it, which, rising at the side, hurt those travelling along the straight road.”

That marital honour too is good, but nevertheless is not to be equated with the best gift of virginity, Master Peter shows in the *Sentences*, saying: “Indulgence” [Note: [Col. 0490D] *Sentences*, book IV, distinction 26: “Indulgence.”] “is taken in different ways: namely, for concession, remission, and permission. In the New Testament, permission is made concerning lesser goods and lesser evils. Of the lesser goods is marriage, which does not merit the palm, but nevertheless [Col. 0490A] serves as a remedy. Of the lesser evils, that is, of venial sins, is intercourse which occurs not for the sake of begetting children but because of incontinence. ‘The former,’ that is marriage, ‘is indulged,’ that is, granted; ‘the latter,’ that is such intercourse, ‘is permitted,’ that is, tolerated, so that it is not prohibited.” For the good of marriage is not preferred to virginity, because marriage is granted as a remedy, whereas virginity will be crowned pre-eminently with glory and honour.

Although, therefore, marriage is good, established by God among the first human beings, and praised and confirmed by Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, we do not doubt that the good of virginity is preferred to marriage. The former is good; the latter is best. Marriage is granted; virginity is only urged [Col. 0490B], not commanded—but urged because it is exceedingly exalted. On this subject Isidore, teacher of Spain, speaks thus in the second book of the *Sentences*, ch. 40:

> “The gift of virginity is twofold, because in this age it loses the anxiety of temporal things, and in the age to come it gains the eternal reward of chastity. The prophet Isaiah testifies that virgins are happier in eternal life, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs’—that is, to those who keep his Sabbaths, who live chastely, who become eunuchs without the knife solely through fear and love of God—‘I shall give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters. I shall give them an everlasting name which shall not perish’ (Isa. 56). Nor is there doubt that those who persevere chaste and virginal become equal to God’s angels. Therefore the beauty of chastity is to be loved; once its delight has been tasted, it is found sweeter than that of the flesh. For chastity is the fruit of sweetness and the inviolate beauty of the saints. Chastity is security of mind and health of body. Hence we read [Note: [Col. 0490D] Supply: “we read.”] that certain *gymnici*, that is, philosophers among the gentiles, practised perpetual abstinence from Venus, lest they break their strength through lust. For a luxurious life quickly weakens and swiftly brings a person, broken down, to old age. Every sin receives the healing of its wound through repentance. But if virginity falls, it is in no way restored. For although repentance receives the fruit of pardon, it does not in any way recover its former incorruption.

[Col. 0490D] “It should further be known that a virgin in body but not in mind, as St Isidore says, has no reward in the promise. Hence, when the Saviour comes for judgment, he will say to the foolish virgins: ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you’ (Matt. 25). For where, judging, he finds a corrupted mind, he will undoubtedly condemn bodily incorruption. Therefore bodily incorruption profits nothing where integrity of mind is absent; nor is it of any value to be clean in body when one is defiled [Col. 0491A] in mind. Many of the reprobate know no contagion of carnal corruption; yet just as they are unfruitful in body, so they remain barren in mind of the fruitfulness of good work. They would rightly rejoice in virginity if they did not serve other wicked deeds. A person who professes continence but does not withdraw from earthly desires, though the luxury of the flesh does not defile that person, is nevertheless stained by the diverse activity of worldly conduct. Virgins who glory in their own merits are also compared to hypocrites, who seek outwardly the glory of good work which they ought humbly to possess inwardly in their conscience. Such persons do not attain the heavenly promises, because they themselves deprive themselves of virginity’s reward. For this is what it means in the Gospel that the virgins have no oil in their vessels (ibid.) [Col. 0491B]: they do not preserve inwardly in their conscience the testimony of good work, but boast openly before human beings, not in heart before God.”

Thus the authorities of the Old and New Testament, O Heraclite heretics, praise the honourableness of marriage and utterly condemn you, who reject it, in your false assertion. The Catholic faith is strengthened by the sayings of the holy fathers of the Old and New Testament, and your most mendacious sect is wholly refuted. Therefore, while you condemn marital honour, you denigrate ecclesiastical religion; and while you attempt to alter the norm of Catholic faith, firmly and beneficially established by Jesus Christ, God and man, you plainly make yourselves liable to eternal damnation.

[Col. 0491C] Still persisting in your malice, O heretics, you next assert that little children, although cleansed from original sin through water and the Holy Spirit, nevertheless cannot enter the heavenly kingdom. To this we, O heretics, answer contrariwise: if little children depart this present life before being reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, they will by no means be able to enter the heavenly kingdom. St Isidore attests this in the first book of the *Sentences*, ch. 22:

> “Newborn infants will suffer punishment in hell solely for the guilt of original sin, if they have not been renewed through the washing of regeneration.”

If, then, they pass from this life before being reborn, as has been said, they will undoubtedly be alien from Christ’s kingdom, according to the testimony of Christ himself, who says: “Unless one is reborn of [Col. 0491D] water and the Holy Spirit, one cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3). Therefore little children themselves, who do not yet know how to speak or believe, are baptized while others profess faith for them, lest perhaps they die without baptism and perish.

That sins are remitted in baptism to little children—indeed, to youths and old persons—the wise Augustine attests in the *Enchiridion*, ch. 43, saying: “From a newly born little child to a decrepit old man, just as no one is prohibited from baptism, so no one is who does not die to sin.” [Note: [Col. 0491D] Letter 98; otherwise 22.]

That little children are also joined to the number of the faithful, he declares among other remarks addressed to Peter: “Hold most firmly [Col. 0492A] that, just as little children who die without baptism are enrolled among the number of unbelievers, so those who are baptized are called faithful”—namely, because they are not separated from the fellowship of the faithful, since the Church prays for departed believers. “They are faithful,” he says, “not because of virtue, but because of the sacrament of faith.” Explaining this in his address to Boniface, he says:

> “Although a little child does not yet have that faith which consists in the will of believers, nevertheless the sacrament of faith itself—that is, baptism—makes the child faithful. Just as the child is answered for as believing, so the child is also called faithful: not by assenting in mind to the reality itself, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality.”

Thus true reasoning clearly declares, O Heraclite heretics, that little children cleansed from original sin through baptism can enter the heavenly [Col. 0492B] kingdom, and shows that you who deny this have lied in your assertion.

To strengthen the Catholic faith still more and to destroy your most mendacious sect completely, let us all hear together what Jesus Christ, God and man, says concerning little children: “Allow the little children to come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. 19). What dignity or power belongs to the one who says this? He is the King of kings and Lord of lords, who redeemed the human race by his most precious blood, and through whom all the elect attain the heavenly kingdom. For this reason he descended from the bosom of the Father: that he might redeem his elect from the hand of the ancient enemy; for this he ascended [Col. 0492C]: that he might raise them with himself into heaven and prepare dwellings for them according to the merits of each. In him all things in heaven, sea, and earth were created (Col. 1); he is the way, truth, and life (John 14), upon which all saints walk with unharmed feet and attain the joys of Paradise. Through him, the supreme priest of the holy Church, God the Father created, governs, and rules all things. Without him no one can do any good thing or be able to ascend to behold the brightness of God the Father himself. To him God the Father has committed all judgment; on the last day he will give every person either reward or punishment according to deeds.

This one, therefore, so great and such as he is—almighty and immeasurable, indeed judge of the living and the dead, and with the same Father and the Holy Spirit king of all ages—said to his disciples: “Allow little children to come to me, and do not forbid them; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (John 18). [The citation is printed thus.] In saying, then, “Allow little children to come to me,” he plainly shows that little children released from the bonds of original sin by the water of baptism are to be joined to the children of the holy Church. Likewise, when he subsequently said that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these, he undoubtedly and manifestly refuted your most mendacious assertion, you who deny that they can enter the heavenly kingdom. Therefore believe without doubt that little children renewed through baptism can enter the heavenly kingdom, and recognize that you have been deceived and have lied in your most mendacious sect.

[Col. 0493A] Perhaps in response you say to us, O heretics, that if little children reborn through water and the Holy Spirit are to enter the heavenly kingdom, the greatest part of the heavenly Jerusalem will be filled from among little children or infants. But we answer this: there is no doubt that all infants who are baptized, released from original sin, and still free from actual sins can enter the heavenly kingdom; but this must not be affirmed of all who already speak and delight in blasphemies, curses, abusive language, and reproaches.

St Gregory asserts this in the *Dialogues*, saying: [Note: [Col. 0493D] *Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 18.]

> “Although all baptized infants who die in infancy must be believed to enter the heavenly kingdom, it must not be believed that all little children who [Col. 0493B] can already speak enter the heavenly kingdom; for some are shut out from entrance to that heavenly kingdom by their parents, if they are badly brought up. For a certain man, very well known in this Roman city, had, three years ago [Note: [Col. 0493D] The edition reads: “a three-year period.”], a son, I think about five years old. Loving him too carnally, he brought him up indulgently. And this little child, grievous to say, whenever anything opposed his inclination, immediately used to blaspheme the majesty of God. Struck down in the mortality three years ago, he came to death. As his father held him in his lap, the boy, with trembling eyes, saw evil spirits coming to him—as those who were present testified—and began to cry: ‘Keep them away, father; keep them away, father!’ Crying out, he turned his face aside in order to hide himself from them in his father’s lap. When his father saw him trembling and asked what he saw, the boy added: ‘Moorish men—that is, black men—have come and want to take me away.’ Having said this, he immediately blasphemed the name of Majesty and gave up his soul. Thus, in order that the Almighty might show for what guilt he had been handed over to such *exauctoribus* [perhaps “deprivers”; the reading is uncertain] [Note: [Col. 0493D] The edition reads “executioners” (*exsecutoribus*) instead of *exauctoribus*.], he allowed him to repeat in dying what his father had refused to correct in him while living; so that he who had long lived blasphemously through the patience of the Divinity might at length blaspheme and die through the judgment of the Divinity, and so that his father might recognize his own guilt, since, by neglecting the soul of his little son, he had nourished not a little child but a sinner for the fires of Gehenna.”

[Col. 0493D] Therefore little children and infants, as has often been said, who have been freed from original sin through holy baptism, can enter the heavenly kingdom. But if they are badly brought up by their parents, become cursers and blasphemers, they will not be able to enter it, as Paul the Apostle testifies: “Cursers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). Yet hold most certainly that little children baptized with holy baptism and brought up religiously and properly by their parents can enter the heavenly Jerusalem; indeed, that by the grace of God the kingdom of heaven belongs to these little children. Concerning the blasphemies and slanders by which you have denigrated the holy Church [Col. 0494A] and blasphemed its ministers, humbly repent. Entrust yourselves with devout minds to the ministers of that holy Church; reveal in penitence and confession of heart the stains of leprosy—that is, the errors of heretical perversity—and receive with all your heart, under their judgment, the colour of true salvation—that is, the teaching of ecclesiastical religion—so that it may not happen that you perish with heretics, but that with the children of the same holy Church you may attain the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

§ XXXIII.—

Cathari who gloried in their own purity and rejected repentance are refuted by the preaching of Christ and John. The same people, who accused widows entering a second marriage as though of adultery, are refuted by the testimonies of Scripture, especially Paul. Something is said concerning the praise of virginity, divorce, and rites used in the blessing of marriages.

The Cathari—[Note: Col. 0494D: *Cathari*]—are also among those heretics who malign the body of Christ, that is, the holy Church. But let us hear what St Isidore says of them in Book VIII of the *Etymologies* (ch. 5):

> “The Cathari,” he says, “named themselves thus on account of purity, boasting of their merits. They deny pardon of sins to penitents and proclaim themselves purer than others. If they wished to understand their name, they would call themselves unclean rather than clean. Among their other errors, they condemn widows who remarry as though they were adulteresses.”

These Cathar heretics too, who boast of their merits and deny pardon of sins to penitents, bear, as it were, leprosy in their body when they malign the religion of the holy Church, which is Christ’s body. For those sin against God and against the Church who despair that penitents can obtain pardon from the merciful God. But they are wholly mistaken in this false assertion of theirs, because every penitent who humbly confesses sins to God undoubtedly obtains forgiveness from him. And, lest you doubt that what we say is true, O heretics, we wish to prove it by the authorities of the holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments.

For if penitents, who thereafter withdraw from evil, could not obtain pardon of sins, St Jerome would never have said, for the consolation of penitents:

> “Penance,” he says [Note: Col. 0494D: IV *Sentences*, distinction 14, *Post haec*], “is the second plank after shipwreck. For if anyone, by sinning, has ruined the garment of innocence received in baptism, he may recover it by the remedy of penance. The first plank is baptism, in which the old man is put off and the new put on; the second is penance, by which we rise after a fall, while the returning oldness is driven away and the lost newness restored. The preaching of John the Baptist began with penance, when he said: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near’ (Matt. 3). What the herald taught, Truth himself afterward preached, beginning his discourse with penance. Penance is so called from punishing, by which a person punishes the unlawful acts he has committed.

[Col. 0495A] “Moreover, it should be known that the power of penance is conceived from fear, as Isaiah testifies when he says: ‘From fear of you, Lord, we have conceived and borne the spirit of salvation’” [Note: Col. 0495D: Isa. 26:18, according to the Septuagint.].

But what is penance? “Penance,” says St Ambrose, “is to lament past evils, and, in lamenting them, not to commit them again.” For one who laments certain sins in such a way as still to commit others either does not know how to do penance or pretends to do so. “For what profit is it,” says St Gregory, “if someone weeps over sins of lust while still panting in the heats of avarice?” Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain, also says in his book *On the Supreme Good* [Note: Col. 0495D: Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 16]:

> “He is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he repents of; nor does the man who does this seem humbly to beseech God, but proudly to mock him. ‘A dog,’ he says, ‘returns to its vomit’ (2 Pet. 2), and the penitent [Col. 0495B] to sin.”

Let us also hear what Isaiah says to sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1). The person who laments what is past and does not commit again what ought to be lamented is washed and clean. The person who laments what he has done, but after his tears repeats what he had bewailed, is washed but not clean. Likewise St Augustine, in the book *Soliloquies*, says:

> “Penance is empty when a subsequent fault defiles or stains it. Lamentations avail nothing if sins are repeated. It is of no use to seek pardon for evils and then to commit evils anew.”

In the perfection of penance [Note: Col. 0495D: Distinction 16, *In perfectione*], however, three things must be observed: compunction of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. Hence John Chrysostom says:

> “Perfect penance compels the sinner willingly to endure everything, so that there may be contrition in his heart, confession in his mouth, and complete humility in his deeds. This is fruitful penance: as we offend God in three ways—namely, by heart, mouth, and hand—so we may make satisfaction in three ways. For there are three kinds of sin, as St Augustine says in his discourse on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount [Note: Col. 0495D: Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, Book I, ch. 12], namely in the heart, in the deed, and in habit; or in [Note: Col. 0495D: Neither Augustine nor the Master has ‘or in words.’] words, as it were three deaths. One is as though in a house (Matt. 9), namely when lust is felt in the heart; another is as though already borne outside the gate (Luke 7), when consent proceeds into action; the third, when the mind is weighed down as by the mass of an evil habit, or armed with the shield of harmful self-defence, as though already rotting in a tomb” [Note: Col. 0496D: Thus Augustine; but the Master has “stinking.”] (John 11).

These three kinds of sin were signified by the three dead persons whom the Lord is recorded to have raised. To this threefold death, therefore, a threefold remedy is applied, as stated above: confession, contrition, and satisfaction. The prophet Joel commends compunction to us, saying: “Rend your hearts, not your garments, and turn to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful” (Joel 2), etc. Solomon, however, approves confession, saying: “The just man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18). For he truly confesses who accuses himself of having sinned, who, abhorring [Col. 0496A] the evil he did, lays it to his own charge. Satisfaction is commanded by John the Baptist, where he says: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Matt. 3).

By these and similar authorities of the Old and New Testament, O Cathar heretics, who deny that sinners can obtain forgiveness through penance, the folly of your most deceitful sect is rejected and the Catholic faith is in every way strengthened. The aforementioned testimonies of the holy Fathers unquestionably affirm that sinners can obtain pardon of sins from almighty God through true penance; and they plainly prove that you, who obstinately deny this, have lied in your assertion. For unless Jesus Christ himself, God and man, had decreed to grant sinners pardon through penance, he would never have preached penance aloud to the crowds following him: “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). Therefore, when he preaches penance aloud to the people, he wholly nullifies your utterly damnable sect.

Perhaps you ask, O heretics, what true penance is, and what fruits are worthy of penance. Know, therefore, O heretics, that true penance is to weep over evils committed and not to commit again what must be lamented. Fruits worthy of penance occur when the quality and quantity of punishment correspond to the quality and quantity of the fault. The Venerable Bede explains this in his book *Sentences*, saying:

> “The fruit of a good work ought not to be equal for one who has sinned not at all or less, and for one who has fallen more grievously.”

Let us also hear what St Augustine says *On the Discernment of Penance* in the book *Sentences*:

> “Let him consider the quality of the crime with respect to place, time, persistence, variety of person, the temptation by which he committed it, and the repeated performance involved in those very vices. The fornicator ought,” he says [Note: Col. 0496D: Supply here: “to repent.”], “to repent according to the eminence of his rank or office, or according to the station of the prostitute, according to the manner of his act, and how he committed the shamefulness: whether in a holy place; whether at a time appointed for prayer, such as festivals and fast-days; and let him consider how long he persisted in sin, grieving that he sinned persistently, and how great the assault was by which he was overcome. For there are those who [Note: Col. 0496D: Supply ‘not’; but all manuscripts lack this negation, as the Maurist editors observe, and this is also confirmed by ours.] are not merely overcome, but freely offer themselves to sin; they do not await temptation, but anticipate pleasure. Let everyone examine with himself how often, by repeated acts of vice, he sinned pleasurably. All this variety must be confessed and lamented, so that, when he has recognized that he is a sinner, he may quickly find God propitious. In recognizing also the increase of sin, let him discover at what age he was, of what wisdom and rank. Let him dwell upon each of these matters and perceive the measure of the crime, cleansing with tears every quality of the vice; meanwhile let him mourn the virtue which he lacked. For one must grieve not [Col. 0497A] only because one sinned, but also because one deprived oneself of virtue. Let him grieve also because, offending in one point, he became guilty of all. For he proved ungrateful, who, though full of virtues, did not fear God at all. In this, indeed, every sinner becomes more blameworthy: the more acceptable he had been to God before sinning. Adam sinned more grievously before God because he abounded in every good. In another way also, one who offends in one point becomes guilty of all, because every virtue suffers injury from one vice. Therefore let the penitent place himself under the judgment and authority of the priest, reserving nothing of himself for himself, so that, at the priest’s command, he may be ready to do everything for recovering the life of his soul that he would do to avoid bodily death; and let him do this with desire, because he recovers life without end—that is, eternal life. For one who is to become immortal ought joyfully to do what one destined to die would do in order to postpone death. Let him always pray to God and offer God contrition of heart, and then whatever he can from his possessions. Then let him securely offer what he offers to God and priest: ‘The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings’ (Gen. 4). He first said ‘upon Abel,’ and then ‘upon his offerings.’ Therefore, in the judgment of the heart, the alms of the giver must be weighed; one must consider not how much is given, but with what mind and affection one gives what one can. Whoever, therefore, wishes to redeem his sins by an offering of temporal goods must first offer his mind to God.

> “Let him also beware, led by shame, of dividing his confession within himself, wishing to disclose different matters to different priests. For some conceal from one priest what they reserve for disclosure to another; this is to praise oneself [Col. 0497C] and incline toward hypocrisy, and always to lack the pardon which they vainly think they will reach—or to which [the reading is uncertain: *vel ad quam*]. Let him also beware of approaching the Lord’s body before he is strengthened by a good conscience; and let him grieve that he does not yet dare to receive the saving food which he greatly desires. Let him also abstain from games and worldly spectacles if he wishes to attain the grace of perfect remission.”

These are fruits worthy of penance, O Cathar heretics, ensnaring the captive soul and preserving it in the liberty of the glory of the children of God. Moreover, as St Augustine says, let the soul seek worthy fruits, even if they are not fruits worthy of penance. That is, more plainly: let the soul of its own free will submit itself to spiritual disciplines, by which, once instructed, it may withdraw from sin; and though it has not sinned gravely and penance has not been imposed upon it for more serious sins, let it nevertheless repent of lighter sins with voluntary devotion and strive to serve God. For, as St Augustine says, there are fruits worthy of virtues which are insufficient for penitents. Penance demands weightier fruits, so that the dead person may obtain life through grief and groaning. From this it is shown which are fruits worthy of penance, by which true satisfaction is fulfilled; and that not all worthy fruits are fruits worthy of penance—this being understood of that penance which is required for greater crimes. For what suffices for those who sin less or little [Col. 0498A] does not suffice for those who offend grievously.

Moreover, it should be known that, just as there are fruits worthy of penance and true satisfaction, so there are unworthy fruits and false satisfaction—that is, false penance. Hence St Gregory says: “We call those penances false which are not imposed according to the authorities of the saints in proportion to the character of the crimes.” Therefore, if a soldier, merchant, or person devoted to an occupation which cannot be carried on without sin comes to penance ensnared in graver faults; or if someone unjustly keeps another’s property, or harbours hatred in his heart: let him recognize that he cannot do true penance unless he abandons his business or occupation, puts hatred away from his heart, and restores the goods which he has unjustly taken [Col. 0498B]. Yet let him not despair; meanwhile we urge him to do whatever good he can, so that God may enlighten his heart unto penance.

If someone perhaps asks what satisfaction is sufficient for venial sins, St Augustine shows this in the *Enchiridion*, saying:

> “For daily, brief, and light sins, without which this life cannot be lived, the daily prayer of the faithful—namely the *Our Father*—makes satisfaction. For it belongs to them to say: ‘Our Father who art in heaven’ (Matt. 6), etc.”

For this prayer removes these least and daily sins; it also removes those from which even a life of the faithful person, though wickedly lived, departs when changed for the better by penance—if, as “forgive us our debts” is spoken truthfully, so also “as [Col. 0498C] we forgive our debtors” is spoken truthfully [Note: Col. 0497D: Supply “that is,” and note that these manuscripts have the particle *si* (“if”), which Augustine’s editors observed to be absent from all their manuscripts.]: if what is said is done, because it too is an almsgiving wholly to forgive penitents. From these and the other preceding matters it is now easy to understand what satisfaction must be offered for venial sins. The Lord’s Prayer, with some fasting and almsgiving, is sufficient, provided that contrition of heart precedes and confession is added if opportunity is available. But for graver sins not only these things must be employed as satisfaction, but much greater measures, more vigorously and strictly; because, as St Augustine says, to do penance it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also makes satisfaction to the Lord for what has been done through the sorrow of penance, [Col. 0498D] through the groaning of humility, through the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with alms cooperating.

[Note: Col. 0498D: Distinction 17, *Jam sed quod*.] Perhaps someone asks whether it is sufficient to confess sins to God alone, or whether one must also confess to a priest. But whoever asks this should know that it is proved not only by the authority of St James the apostle—“Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5)—but also by many testimonies of others, that sins must be confessed to God and, if time permits, to priests. St Augustine says [Note: Col. 0498D: Sermon 351 (otherwise 50), among the fifty homilies]:

> “Let a man judge himself while he can, and turn his will and conduct to what is better [Col. 0499A] [Note: Col. 0499D: Augustine reads: ‘Therefore let a man judge himself in these matters voluntarily, while he can, and turn his conduct to what is better.’ The Master, however: ‘Let a man judge himself voluntarily while he can,’ etc.], lest, when he can no longer do so, he be judged against his will by the Lord. And when he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of a most severe but most beneficial remedy, let him come to the priests [Note: Col. 0499D: Both Augustine and the Master here have *antistites*, ‘bishops/prelates’.], through whom the keys are administered to him in the Church—that is, penance is imposed. As a good son now beginning to be such, preserving the order of the maternal members, let him receive from those set over the sacraments the measure of his satisfaction, devout and suppliant in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart.”

Likewise Pope Leo, to Bishop Theodore [Note: Col. 0499D: Editions of the books of the *Sentences* omit “to Bishop Theodore.” Perhaps this is the first place from which we may suspect that Martin also had Gratian before him: for Gratian cites Theodore, to whom Leo the Great addressed the letter [Col. 0500D]. Unless the manuscript of the *Sentences* consulted by the author contained the words lacking in the editions, he could have read them nowhere except in Gratian; for we assert without doubt that Martin did not see the works of the supreme pontiff himself.]:

> “The manifold mercy of God,” he says [Note: Col. 0500D: Letter 108, otherwise 83], “so aids human falls that hope of life is restored not only through baptism but also through penance; the supports of the divine will being so ordained that they cannot obtain God’s forgiveness except through the supplications [Col. 0499B] of priests. For Christ gave this power to the rulers of the Church: that they should assign the satisfaction of penance to those who confess, and should admit the same persons, cleansed by salutary satisfaction, to communion in the sacraments through the gate of reconciliation.”

Likewise St Augustine, in the book *On Penance*:

> “Let one who repents repent altogether and show his sorrow by tears; let him present his life to God through the priest; let him forestall God’s judgment by confession.”

It may also be asked whether it is permissible to confess sins to a priest by messenger or in writing. St Augustine forbids this, expounding the Lord’s saying:

> “For the Lord commanded lepers who were to be cleansed [Col. 0499C] to show their faces to the priests, teaching that sins must be confessed in bodily presence, not disclosed in writing.”

For the Lord said to the lepers: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17). He did not say, “Let one go for all”; rather, he said: “All of you go and show yourselves to the priests.” As though he said: Do not send another messenger to offer in your stead the gift ordained by Moses [Note: Col. 0500D: “By Moses.”]; but you who sinned must yourselves be ashamed. For shame itself has a share in recompense [Note: Col. 0500D: Editions read “remission.”]. From the foregoing, therefore, it is shown clearly enough that a sinner may not confess sins by messenger or by letter.

It is also customary to ask whether one may confess to a neighbour—that is, a layperson—if a priest is absent by chance. To this one may rightly answer that the examination of a priest must diligently be sought, because God granted priests the power of binding and loosing; and therefore what they forgive, God also forgives. Yet if a priest is absent, confession should be made to a neighbour or companion; but everyone should take care to seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose. For one who judges the crimes of others must be such a person. Hence St Augustine says in the book *On Penance*:

> “Whoever wishes to confess sins so as to find grace should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose, lest, having been negligent concerning himself, he be neglected by one who mercifully warns him and asks that they may not both fall into the pit which the foolish man refused to avoid. So great is the force of confession,” St Augustine says, “that, if a priest is lacking, one should confess to a neighbour. For it often happens that a penitent cannot be ashamed before the priest whom he desires, because neither time nor place affords him access. Although the person to whom he confesses sins lacks the power to loose and free him, yet the one confessing his offence to a companion is worthy of pardon by reason of his desire for a priest. For the lepers were cleansed while they went to show their faces [Col. 0500B] or themselves to the priests (ibid.), before they reached them. Hence it is clear that God looks to the heart when necessity prevents persons from reaching priests.”

It is now entirely clear how detestable is silence about sin and, conversely, how necessary confession is. Confession is the testimony of a conscience that fears God. For one who fears God’s judgment is not ashamed to confess sin. Perfect fear removes all shame; confession of sin entails shame, and that shame itself is a very severe punishment. It has plainly been shown to you, O Cathar heretics, that through humble confession and worthy satisfaction a penitent can obtain remission of sins from almighty God [Col. 0500C]. Competent witnesses of the Old and New Testaments agree truthfully that God mercifully grants pardon to those who truly repent; and they prove that you who deny this possibility have wholly lied in your assertion. Thus the Catholic faith is more firmly strengthened by the most truthful testimonies of the holy Scriptures, and your most deceitful sect is entirely nullified.

Furthermore, persevering still in your malice and maligning the religion of the holy Church, you say that widows joined again in marriage ought to be condemned as adulteresses. “There are many examples of widows,” as St Isidore says in the second book *On the Kinds of Offices* [Note: Col. 0500D: Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 19], “of whom the first mentioned in the Old Testament is Naomi (Ruth 1). We also read of another widow to whom Elijah was sent (3 Kgs. 17). It is also written of the widow who, under King Antiochus, suffered martyrdom with her seven sons for God’s law (2 Macc. 7). That admirable widow Judith too exults, who, preserving her chastity and overcoming the enemy Holofernes, prince of the Assyrians, won a triumph (Judith 8). In the New Testament Anna is the first [Col. 0501A] widow mentioned, who recognized the Lord. For she deserved to recognize the grace of his divinity before she could hear his word (Luke 2). Her rank, indeed, as St Isidore says, is almost joined to virginity. Hence the widow was first to recognize the Christ whom the Virgin bore. Happy, therefore, is the widow, because experienced; most happy is the virgin, because untouched [Note: Col. 0501D: The editions differ greatly: ‘Happy, therefore, is the virgin because untouched; strong is the widow because experienced.’]. Both assuredly have a reward with God; the former greater, the latter following [Note: Col. 0501D: Thus the editions fittingly accord with the preceding sense; but Martin, whose reading differs greatly, should have altered the antithesis thus: ‘The latter greater, the former following.’]. But the Apostle calls her a widow who, after the marriage to one husband has ended [Note: Col. 0501D: Editions: “after the bed of one marriage has been cut off … renounces her sex.”], thereafter renounces sexual relations. For he says: ‘Let a widow be chosen, not less than sixty years old, the wife of one husband’ (1 Tim. 5). It follows, therefore, that she who has been bound to many husbands lacks the name of widow.

“But the same Apostle expressly set forth what kind of widows they ought to be, saying: ‘Having testimony in good works’; namely, in this manner [Note: Col. 0501D: Here too the editions differ greatly, reading: ‘namely, like Tabitha.’ Our manuscript is undoubtedly corrupt.]: if she has brought up children—understand, for God; if she has received strangers; if she has washed the feet of the saints; if she has ministered to those suffering tribulation—that is, the sick or those placed in prison; if she has pursued every good work (ibid.). And, to summarize all in brief, let them be examples of good living in all things. Again: ‘Older women likewise in holy dress’ (Titus 2): that is, he wishes even their gait, movement, countenance, and silence [Note: Col. 0501D: Supply, from the editions: “their speech.”] to display a certain dignity of sacred continence. After this he adds concerning these same widows: ‘Not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, but using little.’ For those ages which enjoy bodily luxury are accustomed to give themselves to wine for the sake of lust. After this [Col. 0501C] St Paul added concerning widows that they should be good teachers—that is, that they should teach prudence (ibid.). He did indeed permit them to teach, but women, and not in church but privately. For this class of women is apt to be garrulous, and he says this vice arises from idleness. For, living in idleness, they learn to go about from house to house (1 Tim. 5): that is, held back by no fear and subject to no husband’s authority, they run about not merely idle but also inquisitive, speaking what they ought not.

> “The Apostle declares that widows who, after undertaking a purpose of continence, desire to marry incur condemnation. ‘For when,’ he says, ‘they have become wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, having condemnation because they have made void their first faith’ (ibid.), namely because they did not abide by what they first vowed. Many of them are restrained from marrying not by love of a noble purpose but by fear of open disgrace. Therefore those who wish to marry [Col. 0502A] do not marry because they cannot do so without punishment; but it would have been far better if they had not vowed and had married than if they burned—that is, were consumed by the hidden flame of desire—regretting their profession and weary of their confession. Unless, corrected, they direct their hearts and again overcome lust through fear of God, they must be numbered among [Note: Col. 0501D: Editions read “in.”] the dead, whether [Note: Col. 0502D: The editions read better: “if.”] they live in pleasures. Hence the Apostle says: ‘She who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives’ (ibid.).”

Therefore widows who have not vowed continence to God may marry again and again; but we say that those who have already professed chastity cannot marry further. Thus it is good to marry and beget children, but far better to abstain for the love of God. Therefore, O Cathar heretics, you ought not to condemn [Col. 0502B] what is good—namely marriage—but to commend and praise what is better—namely chastity.

I do not want you to be ignorant, O heretics, that God’s first pronouncement commanded increase and procreation; the second commended continence. [Note: Col. 0502D: From Isidore, ibid., ch. 18.] For the saying, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1), no longer has its place, because another saying has now supervened: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing!” (Matt. 24). And [Note: Col. 0502D: Here Isidore altered the Vulgate’s words, “the time is short,” after the manner of Tertullian, to “the time is now gathered in.” Our author, however, does not seem to have understood them as belonging to sacred Scripture, but took them as Isidore’s words.], because that time is now gathered in, it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none (1 Cor. 7). And, unless I am mistaken [Note: Col. 0502D: Perhaps *ni* or *nisi*, “unless,” as in the editions.], both pronouncements are of one and the same God. It is indeed God himself who, in the beginning, sent forth the seed of the human race, loosening the reins of marriage until the world should be filled; he himself, now at the end of the ages, has restrained what he sent forth and recalled what he allowed. Solomon foresaw this in the Spirit when he said: “A time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces” (Eccl. 3). As if he said more plainly: It belongs to the old command that the earth be filled with offspring, but to the new that heaven be filled with continence and virginity.

This prize is, however, known to be so arduous and exalted that, according to Matthew’s Gospel, the Apostles said to the Lord: “If this is a man’s case with his wife, it is not expedient to marry.” [Note: Col. 0502D: The material enclosed in brackets is absent from the editions and disrupts the discourse; for after “to marry,” Isidore rightly says: “The Lord replied: ‘He who can receive it, let him receive it.’”] [The Lord answered them: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it is given.” It follows: “There are some eunuchs who were born thus from their mother’s womb” (Matt. 19). As if he said more plainly: There are eunuchs—that is, continent persons—who were born thus from their mother’s [Col. 0502D] womb, without instruments, because of a frigid constitution; and there are eunuchs made by men. Neither group has a reward, because they are so not by choice but by necessity.
