And there are eunuchs who [Col. 0503A] have made themselves eunuchs—that is, who of their own will have devoted themselves to chastity—for the kingdom of heaven. He adds again, saying:] “He who can receive it, let him receive it.” This is the voice of one exhorting, not commanding. As though he said: Let each person consider his strength, whether he can fulfill the precepts of virginity and chastity. Therefore not all can be chaste—that is, not all can fulfill the command of continence—because it is not given by God to all, nor is ascent to the reward of continence granted to all. Thus this is not a command concerning continence, but a counsel. Virginity is not imposed in such a manner as to be a necessity; rather, it is praised because it can exist voluntarily. The Apostle Paul testifies to this, saying: “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord” (1 Cor. 7). And again: “I think, therefore, that this is good because of the present necessity: that it is good for a person to remain thus” (ibid.).

But those who cannot bear the temptation of the flesh, as St Isidore says, must seek the harbour of marriage if they have not vowed chastity. Hence the same Apostle says: “He who does not restrain himself, let him marry. For it is better to marry than to burn.” And again: “If you have taken a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin” (ibid.). You have free will: if you do not wish to be greater, be at least lesser. For lawful marriage, as St Isidore says, is not sin; but because of worldly care, those who marry can scarcely keep God’s law. The Apostle says in another sense that those do not sin when they marry who have not yet vowed chastity to God [Col. 0503C]. For one who has promised, even in his heart, to be continent will be condemned if he does otherwise, because, as the same Apostle says, he has made void his first faith (1 Tim. 5). What was lawful by nature, he has made unlawful for himself by a vow, as Ananias and his wife Sapphira were not permitted to keep anything back from the price of their property, for which cause they were struck down by sudden death (Acts 5). Therefore, as stated above, different classes of virgins are mentioned in the Gospel; but possession of the kingdom is assigned especially to those who have made themselves eunuchs without iron for the love of God—that is, not those compelled by the necessity of incapacity, but those whom holy devotion makes continent.

How great is the gift of holiness in virgins is shown by St John the Evangelist, who writes that only those who have not been defiled by union with women cleave to the Lamb’s footsteps [Note: Col. 0503D: John’s testimony is absent from the editions.]: “These,” he says, “are they who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. These follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. 14). These, as St Isidore says in the book *On the Kinds of Offices*, are the twelve times ten [Note: Col. 0504D: Editions read “twelve times twelve.”] thousand holy harpists, of spotless virginity in body and inviolate chastity in heart. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, whom no one except virginity alone dares or is able to follow. The other faithful who have lost bodily virginity also follow the Lamb, but not wherever he goes [Col. 0504A]; rather, wherever they themselves can—that is, insofar as it has been granted them. Therefore care must be taken lest so great a gift of holiness be corrupted by pride. For virginity exalts many, and continence lifts them up.

Let us hear what St Isidore says in this place:

> “Humble married persons follow the Lamb more easily—if not wherever he goes, certainly wherever they can—than proud virgins. For how will they follow one whom they refuse to approach? Or how will they approach one to whom they do not come, so as to learn how meek he is and humble of heart? Therefore let virgins go to the height of the heavenly homeland on the foot of humility. Let them follow Christ by perseveringly keeping what they have ardently vowed, so that, with integrity professed and preserved, [Col. 0504B] they may also correspond in their other conduct; without these virtues virginity undoubtedly remains idle and empty. For good actions, when added to virginity, display to human beings an angelic life and the manners of heaven upon earth. Certainly, as St Jerome says, to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly life but a heavenly one. Hence to acquire angelic glory in the flesh is a greater merit than to possess it. For to be an angel belongs to blessedness; but to be a virgin belongs to virtue, since one strives by one’s powers with grace to obtain what the angel possesses by nature.”

Thus those are proved to be virgins who imitate the angelic life on earth, and who serve continence in such a way that they are weighed down by no crimes and no burden of earthly concern. For the marriage bond produces care of the world, as the Apostle Paul says: “I want you to be without care” (1 Cor. 7). And again: “He who is without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but he who is with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and is divided” (ibid.). Hence it is recognized that a vow of continence impeded by the hindrance of worldly cares cannot perfectly please God. “For it profits virgins nothing,” as St Isidore says in the book *On the Kinds of Offices*, “to be free from the act of the flesh while bound by worldly cares, except that they acquire greater punishments for themselves, because they do not overcome the world although they were able to overcome the flesh.

[Col. 0504D] “It is asked why female virgins are veiled at the blessing. The reason for this is as follows. Women are in no way appointed to ecclesiastical ranks or offices. They are not permitted to speak or teach in the Church, nor to touch or offer the chalice or paten, incense, or claim any share whatsoever in a male or priestly office. Therefore only this is granted them: because she is a virgin and has resolved to sanctify her flesh, she is granted the favour—that is, the permission—of the veil, so that she may enter the Church as a conspicuous or distinguished person, display the honour of her sanctified body in the freedom of her head, and wear a mitre on her head like a crown of virginal glory.”

[Col. 0505A] Therefore, as was said above, if a virgin has not professed virginity and lawfully marries a man, she will not sin, according to the judgment of the Apostle Paul; yet it will be much better if, for love of Christ, she preserves her virginity undefiled all her days. I want you to know, O Cathar heretics, who say that widows who marry are to be condemned as adulteresses: if a virgin marries and, after her husband’s death, remains a widow, then, if she is unwilling or unable to remain continent, she may marry another man again. Thus Paul, the teacher of the churches, because of incontinence commands remarriage, saying: “It is better to marry than to burn” (ibid.). Indeed, it is better to marry one man again than, in order to satisfy lust, to commit fornication with many.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Also from Isidore, ibid., ch. 20.]

For the fact that spouses are blessed by a priest in the very joining of marriage was done by God at the first creation of humankind. For it is written: “And God made man; in the image of God he made him; male and female he created them; and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1). By this likeness, therefore, that which was then done in paradise is now done in the Church.

And the fact that women who are lawfully marrying are attended by women who have had one husband—

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Edition: *univirae*, “women of one husband.”]

—that is, on account of monogamy; and, though it is for the sake of an auspice, nevertheless, as Blessed Isidore says, it is a good auspice.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] From the same work, *Etymologies*, book IX, ch. 7.]

She is called a *pronuba* because she presides over those marrying and also joins the bride to her husband. She is also called a *paranympha*. For *nympha* means a bride at a wedding, and also a nymph in connection with the office of bathing; it is likewise joined to the term for a woman marrying. A *monogamus* is so called because he has married only one woman. For among the Greeks μόνος (*monos*) means “one,” while γάμος (*gamos*) means “marriage.” A bigamist, trigamist, and quadrigamist are named from the number of wives: as though a husband of two, three, or four wives.

[Note: [Col. 0505D] Again from *Ecclesiastical Offices*.]

The fact that these same women are veiled while being married is so that they may know themselves to be subject and humble toward their husbands. Hence the veil itself was popularly called *mavors*—

[Note: [Col. 0505D] *Mavors*.]

—that is, Mars—

[Note: [Col. 0505D] *Mars*.]

—by the ancients, because it was, as it were, a sign of marital dignity and authority; for “the husband is the head of the wife” (1 Cor. 11). They are also veiled when they marry so that they may recognize the modesty proper to womanhood, since what follows thereafter is something of which they ought to be ashamed. Thus Rebekah, when she was being led to Isaac, her bridegroom, as soon as she saw him did not await kisses of greeting, but immediately, sensing what she was to become, covered her head with a mantle (Gen. 24). Hence brides too are called *nuptae*, because they veil their faces. For *obnubere* means “to cover over”; hence clouds too are called *nubes*, because they cover the sky.

[Col. 0506A] Moreover, it should be noted that in the times of the earlier Fathers—namely Blessed Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and Saint Isidore—spouses came before the altar and, with their knees bent, were bound together by a deacon with the bond of a single ribbon. Thus, after the blessing, those marrying were joined to one another by one bond through a levite, so that they might not break apart the compact of conjugal unity. The fact that this same ribbon was interwoven with white and purple was meant to signify that white represented purity of life and purple the posterity of blood; by this sign both parties were admonished that the rule of continence should be observed for a time, and that afterward the marital due should not be withheld.

For what the Apostle says to married persons—“Abstain for a time, that you may be free for prayer” (1 Cor. 7)—was indicated by the whiteness of the ribbon. But what he adds, “and return again to the same,” was shown by its purple color. The ring first given by the bridegroom to the bride is given either as a sign of mutual faithfulness or, more particularly, so that by this pledge their hearts may be joined in love. Hence the ring is placed on the fourth finger, because from it, as is said, a certain vein of blood reaches to the heart. In ancient times, however, as Blessed Isidore says in the book *On the Kinds of Offices*, no more than one ring was given, lest plurality diminish a single love. Among the Israelites, moreover, it was unlawful to give a girl to a man before the maturity signified by manifest blood.

[Col. 0506C]

[Note: [Col. 0505D] These matters are from book IX of the *Etymologies*, ch. 6.]

Among the ancients, four qualities were sought in choosing husbands: virtue, lineage, beauty, and wisdom. Of these, wisdom is more powerful in awakening love. Virgil relates these four concerning Aeneas—

[Note: [Col. 0505D] *Aeneid* IV, 10.]

—by which Dido was moved to love him.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] Another manuscript: “Elisa Dido.”]

By beauty:

> What a bearing he has in face!

[Note: [Col. 0506D] “Whom,” not “what.”]

By courage:

> With a brave breast and arms!

[Note: [Col. 0506D] “What,” not “with.”]

By speech, that is, wisdom:

> Those things by which he, tossed by the fates, was recounting what wars had been endured!

[Note: [Col. 0506D] “Alas,” not “those.”]

By lineage:

> I indeed believe—and my belief is not vain—that his race is of the gods.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] The pronoun *mihi* (“to me”) is absent from Virgil, Isidore, and another manuscript.]

[Col. 0506D] Likewise, in choosing a wife four things impel a man to love: beauty, lineage, wealth, and good character. Yet it is better that character rather than beauty be sought in her. Now, however, women are sought whom wealth or appearance, not uprightness of character, recommends.

[Note: [Col. 0506D] These matters again are from *Ecclesiastical Offices*.]

The question is not how chaste a woman may be, but rather how beautiful; one who both feeds the desire for lust and draws after herself the sighs of all.

[Col. 0507A] “For a beautiful woman,” as a certain wise man says,

[Note: [Col. 0507D] Theophrastus, in Jerome, book I *Against Jovinian*.]

“is quickly loved; and she whom many love is difficult to guard.”

It has already been sufficiently shown above that a wife cannot be dismissed by her husband except for the cause of fornication. For “he who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. 18). If, therefore, a wife is caught in adultery, she may freely be dismissed by her husband. But what if the wife is barren, ugly, aged, foul-smelling, drunken, irascible, wasteful, foolish, gluttonous, wandering, quarrelsome, abusive, bleary-eyed, or follows depraved habits? Whether you wish it or not, O young man, you must keep her; whatever kind she may be when accepted, she must be retained. For when you were free, you voluntarily delivered yourself into servitude.

Therefore faithfulness must be kept by each toward the other; indeed, a husband ought by the example of continence to teach his wife to conduct herself chastely. For it is unjust to demand what you cannot provide. For “the husband is the head of the wife” (1 Cor. 11). But where a wife lives better than her husband, the household hangs head downward. Therefore the husband, who is the head, ought to go before his wife in good works, so that she may imitate her husband and follow him as her head, just as the Church follows Christ her bridegroom.

The Apostle exhorts married persons to abstain from sexual intercourse for the sake of prayer and, by mutual consent, to observe times of consecration, that they may devote themselves to prayer without bodily impediment (1 Cor. 7). For in the Old Testament all were first sanctified from women, and thus were worthy to stand before God as he descended upon the mountain (Exod. 19).

[Col. 0507C] The same Apostle likewise exhorts women to be subject to their husbands (1 Cor. 14). For many women, toward husbands of lesser understanding who abound in wealth and nobility, do not remember God’s sentence, by which they ought to be subject to them (Eph. 5). For the Lord says to the woman: “You shall be under your husband’s power, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. 3). Therefore the precepts of Holy Scripture must be obeyed, and a husband served with a servitude that is in some measure free and full of love. For man was not created for woman, but woman for man (1 Cor. 11). And since the husband is the head of the wife, Christ is the head of the husband (ibid.), when a wife does not submit to her husband—that is, to her head—she is guilty of the same sin, as Blessed Isidore says,

[Note: [Col. 0507D] As above, *On Offices*.]

as is the husband if he does not submit to Christ, his head.

[Col. 0507D] The word of the Lord is blasphemed either when God’s first sentence is despised and treated as nothing, or when Christ’s Gospel is dishonored: when, contrary to the law and faith of nature, a woman who is Christian and subject under God’s law desires to rule her husband, although even pagan women serve their husbands under the common law of nature. Therefore the law of nature and of God is preserved if a woman is subject to her husband. Conversely, if she wishes to command her husband, the order of nature is corrupted, and that household lies wretched and perverse.

At this point I admonish you, O Cathar heretics, who condemn widows as adulteresses if they marry:

[Col. 0508A] patiently hear what I say. Hold it as certain, then, and do not doubt at all, that not only first and second marriages are lawful, but that third and fourth marriages also are not to be condemned. Therefore, that you may not doubt the truth of what we say, we prove it by the authorities of the holy Fathers. Let us hear what Blessed Augustine says in *On the Good of Widowhood*.

[Note: [Col. 0508D] Augustine, *On the Good of Widowhood*, no. 15.—*Four Books of Sentences*, distinction 42, “It should be known.”]

“The Apostle,” he says, “allows second marriages as altogether lawful. But people commonly raise a question about third, fourth, and still more numerous marriages. Yet who would dare to define what I do not see the Apostle himself defining? For he says: ‘If her husband has fallen asleep, let his wife marry whom she wishes’” (1 Cor. 7).

Let us listen carefully, O Cathar heretics, to what Blessed Augustine says on this passage in his book *On Holy Widowhood*.

[Col. 0508B] “The Apostle did not say, ‘if her first, second, third, or however-numbered husband has fallen asleep’; nor should you define what the Apostle himself did not define. Therefore,” he says, “to answer briefly: I ought neither to condemn such marriages, nor to take away from them the modesty that shrinks from their number; nor, against the sense of human modesty, do I dare to say, ‘Let them marry as often as they wish’; nor from my own heart, apart from the authority of Scripture, to condemn marriages of however great a number.”

Thus, in that Blessed Paul permits second marriages and does not object to third, fourth, and fifth marriages, while Augustine, the teacher of the churches, does not presume in any way to prohibit them, your lying assertion, O heretics who condemn widows if they marry, is plainly refuted,

[Col. 0508C] and the Christian religion is unquestionably confirmed.

Let us also bring forward Blessed Jerome, the guardian of the Catholic faith and its most faithful defender, and hear from him whether a widow ought to marry again after her husband’s death.

[Note: [Col. 0508D] *Four Books of Sentences*, ibid.]

“I,” he says, “proclaim in a free voice that a twice-married woman is not condemned in the Church, nor indeed a thrice-married woman; and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth or sixth husband as a second. Yet the Apostle excludes twice-married men from priestly honor, but does this not because bigamy is a vice, but on account of the force of the sacrament: that there may be one wife of one husband, just as one Church belongs to one Christ” (1 Tim. 3).

Therefore, as has often been said, O Cathar heretics who condemn widows as adulteresses if they marry:

[Col. 0508D] marriage is good, but it is better to vow chastity to God for the sake of the heavenly kingdom. Marriage is good; to live continently is better; but far better and happier still is to persevere in virginity until the day of death, for love of God and desire of the heavenly kingdom. Thus a widow, after her husband’s death, has permission to marry lawfully again and again, if she is unwilling to remain continent.

Therefore, to refute completely your most false assertion and more and more to confirm the religion of the Catholic Church, let us bring Blessed Augustine forward and hear together all that he says to us about the good of widowhood.

[Col. 0509A] “Widows,” he says, “who do not remain continent should marry before they profess a vow of continence to God.” Thus, in that Blessed Augustine commands widows to marry if they are unwilling to remain continent, he demonstrates in every respect that you, O heretics who assert that they must be condemned if they marry, are lying.

Since, therefore, you irreverently disparage the religion of the holy Catholic Church—namely, by denying that sinners can obtain pardon through penance; by condemning widows if they marry; and by proudly despising the ministers of that same holy Church, while never ceasing to defame them with blasphemies and insults—you make yourselves liable to eternal condemnation. Therefore humbly perform penance before God and the priests of the holy Church for your past blasphemies; lay aside, by the judgment of those same priests, the stains of lasting leprosy—that is, the blasphemies of heretical perversity. Receive with devout mind the color of true salvation, namely the rule of ecclesiastical religion, so that, believing rightly and doing good works with the children of that same holy Church, you may attain the prize of eternal blessedness. Amen.

XXXIV.—

It is shown against the Aerian heretics that prayers, alms, and the sacred offering of Christ benefit the faithful departed, through examples taken from Gregory’s *Dialogues*. Testimonies from the books of Maccabees and from the Apocalypse of John are also adduced on this point. Costly tombs and funeral pomp are consolations of the living rather than relief for the dead. Burial in churches, however, is beneficial when prayers are offered for the departed in remembrance of them. Holy people

[Col. 0509C] and angels hear our prayers and intercede that our prayers too may be heard by God.

The Aerian heretics also bear leprosy, as it were, in their body when they irreverently disparage the sacraments of the Catholic Church, which is Christ’s body. But let us hear what Isidore, the teacher of the Spanish lands, says about them in book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Etymologies*: “The Arians,” he says, “are named from a certain Aerius, who, among the other doctrines of his perversity, scorns to offer sacrifice for the faithful departed. These heretics also—as I read in a certain writing—forbid their followers to offer sacrifice for the faithful departed.”

Therefore these Aerians, together with their master Aerius, are rightly numbered among heretics by Catholic men,

[Col. 0509D] since they not only refuse to receive the sacraments of ecclesiastical religion, but also shamelessly revile those who receive them with devout mind. They are clearly deceived in their most lying sect when they forbid sacrifices to be offered to God for the faithful departed. Therefore, in order to refute the doctrines of their heretical perversity, it is necessary to bring forward testimonies from the Old and New Testaments.

Let Blessed Augustine, the most powerful hammer of heretics, come into our midst, and graciously show us whether alms or sacrifices offered to God by the faithful for the salvation of their dead benefit them. For he says:

[Note: [Col. 0509D] *Four Books of Sentences*, distinction 45, “Furthermore.”]

“The period extending between a person’s death and the final resurrection holds souls in hidden receptacles, each according as it is worthy either of rest or of suffering, according to what it acquired in the flesh while it lived.”

[Col. 0510A] He continues: “Nor should it be denied that the souls of the departed are relieved by the piety of their living kin, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them or alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while living, merited that they might benefit them afterward. For there is a manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death. Yet there is a condition so good that it does not require them, and again one so evil that, once this life has passed, it cannot be helped even by these things. Accordingly, all merit is acquired here,

[Col. 0510B] through which someone may be burdened or relieved after this life. But let no one hope to merit from God after dying what he neglected here. Therefore the things which the Church repeatedly does in commending the dead are not contrary to that apostolic statement: ‘We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ’ (Rom. 14), ‘that each may receive according to what he has done through the body’ (2 Cor. 5), whether good or evil. For each person acquired even this merit while living in the body: namely, that these things might benefit him. For they do not benefit everyone. And why not, except because of the difference in life which each led in the body?

“When, therefore, sacrifices at the altar or alms of whatever sort are offered for all baptized persons, they are thanksgivings for the very good and propitiations for those not very bad. But even for the very bad, if they are no help to the dead, they are nevertheless some consolation to the living. Yet for those whom they benefit, they benefit either so that there may be full remission, or at least that the condemnation itself may be more tolerable.

[Col. 0510C] Therefore there is no doubt that the dead are helped by prayers, by the saving sacrifice of the holy Church, and by alms offered for their spirits, so that the Lord may deal with them more mercifully than their sins deserved. For this the whole Church observes as a tradition: that, when those who died in the communion of the Lord’s body and blood are commemorated in their place at the sacrifice itself, prayer is made and this sacrifice is offered for them as well.

“Therefore it must not be doubted that these things benefit the departed—but those who lived before death in such a way that these things can be useful to them after death. For those who have departed the body without faith working through love (Gal. 5) and without its sacraments are vainly given such offices of piety by their own people, since while here they lacked its pledge: they did not lay up mercy for themselves, but wrath. Therefore, when their family does some good for them, new merits are not acquired for the dead; rather, these subsequent things are rendered in accordance with their preceding merits. For no one who ends this life can have after it anything other than what he merited in it.”

[Col. 0511A] Behold, O Aerian heretics, whom and in what manner those things which holy mother Church does for the faithful departed benefit. They aid the moderately wicked in mitigating punishment, and the moderately good toward complete absolution: those who do not possess merits of such perfection that they need no help through the poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven (Luke 6), whom they made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity (Luke 16), and whose perfection is so great, as Blessed Augustine says,

[Note: [Col. 0511D] Rather, Peter Lombard: he, not Augustine, says this. The Benedictines’ note on the *Enchiridion* of the Holy Father, no. 29, letter C, must certainly be consulted.]

that they need no such aids, as do the apostles and martyrs. Blessed Augustine therefore asserts beyond doubt that prayers, alms, sacrifices, and the other offices of piety benefit the faithful departed; and he openly shows that you, O Aerian heretics who deny this, are lying.

[Col. 0511B] Perhaps you ask, O senseless heretics, about two equally good persons—one rich and the other poor—equally but moderately good, who need the aforementioned suffrages and have equally merited to be helped after death. For one of them, the rich person, many special prayers from relatives and common prayers from the Church are made, together with many gifts of alms; for the poor person, only the Church’s common prayers are made. You ask, therefore, whether the poor person is helped by fewer aids just as much as the rich person by more abundant ones. But if he is not helped equally, then he is not repaid according to his merits. For he merited equal help because they were equally good. But if he receives as much suffrage as the rich person, what did the many good things specially done for the rich person contribute?

[Col. 0511C] Certainly, O heretics, your question may be answered thus: special and general suffrages availed the rich person in obtaining forgiveness of sins; the general prayers alone, celebrated by the Church in charity for all the faithful, availed the poor person in obtaining pardon for sins. The distribution of many alms, together with the general aids of the Catholic Church, benefits the rich; good will, together with the common prayers and sacrifices of that same holy Church, benefits the poor. Yet it may be said that the more numerous aids gave the rich person swifter absolution, not fuller absolution.

Therefore hold without doubt, O Aerian heretics, that the souls of the faithful departed can be helped by alms, prayers,

[Col. 0511D] sacrifices, and the other aids of holy Church, and can obtain pardon for sins. And, so that you may not doubt the truth of what we say, we prove it by authoritative examples. Let us then bring forward Blessed Gregory, an eminent teacher, and hear together with devout mind what he says to us concerning the benefit of alms.

“A certain soldier,” he says,

[Note: [Col. 0512D] Book IV of the *Dialogues*, ch. 36.]

“in this Roman city was struck down and came to his end. Drawn out from the body, he lay lifeless, but soon returned and told what had happened to him in that world. For, as the event then became known also to many,

[Col. 0512A] he said that there was a bridge under which ran a black and murky river, exhaling a cloud of intolerable stench. But after the bridge there were pleasant and green meadows adorned with fragrant flowers of herbs, in which gatherings of people clothed in white appeared to be present. And there was such a sweet scent in that place that the fragrance itself satisfied those walking and dwelling there. There were dwellings of various kinds there, each full of immense light. There a house of marvelous grandeur was being built, which appeared to be constructed of golden bricks, though it could not be learned whose it was.

“Some dwellings stood upon the bank of the river mentioned above. Some were touched by the cloud of rising stench, while others were not touched at all by the stench rising from the river.

[Col. 0512B] The test upon the bridge was this: whoever among the unjust wished to cross it slipped into the dark and foul-smelling river. But the righteous, whose guilt did not impede them, came by it with safe and unhindered step to the pleasant places.”

What, then, does that house which appeared to be built of golden bricks in the pleasant places signify, and who are its builders, O Aerian heretics who forbid sacrifices and alms to be offered for the faithful departed? Let us consider this more attentively.

[Note: [Col. 0512D] Ch. 37.]

“For from what was shown in the vision itself about whoever the man may be for whom that dwelling was being built from gold, it is clearly understood what he was doing. For since he will merit the reward of eternal light through the generous distribution of alms,

[Col. 0512C] it is evident that he is building his house with gold. For the same soldier who had seen the things mentioned above related that old men and young men, boys and girls, were carrying those same golden bricks for the building of the house. From this it is inferred that those to whom mercy was shown here appeared there as the builders themselves.”

Therefore, if one who in the present life gives alms to the poor for love of God prepares for himself a dwelling full of light in eternal blessedness, it is evident that you are lying in every respect in your assertion, O heretics, who deny that alms and sacrifices benefit the souls of the faithful departed. For the aids of the living benefit the faithful departed, as has been said—

[Note: [Col. 0512D] Thus the manuscript.]

—but only those who, while living, merited that they could benefit them after death.

[Col. 0512D] What do you say to this, O heretics? What do you propose or object? Do you now, on the basis of the foregoing testimonies and examples, unquestionably believe that works of piety by the living benefit the souls of the departed? Or do you still remain doubtful in your most lying unbelief? But if you say that you still persist in your damnable sect, if you still deny that the suffrages of the living can benefit the souls of the faithful departed, then to overcome your unbelief

[Col. 0513A] and confirm the truth of the Catholic religion, we shall introduce example after example.

Therefore, that you may no longer doubt that prayers and alms can benefit the souls of the faithful departed, I urge you to listen carefully to the example offered by Blessed Gregory. “When I was,” he says,

[Note: [Col. 0513D] Ch. 40.]

“a young man and still in lay dress, I heard elders who knew the matter relate that Paschasius, a deacon of this Apostolic See—whose very sound and lucid books on the Holy Spirit are extant among us—was a man of marvelous holiness, especially devoted to the works of almsgiving, a friend of the poor and a despiser of himself. But in the contention which, through the burning zeal of the faithful, arose between Symmachus and Laurence, he chose Laurence for the pontificate.

[Col. 0513B] Though he was unanimously defeated by all, he nevertheless persisted in his opinion up to the day of his death, loving and preferring the man whom the Church, by the judgment of the bishops, had refused to set over her.

[Note: [Col. 0513D] “By all.”]

“When Paschasius had died during the time when Symmachus was bishop of the Apostolic See, a demoniac touched his dalmatic placed beneath the bier and was immediately healed. Much later physicians advised Germanus, bishop of Capua, to bathe in the springs at Angulana for his bodily health. Upon entering these baths, he found the aforesaid deacon Paschasius standing and serving in the heat of the baths. At the sight he was greatly astonished and asked what so great a man was doing there. He replied:

[Col. 0513C] ‘I have been assigned to this penal place for no other reason than that I agreed with the party of Laurence against Symmachus. But I beg you, pray to the Lord for me; and you will know that you have been heard if, when you return here, you do not find me.’

“Bishop Germanus, a man of God, thereupon devoted himself to prayer; after a few days he returned, but did not find Paschasius in that place. For because he sinned not through malice but through an error of ignorance, he was able to be cleansed from sin after death.”

Tell us, O senseless Aerian heretics, why could he be cleansed of sin after death, except because by the generosity of his almsgiving he obtained this: that he might then merit pardon when he could no longer perform

[Col. 0513D] any good work?

By these and similar most true examples, Christ’s faithful people are especially strengthened in the Catholic faith, more devoutly encouraged to do good, and your execrable sect is altogether refuted and rendered futile. It is also plainly made clear that the aforesaid Paschasius, deacon of the Roman Church, deserved to be freed from sin and its punishment because in his life he devoted himself to the distribution of alms and to other works of mercy. Therefore recognize that you, O Aerian heretics, have lied in your superstitious assertion, and cease any longer to deny that prayers, sacrifices,

[Col. 0514A] and alms can benefit the souls of the faithful departed.

I wonder with what face, O mad heretics, you presume to say that the suffrages of the living do not benefit the souls of the faithful departed in obtaining pardon for sins, when the souls of the departed themselves sometimes seem to request these things. For if faults are not incapable of being dissolved after death, prayers, alms, and especially the offering of the saving sacrifice are often of great help to souls even after death. Therefore, to refute your most lying sect and confirm the religion of the Catholic Church, we can prove by examples the things we have set forth. Let us then hear what Blessed Gregory says in the fourth book of the *Dialogues* concerning a priest of venerable life.

[Col. 0514B] “I learned,” he says,

[Note: [Col. 0514D] Ch. 49.]

“on the testimony of Bishop Felix, that there was a certain priest living in the diocese of the city of Centumcellae, who presided over the church of Blessed John situated at a place called Tauriana. Whenever bodily necessity required, this venerable priest was accustomed to bathe in that same place where hot waters produce great vapors. One day, when he entered, he found an unknown man prepared to serve him: to remove his footwear from his feet, take his garments, offer him a towel when he came out of the heat, and perform every service with great attentiveness.

“When this had happened frequently, one day as the priest was going to the bath, he said to himself:

[Col. 0514C] ‘I ought not to appear ungrateful to the man who so devoutly serves me in bathing; I must bring him something as a gift.’ He then took with him two loaves from the offerings. As soon as he arrived at the place, he found the man and, as usual, received every service from him. He bathed; and when, now clothed, he wished to depart, he offered to the man serving him what he had brought, as a blessing, asking him kindly to receive what he offered out of charity.

“But the other, sorrowful and distressed, replied: ‘Why do you give these things to me, father? This bread is holy; I cannot eat it. For I whom you see was once the lord of this place, but for my sins I have been assigned here after death.

[Col. 0514D] If, however, you wish to help me, offer this bread to almighty God for me, that you may intercede for my sins. And know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and no longer find me.’

“At these words he disappeared. And the one who appeared to be a man made it known, by vanishing, that he was a spirit. The venerable priest himself afflicted himself with tears for him during an entire week, offered the saving sacrifice daily, and afterward returned to the bath, where he no longer found him.”

From this, O Aerian heretics, enemies of truth, you can clearly gather how greatly the immolation of the sacred offering benefits the souls of the faithful departed, since the spirits of the dead themselves urgently request it from the living and indicate by signs that through it they deserve to be absolved.

[Col. 0515A] Therefore, as you see, O heretics, by these most true authorities and examples the Christian religion is more and more strengthened, while your damnable sect is unquestionably refuted and rendered futile. For if the good works of the living—namely prayers, alms, and sacrifices—did not benefit the souls of the faithful departed, the dead would never request them so diligently from the living. But because, all doubt put aside, the suffrages of the living benefit departed souls, they request these things from the living as necessary.

What do you say to this, O heretics? What do you answer or object? Do you now give credence, on the basis of such very clear

[Col. 0515B] examples, that the aids of the living benefit the souls of the departed? Or do you still intend to remain in your damnable unbelief? Therefore, if you say that the examples of truth mentioned above do not yet suffice for you, but you remain doubtful about accepting the rule of ecclesiastical religion, then, in order wholly to overcome your most lying assertion and to confirm in every respect the truth of Catholic teaching, we shall introduce other sufficiently authoritative examples. Let Blessed Gregory, a man of great reverence in the Church of Christ, therefore come forward again and teach us, by examples of events that occurred, for the instruction of the whole Church, whether works of piety performed by the living in the present world can benefit the souls of the faithful departed.

[Col. 0515C] “In my monastery,” he says [Note: [Col. 0515D] Chapter 55.], “I remember that, three years ago, the event I am about to relate occurred. A certain monk named Justus had been trained in the art of medicine. While I was living in the same monastery, he regularly attended me with great care and used to keep watch during my frequent illnesses. He was then overtaken by bodily sickness and brought to his end. In this affliction he was attended by his own brother, named Copiosus, who even now in this city of Rome earns the wages of temporal life by the same medical art. But when the aforesaid Justus knew that he had reached his end, he informed his brother Copiosus that he possessed three gold coins secretly. This, however, the brothers could not conceal. [Col. 0515D] Searching carefully and examining all his medicines, they found the same three gold coins hidden in a medicinal preparation. As soon as this was reported to me, I could not bear with equanimity so great an evil in a brother who had lived among us in common. For it had always been the rule of our monastery that all the brothers should live so communally that none of them was permitted to possess anything as his own.

“Then, struck with excessive grief, I began to consider both what I should do for the cleansing of the dying man and what provision I should make by way of an example for the brothers who were alive. So, having summoned to me the worthy steward of the monastery, named Pretiosus, I said: ‘Go, and let none of the [Col. 0516A] brothers join himself to that dying man, nor let him receive a word of consolation from any of them. But when, at the point of death, he asks for the brothers, let his own fleshly brother tell him that he is abhorred by all the brothers because of the gold which he possessed secretly, so that at least in death the bitterness may pierce his mind on account of his guilt and cleanse him from the sin he committed. When he has died, moreover, do not place his body with the bodies of the brothers; instead, dig a pit in the dung-heap and cast his body into it. Then throw upon him the three gold coins which he left, all crying together: “May your money be with you unto destruction” (Acts VIII); and thus cover him with earth.’

“In both these measures I wished to benefit one person—the dying man—and the other—the brothers who lived: [Col. 0516B] so that the bitterness of death might free him from his guilt, and so that the severity of this condemnation of avarice might keep them from being implicated in such guilt. And so it was done. For when that monk came to death and anxiously sought to commend himself to the brothers, and none of the brothers deigned to come near or speak to him, his fleshly brother told him why he was abhorred by all. He immediately groaned deeply over his guilt and, in that very sorrow, departed from the body. He was buried as I had directed.

“But all the brothers, disturbed by this judgment upon him, began each to bring forth into the common store every last trifling and worthless thing which they had always been permitted by the rule to possess, and they greatly feared lest they might have anything in their possession for which they could be reproved. When, after his death, [Col. 0516C] thirty days had now passed, my mind began to feel compassion for the deceased brother; with grievous sorrow I reflected upon his punishments and sought whether there might be some remedy for his deliverance. Then, summoning to me the same Pretiosus, steward of our monastery, I said sadly: ‘For a long time that deceased brother has been suffering in fire. We must therefore bestow some act of charity upon him and help him, as far as we can, to be delivered from punishment. Go, therefore, and from this day onward take care that the sacrifice be offered for him for thirty consecutive days, so that no day whatever may be omitted on which the saving victim is not immolated for his absolution.’ He immediately departed and obeyed.

“While we were occupied with other concerns and were not counting the passing days, [Col. 0516D] the same deceased brother appeared one night in a vision to his own brother Copiosus. When Copiosus saw him, he asked, saying: ‘What is it, brother? How are you?’ He replied: ‘Until now I was badly off, but now I am well, because today I received communion.’ Copiosus went at once and reported this to the brothers in the monastery. The brothers unlawfully [Note: [Col. 0516D] *Sollicite*, ‘carefully.’] counted the days and found that it was precisely the day on which the thirtieth offering for him had been completed. And since Copiosus did not know what the brothers had been doing for him, and the brothers did not know what Copiosus had seen concerning him, when at one and the same time [Col. 0517A] he learned what they had done and they learned what he had seen, the matter became plainly clear through the agreement of vision and sacrifice: the deceased brother had escaped punishment through the saving victim.”

Therefore, lest the words of the dead seem doubtful to us, O Arian heretics, these deeds of the living confirm them. So long as the soul of that deceased brother remained without the saving victim, it endured, as we believe, a most grievous punishment; but after the victim of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, Redeemer of the world, had been offered for it, it deserved to be freed from punishment. Through the fault of avarice, indeed, he fell into danger of soul; but through the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ he was able to escape it. Since, therefore, the offering of the saving victim could benefit that brother’s soul [Col. 0517B] after death, it plainly proves that you who obstinately deny this have lied in your assertion. What then remains, except that you should faithfully believe with us that the suffrages of the living can benefit the souls of the faithful departed, and humbly repent of the blasphemies you have uttered? Certainly, if you persist in this folly, if you remain unbelieving toward the sacraments of the holy Church, if you dare further to disparage ecclesiastical religion, if you continue to contradict so evident a truth, if you remain doubtful concerning this most sacred saving medicine for the living and the dead, you will utterly perish from the company of the saints.

But if, despite such utterly true examples, you still say that the victim of the most sacred [Col. 0517C] body of Christ cannot benefit the souls of deceased Christians, we shall establish by authoritative examples, in order to overcome your unbelief and confirm the religion of the holy Church, that the most sacred offering of Christ’s body benefits not only the souls of the dead but also those still living in this world. Let blessed Gregory therefore come forward and teach us by examples whether the offering of the saving victim advances not only the dead but also the living toward salvation and deliverance.

“We have heard,” he says [Note: [Col. 0517D] Chapter 57.], “of a certain man held captive among enemies and bound in chains, for whom his wife was accustomed to offer sacrifice on certain days. After a long time he returned to his wife and made known to her on which days [Col. 0517D] his chains had been loosed; and his wife recognized that those were the days on which she had offered sacrifice for him.”

Recognize, then, O foolish heretics, slow of heart to believe, that the saving victim benefits not only the dead but also the living; and cease further to attack the religion of the holy Church with your poisonous tongue. For the offering of the saving victim most certainly frees both the souls of the faithful departed from the bonds of sins, and spiritually refreshes Christ’s faithful still living in the body, delivers them from innumerable tribulations, and raises them to desire the joys of the heavenly homeland. Thus, in the fact that the aforesaid man, held captive among enemies, was repeatedly freed from chains by the power [Col. 0518A] of the offered sacrifice, your lying assertion—which obstinately denies that this can occur—is openly refuted and condemned. By the power of the sacred offering, the Christian people are especially strengthened in faith in the holy Trinity—namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and are very often delivered by that most merciful Father, God, from impending disasters and dangers; and the souls of the faithful departed, who while placed in this present life deserved this, are without doubt released from the bonds of sins.

But if, O demented heretics, you still refuse to give credence to the utterly true examples cited above; if you still resolve to remain in your damnable sect: to overcome your lying assertion [Col. 0518B] and establish beyond doubt the truth of the Catholic religion—namely, that by the saving sacrifice of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ not only are the souls of the dead stripped of the stains of sins, but those still living in the flesh are also rescued from dangers—blessed Gregory introduces another utterly true testimony of an event:

“Agatho,” he says [Note: [Col. 0517D] As above.], “bishop of Panormus, as many faithful and religious men have testified and still testify to me, was commanded in the time of my predecessor Pelagius of blessed memory to come to Rome. He encountered the force of an excessive storm, so that he despaired of being able to escape such danger from the waves. His sailor, named Baruca, who now performs the office of cleric in that same Church, was steering a small boat behind the ship. [Col. 0518C] When the rope broke, he suddenly disappeared amid the heaps of waves with the same small boat which he was steering. The ship in which the bishop was travelling at last, after many dangers, reached the island of Ostia, battered by the waves [Note: [Col. 0518D] *Quassata*, ‘shattered/battered.’].

“On the third day, when the bishop saw no sign in any part of the sea of the sailor who had been snatched away from him in the small boat, he was deeply distressed and believed him dead. Yet he rendered him the service of charity which he owed to the dead: he ordered that the sacrifice of the saving victim should be offered to almighty God for the absolution of his soul. When this had been offered, the ship was repaired, and he proceeded to Italy. Upon reaching the Roman port, he found there the sailor whom he had believed dead when he was swept away in the small boat. [Col. 0518D] It should be noted that the common name for a *carabus* is a little boat.

“The bishop then rejoiced with unexpected exultation and asked him how he had been able to live for so many days amid the danger of that great sea. The sailor explained how often he had been tossed in the waves of that storm with the small boat he steered, how he had swum with it as it filled with water, and how often, when it was overturned from above downwards, he himself had sat upon its upturned bottom. He further related that, after doing this unceasingly day and night, when his strength had altogether failed from hunger and toil alike, divine mercy had preserved him in the following manner. He still testifies to it even now, [Col. 0519A] saying: ‘Struggling in the waves and failing, I was suddenly weighed down by a heaviness of mind, so that I was neither sunk in sleep nor thought myself awake. And behold, while I was in the middle of that sea, someone appeared and brought me bread for refreshment. As soon as I ate it, I recovered my strength. Not long afterwards, a passing ship came, took me up from that danger of the waves, and brought me to land.’

“On hearing this, the bishop asked on what day it had happened; and he discovered that it was the very day on which the priest on the island of Ostia had immolated for him the victim of the sacred offering to almighty God.”

What do you say to these things, O Arian heretics, who forbid sacrifice to be offered for the souls of the faithful departed? What do you answer? Beyond doubt, [Col. 0519B] you are not only defeated but also deserve condemnation in your lying assertion, since with proud minds you disdain to give the assent of faith to such utterly true, mutually concordant examples that the offering of the saving victim benefits faithful living persons and the faithful departed. For when the aforesaid sailor declared that, on the day when the priest, though far away, offered sacrifice to almighty God for him, he received bread from someone—namely, an angel—recovered strength as soon as he ate, and escaped unharmed from so great a danger through the power of that sacrifice, this openly shows that you who obstinately deny that this can happen are liars and superstitious persons.

I believe that this is so openly done concerning the sacrifice of Christ’s body for living persons [Col. 0519C] who do not know it, in order that it may be shown to you, O heretics, and to all those for whom these things are done without their knowledge, that, if their sins are not irremissible, the victim of the sacred offering can benefit both the living and the dead for absolution.

It must be known, as has often already been said, that the sacred victims benefit those who, while living, obtained that good works performed here by others on their behalf might aid them even after death. “Meanwhile, however, it must be considered,” as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0519D] Chapter 58.], “that the safer course is for each person to do for himself while he lives the good which he hopes will be done by others after his death. It is more blessed to leave prison free than to seek freedom after chains. Therefore we must despise the present world with our whole mind, especially because we now see it slipping away; [Col. 0519D] daily offer God sacrifices of tears, daily immolate the victims of his flesh and blood. For this victim alone saves the soul from eternal destruction, because through the mystery it renews for us the death of the Only-begotten Son—he who, though risen from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. VI). Yet, as blessed Gregory says in the book of the *Dialogues*, though living immortally and incorruptibly in himself, he is again immolated in this mystery of the sacred offering. There his body is received; his flesh is distributed among the peoples for salvation; his blood is poured out no longer into the hands of unbelievers but into the mouths of the faithful [Col. 0520A]. Let us therefore consider what kind of sacrifice this is for us, which always imitates the passion of the Only-begotten Son of God for our absolution. For what believer could doubt that at the very hour of immolation, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened, choirs of angels are present in that mystery of Jesus Christ, the lowest things are joined to the highest, earthly things are united with heavenly, and one thing is made out of visible and invisible realities?

“But,” as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0520D] Chapter 59.], “it is necessary that, when we do these things, we sacrifice ourselves to God in contrition of heart; for we who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion ought to imitate what we perform. Then the victim offered to God on our behalf will truly be such when we have made ourselves into a victim. But we must take care [Col. 0520B] that even after the times of prayer, insofar as we are able by God’s gift, we preserve the mind in the same strength and weight; lest a wandering thought afterwards dissipate it, lest empty gladness of mind creep in, and lest the soul through negligence of wandering thought lose the gain of compunction. Thus Hannah deserved to obtain what she had asked, because after her tears she kept herself in the same strength of mind. Of her it is written: ‘And her face was no longer changed in different directions’ (1 Kings I). Since, therefore, she did not forget what she had asked, she was not deprived of the gift for which she had prayed.”

Do so many testimonies and examples of truth suffice for you, O Arian heretics, or do you still seek further testimonies from the Old and New Testament [Col. 0520C] in order to overcome your unbelief and establish the truth of Catholic religion? If this is what you desire, I urge you to hear carefully what Judas Maccabaeus did for those who had fallen in battle. For the utterly true account of that time says: “The most valiant man Judas, having taken up a collection, sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to Jerusalem, to be offered there for the sins of the dead” (2 Maccabees XII). For he thought rightly and religiously concerning the general resurrection when he commanded money to be offered to God for the sins of those who had perished in battle. He did not yet know the precepts of the New Testament, and yet by faith and deed he already prefigured the religion of the Catholic Church.

Since he undoubtedly hoped that those who had died in battle while fighting for the law, the temple, and the holy city would rise again, [Col. 0520D] and believed that pious good works would benefit their souls, he therefore offered gifts to almighty God for them. Had he not most certainly believed that they would rise again, he would never have offered oblations to the Lord for them. But because he considered that those who had received sleep—that is, death—with piety, namely in defense of the law and of their fellow citizens, had the best grace laid up with God, he offered an oblation of silver for them, that they might obtain a swifter remission of sins. He therefore thought rightly and religiously concerning the resurrection, since he offered gifts to God before the altar for the absolution of souls.

Subsequently praising this thought, [Col. 0521A] holy Scripture says: “Therefore it is a holy and salutary thought to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins” (ibid.). As though it said more plainly: It is a holy thought—that is, pleasing to God—and salutary—that is, beneficial—to pray for the faithful departed: namely, to offer for them prayers, alms, and sacrifices to God. These would certainly not be beneficial if, as you lie, O Arian heretics, they did not profit the souls of the faithful departed. Thus the most valiant man Judas believed that all human beings would rise again and did not doubt that the suffrages of the living benefit the souls of the faithful departed; therefore he offered gifts to God for their absolution. In this, then, that he undoubtedly hoped for the general resurrection and with devout mind offered to God at the altar sacrifices and alms [Col. 0521B] for the souls of those who had received sleep with piety—that is, while defending their homeland and fellow citizens—he openly proves that you who deny these things can occur have lied in your assertion. As you see, O heretics, the authorities of the Old and New Testaments agree with one another and utterly condemn your detestable sect.

What do you say, O Arian heretics, or what do you answer to these things? I would like to know what will or what faith you possess. Do you not yet give credence to so many testimonies of truth, or do you still intend to remain in your damnable unbelief? If, therefore, you do not yet believe the authorities of the Old and New Testaments, if you do not give credence to the utterly true examples that truly pious and devout [Col. 0521C] works of the living benefit the souls of the dead, you ought at least, putting aside all doubt, to believe the testimony of an angel. Therefore, that the holy religion of the Catholic mother Church may be especially strengthened and your utterly lying sect more clearly condemned, let the testimony of the angel, truly delivered through John the Evangelist, be brought forward for us all to hear together.

Let us therefore consider carefully what blessed John heard in the Apocalypse—that is, in the revelation—not from a human being but from an angel. “I heard,” he says, “a voice from heaven saying to me: ‘Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord’” (Apocalypse XIV). I do not wish you to be ignorant, O Arian heretics, that this voice pertains not only to blessed John but also to all the faithful who await the reward of eternal blessedness. But let us hear more fully what blessed John heard from the angel: “I heard,” he says, “a voice from heaven saying to me: ‘Write: Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord.’” As though the angel were speaking more plainly to blessed John, saying: Since I have spoken of the torment and misery of the wicked, do not despair of the blessedness of the good; rather, write these things in your heart or commit them to letters, that they may reach posterity. For truly blessed are those dead who die in the Lord—that is, in confession of the Lord—namely, when the body is separated from the soul.

It follows: “From henceforth, the Spirit says that they may rest from [Col. 0522A] their labors” (ibid.). As though he said: “From henceforth,” that is, from the present time or from the time of the resurrection, the Spirit—namely, the whole Trinity, since God is Spirit—now says that they may rest, that is, suffer no longer the labors which they have endured until now. “For their works follow them,” that is, the reward of their works follows them. As though he said more plainly: While they were in the world, greater tribulations contributed to a greater crown, and for that reason they were thought to have been rejected by God. But they will suffer no more; and their works—namely, those which they themselves performed while still in this present life, or which were piously offered to the Lord on their behalf after their death—will follow them, that is, will benefit them in attaining the reward of eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0522B] What the authorities of the Old and New Testaments establish concerning the suffrages of the living and the absolution of the souls of the faithful departed, O foolish Arian heretics, slow of heart to believe, the heavenly voice testifies; and, as you see, it openly refutes your damnable sect. The utterly true testimonies of the holy Fathers, ancient and modern, confirm that pious and religious deeds of the living benefit the faithful departed; the heavenly voice affirms the same things; and it proves at once that you who obstinately deny that these things can occur are false witnesses in your lying assertion.

Hear, therefore, O Arian heretics, what I say; listen to what I speak; carefully attend to what I exhort for [Col. 0522C] your salvation. Since you are entirely convicted not only by the authorities of divine Scriptures but also by the testimony of the angelic voice, you must humbly repent of your blasphemies, by which until now you have irreverently disparaged the sacraments of the holy Church with polluted mouth and faithless heart. You must faithfully believe that the whole Catholic religion of that same holy mother Church was instituted by Jesus Christ, Son of God and man, and consecrated by the Holy Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son; and you must devoutly receive it through the ministers of that holy Church, so that you may attain with the assemblies of the faithful to the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Unless you depart from this folly in the present world, you will utterly perish in the future [Col. 0522D].

Perhaps you also ask, O Arian heretics, whether an expensive burial benefits a wicked rich man, or whether a mean—or no—burial harms a pious poor man. Blessed Augustine says in his sermon *On the Words of the Apostle* [Note: [Col. 0521D] IV Sentences, distinction 45, “On funeral pomp.”]:

“Funeral pomp, the procession of obsequies, and costly care for burial are some sort of consolations for the living, not aids to the dead. The throng of servants, we believe, furnished splendid obsequies before the eyes of men for that rich man clothed in purple; but the ministry of angels rendered far more splendid service before the Lord to that poor man covered with sores, whom they bore up not into a marble tomb but into Abraham’s bosom. [Col. 0523A] Nevertheless, the faithful ought to take care to bury their dead and construct tombs, because these acts are reckoned among good works in the holy Scriptures. Those who did this and rendered this service were praised, not only in relation to the bodies of the patriarchs and other saints but also in relation to the body of the Lord himself. Let people therefore fulfill toward their own these duties of the final service and these alleviations of their human grief. Yet they should procure more diligently and earnestly those things which aid the spirits of the departed: namely, oblations, prayers, and alms.”

Therefore, that you may not doubt that an expensive burial cannot benefit a wicked rich man, O Arian heretics, I urge you carefully to hear what blessed Gregory relates.

“A venerable man of holy life,” he says [Note: [Col. 0523D] Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 32.], “Maximianus, [Col. 0523B] bishop of Syracuse, who for a long time was head of my monastery in this city, used to tell the following story. A certain municipal councillor there, on the most sacred Paschal Saturday, received in baptism the little daughter of a certain man.”

Municipal councillors, as blessed Isidore says in the book of the *Etymologies* [Note: [Col. 0523D] Book IX, chapter 4.], are the same as decurions; they are called *curiales* because they administer and perform civic duties.

“The aforesaid councillor, after fasting, returned home and became very drunk with wine. He asked that this same girl, his goddaughter, remain with him, and that night he violated her—an unspeakable thing. When morning came and he arose, being guilty, he began to think of going to the baths, as though the water of the bath could wash away the stain of his sin. He went and washed, but began to fear entering the church. Yet if he did not go to church on so great a feast day, [Col. 0523C] he was ashamed before people; if he went, he dreaded God’s judgment. Thus human shame overcame him, and he went to church. There he began to stand trembling and afraid, suspecting at every moment the hour when he would be handed over to an unclean spirit and tormented before all the people. Though he was greatly afraid, nothing adverse happened to him in that celebration of the Masses. He went out rejoicing and, on the following day, entered the church now more confidently.

“For six successive days he went about happy and secure, thinking that either the Lord had not seen his crime or had mercifully pardoned it after seeing it. But on the seventh day he died a sudden death. When he had been committed to burial, a flame issued from his tomb before the eyes of all for a long time [Col. 0523D] and burned his bones until it consumed the entire tomb, so that the earth which had been heaped upon the grave appeared hollowed out. By this deed almighty God showed what his soul endured in secret, since flame consumed even his body before human eyes. In this matter he also deigned to give us who hear it an example of fear, that from this consideration we might infer what a living and feeling soul suffers for its guilt, if even senseless bones are burned by so great a punishment of fire.”

As has been said above, therefore, O Arian heretics, neither will an expensive burial benefit a wicked rich man, nor will a mean burial harm a pious poor man. For one who departs from this world in faith and love of Christ passes, as we believe, into eternal rest; therefore nothing harms him, even if he happens to be buried in a despised place. But one who, by living badly, separates himself from faith in and love of God, if he departs this world persevering in his wickedness, gains no benefit at all, even if his body receives an expensive burial, while his soul passes into eternal damnation.

Perhaps you ask, O Arian heretics, whether it benefits souls if the bodies of the dead are buried in churches. But if you ask this, let blessed Gregory answer you: “When grave sins,” he says [Note: [Col. 0523D] Chapter 50.], “[Col. 0524B] do not weigh them down, it benefits the dead to be buried in churches, because their relatives, whenever they gather at those sacred places, remember those whose tombs they see and pour out prayers to the Lord for them. But the bodies of those whom grave sins weigh down are placed in churches not for absolution but rather for a greater accumulation of condemnation. This,” blessed Gregory says, “we shall better show if we briefly relate what occurred in our own days.

“[Note: [Col. 0524D] Chapter 54.] A venerable man of holy life, Felix, bishop of Porto, was born and raised in the province of Suavinium [Note: [Col. 0524D] Sabinium.]. He testifies that there was in that place a certain nun who had bodily continence but did not avoid insolence of tongue [Col. 0524C] and foolish speech. When she died, she was placed in the church. That same night the church keeper saw in a revelation that she was led before the sacred altar, cut in two through the middle, and that one part of her was burned with fire while the other remained untouched. When he arose in the morning and told this to the brothers, and wished to show the place where she had been consumed by fire, the scorching by the flames appeared on the marble before the altar as though that woman herself had been burned there with bodily fire. From this it is plainly understood that those whose sins have not been forgiven here cannot after death be helped by sacred places to avoid the judgment of God.”

Therefore those who live wickedly in the present life [Col. 0524D] and neglect to amend their lives, if their bodies are buried in churches after death, are not relieved from impending punishments by being placed in a consecrated site or by the presence of holy relics; rather, their souls and bodies are more heavily burdened. Furthermore, it must be known that not only are the souls of the wicked more grievously tormented because their bodies are buried in churches, but ecclesiastical men as well—namely bishops, abbots, and the other prelates of the holy Church—who permit such bodies to be placed in them, whether for money or at the request of relatives, grievously sin against God and his saints whose relics are consecrated in those [Col. 0525A] churches. And lest you doubt, O Arian heretics, that what we say is true, I urge you carefully to hear what blessed Gregory says.

“John,” he says [Note: [Col. 0525D] Chapter 52.], “a distinguished man in this city of Rome, holding the office of prefect, whose truthfulness and seriousness we know, testified to me that the patrician Valerian died in the city called Brixa. The bishop of that city, having received a price, gave him a place in a church where he was to be buried. This Valerian had been frivolous and dissolute into decrepit old age and had scorned to set limits to his wickedness. On the very night on which he was buried, blessed Faustinus the martyr, in whose church his body had been [Col. 0525B] interred, appeared to the keeper and said: ‘Go and tell the bishop to cast out from here the stinking flesh which he has placed here; for, if he does not do so, he himself will die on the thirtieth day.’ The keeper was afraid to confess this vision to the bishop. He was admonished again, but refused to speak. On the thirtieth day, however, the bishop of that city, having returned to bed healthy and unharmed at evening, died a sudden and unexpected death.”

As has already been said above, therefore, those who neglect to amend their sins in the present world are more burdened than relieved if their bodies are entombed in churches after death; and those who bury them there commit an injury against the saints whose relics are placed there. Whoever commits the body of a wicked person to burial in a church dishonours the relics of the saints [Col. 0525C] and provokes God still more to wrath. But if you doubt, O Arian heretics, that this is so as we say, let us again bring forward blessed Gregory and listen more attentively to the example of an event which he sets before us.

“Venantius,” he says [Note: [Col. 0525D] Chapter 53.], “bishop of Luna, and the distinguished nobleman Liberius testify that they know and that their people were present at the event which they relate as having occurred recently in the city of Genoa. There, as they say, a man named Valentinus, defender of the Church of Milan, died. He was a very dissolute man, occupied with every frivolity, and his body was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Syrus. At midnight in that church voices were heard [Col. 0525D] as though someone were being violently driven from it and dragged outside. At these voices the keepers ran and saw two most hideous spirits who had bound the feet of this Valentinus with some fastening and were dragging him from the church as he cried out and shouted loudly. The terrified keepers returned to their beds.

“In the morning they opened the tomb in which Valentinus had been buried and did not find his body. Searching outside the church for where it had been cast, they found it placed in another tomb, with its feet still bound, just as it had been dragged from the church. [Col. 0526A] From this, O Arian heretics, infer that those whom grave sins weigh down, if they arrange to have themselves buried in a sacred place, must also be judged for their presumption; so that sacred places may not free them but may instead accuse them of the guilt of rashness.”

And that you may believe without doubt, O Arian heretics, that what we say is true, I urge you carefully to hear what blessed Gregory says concerning a certain man who, while he lived, neglected to amend his life and was buried in a church.

“What happened,” he says [Note: [Col. 0526D] Chapter 54.], “in this city of Rome is attested by many who live here: a certain leading man of their craft, when he had died, was buried by his wife in the church of blessed Januarius the martyr, beside the gate of Saint Lawrence the martyr. [Col. 0526B] On the following night, his spirit began to cry out from that burial-place, with the keeper hearing: ‘I burn, I burn!’ When he had uttered these cries for a long time, the keeper reported this to his wife. His wife sent to the church men of the same craft to inspect carefully, wishing to discover the condition of his body in the tomb from which such cries arose. Opening the tomb, they found the clothes intact; they are still kept in the church as evidence of this matter. But they found no trace whatever of his body, as though it had never been laid in that tomb. From this, O heretics, it must be inferred with what punishment his soul was condemned, since even his flesh was cast out of the church. What benefit, then, do sacred places give to those buried in them, when persons unworthy of them [Col. 0526C] are divinely cast out even from those sacred places?”

[Note: [Col. 0526D] *Sentences*, distinction 45, “But again.”] Perhaps you also ask, O Aerian heretics, concerning someone moderately good, who needs the aid of sacrifices, prayers, and alms, and who, at the very moment of the world’s consummation, departs together with the rest: can he be saved, since sacrifice, prayer, and almsgiving will no longer be offered for him, nor will he have merits of such perfection that he would not need these aids? Will he, then, be saved? We believe that, as one passing through fire, he is saved by the merits and intercessions of the heavenly Church, which always intercedes for the faithful by prayer and merit, until Christ is fulfilled—that is, until the whole Church, which is Christ’s body, is complete.

[Col. 0526D] Perhaps you also ask, O heretics, how the saints, already glorified in the presence of God, hear the prayers of suppliants and intercede for us with God. Do they hear the prayers of those who beseech them, and do the vows of petitioners come to their knowledge? Know assuredly, then, O heretics, that it is not incredible that the souls of the saints, rejoicing in the hiddenness of God’s countenance through the illumination of the true light, should, in contemplating him, understand the things done outside insofar as these concern either their joy or our help. For, just as our petitions become known to the angels, so also to the saints who stand before God, in the Word of God [Col. 0527A] whom they contemplate. Hence angels are said to offer our prayers and vows to God—not because they inform him, but because they consult his will concerning them.

Thus St Augustine says in his book *On Praying to God*: “Our petitions become known to the angels who are with God, so that in some manner they may offer them to God, and may bring back to us, either openly or secretly, what they have learned, by God’s command, is to be fulfilled.” Hence the angel said to human beings—namely, Tobias and Sarah: “When you were praying, I offered your prayer to God” (Tobit 12).

God’s own perfection suffices for knowing all things. Yet he has messengers—that is, angels—not to report to him things he does not know, but to carry out his will. For there is nothing that he does not know; rather, it is the angels’ good to consult his truth concerning their works [Col. 0527B], and this is what they are said to report to him. It is not that he may learn from them, but that they themselves may announce, through his Word and without bodily sound, even what they will. Sent by him, they go to whom he wills, hearing everything from him through that Word; that is, finding in his truth what they must do, and what, to whom, and when they must announce.

For we too, when praying to him, do not instruct him, since he knows even before we ask. For his Word says: “Your heavenly Father knows what you need even before you ask anything of him” (Matt. 6). Nor did he learn these things in time; rather, before all beginning he foreknew all temporal future things, including what and when we would ask of him, and whom he would or would not hear, and concerning what matters [Col. 0527C]. Therefore, as St Augustine says in the book *On the Grace of the New Testament*, an angel is not said to offer our prayers to God as though God then comes to know what we want and need, since he knows all things before they happen as well as after they have happened (Dan. 13); rather, because a rational creature must refer temporal causes to eternal truth, whether by asking what may be done concerning itself or by consulting what it should do.

But if angels learn our petitions from God through his Word, and whether they are to be fulfilled or not, why should we not believe that the souls of saints contemplating the face of God understand in his truth the prayers of human beings, and which are to be fulfilled and which are not? Hence [Col. 0527D] God is said to hear certain prayers not only when he brings them to effect, but also when it becomes known to the court of angels and holy souls what will or will not happen in the future; or when they recognize something to be in God’s will, they too will it. For they are so devoted to the supreme truth that they can will nothing apart from his will.

The saints, therefore, intercede with God for us: by merit, because their merits aid us; and by affection, because they desire our petitions to be fulfilled. Yet they do not do this unless they have learned that it is to be fulfilled in God’s will. Therefore we pray to them that they may intercede for us—that is, that their merits may aid us, and that they themselves may will our good, because [Col. 0528A] when they will it God wills it; and thus, when they pray, God has mercy on us.

From what has been said, it is clear that God deals more mercifully with some persons than any of their sins deserved—namely, with those who are moderately evil and are helped by the Church’s suffrages. O Aerian heretics, the authority of the Old and New Testaments agrees beyond doubt that the souls of departed believers are helped by the pious works of the living, and utterly condemns you who deny that this can happen.
