The authorities of Holy Scripture plainly confirm that the suffrages of the living—namely prayers, sacrifices, and alms—truly benefit the souls of believers, and openly prove that you have lied in your condemnable assertion.

[Col. 0528B] Therefore humbly repent of the blasphemies by which you have hitherto disparaged the religion of the holy Church. In contrition of heart and true confession, disclose to the priests of that Church the unclean varieties of leprosy—that is, the stains of heretical perversity. With their approval, receive with a devout mind the colour of true salvation—that is, the rule of ecclesiastical religion—so that it may not befall you to perish with heretics and pagans, but that with the worshippers of the Catholic faith you may attain the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

§ XXXV.—

The Lord Christ rebukes in the Pharisees the Coritians, who admitted sexual union after the resurrection. Human beings will therefore rise in the same bodies, but shining with every beauty; [Col. 0528C] nor are these bodies to be defiled by any intercourse, since they have no necessity of dying. The one work remaining to the blessed is to praise God without cessation; there will be no succession of day and night, but perpetual light, promised to the pure in heart.

Moreover, there are certain heretics who bear leprosy, as it were, in flesh and skin, while they try to persuade unlearned people of the fleshly corruptions of the future life: the Coritians [Note: [Col. 0527D] Cerinthians.]—heretics who suppose that the future resurrection consists in bodily pleasure. Truly, these aforesaid Coritian heretics stray far from the path of truth, for they think that after the resurrection men and women will again mingle carnally. They depart greatly from the teaching of the Catholic Church when they assert that, in the age to come, men will have sexual intercourse with women.

Therefore, in order to prove that they have lied in their [Col. 0528D] false assertion, we must set against them the testimonies of Holy Scripture. We exhort you, then, O Coritian heretics, who believe in the resurrection but assert that it will occur in fleshly pleasure, carefully to hear what is said. In believing that all human beings will rise, you agree with the faith of the holy Church; but in saying that after the resurrection human beings will serve the pleasures of the flesh, you depart exceedingly far from the rule of Catholic faith. Therefore, to overcome your condemnable unbelief and strengthen the faith of the Catholic Church, let us bring forward the question of the Sadducees [Col. 0529A] and hear together what Jesus Christ, judge of the living and the dead, answered them.

For Luke the Evangelist says: “Some Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, approached Jesus and questioned him, saying: ‘Moses wrote for us: If a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he dies childless, his brother should take her as wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers among us. The first took a wife and died childless. The next took her, and he too died without a child; and the third took her and died. Likewise all seven, and they left no offspring and died. Last of all the woman also died. In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be? For all seven had her as wife’” (Luke 20).

Hear, then, O Coritian heretics, what the Son of God and the Virgin answered the aforesaid Sadducees, and how plainly he demolished your superstitious assertion. Jesus answered them: “The children of this age marry and are given in marriage; but those who are judged worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor take wives; for neither can they die any more” (ibid.). What could you wish to hear more lucid, more clear, or more plain, O Coritian heretics? God-and-man Jesus Christ openly reveals in this declaration the state of the true resurrection, and shows beyond doubt that you lie when you say that after the resurrection men [Col. 0529C] will again unite carnally with women. By this authority the faith of the holy Catholic Church is greatly strengthened, and the sect of your superstition is utterly refuted.

“The children of this age,” says the Son of God, “marry and are given in marriage; but those judged worthy of that age and of the resurrection from the dead neither marry nor take wives, nor can they die any more.” Why, then, do the children of this age marry and are given in marriage, except to beget children who will succeed them after their death? They therefore marry and are given in marriage so that they may have children whom they leave surviving them. Because they know beyond doubt that they themselves will die, they marry and are given in marriage. Thus marriage is provided for the sake of children, children [Col. 0529D] for succession, and succession because of death in the present age. But in the future age they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, because they cannot die any more. It is plainly superfluous to seek succession through children where no one dies. Therefore no succession of offspring is to be sought after the day of resurrection.

But since you have now sufficiently taught us, O Christ, that those judged worthy of that age will neither marry nor be given in marriage, we ask you to teach us again what they will be like after the resurrection. “They are equal to the angels,” he says, “and are children of God, being children of the resurrection.” In saying, “They are equal to the angels,” he plainly shows that their future manner of life will be spiritual, not carnal [Col. 0530A]. In then saying, “And they are children of God, being children of the resurrection,” he openly demonstrates that they enjoy the vision of God without the stain of corruption. As you see, O Coritian heretics, the Son of God and the Virgin powerfully destroys your wicked assertion by saying that after the resurrection human beings will be equal to angels and children of God.

Thus, contrary to your lie, human beings after the resurrection will by no means need to have sexual intercourse with women, since they will be equal to God’s angels and children of God. After our Lord Jesus Christ had answered the Sadducees’ proposed question concerning the state and condition of the true resurrection, he introduces the authority of the Old Testament against the unbelief of these Sadducees, who deny the resurrection [Col. 0530B]. For he says: “That the dead rise, even Moses showed at the bush, when he calls the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (ibid.).

It is as if he said more openly: Since you, O Sadducees, deny the future resurrection, reject the sayings of the prophets, and question me in order to test me concerning the state and condition of the resurrection, I urge you carefully to hear the testimony of Moses, whose books you accept. Moses said to the children of Israel: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob appeared to me” (Exod. 3). Thus, by the souls of these aforesaid righteous persons—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—he proves that the souls of all human beings do not utterly perish together with their bodies after bodily death [Col. 0530C], but on the last day rise with their bodies and thus live always to God.

“God,” he says, “is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” By the statement, “He is not the God of the dead but of the living,” the resurrection of bodies is also understood—bodies which acted well or ill together with souls. “All,” he says, “live to him.” It is as if he said: God is Lord of all, and he himself is the true life of all who live. Yet the good live to him by grace and by his good pleasure; the wicked only by essence. The good live to God because God prepares and approves their life; the wicked live to him because he does not fail to know their pride. Hence the Psalmist says: “For the Lord is exalted, and he regards the humble; and he knows the high”—that is, the pride of the wicked—“from afar” (Ps. [Col. 0530D] 137). For everyone who sins is proud; one who does forbidden things holds the divine commandments in contempt. If, therefore, the Lord utterly ignored the wicked, he would not judge or condemn them at all. So too Christ’s faithful urge one another in the Office of the Dead, saying: “Let us adore the King to whom all things live.”

What do you say to these things, O Coritian heretics, you who say that after the resurrection human beings will have intercourse with women? What do you answer? Beyond doubt, you have been defeated in your lying assertion. How can men after this life unite carnally with women when they will no longer have the power to sin? Their bodies will rise, as we believe, with their generative members, but not subject to any pleasure or [Col. 0531A] necessity of marriage. They will have sexual organs, but will entirely lack the pleasure and act of intercourse. Where there will be neither necessity of dying nor power of sinning, there will beyond doubt be no fleshly pleasure of intercourse [Note: [Col. 0531D] *Sentences*, distinction 49, “After the resurrection.”].

Neither the good will have a will, nor the wicked a power, to sin, nor will either have any condition of dying. The former will live happily in eternal life; the latter will endure unhappily in eternal death, without power to die. Both are without end; but the former will remain in blessedness, one more eminent than another, while the latter will remain in misery, one more tolerably than another. Just as the good will be glorified differently, some more and some less, so the wicked will be punished differently in hell.

Hence St John Chrysostom says: “Just as in my Father’s house—that is, in the kingdom of heaven—there are many dwelling places [Col. 0531B] and differences of rewards, so in Gehenna there are different dwelling places—that is, differences of punishments. Yet all will suffer eternal punishment, just as all the elect will receive the same denarius which the householder gave to all who worked in the vineyard” (Matt. 20).

It should be noted that by the name *denarius* something common to all the elect is understood: namely eternal life, that is, God himself, whom all will enjoy, though unequally—that is, differently. For just as the glorification of bodies will differ, so the glory of souls will differ. “Star differs from star” (1 Cor. 15): that is, one elect person differs from another in brightness of mind and body. Some will contemplate God’s form more vividly and clearly than others, and this difference in contemplation [Col. 0531C] is called a diversity of dwelling places. Thus the house is one, namely the denarius is one; but there is a diversity of dwelling places there, that is, a difference of brightness. This one and highest good, the blessedness and life of all, is God himself. All the elect will enjoy this good, but some will enjoy it more fully than others, seeing face to face, not “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13). To have life, therefore, is to see life: that is, to know God in direct vision. Hence Christ, speaking to God the Father in the Gospel, says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17).

Perhaps you ask, O Coritian heretics, whether after the resurrection the elect will be naked or clothed. Let us all hear together what Master Anselm [Col. 0531D] answers: “The elect,” he says [Note: [Col. 0531D] Book III of the *Elucidarium*, ch. 16], “will be naked after the resurrection, yet they will shine with every beauty, and they will be no more ashamed of those more private members than they are now of their lovely eyes. Yet salvation and joy will be their garments. For the Lord will clothe their bodies with a garment of salvation and their souls with a covering of joy. And just as here there are different kinds of flowers—for example, whiteness in lilies and redness in roses—so it is believed that there will be different kinds of colours in the bodies of the saints, so that martyrs will have one colour, confessors another, and [Col. 0532A] virgins another; and these will be reckoned as garments.”

Perhaps you ask, O Coritian heretics, whether after the resurrection the elect will do anything. But if you wish to know this, know that they will do nothing, but will rest and see God, and praise him for ages of ages. For the saints to praise God in the heavenly homeland is simply to rejoice in his vision. Hence the exultant Psalmist says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; they will praise you for ages of ages” (Ps. 83). The joys of the saints, then, will be those “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (Isa. 64).

“These joys,” says Master Anselm in the *Elucidarium* [Note: [Col. 0531D] As above, ch. 17], “are eternal life, everlasting blessedness [Col. 0532B], and sufficiency of all good things without any want. They will have,” he says, “seven spiritual gifts of the body and seven of the soul. In the body: beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, immortality, and power. In the soul: wisdom, friendship, harmony, will, honour, security, and joy” [Note: [Col. 0532D] Ch. 18.]. “Moreover, their beauty will be like the brightness of the sun. Hence it is said: ‘The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father’” (Matt. 13) [Note: [Col. 0532D] *Sentences*, distinction 48, “At the coming.”].

When heaven has been made new and earth new, then, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun sevenfold—that is, like the light of seven days (Isa. 30). For as much as the sun shone in the first [Col. 0532C] creation during the seven days before the first human being’s sin, so much will it shine after judgment. The light of the sun and moon, and of the other stars, was diminished through the first human being’s sin; but then it will receive the reward of its labour, because it will shine sevenfold. There will then be no alternation of day and night, but only continuous day.

Hence Zechariah the prophet, one of the twelve prophets, says: “There will be one day, known to the Lord, neither day nor night; and at evening time there will be light” (Zech. 14). That is, there will then be no variation of day and night, but continuous day and light. If, therefore—as is true—the righteous will shine after the resurrection like the sun, which will then shine seven times more brightly than now, there is no doubt that Christ’s body is brighter than the sun [Col. 0532D], being the body of the Creator rather than of a creature [Note: [Col. 0532D] Again from the *Elucidarium*, ch. 18.].

Let us also hear what the Apostle promises to holy people in this place: “Christ will transform our lowly body to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). Holy human beings are also temples of God. Therefore, if the bodies of the saints are to be conformed to Christ’s glorious body, which is more splendid than the sun, and God will dwell in them as in temples, then the temples of God must be more beautiful than the sun.

Know, then, O Coritian heretics, that you have lied in your assertion, you who say that holy people, after their resurrection and association with God’s angels, will again [Col. 0533A] serve the work of marriage. For they will by no means be able any longer to unite carnally with women, because all together will be the temple of God. They will utterly lack both the power of sinning and the pleasure of intercourse.

“If, as the Venerable Bede says in a certain homily, they cannot be raised to heaven on the day of resurrection unless they are chaste in body, nor after the resurrection be able to behold the essence of the divine majesty unless they are pure in heart,” then with what recklessness, O senseless Coritian heretics, do you say that those judged worthy of eternal blessedness can be defiled by the stains of fornication? For if, as St Paul says, “fornicators will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6), how will human beings after the resurrection devote themselves to fleshly pleasure—which it is indeed wicked to believe or say? And if, as is true, every fornicator has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God (Eph. 5), by what madness do you think, O foolish and malicious heretics, that the children of the resurrection can wish, or be able, to mingle carnally with women?

Thus clear reason, as you see, proclaims the condition of the true resurrection and most plainly demonstrates that men after the resurrection will no longer unite carnally with women. The authorities of the Old and New Testaments confirm beyond doubt that all human beings will rise with their bodies; but they utterly deny that these children of the resurrection will have any desire for marriage or fleshly intercourse. Know, therefore, that up to now [Col. 0533C] you have thought wrongly about the state and condition of those rising, uttered falsehoods against the faith of ecclesiastical religion, and plainly lied in your most lying assertion.

Make satisfaction to God and the priests of the Catholic Church by humbly repenting and producing fruits worthy of repentance for such sacrilegious and perverse blasphemies. Thus it may not happen that you perish through heresies and schisms by thinking perversely, but that, by believing rightly through the most true teaching of this holy Church, you may deserve to attain the happiness of the heavenly homeland. Show the varieties of leprosy—that is, the diverse blasphemies of heretical perversity—to the same priests of the Catholic Church in pure confession; and, by their judgment and approval, receive with a devout mind the colour of true salvation, namely the discipline of ecclesiastical religion [Col. 0533D], so that by believing rightly and doing good works you may be admitted with the children of that holy Church to the vision of supreme peace. Amen.

§ XXXVI.—

The testimony of the apostle James openly refutes the Aetians, who assert that no sin is imputed to those who have faith. Therefore, those who believe are called saved, provided that faith works through love.

For the Aetian heretics bear leprosy in flesh and skin, because they say that sins cannot be imputed to persons remaining in faith, however carnally they live. Let us hear, then, what St Isidore says about these aforesaid Aetian heretics. “The Aetians,” he says [Note: [Col. 0533D] Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 5], “are named after the heretic Aetius; likewise the Eunomians are named after a certain dialectician Eunomius, a disciple of that same Aetius, and by his name they became better known. These, as has been said, declare that no sin is imputed to those who remain in faith.”

Accordingly, these aforesaid Aetian heretics are rightly numbered among heretics, since they assert that human beings can be saved through faith alone. Yet they are no less greatly mistaken in their sect, believing that persons who live carnally may be saved by faith alone without amendment to a better life. Therefore, lest we be severely reproved at the strict Judge’s examination for our silence, we must oppose the truest testimonies of Holy Scripture to their false assertion and establish the religion of the Catholic Church. We exhort you, then, O Aetian [Col. 0534B] heretics, who say that human beings serving the pleasures of the flesh can be saved by faith alone without good works, diligently to hear what St Isidore says in the second book *On the Supreme Good*.

“Faith without works,” he says [Note: [Col. 0534D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 2], “is empty, and one who is not adorned with good works vainly flatters himself on the basis of faith alone. Those who have knowledge of God through faith, yet are darkened by wicked works, follow the example of Balaam, who, while falling through perverse action, had open eyes through the faith of contemplation” (Num. 22).

Thus, in saying that faith is empty without good works, blessed Isidore most plainly destroys your most lying sect, O Aetian heretics, who claim that persons living carnally can obtain pardon from almighty God through faith alone. By Balaam’s example, all who believe in God and live wickedly also have opened eyes through faith; but because they serve the pleasures of the flesh, they fall into the danger of their souls [Col. 0534C]. What is it to live carnally? To spend this mortal life in revelries, drunkenness, and fornications. And, as St Paul the Apostle testifies: “Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5). Therefore, contrary to your lie, O Aetian heretics, sins will not fail to be imputed to those who remain in faith if they live wickedly; unless they humbly repent and produce fruits worthy of repentance, they can by no means obtain pardon for sins.

To overcome your unbelief also and establish the truth of Catholic religion [Col. 0534D], let us bring forward blessed James and reverently hear his testimony, O Aetian heretics.

“What profit is it, my brothers,” he says, “if someone says that he has faith, but does not have works? Can faith save him?” (Jas. 2). It is as if he said more openly: You ought to persist in good works, because those who believe that faith alone is sufficient for salvation are deceived. Just as words of kindness alone do not refresh a naked or hungry person unless food and clothing are given, so faith preserved only in words does not save a human being.

“Can faith save him?” Faith without works is vain and therefore cannot save; but faith which works through love saves. For example: “If a brother or sister is naked and lacks daily food, and one of you says to them, ‘Go in peace, be warmed and filled,’ but you do not give them what is necessary, what profit is it?” It is as if he said: If you do not provide a needy brother with what is necessary for him, how does your love benefit him? “So faith also,” he says, “if it does not have works, is dead in itself.” It is as if he said: So faith, if it does not have works by which it may be made alive, is dead in itself—that is, against itself—because it has not fulfilled in works what it promised in words.

“But someone says”—that is, someone may say—“You have faith, and I have works.” It is as if he said more openly: You have faith without works, and I have works of faith. “Show me [Col. 0535B] your faith without works, and I will show you my faith from works.” It is as if he said: Since you have no works, show me, if you can, your faith without works by some certain signs, so that I may believe you faithful; and if, in the absence of works, you cannot, I will show you my faith from works—that is, by the works I have I can prove that I am faithful.

“You believe that God is one; you do well. The demons also believe—and tremble.” It is as if he said more openly: You believe that God is one; you do well, and I do not disapprove; but it is still not enough. And lest you think that you do anything great: the demons too believe that God is truly God; and what is more, they tremble. For it is written: “Demons came out from many people, crying out and saying, ‘You are Christ, the Son of God’” (Luke 4). Likewise the legion that beset the man cried out in fear: “What have I to do with you, Son of the Most High God? I adjure you by God, do not torment me” (Mark 5). Those, then, who do not believe that God exists, or do not fear him whom they believe, are slower and more insolent than demons.

“But do you wish to know, O empty man, that faith without works is idle?” (Jas. 2). It is as if he said: I will use not only arguments but also an example, to show that faith without works is idle. “Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac upon the altar?” Although Abraham was righteous through the faith he possessed, yet he was justified more fully through the works he added; if he had not done them, he would have lost the merit of his earlier faith. “He was justified by works.” By which works? Namely, by “offering his son Isaac upon the altar” (Heb. 11). For he judged that God was able to raise the dead.

With the truest arguments blessed James proves that faith without works is dead, so as more clearly to invite people to good action. He also proposes an elegant example of good action drawn from the patriarch Abraham to those who had believed because of circumcision, so that, as good children, they may imitate their good father in trial and action. Great indeed was the trial when he was commanded to kill his son; great was the faith when he believed that even from a dead son he could receive offspring; great was the work when he did not hesitate to offer his most beloved son [Col. 0536A].

You see, therefore, O Aetian heretics, that faith cooperated with Abraham’s works, that faith was brought to perfection by works, and that Scripture was fulfilled which says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God” (Jas. 2). Abraham’s faith led him to works; through works that faith itself was increased and proved; and thus, through the faith which led to works, the truth of Scripture is evident when it says: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” He believed the one who promised him a son and commanded him to sacrifice that same son. Since he offered the one in whom he had received the promise, the great power of faith is evident: if he offered him, he believed that the promise would be fulfilled, because he believed God powerful to raise the dead.

[Col. 0536B] By the aforesaid authorities, O Aetian heretics, you can plainly understand that faith alone, without good works, can by no means suffice to cleanse sins for those who live carnally. Sins are imputed to those who live carnally, although they remain in faith; and unless they join good works to faith, they are not cleansed from sins by faith alone. As St James testifies above, faith without good works is idle and cannot at all free persons who live wickedly from the filth of sins. Therefore, contrary to your lie, O Aetian heretics, sins will not fail to be imputed to those who live carnally even if they remain in faith; but, what is more serious, unless they add good works of faith and produce fruits worthy of repentance, they cannot be saved at all.

[Col. 0536C] Perhaps, O heretics, you object to us here what the Lord commanded his disciples when he was about to ascend into heaven, saying: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16). Perhaps, O heretics, not fully understanding the subtle meaning of Holy Scripture and still persevering in your unbelief, you seize upon the preceding verses as an occasion for your error, saying: When the Lord sent his disciples to preach the Gospel to every creature, he did not say, “Whoever reforms his carnal life or repents of his sins will be saved”; but only, “Whoever believes [Col. 0536D] and is baptized will be saved.” Since we know that Christ uttered this saying, we therefore believe that sins are not imputed to persons living carnally if they remain in faith, even by faith alone without good works.

In answer, we say to these things, O senseless heretics, that the Lord’s statement, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved,” must be understood of perfect faith, which works through love, not of idle faith which is dead in itself, as St James the Apostle testifies when he says: “As the body without spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2). Therefore, whoever firmly believes in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and joins good works to faith, will beyond doubt be saved. But whoever, by living carnally [Col. 0537A], neglects to add the right works of faith cannot be saved.

Hence John the Evangelist says: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and truth is not in him” (John 14). Likewise God-and-man Jesus Christ himself says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7). It is as if he plainly said: Not the one who holds faith merely in words, but the one who fulfils it by good works—namely vigils, prayers, alms, and other works of mercy—does the will of my Father who is in heaven; that person will enter the kingdom of heaven.

Hence Paul says of certain false believers: “They profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1). Both are necessary: the work must be proved by speech and speech by works. Hence St Paul also says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3), that is, in love, because the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and the Son. Truly to say, “Jesus is Lord,” is to believe in the heart, confess with the mouth, and bear witness in works. For one without the other is denial. Although those who live carnally remain in faith, nevertheless, unless they produce fruits worthy of repentance or join works worthy of faith to it, sins will be imputed to them, and they certainly cannot be cleansed from them by faith alone.

[Col. 0537C] Know, therefore, O Aetian heretics, that you have lied in your lying assertion; and no longer disparage the religion of the Catholic Church. Reveal to the priests of that same holy Church the stains of foul leprosy—that is, the blasphemies of heretical perversity—in true confession; and, with their approval, receive with devout mind the colour of health, namely the rule of right living, so that by right belief and good works you may attain the fellowship of God’s elect. Amen.

§ XXXVII.

The Luciferians and Arabians say that the human soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh and is mortal. The most lucid testimonies of Augustine and others refute them. Solomon’s meaning in Ecclesiastes is explained.

[Col. 0537D] It must further be known that those heretics bear leprosy, as it were, in the scar of a healed wound, in whom, after the knowledge of medicinal grace—by which the Son of God and of the Virgin mercifully healed the most grievous wound of the human race—and after the manifestation of the true faith which they received from God and man, Jesus Christ himself, some sign of their former error or of their old dogma of faithlessness again arises in that very scar. Indeed, whoever, after coming to know the Catholic faith, teaches something else or takes up something else contrary to the rule of evangelical instruction contracts the stain of heretical perversity. Whoever refuses to receive the sacraments of the Church’s religion, or defiles those already received by disparagement and evil living, departs far from the path of truth.

[Col. 0538A] They also bear living leprosy in the flesh who hold some false belief concerning the soul, which is the life of the body: as do the Luciferian heretics, who say that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh; or the Arabians, who think that the soul dies together with the body. But let us hear what St Isidore says of the aforesaid Luciferian heretics in Book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Etymologies*:

“The Luciferians,” he says, “take their origin from Lucifer, bishop of Sirmium [Note: [Col. 0537D] Sardinia.], who condemned those Catholic bishops who, during the persecution of Constantius, had consented to the faithlessness of the Arians and later, having been corrected, chose to return to the Catholic Church, repudiating both what they had believed and what [Col. 0538B] they had pretended to believe. The Catholic Church, their mother, received those aforesaid Catholic bishops—already cleansed by repentance—into her maternal bosom, as she received Peter after his weeping for his denial (Matt. XXVI). These aforesaid Luciferians, therefore, proudly taking exception to this charity of holy mother Church and refusing to receive them, withdrew from the communion of the Church; and with Lucifer himself, their author, ‘who rose in the morning’ (Isa. XIV), deserved to fall from the state of uprightness. They are called Arabians because they arose in Arabia, maintaining that the soul dies together with the body and that both rise again on the last day.”

Therefore the Luciferian heretics, who said that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh, and the Arabians, who thought that it dies together with the body, have strayed exceedingly from the rule of ecclesiastical teaching. They were rightly numbered among heretics, since they said that the soul, made in the image of God (Gen. I), is mortal and propagated from the nature of the flesh.

“For the human soul,” as St Isidore says in the book *On the Supreme Good* [Note: [Col. 0538D] Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 12.], “is not the human being; rather, only the body made from the earth is the human being. Yet by dwelling in the body, the soul takes the name ‘human being’ from its participation in the body; thus the Apostle calls the soul, not the flesh, ‘the inner human being,’ created in the image of God.”

If, then, the soul is not by itself a human being but, dwelling in the body, receives the name of human being from its participation in the body, it is clear that it is not corporeal: that is, it is not propagated from the substance of flesh, but, after the body’s formation, is created by God and joined to the body. [Col. 0538D] Know, therefore, O Luciferian heretics, that you have lied in your argument, and presume no longer to maintain that souls are propagated from carnal substance.

“As angels are,” says St Isidore, “so also are souls. For they have a beginning, but no end.” Thus, in saying that souls have no end, he most plainly refutes you also, O Arabian heretics, who assert that they die together with their bodies, in your utterly false assertion. We believe rational natures to be immortal, because they lack flesh and have nothing through which they may fall, so as to need resurrection after ruin.

[Col. 0539A] Still more clearly than light, St Augustine, the most faithful defender of the Catholic faith, demonstrates that you, O Luciferian and Arabian heretics, have lied in your assertions, saying [Note: [Col. 0539D] *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 4.]:

“We do not hold that human souls existed from the beginning among the other rational natures, nor that they were created together, as Origen said; nor are they sown together with bodies after intercourse, as the Luciferian and Cyril maintain. Rather, we say that the body alone is sown through the union of marriage, is congealed in the womb by God’s direction, and, once it has been joined together and formed, the soul is created and infused into the now-formed body, so that in the womb a human being, consisting of soul and body, may live and emerge from the womb alive and filled with human substance. As St Augustine says, [Col. 0539B] God alone, the Creator of all things, knows the creation of the soul.”

St Isidore also testifies in Book I of *On the Supreme Good* that the soul was not created together with the other rational natures from the beginning, saying [Note: [Col. 0539D] As above.]:

“The soul is neither a part of the divine substance or nature, nor does it exist before it is joined to the body; rather, it is created when the body is created, with which it seems to be joined.”

By these authorities, O heretics, your lying and stubborn assertion—that souls are propagated from the substance of flesh and die together with their bodies—is wholly overthrown, and the teaching of the Catholic faith is strengthened in every way.

I also urge you, O Arabian heretics, carefully to hear how openly St Augustine, in the book [Col. 0539C] *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, destroys the perverse assertion of your teacher, the Arabian, who said that the soul dies together with the body. For he says [Note: [Col. 0539D] Chapter 15.]:

“We believe that humanity alone has a substantial soul, which, even when stripped of the body, lives and retains its senses and faculties in full vigour. Nor does it die with the body, as the Arabian asserted; nor after a short interval, as Zeno said; for it lives substantially.”

He continues [Note: [Col. 0539D] Chapter 16.]:

“Nor do we believe that there are two souls in one person, as the heretic Jacob and others among the Syrians wrote: one animal soul, by which the body is animated and which is mingled with the blood; and another spiritual soul, which supplies reason. Rather, we say that [Col. 0539D] there is one and the same soul in a human being, which both gives life to the body by its fellowship and governs itself by its reason, possessing within itself freedom of choice, so that in its own substance it may knowingly choose what it wills.”

[Note: [Col. 0539D] Chapter 17.] “But the souls of animals are not substantial; rather, they are born with the flesh itself, through the flesh’s vitality, and end with the death of the flesh. Therefore they are not governed by reason, as Plato and Alexander thought, but are led by every impulse of nature. The human soul, however, does not die with the flesh, because [Col. 0540A] neither is it sown with the flesh, as St Augustine said above [Note: [Col. 0540D] Chapter 18.]; rather, when the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, it is created and infused by God’s judgment, so that the human being may live within the womb and thus come forth into the world by birth.

“A human being consists of two substances,” as St Augustine says in *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas* [Note: [Col. 0540D] Chapter 19.], “namely, soul alone and flesh: the soul with its reason, and the flesh with its senses. Yet flesh does not move those senses apart from fellowship with the soul, while the soul retains its rational faculty without flesh.”

Augustine, in *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “There is not,” he says [Note: [Col. 0540D] Chapter 20.], “a third element in the substance of a human being, namely spirit, as Didymus contends; rather, spirit is the soul itself. It is called spirit either because of its spiritual nature or because [Col. 0540B] it breathes in the body. It is called soul because it animates the body, either for living or for giving life. But the third ‘spirit’ introduced by the Apostle together with soul and body, we understand to be the grace of the Holy Spirit, which the same Apostle prays may remain whole within us (I Thess. V), lest through our fault it be diminished or driven from us; for ‘the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit’ (Wis. I).”

The doctors of the Catholic Church, O heretics, sufficiently instruct us concerning the creation and immortality of the soul, and most openly refute you who assert that it is generated through intercourse and dies with the body. Taught inwardly by the Holy Spirit, they strengthen the condition of the holy Church with most true arguments and mightily overcome its adversaries—heretics, pagans, and Jews—with spiritual weapons.

[Col. 0540C] So that your lying assertion may be more evidently overcome and the teaching of mother Catholic Church be strengthened more and more on every side, let us bring St Gregory forward and hear together, O heretics, whatever he tells us. Speak, holy Gregory; speak concerning the state of the soul, as you know it: whether it wholly fails together with the body on the day of death, or lives forever after the death of the flesh, so that the Arabian and Luciferian heretics, convicted by your testimony, may recoil from the falsehood of their perversity and believe with us in harmonious accord the truth of ecclesiastical teaching.

“Almighty God,” he says [Note: [Col. 0540D] Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 3.], “created three living spirits: one not clothed in flesh; another clothed in flesh but not dying with the flesh; and a third clothed in flesh and dying with the flesh. The spirit not clothed in flesh belongs to angels; the spirit clothed in flesh but not dying with flesh belongs to human beings; the spirit clothed in flesh and dying with flesh belongs to beasts of burden and all irrational animals. Therefore, as the human being is created in the middle, inferior to an angel and superior to a beast, so the human being has something in common [Col. 0541A] with what is highest and something in common with what is lowest. For the human being shares the immortality of spirit with the angel and the mortality of flesh with the beast, until even this mortality of flesh is swallowed up by the glory of the resurrection and, cleaving to the spirit, the flesh is preserved forever, because the spirit itself, cleaving to God, is preserved in God. Yet even in the reprobate that flesh does not wholly perish amid punishments, because it continues by perpetually perishing, so that those who sinned in spirit and flesh, while always living essentially, may be punished without end in flesh and spirit.”

When St Gregory, O heretics, distinguishes with such subtlety between the spirits of angels, human beings, and beasts, what else does he do but utterly destroy your most lying sect? For when he asserts that the human spirit is clothed in flesh but does not die with it, he openly shows that you who call it mortal have lied in your argument.

[Col. 0541B] Perhaps at this point, O heretics, you ask us: If the human spirit is immortal and unlike the spirits of beasts, what is the meaning of Solomon’s saying: “I said in my heart concerning the children of men, that God might test them and show them to be like beasts. Therefore,” he says, “one destruction belongs to humans and beasts, and the condition of both is equal” (Eccles. III)? Still pursuing the same thought subtly, he adds: “As a human dies, so they also die; all breathe alike, and a human has nothing more than a beast” (ibid.). And he further gives this general statement: “All are subject to vanity, [Col. 0541C] and all go to one place. They were made from earth and together return to earth” (ibid.).

Let St Gregory come forward again and answer your question, O heretics. Let us all hear what he says:

“The book of Solomon,” he says [Note: [Col. 0541D] Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4.], “in which these things are written, is called *Ecclesiastes*. Now *Ecclesiastes* properly means ‘preacher.’ In a public assembly a judgment is pronounced through which the sedition of a tumultuous crowd is restrained. And when many hold differing views, they are brought to one judgment through the preacher’s reasoning. This book is therefore called *Ecclesiastes* because Solomon in it, as though taking upon himself the mind of a turbulent crowd, says by way of inquiry things which an inexperienced mind may perhaps think under temptation. For as many judgments as he raises, as if by inquiry, so many persons with differing views does he assume within himself. But the true preacher, as though with outstretched hand, quiets the tumult of them all and recalls them to one judgment when, at the end of the same book, he says: ‘Let us all together hear the conclusion of the discourse: Fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole human being’ (Eccles. XII). If he had not assumed the persons of many in that book through his manner of speaking, why did he urge all together with himself to hear the conclusion of the discourse? Therefore, he who says at the end of the book, ‘Let us all together hear,’ himself testifies that, assuming within himself [Col. 0542A] the persons of many, he did not speak as though alone.

“Hence, in the same book some things are raised by inquiry, while other things are answered by reason [Note: [Col. 0541D] Supplement from the edition: other things he brings forth from the mind of one tempted and still devoted to the pleasures of this world [Col. 0542D]—other things, etc.]; other things are those in which he discusses what belongs to reason and restrains the soul from pleasure. Thus he says there: ‘Therefore this seemed good to me: that one should eat and drink and enjoy gladness from one’s labour’ (Eccles. V). And much farther below he adds: ‘It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting’ (Eccles. VII). For if it is good to eat and drink, it would seem better to go to a house of feasting than to a house of mourning. From this it is shown that he introduced the former statement in the person of the weak and inexperienced, but added the latter as a judgment of reason. For he at once explains the reasons [Note: [Col. 0542D] Supplement: causes.] of reason itself and shows the usefulness of the house of mourning, saying: ‘For in it the end of all human beings is remembered, and the living person considers what is to come’ (ibid.).

[Col. 0542B] “So too our preacher, as though speaking from the mind of the weak—that is, of those with less understanding—sets forth the judgment of human conjecture when he says: ‘One destruction belongs to human beings and beasts, and the condition of both is equal. As a human dies, so they die; all breathe alike, and a human has nothing more than beasts’ (Eccles. III). Yet afterward he gives his own judgment as a definition of reason, saying: ‘What advantage has the wise person over the fool, and what advantage has the poor person, except that he goes there where life is?’ (Eccles. VI). Therefore he who said that a human has nothing more than beasts, himself again determined that the wise person has something more—not only [Col. 0542C] than beasts, but even than a foolish human being—namely, that he goes there where life is. By these words he first indicates that this is not the life of human beings here, which he testifies exists elsewhere. Therefore, O heretics, this is what human beings have more than beasts: beasts do not live after death, but a human being then begins to live when, through the death of the flesh, that person finishes this miserable life.

“The true preacher himself says much farther below: ‘Whatever your hand is able to do, do earnestly; for there will be neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in hell, whither you hasten’ (Eccles. I). How, then, is one destruction shared by humans and beasts and their condition equal? Or how has a human being nothing more than beasts, when beasts do not live after the death of the flesh, whereas the spirits of human beings, led to hell after the death of the flesh for their evil deeds, do not die even by that death?”

It is therefore clear that human souls do not wholly perish with their bodies through the death of the flesh, but live immortally and, after death, receive from God, the most just Judge, either reward or punishment according to their works. You must therefore confess, O Luciferian and Arabian heretics, that you have lied in your assertion, since you say that human souls are propagated from the substance of flesh and [Col. 0543A] end together with flesh through death. The holy fathers of the Old and New Testaments agree truthfully with one another concerning the creation and immortality of the soul, and reasonably defeat you in your most lying sect, who deny these things. Therefore humbly reveal before the priests of the Catholic Church the leprosy of your long-standing foulness—that is, the stains of heretical perversity—in repentance; and, by their judgment, make satisfaction to God with all devotion for the blasphemies by which you have hitherto blasphemed the religion of that same holy Church. With their approval, reverently receive the colour of true health, namely the saving teaching of evangelical instruction, so that you may not perish with your teachers Lucifer and the Arabian, but through right belief [Col. 0543B] and good works may attain with the children of that same holy Church the blessedness of the heavenly homeland. Amen.

§ XXXVIII.—

The various sects of heresies are denoted by the different colours of leprosy. The Church repels them all from herself, until she reconciles them through the priests when they renounce their errors. Let the Jews, therefore, cease their slanders; indeed, let them acknowledge the Church alone as the virgin and bride whom Christ the Bridegroom has called to eternal life, rejecting the adulterous Synagogue—as Ezekiel foretold.

[Note: [Col. 0543D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, chapter 11.] The Manichaean heretics also have leprosy in the scar of a burn: they burn their bodies with the empty torment of abstinence and, through unbelief, produce in themselves not purity but leprosy. Of such persons the Apostle preached thus: “They depart,” he says, “from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, and having their conscience seared” [Col. 0543C]—“forbidding marriage and abstaining from foods which God created to be received” (I Tim. IV).

But the Law further sets forth the colours of leprosies: pale, reddish, white, livid, and black when flowering. Thus, when it speaks of pale leprosy, it denotes a weak and fragile faith of the soul, which, having lost the colour of sound health, languishes in infirmity. When it shows reddish leprosy, it displays one infected with the blood of murder. When it speaks of white leprosy, it indicates those heretics who call themselves pure, or others who boast in a false name, such as Pelagius and Novatus. When it mentions black or livid leprosy, it execrates envy and spite. [Col. 0543D] When it indicates black leprosy, it abominates a conscience blackened by the performance of sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0543D] Edition: smoke.] and by the pyre of idolatry. But when it says that the leprosy is flowering [Note: [Col. 0543D] “Flowering.”] over the whole skin and covering [Note: [Col. 0544D] “Covering.”] the entire surface of the body from head to foot, it indicates the crime of avarice; for it permits a person to be flourishing and joyful, fortunate in this world, and to appear rich in this age. For this plague of avarice frequently stains the whole human race, as though an entire body, with the contagion of this error.

In the leprosy that has a mixture of redness or pallor, it marks the person who, being weak-minded and deceitful, readily bursts into rage and quickly commits perjury through instability of character. Pallor denotes the liar; redness reveals anger. There is also a leprosy of sin, cleansed by the offering of sacrifices—that is, by a contrite and humbled heart: “For a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. L). There is also that of idolatry, washed away by the water of baptism. There is also that of heretics, which remains outside the camp for seven days’ purification—that is, it is purified through knowledge of the sevenfold Spirit. There is one removed by the priest’s inspection, that is, through teaching. But the kind of leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all belongs to those who sin against the Holy Spirit and say that one who repents cannot obtain forgiveness. Of these Truth says: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither [Col. 0544B] in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. XII).

The command that lepers leave the camp and remain outside until their leprosy is cleansed (Lev. XIII) means that heretics ought to withdraw from the Church until they are cleansed of their own error and thus return to the Lord. Such persons are commanded to sit, awaiting the cleansing of their leprosy, with torn garments, uncovered heads, and covered [Note: [Col. 0544D] Correctly in the edition: “with the mouth covered,” or shut, as below.] mouths. Their garments are torn, that is, all secrets are made manifest; their heads uncovered, so that their nakedness may be seen by all; their mouths shut, lest they further teach or speak impiously.

But Scripture further adds that leprosy may be in the walls of a house (Lev. XIV), by which the heresy of heretics is signified and which ought to be cleansed by a priest. [Col. 0544C] Leprosy in warp or garment (Lev. XIII) signifies sins committed outside the body, or sins perpetrated in the body itself. For the warp is understood as the human soul, and the weft as the sensations of the most delicate body.

All the aforementioned heretics, O Jews, mother Catholic Church repels far from herself as though they were lepers. She in no way permits them to approach her unless they have first cast off the error of heretical perversity. Such persons must be avoided by churchmen to such a degree that, if it may be done, having withdrawn far away, they should cry out to Christ with great cries of compunction, believing rightly and humbly confessing their sins, and should ardently desire to be joined to the faithful people. First, then, they must recognize their error; next, with tears, invoke the supreme priest, who has passed through the heavens (Heb. IV), Jesus Christ, so that, visiting them inwardly by his grace and cleansing them from the leprosy of unbelief, he may deign to send them to the priests of the holy Church. Thus, with those Church priests approving, they may receive the colour of true health—that is, the true teaching of ecclesiastical religion. Christ did not send lepers to the priests (Matt. VIII) so that the priests might give them health, since they had already been made whole before reaching them (Luke XVII), but so that the priests themselves might judge them clean. [Col. 0545A] For Jesus Christ, the true priest, had already in his free goodness bestowed on them the grace of health, so that they were cleansed on the way, when he sent them to the priests.

It should be noted that the Jewish priesthood was a figure of the future lawful priesthood which now exists in the Church, by which all who belong to the body of Christ, the supreme and true Prince of priests, are consecrated. “For all things happened to them in figure,” as the Apostle says (I Cor. X). Therefore whoever has been defiled by heretical perversity, pagan superstition, Jewish faithlessness, or even fraternal schism—as though by the various colours of leprosy—that is, whoever lacks Christ’s grace, must come to the Church and show the priests the true colour of faith which that person has received. The Lord himself heals and corrects the remaining vices, as maladies of the soul and, as it were, of its limbs and senses, inwardly in the conscience and understanding. Finally, even Paul, though he heard the Lord’s voice saying, “Why do you persecute me? I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you persecute” (Acts IX), was nevertheless sent to Ananias [Note: [Col. 0545D] Perhaps “to Ananias”; but it will be better to say that Ananias was sent to him, for this is what the sacred text establishes—not that Saul was sent [Col. 0546D] to Ananias.] in order to receive the sacrament of the true priesthood now established in the holy Church and the teaching of the Catholic faith, and in order that his true colour might be approved by that same Ananias. Likewise Cornelius the centurion was expressly instructed by an angel to send for the blessed apostle Peter and receive from him the teaching of the Christian religion (Acts X).

[Col. 0545C] Therefore whoever, as said above, has been defiled by heretical perversity, pagan superstition, or Jewish faithlessness, should humbly come to the priests of the Catholic Church, cast from the mind the stains of leprosy—that is, the blasphemies of heretical perversity—and, with the approval of those same priests, receive with devout mind the colour of sound health, namely the true rule of ecclesiastical religion. Unless one enters through the gate of holy mother Church, one can by no means belong to the body of Jesus Christ, the supreme priest.

Therefore, O Jews, holy Church does not, as you falsely say, receive lepers—that is, persons covered with stains of heretical perversity—but drives them far from herself with all earnestness. She has no communion with them, but carefully abominates and publicly anathematizes them. Nor without reason does mother Catholic Church shudder at them and separate them from the communion of the faithful, since the Lord says of them in an open utterance through the prophet: “Though Moses and Samuel should stand before me, my soul is not toward this people. Cast them out from before my face, and let them depart” (Jer. XV). By Moses and Samuel we also understand the Law and the Prophets. Although heretics may strive to fulfil these in deed, nevertheless because of the impiety of their error they are cast from the face of God and separated from the assemblies of the righteous.

Know, therefore, O Jews, that you have lied in your assertion, [Col. 0546A] and cease henceforth to assail holy Church, which is truly the bride of Christ, with blasphemies and false objections. For the Church herself, virgin and mother, loving her bridegroom Jesus Christ above all things, believing without doubt that he is one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and following his footsteps with all her heart’s desire, willingly suffers adversities for his love: she is blasphemed by heretics, mocked by Jews, dishonoured by pagan tongues, and attacked by swords. But, solicitous for the love of the same Jesus Christ, her beloved bridegroom—strengthened by his aid, rejoicing in his promise, taught by his example—she patiently suffers adversities; freely performs good works; despises earthly things; desires heavenly things; and continually raises herself by hope and desire [Col. 0546B] to joys above.

And so that you, O wretched and pitiable Jews, may not doubt that what we say is true, I urge you to hear carefully what the daughters of Jerusalem say in wonder concerning her in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” [Note: [Col. 0546D] Gregory, on this passage.] (Cant. VII). For the Church herself, virgin and mother, the bride of Christ, comes up from the wilderness because, placed in the exile of this pilgrimage, she tends in mind and thought toward heavenly joys. Thus the blessed apostle Paul, sprung from the tribe of Benjamin, educated at the feet of your teacher Gamaliel, and called by Christ from heaven—whom you neither ought nor can resist—said in the person of the faithful: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Therefore the holy Church, redeemed by Christ’s blood, abounds in delights because, intent upon meditations on the holy Scriptures, she continually nourishes her mind with heavenly food. She leans upon her beloved because, trusting in the aid of Christ alone, she is brought by his gift from exile to her homeland and from prison to the palace. For the Son of God and of the Virgin himself says to all the faithful: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

But from where, O unhappy Jews, did this bride of Christ herself receive the ability to ascend from lower things to higher, from wilderness to kingdom, from earth to heaven? The beloved himself, namely the Son of God and of the Virgin, makes this plain when he speaks to the same holy Church, his bride, saying: “Under the apple tree [Col. 0546D] I raised you up” (Cant. VIII). What is signified by the apple tree except the holy cross, which bore that apple—that is, Christ—of whom the bride herself, namely holy Church, says above: “As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons” (Cant. II)? Therefore Christ raised up his bride under the apple tree because, set upon the cross, he called to eternal life the Church subject to him: namely, that she might rise from the sleep of death and, crucifying herself with him, hasten to a new resurrection. Hence he says to every soul that is dead [Note: [Col. 0546D] Correct from the edition: “to every soul that is dead.”]: “Awake, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. V). To some [Col. 0547A] also [Note: [Col. 0547D] Supplement: “who.”] who had already risen, he says elsewhere: “If you have risen together with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Col. III).

Under the tree of the cross—that is, through Christ’s passion and resurrection—holy Church received, as has been said, the means by which she might ascend to higher things; and under the same cross—that is, in Christ’s passion—the faithless Synagogue committed a most grievous sin, through which she descended to lower things. Holy Church willingly heard Christ’s preaching and believed him to be true God and true human being; therefore through the same bridegroom she deserved to ascend to heaven. But because the Synagogue knew beforehand from the Law and Prophets that he would come, saw him working miracles, heard him preaching, and not only refused to receive him reverently but even fastened him to the cross without cause, she therefore incurred the darkness of ignorance and fell from the state of uprightness into the abyss of evils.

That the unbelief of the Synagogue, O Jews, crucified Christ and thereby contracted for itself and its posterity the stain of condemnation, the beloved himself—namely the Son of God and of the Virgin—plainly testifies, speaking to the same holy Church, his bride: “There your mother was corrupted; there your mother who bore you was violated” (Cant. VIII). The Synagogue, the mother of the Church, is said to have been corrupted under the apple tree because, when she fastened Jesus Christ, the Saviour of humankind, specially sent to her by God the Father, to the wood of the cross, she corrupted herself by an unspeakable crime. He emphasizes the greatness of this crime when he repeats: “There your mother who bore you was violated.”

You must therefore believe without doubt, O Jews, that Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, promised in the Law and the Prophets, has long since come; that he was born of the Virgin, suffered the Passion for the redemption of the world, tasted death upon the cross, rose from the dead on the third day, ascended to heaven while his disciples watched, and now sits reigning at the right hand of God the Father; that he changed the condition of your mother, the adulterous [Note: [Col. 0548D] “Of the adulteress.”] Synagogue, set an end to the carnal commandments of the Law, chose holy Church as his bride, richly endowed her with special gifts, and summoned her to the blessedness of the heavenly homeland—indeed, what is far more glorious and happy, [Col. 0547D] raised her up to behold the face of his Father. In the womb of the Virgin he mercifully and wondrously betrothed her to himself, and seated her with himself at the right hand of God the Father. He himself, who is the true refreshment and the true sun of angels, became the head of the whole Church in the end of the ages.

In response to these things, O Jews, you object to us that it seems incredible to you that through Christ, whom your fathers crucified, the condition of the Synagogue could be changed, or that the Church could be chosen from uncircumcised nations. You also say that the same Synagogue was anciently established by the Lord through the legal commandments given by Moses [Col. 0548A], and therefore cannot in any way be changed from its condition until the end of the world.

To what you object, O Jews, we make this reply: that truly God almighty, who gave the Law through Moses, himself through his most beloved Son changed the ceremonies and precepts of the carnal Law, and commanded that they be fulfilled more perfectly in a spiritual sense. For he did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it more perfectly (Matt. 5). Therefore, in order wholly to overcome your most mendacious unbelief and to establish the truth of the Church’s religion, it is necessary for us to introduce the testimonies of the Law and the prophets. First, then, we wish to prove that your mother, the Synagogue, was corrupted for two reasons: namely, by sacrificing to idols and beneath the tree of the cross. [Col. 0548B] Truly she shamefully corrupted herself when she rendered to idols the worship owed to almighty God; and she damnably violated her faith when, in Jesus Christ—God and man, prefigured in the Law, foretold by the prophets, and sent from heaven by God the Father—she not only refused to believe, but also, to increase her own condemnation, fastened to the cross him who committed no sin and in whose mouth no falsehood was found (Isa. 53).

And so that you, O Jews, may not doubt that what we say is true, I urge you to listen attentively to what the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel to that same Synagogue, your mother, as though in complaint and while recounting the benefits he bestowed upon her from the beginning:

“Your root and your stock [Col. 0548C] are from the land of Canaan. Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite. And when you were born, on the day of your birth, your navel-string was not cut; you were not washed with water for cleansing, nor salted with salt, nor wrapped in swaddling-clothes. Rather, you were cast out upon the face of the earth, in contempt for your life, on the day you were born. But passing by you, I saw you trampled in your blood; and I said to you, when you were in your blood: ‘Live!’ I said, I say, to you: ‘Live in your blood!’ I made you numerous as the growth of the field; and you multiplied and became great. You entered and came to womanly maturity; your breasts swelled and your hair grew; and you were naked and full of shame. Then I passed by you and saw you; and behold, your time was the time of lovers. I spread my garment over you; I covered your shame [Col. 0548D] and swore an oath to you, and entered into covenant with you, says the Lord God. And you became mine. I washed you with water and cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil. I clothed you with embroidered garments, shod you with violet-blue leather, girded you with fine linen, and arrayed you in delicate fabrics. I adorned you with ornaments: I put bracelets on your hands, a necklace around your neck, an ornament above your mouth, rings in your ears, and a crown of beauty upon your head. You were adorned with gold and silver, and clothed in fine linen, embroidered fabric, and many colours; you ate fine flour, honey, and oil, and became exceedingly beautiful. You advanced to royal dignity, and your fame went out among the nations because of your beauty, [Col. 0549A] for you were perfect in my splendour, which I had bestowed upon you, says the Lord God. But trusting in your beauty, you prostituted yourself in your renown; you offered your fornication to every passer-by, so as to become his. Taking some of my garments, you made for yourself high places sewn together here and there; and you prostituted yourself upon [Col. 0550A] them—such a thing has not happened and shall not happen. You took the vessels of your adornment from my gold and my silver, which I had given you, and made for yourself male images and prostituted yourself with them. And you took your many-coloured garments” (Ezek. 16).

## SERMON FIVE. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD.

[Col. 0549]

[Col. 0549B] “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod, behold, Magi came from the east to Jerusalem, saying: ‘Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the east and have come with gifts to worship him’” (Matt. 2).

[Note: [Col. 0549D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 7, ch. 2.]

Jesus in Hebrew, Σωτήρ (*Sōtēr*, “Saviour”) in Greek, is interpreted in Latin as *salutaris*, “saving,” or *Salvator*, “Saviour,” because he appeared as salvation to all nations. The Evangelist also indicates the etymology and interpretation of this name, saying: “You shall call his name Jesus, that is, Saviour, because he himself will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1). For just as Christ signifies king and priest, so Jesus signifies Saviour. Thus it is not any king whatever who saves us, but the Saviour. This word did not formerly exist in the Latin language [Col. 0549C] [Note: [Col. 0549D] See the annotation of Grialius at this passage of Isidore, and Baronius in the *Martyrology* for 9 November.]; yet it could have existed, just as it could when it pleased.

Thus let it be said: “When Jesus, that is, the Saviour, had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of King Herod.” This Herod was not of David’s line, as the other kings who ruled among the Jewish people had been; rather, he was the son of Antipater, of Idumaean descent. For the time had already arrived of which the patriarch Jacob, blessing his son Judah long before, had said: “A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49).

[Note: [Col. 0550D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.]

This passage refers most plainly to Judah. For an unbroken succession of royal rule from his seed remained among the Jews until Christ was born of the Virgin for the redemption [Col. 0549D] of the world. Jewish histories prove this, showing that Herod was the first foreign-born king among the Jewish people, at the time when Christ appeared in the flesh. But if the Jews say that Christ has not yet come, let them show their king from the tribe of Judah. Yet because it is true that Christ has already come, the king from Judah’s tribe has failed, and Herod, a foreigner, obtained the Jewish kingdom. Beyond doubt, if Christ had not come, the Jewish kingdom, as had been promised, would have endured to the present day; a leader would not have failed from Judah’s thigh, nor would Herod [Col. 0550B] the Idumaean have ruled the Jews. Therefore a king did not fail from Judah’s tribe until Christ came, who was to be sent by God the Father for human salvation. But because Christ’s coming benefited not only the Jews but also the nations, the prophecy adds: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the nations.”

It follows: “Behold, Magi came from the east.”

[Note: [Col. 0550D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 8, ch. 9.]

Magi are those who, because of the enormity of their deeds, are commonly called sorcerers. So great is their malice that they shake the elements, disturb minds, and transform human beings into the forms of beasts. From them, indeed, arose divination from entrails, augury, necromancy, and astrology. Necromancers are those through whose incantations the dead seem to be raised and, when questioned, to utter prophecies and answers. For νεκρός [Col. 0550C] (*nekros*) in Greek is translated “dead” in Latin; *mantia* is called divination. *Arioli* are called those who utter wicked prayers around the altars of idols and offer abominable sacrifices, and thus receive the responses of demons. *Haruspices* are so called, as it were, “inspectors of hours,” for they observe days, hours, and years in conducting business and works. *Haruspicia* are, as it were, the observation of birds. *Auguria* are so called as though from the chatter of birds—that is, their cries and language. Again, *augurium* is as though *avigarium*, “the birds’ chatter.” Astronomy is the law of the stars, which by investigating reason traces the courses and figures of the heavenly bodies and the configurations of the stars in relation to themselves and to the earth.

Sortilegists are those who, under the name of a false religion, promise the future through certain divinations which they call “lots of the saints,” or by the inspection of whatever writings. *Salisatores* are so called because, whenever parts of their bodies have twitched, they predict from this some favourable or adverse event. To all these belong magical characters, *scantationes* [perhaps “incantations”], bindings, and *imprecantationes* [perhaps “imprecations”], remedies of an accursed kind, and whatever objects are hung and tied around the neck. In all these things sacrilege is committed and God [Col. 0551A] is provoked to anger. Therefore all such things must be avoided by Christians, rejected with every execration, and condemned altogether.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] Isidore, book 6, ch. 18.]

Magi, then, so full of perversity, would never have come from regions so distant or sought the King of the Jews unless they had been enlightened by the Holy Spirit. Thus this King of the Jews, who was born, inwardly enlightened them with the Holy Spirit and drew them, under the guidance of a star, to worship himself; in them he dedicated to his worship the firstfruits of the nations. The same patriarch Jacob also signified this when, speaking figuratively of Christ in the same prophecy, he said: “Binding his colt to the vine” (ibid.), namely, the Gentile people. The colt, therefore, was the people of the nations, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed. [Col. 0551B] Christ bound this colt—that is, the Gentile people—to the vine when he first led the Magi, who are the firstfruits of the nations, to himself at the star’s disclosure, and joined them by the bond of faith to his Church, which took its origin from Judaea. Nor was this alone enough for him; rather, what is a still greater indication of mercy and grace, he bound them by the bond of charity to the vine of his body and subjected them to the yoke of Gospel discipline.

Ἐπιφανία (*Epiphaneia*) is translated from Greek into Latin as “appearance” or “manifestation.” There are two Epiphanies, that is, appearances: the first, in which Christ at his birth appeared to the Hebrew shepherds, with an angel announcing him; the second, in which he displayed the manger-cradle to Magi from the peoples of the nations, who were to worship him, with the star as their guide. These [Col. 0551C] two walls—Jews and Gentiles, that is—came from opposite directions and made one faith in the stone “which became the head of the corner” (Acts 4), that is, in Christ.

The Magi say: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews?” Just as Christians are named after Christ, so Jews are named after Judah, the son of the patriarch Jacob. Jews are also interpreted as “confessors,” because when Leah bore Judah, she gave praise to the Lord, saying: “Now also for this I will give thanks to the Lord” (Gen. 29). Therefore his name was given from confession, which signifies thanksgiving.

[Note: [Col. 0551D] These are the words of Isidore in book 8, ch. 4 of the *Etymologies*. The following words occur in book 7, ch. 7. Thus what the blessed bishop said concerning the patriarch Judah, Martin applied to the Jews [Col. 0552D]. The holy doctor explains whence the Jews derived this name in book 9, ch. 2.]

But although Jews are interpreted as confessors, they have now lost this name, because, although they confess in words that they know God, in deeds they deny [Col. 0551D] him (Titus 1). The Jews lost the name of confession and praise when they cried to Pilate concerning Christ, “Away, away, crucify him!” and, denying him, said, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). For, as John the Evangelist relates, “He who denies the Son does not have the Father either” (1 John 2). Therefore the name of confessors has been transferred to Christians, because they confess and love Christ insofar as this is possible; and, for love of him, when necessity compels, they surrender themselves to flames and diverse torments.

The Magi, then, with supreme longing sought the King of the Jews—that is, the king of the holy confessors—and deserved to find him whom they had long desired to see. And what king? Certainly not Herod, but the Maker of heaven and earth: namely, he whom God the Father before the ages ineffably begot from himself without a mother, and whom at the end of the ages a Virgin bore from bodily substance without male seed. The Magi desire to worship this King lying in his mother’s lap, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing. The Magi offer gifts to this infant newly born, through whom all the elements subsist. Of this King, indeed, that divine man Balaam—though a Gentile, a magus, and a diviner—sang thus: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Num. 24). The Magi, coming from eastern [Col. 0552B] regions, announced Christ’s birth as the star pointed it out, so that by beholding the star they might reveal him whom the chief master of their art had formerly foretold.

The prophets also foretold this long before. Thus Isaiah says: “At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn apart and mangled, from a terrible people, after whom there was no other” (Isa. 18). He said this because of the exceedingly powerful nation of the Persians, whose might no people then equalled; Magi coming from them brought gifts to Christ. And again: “All shall come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense” (Isa. 60). And the Psalmist says: “He shall live, and gold of Arabia shall be given to him; they shall always worship concerning him; all day they shall bless him” (Ps. 71). Arabia in Greek is interpreted as “chest,” [Note: [Col. 0552D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 14, ch. 3, *sacra*.] [Col. 0552C] because it is a region producing fragrant incense, in whose groves cinnamon and myrrh grow. Arabia is itself also Sheba, named from the son of Cush who was surnamed Sheba. Hence the prophet David also says: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts; the kings of the Arabs and of Sheba shall bring presents” (ibid.). To whom will they bring gifts? Clearly, to our Lord Jesus Christ, over whom, when he was baptized, the Father’s voice sounded from heaven: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

What is this, most beloved brothers, that God the Father says of the Son, “In you I am well pleased,” except that through this he plainly indicates that he was displeased with other human beings? Thus the same almighty [Col. 0552D] Father, speaking in human fashion of sinners—as human beings could understand it—said in the book of Genesis: “I repent that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6). Through this he plainly made known that he was displeased with himself in the human beings whom he had created. Of them David says in the psalm: “They are corrupt and have become abominable in their pursuits; there is none who does good” (Ps. 13).

Therefore the Father was well pleased in our Lord Jesus Christ alone, because among all human beings he did not repent of having created one man, in whom he found no sin whatsoever. As the Psalmist says concerning him: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). Because God the Father was well pleased in him, he set him above everything whatsoever that he created, so that the authority which the same Son of God had eternally with the Father according to the divine essence might be received, at the end of the ages, by the man assumed by the Word, in whom he found no fault. Concerning him the Psalmist again speaks to God the Father, saying: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8). Thus our same Lord Jesus Christ says of himself: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28). Therefore the Father was well pleased in our Redeemer alone, and set him above all that [Col. 0553B] has been created, because he found no stain in him.

Moreover, when he had been baptized, the Holy Spirit appeared above him in the form of a dove. He descended over him in the form of a dove because, in the nature of divinity, he could not be seen by mortals. He was seen in the form of a dove because “discipline will flee deceit and will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1).
