After the Flood, it was not the raven but the dove that brought a branch announcing peace restored (Gen. 8), teaching that the anointing of the Holy Spirit is present only with those baptized in simplicity of heart. The Lord was not first anointed by the Holy Spirit after baptism; rather, the dove is shown so that we may understand that those baptized in his body—that is, the Church—especially receive the Holy Spirit. Rightly, then, [Col. 0553C] does the Father say to the Son: “In you I am well pleased” (Luke 3), because in him there is supreme holiness and simplicity pleasing to me.

[Col. 0554A] Therefore, dearest brothers, greatly fear this pronouncement in which God says: “I repent that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6). For God created man in order that he might render service worthy of him, please him by good conduct, and fulfill his will in all things. But because man preferred his own will to God’s will, he displeased God, lost the delights of paradise, and miserably cast us with himself into this exile of the world. Therefore, beloved, if you desire to return to the delights of paradise, renounce your own wills and strive to fulfill God’s will in everything. Fear God and love him above all things; show charity to one another; flee the enticements of this world as a deadly precipice; choose poverty for Christ’s love; despise riches; prepare yourselves for God’s service with all diligence; love virtues and put vices aside; recall the day of your death; without ceasing wash away with tears your sins and the sins of those whose alms you administer; despise earthly things and long for heavenly things.

But because you can do no good without God (John 15), beseech him with the deep groaning of your heart that he may deign to enlighten you by the light of his charity and lead you to the heavenly homeland to contemplate himself, by that same grace and power through which he deigned to draw the Magi from eastern lands to the cradle of his humanity. He, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect [Col. 0554C] Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON SIX. ON SEPTUAGESIMA.

[Col. 0553]

[Col. 0553C]

[Note: [Col. 0553D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Patriarchs*, ch. 25.]

Moses, of the tribe of Levi, son of Amram, adoptive son of King Pharaoh’s daughter, prophet and leader in Israel, [Col. 0553D] servant and friend of God, called from the flaming yet unconsumed bush and enlightened by the Holy Spirit, was most humble in refusing the office of teacher, obedient in accepting it, faithful and devoted in maintaining it. Moreover, in governing the people he was watchful; in correcting, vigorous; in loving, ardent; in enduring, patient; interceding with God for those subject to him. Finally, endowed with the spirit of prophecy for the instruction of the faithful, he speaks as follows: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1).

The beginning is Christ, who said to the Jews in the Gospel: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8).

[Note: [Col. 0554D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 1.]

In this beginning—that is, in the Son—God made heaven, that is, spiritual people who meditate upon, love, and pursue heavenly things. In the Son he also made earth, [Col. 0554C] that is, carnal people who have not yet put off the earthly man, namely earthly vices, and who still persistently live in their sins. “But the earth was empty and void”: that is, the earth of our flesh was without spiritual teaching. “And darkness was upon the face of the deep”: that is, blindness and the darkness of sin covered our hearts. “But the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”: that is, over our dark and fluid heart, as though over waters, he was already being borne, so that resting in him we might subsist and be made alive by his breath, whose wave would wash us from sins and vices.

And God said: “Let there be light”—namely, angelic nature [Col. 0555A] and the light of faith. It is as though he said more plainly: “Let the illumination of faith appear.” For on the first day he gave the light of faith, because faith in God is first in the conversion of believers. Thus the very first commandment among the precepts is: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6). For this faith the Lord himself deigned to descend from heaven and appear bodily to men. Already then, according to the grace of his foreknowledge, God divided light from darkness: that is, the children of God and of light, separating the righteous from sinners as from darkness. He called the righteous day and sinners night. For that the righteous are called by the name of light, hear the apostle Paul saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Then, on the second day, God arranged the firmament of heaven, [Col. 0555B] that is, the firm foundation of the holy Scriptures in the Church. For the firmament in the Church is understood as divine Scripture, because “heaven shall be folded up like a book” (Isa. 34). And above this firmament God divided the waters: that is, the heavenly peoples of angels, who do not need the firmament of the Scriptures in order, by reading God’s word, to know that they always behold God’s face with supreme love. But he placed this firmament of his Law above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that by looking up to it they may learn how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the upper and lower waters.

After this, on the third day he gathered together the salty lower waters, that is, unbelieving people [Col. 0555C] tossed by the waves of carnal temptations. And he separated from them the dry land: that is, the faithful people thirsting for the fountain of living water, namely Christ. Then, on the fourth day, the lights of sun, moon, and stars, fixed in the firmament of heaven, shone forth: that is, the evangelists and teachers of Holy Scripture, united in exposition and showing the light of wisdom to those below. At the same time there also came forth the whole host of glittering stars, that is, the abundance of diverse virtues in the Church. Shining in the darkness of this life as though in the night, they distinguish in this firmament of Scripture sensible things from intelligible things, as light belonging to the perfect from darkness belonging to little ones; and they exist in the signs of virtues and miracles. They also serve for times and years, because preachers live and pass away in their own times, but the word of the Lord remains for ever.

Why, moreover, did the earth first bring forth vegetation and the heavenly lights then come into being, except because good works come first, and then comes the illumination of light for contemplating the form of heavenly power? Meanwhile, on the fifth day living creatures that creep in the waters were made: that is, people recalled to life through the sacrament of baptism. Birds were also made: that is, holy souls flying toward things above. After this, on the sixth day the earth brought forth a living soul, because when Christ came in the flesh, our flesh refrains from dead works. The earth gave birth to the green shoots of virtues, according to their kind: that is, by imitating the life of the saints. Hence the Apostle says: “Be imitators of me” (1 Cor. 11). Thus [Col. 0556A] we live according to our own kind when in good works we imitate holy men as though they were our neighbours.

Then the earth brought forth beasts, that is, people living in secular power or in the fierceness of pride; likewise cattle, namely faithful people who remain in simplicity of life. The earth also brought forth harmless serpents—not those poisonous ones who place themselves among this world’s desires, but holy men, discerning good from evil through the liveliness of their astuteness and, insofar as is lawful, creeping—that is, examining earthly things through which they understand eternal things. After this God made man in his image and likeness: the body of man in the image of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the soul in the likeness of his divinity. [Col. 0556B] For this reason he made this man—the perfect man—who works righteousness not by imitating any particular holy men, but by contemplatively beholding Truth itself, in order to understand and follow that Truth in whose image he was made. This man also received power over the fish of the sea, birds of heaven, cattle, beasts, and serpents, because everyone made spiritual and made like God, as the Apostle says, “judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore God formed man from the mud of the earth and breathed into his face the breath of life: that is, the substance of a soul through which he might live. He created it not from any bodily or spiritual material, but from nothing. Now the Lord God had planted from the beginning a paradise [Col. 0556C] of delight, in which he placed the man whom he had formed. Although this paradise is a type of the present or the future Church, it is nevertheless a place situated in eastern regions. The word *paradisus* is Greek: in Greek it is understood in Latin as “garden.” In Hebrew it is called Eden, interpreted “delights”; all these words combined make “garden of delights.” For paradise is planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree, and also has the tree of life. In this paradise there is never cold, never summer, but perpetual pleasantness. From the middle of this paradise a spring goes forth, watering all its trees, and is thus divided into four rivers that arise from it.

Therefore God took man [Col. 0556D] and placed him in the paradise of delight which he had planted from the beginning. Man was created outside paradise and placed in paradise after his creation, to signify by this that he would not remain there for a long time: “that he might work and keep it,” that is, that he might fulfill God’s will and keep his command. After this the Lord cast a sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, and formed it into a woman. God did not create man and woman at the same time, but first man and then woman from man, so that God’s image might be displayed in man: for just as God is the principle of the creation of all things, so man would become the principle of the generation of all human beings. God also willed human beings to descend from one man so that, knowing themselves all to be from one man, [Col. 0557A] they might love themselves as one.

The woman was formed from the man’s side in order to show that she was created for the fellowship of love; otherwise, if she had been made from his head, she might seem to be mistress, but if she had been formed from the man’s feet, perhaps she would be subjected to servitude as a slave. Therefore, since woman is neither mistress nor slave but companion, she was rightly formed neither from the head nor the feet, but from the side, so that the man might place beside himself her whom he knew had been taken from his own side. The rib from which the woman was formed as the man’s helper was taken from the side of the sleeping Adam for two reasons. First, so that he might feel no pain; second, so that in this work divine power might be praised—the power which opened the side [Col. 0557B] of a sleeping man and yet did not awaken him from the slumber of rest. In this it also prefigured the mystery of Christ and the Church.

Then God said to Adam: “Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.”

Dearest brothers, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is the choice of one’s own pleasure [Note: [Col. 0557D] “Will.”], placed in the middle of us in order to know good or evil. Whoever, leaving God’s grace, tastes of this tree—that is, of this choice—shall die the death: that is, shall perish from the fellowship of God’s elect. The crafty serpent historically signifies the devil, who is called serpent because he moves by winding craftiness. But why did the serpent—that is, the devil—deceive through the woman [Col. 0557C] and not through the man? Because we are led into sin through the delight of carnal weakness, not through the strength of spiritual understanding. We understand the serpent as the devil’s suggestion; the woman is carnal sensation; and the man is the reason of spiritual strength. Thus when a suggestion of sin meets us, it is as though the serpent speaks. If the flesh delights in consenting to that evil suggestion, the woman already, as it were, consents. But if the devil’s suggestion is restrained and expelled from thought, it is as though the woman alone eats the forbidden tree. But if the flesh, delighting—that is, the woman—eats the very sin which the serpent, that is, the devil, suggests, and the human mind consents to commit that sin, then the man too has, as it were, been deceived. The woman has given food to the man when the rational mind has given consent to sinning through the flesh’s delights. Then, indeed, a human being is rightly separated from the blessed life and expelled, as it were, from paradise. The sin is also imputed to him even if it is not carried out in deed; for [Col. 0558A] although there is no guilt in the outward act, the conscience is nevertheless held guilty in consent.

Thus let it be said: “Eat from every tree of paradise; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil do not eat.”

Therefore, beloved, just as our first parent was commanded not to eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, so we too are commanded not to touch it, lest perhaps we die. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, as we have already said above, is the choice of one’s own will, placed in the middle of us. Therefore let us not touch the forbidden tree: that is, let us not wish to be proud on account of the nature of our free choice, which is placed in the middle of us, lest afterwards, deceived, we experience knowledge of good and evil. Let us not, then, exchange the knowledge of doing good for transgression of the commandment. [Col. 0558B] Let us therefore eat from every tree of paradise, by which are signified the spiritual delights of God’s kingdom.

“Do not love the world, therefore, my brothers and lords, nor the things that are in the world; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition” (John 2).

[Note: [Col. 0557] Book *On Salutary Instructions*, ch. 13, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. 6.]

These are the three things which cast Adam and Eve out of the paradise of delights into this miserable exile; for, unless love of God had failed in them, they would never have begun to love, indeed would not even have believed, the counsel of the serpent who gave evil advice. Thus the desire of the flesh was fulfilled in them when they tasted of the forbidden tree; the desire of the eyes, when they desired their eyes to be opened; and worldly ambition, when they believed that they could become what God is.

[Col. 0558C] Therefore, beloved, it is fitting and very necessary for us to raise the eyes of mind and body from earthly delights, to correct our conduct for the better with diligent effort insofar as we can, and to hasten to acquire every virtue of the good, so that we may obtain God’s mercy and compassion at the opportune time, rejoice ineffably in his promise, and deserve to return to the delights of paradise from which we were expelled—by fasting, keeping vigil, despising visible things, and washing sins away with tears—under the guidance of him who, for the restoration of the human race, deigned to undergo the passion of the cross and to rise from the tomb on the third day; and who, with his disciples looking on, [Col. 0558D] ascended into heaven on the fortieth day and sits at the right hand of the Father: Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong honour, strength, and power with the same Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON SEVEN. ON THE SECOND SUNDAY OF SEPTUAGESIMA.

[Col. 0559]

[Col. 0559A] “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). [Note: [Col. 0559D] *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 11.] With these words Moses, inspired by the Spirit of God, relates that the world was made by God the Creator in one beginning, overthrowing the error of certain persons who supposed that there were several principles without a beginning. Plato, indeed, held that there were three principles: God, the exemplar, and matter; and that these themselves were uncreated and without beginning, while God was, as it were, an artificer, not a Creator. For a creator is one who makes something from nothing. Thus, properly speaking, to create is to make something from nothing. To make, however, is not only to produce something from nothing, but also from material. Hence a human being or an angel is said to make something, but not to create it; and is called a maker or artificer, not a creator. This name properly belongs to God alone, who both makes certain things from nothing and makes certain things from something.

[Col. 0559B] He, therefore, is Creator, craftsman, and maker; but He has reserved the name of creation properly for Himself, while He has shared the other names even with creatures. In Scripture, nevertheless, “creator” is often used in the sense of “maker,” and “to create” in the sense of “to make,” without a distinction of meaning. Yet it must be understood that these three terms—namely, to make, to create, to act—and other such terms cannot be said of God in the same way as they are said of creatures. For when we say that He makes something, we do not understand that any motion in working, or any suffering in labouring, is present in Him, as commonly happens to us.

Let us therefore believe that the cause of all heavenly and earthly creatures, visible and invisible, is none other than the goodness of the Creator, who [Col. 0559C] is living and true; and His goodness is so great that, being supremely good, He wills others to be partakers of that blessedness by which He is eternally blessed—blessedness which can be seen and shared, yet can in no way be diminished. And because no one can be a partaker of His blessedness except through understanding, which is possessed more fully the more it is understood, God made a rational creature, that it might understand the highest good, love it by understanding it, possess it by loving it, and enjoy it by possessing it.

God accordingly distinguished rational creation in this way: one part was to remain in its purity and not be united to a body—namely, the angels; another part was to be joined to a body—namely, souls. Rational creation, therefore, is divided into incorporeal and corporeal: the incorporeal is called an angel, while the corporeal is [Col. 0559D] called a human being, subsisting from a rational soul and flesh. The first cause of creation, then, was the goodness of God. Why, therefore, was a human being or angel created? Namely, because of God’s goodness. Hence [Col. 0560A] blessed Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*: “Because God is good, we exist; and insofar as we exist, we are good.” For what purpose was rational creation also made? Namely, to praise God, to serve Him, and to enjoy Him; in these things it itself advances, not God. For God is perfect and full of the highest goodness, and can neither be increased nor diminished. Thus, the fact that rational creation was made by God must be referred both to the Creator’s goodness and to the creature’s benefit. It is indeed beneficial to the creature to serve God and enjoy Him.

Let Moses, therefore, taught by the Holy Spirit, say: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Who would have believed Moses when he spoke truth concerning the past, had he not also spoken something true concerning the future? For he prophesied concerning the future people of Israel, saying: [Col. 0560B] “The Lord your God will raise up for you from among your brethren a prophet like me; him you shall hear. And it shall be that whoever does not hear that prophet shall be cut off from his people” (Deut. 18). Why, then, did he mingle future things with past, except that, when the things he foretold concerning the future were fulfilled, he might show that what he had said concerning the past was also true?

Beyond doubt, therefore, we believe that he prophesied truthfully concerning past things, because we now see fulfilled the things he foretold concerning the future: namely, that God the Father [Note: [Col. 0559D] “God the Father.”] raised up from the tribe of Judah the great prophet—that is, Christ—and preached through Him to the children of Israel; that He adopted as children those who gave faith to His preaching; and that He cut off unbelievers, both in the present and in the future, from the fellowship of the elect [Col. 0560C]. Let the leader of the Israelite people, inspired by the gift of the Holy Spirit, therefore say: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

“All times,” says blessed Isidore, [Note: [Col. 0560D] *Sentences*, Book I, chapter 6.] “are preceded by divine eternity. Nothing past or future is attributed to God; rather, all things are said to be present in Him, because by His eternity He encompasses all things. Otherwise He would have to be thought mutable, if the succession of times were ascribed to Him. If any times always existed with God, they would not be time but eternity; nor would times change, but remain fixed. It belongs to us, not to God, to have past, present, and future.” [Note: [Col. 0560D] The Master, as above, distinction 2: “Thus it appears.”]

That spiritual and corporeal creation were created simultaneously is shown by Solomon when he says: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. [Col. 0560D] 18), that is, spiritual and corporeal nature. The angels, therefore, were not created earlier in time than that corporeal matter of the four elements. Yet wisdom—that is, [Col. 0561A] the angels—was created before all things, because, although not earlier in time, it nevertheless precedes in dignity.

Augustine also, in his work on Genesis, shows that spiritual and corporeal creation were made together, saying: “By heaven and earth we understand spiritual and corporeal creation, and these were created ‘in the beginning,’ namely, of time; or ‘in the beginning,’ because they were made first. For nothing was made beforehand; nor was time made before spiritual nature, namely angelic nature, and before corporeal nature, that is, that undifferentiated matter of the four elements. These were created with time, not from time or in time; just as time was not created in time, because there was no time before heaven and earth existed.”

Moreover, it must be known that “there are two things in the Creator [Note: [Col. 0561D] Isidore, as above; and he reads, “creatures.”] [Col. 0561B] to which the succession of times cannot apply: namely, the angels, because they cleave to the immutable Creator; and that formless matter before all these things which now revolve temporally were formed from it. Time, therefore, pertains not to those creatures above the heavens, but to those beneath heaven. For times do not come to or succeed one another for angels, but for us who dwell beneath heaven in this frail world. Thus no times existed before the beginning, because time itself is a creature and must be believed to have been made at the beginning of the world.”

Hence blessed Isidore says: [Note: [Col. 0561D] Chapter 7.] “It is called ‘beginning’ because from it the commencement of the universe began. Times possess no bodily extension, for they almost pass away before they arrive. Therefore [Col. 0561C] there is no permanence of times among things, because they are changed by the swift movement of creation. Thus neither a hundred years is one time, nor one year one time, nor one month one time, nor one day, nor one hour one time. Therefore, while all these things come and pass away in their parts, how can that be called one which is not simultaneous? Whether past or future time exists, as the present does—if it exists, one must know where it is. But observe that all future, past, and present things must rather be sought in the mind: past things by remembering, present things by observing, future things by expecting. These things are not so in God, to whom all things are present at once.”

The world, therefore, consists of visible things, yet things capable of investigation; but the human being, composed from the totality of things, is in a certain brief fashion another world. The character of the world is to be considered in one human being. For just as a human being moves through the stages of life toward an end, so the world declines through being stretched out in time; since that by which human beings and the world appear to grow is also that by which each is diminished.

Isidore says: [Note: [Col. 0561D] Chapter 8.] “It is said in vain that, after so great a stretch of time in which God was idle, a new thought arose in Him to make the world, when the construction of this world remained in His eternal counsel [Col. 0562A] and no time existed before the beginning, but eternity. Some also say: ‘What was God doing before heaven and earth came to be? Why did a new will arise in God to create the world?’ But no new will arose in God, because, although the world did not exist in actuality, it always existed in eternal reason and counsel.”

Now we must carefully consider [Note: [Col. 0561D] The Master, as above: “It has now been shown.”] where angelic nature was created. The testimony of certain authorities clearly shows that angels were in heaven before the fall, and that some fell from there through pride, while others who did not sin remained there. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Here “heaven” does not mean the firmament [Col. 0562B] made on the second day, but the radiant heaven called the empyrean—that is, fiery by reason of splendour, not colour—which was immediately filled with angels, and which lies above the firmament. Of this heaven Scripture says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

Strabus says: “Here he does not call the visible firmament ‘heaven,’ but the empyrean, that is, fiery or intellectual heaven, which is called so not from heat but from splendour, and which, as soon as it was made, was filled with angels.” Hence the Lord says to Job: “Where were you when the morning stars praised me and all the sons of God rejoiced?” (Job 38). He calls those same angels “morning stars,” for they praise God unceasingly. Of this heaven also the Venerable Bede says: “This higher heaven, removed and set apart from the revolution [Col. 0562C] of the world, was filled with holy angels as soon as it was created. For the heaven in which the luminaries are placed was made not in the beginning, but on the second day.”

“Heaven,” says blessed Isidore, [Note: [Col. 0561D] *Etymologies*, Book III, chapter 31; and Book XIII, chapter 4.] “is so called because, like a chased vessel, it has the lights of the stars impressed on it like signs; for a chased vessel is said to be one that shines with raised figures. God distinguished it with bright luminaries and filled it—with the sun and moon shining upon the globe—and adorned it with the glittering signs of twinkling stars. Heaven is also called so from concealing the things above. In Greek it is called *Ouranos*, *apo tou horasthai* (ἀπὸ τοῦ ὁρᾶσθαι), that is, “from being seen,” because the air is transparent and clearer for viewing. In Holy Scripture [Col. 0562D] heaven is called the firmament because it is made firm by the course of the stars and by stable, fixed laws. At times ‘heaven’ is also taken for the air, where winds and clouds, storms and whirlwinds arise. Hence Lucretius: ‘Heaven, which is called air.’ The Lord [Note: [Col. 0562D] Isidore reads: “And the psalm calls them birds of heaven”; but birds of heaven are often mentioned both in the Psalms and in the Gospel, as may be seen in Psalms 8 and 103, and in Matthew chapters 8 and 13, Mark 8, and Luke 13.] also calls them ‘birds of heaven’ in the Gospel, though it is clear that birds fly in the air. We too customarily call this air ‘heaven’; for when we ask whether it is clear or cloudy, we sometimes say, ‘What is the air like?’ and sometimes, ‘What is the heaven like?’”

[Col. 0563A] [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Master, as above: “Here it is customary to ask.”] It is customary here to ask: if angels were in the empyrean heaven as soon as they were made, how is it that, as we read in Isaiah, Lucifer says: “I will ascend into heaven, and exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14)? But there he calls heaven the loftiness of God, to which he wished to make himself equal, as though he said: “I will ascend into heaven,” that is, to equality with God.

Hence Augustine says on Genesis: “God made all things very good. God made angelic nature good; and because it would be unjust for God to condemn in anyone, on any ground of merit, what He created, we must believe that not nature but an evil will is punished.” Again he says: “The opinion that the devil never stood in the truth, never lived a blessed life, but fell from the beginning, must not be understood so that he is thought to have been created evil by the good God, because he is said to have fallen from the beginning. For he would not fall if he had been made such—that is, evil. From whom could he fall? Therefore, having first been made good, he immediately turned himself away from the truth, delighting in his own power; and he neither tasted the sweetness of the blessed life nor wholly came to loathe it, but lost it by refusing to receive it.”

Here he plainly declares that angels were created good, that they fell after their creation, and that there was some interval, however very brief, between creation and the fall.

[Note: [Col. 0563D] Distinction 4.] After this it must be considered whether God created angels perfect and blessed, or miserable and imperfect. To this it may be said that they were created neither in misery nor in blessedness. For they could not have been miserable before sin, because misery comes from [Col. 0563C] sin; if there had been no sin, there would have been no misery. Nor were those who fell ever blessed, because they were ignorant of their own outcome—namely, of sin and of future punishment.

Augustine says: “How could they be blessed when uncertain of their own damnation or salvation—when they had neither hope that they would be changed for the better, nor hope of persevering in the love of God? Or how can those be blessed whose blessedness is uncertain? Therefore God revealed neither the future evil to those who were to sin, nor the future good to those who were to remain. Accordingly, neither those who fell were ever blessed, nor those who remained, until their confirmation.”

What, then, were angels like at creation? It has already been shown: namely, good and not [Col. 0563D] evil; just, that is, innocent; and in a certain sense perfect, because they were well made by God; yet imperfect in another sense, because they had not yet been confirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] Distinction 5: “They possessed.”] Nevertheless, all angels possessed free choice, which is the free power and capacity of rational will. For by the will they could choose whatever they wished, and by reason they could judge—that is, discern; in these things free choice consists. They were not created willing either to turn away or to turn back, but capable of willing this or that. After creation, however, some chose evil by spontaneous will, while others chose good. Thus God distinguishes light from darkness, as Scripture says, [Col. 0564A] that is, good angels from evil; and He called the light day and the darkness night, because He enlightened the good angels by adding His grace, but blinded the evil angels—not because grace previously bestowed upon them was withdrawn, but because it was never bestowed upon them, that they might turn back, as their faults required.

The fault of those who fell may plainly be recognized in this: although without grace they could not advance, and had not yet received it, yet through what had been bestowed on them at creation they could avoid falling—that is, they could stand. For nothing compelled them to fall; rather, they turned aside by their own spontaneous will. Had they not done so, what was given to others would assuredly have been given to them also.

[Note: [Col. 0564D] Distinction 6.] Furthermore, it must be known that, just as some of the greater and some of the lesser angels remained, so some from each rank fell; and among these was one of more excellent nature than all the other fallen angels, as authorities show. For blessed Job says: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). And in Ezekiel we read: “You, Cherub, seal of likeness, full of knowledge, perfect in beauty, were in the delights of paradise” (Ezek. 28). Explaining this, Gregory says: “The more subtle his nature, the more fully is the image of God shown to have been impressed upon him.”

Likewise, in Ezekiel: “Every precious stone was your covering” (ibid.), that is, every angel was, as it were, his covering. For, as Gregory says, in comparison with the others he was brighter than all the rest; hence he was called Lucifer, as Isaiah testifies: “How [Col. 0564C] have you fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning?” and so forth (Isa. 14). This is to be understood not as a single order but as a single angel. According to Isidore’s testimony, after he was created, considering the eminence of his nature and the depth of his knowledge, he grew proud against his Creator to such an extent that he wished to make himself equal to Him. Of him Isaiah says: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; and I will be like the Most High” (ibid.). He desired, indeed, to be like God not through imitation but through equality of power.

By the merit of such great pride he was cast down from the empyrean heaven, in which he had been created with the others, into this dark air, together with all the companions of his perversity. For John says in the Apocalypse: “The dragon, falling from heaven, drew down with him a third part of the stars” [Col. 0564D] (Apoc. 12). Thus that Lucifer, greater than the others, did not fall alone; many others fell with him, having consented to him in evil. This dwelling-place of dark air received them as they fell, and this occurred for our testing, that it might be an occasion of discipline for us. Hence the Apostle says: “Our struggle is against the principalities and powers of this world, and against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). For demons, who are spiritual and wicked, dwell in this troubled air near us, which is called heaven. Hence the devil is called the prince of the air.

[Col. 0565A] They have not been permitted to dwell in heaven, because it is a bright and delightful place; nor on earth with us, lest they afflict us too severely. Rather, according to the teaching of the Apostle Peter handed down in the Catholic Epistle, they have been assigned this dark air as a prison until the time of judgment (2 Pet. 2). Then they will be thrust down into the abyss of hell, according to the saying: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

Furthermore, it must be known that, just as among good angels some preside over others, so among evil angels some are set over others and some are subject to others. As long as the world endures, angels preside over angels, human beings over human beings, and demons over demons; but in the future every preeminence will be abolished, as the Apostle teaches [Col. 0565B] (1 Cor. 15). According to the degree of greater or lesser knowledge, demons also have various higher and lower ranks of authority. For some spirits preside over one province, others over one person, and still others over one vice. Hence there is said to be a spirit of pride, a spirit of lust, and the like, because a demon can most readily tempt human beings through the vice from which it is named.

This is also why riches are called by the name of a demon, namely *mammon*. For *mammon* is the name of a demon, and riches are called by that name in the Syrian language. This does not mean that the devil has power to give or take away riches as he wishes, but that he uses them to tempt and deceive human beings.

Concerning Lucifer, however, some hold that he is bound in hell and has no present access to tempt us, as is written in the Apocalypse: “When the thousand years have been completed, Satan will be released from his prison and will go forth and deceive the nations” (Apoc. 20). This will occur in the final time of Antichrist, when there will be such great tribulation that even the elect, if possible, may be led astray (Matt. 24). They say that he has been bound there since the time when he tempted Christ in the desert, or during the Passion, and was conquered by Him. They believe that he tempted and overcame the first human being, and tempted the second—that is, Christ—but was overcome by Him, and is therefore held bound in hell.

The power to tempt others again also seems to be taken from demons who are conquered by saints living justly and chastely. Hence Origen says: “I think, indeed, that if the saints resist demons, the instigators of vices, and conquer them in battle, it is no longer permitted for that spirit which has already been conquered by a saint to attack another human being.” Some understand this to refer to the particular great vice in which it was overcome: for example, if it tempts a holy man concerning pride and is conquered, it may no longer tempt him or anyone else concerning pride.

[Note: [Col. 0565D] Distinction 7: “Therefore not.”] Furthermore, it must be known that good angels, after confirmation, could not sin by nature as they could before—not because their choice was weakened by grace, but rather because it was so confirmed that a good angel can no longer sin through it. [Col. 0566A] This is certainly not from free choice itself, but from God’s grace. For both angel and human being were created such that they could incline to either side; but afterward good angels were so confirmed by grace that they cannot sin, and evil angels so darkened by vice that they cannot live well.

Although evil angels are so obstinate in malice, they have not been wholly deprived of keen understanding. “For,” as Isidore relates, “demons are strong in a threefold sharpness of knowledge: in the subtlety of their nature, partly in experience of the times, and partly in revelation from higher spirits. Magical arts are practised through their knowledge; yet both their knowledge and power have been given by God, either to deceive the deceitful, to admonish the faithful, or to exercise and test the patience of the righteous.”

Hence [Col. 0566B] blessed Augustine says: “I see what may occur to weak thought: namely, why these miracles are done by magical arts. For Pharaoh’s magicians also made serpents, and many other things besides (Exod. 7). But it is still more remarkable how the power of the magicians, which could make serpents, utterly failed when it came to the tiniest flies, that is, gnats. There the magicians failed, saying: ‘This is the finger of God’ (Exod. 8). Certainly those evil angels must not be called creators because the magicians made frogs and serpents through them, for they did not themselves create them. God alone is Creator of all visible and invisible creatures. Why, then, could the magicians not make gnats, except because the greater dominion of God, forbidding them through the Holy Spirit, was present? [Col. 0566C] This the magicians themselves confessed, saying: ‘This is the finger of God.’” That is, the manifest power of God performs these miracles.

“This vanity of magical arts,” says blessed Isidore, [Note: [Col. 0565D] *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 9.] “prevailed for many ages throughout the whole world from the tradition of evil angels, through a certain knowledge of future and infernal things and their invocations. Divination from entrails, augury, the things called oracles, and necromancy were also invented. Nor is there any wonder in the tricks of magicians, whose arts of maleficence so flourished that they even resisted Moses with very similar signs, turning rods into dragons and waters into blood. The first magician was Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, whom Ninus, king of the Assyrians, killed in battle. Aristotle wrote of him that the testimony of his books showed two million verses composed by him. Many centuries later Democritus expanded this art, at the time when Hippocrates’ discipline of medicine also flourished. There is also the famous sorceress Circe, who is said to have changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts. [Note: [Col. 0566D] Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.70.] We also read of the sacrifice which the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus, from which whoever partook was changed into the forms of beasts. From this it appears beyond all doubt that the noble poet wrote of a certain woman who excelled in magical arts.

[Col. 0567A] “She,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0567D] *Aeneid*, Book IV, line 487.] “undertakes by spells to release the minds

Of whom she will; but [Note: [Col. 0567D] The manuscript less correctly has “he says.”] upon others to bring hard cares;

To stop the rivers’ waters, and turn the stars backward;

And to summon the [Note: [Col. 0567D] The manuscript has “will shake the nocturnal [spirits].”] nocturnal spirits. You will see

The earth bellow beneath your feet, and ash trees descend from the mountains.” (*Aeneid*, Book IV, 487.)

“What more need be said? If it is permitted to believe, [Note: [Col. 0567D] Isidore seems to have hesitated in this highly celebrated question, vigorously debated from the earliest centuries among the foremost Fathers of the Church. Their testimonies are weighed by the learned Natalis Alexander in Dissertation 23 of his *Ecclesiastical History of the Old Testament*, and by Augustin Calmet in the work entitled *On Samuel Presented to Saul by an Apparition*. Both these, as well as other more recent critics, incline to the opinion finally followed by the great Father Augustine, prompted by the authority of Ecclesiasticus 46:23: namely, that the real Samuel made himself visible to Saul. We therefore wonder that Theodoric Ruinart, in his note on the Acts of St Pionius the Presbyter, appears not only to approve the contrary opinion—which we do not oppose—but even to claim Augustine as its follower in the book *On Diverse Questions to Simplicianus*. In that work Augustine is wholly tentative; but in the later works *The Eight Questions of Dulcitius* and *On Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, he adopts the opinion already stated. Its supporters, besides Augustine, are Ambrose, Origen, Justin Martyr, and all the others listed by Natalis and Calmet.] a pythoness was able to summon the soul of the prophet Samuel from the depths of hell and present it to the sight of the living—if, however, we believe it was the prophet’s soul, and not some phantasmal deception wrought by Satan’s fraud.”

Prudentius also says of Mercury: [Note: [Col. 0568D] Book I, *Against Symmachus*.]

> It is said that by the controlling power of his wand he recalled extinguished souls  
> [Col. 0567B] into the light [lacuna],  
> but condemned others [Note: [Col. 0568D] Manuscript: “others” in the masculine.] to death.

“And shortly afterward he added:

> For with magical murmur he knew how to raise thin shapes,  
> and skilfully charm sepulchral ashes.  
> The harmful art likewise knows how to rob others of life.”

Therefore, in all the things mentioned above, the art of demons has arisen from a destructive association of human beings and evil angels. Hence Christians must avoid all such things, utterly reject them with every execration, and condemn them.

“Holy angels,” says blessed Isidore, [Note: [Col. 0568D] *Sentences*, Book I, chapter 10.] “take from the upper air the bodies in which they appear to human beings, and assume a solid form from the heavenly element, through which they may show themselves more clearly to human sight.” [Note: [Col. 0568D] The Master, *Sentences*, Book II, distinction 8.] Such bodies are preserved for the good angels who [Col. 0567C] remained, so that in them they may do good and suffer no evil. They are of such fineness that mortals cannot see them unless they are clothed in some denser form; having assumed it, they are seen, and having laid it aside, they cease to be seen.

But at their fall the bodies of evil angels were changed into the inferior condition of denser air. For just as they were cast down from a more worthy place, namely heaven, to an inferior place, namely dark air, so those heavenly and more subtle bodies which they previously possessed were transformed into inferior and denser bodies, in which they can suffer torments. Good angels, then, with God preparing them, assume bodies from the upper air in order to fulfil the ministry enjoined upon them by God; and after accomplishing it, they lay aside the bodies in which [Col. 0568A] they appeared to and spoke with human beings.

Furthermore, it must be known that angels sometimes speak to human beings in the person of God without distinction of any Person; but sometimes in the person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Nor must it be doubted that God appeared to human beings in bodily forms, as Augustine demonstrates in the second book of *On the Trinity*, comparing various testimonies of Scripture from which he proves that God appeared in bodily figures, and that speech was sometimes made to them in the person of God without distinction, and sometimes with distinction.

Let us therefore hold without doubt that God never appeared to mortals in the form of His essence, as He says to His servant Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). And as is said in the Gospel of John: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1). For nothing visible is not mutable. Therefore, since the substance or essence of God is in no way mutable, it can in no way be visible through itself. Consequently, all those things seen by the fathers—that is, patriarchs and prophets—when God made Himself present to them, were evidently brought about through a creature. Although we do not know how God made these things through the ministry of angels, we nevertheless say that they were made through angels.

I therefore dare to say confidently that neither God the Father, nor His Word, nor His Holy Spirit—who is one God—is in any way mutable by that which He is and is Himself; and for that reason He is still less visible [Col. 0568C].

It also seems worthy of consideration whether demons enter human bodies substantially and insinuate themselves into their souls; or whether they are said to enter because, by God’s permission, they exercise there the effect of their malice, oppressing and tormenting souls, or drawing them into sin according to their will. The Gospel plainly declares that they enter human beings and, when expelled, depart from them, recounting demons that entered certain persons and were cast out by Christ. But whether they enter according to substance, or are said to enter because of their evil effect, is not so clear.

On this subject Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0568D] The highly learned Benedictine revisers of the works of St Augustine note in the Appendix, volume VIII, that the Master of the Sentences very often cited this book under Augustine’s name, except in one Louvain edition at this place. But since there are several Louvain editions of the *Sentences*, it would not have been useless for them to identify the one they saw. We have examined a Louvain edition of 1552, printed by Bartholomaeus Gravius and Augustine, and it does not cite Gennadius here. We have also seen two others: a Venetian folio edition of 1514, printed by Gregorio de’ Gregoriis, and a Lyons octavo edition of 1527, printed by Jean Moylin; in this chapter they attribute the book to Gennadius, not Augustine. The codex examined by B. Martin cited Gennadius here, though elsewhere it often attributes the book *On Dogmas* to Augustine.] [Col. 0569A] says in *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “We do not believe that demons assail the soul substantially by energy or operation, but by application and oppression. But to be united to the mind is possible only for Him who created it, who, subsisting incorporeally by His own nature, is capable of His creature.” Bede also, commenting on the place in the Acts of the Apostles where Peter says to Ananias, “Why has Satan tempted your heart?” (Acts 5), observes that he did not say, “Why has he entered?” but, “Why has he tempted?”

It should be noted that nothing can fill human minds in respect of substance except the creating Trinity. Satan fills someone’s heart not by entering him or his understanding, nor by entering through the doorway of that person’s heart—for this power belongs to God alone—but by craftily and deceitfully drawing [Col. 0569B] the soul toward an affection for malice, through thoughts and incitements to vices, with which he is full. Thus Satan entered Ananias’s heart not by entering, but by introducing the force [Note: [Col. 0570D] More correctly, “venom.”] of his malice. These authorities show that demons do not enter human hearts substantially, but through the effect of malice; they are said to be driven out when they are not permitted to harm.

[Note: [Col. 0570D] Distinction 9.] After what has been said, it remains to learn what Scripture says concerning the orders of angels. Dionysius teaches that there are three orders of angels, placing three ranks in each order. There are three higher, three lower, and three middle ranks. The higher are seraphim, cherubim, and thrones; the middle, dominions, principalities, and powers; the lower, virtues, archangels, and angels.

[Col. 0569C] An order of angels is called a multitude of heavenly spirits. Seraphim are called those who burn with charity beyond the others. *Seraphim* means “burning” or “kindling.” Cherubim are called those who surpass the others in knowledge; *cherubim* means “fullness of knowledge.” A throne is a seat; and thrones, as blessed Gregory says, are those who are so filled with divine grace that God sits in them and decrees His judgments through them. Dominions are called those who surpass principalities and powers. Principalities are those who arrange for their subjects what must be done, and preside over them in carrying out the divine mysteries. Powers are those who have received more power than others in their order, so that the hostile forces subject to them may be restrained by their authority, lest they be able to tempt human beings as much as [Col. 0569D] they desire. Virtues are those through whom signs and miracles are frequently performed. Archangels are those who announce greater things; angels, those who announce lesser things.

But since there are only nine orders, nor would there have been more even if those who fell had remained, readers ask how Scripture can say [Col. 0570A] that a tenth order is to be completed from human beings. Gregory says that human beings are to be assumed into the angelic orders: some into the order of the higher ranks, namely those who burn more intensely with charity; others into the order of the lower ranks, namely those who are less perfect. From this it is clear that a tenth order is not to be formed from human beings, as though there were nine orders of angels and a tenth of humans; rather, human beings are to be placed in the angelic orders according to the quality of their merits. Therefore, what is read—that the tenth order is to be completed from human beings—may be understood in this sense: that what fell away from the angels will be restored from human beings, since so many of them fell that a tenth order might have been made from them. For this reason the Apostle says that all things in Christ are restored, those in heaven and those on earth [Col. 0570B] (Col. I); because through Christ the human race has been redeemed, from which comes the restoration of the angelic ruin. Yet a human being would be saved no less even if an angel had not fallen. Human beings are admitted to blessedness not according to the number of those who fell, but according to the number of those who remained.

Hence Gregory:

> “That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings; and we believe that as many of the human race ascend to it as there are angels remaining there, as it is written: ‘He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God’ [Deut. XXXII].”

[Note: Col. 0570D: Homily 34 on the Gospels.]

[Note: Col. 0570D: The Master reads “angels,” as do the Septuagint, the Old Italic, and many others cited by Sabbatier on this passage. How Martin derived this particular reading, “sons of God,” is unknown to us.]

Whence also blessed Isidore says:

> “The number of the good angels, diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be made up from the number of the elect [Col. 0570C] among human beings; that number is known to God alone.”

[Note: Col. 0570D: Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 10.]

It must also be investigated [Note: Col. 0570D: Distinction 10.] whether those heavenly spirits are sent forth to announce outward matters. Isaiah likewise says: “One of the seraphim flew to me” (Isa. VI). This is the highest and most excellent order; therefore, if messengers are sent from that order, there is no doubt that messengers are also sent from the others. Hence the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service?” (Heb. I). On the strength of these testimonies some maintain that all angels are sent. Yet it should not seem unworthy that even the higher angels are sent, since he who is the Creator of all descended to these lower things.

Moreover, it should be known [Note: Col. 0570D: Distinction 11.] that good angels are appointed for the guardianship of human beings, so that each [Col. 0570D] of the elect has an angel specially assigned for his progress and protection. Therefore Truth himself, in the Gospel, forbidding offence against little ones, says: “Their angels always behold the face of the Father” (Matt. XVIII). He calls them *their* angels because they have been appointed for their protection. Jerome says on this passage:

> “Great is the dignity of souls: each one has, from the beginning of its birth, an angel assigned for its guardianship.”

Gregory also says:

> “Each person has one good angel appointed for protection and one evil angel for trial.”

Therefore, although all good angels desire our good and generally devote themselves to the salvation of all the faithful, the one assigned to a person’s guardianship especially exhorts him to good, as is read of Tobias’s angel (Tob. III) and of Peter’s angel in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XII). Likewise, although evil angels desire human evil, the one appointed for a person’s trial more strongly urges that person toward evil and presses more forcefully to cause harm. Let these statements concerning the condition of angelic nature suffice.

[Col. 0571B] It remains to set forth something concerning the creation of the other things also, [Note: Col. 0571D: Distinction 12.] and especially concerning the division of the works of the seven days. “In the beginning,” Scripture says, “God created heaven,” that is, the angels, “and earth,” namely, the matter of the four elements, still confused and unformed. The Greeks called this *chaos*. He also calls that earth “the abyss,” saying: “And darkness was upon the face of the abyss,” because it was confused and mingled. That earth—that is, unformed matter—was also called water, over which the Spirit of the Lord was borne, just as an artisan’s will is borne over the things being fashioned.

Augustine says:

> “Darkness is not something; it is simply the absence of light. Just as silence is not some thing, but where there is no sound it is called silence; and nakedness is not some thing, but where there is no covering upon the body it is called nakedness; likewise emptiness is not something, but a place is said to be empty where there is no body, and emptiness is the absence of a body.”

Observe therefore, reader, that here Augustine says darkness is not something, whereas elsewhere darkness is named among the created things that bless the Lord, where it is said: “Bless the Lord, light and darkness” (Dan. III). Thus he says that darkness was then upon the face of the abyss because the light was lacking, which, if it had been present, would have rested above and been poured over it. But God had not yet adorned his work with the grace of light, which was later formed on the first day, when the Lord said: “Let there be light,” and light was made. Thus God divided light from darkness and called the light day and the darkness night (Gen. I).

[Col. 0571D] But if it is asked what kind of light that was—[Note: Col. 0571D: Distinction 13: “If it is asked.”] bodily or spiritual—we answer what we read as handed down by the holy Fathers. Augustine says that this light may be understood as bodily or spiritual. If it is understood spiritually, the angelic nature is meant: it was first unformed, but afterward formed when, turning to the Creator, it clung to him in charity. Its formation too is shown when it is said: “Let there be light, and light was made.” Thus this angelic nature was first darkness and afterward light, because it first possessed formlessness and imperfection, and then formation. Thus God divided light [Col. 0572A] from darkness.

[Note: Col. 0571D: In place of the authority of Augustine inserted here by the Master [Col. 0572D], blessed Martin introduced a passage from Isidore.]

Hence our patron, blessed Isidore, says:

> “Darkness should not be believed to possess substance because the Lord says through the prophet, ‘I am the Lord, forming and creating darkness’ (Isa. XLV). Rather, angelic nature which did not transgress is called light, while that which transgressed is designated by the name of darkness. Hence light is divided from darkness in the beginning. But because he created both the one and the other, he is therefore said to form light and create darkness; nevertheless, he not only created but also formed the good angels, while he only created the evil angels and did not form them. This must also be understood concerning good and evil human beings.

> “But if that light was bodily—which is certainly probable—it is understood to have been a luminous body, like a shining cloud, formed not from nothing [Col. 0572B] but formally from pre-existing matter, so that it might be light and possess the power of shining. With it the first day arose, since before light there was neither day nor night. That light therefore occupied the role and place of the sun. In its rising it revolved, distinguishing night and day. It is consequently probable that light first appeared where the sun appears as it travels in its daily course, so that, moving along the same path and first descending toward its setting, it made evening; then, recalled to its rising, it illuminated dawn—that is, morning. Thus God divided the light from the darkness and called the light day and the darkness night.”

[Note: Col. 0572D: Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 8.]

Therefore evening came first, and afterward morning; and thus one day of twenty-four hours was completed, [Col. 0572C] namely, the natural day, which had evening but not morning. Morning is called the end of the preceding day and the beginning of the following day: it is dawn, which has neither full light nor utter darkness. Therefore the first day did not have morning, because no preceding day existed whose end might mark the beginning of the following day; and especially because, once light appeared, a full and brilliant day immediately came upon the earth, beginning not with dawn but with full light, and completed by the morning of the following day.

Hence Bede, on Genesis:

> “It was fitting that the day should begin with light and extend to the morning of the following day, so that it might signify that the works of God began in light and were completed in light. The remaining days, however, had morning and evening: each began at its own morning and extended to the morning of the other [Col. 0572D] day.”

This is the natural order for distinguishing days: a day is distinguished and counted from morning to morning. Later, however, it was mystically ordained that a day should be reckoned from evening to evening and that the day should be joined with the preceding night in the calculation. Someone may perhaps ask: Why was the sun made if that light was sufficient for the day? One may answer: because, when the sun was made, the day’s light was increased. For afterward the day shone with far greater light than before.

Furthermore, it must be investigated how we should understand what Scripture says: “God said”—whether he said it temporally, or with a vocal sound, or in some other [Col. 0573A] manner. Augustine teaches in his work on Genesis that God spoke neither with a vocal sound nor temporally; for if temporally, then mutably. And if the voice of God is said to have sounded bodily, he had neither a tongue by which to speak nor anyone who needed to hear and understand.

Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain, says:

> “God did not say, ‘Let heaven be made in the beginning,’ as we fleetingly say, ‘Let something be made.’ Rather, it was said eternally in the one Word. If ‘Let there be’ had been spoken by God fleetingly, there would surely already have been some creature from which such a voice might be produced. But because before he said, ‘Let there be,’ no creature existed, that ‘Let there be,’ which was uttered in the eternity of the Word, was not pronounced in the sound of a voice. Therefore the voice of God is rightly referred to the nature of the Word, through whom all things were made.”

[Note: Col. 0573D: Here the Master lacks both this and the other passage from Isidore.]

God therefore said, “Let there be light,” and so forth, not temporally and not with a vocal sound, but in the Word co-eternal with himself; that is, before all times he begot the Word, in whom he possessed and eternally ordered that this should come to be in time, and in whom it was made. Therefore evening and morning came to be: one day.

Hence blessed Isidore says:

> “The first day made was the angels, who, to indicate unity, is called not the first day but one day; and for that reason it is always repeated in the account of creation. This day—that is, angelic nature—when it contemplated creation itself, in some sense was becoming evening; yet it did not remain in the contemplation of it, but referred its praise to God, and, beholding it more excellently in the divine reason, immediately became morning. But if, neglecting the Creator, it remained in the sight of the creature, it would no longer be evening but certainly night.”

[Note: Col. 0573D: Ibid.]

As the creature knows itself better in God than in itself, this knowledge of itself—which is greater in God—is called day and light. Its knowledge of itself in itself, however, compared with that which is in God, is far inferior and is called evening. Therefore morning followed evening because, when the creature recognized that its self-knowledge did not suffice for it to know itself more fully, it referred itself to God, in whom, by knowing itself, it became more perfectly day.

Concerning the work of the second day, on which the firmament was made [Note: Col. 0573D: Distinction 14.]:

God also said: “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters.” And he divided the waters that were beneath the firmament from those that [Col. 0573D] were above the firmament. It should be known, as venerable Bede says on Genesis, that the creation described here is of that heaven in which the stars are fixed. Beneath it are waters in the air and on the earth, and above it are other waters, of which it is said: “You cover its upper regions with waters” (Ps. CIII). Therefore the firmament, namely the starry heaven, being in the midst of the waters, may be believed to have been made from waters. For crystal, a stone of great hardness and transparency, is made from water. But if anyone is troubled by how waters, fluid by nature and liable to flow downward, can remain above heaven, I remember that it is written of God: “He binds the waters in his clouds” (Job XXVI). He who binds beneath heaven waters temporarily held in the vapours of clouds can also suspend waters above the sphere of heaven, not with vaporous thinness but with icy solidity, lest they fall. What they are like and for what purpose they were created, he who created them knows.

It is also asked [Note: Col. 0573D: Ibid.: “It is also customary to ask.”] whether heaven stands still or moves. If it moves, they ask, how is it a firmament? But if it stands still, how do the stars fixed in it revolve? Yet it may be called a firmament not because of standing still, but because of firmness, or because it is the impassable boundary of the waters. And if it stands still, nothing prevents the stars from moving and making their circuit.

Hence the eminent teacher Isidore says:

> “*Aethera* is the place in which the stars are, and it signifies that fire which has been separated upward from the whole world. Strictly speaking, *aether* is the element itself; *aethera*, however, is the brightness of the ether, and the word is Greek. The sphere of heaven is so called because its form is rounded. Everything of that kind is called a *sphaera* by the Greeks from its rolling motion, as are the balls with which children play. For philosophers say that heaven is convex on every side in the shape of a sphere, equal in all its parts, enclosing the earth poised in the middle mass of the world. They say that it moves, and that, with its motion, the stars fixed in it travel round from east to west, making shorter circuits near the north.

> “The axis is a straight northern line passing through the middle ball of the sphere [Col. 0574C]; and it is called an axis because upon it the sphere turns like a wheel, or because the wagon is there. The poles are the extreme parts of the axis; they are called pivots because heaven turns through them. The poles are the circles that run through the axis. One is northern, never sets, and is called Boreas; the other is southern, never seen, and is called *austronotius*. They are called poles because they are the circles of the axes, named from the practice of wagons, namely from polishing. But the northern pole is always visible, and the southern is never visible, because the right-hand regions of heaven are pressed higher by the south wind. The convex parts are the outermost regions of heaven, so called from their curvature; for what is convex is curved, sloping, and bent round in a circular form. The Milky Circle is a path visible in the sphere, named from its whiteness because it is white. Some say that it is the path traversed by the sun and that it shines in this way from the passage of its radiance.”

[Note: Col. 0573D: This authority too is not found in the Master. Col. 0574D: Book XIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5. “*Aethera*”: rather, *aether*, for *aethera*, as used here, is something else.]

> “This habitation of heaven, divided into circular zones, has allowed certain regions to be inhabited because of their temperate climate, but has denied others because of excessive cold or heat. There are five zones, called zones or circles because they exist in the revolution of the sphere. The first circle is called Arctic because within it are seen the signs of the Bears [Col. 0575A], which our people, imagining them in the shape of bears, call the northern constellations. The second circle is called the summer tropic because, when the sun makes summer for northern regions in that circle, it does not pass beyond it but immediately returns; hence it is called tropic. The third circle is the winter circle, called by the Latins the equinoctial because, when the sun comes to that orbit, it produces the equinox. For *hiemerinus* in Latin means day and night; at this circle one half of the sphere is seen. The fourth circle is called Antarctic because it is opposite to the circle we call Arctic. The fifth circle is the winter tropic, called by the Latins wintry or brumal, because, when the sun comes to that circle [Col. 0575B], it causes winter for those in the north and summer for those dwelling in the southern regions.”

[Note: Col. 0574D: Isidore, chapter 6.]

Having briefly stated these matters concerning the sphere of heaven and the five zones from blessed Isidore, we must again say something, for the readers’ benefit, about the work of the third day as explained by the holy Fathers:

God also said: “Let the waters under heaven be gathered into one place, and let dry land appear.” [Note: Col. 0575D: The Master, in the place cited above: “There follows.”] The work of the third day is the gathering of waters. The waters under heaven were therefore gathered into one basin, so that the light which during the preceding two days had surveyed the waters with brilliant light might shine more brightly in the clear air, and so that the earth which was hidden might appear, and, being moist with waters, might become dry and fit for producing shoots.

[Col. 0575C] Concerning the work of the fourth day, when the luminaries were made, let us add something again. God also said: “Let there be luminaries in the firmament of heaven, and let them divide day and night.” Therefore, because heaven excels the other elements in beauty and was made before the others, it is adorned before the others with sun, moon, and stars on the fourth day. These were made to illuminate the lower part, namely the earth, lest it be dark for its inhabitants. Provision was thus made for human weakness: as the sun moves around, human beings might enjoy the alternation of day and night because of the need for sleeping and waking. This was also done lest the night remain unattractive, but that human beings might be comforted by the moon and stars when the necessity of working or walking at night [Col. 0575D] lay upon them, and because certain animals cannot endure light.

But it is customary to ask how the following should be understood: “Let them be for signs and seasons, and days and years.” We should answer that by the seasons produced through the stars we must understand not intervals of hours but changes in atmospheric conditions, because such signs are made known to us as are days and years, which we commonly know. For signs of fair or stormy weather and seasons arise; and by them we distinguish the four seasons of the year: spring, summer, autumn, and winter.

[Note: Col. 0575D: Distinction 15.]

Concerning [Col. 0576A] the work of the fifth day, when God created birds and swimming creatures from the waters:

God said: “Let the waters bring forth the creeping thing of living soul, and birds above the earth,” and so forth. The work of the fifth day is the formation of fish and birds, by which two elements are adorned. From the same matter—that is, from waters—he created fish and birds, raising the flying creatures into the air, but sending the swimming creatures back into the deep.

Concerning the work of the sixth day, when animals and creeping things of the earth were created:

God also said: “Let the earth bring forth living soul: cattle, creeping things, and beasts according to their kinds.” The work of the sixth day is described when the earth is said to be adorned with its animals. It is customary to ask concerning venomous and harmful creatures whether they were created after human sin for punishment, or whether they were instead created harmless and afterward began to harm sinners. Certainly it may be said that, when created, they would have harmed no human being if he had not sinned. They began to harm for the punishment of vices, or for the testing and even perfecting of virtue. Thus they were created harmless, but because of sin they became harmful.

Hence blessed Isidore says:

> “Evil was not created by the devil but invented by him; and therefore nothing is evil, because without God nothing was made. But God did not make evil (Wis. I). There was nowhere, nor ever, evil from which the devil might be made evil; rather, because it is a vice, when he was a good angel he became evil through pride, and therefore evil is rightly said to have been invented by him. There is no nature of evil [Note: Col. 0576D: Add ‘it is evident,’ from Isidore, and the sense will be more complete.], because every nature is either unchangeable, as God is, or changeable, [Col. 0576C] as a creature is. But evil is no nature because, entering a good nature, it makes it vicious. When it departs, the nature remains and the evil which was present is nowhere.

> “From the fact that vice harms nature it is recognized that vice is not nature, because nothing natural harms. When a good nature is condemned because of an evil will, that evil will itself testifies to the goodness of nature: it testifies so greatly that God does not leave it unpunished for evil. Heretics believe that the mind was created by God and vice by the devil. Hence they suppose two natures, one good and one evil. But vice is not a nature; though it truly comes from the devil, it was nevertheless not created by him. For what reason did God permit a state of evil to arise, except that he might adorn the good of nature from contrary evils?

> “This device is also found in speech. It is called *antitheton*, which in Latin is called ‘opposed’ or ‘counterposed’; and it produces beautiful expression when contrary things are immediately set forth in place of favorable things. Thus evil is mingled among things so that the good of nature may excel by comparison with evil. God made all things very good. Therefore nothing is evil by nature, since even those things which appear punitive among creatures, if used well, are both good and beneficial; if used badly, they harm. [Col. 0577A] Thus a creature must be judged not good from our use of it, but very good from its own nature. If you shave a man’s eyebrow, you remove a small thing, but introduce ugliness into the whole body. So too, if in the universe of creation you call even the least worm evil by nature, you do injustice to the whole creation.

> “All evils were transmitted through the sin of the first human being as punishment to the entire human race. Hence whatever appear to be evils rage among us partly because of our origin, partly because of fault. Perverse people call many things among creatures evil: fire because it burns, iron because it kills, a wild beast because it bites. But, not attending to their benefits, a human being accuses in them what should rather be imputed to himself: for because of his sin these things became harmful to him, though before sin they had in part been subjected to that human being. Therefore, through our fault and not through their nature, things that harm us are evil to us.

> “For though light is good, it is harmful to diseased eyes; in that case the defect is in the eyes, not in the light. So too with the rest. When a human being is scourged by the stings of creatures and the adversities of the elements, the punishment of sin requires that the human being who was proud against God should suffer adversity from things below himself. Hence it is read in Wisdom: ‘The world of the earth will fight for God against the foolish’ (Wis. V). It is therefore deservedly because of sins that things naturally beneficial are changed into adversities for human beings. Hence Solomon also says: ‘Creation burns fiercely in punishment against the unjust, and is gentler in doing good to those who trust in God’ (Wis. XVI).

> “Thus flesh will not be subject to soul, nor vices to reason, if the mind is not subject to its Creator. But all things below us are rightly subjected to us when we are subjected to him by whom they have been subjected to us. For even the things that appear subject to one who is not subject to God are rather those to which that person is subjected, because he subjects his will to the love of things which he thinks are subject to him. Therefore, as was said above, animals were created harmless, but through sin they became harmful.”

[Note: Col. 0575D: Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 9. Col. 0576D: You will seek this passage in the Master in vain.]

There follows: “God completed his work on the seventh day, and rested from all his work which he had accomplished.” [Note: Col. 0577D: The Master, cited above: now concerning the seventh day.] God is said to have rested on the seventh day, not as though weary from working, but he rested from all work because he ceased to make a new creature. [Col. 0577D] For to rest is said to mean to cease. Hence it is read in the Apocalypse: “The living creatures had no rest, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy’” (Apoc. IV), that is, they did not cease to speak. He is therefore said to have rested because he ceased to make kinds of creatures. Yet even now, as Truth says in the Gospel, the Father works with the Son (John V), administering the same kinds which were then established. For the Creator’s power is the cause of the continued existence of every creature. Thus the saying, “My Father works until now, and I work,” signifies the governance of the whole creation.

Therefore, God is said to have created nothing new on the seventh day, unless perhaps he is said [Col. 0578A] to have completed his work on the seventh day because he blessed and sanctified it, as Scripture says: “God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it” (Gen. I). For blessing and sanctification are a work. Solomon too performed a work when he dedicated the temple. Thus God is said to have sanctified and blessed that day because he endowed it with a mystical blessing and sanctification above the rest. Hence it is said in the Law: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX).

There follows: “God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good.” All things were indeed naturally good and had no defect in their own nature. The things God created are each individually good. Taken together, however, they are very good, because from all of them consists the wonderful beauty of the universe, in which even that which is called evil, being well ordered and placed in its own position, more conspicuously commends its goods, so that they may be more pleasing and praiseworthy.

Hence blessed Isidore says:

> “Creation was not seen by God seven times and praised seven times, since before it was made it was perfectly seen by him. But when we see and praise individual things, it is as though he sees and praises through us, as in the saying: ‘It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father’ (Matt. X). Therefore, just as he speaks through us, so he sees and praises through us; yet through himself he sees eternally and everlastingly, but through us temporally. Observe that creation is universally called very good in the beginning, but individually only good, because the members of a body, though individually good, nevertheless constitute a greater good when all together make one very good body.”

[Note: Col. 0577D: Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 8.]
