There follows concerning the creation of the human being [Note: Col. 0578D: Distinction 16.]. Here these matters seem to require consideration: why a human being was created, how he was established, what he was like, and how he was made; then how he fell, and finally how and through whom he was restored.

God also said: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” In the phrase “Let us make,” the one operation of the three persons is shown. But in the phrase “in our image and likeness,” the one and equal substance of the three persons is shown. For this is said from the person of the Father to the Son and the Holy Spirit. He did not [Col. 0578D] say this to the angels, as some suppose, because God and angels do not share one and the same image or likeness. In this passage, “image and likeness” are understood either as the uncreated essence of the Trinity, according to which the human being was made, or as the created image and likeness in which the human being was made and which was created together with the human being.

Hence the Apostle says: “Man indeed is the image and glory of God” (I Cor. XI). Blessed Isidore says:

> “The human being is a great portion of the whole creation, and surpasses the rest by as much as he is nearer to the divine image. How greatly a human being surpasses other creatures in the dignity of virtue is learned from the very reverence of his creation: God said that all things should be made, and they were made; but when he wished to create [Col. 0579A] the human being, he did so with a certain deliberation of eternal counsel, saying, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’

> “Because we were naturally made good, by the deserved consequence of fault we have in a sense been made evil contrary to nature. As God foresaw that man would sin, so he also foresaw how he would restore him by his grace, although man could perish through his own choice. Adam and Eve were originally created together; but afterward the woman was formed specially from the side of the man. They were created together in the order of reason, certainly, not in one and the same moment of time. The man was made in the image of God; the woman, however, was formed in the image of the man, and for that reason is subject to him by the law of nature. Woman was created for the help of man; but man was made for his own sake.”

[Note: Col. 0578D: Ibid., chapter 11.]

The human being was therefore made in the image and likeness of God with respect to the mind, by which he surpasses irrational animals. He is in the image because of memory, understanding, and love; but in the likeness because of innocence and justice, which naturally belong to the rational mind. Or the image is considered in the knowledge of truth and the likeness in the love of virtue. Or the image is in other virtues, while the likeness is in essence, because it is immortal and indivisible.

Hence Augustine says:

> “The soul was made like God because God made it immortal and indissoluble. Image therefore belongs to form, likeness to nature. Thus the human being was made, according to the soul, in the image and likeness not of the Father or the Son or even the Holy Spirit individually, but of the whole Trinity. In this sense too the human being is said, according to the soul, to be the image of God, because the image of God is in him; just as a panel and a painting are called an image because of the picture which is upon them, and the panel itself is called an image together with it. Therefore the human being was made in the image of God; but the Son is image, not made in the image, because he is begotten, not created, equal and unlike in nothing. The human being was created by God, not begotten—not equal by parity, but approaching through a certain likeness.”

[Col. 0579C]

Several questions are commonly asked concerning the origin of the soul [Note: Col. 0579D: Distinction 17.], namely, from what it was created and what grace it possessed in its creation. Just as the formation of the human being according to the body is described when it is said, “God formed [Col. 0579D] man from the mud of the earth,” so the making of the same human being according to the soul is described when it is added: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life.” God formed the body from the mud of the earth and breathed a soul into it—not that he blew with his throat or formed the body with hands. God is spirit and is not composed of the features of bodily members. Therefore we must not think carnally that God formed the body with corporeal hands and breathed into man with his throat. Rather, he formed the human being’s body from the mud of the earth by commanding and willing—that is, he willed and commanded by his Word that it should be so made.

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a soul”: that is, he created the substance of the soul [Col. 0580A], in which the human being might live, not from any bodily or spiritual matter but from nothing.

Hence blessed Isidore says:

> “The soul is not a part of the divine substance or nature, nor does it exist before it is joined to the body; rather, it is created when the body is created, with which it seems to be mixed. The opinions of philosophers say that the soul exists before it is born in the body, but no evidence establishes this as true. For we ourselves do not know whether we existed before, nor do we have any human guide [the reading is uncertain]. Therefore we should not seek what, when sought, is more deserving of ridicule. Pagans and heretics attempt to dispute about the soul; but how can they rightly think anything about it when they do not know the Author in whose image it was made? Hence they have said many things deserving of error.

> “[Col. 0580B] Some heretics also thought that God created the soul from his own substance, stubbornly adhering to the words of Scripture which say: ‘He breathed into his face the breath of life.’ For when a human being breathes, they say, he emits breath from himself. Therefore, since God is said to have breathed a breath into the face, it is understood that he sent forth from himself the human spirit—that is, from his own substance. But those who say this do not understand that ‘he breathed’ is said tropically, that is, figuratively: he made the human breath, namely the soul. For to breathe is to make breath. Therefore those who suppose that the soul is a part of God must not be heard. For if it were so, it could be deceived neither by itself nor by another, could not be compelled either to do or to suffer evil, and could change neither for better [Col. 0580C] nor for worse.”

But it is customary to ask whether souls are created in the body or outside the body. Some say that the human soul is created in the body, explaining the words, “He breathed into his face the breath of life,” thus: he created the soul in the body, so that it might give life to the whole body. For he specifically mentioned the face because this part is furnished with senses for beholding higher things. Therefore it must be known with complete certainty that souls are created in the body: in creating them God infuses them, and in infusing them creates them.

It should further be noted that God did not create the human being by stages of age, as he now forms one in the mother’s womb, but suddenly made him in the age of manhood. Hence [Col. 0580D] Augustine says in his work on Genesis:

> “Adam was immediately made at the age of manhood, and this according to higher, not lower, causes—that is, according to the will and power of God—just as Moses’ rod was immediately changed into a serpent.”

God therefore took the man thus formed and placed him in the paradise of delight, as Scripture teaches (Gen. II), which He had planted from the beginning. By these words Moses plainly indicates that man was created outside paradise and afterwards placed in paradise. This is said to have been done because he was not to remain there permanently, so that this should be understood as signifying not nature but grace. Paradise, however, is understood as a local and bodily place, in which man was placed and spoke. There are three general opinions concerning paradise: one, namely, of those who wish paradise to be understood only bodily; another, of those who understand it only spiritually; a third, of those who understand paradise in both ways.

[Note: [Col. 0581D] After this one should perhaps read: “I confess that the third opinion pleases me: that man was placed in a bodily paradise. Now it must be considered from what beginning paradise was planted, which from that beginning, etc.” Thus the sense is more suitable and more in agreement with Augustine, Bede [Col. 0582D], and the Gloss, from whom the Master took these things, and our author from him.]

Now it must be considered from what beginning paradise was planted. Hence the Venerable Bede:

> “That man was placed in a bodily paradise, which may be understood as planted from that beginning when, after the waters had been removed, He commanded the whole earth to produce grass and trees. Although it bears a figure of the present or future Church, it must nevertheless be understood to be a most pleasant place, great with fruitful trees, watered by a great spring. But what we call ‘from the beginning,’ the ancient translation calls ‘toward the east.’ Hence they maintain that it lies in the eastern region, secluded and elevated, with a great expanse of sea or land intervening between it and the regions inhabited by men, reaching up to the lunar sphere. Therefore even the waters of the Flood did not reach it.”

Concerning this, blessed Isidore says:

[Note: [Col. 0582D] Book XIV of the *Etymologies*, ch. 3.]

> “Paradise is a place situated in the eastern regions; its name, translated from Greek into Latin, means ‘garden’; in Hebrew it is called *Eden*, which in our language is interpreted ‘delights.’ Combined, the two make ‘garden of delights.’ For it is planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree, and it also has the tree of life, from whose fruit whoever eats shall always remain immortal in the same state. Of it it is said: ‘See lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live for ever’ (Gen. [Col. 0581C] III). It is a place distinguished by every delight, inaccessible to human beings because it is surrounded by a fiery wall reaching to heaven. There is no cold there, no summer, but the perpetual mildness of spring. From its midst a spring rises and waters the whole paradise; it is divided into four rivers, which flow below paradise into the earth, though they are carried onward through far-distant regions.”

[Note: [Col. 0582D] Isidore, Book XIII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 21.]

> “For the river Ganges, which Sacred Scripture calls Phison, rises from Mount Oreabares and proceeds toward the regions of India. It is called Phison—that is, ‘multitude’—because it is filled by ten great rivers joined to it, and, flowing eastward, is received by Ocean. It is called Ganges from Gangarus, king of India. It is said to rise like the Nile and burst forth over the lands of the East.  
> 
> The river Geon, [Col. 0581D] like the Ganges, comes forth from paradise near Mount Atlas, but is immediately swallowed up by the earth. Running through Persia by a hidden course, it pours forth again on the shore of the Red Sea; circling Ethiopia, it flows through Egypt and, divided into seven mouths, enters the great sea near Alexandria. It is called Aeeon because, through the increase of its overflowing, it irrigates the land of Egypt. For *gē* in Greek means ‘earth’ in Latin. Among the Egyptians it is called Nile because of the mud which it carries, which produces fertility. Hence [Col. 0582A] it too is called Nile, as though *neaniai naaion* [reading uncertain]. Formerly, indeed, the Nile was called *Nelo* in Latin. It appears in Lake Nilides, from which Egypt receives it toward the south; there, driven back by northern winds, it swells as the waters are thrust backward and causes Egypt’s inundation.
> 
> “The river Tigris of Mesopotamia, rising from paradise and proceeding toward the Assyrians, after many windings flows into the Dead Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, running with the extreme swiftness of the beast.
> 
> “The river Euphrates of Mesopotamia rises from paradise, is exceedingly rich in gems, and flows through the midst of Babylon. It received its name from crops or abundance. For *Ephrata* in Hebrew is interpreted ‘fertility.’ The Euphrates in some places irrigates Mesopotamia as the Nile does Alexandria. Sallust, a most reliable author, asserts that the Tigris and Euphrates flow from one spring in Armenia; proceeding by different routes, they divide far apart, leaving between them a space of many miles. Yet the land enclosed by them is called Mesopotamia.”

In this paradise, therefore, as was said above,

[Note: [Col. 0582D] The Master, as above.]

there were trees of various kinds, among which one was called the tree of life, while another was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The tree of life was so called, as the Venerable Bede teaches, because it had divinely received this power: whoever ate of its fruit would have his body strengthened by stable health and perpetual soundness [Col. 0582C], and would not decline into worsening or decay through any sickness or frailty of age.

But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil received this name not from its nature but from the occasion of the event that afterwards followed. That tree was not evil; but it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, after the prohibition, transgression was to occur in relation to it, by which man would learn through experience what lay between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. Thus the name was not given because of a fruit that might be known from it, but because of the event following transgression. Before touching this tree, man knew good and evil: good through prudence and experience, but evil through prudence alone. He came to know it through experience [Col. 0582D] when he usurped the forbidden tree, because by experiencing evil he learned what lay between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience. But if the first parents had been obedient and had not sinned against the commandment, it would nevertheless not have been called any less the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because this would have resulted from its use if it had been usurped. Man, therefore, was forbidden the tree, which was not evil; there even the preservation of the commandment would have been good for him, while transgression would have been evil.

It follows: “The Lord cast a sleep upon Adam.” [Col. 0583A] “And when he had fallen asleep, He took one of his ribs and formed it into a woman.” Here one must consider

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Distinction 18.]

why God did not create man and woman together, as He did the angels, but first the man and then the woman from the man. It was so, namely, that there might be one beginning of the human race, so that in this both the devil’s pride might be confounded and human humility exalted by likeness to God. For the devil had desired to be a principle other than God; and therefore, so that his pride might be struck down, man received as a gift what the devil perversely wished to seize but could not obtain. Through this the image of God appeared in man. For as God is the principle of creation for all things, so man is the principle of generation for all human beings. God also wished all human beings to arise from one man, [Col. 0583B] so that, while all recognized themselves to be from one, they might love themselves as though one.

The woman was formed not from just any part of the man’s body but from his side, to show that she was created for companionship in love; lest, if she had been made from his head, she might seem to be set above the man for dominion, or, if from his feet, to be subjected to servitude. Therefore, because she is proved by right to be neither mistress nor slave, but companion, she was to be brought forth neither from the head nor from the feet, but from the side, so that he might know he ought to place beside himself her whom he had learned was taken from his own side.

Not without reason, too, was the rib taken from the sleeping rather than the waking man, from which woman was formed [Col. 0583C] as the man’s helper in generation. This was so that he might be shown to have felt no pain, and that the wondrous work of divine power might be demonstrated: it opened the side of a sleeping man and nevertheless did not awaken him from the sleep of rest. In this work also the mystery of Christ and the Church was prefigured; for as woman was formed from the side of the sleeping man, so the Church comes from the sacraments which flowed from the side of Christ sleeping on the cross—namely blood and water—by which we are redeemed from punishments and washed from sins.

Thus from the substance of the rib alone, without any extraneous addition, multiplied in itself by divine power, the woman’s body was made, by the same miracle through which later five thousand men were fed from five loaves of Jesus multiplied by heavenly blessing [Col. 0583D] (Mark VI). It must also be known that, although the formation of the woman was effected through the ministry of angels, the power of creation must not be attributed to them. Angels cannot create any creature. God alone—that is, the Trinity—is Creator. Therefore the woman was made by God, even if the rib was supplied through angels.

Man in his first state was rational,

[Note: [Col. 0583D] Distinction 23: “And indeed.”]

having discernment of good and evil. It is reasonably thought that, immediately upon being created, he received knowledge of created things and cognition fitting to his first perfection. Before the Fall he also possessed a threefold knowledge: of things made for his sake, of the Creator, [Col. 0584A] and of himself. He had knowledge of things, since it was neither the Creator Himself nor any angel, but man himself, who assigned names to all animals, in order to show that he possessed knowledge of each one. Of all the things created for him and to be governed and ordered by him, God granted him knowledge and entrusted him with foresight and care, so that they might be subjected to his dominion and governed by his reason; thus he might know how to provide necessities for those from which he was to receive the benefit or assistance of temporal life. For, as the Apostle says: “Is God concerned for oxen?” (I Cor. IX).

The first man is also believed to have had knowledge of his Creator. For he knew by whom he had been created, through a certain inward inspiration by which he contemplated God’s presence; yet not as excellently as the saints shall see after this life, nor in an enigma as we see in this life. Man likewise had such knowledge of himself that he was not ignorant of what he owed to one above him, to an equal, and to one below him. He understood also his condition and order: why and what kind of being he had been made, how he ought to proceed, what he ought to do, and what he ought to avoid. If he had not possessed this knowledge, he would not have been guilty of transgression. But neither man nor angel was in any way foreknowing of his own fall.

[Note: [Col. 0584D] Distinction 19: “Several questions are commonly asked.”]

In the first state, namely before sin, man had the power to die and the power not to die; and this was the first immortality of the human body, namely the power not to die. In the second state, namely [Col. 0584C] after sin, he had the power to die and the inability not to die, because in this state there is necessity of dying. In the third state he will have the inability to die, because impossibility of dying belongs to that state; this will be by grace, not by nature. Man is said in the first state to have been made “into a living soul,” that is, giving life to the body, though through the support of food. Before sin, he had from the tree of life the power not to die, not from nature. For this reason he is said to have been able not to die: he was able to use the tree of life, by not eating from which he would die.

[Note: [Col. 0584D] Distinction 20.]

If the first human beings had not sinned, they would have entered into union without sin and stain in the bodily paradise; there would have been an unstained marriage-bed and intercourse [Col. 0584D] without concupiscence, and they would have commanded their sexual organs as they did their other limbs, so that they would have felt no unlawful movement there. Just as we bring other bodily members to other members—for example, the hand to the mouth—without the burning of lust, so they would have used their sexual members without the itching of the flesh. For this deadly sickness attached itself to human members as a result of the sin of transgression.

But concerning the time at which they would be transferred to spiritual and heavenly life, Scripture hands down nothing certain; and therefore it is uncertain whether, after the parents had begotten children and the righteousness of human duty had been fulfilled, they would be transferred to a better state, not through death [Col. 0585A] but through some change; or whether the parents would remain in some state of life, using the tree of life, until their children reached the same state, and then, once the number had been completed, all would together be transferred to better things, so as to be like the holy angels in heaven.

Why, then, did they not cultivate paradise? Because immediately after the woman’s creation transgression took place, and they were expelled from paradise. Some teachers reasonably hold that the children of the first parents would have been born small and then, over intervals of time, would have received growth in stature and the use of their limbs under the same law by which we now see birth ordered; thus in them an age for walking and speaking would have been awaited, as now in us. This would certainly not have been imputed to a fault, but to the condition of nature.

[Col. 0585B] It is asked whether, just as infants would have been born small in bodily stature, they would likewise have been born small in mental understanding and advanced with the passage of time in understanding and knowledge of truth; or whether they would have been perfect in these matters as soon as they were born. The reasonable answer is this: just as they would have advanced over the passage of time in bodily stature and use of limbs, so at the beginning of birth they would have been imperfect in understanding, and would have advanced in understanding and knowledge through intervals of time until perfection. Such was the constitution of man before sin, according to the condition of the body: he was to be transferred from this state, together with all his offspring, to a better and worthier state, where he would enjoy the heavenly and eternal good prepared for him in heaven. For as man is compounded [Col. 0585C] from a twofold nature, so the Creator prepared two goods for him from the beginning: one temporal and the other eternal; one visible and the other invisible; one for the flesh and the other for the spirit. And because “the natural comes first, then the spiritual” (I Cor. XV), He first gave the temporal and visible good, but promised the invisible and eternal good and set it forth as something to be sought through merits.

Now something must be said concerning the devil’s envy,

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Distinction 21.]

by which he approached man. Seeing that man could ascend through the humility of obedience to the place from which he himself had fallen through pride, the devil envied him. He who had first become a devil—that is, one cast downward—through pride, became Satan—that is, an adversary—through the zeal of envy.

[Col. 0585D] Why, then, did he first come to the woman? Namely, because he knew that reason was less vigorous in her than in the man. His malice, timid in testing virtue, attacked human nature in the part where it appeared weaker, so that, if perhaps he prevailed there in some measure, he might afterwards proceed more confidently to assault—or rather overthrow—the other part, which was stronger. He first tested the woman when she was alone, in order first to try in her the whole force of his temptation.

Why did the devil come in an alien form to tempt? Because he could not harm them by force, he turned to fraud, in order to trip up man by deceit whom he could not overcome by strength. [Col. 0586A] Yet, lest his fraud be too evident, he did not come in his own appearance, lest he be openly recognized and thus repelled. Again, lest the fraud perhaps be too concealed to guard against, and man seem at the same time to suffer an injury if God allowed him to be deceived in such a manner, he was permitted to come in an alien form, but one in which his malice could readily be detected.

Why did he come to tempt only in the form of a serpent? One must answer that his not coming in his own form was due to the will of the same evil enemy himself; but his coming in a form suited to the character of his malice was brought about by divine action. Thus he came to the woman in a serpent, though perhaps he would have preferred to come in the appearance of a dove; but it was not fitting that that evil spirit [Col. 0586B] should make odious to man the form in which the Holy Spirit was to appear.

Why is the serpent called more cunning than all the animals of the earth? Namely, because, as Augustine says, evil angels, although cast down through pride, nevertheless surpass all beasts by nature owing to the eminence of reason, although the serpent can be called most wise not because it has a rational soul but because of the devil’s spirit. Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*:

> “It must not be thought that the devil chose the serpent through which he might tempt; rather, when he wished to deceive, he could not do so except through the animal through which he was permitted. The will to harm is in him, but the power is from God. The devil spoke through the ignorant serpent as he speaks through the possessed or the frenzied. For he used the serpent as though it were an instrument, moving its nature to produce the sounds of words and signs by which he might display his will. Therefore the serpent neither understood those things nor was made rational. It was called most cunning because of the devil’s craftiness. Thus the serpent spoke as Balaam’s ass did (Num. XXII), but that was angelic and this was diabolical. The woman therefore did not shrink from the serpent because she thought it had received from God an office of speech.”

The temptation took place in this way. Standing before the woman, the proud enemy did not dare to proceed at once to persuasive words, fearing detection; instead, he approached her in the form of a question, so that from her response he might gather how he could advance in malice. “Why,” [Col. 0586D] he said, “did God command you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman answered him: “We eat of the fruit of the trees which are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of paradise, He commanded us not to eat it or touch it, lest perhaps we die.” In this saying she gave room for temptation when she said, “lest perhaps we die.” Therefore the devil immediately said to the woman: “You shall not die at all. For God knows that on whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

Observe the sequence in the progress of human ruin. First God said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die the death.” Then the woman [Col. 0587A] said: “Lest perhaps we die.” Finally the serpent said: “You shall not die at all.” God affirmed; the woman spoke as though doubting; the devil denied. Therefore she who doubted departed from the One affirming and drew near to the one denying—that is, to the devil.

The ancient enemy tempted man in three ways: by gluttony in persuading him to eat, when he said, “On whatever day you eat”; by vainglory in promising divinity, when he said, “You shall be like gods”; and by avarice in promising knowledge, when he said, “You shall know good and evil.” Gluttony is an immoderate appetite for food; vainglory, love of one’s own excellence; avarice, an immoderate desire for possession. It is not merely a desire for money, but also for eminence and knowledge, when exaltation is sought beyond measure. Therefore man, who had an instigator toward evil, not unjustly had a restorer toward good. But because the devil sinned without anyone’s temptation, he ought not to be helped through another, nor could he be helped through himself; thus his sin proved incurable. Human sin, however, as it had its beginning through another—that is, through the devil—so fittingly had its remedy through another, that is, Christ.

Here it seems necessary to investigate carefully the origin and root of that sin. Some think that a certain self-exaltation in the human mind preceded it, through which he yielded to the devil’s suggestion. Augustine seems to intimate this in *On Genesis*, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0587D] Distinction 22.]

> “It must not be thought that man was cast down from the state [Col. 0587C] of rectitude unless a certain exaltation requiring repression had first occurred in him, so that through the humility of sin he might know how falsely he had presumed concerning himself; and that neither angelic nor human nature is in a good condition if it departs from its Maker.”

Finally, the woman, not content with the serpent’s suggestion, saw that the tree was good for eating and beautiful to behold, not believing that she could die from it; or perhaps she thought God had said this for some symbolic reason. Therefore she ate, and gave to her husband—perhaps with some persuasion, which Scripture leaves to be understood; or perhaps persuasion was unnecessary, since the man did not see her dead from eating that food. Therefore, just as the devil was not permitted to tempt the woman except through the serpent, so neither was he permitted to tempt the man except through the woman; so that as God’s command came through the man to the woman, so the devil’s temptation might pass through the woman to the man.

It is commonly asked whether such self-exaltation, love of one’s own power, existed in the man as in the woman. The answer is that Adam was not deceived in the manner in which the woman was. He did not think true what the devil suggested. Yet he may be believed to have been deceived in this: he considered a venial offence what was mortal. But he was not deceived first, nor in the same point as the woman, namely in believing that God had forbidden them to touch the tree because, if they touched it, they would become like gods. Thus some self-exaltation may have been present in his mind [Col. 0588A] immediately after the temptation, by which he wished to try the forbidden tree when he did not see the woman dead after receiving that food.

Hence Augustine, *On Genesis*: Although the Apostle shows that Adam was a transgressor when he says, “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V), he nevertheless denies that he was deceived when he says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman” (I Tim. II). Therefore, when questioned, he did not say, “The woman deceived me,” but, “She gave me, and I ate.” But the woman said: “The serpent deceived me.” The Apostle called this deception properly that through which what was being urged, although false, was thought true—namely, that God had forbidden touching that tree because, if they touched it, they would become like gods, as though He who had made them human beings begrudged them divinity. Adam [Col. 0588B] therefore was not deceived, because he did not think true what the devil urged, even if he touched the tree—that is, he did not believe himself able to be made equal to God.

From this it can plainly be seen which of them sinned more, Adam or Eve. The woman seems to have sinned more, for she wished to usurp equality with divinity and, lifted up by excessive presumption, believed that this would happen. Adam, however, did not believe this; and he considered repentance and God’s mercy when, yielding to his wife’s manner, he consented to her persuasion, unwilling to grieve her and leave her estranged from him, lest she perish. He judged the offence to be venial, not mortal. Therefore, after the woman had been deceived and eaten and had given to him that they might eat together, [Col. 0588C] he was unwilling to grieve her, whom he believed would waste away without his consolation and perish estranged from him.

He was joined to her not by fleshly

[Note: [Col. 0588D] The Master: “overcome.”]

concupiscence, which he had not yet felt, but by a certain friendly good will, through which it often happens that God is offended lest a friend be offended. That he ought not to have done this is shown by the just outcome of the divine judgment. From these things it may therefore be understood that the woman sinned more, for in her was the presumption of greater pride; she sinned against herself, her neighbor, and God. The man, however, sinned only against himself and God. It is also inferred that the woman sinned more because she was punished more severely, when it was said to her: “In pain you shall bear children,” and so forth. Although Eve sinned through ignorance in believing true what the devil urged, nevertheless [Col. 0588D] she was not ignorant that it was God’s command and that acting otherwise was sin; therefore she could not be excused from sin through ignorance. For there is an ignorance that excuses the sinner and an ignorance that does not excuse. Moreover, there is vincible ignorance and invincible ignorance. Every excuse is removed where the commandment is not unknown.

There is a threefold ignorance: that of those who are unwilling to know although they can, which does not excuse and is sin; that of those who wish to know but cannot, which excuses and is a punishment of sin, not sin itself; and that of those who simply do not know, neither refusing nor proposing to know, which excuses no one fully [Col. 0589A] but perhaps results in less punishment. Hence blessed Augustine:

> “Excuse is taken away from those who know the commands of God—the excuse which people usually derive from ignorance. And although it is more serious to sin knowingly than unknowingly, one should not therefore flee to the darkness of ignorance in order to seek excuse in it. For it is one thing not to know and another to be unwilling to know: in those unwilling to understand, ignorance itself is sin; but in those unable to understand, it is the punishment of sin. But the ignorance belonging not to those unwilling to know, but to those who simply do not know, excuses no one in such a way that he does not burn in eternal fire, though perhaps he burns less.”

The woman, therefore, had no excuse from ignorance, since she knew the commands and was not ignorant that it was sin to act otherwise.

[Note: [Col. 0589D] Distinction 23: “Furthermore.”]

But why did God create those whom He foreknew would be evil? Namely, because He foresaw what good He would make from their evils. For He made them in such a way as to leave them the means by which they might do something; if they acted culpably, they would find Him working praiseworthily from themselves. Thus they have an evil will from themselves, but from Him a good nature and a just punishment.

Nor should this be passed over:

[Note: [Col. 0590D] Distinction 24.]

the order and progress of temptation now exists in every human being such as once occurred in the first human beings. For as then the serpent suggested evil to the woman, she consented, and then gave it to her husband, and thus [Col. 0589C] the deed was completed, so now in us the sensual motion of the soul stands for the serpent, the lower part of reason for the woman, and the higher part of reason for the man. This is the man who, according to the Apostle, is called “the image and glory of God”; and that is the woman who, according to the same Apostle, is called “the glory of man” (I Cor. XI). Between this man and this woman there is, as it were, a spiritual marriage and a natural bond: the higher part of reason, like the man, ought to preside and rule; the lower part, like the woman, ought to be subject and obey. Therefore, according to the Apostle, the man ought not to have a veil, but the woman ought (ibid.).

And as among all the animals no helper resembling man was found, but one was taken from him to be formed for him in marriage, so among the parts of the soul [Col. 0589D] which we share with beasts no helper resembling our mind is found. From this, therefore, one may understand how there exists in the human soul an image of that marriage, and how these three—the man, the woman, and the serpent—are present spiritually in each of us.

It remains to show how sin is completed in us through these three. If careful attention is given, it may be recognized here what mortal and venial sin are in the soul. For as there the serpent suggested to the woman and the woman to the man, so in us the sensual motion which we have in common with beasts, when it has conceived the enticement of sin, suggests, like a serpent, [Col. 0590A] to the woman, namely to the lower part of reason, that is, the reason of knowledge. If she consents to the enticement, the woman eats the forbidden tree. Afterwards she gives of the same thing to the man, when she suggests the same enticement to the higher part of reason, that is, the reason of wisdom. If it consents, then the man too tastes forbidden food with the woman.

Therefore, if the enticement of sin is retained only in sensual motion, the sin is venial and very slight. But if the lower part of reason consents, so that it is held merely by the pleasure of thought, without a will to carry it out, the woman alone eats, not the man; by whose authority the will is restrained from proceeding to action. But if there is a full will to carry it out, so that, if opportunity is present, it is brought to effect, the man also eats, because the higher part [Col. 0590B] of reason consents to the enticement; then the sin is damnable and grave.

When, however, the woman tastes without the man, the sin is sometimes mortal and sometimes venial. If the sin is not retained long in the pleasure of thought, but as soon as the woman has touched it is repelled by the man’s authority, it is venial. But if it is retained long in the pleasure of thought, even if the will to carry it out is absent, it is mortal; and for it both the man and the woman—that is, the whole person—will be condemned, because even then the man did not restrain the woman as he ought, and may thus be said to have consented.

We have written these things summarily as they were long ago expounded by the holy Fathers. Now, if it please you, dearest brethren, let us briefly set down again for your benefit what the things said above signify.

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Allegorically, heaven is the angels and earth is human beings; heaven is prelates and earth subjects; heaven is the perfect and earth the imperfect; heaven is contemplatives and earth the active; heaven also is spirit, earth is body. The creation of the primordial light is knowledge of sin. The firmament between the upper and lower waters is the division between vices and virtues. The gathering of the lower waters is the restraining of vices. The production of plants is the performance of good works. The creation of the two lights is recognition of perfect virtue. Fish are good action; birds, contemplation; the creation of animals, the restoration of bodily senses; Adam’s formation, the perfection of a righteous person; Adam in paradise, the righteous person in heaven.

[Col. 0590D] The primary light before the sun signifies the Law before grace, John before Christ, beginning before perfection, grace before the glory of angels. For as the primary light was earlier than the sun in time but less in brightness, so the Law before grace, John before Christ, beginning before perfection, and grace before glory are understood as prior in order, yet far inferior in perfection. The upper waters signify the good who are to be saved; the lower waters, the evil who are to be damned. Of the upper waters it is said: “Bless the Lord, waters that are above the heavens” (Dan. III), because the elect will not cease eternally to praise the Lord’s name. But of the lower waters it is said: “Let the waters be gathered [Col. 0591A] into one place” (Gen. I), because the reprobate, now dispersed throughout the whole world, shall be gathered into hell for punishment.

The holy teachers customarily understand Christ by the sun, the Church by the moon, and individual faithful persons by the individual stars. They understand Christ by the sun because, as the sun is perfect in itself and is not diminished, so Christ, because He is immeasurable, cannot be increased, and because He is eternal, cannot be diminished. The Church is signified by the moon because, as the moon is brought to fullness by daily increase, so the body of the Church is brought to completion as members are added to it through succeeding grace. And as the moon receives light from the sun, so the holy Church receives justification from Christ. The faithful are signified by the stars because they too are lights of heaven, as Paul said of himself and those like him: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). And again: “You shine as lights in the world” (Phil. II).

Therefore the sun is Christ, the moon is the Church, and the stars are the faithful. Fish signify the evil, birds the good. Fish signify the evil because they remain in the place in which they were created; birds signify the good because they ascend to a higher dwelling-place. The evil remain in the fault in which they were born; the good ascend through grace to the glory for which they were reborn. The evil have the wings of sins; the good, the wings of virtues.

The good sing divine praises in modulated voices; the evil, in whose mouth there is no beautiful praise, are silent. [Col. 0591C] The paradise of delights signifies the Church, in which there are diverse delights and joys: some through the abundance of graces, some through the fragrance of virtues, some through the manifold variety of good works, some in contemplation of the heavenly homeland, some in the melody of divine praise, some in the sweetness both of eternal recompense, and some in hope of future reward. The spring which is in paradise signifies Christ.

For the fountain of wisdom is the Word of God, that is, the Son of God. Whoever therefore comes to this fountain—that is, to the Word of God and to wisdom—finds life and draws salvation from the Lord (Prov. VIII). The four rivers flowing from the fountain are the four Gospels of Christ, [Col. 0591D] by which the garden of holy Church is watered and made fruitful, so that it may grow and bear fruit. They fittingly flow around diverse lands, because they gather into the unity of faith diverse peoples formerly intent upon earthly things. The tree of life likewise signifies Christ. For he himself says: “Whoever eats me lives because of me” (John VI). And again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). If, therefore, we eat of him, we have eternal life, as he himself said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John VI). Therefore Christ is both tree and fountain. He is a tree because he satisfies us with the fruit of life; a fountain because he gives us drink of the water of wisdom.

But it is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, if we keep its command, we experience good; if we transgress it, [Col. 0592A] we experience evil. For paradise is the Church; delight is grace; the fountain is Christ; the four rivers are the four Gospels; eating of the tree is transgression of the commandment. The earth from which the first man was made signifies the virgin from whom the second man was born. Virgin earth: the Virgin Mary. Therefore, just as the human body was made from virgin earth by a divine operation, so the Word of God is believed to have become incarnate from the Virgin Mary by a divine operation. Adam’s body, taken from the earth, was without the stain of sin; and Christ’s spotless body was born from Mary. Adam was made on the sixth day, and Christ was born in the sixth age, suffering on the sixth day of the week, at the sixth hour of the day. Adam fell asleep so that Eve might be made from his side; Christ was put to sleep in death so that the Church might be redeemed by [Col. 0592B] his blood. Adam was bridegroom, and Eve, made from him, was bride; Christ is bridegroom, and the Church is bride, redeemed by him. Adam ought to have presided over and governed Eve; Christ presides over and governs the Church. Thus, in the likeness of Adam and Eve, Christ and the Church, God is the bridegroom of every faithful soul. Adam signifies the spirit; Eve, the flesh. Therefore, just as Adam ought to govern Eve, so the spirit ought to govern the flesh; and just as Adam was to beget children through Eve, so the spirit ought to propagate good works through the flesh. The serpent signifies the devil; the apple, earthly delight. Therefore, just as the serpent deceived Eve with the apple, so the devil entices and seduces the unreasoning flesh with earthly delight. And just as Eve led Adam to eat the apple, [Col. 0592C] so the flesh sometimes draws the spirit into consenting to sin. And just as Adam and Eve are cast out of paradise, so both—the flesh, that is, and the spirit—are cast out of paradise, that is, from the state of their good; for the spirit is afflicted through an evil conscience, and the flesh is punished by punishment.

The six days signify the labor of good work; the seventh expresses the rest of eternal blessedness. For God completed his work in six days, and on the seventh day rested from all his work. So too we ought in the present age to labor in the performance of good works, so that in the future we may rest in the Sabbath of recompense.

After Adam and Eve were cast out of paradise through [Col. 0592D] the fault of disobedience, Adam knew his wife Eve and begot Cain. Then he begot Abel, whom Cain killed. Afterwards Cain became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth. Adam, the parent of the human race, signifies God, by nature the God of all things chosen, and by grace the Father of all the elect. He is God to the former because he is Creator; Father to the latter because he is Redeemer. Eve signifies the Synagogue, whom God had espoused to himself, from whom in a certain manner he also begot Cain and possessed a son—namely, the ancient people, of whom he himself said: “Israel is my firstborn” (Exod. IV). He likewise begot innocent, righteous Abel, that is, Jesus Christ our Lord. Abel was righteous and innocent; Christ “did no sin, neither was deceit found in [Col. 0593A] his mouth” (I Pet. II). Abel, the first righteous man in temporal order, offered a sacrifice to God; Christ, the first righteous man in excellence of holiness, offered his own flesh immaculate to God. The Lord looked upon the offering of righteous Abel, and looked upon Christ’s Passion, which he mercifully undertook for the redemption of humankind. Thus Abel signifies Christ, Cain the Jewish people. Cain killed Abel; and the people of the Jews fastened Christ to the gibbet. After fratricide Cain became a wanderer and fugitive; and after the Passion of Christ, his brother according to the flesh, the Jewish people were scattered throughout the whole world. Also, after the likeness of Cain persecuting and Abel suffering, the flesh persecutes the spirit, the impious person the righteous, vice virtue, malice goodness, evil good. [Col. 0593B] Seth signifies Christ; Cain, the devil. The sons of Seth are the elect; the sons of Cain, the reprobate. The daughters of men are carnal pleasures; the union of spouses, the dishonorable use of worldly things; the giants of the earth, the pride of life.

Enos, third from Adam, who began to call upon the name of the Lord, signifies those who are perfect in faith in the holy Trinity. Enoch, seventh from Adam, who pleased God, signifies those who have been sanctified by the gifts of spiritual grace, cleansed from sins and vices. But who in this present life can perfectly avoid sins unless, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, they have been forgiven the faithful? For in him forgiveness of sins is bestowed upon the children of the Church, as the Lord says through the prophet: “I will pour upon you clean water, [Col. 0593C] and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements, and I will give you a new spirit” (Ezek. XXXVI). For, propagated in this world from our first parents, we had contracted original sins from them, to which we thereafter added many actual sins; and yet, with blind minds oppressed by carnal desires, we did not perceive our guilt clearly. But Jesus Christ, coming to us from the bosom of God the Father, showed us that we were bound by the chains of sins. Hence our blessed Isidore—indeed, the teacher and patron of all Spain—says:

> [Note: [Col. 0593D] *Sentences*, Book I, ch. 14.] “The first gifts of God are those by which he shows us that we are guilty before ourselves; for while we lay under the charge of guilt, we believed ourselves righteous.”

Therefore the Son of God showed us, by proclaiming it, that we are sinners; but by dying he displayed himself as merciful, [Col. 0593D] when, through the Holy Spirit given in baptism to the children of the Church, he remitted sins. He is therefore righteous and merciful: righteous, that through justice he may punish unbelievers; merciful, that he may forgive sins to those who hope in him. Blessed Job desired the coming of this most just condemner of the impious and most gracious receiver of the godly, when, drawing long sighs from his inmost breast, he said: “Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance” (Job VI).

Gregory:

> [Note: [Col. 0594D] *Morals*, Book VII, ch. 2.] “Who else is denoted by the name of the balance but the mediator of God and men, who came to weigh [Col. 0594A] the merit of our life and brought with himself both justice and mercy, yet, with the scale of mercy outweighing the other, lightened our sins by sparing us? For in the hand of the Father he was made, as it were, a balance of wonderful equilibrium: on one side he suspended in himself our calamity, and on the other our sins. By dying he made known that calamity is of heavy weight; by remitting sin he showed that it is light in the sight of mercy. For this was the first gift he granted by grace: he made our punishment knowable to us.
>
> “For man, made to contemplate his Creator, but cast down from inward joys by his deserved sins, falling into the misery of corruption and suffering the blindness of exile, endured the punishments of his guilt and did not know it. Thus he believed exile to be his homeland, and so, beneath the [Col. 0594B] burden of corruption, he rejoiced as though in the liberty of salvation. But he whom man had left within appeared without as God, having assumed flesh. And when he presented himself outwardly, he called back inward the man expelled without, so that he might now see his losses and now groan over the punishment of his blindness. Therefore the calamity of man appeared heavier in the balance, because he recognized the evil he suffered only in the presence of the Redeemer. For, not knowing the light, he pleasantly endured the darkness of his condemnation. But after he saw what he might love, he understood also what he might grieve over. And he felt as grievous what he suffered when the sweetness of what he had lost was made known.
>
> “Therefore let the holy man, filled with the abundance of the prophetic spirit, speak in his own voice and in that of the human race: [Col. 0594C] ‘Would that my sins, by which I deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, were weighed in a balance.’ This calamity appears heavier than the sand of the sea. It is as if he were plainly saying: The evil of our condemnation is thought light because it has not yet been weighed by knowledge of the Redeemer’s justice. But would that he come and suspend the misery of so great an exile in the scale of his mercy, and teach us what we should seek after exile. For if he shows what we have lost, he makes clear how grievous is what we endure. This same calamity of our pilgrimage is aptly compared to the sand of the sea. For the sand of the sea is cast outward by the surging of waves, because sinful man, while he endures the shifting waves of temptations, goes forth from his inward self. And the sand of the sea is of great weight. But the calamity of man [Col. 0594D] is said to be heavier than the sand of the sea, because it is shown to have been hard when guilt is lightened through merciful Christ. Whoever therefore recognizes the grace of the Redeemer, whoever loves the return to the homeland, groans as one instructed beneath the burden of pilgrimage. After the desire for the balance there rightly follows: ‘Therefore my words are full of sorrow.’ Whoever loves pilgrimage as homeland does not know how to grieve even amid sorrows. But the words of the righteous are full of sorrow, because while he endures present things, he sighs in speech for something else. He sees all that he suffered in sin, and, in order to return to the state of blessedness, carefully weighs the judgments by which he is afflicted.
>
> “[Col. 0595A] Hence there follows: ‘For the arrows of the Lord are in me.’ By the name of arrows are sometimes denoted words of preaching, sometimes the sentence of chastisement. The utterances of preaching are expressed by arrows because, in striking vices, they pierce the hearts of those who live badly. Of these arrows it is said at the coming of the Redeemer: ‘Your arrows are sharp; peoples shall fall beneath you’ (Ps. XLIV). Isaiah also says of them: ‘I will send from among them those who have been saved to the nations, to the sea, to Africa, to Libya [Note: [Col. 0595D] Lydia.] drawing the bow, to Italy and Greece’ (Isa. LXVI). Again, a blow of chastisement is signified by arrows, as Elisha says to King Joash: ‘Shoot an arrow.’ And when he shot it, he said: ‘You shall strike Syria until you have destroyed it’ (IV Kings XIII). Therefore the holy man, who beholds the misery of [Col. 0595B] his pilgrimage—indeed, of the whole human race—because he groans beneath the stroke of the Lord’s chastising judgment [Note: [Col. 0596D] “chastisement” (*animadversione*)], says: ‘Therefore my words are full of sorrow, because the arrows of the Lord are in me.’ It is as if he plainly said: I do not rejoice in the condemnation of exile, but, placed under judgment, I grieve because I recognize the force of the blow. Yet there are many whom torments torture but do not amend.
>
> “Against this there fittingly follows: ‘Whose indignation drinks up my spirit.’ What is the spirit of man but the spirit of pride? The arrows of the Lord drink up the spirit of man when the judgments of heavenly chastisement restrain the afflicted mind from pride. Thus the arrows of the Lord [Col. 0595C] drink up man’s spirit because they draw inward one intent upon outward things. David’s spirit had been drunk up when he said: ‘When my spirit failed from me, you knew my paths’ (Ps. XLI). And again: ‘I refused to be comforted in my soul; I remembered God’ (Ps. LXXVI). Therefore the indignation of the arrows drinks up the spirit of the righteous, because heavenly judgments, as they wound the proud whom they find in sins, change them, so that the pierced mind may abandon its hardness and the blood of confession may flow from a saving wound. For they consider whence and whither they have fallen; they consider from how great a blessedness they have fallen into the torments of their corruption. Nor do they merely groan over what they endure; they also fear what the strict Judge threatens sinners with from the fires of Gehenna. [Col. 0595D] Hence there rightly follows: ‘And terrors wage war against me.’ The mind of the righteous not only considers what it endures, but also fears what remains. It sees what it suffers in this life and fears lest, after this life, it suffer more grievous things. It mourns because, in the exile of this blindness, it has fallen from the joys of paradise; it fears lest, when exile is left behind, eternal death should follow. It already endures the sentence in punishment, but still dreads from guilt the threats of the Judge yet to come. Thus the Psalmist says: ‘Your wraths have passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me’ (Ps. LXXXVII). For after the wrath of the inward Judge passes over us, terrors also trouble us, because we already suffer one thing from condemnation [Col. 0596A] and still fear another from eternal vengeance. Therefore we recognize that our calamity is heavier than the sand of the sea, because, in withdrawing from God through sin, we groan bitterly under the burden of pilgrimage. The graver the things we suffer for our sins in this pilgrimage of exile, therefore, the more quickly we ought, by persevering in good works, to desire release from it and return to our homeland. Let us carefully weigh the goods that we lost in our first parents and the evils that we endure in this exile of the present life; and let us labor with all diligence that we may attain the state of blessedness. Therefore let our words, as blessed Job declared before, be full of sorrow, and with tears, supreme longing, and devotion let us say to God with the Prophet:”

[Col. 0596B] “To you praise is due, O God, in Zion; and to you a vow shall be paid in Jerusalem” (Ps. LXIV).

This is a psalm of David. It is also a song of Jeremiah, Haggai, and Ezekiel concerning the word of pilgrimage, or concerning the people of the migration, when it began to depart. As is read in the history of Kings, Nebuchadnezzar king of the Babylonians took the children of Israel captive and, after Jerusalem had been overthrown, transferred them to Babylon. They were held in that captivity for seventy years. The literal cause of this captivity was a statement made in Nebuchadnezzar’s court. There, when it was said that all nations ought to be subject to him, it was said that the Jews were rebellious; and therefore he took them captive. Jeremiah foretold this captivity before it came, saw it when present, and lamented it after it was past in the Lamentations with its fourfold alphabet. [Col. 0596C] Jeremiah also prophesied that after seventy years the people would return to Jerusalem. Among the captives, moreover, there were certain prophets, namely Haggai and Ezekiel and others, who understood and foretold the return from Babylon to Jerusalem; and some of them, with others, returned to Jerusalem by permission of Cyrus king of the Persians. Thus, at the exhortation of Haggai and other prophets, the Temple was restored. But since all these things happened to them in figure, they should rather be applied spiritually to us.

We must therefore know that there are now two spiritual cities: one of the wicked, which begins with Cain and is called Babylon; the other of the good, which [Col. 0596D] began with Abel and is called Jerusalem. Hence blessed Augustine says: “Desire makes citizens of Babylon, but charity makes citizens of Jerusalem. Though they are mingled in body, they are nevertheless separated in mind; one of them journeys in the other and is held captive there.” For as long as we are held, or are, in the body, we are “away from the Lord” (II Cor. V), since we sigh from Babylon toward Jerusalem—that is, from the world and from the body of death and sin toward heaven. The cause of this pilgrimage and sighing was the word which the devil spoke to the first parents: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. III). Hence Augustine, the eminent teacher, says: “He begins to go out, or return, from this captivity [Col. 0597A] who begins to love. For charity moves the foot toward return.” And as the children of Israel returned, when the seventy years had been completed, under Jesus the high priest, so we too, led by Christ, who according to Luke was born in the seventy-seventh generation (Luke III), begin to return, until in the future, when the sevenfold course of this life has been completed, with the goats placed on the left, we are set at the right hand of God (Matt. XXV). The aforesaid prophets understood that this spiritual return was figured by no actual event, and especially rejoiced over it. Hence “song” is placed in the title. Its sense is this: a song is rejoicing, the voice of a people returning from migration—that is, a people which migrated from heaven to earth, from perfection to confusion—or concerning the word of pilgrimage, [Col. 0597B] that is, concerning the people made pilgrims by that saying: “You shall be like gods.” This song was uttered when they began in mind to depart from the Babylon of this world; it is not a song because they became pilgrims, but because they begin to return. Hence blessed Augustine says: “He begins, then, to go out of Babylon who begins to love God and neighbor. Charity, as was said above, makes a citizen of Jerusalem, but desire a citizen of Babylon; and although they are mixed in body, they are separated in longing.” This, then, as we have said, is the song of Jeremiah, Haggai, and Ezekiel. Jeremiah is interpreted “exalted,” and signifies those who say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Haggai is called “the feast of God,” [Col. 0597C] and signifies those “rejoicing in hope” (Rom. XII), who celebrate a feast-day for the Lord in the remnants of their thoughts (Ps. LXXV). Ezekiel, moreover, is interpreted “God strengthened me,” and signifies those strengthened in God. This song belongs to such persons. Therefore the prophet’s purpose is to console us in this exile, lest anyone despair, because he assures us of the return, through whom it comes about, and what riches belong to those who return.

Thus, in the voice of those returning, the joyful Prophet sings, saying: “To you praise is due, O God, in Zion,” etc. Augustine:

> [Note: [Col. 0597D] Perhaps Alcuin. Although Martin derived this argument concerning the three septuagesimas from the *Gloss*, Augustine’s name appears here rather incongruously; for nothing is more foreign to him than this whole doctrine of Septuagesima and the singing of Alleluia, which is purely Roman. The African Church never knew the Sunday of Septuagesima, nor did it, like the Spanish and Roman Churches, fall silent in its singing of Alleluia from that Sunday until Holy Saturday; rather, at all times—Sundays excepted—and during the fifty days after the Resurrection, as may be seen in Augustine himself, Letter 55 (otherwise 119), chs. 15 and 17, near the end, and in Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Book I, ch. 13. Alcuin, however, in *On the Divine Offices*, in the chapter on Septuagesima, adduces statements similar to these; undoubtedly the glossographer copied from him the materials discussed here.]
>
> “Because we have mentioned Septuagesima, we must know that three septuagesimas are remembered in holy Church: one signified, and two signifying. One preceded in figure, namely the septuagesima of the Jewish captivity; the other [Col. 0597D] is observed by the Church in representation, beginning with *The sorrows of death surrounded me* and ending on Holy Saturday. The Church observes it as a representation of our spiritual captivity, in which we are captives while we are absent from the Lord in the body (II Cor. V); this captivity was prefigured by the septuagesima of the Jews. And just as before the end of the seventy years the Jews received leave and opportunity to return by Cyrus’s permission, and when the same seventy years were completed returned fully under the leadership of Jesus, so before the end of this sevenfold course of pilgrimage we too have been granted freedom to return through Jesus, by whose death we have already been redeemed in respect of our souls and saved in hope. But when the sevenfold course of this life is completed, we shall be wholly free, glorious in both persons.
>
> “Hence the Church, setting forth the miseries of our sojourn from *The groans of death surrounded me* until the Paschal Sabbath, is silent concerning songs of joy—namely Alleluia, *Glory to God in the highest*, and the like. On the Paschal Sabbath, however, since through Christ’s Passion it has now obtained the possibility of returning and therefore rejoices in hope, it sings Alleluia. But because it is still weighed down by the mass of corrupt flesh [Col. 0598B] and suffers the ambushes of robbers, after Alleluia there remains the Tract: ‘Praise the Lord, all nations.’ And because we must still be drawn onward by labors, in the following week we sing the Gradual with Alleluia, advancing by a laborious path and therefore sorrowful in reality, but joyful in hope. Yet on Saturday in White, as though the septuagesima of this captivity had ended, we sing two Alleluias more fully, joyful over the twofold robe of our glorification with which we shall be glorified in the future. Now, however, partly freed and joyful in hope, as though returning from Babylon, we sing: ‘To you, O God, praise is due in Zion.’ He sings this who truly loves God. Where? In Zion, that is, in the heavenly homeland, where we now are in hope; and therefore we do not sing in Babylon, where [Col. 0598C] we have hung up our instruments. And this is the sense: Those who are in Zion either in mind or in reality are fittingly to praise you. For “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV). ‘And to you a vow shall be paid’: that is, the immortal soul and body, in Jerusalem, that is, in the heavenly homeland. Here in the present life we make vows by good works and thoughts; there we shall pay them by praising God for both.”

Note that the heavenly homeland is Zion, and it is also Jerusalem. It is as if he said: O God, a vow shall truly be paid to you, because all [Note: [Col. 0598D] The manuscripts wrongly read *sumus*, “we are.”] flesh—that is, human beings of every kind, namely poor and rich, men and women, learned and unlearned, children, young people, and old people—shall come to you, who took the firstfruits from our flesh, that is, assumed flesh free from sin. This is the tithe of the tithe which, under the old law, was given by lesser persons to the high priest. This is also the light cloud upon which the Lord ascended in order to enter Egypt (Isa. XIX). Therefore, O Lord, eagles shall gather to you, as to a body, so that the whole burnt offering may be completed.

Therefore, most beloved brothers, we ought to sigh to him from the pilgrimage of this world and lift the eyes [Col. 0599A] of our mind to him, who deigned to redeem us by his most precious blood and, seated at the right hand of God the Father, does not cease mercifully to admonish us that we may follow his footsteps without stumbling. And because praise is due to him in Zion, that is, in the heavenly homeland, let us render him our vows by good thoughts, words, and works, as the Prophet says: “Make vows and render them to the Lord your God, all you who bring gifts around him” (Ps. LXXV). Let us devoutly implore his kindness, so far as we can, that he may forgive us our sins and grant us strength to work well. We rise to good works with labor, but slide easily into vices; for even our own action, though it seems upright, cannot at all save us unless divine goodness goes before us by lifting us up [Col. 0599B] and sustains us by sparing us.

Who could ever be saved by his own merits if the weight of divine justice pressed him? [Note: [Col. 0599D] The manuscripts: “were pressing him” (*premeretur*).] Hence blessed Job, carefully considering the strictness of the divine examination and confessing himself a sinner, said to God in mourning with a deep groan of heart:

“**I have sinned. What shall I do to you, O guardian of men?**” (Job VII.)

Gregory:

> [Note: [Col. 0600D] *Morals*, Book VIII, ch. 19.] “See: he confesses the evil that he did, but does not find what good he ought to offer God in recompense, because any strength of human action is weak to wash away guilt unless the mercy of one who spares sustains it and the justice of one who judges rightly does not press it down. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: ‘Your mercy is better than lives; my lips shall praise you’ (Ps. LXII). Therefore God’s mercy is better than lives because, however innocent we may seem, our life does not set us free before the strict Judge unless the kindness of mercy remits to it the debt of its guilt. Or certainly, when he says, ‘What shall I do for you?’ he clearly shows that these very good things which we are commanded to do benefit not the commander but ourselves. Hence the Psalmist again says: ‘You have no need of my goods’ (Ps. XV). The humility of our helplessness is expressed when God is called the guardian of men; because if his guardianship does not protect us, the watchful eye of our own vigilance sleeps before the snares of the hidden enemy. The Psalmist again testifies to this when he says: ‘Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it watches in vain’ (Ps. CXXVI). For through ourselves we fell, but by our own powers we cannot rise again. The fault of our own pleasure cast us down once, but the punishment of fault presses us down more grievously every day. We strive to rise to lost uprightness by the efforts of our endeavors, but we are weighed down by the burden of our merits. Hence there fittingly follows: ‘Why have you set me as contrary to you, and I have become burdensome to myself?’ Then God set man as contrary to himself when man abandoned God by sinning. For, captured by the serpent’s persuasions, he became the enemy of him whose commands he despised. But the just Creator [Col. 0600A] set him as contrary to himself because he counted him as an enemy on account of pride. Yet this very opposition of guilt became for man the burden of punishment, so that he who, as the good servant of God, rejoiced in the freedom of incorruption, might serve in misery, though free, his own corruption. For, abandoning the health-giving citadel of humility, he came through pride to the yoke of weakness and, by raising the neck of his heart, placed it beneath that yoke. Because he was unwilling to be subject to divine commands, he laid himself low beneath his own necessities. We shall show this better if we set forth what he endures when cast down: first the burdens of the flesh, then those of the mind.
>
> “For, not to mention that he endures pains, gasps in fevers, and is bound by a certain sickness of his own: this very state of our body which is called health is sickness. For it wastes away in idleness and fails under work; failing through hunger, it is restored by food in order to subsist; growing sluggish through refreshment, it is relieved by abstinence in order to remain vigorous; [Col. 0600B] it is sprinkled with water lest it dry up; it is dried with cloths lest it dissolve through excessive soaking itself; it is invigorated by labor lest it grow torpid through rest; it is refreshed by rest lest it collapse under the exertion of labor; exhausted by vigils, it is restored by sleep; oppressed by sleep, it is shaken awake by vigils lest it be wearied more grievously by its own rest; it is covered with clothing lest it be pierced by the adversity of cold; failing for want of sought warmth, it is refreshed by the breath of breezes. And while it finds troubles from the very means through which it sought to avoid troubles, grievously wounded, so to speak, by its own medicine, it languishes.
>
> “Therefore, even when fevers are removed and pains cease, our very health is a sickness which never lacks a need of treatment. For as many comforts as we seek for the use of living, so many remedies, as it were, do we apply to meet our sickness. But the remedy itself becomes a wound, because, clinging a little too long to a carefully sought remedy, we fail more grievously through that which we prudently prepare for restoration. Surely presumption ought thus to have been corrected; pride thus laid low. For we who once assumed an exalted spirit, behold, carry daily a sorrow that is sinking away. Our very mind also, shut out from the secure joy of its inward secret place, is now deceived by hope, now vexed by fear, now cast down by enduring pain, now raised up by false cheerfulness. It stubbornly loves transitory things and is incessantly worn away by losing them, because they are continually changed by their rushing course. Subject to mutable things, it is changed from itself; for, anxiously seeking what it lacks, it acquires it, and when it has begun to possess it, it grows weary of possessing what it sought. It often loves what it had despised; it despises what it loved. With labor it learns eternal things, but immediately forgets them if it ceases from labor; it seeks long in order to find some little thing of the highest realities. But quickly slipping back into its accustomed ways, it does not persevere even a little in the things it has found. Desiring instruction, it scarcely overcomes its ignorance; but once instructed, the glory of knowledge fights more grievously against it. It scarcely subjects to itself the tyranny of its flesh; nevertheless it still endures within [Col. 0601A] the images of guilt, whose outward works it has now restrained by overcoming them. It rises in the inquiry after its Creator, but the friendly darkness of bodily things confounds it when struck back. It wishes to see how an incorporeal being governs a body, and cannot; it wondrously seeks what it cannot sufficiently answer itself, and fails in ignorance beneath what it prudently seeks.
>
> “It finds itself both spacious and narrow, while considering what estimate it ought truthfully to make of itself. It does not know that, if it were not spacious, it would by no means seek something so investigable; and again, if it were not narrow, it would at least find the very thing which it seeks.
>
> “Therefore it is well said: ‘You have set me as contrary to you, and I have become burdensome to myself’; because, while rejected man endures troubles from the flesh and [Col. 0601B] questions from the mind, he clearly carries the heavy burden of himself. He is pressed on every side by sicknesses and driven hard on every side by weaknesses, so that he who, having forsaken God, believed himself sufficient for his own rest, might find in himself nothing but the tumult of disturbance and seek to flee from himself once found—yet, having despised his Creator, might have nowhere to flee. A certain wise man, carefully considering the burden of this weakness, well said: ‘A heavy yoke lies upon the children of Adam from the day they come forth from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all’ (Ecclus. XL). Blessed Job, therefore, considering these things and groaning over why they were so ordered, does not find fault with justice but seeks mercy, so that by humbly asking he may knock for what divine compassion may change by sparing. It is as though he plainly said: [Col. 0601C] Why do you despise man as though he were contrary to you? For I know with certainty that you do not wish even him to perish whom you seem to despise. Hence he fittingly expresses still further both the humility of confession and the voice of free inquiry, saying: ‘Why do you not take away my sin, and why do you not remove my iniquity?’ By these words, surely, what else is intimated but desire for the awaited Mediator, of whom John says: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world’ (John I)? Or certainly, sin is then fully taken away from the human race when our corruption is changed through the glory of incorruption. For we cannot be free from guilt as long as we are held in this body of death. Therefore he desires the Redeemer’s grace, or the firmness [Col. 0601D] of resurrection, who hopes that his iniquity will be wholly taken away. Hence, immediately adding both the punishment which he deserved from his origin and the judgment which he fears from his own action, he says: ‘Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust, and if in the morning you seek me, I shall not remain.’ To the first sinful man it was said: ‘You are dust, and to dust you shall return’ (Gen. III). By “morning,” however, is meant that manifestation of minds which will be shown at the coming of the Judge when thoughts are laid open, as it were after the darkness of night. Of that morning the Psalmist says: ‘In the morning I shall stand before you and shall see, because you are not a God who wills iniquity’ (Ps. V). God’s seeking a man is to examine him by subtle questioning and, examining him strictly, to judge him. Blessed Job, therefore, considering the losses of human [Col. 0602A] abasement, sees that in the present he is already pressed by punishment and is yet more heavily oppressed by future things, and says: ‘Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust, and if in the morning you seek me, I shall not remain.’ It is as if he mourned more plainly, saying: In the present, indeed, I already suffer the death of the flesh, and yet I still fear, from the judgment to come, the more grievous death of your strict sentence. I endure destruction because of fault; but when I come into judgment, I fear that my faults will be restored and that I shall suffer after destruction. Therefore, considering outward death, let him say: ‘Behold, now I shall sleep in the dust’; and fearing inward death as well, let him add: ‘And if in the morning you seek me, I shall not remain.’
>
> “For however greatly the elect may excel in righteousness, they are by no means sufficient to secure their own innocence if they are strictly examined in judgment. But they now find this as consolation for their election: they humbly know that they cannot suffice by themselves. Therefore beneath the covering of humility they hide themselves from the sword of so great a chastisement; and the more they tremble in continual fear while awaiting the terror of the coming Judge, the more they are continually made ready. They diligently prepare themselves to serve God; but since no one is perfect, placing no confidence at all in their own righteousness, they await God’s judgment with fear.”

For if the first man, placed in paradise, had obeyed God, the necessity of sinning would not weigh upon the elect. But because he, heeding his wife’s voice, refused to obey God, the elect in this mortal pilgrimage cannot live without fault, even if they wish to do so. [Col. 0602C] Hence we read in Job: “No human being is without sin, not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day” (Job 14). Therefore the first man sinned through disobedience, and all who are born from his stock are bound by the chains of original sin. Since, then, he chose to heed the voice of the woman rather than the voice of God, he unhappily corrupted the honour which God had bestowed upon him in his first creation.

God therefore created man in great dignity, when He established him as ruler over all living creatures beneath Himself. Great indeed was the dignity of one whom God fashioned with His own hands—that is, by His own power—and whose soul He created by breathing it in.
