Surely that which God’s hand [Col. 0602D] specially made and His breath gave life could not be slight and superfluous. God therefore breathed into the face of man the breath of life and set him over the birds of heaven and all the living creatures of earth. For what purpose? Namely, that he might serve God, rule created things, obey God, compel creation to serve him, know God, and receive from creation the support of life.

Man, then, was created in great dignity, as we have said: so that he might excel all living creatures, serve God alone, rule the world, zealously keep the Lord’s commandments in order to merit eternal blessedness, and have within his power both obedience to the commandments and contempt for them. God therefore left him in his own power, so that, if he wished to keep the commandments, he might live; but if he did not wish to do so, he would have no excuse for transgression [Col. 0603A] and would consequently pay the penalties justly according to his deserts. He had received great gifts from God’s goodness; but because he scorned to obey Him, having lost his dignity he incurred the sentence of death and curse.

He had, then, no excuse for the guilt of his transgression, because he sinned not in ignorance but deliberately—that is, knowingly—and therefore proved ungrateful for God’s benefits. For he ought to have obeyed God all the more devotedly, inasmuch as he had received greater gifts from the abundance of His goodness. For this reason all living creatures of the earth were made subject to him: that he himself might humbly be subject to the Creator of all. And as creation, by God’s command, unceasingly renders service to man, so man ought to offer devoted service to God.

But what is more unfitting, or more wretched, [Col. 0603B] than daily to exact from creatures the support of life, yet to despise the Ruler of heaven and earth, who in His free goodness created for humankind all things that are under heaven? Alas! God appointed man ruler over all living creatures, while man despises God in his deeds. In His own kindness God set man over every creature beneath heaven, while man through his perverse will despises God, by whom all these things were made subject to him. In forming man, God bestowed great dignity upon him; man, despising God, holds His commandments cheap. Loving man, God placed him over every living creature; man—that is, the human race—forgetting God, worshipped idols.

Since, then, proud man [Col. 0603C] despised God, he lost the privilege of dignity and brought condemnation upon himself. Yet, although he scorned the Lord’s commandment, creation still renders him service. He ceaselessly demands from creatures the support of life, while denying obedience to his Creator.

You therefore, O man, sin gravely in this matter; you commit a grave offence; you bind yourself with grave and inexcusable guilt, when you despise the Creator and rule His creatures. You do not wish to serve the Creator, yet you compel creation to serve you. Everything beneath heaven that He created serves you, and you deny service to Him. Thus you sin doubly; you offend twice: for you not only fail to render fitting obedience to the Creator, but also prove ungrateful for His benefits. You heap sin [Col. 0603D] upon sin, because you refuse both to serve Him and to give the thanks due for the gifts bestowed on you.

Why do you not fear the power of Him by whose strength you stand, whose benefits you enjoy, whose gifts refresh you, whose right hand sustains you, and whose mercy bears with you although you are evil? It would indeed have been good and beneficial for you to dread His omnipotence and obey His commandments. You, then, who are rebellious against the Creator of all and rule His creatures; who despise the Lord and compel creation to obey you; who do not fear God’s power, yet enjoy His benefits; who exercise dominion over the things beneath heaven and deny service to Him by whom these things were subjected to you; who do not know Him [Col. 0604A] from whose hand you continually receive life’s provisions; who turn your back rather than your face toward Him by whose aid you are sustained; who cast behind your back Him by whose providence you are governed—fear the Lord, who mercifully endures you and is patient, lest at His coming you find Him a strict and severe judge.

Fear, I say, the Lord from whom you receive many good things, lest, when He comes to judge the world, He destroy you with the ungodly. Be watchful lest you pass over any of His commandments and, as a transgressor, incur His wrath. Obey all His commandments, so that on the day of strict examination you may be gathered among the elect sheep. Keep the Creator’s commands before your eyes, so that at the last time you may deserve to be placed at His right hand. For God will be gracious to you if you amend [Col. 0604B] your life promptly. You will immediately obtain His grace if you devoutly obey His commands. Perform His commandments, therefore, in all things, that you may escape His wrath. Correct your vices while He patiently waits for you, lest His sentence punish you severely. Let the terror of His just judgment call you back from guilt, lest His verdict condemn you as incorrigible. Let the delay of Him who waits correct you, lest the justice of Him who judges overwhelm you. You will have Him continually gracious if at last, turning back, you amend yourself. You can very easily have God propitious if you change your manner of life for the better.

The more slowly you resort to repentance, the more culpable you make yourself before God. For from one to whom money is lent over a long period, it is demanded with interest. Therefore, the longer [Col. 0604C] you ungratefully make use of God’s benefits through the extended course of your life, the more heavily you bind yourself in chains of condemnation. Nor will you now be able to have any excuse for disobedience unless you speedily approach Him in true repentance.

What, then, will you repay Him for all that He has bestowed upon you? What will you render Him in return for His gifts, who has no need of your goods? What can you worthily offer the supreme Maker, O poor little man, who always abounds in unfailing treasures? What can you adequately repay to Him, you earth and ashes and food for worms, whose is all the earth and its fullness? (Psalm 23). For God’s benefits bestowed upon you exceed both number and your deserving. You cannot count them because of their multitude, for they are exceedingly many. They exceed measure because they transcend all limit. [Col. 0604D] They cannot be conceived or comprehended by the human mind. You cannot match your merits to God’s gifts, nor fully understand them by your own intelligence.

Just as your understanding does not suffice to investigate the benefits God has granted you, so your knowledge is insufficient to praise them. The greatness of God’s benefits surpasses the thoughts of hearts, and the innumerable multitude of His gifts exceeds the praises of the tongue. Even if you should strive to spend the whole course of your life in God’s praises, continually render Him thanks, and serve Him with all your strength, still your services could not compensate for His gifts.

What then? Must praise cease? [Col. 0605A] Must good works be abandoned? By no means. Rather, throughout all the time of our life we ought to devote ourselves most earnestly to good works, praise God with a pure mind, cling to Him with all our heart, render innumerable thanksgivings, and raise pure prayers to Him. Yet this is not because by such virtues we can compensate for what we owe to divine benefits, but so that the will of our heart may be manifested in these endeavours, and that what our weakness cannot accomplish, the will of devotion may obtain through grace.

Although, therefore, a person is subject to divine power, strives to fulfil His commands in all things, holds the right faith in conduct, keeps the law, loves righteousness, practises virtues, despises vices, washes away sins with tears, and, if possible, [Col. 0605B] surpasses human merits, yet all this is little and brief in comparison with God’s gifts—those which in His free goodness He has bestowed upon us unworthy people in this life, and those which He has prepared in the heavenly homeland if we are obedient to Him and love Him in all things and above all things. Hence the Apostle says: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what things God has prepared for those who love Him” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore, just as through the disobedience of our first parent Adam we were driven from the delights of paradise, so through the ineffable mercy of God we believe that we shall come to the joys of paradise. And just as contempt for God’s commandments made us exiles from paradise’s loveliness, so the obedience of Jesus Christ, our deliverer, [Col. 0605C] enabled us to attain the good things which through Him God the Father prepared for those who love Him. Through the transgression of the first man we came into the misery of this exile; but through the humility of our Redeemer we obtained eternal life. For He humbled Himself, becoming obedient to God the Father unto death (Phil. 2), in order to lead us to the blessedness of paradise. Through Adam’s sin we unhappily fell from the dwellings of paradise; but through the righteousness of Jesus Christ our Saviour we have undoubtedly risen to the hope of eternal blessedness. The ancient enemy, envying our blessedness, stripped us of the robe of immortality; Christ, God and man, pitying our weakness, raised us through Himself to behold the face of His Father. Amen.

[Col. 0605D] We have also inserted in this sermon certain matters concerning the Sunday of Septuagesima which we find ordained by the holy Fathers in ecclesiastical books: first, what these days signify; second, where they begin and where they end; third, their institution; fourth, their offices.

Septuagesima, then, represents the time of departure, which was a time of punishment and guilt. Therefore on the first Sunday the history of the book of Genesis begins to be read, and it is read as far as the Sunday entitled “in the Passion of the Lord,” where the departure and error of the first parents are treated. A “departure” is said to occur when someone turns aside from a holy and just command laid upon him.

Therefore, on Saturday [Col. 0606A] at Vespers before Septuagesima, we lay aside the Alleluia, and at the Paschal Vigil we take it up again. It is called Septuagesima because it has seven times ten days. This Septuagesima which the present Church observes represents the seventy years during which Israel was in Babylonian servitude. For just as they laid aside their instruments, saying, “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm 136), so we too lay aside songs of praise.

But after permission to return was given them by Cyrus, king of the Persians, in the seventieth year—[Note: [Col. 0605D] The manuscripts erroneously read “sixtieth.”]—they began to rejoice. So we sing Alleluia on the Saturday of Easter, representing their joy. Yet they laboured greatly in preparing for their return and gathering their little bundles; [Col. 0606B] and we likewise immediately add the Tract after the Alleluia, namely, “Praise the Lord,” which signifies labour. As they returned joyfully but were wearied by the toil of the journey, so throughout the Paschal week we sing the Gradual with Alleluia, signifying labour by the Gradual and joy by the Alleluia. Finally, when they entered their homeland, they received full joy; and we sing two Alleluias on the Saturday on which Septuagesima ends.

Moreover, our seventy days and their seventy years, as it were a single history, figure the exile of the entire human race [“of the whole human race”] from Adam to the end of the world. This exile is enacted by the cycle of seven days and contained under seven thousand years, so that we understand seventy days, or seventy years, or seventy hundreds of years. For from the beginning of the world to the Ascension of the Lord we reckon six thousand years. Whatever time follows thereafter until the end of the world is included under the seventh millennium, [Col. 0606C] the number of which God alone knows.

Therefore, just as the children of Israel were delivered from Babylonian bondage through Cyrus in the seventieth year, so in the sixth age of the world we have been redeemed through Christ from the slavery of the devil, the robe of innocence being restored to us through the remission of baptism. Hence on the Saturday of Easter we sing Alleluia, rejoicing already in hope of eternal rest and recovery of our homeland. Israel laboured in accomplishing its return and while returning; and we too in the present Church must labour toward the fulfilment of the ten commandments of the law. But when the time of our exile has ended and we have reached our homeland, then both robes will be adorned, when body and soul are glorified together. This is figured by the two Alleluias sung at the end of Septuagesima.

Sexagesima means six times ten and signifies the time of the Church’s widowhood and her grief through the absence of the bridegroom, although Christ is present to us according to His divinity. Hence He says: “I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28). Yet according to His humanity He is in heaven and sits at the right hand [Col. 0607A] of God the Father.

Nevertheless, six works of mercy are given here to the bride as remedy and consolation: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, visiting the sick, clothing the naked, and receiving poor persons and pilgrims as guests. A seventh is added according to Tobit, namely, burying the dead (Tob. 12). These are given to the bride, that she may exercise herself in them and, through their observance together with that of the Decalogue, merit to have her bridegroom’s door opened to her and to enjoy His delightful embrace.

Quinquagesima is so called because it means five times ten, [Col. 0608A] and signifies the time of remission, just as in the Old Testament the fiftieth year was called the year of remission. Hence in this season the fiftieth psalm, namely, “Have mercy upon me, O God,” is especially sung—the psalm of penitence and remission. Therefore we fast during this season that we may obtain forgiveness of sins, through Him who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages.

## EIGHTH SERMON: FOR SEXAGESIMA

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607B] [Note: [Col. 0607D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, ch. 4.] Noah, son of Lamech, tenth from the first man Adam, the second father and restorer of the world, was found righteous before God, patient in hope, and wise in his works. Commanded, he built the ark; warned, he entered it; he did not dread the turbulent [Note: [Col. 0607D] “Turbulentos”: “turbulent [waves].”] waves of the flood, nor fear the crashes of the winds or the murmurings of the clouds. He is borne along by storms and is not submerged; he is associated with serpents and beasts, nor do the wild beasts rashly submit their necks to anyone, while birds render service to him. For he sent out a bird and waited for its return, but was deceived by the faithless treachery of the raven; deservedly he is instructed by the dove, bearing in its beak a branch of the tree of peace.

For God found him righteous in that generation. To him He also disclosed the secret of His counsel, when in His high and just judgment He wished to wipe out human beings from the face of the earth; for He said: [Col. 0607C] “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. 6). Repentance does not, indeed, apply to God, but He speaks according to our manner; for we are accustomed to be pierced by repentance when we see our deeds turned contrary to our intention. He said that He repented of making man when He saw man, by sinning, degenerate from the uprightness of his creation. God therefore rightly said that He repented concerning the people whom He had created, because He saw the earth filled with their wickedness.

But because, dearest brothers, we have briefly set forth these matters, it is fitting that we explain more fully for your benefit certain points from the history of blessed Noah. This man, as holy Church sings of him—[Note: [Col. 0607D] You will find these words in the second responsory of the first nocturn at Matins on the Sunday of Sexagesima, except for the words “and in his works he signified Christ.” [Col. 0608D] But the responsory is taken from sacred Scripture, Gen. 6:9.]—was righteous and perfect, walked with God, and in his works signified Christ.

Noah is interpreted “rest,” [Col. 0607D] because under him all former works rested through the flood and came to an end. Therefore his father, giving him the name Noah, said: “This one gives us rest from all our works upon the earth which God has cursed” (Gen. 5). [Note: [Col. 0608D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 7, here transcribed almost word for word.]

[Col. 0608B] Noah, then, is interpreted “rest,” and the Lord says to His disciples: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11). Noah alone is found righteous in that generation, and seven souls are assigned to him, because Christ alone is found righteous and perfect in the human race; and seven Churches are granted to Him because of the sevenfold enlightening Spirit in the one Church.

Noah is delivered through water and wood; for wood and water signify the cross and baptism in holy Church. As he with his household is saved through water and wood, so Christ’s family is marked through baptism and the passion of the cross, and delivered from eternal condemnation. Noah built the ark from incorruptible timbers; Christ builds the Church [Col. 0608C] from persons who will live forever.

This ark represented the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. The fact that the ark itself is commanded to be made of squared timbers signifies the stable life of the saints, ready for every good work. Whichever way you turn a squared timber, it will without doubt remain unmoved and firm. The ark’s timbers, moreover, are joined inside and outside with pitch, so that the endurance of charity may be signified in the bond of unity: lest, when scandals tempt the Church, whether from those who are within or those who are without, the brotherly union should yield and the bond of peace be broken. For pitch is a most powerful and fiery glue, signifying the ardour of love and the force of great strength for maintaining spiritual fellowship. Pitch binds the ark together, while charity and the love of the saints bind and strengthen the Church.

The fact that the ark is three hundred cubits long signifies that the Church of Christ extends through six ages of the world. In the first age of the world Christ is prefigured in the death of Abel and the birth of Seth. In the second He is foreshown in types and riddles. In the third He is foretold by the sayings of the patriarchs. In the fourth He is declared by the testimonies of the Law to be about to be born, suffer, die, rise again, ascend into heaven, and come thence to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. In the fifth He is proclaimed by the heralding of the prophets. In the sixth He is openly shown by the Gospel to have already come. For six times fifty make three hundred, which is the whole duration of the world.

The fact that the ark’s width extends to fifty cubits signifies that, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, the Holy Spirit is poured out in the Church of the faithful to enlarge its bounds. Therefore the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into [Col. 0609B] our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). The fact that its height rises to thirty cubits signifies that Christ, who is the height of the Church, at the age of thirty consecrated the teaching of the Gospel. For He Himself testifies that He came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5).

The fact that the same ark is brought to completion above in a single cubit teaches that the unity of holy faith must be maintained, without which no one is delivered from eternal condemnation. The fact that an entrance is made for it in the side signifies that no one is worthy to enter the Church except through the sacrament of forgiveness of sins, which flowed from Christ’s opened side.

The fact that the lower levels of the ark are constructed with two chambers and three chambers signifies that the Church is gathered from all nations in a twofold multitude, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision; or in a threefold multitude, on account of Noah’s three sons, from whose offspring the entire world was filled. These are called the ark’s lower parts because the diversity of nations belongs to this earthly life. But at the summit all are completed in one, and this diversity does not exist in God’s kingdom, because Christ is all in all (Col. 3), completing us, as it were, above in a single cubit through heavenly unity.

The fact that every kind of animal is enclosed in the ark signifies that a congregation is formed in the Church from all nations. The sheet shown also to Peter signifies that clean and unclean animals are there, just as good and evil people participate in the Church’s sacraments. The clean animals are in sevens and the unclean by twos, not because evil people are fewer than good in the Church, but because good people preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace without discord. Holy Scripture commends the Holy Spirit by a sevenfold operation: namely, wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord (Isa. 11). Hence the number of fifty days pertaining to the coming of the Holy Spirit is completed in seven sevens, which make forty-nine, with one added. Therefore it is said: “Be diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4). Evil people, however, in the number two, are prone to schisms and are in a manner [Col. 0610A] shown to be divisible.

The fact that Noah himself is named eighth with his household signifies that Christ, who is the hope of our redemption, rose from the dead on the eighth day—that is, the first after the Sabbath—which is the third day from the Passion and, in the number that revolves through all time, both first and eighth. The fact that the flood came seven days after Noah entered the ark signifies that people are baptized for the remission of sins into the hope of future rest, signified by the seventh day. The fact that all flesh supported by the earth was consumed by the flood outside the ark signifies that outside the fellowship of the Church, the water of baptism, though it is the same water, not only [Note: [Col. 0609] We have corrected this from Isidore, since both manuscripts lack this negation.] has no power to save, but rather has power to destroy.

The fact that it rained for forty days and forty nights and all flesh was destroyed indicates that every guilt of sins is committed against the ten commandments of the Law throughout the whole world, which is contained in four regions. For ten multiplied by four makes forty. The fact that Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord told him to build the ark signifies that the Church was built in the fifth age of the world. The fact that the ark was constructed over one hundred years shows that the Church is preached through all ages. These hundred years signify the entire time of this world. The fact that Noah was six hundred years old when he entered the ark signified that in the sixth age of the world, in the manifestation of the Gospel, the Church’s perfection is fulfilled—the Church which [Col. 0610C] delivers us from the world’s waves.

The fact that Noah entered the ark in the second month of the six hundredth year signifies the same sixth age. For two months are contained in the number sixty. From the number six derive the names sixty, six hundred, six thousand, six hundred thousand, six hundredfold, and whatever further numerical and infinite increases rise by greater degrees under the same designation. The mention also of the twenty-seventh day of the month pertains to the signification of the same squareness already explained in the squared timbers. Here, however, it shows this more clearly: because it teaches that the Trinity makes us ready for every good work—that is, as it were squared—in memory, because we remember God; in understanding, because we know Him; and in will, because we love Him. For three times three are nine, and three times nine make twenty-seven, the square of the number three.

The fact that the ark rested and came to rest in the seventh month after the flood began signifies the sevenfold rest of the Church’s repose. The water increased fifteen cubits above the heights of the mountains. Eight and seven make fifteen: eight signifies resurrection, while seven signifies eternal rest. The fact that the raven, sent from the ark after forty days, did not return signifies the most foul people of worldly desire, who, after receiving baptism, bind themselves so tightly to earthly cares that they do not yet return to the Church through good works.

The fact that the dove, sent out, returned because it found no rest shows that under the New Testament rest is not promised to the saints in this life, but in the life to come. For it is sent out from the ark after forty days, a number signifying the life lived in this world. Then, after seven days, the dove is sent out, on account of that sevenfold spiritual operation, and returns with the fruitful shoot of the olive. This signifies that even some baptized persons outside the Church can be brought into the fellowship of unity if, at a later time, the richness of charity, like evening, is not lacking to them in the dove’s beak, as it were in the kiss of peace. The fact that, after another seven days, it was sent out and did not return signifies the rest of the saints with the Lord in the heavenly homeland.

The fact that, when Noah’s six hundred years [Col. 0611B] of life had been completed, the roof of the ark was opened signifies that in the sixth age the hidden sacrament and promise will be revealed. The fact that the earth is said to have dried on the twenty-seventh day of the second month signifies that the necessity of baptizing had already ended in the number of the eighth or seventh day; for the twenty-eighth is the twenty-seventh day of the second month. That number comes from the union of spirit and body; it contains seven eights with one added on account of the bond of unity by which the universal Church is joined.

Why do those who entered separately leave the ark joined together? For thus we read: “Noah entered the ark, and his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons” (Gen. 7). Why, then, are the men and women mentioned as entering separately, except because in this pilgrimage “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5)? Afterwards, however, Noah and his wife, his sons and his sons’ wives leave. That is, males and females joined together, because at the end of the world and in the resurrection of the righteous the body will cleave to the spirit in complete and perfect peace, with no need of mortality or resisting concupiscence.

The fact that all animals are given them for food, as Peter is told concerning that sheet, “Kill and eat” (Acts 10), signifies that one is commanded to eat after the blood has been poured out, lest one’s former life, as if strangled, be retained in the conscience, but instead may have, as it were, an outpouring of blood through confession by the mouth.

The fact that God established a covenant between Himself and human beings and every living soul, that He would not again destroy it by a flood, signifies the rainbow which appears in the clouds and never shines except from the sun. For those do not perish in the flood who recognize the glory of Christ in the prophets and in all divine Scriptures, as it were in clouds, and do not seek their own glory.

Dearest brothers, as has already been explained above by the Fathers, this ark prefigured the Church, which floats upon the waves of this world. Holy Church floats amid this world’s storms; yet with Christ as helmsman, it overcomes every adversity. It is battered by adversities on every side, yet it is not shaken. It is attacked from every quarter by enemies and false brothers, [Col. 0612A] yet by partly enduring and partly resisting it is never conquered. It is often attacked by enemies, given offence by Jews, mocked by pagans, and nevertheless pours forth prayers to the Lord for them without ceasing, that they may be delivered from eternal condemnation.

In time of persecution it willingly suffers, even to the shedding of blood, for Christ’s love; but in time of peace it disciplines itself by fasts, vigils, abstinence, and prayers. In time of persecution it is afflicted by the swords of enemies; in time of peace it crucifies itself with its vices and desires. Holy Church, faithfully following the footsteps of Jesus Christ her bridegroom, endures patiently and strongly conquers every adversity for the sake of the rewards of eternal recompense.

Thus the holy Church of the elect has roses in time of persecution [Col. 0612B] and lilies in peace. By roses we understand the holy martyrs who shed their blood for Christ’s name; by lilies, the holy confessors, who, resisting their own pleasures and overcoming the vices of the flesh, became martyrs without the sword. Hence Solomon, figuratively speaking in praise of Christ under the person of this same Church, says: “His lips are lilies, dripping first myrrh” (Song 5). [Note: [Col. 0611D] Gregory, on this passage.]

For what do we understand by the lips of the bridegroom, namely Christ, except the confessors themselves of whom we have spoken—that is, the preachers of the Church? While they preach the deaths of martyrs, they drip, as it were, myrrh for the seasoning of flesh that must be mortified. This myrrh is rightly called “first,” because none is mortified as that person is who is brought to an end by martyrdom for Christ. “First” is said not with reference to time but to dignity.

Why are the lips of the bridegroom, namely Christ, called lilies, except because those through whom Christ speaks must be pure and through them a good fragrance must be spread abroad? Among these was the Apostle Paul, who said of himself and his companions: “We are a sweet fragrance to God in every place, among those who perish and among those who are saved” (2 Cor. 2).

Therefore, as we have said above, holy Church has roses, that is, martyrs, in time of persecution, and lilies, namely confessors, in time of peace. The redness of roses signifies the blood of martyrs. Hence it is said in praise of the Church: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of orchards” [Col. 0612D] (Song 4). What does holy Church send forth except holy words together with holy works, by which it begets and nourishes children? [Note: [Col. 0612D] Also from Gregory, on this passage.]

While it leads some of them even to martyrdom and trains others in holy conduct, it sends those reddened by the blood of martyrdom to the eternal homeland, and leaves the others, living in holy works, to their neighbours as examples of holiness. What else does it send forth except pomegranates and fruits of orchards? For pomegranates contain a multitude of seeds beneath a red rind, while orchard fruits have within themselves the sweetness of refreshment. Thus holy martyrs, while they labour beneath the fire of tribulation and do not hesitate outwardly to shed their blood for Christ, gather inwardly within their minds a multitude of virtues.

Likewise, all holy persons who live in the Church’s peace bear the fruits of orchards, because in completing holy works they offer their neighbours examples by the display of which those who wish may refresh themselves. All the saints in the Church, whether they burn in the fire of suffering or grow while resting in the Church’s peace, never cease, while they live, to make themselves a paradise of sweetness and delights by the fragrance of holy virtues.

Let the holy Church of the elect, therefore, be called full of flowers. In war it has roses, and in peace lilies. Doctors of the Church are rightly signified by the name of lily, for they must preserve alike chastity of body and purity of mind. To them it is said: “Let your loins be girded” [Col. 0613B] (Luke 12). For teachers of the Church must take care both to shine before God in the purity of chastity and, by the light of good works, to offer people examples of good living. By preserving bodily chastity they in some manner draw near to God; by providing their neighbours with examples of a good life, they increase for themselves the rewards of eternal recompense.

“Angels” in Greek means “messengers” in Latin. Therefore all who discharge the office of teachers are rightly called angels, because they announce God’s will to human beings.

Accordingly, beloved, we must return to the matters which we set forth at the beginning of this sermon concerning the labours of blessed Noah and the Flood. For, although we have said something, however briefly, about the teachers of the Church, [Col. 0613C] once we had set out on that course we wandered a little too far afield. God, supremely just and good, by the Flood wiped out the human race from beneath heaven according to his high counsel; but is he therefore to be thought unjust? By no means. What pleases a just Judge cannot possibly be unjust. Hence blessed Jerome, a man most learned in the Holy Scriptures, says:

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] In Nahum, chap. 1, explaining the words: “A second tribulation shall not arise,” or “God will not take vengeance twice for the same thing.”]  
> If God seems to us cruel, harsh, and bloody because he destroyed the human race in the Flood, rained sulphur and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah, drowned the Egyptians in the waves, and laid the corpses of the Israelites low in the wilderness, know that he inflicted present punishments upon them for this reason: that he might not punish them eternally in the fires of Gehenna.

Thus the Lord also says elsewhere: “My eye spared them, [Col. 0613D] lest I should kill and destroy them in the mountains” (Ezek. 20). But how did he spare those whose corpses lay in the wilderness, and of whom, except Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh—

> [Note: [Col. 0613D] Caleb Jephone]

—not one entered the land of promise? From this we understand that they live, that they were not reserved for eternal punishments, and that they were not erased from the book of the living. Must they therefore be thought to have perished because they were not brought into the promised land? Far from it! God must not be thought cruel, but merciful; for he is supremely compassionate and kind. Therefore in this life he chastises whom he wills, [Col. 0614A] lest he punish them eternally.

> [Note: [Col. 0614D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chap. 2.]

God looks in a twofold manner: either toward pardon or toward vengeance. Toward pardon, as with Peter; toward vengeance, as when he testifies that he will descend and visit the deeds of the Sodomites. God strikes those whom he wills in three ways: the reprobate for condemnation; the elect whom he sees erring, for purification; and the righteous, to make the glory of their merits known. Egypt was struck in the first way, for condemnation; poor Lazarus in the second, for purification; Job in the third, for testing. Therefore God corrects with the scourge of justice in the present those elect whom he sees erring, so that he may rescue them from eternal condemnation in the future. Often almighty God patiently endures sinners, that he may find fewer to condemn.

[Col. 0614B] God also sees some unwilling to be corrected of their own choice, and scourges them temporally, lest, persevering in their wickedness, they be punished eternally. For some, temporal affliction begins here, and eternal damnation will accompany them in the future. Others, while they wait too confidently upon God’s patience, take no care to put an end to their crimes; and while they put his kindness to the test, they provoke him still further to anger. Blessed Peter was speaking of these when, in his Epistle, he said to certain believers concerning Christ: “Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might offer us to God; put to death indeed in the flesh, but made alive in the Spirit” (1 Pet. 3). In that Spirit the Son of God came spiritually [Col. 0614C] and preached to those who were in the flesh—

> [Note: [Col. 0614D] See what we say in Part III, where our author expressly expounds the Epistle of blessed Peter.]

—or held in prison: “who had once been unbelieving, when they awaited God’s patience in the days of Noah while the ark was being built, in which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water” (ibid.).

Almighty God, whose nature is goodness and whose work is mercy, did not cease to invite the human race: before the Law through the patriarchs; under the Law through the prophets; and in the time of grace through his Son. He did so lest, by living wickedly any longer, it should finally perish in its crimes. Hence blessed Peter now says: “The Son of God, coming spiritually, preached to those who were in the flesh,” that is, held in carnal desires or in the prison of unbelief. “Who had once been unbelieving,” namely, [Col. 0614D] they had not believed God when he threatened through Noah: “when they awaited God’s patience in the days of Noah while the ark was being built”; that is, when God’s patience invited them to repentance, sparing them during the hundred years in which Noah built the ark, by which what was to happen to the world was shown. They did not employ God’s patience for repentance, but awaited it as though it would last forever, and never thought that it would fail.

Those whose understanding is darkened by darkness are rightly said to be confined in prison in this life; and in this inner prison [Col. 0615A] of the mind they are burdened by unrighteous deeds, until, released from the flesh, they are cast into the outer darkness of eternal condemnation. The righteous too have a prison in this world, namely, that of tribulations; the reprobate, however, have that of vices.

Therefore that Son of God who, coming in the flesh, preached to the world in our times, also preached before the Flood to those who were then unbelieving and had lived carnally, so that they might be corrected from their errors. For he was present through the Holy Spirit in Noah and in the other holy Fathers, through whose good manner of life he preached to other wicked people, that they might turn from their iniquities to good things. It follows: “In the days of Noah, while the ark was being built, in which a few who believed God, that is, eight souls, having hope of the eighth [Col. 0615B] resurrection, were saved through water in the Flood.”

As the ark was built of smoothed timbers, so the Church is built through the shaping of faithful souls. And as few were saved through water while the world perished, so, in comparison with those who perish, the number of the elect is small: “for narrow is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it” (Matt. 7). The fact that the water of the Flood saved no one placed outside the ark, but killed them, signifies that every heretic, even if possessing the sacrament of baptism, is to be drowned to hell not by waters other than those by which the ark is lifted to heaven, but by those very waters. By those drowned in the Flood is signified the putting to death of the flesh; by those who were saved is signified the quickening of the Spirit. Noah, whose name is interpreted [Col. 0615C] “rest,” signifies Christ, who gives rest of soul to his faithful.

He adds again, saying: “And baptism, which is of like form, now saves you also.” As if to say: What baptism now does—namely, baptism saves—I call of like form, that is, altogether resembling that ark; because whatever was done there carnally is done here spiritually, namely within the holy Church. “Not the removal of filth from the flesh, but the inquiry of a good conscience toward God.” That is, it is not enough for one being baptized to have a good conscience unless, in response to the Church’s question, he shows his faith; and this is through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6), cleansed from [Col. 0615D] vices through the water of regeneration.

I do not say that baptism can save a Christian where there is only removal of the filth of the flesh—where the flesh alone is outwardly washed, as heretics too possess it, washing away outwardly the bodily dirt but not inwardly that of vices—but where there is the inquiry of a pure conscience: that is, where the good conscience of the person being baptized is questioned and required for baptism. Such baptism saves; the other kills and condemns. The questioning that is made and tends toward God through a good conscience makes many believers one in God.

But why, dearest friends, are we astonished at the outward Flood [Col. 0616A] by which God destroyed the human race? If we consider ourselves rationally, we can find it within ourselves. Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain, says:

> [Note: [Col. 0615D] *Sentences*, book I, chap. 13.]  
> Man, why do you marvel at the height of the stars and the depth of the sea? Enter into the abyss of your own mind, and marvel if you can.

Let us therefore enter the abyss of our breast and consider there a most dangerous flood. Every human being suffers within his heart a certain flood of desire, from which no one is freed except through the ark of faith: so that the evil person walking upon dry land is drowned, while the good person, plunged into the depth of the sea, is not killed. Truly dangerous is the shipwreck which, as we have said, takes place within the dwelling-place of the breast. Woe to the person who is endangered there—that is, who is seduced by unlawful thoughts! [Col. 0616B] No harbour is safe for such a one, no anchorage secure, no calm safety exists for one tossed inwardly by the surges of his desire and swallowed by the insatiable whirlpool of lust.

Here we may observe three kinds of people: those who have the Flood within but have no ark; those who have both Flood and ark within, but are not in the ark; and those who have both Flood and ark and remain in the ark. In the Flood without an ark are unbelievers, whom carnal desires envelop and who know no life other than this passing life. Those who have an ark in the Flood but do not remain in it are those who have already learned through faith to believe that, after the end of this changeable condition, an unchangeable life will come, but who subject their minds, setting that aside, to the delight of temporal things.

Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Luke 12). As if he said: Where your desire is, there also is your heart. Without doubt, the dwelling of the inner person is where thought turns; for each person is said to dwell according to the inner person where he is occupied in thought.

[Col. 0616C] Therefore those who establish their heart’s delight in the vanity of this world, although they possess the ark of faith, are nevertheless shipwrecked within. Although someone may boast that he has faith, he cannot be saved if he does not join to faith its right works. Hence blessed James says: “Faith without works is dead” (James 2). What, then, does it benefit them to possess an intact ark—that is, faith—and amid the waves, that is, [Col. 0616D] amid evil works, not merely to suffer shipwreck but to make it willingly? What does it benefit them to know truth and love falsehood, and through evil works break the ark, that is, faith? Such people are not truly faithful.

Do you wish to know what true believers are like? Hear what one of them was like, and understand that all were such in faith and action. For those who are one in faith and truth cannot be unlike. Hear, then, what is said of him in the Psalmist’s voice: “The law of his God is in his heart” (Ps. 36). This is to have the ark within; and, because perhaps this is not enough, hear what he adds again: “His will is in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 1). This is to dwell in [Col. 0617A] the ark: namely, to have a perfect will in God’s commandments. That person is perfect who loves what he believes, so that he possesses faith working through love, which conquers the world.

This is the ark in which we must be saved. It can be carried by the waters of temptations but can in no way be submerged, because in this manner it struggles indeed under necessity, but does not yield to it through covetousness. This is what is said in the Psalm: “This sea is great and wide, in it are creeping things without number, little animals with the great; there ships will pass through” (Ps. 103). The sea within us is desire for this world; and whatever pleasures may be found in it are mingled with many bitter things, which flow downward in [Col. 0617B] our heart according to carnal inclination. Creeping things are carnal thoughts, deformed by the foulness of diverse vices. When we admit them as they come disorderly into our heart, we fill our inward parts, as it were, with monstrous creeping things.

The ship is that spiritual ark, namely our faith, which, suspended inwardly on high, treads underfoot worldly desires and the unlawful longings of the flesh. By “ships” he means many souls faithfully joined to Christ. For many souls, because of one faith and love, are one soul, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4); and one faith is many faiths because of many faithful souls. How can it be said, “Your faith has made you well” (Mark 10), and “my faith,” and “that person’s faith,” when Catholic faith is nevertheless one? Therefore the ship of faith alone crosses the sea; the ark alone escapes the Flood. If we wish to be saved, it must not only be within us, but we must remain within it.

Therefore let no one, trusting in his own conduct, say to his conscience: “What have I to do with this ark? The Flood of carnal desire has dried up within me.” One who stands outside does not know what is happening within. But if a person returns to his heart, he will find there a stormy expanse of sea—that is, a sea stirred by the storms of violently surging passions and evil desires—which sink the mind downward as often as they subject it to themselves through consent. For in every person, as long as he lives this corruptible life, in which the flesh desires against [Col. 0617D] the Spirit (Gal. 5), this Flood exists, or rather every person is in this Flood. But the good are in it like those borne over the sea by ships, while the wicked are in it like shipwrecked persons engulfed by waves.

Let us therefore hold fast, beloved, to upright faith joined with good works, certain hope of eternal blessedness, and perfect charity, which believes and endures all things. For the Apostle Paul says of charity: “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things, and never fails” (1 Cor. 13). You ought, therefore, to imitate these four virtues of charity, so that, [Col. 0618A] following the footsteps of the holy Fathers who advanced through these same virtues, you may be able to be joined to their fellowship.

> [Note: [Col. 0617D] Augustine, Sermon 106 in the Appendix, vol. V; otherwise Sermon 46, *On Time*; or, in other editions: *Treatise on the Four Virtues of Charity*, vol. IX [Col. 0618D].]

First, you should observe how charity itself, containing all things as though it were the four cardinal points of the world, took possession of the whole world through the evangelists preaching Christ’s truth. Let us, if you please, seek examples among certain saints—those possessed by these virtues of holy charity—so that we may assign each of the virtues individually to each of them, while recognizing that all are present in all. Everyone who endures devoutly believes; and whoever rightly believes hopes for something. Thus whoever hopes endures, lest he fall from hope. But let us now see who these persons are and, for your benefit, bring forward their persons and examples.

The virtue of charity which bears all things shone forth [Col. 0618B] in holy Noah, when, with the Lord at once commanding and helping, he endured his labours and escaped the dangers of the Flood. Charity believes all things in holy Abraham; it hopes all things in the other Fathers, namely patriarchs and prophets, from whose offspring Christ descended according to the flesh. Charity also endures all things in the Head himself, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is true charity and never fails from him. Nor, beloved, should your charity judge the other saints strangers to these virtues. Though, because of the brevity of time and the sermon undertaken, they are omitted, understand nevertheless that Christ is in all, and all are founded in Christ.

But now let us see how holy Noah possessed, or was possessed by, the virtue of charity which bears all things [Col. 0618C] in Christ and in his saints. God foretells to him that, as human wickedness increased, he would destroy them from the face of the earth by a Flood. Immediately, when warned, he flees to wood; leaving the pleasant face of the fields, he shuts himself into the narrow confines of the ark. Then the holy man endures the roaring of heaven, the sound of waters, and the violence of storms. And after all this, he who had been accustomed to rejoice in human companionship becomes in some fashion the companion of serpents and wild beasts. Yet this man is not alarmed because wild beasts are with him in the ark. Rather, there wildness recognizes its order, in which humanity had recognized itself; and the beasts obey the commanding human being because they recognize that the human being has obeyed his higher Lord.

[Col. 0618D] In Noah it was shown what Adam lost by despising God’s command, and it was demonstrated that human beings can rule even beasts if they submit in obedience to their Creator. Hence blessed Isidore, eminent teacher and our patron, says:

> [Note: [Col. 0618D] *Sentences*, book I, chap. 9.]  
> When a human being is struck by the assaults of creatures and the adversities of the elements, the punishment of sin requires this: that one who proudly rebelled against God should suffer adversities from things beneath him. Hence we read also in Wisdom: “The whole world will fight for God against the senseless” (Wis. 5). Therefore, deservedly because of sins, things naturally favourable are changed into adversities for human beings. Hence Solomon also says: “Creation burns fiercely in punishment [Col. 0619A] against the unjust, and is gentler in doing good to those who trust in God” (Wis. 16).

Therefore the flesh will not be subject to the soul, nor vices to reason, if the mind has not been subjected to its Creator. But then all things beneath us are rightly subjected to us when we are subject to him by whom they have been subjected to us. For even those things which appear to be subject to one who is not subject to God instead subject him, when through love of them he enslaves his will to things which he thinks subject to himself. Therefore the animals were rightly subject to this most blessed man, because he himself was subject in mind and body to almighty God.

Holy Noah therefore waits for the end of the Flood and endures hardships; nor, before the business of the beasts is finished, does he leave the ark. The good person endures evil and perseveres with great constancy of heart until at the end they are separated even bodily. Therefore, whatever soul you are that wishes to possess the virtue of charity which bears all things, leave the world and flee to the wood of the cross. Do not fear the storms and whirlwinds of this Flood, for you will not be drowned if you are borne by the wood. He who deigned to create all things from nothing knows how to steer. Let only the virtue of charity which bears all things be present, and no thing will be able to tear you away from the firmness of the ark.

[Col. 0619B] Remain good and endure the wicked. For it is better that, being within, you endure the wicked for the sake of the good, than that, going out and sparing them, you leave both the good and the wicked. Therefore, if beasts are with you—that is, if there are with you in the Church persons teaching perversely, holding false opinions, heretics, schismatics, or even evil Catholics themselves who, in the manner of beasts, seek to devour souls—let them be endured until the end of the age, as though until the end of the Flood. Though they roar, gnash their teeth, and seek with every effort to break the ark itself, do not be afraid. For when the Flood is ended, an empty and thorny wilderness will seize them, but a fertile and pleasant land will receive you. After the end of the age, the ungodly will be carried away into outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 25), while the land of the living will receive the godly.

For that holy man himself, after the end of the Flood and of his labour, offered God a sacrifice of sweet savour, but from clean animals, not unclean ones (Gen. 8). For clean and unclean animals alike could float in the ark, but the unclean—that is, the wicked—did not attain God’s sacrifice.

[Col. 0619D] It is fitting, therefore, beloved, that while we recount the deeds of strong men, we should call to mind our own faint-heartedness and weakness; and, advancing along the very path by which we know they have already progressed, follow them with all earnestness, lest we abandon what we have begun before, with Christ’s help, we are able to attain their fellowship.

“Patriarch” means “chief of the fathers.” For *archos* in Greek is called *princeps* (“chief”) in Latin. This most blessed patriarch, therefore—the chief of the fathers, second after Adam—proved obedient in commands, patient in adversity, and persevering in good works. By these three [Col. 0620A] virtues he pleased God. He endured adversities bravely, brought the work he had begun to completion, was pleasing to God by obedience, overcame dangerous events by patience, and completed by perseverance the work laid upon him by God. By obeying, he deserved to have God propitious; by patiently enduring, he escaped the danger of the Flood; by persevering, he renewed the entire human race.

What, dearest brothers, shall we say when this most holy patriarch appears glorious on the day of strict examination, exalted in the choir of patriarchs, enriched with heavenly rewards, adorned—as it were—with a gleaming crown of gold and precious gems, clothed in the robe of immortality, radiant with an angelic face and splendour? What shall we say on that day, we who are stirred to good works neither by the examples of the saints, nor roused by promises, nor terrified by threats? What will become of us sinners, who are sluggish in God’s service and anxious in earthly affairs, lukewarm in spiritual duties and frozen in idleness, yet zealous in fulfilling the desires of the flesh?

What then? Must we spend the whole course of our life in lowly, earthly pleasures? Or must we not, who until now have obeyed our own will rather than God’s, rise from the sleep of torpor and negligence while it is day? Or are examples of the saints set before us to be read merely that we may take delight in hearing them, and not rather that we may follow their footsteps with our whole mind? Far from it! Therefore, while there is time for good works, we must rise all the more earnestly [Col. 0620C] because we remember that until now we have been more negligent in God’s service. Thus most blessed James says:

> [Note: [Col. 0619D] These are the words of St Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, 2:13; following him, James said: “Be doers [Col. 0620D] of the word, and not hearers only,” and so forth, chap. 1:22.]  
> “It is not hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but doers of the Law will be justified.”

Let us therefore examine more closely the deeds of this Noah, our father, and take from him examples of good living. As was said above, he shone especially in three virtues: obedience, patience, and perseverance. By these he pleased God, overcame adversity, and completed a good work. If you have these virtues, beloved, show them by worthy conduct; if you do not have them, ask them from God, “who gives and does not reproach,” and they shall be given you (James 5). First, then, obey your superiors without pretence [Col. 0620D] (Heb. 13), and take care to fulfil their will in good things rather than your own. You especially vowed this to God and to the abbot when you first entered the order; without it you cannot please God at all.

Therefore, if you desire to please God and receive from him the rewards of eternal life, obey your superiors and show them reverence in all things. For they keep watch as those who will render an account for your souls, and labour without ceasing so that they may bring you with them to eternal joys. As a most kindly father cares for his own children in food, drink, and clothing, so they provide for you in spiritual duties as well as temporal affairs, that, if possible, free from want of bodily necessity [Col. 0621A] and with the stumbling-blocks of temporal life subdued, you may serve God.

Likewise divine grace moves them anew to concern for the advancement of your salvation. As an eagle guards her young by hovering over them lest anything harm them, and incites them to fly, so their care watches over you, lest any of you depart from the way of truth by sinning, lest the ancient enemy deceive you by some fraud and lead you with him—as God forbid—to destruction. Your prelates also, so to speak, urge you to fly when by their sweetest admonitions they exhort you to abandon low things, seek high things, despise earthly things, and desire heavenly things.

Again, beloved brothers, if you desire to attain fellowship with blessed Noah, be imitators of that admirable patience by which he could live with serpents and the most savage beasts. He endured the roaring [Col. 0621B] and growling of lions; you, patiently endure the complaints of foolish brothers. The roars of beasts and hissing of serpents did not disturb him; let not the slanders and whisperings of companions cast you down from the state of true patience. Let not human malice conquer you, for neither did the rage of beasts conquer him nor the fierceness of untamed animals terrify him.

[Col. 0622A] Therefore, if you wish to imitate wholly the footsteps of this holy man, you must be readier to endure injuries than to inflict them. Overcome with a tranquil mind both the evils of neighbours and the adversities of this present life; reject prosperity; refuse to repay evils with evils. Love friends in God; patiently endure enemies for God’s sake. Moreover, beloved, perseverance in good works is necessary for you; otherwise all your pursuits and works will fail like smoke, with fruitless labour. Hence it is said: “Whoever perseveres unto the end, that one will be saved” (Matt. 24). For our works then please God when we complete with a persevering end the good which we begin. Of those who do good without perseverance Scripture says: “Woe to those who have lost endurance!” (Sir. 2), that is, those who have not completed a good work.

Therefore, beloved, do not abandon before the day of death the good work [Col. 0622B] which you have begun, so that with blessed Noah you may deserve to share eternal blessedness and behold the one true God in three persons. May he deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Ninth Sermon: On Quinquagesima

[Col. 0621]

[Col. 0621C]

> [Note: [Col. 0621D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chap. 6.]

Abraham, father of nations, son of Terah, of the lineage of Shem and Chaldean by nation, was the first in faith in the Holy Trinity; a voluntary exile; obedient in commands; believing in promises; poor in his homeland; wealthy as a wanderer; victorious in battles; and generous in victory. Moreover, he overcame five kings, stripped them of spoils, and brought back his captive kinsman. This man is said to have been of such great wisdom and holiness that he deserved even to be called the friend of God. This holy man also signified Christ in his deeds.

While this most blessed man still dwelt in the land of the Chaldeans, God visited him, saying: “Go out from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and go into the land which I shall show you” (Gen. 12).

> [Note: [Col. 0621D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chap. 10.]

But who else than Christ went out [Col. 0621D] from his own land and kindred, to be enriched among strangers and become a great nation, leaving the land and kindred of the Jews, and now prevailing, as we see, among the peoples of the nations? But we too, after Christ’s example, must go out from our land—that is, from the possessions and earthly riches of this world. We must also go out from our kindred—that is, from evil conduct, wicked habits, and former vices which, clinging to us from our birth, are joined to us as if by a certain relationship and blood kinship. Or we must go out from our father’s house: that is, by renouncing every remembrance of the world, we may be enlarged among God’s people and, when the time comes, brought into the land of the heavenly promise.

Now two promises are given to Abraham. One is that his seed will possess the land of Canaan, when the Lord says to him: “Go into the land which I shall show you, and there I will make you into a great nation.” The other promise is far more excellent than this first one, because it concerns not carnal but spiritual seed. By it he is father not of one Israelite nation, but of all nations that follow faithfully in his footsteps. This began to be promised in these words, God saying: [Col. 0622D] “And in you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.”

Therefore Abraham, leaving the land of the Chaldeans, came to Shechem according to the Lord’s command. Driven thence by the scarcity of famine, he went down into Egypt, where he said without lying that his wife was his sister, since he had taken her from his own lineage.

> [Note: [Col. 0622D] Isidore, ibid., chap. 11.]

Returning from Egypt, whither he had gone, he parted from Lot, his brother’s son, without loss of charity, avoiding discord. Then he freed Lot, captured by the five kings who had invaded Sodom, taking with him into battle three hundred and eighteen home-born servants, by whom he defeated them.

And what does this victory of Abraham over the five kings signify, whom that father of faith overcame with God’s help, except that our faith may be so strengthened in the ruling spirit as to subject the same number of our bodily senses to the Word of God? For as he won victory over kings on behalf of his kinsman, so faith, victorious on behalf of the soul, triumphed over the outer human being. And because he defeated the hostile princes not by a multitude of peoples or the strength of legions, but with only three hundred and eighteen companions, God supplying him help, this foreshadowed that Christ’s Passion would free us from the dominion of the five carnal senses, which had formerly taken us captive through diverse vices to the destruction of our souls.

[Col. 0623B] As Abraham returned from the slaughter of the enemies, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God, at once met him—begotten of an unutterable parent—and blessed Abraham, offering bread and wine to God as a sacrifice. The Hebrews say that this man was Shem, son of Noah, Abraham’s great-grandfather. For he is the father of fathers, namely the origin of prophets and apostles; he is the one who, by the blessing of filial piety, deserved to be lord over his brother, and who, walking backward, covered his father’s nakedness. He did not mock him while drunk, as did the shameless and reprobate son, but modestly covered him. Thus it immediately became a law among the Jews that sons should never see their parents naked.

In the type of the true sacrifice, he was the first to offer God a victim of bread and wine [Col. 0623C] from the fruits of the earth, because priesthood and kingship belonged by right to firstborn sons before Aaron exercised the priesthood. He was also the first of all after the Flood to found the city of Salem, in which he reigned. It was afterwards called Jebus or Solyma and is now, by a derived name, called Jerusalem. He lived six hundred years and survived until the seventieth year of Isaac’s life; he died and was buried in his city Jerusalem.

This king is also called “king of righteousness”; but he is called king because he ruled Salem, and righteous because, discerning the sacraments of the Law and the Gospel, he did not slaughter animal victims but offered an oblation of bread and the cup to God as a sacrifice.

> [Note: [Col. 0623D] Isidore, ibid.]

The Apostle Paul, mentioning this Melchizedek as “without father, without mother,” says figuratively [Col. 0623D] that he signified Christ (Heb. 7). For Christ alone was begotten from the Father without a mother according to divinity; he was from a mother without a father according to humanity. He also is the eternal priest, to whom God says through the Psalmist: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). This is indeed because of the sacrament of the mystery which he commanded Christians to celebrate in memory of himself: that, not according to Aaron, with victims of animals, but through the offering of bread and wine—that is, the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood—we should offer sacrifice through him to God the Father.

And because the great patriarch, after the blessing, offered Melchizedek the priest tithes of all his possessions, [Col. 0624A] he knew spiritually that there would be a better priesthood among the people of the nations than the Levitical priesthood that was to arise from himself, and that the priesthood of the Church, having uncircumcision in Abraham’s circumcision, would bless the priesthood of the Synagogue. For one who blesses is greater than the one blessed. Hence the priests born from Abraham’s seed—the brethren whom they blessed, that is, the people, or those who gave them tithes according to the command of the Law—truly obeyed them as their greater and more eminent persons.

The name itself, Melchizedek, means “king of peace and righteousness,” and this is fittingly referred to Christ. For he is king of peace, because through him we are reconciled to God and have harmony with the angels. Truly he is king of righteousness, because he came to distinguish the holy from the ungodly now and on the last day. He is likewise both priest and king: because for the redemption of all he offered himself as a victim to God the Father; and, as true king, he rules his people in the present age and will judge them in the age to come.

> [Note: [Col. 0624D] Isidore, ibid., chap. 12.]

After this victory the word of the Lord came to Abraham in a vision, while he was anxious about his descendants and did not see a son being born to him. And although he retained the promise made to his seed, a twofold figure of his promised seed was immediately given him: it would be like the sand of the sea or like the stars of heaven. God therefore led Abraham outside, showed him the stars of heaven, and said: “Thus will I make your seed” (Gen. 15): that is, the Christian people, of whom you stand as father in faith. Thus will I make it [Col. 0624C] shine with the light of resurrection.

Then he showed him the sand of the sea and said to him: “So shall your seed be in multitude.” That is, the Jewish people will indeed be numerous, but barren and unfruitful like the sand of the sea. After this, when God promised him again that he would become possessor of the promise, a sign of this sort was given in these animals: “Take for me,” he said, “a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, together with a turtledove and a dove.” Abraham therefore took all these, divided them down the middle, and set the two halves opposite one another; but he did not divide the birds. And birds of prey descended upon the carcasses, and Abraham drove them away. And when the sun was setting, dread fell upon Abraham, and a great dark terror seized him [Col. 0624D]; and a smoking furnace appeared, and fire passing between those divided pieces. And it was said to him: “Know certainly that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own; and they shall afflict it and subject it to bondage for four hundred years” (ibid.), etc.

This, then, is the manner of Abraham’s promised seed, and this is the figure and allegory of the history mentioned above. By the heifer is signified the Israelite people placed beneath the yoke of the Law; by the she-goat, that same people as destined to be sinful; by the ram, that same people as destined to reign. These animals are called three-year-old because, passing through the divisions of time from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham [Col. 0625A], and from the time of Abraham to David, that people grew up as if passing through a threefold age. But by the turtledove and dove are signified the spiritual peoples within it, the undivided children of promise and future heirs of the kingdom. Their temporal years are therefore left unmentioned, because, meditating on eternal things, they have passed beyond temporal desires.

But what does it mean that the three animals are divided, their parts set against one another, except that carnal persons, both then among that people and now, are divided among themselves? The birds, however, are not divided because spiritual men are undivided. They devise no schisms and are not led astray by heretics; but peace is within them, whether they withdraw from crowds like the turtledove or live among them like the dove. Yet each bird possesses innocence [Col. 0625B] and simplicity, and denotes the holy way of life of God’s servants.

The birds descending upon the divided carcasses signify unclean spirits, which delight in receiving, as it were, their food from the division of carnal people, while they desire them to be condemned through the sin of discord. For just as the Son of God is nourished by the progress of the righteous, so the devil insatiably and ardently desires the condemnation of the faithful. Abraham’s driving away the descending birds signifies that, through the merit of the saints, many carnal persons devoted to worldly life are to be delivered from afflictions at the end of the world.

The dread that fell upon Abraham at sunset, and the great dark terror that seized him, signify the great disturbance that Antichrist will bring upon the saints near the end of this age [Col. 0625C], concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “Then there shall be great tribulation, such as has not been from the beginning” (Matt. 24). The further statement, “When the sun had set, a dark gloom came, and a smoking furnace and a lamp passing between the divided pieces appeared,” signifies the coming day of judgment, when the peoples of the saints and of the wicked will be separated by fire.

The words spoken to Abraham—“Know certainly that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall reduce them to bondage and afflict them for four hundred years”—were most fittingly revealed to us as referring to the people of Israel, who were to serve in Egypt. Yet this must not be understood as meaning that the children of Israel served under the Egyptians for four hundred years [Col. 0625D], but that this number was completed in the same affliction when reckoned from the time at which God made these promises to Abraham.

[Note: [Col. 0625D] Isidore, ibid., ch. 13.] Already then, because of the future sojourning, lest his seed should mingle with the other nations, circumcision was given him as a sign in these words: “Every male among you shall be circumcised; the child eight days old shall be circumcised among you, whether home-born or purchased. But the male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has made my covenant void. Nor shall Sarah be called Sarai, but Sura; and I shall give you a son from her, and I shall bless him, and he shall become nations, and kings of nations shall arise from him” (Gen. 17).

Here the promise concerning the calling of the nations is now made clear: namely, in Isaac, the son of promise—by grace, not by nature—since the history relates that he was to be born of an aged father and a barren mother. And because the offspring was to come, not through the generation represented in Ishmael, but through Isaac, circumcision was commanded by God at that point: when the son was promised as to be born from Sarah in a type of the Church, not when Ishmael, who in his birth and conduct bore the type of the Jews, was born.

But what else does circumcision signify except nature renewed through baptism after the stripping off of the old man in Christ? And who is the eighth day except Christ, who, when the week was completed—that is, after the Sabbath—rose again, now to live forever? The fact that he commands not only sons but also servants, home-born and purchased, to be circumcised shows that the grace of redemption pertains to all. There the names of the parents are changed, and everything resounds with newness. For Abram was formerly understood to mean “exalted father,” while Abraham is understood as “father of nations”; by this name it was foretold that many nations would follow in the footsteps of his faith.

But what is meant by the statement: “The male who is not circumcised on the eighth day—that soul shall perish from his people because he has made my covenant void”? Why does the soul of the uncircumcised child perish, when he himself did not make God’s covenant void, but those who neglected to circumcise him did so? Is it not to signify that [Col. 0626C] little children broke God’s covenant in the first man, not by their own act but by their origin, in whom all sinned? Infants are born sinners, not properly but originally; unless regeneration frees them, his soul will perish from his people—that is, from the assembly of the saints—because he made God’s covenant void, when he too sinned originally in Adam.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] Augustine, Sermon 106, as above.] But let us now at last pass on from this, so that we may say something about the power of charity by which most blessed Abraham deserved to please God. Let Abraham, then, that father of nations and beloved of God, teach us by his example to possess the power of charity, which “believes all things and hopes all things” (1 Cor. 13), in all the saints. At the Lord’s call he did not hesitate even once to leave his homeland, dwelling-place, house, and family; everything was left behind in order to obey the Lord’s command. “Go forth,” God said to him, “from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I shall show you.”

This holy man did not deliberate within himself or say, “Where am I going? To what land shall I entrust myself?” Rather, as soon as he heard, he rose, ran, hurried, hastened. He did not see the land of promise, but by believing he held it securely. He walked on the straight road and did not turn aside elsewhere than he ought with wandering steps, because the one who sent him to an unknown land provided him guidance; nor did he deceive him [Col. 0627A]. The reward is rendered to the believer: according to the Lord’s command, he reaches the land entrusted to him. He is enlarged and multiplied; from poor he becomes rich, from insignificant powerful. He is enriched with every good thing, and in him is fulfilled what the Lord promised his disciples in the Gospel, where he says among other things: “If anyone leaves house, or fields, or parents for my name’s sake, he shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19).

The reward of faith is further increased, and a son is promised to the old man. The power of charity is present: it believes all things, hears, rejoices, and loves more deeply. He receives a son from a barren wife, whom barrenness and age had already deprived of hope of childbearing; and in him he holds most firmly, without hesitation of mind, the blessing promised to all nations [Col. 0627B]. Yet charity still tests him and commends him when tested, because, as the outcome shows, he prefers nothing to God.

God calls to him from heaven, saying, “Abraham, Abraham.” And he, like an obedient servant and one loving God above all things, immediately answers: “Behold, I am here.” And the Lord says to him: “Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of vision, and there offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I shall tell you” (Gen. 22).

But to what place did Abraham proceed in order to sacrifice his son, and on what mountain, according to the Lord’s command? On Mount Orie, namely, in the thickets of Sabeth, which is interpreted “brambles” or “thorn-brake,” having bent branches within itself. Abraham therefore ascended this mountain to sacrifice his son, at the Lord’s command. Yet not even this command troubled or broke the faithful servant [Col. 0627C]; for the power of charity was present in him, which believes all things, willingly endures adversity for God, and despises prosperity.

At once he goes home, saddles the ass, cuts wood, takes sword and fire, brings the boy with him, and proceeds to the place. Then Isaac, attentive as he walked along, questioned his father, saying, “My father?” And he replied, “What is it, my son?” And the son said, “Behold, there are fire and wood; but where is the victim for the burnt offering?” He answered, “God will provide himself the victim for the burnt offering, my son.”

I see a great mystery here, in the father’s answer to his son. Abraham bore one thing in his heart and promised another thing to his son; yet what the father promised did not deceive the son, nor did any weakness alter Abraham’s heart from its purpose [Col. 0627D]. What more need be said? He proceeds, sees the place from afar, and, immediately stationing the servants there, speaks these words to them: “Sit here with the ass; the boy and I will hasten over there, and, after we have worshipped, we shall return to you.”

O holy Abraham! What is this that you said to your servants, when, by God’s command, you had resolved to do something else concerning the boy? Do you deceive yourself by these words, or your servants? By no means. Rather, I see that the things I say or do prophetically are wrought and spoken in me by the power of charity, which believes all things. For I hear it speaking inwardly to my heart without sound of voice [Col. 0628A], and saying to me something like this: “Although, in unquestioning faith that he will rise again, you lead the boy to be sacrificed with full and perfect resolve, yet your son is not consumed in this sacrifice, because the resurrection is reserved for the Son of God.”
