The apostle James fittingly recalls the faith of this holy man for our instruction: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness, and he was called the friend of God” (Jas. 2). As we know, union of minds makes friends, and division makes enemies. Hence I have read that a certain sage of this world said in a certain writing: “To desire the same things and to reject the same things—this, and this alone, is firm friendship” [Note: [Col. 0627D] Sallust, *On Catiline*, p. 26, Regia Hispaniarum Inferiorum edition.]. [Note: [Col. 0627D] “That is the old law of just and true friendship: friends should always desire the same things” [Col. 0628D]. Cicero, *Oration for Gnaeus Plancius*.]

Thus, as we have said above, union of minds makes friends and division makes enemies. Do you wish to know how this saint united his mind to God, so as to become and be called his friend? For just as God the Father “did not spare his only Son but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8), so he too did not spare his only son, but with his whole heart offered him for sacrifice at the command of the one who had given him. But let us hear what follows.

For, with the help of the Lord our God, it delights us to give you a full understanding of this history. After leaving the servants behind, the father comes with his son to the place of sacrifice; he builds an altar, arranges the pile, binds his son’s hands, lays him upon the altar above [Note: [Col. 0628D] Above.] the wood, sets aside the dictates of human fatherly affection, puts on the terrible constancy of a priest, and draws the sword in order to kill his son [Col. 0628C].

What do you observe here, brothers? What do you see or understand? I confess that we perceive nothing human here, because we recognize that everything is divine. And that son, who a little earlier had asked for the sheep, feels these things being done to him in profound silence and bears all of them so patiently; he does not contradict his father in any respect, as though he were already that lamb who wished to be led like a sheep to slaughter for us, and “like a lamb before its shearer was without voice, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53).

O holy Isaac, whom your father, by divine command, laid upon the pile of wood, disclose to us this great secret of your silence. A little earlier you felt nothing being done to you and asked your father for a ram; now your hands are bound, you are placed upon the altar, you are in a manner suspended upon wood [Col. 0628D], and now in silence you hide yourself in the stillness of silence. “I am silent,” he says. “Tell us why, I beg you, so that you may disclose to us the reason for your silence.” “Do you wish,” he says, “to know why I am silent and send forth no tearful voice of complaint against God or my father? It is because I bear the figure of him who lays down his life for the salvation of the whole world willingly, not by necessity.”

In this great mystical sacrament of faith, holy Abraham was shown to be tested, the son was delivered in the present event, and Christ too was prefigured. Therefore, if there is any soul that desires to follow in the footsteps of the faith of our father Abraham, go forth from your land [Col. 0629A] and from your kindred; leave your people and your father’s house—that is, firmly renounce the devil, his pomps, and his angels—and follow the straight way that leads you to the best land, where you may become rich and eminent and become Abraham’s companion, that is, in the heavenly homeland. But when you have done all these things, if the power of charity, which believes all things, is in you, it will still test you and crown you when tested.

God asks from you a burnt offering: namely, the pure and spotless sacrifice of your one beloved. What does he ask from you? The very thing said to Abraham: “God said to Abraham: Give me your one beloved.” Wisdom says to you: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 25). That one beloved is our mind. Why are you afraid to offer your heart? Offer to the Lord your God the sacrifice [Col. 0629B] of a contrite heart, and say with the Prophet: “You will not delight in burnt offerings; a sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50). When such a sacrifice has been offered and accepted by God, you will fear nothing; and what you offer will not perish, but will remain whole.

Meanwhile, dearest brothers, since [Note: [Col. 0629D] Supply: “since.”] we have said something about the virtues and labours of our most glorious father Abraham, it is fitting that we should call ourselves to remembrance and, beholding his holiness and perfection, rebuke within ourselves our own negligence. For then we profitably set the lives of the saints before the eyes of the mind, if by imitating them [Col. 0629C] we detest vices and take examples of good living. The more often we discern, by reading, the life of the perfect, if we are not stirred by their examples to act well, the more blameworthy we shall be found at the judgment of the strict Judge. Without doubt, we become guilty of the greater crime if we neglect to do the good that we know. He heaps guilt upon himself who refuses to do the good he has learned.

Let it therefore delight us all to hear what God said to our father Abraham: “Go forth from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land which I shall show you.” What do you understand in this command of the Lord, brothers? Do you think that the Lord commanded Abraham alone to leave his land, rather than commanding us through him, so that, stirred by his example [Col. 0629D], we might go forth from our own land, so to speak—that is, from earthly vices and desires—renouncing sins and depraved habits, be enlarged among God’s people, and attain the promise of the heavenly reward?

We too must go forth from our kindred—that is, from evil conduct—and from our father’s house, namely from every carnal affection and pleasure; and through the path of virtues we must arrive at the land of promise, according to the Lord’s command. Yet, beloved, I do not wish you to be ignorant that unless you travel by the way of virtues, you cannot arrive at the land of promise, that is, the heavenly homeland. For lovers of this world descend into hell by the way of vices [Col. 0630A], but friends of God ascend to heaven by the way of virtues. Just as the desire of this present age, which is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6), casts souls headlong into hell, so its contempt undoubtedly raises them to heaven; and just as friendship with the world makes people enemies of God, so contempt for it makes them friends.

Therefore, dearest brothers, while we strive more to pursue the desires of the flesh than to fulfil God’s commands, we dwell in our land—that is, in Ur of the Chaldeans, in the fire of vices. When we are anxious about earthly affairs and sluggish in spiritual duties, we have not yet gone forth from our kindred and our father’s house. Thus, beloved, as we have already said above, God called not Abraham alone [Col. 0630B] to leave his land, but also us, so that by renouncing the world we may be fit for the heavenly homeland. For he who said to Abraham, “Go forth from your land and from your kindred,” also said to us: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). And he who said to Abraham, “Come into the land which I shall show you, and I shall make you into a great nation,” undoubtedly promises us all in common, saying: “Whoever leaves father and mother, brothers and sisters, for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19); and again: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there my servant shall be also” (John 12).

What do these promises of the Lord seem to you, brothers [Col. 0630C]? Did God promise great things to him but small things to you? By no means. He undoubtedly promised him great rewards, but if you follow him with your whole heart, he has not promised you insignificant things. Let us therefore compare, if you please, some of the things that God promised to him and to you. God promised him the land of Canaan, and possession for his seed; but to us, a heavenly dwelling. God made him, through faith, the father of many nations; you beget many by examples of spiritual life, when you raise them up by salutary admonitions and lead them to the knowledge of God.

To him it was said: “In your seed,” that is, in Christ, “all nations of the earth shall be blessed.” You frequently beget the very Son of God when, by preaching, you nourish his knowledge, faith, and love in the hearts of your hearers; by admonition you increase them; by promising the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0630D], you strengthen them. Of this Scripture says: “Those who nourish him shall be kings and queens” (Isa. 49). He himself also says of himself: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12). By obeying God’s voice, Abraham was called the friend of almighty God; the same God and Son of God speaks to you: “You are my friends if you do the things which I command you” (John 15).

He was poor in his native land and rich in the land of promise; but God promises you, if you are poor in spirit and love him, ineffable riches [Col. 0631A] which eye has not seen nor ear heard, if you obey his voice. What voice? Do you wish to hear which? “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16).

Therefore renounce, beloved, in accordance with the Lord’s command, all that you possess: namely, every desire of the flesh and pleasure of this present world, the devil and his pomps and works. Strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new (Col. 3), “created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4). Having taken up the cross, follow not only the footsteps of Abraham but, what is far better and far more blessed, the footsteps of Jesus Christ your master [Col. 0631B], as far as you are able.

Perhaps you say, “By what path, and to where?” By the way of blessing and virtue, of which the Prophet speaks in the Psalms: “The lawgiver shall give blessings; they shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83). He appropriately said that one can arrive at heaven by the way of virtues, since the ungodly descend into hell by the way of vices. He rightly said that one ascends to see the God of gods in Zion, because only the purified eyes of the saints shall be able to see him in his essence.

It should certainly be noted that this most faithful patriarch was never admonished by any prophet, no preacher was ever sent to him, and yet at one command of the Lord he left land, kindred, paternal house, and all relatives, ready to fulfil the word [Col. 0631C]. What shall we say to these things, beloved, we who have been forewarned by the examples of the patriarchs, taught by the prophecies of prophets, instructed by the proclamations of the apostles, educated by the writings of the evangelists, and, what is nobler and more blessed still, nourished and brought up from infancy as with heavenly richness even by the preaching of the Lord himself [Col. 0632A], and yet are sluggish in obeying his voice?

It is time, then, beloved, to rise from the sleep of sloth and indolence, cast sluggishness from our minds, cease to devise delays in doing good, and hasten joyfully and girded up by the way of virtues toward the land of promise—that is, the heavenly homeland—where the Lord has gone before us and calls us. Yet we must know that this way is not travelled with bodily steps but by good habits; not by departing from one’s homeland but by living well in it; not by taking the broad road but the rough and exceedingly narrow one; not by loving vices but virtues; not by pursuing carnal but spiritual things; not by seeking visible but invisible things; not by preserving hatred, anger, or discord in the mind [Col. 0632B], but by maintaining perfect charity toward friends and enemies; by detesting avarice and giving alms with a generous hand; by uprooting pride and self-exaltation from the mind and planting there profound humility; by detesting lust with all impurity and embracing with all one’s strength purity of mind and body; by despising all things under heaven and longing with supreme desire for those things above the heavens; and finally by fixing the eye of the mind upon the highest good, almighty God.

This, beloved, is the royal and straight way. “While you have the light, walk in it” (John 12), and do not turn aside from it either to the right or to the left (Prov. 4), because it will lead you without stumbling to the land of promise, that is, to the joys of heavenly life, through him who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TENTH SERMON. AT THE BEGINNING OF THE FAST.

[Col. 0631]

[Col. 0631D] Almighty God, dearest brothers, seeing us travel over the precipices of vices and observing us draw away from him by evil living, loving conversion more than the death of sinners, mercifully admonishes us through the prophet Joel that we may return to him in repentance, saying: “Return to me with all your heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning” (Joel 2), etc.

Therefore, beloved, let us not delay in turning to God, because he is ready mercifully to forgive us our sins. He who kindly invites us to return to him wishes to grant pardon; he who calls us to repentance commands us, as a most merciful Lord, to return to him; and, as a most loving Father, he forgives the sins of those who return to him [Col. 0632D]. For if he had not wished to spare us, he would never have invited us to repentance. “Return to me,” he says, “with all your heart.” He does not say, “Return to me in part,” but “with all your heart,” that is, with all your understanding, all your memory, all your will, and all your love.

From where shall we return, and to whom? From slavery to the devil to God; from the dominion of the most cruel enemy to the sweetest Lord; from the rule of the foe to the most loving Father; from the hand of the most cunning robber to the most merciful deliverer; from evil to the highest good; from this wicked age to paradise; from earth to heaven; from the conduct of perverse people to the fellowship of angels; from prison to a palace [Col. 0633A]; from the theatre to a kingdom; from low things to high; from vices to virtues; from injustice to righteousness; from misery to blessedness; from toil to rest; from sorrow to joy; from everlasting death to eternal life.

And how shall we return to God? Namely, in fasting, weeping, mourning, and the rending of the heart. Teaching elsewhere how we ought to return to God, cast away the darkness of vices, and walk honourably before him in the day of virtues, the apostle Paul says: “The night has gone before”—that is, the night of error—“the day,” that is, the light of Christ’s evangelical preaching, “has drawn near. Let us therefore cast off the works of darkness” (Rom. 13), namely sins and the vices of the flesh, which lead the soul into eternal darkness, “and put on the armour of light,” of which he says: “By the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left” [Col. 0633B] (2 Cor. 6), so that “we may walk honourably as in the day,” that is, in Christ or in Christ’s teaching, “not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and shameless acts, not in strife and envy; but put on” (Rom. 13)—that is, imitate—the new man, our Lord Jesus Christ, fulfilling his new commands in deed.

Therefore, what the Lord says, that we should return to him in fasting, weeping, and mourning, is what Paul preaches to us: that we should not walk in revelries and drunkenness, nor in beds and shameless acts, but honourably, and that in the day, that is, in the splendid teaching of Christ, who is the true Sun of righteousness and the day of eternity. Similar also is what Peter, prince of the apostles, says when exhorting the faithful: “I beseech you, as strangers [Col. 0633C] and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2).

Let us therefore recognize and reflect, dearest brothers, with what honour an embassy from almighty God ought to be received by us [Note: [Col. 0633D] From the book *On Salutary Instructions*, ch. 9.]. If an embassy from an earthly king, or a letter or seal, came to us, would we not immediately, setting aside other concerns, receive the letter with ready will and every devotion, and strive to fulfil it when we had read it? And behold, the King of heaven and earth, the Creator of all creatures, our Redeemer and Restorer, has deigned to send us his letter through his prophet Joel—not to seek from us any service necessary to himself, but to make known what may benefit our eternal salvation [Col. 0633D]. Let him therefore show us how he commands us to return to him.

“Return,” he says, “to me with all your heart,” and the rest. These commands, dearest brothers, are exceedingly profitable and worthy of all acceptance; without them no one can attain the homeland of eternal brightness. These most health-giving commands of God bring their fulfilers to eternal joys; this saving admonition is evidence of divine love. For unless he loved us, however wicked we are, as a most loving Father, he would never invite us to return to him.

Therefore, with the utmost devotion we ought to receive the letter he sent us through the prophet, because one who despises the commands of the physician kills himself [Col. 0634A]. [Note: [Col. 0633] “He kills himself who does not wish to observe the physician’s commands.” Augustine, *Tractates on John*, 12.] Certainly, one who despises God’s commands tends not toward life but toward perpetual death. Truly, contempt for God’s commands drags a person not to rest but to eternal torments. The embassy of almighty God must therefore not be despised, but embraced with the greatest love and fulfilled in deed with the highest diligence.

“Return,” he says, “to me with all your heart.” It is as though he said: “If you wish to return to me, do not do so deceitfully, but return with all your heart. For fear and love of me, despise the riches of this passing life. If you truly wish to leave the world and return to me, reject the delicacies of foods and softness of clothing. If you wish to cling to me with your whole heart, first do penance for sins committed [Col. 0634B]. Let it grieve you not only that you committed sins, but also that you did not do the good that you ought to have done. Mortify your bodies with fasts; wash the stains of sins with tears. Let the flesh fast from food and the mind from vices. By abstinence from food the flesh is weakened, but the spirit is strengthened. Let the body serve through fasting and vigils, while the mind devoutly attends to prayer. Let the outward person be exercised by abstinence and vigils, while the inward person is raised to contemplation of its Creator. Let the hand be occupied in works of mercy, and let the mind inwardly attend to divine contemplation. Let sackcloth cover the body’s members within; let the hand give alms to the poor. Let ashes and a mournful garment envelop the body, while the mind has compassion on the needs of the wretched [Col. 0634C]. Let the roughness of sackcloth prick the flesh; let tears wash away the stains of sin. In penitence, let the sackcloth cover limbs rendered unsightly and wasting away, while the eye pours forth streams of tears.”

Again the prophet continues: “Return to the Lord your God, for he is kind and merciful, relenting concerning evil.” It is as if the prophet more openly exhorted the people to repentance in the Lord’s words: “Return to God with all your heart”—not only with the lips, but with all understanding, will, and action; in fasting, that you may be satisfied in the future; in weeping, that you may laugh; and in mourning, that you may be comforted. And “rend”—that is, open—your hearts through confession of faith, which are like skins full of sins and, unless willingly torn open, will burst; “and not your garments,” as it is the custom of the Jews to do in time of sorrow or distress.

And thus return to the Lord your God, whom sins have made estranged; and do not despair, even if your offences have been great. For he is kind and merciful—naturally compassionate and unwilling that sinners should die, but rather repentant; patient and “of great mercy,” that is, he does not punish immediately but waits; “relenting concerning evil,” that is, granting mercy after repentance for evils. “Relenting concerning evil” (Matt. 6), he says—that is, concerning the affliction of penitents, according to the words, “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” [Col. 0635A]. And again: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos 3).

But because he had called the Lord merciful and patient, lest the greatness of mercy should make people negligent in doing penance, the prophet adds in the form of a question: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” It is as though he said: “I exhort you to repentance and proclaim God’s mercy; but because we cannot penetrate the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, I moderate my assertion: I pray rather than presume.”

It follows: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” As if he said: Who knows whether he may turn from anger, that is, to mercy, and forgive our sins, and leave behind—[Col. 0635B] that is, grant after himself, that is, after vengeance and his scourge—a blessing, namely, remission of sins? “Who knows,” he says, “whether God may turn and forgive?” This is impossible or difficult to know; and therefore it is safer to do penance than to remain in guilt. And, having received forgiveness, we shall offer sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God. Hence the Psalmist: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Ps. XLIX).

Again he adds: “Sound the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast, call an assembly, gather the people, sanctify the Church, assemble the elders, gather the little children and those who suck the breast.” In this place the divine word exhorts preachers and prophets to preach repentance before the hostile sword comes, or [Col. 0635C] any other plague that destroys crops. As if he said: Above I warned you to repentance both by reminding you of the enemies’ cruelty and by recalling my mercy; now, however, again and again I command: “Sound the trumpet in Zion,” that is, publicly preach repentance in the Church; sanctify the fast by good will, prayer, and works; call an assembly, a synod or congregation; gather the people, so that he who wandered scattered from God may, when gathered, serve God; sanctify the Church, so that none in it may be unclean or unsanctified, lest the whole mass be corrupted by evil leaven (Gal. V); assemble—that is, choose—elders, both in age and in wisdom, in good character and knowledge, so that they may furnish others with [Col. 0635D] an example of good living and instruction. Or the elders are commanded to be gathered so that at least at the end of life they may repent. Gather the little children, to whom it is said: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. III); and those who suck the breast, concerning whom the Prophet says: “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Ps. VIII). Therefore let there be no age that does not turn to God, because no one on earth—not even an infant one day old—is without sin (Job XIV, according to the Septuagint); if one is not bound by actual sin, one is bound by original sin.

It follows: “Let the bridegroom go out from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room”—namely, so that they may fast and not serve the work of marriage, but devote themselves [Col. 0636A] to prayer.

Again he says: “Between the porch and the altar the priests, the ministers of the Lord, shall weep.” There were two altars: one in the temple, called the altar of incense, and another in the portico before the doors of the temple, the altar of burnt offerings. Hence it is now said, “between the porch and the altar,” that is, in the space between the altar of incense and the altar of burnt offering. Let “between the porch and the altar” therefore be understood as in the portico that covers the inner house: in a place suitable for repentance and confession the priests wept, those who say with the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. XI). They are ministers of the Lord, who ought to weep with those who weep and urge others to weeping, and “they shall say,” that is, he teaches what the priests should say and how [Col. 0636B] they ought to implore God: “Spare, O Lord, spare your people, and do not give your inheritance over to reproach, that the nations may rule over them.” As if they said: Spare, O Lord—that is, forgive sins; spare your people, now already yours because it repents, though formerly not yours while it sinned; and do not give your inheritance, namely Israel, over to reproach, so that they may serve the nations. “That the nations may rule over them”: namely demons, who rule over us while we are unrepentant.

Again he adds, saying: “Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’” As if he said: Why should those peoples who are compared to the caterpillar, locust, beetle, and blight say, “Where is their God?” That is, why do you permit the peoples to say, “Where is their God,” whom they thought their defender [Col. 0636C] and helper? Why does your God not help you? [Note: [Col. 0635D] For this is what they said to the captives.]

It follows: “The Lord was jealous for his land and spared his people.” As if he said: When the people and priests had fulfilled the things mentioned above, God loved his land, which he had formerly despised. Or, more plainly: “The Lord was jealous for his land,” namely, he took vengeance, because he first scourged his people; but afterward, appeased by their repentance, he spared his people. “And the Lord answered and said to his people.” He answered not words only, but deeds—that is, their repentance. God so spares a people doing penance that he considers them worthy of his response; and we see this happen daily in the Church.

And the Lord said to his people: “Behold, I will send [Col. 0636D] you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them; and I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations.” As if he said: Behold, I who sent upon you, when you sinned, the caterpillar, beetle, blight, by which all your crops were laid waste, have now through repentance turned to mercy; I shall deliver you from the Assyrians, and if you persevere in good things, I shall fill you with every good. Or, more plainly: “I will send you grain,” namely, the bread that came down from heaven; “and wine, which gladdens the human heart” (Ecclus. XL); and oil, which makes the face cheerful (Ps. CIII); “and you shall be filled with them,” so that the old sadness of sins may be tempered by the joy of grain, wine, and oil—that is, of virtues [Col. 0637A].

Allegorically, every soul is the Lord’s land, in which he sows. But if it bears tares, that is, vices, it offends the Lord; if, however, it repents and says, “Spare, O Lord,” the Lord is jealous for his land and deigns to comfort it with his word, saying: “I will send you grain, wine, and oil”—namely, virtues by which you may do good works and avoid sins.

It follows: “And I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations; and him who is from the north I will remove far from you and drive him into a land without a way and desolate.” As if he said: I will no longer give you up as captives to reproach among the nations, and him who is from the north, namely the people of the Assyrians dwelling in the northern regions, I will remove far from you; and if he comes, I will drive him into a land [Col. 0637B] without a way—that is, into some nation deserted by God, in which the Holy Spirit does not dwell—and desolate, because it has no knowledge of God.

According to the literal sense, it is not the north wind but the south wind that commonly brings locusts: for they do not come from cold but from heat. But because he was speaking of the Assyrians under the likeness of locusts, he introduces the north, so that we may understand not real locusts but Assyrians and Chaldeans. Hence it is said: “From the north evils shall blaze forth upon the inhabitants of the land” (Jer. I). “I will no longer make you a reproach among the nations,” namely among those of whom he said above, “a people numerous and strong,” and so forth; or “among the nations,” that is, among demons, whence this saying: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and rulers of this darkness, [Col. 0637C] against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). He preserves the metaphor and speaks according to the geography of the province, as though he appeared to speak of locusts and not enemies.

For Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0637D] On Joel, chapter II; but from the *Gloss*, as our Martin always drew these things.] that in his time there was a swarm of locusts which, afterward, through God’s mercy, when priests and peoples cried between the porch and the altar—that is, between the place of the cross and the resurrection—“Spare, O Lord, your people,” were, as a wind arose, cast headlong into the first and the last sea. But when heaps of dead locusts were thrown back from the waves to the shores by the force of the sea, rot and noxious stench arose, which, corrupting the air, brought pestilence upon human beings and beasts.

Again he adds, saying: “Its face toward the eastern sea [Col. 0637D] and its end toward the last sea.” As if he said: I shall turn the face of that most savage nation, so that its first part may be toward the eastern sea, where Sodom and Gomorrah formerly stood, together with other cities which were turned into the sea called the Dead Sea because no animals live in it. And I shall turn its farthest part toward the sea that is to the west and leads toward Egypt, upon whose shore are Gaza, Ascalon, Ashdod, Joppa, Caesarea, and other cities.

> “This same Dead Sea, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0637D] *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 19.], is called the Lake of Asphalt because it produces nothing living [Col. 0638A] and receives nothing of the race of living things. For it has no fish, nor does it permit birds accustomed to water and delighted by the practice of diving. Indeed, whatever living creature you try to submerge, however skillfully immersed, immediately springs back; and, though violently thrust down, is at once cast up. Nor is it moved by winds, because bitumen resists the storms and keeps all the water still; nor does it permit navigation, because everything lacking life sinks into the depths; nor does it support any material except that which is coated with bitumen. [Note: [Col. 0638D] The very learned Grialius conjectures that Isidore wrote *incrustatur* (“is coated”), not *illustratur* (“is made bright”).] They report that a lighted lamp floats upon it, but when its flame is extinguished it sinks. This is also called the Sea of Salt, or the Lake of Asphalt—that is, bitumen—and it lies in Judaea, between Jericho and Zoar. Its length extends to the Zoars of Arabia for [Col. 0638B] seven hundred [Note: [Col. 0638D] Isidore: five hundred.] and eighty stadia; its breadth is one hundred and fifty stadia as far as the neighborhood of Sodom.”

The Prophet therefore calls the Dead Sea the eastern sea, and the Last Sea the western sea. Mystically, the first part of that most savage nation—that is, the assault of demons—is turned toward the eastern sea in those who open to it the gate of sin; and its last part toward the western sea, in those, that is, with whom the Assyrian—the devil—has remained to the end of life.

Again he says: “Its stench shall rise, and its rot, because it acted proudly.” According to the letter, this happened to the Chaldeans in Hezekiah’s time, when in one night one hundred and eighty-five thousand were killed by the angel in the camp; and that part of the camp facing the eastern sea, that is, toward Sodom, was slain, together with the rear part looking toward the sea leading to Egypt. Their bodies were consumed by fire and reduced to earth. What follows concerning the stench is to be understood not of the bodies of the Assyrians but mystically: “Its stench shall rise,” he says, in those who promise themselves great things and fall through pride, lest frail man be secure; “and its rot shall rise,” because the more one increases in virtues, the more one should fear falling through vices.

It follows: “Do not fear, O land; exult and rejoice, for the Lord has magnified himself by acting.” Above, having threatened, he promises prosperity and turns tears into laughter. As if he said: Rejoice, O land, [Col. 0638D] and be glad in the Lord’s promises, because you had lost God’s seed through your dryness; for the Lord has magnified himself by showing mercy to you, so that even the beasts, which above were said to have perished through hunger and thirst, may multiply, and the wildernesses may be filled with joyful new fields, because the people have turned to repentance.

“Do not fear, beasts of the region, for the beauties of the wilderness have sprouted, because the tree has borne its fruit; the fig tree and the vine have given their strength.” As if he said: Do not fear, beasts of the region—that is, faithful people predestined for the pastures of eternal greenness, who feed upon the sweetness of God’s word—[Col. 0639A] for the beauties of the wilderness have sprouted, namely the Gentiles, who, having received the seed of evangelical preaching, have borne fruit a hundredfold. The tree also has borne its fruit: namely, the tree of the cross has borne the fruit of Christ’s Passion. The fig tree, that is, the Holy Spirit, and the vine, namely the word of God, have given their *virtus*, that is, abundance.

Again, congratulating those converted to God by repentance, he says: “And you, children of Zion, exult and rejoice in the Lord your God, because he has given you the teacher of righteousness, and will cause the early and the latter rain to come down upon you as in the beginning.” Or, more plainly: You especially, children of Zion—that is, of the Church—rejoice through repentance, you who were formerly estranged from God by sins; and rejoice in the Lord [Col. 0639B] your God, not in the delights of this world, because he has given you the teacher of righteousness, namely Christ, who will teach you all truth (John XVI), and will cause the early rain to come down upon you—the former teaching of faith, namely that of the Old Law—and the latter rain, namely the New Testament, as in the beginning of blessing.

In the literal sense, the early rain is that which comes when the crop is sown, while the latter rain comes when the crop must be gathered. Mystically, the early rain is faith, while the latter is the perfection of works; or the early rain is the knowledge of God given after faith, and the latter rain the fullness of that same knowledge.

It follows: “And the threshing-floors shall be filled with grain, and the winepresses shall overflow with wine and oil; and [Col. 0639C] I will restore to you the years which the locust, beetle, blight, and caterpillar have consumed—my great strength which I sent against you—and you shall eat plentifully and be satisfied, and you shall praise the name of your God, who has dealt with you in mercy and wonders; and my people shall never be put to shame, and you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel.”

As if he said plainly: The threshing-floors shall be filled with grain—that is, there will be such abundance of crops that, after you are satisfied, much will remain on the floors and in the winepresses; and the winepresses shall overflow with wine and oil. He will make you abound in the fruits of virtues. By this expression great abundance is indicated, so that they may also supply others with what is left over to themselves. “I will restore to you the years which the locust, beetle, blight, and caterpillar consumed”: that is, I shall not allow the fertility which you lost in past [Col. 0639D] years to perish. For as many years as you endured famine, for so many years I shall again double the crops.

“I will restore to you the years which the locust, beetle, blight, and caterpillar consumed”—the caterpillar which scarcely moves and is crushed by a slight touch, in which both God’s great strength and human frailty are displayed, as also by the gnats in Egypt, which are so small that they can scarcely be seen. God could indeed have covered all things with a flood or burned them with lightning; but through such tiny creatures he displays both his power and our frailty. For if these are stronger than a human being, why does earth and ashes boast?

“I will restore to you the years which the locust, beetle, blight, and caterpillar consumed—my great strength [Col. 0640A] which I sent against you”: namely demons, who are avengers of those who work evil, such as the one who deceived Ahab [Note: [Col. 0639D] *Achab*] (3 Kings XXII), and the one who tormented Saul (1 Kings XVIII). Paul hands sinners over to torturers of this kind for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. V).

Novatian and certain other heretics say that after sin a person cannot through repentance be restored to the former state. This error is plainly destroyed in this passage, since the Lord receives penitents so fully that he calls them his people, declares that they shall not be put to shame, says that he will dwell in their midst, and that they will have no other God but will trust with their whole heart in him who remains in them for ever.

Truly, just as almighty God is essentially [Col. 0640B] good, so he is merciful and compassionate toward those who turn back; and just as he justly punishes those who persevere in evil, so he kindly receives those who return to him through repentance. It is therefore necessary, beloved, that we praise God’s justice in all things and recall with tears into what misery we have fallen from the beginning of our creation. Let us confess that we are sinners, and let us bring before the eyes of our mind, with weeping, the miseries into which we have fallen. And with blessed Job, who mourns not only his own unhappiness but that of the whole human race, let us say: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not perish at once when I came forth from the womb? Why was I received upon knees? Why nursed at breasts?” (Job III).

Blessed Job does not say this because he wishes himself to have been miscarried, but in order to show by mourning in what ways the first human being, sinning in paradise, miserably cast us down with himself into the exile of this world. For the more attentively he considers the fall of the human race, the more bitterly he laments its calamity.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0639D] *Morals*, book IV, no. 49.] says: “(The ancient enemy tempted the first human being in paradise in three ways: namely, suggestion, temptation, and consent. [Note: [Col. 0640D] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from Gregory.]) Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and in four ways it is brought to completion in deed. In the heart it is committed by suggestion, delight, consent, and defense: now secretly, now openly, now by habit, now by despair. Suggestion comes through the adversary, delight through the flesh, consent through the spirit, and the boldness of defense through pride. For guilt, which ought to terrify the mind, [Col. 0640D] exalts it; and, by casting it down, raises it up, yet by raising it up more grievously overthrows it.

“Thus the ancient enemy shattered the uprightness of the first human being by these four blows. The serpent suggested; Eve took delight; Adam consented, and, when questioned, through boldness refused to confess his fault. What was done in the first parent of our race is enacted daily in the human race. The serpent suggested, because the hidden enemy secretly suggests evils to human hearts. Eve took delight, because carnal sense immediately submits itself with delight to the serpent’s words. But Adam, set over the woman, gave consent, because, while the flesh is carried away in delight, the weakened spirit also bends from its uprightness. [Col. 0641A] And Adam, when questioned, refused to confess his fault, because the very spirit which is separated from truth by sinning is, by the boldness of its fall, more wickedly hardened.

“Sin is likewise completed in deed by the same four modes. First hidden fault is committed; afterward guilt is revealed even before human eyes without shame; then it is brought into habit; and finally it is nourished either by the deceptions of false hope or by the obstinacy of wretched despair. Blessed Job therefore considers these modes of sin, which occur secretly in the heart or are openly perpetrated in deed, and laments the degrees of sins into which all of us—indeed the whole human race—have fallen, saying: ‘Why did I not die in the womb? Why did I not [Col. 0641B] perish at once when I came forth from the womb? Why was I received upon knees? Why nursed at breasts?’

“For the first womb of conception was the tongue of evil suggestion. But the sinner would die in the womb if a person recognized himself as destined to die at the very suggestion. Yet he came forth from the womb because, after the suggestive tongue conceived him in sin, delight immediately drew him outward. After coming forth he was received on knees, because, when he came out into the delight of the flesh, he doubtless completed the fault by the consent of the spirit, made subject to all the senses, as though set upon knees. But, received on knees, he was also nursed at breasts. For when the spirit is enslaved to the senses in consenting to fault, many arguments giving confidence follow, which nourished the soul born in sin with poisonous milk, and fostered it with soothing excuses lest it fear [Col. 0641C] the harsh punishments of death.

“Hence the first human being after his fault became bolder, saying: ‘The woman whom you gave me—she gave me, and I ate’ (Gen. III). He had fled to hide himself through fear; yet, when questioned, he made himself known. How much he swelled even while afraid! For when the present punishment arising from sin is feared, while the lost face of God is not loved, that fear springs from arrogance, not humility. The person who would not abandon sin if it could go unpunished is proud.

“Therefore fault, as has been said, is committed in deed by the same four ways by which it is committed in the heart. Blessed Job, mourning most bitterly not only himself but also the human race, recalling to all of us the sins through which we were expelled from the delights of paradise, and at the same time giving a useful example of mourning, says: ‘Why did I not die in the womb?’ and so forth. The womb of the sinning human being is the hidden fault which secretly conceives the sinner and conceals its guilt in darkness. ‘Why,’ he says, ‘did I not perish immediately when I came forth [Col. 0641D] from the womb?’ One goes out from the womb when a sinner is not ashamed to commit openly what he committed in secret. Those of whom the prophet said, ‘They proclaimed their sin like Sodom and did not hide it’ (Isa. III), had, as it were, come forth from the womb of their concealment.

“It follows: ‘Why was I received upon knees?’ Because, when the sinner is no longer ashamed of his iniquity, he is strengthened in that same iniquity by the supports of most evil habit. The sinner is cherished as if on knees, so that he may grow, while fault is strengthened by habits so that it may flourish.

> “Why nursed at breasts? Because, when one has begun to bring one’s fault into practice, one feeds oneself either with false hope of divine mercy or with the open misery of despair, so that one may by no means return to correction, since one imagines one’s maker to be merciful to oneself in an unruly way, or fears in an unruly way what one has done. Therefore let the blessed man look upon the fall of the human race and consider by what precipices it has been plunged into the pit of iniquity, saying: ‘Why did I not die in the womb?’—that is, why was I unwilling to mortify myself from the life of the flesh? ‘Why did I not perish immediately when I came forth [Col. 0642B] from the womb?’—that is, after I came forth into open iniquity, why did I not at least recognize myself as lost? Certainly, in its own judgment the human race would have perished if it had recognized itself as lost in its guilt. ‘Why was I received upon knees?’—that is, even after open fault, why did habit still receive me into it, making me stronger for wickedness and fostering me by sustaining my evil practices? ‘Why nursed at breasts?’—that is, after I came into the habit of sin, why did I nourish myself into more atrocious wickedness, either by confidence in false hope or by the milk of wretched despair?

> “For when fault has come into practice, the mind, even if it desires to do so, resists it more weakly, because as many times as it is bound by evil repetition, so many bonds, as it were, bind it to the mind. Thus, when the darkened mind cannot free itself, it turns toward certain consolations of false comfort, promising itself that the coming Judge will be so merciful that he will not entirely destroy even those whom he finds blameworthy. What makes this worse is that the speech of many like persons agrees with it, even magnifying evil deeds with praise; thus fault, nourished by approval, grows without ceasing. A wound that seems worthy of the reward of praise is neglected rather than cured. Hence Solomon says: ‘My son, if sinners nurse you, do not consent to them’ (Prov. I). For sinners nurse when they offer enticements toward evils to be committed, or extol by approval evils already committed. [Col. 0642D] Is not he nursed of whom the Psalmist says: ‘For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the unjust person is blessed’ (Ps. IX)?

> “It should also be known that the first three modes of sinners are more easily corrected according to the order of their descent, whereas this fourth is corrected with greater difficulty. Hence our Redeemer raised the girl in the house (Mark V), the young man outside the gate (Luke VII), but Lazarus in the tomb (John XI). For one who lies hidden in sin is still dead. One whose iniquity is openly brought out to the shame [Note: [Col. 0641D] Gregory: ‘to shame.’] of public perpetration is already, as it were, being carried outside the gate. But one who is weighed down by the mound of burial is burdened by committing wickedness through the practice of habit [Col. 0643A]. Yet the Lord in mercy calls such persons back to life, because divine grace often illumines by the light of its regard not only those dead in hidden iniquities but also those dead in open iniquities and crushed under the weight of evil habit.

> “But our Redeemer learns of the fourth dead person from disciples reporting [Note: [Col. 0643] Gregory has ‘a disciple reporting,’ and this is more correct, for the Lord speaks to only one person.], yet does not raise him, because it is exceedingly difficult for one whom flattering tongues receive even after the practice of evil habit to be recalled from the death of his mind. Concerning him it is well said: ‘Let the dead bury their own dead’ (Luke IX). The dead bury a dead person when sinners press sinners down with approval. For what else is it to sin than to die? But those who exalt a sinner with praise hide one who is dead beneath the mound of their words. Lazarus too was dead, but he was not buried by the dead. Faithful women had covered him over, and they announced his death to Jesus Christ, the giver of life. Therefore he immediately returned to the light, because when the mind dies in sin, it is more quickly restored to life if living thoughts attentively attend to it—thoughts which recall it from unlawful works by recommending good, and restore it with them to eternal life by doing what is right.”

Therefore let the stinking dead person—that is, one who perseveres in sin and is weighed down by the mound of false flattery—quickly cast off through divine inspiration the works of darkness, and rise from the death of despair or habit by humbly repenting of past faults. Let him abandon the long habit of sinning [Col. 0643C] and hope for salvation from God’s goodness. Let him leave the practice of evil action as soon as possible and raise himself without doubt to hope in divine mercy. Let him abandon the wickedness of a perverse life and await forgiveness for his sins. Let him entirely extinguish the enticing affections of the flesh, diligently exercise himself in good works, and fix the hope of his salvation upon God’s mercy.

Let each person therefore correct his neighbor, lest he persevere in evil, and urge him to do good. Sinners must be rebuked for their evil actions, not exalted with false praises. Hence it is said: “The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins.” Therefore whoever wishes to bring sinners back to the way of salvation, which is Christ, should labor to recall their evils to their minds, as the Lord powerfully admonishes the ruler of the Church [Col. 0643D] through the prophet, saying:

“Cry aloud; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and declare to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isa. LVIII).

As if God, who does not desire the death of sinners but that they turn and live (Ezek. XVIII), commanded a teacher of the Church—indeed, the whole order of teachers—under the person of Isaiah, saying: Cry aloud; do not cease from preaching. Raise your voice like a trumpet, so that you may be heard by all; and declare to my people their abominable crimes: namely idolatry, murders, thefts, false testimonies, and things like these; and to the house of Jacob their sins, damnable though they are, since they may still repent.

[Col. 0644A] But where the command is given to the entire college of apostles, “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. XL), neither a horn nor a trumpet is taken up; rather, he is commanded to ascend a mountain and make a resounding proclamation with his own voice.

Here, however, because those to whom the message must be announced are sinners and are below, he is not commanded to ascend the mountain, but only to raise his voice like a trumpet and announce the punishments to come, because they are to be raised as the dead are raised. Hence blessed Paul says: “The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise” (1 Cor. XV).

Truly almighty God is naturally compassionate and merciful, who calls even sinners and unworthy persons his people. As if he said: Let the Jews see what a Father they lost through their deserving sins—a Father who calls his people even those who departed from him by sinning.

It follows: “For they seek me from day to day, and desire to know my ways, like a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God.” As if God were speaking more plainly about the Jews: They seek me from day to day—that is, daily—with their mouth, though not with their heart, gathering at the temple and synagogues, enquiring into the law given by me through Moses, and desiring to know my ways: namely, my actions and wills. And they do this like a nation that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God. They did not perform righteousness because they worshipped idols, and they forsook the judgment of their God, namely the Law or true faith, by which the righteous person lives; nevertheless they desire to know God’s ways.

As if God said more plainly to them: You have not done righteousness and have forsaken my judgment. Why, then, should I hear you as I hear those who today in the Church perform righteousness, living justly and devoutly (Titus II) and confessing Christ as true God and true man? Because you honor me with lips only, while your heart departs far from me (Matt. XV), you do not truly seek me day by day but seek me deceitfully; and because you are unwilling to do what I command, you cannot at all obtain the effect of your petition, because you ask badly (James IV).

“Like a nation,” he says, “that has done righteousness and has not forsaken the judgment of its God.” Righteousness is understood as Christ, who justifies all, and God the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son (John V). Therefore the Jews did not perform righteousness and forsook judgment, because they denied Christ, who is everlasting righteousness that looked down from heaven (Ps. LXXXIV), saying: “He is not” (Ps. XIII).

Again he adds: “They ask me for judgments of righteousness, and desire to draw near to God.” Behold another presumption of the Jews. For, as though trusting in a good conscience, they demand just judgment, according to the saying: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. XXV). “They ask me,” he says, “for judgments of righteousness.” As if he said: They ask me to render judgments of righteousness, and as though I do not hear them because they desire to draw near to God, not in deed but in voice alone. Hence it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, [Col. 0645A] but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV). For one draws near to God not by place, but by merit.

The Jews, boasting in false righteousness, accuse the God of righteousness as though he did not regard good works, saying: “Why have we fasted and you have not looked upon it? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known it.” They have forgotten the ancient history: the Lord did not regard Cain’s offerings (Gen. IV), because he did not deal rightly with his brother, toward whom he envied God’s love.

“Why,” they say, “have we fasted and you have not looked upon it? We have humbled our souls and you have not known it?” Woe to those who think hunger is a virtue. Hence: “I fast twice on the Sabbath” (Luke XVIII). As if they said more plainly: Why have we fasted, and have you not regarded our fast as acceptable? We have humbled—that is, afflicted—our souls by fasting, [Col. 0645B] and you have not looked upon it—that is, it has not pleased you.

The Lord answers them: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own will is found, and you exact payment from all your debtors.” As if he said: I do not regard your fasts because they are without mercy; nor do you fast for me, but for human praise and vain glory. Perhaps the Jews often fasted in order to devote themselves to exacting debts. As if the Lord said more plainly: Behold, on the day not of my fast but of yours, your carnal pleasure is found, namely in more lavish foods; but my will is not found there in good works, because while you exact all your debtors, you devote yourselves not to fasts and prayers but to exacting [Note: [Col. 0645D] Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 16, correctly reads: “Nor does one who asks back from a debtor what one has given do anything unjust; but it is fitting that whoever mortifies himself in penitence should also deny himself even what is rightfully due to him. Thus, when we are afflicted and penitent, God forgives what we have done unjustly, if for love of him we remit even what is rightfully due to us.” [Col. 0646D]] debts. In this also, that you exact from debtors who do not possess the means, you commit violence against me.

A fast acceptable to God, therefore, is fulfilled not only by abstaining from foods but also from unlawful works.

Again adding, he says: “Behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and strike wickedly with the fist.” As though he plainly said: Behold, your outward person fasts for quarrels and disputes; but the inward person feeds on the flesh of the dragon, which was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia (Ps. 73). You also exact what you have not lent, and, on the other hand, wickedly strike with the fist those who resist. Therefore God does not rebuke fasting, but the things that harm fasting. Lest, therefore, He seem to disapprove fasting, as a most loving Father He says in counsel: “Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high.” As though He said: If you wish Me to hear you [Col. 0645D], do not fast without works of mercy as you have done until this day; nor for the praise of men, praying in synagogues and at the street corners in order to be seen by men. Rather, enter your chambers and, with the door shut, pray truly to your Father, so that your cry may be heard on high (Matt. 6).

Again, teaching how they ought to fast, He says: “Is this the fast that I have chosen: for a man to afflict his soul for a day?” As though He said more plainly: Is the fast that I have chosen such as you practice—namely, throughout the whole day not [Col. 0646A] to amend your evil conduct, but to afflict one’s soul by abstaining from food, not from unlawful deeds? “Is it to twist his head like a circle, and spread sackcloth and ashes?” As though He said: Is it to twist your head like a circle, namely by bowing it to the feet, or in a circle like monks, merely outwardly; to put on sackcloth and spread ashes beneath yourself? These things are indeed good, if done with a good disposition. Having shown what sort of fast the Lord reproves, He also shows what sort He praises when there follows: “Would you call this a fast, and a day acceptable to the Lord?” No. Rather, this is the fast that I have chosen: “Break the chains of wickedness; loosen the oppressive bundles.”

Here the Seventy Interpreters plainly rendered, instead of “chains” and “bundles,” [Col. 0646B] “tear apart every written instrument of injustice”—that is, false debt-documents, by which they often wickedly oppressed the poor. For if it is wicked to demand a debt from those unable to repay, much more so is it wicked to demand it from those who owe nothing. As though it were plainly said: Break the chains of wickedness—that is, the false documents by which they claimed that poor persons were bound. Loosen the oppressive bundles—that is, the false debt-documents by which moneylenders oppressed the innocent. In this passage He does not forbid one to recover what is one’s own; rather, He shows that it is wicked to extort by force from those who cannot repay, or to exact debts from those who do not owe them. Yet the Lord, who came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (Matt. 5), forbids in His Gospel everyone to demand back what is his own.

In the moral sense, by “chains of wickedness” [Col. 0646C] and “oppressive bundles” we understand sins, which we are commanded to forgive our neighbours on the day of fasting, so that God may forgive us and we may confidently say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6), etc. It follows:

“Release as free those who are broken, and break every yoke.” As though He said: Release from slavery those who sold themselves because of hunger, and those who have been crushed by long servitude. As was said above, the Jews often kept the poor in slavery beyond the appointed term. “Break every yoke”—that is, every burden of slavery, or of sin.

Again adding, He says: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house.” As though He said: Not another’s bread, but your own. And if you cannot [Col. 0646D] give all of it so that it may benefit many, at least break it for one hungry person. Do not plead poverty because you do not possess many loaves: share even from that one loaf with the poor. Hence it is said: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 111). Give to the poor what you would have eaten had you not fasted, so that your fast may not be profit for your purse but satisfaction for a soul and spiritual nourishment. Bring the needy and homeless—those from whom you expect no return—into a rented house, even if you do not have one of your own [Col. 0647A]. If you do not have bread, offer shelter, and receive heaven. Thus blessed Peter says: “Be hospitable to one another without complaining” (1 Pet. 4).

[Note: [Col. 0646D] Since the reading of the Vulgate, according to which we are commanded to bring the needy merely into “our house” [Col. 0647D], seems incompatible with this interpretation, Jerome rightly introduced the Hebrew reading, from which—because it lacks the adjective “your”—he drew that sense. The gloss-writer follows the holy doctor in this exposition, and our Martin follows him, as always. [Col. 0648D]]

Perhaps someone says: “I have no debtors; what shall I do, so that my fast may be accepted?” Whoever says this should break his bread for the hungry and bring needy wanderers into his house, and his fast will be acceptable. Allegorically, we break bread for the hungry when we make known to others the faith of Christ, who is the living bread (John 6), and Holy Scripture, which is our spiritual food. We bring the needy and wandering into the house when we recall those in discord to fraternal peace and the unity of charity.

It follows: “When you see the naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own flesh.” As though it were said more plainly: When you see one naked—[Col. 0647B] namely, naked of faith, virtues, and good works—clothe him by word and example, according to that saying: “He who has two tunics, let him give to him who has none” (Luke 3). And do not despise your own flesh—that is, a sinner like yourself—considering yourself, lest you too be tempted (Gal. 6). As though He said: In every necessity recognize your neighbour as like yourself: mortal and liable to suffering. Hence it is said: “By attending to your own condition, you will not sin” (Job 5).

In the tropological sense, the person who fasts from every evil and desires his fast to be regarded must not only turn away from evil but also do good: he must break every bond of iniquity by which the simple have been bound through the deceits of heretics. Hence it is said: “Those turning aside into their bonds, the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity” (Ps. 124). Such broken persons [Col. 0647C] an ecclesiastical man ought to release, and he ought to tear apart every written instrument of the heretics. Hence the prophet says: “Woe to those who write iniquity” (Isa. 10), etc.

[Note: [Col. 0648D] Neither the Gloss nor our author states whence this reading was taken, since neither the Vulgate, nor Jerome on this passage, nor the Seventy supports it. Nonetheless, it was transferred from Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah, chapter 68.]

He should also break the bread of doctrine for the hungry. For the Lord handed the broken loaves to the apostles, leaving them in the Gospel not whole as they had been in the Law, but divided and broken—in seven baskets and twelve hand-baskets (Matt. 14)—so that they might have something to distribute to the poor. Those who lack the warmth of faith and, outside the Church, grow cold in the frost of unbelief, he should bring in as needy strangers into the house of the Church and cover with the cloak of incorruption, so that, clothed in Christ’s tunic, they may not remain naked in tombs—as we read of the man possessed by a legion of demons, who dwelt among the monuments of the dead [Col. 0647D] naked. When he has done these things, he will not despise his own flesh, that is, especially the members of the household of faith, whom the Seventy Interpreters called “the household members of your seed.”

Again adding, He says: “Then your light shall break forth as the morning, and your healing shall arise swiftly.” As though He said: When you have done the things stated above, then your light shall break forth like the sun in the morning, and your healing—that is, the remission of sins—shall arise swiftly. As the morning light dispels darkness, so the light [Col. 0648A] of truth drives away error.

Again He says: “Your righteousness shall go before your face, and the glory of the Lord shall gather you.” As though it were said more plainly: Your righteousness—that is, your good works—will go before you into the presence of the Judge or into eternal blessedness; and the glory of the Lord—that is, the Son of God, of whom it is said in the Psalms, “Arise, my glory” (Ps. 56)—will gather you into the protection of mercy. Righteousness, which is Christ and justifies all, will go before you unto glory. Hence it is said: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14). And the glory of the Lord, namely Christ Himself, will gather you—that is, receive you to Himself—who said: “Where I am, there my servant also shall be” (John 12). “He will gather you,” it says, so that you may be glorified before God and men.

It follows: “Then you shall call, and the Lord shall hear.” As though He said: You will call with heart, mouth, and deed; and the Lord, whose will you have done, will hear you—that is, will answer you with benefits. “You will cry, and He will say: ‘Behold, I am present’”—present to reward you, who was present to aid your good work.

Again, admonishing how one should amend oneself and have mercy on one’s neighbours, He says: “If you remove from your midst the chain, and cease to point the finger and speak what is unprofitable; when you pour out your soul to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, your light shall rise in darkness, and your darkness shall be like noon.” As though it were said more plainly: If you remove from your midst the chain of sins, of which it is said, “The cords of sinners have entangled me” (Ps. 118); and cease to point the finger—that is, to mark out your neighbours [Col. 0648C] or speak against them—this means not only that you should neither think nor do these things, but that you should not slander your neighbour. And if you cease to speak what is not profitable but harmful; if, in abundant mercy, you pour out your soul—that is, a willing compassion—to the hungry, giving bodily or spiritual bread; and if you satisfy by whatever benefit a soul afflicted by any distress, not merely supporting it but, if you can, satiating it: then your light, that is Christ, shall arise to drive away the darkness of your sins, and your darkness, that is your sins, shall be like noon—that is, like the brightness of righteousness. Hence it is said: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

Also adding, He says: “The Lord your God will give you rest always, and fill your soul with splendours [Col. 0648D], and set free your bones.” As though He said: When your darkness has become like noon, then the Lord your God will also give you eternal rest, fill your soul with splendours—namely virtues, or the vision of the Godhead—according to David’s saying: “With you is dominion in the day of your power, in the splendours of the saints” (Ps. 109); and He will set free your bones—that is, your virtues, lest they fail—or will raise your body on the day of judgment and deliver both it and your soul [Col. 0649A] from everlasting fire.

It follows: “You shall be like a watered garden, and like a fountain of waters whose waters do not fail.” The watered garden is the paradise of delight, planted by the Lord God in the beginning—that is, the Church. The fountain in the middle of paradise is Christ, whose waters of spiritual teaching do not fail and irrigate the Church; and this is what it means: “You shall be like a watered garden.” O faithful soul, or holy Church! Let it therefore be said more plainly: O faithful soul, or holy Church, you shall be like a watered garden, distinguished by the flowers of virtues and the fruits of good works; and like a fountain of spiritual waters—that is, like Christ your head. For “when He appears, we shall be like Him” (1 John 3), whose waters do not fail, because “heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” [Col. 0649B] (Mark 13).

“And ancient wastes shall be built up in you; you shall raise up foundations from generation to generation.” The Jews refer this to the restoration effected under Zerubbabel and Jesus the high priest, or to that restoration which they foolishly imagine will occur at the end; but it is better and truer referred to the Church. By the foundations of the Church he means the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and those like them. Hence the Psalmist says: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the dwellings of Jacob” (Ps. 86). Thus the foundations of the Church are the holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments. But Christ is the foundation of all, other than which, as Paul says, no one can lay another (1 Cor. 3).

Let it therefore be said more plainly: O Church! [Col. 0649C] besides the things mentioned above, the ancient wastes—that is, the assemblies of the Jews, which had been deserted because of unbelief—shall be built up in you through faith. You shall raise up the foundations from generation to generation of both peoples, by believing and confessing Christ to be true man and true God.

He also addresses the teacher of the Church in congratulation, saying: “You shall be called a builder of hedges, turning aside the paths of iniquity.” As though He said: O teacher of the Church, you shall be called a builder of hedges—that is, of holy doctrines, by which the Church is fortified—turning the paths of iniquity, that is, of errors, toward true peace and rest, which is Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] You will find this reading in none of the published versions. But Cassian, *Conference* 14, chapter 13, reads it in the same way, though it did not please Peter Chacon, who wished to emend it to “into rest.” [Col. 0650D]]

Again adding, He says: “If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath, from doing your own will on my holy day, and call the Sabbath delightful and the holy day of the Lord glorious, and glorify Him by not following your own ways, nor pursuing your own will, nor speaking a word: then you shall delight in the Lord, and I will lift you up above the heights of the earth, and feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father.” As though He said: If you turn your foot back from the Sabbath, lest you transgress—that is, lest you do evil on the Sabbath day or do your carnal will on My holy day, which must be observed at all times—and if, keeping Sabbaths dedicated to the Lord, you are called a delightful Sabbath, that is, [Col. 0650A] acceptable to God, and a glorious holy thing of the Lord, that is, pure; and if in your works you glorify Him, namely the Sabbath day, by not following your own ways—that is, wicked actions—and by having your own will not found in you, so that you sin neither in deed nor in intention, and do not speak an idle word: then, when you have done the things stated above, you shall delight in the Lord, not in worldly things. Hence it is said: “Delight in the Lord, and He will grant you the requests of your heart” (Ps. 36).

“I will lift you up above the heights of the land of the living,” namely into eternal blessedness, that is, into the exaltation of eternal stability; for this alone is the immovable and solid element. Hence it is said to Lot: “Save yourself on the mountain” (Gen. 19). “And I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father,” namely with the true heavenly homeland [Col. 0650B] which I gave to Jacob, whose son you are through faith and works, overthrowing vices and sins. For everyone is called the son of the one whom he imitates. We therefore overthrow sins and vices when, in true repentance, we fast not only from food but also from vices.

For through fasts and works of mercy vices are overthrown. Our fast becomes acceptable when the mind inwardly burns with love of God and neighbour and the hand outwardly willingly serves the poor. We offend in many things; but through humble repentance we believe that we obtain pardon from God. He inwardly and outwardly sees not only our thoughts but all our works with exactness; yet He mercifully forgives us when we grieve over committing sin. He considers all [Col. 0650C] our deeds, with no obstacle impeding Him, but through the compunction of tears mercifully remits our faults. Hence blessed Job, carefully understanding the excellence of divine knowledge and humbly asking pardon for his sins, said to God:

“You have indeed numbered my steps, but spare my sins” (Job 14).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0650D] *Morals*, book 12, no. 20]: “God numbers our steps when He marks each of our individual deeds for recompense. For what is signified by steps except each of our actions? Almighty God therefore both numbers our steps and spares sins, because He examines our deeds minutely and yet mercifully remits them to the repentant. He also sees hardness in sinners, [Col. 0650D] yet, through grace going before, softens it unto repentance. Thus He enumerates faults when He turns us to mourn over each particular thing that we have done. He mercifully remits them because, while we punish ourselves, He by no means judges them in the final examination. Paul bears witness, saying: ‘If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged’ (1 Cor. 11). Hence it is further added: ‘You sealed my offences as though in a bag, but healed my iniquity.’

“Our offences are sealed as though in a bag because whatever we do outwardly, unless we wash it away by intervening repentance, is kept, hidden away under a certain concealment, in the secret judgments of God [Col. 0651A], so that at some time it may emerge from the seal of secrecy into the public judgment. Hence it is also said through Moses: ‘Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasures? On the day of vengeance I will repay them’ (Deut. 32).

“But when we are worn down by the scourge of discipline for the evil that we have done, and mourn it through repentance, He seals and heals our iniquity, because He neither leaves it unpunished here nor preserves it to be punished at judgment. He therefore seals offences because He carefully attends to them here in order to strike; but He heals them because through the scourge He utterly remits them. Thus He healed by sealing the iniquity even of that persecutor whom He had struck down to the ground, when He said of him to Ananias: ‘This man is a chosen vessel for me, to bear my name before kings, nations, and the children of Israel. For I [Col. 0651B] will show him how much he must suffer for my name’ (Acts 9). For when He threatens future sufferings for transgressions already committed, He was surely keeping in mind what the man had sinned; yet He had undoubtedly healed his offences by sealing them, since He called him a chosen vessel.

“Or, certainly, our sins are sealed in a bag when we continually weigh with an attentive heart the evil that we have done. For what is the human heart but God’s bag? When we carefully observe how greatly we sin, we carry our sins as though sealed in God’s bag. Did not David keep his sin sealed in the bag when he said: ‘I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me’ (Ps. 50)? And because our merciful Creator remits the faults that we recognize by considering and repenting of them, He rightly adds after ‘offences sealed in a bag’: ‘But you healed my iniquity.’ As though He openly said: The things which you now seal so that I may see them in repentance, you undoubtedly do so that they may not be seen at recompense. For through repentance sins are blotted out like a cloud and annulled like mist, lest they appear at judgment. Through contrition of heart and worthy satisfaction for sins committed, we believe that we obtain forgiveness of sins and do not doubt that we draw near to God, from whom by sinning we had withdrawn far away.”

Therefore, in these days of holy Lent it is necessary, dearest beloved, that we chastise our bodies with fasts and vigils if we seek to have God propitious to us. Let us seek Him by persisting in good works [Col. 0651D], so that we may be able to find Him gracious on the day of need. Yet we should know that one who has not sought Him by doing good in the present life will by no means be able to find Him in the life to come, as the prophet Isaiah testifies, saying:

“Seek the Lord while He may be found; call upon Him while He is near” (Isa. 55). As though He said: Seek the Lord by faith, work, and simplicity while He may be found—that is, while you live, while there is room for repentance. Call upon Him in truth while He is near, namely while we have time. Hence blessed Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). Now God can be found through the merit of faith, but cannot be seen; in the future He will be seen, yet will not be found by sinners [Col. 0652A]. As though He said: Seek the Lord with your whole heart while He is near, lest through your vices He depart from you—He who draws near to those drawing near to Him and joyfully meets the returning son (Luke 15). Therefore seek Him by doing good in this present age, if you seek to find Him gracious in the future.

It follows: “Let the wicked abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and He will have mercy on him; and to our God, because He is abundant in forgiveness.” As though He plainly said: Let the wicked abandon his crooked way—that is, turn away from evil and do good—and let the unjust man abandon his most evil thoughts, of which it is said: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9). Let him return by good works to the Lord, who does not desire the death of the sinner [Col. 0652B] but rather that he be converted and live (Ezek. 18); and to our God, because, as a most merciful Father, He is abundant—that is, greatly merciful—in forgiving.

Again adding, He says: “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways.” As though He plainly said: Do not think that what I promise is difficult; consider that there is a great difference between my counsels and yours, and as great a diversity of will as of nature. As though He said: I both will and can have mercy, because my thoughts are not changeable as your thoughts are changed for the worse. Thus it is written in the book of Psalms: “The Lord frustrates the counsels of the nations; He rejects the thoughts of peoples and rejects the counsels of princes” (Ps. 32). But of my thoughts [Col. 0652C] it is said: “The counsel of the Lord stands for ever, the thoughts of His heart from generation to generation” (ibid.). Therefore, says the Lord, my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your crooked ways my straight ways; for as the heavens are raised above the earth, so my ways are raised above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts. As though He said: As the heavens of angels are raised above the earth of men, so my straight ways are raised above your crooked ways, and my immutable and inscrutable thoughts above your thoughts, because they are vain. Of them it is said: “They devised plans which they were unable to establish” (Ps. 20).
