By another comparison Isaiah shows that He is abundant [Col. 0652D] in forgiving, saying: “As rain and snow come down from heaven and do not return there again, but soak the earth, water it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth.” As though He plainly said: As rain and snow come down from heaven—that is, evangelical teaching from the clouds, namely the apostles—and do not return there again, but soak the earth, that is, the hearts of earthly people, with love of God and neighbour, and water it with the living water of which it is said: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7), and thus cause it to produce the fruits of righteousness; and give seed to the sower—that is, spiritual children to the preacher of God’s word, for “those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125)—and bread [Col. 0653A] of spiritual teaching to the one who eats, namely the one exercising himself in holy disciplines. Hence it is said: “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you shall find it” (Eccl. 11): that is, pour out the bread of your teaching and spiritual grace upon all, and in the end you shall receive rewards.

“So shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth.” Here God the Father makes a promise concerning the salvation of Jews and Gentiles. As though God the Father spoke more plainly, saying: “So shall my Word be which goes forth from my mouth,” namely my Son, who “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with me, and the Word was God” (John 1). When the fullness of time comes, He will accomplish all the things stated above: “The Word,” He says, “which shall go forth from my mouth,” according to that which is written in Proverbs: “I came forth from the mouth [Col. 0653B] of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24).

Otherwise: “The word which goes forth from my mouth” means from the mouth of the prophets and apostles, through whom Christ will be preached to the peoples. For Christ is the mouth of God the Father, through whom God the Father was made known to the world. Hence He says to Him in the Gospel: “Father, I have made your name known to men” (John 17). The holy preachers were also the mouth of Christ, who preached Him throughout the whole world.

It follows: “It shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in those things for which I sent it.” As though God the Father said: After the Word coeternal with me, which goes forth from my mouth to free the human race, has fulfilled my will in the last days, it will return again to me [Col. 0653C] with the kingdom acquired and sit at my right hand, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). “It shall not return to me empty,” He says, “but shall accomplish all that I have willed concerning the redemption of the human race.” Hence that Gospel saying: “The Father has not left me alone, because I always do those things that please Him” (John 8). “And it shall prosper in those things for which I sent it.” As though He said: It shall also prosper according to His humanity in those things for which I sent it, namely in preaching and converting peoples to faith. Hence it is said: “And Jesus advanced in age and wisdom before God and men” (Luke 2).

Therefore, as has been said above, let the wicked abandon his crooked way and the unjust man his most evil thoughts [Col. 0653D], and return with his whole heart to the Lord in repentance, mourning during this season of fasting not only grave sins but also venial sins; because many slight sins make [Note: [Col. 0653D] The same opinion is explained in the same words by Isidore, *Sentences*, book 3, chapter 18. Augustine also says near the end of *Tractates on John*, tractate 12: “If many small sins are neglected, they kill.” And in the *Sermon on the Ten Strings*, chapter 11: “Do not despise those daily sins because they are smaller; fear them because they are more numerous . . . They are small, not great . . . yet many small beasts often kill,” etc. Yet, although these things are so, it must certainly be maintained what St Thomas asserts: that it is false to understand a venial sin becoming mortal as though one mortal sin were integrally constituted from many venial sins; for all venial sins in the world cannot have as much guilt as one mortal sin. . . . But if this is understood to mean that many venial sins make one mortal sin dispositively, it is true. Augustine, Isidore, and Martin speak in this sense. [Col. 0654D]] one great sin, just as immense rivers commonly grow from [Col. 0654A] minute and small drops.

But lighter sins—that is, venial sins—if they are not forgiven by repentance in this age, will be purged by a passing fire in the age to come. More grievous or criminal sins, however, if they are not forgiven here by daily tears and worthy satisfaction, will nevertheless be incapable of absolution and condemnable in the future. Hence the apostle Paul says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon it gold, silver, precious stones, hay, wood, straw, each one’s work will be made manifest; for the day of the Lord will reveal it, because fire will test each one’s work. If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward; and [Col. 0654B] if anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss, but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3).

[Note: [Col. 0654D] See Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapters 15 and 16; *Enchiridion to Lawrence*, chapter 68; and Question 1 of *Questions Addressed to Dulcitius*. Consult also the work *On the Order of Created Things*, attributed to Isidore, chapter 14, in the Acheryan *Spicilegium*, vol. 1.]

Many people, badly misunderstanding this passage, are deceived by false security, believing that they build capital sins on the foundation of Christ and that those sins can be purged by a passing fire, so that afterwards they may attain eternal life. This interpretation, dearest brothers, must be corrected, because not capital sins but slight sins are purged; for those who thus flatter themselves concerning that passing or purgatorial fire deceive themselves.

Yet some things must be mentioned concerning greater and lesser sins, lest anyone try vainly to excuse himself and say: “I do not know what venial or criminal sins are.” Let us therefore briefly name certain venial and criminal sins, lest we cause sinners to despair. Namely: sacrilege, murder, adultery, false witness, theft, perjury, robbery, avarice, pride, anger, drunkenness, and whatever things are of that kind. If, therefore, anyone recognizes that these more grievous sins rule over him, unless he repents worthily and long beforehand corrects them with tears, sighs, fasts, and generous almsgiving, he cannot be purged in that passing fire, but, as we believe, will burn in everlasting fire.

It is called a passing fire because the souls of certain elect persons are believed to pass through it to rest; or because it itself will pass away and will not remain forever. Although lesser sins are known to many, let us nonetheless mention some of them for the less understanding. Whenever we take more food or drink than necessary; if someone speaks or keeps silence more than is fitting; if he harshly rebuffs a poor person who begs importunately; if, while sound in body and others are fasting, he presumes to eat [Col. 0655A] a meal; if, given over to sleep, he rises late for church; if, having a wife, he knows her other than for the desire of children; if he does not visit prisoners and the sick; if he does not recall the discordant to concord; if he occupies himself with idle words; if he swears rashly; if he curses anyone, though it is written: “Neither those who curse shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6); or if he sometimes thinks unlawful things: these and similar matters belong to the lesser sins, without which this present life cannot be passed. Therefore they must be continually redeemed by prayers, more generous almsgiving, fasts, and other works of mercy—especially through the forgiveness of those who sin against us.

Whatever of these least sins—that is, venial sins—is not redeemed by us in this age [Col. 0655B] must be purged by a passing fire. But if we truly repent, are afflicted by tribulations for God’s sake, give thanks to God in adversities, and confess that we suffer less than we deserve, these sins are purged in this age, so that in the age to come the purgatorial fire finds little or nothing to burn. For, as holy teachers assert, we shall remain in that purgatorial fire until the sins which we have committed are consumed. They also say that this fire is harsher than anything that can be seen, felt, or imagined as punishment in this present age.

Gregory likewise, in the book of the *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0655D] Book IV, ch. 39.], replying to Peter [Col. 0655C] when he asked whether purgatorial fire is to be believed in after death, adduces very suitable testimonies not only concerning purgatory but also concerning eternal fire, and says:

> “Walk,” says the Lord, “while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12). Through the prophet also the Lord himself says: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49); and likewise the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55). Explaining this, the Apostle Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6). Solomon also says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do earnestly; for there will be neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in hell, whither you are hastening” [Col. 0655D] (Eccles. 9). David too says: “For his mercy is for ever” (Ps. 105). From these sayings it is certainly clear that as each person departs hence, so he is presented at judgment. Yet concerning certain light faults, it must be believed that there is a purgatorial fire before judgment, because Truth says: “If anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12).
>
> “In this saying it is given to understand that certain faults can be remitted in this age, and others in the age to come. For when remission is denied of one thing, the consequent meaning is plainly that it is granted concerning certain others. Yet, as I have said, this must be believed possible only in small and very slight sins: such as habitual idle speech, excessive laughter, or the sin involved in managing household affairs—which scarcely can be conducted without fault even by those who know how they ought to avoid fault—or an error of ignorance in matters not serious. All these burden a person even after death, if they have not first been remitted while one is still in this life.
>
> “For when Paul says that Christ is the foundation and adds: ‘If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble: the fire shall test what sort each person’s work is. If anyone’s work which he has built upon it remains, he shall receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he shall suffer loss; but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire’—although this can be understood of the fire of tribulation applied to us in this life—nevertheless, if anyone understands it of the fire of future purification, he must carefully consider that Paul said one may be saved through fire, not if one builds upon this foundation iron, bronze, or lead—that is, greater sins, and therefore harder and then incapable of being dissolved—but wood and stubble, that is, sins very small and very light, which the fire easily consumes.”

[Note: [Col. 0655D] What we enclose in brackets is absent from Gregory and seems superfluous; for Paul explains the other testimony from Isaiah, not this one.] [Col. 0656D]

Nevertheless, this must be known: there, no one will obtain even purification from the least sins unless, while still in this life, he has deserved it through good works, so that he may obtain salvation there. Therefore, dearly beloved, if we seek to escape the burning of both fires—the purgatorial and the eternal [Col. 0656C]—we must avoid not only grave but also light sins. If we desire to be freed from the fires of the life to come, we must correct our life not only of graver but also of lighter faults. Let us amend our sins by pure confession while we still live, lest after this life we be handed over to the fires of Gehenna. Sins are indeed wounds of the soul.

Therefore, in this holy fast, while we have time, let us apply the medicines of repentance to the wounds of the soul, lest, suddenly overtaken by the day of death, we seek an opportunity for repentance and be unable to find it. For permission for repentance is granted us only in this day of salvation. Whoever has not devoutly embraced it in this acceptable [Col. 0656D] time will by no means be able to find it in the future. Hence blessed Job, among other things which he uttered for the instruction of holy Church, says: “For it is no longer within a man’s power to come to God in judgment” (Job 34).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0656D] *Morals*, Book XXV, no. 12.]:

> “This verse requires discussion all the more because, if what it says is neglected, the pain is sharper. Here, indeed, is not signified that judgment which punishes by eternal retribution, but that judgment conceived in the mind and dissolved through confession. For whoever fears being condemned by that judgment does not desire to come to it.
>
> “Therefore, when it is said, [Col. 0657A] ‘For it is no longer within a man’s power to come to God in judgment,’ it is certainly shown that there is a kind of judgment which at some time is desired even by the condemned and reprobate. And what is that judgment except the one of which the Apostle Paul says: ‘If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged’ (1 Cor. 11)? And of which it is said through the prophet: ‘There is no judgment in their paths’ (Isa. 59); and of which David says: ‘The honour of the king loves judgment’ (Ps. 98). That is, because one who already honours the Lord by faith should carefully judge what he owes him in conduct.
>
> “Hence it is again written: ‘Judge before the Lord, and wait for him’ (Job 35). One judges before the Lord who beholds the Lord in the heart and, under his presence, distinguishes one’s actions by careful inquiry. Each person awaits him the more securely [Note: [Col. 0657D] Perhaps *more securely*, as in the edition.] insofar as, suspecting himself, he examines his life daily. For one who comes to his eternal judgment is no longer judged before him, but by him.
>
> “Concerning this judgment of the mind, the Lord says to the soul that has forgotten it through the prophet: ‘Bring me to remembrance, that we may be judged together; declare what you have, that you may be justified’ (Isa. 43). Each person’s mind ought carefully to examine both its own case before the Lord and the Lord’s case against it. It ought cautiously to weigh both what goods it has received from him and what evils it has perversely returned for his goods. The elect certainly never cease to do this every day.
>
> “Thus Solomon rightly says: ‘The thoughts of the righteous are judgments’ (Prov. 12). For they approach the chamber of the Judge within the breast of the heart and consider how strictly he will one day strike, though he waits patiently for long. They fear in the deeds which they remember having done; by weeping they punish what they understand themselves to have committed. They fear the subtle divine judgments even concerning things which perhaps they are unable to perceive in themselves. For they see that God sees what they themselves do not see in themselves by their humanity. They behold the strict Judge, who strikes the more severely the more slowly he comes.
>
> “They also contemplate the assembly of the holy Fathers seated together with him. They reproach themselves for having despised their examples or sayings; and, constrained in this secret court of inward judgment by the very execution of their own mind, they strike in repentance what they committed in pride. There [Col. 0657D] they enumerate against themselves whatever attacks them; there they heap before their own eyes everything that they must bewail; there they consider whatever can be decreed through the anger of the strict Judge; there they suffer as many punishments as they fear to suffer.

> “Nor does this judgment conceived in the mind lack any instrument needed more fully to punish its guilty persons: conscience accuses, reason judges, fear pleads [Note: [Col. 0658D] Perhaps *binds* or *restrains*, as in Gregory.], and sorrow tortures. This judgment punishes the more certainly because it rages more inwardly, since it does not come from external things. For when anyone begins to bring the case of this examination against himself, he [Col. 0658A] is himself the examiner who presents the case; he is himself the accused who is presented. He hates the person he remembers having been; and he who now is pursues himself, the person he was. Thus, from the same person there arises in the mind against oneself a conflict which brings forth peace with God.
>
> “The Lord sought this conflict of the heart when he said through the prophet: ‘I attended and listened: no one speaks what is good; no one does repentance for his sin, saying, “What have I done?”’ (Jer. 8). The Lord was appeased by this conflict of the human heart when he spoke concerning King Ahab, accusing and reproving himself, to his prophet: ‘Have you seen Ahab humbled before me? Therefore, because he has humbled himself for my sake, I will not bring evil in his days’ (3 Kings 21).
>
> “Therefore, since it lies in our power to undergo the inward judgment of our mind against ourselves, let us accuse ourselves by recalling what we have been; let us torture ourselves by repentance; while it is permitted, let us not cease to judge what we have done. Let us carefully hear again what is said: ‘For it is no longer within a man’s power to come to God in judgment.’ For it is characteristic of the reprobate always to do evil and never to reconsider what they have done. They pass through everything they do with a blind mind and do not recognize their deed except when they have been punished.
>
> “On the contrary, it belongs to the elect to examine their actions daily from the very source of thought and to dry out from their depths everything that flows forth turbidly. For just as we do not perceive how our limbs grow, the body increases, appearance changes, and the blackness of the hair becomes white in old age—though all these things take place in us without our knowing [Col. 0658C] them—so our mind, through the successive moments of living and the very practice of cares, is changed from itself; and we do not recognize this unless, sitting watchfully over our inward self, we daily weigh both our advances and our failings.
>
> “For to remain in this mortal life is itself, as it were, to proceed toward old age. When the mind is left unexamined, it is lulled into a kind of senile numbness; neglecting itself and imperceptibly losing the strength of its purpose, it grows old from the form of its former strength while it does not know it. Hence it is said through the prophet under the figure of Ephraim: ‘Strangers have devoured his strength, and he knew it not; gray hairs also are scattered upon him, and he himself did not know’ (Hos. 7).
>
> “But when the mind seeks itself and examines itself subtly in repentance, washed from its very old age by tears and kindled by sorrow, it is renewed; and what had almost become old grows warm anew through the supplied exercises of inward love. Hence the Apostle Paul, as the practice of mortal life makes old, admonishes his disciples, saying: ‘Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God was created in righteousness and holiness of truth’ (Eph. 4). But for doing these things, the examples of the Fathers and the precepts of sacred Scripture greatly help us.

> “For if we examine the works of the saints and give ear to divine commands, some things follow from what we have contemplated and others from what we have heard; and our heart is not [Col. 0659A] bound in numbness while it is stirred to imitation. Hence Moses is rightly told: ‘The fire on the altar shall always burn, which the priest shall feed by laying wood upon it every morning, day by day’ (Lev. 6).
>
> “The altar of God is our heart, in which fire is commanded always to burn, because the flame of charity must rise unceasingly from it to God. Every day the priest must lay wood upon it lest it be extinguished. For every person endowed with faith in Christ has surely become a member of the High Priest, as the Apostle Peter says to all the faithful: ‘But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood’ (1 Pet. 2); and as the Apostle John says in the Apocalypse: ‘You have made us a kingdom and priests to our God’ (Rev. 5).
>
> “Therefore, as a priest feeding the fire on the altar, each believer must daily lay on wood; that is, lest the flame of charity [Col. 0659B] fail within him, he must not cease to gather in his heart both the examples of those who went before and the testimonies of sacred Scripture. For to supply, in the exercise of charity, either the examples of the Fathers or the Lord’s commands is like supplying fuel to a fire.
>
> “Since our inward newness itself grows old daily through the conduct of this life, this fire must be fed with wood, so that, while it wastes away through the practice of our oldness, it may revive through the testimonies and examples of the Fathers. And it is rightly commanded there that wood be gathered every morning, day by day. For this is done only when the night of blindness is extinguished; or certainly because morning is the first part of the day, each believer, setting aside thoughts of the present life, should first consider [Col. 0659C] how he may, by whatever efforts he can, kindle the devotion of charity which is already beginning to fail within him.
>
> “For this fire upon the altar of the Lord—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is carefully restored by the examples of the Fathers and the Lord’s testimonies. It is then suitably added: ‘And, after the holocaust has been placed upon it, he shall burn above it the fat of the peace-offerings.’ For whoever kindles this fire of charity within himself surely places himself as a holocaust, because he burns up every judgment by which he had lived badly within himself. When he considers inwardly his thoughts and sacrifices his reprobate life by the sword of transformation, he places himself upon the altar of his heart and kindles himself with the fire of charity.
>
> “From this sacrifice of peace-offerings the fat gives forth fragrance: that is, the inward richness of the new life makes peace between us and God, and gives us a most sweet fragrance. But because this same charity remains inextinguishable in the hearts of the elect, it is aptly added: ‘This is a perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar.’ This fire will indeed never fail from the altar, because even after this life the fervour of charity increases in their minds. For inward contemplation brings it about that the more the almighty God is seen, the more he is loved.

> “That we are delivered from the depth of this life with the help of divine admonitions and the examples of earlier Fathers is also signified well through the prophet Jeremiah, cast into a pit. In order that he may be raised from the pit, ropes and old rags are lowered to him [Col. 0660A] (Jer. 38). What do the ropes signify except the Lord’s commands? Because they both convict and rescue us when we are engaged in evil action, they bind and draw us, constrain and raise us, as it were.
>
> “But lest one bound by these ropes be cut while being drawn up, old rags are also lowered. This means that, lest the divine commands terrify us, the examples of the ancient Fathers strengthen us; and by comparison with them we presume that we can please God, though we fear this because of our own weakness. Therefore, if we hasten to be lifted from this depth, let us be bound with ropes—that is, be constrained by the Lord’s commands. Let old rags be present, by which the ropes may be held more securely: that is, let us be strengthened by the examples of those who went before, lest subtle commands wound us, weak and fearful as we are, while they raise us.
>
> “The Apostle Paul added certain old rags, as it were, when, in raising up his disciples by spiritual commands, he supplied examples of the ancients, saying: ‘The saints experienced mockings and scourges, moreover bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and died by the slaughter of the sword’ (Heb. 11). And a little later: ‘Therefore, having so great a cloud of witnesses set over us, laying aside every weight and the entanglements of sins, let us run with patience to the contest set before us’ (Heb. 12). And again: ‘Remember your leaders, who spoke to you in the name of the Lord the word of salvation; considering the outcome of their manner of life, imitate their faith’ (Heb. 13).
>
> “Above, while speaking spiritual commands, he had sent down ropes, as it were; afterward, recalling the examples of the elders, he applied old rags. Therefore, stirred by so many voices of commands and aided by so many comparisons of examples, let us return to our hearts. Let us examine everything we do; and whatever in us offends against the rule of divine righteousness, let us accuse, so that before the strict Judge our very accusation may excuse us.
>
> “For in this judgment of our mind we are absolved the more quickly the more strictly we hold ourselves guilty. Nor must time be wasted for these acts while there is leisure, because after the time of this life there is no leisure for them. For this little verse is not said in vain: ‘For it is no longer within a man’s power to come to God in judgment.’ We are reminded that we shall then be unable, lest we neglect now what [Col. 0660D] we are able to do.
>
> “But worldly business occupies us, continually set before us, turning the eye of the mind away from the consideration of ourselves. In these visible things which we behold, our heart is scattered outside itself; and, occupied outwardly, it forgets what is being done inwardly concerning itself. The divine voice pierces it with its terrible judgments as with nails, so that it may awaken; so that a human being, at least struck by fear, may dread the hidden judgments concerning himself which, weighed down by numbness, he disregards.
>
> “For, as we said above, the mind, badly accustomed by the very practice of its old life, is weighed down and falls asleep, as it were, in the external things for which it waits. Once it has poured itself outward to desire visible things, it has vanished inwardly from contemplating invisible things. Hence now it is necessary that the mind which is scattered through visible things be struck by judgments concerning invisible things.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, while it lies in our power to come to God in judgment, we must humbly undertake repentance for sins past, lest, deceived by the vain security of the mind, we suddenly be carried off to punishments. For, as has already been said, if we do not willingly come in this life to the judgment of conscience, we shall come unwillingly in the life to come to the judgment of eternal condemnation.

Let us therefore willingly judge ourselves in this age through pure confession, lest we be condemned in the future because of hardness of mind and an unrepentant heart. But what is repentance, and what benefit is there in it? Repentance is the second plank after shipwreck [Col. 0661B], as blessed Jerome says; for if anyone, by sinning, has spoiled the garment of innocence received in baptism, he can recover it by the remedy of repentance. [Note: [Col. 0661D] *Sentences*, Book IV, distinction 14: “After these things.”]

The first plank is baptism, in which the old person is put off and the new put on; the second is repentance, by which we rise after a fall, when returning oldness is driven away and lost newness is resumed. There is an inward repentance and an outward repentance. Outward repentance is a sacrament; inward repentance is a virtue of the mind. Both are causes of salvation and justification.

John’s preaching began with repentance: “Do repentance, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3). What the herald taught, Truth himself afterwards preached. Repentance (*poenitentia*) is so called from repenting (*poenitendo*), by which someone punishes the unlawful acts he has committed. Repentance is also, as blessed Ambrose says, “to bewail past evils and not again commit what must be bewailed.”

Likewise Gregory [Note: [Col. 0661D] St Gregory, Homily 34 on the Gospels; whence the Master took this: “To do repentance is to bewail evils committed and not commit what must be bewailed.”]:

> “To repent is to weep for sins previously committed and not commit what must be wept for. For anyone who bewails some sins in such a way as nevertheless to commit others either does not know how to do repentance or pretends to do it. For what good is it if someone bewails sins of lust and still pants with the heats of avarice?”

Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain [Note: [Col. 0662D] *Sentences*, Book II, ch. 16.]:

> “He is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he repents of; and he does not appear to beseech or ask God as one subject to him, but to deride him in pride. A dog has returned to its vomit, and [Note: [Col. 0662D] Isidore has: “and the penitent to sin.”] the penitent to sin.”

Many shed tears without ceasing and nevertheless do not cease from sinning. Whoever therefore already knows how to bewail his sins [Col. 0661D] must withdraw from sins with the whole effort of his mind. This is what the prophet Isaiah commands sinners, saying: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1). Washed and clean is the person who both bewails the past and does not again commit things to be bewailed. The one who bewails what he has done but does not abandon it is washed but not clean, and after tears repeats what he had wept over.

For repentance which subsequent fault defiles or stains is empty. Laments profit nothing if sins are repeated. It is of no avail to ask forgiveness for evils and to repeat evils anew. Likewise blessed Gregory: “He who bewails sins and nevertheless does not abandon them subjects himself to a heavier punishment.” Likewise blessed Augustine, on the need not to repeat sins, says:

> “Care must be taken lest anyone suppose that those wicked crimes—such as those who commit them do not obtain the kingdom of God—are to be committed daily and redeemed by daily alms. Rather, one’s life must be changed for the better, and by alms God must be propitiated for past sins; not, in a sense, bought off so that it may always be lawful to commit them with impunity.”

Likewise Pope Pius says: “It profits a person nothing to fast, pray, and perform other works of religion unless the mind is recalled from iniquity.” Therefore, as we wrote above, he is a mocker, not a penitent, who bewails what he has committed in such a way that he does not cease to commit, in will or deed, what ought to be bewailed. He also who repeats after tears what he wept over is washed for a time [Col. 0662B], but is not clean; that is, such cleanness is not sufficient for salvation, because it is momentary and not enduring.

Likewise, the statement, “Repentance which subsequent fault defiles is empty,” is to be understood thus: it is empty, namely, lacking the fruit proper to itself, when subsequent fault defiles it. The fruit of repentance is avoidance of Gehenna and attainment of glory. For that repentance, and also prior good deeds, are killed by a subsequent sin, so that they do not receive the reward which they deserved and which they would have had if sin had not followed.

Thus, as blessed Augustine says: “To repent is to keep punishment, so that one may always punish in oneself by avenging what one committed in sinning.” The person keeps punishment who always takes vengeance upon himself for what he grieves to have committed. [Col. 0662C] Repentance, therefore, is vengeance continually punishing in oneself what one grieves to have done. But what remains for us except to grieve throughout our whole life? For where grief ends, repentance also fails. But if repentance ends, what remains of forgiveness? Hence blessed Augustine: “Let each person rejoice and hope in God’s grace as long as he is sustained by repentance.”

Solemn repentance, as blessed Ambrose says, is that which takes place publicly outside the church—that is, at the church door, in ashes and sackcloth. It is imposed only for graver, dreadful, and public offenses. It is not to be repeated, out of reverence for the sacrament, lest it become cheap and contemptible in people’s eyes. Blessed Augustine says of it [Note: [Col. 0662D] Letter 153, alternatively 54.]:

> “Although it has been cautiously and beneficially provided that the place of that most humble repentance be granted once in the Church, lest the medicine, becoming cheap, be less useful to the sick—though it is more salutary the more contemptible it is—yet who would dare say to God: ‘Why do you still spare this person, who after the first repentance has again bound himself in the snares of iniquity?’”

Therefore repentance must be repeated if graver sins are again repeated, but not solemnly as the first time, lest it become cheap. Origen likewise says of this solemn repentance imposed for graver crimes:

> “If some mortal fault be found in us which does not consist in a mortal crime or blasphemy against the faith, but in a fault of speech or conduct, this fault can always be repaired, and one is never forbidden to do repentance for such things. But it is not so with graver crimes. For in graver crimes, opportunity for repentance is granted only once. Common sins, however, which we frequently incur always admit repentance and are always redeemed.”

By “common sins” he means venial sins, and perhaps certain mortal sins less grave than others, which, as they are frequently committed, are likewise frequently redeemed through repentance. But for graver crimes solemn repentance is undertaken only once; for if they are repeated, repentance too is repeated, but not solemnly.

[Col. 0663B] [Note: [Col. 0663D] Distinction 15.]

There are some who repent of having sinned, yet reserve for themselves altogether certain vices in which they delight, not observing that the Lord delivered from the demon one who was both mute and deaf. Hence blessed Augustine says:

> “By this the Lord teaches us that we are never healed except from all sins. For if he had wished sins to be healed in part, he could have made whole the one who had seven demons after expelling six; but he expelled seven, in order to teach that all crimes must be cast out together. When he casts a legion of demons out of another person, he leaves none of them to possess the one delivered, showing that even if sins should be a thousand, one must repent of all of them.
>
> “For the Lord never healed anyone whom he did not wholly deliver. He healed the whole person on the Sabbath, both the body from every infirmity and the soul from every contagion, showing that the penitent must grieve at once for every crime. For I know that the Lord is an enemy to every criminal. How then will one who reserves one crime receive forgiveness for another? He would obtain forgiveness without the love of God, without which no one has ever found grace. For he is God’s enemy while he shows himself to persevere in sins. It is a kind of impiety of unbelief to hope for half forgiveness from him who is righteous and justice itself. Thus one would find grace without true repentance.
>
> “True repentance strives to lead to baptismal purity. The rightly penitent person must wash away, at least by the tears of the mind, whatever defilement he has contracted after purification. But hard indeed is the person [Col. 0663D] whose eyes do not reveal the pain of his mind. Let him know himself culpably hard who weeps for the harsh losses of temporal things or for a friend’s death, but does not show sorrow for sin in tears.”

Hence blessed Augustine, admonishing penitents, says:

> “Penitents, if you are truly penitents and not mockers, change your life for the better and be reconciled to God. Do you do repentance, bend your knees, and laugh? You mock God’s repentance. If you do repentance, repent; if you do not repent, you are not a penitent. Therefore, if you repent, why do you again do evil? If you repent of having done evil, do not again do evil. If you still do it, you certainly are not penitent.”

Pope Innocent plainly indicates what false repentance is, saying:

> “We admonish our brothers, namely bishops and priests, not to permit the souls of laypeople to be deceived by false repentances and dragged into hell. False repentance is evidently present when, many sins having been disregarded, repentance is done for one alone; or when repentance is done for one in such a way that the person does not depart from another.”

Therefore, only that repentance is true which removes sin; and only that removes sin which corrects it. If at any time a brother so sins against a brother that he is unable to repair what he has sinned, it can be forgiven him. For someone may unjustly take from another what he cannot restore, such as an eye or life and the like; yet, if he repents with the love of fitting satisfaction, he receives forgiveness of the sin.

Yet no one should suppose that a person who has unjustly taken another’s property, which he can restore, repents of that sin or obtains forgiveness unless he restores what he has taken. So long as the thing on account of which the sin occurred is not returned, when it can be returned, repentance is not done but feigned. [Col. 0664B]

[Note: [Col. 0663D] Distinction 16.]

In the perfection of repentance three things are to be considered or observed: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. Hence John Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 0664D] “Golden” or “Chrysostom.”]:

> “Perfect repentance compels the sinner willingly to endure all things, so that contrition may be in his heart, confession in his mouth, and complete humility in his conduct.”

This is fruitful repentance: as we offend God in three ways, namely by heart, mouth, and hand, so we make satisfaction to God in three ways. For there are three kinds [Col. 0664C] of sin, as blessed Augustine says: in the heart, in deed, and in habit; or, as it were, three deaths. One is as if in the house, namely when the heart consents to lust; another as if already carried beyond the gate, when consent proceeds to action; the third when the mind is weighed down as by a mass of evil habit and armed with the shield of harmful self-defense, as if already rotting in the tomb.

These are the three kinds of dead persons whom the Lord is read to have raised. This threefold death is met by a threefold remedy: contrition, confession, and satisfaction. Contrition is commended to us, as the Prophet says: “Rend your hearts and not your garments,” etc. (Joel 2). Confession is commended where it says: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. 18). For that person truly confesses who accuses himself, imputing evil to himself with abhorrence.

The Psalmist, inviting us to confession, says: “Pour out your hearts before him, because God is our helper for ever” (Ps. 61). As though he said: Empty your hearts before God, not before people, because he sees when we make true confession. Pour them out, I say, by tearfully entreating, humbly confessing, truthfully repenting, and not hoping deceitfully. Or “pour out before him,” that is, before his regard, or so that he may receive it; or “pour out,” that is, transcend your hearts, so that you may be able to think of him.

As if he said plainly: Whatever you conceive apart from God passes away; he remains. Pour out upon him whatever anxiety your heart conceives [Col. 0665A]. Therefore pour out your hearts before him, because what you cannot do by yourselves, he will do. He is our helper, leading us into eternity, mercifully calling, justifying, and preserving us.

Satisfaction too is commanded by John when he says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3): namely, that the quality and quantity of punishment correspond to the quality and quantity of the fault. Therefore discernment in repentance is very necessary, so that one does what Augustine teaches, saying:

> “Let a person consider the quality of the crime in its place, its time, its continuance, the variety of the person, the temptation under which it was committed, and the manifold execution of the vices themselves. One who has committed fornication must repent according to the excellence of his rank or office, according to the character of the prostitute, and according to the manner in which he used his body for shameful conduct: whether in a sacred place or at a time appointed for prayer, such as festivals and fast-times.
>
> “Let the penitent also consider how long he persisted in sin, and bewail that he sinned persistently; and how great was the assault by which he was overcome. For there are some who are not merely overcome, but freely offer themselves to sin: they do not wait for temptation but anticipate it by will. Let the penitent also examine within himself with how manifold an exercise of vice he sinned with delight.
>
> “All this variety must be confessed and bewailed, so that when he recognizes what sin is, he may quickly find God propitious. In recognizing the aggravation of the sin, let him consider what degree of wisdom and age, and what rank, he had. Let him dwell upon each of these matters and, by tears, feel out the measure of the crime, cleansing every quality of vice. Let him also bewail the virtue which he lacked; for one must grieve not only because one sinned, but because one deprived oneself of virtue. Let him also bewail that, by offending in one matter, he became guilty of all.”

For he proved ungrateful who, though full of virtues, did not fear God at all. For the more acceptable a sinner is to God, the more blameworthy he becomes in sinning. Thus Adam sinned the more because he abounded in every good. In another way also, the one who offends in one point becomes guilty of all, because every virtue suffers damage from a single vice. Let the penitent place himself wholly under the judgment and authority of the priest, reserving nothing of himself for himself, so that, at the priest’s command, he may be ready to do for the recovery of the soul’s life whatever he would do to avoid bodily death [Col. 0665D]; and let him do this with desire, because he recovers everlasting life. For one who is to become immortal ought gladly to do what one who is dying would do in order to postpone death. Let him always pray to God and offer God a pure mind and contrition of heart. Then, if he can offer anything from his possessions, let him offer it confidently: “The Lord had respect unto Abel, and to his gifts” (Gen. IV). He mentioned Abel before his gifts. Therefore the giver’s alms must be weighed by the judgment of the heart: one must consider not how much he gives, but with what mind and affection he gives what he can [Col. 0666A]. Therefore, whoever wishes to redeem his sins by an offering of temporal goods must first offer his mind. Let him beware, lest, prompted by shame, he divide his confession within himself and wish to disclose different matters to different priests. For some conceal from one priest what they reserve to disclose to another; this is to praise oneself, to tend toward hypocrisy, and always to lack the forgiveness which they vainly imagine they will attain. Let him beware also not to approach the Lord’s body before he has strengthened his conscience by good works, and grieve because he does not yet dare to receive the saving food which he greatly desires. Let him also refrain from the games and spectacles of the world if he wishes to attain the grace of perfect remission. These are fruits worthy of repentance, freeing the captive soul [Col. 0666B] and preserving it in freedom. And just as there are worthy fruits of repentance and true satisfaction, so also there are unworthy fruits and false satisfaction—that is, false repentance—of which blessed Gregory says:

> We call those repentances false which are not imposed, according to the authorities of the saints, in proportion to the nature of the crimes. Therefore, if a soldier, a merchant, or one devoted to some occupation which cannot be practiced without sin, comes to repentance entangled in graver faults; or if one unjustly retains another’s goods, or bears hatred in his heart: let him recognize that he cannot perform true repentance unless he leaves his business or abandons his occupation, casts hatred out of his heart, and restores the goods which he has unjustly taken. Yet let him not despair. Meanwhile, whatever good he can do [Col. 0666C], we exhort him to do, so that God may enlighten his heart unto repentance.

What satisfaction is sufficient for venial sins, Augustine indicates in the *Enchiridion*, saying:

> For daily, brief, and light sins, without which this life is not lived, the daily prayer of the faithful makes satisfaction; for it belongs to them to say, “Our Father, who art in heaven; hallowed be thy name” (Matt. VI), and the rest. This prayer wholly removes these least and daily sins; it also removes those sins from which the life even of believers, though wickedly lived, departs when it is changed for the better through repentance. If it is truthfully said, “Forgive us our debts [Note: [Col. 0665D] Something is lacking here for completeness of sense: ‘Let it be said as truthfully as we too forgive our debtors [Col. 0666D].’],” that is, if what is said is done, since it too is an alms to forgive completely those who seek pardon.

For doing repentance, as blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0666D] Distinction 17, “But to priests.”], it is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil deeds, unless one also makes satisfaction to the Lord for what has been done through the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, the sacrifice of a contrite heart, with alms cooperating. Therefore, let one who repents repent wholly, and show his sorrow by tears. Let him present his life through the priest; let him anticipate God’s judgment by confession. Thus it is not sufficient to confess sins to God without a priest, nor is one truly a humble penitent if he does not desire and seek the priest’s judgment.

But is it equally effective to confess to a companion or neighbor [Col. 0667A], at least if a priest is absent? Certainly, it may be said on this point that the examination of a priest is to be diligently sought, because God granted priests the power of binding and loosing; and therefore those whose sins they forgive are also forgiven by God. Nevertheless, if a priest is lacking, confession is to be made to one’s neighbor or companion. Hence blessed Augustine says:

> Whoever wishes to confess sins, so as to find grace, should seek a priest who knows how to bind and loose; lest, when he has been negligent concerning himself, he be neglected by the one who mercifully warns and entreats him, lest both fall into the pit which the fool was unwilling to avoid.

But Bede distinguishes between the confession of venial and mortal sins, saying: “Let us disclose daily and light sins to equals; but graver sins to a priest, namely a bishop [Col. 0667B], and let us take care to cleanse them in whatever time he appoints; for sins cannot be forgiven without the confession of amendment. Yet grave sins also must be disclosed to equals when a priest is absent and danger presses.” Nevertheless, it is safer and more perfect to disclose both greater and lesser sins to priests and seek from them the counsel of medicine, since to them the power of binding and loosing has been granted.

Furthermore, it must be known that what is secret ought not to be made public before many. For just as public sins require a public remedy, so hidden sins are cleansed by secret satisfaction and private confession. Nor is it necessary that what we have once confessed to a priest should be confessed again; but we must continually confess it to the true Judge with the tongue of the heart [Col. 0667C], not of the flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Distinction 19.] It must also be known that no one ought to exercise the office of priest unless he is free from those sins which he judges in others; otherwise he condemns himself. Wise Augustine describes what sort of person one appointed judge of others ought to be, saying:

> Let the priest to whom every sinner is brought, before whom every sickness is set, be judged in none of those things which he is ready to judge in another. For one who judges another while himself subject to judgment condemns himself. Let him therefore know himself and cleanse in himself what he sees offered to him in others. Let him take care to cast away from himself whatever he finds harmful in another. Let him heed that “he who is without sin, let him first cast a stone at her” [Col. 0667D] (John VIII).

Let the spiritual judge beware that, just as he has not committed the crime of wickedness, so he does not lack the gift of knowledge. He must know how to discern whatever he ought to judge. Therefore a diligent investigator wisely asks the sinner about what he perhaps does not know, or wishes to conceal through shame. Once the crime is known, he does not hesitate to investigate its variations: the place, the time, and the other matters written above. When these are known, let the master himself be kindly, ready to raise the penitent up and mercifully to bear the penitent’s burden with him; let him have gentleness in affection, discernment amid variety, and teach perseverance.

[Note: [Col. 0668D] Distinction 20.] It must also be known that the time for repentance extends to life’s final moment [Col. 0668A]. No one must be despaired of while he remains in this life or in this body, because what is deferred through lack of confidence in youth is sometimes accomplished by more mature counsel. Yet blessed Augustine writes thus concerning those who put off repentance:

> If someone placed in final necessity wishes to receive repentance, receives it, and, reconciled, immediately departs this life, I confess to you that we do not deny him what he asks; but neither do we presume that he departs well. If he departs securely, I do not know. We can give him repentance, but not assurance. Will he be condemned? I do not say so; but neither do I say that he will be delivered. Do you then, O man, wish to be freed from uncertainty? Do repentance while you are well. If you do so, I tell you that you are secure, because you have done repentance at a time when you were able to sin. If you wish [Col. 0668B] to do repentance when you can no longer sin, your sins have left you; you have not left them.

Again, there are two possibilities: either you are forgiven or you are not; which of these will be yours I do not know. Therefore hold fast to what is certain, and leave what is uncertain: love God above all things, and repent that you have done evil. One who repents late ought not merely to fear the Judge but also to love him, because no one can be saved without charity. Therefore, one who repents should not only fear punishment but also yearn for glory. If such conversion happens to someone even at the end, one must not despair of his forgiveness. But because so just a conversion is scarcely or rarely found, one ought to fear for the late penitent. Since there are many things which hinder and draw back the weak, it is most dangerous [Col. 0668C] and close to destruction to delay the remedy of repentance until death.

But even if one thus converted lives and does not die, we nevertheless do not promise that he will escape every punishment; for he who postponed the fruit of conversion to another age must first be purified by the fire of purification. Though this purgatorial fire is not eternal, it is nevertheless marvellously severe: it exceeds every punishment that anyone has ever suffered in this life, although martyrs endured many torments for Christ. From this it is sufficiently shown how dangerous it is to postpone repentance until life’s end. Yet if true repentance is found even then, it frees the person and obtains life for one who is dying, though not so that he feels no punishment—unless perhaps the intensity [Col. 0668D] of his groaning and contrition is so great as to suffice for the punishment of the offence. Therefore, although it is difficult for repentance to be true when it comes so late, when agony binds the limbs and pain overwhelms the senses so that a person can scarcely think of anything, still late repentance is better than none. For if repentance comes at life’s final breath, it heals and liberates. The thief’s repentance was very late, but pardon was not late; yet although the thief deserved pardon at the end for every crime, he did not thereby give the baptized authority to sin or to persevere in sin.

But if the question concerns those who do not complete repentance in this life—whether they will pass through fire [Col. 0669A] there, as though to complete what they did too little here—we say that the same must be thought of these as of those who repent at the last moment. For if there is such contrition of heart and reproach for the offence as suffices to punish the sin, they pass free from other punishments into life. But those whose hearts are not so contrite and who do not groan sufficiently for sin, if they die before completing repentance, will experience purgatorial fire and be punished more severely than if they had completed repentance here. “For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. X). For God, being merciful and just, out of mercy forgives the penitent, not reserving sin for eternal punishment; but in justice he does not leave an offence unpunished: either the human being punishes it, or God does. The human being [Col. 0669B] punishes it by repenting; God, by handing the human being over to punishments.

Repentance is inward and outward. Therefore, if inward repentance is so great that it is a sufficient requital for sin, God, who knows this, requires no further punishment from one who repents in this way. But if inward repentance does not suffice for the avenging of sin and outward repentance is not completed, God, who knows the kinds and measures of sins and punishments, will add a sufficient punishment. Therefore every sinner should strive so to correct offences that after death he need not undergo punishment. Some mortal sins become venial in repentance, though they are not immediately healed. A sick person would often die if he were not treated; yet he is not healed immediately after treatment. He languishes [Col. 0669C] though he will live, when formerly he was going to die. But one who dies unrepentant dies utterly and is eternally tormented. For if he were always to live, he would always sin.

But if the question concerns one who has completed the imposed satisfaction which, through the priest’s negligence or ignorance, was not proportionate to the sin: is he, on departing this life, free from every punishment? I give the same answer as I gave above concerning the one who did not complete repentance. If there is such a lament of inward sorrow as suffices for the punishment of sin, he is wholly freed; but if inward sorrow together with the imposed penalty is insufficient, God will add punishment. That inward sorrow sometimes suffices for the punishment of sin is certainly demonstrated in that thief [Col. 0669D] who, by contrition and confession of mind alone, deserved to enter paradise immediately when he was converted.

Moreover, the law of satisfaction is not to be imposed on those who are dying. Hence Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, says:

> From the sick who are in danger of death, a pure confession of sins must be sought; nevertheless, no measure of penance is to be imposed upon them, but it must be made known to them. And with the prayers of friends and the distribution of alms the burden of repentance is to be lightened, should they perhaps depart; but if they recover, they should diligently observe the measure of penance imposed by the priest.

Furthermore, it must be known that a priest ought not to reconcile penitents without consulting the bishop, unless extreme necessity compels [Col. 0670A]. Hence in the Council of Carthage: “For any penitent whose crime is public and has stirred the whole city, hands shall be laid upon him before the apse, that is, the entrance of the church.” Likewise Bishop Aurelian says: “If anyone is in danger and wishes to be reconciled to the divine altars, if the bishop is absent, the priest ought to consult the bishop and then, by his command, reconcile the person in danger.” Therefore, without consulting the bishop, a priest cannot reconcile those excommunicated or publicly doing penance. Just as a priest can consecrate virgins by the bishop’s command, so he can reconcile penitents.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since for your instruction and admonition [Col. 0670B] we have set down the distinctions of repentance established and firmly defined by the holy teachers, it is fitting that at the beginning of this holy fast we punish, by bitter weeping, humble repentance, and worthily making satisfaction to God through good works, the sins which throughout all our life we have negligently and pleasurably committed, lest by persisting long in evils we end our life [Note: [Col. 0669D] Book *On Saving Counsels*, chapter 38.]. For all laypeople, clergy, monks, and all believers ought to have hope, charity, and humility; to serve God with their whole heart; to make true satisfaction for sins; and to perform worthy repentance, because the most merciful Lord is accustomed kindly to forgive those who flee to repentance.

But let us not be so confident in the Lord’s mercy as to add sins to sins, nor say: “So long as the age of our flesh is vigorous, let us indulge our desires; and finally, in old age, let us repent of our evils. For the Lord is kind and merciful and will remember our deeds no more.” I beg you, dearest brothers, let us not think such things. For it is supreme folly to think them and damnable for anyone to wish to seek from God such a license, the beginning of which is to separate us from God. Therefore, I say, let us not think such things, especially since we do not know on what day we shall die. Not all people die in old age; rather, they depart from this world at different ages. And in whatever actions each person is found, as blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0669D] The same author, *Exposition 1 on Psalm XXXVI*: “As you depart from this life, so you are restored to that life.”], in those same actions he shall be judged when his soul has departed from the body. Hence it is said: “Where I find you [Col. 0670D], there I shall judge you.” And again: “No one in hell will confess to you” (Ps. VI). Therefore let us hasten, while there is time, to turn to God through repentance, if we truly wish to obtain pardon [Note: [Col. 0670D] Book *On Saving Counsels*, chapter 35.].

Let the last day always be before our eyes; and when we have risen at dawn, let us not be confident of reaching evening. When we have laid our limbs upon the bed, let us be uncertain of the coming of daylight. Then we shall most easily restrain our body from vices and unlawful desires. Let our flesh always be subject to the soul, serving its mistress as a maidservant. Let us not give unlawful strength to our body, lest it wage war against the spirit [Col. 0671A]; but let the flesh always be subject, so that it obeys the commands of the Holy Spirit. Nor let us permit the maidservant to grow fat, lest she despise her mistress, namely the soul; rather, let her be made a servant, obedient to its will in all things. For just as bridles must be put upon horses, so our bodies must be bridled and restrained by fasts and prayers. Hence blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0671D] Ibid.]:

> Just as charioteers, if they loosen the reins, are carried over precipices, so the soul together with its body slips down to the precipices of hell if we do not put a bridle upon it.

Therefore let us be good and skilled charioteers of our body, so that we may travel by the straight way. Excessive food greatly harms not only souls but bodies too, and brings them into sickness. For through excessive greed for food [Col. 0671B] [Note: [Col. 0671D] Ibid., chapter 36.] and intemperance in drink, the strength of the stomach is usually broken; and abundance of blood and bile, along with very many illnesses, are contracted through plentiful eating. For as these things are necessary to soul and body, so moderation is the remedy for both. And if not at every time, at least during these most sacred days of fasting, let us, as far as we can with God’s help, flee the pleasures of the world and abundance of food, lest perhaps—God avert it—we seek a drop of water amid the tormenting flame and receive no refreshment. For, as the Apostle says, “The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to one another” (Gal. V).

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Beautifully Leo the Great, Sermon 8, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*: “Daily experience,” he says, “proves that the sharpness of the mind is dulled by the satiety of the flesh and the vigor of the heart blunted by excess of food; so that the pleasure of eating is even opposed to bodily health, unless the rule of moderation withstands the enticement and withdraws from pleasure what would become a burden.”]

The flesh is a wretched beast which weighs down the soul, as the Apostle says: “Those who are in the flesh,” that is, those who live according to the flesh, “cannot please God” (Rom. VIII) [Col. 0671C]. Likewise our Lord Jesus Christ, Truth itself, says to his disciples: “The spirit indeed is willing,” namely for doing good, “but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI). For our flesh always wants to be strong in wickedness, but in abstinence—that is, fasting, prayer, vigils, and other good works—it pretends to be weak. Our flesh is what plunges us into the pit of vices, as the Apostle says: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth, namely fornication, impurity, anger, strife” (Col. III), and the other things which follow. And again: “Make not provision for the flesh in your desires” (Rom. XIII). Therefore let us mortify our flesh [Col. 0671D] through abstinence, fasting, vigils, and prayers, lest through evil desires it lead us into the devil’s temptation. Flesh was given to us as a war against the soul: if it is mortified, it leads to life; if nourished, it prepares itself for war against the soul. Hence blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0671D] *On Saving Counsels*, chapter 64.]:

> I praise the person who can have power over his flesh [Col. 0672A]; but we, while fearing the weakness of the flesh, neglect the salvation of our souls.

Therefore, let one who has an abundance of banquets consider the punishment of the rich man burning in torment, whose poverty amid the fires of hell was as great as his abundance of feasts had been here (Luke XVI). In this world he refused to hunger and thirst; therefore there, thirsty amid flames, he sought a drop of water and did not deserve to receive it. Likewise the bodies of the three youths did not burn in the furnace of blazing fire because they were abstinent (Dan. III): that is, they despised the riches of food.

There are four kinds of distinction in the appetite of gluttony, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0671D] Garsias Loaysa says that the whole substance of this statement, at chapter 42 of Book II of the *Sentences*, is drawn from Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXX, chapter 13. But Gregory adds a fifth kind: “It must further be known,” he says, “that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways,” etc. Yet although Isidore in this place distinguishes only four kinds of gluttony, he nevertheless explains five kinds of it in Book II of the *Differences*, no. 40—namely, the very kinds which Gregory explains in the passage cited.]: what is desired, when, how much, and how. “What” concerns the thing itself [Col. 0672B] which is desired. “When” applies if something is desired before the lawful time. “How much” refers to excess. “How” is ascribed to the impatience of haste. Often we taste more carefully prepared foods without the concupiscence of gluttony, and take cheap and common food with eagerness to eat; thus it comes about that not the quality of the foods is at fault, but what is taken with the desire of eating is counted as vice. Certainly, if we eagerly desire what is not permitted; or if we seek with especial care permitted things prepared at elaborate expense; or if we do not wait for the lawful time of eating, we incur the vice of gluttony.

For this reason our first parents lost the delights of paradise and the rewards of immortality, because they ate the forbidden food of the prohibited tree [Col. 0672C] (Gen. III). Esau, because he eagerly desired lentils, sold his birthright (Gen. XXV). And because animals do not keep the proper time for eating, they are irrational. Therefore one who greedily devours even cheap food is not abstinent. “Their throat is an open grave,” says the Psalmist (Ps. XIII). Likewise he is soft and self-indulgent who, despising what is at hand, delights in costly and foreign foods. The fish is caught on the hook through bait; the bird is caught in snares by the sight of food [Note: [Col. 0672D] “In traps” (*muscipulis*).]. Beasts that are vigorous or strong by natural power rush into the pit through desire; food deceives those whom nature does not soften [Note: [Col. 0672D] Isidore, Book II of the *Sentences*, final chapter.].

Yet immoderate fasts must not be imposed upon the body, lest, when the flesh is weighed down too heavily [Col. 0672D] by the burden of hunger, it afterward be unable to do good, even though it does no evil; and lest what is constrained to lack the habit of evil together with the performance of good, through being pressed too hard, perish. Therefore the bodily material must be moderated by watchful discernment: so that it is neither wholly extinguished nor immoderately relaxed. For however much anyone may love holiness [Col. 0673A], he is nevertheless unable to carry out the beginning of the work in which he seeks to serve by the intention of his heart. Excessive bodily weakness also breaks the powers of the mind, causes the intellect to wither, and through infirmity cannot accomplish anything good. Hence blessed Isidore says in the second book of the *Sentences*: “No one can attain perfection when excessive weakness of the flesh prevails.”

Some tear their bodies with extraordinary hunger, “disfiguring,” as the Lord says in the Gospel, “their faces, so that they may appear to men to fast” (Matt. VI). Their faces grow pale, their bodies are worn away, they draw deep sighs from their hearts, and even before death deliver themselves to deadly torments. Yet these wretches pursue so great an exercise of labor not for God’s love but solely for the admiration of human praise [Col. 0673B]. Therefore this good of abstinence must not be counted a virtue in such people, but a vice, because they use good things badly.

Fasting too is despised when it is renewed in the evening by a surfeit of food. Abstinence cannot be reckoned where fullness of the belly follows. For the person who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening in order to fill his gluttony chews over feasts in his thoughts all day. Therefore this is perfect fasting: when the mind prays inwardly, the body fasts from food, and the hand refrains from unlawful deeds. For by fasting prayer more readily penetrates heaven. Fasting and almsgiving love to remain hidden, so that God alone, who sees all things, may reward the merit of good works. For those who do them before public display are by no means justified by God, because according to the Gospel saying [Col. 0673C] they have received their reward. Thus fasts joined with good works are acceptable to God. But those who abstain from food and act wickedly imitate demons, who have no food and yet always possess wickedness. One abstains well from food who also fasts from deeds of malice and from worldly ambitions.

Therefore, dearest brothers, as the Lord says, “Do not become sad like hypocrites” (ibid.), but be cheerful like true Christians; for as God loves a cheerful giver (II Cor. IX), so he also loves a cheerful faster. Therefore fast, sweetest brothers, not for human favor but for eternal glory; not for the praise of men but for hope of heavenly goods; not for the world [Col. 0673D] but for God; not as pleasing men but as serving God.

> For when a person truly prays and fasts, then by spiritual effect he is joined to angels. Through fasting also, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0673D] Book II of the *Sentences*, final chapter.], the hidden mysteries of heaven are revealed and the secrets of the divine sacrament are disclosed.

Thus Moses, leader of the people of Israel, first fasted for forty days and forty nights (Deut. IX), and so deserved to receive the law from the Lord. It was fitting that he should first abstain from bodily food, so that afterward he might worthily be instructed in the divine commandments. So Elijah, fasting forty days, withdrew into the wilderness; and standing at the entrance of the cave, he saw a great vision of God [Col. 0674A], which he was unable to bear, and covered his face with his cloak (III Kings XIX). So Daniel, through an angel’s revelation, deserved to know the sacraments of the mysteries (Dan. X). For this virtue displays manifestations of angels and reveals their announcements. Thus Daniel himself, desiring to know the things to come in the future age and commending fasting while leaving posterity a most useful example of fasting, says: “I, Daniel, fasted for three weeks of days; I ate no bread of desire, and wine and flesh did not enter my mouth” (ibid.). Likewise the three youths who despised the rich foods of the royal table (Dan. I), and ate vegetables in fasting, strengthened by divine power and armed with the weapons of faith, extinguished the flame of the burning furnace [Col. 0674B] (Dan. III). So too the holy apostles, after the ascension of the Bridegroom, namely Christ, into heaven, persevered in prayer and fasting and sowed the teaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world (Acts I).

Therefore, dearest brothers, do not become, as the Lord says in the Gospel, like sad hypocrites, who, while fasting, disfigure their faces so that they may appear to men to fast (Matt. VI). They disfigure their faces because they do not fast devoutly for God, but in order to receive a temporal reward from human beings. They do not fast in order to obtain remission of sins, but in order to be honored by mortals. They fast sadly, not to redeem their sins, but to please flatterers. Therefore fast, not as sad hypocrites, but as joyful true Christians; not as heretics, but as children of the Church; not as gaining praise from men, but as awaiting a heavenly reward from God; not as lying to God and men, but as those who truly desire to please God; not as heretics withdrawing from the unity of the Church, but as Catholics preserving the true faith.

Break your bread for the hungry, and kindly bring the poor into your home. Give garments to the naked, and do not despise your flesh, so that your light may rise like the morning: namely, the light of a good work or of eternal brightness. Anoint your head, namely Christ, through pure, singular, and perfect love; through compassion for neighbors; through mercy toward the poor; through [Col. 0674D] generous almsgiving. Let each also wash his face—that is, the sight of his soul—so that it may be clean for contemplating God: clean from every stain of sin and impure thought, from every error of heretical depravity, from every contamination of vices and blindness of unbelief.

Otherwise: “Wash your face” (ibid.), that is, adorn the Church or the altar with all diligence and all devotion. For just as the face—namely, the look and countenance—is the glory and beauty of the whole body, so the Church and the holiness of the altar are the countenance and glory of the one body of all faithful Christians. Therefore, let each person wash—that is, adorn, raise, exalt, honor, and glorify—this face, the holy Church, according to his means [Col. 0675A]. And let him do so to the praise and glory of the head of this body, namely Christ, who is head of the whole Church (Col. I) and sits at the right hand of the Father (Heb. X).

Likewise, store up treasures for yourselves not in this age, where thieves break in and steal, but in heaven, where the thief does not approach and where rust and moth do not corrupt (Matt. VI). Store up all together for yourselves treasures of faith, charity, mercy, and piety; but let others to whom it has been given store up treasures of virginity; others, of purity and chastity; others, of vigils, fasts, prayers, and almsgiving. Dearest ones, lay up these treasures for yourselves in heaven, where the spirits and souls of the righteous contemplate God [Col. 0675B]—God, I say, the most generous rewarder, whom the choir of holy angels serves, before whom the multitude of archangels stands, whom the entire host of heavenly orders praises without end. If you truly and diligently lay up these treasures of good works in heaven, you will have ready the most merciful Father and Lord as giver of your reward.

Indeed, according to the Lord’s saying, where the treasure of the children of humankind is, there also is their heart (ibid.). Thus, just as one who stores treasure on earth is anxious lest, after going far from home, he lose the treasure he left behind, and therefore hastens to return from his journey as quickly as possible [Col. 0676A], so too one who stores treasure in heaven desires to reach more quickly the riches he has sent there. Therefore, dearest brothers, lay up treasures of good works in heaven and fix there the intention of your minds, so that you may rightly say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Let our heart always meditate on heavenly promises. Let us transfer all earthly things which we possess into heavenly dwellings, so that, when we depart from this world, we may enjoy heavenly goods through God’s ineffable grace.

For, as blessed Augustine says:

> We believe that, when our soul has been released from the bond of the flesh, if we have lived well and rightly before God, the choir of holy angels will immediately come to meet us, and the companies of all the saints will be joined to our embraces [Col. 0676B] and lead us to worship the true Judge. If, while we live in the body, we do what pleases God, as has now been said, then peace will be round about us; and when we have cast off the burden of flesh, the Holy Spirit will grant us a dwelling in heaven—he to whom we had shortly before made a dwelling within the lodging of our body. And, glad and rejoicing, we shall await the day of future judgment, in which the souls of each will receive their deserts for their deeds: through him who, God in perfect Trinity, lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Eleventh Sermon, for the First Sunday of Lent

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675C] “Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterward he was hungry” (Matt. IV). The Son of God could indeed, if he wished, have powerfully cast off or repelled his tempter. But he allowed himself to be tempted in order reasonably to conquer him and to teach us to overcome our temptations. Therefore the devil first attacked him through the desire of the flesh, that is, through gluttony, when he said: “Command that these stones become bread.” And because wisdom always acts wisely, he set the shield of authority against the missile of the ancient enemy, saying: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God.”

Then he tempted him through vainglory, when he took him up upon the pinnacle of the temple and persuaded him [Col. 0675D] to cast himself down. He replied most fittingly: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Finally, he tempted him through greed for temporal things, when he showed him all the kingdoms of the world upon a mountain and said: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me.” But he breaks the enemy’s weapon with the sword of God’s word, when he says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve.” And so, [Col. 0676C] when the enemy had been defeated, angels came and ministered to him.

From these three snares of vices the evangelist John wishes to call us back, when in his Epistle he says with fearful emphasis: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world; for everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life. And the world passes away, and its concupiscence” (1 John 2). This world is especially an enemy of the human race: it blinds the eyes of the mind, allures its intention by false goods, and incessantly draws it back by its pleasures from the love of the heavenly kingdom. For the world itself subjects to the slavery of the devil those human beings who were created in God’s image and to serve God, and separates them from the love of God [Col. 0676D]. This is attested by the Apostle James, who says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be made an enemy of God” (James 4). People therefore serve the devil because they love the world—that is, the things that are in the world. But those who perfectly despise the world’s delights undoubtedly love God above all things. Thus, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0675D] Book III of the *Sentences*, chap. 16]: “All things in this world are opposed to God’s servants, so that, when they experience these adversities, they may be stirred more ardently [Col. 0677A] toward heavenly longing.” Surely it is fitting that one who truly loves God should despise the world.

In this age holy men are guests and pilgrims. Hence the Son of God rightly rebuked the Apostle Peter because he wished to make a tent on the mountain (Matt. 17). Therefore the saints have no tent in this world, for their homeland and dwelling are in heaven. Holy men consequently desire to despise the world and to draw the movement of their minds back to things above, so that they may gather themselves there from where they have flowed away, and withdraw themselves from where they have been scattered. If, therefore, we wish to rise to the love of God, we must first hold cheap, in comparison with him, all things that are in the world; for if we love them, we shall be made enemies of God.
