Thus everything in the world [Col. 0677B] is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life.

[Note: [Col. 0677D] Sermon 31 to the brethren in the desert, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VI.] Let us therefore speak, if you please, of each in turn. The pleasures of the flesh are those which the flesh seeks through unlawful impulse: gluttony, drunkenness, lust, excessive sleep, gazing, laughter, and other such things. Because the flesh is nearer to us, the world first attacks us through its vices. For the more familiar an enemy is, the more harmful he is; and many have fallen through its vices. Adam fell through gluttony; Lot through drunkenness; Solomon through lust. We must always oppose gluttony by abstinence, for it was the beginning of our captivity and the fosterer of other pleasures, since lust and drowsiness arise from it [Col. 0677C]. It is also very often the cause of serious illnesses and the consumption of great wealth.

Hence blessed Isidore, our patron, says [Note: [Col. 0677D] Book III of the *Sentences*, chap. 41]:

> “No one can undertake spiritual warfare unless he has first subdued the desires of the flesh. Nor can a mind be free for contemplating God when it eagerly pursues the desires and cravings of this world. For the eye that is shut in by the dust of concupiscence cannot behold things on high. Therefore avarice and the love of money are worse than every sin. Hence it is said through Solomon: ‘Nothing is more wicked than to love money; for such a person makes his own soul saleable, because in his lifetime he casts away his inmost parts’ (Sirach 10).”

Covetousness, therefore, is the material of all crimes. Hence Paul also says: “The root of all evils is covetousness; in seeking it, some have wandered from the faith” [Col. 0677D] (1 Tim. 6). Let the root of crimes therefore be cut down, lest the remaining offspring of vices sprout forth. The first snare, then, is the concupiscence of the flesh, because it is the root of all evils.

The second snare is called the concupiscence of the eyes: namely, the desire for outward things—for gold, silver, and other desirable possessions—because through the eyes the desire for them is conveyed inwardly to the soul [Col. 0678A]. There are many whom the devil does not hinder by the pleasure of the flesh, yet he allures their eyes through the craving for outward things. Money is God’s creation; yet God is not angered because his creation is loved, but because it is preferred to himself. Why then, O man, do you admire the appearance of a creature more than the beauty of the Creator? Why do you love the creature more than him who gave beauty to creatures? You also maintain a disordered love when you honor the creature more than the Creator. You do not think rightly of God if you put love of the creature before love of the Creator. We must therefore despise all temporal things, but love above all things the highest good, which is God. Man most rightly loves him above all things who created everything under heaven to serve humankind [Col. 0678B].

Let us not therefore put our trust in this world’s riches, for they cannot free us from eternal punishments. Hence Solomon says: “Riches will not profit on the day of vengeance, but righteousness will deliver from death” (Prov. 11). He calls the day of vengeance the time when, at the end, God will hand over those who despise him to the fires of hell. Accordingly, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0677D] Book III of the *Sentences*, chaps. 59 and 16], what is possessed with great love is lost with grievous sorrow; but we suffer less in losing what we love less in possessing. What, indeed, is more laborious in this life than to burn with earthly desires? Or what is safer here than to desire nothing of this age? Those who love this world are disturbed by its turbulent cares and anxieties [Col. 0678C]; but those who hate it and do not pursue it, enjoying the tranquillity of inward rest, already begin in some manner to possess here the repose of the future peace which they await there.

The third snare is the pride of life. When the devil cannot subdue some righteous person either by the concupiscence of the flesh or by the craving for outward things, he nevertheless strives to strike down every perfection of religious life with the dart of pride. Blessed Augustine testifies to this, saying [Note: [Col. 0677D] Book *On Saving Counsels*, chap. 32]: “The labors of many years—prayers, almsgiving, fasts, and vigils—if they end in pride, are reckoned as nothing before God.” Pride, then, is the first vice, yet it remains the last to be conquered. Hence it is said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Sirach 10).

[Col. 0678D] Now [Note: [Col. 0677D] Our author has excerpted all this from the book *On Saving Counsels*, chaps. 18 and 19, which circulates under Augustine’s name but whose true author is Paulinus of Aquileia, as the Benedictines show in the Appendix, vol. VI, p. 191, Paris edition.], just as humility makes human beings like the holy angels, so pride made demons out of angels. From pride arise heresies and schisms, slanders, envies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, resentments, ambitions, self-exaltations, presumptions, boasting, verbosity, vanity, restlessness, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind, which would take too long to enumerate individually. Covetousness likewise makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunken, greedy, [Col. 0679A] rapacious, sexually immoral, adulterous, violators, incestuous, depraved, and countless others, through which the devil is accustomed to cast down the human race.

Moreover, pride and covetousness, as blessed Augustine says, are so much one evil that pride cannot be found without covetousness, nor covetousness without pride. For every sin is nothing other than contempt for God, by which we despise his commandments; and nothing other than pride persuades a person to this. And, as blessed Augustine clearly shows, it is the beginning, end, and cause of all sins; it is not only sin itself, but no sin could have been, can be, or will be without it.

[Note: [Col. 0679D] Ibid., chap. 13.] These, then, are the things that cast Adam and Eve out of the paradise of delights into this miserable exile: [Col. 0679B] namely, the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition. For unless the love of God had failed in them, they would never have begun to love—indeed, would never even have believed—the counsel of the serpent who gave evil advice. The concupiscence of the flesh was thus fulfilled in them because they tasted of the forbidden tree; the concupiscence of the eyes, because they desired that their eyes should be opened; and worldly ambition, because they believed that they could become what God is. Therefore the Apostle, wishing all of us to beware of these three kinds of vice, which altogether bring the soul to eternal death, said: “Everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and worldly ambition” (1 John 2).

In those two human beings the entire human race was originally condemned, as blessed [Col. 0679C] Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0679D] Ibid., chap. 14]. They would not have eaten of the forbidden tree unless they had desired it; nor would they have desired it unless they had been tempted; nor would they have been tempted unless they had been forsaken; nor would they have been forsaken by God unless they had first forsaken God; nor would they have forsaken God unless they had been proud and culpably neglected the likeness in which they had been made. Therefore they are believed to have died, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, on the day when the necessity of dying was made penal in them.

We have written this, though briefly, concerning the fall and condemnation of the first human beings so that we may escape their exile or punishment [Note: [Col. 0680D] Ibid., chap. 15]. For although we have been born carnally from Adam, we ought not imitate him, but rather our Lord Jesus Christ, in whom we were reborn through baptism and in whom we live spiritually. [Col. 0679D] What is it to imitate Adam except to condemn ourselves to perpetual death through fleshly lusts and desires? And what is it to imitate Christ except to mortify fleshly lusts and desires, and to reign happily with Christ, who redeemed us by his precious blood?

It is therefore fitting, dearest brethren, and greatly necessary for us, that we flee the fall and condemnation of the first human beings, and, mortifying fleshly desires insofar as possible, follow the footsteps of Jesus Christ our Lord. With every spiritual effort let us mortify our members which are upon the earth—that is, fleshly vices—so that we may be able to attain the delights of paradise, from which we were expelled through the fault of the first human being [Col. 0680A]. At every time, and especially in these holy days of fasting, let us hasten to amend through humble repentance and worthy satisfaction not only the crimes or sins we have committed, but also those things we have thought unlawfully. For we shall render an account not only of graver or manifest sins, but also of lighter and hidden offenses.

For, conceived in iniquities and born in sins, we altogether need to be cleansed by contrition and tears from both grave and hidden sins. But who fully understands hidden offenses or sins? No one but God alone, as the Psalmist testifies: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. 7). He searches hearts because he knows what each person thinks [Col. 0680B]. He searches the reins because he knows what delights each one. Even those things which are hidden from us within ourselves are perfectly open to God. Whoever, then, desires in this present life to be cleansed of manifest and hidden sins should, bathed in tears and clinging to his knees, cry out with blessed Job and say: “How many are my iniquities and sins? Show me my crimes and offenses” (Job 13).

This is as though he said openly: “You, God, who know all things, show me my iniquities and sins, my crimes and offenses.” This is the labor of the righteous in this life: to discover themselves and, having discovered themselves, to carry themselves by weeping toward better things. Explaining this, blessed Gregory—whom God endowed with great wisdom [Col. 0680C]—says [Note: [Col. 0680D] Book XI of the *Morals*, chap. 21]:

> “Although John the Apostle declares that there is no difference between iniquity and sin, saying, ‘Iniquity is sin’ (1 John 3), nevertheless ordinary usage gives *iniquity* a stronger force than *sin*. Every person freely confesses himself a sinner, but sometimes is ashamed to call himself iniquitous. Between crimes and offenses there is this difference: a crime exceeds even the weight of sin, whereas an offense does not exceed the weight of sin. For when the Law commands a sacrifice to be offered, it plainly prescribes this both for sin and for offense. A crime is sometimes in an act, whereas an offense is usually in thought alone. Hence the Psalmist says: ‘Who understands offenses?’ (Ps. 18). Sins of deed are recognized more quickly because they are seen outwardly. But sins of thought are more difficult to understand because they are committed invisibly [Col. 0680D]. Thus, if darkness were seen, offenses would be understood. To see is to withdraw from darkness, and to understand is to cease from offense. This is said of those who are in offenses, just as it is said of those who were in darkness. For who understands offenses as they must be understood—that is, so as to avoid them? There are indeed few such people, and none by themselves; hence the saying: ‘No one avoids a vice unless it is known.’ ‘Cleanse me from my hidden faults,’ he says, ‘and spare your servant from those of others’ (ibid.).”

This is as though he said openly: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults,” that is, from original offenses, which have secretly come down to us from the first parents as though by hereditary right [Col. 0681A]; “and from those of others,” that is, from those which I did not contract from my parents—namely, those which I afterward added—“spare me, your servant,” since you did not spare your freedman, that is, Adam.

Alternatively: sin was hidden when the devil sinned, because through pride he possessed it secretly, as though in his heart and from himself. The sin through which Adam fell was another’s, because he yielded when tempted by the devil, who was an outsider. Alternatively: “Cleanse my heart from my hidden faults,” that is, from evil thoughts; and “spare me from those of others,” that is, from the evil persuasions of others, lest I consent to them. Spare me, your servant, since you did not spare your freedman Adam from another’s persuasion, when he refused to obey your commands, wishing to be free like gods. This could be stated more plainly as follows: “For this reason I ask you to cleanse me from my own [Col. 0681B] offenses and to spare me from those of others: because if they do not rule over me, then I shall be spotless”—that is, free from mortal sin, which defiles body and soul.

> “Therefore, whoever, anxious with the desire for eternal life, wishes to appear pure before the coming Judge examines himself now all the more closely, because he considers that he must then stand free before that terror. Where he is displeased with himself, he asks that it be shown to him, so that by repentance he may punish it in himself; judging himself here, he may become exempt from judgment. But amid these things we must consider how great is the punishment of our pilgrimage, since we have come into such blindness that we do not know ourselves. We commit evils, yet do not promptly detect them, even when committed [Col. 0681C]. For the soul, shut out from the light of truth, finds nothing in itself but darkness, and often extends its foot into the pit of sin without knowing it. It suffers this solely from the blindness of its exile: driven away from the Lord’s illumination, it has lost the ability to see itself, because it did not love the face of its Creator.

> “It follows: ‘Why do you hide your face and reckon me your enemy?’ (Job 13). The human race possessed contemplation of the inward light in paradise; but, pleasing itself, it lost the light of its Creator when it withdrew from him, and fled from his face to the trees of paradise, because after its sin it feared to see him whom it had been accustomed to love. But behold: after sin it came to punishment, and from punishment it returns to love; for it has discovered what the fruit of sin was, and, stirred by punishment, seeks that face which it feared in sin [Col. 0681D], so that it may now flee the gloom of its own blindness and greatly dread the very fact that it does not see its Creator. Moved by this desire, the holy man, in the person of the whole Church, cries with tears: ‘Why do you hide your face and reckon me your enemy?’ If you looked upon me as a friend, you would not deprive me of the light of your vision.

> “Then, following the instability of the human heart, he adds: ‘Do you display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue dry chaff?’ What is man but a leaf, since in paradise he fell from the tree? What is he but a leaf [Col. 0682A], since he is carried away by the wind of temptation and lifted by the gusts of desires? As many temptations as the human mind suffers, so many gusts, as it were, move it. Anger often disturbs it; when anger subsides, foolish joy succeeds. It is reproved by the spurs of lust and inflamed by the heat of avarice, far and wide, to seek earthly things. At one time pride raises it up; at another, disordered fear casts it down to the lowest places. Therefore, because man is lifted and led by the gusts of so many temptations, he is rightly compared to a leaf. Hence Isaiah fittingly says: ‘We have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities have carried us away like the wind’ (Isa. 64). Iniquity carried us away like the wind because, not fixed by any weight of virtue, it lifted us into vain joy.

> “After the leaf, man is also rightly called chaff [Col. 0682B]. He who was a tree at his creation made himself a leaf in temptation; but afterward, in his humiliation, he appeared as chaff. Because he fell from on high, he is a leaf; because through the flesh he was close to the earth, even when he seemed to stand, he is described as chaff. But because he lost the greenness of inward love, he is now dry chaff.

> “Let the holy man, therefore, consider how worthless man is and how exacting God is, and say: ‘Do you display your power against a leaf carried away by the wind, and pursue dry chaff?’ It is as though, lamenting not only himself but the entire human race, given over to such instability and fickleness, he said: ‘Why do you assail with such strictness one whom you know to be so weak in temptation [Col. 0682C]? We shall be wholly unable to bear the sentence of your judgment if you wish to judge us with such exactness. The frailty of the human race will not be able to endure the weight of your strictness if you judge us with such rectitude. If you write bitter charges against us because of original or actual sins, you will immediately consume us. For you justly consume both the innocent and the ungodly. The innocent person is rightly consumed by you because, when his innocence is examined more clearly and compared with your innocence, it is reduced to nothing. The ungodliness of the ungodly is likewise consumed by you because, when it is uncovered and judged by the subtlety of your examination, it is condemned. Therefore, ‘If you observe iniquities, O Lord, who shall endure?’ (Ps. 129). We therefore beseech you, most gracious Creator of the human race [Col. 0682D], to temper the sentence of your judgment through your ineffable mercy.’”

But since we fear the judgment of almighty God, it is necessary, dearest brethren, that, following the counsel of the Apostle Paul, we cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light, so that, once the gloom of night has been expelled and the darkness of ignorance and negligence driven away, we may walk honorably in the day—that is, in Christ—and may perform in the night not the works of night but the works of day, because we are called children of light (Rom. 13). For, as blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0681D] Book *On Saving Counsels*, chap. 59], let not our senses become numb through the pleasure of sleep [Col. 0683A], nor let vain phantasms mock our souls, nor let repose, with our bodies weighed down by the warmth of bedding, incline us toward deep torpor. Rather, by watching, praying, singing psalms, and fasting, let us fight against the devil, our adversary; and, that we may feel the great light of evangelical teaching poured into our hearts, let us perform in this valley of tears not the works of night but those of day.

What ought we to do in the blindness of this night except capture the captor and follow the Liberator? We capture, as it were, the enemy of the human race himself when we overcome his temptations by our conduct. At his coming the Son of God not only captured the captor of the human race, but also gave his servants power to tread upon all demons (Luke 10). Scripture also says elsewhere: “The Lord will quickly crush [Col. 0683B] Satan under your feet” (Rom. 16). Therefore he who is crushed beneath the feet is, as it were, taken captive when defeated.

This author of all wickedness tempted and conquered the first human being; and he presumed to tempt the second, that is, Christ, the Son of God and man, but in tempting him he was defeated and fell before him. The Son of God and of the Virgin, stronger than he and mightier in battle, conquered that strong man armed, who guarded his own court in peace (Luke 11), took him captive, stripped him of his weapons, plundered his goods, and, as we believe, bound him with fiery chains in the depths of hell. Of him blessed John the Evangelist says in the Apocalypse: “After a thousand years,” that is, in the time of Antichrist, “that dragon, who is the devil and Satan, will be released from his prison, and will go out and deceive many nations, namely Gog [Col. 0683C] and Magog” (Rev. 20), when the tribulation will be so great that, if possible, even the elect will be moved (Matt. 24).

But if they are elect, how are they to be led into error? [Note: [Col. 0683D] Isidore, Book I of the *Sentences*, chap. 25.] They will go briefly into wavering error because of the multitude of signs, but they will not be cast down from their steadfastness by the shock of terrors and signs. Gog and Magog are two peoples dwelling in the north, whom he will first deceive and with whom he will conquer others. By Gog, which is interpreted “covered,” we understand all hidden persecutors of the Church; and by Magog, which is interpreted “uncovered,” open persecutors. The number of Gog and Magog is as infinite as the sand of the sea; they are barren and unfruitful in good works.

[Col. 0683D] In the night of this present age, therefore, through Christ’s passion and resurrection we capture the devil, as has been stated above, whenever we resist his many kinds of temptation and renounce evil deeds. The devil is quickly conquered by those strong in Christ’s faith, and his fragile weapons are easily broken. That demons conquered by holy people who live justly and piously no longer have the power to tempt others is written thus in the book of the *Sentences* [Note: [Col. 0683D] II *Sentences*, distinction 6]:

> “It seems that demons who are conquered by holy persons living justly and chastely are deprived of the power of tempting others further.”

Hence Origen the African also says:

> “I think indeed that the saints, resisting these demons—that is, inciting and conquering them—defeat the army of demons and, as it were, kill very many of them, so that it is no longer permitted for that spirit which is conquered by some saint through chaste and modest living to assail another human being again.”

Master Anselm also, a wise and catholic man, maintains this when he answered a disciple who asked such a question:

> “Demons preside over each vice, and under them they have countless attendants who continually entice souls to vices and report human evils to their prince with loud laughter. Yet if one of them, fighting, is conquered by one of the righteous, he is immediately thrust back [Col. 0684B] into the abyss by that person’s guardian angel and is no longer permitted to engage any of the righteous, though another is substituted in his place by the prince of demons. For example, just as a human being conquered by the devil was immediately expelled from paradise, so, whenever a demon is overcome by holy men, he is at once put to shame and confined in Tartarus.”

We have adduced these testimonies from holy and authoritative books, dearest brethren, so that you may understand more readily that, if we live according to Christ’s commandments, we capture in the night of the present life, with Christ as author, the captor—that is, the ancient enemy—as Augustine, the teacher of the churches, says.

What else should we do in this night [Col. 0684C] except uproot from our hearts pride, the root of all evils, and introduce into our minds humility, through which we can be exalted to glory? Through the just consequence of pride the devil fell from heavenly blessedness, and through humility man ascends to heaven. Therefore those who are lifted up by their virtues imitate the devil and fall more grievously because they fall from a height. Hence blessed Isidore, our patron, says [Note: [Col. 0683D] Book II of the *Sentences*, chap. 38]:

> “Just as pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of every virtue. It is first in sin and last in the conflict. For it either casts down the mind through sin at the beginning, or at the very end casts it down from its virtues.”

Blessed Ambrose, held in great reverence in Christ’s Church, also says [Note: [Col. 0683D] Rather, Julianus Pomerius, in Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chap. 3. Paulinus of Aquileia later inserted this statement [Col. 0684D] into Book *On Saving Counsels*, chap. 18, a work attributed in the age of Martin to Ambrose or, rather, Augustine, as we have already said, and from which we believe it was copied here.]:

> “Pride made demons out of angels; humility, however, makes human beings like the holy angels. Pride causes God’s commandments to be despised; humility causes them to be kept.”

Let us therefore embrace profound humility with the greatest zeal, for it advances the faithful to eternal joys [Col. 0684D].

What again should we do in the night of this unstable life except drive away from ourselves the prince of all vices, that is, the devil, and receive the fountain of all goods—God, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who is of such inestimable [Col. 0685A] beauty, such ineffable sweetness, such honeyed delight, and such immense goodness, that all citizens of the heavenly homeland are satisfied from him? He is the fountain and origin of all goods, because in him the foundation of the four elements subsists.

Truly God the Father is the fountain of all goods: before all ages he begot from himself a Son equal to himself, whom he appointed heir of all things, both heavenly and earthly (Heb. 1), pertaining to eternal life. The Son himself also, true and consubstantial with God the Father, is the purest fountain of all goods; he sent to his disciples, grieving at his bodily departure, the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and from himself. Hence he says of himself in the Gospel: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” [Col. 0685B] (John 7). Explaining this, the Evangelist says: “He said this concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in him were to receive” (ibid.).

He, therefore, is an unfailing fountain, because in him persons journeying toward the heavenly homeland are strengthened, and from him the spirits and souls of the righteous are refreshed, while they always see him face to face at the Father’s right hand. Pilgrim human beings taste him according to their measure, lest they fail on the road; angels in their homeland spiritually eat him with full mouth and without weariness. He is food for the journey of those hastening to eternal joys; he is refreshment for those resting in the kingdom of heaven. Through him the faithful advance in good works; without him they can do nothing good. He is the way by which all saints hasten [Col. 0685C] to heaven; the holy angels see him reigning at the Father’s right hand and desire to see him. In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2), and all heavenly orders are sufficiently refreshed from him. In him are all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge (ibid.); he is the pleasantness and sweetness of all who are predestined for eternal blessedness. For he is eternal and without beginning, through whom God the Father created all things from nothing (John 1). Whoever sees the Son of God sees the Father also (John 14), because he has the same divinity as the Father. The Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and the Father and Holy Spirit are in the Son; for there are not three gods, but one true God, in whom we live, move, and are (Acts 17).

[Note: [Col. 0685D] *On Saving Counsels*, chap. 59.] Therefore, sweetest brethren, in the night of this present life, as has already been said, let us drive away from ourselves the prince of all vices, namely the devil, and receive the fountain of all goods—God, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—that we may deserve to be received by him and admitted to his eternal banquet. Let us also call to mind the good things prepared for us by him who calls us to himself daily; and let us receive his sweet yoke (Matt. 11) and his light burden, for he mercifully lifts the weights of our sins. Let us therefore, as has been said above, put away the works of darkness and put on the armor of light (Rom. 13).

But what is putting away the works of darkness except renouncing the pomps of the devil and his angels [Col. 0686A]? And what is it for us to put on the armor of light except to believe in God the omnipotent Father, who is truly the fountain of all goods and enlightens every person coming into this world? (John 1). Therefore, while we have the light, let us believe in the light, so that we may be children of light (John 12). With him, as the Psalmist says, is the fountain of life, and in his light we shall see light (Ps. 35). With God the Father indeed is the fountain of life, namely Christ, who with that same Father and the Holy Spirit is one true God. For he himself says in the Gospel: “Whoever comes to me shall not hunger; and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6). And again: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). And again: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven [Col. 0686B]. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever; and the bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6).

He himself also testifies in the Gospel that he is the true light from the true light, that is, from God the Father. “As long as I am in the world,” he says, “I am the light of the world” (John 9). Elsewhere: “Whoever follows me does not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8). Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is fountain from fountain, God from God, true light from true light. He came to us in the flesh in order to moisten our parched hearts and water our thirsty throats with the dew of spiritual teaching. He who watered the thirsty will satisfy those who hope in him, because he is the fountain, and in his light we shall see light.

In this homeland a fountain is one thing and light another. But in Christ, what is fountain is also light [Col. 0686C]. He is the living fountain from which those who hunger and thirst for righteousness are satisfied (Matt. 5). He is also the true light illuminating the holy Church. From himself he enlightens those who believe in him, and he refreshes those who reach him. Therefore, because he is light, let us tirelessly raise the eyes of our hearts to him; and because he is an unfailing fountain, let us unceasingly desire to be satisfied from him in eternal blessedness.

Therefore, dearest brethren, as has been said above, in the night of this pilgrimage it is fitting that we thirst with the greatest longing for the fountain of life, namely Christ; that we cast off the works of darkness, put on the armor of righteousness, and perform in the night not works of night but works of day. First, however, sweetest brethren [Col. 0686D], if you please—indeed, because it pleases us—let us examine and diligently investigate who or what the devil is, and what injury he has brought upon us.

The devil is an angel separated from God through pride. He did not stand in truth, but as soon as he swelled up against God, he fell irrecoverably. He is both father and teacher of falsehood, because falsehood was first devised by him, and he himself is falsehood, as the most truthful Truth, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, testifies in the Gospel of John, saying: “The devil was a liar from the beginning, and a murderer, and did not stand in truth” (John 8). Therefore he is the head and culmination of falsehood; deceived by himself, he hastens by every means to deceive us.

He is the adversary of the human race [Col. 0687A], the inventor of death, the founder of pride, the root of evil, the head of crimes, the prince of all vices, and the persuader of shameful pleasures. When he saw that first human being formed by God—the father, as has often been said above, of us all—and saw him made in God’s image, adorned with chastity, governed by temperance, surrounded by charity, and clothed with immortality, he was jealous and envious that an earthly human being had received such blessedness, which he himself, though an angel, is known to have lost through pride. That insatiable murderer immediately stripped us and our parents of goods so great and such as these, and moreover expelled us from the joys of paradise.

For at the outset the devil robbed us of many goods: chastity [Col. 0687B], self-control, patience, gentleness, charity, and immortality. He thus made us wretched and naked, mocked us as clothed in his rags—that is, vices—subjected us to his cruel dominion, and bound the entire human race to himself in the chain of his deadly persuasion. He stripped us of chastity and girded us with unchastity; he stripped us of temperance and made us intemperate. He stripped us of charity and clothed us with malice; he stripped us of immortality and offered us death. He wrapped us and our descendants in these most shameful and wretched rags and left us half alive, when he inflicted mortal wounds upon our minds.

That first parent of ours, besides the other miseries of human frailty which he justly incurred because of the sin of transgression, also incurred the punishment of corruption and a diminution of free choice. [Note: [Col. 0687D] *Sentences*, II, dist. 25, “Unde.”] For through that sin the natural goods in man were corrupted, and the gratuitous goods taken away. This is the man who, going down to Jerusalem, was wounded and stripped by robbers (Luke 10). He was wounded, indeed, as blessed Augustine says, in his natural goods, of which he was not deprived—for otherwise restoration could not take place—but stripped of the gratuitous goods which grace had added to the natural ones. These are the good gifts and perfect presents: some of them, as has been said, namely the natural goods—intellect, memory, reason, intelligence, freedom of choice—were corrupted by sin; others, namely the gratuitous goods—good will, justice, faith, hope, charity, and the remaining virtues—were removed. They are called gratuitous because they are granted to us through divine grace.

Therefore freedom of choice was in part corrupted through sin and in part lost. Hence blessed Augustine says: “By making bad use of free choice, man lost both himself and it.” For when he sinned by free choice, free choice was lost through the victory of sin. “For whoever has been conquered by someone is also enslaved to him.” He says that man lost free choice, not because after sin he did not possess free choice, but because he lost the liberty of choice—not every liberty, indeed, but freedom from misery and from sin. [Col. 0688A] There are, then, three kinds of liberty: freedom from necessity, from sin, and from misery.

Freedom from necessity could no more be compelled then than it can now. Therefore the will is deservedly judged before God, since it is always free from necessity and can never be forced. Where necessity is, there is no liberty; and where there is no liberty, neither is there will, and thus neither merit. This liberty belongs to all alike, both good and evil.

There is another liberty, namely freedom from sin, of which the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3); and of which Truth says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8). This liberty frees from the slavery of sin and makes people servants of righteousness; just as, conversely, the slavery of sin [Col. 0688B] makes people free from righteousness. Hence the Apostle: “Having been freed from sin, you became servants of righteousness” (Rom. 6). And again: “When you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness” (ibid.). Man therefore lost this liberty by sinning, as blessed Augustine says above: “By making bad use of free choice, man lost both himself and it,” because through sin liberty was lost—not freedom from necessity, but freedom from sin. “Whoever commits sin is a servant of sin” (John 8).

Hence blessed Augustine says: “Only those whom the Son frees and restores through grace possess this liberty, which is freedom from sin; not, however, in such a way that they are altogether without sin in this mortal flesh, but so that sin does not rule or reign in them.” This, therefore, is the good and true liberty which produces a good servitude, namely service to righteousness.

[Col. 0688C] Again, there is freedom from misery, of which the Apostle says: “Creation itself also will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. 8). [Note: [Col. 0688D] The Master, ibid., “Est iterum.”] Man possessed this liberty before sin, because he was free from every misery and touched by no affliction; and he will possess it more fully in the blessedness to come, where he cannot be miserable, either in body or in soul. In this life, certainly, which lies between the first sin and final confirmation, no one is free from misery, because no one is without sin’s punishment.

From what has already been said it is clear in what respect free choice was diminished or corrupted by sin: before sin, man had no difficulty or obstacle, arising from the law in his members, in doing good; no impulse or incitement to evil. Now, however, through the law of the flesh he is hindered from good and incited to evil, so that he cannot will and accomplish good unless he is freed and helped by grace; for, as the Apostle says, “Sin dwells in the flesh” (Rom. 7). Thus the first man—and indeed the whole human race—was wounded in its natural goods and stripped of gratuitous and excellent gifts.

Blessed Job, whose name is interpreted “sorrowing,” lamented these wounds of the whole human race when he said: “He surrounded me with his spears; he wounded my loins together; he did not spare and poured out my inward parts upon the ground” (Job 16). In this passage blessed Job laments not only his own wounds of temptation, [Col. 0689A] but also those of the Church’s members; therefore these words must be understood spiritually, not carnally. Thus, as blessed Gregory explains, [Note: [Col. 0689D] *Morals*, Book XIII, ch. 6] holy Church is surrounded by the spears of the ancient enemy when, in her members, she is assailed by the darts of temptation from that same cunning assailant.

We are rightly said to be surrounded by spears because the ancient enemy attacks us on every side with the wounds of temptation. Often, when gluttony is restrained in order that lust may be subdued, the sting of vain glory strikes the mind. But if the body is not worn down by the affliction of abstinence, he kindles flames of lust against the mind. Often, while we strive to preserve frugality, we fall into stinginess. And often, while we distribute our possessions lavishly, we are led into avarice, because we seek again to gather what we may give away. Therefore, since the darts of the ancient enemy assail us everywhere, it is rightly said: “He surrounded me with his spears.”

And since every sin is suggested by the cunning enemy, but committed by our consenting to his suggestions, it is fittingly added: “He wounded my loins together.” For lust is in the loins. Thus one who desired to drive the pleasure of lust from the heart, or extinguish it, preached to his disciples, saying: “Gird up the loins of your mind in chastity” (1 Pet. 1). When, therefore, the ancient enemy draws the faithful people into lust, he undoubtedly strikes man in the loins. It should also be noted that he did not say, “He wounded,” but, “He wounded my loins together.” Just as *to speak* may at times be the act of one person, [Col. 0689C] while *to converse* is that of two, or perhaps many, so the ancient enemy, because he does not drag us into guilt without our will, is said not to wound our loins but to wound them together with us. For what he wickedly suggests to us, we ourselves, following him of our own will, carry out; and thus we wound ourselves, as it were, together with him, because we are jointly led by free choice to commit evil.

“He did not spare,” he says—as though he meant: “He did not cease.” “And he poured out my inward parts upon the ground.” What else should we understand by the inward parts of holy Church but the minds of those who contain within themselves certain of her mysteries and serve the innermost sacraments? But when the ancient adversary draws certain faithful persons, who seemed to serve the interior sacraments, into secular business, he undoubtedly pours their inward parts [Col. 0689D] upon the ground, because he tramples into the lowest things those who had formerly been engaged in hidden and spiritual works.

It follows: “He cut me down with wound upon wound.” In her weak members holy Church is cut down with wound upon wound when sin is added to sin, so that guilt is more violently aggravated. For whom avarice draws into robbery, robbery leads into deceit, so that the committed offense may also be defended by falsehood: what is such a person but one cut down with wound upon wound? Hence it is also well said through the prophet: “Cursing and lying, murder and theft and adultery have overflowed, and blood has touched blood” [Col. 0690A] (Hos. 4). Sin is customarily signified by the name “blood.” Thus one who desires to be freed from sins cries through repentance: “Deliver me from bloodguilt.” Blood therefore touches blood when one offense heaps up another.

And because, when wound is added to wound, the forces of the ancient enemy grow mightily against us, it is rightly added: “He rushed upon me like a giant.” An enemy is easily resisted if he is not consented to, whether in many falls or for a long time even in one. But if the soul has become accustomed to submit to his suggestions, the more frequently it subjects itself to him, the more unbearable it makes him to itself, so that it cannot resist him; for the malicious adversary fights against a person overcome through corrupt habit as though with the strength of a giant.

Yet holy Church often calls the minds of the faithful back to repentance even after sins have been committed, and cleanses the sins of action by the virtue of voluntary affliction. Hence it is well added: “I sewed sackcloth over my skin, and covered my flesh with ashes.” What should be understood by sackcloth and ashes but repentance? What by skin and flesh but sin of the flesh? Therefore, when some return to repentance after a fall of the flesh, sackcloth is, as it were, sewn over the skin. And the flesh is covered with ashes, because the guilt of the flesh is covered through repentance, lest it come to punishment in the examination of the strict Judge.

Thus Adam—and in him the whole human race—was wounded by robbers, namely the ancient enemy and his satellites, and stripped, as stated above, of natural goods and gratuitous gifts, because he obeyed that enemy’s wicked suggestions more than the saving commands of the Creator. Departing from Jerusalem, that is, from the vision of heavenly peace, and going down to Jericho, that is, inwardly becoming proud and falling away from the love of God, he entered this mortal life and fell among robbers: he encountered the devil and his angels, hostile to him. Having inflicted wounds upon him, stripped him of virtues, and left him half-dead, they departed, having corrupted his mind by tempting it with the allurements of this world.

Moreover, it should be known that there are two kinds of temptation: interior and exterior. [Note: [Col. 0690D] *Sentences*, II, dist. 21.] Exterior temptation occurs when evil is visibly suggested from without by a word or some sign, so that the person to whom it is made may incline to consent to sin; and such temptation comes from [Col. 0690D] the adversary. Interior temptation occurs when evil is invisibly suggested within us; this temptation sometimes comes from the enemy and sometimes from the flesh. For the devil invisibly suggests evils, and from the corruption of the flesh an unlawful motion arises and a perverse titillation is born. Therefore the temptation arising from the flesh is not without sin; but the temptation of the ancient enemy, unless consent is given to it, is not sin, but material for the exercise of virtue.

The interior temptation of the flesh is more difficult to conquer, because the inward assailant is strengthened from what is our own against us. Therefore man, who fell when assailed by exterior temptation alone, deserved punishment all the more severe because he had been overthrown by a lighter impulse. Yet because he had some, though slight, occasion for falling, he could through God’s grace receive help toward pardon, so that he might be raised by another, having fallen through another. Thus one who had an instigator to evil rightly had a restorer to good. But the devil, because he sinned without anyone’s temptation, ought not to be helped by another, nor could he help himself; therefore his sin was incurable. Human sin, however, just as it had its beginning through another, so also fittingly had its remedy through another.

Therefore angelic nature, since it had not wholly perished but had endured in part, was not redeemed [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 0691D] “Here is lacking: ‘but human nature had wholly perished, and therefore, lest it perish altogether, it was redeemed in part, so that [Col. 0692D] thereby, etc.’”] Thus the angelic ruin might thereby be made good. Hence blessed Augustine says: “It pleased the Creator and Redeemer of the universe that, since the multitude of angels which had perished by forsaking God had not wholly perished, that part which had perished should remain in everlasting perdition; while that which had remained with God when the other forsook him should forever rejoice, with full certainty, in its known fidelity. Should not rational creation, which had perished wholly—for it had perished wholly in sins and punishments—be restored in part, so that what that fall had diminished might be supplied to the angelic fellowship?” For this is promised to the saints: that “they shall be equal to the angels of God in heaven” (Luke 20).

Furthermore, it should be noted that man would not have been so easily cast down from the state of uprightness unless some pride requiring repression had first preceded in him, so that through the humility brought by sin he might learn how falsely he had presumed concerning himself, and that nature is not well when it departs from its Creator. For angelic or human nature, as soon as it departed from its Maker, was ill, because it came to deformity: that is, it lost the dignity in which it had been created. In one fall of pride, while they set themselves beside God in arrogance, both the angel fell and man lost the delights of paradise. [Note: [Col. 0692D] Isidore, *Sentences*, Book I, ch. 10.] But man, returning to repentance, recognizes that he is inferior to God; whereas the devil, not content merely with having fallen by judging himself God’s equal, even declares himself superior to God, according to the Apostle’s statement, who says of him under the person of Antichrist: “He opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshipped” (2 Thess. 2).

Thus man, wounded by robbers, half-dead, and stripped of virtues, is left on the road of this wretched [Col. 0691D] life, and for five thousand years receives the comfort of no one. He tasted the forbidden food and heard from God: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3). He turned his eyes from the brightness of God’s majesty and fell into the darkness of this world. The wretch despised the delights of paradise, and his field brings forth thorns and briars instead of grain. The robbers took from him the robe of immortality and honor, and he was clothed with the skin-garment of mortality and weakness. And because he proudly wished to be like God, he became mortal and weak. After sin he knew himself to be naked, that is, stripped of virtues. Set in paradise, he despised the divine commands; cast out of paradise, his posterity worshipped idols. He despised God his Maker and fell into an abyss of evils, so far that he even rendered service to demons.

Appropriately, he lies wounded by robbers not on the road but outside the road, because he is far from God. He would not lie outside the road, but would indeed stand on the road, if in sinning he had not departed from God. He is left half-dead because, having lost the gratuitous gifts, he is wounded in natural goods. He lay half-dead because, when he presumed to eat the forbidden fruit, he condemned himself to death in accordance with the Lord’s sentence; and in that one sin he committed six capital sins, by which he involved the six ages of his posterity in death.

His first sin was pride, when he desired to be [Col. 0692B] equal with God; and therefore he was made weaker in all respects, though he had been set over all creatures under heaven. Hence Scripture says: “Everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God” (Prov. 16). The second was disobedience, because he had formerly been subject. Concerning it Samuel the prophet says: “To rebel is like the sin of divination, and to refuse obedience is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). The third was avarice, when he coveted more than had been granted to him, and therefore justly lost all that had been granted. Hence the Apostle, admonishing certain disciples, says among other things: “Put to death your members which are on earth: namely, evil desire and avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3). The fourth was sacrilege, when he stealthily took what was forbidden in a sacred place, as though by theft; and therefore he deserved to be excluded from the sanctuary. Of this it is said: “Whoever profanes holy things shall be banished from holy things.” The fifth was spiritual fornication: for his soul was joined to God, but when, having rejected God, he admitted the devil, he committed adultery, as it were, with a stranger, and therefore lost the friendship of the true bridegroom. Of this spiritual fornication the Psalmist speaks to God, saying: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72). The sixth was homicide: namely, he consigned himself to death in accordance with the Lord’s sentence: “On whatever day you eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall die the death” (Gen. 2). And Scripture says of this: “Whoever kills procures eternal death for himself.”

[Col. 0692D] Thus the inner man immediately died and lay buried in the tomb of the body. Truly, then, that wretched man was wounded and stripped by robbers and left half-dead when he was deceived by the most wicked and deceitful spirit. Let the Samaritan therefore approach: the guardian of the human race, the wisest physician of the sick, the most compassionate comforter of the sorrowing, the most merciful restorer of the fallen, the most diligent seeker of lost sheep, the strongest defender of those who flee to him—the Son of God, sent by God the Father for the redemption of humankind—and say: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3).

As soon as Adam sinned in paradise, the most gracious Creator and most merciful Restorer began to seek him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” He sought us, not because we loved him, but because he first loved us (1 John 4) and gave himself up for us (Eph. 5). The almighty Creator, gracious and merciful, long cried in paradise, “Adam, where are you?” Yet he did not receive from him the answer he desired, because Adam attempted to turn the blame back upon the Creator; and therefore he fell into the wretched exile of this world. He despised the most truthful words of the Creator and believed the most deceitful words of the most cruel enemy. He rejected the Creator and encountered the robber.

At last Adam—that is, the human race—half-dead and stripped, cries from the depths to the Lord for five thousand years, that he may be delivered from the harshest oppressions of the ancient enemy. Therefore, through long ages, sending forth from his inmost breast most bitter sighs mingled with tears, he prays to the Creator of heaven and earth, saying: [Note: [Col. 0693D] These are the fourth and sixth antiphons of the seven major antiphons at the *Magnificat* before the Nativity of the Lord, which, as Clichtoveus says, the whole human race pours out to the Son of God, continually pressing him with entreaties that he, so long awaited, may at last after such delay come into the world and by his visitation free human nature from captivity to the devil, the prison of sin, and the darkness of errors.]

“O King of the nations, and their desire, and cornerstone, who make both one: come, save the human being whom you formed from clay!” And again: “O Key of David and scepter of the house of Israel, who open and no one shuts, who shut and no one opens: come, and bring out the captive from the prison-house, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.” [Note: [Col. 0694D] *Book on Saving Teachings*, ch. 57.]

Adam also, wounded and half-dead—that is, the human race confessing its sin—humbly entreats God through the Prophet for deliverance from the most cruel dominion of the ancient enemy, saying: “I have wandered like a lost sheep; seek your servant, O Lord” [Col. 0693C] (Ps. 118). And again: “Save me from the mouth of the lion and from the horns of the unicorns” (Ps. 21). And again: “Refuge has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Ps. 141). “I look to the left, and behold, the devil howls like a wolf, gnashes like a lion, and, on the other side, barks like a dog. I cry to you, O Lord: You are my hope, you are my portion in the land of the living” (ibid.). “Hear, O Lord, my prayers, and bring me out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth” (Ps. 39).

The prophet Isaiah awaited with supreme longing the time of human redemption; bathed in tears, he said to God: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down” (Isa. 64), namely, to free the nations. And again: “I beseech you, Lord, send whom you are going to send” (Exod. 4), etc. Therefore, for the deliverance of this sheep the holy fathers of the Old Testament—namely the patriarchs and prophets—cried to the Lord, saying: “Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45). And again: “O Creator of heaven and earth, we pray that you fulfill the office of the supreme Shepherd, and that the hundredth sheep of your flock may not perish.” [Note: [Col. 0694D] Ibid., ch. 58.] “Pursue the lion, namely the ancient enemy, who has seized your sheep. Let the lion be crushed, and let the sheep be snatched from his jaws. And now, O Lord our God, our Creator, our Father, long has your sheep been carried away over diverse precipices, [Col. 0694A] and why, most merciful Father, do you not redeem it? Stir up your power and come, that you may deliver it from the hand of the enemy. O Lord, while you are so powerful to free it, why do you remain silent so long?”

To this the Lord says through the prophet: “I have been silent, I have been silent; but I shall not always remain silent, for my hand increases judgment” (Isa. 42). Let the Creator therefore mercifully approach the creature, the Maker his work, God the human being, the Samaritan the wounded man, the physician the sick man, grace the wretched man, and pour oil and wine into his wounds.

Let the Samaritan, therefore—that is, the Son of God—make his journey: let him descend from heaven into this world, sent by God the Father; and, mercifully drawing near to the wounded man by assuming human nature, [Col. 0694B] let him provide care for his salvation. Through the Incarnation, let him become akin to the half-dead man, while in divinity he remains by nature co-eternal with God the Father. Let him see the stripped and infirm man and, moved with compassion, bestow upon him the antidote of reconciliation. Let the Son of God graciously descend from the Father’s bosom, unite himself—that is, join humanity to his divinity—and offer the medicine of his death, so that he may be not only one who reveals the wound but also its healer.

This Samaritan, namely the Son of God, is rightly interpreted “guardian,” for he is sent by God the Father into this world to guard and govern together the flock of all the faithful. The Prophet humbly implored this Samaritan when, fearing that he might fall among these robbers, he said: “Guard me from the snare which they have laid for me, and from the stumbling-blocks of those who work iniquity” (Ps. 140). And again: “They stretched cords into a snare; beside the road they set a stumbling-block for me” (Ps. 139). For the devil and his satellites prepared a snare beside the road, into which Adam and his descendants miserably fell.

Therefore let our Samaritan, descending by compassion along the same road, namely that of this present life, draw near; and, pouring in oil and wine, bind up his wounds, not refusing to assume in every respect the sacraments of our salvation. Although he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth, yet, in order to wash us from original sins, let him humbly hasten to baptism. In order to teach us to conquer the devil’s temptations, let him not refuse to be tempted by the devil. In order to teach his Church to fast, let him complete a fast of forty days. In order to show that he assumed true flesh from the Virgin, let him afterward hunger; and in order to prove that he possesses by nature from God the Father the substance of divinity, let him powerfully and wisely conquer his tempter, the devil. Let him graciously approach the Passion, bear our sins in his body upon the wood, and, in order to deliver us from the power of the ancient enemy, rise from the dead on the third day.

To this the Son of God says: “Sent by God the Father, [Col. 0695A] I come from heaven into this world. For what purpose? Namely, to break the yoke of human captivity and bind the wounds of the transgressor Adam. Behold, I graciously come to baptism for the salvation of humanity, though I am subject to no guilt of any sin. I willingly allow the Holy Spirit to lead me to the high mountain, and, when tempted, I shall rightly conquer the ancient enemy, who enviously expelled the first man from paradise. Therefore I patiently permit the tempter to approach me, so that all who believe in me may learn to overcome the temptations of that same ancient enemy. Moreover, to instruct my bride, namely holy Church, I shall myself complete the fast of forty days. But because I possess one substance of divinity by nature with the Father, I remain forty days without bodily food; and again, because I drew the natural substance of flesh from my Virgin Mother, I afterward hunger. I also mercifully and willingly approach the Passion, so that I may redeem the human being whom I created from nothing with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Behold, I hang between two robbers in the middle upon the cross, and, pitying wretched and wounded Adam, again cry: ‘Adam, where are you?’”

To this Dismas, the robber hanging at Christ’s right hand, recognizing that he was the Son of God and had descended from the Father’s bosom for humanity’s salvation, replied with tears, as though in Adam’s person, saying: “Lord, I am on the cross, and indeed I receive things deserved according to my merits. I do not excuse myself; I have deserved what I endure; I suffer by a just judgment. I seek mercy: ‘Remember me when you come into your kingdom’” (Luke 23).

As though the robber, in Adam’s person, were praying to Jesus Christ our Redeemer hanging on the cross, saying: “O most merciful Shepherd, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit formed me from the clay of the earth, I beseech you, grant pardon to me, a sinner, and make me attain with you the delights of paradise which I lost long ago through the devil’s envy. I know clearly that you came to lay down your life upon the cross for your sheep; therefore I pray that you make me attain the beauty of paradise. I confess that contrary to your decree I tasted the forbidden food; but, cast out of paradise, I experienced many evils. [Note: [Col. 0695D] “Many evils.”] I put the fruit to my mouth against your will, and therefore in this exile of the world I endured many [Col. 0695D] adversities. I was disobedient to you, God, Creator of all things, and obeyed the death-dealing suggestions of the devil; therefore I bore his most grievous yoke through many ages. I abandoned you, God, my most compassionate Father, and clung to the most cruel tyrant. Because I despised your most saving command, I eat my bread in the sweat of my face. You justly cursed the earth for the works of my hands, and therefore it brings forth thorns and briars for me. I sinned grievously; I sinned unhappily; I sinned wretchedly. I lay my sins open before you, confess my crimes, declare my offenses. Therefore I beseech you, my God: do not forget me to the end, do not abandon me forever, do not leave me any longer in the power of demons unto destruction. Although I have sinned grievously against you, nevertheless you are compassionate, you are merciful, you are abundant in pity. Show your mercy in me. Let pardon be open to me; let forgiveness also be open. I do not excuse myself, as I did before in paradise. I do not defend my crimes, vindicate my sins, or conceal my offenses. The evil I have done displeases me. Receive, I pray, the voice of one confessing; attend to the voice of one praying; hear the voice of a sinner crying aloud. Do not abandon me forever, O Lord, but remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23).

Since, therefore, Dismas the robber hanging on the cross offered Jesus Christ a true confession, as though in Adam’s person, that same most gracious [Col. 0696B] Shepherd did not impose on him a sentence of vengeance, but mercifully restored the homeland of paradise which he had lost by sinning, saying: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (ibid.). As though he said more plainly: “Today, through humble confession, you shall be with me in paradise, from which you fell through obstinate self-excusing. You voluntarily committed sin and wished perversely to turn it back upon me; therefore you did not deserve to remain long in paradise. Because you obeyed the voice of your wife rather than my voice, I cast you out from the beauty of paradise. With great disgrace you were driven from the delights of paradise and, as you say, afflicted by long exiles. You did not turn your face toward me but your back, and fell downward as far as hell. Pitying [Col. 0696C] your miseries, therefore, I descended to free you from infernal punishments. Greatly compassionate toward your calamities, I came down to earth to restore you to your former rank. I shall also give you the first robe, namely that of immortality, which you lost through the guilt of transgression.” [Note: [Col. 0695D] *Prayer of the Church.*] “For through the gift of grace you shall receive a greater happiness than you lost through the desire of vain glory. By the price of my blood I redeem you from the devil’s slavery and restore you to liberty. For this purpose I permit my body to be suspended upon the cross: that I may bring you to the fellowship of the citizens above.”

As though Adam, in the person of the whole Church, replied to Jesus Christ the Son of God hanging upon the cross, saying [Note: [Col. 0696D] From the hymn for the Ascension of the Lord at Vespers.]:

> O most gracious Shepherd! O most merciful  
> > Redeemer!
>
> What mercy overcame you,
>
> That you should bear our crimes,
>
> Suffering a cruel death,
>
> To raise us up from death?

What compassion overcame you, that you should descend from the Father’s bosom to earth to wash away the stains of our crimes? For your goodness compelled you, mercifully pouring out your own blood upon the cross, to deliver us from eternal condemnation. Your perfect charity also compelled you so greatly that you not only redeemed us from the devil’s power, but, placing us upon your shoulders, carried us back to the flock of the heavenly sheep. [Col. 0697A] We have never done any good whatever by which we might deserve to share in such blessedness; but your greatest kindness did not restrain its mercies in its wrath.

Consider, dearest brothers, God’s ineffable mercy toward human misery. When God approaches the human being and the human being confesses sins to him, the mercy of the approaching God and the truth of the confessing human being meet one another. And because mercy finds the truth of righteousness, no place is left for accusation. Rather, while righteousness consents and peace itself gives a kiss, reconciliation takes place between the merciful God and wretched man through mercy’s working and justice’s permission, when the Son of God immediately and mercifully says to the robber: “Today you shall be with me in paradise.”

[Col. 0697B] Therefore, sweetest brothers, let us give thanks to God the Father, to his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Holy Spirit, because indeed, as the Apostle says, “our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin” (Rom. 6). For all flesh upon earth had corrupted its way (Gen. 6); and therefore the Son of God graciously ascended the cross in order to crucify it in himself. He also drew incorrupt flesh from the Virgin, through which he might deliver us from the corruption of the flesh. For flesh had corrupted the entire world and sold it to the devil for a trifling price, namely the fruit of a single tree. Although flesh was a maidservant, it nevertheless compelled its mistress—that is, the soul—to serve it. Of this the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5), etc.

From the first man Adam until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, flesh had corrupted all people so thoroughly that scarcely anyone could resist its will. Hence the Apostle, in the person of the old man, said: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7). It has five ministers, by whom it enslaved both itself and its mistress, namely the soul, and subjected the whole world to the devil’s dominion. For when anyone, abandoning righteousness, sins—whether delighted by eating, deceived by seeing, drawn by hearing, enticed by smelling unlawful things, or committing evils with the hands—he is led captive by these five ministers. [Col. 0697D] Hence it is said: “Whoever commits sin is the servant of sin” (John 8).

By these five ministers, that is, the five bodily senses, flesh, as has already been said, overcame human beings; and man, though placed in paradise, succumbed. But it first attacked the woman, as the weaker part. In this way the woman sinned through the five bodily senses. With her ears she received and consented to the devil’s persuasion, when he suggested such things, saying: “On whatever day you eat of it, your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3). You have heard, dearest brothers, how the woman succumbed through hearing; now observe how she was deceived by smell and sight. For Scripture says: “The woman saw that the tree was good and pleasant for eating, beautiful to the eyes [Col. 0698A] and delightful in appearance.” When it says “pleasant,” she was captured by smell; when it says “beautiful to the eyes,” she was ensnared by sight.

Two ministers remain, who perpetrated the entire crime: namely touch and taste. Thus through those five ministers, that is, the five bodily senses, flesh wickedly completed what it had unlawfully begun. For Scripture says: “The woman took of its fruit and ate.” The hand took; the mouth ate; touch ministered; taste completed the sin. Therefore, when the origin of all human beings had been cast down and wounded, those ministers, namely the bodily senses, thereafter subjected the whole world to themselves. Seeing, then, that flesh was conquering the whole world and that the maidservant had subjected her mistress, namely the soul, to herself, almighty God the Father sent his most beloved Son, who would free the whole world from this captivity.

Accordingly, Abraham’s victory over the five kings prefigured this: aided by divine help, that father of faith overcame them, because our faith has been so strengthened in the governing Spirit that it may subject the same number of senses in our body to the word of God. For just as he proved victorious over kings on behalf of his neighbour, so faith triumphs over the human being on behalf of the soul. And the fact that he defeated the opposing princes not with a multitude of soldiers nor with the strength of legions, but with only three hundred and eighteen companions, signified that Christ’s Passion was to free us from the dominion of the five carnal senses, which had previously overcome us by holding us captive through various vices [Col. 0698C]. Therefore, whoever subjects the five bodily senses to reason conquers, as it were, five kings.

The Son of God therefore put on our hostile flesh without sin, in order to fight with it and restrain it, and to weaken its servants—the five senses—that thereafter they might be able to resist it, that is, the flesh, and govern their mistress, namely their soul. Thus our most valiant warrior chose a fitting punishment, in which he might crucify the enemy—our flesh—and punish and correct our senses for good works. The eyes of the Son of God and of the Virgin, hanging upon the cross, saw the greatness of the punishment and felt the darkness of death. His ears heard the most shameful insults uttered by the Jews. His mouth said, “I thirst” (John 19) [Col. 0698D], and tasted the bitterness of gall and vinegar in recompense for the food of the forbidden tree. His hands were fastened to the cross with nails. Indeed, all the flesh suffered there, so that thereafter it might be wholly subject to us and always obey the will of the soul.

Then was fulfilled what the prophet David, speaking in the person of Christ, said long before: “What I did not take away, then I was paying back” (Ps. 68). He certainly suffered for the sins of the human race, though he had never at all committed any sin. The angel committed robbery by apostatizing from God, when he said: “I will set my seat in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). The first parent committed robbery when he consented to the devil and offered the cup of pride—death—to himself and to his descendants. For he strove to be God and came to be proud. This sin the Son of God and of the Virgin discharged in his flesh—not with an armed hand, but by having that flesh pierced by the wood [Col. 0699A]. Certainly he bore not his own sins but ours in his body upon the wood, so that, dead to sins, we may live to righteousness; “by whose wound we have been healed” (1 Pet. 2). [Note: [Col. 0699D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, ch. 13.]

The devil was thus deceived in the death of the Son of God and man, as a bird is deceived. For Christ displayed the mortality of his flesh, which the malignant enemy desired to destroy, but concealed his divinity as a snare, by which he might entangle him, like an unwary bird, in a wise trap. For unless innocent Christ had been killed, the human being, enslaved to the devil through transgression, would not have been released. While the devil attacked in Christ the flesh of humanity, which lay open to view, he was caught, as it were, by the hook of Christ’s divinity, which was concealed.

In Christ, as blessed Isidore says, the hook is divinity; the bait is flesh; and the line is the genealogy recited from the Gospel (Matt. 1) [Col. 0699B]. God the Father holds this line, of whom the Apostle speaks: “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). Luke too, weaving the line of Christ’s descent upward from the lowest to the highest, begins with Joseph and ends in God, when he says, “who was of Heli”; and, following the line of descent, says, “who was of God” (Luke 3).

Therefore our old man was crucified together with Christ. That is, our flesh was crucified—made weak upon the cross—lest it wage war against the soul, its mistress. He weakened it so that it might not rise proudly against the soul; and he strengthened it so that it might resist sins and vices. He broke its powers so that it might not draw the soul with itself into destruction, and strengthened it [Col. 0699C] so that it might labour diligently in good works.

As has often been said, through the fault of disobedience the first man administered death to all his descendants; but the Son of God and of the Virgin, by the Father’s grace, restored life to them. The first man, departing from God, fell among robbers with all his offspring; the Son of God, coming from the Father’s bosom, mercifully rescued him from them. Descending from Jerusalem through the fault of the first man—that is, departing from heavenly brightness—the human race suffered mortal wounds from robbers on the road of this world; but the Son of God and of the Virgin, hanging upon the cross, became for it the medicine of eternal salvation.

No patriarch and no prophet, however justly and devoutly he lived, however wholly he loved God in his heart, however much he foreknew of God’s future works through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, could nevertheless rescue the human race from the death of perpetual damnation [Col. 0699D]. Not even the law itself, which restrained the Jewish people from evil by the fear of temporal punishment, commanding that eye be restored for eye, tooth for tooth, and loss for loss (Exod. 21), could deliver it. Thus it could in no way have been rescued from eternal destruction unless Jesus Christ, who truly is the salvation of all nations, had been sent by God the Father for the redemption of the world. Concerning him, foreknowing that he would come, the Prophet says: “Our salvation will come quickly, and it will break the yoke of our captivity.”

[Col. 0700A] [Note: [Col. 0700D] Isidore, *Questions on Kings*, IV, ch. 4.] Elisha the prophet, whose name is interpreted “salvation of the Lord,” prefigured this true physician of the human race in his deeds. When he wished to raise the child, he first sent his staff through his servant; because the child did not rise by it, he afterward went to him in person. Elisha’s staff, sent through the servant to raise the dead person, is therefore the Law; yet the dead person did not rise through it. Elisha himself then came after his servant, and, being of perfect age or stature and fully grown, reduced his own size and fitted himself to the dead child. That is, he placed his mouth upon the child’s mouth, his eyes upon the child’s eyes, his hands upon the child’s hands, and his feet upon the child’s feet; and the flesh of the child grew warm (4 Kings 4).

The child yawned seven times and opened his eyes [Col. 0700B]; and thus he who had been dead rose. “All these things,” as the Apostle says, “happened to them as a figure” (1 Cor. 10). Therefore our Elisha, that is, the Son of God, sent through his servant Moses a staff—that is, the Law—to raise the one dead in sins, namely the human race. But because the staff of the Law could not give life to the human race, Elisha himself came, that is, the Son of God; and he reduced his greatness to the littleness of the dead person, because, obeying God the Father in all things—namely, by assuming human nature and being found in appearance as a man (Phil. 2)—he fitted himself to the dead.

“He placed,” it says, “his mouth upon the child’s mouth.” That is, he breathed into it the mysteries of evangelical teaching; “and his eyes upon the child’s eyes,” providing every good thing for it through the affection of compassion [Col. 0700C]; “and his hands upon the child’s hands,” gradually raising it by the hand of mercy from dead works to the knowledge of its Creator; “and his feet upon the child’s feet,” establishing it firmly upon the foundation of his faith; “and he lay upon him”—that is, in the Passion, he redeemed from demonic dominion the one dead in sins by suffering for him; “and the flesh of the child grew warm,” with the fire of divine love; “the child yawned seven times,” that is, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit it devoutly breathed toward good works; “and he opened his eyes,” namely the eyes of the heart, to know the truth, which is God, and to recall the benefits which God had bestowed upon it in his gratuitous goodness. Thus, having fitted himself to the dead person, the dead person rose: that is, the human race rose from perpetual death [Col. 0700D].

In this manner the Son of God rescued the human race from eternal death, raised it to hope of pardon, and stirred it to earn eternal joys.

Therefore our Redeemer, as a merciful and wise physician, compassionately bound the wounds of the human race which had been inflicted on it by robbers. The words of his preaching and the blood of his Passion are healing remedies for the wounds of sins. For he himself, coming from the Father’s bosom for the salvation of humankind, bound the wounds of the human race: he restrained sinners by reproving them, humbled the proud, checked the exalted, forbade idle words, and commanded vain and useless thoughts to be driven from the heart.

He binds up the wounds of sins when he strikes sinners with the terror of punishment but promises hope of pardon to the penitent [Col. 0701A]. He binds wounds when he threatens the torments of hell to those who do evil and exhorts those departing from evil to do good. Did he not restrain the wounds of sins when he proclaimed terribly in the Gospel: “Those who have done good will go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire” (Matt. 25; John 5)?

The Son of God, as a merciful and devout physician, pours oil and wine into the wounds of the human race. When he promises sweet things, he pours in oil; when he commands harsh things, he pours in wine as well. When he preaches pleasant things, he soothes the souls of his hearers; but when he announces grave things, he frightens them. Thus he binds the wounds of sins when he commands: “Repent” [Col. 0701B] (Matt. 3). He pours in oil when he adds: “The kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid.). And again: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10). He also pours in wine when he says: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. 3). And again: “If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it away from you. It is better for you to enter into life”—that is, into the kingdom of heaven—“maimed or lame, than, having two hands or two feet, to be cast into eternal fire” (Matt. 18), where “the worm of the wicked will not die, and the fire will not be extinguished” (Mark 9).

Nor was it sufficient for the Son of God and of the Virgin merely to bind up the wounds of the wounded man. Mercifully placing him upon his own beast, he led him to an inn and, as a devout and wise physician, cared for him [Col. 0701C]. He placed him upon his own beast because, mercifully assuming human nature, he bore our sins in his body upon the wood (1 Pet. 2). Thus our flesh, which he assumed from the incorrupt Virgin, was his beast, in which he deigned to come to us, defeat the ancient enemy, and rescue us from his tyranny.

He compassionately placed us upon his beast and brought us to the inn, because through faith in his Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection he introduced us into the holy Church, and commanded us to live in imitation of himself, saying: “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5).
