And blessed Peter the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps; he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2) [Col. 0701D]. Blessed Paul also exhorts us to live in imitation of God, saying: “Be imitators of God, as most beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour” (Eph. 5).

Therefore he placed us upon his beast: that is, he bore our sins in his body while offering himself, without stain, as a sacrifice to God the Father upon the altar of the cross. He introduced us into the inn—that is, into the Catholic Church—through faith in his Incarnation; commanded us to live according to the rule of evangelical teaching; bound up the wounds—that is, the sins inflicted on us at the devil’s instigation—by restraining them through reproof [Col. 0702A]; and moreover poured in oil and wine, promising the rewards of eternal blessedness to those departing from evil, while striking sinners with terror of Gehenna.

For this reason also he allowed himself to be led by the Holy Spirit into the desert mountain, so that, being tempted, he might overcome the tempter, the devil, and restore to the delightfulness of Paradise the human being whom that same malignant enemy had expelled from Paradise by temptation. The devil conquered the first human being by tempting him; but, daring to tempt the Son of God and of the Virgin, he was conquered and fell. He who gloried in the fall of the first man is put to shame, conquered by the second man. He through whose envy the first man was expelled from the joys of Paradise, being overcome by the Son of God and of the Virgin, is thrust down into the depths of hell.

That very author of all malice, by the same means through which he rejoiced to have made the first human being captive, is conquered by the second man, Christ, and is held captive in the lake of eternal fire [Col. 0702B]. He acted proudly toward the first human being, but the God-man rightly overthrew him. Thus, by the wondrous and merciful dispensation of almighty God, it was brought about that the same malignant enemy should be caught at the very entrance through which he had entered and held us captive, and should depart from our hearts through the mystery of the Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection of Jesus Christ, God and man.

Moreover, it should be known that the Son of God could indeed have cast him headlong into the abyss by a word alone, just as he had previously caused him to fall from heaven; but he chose rather to conquer him by the authority of Scripture alone and rationally rebuke him, saying: “Get behind me, Satan; you shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Matt. 4) [Col. 0702C].

But that most venomous serpent and insatiable murderer from the beginning did not stand in the truth. As soon as he was created, he grew proud against God and wished to be made equal to him; immediately cast out from heaven, he fell. Seeing himself surpass all the orders of angels in glory and beauty, he despised them all and wished to be God’s equal—indeed, his superior. He wished, against God’s will, to seize a better rank than the one God had given him and to rule the other hosts of angels by tyranny. He was therefore driven from the palace and cast into prison. As he had formerly been most beautiful, so afterward he became blackest; and he who had formerly been most splendid became afterward most dark; he who had formerly been praiseworthy in honour became afterward accursed in every horror [Col. 0702D].

Thus he was cast out of heaven, full of pride, envy, anger, and hatred, concerning whom a voice fallen from heaven says in the Apocalypse: “Woe to you, earth and sea, because the devil has come down to you in great wrath, knowing that he has but a short time” (Rev. 12). This is as if it were said more plainly: Woe—that is, misery, pain, captivity, and damnation—is yours, O earth, namely you who pursue earthly things, and yours, O sea, namely you who are tossed upon this great and wide sea, in which are creeping things without number (Ps. 103). For the devil has come down to you—that is, to your harm—with great anger at the loss of heavenly happiness or dignity, knowing that he has but a short time: that is, that he will be allowed to exercise this power of tempting only for a little while [Col. 0703A], and afterward will shortly be thrust down into hell.

That malignant enemy, then, not only wished in heaven, despising all the angelic powers, to make himself equal to God, the Creator of all things; he also dared to tempt the Son of God and man in the desert. Because he wished to become like the Most High in heaven, he was cast down to earth; and again, because he tempted the Son of God in the desert, he fell into the depths of hell. [Note: [Col. 0703D] *Sentences* II, distinction 6, “On Lucifer.”] Some think that, from the time he tempted Christ, he has been held bound in hell. They say that this is the one who also tempted and conquered the first human being, and who held the rulership of this world for five thousand years, that is, until the coming of Christ. Hence we read in the Gospel that the Lord said: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” [Col. 0703B] (John 12).

It follows: “Then the devil left him; and behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4). Without doubt, the devil left God because, created in heaven, he preferred through pride to depart from him rather than cling to him through love. He despised eternally beholding the most brilliant light of God’s countenance and fell into the gloom of this world. He was unwilling to lead the blessed life in heaven with the holy angels, and therefore did not deserve to remain there longer. He would not happily contemplate the face of his Creator, and so miserably suffers the darkness of this world. Created in heaven, he immediately swelled with pride and turned himself from the light of truth. He hated light and incurred darkness.

Therefore, unwilling in heaven to be subject to God, he departed from him, conquered and confounded, when he dared in the desert to tempt the Son of God and man [Col. 0703C]. The devil thus left his Creator; and, as his sins deserved, he was left by him and delivered forever to eternal fire. He was separated from God and divided against himself; therefore his dominion will not stand. For, as the Lord says to blessed Job, he is “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41), with whom he is to be cast into the lake of fire and sulphur, Gehenna (Rev. 20), as John the Evangelist also says in his Apocalypse. “When he is lifted up,” namely on the day of judgment, “the angels will fear, and being terrified they will be purified.”

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Maximus of Turin, Homily 2, *On the Fast of Lent*, near the end.] It was therefore necessary that the malignant spirit should depart from tempting him in whom he could not find even a trace of his own wicked will [Col. 0703D]. The very author of all malice marvelled, after so many ages—namely, near the end of the world—that he had found a man possessing none of the desires of human frailty. He saw a man born in the flesh who had absolutely no defect of carnal corruption. For he had taken the natural substance of flesh from a Virgin, but was wholly ignorant of the vices of the flesh. A woman’s childbirth provoked the devil to tempt Christ, but the integrity of the mother terrified him. [Note: [Col. 0703D] The same author, Homily 1.]

The form of a human body persuaded the most cunning enemy to go out to battle [Col. 0704A], but the true Son of God and of the Virgin rightly forced him, defeated, to withdraw. Therefore the hesitant tempter seeks soft and deceptive temptations. For although he beheld in Christ the appearance of a carnal human being, the presence of Christ’s divinity nevertheless stirred him to suspect that he was more than human. The Virgin Mary had indeed borne him, but had not conceived him from male seed. Therefore, when the ancient enemy saw Christ produced by so great a miracle and by so unprecedented a manner, he was, I think, silently considering within himself and saying in wonder:

> Who is this who, without my knowing it, has entered this world apart from the natural manner of birth? I see his mother, but I do not know his father on earth. A woman bore him, but she did not conceive him from a mortal man. I marvel, therefore, how a woman could bear him without marital intercourse. I behold a real human being, born outside the customary law of birth. Yet though he lacks nothing of human nature, he has no carnal desire. Through all ages it has never been heard that a human being was born from a woman and had no defect. From the beginning of the world no one born of a woman has lived without sin or been able to rescue his own soul from my hand. Who, then, is this who, born from a woman and living among sinners, is found cleansed from every stain of sin? He is begotten from a mortal mother and yet is not defiled by any contagion of sin.

That malignant enemy therefore withdrew, defeated, confounded [Col. 0704C], and uncertain, unable fully to know whether the one he had tempted was God and man or merely a human being. But afterward he knew him more fully when he saw him raising the dead, giving sight to the blind, cleansing lepers, preaching the Gospel to the poor (Matt. 11), and performing the other works worthy of God. Hence our blessed patron Isidore says: [Note: [Col. 0704D] *Sentences*, book I, ch. 14.]

> Although the devil did not know the order of our deliverance, he nevertheless knew that Christ had come into this world for the salvation of humankind; but he did not know that Christ would redeem us by his death, and therefore killed him. For if he had known that Christ would redeem the human race through death, he certainly would not have slain him. That the devils knew that Christ had come for the salvation of the human race is taught by the testimony of the Gospel: when they saw him shining in the sublimity of his powers, they were terrified in recognizing him and said: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Luke 4).

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Maximus of Turin, Homily 2, *On Fasting*, near the end.] Therefore, when that artificer of all deceit had withdrawn, angels came and ministered to him. The services of angels teach us, dearest brothers, how greatly the glorious victory of our Redeemer should be glorified by us. The ministry of the citizens of heaven shows with what reverence the noble triumph of the eternal King ought to be celebrated. The devil marvelled that he had found [Col. 0705A] a man with no contagion of sin; the angels rejoiced that the most cunning tempter had been conquered by the Son of God and man. The devil was unwilling to be defeated in his purpose; the angels rejoiced in the noble triumph of our Redeemer. Satan recoiled in the utmost shame of defeat; and behold, the angels approached with the highest reverence and ministered to that same Son of God and of the Virgin. [Note: [Col. 0705D] Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels.]

What else is shown by this but both natures in one person? Because he is true man, the devil tempts him; [Note: [Col. 0705D] St Leo, Epistle 28 (otherwise 24): “The one whom diabolical cunning tempts as man is served by angelic ministries as God.”] and because he is true God, angels minister to him. As man he is tempted by the devil; as God, ministry is rendered to him by angels. He is truly man, whom the devil dares to tempt; and that same one is truly God [Col. 0705B], from whom the devil departs defeated. When the devil withdraws, the holy angels reverently serve him, because he is indeed the one through whom all the elements subsist. Nor is it surprising that the holy angels joyfully minister to him, since God the Father ineffably begot him from himself before all ages. [Note: [Col. 0705D] Gregory, ibid.]

Let us therefore recognize our nature in him, for unless the devil saw him as a human being, he would not tempt him. Let us venerate his divinity in him, for unless he were God above all things, angels could in no way minister to him. According to the frailty of our assumed humanity, he hungered; but according to the omnipotence of his divinity, he conquered the devil’s temptations. [Note: [Col. 0705D] Maximus of Turin, Homily 4, *On Fasting*, near the end at [Col. 0706D].] But the most valiant champion, who was waging a new war against the tyrant for our life and liberty [Col. 0705C], was neither broken by soft flattery nor moved by the harshest insults; rather, he answered every temptation of the enemy in such a way that the malignant enemy might not discover, in the one same God and man, the mystery of the heavenly sacrament.

Therefore, dearest brothers, following the example of the Lord’s contest and victory and guarding against the devil’s snares, we must take up spiritual arms and manfully prepare ourselves for battle against this same adversary of the human race. [Note: [Col. 0706D] The same author, ibid., at the beginning of the homily.] This contest, which our Lord Jesus Christ undertook with the most cunning tempter, served our salvation. For those whom long ago paternal transgression, through the serpent’s persuasion in Paradise, cast down into death [Col. 0705D], the Lord’s triumph now raised to life. He conquered for us, who deigned to hunger for us. In conquering, he taught us to conquer diabolical temptations.

Therefore, if the elect are tempted, let them not be discouraged on that account, because the adversities they suffer profit them, provided that they are not conquered. [Note: [Col. 0706D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, ch. 5.] God alone must be feared. For even if the ancient enemy desires to tempt God’s servants, he cannot tempt them beyond what the divine will permits [Col. 0706A]. Although unwilling, the devil nevertheless serves the benefit of the saints when, through his temptations, he does not deceive them but rather trains them. For the temptations which that malignant enemy sets in motion for human ruin are sometimes turned by the Son of God, to saving advantage, into the exercise of virtues. And although the devil always desires to bring temptations upon righteous people, he can in no way achieve what he desires unless he receives power from God.

The devil deludes the minds of the reprobate by tempting them with many deceptive appearances of vices. Now he deceives with promises; now he entices with transitory things as though they were necessities. Hence Isidore, the teacher of Spain, says in the second [Note: [Col. 0706D] Rather, the third, as above.] book of the *Sentences*:

> The devices of machinations and the seeds of evil thoughts which the devil pours into human hearts so often entangle the mind, caught on every side, that from whatever direction anyone attempts to escape, he cannot get out without danger; as, for example, if you swear to do something which, if you do it, is sinful, while if you do not do it, you are guilty and perjured. [Note: [Col. 0706D] There: “guilty of perjury.”]

Thus the devil prepares snares on every side until he finds a way by which to deceive us when unwary.

Therefore, sweetest brothers, following the counsel of the blessed Apostle Paul, we must take up the armour of God, by which we may resist the devil and stand perfect in all things (Eph. 6). Seeing a great conflict rise against us, since “they have laid a stumbling block for us beside the way” (Ps. 139), and invisible enemies press round about us, the Apostle exhorts us to take up the armour of God against them [Col. 0706C]. For our enemies are many, and they desire to wound us with countless darts. They are many and most cunning; if they find us without arms, they seize their darts and hurl them more fiercely at us. These enemies are such that it is neither useful to make peace with them nor right to enter into a covenant with them. Of such enemies the Lord commanded the Israelite people: “Beware lest at any time you enter into a covenant with them” (Exod. 23).

To enter into a covenant with invisible enemies is to fulfil their wicked suggestions by living badly and to live in them with delight and perseverance. And what we must lament and grieve: other enemies die, but these invisible enemies always live. They live, I say, not in soul but in malice; not in God but in fraud and deceit; not happily but unhappily. Of them David says: “But my enemies live, and are strengthened against me; and those who hate me unjustly are multiplied” (Ps. 37) [Col. 0706D]. Visible enemies die, and though they have brought us many tribulations, they are checked by their final death; those who afflicted us come to rest and come to an end. But our invisible enemies neither die in this way nor end their malice: they always live, always attack, always assail us. “Often,” David says, “have they attacked me from my youth” (Ps. 128).

Let us therefore hear the Apostle Paul exhorting us all by his preaching to spiritual battle: “Put on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Eph. 6) [Col. 0707A]. Whoever wishes to fight against the devil and overcome his temptations after the example of the Lord should earnestly strive to despise the pleasures of this world and fervently raise devotion in prayer. Let him be girded with spiritual arms and free of earthly desires and occupations. For when, with divine help, we bravely confront the devil’s most cunning temptations, we easily conquer him. But when we are soft and lax in God’s service, that enemy who had already been conquered pursues us again.

Moses prefigured this spiritual battle when he and his servant Joshua fought against the Amalekites [Col. 0707B]. Moses fought by prayers, standing on the summit of the mountain; Joshua and the children of Israel fought on the plain with weapons of war. Moses, with uplifted hands, prayed to God to grant victory to his people; Joshua, armed for battle, fought Amalek, supported by the aid of the children of Israel. Moses prayed with hands raised, and while he did this upon the mountain Joshua fought the enemies in the foremost line of battle. Aaron and Hur supported Moses’ hands from either side; Joshua with his companions struck back the adversaries with all his strength. [Note: [Col. 0707D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 25.]

Moses, holding [Note: [Col. 0707D] Perhaps: “holds … raises.”] the rod and lifting his arms to heaven in the form of a cross, conquers the enemies. Likewise, the devil, seeking to bar the faithful from the way to the heavenly homeland, is overcome by the sign of the Lord’s cross [Col. 0707C]. While Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them, Amalek prevailed (Exod. 17). For when we lift our deeds toward heaven, the rulers of darkness are subjected beneath our feet, as the Lord promised; but when, as those praying with lowered hands—that is, pursuing an earthly manner of life—we relax, the enemy who had already been conquered pursues us.

But Moses sits upon the stone of which it is written in Zechariah that it had seven eyes (Zech. 3), which Samuel also calls “the stone of help” (1 Sam. 7); and Aaron and Hur support both his hands, like the two peoples or the two Testaments, so that malignant enemies may not prevail against God’s people [Col. 0707D]. Therefore, as has already been said above, whoever desires to conquer the ancient enemy must not lay down spiritual arms until he reaches victory. Let us therefore quickly take up the Lord’s arms and, with God’s help, rise against the enemy. Readiness for the encounter will readily give victory; and that fearful one, though he cannot be seen, yields to those who bravely resist with those divine arms by which he was conquered.

Hence blessed James says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4). This is as if he said: “Be subject to God”—that is, fulfil his will—“resist the devil when he suggests evil, and then he himself will flee from you” [Col. 0708A]. He was permitted to rage against Job, but only so that the righteous man might be tested and the wicked man punished. He desires to take from us the heavenly homeland; he wishes to slay our souls and draw them with himself into damnation.

Fight, therefore, dearest brothers, for your homeland—that is, for the land of the living. Fight for your souls, lest he draw them with himself into eternal destruction. Put on the armour of God, so that you may be able to fight against the devil’s snares. In order that you may know what the armour of God is, consider the armour of an earthly soldier. These are the weapons of an earthly soldier going into battle.

An earthly soldier going to war needs a horse to carry him into battle. The horse must be ready and strong, able to run swiftly and carry the armed soldier easily and rapidly into the fight [Col. 0708B]. The worldly soldier also needs a bridle, saddle, spurs, and stirrups. [Note: [Col. 0708D] “Stirrups” (*stapedis*).] Moreover, he needs a breastplate, shield, helmet, sword, and scabbard; also a lance with which to pierce enemies who resist him. With these weapons the worldly soldier is armed, and trusting in them he is encouraged for battle.

The soldier of Christ likewise needs armour, in order to fight against the temptations of the ancient enemy and against the vices of his own flesh. First of all, he must have a horse on which he may be carried readily into battle. For what is this our horse except our body, over which the spirit presides as rider and governor, moderating and directing its impulses? A horse, being an irrational and spirited animal, if it lacks a rider and governor, will readily rush by its own impulse into danger. So too our body, like a spirited and unruly horse, unless governed by the presiding spirit, will readily go to ruin and perish by its own impulse [Col. 0708C]. But we ought not to follow the impulse of the flesh, but the impulse of the spirit. Of this it is written: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there the living creatures went” (Ezek. 1).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0708D] Homily 5 on Ezekiel]: In the elect and the reprobate, the impulses are different: the impulse of the spirit in the elect, the impulse of the flesh in the reprobate. The impulse of the flesh drives the mind toward hatred, pride, impurity, plunder, outward glory, cruelty, faithlessness, despair, anger, quarrels, and pleasures. But the impulse of the spirit draws the mind toward charity, humility, continence, [Col. 0708D] generosity in mercy, inward progress, works of piety, faith in eternal things, hope of the joy to come, patience and peace, consideration of immortal life, and tears. Therefore we must always take great care to consider everything we do, and to consider where the impulse leads us: whether our thought is driven by the impulse of the flesh or by the impulse of the spirit. For to love earthly things, to prefer temporal things to eternal ones, to possess outward goods not for necessary use but to desire them for pleasure, to seek revenge upon an enemy, and to rejoice at an enemy’s downfall—this is the impulse of the flesh. Conversely, to love heavenly things, to despise passing things, [Col. 0709A] to seek earthly things not for the flesh’s delight but for necessity’s use, and to grieve and weep over an enemy’s death—this is the impulse of the spirit. Therefore all who continually exercise themselves in these virtues rightly fulfil what is said of the holy living creatures: “Wherever,” he says, “the impulse of the spirit was, there they went.”

But we should know that the impulse of the flesh often disguises itself beneath the covering of a spiritual impulse; and thought itself lies to itself, claiming to act spiritually when it acts carnally. For often someone, overcome by the goads of anger, is inflamed against an offender, under zeal for avenging justice, beyond what is necessary. Passing beyond the bounds of justice into vengeance, he acts cruelly while supposing that he acts justly. Thus the impulse of the flesh is veiled for him under the appearance of the spirit, when even that which is believed to be done justly [Col. 0709B] is not kept under the restraint of discernment. And often another, pursuing excessive gentleness, sees the faults of those subject to him and refuses, out of misplaced favour, to correct them with zeal; by not correcting them he causes them to multiply grievously. Thus his mildness becomes hostile both to himself and to those subject to him, because through sluggishness of mind, which he counts as patience, he is carried by the impulse of the flesh away from the impulse of the spirit.

Therefore our first thought ought to examine us by searching our heart, lest we be led into certain actions by an open impulse, lest the mind, seduced by corrupt pleasures, recognize evils as evil and yet commit them. Secondly, vigilance must make us watchful lest the impulse of the flesh secretly insinuate itself under the semblance of the impulse of the spirit, and represent to us as virtues the faults that we commit. [Col. 0709C] We should know, indeed, that sins are more serious when they imitate virtues by assuming their appearance. Openly recognized sins cast the mind down into shame and lead it to repentance; these others not only do not humble it to repentance, but even exalt the mind of the doer, because they are considered virtues.

Therefore, dearest brothers, as was said above, we ought not to follow the impulse of the flesh but the impulse of the spirit. The flesh has its own impulse, and so does the spirit. The impulse of the flesh drives toward vices; the impulse of the spirit urges toward virtues. The impulse of the flesh provokes the mind toward evil, but the impulse of the spirit toward doing good. Therefore the impulse of the spirit must be followed, and that of the flesh restrained. For the impulse of the flesh [Col. 0709D] creeps along the precipices of lusts, whereas the impulse of the spirit climbs heaven in a swift endeavour.

You therefore, servant of God, be a good rider of your horse—that is, of your body—so that it may not cast you headlong into the pit of vices, but raise you to the heights of virtues. Check the impulse of your body, knowing that “the Lord cast the evil horse and its rider into the sea” (Exod. XV). Restrain your fleshly horse, lest it carry its rider—that is, the soul—with it into destruction. You also know that it is written thus in the Psalm: “A king is not saved by great strength, and a giant shall not be saved by the abundance of his strength” (Ps. XXXII).

By the king [Col. 0710A] we mean the one who knows well how to govern his body. “A king,” he says, “is not saved by great strength”: that is, one who governs his flesh is not saved if he presumes upon himself. “And a giant shall not be saved in the abundance of his strength”: plainly, one who resists fleshly desires, or attacks the devil and his angels, is not saved if he presumes upon his own strength. For the horse—that is, the human being—is deceitful for salvation unless God is his rider; because “it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). The horse is deceitful—that is, the human body, which is without understanding like a horse, and which, without a rider, that is, without the governance of the soul, is borne over precipices. It is deceitful for salvation because it obstructs the soul.

Similar is what blessed Job says of God: “He loosens the belt [Col. 0710B] of kings and binds their loins with a rope” (Job XII). This is said of those who rightly govern unlawful impulses and afterward presume upon themselves. He loosens the belt of kings: namely, he allows those who presume upon themselves in what they do to fall into sin—Peter, who denied the Son of God (Matt. XXVI); Thomas, who said, “Let us all die with him” (John XI), yet when he saw that same Son of God and of the Virgin being seized, immediately fled; and John, who shortly before had reclined at supper upon the breast of that same Lord and his Master (John XXI), but fled naked, leaving behind his linen cloth (Mark XIV). [Note: [Col. 0709] But it is uncertain whether he was John, although the holy Fathers Chrysostom, Ambrose, Gregory, and Bede follow this opinion.] Yet Almighty God does this for their benefit, while he girds their loins with chastity and steadfastness.

[Col. 0710C] Thus the king is saved not by great strength, and the giant is saved not by the abundance of his strength (Ps. XXXII), but by the help of heavenly grace. Therefore the horse is deceitful for salvation—that is, the impulse of the body—unless it is moderated by the strength of the presiding spirit. We have, then, the body as horse, the spirit as rider, and reason as bridle. By reason’s moderation, as though by reins, the rider, the spirit, ought to curb and restrain the brute and irrational motions of the body, lest the horse rush headlong and carry away the spirit. To this the Psalmist exhorts us, that we may live rationally, saying: “Do not become like horse and mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI). As though he plainly said: You, created by God in such great dignity above other animals and, through God’s mercy, [Col. 0710D] placed in such great honour, live intelligently and rationally. As though he said: You who were created in God’s image, do not through your own fault become like horse and mule; do not endure another rider; do not carry the burden of another master. For a horse, because it lacks discernment, carries its own rider just as readily as another’s; and a mule equally bears the burden of another as that of its own master who possesses it.

Alternatively: Do not be without a shepherd; do not, wantonly rushing over precipices, wander through byways, as horse and mule do when they are without a shepherd. Or: do not presume upon your own powers, you who have understanding, as do horse and mule, which have no understanding. Therefore the rider, the spirit, ought to restrain the impulses of the body with the bridle of reason. Hence the Psalmist prays to God: “With bit and bridle,” he says, [Col. 0711A] “bind fast their jaws, those who do not draw near to you” (ibid.). As though he said: In great restraint or humility, O Lord, bind fast their jaws; that is, suppress their proud speech, that they may learn not to boast of their own merits but through humility to confess their sins to you. Crush their pride; set in their mouths the words of your law, which may restrain from pride and wandering course those who go about in a circuit and do not draw near to you.

Therefore, as stated before, we have the body as horse, the spirit as rider, reason as bridle, and the profession of chastity as bit. With a bit the horse is tied to the manger, where it eats hay and is renewed with fodder. So too the horse of our profession is tied, as it were by the indissoluble knot of a bit, to the Lord’s manger, where it is fattened with the food of the divine word. Hence the Psalmist joyfully speaks to God: “How sweet,” he says, “are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). The words of God are sweet to those who renounce the world and, through charity, long for their heavenly homeland. The upright in heart rejoice in reading or hearing God’s words as one who finds great spoil (ibid.). Thus the holy animals are bound by the bit—that is, by the profession of chastity and innocence—to God’s manger, and there they are nourished by the sweetness of the holy Scriptures. [Col. 0711C] The bond of the bit holds the horse back, lest it be able to leave the stable. Thus a cleric who in his fickleness wishes to roam in a wandering mind through the fields of wantonness, the marshes of luxury, the precipices of drunkenness, and the heights of excess, is held to the Lord’s manger by the bond of his profession. He would act far more wisely if he stood willingly at the Lord’s manger and did not loosen or break the knot tied by the strong hand of the Lord.

There follows the saddle, in which the spirit ought to rest; by this we understand repose of mind. For repose of mind is a pleasant and soft kind of seat for the spirit. “Upon whom shall the spirit rest, except upon the humble, quiet, and trembling at the words of God?” (Isa. LXVI). Therefore, if we wish to be exalted with Christ, [Col. 0711D] we must first be humbled with him. For he descended in mercy because man fell through pride. If, then, we seek the spirit’s place or seat, “his place has surely been made in peace” (Ps. LXXV). But if our mind is disturbed by the unrest of murmuring, anger, or rage, it does not possess a saddle or soft bedding upon which the spirit, lover of peace, ought to sit.

Two stirrups hang at right and left, upon which the strong rider leans; by them adversity and prosperity are understood. These two stirrups are prosperity and adversity: prosperity stands on the right, but adversity on the left. Therefore every soldier of Christ should lean firmly upon these stirrups, lest he be proudly lifted up by prosperity’s favour or broken by fear of adversity. The spiritual soldier, proceeding to battle against the strong armed enemy, if he leans with all his strength upon these stirrups, will easily obtain victory with God’s help.

A soldier going to battle also needs spurs, which may rouse the heart of the horse when it grows slack and indolent, so that, encouraged, it may rush upon the enemy in an ardent course. The soldier of Christ has two spurs: the examples of the holy Fathers of both Testaments. Whenever we look upon them, we are carried more swiftly to the Lord’s warfare and more keenly stirred against the enemy. The examples of the saints give us courage to run, that we may thus run “after the fragrance of the Lord’s ointments” (Cant. I), so as to attain the prize of eternal blessedness (Phil. III). For we are often lukewarm and negligent [Col. 0712B] in fasting, prayer, or vigils; we often fail in body and mind. But if we look to the lives and examples of the saints, we are immediately aroused, encouraged, and strengthened for every work of righteousness.

Yet we should know that no one runs after the fragrance of the ointments unless he is drawn; for one whom divine grace does not help is weighed down by the burden of his own corruption. Divine grace indeed comes before us, and, showing us the sweetness of inward things, pierces us with compunction concerning outward things. Then the mind, entering into those inward things, despises temporal things for love of them. Thus the one who is drawn runs, because willingly following the bond of love, strengthened by love of grace, he passes every obstacle without burden. Nor is it strange that he follows the fragrance [Col. 0712C] of ointments; for when the sweetness of spiritual gifts is perceived, what is there in this temporal world whose desire can hold back the holy soul, Christ’s bride, from hastening thither? There it rejoices in the mildness of the ointments, and while it breathes through the nostrils of discernment, charity has a sweet fragrance to it. Therefore soldiers of Christ need spurs—namely, the examples of the holy Fathers who went before—stirred by which they may run more swiftly to spiritual battle and be more diligent in doing good.

Having set these things forth, let us come to the spiritual armour of Christ’s soldier. The spiritual soldier needs a breastplate, so that, with his body armoured, he may not fear showers of missiles or the thrusts [Col. 0712D] of a spear. But what is the breastplate of Christ’s soldier? Clearly, righteousness, of which the Apostle says: “Put on the breastplate of righteousness” (Eph. VI). For this breastplate the Psalmist also earnestly entreats God: “Let your priests,” he says, “be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI). A breastplate is woven of iron scales, which cling to one another and by continuous interlocking make up that scaled tunic. The breastplate of righteousness is suitably compared to this: it is woven from diverse virtues as from scales. Perfect charity is righteousness; blessed Paul declares that it consists of various virtues connected with one another by a certain kinship and nature. “Charity,” he says, “is patient” (I Cor. XIII): behold one scale, as it were, of the breastplate of righteousness. He weaves another to it when he says, “It is kind.” Accordingly, the scales cling together and are woven in fitting sequence when it is said: “It does not envy, does not act perversely, is not ambitious, is not puffed up, is not provoked, thinks no evil” (ibid.), [Col. 0713A] and the rest that the Apostle adds to the weaving of this spiritual breastplate. For this is the breastplate of righteousness, which the devil’s fiery arrows cannot break or pierce.

A helmet is also added to the armour of God. The helmet is that of which the Apostle speaks: “the helmet, namely, of hope and salvation” (I Thess. V). The helmet rests over the head, protects the brain, and defends it from the blow of a flashing sword. In the same way hope of heavenly glory rests over the head of our soul—that is, over the mind; with its gentle covering the soul’s head is both covered and fortified. A shield is also most necessary: it must not yield to the impact of an onrushing spear and must keep the body unharmed. So too the Lord crowns and covers his soldiers with the shield of his good will, as David rejoicing says to that same Lord in the Psalm: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. V). By the grace of his good will, the Lord covers and crowns us with the shield set round about us, lest any part of the body, so covered, be exposed to missiles.

Let a sharp sword also be given to the spiritual soldier, so that nothing may be lacking to God’s armour. Hence the Apostle says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). Therefore the word of God is the spiritual sword that cuts away vices, a sword sharp and penetrating. Thus blessed Paul says to the Hebrews: “The word of God is living and effectual and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, [Col. 0713C] reaching even to the division of soul and spirit,” etc. (Heb. IV).

Dearest brothers, how penetrating is this sword, how effectual, how sharp—the sword that cuts off every fleshly affection of the soul! This is the sword of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X). For he came to separate father from son and mother from daughter, to cut us off from love of the world. He breaks the affection and cuts away the love that nature had produced in us toward parents and our own flesh. For if you still love your parents or your flesh beyond due measure, you do not possess God’s sword, nor has God’s sword struck you. For God’s sword, striking the mind, separates it from excessive love of the flesh and from love of parents. Both are vices.

[Col. 0713D] For if you love your flesh and indulge it with richer food, very many vices spring up from it as you nourish it without measure. But if you love your parents carnally, and fortune smiles upon them, you rejoice in a certain vain glory and cannot love perfectly the law of the Creator. The mind grieves and cannot rise to contemplation of the Creator. But if someone speaks an insult to them or inflicts loss upon them, you burn wholly against him and, as most wicked petitioners, call down many evils upon him.

Therefore, dearest brothers, receive the sword of God’s word, if you are soldiers of Christ, that it may cut off harmful affections from your souls. But this sword has a sheath in which it is stored, effectual and living. What is it? Surely the letter is its sheath, in which [Col. 0714A] the spiritual meaning of God’s word lies hidden. As the sword is in its sheath, so spiritual sense lies hidden in the letter. Therefore let Christ’s soldiers know how to draw the sword from its sheath, that they may be counted among the children of Israel who are proclaimed “mighty men and most skilled in wars” (Cant. III).

Let ecclesiastical soldiers also have spears, by which they may more completely overcome invisible enemies. I think the spear is most rightly called prayer, which David prayed might be directed before God like incense: “Let my prayer,” he says, “be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL). Moses directed this spear—that is, prayer—against the Amalekites when, with prayers and hands stretched and raised on high, he overcame them (Exod. XVII). Whenever he lowered this spear, namely prayer, [Col. 0714B] Amalek overcame the children of Israel. Amalek still fights against us and does not permit us free passage to the land of promise. As stated above, Amalek in this battle signifies the devil, who resists us upon the way as we journey toward the eternal homeland. When we leave Egypt—that is, the fleshly manner of life—he meets us armed and lays snares in the course of this present life. Therefore let us direct the spear of prayer against him and, following Moses’ example—that is, through the persistence of good works—overcome him. This spear greatly terrifies our enemy if it is hurled with a strong arm. If it is directed with the soul’s whole effort, the enemy does not escape the blow of its approaching point.

These, dearest brothers, are the spiritual and mighty weapons of Christ’s soldier, which, as the Apostle exhorts, we must put on (Rom. XIII). If that strong armed one sees us clothed in them, overcome by terror at the weapons, he will flee. Therefore shoot the burning arrows of prayers against the snares of demons. The frequency of prayers overcomes the devil’s temptations. The power of pure prayer repels diabolical assaults. Continual prayer breaks diabolical darts.

Therefore, sweetest brothers, let us fight manfully with these weapons; let us fight lawfully, so that, with God’s help, we may both conquer the devil and receive the desired crowns from the Lord’s hand. “For no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (II Tim. II). Therefore, while we have time, let us not neglect the salvation of our souls, but let us strive with utmost vigilance [Col. 0714D] to spend the remaining course of our life in good works. It is greatly beneficial for us, beloved, to beware of that night in which no one can work (John IX). Only in this present time is it lawful for us to devote ourselves to good works. For in the life to come the exercise of work is no longer sought; the recompense of merits is awaited.

Let us also question blessed Paul, and together hear what he says to us about this present time. Say, holy Paul the Apostle, say, we beseech you: what do you think of this present time, and what ought we to do in it?

“Behold,” he says, “now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation, giving no offense to anyone, that our ministry may not be blamed” (II Cor. VI). As though he plainly said: Behold, now is the acceptable time, which was not in the old law; behold, now is the day of salvation—not tomorrow, nor a year from now, but now is the day of salvation, because it is uncertain to us whether tomorrow we shall be permitted to do good. The night comes when no one can work (John IX). Therefore the acceptable time and the day of salvation are in this life, in which good works—namely fasting, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving—are acceptable to God. Let us therefore strive in this present time to sow good works, so that in the future we may be able to receive the fruit of eternal reward.

It follows: “Giving no offense to anyone, that our ministry may not be blamed.” As though he said: We exhort you to give no one any occasion for offense by evil living, whether in word or example, so that our ministry [Col. 0715B]—that is, apostolic teaching—may not be blamed because of you. Hence elsewhere this most wise Apostle, admonishing certain disciples, says: “Let not the good name be blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.” [Note: [Col. 0715D] In the Epistle to the Romans, II.24: “The name . . . of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.” Augustine and others: “among the Gentiles,” XIV.16: “Let not . . . our good be blasphemed.” The authority appears to have been conflated from these two passages. [Col. 0716D] Does not James II.7 read: “They” (the rich) “blaspheme the good name”?]

One who lives wickedly offends God and his neighbours, because he both causes the Church’s religion to be reproached among unbelievers and offers the children of the Church an example of depravity. As though it were said more plainly: Preserve with the utmost devotion the teaching of Christ handed down to you by me and by my other fellow-workers, lest perhaps, if you act otherwise—that is, if by wicked living you become transgressors of apostolic instruction—the blame be imputed not so much to you as to our ministry.

“But in all things,” he says, “let us show ourselves as ministers of God.” Ministers of God ought to be conformed to God’s commands, according to what he says elsewhere: “Be imitators of God, as most beloved children,” etc. (Eph. V). God’s ministers must, so far as possible, abstain from every stain of actual sin, be perfect in God’s ministry, and by words and examples raise human minds from earth to heaven in imitation of God and of the man Jesus Christ. Hence it is said: “He who ministers to me, let him follow me” (John XII). He is truly God’s minister who both lives well and kindles others to do good by preaching. [Note: [Col. 0716D] “By preaching.”] Surely that person shows himself God’s minister who always strives to live justly and to have many companions in God’s way.

Again he adds: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God.” As though he more plainly exhorted his fellow disciples—indeed, all [Col. 0715D] of us—saying: In all our works and in our whole conduct, let you and I show, that is, offer, ourselves to God without reproach as ministers of God. In what way? Namely, “in much patience, in tribulations, in necessities, in distresses, in stripes, in prisons, in tumults, in labours, in vigils, in fastings, in chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit.”

In so many adversities, in so many hardships of this present age, Christ’s burden and rest are light for believers, because the Holy Spirit gives life within and hope of future blessedness softens all things. Christ’s love makes every immense and heavy torment easy and almost nothing. “Let us show ourselves,” he says, “as ministers of God.” How? Namely, “in much patience,” so that we are not moved even a little by anger against those who unjustly inflict injuries or insults upon us; “in tribulations,” namely in various afflictions of body and soul; “in necessities,” in the daily needs of food and clothing; “in distresses of mind,” namely anxiety and fear; “in stripes, in prisons,” that is, should it happen that we are scourged or put into prison for love of Christ; “in tumults,” that is, in the disturbances raised against us by the enemies of Christ’s cross, whom this Apostle elsewhere laments, saying: “But now, I say it weeping, [Col. 0716B] they are enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil. III); “in labours, in vigils,” namely by working with our own hands day and night for the benefit of many.

Hence, advising certain disciples, he says: “Rather, let each one labour with his own hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need” (Eph. IV). And again, offering himself as a model of humility to the Church’s ministers, he says: “When we were among you, we were not disorderly; nor did we eat bread from anyone without payment, but in labour and weariness, working night and day, lest we burden any of you—not because we lacked authority, but that we might give ourselves to you as a pattern for imitating us” (II Thess. III).

“In chastity,” he says: namely, in preserving and guarding purity of mind and body, which is acceptable to God, exceedingly pleasing to angels, and greatly lovable to holy people. For, as Scripture says, “Without chastity no one shall see God” (Heb. XII)—that is, the essence of the divine majesty. For every fornicator, as the Apostle says, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God (Eph. V). “In knowledge,” namely of the Scriptures, so that we may know with purity and not be wise beyond what is fitting; or so that we may not be ignorant how we ought to conduct ourselves among the household of faith and among the adversaries of the Gospel. “In long-suffering,” namely of expectation, so that we may both devoutly fulfil the things commanded us and await with long-suffering and patience, amid this world’s pressures, the eternal blessedness promised to us by God.

[Col. 0716D] “In kindness,” so that we may be kind and gracious according to God; not like those who deceive innocent hearts through sweet speeches, but like the Bridegroom of the Church in the Song of Love, of whom it is said: “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable” (Cant. V). He is surely kind whose words always preserve uprightness and water the hearts of hearers with the sweetness of spiritual teaching. He is kind and gracious whose tongue does not produce bitterness but instead, by preaching, pours love and the Creator’s sweetness into the minds of neighbours. “Let all bitterness,” says [Col. 0717A] the Apostle, “be taken away from you with all malice” (Eph. IV). Therefore God’s servant ought to be gentle and gracious, so that what was said above may rightly be applied to him: the Bride, that is the holy Church, praising the Bridegroom, namely Christ, says in the Song: “His throat is most sweet, and he is altogether desirable.” And again: “His tongue is the sweetness of honey; his lips are a dripping honeycomb” (Cant. IV). And all this is “in the Holy Spirit,” who “works all things in all” (I Cor. XII), so that these things may be done sincerely and according to the Lord’s will.

It follows: “In charity unfeigned.” We call that charity feigned which does not preserve enduring friendship. Hence it is said: “Charity that can be abandoned was never true.” [Note: [Col. 0717D] This sentence, expressed in precisely the same words, occurs in Paulinus of Aquileia’s *On Saving Precepts*, chapter 7; concerning it, consult, if you wish, John Francis Madrisius in the most recent edition of the works of the Blessed Father. [Col. 0718D]] This holy Apostle says of perfect charity: “Charity never fails.” [Col. 0717B] Therefore charity which does not preserve enduring friendship is evidently feigned. For the proof of love is the performance of a deed. True charity, then, is said to be that which is demonstrated by good works. For charity that denies God by evil living or abandons its neighbour in need was never true.

“In the word of truth”: namely, by preaching to peoples, that they may rightly believe in one living, true, and almighty God; fulfil his will; truly and devoutly devote themselves to good works; prudently reject the subtleties of heretics; despise the doctrines of philosophers; and firmly hold and defend the Catholic faith in heart, word, and deed—even, if necessary, to the shedding of blood. “In the power [Col. 0717C] of God,” he says: that is, that we should not boast of our merits; nor, even if we advance so far as to perform miracles by divine power, should we trust in our own works, but firmly place our hope in God’s power, from whom all good things proceed. For by trusting in God’s power, we can conquer the temptations of the ancient enemy, patiently endure bodily pains, and bravely overcome this world’s adversities.

It follows: “Through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left.” As though he said: We who journey toward the heavenly homeland by faith, hope, and charity must take up the weapons of righteousness, by which, as was said above, equipped on either side, we may overcome alike prosperity and adversity: namely, that we may neither be lifted up in prosperity [Col. 0717D] nor broken in adversity. He bears the weapons of righteousness on the right who is not lifted up in prosperity; he bears them also on the left who is not broken in adversity. The prosperities of this present world are more to be feared than adversities, because prosperity casts down God’s servants, whereas adversity instructs them. All the tribulations of this life are compared to passing waters, precisely because whatever tribulation may occur in this life does not remain but quickly passes.

Again he adds: “Through glory and dishonour,” namely, of the Gospel, so that we may not be ashamed to preach to all nations throughout the world Jesus as born, suffering, crucified, dead, buried, and [Col. 0718A] raised again, as he himself, the Son of God and man, said to his disciples: “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI). Paul was not ashamed to preach the Gospel’s dishonour when he confidently said to his hearers: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Rom. I). And again: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II). And exhorting Timothy to preach, he says: “Do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ” (II Tim. I). Again he preached the Gospel’s glory when he said to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0718D] Galatians.]: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. VI). And again: “We see,” he says, “Jesus Christ, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour, so that by the grace [Col. 0718B] of God he might taste death for human beings. For it was fitting that he, for whom are all things and through whom all things were made, who had brought many sons to glory, should perfect through suffering the author of their salvation” (Heb. II).

And again, writing to the Colossians, he says: “We give thanks to God the Father, who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his charity, in whom we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature. For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and in him. He is before all things, and all things subsist in him. And he is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he may hold the first place—Jesus Christ our Lord” (Col. I).

Alternatively: “Through glory and dishonour.” As though it were said more plainly: Let us show ourselves as ministers of God through glory and dishonour; that is, if we are glorious in human eyes or lowly and contemptible, let us neither be puffed up on that account nor yield to it or grieve. “Through ill repute and good repute”: that is, if we are defamed for some crime, let us not be broken; or, if we have a good reputation for a good work, let us not be lifted up, but let the state of our mind always remain unbending through God’s power. Therefore let us learn to be humble amid prosperity and strong amid adversity: namely, to fear falling through pride in prosperity, [Col. 0718D] and to trust that we can overcome adversity through God’s power.

“As deceivers,” he says, “and yet true.” Among some people the Apostles were considered deceivers; among others they were thought not only truthful but even gods, who wished to offer sacrifice to them and burn incense (Acts XIV). They had also been appointed for the enlightenment of the Gentiles, yet some received them not as truthful apostles but afflicted them as deceivers and unknown persons. Before God they were indeed truthful, but among the foolish they were judged liars. Therefore let us not be proud because of good repute, nor grieve because of bad.

[Col. 0719A] It follows: “As unknown, and yet well known.” Unknown to God are the reprobate; known, however, are the approved. As though he said: Although we are known to God, as persons sent by him, yet by wicked people we are considered unknown—that is, alienated from God. Alternatively: “As unknown, and yet well known”: that is, to ungrateful and faithless people we are as though unknown; but to the just and faithful we are known—that is, received with reverence. “As dying,” he says, “and behold, we live.” As though he plainly said: In the opinion of some we are as dying—that is, falling from vice into vice—and yet we live for God in good works. Alternatively: “As dying, and behold, we live”: by the severity of punishments we seemed to be dying unto despair; and behold, strengthened by God’s grace, we have been restored to health and repaired for preaching [Col. 0719B] better than before. Thus enemies thought that they would not escape the threats of the wicked; but they themselves were protected by God’s aid from present and future death.

Adding again, he says: “As chastened, and not put to death.” Blessed is almighty God, who permits his servants to be chastened with scourges and blows in this present age, in order to deliver them from everlasting condemnation in the age to come. Hence it is said: “Therefore we are corrected by the Lord, that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Cor. 11). “As chastened,” he says, “and not put to death.” This saying of the Apostle may also agree with what David, the most glorious of prophets, says in the Psalms: “The Lord severely chastened me, and did not hand me over to death” (Ps. 117 [118]). As though he said: He chastened me [Col. 0719C] in the present, so as not to hand me over to eternal death. Therefore, although the holy Apostles were sometimes chastened by the assaults of raging persecutors, God did not permit them immediately to die bodily, lest the Church, placed amid the storms of persecutors, should seem altogether bereft through their death. Although many martyrs are killed by unbelievers, the Church nevertheless does not die; rather, she is scourged by various adversities in order to be corrected.

It follows: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.” “As sorrowful,” he says: that is, we are not truly sorrowful because of the blows inflicted upon us, but only as if sorrowful, because this momentary sorrow produces eternal and spiritual joy. He did not say, “truly sorrowful,” or “always sorrowful,” but “as”—that is, we are not truly sorrowful over momentary torments, but always rejoice in the hope of eternal reward. Concerning such persons David, king and prophet, speaks, saying: “They went forth and wept, scattering their seed; but they shall come again with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. 125 [126]). For momentary weeping will pass away with an end, and eternal joy without end will come.

And the blessed Apostle Peter, exhorting all the children of the Church to endure suffering, said: “Now for a little while, if need be, you are made sorrowful in various trials, so that the testing of your faith, much more precious than gold which is tested by fire, may be found unto praise and glory and honour at the revelation of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1).

Adding again, [Col. 0720A] he says: “As needy, yet enriching many.” Many appear to lack earthly goods, yet by their admonition and preaching they make many abound. Many do not possess earthly riches, but through the owners of riches they cause many alms to be given. Blessed Peter likewise seemed to possess nothing, and yet through preaching he gave many alms when he said to the faithful peoples: “Above all, maintain continual mutual love among yourselves, because love covers a multitude of sins. Be hospitable to one another without murmuring. Let each administer to another the grace which he has received, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 4). Blessed Paul likewise possessed none of this world’s riches, and yet enriched many [Col. 0720B] when he said to those possessing riches: “Let brotherly love remain among you, and do not forget hospitality; for by this holy and praiseworthy work some have pleased God by receiving angels as guests” (Heb. 13).

Thus these persons, and those who follow their example, are “as having nothing, and yet possessing all things”: not only because through the hands of the rich they make many wealthy, but also, what is greater, because they possess the masters of riches themselves. For it is of greater dignity and power to possess the masters of riches than to possess riches. Alternatively: “As needy, yet enriching many.” As though he said: In the judgment of some, we are as needy of true goods. But because grace has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0720C] (Rom. 5), we enrich many with spiritual riches. “As having nothing,” he says, “and possessing all things.” The Apostles’ glory was to possess absolutely nothing, to be free from anxiety, and to possess both things and their owners.

Let it also be our glory, dearest brothers, especially in these days of holy Lent, to live soberly, justly, and devoutly (Tit. 2); to reject bodily pleasures, despise earthly things, desire heavenly things, and apply ourselves to good works not only in this acceptable time but on every day of our lives. Therefore let us fight manfully with the weapons of righteousness, and not abandon the good works we have begun until, with God’s help, we attain victory.

[Col. 0720D] Furthermore, it should be noted that we must fight not only against the temptations of the ancient enemy, but also against vices both carnal and spiritual. Indeed, God typologically forewarned the children of the Church concerning this spiritual battle when he said to the people of Israel, while they were still situated in the wilderness:

“When the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are to possess, and destroys many nations before you—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations more numerous and stronger than you, and delivers them to you, you shall strike them down unto extermination” (Deut. 7).

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Isidore, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, ch. 16.]

These seven nations [Col. 0721A], said to be stronger, are the seven principal vices. Every spiritual soldier is admonished, by overcoming them through God’s grace, to eradicate them utterly. The reason they are said to be more numerous is that there are more vices in our flesh than virtues in the soul; thus, in the list seven nations are counted, but in the account of their overthrow they are mentioned without a numerical designation. For it reads: “And he shall destroy many nations before you.” More numerous than Israel is the people of carnal passions, which proceeds from this sevenfold fountain and root of vices.

These are the seven principal, or capital, vices which, as John Chrysostom says [Note: [Col. 0721D] Martin adduces Chrysostom for no other reason than that he found him cited in the *Master of the Sentences*, at the passage below, “Furthermore.” But since that most holy Father never said anything of the kind, and since John Cassian in Conference 5, chapter 16, begins thus: “These are the seven nations”—namely, the seven capital vices, concerning which he treats there and in the preceding and following chapters—“whose lands the Lord promises that he will give to the children of Israel when they have gone out from Egypt,” we do not doubt that Cassian should here be substituted for Chrysostom. From Cassian Isidore excerpted the aforesaid chapter of his *Questions*, and from blessed Isidore, as always, our Martin.], are represented by the seven nations above mentioned: namely, *castrimargia* [Note: [Col. 0722D] *Gastrimargia*.], that is, gluttony; fornication; [Col. 0721B] *philargyria*, that is, avarice; anger; *acedia*, that is, sorrow; *cenodoxia*, that is, vain glory; and pride.

From *gastrimargia* arise quarrels and drunkenness. From fornication arise obscene speech, buffoonery, frivolous entertainments, and foolish talk. From *philargyria* arise lying, fraud, thefts, perjuries, the desire for shameful gain, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity. From anger arise murders, clamour, and indignation. From *acedia* arise idleness, sleepiness, importunity, restlessness, wandering about, instability of mind and body, loquacity, and curiosity. From *cenodoxia* arise disputes, heresies, boastfulness, and a presumptuous craving for novelty. From pride arise contempt, envy, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many other like things. From these, as though from seven fountains, all the deadly corruptions of souls flow forth [Col. 0721C].

[Note: [Col. 0722D] *Sentences*, II, distinction 42: “Furthermore, it should be known.”]

These are called capital vices because all evils arise from them. For there is no vice which does not derive its origin from one of them. Yet all evils arise from pride, which, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 0722D] *Morals*, book 31, ch. 17.], is the root of every evil. Of it it is said: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). Pride is the love of one’s own excellence, and it has four kinds. The first is when someone attributes to himself the good that he possesses. The second is when he believes it has been given by God, yet believes it was given for his own merits. The third is when he boasts of possessing what he does not possess. The fourth is when, despising others, he wishes to appear singularly distinguished. Pride is therefore rightly called the root of every evil.

But the Apostle’s statement seems opposed to this: “The root of all evils,” he says, “is covetousness” (1 Tim. 6). How then is pride the root and beginning of every sin, if covetousness is the root of all evils? Yet both statements are rightly understood if both expressions are taken to include the kinds of individual sins, rather than every individual instance of those kinds. For there is no kind of sin [Col. 0722A] which does not sometimes arise from pride. Hence blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0722D] *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 38.]: “Everyone who sins is proud; for the person who does forbidden things holds the divine commandments in contempt.” Nor is there any sin which does not sometimes descend from covetousness. Some people become proud through covetousness, and others become covetous through pride. Hence Augustine, that outstanding teacher, says: “There is a person who would not be a lover of money unless by it he thought himself more excellent; and therefore, in order to surpass others, he desires riches.” Thus covetousness arises from pride. And there is someone who would not love to excel unless he believed that by excelling he would possess greater riches. Therefore he strives to excel because he loves to possess riches. From this pride arises—that is, the love of excellence—from covetousness. [Col. 0722B] It is clear, therefore, that covetousness sometimes arises from pride, and pride sometimes from covetousness; and so each is rightly called the root of all evils.

[Note: [Col. 0722D] Isidore, *On Deuteronomy*, as above.]

Although vices are much more numerous than virtues, nevertheless, once those seven principal vices are overcome, from whose nature other vices proceed, all the rest at once fall quiet and are destroyed together with them in perpetual extermination. That these plagues are stronger than virtues we ourselves perceive through nature’s manifest opposition. For the delight of carnal passions fights more vigorously in our members than the pursuit of virtues. Virtues are acquired only through God’s grace and with the utmost contrition of heart and body; likewise, vices can in no way be overcome unless they are attacked with the greatest zeal and vigilance.

The command to possess healthfully the territories of these destructive nations is understood thus. Each vice has its own dwelling-place in our heart. But when vices have been overcome by the Israelite people—that is, by virtues in combat—the place that the desire, or spirit, of fornication held in our heart will thereafter be occupied by chastity. Patience will claim the person whom fury had provoked to quarrelling. Joy, wholesome and full of gladness, will possess the person whom worldly sorrow had seized unto death. Strength will fortify for good works the person whom *acedia* was devastating. Humility will render devoted to the service of God [Col. 0722D] the person whom pride was dangerously exalting. Thus, once the individual vices have been expelled, the children of Israel will possess their places—that is, the contrary affections; namely, the virtues, the souls that see God, will healthfully occupy them.

But among these things it must be observed that certain virtues, when they do not serve discretion, turn into vices. For justice, when it often exceeds measure, produces the savagery of cruelty; and excessive compassion gives birth to the relaxation of discipline. Likewise, in some people, as our blessed patron Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0723D] Isidore, *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 34.], vice is born from virtue when someone glories in the merits of chastity and abstinence. For one who gives alms for the sake of vain glory turns virtue into vice. Likewise, one who is arrogant because of wisdom, one who takes a reward for justice, and one who turns to his own praise, or applies to evil uses, some gift of God which he has obtained—such a person undoubtedly makes evil out of good. But the discernment of a prudent person diligently provides against doing good intemperately and thereby passing from virtue into vice.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] The same author, ibid., ch. 37.]

Therefore contrary virtues must be brought into battle against the assaults of vices. Against impurity of heart, cleanness must be employed; [Col. 0723B] against hatred, love must be prepared; against anger, patience must be set; against fear, the power of confidence; against sluggishness, the warfare for heaven; against sorrow, joy; against *acedia*, fortitude; against avarice, generosity; against pride, humility. Thus the individual virtues restrain the vices that arise against them; and, by the power of divine love, they extinguish every seed of vices amid the movements of temptations.

Abstinence subdues lust. For the more the body is weakened by hunger, the more the mind is recalled from unlawful desire. Endurance fights against anger. Anger kills itself; but patience, by enduring, bears away the victory. The hope of eternal joy overcomes the grief of sorrow, and the interior sweetness soothes the person whom an agitated mind afflicts over outward things. Love is prepared against envy, and the tranquillity of gentleness is applied against the fires of anger. The proud person imitates the pride of the devil; Christ’s humility is set against it, by which exaltation is humbled.

As stated above, pride is the queen and mother of the seven principal vices. These same seven principal vices give birth to many sins from themselves, because they are joined to one another by a kind of kinship, so that one arises from another. As pride, prince of the seven vices, subjects us to the power of vices, so Christ, full of sevenfold grace, snatches us away from their dominion; those whom the former enslaves by sevenfold vice, the latter frees by the gift of sevenfold grace. Truly, he mercifully frees us when he grants us spiritual weapons and strengthens us by gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0723D] to overcome both the temptations of the ancient enemy and the vices of our own flesh.

Therefore, dearest brothers, attend diligently to yourselves, lest you make vices out of virtues, and be conquered by the same enemy—God forbid!—with the very weapons by which you strive to conquer him. Take careful forethought lest you do good intemperately—that is, lest you turn virtue into vice. First, vices must be uprooted in a person; then virtues must be planted. Therefore with the utmost zeal and the utmost devotion continually raise the eyes of your mind to the true light, which is God; and, bathed in tears, pour out prayers before him [Col. 0724A], that he may deign to grant you the discernment by which to distinguish virtues from vices, good from evil, good from better, and evil from worse. For the eye of the mind is the virtue of discernment.

Blessed Job did this figuratively when, rising early, he offered burnt offerings to God for each of his children (Job 1). Since whatever was written was written for our instruction (Rom. 15), we too must offer burnt offerings in his temple for each of the children, so that all our works, through the ordering of the Holy Spirit, may be acceptable in God’s sight. Let us therefore bring forward the blessed Gregory, magnificent defender of the Catholic faith [Col. 0724B], and carefully hear how he expounds the verse just mentioned, that we may strive to fulfil it devoutly.

[Note: [Col. 0724D] *Morals*, book 1, ch. 18.]

“We rise early,” he says, “when, flooded with the light of compunction, we leave behind the night of our humanity and open the eyes of our mind to the rays of the true light. And we offer a burnt offering for each child when, for every virtue, we sacrifice to the Lord the offering of our prayer: lest wisdom exalt us; lest understanding, in its subtle course, go astray; lest counsel, in multiplying itself, bring confusion; lest fortitude, by imparting confidence, rush headlong; lest knowledge, by knowing without loving, puff us up; lest piety, by inclining itself beyond rectitude, twist us aside; lest fear, by trembling beyond what is right, sink us into the pit of despair. Therefore, when we pour out prayers to the Lord for every virtue, that it may be as pure as it ought to be, what else do we do but offer a burnt offering for each one according to the number of the children? For a burnt offering is called ‘wholly burned.’ To offer a burnt offering, therefore, is to set the whole mind aflame with the fire of compunction, so that the heart may burn upon the altar of love and, as it were, burn away the stains of thought, the sins of one’s own offspring.

“But no one knows how to do these things except those who, before thoughts issue into action, diligently observe and restrain their inward motions. No one knows how to do these things except those who know how to fortify the mind with manly watchfulness. Thus Ish-bosheth is rightly said to have been slain by an unexpected death; Sacred Scripture testifies that he had not a male doorkeeper in his house, but a female doorkeeper, saying: ‘The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and [Col. 0724D] Baanah, came at the heat of the day into the house of Ish-bosheth, who was sleeping upon his bed at noon. They entered the house, and the female doorkeeper of the house, while cleaning wheat, fell asleep. Therefore, taking ears of wheat, they entered secretly and struck him in the groin’ (2 Kings [2 Sam.] 4).

“The female doorkeeper cleans wheat when the mind’s guard, by discernment, separates virtues from vices. If she falls asleep, she admits plotters to the death of her own lord; for when the vigilance of discernment ceases, it opens a way for evil spirits to kill the soul. When they enter, they take the ears of wheat, because they immediately remove the shoots of good thoughts; and they strike and kill in the groin. To strike in the groin is [Col. 0725A] to pierce the life of the mind through the delight of the flesh. Nor would this Ish-bosheth have succumbed to this death if he had not stationed a woman—that is, a weak guard—at the entrance of his house, that is, at the entrance to the mind. A strong and manly faculty must indeed be placed at the gates of the heart: one oppressed neither by the sleep of negligence nor deceived by the error of ignorance.

“Thus Ish-bosheth is rightly named, for he is exposed to hostile swords through a woman guard. For Ish-bosheth means ‘man of confusion.’ The man of confusion is one who is not fortified by a strong guard over the mind; for while he thinks that he is performing virtues, vices creeping in kill him unawares. Therefore the entrance of the mind must be fortified with every power, lest plotters at any time penetrate it through the opening of neglected thought. Hence Solomon says: ‘Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds’ (Prov. 4). It is fitting, therefore, that we govern the virtues which we practise with the greatest care from the source of intention, lest they spring from an evil origin, even though the things they display are right.”

Therefore, dearest brothers, as was said above, take careful forethought lest you do good intemperately—that is, lest you turn virtue into vice. Let your hearts exercise themselves through the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left, so that glory and dishonour, ill repute and good repute, may neither exalt you through prosperity nor disturb you through adversity. At all times, and especially in these days of holy Lent, extend your hands to works of mercy, so that your fast may be acceptable in God’s sight.

[Col. 0725C] Therefore, when you extend your hands to give alms, do not fear to endure poverty in this world, because in the Lord of all things you possess all things. Christian poverty should not fear to lack earthly goods, when it has been granted to possess God, who possesses all things. One for whom the Lord is not enough is exceedingly avaricious. Hear what the Lord says in the Gospel to the rich miser: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; whose then will be the things you have prepared?” (Luke 12). David the prophet likewise, detesting avarice, says in the Psalm to the rich person who stores up treasure on earth: “He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it” (Ps. 38 [39]).

[Note: [Col. 0725D] Sermon 60 *On Scripture* (otherwise 50 *On the Seasons*).]

Let blessed Augustine, the hammer of heretics, come forward and, according to the wisdom given him by God, expound this verse for us. “Behold,” he says, “the whole human race is like one man who has failed in his case, lost counsel, wandered from the path of sound understanding: he heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it. What is more senseless? What more unhappy? Does he gather it for himself? No. Why not for himself? Because he is going to die; because this present life passes away; because the treasure endures while the one gathering it quickly passes away. A human being is vainly troubled because he heaps up treasure, gathers, labours, and keeps watch amid cares.

“You who heap up treasure in this world are harassed by labours in the day and tormented by fears in the night, namely so that your purse may be filled with coins while your soul burns with anxious cares. You are troubled, and, as it is written in the Psalm: ‘Every human being is vainly troubled’ (ibid.). While you keep watch over earthly cares, you incur peril to your soul. Let us therefore set individual deaths against individual gains—deaths, I mean, not of bodies, but of evil thoughts. Thus, so that gold may come in, faith perishes; so that you may be clothed outwardly, you are stripped inwardly.

“But let us pass over these things and omit others; let us pass over adversities and consider prosperity alone. Behold, you heap up treasure; behold, gains flow in from every side, and coins run together like streams. Where poverty burns, abundance flows from every side. Do you not know that it is written in the Psalm: ‘If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them’ (Ps. 61 [62])?
