Behold, you acquire much; you do not labour without profit; yet you are vainly troubled. Perhaps you will say to me: ‘Why am I vainly troubled? Behold, I fill purses with money; my storehouses can scarcely contain what I acquire. Why, then, am I vainly troubled?’ I say that you are vainly troubled because you heap up treasure [Col. 0726B] and do not know for whom you gather it. Or, if you know for whom, I beg you, tell me. Tell me: for whom do you heap up treasure? ‘For myself,’ you say. Do you dare to say this, O person destined to die?

“To say that you heap up treasure for your children is great piety—indeed, great vanity. You, who are dying, heap up treasure for those who are dying. But if you gather riches for yourself, you are vainly troubled, because in dying you lose them. Why then do you gather things destined to perish, O you who are destined to perish? Why collect perishable things when you yourself cannot remain long? Or, if you do this for your children, they will succeed you, not remain forever. For what kind of children do you gather it? Beware lest perhaps what your avarice has gathered their luxury may destroy; lest your son squander and lose what you gathered through labour. Perhaps you heap up treasure for a thief or robber. Perhaps he will come in one night, find the treasure gathered and prepared through so many days and nights, and carry it away with him. For cruel hostility finds ready for itself many things which empty vanity has gathered.

“You see, then, that Truth has truly said that vanity is vainly troubled. For even this very statement of yours—‘Perhaps I gather it for my children’—you do not dare, I am certain, to say with confidence; rather, you speak as though in doubt, because you do not know for whom you gather it. You have therefore failed in your case. You cannot find what to answer me, nor can I find what to object to you. Let us both seek, then; let us both ask for counsel. Let us both listen to Jesus Christ, who gives the truest counsel to all: ‘Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where rust and moth destroy, and where thieves dig through and steal. But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys [Col. 0726D] and where thieves do not dig through or steal’ (Matt. 6).”

It is fitting, therefore, beloved ones, that we devoutly hear these words of our Lord Jesus Christ and, following his counsel, lay up our riches not in an underground hiding-place but in heavenly treasures, through the hands of the poor and through the other works of mercy. For he himself, the Son of God and of the Virgin, is the angel of great counsel, whom God the Father sent from heaven to reconcile the human race to himself. He too, when he comes for judgment, will openly say, with all hearing, to those who gave alms: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. [Col. 0727A] 25), etc. But those who refused to assist the wretched from their resources will hear from him: “Go, cursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil” (ibid.), etc.

Consider, dearest brothers, that the just are to receive the kingdom because they showed mercy to the wretched from the benefits bestowed upon them by God. But the wicked are to be hurled into hell with the devil and his angels because they not only failed to show mercy to the poor from their resources, but, more gravely, cruelly oppressed widows and orphans. The good, as faithful Christians, did not despise the words of the Lord, but gave alms to the needy while confidently awaiting God’s promises; and therefore they will be transferred from earth to the company of angels. But the wicked, doing none of these things and keeping none of the Lord’s commands, will be assigned to eternal fires.

For almsgiving is a great remedy against the wounds of sins, because “as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Ecclus. 3). Again, approving almsgiving, Scripture says: “Hide alms in the bosom of the poor, and it shall pray to the Lord for you” (Ecclus. 29). Daniel the prophet likewise, urging King Nebuchadnezzar to give alms, said among other things: “O king, accept my counsel, and redeem your sins with alms” (Dan. 4). Tobit too, exhorting his son in the fear of God and praising the effect of almsgiving, said: “My son, give from your substance to the poor, because [Col. 0727C] almsgiving delivers from death and does not allow the soul to enter into darkness” (Tob. 3). There are many other testimonies of divine utterance showing that almsgiving is very powerful for extinguishing and blotting out sins.

Of the reprobate it is said in the Book of Wisdom: “Their iniquities will confront them” (Wis. 4). And blessed James, severely rebuking those devoted to avarice, says: “Judgment without mercy to the one who does not practise mercy” (Jas. 2). But of the just it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

Therefore, sweetest brothers, willingly give the poor earthly bread, so that you may gain heavenly bread. For the Lord Jesus Christ is the living bread: “I,” he says, “am the living bread that came down from heaven” [Col. 0727D] (John 6). How, then, will he give himself to you if, for love of him, you have not given earthly bread to the poor? For the true bread himself says: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6). How, then, shall it be given to you if you close the bowels of mercy to those in need? How do you suppose that you will receive from him the reward of eternal blessedness if you refuse to assist the poor from your possessions?

It is fitting, therefore, that you bestow benefits upon the needy according to your means, since you yourselves are needy. For God needs nothing and is therefore truly Lord. Hence the Psalmist says: “I said to the Lord: You are my God, because you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15 [16]). Although he is God and the true Lord [Col. 0728A], and has no need of our goods, nevertheless, in order that we might do some good for love of him, he deigned to hunger in his poor. Let Christ’s faithful, therefore, hear briefly and consider worthily how great a merit it is for Christians to have fed Christ when he hungered, and what a crime it is to have despised Christ in his needy poor.

Repentance for sins indeed changes a person for the better, because it makes the unjust just. Yet even repentance itself seems to be of no benefit if it is barren and devoid of works of mercy. The herald of truth bears witness to this, for he said to the crowds coming to him: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come? Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3). And again: “Already the axe has been laid to the root of the tree. Every tree which does not produce good fruit [Col. 0728B] will be cut down and cast into the fire” (ibid.). Whoever, therefore, has not produced fruits worthy of repentance vainly thinks that by barren repentance he can deserve forgiveness of sins.

What these fruits are, he immediately shows. For after these words the crowds asked him: “What, then, shall we do?” As though they said more openly: “What are these fruits which you exhort us to produce?” In answer he said to them: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give to one who has none; and whoever has food, let him do likewise.” What could be said more plainly, dearest brothers? What more certain? What more evident? What else, then, does what he said above mean—“Every tree not producing good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire”—than what those on the left will hear, namely: “Go into the eternal fire, [Col. 0728C] for I was hungry and you did not give me to eat” (Matt. 25), etc.?

Mercy, therefore, sweetest brothers, as said above, delivers from death and does not permit the soul to enter destruction.

[Note: [Col. 0727] Augustine, Sermon 310 in the Appendix, vol. V; otherwise Sermon 47 among the fifty homilies.]

It pleads on the day of judgment, as blessed James testifies in his epistle: “Mercy,” he says, “triumphs over judgment” (Jas. 2). Again he says: “Judgment without mercy to the one who does not practise mercy” (ibid.).

Furthermore, it should be noted that mercy must be such as is accepted, not rejected; such as cleanses sins, not burdens the soul; by which, so to speak, we make God our debtor, rather than one which makes us guilty before the Lord. Thus Solomon says: “My son, honour the Lord from your just labours” [Col. 0728D] (Prov. 3). Those who give alms from the goods of others will say on the day of judgment: “O Lord, did we not give alms in your name, feed the poor, clothe the naked, receive strangers, and do everything that you commanded?” (Matt. 7). As though the Lord were to answer them: “You say that you gave alms to the poor; why do you not mention the robberies that you committed? You remember those whom you fed, but do not recall those whom you killed. Those whom you once clothed rejoiced, while those whom you despoiled mourned. You remember those whom you received as guests, but you have forgotten how many people you drove from their dwellings [Col. 0729A]. For I commanded mercy to be done; I did not command frauds and robberies. One fellow citizen was filled, while another was tormented by hunger. That poor person did not know the source of what he received from your hands. He ate and said: ‘The Lord gave him to me.’ But that most wretched person to whom you were doing injury groaned with tears, and the Lord heard his groaning. You rob others’ goods and give alms from robbery; but the wretched person from whom you take what is his utters bitter cries and sobs. You refuse to hear him and turn your face from him. For you have forgotten the voice of the wise man, sounding terribly and threateningly: ‘He who turns away his face from the poor will himself call upon the Lord, and the Lord will not hear him’” (Prov. 21).

Therefore, beloved brothers, minister to the poor from your own just labours, for the love of God. Do not take from one person what you give to another, nor display yourselves as merciful by means of the spoils of others. For what good does it do if you refresh one person from what you strip from another? Such almsgiving condemns; it does not save. It does not erase sins but multiplies them. Therefore, dearest brothers, strive to give such alms as may worthily avail to extinguish your sins. Give alms not from robbery but from your just substance, so that you may deserve to receive their fruit in the heavenly homeland. Hide just alms in the bosoms of the poor, so that, aided by their prayers, you may attain eternal riches. For almsgiving [Col. 0729C] devoutly and cheerfully offered to a poor person wholly extinguishes the sins of the giver. But one who gives alms reluctantly loses the reward.

Hence blessed Augustine says:

[Note: [Col. 0729D] *Exposition on Psalm 42*. But thus: “If you give bread while sorrowful, you have lost both the bread and the merit.”]

“If you gave alms sorrowfully, you have lost both the alms and the reward.”

Blessed Isidore affirms this in the second book of the *Synonyms*:

[Note: [Col. 0729D] Chapter “On the Brevity of This Life,” near the end.]

“He who stretches out his hand with sorrow loses the fruit of recompense. For there is no mercy where there is no goodwill.”

Moreover, it should be noted that there are many kinds of almsgiving which, when we perform them, help to procure the forgiveness of our sins. [Note: [Col. 0730D] Augustine, *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, ch. 72.] Thus not only does one who gives food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, clothing to the naked, lodging to the traveller, a hiding-place to the fugitive, visitation to one in prison, consolation to the sorrowful, ransom to the captive, transport to the disabled, guidance to the blind, healing to the sick, a road to the lost, counsel to the doubting, and whatever else the needy require; but also one who grants forgiveness to a person sinning against him performs almsgiving.

Therefore, dearest brethren, since during these days of holy Lent we ought, by the weapons of righteousness at the right hand and at the left, following the example of our Redeemer, to fight against the ancient enemy, we must devote ourselves earnestly to fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. For fasting kills and gives life. [Col. 0730A] It kills the flesh; it gives life to the soul. It extinguishes vices and nourishes virtues.

Hence the holy Church, speaking in the Song of Songs of her members who lawfully contend against the ancient enemy and his temptations, says: “My fingers are full of the finest myrrh” (Song 5). For as several fingers are divided from one hand, so in the single holy way of life of a righteous person diverse virtues are found through discernment. [Note: [Col. 0730D] Gregory, on this passage.] The virtue of generosity is one thing, that of abstinence another; the work of humility one thing, that of free rebuke another. We do one thing when we restrain ourselves in silence for our own edification, and another when we speak to our neighbours for their benefit. But the fingers are said to be full of the finest myrrh, because in everything done it is always [Col. 0730B] necessary to maintain mortification of the flesh. And this is rightly called the finest when, in every suggestion incessantly offered by the enemy, carnal pleasure is guarded against lest it be admitted.

Fasting, then, as was said above, extinguishes vices and nourishes virtues. Fast therefore, beloved, not only from food but also from vices; for fasting from vices is holier than fasting from food. It is more blessed to cease from vices than to abstain from food. For, as Isidore, doctor of the Spanish lands, says: [Note: [Col. 0730D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 44.] “Those who abstain from food and do evil imitate demons, who have no food, yet always possess wickedness.” Fasts joined with good works, therefore, are useful to the children of the Church and acceptable to God. Certainly that person fasts well who moderates his stomach [Col. 0730C] against excesses of food and keeps his body apart from the filth of vices. Fasting from food and abstinence from sins are two good things. To fast from food and abstain from vices is a double good. Fasting from food together with abstinence from sins makes a person near and acceptable to God.

Hence in the Old Testament the Nazirites are commanded neither to drink wine or strong drink, nor to eat or drink anything from grapes, nor even raisins or vinegar derived from wine (Num. 6). What, then, is signified by the name of the Nazirites except the life of those who abstain and exercise self-restraint? In wine, luxury is forbidden them; in strong drink, every earthly pleasure is cut off. For strong drink is made from various kinds of material, just as pleasure arises from diverse passions of the vices. Thus those drink no wine but drink strong drink who pretend to possess certain shadows and images of virtues in order to deceive people. Those eat raisins who are marked with the pallor of abstinence before human eyes so that they may be praised by people. But those drink vinegar who, after a life of holiness, fall back into the oldness of former vices and take delight in the corruption of their old wickedness.

Therefore, in order that your fasting, beloved brethren, may be acceptable to God, let it be pure, sober, [Col. 0731A] devout, holy, chaste, and full of works of mercy. Let wine—indeed, the poison—of luxury be far from your minds; let the strong drink of earthly pleasure depart; let raisins be absent, that is, love of empty glory; let vinegar be far away, namely the corruption of old malice and wickedness. For “Nazirites” is interpreted “holy.” Be holy, therefore, because the Lord your God is holy. Sanctify the fast, according to the counsel of the prophet Joel (Joel 1). But what is it to sanctify a fast? It is to restrain the body from excess of food; to persist fittingly in vigils and prayers; to curb the tongue from cursing, lying, and perjury; to restore peace and concord among brethren; and willingly [Col. 0731B] to stretch out the hands to console the poor and to perform the other works of compassion. To sanctify a fast is to offer God a worthy abstinence of the flesh, joined to other good works. [Note: [Col. 0731D] Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels.] Therefore, during this time of holy fasting, let anger cease, let quarrels be laid to rest, and let neither abuse nor curses be heard anywhere. In vain, moreover, is the flesh worn down by fasting if the mind is not restrained from its depraved pleasures. The prophet says: “Sanctify the fast.” [Note: [Col. 0731D] Maximus of Turin, Homily 1, *On the Fast of Lent*.] For that person sanctifies the fast whose heart is turned aside from the straight path neither by the flattery of the rich nor by small or great gifts from dependants. One sanctifies the fast who receives no reward in this present life for righteousness. One sanctifies the fast who restrains the stirrings of raging anger by gentleness of mind. One sanctifies the fast who, out of love for chastity, refuses to look upon forms of luxury. One makes the fast holy whose justice is not cheapened for a price. One rightly sanctifies the fast who cleanses his heart from unlawful and unclean thoughts. One sanctifies the fast who patiently bears insults and curses inflicted by neighbours. One sanctifies the fast who calms the uproar of disputants by the sweetness of peaceful speech. One sanctifies the fast who provides relief for the needs of the poor according to the measure of his means. Finally, that person perfectly sanctifies the fast who subjects himself in all things to the divine commandments and drives diabolical temptations from his heart.

Moreover, it should be noted that, as blessed Isidore says, [Note: [Col. 0731D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 44.] then fasting is perfect and reasonable [Col. 0731D] when our outward person fasts while the inward person prays. For through fasting prayer easily penetrates heaven.

Therefore, if you wish, [Note: [Col. 0731D] Blessed Augustine, *Exposition on Psalm* 42: “Do you wish your prayer to fly to God? Give it two wings.” [Col. 0732D] Fasting and almsgiving. The same author, formerly *Sermon on the Seasons* 59, now 62 in the Appendix to vol. V: “Whoever wishes his prayer to fly to God should give it two wings, namely almsgiving and fasting.”] beloved, for your prayer to fly to God, give it two wings: fasting and almsgiving. By the humiliation of fasting and the generosity of almsgiving you will readily obtain the fulfilment of your petition. If we chastise our flesh by fasting and willingly stretch out our hands [Col. 0732A] to perform almsgiving, we shall swiftly obtain from the divine mercy what we ask in prayer.

Therefore, beloved brethren, we for whom our invincible champion, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, consecrated this venerable Lent, rejecting carnal desires, should so chastise our members with fasting and vigils that we may fatten our souls with virtues. If we wish our souls to be filled with spiritual delights, “as with fat and richness” (Ps. 62), it is first fitting for us to abstain from carnal desires. In this mortal body we ought to hunger and thirst for righteousness, so that we may deserve to be satisfied in eternal blessedness. Hence we know that King David spoke with supreme longing: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41.) And again: “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh did so for you” (Ps. 62). The flesh, as blessed Isidore says, [Note: [Col. 0732D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 44.] thirsts for God when, for the sake of God’s love, it dries up through fasting. Likewise, the soul truly hungers and thirsts for God when, withdrawing as far as possible not only from grave but also from venial sins, it longs with utmost desire to attain the joys of eternal felicity. It thirsts for God when, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, it earnestly desires to pass from the active to the contemplative life. [Note: [Col. 0732D] Maximus of Turin, Homily 3, *On Fasting*.] Let ruinous luxury, then, fast within us; let the costly gluttony of the belly fast; let every perverse iniquity fast; let hateful contention fast; let us fast [Col. 0732C] from feasts, and especially from vices. Let us so moderate ourselves in food and be so sober in wine that no drunkenness of pleasures or iniquity rules us, but that we show ourselves such as to be worthy of obtaining pardon for sins. For what profit is there in observing the period of forty days of fasting and not keeping the rule of the fast? What profit is there in abstaining from banquets yet spending the day in lawsuits and quarrels? What profit is there in not eating bodily foods and occupying the hours of the day with unlawful deeds? What profit is there in not eating one’s own bread and violently seizing the food of one’s neighbours? The fast of a Christian ought to be refreshment for the poor, nourishment for concord and peace. How can one suppose that he pleases [Col. 0732D] God by fasting when his tongue is defiled with lies? Nor does one who lends his money at interest sanctify his soul by abstaining from food (Ps. 14). Those also fast rightly and fittingly attend holy Church in order to pray who do not entangle themselves in the deadly snares of usury and other vices. One prays rightly before God while fasting whose heart is not stained by the blot of uncleanness or torn by the plague of envy. One also strikes his breast well, confessing his sins in prayer, [Col. 0733A] who drives from it every frenzy of malice. This, dearest brethren, is religious fasting. This is the nourishment of the souls of the faithful: namely, that chastity may sanctify our fast, patience adorn it, kindness cherish it, mercy gladden it, and humility commend it. [Note: [Col. 0733C] Maximus, Homily 4, at the end.] Therefore, dearest brethren, if we wish with Christ’s help to overcome the devil, if we desire to reign with God after passing from this world, if we wish to celebrate the most sacred day of the Lord’s Resurrection, let us moderate our bodies from food and drink according to our ability, but let us fast from vices with all our strength.

It is customary to ask: since in this Lent we imitate Christ’s fasting, why do we not fast at the time when he is said to have fasted? For Scripture has handed down [Col. 0733B] that immediately after baptism he began his fast. There are, then, four reasons why we continue our fast until Easter. The first reason is that we desire thus to rise with him, because he suffered for us (1 Pet. 2), and we ought to suffer with him; and therefore we fast before Easter, so that resurrection may immediately follow the Passion. The second reason is that by this we may imitate the children of Israel, who first came out of Egypt at that time and later came out of Babylon at that time; this is proved from the fact that both the former and the latter celebrated the Passover immediately when they came forth. The third reason is that the heat of lust is accustomed to inflame us more in springtime. Therefore, in order to restrain the heat of the body, we customarily fast more at this time, and especially so. The fourth reason [Col. 0733C] is that immediately after the fast we ought to receive the body of the Lord, so that we may mystically receive the paschal sacraments. That is to say: just as the children of Israel afflicted themselves before eating the lamb and ate wild lettuces—that is, bitter ones—so we too must first afflict ourselves in penitence, [Col. 0734A] that we may be deemed worthy to eat the Lamb of life.

Jesus, therefore, as was said above, was led into the wilderness by the Spirit, namely the Holy Spirit, in order to be tempted by the devil. And among other things the devil set him upon the pinnacle of the temple and said to him: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down” (Matt. 4). The Lord answered him: “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (ibid.). This saying is not to be understood as some suppose, as though he had said: “You must not tempt me, for I am your Lord and God.” Had he said this, the devil would immediately have recognized him as his Lord and God. For the devil was always striving to discover, in whatever manner he could, whether he was God or man. If he recognized God, he would withdraw; if man, he would lay hands upon him. Yet the devil could never perfectly discover this, [Col. 0734B] even when Christ was dying upon the cross, when he thought that he would receive Christ’s soul. Therefore, when he said, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” it must be understood as though Jesus Christ were saying this of himself: “I ought not to tempt my Father, who is my Lord with respect to my humanity and my God with respect to the essence of divinity. I ought not to tempt him, I say, since by reason and free will I have what I ought to do.” One tempts God who so presumes upon grace as to attribute nothing to free will; for example, if someone standing upon the summit of a tower throws himself down, saying that he cannot die unless God wills it, though by free will he possesses what he ought to do. Therefore, O sweetest brethren, let us all together beseech this same Lord Jesus Christ, that as [Col. 0734C] he deigned for our sake to be born, tempted, suffer, die, and rise again, so he may through himself bring us to the heavenly homeland. He who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity for all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON TWELVE. IN LENT

[Note: [Col. 0733D] In the index of sermons it is headed: “Another sermon on the first Sunday of Lent.” This is more suitable to the following sermons, which are likewise marked here as for the second, third, and fourth Sundays.]

[Col. 0733]

[Col. 0733D] [Note: [Col. 0734D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, ch. 69.] Paul, born of the tribe of Benjamin, educated at the feet of Gamaliel, first an advocate of the Jews and afterwards an apostle of the Gentiles, called by Christ from heaven and struck down upon the earth, made from a wolf into a sheep; caught up to the third heaven, plunged into the depths of the sea by day and by night—thus spoke for our exhortation: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation; giving no offence to anyone, lest our ministry be blamed” (2 Cor. 6). Dearest brethren, I want you to know that, in calling it “the day of salvation,” the Apostle shows that there are two days: the day of time and the day [Col. 0734D] of eternity. The day of time is that in which all things under heaven run their temporal course; the day of eternity is that in which angels and the souls of saints live eternally in heaven. The day of time is that in which the things belonging to this world come to nothing; the day of eternity is that in which everything above the heavens endures eternally. The day of time is in this life; the day of eternity is in the life to come. Why, then, does the Apostle say, “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation,” when this life ought rather to be called death than life? Or why is it called a day of salvation in this temporal condition, when this day is full of sorrow [Col. 0735A] and toil? Beyond doubt, tribulation and distress are common to all people in this life. There is no one in this present life who does not grieve and groan, no one who does not sigh, no one who does not endure miseries. Everywhere is death, everywhere mourning, everywhere desolation. Hence divine Scripture says: “The children of Adam are born for toil and sorrow” (Job 5). Again, elsewhere it says: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40). How, then, is this life called the day of salvation or an acceptable time, when it is indiscriminately full of such great evils? Or would it not more fittingly be called the day of salvation in the life to come, which is full of every happiness and joy? For there no one dies, no one falls ill, no one is harmed, no one [Col. 0735B] suffers injury, no one is angry, no one is despised, no one is tempted. There no one envies a neighbour, no one hates an enemy, no one gives another a cause of stumbling. There is no poor person there, no needy person, no orphan, no beggar, no hungry person. Never is the voice of lamentation heard there, nor mourning nor weeping. There is no night there, no harshness of cold, no heat of summer, no winter clouds. There is no massing of clouds, no force of winds, no crash of hail, no terror of thunder, no violence of storms. There are the ineffable joys of the saints, because “eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). There all the saints will shine in every splendour, [Col. 0735C] clothed with the garment of salvation and the robe of gladness; theirs will be eternal salvation and joy, perpetual life and blessedness, an abundance of every good without any want. Their brightness too will be like the beauty of the sun, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 13). Hence the Apostle also says: “He will transform the body of our humiliation, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). Therefore, if the bodies of the saints are conformed to Christ’s glorious body—which is brighter than the sun—and God dwells in them as in temples, the temples of God must be more splendid than the glory of the sun. O how most glorious is that heavenly homeland, in which the harmonies of heaven, the choruses of angels, the new songs of the innocent, and the sweetest [Col. 0735D] instruments of the saints resound without ceasing! O how desirable is that heavenly homeland in which God, the fountain of all goods, abides, refreshing from himself all who dwell there in full sufficiency! O how most glorious is that God, the fountain of all goods, from whom the fragrance of sweetness streams forth, who satisfies all who behold him and ineffably intoxicates them with the abundance of his love!

How, then, does the Apostle say of the present life, “Behold, now is the day of salvation,” when the future life is full of innumerable goods and this present life abounds in such great evils? Or why is it called an acceptable time, in which we suffer so many adversities and finally die with no possibility of return? Yet, dearest brethren, [Col. 0736A] the Apostle speaks truly, because now is the acceptable time in which we can gain the remission of our sins through penitence. Truly, the day of our salvation is in this life, in which we can obtain forgiveness of all offences through good works. Only in this present life is it permitted to do good. For in the future life work is no longer required of us, but the recompense of merits is awaited. Therefore, one who desires to reign with Christ in the heavenly homeland must first devote himself to good works. [Note: [Col. 0735D] Gregory, Homily 37 on the Gospels.] For great rewards are not reached except through great labours. Hence the Apostle Paul: “He will not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. XXV). And blessed Isidore: “We endure many sweats in order that we may be able to reach heaven.” Let it therefore be said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” It is fitting, then, beloved, that while we still live in this mortal body, we seek from almighty God through tears and pure prayers the reward of eternal salvation. Let us change our dress to ashes and sackcloth, and amend what we have hitherto done negligently in God’s service while we still live in this world, because there is no redemption in hell. In this present time let us strive to please God by good works, because in the age to come almsgiving and fasting will not be acceptable before God. Therefore, while there is time, let us do whatever good we can, lest, if we are unwilling when we can, perhaps we shall be unable when we wish. Hence the Lord says: “Night comes [Col. 0736C] when no one can work” (John 9). In the future life penitence profits nothing; there tears avail nothing, nor sighs. There is then no place for pardon, no freedom for penitence stands open, no recourse to confession exists, no opportunity for correction is given, no return to forgiveness. Meanwhile, it is fitting that we call to mind the saying of the wisest Solomon: “Whatever good things your hand finds to do, do them earnestly; for neither wisdom nor knowledge nor reason nor any work has value among the dead, whither you are hastening” (Eccl. 9). Therefore, dearest brethren, while we still have freedom to do good, let us persist in spiritual pursuits, lest perhaps on the last day we perish with the lukewarm, the idle, and the wandering. Or do you perhaps think that [Col. 0736D] you can at once rejoice with the world in the present life and with Christ in the future? Do you think that in this present life you can at once serve earthly pleasures and afterward live eternally with God’s saints in the heavenly homeland? [Note: [Col. 0735] Isidore, Book II of the *Synonyms*, chapter “On the Brevity of This Life.”] It is difficult to love God and the world at the same time. It is impossible to serve simultaneously the cares of heaven and those of earth. One does not love God perfectly if one fixes one’s love upon the pleasures of this world. Hence John the Evangelist says: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2). Perhaps you think that holy people acquired the kingdom of God through enjoyment of temporal things, rather than through tribulation? [Col. 0737A] For we read of the Apostles themselves that they served God in hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness, in many vigils (2 Cor. II). The martyrs too reached the heavenly kingdoms through the many torments they endured for Christ’s name. The holy confessors likewise, advancing along the way of religious life and firmly restraining themselves in God’s service, became sharers in heavenly goods. Virgins dedicated to God also, although frail in sex and age and of great tenderness, nevertheless reached the rewards of eternal blessedness by patiently enduring adversities for Christ. Certainly, all saints who have already reached the heavenly kingdom first endured struggles in their bodies for God’s sake, except little children who do not yet know the difference between good and evil. But why do we speak of human beings, when our Redeemer himself, who came into the world without sin, did not leave this world without the penalty of suffering? If the Son of God himself, who never committed sin, first underwent the sentence of suffering before entering into his glory, how do we wretches, full of every iniquity, seek to reach the heavenly homeland without the struggle of labour? And certainly the Son of God suffered not for himself but for us, leaving us an example that we might follow in his footsteps (1 Pet. 2). Hence he himself says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16). To follow is to imitate; and what is it to imitate Christ except to mortify within ourselves carnal lusts and [Col. 0737C] desires? That person truly follows Christ who willingly suffers the adversities of this world for love of him. Hence in the Song of Songs it is said in his praise: “His locks are like the upraised branches of palm trees, black as a raven” (Song 5). [Note: [Col. 0737D] Gregory, on this passage.] By the locks—that is, the hair—of Christ, what are we to understand except all the faithful, who, while keeping faith in the holy Trinity in their minds and cleaving to God, fulfil in work what they believe in heart, and, as it were, confer honour by hanging upon Christ’s head? The palm, however, rises very high in growing and signifies victory by its meaning. Therefore Christ’s locks are like the upraised branches of palm trees because the servants of God, while always raising themselves to the heights of virtues, are at times led by God’s grace [Col. 0737D] to victory, since they conquer earthly desires together with their delights. Christ’s locks are black like a raven because all the faithful, although they raise themselves toward heaven by virtues, nevertheless recognize that they are sinners. The raven, it is said, does not wholly recognize its young or feed them fully until their plumage turns black. The raven looks at its young from afar and is unwilling to approach them more closely until it sees them grow black in feather. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ especially recognizes and loves his elect as sons when he sees them willingly suffering the adversities of this world in likeness to himself. Then above all he nourishes those who believe in him with the dew of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0738A] and refreshes them with the sweetness of his love, when he sees them, through fasting, vigils, and abstaining from fleshly vices, as it were becoming black in imitation of his Passion.

Therefore, beloved, if you are striving toward likeness to Jesus Christ, mortify your bodies by abstinence and fasting on this day of salvation. If you desire to imitate Jesus Christ, subdue your flesh through fasts and abstinences for love of him in this acceptable time. Beyond doubt, if for love of him you endure adversities in this life, you will reign with him in the heavenly homeland, as the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2). If in this world you serve him by almsgiving, vigils, sacrifices, and other good works, after this life, in the heavenly [Col. 0738B] kingdom where he is, you also shall be. For he himself said: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my servant shall be” (John 12). Therefore, beloved, do not be reluctant to fast, so that you may enter Christ’s banquets of eternal life. Yet one fasts well from food only if one also ceases from depraved deeds and worldly desires. Hence blessed Isidore, our patron, says: “Whoever abstains from food and acts wickedly imitates demons, who have no food, yet always possess wickedness.” How does one think he is fasting when, by grumbling, he devours the raw flesh of his brethren? Or how does one say that he abstains from food when, by slander, he gnaws the limbs of his neighbours like a dog? How does one suppose he pleases God by fasting from food when he never ceases to scandalize his brethren by grumbling, slandering, [Col. 0738C] and whispering? By such fasts sins are not erased but are increased all the more. Nor does one redeem his sins by fasting who, abandoning the study of reading and prayer, gives his attention to disputes and idle tales. That person too fasts uselessly who readily stirs up quarrels and discord against his brethren. Of such persons the Lord says through the prophet: “Behold, you fast for strife and contention, and strike wickedly with the fist” (Isa. 58). One strikes wickedly with the fist who abuses his neighbour in public. Nor is one believed to fast well who refreshes himself at supper until the belly is distended. There can be no reckoning of fasting where, at the hour of supper, the belly is filled with food beyond measure. Hence blessed Isidore again says: “The fast is despised when it is renewed in the evening by a filling [Col. 0738D] of food. For abstinence is not to be reckoned where fullness of the belly follows immediately.” All day long one chews over feasts in thought who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening to satisfy his gluttony. The prophet rebukes such people, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your pleasure is found” (Isa. 58). “Pleasure” means luxuries. Such fasts, then, do not please God but provoke him more greatly to anger. Fasts with good works are therefore acceptable to God and useful for the remission of sins. This, then, is perfect fasting: when the servant of God prays inwardly, fasts outwardly, and restrains his tongue [Col. 0739A] from idle speech. Then our fast truly pleases God, when the mind inwardly abstains from vices and the flesh outwardly from food. Then prayer more easily penetrates heaven when the servant of God bears his body dry through abstinence and keeps his tongue silent. For our mouth becomes as far distant from almighty God in prayer as it is more polluted by foolish speech. Let the body, therefore, be chastised from vices by abstinence from food, and let the tongue be restrained from idle words through the observance of silence. Let a measure of abstinence be applied to the body, lest the fire of luxury grow strong within it; but let the bridle of silence be imposed upon the tongue, lest a harsh word proceed from it. Let the flesh be moderated from food by abstinence, lest it grow proud against the soul; but let the tongue be restrained [Col. 0739B] from superfluous talk, lest it burst forth into the vice of frivolity. For where the belly is filled with food, there the fire of luxury is utterly kindled. But the fire of luxury does not burn a body broken by abstinence.

It follows: “Giving no offence to anyone, lest our ministry be blamed.” Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “It is evil for the person who eats through an occasion of stumbling” (Rom. 14). And again: “Do not by your food destroy the one for whom Christ died” (ibid.). Therefore one gives offence to his brethren who eats through an occasion of stumbling. Who is the one who eats through an occasion of stumbling? Namely, the one who prepares more delicate foods for himself. Without doubt, that person eats through an occasion of stumbling [Col. 0739C] who despises the common foods and prepares better ones outside the community to satisfy his gluttony. Likewise, one gives offence to others who separately prepares more elaborate provisions for himself to satisfy the desires of *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony, as though what is common to the brethren could not suffice him. It is evil, therefore, for the person who eats through an occasion of stumbling, because through the greediness of his belly he gives his brethren an occasion to grumble. He eats badly who causes others to grumble over his food. Yet, as the same Apostle says: “Food is for the belly and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6).

Alternatively: “Giving no offence to anyone, lest our ministry be blamed.” It is as though he plainly said: [Col. 0739D] Keep Christ’s commandments with every care, but withdraw from sins and vices, lest others be scandalized by your transgression. For if you live chastely, soberly, and piously (Tit. 2), you can lead others with you to the kingdom of heaven. But if you neglect to fulfil Christ’s commandments and cleave to sins and vices, you will give others offence by your depraved way of life, because through you the ministry of Gospel preaching will be blamed.

We cannot utter this judgment, dearest brethren, without grievous groaning, because today, by living badly, we cause the ministry of the Christian religion to be blamed. We who ought through good works [Col. 0740A] to shine like lights for people give them today an example of perverse life. Worldly people no longer say, “Let us enter a monastery so that we may save our souls there”; rather they say, “It is better for us to remain in the world.” They also say: “Why should we leave the world and enter a monastery, when it is full of envy, hatred, and slander?” Do they say this, dearest brethren, without cause? By no means. For we are no longer religious but self-indulgent. We care more about filling our bellies with food than serving God in psalms and hymns. In feasts and clothing we seek softness and pleasure. Once we have eaten our fill, we do not enter the private chamber so as to pour out prayers silently before the Lord for the remission [Col. 0740B] of the sins of those whose alms we eat; rather, we prefer to seek the conversation-room, so that there we may hear laughter and jokes, vain and superfluous words, and rumours of the world. Yet the Lord promised consolation not to those who laugh but to those who mourn. Nor did he say, “Blessed are those who laugh,” but “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5). Elsewhere he says to those who laugh wickedly: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6). Hence blessed James also says: “Be miserable and mourn, because your laughter will be turned into mourning and your joy into sorrow” (Jas. 4). But of those who truly mourn their sins he says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” What follows? Beyond doubt, by living in this way we give offence to many [Col. 0740C] and cause the ministry of holy Church to be blamed. While we live badly, we condemn ourselves and scandalize others. Those who set before others examples of depraved conduct from themselves sin grievously against God. That this is so Isidore, doctor of the Spanish lands, affirms, saying: [Note: [Col. 0739D] Book III of the *Sentences*, ch. 38.] “Worse are those who corrupt the life and morals of the good either by teachings or by wicked examples than those who plunder the property and estates of others. Robbers plunder goods that are outside us. But those who corrupt their neighbours’ morals through wicked examples or perverse teaching themselves properly lead down to hell, as damned captives with them, those whom they deceive. Far worse are those who take away good morals than those who seize earthly things, because good morals are human beings’ riches. Certainly those who seize human souls are worse than those who seize earthly possessions. The harms done to morals differ greatly from the losses of temporal things. Why? Because temporal things are outside us, whereas good morals are within us.” Therefore, for all whom we destroy by the example of our depravity, we shall without doubt render an account. We must therefore have a good testimony from those who are outside and from those who are within. A good life is necessary for our own sake, but a good reputation for the sake of others.

Dearest brethren, as we have already said above, it is far better for us to ascend to heaven by the narrow and strait way than to descend to hell by the broad and spacious one [Col. 0741A]. Therefore, if the greatness of the heavenly rewards delights you, do not let the struggle of labours dismay you. If you desire to receive unfading crowns from the Lord’s hand, discipline your bodies with fasts. If you truly long for the delights of the heavenly homeland, persevere day and night in prayers and vigils. If you wish to attain fellowship with the citizens above, preserve chastity of mind and body. If with the whole desire of your mind you seek to be intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house, [Col. 0742A] drive from your hearts the love of earthly pleasure. If you wish by vow and desire to attain the sweetness and satisfaction of the eternal fountain—that is, the vision of God—raise the eyes of your mind to that heavenly homeland, in which angels and the souls of the saints are satisfied from the same fountain and desire to be satisfied, so that you too may deserve to be satisfied from it without end, through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Thirteenth Sermon. Second Sunday in Lent

[Note: Col. 0741D. In the index: Sermon for the Second Sunday in Lent.]

[Col. 0741]

[Col. 0741B] [Note: Col. 0741D. Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, ch. 7.] Isaac, son of the holy patriarch Abraham by promise, born in the land of Canaan, called the eternal seed, renowned for the chastity of married life, inclined to graciousness and prepared to forgive: he did not drive out with weapons those who excluded themselves, but overcame himself by patience; he received penitents with kindness; and through fear of God he showed such honour to his father that he willingly approached the altar to be sacrificed, and, as a figure of Christ, did not refuse death.

But since, dearest brethren, we have briefly set these matters forth, it is fitting that, for God’s honour and the benefit of your instruction, we should survey his deeds more fully. [Note: Col. 0741D. Id., *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 17.] Thus, when Abraham was one hundred years old, his wife Sarah bore him a son, whom he named Isaac in accordance with the divine prediction. When his mother saw him playing with [Col. 0741C] Ishmael, she took offence; understanding in this a spiritual mystery, she immediately spoke to Abraham, saying: “Cast out the slave-woman and her son; for the son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Gen. 21).

We must now ask why Sarah had formerly wished her husband to receive a son by the slave-woman (Gen. 16), and why she now commands that he be expelled from the house with his mother. She did this, certainly, not inflamed by jealousy, but commanded it under compulsion of prophetic mystery. For Hagar, as the Apostle says, bore in slavery the carnal people. But Sarah, the free woman, bore the people called not according to the flesh but in freedom, because Christ called it in freedom (Gal. 4). Thus by this mystery [Col. 0741D] the former people, begotten into slavery to sins, was prefigured as not remaining for ever in the house of Sarah [Note: Col. 0741D. Isidore reads “Sarah’s”; Martin, vol. I, fol. 225.], that is, in the Church; nor as heir of the Christians; nor as destined to possess the kingdom of heavenly glory together with the noble son, that is, the faithful people.

When Abraham therefore led Hagar out of his house, he took bread and a skin of water and gave them to her; he placed the child upon her shoulder [Col. 0742B] and thus dismissed her. Hagar went out carrying the child on her shoulder and wandered through the wilderness. When, overcome by thirst, she had cast her dying son beneath a tree, an angel of the Lord appeared to her and showed her a fountain of water. She gave her son drink, and he gradually began to recover his strength (Gen. 21).

What then does it signify that Hagar, as she departed, placed the child upon her shoulders, except that the sinful and foolish people burdened the neck of their mother, the Synagogue, when at Christ’s Passion it cried: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 15 [an apparent citation error for Matt. 27:25])? The loaves, moreover, indicated either that the old priesthood [Note: Col. 0741D. Isidore more fully: “That the old priesthood carried with it, as is written, the loaves of presentation [Col. 0742D], and that they would grow old. But the water-skin, which fails, signified Jewish purification as destined to fail, or their carnal teaching,” etc. Martin somewhat differently in vol. I, as above.] or carnal teaching was enclosed in dead skin—that is, in the flesh of the old man, condemned by the sentence passed for transgression—which neither [Col. 0742C] satisfies thirst nor supplies refreshment, but, lukewarm in heat, provokes those who drink it to vomit.

That Hagar wanders with her son in the wilderness of Beersheba signifies that the synagogue, with all its people, was expelled from its own land and wanders throughout the world without priesthood or sacrifice, wholly ignorant of the way which is Christ. That her son perished from thirst shows the people to have no spiritual purification. But that she cast her son down dying of thirst beneath a tree, and then, when the angel showed her, saw the fountain, signifies that some from that people would obtain beneath the shadow of the wood of the cross [Note: Col. 0742D. Isidore: “would seek refuge.”] the refreshment of salvation.

It should be known that four persons in the Old Testament were called by their own names before they were born, without any veil: namely Ishmael, Isaac, Solomon, and Josiah; and in the New Testament two: John and Christ. That the boy Ishmael weeps and the Lord hears him, and that, when the angel shows him, he sees the fountain, is said of those Jews who are converted to Christ and, weeping over their past errors, are heard; with the eyes of their heart opened, [Col. 0743A] they behold the fountain of living water—that is, Christ, Son of the living God—who himself speaks in the Gospel: “I am the fountain of living water. If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John 7). And again: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst” (John 4). Hence Ishmael is interpreted “hearing.” This angel, moreover, is a likeness of Elijah, through whom this people will believe at the end of the world.

Accordingly, it is said through Malachi: “Behold, I will send you Elijah, who shall turn the hearts of fathers to their children,” etc. [Note: Col. 0743D. Gloss on this passage.] The Jews say that Elijah will come before their Christ and restore all things. Hence the Pharisees put to Christ in the Gospel the question whether Elijah is to come. He says to them: “Elijah indeed will come, and has already come” (Matt. 17:12), [Col. 0743B] understanding John in Elijah, John who was sent before his face.

Therefore let it be said: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he shall turn the hearts of fathers to their children, and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest perhaps I come”—namely, to judge—“and strike the earth with anathema,” separating sheep from goats (Mal. 4). After Moses, that is, after the Law which must be observed spiritually, he says that Elijah is to be sent. In him prophecy is signified: before the Lord strikes the earth with anathema at the judgment, he will send the choir of prophets, signified in Elijah, whose name is also interpreted “My God,” and who is from the town of Tishbe, a name meaning conversion to repentance.

This Elijah will turn the hearts of the fathers—namely Abraham, [Col. 0743C] Isaac, and Jacob, who held the true faith, and of the other prophets—to the instruction of their descendants concerning faith in the Saviour, in whom they too believed; and the hearts of the children to their fathers, because they will receive the faith which those fathers held. Or, he will turn the heart of the Father to the son—that is, God’s heart toward the person who has received the Spirit of adoption—and the hearts of the faithful, that is, the children, to their Father God, so that they may fulfil his will in all that he commands.

If Elijah does not first turn the hearts of the fathers to their children and the hearts of the children to their fathers, when the Lord’s day comes—great for the righteous and terrible for the unrighteous—the true Judge will strike with anathema not heaven, that is, not those who dwell in heaven in thought and deed, but earth: those who do earthly and wicked things.

[Col. 0743D] But because the angel of the Lord immediately called Hagar, saying, “Arise, take up the boy, for I shall make him into a great nation” (Gen. 17 [an apparent citation error for Gen. 21]), this signifies either the numerous Jewish people, or that those from among them who believed in Christ would attain for ever the glory of the heavenly kingdom. Since Scripture first shows the angel who speaks to Hagar to be an angel and then God, it must be believed that he was the Son of God, who always spoke through the Law and the prophets, and who was called an angel because of obedience to the Father’s will. The Son of God, [Col. 0744A] according to the Father’s nature, is God, because he is truly God just as the Father himself is God.

[Note: Col. 0743D. Isidore, as above, ch. 18.] Abraham is then commanded to sacrifice his only son at a distance from home, on one of the mountains. Obeying God, he fulfilled the command: he saddled the ass, loaded the wood, sent the servants far away, and went up alone with his son. He reached the place on the third day. Before the son came to the place of sacrifice, he himself, who was to be sacrificed, carried the wood. Then Abraham, armed with a sword and already almost striking, was warned to spare his son; yet he did not depart without sacrifice and without blood being shed. For a ram appeared, caught by its horns in a thicket, and was sacrificed. When the sacrifice had thus been completed, Abraham was told: “I will bless you, and multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand [Col. 0744B] of the sea,” etc. (Gen. 22).

[Note: Col. 0744D. These words are not from Isidore.] Why was this ram caught by the horns and not by the fleece, except because it prefigured Christ suffering for human salvation? It was done, therefore, because of the figure of Christ: his strength, that is, his divinity, was caught among the thorns of the Jews’ sins, where strength is most tightly bound and does not suffer before the Passion. But its fleece burns more quickly in the fire: that is, the flesh in the Passion. “Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies, and in you shall all nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice” (ibid.).

[Note: Col. 0744D. Isidore, as above.] Now then, beloved, it remains to see what lies hidden beneath the mystery of this sacrament. For this Abraham, when he led his only son to sacrifice, bore the person of God the Father. But why does an old man receive him, when God does not grow old? Because the announcement itself concerning Christ had in a manner grown old when Christ was born into this world. It was begun in Adam, where it was said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2): that great sacrament, namely, in Christ and in the Church (Eph. 5).

And the sixth age of the world was completed, signified by Abraham’s old age, because this mystery of God had already been long; and Sarah’s old age had been prefigured in God’s people, that is, in the multitude of prophets. The same point is signified by Christ’s being born at the end of the ages from the very people of the holy Fathers. Her barrenness, moreover, intimates that in this age we have been saved in hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born; because at the end of the ages the Church of the Fathers [Col. 0744D] produced fruitfulness by God’s marvellous grace, not by nature, and from her virginal womb we have been reborn.

The following history must now be examined and treated more closely, to see what it foreshadows figuratively in sacramental image. For who was figured in Abraham by that sacrifice, as has been said, except the exalted Father? And who in Isaac except Christ? For as Abraham offered his only and beloved son to God as a victim, so God the Father delivered up his only-begotten Son for us. And as Isaac carried the wood upon which he was to be laid, so Christ bore upon his shoulders the wood [Col. 0745A] of his cross, upon which he was to be crucified.

The two servants who were sent away and not brought to the place of sacrifice signified the Jews. Since they lived slavishly [Note: Col. 0745D. The manuscripts corruptly read *venirent*, “they might come.”] and thought carnally, they did not understand Christ’s Passion, and therefore did not arrive at the place of sacrifice. Why two servants? Because that people itself was to be divided into two parts. This occurred when Solomon sinned, when the same people was divided in the place of the kingdom, not through an error of piety (3 Kings 11); and to these it is frequently said by the prophets: “Israel, the adversary,” and “Judah, the transgressor.” [Note: Col. 0745D. See vol. I, fol. 234.]

That ass signifies the senseless folly of the Jews, by which they kick against Christ their Lord. This senseless Jewish folly bore in the Law Christ’s sacraments, yet wholly failed to understand what it bore. As for the words addressed to them: “Wait here with the ass; after we have worshipped, we shall return to you” (Gen. 22), hear the Apostle saying to the Romans: “I do not want you, brethren, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own eyes: that blindness has happened in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. 11).

It is as though he said more plainly: I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery—that is, God’s hidden judgment; I call it a mystery lest you think that you can investigate it by your own intelligence. For blindness has happened in part to Israel: not to all, nor by nature, but in part; until the whole fullness of the Gentiles should enter. “Until” denotes both cause and limit; and thus, after it has entered, all Israel, through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch and emulating the Gentiles, should be saved. His saying “until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” seems to define the blindness and also to offer some reason why the blindness occurred; and by calling it a mystery he says that the reason why God does this is hidden from them. Yet the Lord seems to have done this in order to take away any cause for boasting; and we can state this at a deeper level.

God established all the angels in great dignity. Some of them had not yet experienced their own frailty; believing that they possessed such dignity from themselves, they turned to pride and were cast away by the God who created them. In their fall, the others who had not consented, remembering that their own nature was weak as far as they themselves were concerned, were so strengthened that they attributed their dignity not to themselves but to God alone. They would never have been fully strengthened had the others not fallen, for they too, as we believe, would have become proud because of their dignity.

Likewise, God created humankind in great dignity; humanity too had not yet experienced its own frailty and similarly fell through pride. If it had not fallen, mercy would not have come to the others, because, trusting in their own dignity, they would have become proud. Therefore after Adam he allowed all alike to be blinded, so that if anyone were afterwards enlightened, that person would have nothing from which to become proud or boast. He did indeed enlighten Abraham [Col. 0746A] and certain other fathers, who, recognizing their own frailty and that of others, would not grow proud because of that enlightenment, but would rather give thanks to God.

But after he himself came in the flesh, in order to preserve humility, he enlightened not the Jews but the Gentiles. For if he had immediately called the Jews to faith, because the Jews had possessed knowledge of God and had done certain good works, perhaps they would have had a cause—though an unjust one—for pride, a cause from which the Gentiles could in no way have been proud. Thus after a long blindness they will be enlightened, so that they may have nothing of which to boast.

[Note: Col. 0746D. Isidore, ibid.] What, then, is the blindness? Namely: “Wait here with the ass.” “Until,” he says, “the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.” This means: “After we have worshipped, we shall return to you”—that is, after the sacrifice of the Lord’s cross has been fulfilled and preached among the Gentiles, so that the fullness of the Gentiles may enter. And what is “we shall return to you”? “And thus,” namely, “all Israel should be saved.”

The three days in which they came to the place of sacrifice signify the three ages of the world: one before the Law, another under the Law, and the third under grace. Before the Law was from Adam to Moses; under the Law, from Moses to John. From the Lord onward, and throughout all that remains, is the third day of grace. In this third age, as though after three days, the sacramental mystery of sacrifice was completed. Then Isaac, with his feet bound, is placed upon the altar, and the Lord, suspended on the wood, is fastened to the cross. But what was figured in Isaac was transferred to [Col. 0746C] the ram. Why? Because Christ is the sheep. He is himself both Son and lamb: Son because he was born; ram because he was sacrificed for the world’s salvation.

But what does it mean that the ram was caught by its horns, except that it signified the horns of the cross? For the two pieces of wood are so joined that in them the sign of the cross is displayed, as it is written of him: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. 3). Therefore the ram, caught by its horns, signified the crucified Lord; the thicket, however, means thorns. The thorns therefore designated the wicked and sinful men who hung the Lord upon the cross. Thus the Lord hung among the thorns of the Jews’ sins, as he himself says through Jeremiah: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins.” Others understood this ram, bound by its horns in the thicket, as the same [Col. 0746D] Christ crowned with thorns by the Jews before he was sacrificed.

When the sacrifice was completed, Abraham was immediately told by the angel: “In your seed shall all nations of the earth be blessed, because you obeyed my voice” (Gen. 22). For when was this fulfilled, except when that great ram cried with the prophet’s mouth in a loud voice: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21)? Then also was fulfilled what is said in the same psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord; and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence. For the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule over the nations” (ibid.).

After Abraham sacrificed the ram for Isaac, [Col. 0747A] he called that place “The Lord sees,” because the Lord made himself seen there, since by the Incarnation he made himself visible. Sarah then died in the one hundred and twentieth year of her life; and after buying a field from Ephron, Abraham buried her in it (Gen. 23). But what does it mean that Sarah is buried in the double tomb, except that the soul which lives to God and dies to the world is received into a twofold rest of life: in the action of good work and in contemplation of the divinity?

[Note: Col. 0747D. Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 19.] Abraham was old and full of days. He said also to his oldest servant, who had charge of all that he possessed: “Put your hand,” he said, “under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the God of heaven and earth that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites [Col. 0747B], but will go to my land and kindred, and take from there a wife for my son Isaac” (Gen. 24).

But what does it mean that Abraham, requiring the assurance of an oath, said to his servant: “Put your hand under my thigh, that I may make you swear by the God of heaven and earth”? What has the God of heaven to do with Abraham’s thigh, except that the sacrament of the matter may be recognized? What else is understood by the thigh except descent? What then was that oath, except that it signified that the God of heaven would come in flesh from Abraham’s line? This elder servant bore the image of the Law, through which the Church, Christ’s bride, was betrothed; yet because of its antiquity it is called the elder.

The servant therefore went to Mesopotamia, [Col. 0747C] to the city of Nahor.

[Note: Col. 0747D. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIV, ch. 3.] Mesopotamia is called “the land between rivers” by etymology, because it is enclosed by two rivers. On the east it has the Tigris, and on the west the Euphrates. It begins in the north between Mount Taurus and the Caucasus; Babylon follows it on the south, and then Chaldea. At Babylon is the city of Babylonia, from which it is named, so famous that Chaldea, Assyria, and Mesopotamia at times passed under its name and were subject to its dominion. As blessed Stephen asserts in the Acts of the Apostles, Abraham first lived in the city of Haran (Acts 7).

[Note: Col. 0747D. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XV, ch. 1.] Haran is a city of Mesopotamia beyond the city of Edessa, founded by the Parthians, where the Roman army was once slaughtered and the commander Crassus [Col. 0747D] captured.

[Note: Col. 0747D. Isidore, *On Genesis*, as above.] The servant therefore went, as has been said, to Mesopotamia, to the city of his lord Abraham’s brother; and he stood beside a fountain, seeking a bride for his lord’s son. So too the Law, which follows faith, comes to the fountain of baptism; and there, while it prays, the virgin Rebecca—that is, the Church—meets it. Rebecca sees the servant, that is, the prophetic utterance, and takes down from her shoulder the water-jar, namely the lofty eloquence of the world; and she inclines it toward the humble prophetic utterance. [Col. 0748A] Then she receives the ornaments of faith and conduct, receives the golden meanings of the Scriptures and the bright eloquence of silver; and thus Rebecca, following the servant, comes to Isaac her bridegroom. So the Church, following the prophetic utterance, comes to Christ.

Yet she is led upon a camel’s back, because the Church hastening to Christ from the Gentiles is found amid the twisted and vicious habits of her former life. When she sees Isaac, she descends from the camel, because, having recognized the Lord, the Gentile people abandons its vices and comes down from lofty pride to the depths of humility. She also veils herself modestly with a cloak, because the Church is ashamed before him of the errors of her former life. Isaac’s going out into the field as the day was already declining signifies that at the end of this life’s time [Col. 0748B] the Son of God, coming as it were at the day’s end, went forth outside into the field. Although invisible in his divinity, he nevertheless came visibly into this world and gathered the Church from among the Gentiles.

The Church found him at the well of vision, that is, in contemplation and understanding of truth, where it may receive a loftier understanding, or at the washing of water, where it may be cleansed from sins. Thus thereafter, cleaving to Christ its bridegroom, it is united with him in glory, eternity, and kingdom.

[Note: Col. 0747D. Isidore, *On Genesis*, ch. 20.] What does it mean that, after Sarah’s death, Abraham took a wife named Keturah? (Gen. 25.) Did he do this through lack of self-control, although he was now advanced in years? Far be it from us to suppose that he did this for [Col. 0748C] begetting children, when God had promised him seed like the stars of heaven, and had promised Isaac as his son. What then does this Keturah mean, except that as Hagar and Ishmael prefigured the carnal persons of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons signified heretics, who think themselves to belong to the New Testament?

Yet both women are called concubines; Sarah alone is always called wife. So we read in the Song of Songs: “One is my dove, my perfect one, my immaculate one, my beautiful one” (Song 6), etc. Abraham gave all that he possessed to his son Isaac; but to the sons of the concubines he gave gifts and separated them from Isaac. What does this signify except that certain gifts are given even to the sons of concubines, that is, to carnal persons; but heretics and Jews, namely, do not attain [Col. 0748D] the promised kingdom, because they pursue carnal gains and not spiritual rewards? Apart from Isaac, there is no heir of Abraham—certainly, because not the children of the flesh but the children of promise are reckoned as seed.

Then Abraham died, old and full of days, one hundred and seventy-five years old; and he was buried in the double cave, in the inner part of which Hebrew tradition testifies that Adam was laid. [Note: Col. 0748D. Isidore indeed extracted this entire chapter 20 from Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI, ch. 34, as John Grialius says; but what he says concerning Adam’s burial Augustine reports neither there nor elsewhere. Indeed, in the sermon transmitted under Augustine’s name [Col. 0749D] (no. 6 in the Appendix, vol. V; otherwise no. 71, *On Time*), Adam is asserted to have been buried at the place of Calvary, where the Lord’s cross was fixed. Although Jerome, in his commentary on Matthew, ch. 22, does not approve this opinion, affirming the other view to which Isidore here subscribes, it is nevertheless supported by the testimonies of Origen (Tertullian, also cited by the Benedictine revisers of Augustine’s works, nowhere speaks on this subject), Basil, Ambrose, and Chrysostom. See the notes of those monks on the aforementioned sermon, and Juan de Villalpando, *Apparatus of the City and Temple of Jerusalem*, part I, book I, ch. 9, where other testimonies of the Fathers are gathered, though of doubtful authority, except that of Epiphanius, *Heresy* 46, ch. 5, and another of Jerome, Epistle 44, from Paula to Marcella; that latter, however, is narrative rather than assertive, for the holy doctor’s mind is made clear in his passage on Matthew. See Serarius, question 5 on Joshua ch. 44.]

[Col. 0749A] [Note: Col. 0750D. Isidore, ch. 21.] When famine afterwards arose over the land, Isaac went, by the Lord’s command and blessing, to Gerar, to Abimelech king of the Philistines (Gen. 26). There, from fear, he pretended that Rebecca his wife was his sister. The foreign king learned that Rebecca was Isaac’s wife when he saw him playing with her. What then does it mean, in the sacrament of Christ and the Church, that so great a patriarch played with his wife and that the king of that land thereby learned of their marriage?

Let anyone surely take care, lest through error he sin in some other way in the Church, if he diligently contemplates in the holy Scriptures the secret of her husband. He will find that Christ concealed for a while his majesty, in which in the form of God he is equal to the Father, under the form of a servant, so that human weakness might be capable of him and he might be able to adapt himself suitably [Col. 0749B] to that marriage. For what could be more absurd—or, rather, more fittingly adapted as a foreshadowing of things to come—than that a prophet of God should play some carnal game so as to win his wife’s affection, when the very Word of God was made flesh in order to dwell among us? (John 1).

[Note: Col. 0750D. Isidore, ch. 22.] After this Scripture relates that Isaac began to dig the wells which the servants of Abraham his father had dug; and the Lord blessed him, and he became exceedingly great. But the Philistines, envying him, stopped them up by filling them with earth (ibid.). Who is this Isaac except the Saviour of the world, who, when he descended into this torrent of Gerar, wished to dig for the first human being the wells which the servants of his Father had dug—that is, Moses [Col. 0749C] the lawgiver, David, Solomon, and the prophets, who dug the wells of the Law, that is, wrote the books of the Old Testament? Yet these wells had been filled with the earthly and filthy impurity of their carnal understanding.

When Isaac—that is, the Son of God—wished to cleanse them, he showed that whatever the Law and the prophets said, they said without doubt about him. The Philistines disputed with him—that is, the Jews alienated from the kingdom of God. And Isaac departed from them, that is, Christ from the Jews. For he cannot be with those who refuse to have living water in the wells, that is, spiritual teaching, but instead earth, namely carnal uncleanness. Hence comes the saying: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23).

Isaac therefore dug a new well—rather, Isaac’s servants dug it. Isaac’s servants are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John; Peter, James, Jude, and the apostle Paul. All these dug the well of the New Testament and found living water, which is “a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4). Yet those who think earthly things still quarrel [Col. 0750A] over these wells: they allow neither the new to be established nor the old to be cleansed; disputing against the Gospel wells, they contend and resist the truth. To them it is said: “Since you have judged yourselves unworthy of the grace of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

After this Isaac dug a third well and called the place “Breadth,” saying: “Now the Lord has enlarged us and made us increase upon the earth” (Gen. 26). Truly Isaac—that is, the Son of God—has been enlarged; he has filled the whole earth with knowledge of the Trinity and established the breadth of the Church throughout the world. For formerly God was known only in Judaea and his name was great in Israel (Ps. 75). But now his sound has gone out into all the earth and his words to the ends of the world (Ps. 18).

Isaac’s servants, that is, the holy apostles, went throughout [Col. 0750B] the entire world and dug wells: that is, they taught everyone and showed the teaching of the Gospel, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28). But what does it mean that Isaac gave the wells of Abraham, which he opened, the same names that his father had given them, except that Moses is still called Moses among us, every prophet is called by his own name, and, as it were, the names of those same wells are not changed?

This is the mystical sense. Morally, however, Isaac is described as digging wells among foreign peoples and finally as finding water. By this example we learn that, set amid the distress of this pilgrimage, we should penetrate the depths of our thoughts; and that until the water of true understanding answers us, the hand of our inquiry must never grow slack in drawing out the water of the heart. Yet hostile foreigners fill these wells with earth, because unclean spirits, when they see us diligently digging, add to us the accumulated thoughts of temptations.

[Note: Col. 0750D. Isidore, ch. 23.] Therefore, when Isaac asked the Lord that his barren wife might bear children, the Lord granted what he had asked. But as the birth approached, the twins enclosed in her womb struggled together; and, while she was distressed, Rebecca questioned the Lord, desiring to know the outcome. The answer was given her: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from it; and one people has overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25).

That this happened figuratively is known even to the unbelieving Jews themselves: how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and how the Jewish people, greater in time, serves the lesser Christian people. Indeed, [Col. 0751A] this may also be said of each one of us: two nations and two peoples are within us, namely vices and virtues. But one is the lesser and the other the greater. For there are always more evil people than good, and vices are more numerous than virtues. Yet within us also, by God’s grace, one people overcomes the other: virtue excludes vice, and the greater serves the lesser—that is, vice yields to virtue. For flesh serves spirit and vice yields to virtue when sensuality is subjected to reason.

Esau came forth first, red and wholly like a hairy skin. Then his brother Jacob came forth, and his hands were grasping Esau’s heel. Jacob is interpreted “supplanter of his brother,” either because at birth he seized the sole of his brother who was being born, or because afterwards he deceived his brother by craft. [Col. 0751B] Hence Esau said: “His name is rightly called Jacob; behold, he has supplanted me a second time” (Gen. 27).

But why was Esau wholly red and hairy, except because the former people was stained by the blood of the prophets and of Christ, and was surrounded by the filth of sinful wickedness? The lesser held his heel because, in the mystical sense, he was to overcome the greater people.
