For Esau’s selling his birthright to his younger brother for food, and later being deprived of the paternal blessing promised to him, signifies that same Israelite people, which God, as the book of Exodus indicates, called his firstborn (Exod. 4). Because of the gains of this present age, it lost not only the honour of its primacy [Col. 0751C] but also did not deserve to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom. The Lord in a sense reproaches it for this when he says: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21).

The birthright itself was the priestly garment, in which the elder sons, clothed and with their father’s blessing, offered victims as high priests in the presence of almighty God. Since Esau was the firstborn, he came first in honour and in allotment, because the larger share was given to firstborn sons along with the blessing; as we read that Jacob, blessing his sons, said to Reuben: “Reuben, my firstborn, greater in authority, first in gifts” (Gen. 49). The Jews were deprived of this gift through the desire of earthly love, together with the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0751D] There follows next the blessing itself of Jacob. What it indicated figuratively, however, must here be explained in the words of the blessed martyr Hippolytus, as Jerome, a man of outstanding learning and teaching, has repeated them. [Note: This is Bishop Hippolytus, whom Jerome often mentions, and of whom he testifies that he did not know the name of the city over which he presided; *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 61.] [Note: Epistle 125 to Damasus, Question 3.]

“Isaac,” he says, “bears the image of God the Father; Rebecca, that of the Holy Spirit; Esau, that of the former people and of Zebulun; Jacob, that of the Church and of Christ. That Isaac is shown to have grown old at the end, and that his eyes were dimmed (Gen. 27), signifies that faith had perished from the world and that the light of religion had been neglected before him. By the fact that the elder son is called for, the Jews’ receiving of the law is understood. That the father loves his food and his hunting signifies people saved from error, whom every righteous person hunts by teaching. The blessing of promise is the word of God and the hope of the future kingdom, in which the saints shall reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath.

“Rebecca, full of the Holy Spirit and knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—that the greater, namely, should serve the lesser—here represents the Holy Spirit. She foretells what is to come in Christ and beforehand considers it prefigured in Jacob when she says to him: ‘Go to the flock and bring me two kids’ (ibid.). She thereby prefigures Christ’s coming in the flesh, in which he would especially set free the kids—that is, sinners—who were held liable by sins. For throughout all the Scriptures kids are understood as sinners.

[Col. 0752A] “That he is commanded to bring [Note: *Bring.*] two signifies the reception of two peoples. That they are tender and good signifies peoples who are teachable and innocent. [Note: Supply: “signifies.”] Esau’s garment is the faith and Scriptures of the Hebrews, first given to them, with which the Gentile people was afterwards clothed. The skins with which his arms are covered signify the sins of both peoples. Christ certainly fastened these with himself upon the cross in the stretching out of his hands, because he bore in his body not his own sins but those of others.

“That Isaac asks why Jacob has come so quickly, and marvels at his voice, signifies the sudden faith of believers in the churches. That pleasing foods are offered to the father by the son means that the sacrifice pleasing to God [Col. 0752C] is the salvation and forgiveness of sinners. That the following blessing speaks of his enjoying the fragrance plainly proclaims the power of the resurrection and the glory of the heavenly kingdom. For he is blessed thus: ‘Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed.’ The world, like a field, is filled with the fragrance of Christ’s name; its blessing comes from the dew of heaven—that is, from the rain of divine words—and from the fatness of the earth, that is, from the gathering of peoples; from an abundance of grain and wine, that is, from the multitude which he gathers through the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood. Peoples from the Gentiles, converted to him, serve him—that is, Christ. Tribes worship him—that is, peoples coming from the circumcision persevere devoutly in his praises and invoke him in holy prayers. [Col. 0752D] He is Lord of his brothers, because Christians rule over Jews.

“Alternatively: he is Lord of his brothers, namely, of the prophets and apostles and of all who believed from the Jewish people. The sons of his mother worship him, because he too, according to the flesh, is a son of the Synagogue. Whoever curses him shall be cursed, and whoever blesses him shall be filled with blessings. Christ, I say, is blessed by the mouth of our faithful people—that is, he is spoken of truthfully; but another is thought by the Jews to be blessed, the one whom they, in their error, await.

[Col. 0753A] “Behold, when the elder son sought the promised blessing again, Isaac was terrified [Note: We have corrected this passage from Augustine and Isidore; for in the manuscripts we found it quite corrupt, namely: ‘Behold, Isaac, suddenly with the promised blessing, was terrified by the elder son.’], and recognized that he had blessed one in place of another. Yet he was not angered by the sacrament disclosed to him; rather, he confirmed the blessing in the son, saying: ‘I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.’ This is Isaac’s first blessing, given to the lesser, Christian people. Yet neither did he reject the elder son; for, ‘when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved’ (Rom. 11).

“The prophecy of the second blessing, however, is this: ‘In the fatness of the earth and in the dew of heaven above shall your blessing be.’ In the fatness of the earth, certainly—that is, in the fruitfulness of lands and in the power of the kingdom—which belonged to that people before they were delivered into the hands of their enemies. ‘And in the dew,’ he says, ‘of heaven shall [Col. 0753B] your blessing be’: that is, in the utterances of God, which were ministered to you by God through the mouths of the saints (Rom. 3). For to them were entrusted God’s utterances and the covenants of the law. ‘You shall live by the sword’: namely, because that people, given over to bloodshed, perpetrated killing against Christ and the prophets, through which guilt it has been scattered throughout the whole world. ‘And you shall serve your younger brother’: that is, you shall pay tribute to the Christian people. A time will come when you shall shake off and loosen his yoke from your neck, when, through recognition of faith, you are converted to Christ’s grace and cast off the burden of the law; when you will no longer be called the servant of the lesser people, but through faith will be a brother.

“Therefore Esau, after his brother’s blessing, deceitfully devised his brother’s death, stirred by the goads of envy. This, plainly, is the Jewish people meditating Christ’s death. It not only delivered the Lord to the gibbet of the cross, but also persecuted those who believed in him, even to the shedding of blood. [Col. 0753C] Jacob, however, fleeing his brother’s deceit, left house, homeland, and parents and went to a distant region to take a wife from his own kindred. In no other way did Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh—that is, the people Israel—and his homeland—that is, Jerusalem—and all the cities of Judaea, go away among the Gentiles to receive the Church from there as his own. Hence it is written: ‘I will call the people not beloved, beloved’ (Hos. 2). And, ‘It shall be in the place where it was said: You are not my people; there they shall be called sons of God’ (Hos. 1).”

If you attend carefully, dearest brothers, to what is said, [Col. 0753D] you recognize around you great gifts of God. Therefore cast out from the eyes of your mind the motes of earthly delight; behold the things mentioned above with a pure gaze of mind, and grasp them by spiritual understanding. “And it shall be,” the Lord says through the prophet, “where it was said, ‘You are not my people’”—that is, the Gentiles—“there they shall be called sons of God”: those, namely, who have been converted to the Lord and reborn through faith in the holy Church.

O happy those to whom it has been granted to be born again of water and the Holy Spirit and to be called God’s sons by adoption! O happy those who have cast off the most grievous yoke of the devil and have deserved to be adopted as God’s sons! O happy those who have been able, by God’s grace, to escape the blindness and obstinacy of unbelievers, [Col. 0754A] and to possess knowledge of their Creator! O God, King of all ages! O God, source of every good! O Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1), who do not disdain to call even your unworthy servants sons! You see us continually doing unworthy things, yet you do not drive us away from your mercy. You constantly see us fall away from your purity and righteousness, yet you do not cease mercifully to invite us to return to you. May every creature in heaven, on earth, and in the sea bless, worship, praise, and exalt you above all forever (Dan. 3), and render you thanksgivings for the countless benefits that you grant us, though unworthy. May all the holy choirs of the righteous and every order of the elect pour out prayers for us before your mercy, that we may be worthy [Col. 0754B] of your promises.

To these things, beloved, let your minds awaken; ponder them in diligent meditation, and let such great and splendid benefits of God never depart from your mind’s remembrance. What greater gift can be conceived than to be called and to be God’s children? And yet, dearest ones, this comes not by our merits but solely by the generosity of divine condescension. Or perhaps have we done some good deed through which we deserved to be adopted as sons? By no means. God, supremely good and merciful, adopted us as sons because of his love alone. No works of ours preceded for which we received such great goods from him; rather, he did this solely by his gratuitous goodness. We were never worthy servants; and unless this had come about through the regard of divine grace, how could we have become sons?

Therefore, beloved, because God the Father adopted you as sons before the foundation of the world, be imitators of him as most beloved children. Love righteousness; hate iniquity, that you may be able to conform to his purity. He himself is supremely righteous and holy; and you, insofar as his grace grants, be holy, so that you may be able to behold his divine essence among the companies of angels. In this you are truly his children: if you also love what he loves, hate what he hates, and do not refuse to suffer adversity for love of him; if you show true love not only to friends but also to enemies; if you love purity of mind and body as though it were fellowship with angels; [Col. 0754D] if you flee fornication and every uncleanness as eternal damnation; if you despise riches, willingly lead a poor life, drive lying and every wicked desire from your heart, and, after all else, reject in word and deed whatever is opposed to sound teaching.

Furthermore, beloved, call to mind the deeds of this holy patriarch Isaac, and draw from his outstanding manner of life examples for living well. For he is recorded to have been of such holiness and integrity that there can be no doubt that in all his life and conduct he prefigured Christ. Though he lived before the law and had not read the Gospel’s commands, he nevertheless fully observed them in his deeds. The Son of God had not yet said in the Gospel, “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6); yet this holy man was always ready for favor and always prepared to forgive his enemies. You therefore, beloved, who read these things in the Gospel, ought all the more fully to carry them out in deed. Cultivate kindly favor toward your neighbors, and according to the Lord’s command forgive if you have any grievance against anyone (Col. 3).

[Col. 0755A] The venerable Isaac did not overcome those who drove him out by arms, but conquered them by patience. But you, as though the Lord dwelt with you and said, “Do not resist evil” (Matt. 5), and, “Whoever takes your tunic, leave him your cloak also” (ibid.), must not return evil for evil. Rather, bestow such good as you can, not only upon friends but also upon enemies. You ought to overcome enemies not by cruelty or malice but by love and gentleness, so that you may be executors of the Lord’s command.

The holy Isaac, leaving a useful example to posterity, kindly received those who had proudly expelled him when they did penance before him; he made a covenant of peace with them and willingly promised that he would not afterwards inflict evil upon them or their children (Gen. 26). By the example of this holy man, then, overcome enemies patiently; kindly receive those who do penance before God and before you; conquer the wickedness of others by gentleness; soften the angry with sweet words; restore the discordant to harmony; invite the contentious to peace; urge those who hate to embrace love; [Col. 0755C] correct those who err, gently or sternly, as reason requires; visit the sick; aid the oppressed; offer comfort to those in prison; bestow benefits upon the poor; strive to console the afflicted; shed tears from the depths of your heart with those who mourn; rejoice with those who rejoice, not childishly but wisely and reasonably; supply necessities to the needy according to your ability.

Earnestly admonish the rich and powerful of this age to fear and love God. Set before their eyes, in preaching, the torments of hell and the joys of paradise, and also the worms that will devour their flesh. Tell them also of the former prosperity and eternal condemnation of that purple-clad rich man of whom the Gospel speaks, so that those who refuse to refresh [Col. 0756A] the poor from the wealth granted them by God—to clothe them and treat them mercifully—may at least, terrified by the punishments of hell or stirred by desire for eternal blessedness, deign to minister to them generously for God’s sake (Luke 16).

This same venerable Isaac also showed honor to his parent—that is, to his father—so completely through fear of God that he carried the wood himself, willingly came consecrated to the altar, and, as a figure of Christ, did not refuse death. Thus the Son of God, coming into this world, showed honor to God the Father by obeying him even unto death; and because he sought not his own glory but the Father’s, he fulfilled his will in all things. Set this pattern before yourselves, beloved; love it; strive to carry it out according to your strength, so that in everything you do rightly [Col. 0756B] you may render glory not to yourselves but to God.

Blessed Isaac rendered honor to his father from childhood by allowing himself to be placed bound upon the altar. But you, to God’s honor, present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God: your reasonable service (Rom. 12). Isaac, to glorify his father, was offered upon the altar of his own accord; glorify God the Father by examples of a good life. When he was laid upon the altar, he uttered no cries of complaint against God who had commanded this, nor against his father. But you, take care to render with all devotion and without any contradiction the things that you have vowed to God. Isaac, seeing such things done to himself, is said to have kept the deepest silence; you, without murmuring or detraction, offer God pure service.

After this Isaac deserved to return safe and unharmed to the land of promise, in which for a long time—namely, one hundred and eighty years—he served God worthily; and he was buried by Esau and Jacob, his sons, in the double cave beside his father. But if, with a perfect mind, you strive to despise earthly things and love heavenly things, and follow Christ’s footsteps through the examples of the righteous, [Col. 0756C] you will be able to reach the bosom of those same patriarchs—that is, eternal blessedness—by the granting of our same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON FOURTEEN. FOR THE THIRD SUNDAY OF LENT

[Col. 0755]

[Col. 0755D] [Note: Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, ch. 8.]

Jacob the patriarch, son of Isaac, born in the land of Canaan, supplanter of his brother, beloved of his mother, living humbly at home, was blessed by his father. When he set out abroad, because he needed the company of people, he deserved the companionship of angels. After he had obtained the blessing of his firstborn brother, he obeyed his mother, yielded patiently to his brother’s anger, left homeland and parents, became an exile, endured long servitude, bore labor, hunger, and cold, served his father-in-law, and as a hired shepherd fed the flock. After waiting a long time, he received his wages not from a division but from the flock’s increase. He wrestled with the Lord and prevailed; he saw God face to face; driven by famine’s scarcity, he descended to Egypt with his distinguished offspring; and, having completed one hundred and forty-seven years, he paid nature’s debt and was buried with his fathers in the tomb which Abraham bought from Ephron.

But since, beloved, we have briefly stated these matters about his life and deeds, let us, if it pleases you—or rather, because it does please you—speak of them somewhat more fully. For we ought to call to mind the lives and deeds of the holy Fathers and frequently to read their examples into the ears of the faithful for the instruction of the holy Church, because many are accustomed to benefit from imitating them.

[Col. 0757B] [Note: Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 24.]

As Jacob was going to Mesopotamia, he came to the place now called Bethel. He placed a great stone beneath his head and, while sleeping, saw a ladder set against heaven, with angels of God ascending and descending upon it. When he saw this, he awoke, anointed the stone, and said: “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28).

[Note: Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 15, ch. 1.]

The Jebusites founded Bethel, a city of Samaria, which was formerly called Luz. But after Jacob, sleeping there, saw the ladder set against heaven, he said, “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven”; for this reason the place received the name Bethel, that is, “house of God.” But when golden calves were made there by Jeroboam, it was called Betheum, that is, “house of an idol,” although it had formerly been called “house of God.” Jacob therefore slept in this place, saw the vision mentioned above, declared that it was the house of God, and immediately departed.

[Col. 0757C] [Note: Isidore, *On Genesis*, as above.]

This sleep of Jacob is the death or passion of Christ, which he endured for the salvation of the human race. The stone at his head, which is in a sense expressly named, likewise signified Christ the Anointed One. For Christ is the head of the man, and God is the head of Christ (1 Cor. 11). For who does not know that Christ is called by a washing? Certainly not a visible washing, but an invisible one.

[Note: Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 7, ch. 2.]

Christ, then, is named from *chrism*, that is, “the Anointed One.” For the Jews had been commanded to prepare a sacred ointment, by which those called to priesthood or kingship might be anointed (Exod. 30). And just as now the purple garment is the insignia of royal dignity for kings, so among them the anointing with sacred ointment bestowed the name and authority of kingship in the Jewish nation. Christians are called from *chrism*, that is, from anointing. For Greek *chrisma* is translated into Latin as *unctio*, “anointing.” This spiritual reality also gave the Lord his name, because he was anointed by God the Father with the Holy Spirit, as the disciples testify while making their complaint in the Acts of the Apostles: “Herod and Pontius Pilate gathered together in this city against your holy Son Jesus, whom you anointed” (Acts 4). He was certainly not anointed with visible oil, but with the gift of grace signified by visible ointment.

[Col. 0758A] “Christ” is not the Savior’s proper name, but a common designation of authority. When he is called “Christ,” the common name of dignity is signified; when he is called “Jesus Christ,” the Savior’s proper designation is shown. Moreover, we read nowhere at all that the name “Christ” existed in any other nation, but only in that kingdom in which Christ was prophesied and from which he was to be born.

[Note: Again in *Genesis*, as above.]

It continues: after Jacob saw the ladder raised up, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon it, he said, “Truly this is the house of God and the gate of heaven.” It is called the house of God because in that land—that is, in Bethlehem—the Son of God was born. It is the gate of heaven because there he descended to earth and from there ascended again into heaven. This ladder, moreover, is Christ, who said: “I am the way” (John 14). Upon it the angels ascended and descended; in them are signified the evangelists and other teachers, who ascend in mind to the divinity of Christ.

When Christ’s preachers ascend to understand his most surpassing divinity, they transcend all creation so that they may find the true God, him who was with God in the beginning, through whom all things were made from nothing (John 1). They descend to him again, that they may find him made of a woman, made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law (Gal. 4), namely those burdened with the yoke of the law. For on that ladder, from earth unto heaven, from flesh unto [Col. 0758C] spirit [Note: Something is missing.], carnal persons become spiritual by making progress, as though ascending, since they live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Spiritual persons also descend to nourish such people with milk, because in a sense they cannot speak to them as spiritual, but as carnal persons.

The Son of God and of man himself is above, in his head; he himself is below, in his body, which is the Church joined to him through faith and action. He therefore is that very ladder, because he himself said: “I am the way.” Thus one ascends to him, that he may be understood in the heights; one descends to him, that he may be nourished as a little one in his members; and through him alone people are raised up, that they may behold him sublimely. Through him they also humble themselves, that they may be able obediently to proclaim him as exalted.

[Col. 0758D] After this vision Jacob continued on his journey and saw sheep and shepherds, a well of living water, and a great stone laid upon it. Figuratively, the sheep standing beside the well signified the peoples of the righteous. Of them the Lord said in the Gospel: “He shall set the sheep at his right hand” (Matt. 25), namely, the innocent and holy people. The shepherds who presided over the sheep designated the holy prophets, who, until the Lord’s coming, governed the people Israel through the overflowing Holy Spirit. The stone placed upon the well bore the figure of the Lord. [Col. 0759A] The well designated the grace of the Holy Spirit, which was to come to the Church from the Gentiles through Christ’s preaching, though it was not yet covered when Christ came in the flesh.

[Note: Isidore, *On Genesis*, ch. 25.]

Jacob, then, going to Mesopotamia took two wives, daughters of Laban, Rebecca’s brother: Leah first, Rachel second, after one week. Then he took Leah’s handmaid Zilpah and Rachel’s handmaid Bilhah, by whom he begot twelve sons and one daughter. By Leah he begot Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun; by Rachel, Joseph and Benjamin; by Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid, Dan and Naphtali; by Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid, Gad and Asher. These are the twelve sons of Israel.

But what did Jacob’s four wives signify, two of whom were free women and two handmaids? We see that the Apostle understands the free woman and the handmaid among Abraham’s wives as two covenants (Gal. 4). Yet the meaning is not readily apparent, since those wives are said to have been two, whereas these are four. Moreover, the sons of the handmaids receive the land of promise together with the sons of the free women. Therefore something else is undoubtedly signified here by the report that those two were these four.

Although Jacob’s two free wives are thought to belong to the New Testament, in which we have been called into freedom, they were not two without purpose. For two lives are proclaimed to us in Christ’s body—that is, in the Church: one temporal, in which we labor; the other eternal, in which [Col. 0759C] we shall behold God’s majesty with the highest exultation. Leah, indeed, is interpreted “laboring”; Rachel, “a beginning seen,” or “true action,” or “sheep.” Therefore this life, in which we live by faith, is laborious and uncertain in its works, and it is not known to what outcome it will reach for the benefit of those for whom we wish to provide. This is Leah, Jacob’s first wife, and therefore she is described as having not sound but weak eyes. For “the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our foresight uncertain” (Wis. 9).

But the contemplative life possesses, in hope of eternal contemplation in God, a certain understanding of truth. This is Rachel. Hence she too is called “beautiful in countenance and fair in appearance” (Gen. 29). Every devoutly zealous person loves her and serves God’s grace for her sake, because our sins, even if they are as scarlet, shall be made white as snow (Isa. 1), as soon as the light of God’s countenance has looked upon [Col. 0760A] us. For Laban is interpreted “whitening,” and Jacob served him for Rachel with the greatest zeal and labor. No one turns to serve righteousness under the grace of forgiveness of sins except in order to live peacefully in the Word, from whom the Beginning, who is God, is seen in contemplation by the pure mind. Therefore Jacob served for Rachel; he did not endure so many labors for Leah. For who at last has loved [Note: “Has loved.”] the toil of deeds and sufferings in works of righteousness? Who has sought that life for its own sake, just as Jacob did not desire Leah?

Yet, although Leah was substituted for him at night, he embraced her for the purpose of begetting children and experienced her fruitfulness, through the ordering of divine providence. [Note: “Through the ordering of divine providence” is absent from Augustine and Isidore.] For because she could not be loved for herself, the Lord first made her tolerable until Rachel might be attained, then commended her because of her children. Thus every useful servant of God, once established under the grace of the whitening of his sins, what else does he ponder in his conversion [Note: The Benedictine revisers of Augustine note that *conversatione* is corrupt and should be replaced by *conversione*, “conversion.”] except the teaching of wisdom? Many think that they will receive it at once after they have practiced the seven commandments concerning their neighbors: [Note: To make up the number seven commandments, St Martin made one of them: “Love … of neighbor, that no one be harmed.” This is found neither in Augustine nor in Isidore, who read: “Many think that they will receive [the teaching of wisdom] at once after they have exercised themselves in the seven commandments … which concern love of neighbor, that no one be harmed: namely, honor your father, etc., down to the final command, where, to complete the number seven, they add: ‘You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.’ When the Lord Christ was asked by the young man what he should do to have eternal life, among the commandments he declared necessary he especially mentioned love of neighbor: ‘Honor your father … and mother … and you shall love your neighbor as yourself’ (Matt. 19:19). Therefore, although the seven commandments of the second tablet truly concern love of neighbor, the singular commandment like the greatest is fittingly counted among them: ‘You shall love your neighbor,’ etc.; or, ‘love of neighbor, that no one be harmed.’]

[Col. 0760B] What are these commandments? Namely, love of neighbor, that no one be harmed: “Honor your father and mother; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not kill; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20). Once these have been observed, after he has adhered to the desired delight of teaching through various trials—as though through the night of this toil of endurance—Leah is unexpectedly joined to him in place of Rachel, and he endures her until he reaches Rachel, if he loves perseveringly, after receiving another seven commandments. It is as though he were told: “Serve another seven years for Rachel,” so that he may be poor in spirit, meek, needy, hungering and thirsting for righteousness (Matt. 5), merciful, pure in heart, and peaceable.

For, if possible, a person would wish to arrive at once at the delightful beauty of contemplation without any endurance of the toil that must be embraced in acting and suffering. This seems to be the meaning of what was said to Jacob: “It is not our custom in this place [Note: Augustine and Isidore: “It is not the custom in our place”—in Isidore, “in this place”—“for the younger daughter to be given in marriage before the elder.”] for the younger daughter to be given to a husband before the elder” (Gen. 29). She who is earlier in time is not inappropriately called the elder. In every instruction, however, the labor of good works comes before the rest of contemplation. [Note: Isidore reads “of man”; Augustine: “In the right instruction of man, the labor of doing what is just comes before the delight of understanding what is true.”] [Col. 0761A] One thing, therefore, must be sought, but many things must be endured for the sake of one. [Note: Augustine and Isidore: “One thing, therefore, must be sought, but for its sake many things must be endured.”]

Thus Jacob has two wives, daughters of Laban, “whitening”; one is loved, but the other endured. The first is made more abundantly fruitful, so that if she is not loved for herself, she may at least be loved for her children. For the labor of the righteous bears the greatest fruit in those whom they beget for the kingdom of God amid the many tribulations they endure while preaching the Gospel. Therefore they are “more abundant in labors, beyond measure in beatings, more often in deaths” (2 Cor. 11). And because they have outward conflicts, griefs, and fears (2 Cor. 7), they call such persons their joy and crown. Faithful children are born to them more easily and more abundantly from that word by which they preach Christ crucified for the salvation of the world.

[Col. 0761B] Rachel, fair in appearance, transcends the mind and sees in the Beginning the Word, God with God (John 1); she wishes to give birth but cannot, “for who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53). Therefore she seeks the leisure of contemplating him and desires to be free of every occupation so as to behold the ineffable divinity; and thus she is barren because she is not pressed by various afflictions. Yet she too sometimes burns with the love of bearing children. For she wishes to teach what she knows when she sees her sister, through the labor of action, abundant in children—and [Note: This passage is corrupt and should be restored from Augustine and Isidore thus: “and she is grieved rather that people run to that virtue by which their needs—Augustine: their weaknesses and needs—are provided for, than to that from which something divine—and Augustine adds, ‘and unchangeable’—is learned.”] she is grieved rather that people run to the virtue by which those whom Leah consoles have their needs met, than to that from which something divine is learned. This grief seems to be figured in what is written: “Rachel was jealous of her sister” (Gen. 30).

Accordingly, because the pure understanding of spiritual substance cannot be expressed in words uttered [Note: “Uttered.”] in the flesh, the teaching of wisdom chose to suggest divine things through whatever bodily likenesses it could, just as Rachel chose a handmaid for her husband so that she might not remain altogether without bearing children. Bilhah, Rachel’s handmaid, is interpreted “grown old.” For bodily images are sometimes conceived [Note: Augustine and Isidore read “old”; below, “are stirred.” The Benedictine revisers of Augustine note that nearly all manuscripts retain “are conceived.”] from the true life, devoted to carnal senses, even when something is heard about the spiritual and unchangeable substance of divinity.

Leah also bears children by her handmaid, inflamed by the desire to have more numerous offspring. We find that Zilpah, her handmaid, is interpreted by the ancients as “a gaping mouth.” [Col. 0762A] [Note: The manuscripts corruptly read *Oriens*, “rising/east.”] Therefore this handmaid represented those whose mouths were open in the preaching of evangelical faith, but whose hearts were not. Of them it is written: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29). And of them the Apostle says: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. 2). Yet in order that even through this conditional handmaid [Note: Isidore and the Louvain edition of Augustine read *conditionem*, “condition.” But the Benedictine revisers note that the Amerbach and Erasmus editions and all their manuscripts read *conditionalem*, “conditional”; no one except St Martin added *ancillam*, “handmaid,” making the sense clearer. The Benedictines similarly explain *conditionalem*: understand “the handmaid with the gaping mouth.”] that free wife of Jacob, Leah the laboring one, might receive children as heirs of the kingdom, the Lord said to his disciples and the crowds: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23).

Hence the Apostle again says: “Whether from pretense or from truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, yes, and I shall rejoice” (Phil. 1), as though saying: “I shall rejoice in the more numerous offspring borne even by the handmaid,” [Note: Augustine and Isidore: “as though rejoicing because even the handmaid is bearing more numerous offspring.” Isidore: “rejoices.” Neither adds “like the free woman.”] [Col. 0762B] like the free woman. But one of Leah’s children was born from Rachel’s favor, when Rachel allowed her husband to sleep with Leah on the night owed to her, in exchange for the mandrakes received from Leah’s son. [Note: The same sources read “to sleep.”] [Note: The same sources read “mandrake apples.”] [Note: Isidore reads “allowed.”]

[Note: Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 17, ch. 9.]

The mandrake is so called because it bears sweet-smelling apples, as large as the Mancian apple; hence the Latins also call it the “apple of the earth.” Poets call it *anthropomorphos*, “human-shaped,” because it has a root resembling the form of a human being. [Note: Isidore: “imitating.”] Its bark, mixed with wine, is given to drink to those whose bodies are cut for healing, so that, as though put to sleep, they do not feel pain. [Note: Isidore: “whose body must be cut for treatment, so that, put to sleep, they do not feel pain.”] It has two kinds. The female [Note: “Female.”] has leaves like lettuce and bears apples resembling plums, [Col. 0762C] [Note: Isidore: “in the likeness of plums.”] whereas the male has leaves like the beet plant. [Note: Isidore: “The male, however, has leaves like those of the beet.”]

What, then, is to be said of this mandrake? [Note: [Col. 0762D] Again on Genesis, as cited above.] I therefore find the thing beautiful, with a sweet fragrance [Note: [Col. 0762D] Augustine and Isidore: “sweet-smelling, but … insipid in taste.”], but a rough taste; and hence I understand that in that mandrake apple a good public reputation is figured. Thus the Apostle says: “He must have a good testimony from those who are outside, and [Note: [Col. 0762D] Neither Augustine nor Isidore reads: “and from those who are within.”] from those who are within” (1 Tim. 3). Although these people understand little, they nevertheless commonly repay the labour of those through whom provision is made for them with both the splendour of praise and the honour of good compunction [Note: [Col. 0762D] The same authors: “the fragrance of good repute.” They do not reach this glory …], lest they outrun, in chaste public glory, those who are in the Church—except those who are [Col. 0763A] occupied amid the dangers and toil of public action. Therefore Leah’s son finds mandrakes [Note: [Col. 0763C] The same authors: “mandrake apples.” Neither reads: “that is, honourableness … namely, possessing the reputation of good fame.”], that is, honourableness: by walking honourably toward those outside, he possesses the reputation of good fame. But that teaching of wisdom which shrinks from the clamour of the crowd is most gently fixed in the contemplation of truth [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same authors: “which, most remote from the crowd’s clamour, is fixed in the contemplation of truth with sweet delight.”], and in sweet delight. Yet it is right that this manner of life too should become more widely known and should earn public glory.

After this Leah says to her sister: “Is it too little for you that you have taken my husband, and do you also wish to take my son’s mandrakes [Note: [Col. 0763D] Augustine and, below, this author: “mandrake apples.”]?” (Gen. 30). By the one husband she signifies those who, being capable through virtue of acting and worthy to have the government of the Church entrusted to them for administering the sacrament of faith, are nevertheless so inflamed with zeal for teaching and for investigating and contemplating knowledge that they wish to withdraw themselves from every burden of activity and to settle in the leisure of learning or teaching [Note: [Col. 0763D] Augustine: *condere*, “hide/place”; Isidore: *considere*, “settle.”].

Thus it is said: “Is it too little for you that you have taken my husband, and do you also wish to take my son’s mandrakes?” It is as though one said: “Is it too little that she keeps in the leisure of a studious life men necessary for the labour of accomplishing affairs [Note: [Col. 0763D] *Gerendarum*, “of carrying out affairs.”], and also seeks public glory?” Therefore, in order to obtain that glory, she justly [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same authors: “justly.”] grants [Note: [Col. 0763D] Supply “Rachel,” according to the same authors.] her husband to her sister for that night: that those fitted by virtue for the laborious government of peoples, even if they had been accustomed [Note: [Col. 0763D] Augustine: “had chosen”; Isidore: “may have chosen.”] to devote themselves to learning, may nevertheless undertake the experience [Col. 0763C] of temptations and the burden of cares for the common benefit of their neighbours. Thus the very learning to which they had resolved to devote themselves is not blasphemed; they gain the good esteem [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same authors: “nor gain from the less learned peoples the esteem,” etc.] signified by those apples; and they acquire what is necessary for exhorting learners. Yet they are indeed compelled to assume this care [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same authors: “that they assume this care, they are compelled by force.”], and are joined to her for this purpose.

This too is sufficiently signified by the fact that, when Jacob came from the field [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same authors: “was coming.”], Leah met him and, taking hold of him, said: “You shall enter in to me this night [Note: [Col. 0763D] Neither reads “this night.”], for I have hired you with my son’s mandrakes” (Gen. 30). It is as if she said: “If you wish to confer a good reputation on the learning [Note: [Col. 0763D] The same authors: “On the learning … do you wish to confer (Augustine: ‘to be conferred’) a good reputation? Do not flee dutiful labour.”] which you love, do not flee the labour of duties.”

[Col. 0764A] Whoever observes these things occurring in the Church will see them, and will experience in examples what we understand in books. [Note: [Col. 0764C] Augustine: “Whoever observes these things … sees them. We experience in examples what we understand in books.” [Col. 0764D] Isidore: “Whoever observes these things … sees them, and we experience in examples what we understand in books.”] Who does not see this happening throughout the whole world: namely, that people come from secular occupations and go to the leisure of knowing and contemplating truth, as though into Rachel’s embrace, only to be overtaken [Note: [Col. 0764D] Augustine and Isidore: “and to be unexpectedly met by ecclesiastical necessity and appointed to labour, as though Leah were saying, ‘You shall enter in to me.’”] by ecclesiastical necessity and the labour of ordination, as though Leah said, “You shall enter in to me, because I have hired you with mandrakes”? (Those who administer this mystery of God, so as to beget children in the night of this world, are commended by the Apostle in that life for the love of which, once converted, they abandoned worldly hope, and from whose profession they were taken up for the sake of begetting children, persevering therein.) [Note: [Col. 0764D] The passage is corrupt and should be restored from the same authors: “While they chastely administer the mystery of God, so as to beget children of faith in the night of this world, even that life is praised by the peoples, for love of which … they abandoned hope … and from whose profession they were taken up for the mercy [Isidore, perhaps better: *ministerium*, ‘ministry’] of governing the people.”]

For in all their labours they act so that the profession by which [Note: [Col. 0764D] The same authors: “to which they had turned themselves, because such …”] they turned themselves, which gave such rulers to the people, may be more widely and clearly glorified; as though Jacob, not refusing [Note: [Col. 0764D] The same authors: “not refusing.”] Leah’s night, might obtain Rachel, sweet with fragrant and brightly gleaming apples. At times Rachel herself also bears children, through God’s merciful favour—though scarcely and only at last [Note: [Col. 0764D] The same authors: “scarcely and only at last.”]—for it is exceedingly rare that “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), and whatever is said concerning this matter piously and wisely, may be grasped [Note: [Col. 0764D] The same authors omit “and,” and below read “may be grasped.”] healthfully, even in part, without the phantasm of carnal thought. [Note: [Col. 0764D] Here Augustine ends.]

In another sense also Victorinus the martyr and other teachers have interpreted Leah and Rachel, in the likeness of the Church and the Synagogue. For they judged that Leah, the elder, bore the type of the Synagogue, because she [Col. 0764C] first bore God’s people. Moreover, where she is read to be pregnant, this signifies that the law given through Moses was covered and sealed. But Rachel is the younger and beautiful one, because she is holy in spirit and body. Her eyes are lovely because they deserved to foresee Christ’s Gospel. She too was barren for so long, until she bore the people of the Synagogue.

Why did Jacob serve for Rachel, yet Leah the elder was substituted for her, unless it was because the Lord, in order to take the Church to himself, first joined the Synagogue to himself? Jacob’s serving for two wives signifies the time of the present life, which unfolds in seven days. In it the Lord also [Col. 0765A] took the form of a servant and became obedient to God the Father unto death. Jacob served for sheep, and our Lord said: “The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life for many,” that is, for his sheep (Matt. 20). Jacob fed sheep; and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). Jacob obtained for himself variegated cattle as the profit of his wages; Christ joined to himself the diversity of different nations. Jacob set three rods, stripped of bark, in the water-troughs so that the sheep of his flock, looking at them, might multiply; and our Lord set before the people, in the water of baptism, the names of the three powers for faith, so that those who behold these with a whole heart may become God’s sheep.

[Col. 0765B] We read [Note: [Col. 0765D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 17, chap. 17.] that the rods which Jacob set before the eyes of the sheep so that they might have variegated offspring were of poplar, almond, and plane tree. The poplar (*populus*) is so called because from its root a multitude of shoots spring up; it has two kinds, one white and one black. The white poplar is so called because its leaves are white on one side and green on the other. (Thus it is two-coloured [Note: [Col. 0765D] The passage is corrupt and should be corrected from Isidore: “Thus it is two-coloured, bearing as it were the marks of night and day, which mark the times constituted by sunrise and sunset.”], bearing as it were night and day, and indicating the times, which are determined by sunrise and sunset.) It also produces resin around the river Eridanus, like [Note: [Col. 0765D] The same authors: “as others relate.”] alum in the regions of Syria. The leaves of this tree are always altered in rain, in which pregnant and moist persons are signified.

Almond is a Greek name; in Latin they are called “long nuts,” whose fruit [Col. 0765C] is soft within and hard without. Some call it *nucicula*, “little nut,” as though it were a smaller nut. Virgil says of it [Note: [Col. 0766D] *Georgics* 1.187.]:

> … when the abundant nut  
> Clothes itself in blossom through the groves …

For before all trees it clothes itself in blossom, but it is slower than the others in producing fruit.

The plane tree (*platanus*) is a broad tree, suitable for writing letters, and is named from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and wide. For the Greeks call “broad” *platos*. Scripture expressed both the name and form of this tree, saying: “Like a plane tree I was spread abroad, or exalted, in the streets” (Ecclus. 24).

Who, then, showed Jacob that he should set rods of this sort, partly stripped of bark, before the eyes of the sheep, [Col. 0765D] so that by looking at them they might conceive and bear variegated young? Surely an angel in a vision of the night; or, as the Hebrews say, through natural science in the manner of the ancients, who say that whatever image they look upon, such offspring they produce. It is accordingly reported that the same thing is done among herds of mares: fine horses are set before the sight of females conceiving, in order that they may conceive and bring forth animals like them. Lovers of doves likewise place painted images of most beautiful doves in the same places where the birds live, so that, their sight being captivated, they may produce similar birds. Hence some order pregnant women to look upon no very ugly faces of animals, such as dog-headed creatures and monkeys, lest, if these meet their eyes, they bear similar offspring. Dog-headed creatures are themselves like monkeys, but their faces are like those of dogs; hence their name. For this is said to be women’s nature: that whatever beings they have looked upon, or conceived in mind, in the very height of sensual pleasure while they conceive, such offspring they bring forth. Indeed, in sexual intercourse an animal transmits forms from without to within; when it has been filled with them, it seizes ugly images and transforms them into its own quality.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chap. 26.] After the long servitude which Jacob endured with his father-in-law for his wives or for wages, the Lord commanded him to return to his own country. Then, without the others knowing, he hastened to fulfil what the Lord had commanded him. But Laban pursued him in anger, found him on Mount Gilead, and sought from her the idols which Rachel had stolen; yet he did not find them.

Where were these idols, and what form did they have? The Hebrews say that these idols were stolen from Ur of the Chaldeans, without Terah’s knowledge, and that they had the form of an old man. Why, then, are they called idols if there was only one?

Because gods are always spoken of in the plural, even if there is one; for thus the first teacher of all wickedness taught when he said: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3). [Note: [Col. 0766D] *Etymologies*, chap. 2.] [Col. 0766C] The Jews say that Ishmael first made an image from clay after the Flood. The Gentiles, however, maintain that Prometheus was the first to make images of men from clay, and that from him arose the art of fashioning images and statues. An idol is an image made and consecrated in human form, according to the interpretation of the word. For *idos* in Greek means “form,” and from it *idolum*, “idol,” is derived by diminution, just as among us *formula*, “little form,” is made. Hence *idolatry*: namely, every service or worship rendered to any idol. Certain Latins, ignorant of Greek speech, ineptly say that *idolum* takes its name from *dolus*, “deceit,” because the devil introduced divine worship of the creature.

[Col. 0766D] [Note: [Col. 0766D] The same author, on Genesis, as cited above.] But what does this signify: that Laban above bears another character, while here he holds the type of the devil? Laban is interpreted “whitening.” Whitening is not inappropriately understood as the devil, because, although he is dark by merit, he transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11) in order to deceive the human race. We may also understand Laban as the present world, which pursues Jacob in anger. Jacob served this world in the person of the reprobate Jewish people, from whose flesh [Col. 0767A] the Lord was born, because it strives to oppress by persecution all the elect who are known to be members of our Redeemer.

Jacob took away the daughter either of the devil or of the world when Christ joined the Church from the nations to himself. He draws her away from her father’s house when he says to her through the Prophet: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44). What is signified by the idols but avarice? Thus Paul says: “Avarice, which is the service of idols” (Col. 3). When Laban came, he did not find the idol with Jacob, because, when the treasures of the world were displayed, the devil found in our Redeemer no traces of covetousness. But what Jacob did not possess Rachel covered by sitting upon it. Rachel, who is also called “sheep,” figures the Church. But what is sitting? It is to seek the humility of repentance. For thus it is written: “Rise after you have sat down” (Ps. 126), etc. Rachel therefore covered the idols by sitting, because the holy Church, following Christ, covered the vice of earthly desire through the humility of repentance. Of this covering of vices the Prophet says in the book of Psalms: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. 31). Therefore Rachel signifies us, who press down idols by sitting, if through repentance we condemn the sins of avarice. This avarice does not befall those to whom the Psalmist says: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 26), but it especially befalls those who, walking amid the blandishments of the world, become effeminate.

[Col. 0767C] Thus also that statement of Rachel is true: “It has happened to me now according to the custom of women” (Gen. 31): namely, she made it known to her father that she had, as it were, her monthly condition. But after Laban had pursued Jacob, found him, and they had spoken together and made a covenant, Jacob took a stone and set it up as a monument. He said to his brethren: “Bring stones” (ibid.); and, gathering them, they made a mound. Laban called it the “mound of witness,” and Jacob the “heap of testimony,” according to the property of each language and speech. For among believers, both Jews and Gentiles, the prominent stone is Christ, a witness among the multitude [Note: [Col. 0767D] A likeness of Christ.]; and the heap of stones is the multitude of believers gathered together in his name and faith.

[Col. 0767D] [Note: [Col. 0768D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chap. 27.] After these things Jacob sends messengers to his brother Esau, and also sends gifts to appease him. Then, after all his household had been brought over the torrent, he himself remained alone. And behold, a man wrestled with him at the very dawn of light. Jacob prevailed and did not let him go until he had extracted a blessing from him (Gen. 32), and received the holy name Israel, in which above all the image of the Lord’s mystery was prefigured.

That man most plainly bore the type of Christ. Yet Jacob prevailed over him because he willed it, in order that the mystery of the Lord’s passion might be foreshadowed. There Jacob was seen, in the type of the Jews—that is, in the offspring of his own body—to prevail [Col. 0768A] over God and, as though with one weak, to enter into conflict with his flesh and prevail in his passion, as it is written in the Gospel: “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23). Yet Jacob obtained a blessing from that same angel whom, as victor, he had overcome, when the angel gave him another name. The giving of this name was surely a blessing. Israel means “Seeing God,” which will be the saints’ reward at the end.

Moreover, the angel touched the width of his thigh and made him lame. Thus Jacob was one and the same person, lame and blessed. For the sinew, or width, of the thigh is the multitude of a race. Many in that stock, degenerating from the faith of their father and departing from the command of their maker, limp along the paths of their error. Of them the Prophet says in the Psalms: “They limped from their paths” (Ps. 17). [Col. 0768B] Yet that people, having its strength taken away, not only limps but also grows numb, so that it can no longer beget children. Finally, when the same patriarch added that he had seen God face to face, though above he related that a man had wrestled with him, this signifies that he who wrestled with Jacob’s people would be both God and man.

Most earnestly, dearest brothers, take heed lest you wish to belong to the number of those who frequently read or hear God’s words yet depart empty from sacred reading, because they do not store those words in the ark of their heart but, through the fickleness of their mind, hand them over to forgetfulness. [Col. 0768C] Therefore preserve in the womb of memory the words of the Lord which you unceasingly receive through the ear of the body, and hasten to fulfil them with good works, so that, for Christ sowing good seed, you may, like good ground, bring forth fruit a hundredfold. Therefore diligently hear what, by God’s gift, we wish to say concerning Jacob’s ladder, which we mentioned above.

As we have already said, this ladder is Christ: the straightest way, reaching to heaven for those who believe in him. Through him, therefore, beloved, ascend to understand his divinity, in which he is equal to God the Father; through him descend to know his true humanity, which he received from the substance of his virgin mother. Through him ascend, loving him with the Father and the Holy Spirit in all things and above all things; through him descend, loving your neighbours in him as yourselves. Through him ascend to heaven, advancing from virtue to virtue; through him descend to earth, bearing your brothers’ burdens. Ascend to him through purity of heart; descend to your neighbour by mercifully supplying his need. Strive to reach him by rendering him true service; but through compassion of mind, according to your ability, assist your neighbour in need.

Again ascend from flesh to spirit and from sensuality to reason; but at times descend through charity to instruct your neighbours. [Col. 0769A] Keep yourselves, as more learned persons, in the lofty citadel of wisdom; but frequently proclaim the fear and love of the Lord to the simpler people. Hold firmly to the right course which you have begun; but do not cease to preach to your neighbours that they should avoid evil and seek good. Do not wish, if it can be done, to go on alone; rather strive to lead many with you to God. Persevere in good works; be watchful lest you fall; and gather others with you on the way of the Lord. [Col. 0770A] Labour, then, to attain fellowship with the citizens above, not alone but with a multitude of spiritual children. Therefore strive by your holy admonitions to beget many children in faith, so that with them you may attain the prize of eternal recompense, through the favour of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Fifteenth Sermon: On the Fourth Sunday of Lent

[Col. 0769]

[Col. 0769B] [Note: [Col. 0769D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chap. 25.] Moses, the servant of God, of the tribe of Levi, son of Amram, became, by the Lord’s appointment, a prophet and leader in Israel. We read that he was adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter, a friend of God, and master of that same king Pharaoh; that he was called by the Lord from the flaming yet unburnt bush. In order to make him an example, God commanded his displayed hand to become lifeless; then, when it was withdrawn, he restored its dead vigour and its former colour, and made Moses’ face radiant through communion with his own speech.

This blessed man humbly declined the leadership of all the Israelite people entrusted to him by the Lord; thereafter he devoutly accepted it, faithfully maintained it, ruled with all vigilance, corrected with discernment, loved ardently, and endured patiently. He interposed himself before God consulting him on behalf of those subject to him, and opposed God when he was angry. [Col. 0769C] For his people’s freedom he exposed his own salvation; he feared neither the threats nor weapons of the most savage king. Indeed, he raised his rod against that king’s serpents and, by God’s hand, struck down his kingdom with ten plagues. First he turned springs and rivers into blood. Then he filled cities with a multitude of frogs and the air with clouds of flies; he brought death upon the cattle, struck men with sores, devastated the land with hail, covered heaven with darkness, and destroyed the firstborn by sudden death.

After this he despoiled the Egyptians; and, when the people had been led out, with a fiery pillar going before them he opened their way. Without delay he divided the sea as he crossed it, checked the masses of water on either side, and afforded the advancing people a dry path for their feet. Then he covered their enemies with the waves and changed bitter waters into sweetness by the touch of wood. Meanwhile he gave heavenly food to hungry Israel and filled the camp-sites with food from birds; moreover, he struck a rock, and the hard stone immediately poured forth abundant streams. He also ascended the summit of Mount Sinai to behold God’s face, endured there forty days of fasting, and on descending burned the calf, struck down the sacrilegious with the sword, handed the law received from God to the people, and established the rite of religion. [Col. 0770B] Meanwhile he waged wars, was famous for victories, and, holding the rod in his hand, overcame the enemies whom he confronted. He healed the deadly bites of asps by the sight of the bronze serpent. Dathan and Abiram he cast down alive into the abyss when the earth’s joints burst open. Finally he ascended Mount Nebo, looked upon the land of promise as the Lord showed it to him, died at the Lord’s command on Mount Abarim, and was buried by him in the valley of Moab (Deut. 34), which is in Arabia. He ruled God’s people in the wilderness for forty years and died at the age of one hundred and twenty. Some, however, attest that he lives because his grave is not found and because he appeared with Elijah to the Lord on the mountain (Matt. 17). But all Holy Scripture most certainly records that he died, not that he was taken away.

Since, beloved, we have briefly set these matters forth for your instruction, it seems fitting to say more fully something concerning his deeds [Note: [Col. 0769D] Many of Moses’ deeds, which are expounded mystically at sufficient length in what follows, remain explained in vol. I, from p. 260.], as we know them to have been expounded by ecclesiastical writers. Moses, as will appear more clearly in what follows, signified Christ in every stage of his life and in the miracles wrought by his hands.

Therefore, as we have already said, when his mother bore him, she did not dare to nurse him because she feared the most savage king, but exposed him on the riverbank; there the daughter of that same king found him and adopted him as her son (Exod. 2). Moses is found on the riverbank so that the Lord also, whose type Moses bore, might be found at the river of washing—that is, at the water of baptism. [Col. 0770D] [Note: [Col. 0770D] The same author, *Questions on Exodus*, chap. 5.] The infant Moses, placed on the riverbank, shows that Christ wept over the sins of the old man whom he had put on. Thus he wept over the city of Jerusalem (Luke 19) and when raising Lazarus (John 11), lamenting the unbelief of the Jews, whom he foresaw would persist in their wickedness.

Pharaoh’s daughter descends to the river for washing and gathers up the infant; the Church from the nations, desiring the sanctification of the saving washing, receives Christ. His mother drove Moses from her house; and the Synagogue, his mother according to the flesh, drove out Christ as though he were an infant and innocent, because he seemed little when he was seen as a man. Pharaoh’s daughter found Moses enclosed in a small vessel of *tibin*, made from many wild twigs; the Church found Christ hidden in the hearts of the saints, who are woven together in unity from the members of many brothers and have all become one body in Christ; and, receiving him with religious observance, they guard him with devout minds.

Meanwhile Moses freed a brother, a stranger, from an Egyptian who was doing him injury. Not allowing this to go unavenged, he defended his brother and killed that Egyptian. [Col. 0771B] That Egyptian bore the figure of the devil, who continually injures us in this our pilgrimage. Christ, as though defending us, destroys him when he restrains his powers, so that he may not harm us as greatly as he desires. That Moses buried the slain Egyptian in sand plainly means that the devil’s now-dead presence lies hidden in those who have no foundation. Hence the Lord builds his Church upon a rock (Matt. 16), and compares those who hear his word and do it (Luke 11) to a wise man building his house upon a rock (Matt. 7), lest it be driven down by temptations and fall. But those who hear and do not act he compares to the foolish man building upon sand, whose house, when struck, suffers a great fall (ibid.).

[Col. 0771C] Then the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush, sending him to that people whom he foreknew would become wicked. There was flame in the bush—that is, among thorns—and the bush was not burned by it. [Note: [Col. 0771D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 17, chap. 7.] The Greeks call it *morus*, which the Latins call *rubus*, because its fruit or shoots are red. The mulberry (*mora*) is a wild fruit-bearing tree, by whose fruit shepherds’ hunger and scarcity in the wilderness are relieved. It is said that its leaves, cast upon a serpent, kill it. The *ramnus* is a kind of bramble, commonly called the Marsian [Note: [Col. 0771D] “Bear-like.”] thorn-bush, exceedingly rough and thorny. A thorn-brake (*sentis*) is so called from its site, that is, uncultivated land in which thorns and brambles grow.

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Again from Exodus, Isidore.] The bush signifies the thorns of Jewish sins. [Col. 0771D] The flame in the bush is the Word, because the law was given to them. The bush was not consumed by the fire, because, when the law was given, [Col. 0772A] their sins were not consumed. Others understand in the same flaming bush the Church inflamed by the persecutions of the wicked and, with it [Note: [Col. 0771D] “her.”] speaking to the Lord, not perishing but being renewed for the better.

That the Lord is read to have appeared to Moses in that bush shows that he appears to believers nowhere other than in the Church. In it no one can stand worthily or see God unless he has put away every earthly and mortal vice, as those sandals removed from Moses signified. This is also figured otherwise by Moses’ being commanded to remove his sandals. For it was the custom of the ancients that, if a bridegroom wished to repudiate a bride, he should be unshod [Note: [Col. 0771D] Isidore perhaps alludes to what is said in Scripture either in Deut. 25:9 or, more likely, Ruth 4:7. But whatever passage he had in mind, we must note that one unshoeing was religious—as that which God commanded Moses and Joshua—and another is called political by the sacred interpreters. The latter kind is the one Isidore mentions here; they distinguish it into penal and non-penal, or confirmatory. Penal unshoeing is imposed on the man who refuses to marry his childless deceased brother’s wife: the widow took off his sandal and spat in his face, in the cited passage of Deuteronomy. Confirmatory or non-penal unshoeing occurs between relatives if one yields his right to another: in order that the transfer might be firm, the transferee himself removed his sandal and gave it to his neighbour; so in the aforesaid passage of Ruth. Therefore, unshoeing can be understood as a sign of repudiation only in the sense that someone would not take his own glory as wife, or would yield to another a female relative whom he might marry, as the kinsman Boaz yielded Ruth the Moabite woman to another. It is thus a repudiation not of a marriage already contracted but of one to be contracted—something more properly called a refusal.]. Therefore Moses is commanded to be unshod, lest he approach the Church, signified in the bush, as though a bridegroom wearing sandals; for this was reserved for Christ, who was the true bridegroom. John speaks of him: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Luke 3). Surely this was said likewise to Joshua and Moses.

[Note: [Col. 0772D] Isidore, as above, chap. 8.] Moses is then sent to free Israel, and says to the Lord: “What sign have I, that they may believe me, that you have sent me?” God says to him: “Cast the rod which you hold in your hand upon the ground.” He cast it down and it became a serpent. Moses was terrified and fled. The Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail; do not fear.” He took hold of it, and it became a rod again (Exod. 4). What does this signify? The serpent persuaded man to death. Therefore death comes from the serpent. [Col. 0772C] Thus the rod in the serpent is Christ in death. Yet Moses was terrified and fled. What is Moses’ fleeing from that serpent except what we read happened in the Gospel? Christ died, the disciples fled, and they departed from the hope in which they had been.

But what was said? “Take hold of its tail.” What is the tail but the latter things? This signifies what is said elsewhere: “You shall see my back parts, but you shall not be able to see my face” (Exod. 33). For first it became a serpent, but when the tail was taken hold of, it became a rod, because first he was killed, but afterwards, when all things had been accomplished, he returned by rising again to what he had been. There, death having been consumed through the restoration of life, nothing serpentine appeared in him, because he will no longer be subject to death at all.

There is also the end of the world in the serpent’s [Col. 0772D] tail, because the Church’s mortality rolls on through the slippery course of time. Some come and others go through death, as through a serpent. Death is a path [Note: [Col. 0773D] The manuscripts initially read *seminata est*, “has been sown,” in agreement with Isidore, who adds “through the serpent”; but an untrustworthy hand corrected it to *semita est*, “is a path,” to follow another manuscript.] through the serpent; but at the final end, as at the tail of the world, we return to God’s hand. When it is grasped, we shall be restored; and, with death, the last enemy, destroyed, we shall be the rod of kingship rising in the right hand of God. [Note: [Col. 0773D] Isidore, chap. 9.]

Another sign is given to Moses. “Put your hand into your bosom,” says the Lord (Exod. 4), and he put it in. “Bring it out,” he says; he brought it out, and it was found white—that is, unclean. For whiteness in the skin is leprosy, not brightness. God’s own inheritance, that is, his people, having been put outside from among the lost, became unclean. Thus the Psalmist speaks of it: “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand from the midst of your bosom unto the end?” (Ps. 73). But he says to it: “Bring it again into your bosom,” and it returned to its colour. So too the Jewish people is now alienated from God’s bosom and has remained outside, unclean; but he will call it back, and it will return to its former colour when it acknowledges the Lord and Saviour. For now blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel might come to be (Rom. 11).

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Isidore, ch. 10.] Then the waters cast upon the earth are changed by Moses into blood; that is, the peoples are changed into faith in Christ’s blood. For the waters, as the Apocalypse says, “which you saw … are nations and peoples” (Rev. XVII).

[Note: [Col. 0773D] Isidore, ch. 11.] After this Moses and Aaron enter before Pharaoh at the Lord’s command, asking that the people of Israel be allowed to go three days’ journey into the wilderness, there to sacrifice to God. What is this three-days’ journey which [Col. 0773C] we must travel, so that, leaving Egypt, we may reach the place where we ought to offer sacrifice? This way is Christ, who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). We must travel this way for three days. For whoever confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth and believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead on the third day shall be saved. This is the three-days’ way by which one comes to the place where sacrifice is offered and a sacrifice of praise is rendered to God. “We shall go,” they say, “three days’ journey, and shall sacrifice to the Lord the abominations of the Egyptians.” For the Egyptians disdain to eat sheep; but what the Egyptians abominate, that the Israelites offer to God. For the simplicity of conscience which the wise of this age—that is, citizens of Egypt—regard as folly, the righteous [Col. 0773D] offer to God as a sacrificial victim; and by that which they see to be rejected and contemptible in the world, they strive to please God. Hence the Apostle: “God chose the foolish things of the world in order to confound the strong” [Note: [Col. 0774D] See our note, vol. I, p. 268.] (I Cor. I).

But from the time when Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God are afflicted more severely. From the time when the word of God has been uttered in a person’s soul, the crafty enemy rises more fiercely and introduces greater vices by which that person may be overcome. Before the word came to rebuke vices, [Col. 0774A] vices reigned in peace; but when the word of God begins to distinguish each person’s condition, then great disturbance arises. [Note: [Col. 0774D] Isidore, ch. 12.]

Then Moses cast down the rod before Pharaoh, and, having become a serpent, it devoured the serpents of the Egyptians; signifying that the Word would become flesh and would annul the serpent’s dreadful poisons. For the rod is a straight, royal word, full of authority and an emblem of power. The rod became a serpent because he who was the Son of God, begotten of God the Father, was born of the Virgin and became the Son of man; and, raised up like a serpent upon the cross, he poured medicine into human wounds. Hence the Lord himself says: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of man be lifted up” (John III), and so forth. For Moses’ rod, turned into a dragon, swallowed the rods of the magicians; and Christ, after the dignity of glory, became obedient unto death (Phil. II), and through that death of the flesh consumed the sting of death, as the prophet testifies in these words: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. XIII).

[Note: [Col. 0774D] Isidore, ch. 13.] God hardens Pharaoh’s heart; that is, after his sin he hardened the devil in such a way that he would never be softened by the compunction of repentance, as is written of him in Job: “His heart shall be hardened like a stone” (Job XLI).

[Note: [Col. 0774D] Isidore, ch. 14.] Although those ten plagues came upon Egypt bodily, they are nevertheless now enacted spiritually in us. For Egypt is a figure of the world, in which waters are changed into blood by the Lord’s command. [Col. 0774C] The waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of philosophers; and they are rightly changed into blood, because they think carnally about the causes of things. But when Christ’s cross reveals to this world the light of truth, it rebukes it by such chastisements that, from the nature of its punishments, the world may recognize the sins it has committed.

In the second plague frogs are produced. By them we judge the songs of poets to be figuratively indicated, since they brought into this world fables of deception in a certain empty and swollen modulation, like the singing and noises of frogs. For a frog is the most talkative kind of vanity. The creature itself has no other use or benefit except that it makes a sound with its voice in wicked and importunate cries. [Note: [Col. 0774D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, XII.6.] Frogs are so called from their chattering, because they make a din [Col. 0774D] about breeding marshes and emit vocal sounds. Some of them are called aquatic, some marsh-dwelling, and some *rubetae*, because they live among brambles and are the largest of all. Others are called *calamitae*, because they dwell among reeds and bushes: the smallest and greenest of all, mute and voiceless. There are also *gradulae* [Note: [Col. 0774D] *Agredulae*.], small frogs that remain on dry ground or in fields, and are so named accordingly. They even prevent dogs from barking when live frogs have been given to them in a morsel.

[Col. 0775A] [Note: [Col. 0775D] Again from the *Questions*, ch. 14.] After this gnats (*ciniphes*) are produced. This creature is indeed borne aloft on wings as it flits through the air; but it is so subtle and small that it escapes the sight unless one looks very sharply. Yet when it settles upon a body, it pierces it with an exceedingly sharp sting, so that one who cannot see it flying immediately feels it wounding. This kind of creature is compared with the subtlety of heretics, who pierce the soul with subtle verbal stings and ensnare it with such cunning that the deceived person neither sees nor understands the source of the deception.

That the magicians ceased at the third sign, saying, “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII), means that they represented heretics and their obstinacy. The Apostle makes this clear, saying: “As Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist [Col. 0775B] the truth: people corrupted in mind, rejected concerning the faith. But they shall proceed no further, for their madness shall be manifest to all, as theirs also was” (II Tim. III). They were exceedingly restless through corruption of mind, but at the third sign they failed, confessing that the Holy Spirit, who was in Moses, was opposed to them. For the Holy Spirit is placed third and is called the finger of God. Thus they too, failing at the third sign, said, “This is the finger of God.” For just as the reconciled and appeased Holy Spirit grants rest to the meek and humble in heart, so, being contrary and hostile, he agitates the proud and harsh with unrest. For those tiny flies signified unrest; under their agitation Pharaoh’s magicians failed and said, “This is the finger of God.”

[Col. 0775C] In the fourth place Egypt is struck with flies. For the fly is a very insolent and restless creature. What else is signified by it but the insolent anxieties of carnal desires? Egypt, therefore, is struck with flies because the hearts of those who love this world are struck by the restlessness of their desires. Moreover, the Seventy Interpreters rendered it *cynomyia* [Note: [Col. 0775D] *Coenomyia*.], that is, the dog-fly, by which dog-like habits are signified, in which the pleasure of the human mind and the lust of the flesh are reproved. [Note: [Col. 0775D] Id., *Etymologies*, XII.8.] *Cynomyia* is Greek; in Latin it is called the dog-fly. [Note: [Col. 0775D] Again from the *Questions*, as above.] For *kynos* is the Greek word for “dog.” In this passage the dog-fly may also signify forensic human eloquence, because people tear one another apart like dogs.

[Col. 0775D] In the fifth place Egypt is struck with the death of animals or cattle. Here the folly and stupidity of mortals are reproved: they imposed divine worship and names upon figures made of wood and stone, not only images of human beings but also of beasts. They venerated Ammon—that is, Jupiter—in the form of a ram, and the Danube in the form of a dog; they also worshipped Apis. Egypt likewise marvels at other monstrous gods; and in those things to which they believed [Col. 0776A] divine worship was due, they saw pitiable punishments.

After this, ulcers with burning blisters are produced in the sixth plague. In the ulcers is reproved this world’s deceitful malice; in the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; in the burning inflammations, the madness of anger and rage. Up to this point they endured such punishments of the world because of the error of their images. [Note: [Col. 0775D] Isidore: “the punishments of the world are moderated by their images.”]

After this come blows from above: voices and thunder, hail and running fire. In the thunders are understood the corrections of divine rebuke, because God does not strike in silence, but gives utterance and sends teaching from heaven, through which the chastened world may recognize its own fault. He also gives hail, by which the still tender growths of vices may be laid waste. He gives fire also, [Col. 0776B] knowing that there are thorns and thistles which that fire must consume—the fire of which the Lord says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and I desire that it should burn” (Luke XII). By it the incitements of pleasure and lust are consumed and uprooted.

That locusts are mentioned in the eighth place is thought by some to mean that, by this kind of plague, the instability of the divided human race is rebuked.
