In another sense, locusts should be understood, because of their mobility, as levity: souls wandering and leaping about amid the world’s pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0776D] Id., *Etymologies*, XII.8.] The locust is so called because it has long feet like a spear. Hence the Greeks call it *astakos*, both the marine and the land creature.

The ninth plague was darkness, either in order that the blindness of their minds might be reproved, or that they might understand that the purposes of divine [Col. 0776C] dispensation and providence are most obscure. For “God made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. XVII); and those who wished boldly and rashly to search it out, attaching one thing to another, fell into thick and palpable darkness of ignorance. Finally, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed: either the principalities and powers and the world-rulers of darkness [Note: [Col. 0776D] Supplemented from Isidore: “or the authors and inventors of false …”] which existed in this world, of false religions, which Christ’s truth extinguished and destroyed along with their promoters through the venerable mystery of his cross. Moreover, as the Hebrews maintain, he executed the following judgment upon their gods: on the night when the people departed, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed, whether by an earthquake or by lightning strikes. [Col. 0776D] Spiritually, however, we say that when we leave Egypt, the vain idols of errors collapse for us, and every cult of perverse doctrines is shaken. [Note: [Col. 0776D] Isidore, on Exodus, ch. 15.] Meanwhile the Passover takes place in the slaughter of the lamb. Christ is slain, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I).

The offertory derives its name from this cause. An offering placed upon the altar and sacrificed by bishops or priests is called *fertum*, and from this the *offertory* is named, as it were “because of the *fertum*.” [Col. 0777A] It is called an *oblation* because it is offered. Divine gifts, indeed, are called the offerings of human beings. For *munera* are services which poor people render to the rich in place of gifts. Thus a *munus* is given to a human being, a *donum* to God. Hence we also call votive offerings in temples *donaria*. They are called *munera* because they are either received or given by hands. There are two things that are offered: namely, a gift and a sacrifice. A gift is whatever is made of gold or silver or any other material. A sacrifice is a victim and whatever is burned or placed upon an altar. Everything given or dedicated to God is given by being spoken, whence it is also called so. Therefore those who think that consecration is signified by dedication are mistaken.

*Immolatio* was so called by the ancients because the victim placed upon the mass of the altar [Col. 0777B] was slain. Hence *mactatio* follows *immolatio*. Now, however, *immolatio* applies to bread and the cup [Note: [Col. 0777D] “To bread … to the cup.”]; *libatio* is the offering of the cup alone. Hence the saying: “And the priest poured out an offering from the blood of the grape” (Ecclus. L). So also one of the secular poets says [Note: [Col. 0777D] *Aeneid*, VII.133.]:

> “Now,” he says, “pour out the bowls for Jupiter.” [Note: [Col. 0777D] “Pour them out.”]

Thus *libare* properly means “to pour out,” and the term is derived from a certain Liber, who discovered the use of the vine in Greece. Concerning the rejection of the old sacrifice, the Lord says through Isaiah: “What use to me is the multitude of your victims? says the Lord. I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fattened beasts; and the blood of calves, [Col. 0777C] lambs, and goats I have not desired” (Isa. I). By using the past tense, “I have not desired,” the Lord shows that he never loved the sacrifices of the Jews, but endured them for a time because of what they signified and, once the true sacrifice had been fulfilled, reckoned them as nothing.

Among the ancients, *hostiae* were sacrifices performed before they went against an enemy; *victimae* were sacrifices offered after victory over conquered enemies. *Victimae* were greater sacrifices than *hostiae*. Others thought that *victima* was so called because it fell when struck by a blow, or because it was led bound to the altars. A holocaust is that in which everything offered is consumed by fire. For when the ancients performed the greatest sacrifices, they used to consume whole victims in the flame of the rites, and these were holocausts. For *holon* [Note: [Col. 0778D] *Olon*.] means “whole” in Greek; *kausis*, “burning.” Thus *holocaustum* means “wholly burned.” Therefore, dearest brethren, we have inserted these matters here so that you may without difficulty recognize the distinctions among sacrifices, *hostiae*, *victimae*, holocausts, immolations, *munera*, and *donaria*.

Therefore, as we said above, the Passover takes place in the slaughter of the lamb. Christ is slain, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). The lamb is sacrificed in the evening; Christ was sacrificed in the evening of the world. Those who celebrate the Passover are forbidden [Col. 0778A] to break the bones; on the cross the Lord’s bones are not broken, as the Evangelist testifies: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John XIX). The doorposts of the Israelites are smeared with the lamb’s blood, lest the destroying angel dare bring destruction; the faithful peoples are marked on their foreheads for the safeguard of salvation by the sign of the Lord’s passion, so that only those may be delivered from destruction who are marked in heart and forehead by the blood of the Lord’s passion. They also proclaim in their deeds: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. IV).

Hence the feast of Passover itself is called a passing-over, because, advancing from worse things to better, we leave dark Egypt behind. But what it says about eating that lamb—“No foreigner shall eat of it; it shall be eaten in one house, and none of its flesh shall be carried outside” [Col. 0778B] (Exod. XII)—must properly be understood concerning the sacrament of Christ’s body, of which that lamb was the figure. We are commanded to feed on that body and blood in one house, that is, in one Church; and it is not to be carried outside, namely among the communities of heretics who wander outside the same unity of the Catholic Church.

Then God commands the people through Moses to ask the Egyptians for goods which they might carry away. [Note: [Col. 0778D] Isidore, ch. 16.] Thus Moses and the departing people despoiled the Egyptians of gold and silver at the command of the Lord, who commanded nothing unjustly. What does this prefigure except that, in the gold, silver, and clothing, certain Egyptian teachings are signified—teachings learned through useless study from the very custom of the Gentiles? Or, whether this signifies that precious souls from among the Gentiles themselves, like vessels of gold and silver, together with their bodies (which are signified by garments), may be freed from this world as from Egypt and, through Moses—that is, Christ—be brought to the land of promise, namely to the heavenly homeland.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] Id., ch. 16.] But the statement that the children of Israel departed Egypt without leaven must be worked out by us in every possible way, if possible: namely, that when we leave the enticements of this world we may not walk in the old leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (I Cor. V), which is the conduct of the new human being after abandoning the first human being with his vices. They indeed ate unleavened bread for seven days; but if we live purely and simply through the seven [Col. 0778D] days in which the world runs its course, always revolving in their order, then every day the lamb is sacrificed for us and the Passover is continually celebrated without the leaven of malice and wickedness—if, renewed, we take no delight in any malice of the old corruption. For what else is leaven except a corruption of nature, which has departed from natural sweetness and been corrupted by adulterous love?

During this dwelling we are commanded always to remember our departure from Egypt; to celebrate the Passover, that is, our passage from worse things to better; and to consecrate to the Lord the firstborn of our womb, [Col. 0779A] that is, the beginnings of our works and of every virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0779D] Isidore, ch. 18.] At that time the Lord appears by night in a pillar of fire and, by day, goes before the people in a pillar of cloud, becoming the guide of their journey. This cloud going before them is Christ, and likewise the pillar: he is upright and steadfast, shining for our weakness; not shining by day but shining by night, so that those who do not see, and those who see, may become blind. The mystery of Christ may also appropriately be understood: in the flesh, as in a cloud, it is as though manifest in daytime; but in judgment it is as in the terror of night, because there will then be a great tribulation of the world like fire, and it will shine for the righteous and burn for the unrighteous.

Then, as the Egyptians pursued them, Moses struck [Col. 0779B] the waters with his rod while the others looked on; they were divided this way and that, and the children of Israel passed through the midst of the Red Sea. What does this signify except baptism consecrated by the blood of Christ? The pursuing enemies with their king, who die behind them, are past sins which are blotted out, and the devil and his attendants, who are drowned in spiritual baptism. The Egyptians press hard in pursuit; sins follow and assail them up to the water of baptism.

The people of God sing a song after crossing the Red Sea, when Pharaoh and the Egyptians have been submerged. Spiritually, after believers rise from the font with their sins extinguished, they give forth a hymn in a voice of rejoicing, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honoured; horse and rider [Col. 0779C] he has cast into the sea” (Exod. XV). Yet this is said better and more worthily by one who, like Mary, has a timbrel in hand—that is, one who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires, and has mortified his members which are upon the earth.

Thereafter, after crossing the sea, the people are led through the wilderness: that is, baptized people, enjoying the promised homeland [Note: [Col. 0779D] This passage seems to have a somewhat obscure sense in the manuscript, which reads: “Baptized people, enjoying the promised homeland through the world, and hoping for what they do not see, are by patience awaiting it, and are with them,” etc. Nor does it appear clearer in Isidore, which reads: “All the baptized pass through the world, not enjoying the promised homeland; but hoping for what they do not see and awaiting it by patience, they are as though in a wilderness, and there are laborious temptations there lest they return,” etc. Our punctuation may explain the passage: just as after crossing the sea the people are led through the wilderness, so baptized people who already enjoy the promised homeland are led through the world: they are led, namely, by patiently hoping for what they do not see and by unfailingly awaiting it in this world as though in a wilderness.], through the world; and, hoping by patience for what they do not see, they await it unfailingly as though in a wilderness. There too are laborious and dangerous temptations, lest they return to Egypt in heart and Christ finally abandon them in the solitude.

After this the people come to the place called Elim, where there were twelve springs of water, as though twelve figures of the apostles, and seventy palm trees [Col. 0779D] as a type of the seventy disciples, by whose preaching [Note: [Col. 0780D] “By whose preaching.”] a multitude of Gentiles hastened to the palm of Christ’s victory.

[Col. 0780A] [Note: [Col. 0780D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, XII.7.] Meanwhile, in the wilderness, because of hunger the people turned and looked from afar upon God’s glory in the cloud; in the evening they saw quail, and on the morning of the following day, manna. Quails are so named from the sound of their voice. The Greeks call them *ortygas*, because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. They also have seasons for their arrival, because, when summer is driven away, they cross the seas. The *ortygometra* is the bird which leads the flock; when it approaches land, a hawk sees and carries it off. Therefore all are concerned to put a bird of another species in charge, so that through it they may avoid the first dangers. They find the seeds of poisonous plants most pleasing food; for this reason the ancients forbade people to eat them. This creature alone, like the human being, suffers from the falling sickness.

For what is signified by the food of birds except divinely sent preaching, which passes through sounding words like true winged birds in flight? By faith those who strive to attain the homeland of the heavenly kingdom are fed by it. [Col. 0780B] ([Note: [Col. 0780D] A remarkably incomplete passage, supplied here from Isidore: “The food of birds may signify the utterances of the old law, which fed the carnal people as with flesh, through words divinely sent as through birds. Hence it is given in the evening, because all things granted to them carnally were destined to have an end. But when the light of faith has been revealed, manna is given to the people. Manna, indeed, etc.”] The food of birds can indeed signify the utterances of the old law, which fed the carnal people as with flesh through words divinely sent, as through birds. Hence it is given in the evening, because all that was granted to them carnally was destined to have an end. But when the light of faith has been revealed, manna is given to the people.)

Manna, indeed, is Christ, who descended from heaven as the living bread and is rained upon the whole world through the cloud of the Gospel—not now upon the murmuring and tempting synagogue, but upon the Church that believes and places hope in him. This is the unfailing manna; this is the bread of heaven and the true food of angels: the Word of God, which feeds corruptible beings incorruptibly. So that a human being might eat it, the Word [Col. 0780C] became flesh and dwelt among us (John I); and those who feed upon it live spiritually. For those who looked carnally upon the old figure died.

Not inappropriately, heavenly utterances are signified by manna; and the interpretation of the name likewise has this sense: *Manhu?* (Exod. XVI) [Note: [Col. 0780D] In vol. I, p. 290, in agreement with Origen, Augustine, and Isidore: “For *manna* means: WHAT IS THIS?”] means “What is this?” For when we hear the law of God read in the Church, we ask the teachers, saying, “What is this?” This manna, moreover, was like a very small seed of coriander and sweet to eat. What is more minute than God’s word, what more subtle, or what sweeter and more delightful than the utterances of God, which are “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. XVIII) to those who hear or read them?

But why is a double portion commanded to be gathered on the sixth day, sufficient also for the Sabbath? This sixth day [Col. 0780D] is the sixth age of the world, in which we now live. In this age, that person gathers a double portion who, in hope of eternal life, both hears and does God’s word. In this age that person stores up a double portion [Col. 0781A] who both lives well and shows mercy to others. What was stored for after the Sabbath decayed. But good works done for the sake of eternal rest remain incorrupt in the world to come. Those, however, who were unbelieving and kept it from morning without regard to the Sabbath, swarmed with worms and rotted. So too those who lay up treasure for the present life and the love of the world swarm with worms that endure forever. These are the worms generated by blind avarice and desire for riches in those who possess money and, seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts against them (I John III). Likewise, one who sins after receiving God’s word finds God’s word itself made a worm that continually pierces his conscience and gnaws the hidden places of his breast. Yet Christ also is a worm, as he says: “I am a worm and not a human being” (Ps. XXI). As he is for some a fall and for others a resurrection, so in manna he is sweetness of honey to believers but becomes a worm to unbelievers.

Then Moses offends the Lord at the water of contradiction and is forbidden to cross the Jordan into the land of promise. Troubled by the people’s murmuring, he struck the rock uncertainly with his rod; but immediately waters flowed and flooded the valleys of the torrents (Ps. LXXVII). In Holy Scripture Moses represents one person or another according to his various miracles; but in this place he held the figure of the Jewish people under the law, which, fastening Christ to the wood, doubted his power [Col. 0781C] and divinity. Therefore, as water flowed from the struck rock for the thirsty, so the wound of the Lord’s passion became life for believers.

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Isidore, ch. 27.] After this, on the forty-seventh day after the people’s departure from Egypt, they came to Mount Sinai; there Moses went up to the Lord, and the Lord came down to him. For the mountain is a figure of the height of contemplation, upon which we ascend so that we may be raised to behold things beyond our weakness. But the Lord descends upon it because, when the saints make great progress, he reveals a little something of himself to their minds.

Then, on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been completed, the law was given to Moses. So too on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s passion, which that Passover prefigured, [Col. 0781D] the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete promised by Christ, descended upon the apostles and [Note: [Col. 0781D] “And upon them.”] those who were with them in the city, one hundred and twenty in number—the age of Moses, [Note: [Col. 0781D] “Having been established.”] and the whole world was filled with evangelical preaching through the divided tongues of believers. There the law is said to have been written by God’s finger, which casts out demons. All the people look there upon voices and lamps, the smoking mountain, thunder and lightning, and the blaring sound of the trumpet. In the voices and thunders the Holy Spirit is understood; in the lamps the brightness of miracles is signified; in the trumpet’s sound the mighty preaching [Col. 0782A] of the saints is understood. All these things were fulfilled at the coming of the Holy Spirit, when all Christ’s disciples thundered forth in diverse tongues by precepts and signs.

Sinai, moreover, is interpreted “bush,” signifying the Church in which the Lord also speaks to Moses. The fact that the Lord, about to give the law, comes down in fire and smoke signifies that he both illumines believers by the brightness of his manifestation and darkens the eyes of unbelievers through the smoke of error. The fact that he is seen in darkness signifies that the impious, who think earthly thoughts, did not recognize him when he descended—that is, when he was born in humility—because of the darkness of wickedness. Therefore he was seen in darkness and gave the law, because to unbelievers who do not follow the truth of his law he spoke as through darkness: “That seeing they may not see, and hearing [Col. 0782B] they may not understand” (Luke VIII).

[Note: [Col. 0782D] Isidore, ch. 29.] God then gives Moses the law of innocence and the knowledge of himself, establishes it in ten sayings, and writes it with his finger on stone tablets. These commandments are arranged so that three concern love of the divine Trinity, and seven concern brotherly love, by which human society is not harmed. The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father when it says: “The Lord your God is one God” (Deut. VI): namely, that hearing this you may worship the one God the Father and not pour out your fornication among many invented gods.

The second commandment pertains to the Son when it says: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Exod. XX); that is, do not judge Christ, the Son of God, to be a creature, [Col. 0782C] because every creature is subject to vanity; but believe him to be equal with the Father, God from God, the true Word with God, through whom all things were made.

The third commandment concerns the Sabbath and pertains to the Holy Spirit, through whose gift eternal rest in heaven is promised us. Since he is called Spirit, the Lord also sanctified the seventh day. In the other days of works sanctification is not named, but only in the Sabbath, where it says: “God rested from all his work” (Gen. II). Therefore this commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit, both because of the name of sanctification and because eternal rest pertains to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it says there: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day. For six days you shall work [Col. 0782D] and do all your works. The seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work on it, but shall rest” (Exod. XX). [Note: [Col. 0782D] See the notes, vol. I, p. 303.]

The six days of works contain the activity of six thousand years. In the seventh, however, is shown the rest and time of that blessed kingdom, which the Jews sin by celebrating carnally. We do not desire this in the faith of deceiving falsehood, since the Lord says through the prophet: “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isa. I). How then could Sabbaths be sanctified which God’s soul hates? That Sabbath, therefore, is sanctified in which eternal rest is promised us after the good works of this life. Thus whatever we do, if we do it for the rest of the age to come, we truly observe the Sabbath.

After these three commandments follows the number seven of commandments pertaining to love of neighbours. The first is on the second tablet and begins with honouring parents, although it is fourth in sequence: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. XX). How, then, is the first commandment the fourth? As stated above, among the number seven which pertains to love of neighbour, it is first on the second tablet. For this reason two tablets of the law were given. Thus children are commanded in this precept to honour their parents and not to be insulting, but to render them the reverence due through filial devotion. For [Col. 0783B] one who does not know how to pay honour to parents—whom can such a person spare or assist? Or how can one love others who hates one’s own people?

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery”; that is, no one is to have intercourse with other women outside the bond of marriage in order to satisfy lust. For one commits adultery in the particular sense when one approaches another woman besides one’s own. The sixth: “You shall not kill.” Not only one who commits homicide, but also one who sees a hungry or naked person and does not assist by providing clothing and food, is held guilty as a murderer. The seventh: “You shall not commit theft,” which is the vice of rapacity. The eighth: “You shall not bear false witness,” which is the crime of lying and falsehood. The ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s wife.” [Col. 0783C] The tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s field or other possessions.” In these precepts he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the desire for possessions.

Thus the first forbids superstition; the second, error; the third destroys love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth shatters fornication; the sixth, cruelty; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth destroys falsehood; the ninth, the thought of adultery; the tenth, the covetousness of the world.

And it should be noted that, as the Egyptians are struck with ten plagues, so the tablets by which the people of God are governed are inscribed with ten commandments. [Note: [Col. 0783D] Isidore, ch. 30.] Why, moreover, was the law written on two tablets, except to signify either the two Testaments or those two commandments—namely love of God and of neighbour—upon which the whole law and the prophets depend? (Matt. XXII.) [Col. 0783D] These are to be expounded in the individual tablets. For one contains the three commandments of God pertaining to charity; the other, the seven pertaining to fellowship with one’s neighbour.

[Note: [Col. 0783D] Isidore, ch. 31.] But why were these tablets of stone, except [Col. 0784A] to signify the stony heart of the Jews? For by the insensibility of stone we understand the stupidity of their hard mind. Hence the prophet: “I shall take away the heart of stone, and shall give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XI). Hence also the Apostle: “Not on tablets,” he says, “of stone, but on tablets of the heart” (II Cor. III). [Note: [Col. 0783D] Supplemented “of flesh” from Isidore, or “fleshy,” from vol. I, fol. 312. In the same place, more in accordance with the same Father, the later reading is: “Nor do these tablets … intend that we should think carnally; but because flesh feels in comparison with stone … therefore an understanding heart is signified by a heart of flesh.” Isidore: “Nor do these tablets … intend … therefore, by the hardness of stone, a heart that does not understand is signified, and by fleshly sensibility an understanding heart is signified.”] These tablets do not intend that we should think carnally; but, in comparison with stone, which lacks sensation, flesh has feeling. Therefore, by the hardness of stone, an understanding heart is signified.

Accordingly, when Moses came down from the mountain with the tablets and heard that the people consecrated to God had turned to idols, judging them unworthy to receive the law, he threw the tablets from his hands. When they were broken, he burned the calf which they had made, cut it into very small pieces, scattered it upon the waters, and gave the people the drink. [Col. 0784B] As some maintain, the Hebrews worshipped the head of the calf, not its body; for the body of the devil consists of all the Gentile peoples, while the calf’s head is the devil. [Note: [Col. 0784D] These words are not Isidore’s.] Moses burned it—that is, Christ burns up idolatry. Therefore Moses crushed and burned the calf so that those who worshipped it as God might see it as dung, and thus no one might deem it worthy of worship.

For this reason the children of Israel worshipped it: it was of varied colour, as though its form had been fashioned or painted. The children of Israel had always been shepherds, loved livestock, and preferred those of varied colour to those of one colour. Therefore they made the form of that calf variegated and painted, and set it before their livestock at the time of breeding, so that, namely, they might please the Egyptians [Col. 0784C] in whose land they dwelt, because they kept their god before them; and so that their livestock might conceive offspring of varied colour, because Jacob had first chosen that colour as his own share from Laban’s sheep.

After this Moses said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, join me.” At once the sons of Levi attached themselves to him. To them he said: “Go back and forth from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each one kill his brother, neighbour, and friend” (Exod. XXXII). [Note: [Col. 0784D] Isidore, ch. 39.] To go from gate to gate is to go from vice to vice, by which death enters the mind, and to range about with the sword of discernment. Moreover, the very number [Note: [Col. 0784D] Isidore: “twenty-three thousand.” But the reading “three thousand,” found also in the Old Italic version and followed tenaciously by Martin here and in vol. I, fol. 361, appears more consistent with Isidore’s intention in this allegorical exposition; for otherwise the number twenty-three thousand cannot signify a threefold form. We do not doubt that the text of the blessed bishop was corrupted either by editors following the Vulgate or by printers.] of three thousand slain indicates the threefold form of sins. For every sin is committed [Col. 0784D] either in thought, word, or deed.

Moses therefore went up the mountain again, and God again gave him the law on other tablets cut in the likeness of the former ones. The earlier tablets represented the image of the ancient law, which did not cease the people’s sin after a long interval. [Col. 0785A] But the other tablets, cut anew after the pattern of the former, bore the figure of the New Testament. These are not broken, in order to show that the utterances of the New Testament are to endure.

What, then, is meant by Moses’ fasting for forty days? His fast has a certain symbolic meaning in the consideration of this number. For Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for the forty-day period. We are commanded by the Law and the Prophets [Note: [Col. 0785D] Supply here: “and by the Gospel itself, which has testimony from the Law and the Prophets.”]—which is why the Saviour shone forth on the mountain between the two persons—that we should restrain our appetite from all the enticements of the world, as by the fast of temperance, for as long as the perfection of the Decalogue is preached through the four regions of that same world, that is, throughout the whole globe: thus ten multiplied four times signifies the number forty. [Col. 0785B]

Furthermore, dearly beloved, observe that the number of the days of the holy Forty Days was instituted not only by the holy Fathers but consecrated also by the Lord Jesus Christ. Moses’ fast for forty days and as many nights on Mount Sinai was accomplished not by his own strength but by God’s ordering grace. Nor could Elijah, even through the strength or refreshment of a single hearth-baked loaf, have walked forty days and forty nights unless God’s mercy had granted this to him (III Kings XIX). The Son of God likewise consecrated this number by fasting in his own person, and commanded that it be observed by his whole Church for the remission of sins.

Therefore these sacred fasts are not to be despised by believers [Col. 0785C] or passed over idly or negligently, since they were instituted not by human will or wisdom, but by divine ordering. Thus no one should neglect to do for the remission of his sins what the Son of God and man—who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found (I Pet. II)—is known to have done in order to give us an example of abstinence.

Yet amid these matters it must be known that fasting weakens the body, strengthens the spirit, multiplies virtues in the soul, uproots vices, moderates nature’s heat, subdues fleshly pleasure, and lifts prayers up to heaven. It is good, therefore, to weary the body by fasts, if charity is preserved in one’s conduct. It is good to restrain vices by fasting [Col. 0785D] if charity remains whole in the mind. Although one fast from bodily food, nevertheless, if one retains hatred of one’s neighbour in one’s breast, or does not refrain from other vices, one cannot obtain forgiveness of sins.

The prophet Jeremiah laments those who abstain from fleshly food in this manner, readily break the bond of love, and do not resist vices, saying: “Those who feasted luxuriously have perished in the streets; those brought up in saffron,” that is, aromatic herbs, “have embraced dung” (Lam. IV).

[Note: [Col. 0786D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, bk. XVII, ch. 9.] Saffron—an aromatic herb—is said to take its name from a Cilician town called Corinthium, although [Col. 0786A] it also grows elsewhere, though not in such quantity or of such quality as in Cilicia; and therefore it takes its name from the more prominent place. For many things have received names from places where they grew more abundantly and in better quality.

Let it therefore be said: “Those who feasted luxuriously,” and so forth. Truly, those who abandon charity and the other virtues, in which they were nourished as it were amid saffron, embrace the dung of transgressions. Hence it is said: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I). Like beasts rotting in dung are those who, amid the stench of their own lust, serve their vices either by desires of the heart under the appearance of virtues or under the garb of holiness. Since there are many who practise fasts and other good works without discernment, do not reject vices, and refuse worthily to repent or weep, the prophet laments them in the person of the Church. For they do not know how to lament themselves [Col. 0786B] and, through love of sinning, do not cease to embrace dung—that is, vices.

“Those who feasted luxuriously,” he says, and so forth, appear to feast luxuriously upon the virtues of the soul, fasts, vigils, prayers, the delights—that is, utterances—of the Scriptures, and the other virtues; and to be nourished amid saffron, when they are affectionately satisfied and enlightened by love of God and neighbour. For the saffron colour signifies the brightness of love. Saffron has the appearance of fire and displays the ardour of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, when charity is lost, the remaining virtues embrace dung and are reckoned as nothing, because from the good fragrance of love for God and neighbour they pass to the stench of hatred and perversity. Hence Paul says: “If I do not have charity, [Col. 0786C] I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII).

There are many who secretly seek pleasures but wish to appear abstinent in public. Within, they conceal disordered worldly desires; outwardly, they show themselves to be despisers of the world. Externally they parade holiness; inwardly they hide vices. Foreseeing their wickedness in the Spirit, the prophet Jeremiah lamented in the person of the same Church, saying: “The iniquity of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and hands did not begin in her” (Lam. IV).

The Church laments, as we have said, the crimes of her people who fall into hypocrisy. His iniquity is greater than the sin of Sodom, because he covers evils by gilding them over and even performs good acts deceitfully. As the people rises up against itself, so the morals and actions of hypocrites contend against themselves; and the good works they perform hypocritically are worse than the vices of Sodom. For when the unclean spirit has gone out of a man, if he returns with more wicked spirits, the latter state of that man becomes worse than the former (Matt. XII). The spirit goes out of a person when he is reborn in Christ. It returns when it finds the soul empty of good work, cleansed from filth by hypocrisy, and adorned with pretences. Then the soul is filled with many unclean spirits, and its iniquity becomes greater than the sin of Sodom.

“The iniquity of my people,” he says—that is, of their vices and [Col. 0787A] deeds—“and she did not lay hands to the fruit of good work”: outwardly adorned with false goods, inwardly filled with vices. Truly, the iniquity of Christians today is greater than that of the Sodomites, because, knowing their Lord’s will and scorning to fulfil it in deed, they sin more grievously than those who had no knowledge of God. Had they known God’s will as fully as we know it, they either would not have committed so great a crime, or at least, in accordance with the Lord’s judgment, would long ago have done penance for their sins in ashes and sackcloth. Hence it is said: “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke XII).

For we see that faith and justice have left the earth; humanity and kindness are nowhere; discord and desire have set [Col. 0787B] the world ablaze; anger and envy are a devouring flame; the Church is ravaged by thefts and frauds; the poor are stripped to the bone; and now almost the whole world lies uncultivated amid thick brambles. The rights of laws are treated as fables; divine and human things, lawful and unlawful, are confused. Countless evils accumulate every day. Therefore our iniquity is greater than that of those who did not know the way of truth and consequently deserved lesser punishments, since they were overthrown in a moment.

A “moment,” as blessed Isidore says, [Note: [Col. 0787D] *Etymologies*, bk. V, ch. 29.] is the smallest and narrowest span of time, named from the movement of the stars. It is the end-point of an hour in brief intervals, when one thing gives way to and succeeds another. *Hora* is a Greek word, though it has a Latin sound. [Col. 0787C] For an *hora* is a boundary of time, just as shores (*orae*) are the boundaries of the sea, rivers, and garments. Thus a moment is all that we live; and by sinning daily we are, as it were, overthrown to punishment in a moment, since we deserve worse things and store up wrath for ourselves on the day of judgment.

There are many who abstain from bodily foods, yet not for God, but in order to receive praise from men. In public they seem to abstain from vices as well as food before others, but secretly they seek pleasures and do things unworthy of and hateful to God. The prophet again laments them when he says: “Her Nazarites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, redder than old ivory, more beautiful than sapphire” (Lam. IV). The Church has her Nazarites [Col. 0787D] whiter than snow and brighter than milk, by whom the life of those who abstain is signified. Snow comes from above; milk from flesh, as it were from below. Thus by snow is shown the brightness of heavenly life; by milk, the ordering of temporal affairs.

The Church, therefore, has Nazarites who through contemplation lead a heavenly life and through the ordering of the active life shine brighter than milk to the praise of the Creator; so that they often surpass in works of virtue those who have maintained a heavenly life or administered earthly matters well. Since through the fervour of the spirit they appear to surpass the lives of the ancient and strong Fathers, it is rightly added: “Redder than old ivory.” While the beauty of redness is praised, the flame of holy desire is expressed. Ivory, moreover, is known to be the bone of elephants.

As blessed Isidore says: [Note: [Col. 0788D] *Etymologies*, bk. XII, ch. 2.] The Greeks suppose that the elephant is named from the greatness of its body, because it presents the shape of a mountain. For in Greek a mountain is called *lophos* (λόφος). Among the Indians, however, it is called from the cry *barro*. Hence its cry is *barritus*, its teeth are ivory, and its snout is called a *promuscis*, because with it it brings food to its mouth; and, protected by an ivory rampart, it is like a serpent. The ancient Romans called them Lucanian oxen: oxen because they saw no larger animal; Lucanian because Pyrrhus first deployed them against the Romans in battle in Lucania. For this kind of animal is suited to warfare. Persians and Indians set wooden towers upon them and fight from these, as though from a wall, with missiles. [Col. 0788B] They are strong in understanding and memory; they walk step by step; they salute with whatever movement they can; they flee from the sea and copulate facing away from one another. When they give birth, they leave their young in waters or on islands because of dragons: the two are enemies, and elephants are killed when entangled by them. They carry their young for two years, give birth no more than once, and bear not several, but only one. They live for three hundred years. Elephants were formerly born only in Africa and India; now India alone produces them.

Let these few remarks about the elephant’s nature suffice, since we must return to what we omitted above. Redness, therefore, as we have said, signifies the flame of spiritual desire [Col. 0788C] of ancient ivory. Sapphire is the colour of the upper air. Thus the whole life of the Nazarites is here briefly expressed: through action they tend toward things above, and through contemplation they appear to surpass the Fathers. But abundance often makes one poor, and a person is more prosperous than is expedient; the mind, often presuming upon itself and yielding to empty favour, becomes darkened, and what seemed to grow white is blackened and fouled. Hence it follows: “Their face has become blacker than coals, and they are not known in the streets” (Lam. IV).

Those who have lost God’s righteousness and seek their own praise become black after their whiteness, because they presume not on God but on themselves. Thus, even without knowing it, they fall into sins and descend from the fire of the mind to the coldness of the body, from the whiteness of life to the blackness of vain flattery; [Col. 0788D] and consequently they become like extinguished coals. For this reason it is said: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. VII). It follows: “And they are not known in the streets,” that is, in the broad expanse of secular life. For nothing is narrower for the human mind than to deny one’s own will and break such desires of the flesh. Hence: “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matt. VII). But nothing is broader than to serve one’s own pleasures and be subject to no such laws. Those are in the streets who seek their own interests. “For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death” (ibid.). But such people are not known in the streets, because they are not what they appeared to be: they were one thing and showed another.

[Col. 0789A] Hence it follows: “Their skin has clung to their bones; it has dried up and become like wood.” By bones strength is represented; [Note: [Col. 0789D] Strength.] by skin, weakness. Thus skin clings to bones when the weakness of vices is regarded as the strength of virtues. Skin clings to bones when outward flattery for deeds supposedly well done is joined inwardly to virtues; when these are united, the reward is lost. And because, deceived by flatteries, they think great things of themselves, they scorn correction. Hence it is said: “It has dried up and become like wood.” For guilt becomes the more insensible in proportion as it is praised as though it were a true virtue. It therefore dries up because no grace flourishes within. Many, when corrected, are as insensible as wood, estranged from the dew of grace and dry. This happens to those who aspire to things too high for themselves and desire to appear holy, but secretly serve vices. Such people are not known in the streets. Spiritual people know that they feign one thing and are another. Outwardly they shine fairer than snow, brighter than milk, redder than ivory; but inwardly they are insensible like dry wood. [Col. 0789B] Hence they are often corrected neither by blandishments nor threats. He adds again:

“It was better for those slain by the sword,” namely, the word of God, “than for those killed by hunger,” namely, hunger for that same word of God. The former are killed in order to live; the latter are killed in order to perish. Hence it is said: “Take up the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). There is a sword by which death kills so that life may follow. There is another which cuts off life and kills the soul. Hence: “My sword has devoured flesh” (Isa. I). There is also the flaming and turning sword [Col. 0789C] for guarding the way to the tree of life. Further, there is a polished and sharp sword, to which it is said: “Return to your sheath” (John XVIII). A sword also passed through the soul of the most holy Mary (Luke II), namely, sorrow at Christ’s Passion.

But the Church rejoices over those who are slain by the sword of God’s word; she grieves for those killed by hunger for that same word. She mourns those whom she knows to have been consumed by hunger or thirst because of the land’s barrenness. Hence it is said: “I shall send among them not a hunger for bread nor a thirst for water, but for hearing the word of God” (Amos VIII). Whoever is destroyed by this hunger will be subject to eternal death, since man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from God’s mouth (Deut. VIII; Matt. IV). As a human being consists of two substances, so he preserves life by two foods. [Col. 0789D] The flesh is sustained by bodily food, and the soul by the divine word. Hence it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke XI). We ask for both, because we daily need both.

The barrenness of the land is the Church’s want, when, as teachers fail, it is not watered with rains of the divine word. The people’s destruction follows the priests’ fault and ignorance [Note: [Col. 0789D] “Ignorance.”] or negligence in teaching.

[Col. 0790A] To this end, dearest brothers, let your minds awaken and ponder these matters without ceasing, so that your good works may be free from the desire for empty glory or boasting. It does not befit servants of God to perform any good work for human fame, but for the reward of heavenly goods. Whoever practises a good work for the sake of popular favour loses the heavenly reward, because, according to the Lord’s judgment, he receives his reward in this world (Matt. VI). Boasting must be guarded against in deeds as well as words. Yet the ruin of anyone who wishes to please himself more than God and obtain praise from human beings must be lamented.

Hence Isidore, teacher of the Spaniards, says: [Note: [Col. 0790D] Isidore, *Sentences*, bk. III, ch. 23.] “Examine yourself, O man, and claim nothing for yourself from what is in you except sins.” It is true that human nature expects to delight in praise, but rightly only if each person is praised in God and not in himself, as it is written: “My soul shall be praised in the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII). [Col. 0790B] Therefore, most beloved, do your works not for human favour but solely for God’s love, so that you may rightly be counted among the Nazarites of the Church. Strive with all earnestness that through contemplation you may be whiter than snow, and through the ordering of active life brighter than milk, to God’s glory. Let the eyes of the mind contemplate God in prayer, but let the intention be clean from the filth of empty glory. Let the mind be fixed on God through contemplation; let the dwelling-place of the heart be cleansed from the dregs of earthly praise. Let a good work have its beginning and end in God, [Col. 0790C] but let the spirit not yield to human favour.

Let your charity, beloved, watchfully attend to this, lest what ought to shine before God become defiled. One does not shine, but is unhappily blackened, who seeks from a good work not God’s praise but his own. They become black as ravens who turn God’s praise back upon themselves. They become like cold coals who praise not God but themselves in good works. It is the height of misery to proceed by the path of virtues toward eternal damnation. No iniquity is greater than for anyone to wish to glory in himself and not in God. Nothing is more unhappy than to defraud God in good works. One defrauds God who, in the good acts he performs, assigns praise not to God but to himself.

Therefore, dearest brothers, apply yourselves with the utmost zeal to good works, and in them [Col. 0790D] take care to render to God, with all reverence, the praise due to him. Reject temporal glory as dung; love God in all things and above all things; and pray to him with every devotion that he may bring you to the fellowship of his elect—God, who lives and reigns in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SIXTEENTH SERMON: ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0791]

[Col. 0791A] [Note: [Col. 0791D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, ch. 38.] Jeremiah, born of the priestly tribe in the village of Anathoth, three miles from Jerusalem, a priest appointed in Judaea and a prophet consecrated among the Gentiles, was known before he was formed, sanctified before he came forth, and was admonished to remain a virgin. He began to preach as a boy, reproving the people for their offences and repeatedly urging them to repentance. But he was often afflicted and bound by the cruel savagery of the people’s unbelief; he was cast into prison and thrown into a pit; and at last he was stoned by the people at Taphnas in Egypt. He was buried in the place where King Pharaoh had lived. Yet because by his prayers he drove serpents from that place and delivered the Egyptians from the harmful bite of asps, the Egyptians themselves honour him with remarkable veneration and the greatest honour, [Col. 0791B] and still devoutly venerate his tomb.

But since we have briefly said these things, beloved, it is fitting that, for your instruction, we speak more fully about some of his prophetic words. Almighty God, merciful and kind, wishing that none should perish but that those returning to him through repentance—not Jews only, but Gentiles also—should be mercifully saved, speaks thus to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and gave you as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. I).

Was Jeremiah in existence before conception, as heretics suppose? By no means. Rather, the Lord foreknew that he would be, [Col. 0791C] he for whom things yet to be done are already done, who calls things that are not as though they were (Rom. IV). Let it therefore be said more plainly: “Before I formed you”—that is, by the act of your mother—in the womb, “I knew you” in foreknowledge; “and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you and gave you as a prophet among the nations,” in accordance with Paul’s words: “When it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, that I might preach him among the nations” (Gal. I).

John also is sanctified in the womb, receives the Holy Spirit, moves in the womb, and speaks through his mother’s mouth (Luke I). [Note: [Col. 0791D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, bk. XI, ch. 1.] *Vulva* (“womb”) is so called as though from *valva* (“door”), that is, the door of the belly, either because it receives seed or because the offspring comes forth from it.

Some understand this passage as referring to the Saviour, who in the proper sense was the prophet of the nations and called every nation through [Col. 0791D] the apostles; who, before he was formed in the virginal womb and before he came forth from the womb, was sanctified in the womb and known to the Father; who is always in the Father, and in whom the Father always is.

[Col. 0792A] The boy Jeremiah answered the Lord: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a boy.” He declines an office which his age cannot bear, with the same modesty by which Moses says that he is of a weak and slender voice (Exod. IV). But Moses is reproved as one of mature and vigorous age; to Jeremiah, however, as to a child, kindly [Note: [Col. 0792D] The gloss: “Pardon is granted.”] admonitions are given, since he is adorned with modesty and shame.

Concerning such preachers who humbly decline the office of preaching, blessed Gregory says: [Note: [Col. 0792D] *Pastoral Rule*, pt. I, ch. 7.] “Some laudably seek the office of preaching, to which others are laudably compelled. Isaiah offered himself freely, saying: ‘Behold, here am I; send me’ (Isa. VI). Jeremiah, however, humbly draws back when he says: ‘Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am a boy.’ [Col. 0792B] Thus different words issue outwardly from each, but not from a different source of love. For there are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbour. Isaiah, therefore, desiring through the active life to benefit his neighbours, seeks the office of preaching; Jeremiah, desiring through the contemplative life to cling to the love of God, refuses to be sent out to preach. The latter feared by speaking to lose the gains of silent contemplation; the former feared by keeping silence to suffer the losses of zealous activity.

“But it must be observed that he who declined did not resist completely, and he who wished to be sent first saw himself cleansed by the altar’s coal, lest either anyone unpurified dare approach the sacred mysteries, or one whom God has chosen proudly oppose him under the guise of humility. Since it is difficult to know [Col. 0792C] oneself purified, the office of preaching is more safely declined. Yet it should not be declined obstinately when the divine will to undertake it is recognized. Moses wonderfully fulfilled both duties: he was unwilling to preside over so great a multitude and yet obeyed. Perhaps he would then have been proud had he fearlessly accepted the leadership, or had he refused obedience to his Creator’s command. Thus subject in both respects, through fear he did not wish to rule peoples, yet, trusting in the strength of the One commanding, he consented.”

It follows: “And the Lord said to me: Do not say, ‘I am a boy,’ because you shall go to all to whom I send you, and shall speak all that I command you.” As if he said: Do not consider your age; a man’s wisdom is his grey hair. Bring willingness to go, and you will have [Col. 0792D] me as companion, by whom you may accomplish all things. “Open your mouth, and I shall fill it” (Ps. LXXX). “Do not fear their face, for I am with you to deliver you.” That is, do not consider the multitude [Col. 0793A] of those to whom and against whom you are to speak, but me, who am with you to deliver you from them. This does not mean that you will be free from persecutions and trials—for you will suffer many things—but that you will overcome everything patiently and not yield.

Again he adds: “And the Lord sent forth his hand”—that is, the Father sent the Son, through whom all things were made—so that the boy, seeing a human likeness, should not be terrified or fear being touched. And the Lord said to me: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth” (Isa. VI). “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. XXX).

Observe that here God’s hand is sent, touches the prophet’s mouth, and says: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.” In Isaiah it is written: “One of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand he had a coal”—that is, a live coal—“which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth” (Isa. VI), and so forth. [Col. 0793B] Because Isaiah was of mature age, had unclean lips, and dwelt among a people with unclean lips, one of the seraphim is sent to touch his mouth, not with his hand but with tongs and a coal, and remove his iniquities. Here, however, God’s own hand is sent, not to remove sins which Jeremiah had not committed in childhood, but to grant him the grace of speaking.

Ezekiel devours a scroll written within and without (Ezek. II), containing both the divine mysteries and the plain historical narrative. Jeremiah’s mouth is touched and the Lord’s words are bestowed, so that he may receive confidence to preach. Again he says: “Behold, today I have set you over nations and kingdoms.” [Col. 0793C] These words seem applicable to Christ. It is as though God the Father spoke to him in these words: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. II), and so forth. Why? So that you may uproot, destroy, ruin, and scatter evils, and build up good things and plant the holy Church.

As we said above, we understand this passage in the person of Christ. For Jeremiah means “the height of the Lord,” he who destroyed the kingdoms of the devil which the devil showed him on a high mountain as his own (Matt. IV), destroyed the hostile powers, and wiped out the written bond of errors on the cross [Note: [Col. 0793D] Supply: “wiping out.”]. Of these things, after the historical truth, the tropological sense says: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples meditated vain things? The kings stood forth and the rulers gathered together as one against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. II).

After these things were uprooted, destroyed, ruined, and cast down to the depths, the Church of God is built and planted. Two joyful things follow the four mournful things mentioned above. Good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed; nor could the best things be planted unless the worst had been uprooted. “Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. XV), and every building not founded on rock but on sand shall be undermined and destroyed by God’s word (Matt. VII). But the Lord, by the breath of his mouth and the appearing of his presence, shall destroy forever every perverse and sacrilegious [Col. 0794A] doctrine. He will scatter and cast down those things which are exalted against the knowledge of God and trust in their own wisdom, which is foolishness with God; so that humble things may be built in their place, and in the place of things above that have been destroyed and uprooted, things suited to ecclesiastical truth may be constructed and planted, concerning which it is said: “You are God’s building; you are God’s field” (I Cor. III).

Again he says: “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah?” By his question the Lord awakens him. “I see,” he says, “a watchful rod.” Of this it is said: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. XXII). As though he said more plainly: Your discipline, which is the rod [Col. 0794B] for the sheep, that is, for simpler peoples; and your staff for the more grown children, namely, those more learned persons who grow from the animal life to the spiritual—these have comforted me, that is, have not afflicted me. The rod is strictness, which crushes vices; the staff is governance, which upholds believers. Paul said of this rod to certain disciples: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV). It must examine sins, strike, and rebuke them; for it rebukes in order to amend. And just as a nut or almond has an exceedingly bitter husk and a very hard shell, so that, when the hard and bitter parts are removed, a most sweet fruit is found, so every correction and labour of self-restraint is bitter at present, [Col. 0794C] but in the end bears a most sweet fruit. Thus the roots of learning are bitter, but its fruits sweet.

Some understand the watchful, nut-bearing rod as the Lord, of whom Isaiah says: “A rod came forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI), and so forth. Hence Aaron’s rod, thought to be dead, is said to have blossomed in the Lord’s resurrection.

The Seventy Interpreters translated “a watchful rod” as “a rod of nuts,” because of the similarity of the words. For “watch,” “watchful,” and “to watch” are called in Hebrew *sachad*, while “nut” is *seched* [Note: [Col. 0793D] Supply: in Hebrew, *sachad*; and “nut,” *seched*.]. Hence in what follows a watchful leopard is designated by this name. The same is written in Daniel according to Theodotion: that the adulterous elders are to be sentenced to cutting and sawing under the trees *schinu* [Note: [Col. 0794D] *Schino*.] and *prinu* [Note: [Col. 0794D] *Prino*.], that is, the holm-oak and the mastic tree. [Col. 0794D] And at the beginning of Genesis, the woman is called by the man named *Is* (“man”) *virago* (“woman-man”), as it were.

And the Lord said to me: “You have seen well, for I shall watch over my word, considering all things, in order to fulfil it.” Those who sin step by step are rebuked, because they refused to be amended by the rod that struck them.

And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And I said: “I see a kindled pot, and its face is from the north.” The kindled pot signifies the king of Babylon and the city of Jerusalem. Hence the Lord says to Job concerning Leviathan: “Smoke goes forth from his nostrils, like that of a kindled and boiling pot. His breath makes coals burn, and flame goes forth from his mouth” (Job 41). For the sharpness of the eyes is injured by smoke. [Note: [Col. 0795D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXIII, chapter 27, after the beginning.] Therefore smoke is not without reason asserted to proceed from the nostrils of Leviathan: through his harmful inspirations, perverse thought arises in human hearts, whereby the mind’s sight is dulled, lest the inward light be seen. For, as it were, he emits darkness by the blast of his nostrils, who in the hearts of the reprobate, by the breathings of his snares, accumulates from the love of temporal life the heat of manifold thoughts; and he multiplies, as it were, balls of smoke, who heaps up the minds of wicked people for the most enormous cares of the present life. The Lord carefully expresses the force of this smoke when He immediately adds: “Like that of a kindled and boiling pot.”

[Col. 0795B] For the pot is kindled when the human mind is stimulated by the persuasions of the evil enemy. But the pot boils when, through consent, it is already inflamed in the desires of that perverse persuasion; and it throws out as many waves, as though boiling, as the number of its wicked impulses which it extends into outward deeds. Let it therefore be said: “I see a kindled pot, and its face [Note: [Col. 0795D] St. Martin consistently follows the reading, “its face from the north,” in conformity with Augustine on Psalm 59, §10: “In a certain … passage it is said, ‘a pot kindled from the north’;” but Gregory the Great adheres to [Col. 0796D] the Vulgate, “its face from the face of the north,” so that he might correctly continue later: “For from the face of the north,” etc. Our author, who adopts the other reading, has not transcribed that period very well.] is from the north.” For from the face of the north the pot of the human heart is kindled when, through the instigation of the apostate spirit, it is inflamed with unlawful desires. For that evil spirit says: “I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). Therefore, the mind which that enemy has once captured, he kindles with evil persuasions or breathings, as with fires set beneath it, [Col. 0795C] so that, content with present things, it may burn without cease after superfluous desires: desiring some things which should be despised, and despising others once they are obtained. Therefore, since the heart inflamed by the instigation of this Leviathan is drawn through various desires, his smoke is rightly declared to resemble a kindled and boiling pot; for the conscience afflicted by his temptations rises in as many boilings as it swells inwardly with thoughts.

It follows: And the Lord said to me: “From the north evil shall be opened” (that is, evils shall blaze forth) “upon all the inhabitants of the earth”: of Judaea, or of the whole earth, concerning whom the Apocalypse says: “Woe upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Rev. 8). For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth but strangers and pilgrims, [Col. 0795D] one of whom says: “I am a stranger and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Ps. 38). The patriarch Jacob likewise said of himself when questioned by King Pharaoh: “Few and evil are the days during which I am a pilgrim upon the earth” (Gen. 44). Solomon also says of this wind: “The north wind is a harsh wind” (Ecclus. 43). Yet it is called “the right” by those who have lost the warmth of faith through its coldness.

It follows: “Behold, I shall summon all the thoughts of the kingdoms of the north,” says the Lord—that is, those subject to the [Col. 0796A] king of Babylon—“and they shall come, and each one shall set”—the city being besieged—“his seat,” that is, his throne or his tent, “at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem,” so that no one may be able to go out, “and against all its walls round about”; and not only against Jerusalem, but also against all the cities of Judah, enclosed by a similar siege. “And I shall speak my judgments with them concerning all their wickedness,” because no sin is unpunished. As though He said more plainly: When the city has been taken, I shall show that my judgments were just and that each received what he deserved. “Concerning all their wickedness,” He says: those who forsook me, their God, and poured libations to foreign gods, whom their fathers did not worship, and adored the idols of the nations—silver and gold, the works of human hands (Ps. 113), [Col. 0796B] that is, the work of their own hands, what they made, not Him by whom they were made. As though they had been delivered into the hands of their enemies not for the other vices to which human nature is subject, but especially for idolatry.

“But you, gird your loins, arise, and speak to them all that I command you.” Job too is commanded to gird his loins like a man. [Note: [Col. 0796D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXVIII, chapter 4.] Sacred Scripture customarily calls those men who follow the ways of the Lord with strong and not slack steps. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened” (Ps. 26), etc. Hence elsewhere it is commanded: “Raise up hands that hang down and feeble knees” (Heb. 12). Thus Wisdom also [Col. 0796C] says in Proverbs: “O men, I cry out to you” (Prov. 8). As though she said plainly: I speak not to women but to men, because those whose minds are weak and unstable cannot receive my words.

To gird the loins is to restrain lust in deed and thought. For the pleasure of the flesh is in the loins. Hence holy preachers are told: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). By the loins, lust is signified; by the lamps, the brightness of good works. Therefore they are commanded to gird their loins and hold lamps. As though they plainly hear: First restrain lust within yourselves, and then show others, from yourselves, examples of good works. But one kind of lust is that of the flesh, by which we corrupt chastity; another is that of the heart, by which [Col. 0796D] we glory in chastity. Let it therefore be said: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job 38), so that he who first conquered the lust of corruption may afterwards conquer the lust of pride; lest, growing proud of chastity, he be inwardly before God’s eyes all the more shamefully lustful, the more humble and chaste he appeared before human eyes. Hence Moses rightly says: “Circumcise the foreskins of your hearts” (Deut. 10), that is: after extinguishing the lust of the flesh, cut off also the pride of the heart.

[Col. 0797A] Therefore Jeremiah is rightly told by the Lord to gird his loins: that he may restrain the lust of the flesh and, when about to preach God’s commands concerning chastity to the people, may not grow proud of chastity. We likewise read that Elijah and John the Baptist had their loins girded with belts (4 Kings 1; Matt. 3). The Apostles too are told, with loins girded, to hold lamps in their hands (Luke 12), namely lamps of evangelical preaching. Whoever is to preach God’s words, therefore, ought to gird his loins. The strength of the devil is in the loins. Hence the saying: “For my loins are filled with delusions, and there is no health in my flesh” (Ps. 37). As though he said: Not only do I sin through my own weakness, [Note: [Col. 0797D] I sin.] but also through the devil’s persuasion, who afflicts the body and wearies the soul with vain [Note: [Col. 0797D] Empty.] imaginings; and [Col. 0797B] therefore there is no health in my flesh. The loins—or the soul—are filled with delusions, and thus there is nothing in the whole person from which joy may arise, until the soul is stripped of delusions and the body clothed with health.

The soul’s delusions are infinite. At times they scarcely permit one to pray: images of bodies present themselves, and you pass from this one to that; forgetfulness comes, you recall this instead of that, and things of this sort. These will be driven away when we see the truth as it is.

With loins girded, let him hear what is written: “Arise, you who sleep, and rise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” (Eph. 5). As though it were said more plainly: Arise, you who sleep, that is, who have forgotten God, who are sluggish and do not know that you are in sins; and rise from [Col. 0797C] the dead, that is, from future condemnation; and Christ shall enlighten you, that is, He shall be your everlasting light, so that ever watchful and rising from sleep, you may do and say what has been commanded.

Almighty God, dearest brethren, seeing that the Jewish people had long persisted in their wickedness, sent the prophet Jeremiah, as was said above, to exhort them to repentance for their past evils, so that, though late, they might fulfil the Lord’s will in good works and escape the evils threatening them in the near future. God is always ready to do good and slow to punish. For although He can punish the guilty without announcement of the coming judgment, He does not do so; rather, even if He has condemned them, He foretells it so that those who were to be condemned through fault may be delivered through repentance.

The Ninevites, sinners condemned by God, had been condemned; for there were still three days, and Nineveh was to be overthrown. God did not wish sinners to perish in silence, but, giving place for repentance, sent a Hebrew prophet to say: “Still three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3), so that those who had been condemned might not perish but, doing penance, might obtain mercy. The Sodomites and Gomorrahites likewise had already been marked out for a dreadful [Note: [Col. 0798D] Another manuscript: “divine.”] destruction, as God’s speech to Abraham showed. Yet the angels did what belonged to them, wishing to save those who judged themselves unworthy of salvation, saying to Lot: “Do you have here any son-in-law, [Col. 0798A] or sons, or daughters?” etc. (Gen. 19). They did not fail to know that they would not follow Lot; but they displayed alike their own kindness and love, and that of Him who had sent them.

We find something similar in Jeremiah. God had condemned Jerusalem for its sins, and this was the sentence: that it should be surrendered to captivity. But since God loves humankind and wills no one to perish, before the time of devastation came He sent this prophet also, to invite them to repentance. He sent him under a second king after the first; He sent him also under a third. Captivity was already threatening, and still God exhorted them to salvation, granting even before a single day an opportunity for repentance. Hence it is written that Jeremiah prophesied until the captivity [Col. 0798B] of Jerusalem and until the fifth month (Jer. 1). The hands of the enemies had already drawn tight their chains, and nevertheless God said these things: Behold, you have been made captives; repent, though late; pray to me, and I shall spare you. I, who gave you over, can rescue you from captivity.

We too, dearest brethren, can understand this concerning ourselves: if we sin, we shall become captives. Hence it is said: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). For handing a sinner over to Satan differs in nothing from the handing over of the Jews to Nebuchadnezzar. And as God gave them over to the adversary because of their frequent impieties, so we shall be given over to the spiritual Nebuchadnezzar because of our sins. Thus Paul says of certain incorrigible persons: “I have handed them over,” he says, “to Satan” (1 Tim. 1)—namely Hymenaeus and Alexander, false teachers and blasphemers. “I have handed them over to Satan,” he says, because Satan cannot torment anyone unless permitted. As though he said: I excommunicated them so that Satan’s kingdom may be excluded from Satan; for the Church is to be gathered from every race of humankind, even from those who, through worldly arrogance and pride, appear far removed from faith and humility.

Do you suppose sinning to be a small evil, that God should hand people over to Satan, who enslaves the souls of those abandoned by God—not, of course, without cause or without judgment? For when He has sent rain upon the vineyard and it has produced or brought forth thorns instead of grapes, what will He do [Col. 0798D] except command the clouds not to rain upon it? (Isa. 5.) Again, almighty God, even after countless sins, desiring us to return to Him through repentance, sets before us the likeness of a defiled woman, saying: “If a man dismisses his wife, and she departs from him and marries another man, shall he return to her again? Shall not that woman be polluted and defiled?” (Jer. 3.) Behold, beloved, an argument of justice is drawn from a woman who has committed adultery and been abandoned; yet, for those who return after their fall, not justice but mercy is shown. Thus we may understand how great is the mercy by which He spares us when we sin, and how great the impiety with which we sin when we do not return even after sin; or what pardon will be granted by Him to the wicked, He who does not cease to call even after fault?

Hence it is said: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of one warning behind your back” (Isa. 30). Therefore we ought to be ashamed before the mercy of Him who calls, if we wish to fear justice; for He is despised with so much graver wickedness, the more He does not disdain still mercifully to call the one who despises Him. God has betrothed the soul to His embraces and therefore desires it to return to Him and do penance. But the more merciful He is who shows the way of salvation after fornication, the more miserable is the harlot—that is, the soul—which refuses to receive the remedy.

It is fitting, therefore, dearest brethren, that we repent before almighty God for past evils, [Col. 0799B] and, while we have light, persist in good works, lest we be assigned afterward to punishments so much the more severe as we have longer despised the kindness of Him who calls. [Col. 0800A] Our captivity, then, is near if we do not repent: we shall be handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and the Babylonians, who are already close at hand. The words of the prophets, of the law, of the apostles, and of our Lord Jesus Christ Himself exhort us to repentance and summon us to salvation. If we listen, we believe Him who said: “And I too shall repent of all the evils which I spoke of doing to them” (Jer. 18). Let us therefore pray to Him together, who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), that in this present life He may grant us to bring forth fruits worthy of repentance; so that, endowed with virtues and cleansed of vices, under His guidance we may be able after our death to attain the joys of eternal life—He who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Seventeenth Sermon: On the Passion of the Lord

[Col. 0799]

[Col. 0799B] The Son of God, beholding the long captivity of the human race and desiring, by the Father’s will, to redeem it through Himself, speaks through the mouth of the prophet Jeremiah concerning His passion to God the Father Himself, saying: “You, Lord [Col. 0799C] Father, have shown these things to me, your Son, according to my humanity; and I have known how I ought to speak and suffer for the liberation of your own.” You have shown me their intentions”—namely, those of the Jews—“and I was like a gentle lamb carried to the sacrifice of the cross, and I did not know,” namely sin, “because they devised schemes against me” (Jer. 11).

Hence it is said: “Him who knew no sin, He made sin for us” (2 Cor. 5). As though He said more plainly: He who never sinned and in whose mouth no deceit was found (Isa. 53), for our sins died on the cross as though a sinner. Not without reason, since the Lord can do whatever He wills, He explains the causes, lest He appear unjust. Hence the Prophet says: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50). “You have shown me, and I have known” is fittingly said, because, according to the Psalmist, “The Lord teaches knowledge to man” (Ps. 93). Hence the same Son of God says in the Gospel: “Call no one master upon earth; for one is your master, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23), who alone instructs human beings. Let it therefore be said: “You have shown me, and I have known.” As though He said: According to my humanity, I could not know these things unless you, Father, revealed them to me, your Son. But when you show them, I shall see each person’s thoughts—what they do and what their disposition is.

[Col. 0800B] It follows: “Let us put”—namely, the wood of the cross—“into his bread,” that is, into the body of the Saviour, who is the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6). “And let us eradicate him from the land of the living, and let his name be remembered no more.” For the Saviour Himself says of Himself in the Gospel: “If a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it brings forth much fruit” (John 12). “Let us put,” they say, “wood into his bread.” But I shall introduce something wonderful. The wood put into His bread made the bread better, that is, made the teaching sweeter, just as the wood put by Moses into bitter water made it sweet (Exod. 15). For before the wood was put into His bread, when there was bread alone and no wood, His sound had not gone out into all the earth (Ps. 18); but after He assumed strength through the wood, the report of His passion was sown throughout all the earth. But I say that the law not understood is bitter water. When, however, [Col. 0800D] the wood of Jesus Christ comes and the Saviour’s word descends into it, it is sweetened.

Again the Son, according to His humanity, calls upon the Father, saying: “But you, Lord Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the reins and hearts, let me see your vengeance upon them” (Jer. 11). The Son according to the flesh speaks to the Father and prays for His judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0799D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 1.] The fourth name of God among the Hebrews is said to be *Sabaoth*, which is translated into Latin as “of hosts” or “of powers.” Of Him it is said by the angels in the Psalm: “Who is this king of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is [Col. 0801A] the king of glory” (Ps. 23). For in this order there are many powers: angels, archangels, principalities, powers, and all the orders of the heavenly host; yet He is Lord of them.

As though the Son of God said more plainly according to His humanity: You, Lord Sabaoth—that is, Lord of hosts—who judge justly by rendering to each one what he deserves and test the reins and hearts, let me see your vengeance upon them, namely upon those who persist in wickedness and do not repent. For I have revealed my cause to you, because I am crucified not through my own desert but through their wickedness. For others, who are ready for repentance, He says: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). But concerning these obstinate persons He says: “Let me see your vengeance upon them.” Of these obstinate persons who depart from God, [Col. 0801B] this prophet said: “Lord, all who forsake you shall be confounded”—that is, forever; “those who depart from you shall be written in the earth,” namely erased from the book of life, “because they have forsaken the fountain of living waters, the Lord” (Jer. 17), who says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). Those whose citizenship is in heaven are written in heaven; those who depart from the Lord are written on earth with those who savour earthly things.
