Truly, whoever comes to Christ—that is, whoever faithfully believes in Him—will have rivers of living water flowing from his belly, because He is the true physician of the human race, true wisdom and salvation. To Him the prophet devoutly cried: “Heal me, Lord, and [Col. 0801C] I shall be healed; save me [Note: [Col. 0801D] Supply: “do.”], and I shall be saved, for you are my praise” (Jer. 17). Many physicians treated the woman with the issue of blood in the Gospel, but she could be healed by none except Him who is the true physician (Mark 5). Therefore the prophet, enduring reproaches from the people and surrounded by snares, desires to be healed and cured by Him whose praise and medicine are true. For He is the true physician, who deigned to suffer many injuries for us sinners. Taught by the spirit of prophecy, Jeremiah foresaw that He would suffer, when in His person he cried to the Father: “Attend to me, Lord, and hear the voices of my adversaries” (Jer. 18), namely of the Jews shouting: “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23).

Again he adds, saying: “My enemies hunted me like [Col. 0801D] a bird without cause” (Lam. 3). This is the voice of the Church, that is, of the body, over whose head—over Christ, namely—waters, that is peoples, overflowed, in order to destroy Him without cause. Christ is the head of the Church (Eph. 5). Hence, in the voice of this same Church, as though disappointed in its hope, there follows: “I have perished,” because the disciples, leaving Him, fled, denied Him, and doubted. Hence the letter *sade* is rightly prefixed, which is interpreted “consolation,” because unless the consolation of the loving shepherd had been present, none of the sheep would have been saved. It is thus clear that the trial of the passion was not without the consolation of the Holy Spirit, who strengthened the despairing, restored faith, and sustained them. Hence it is said: [Col. 0802A] “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22). So far as it lay in Peter himself, he denied; but in God his faith remained. Thus it is fittingly said in the Church’s voice: “I have perished”; yet, through the promise and foreknowledge of the loving master, faith lives unconquered.

Consolation, moreover, occurs in many ways. Scripture consoles, and the mercy of the judge, and the penalty paid for sin. Hence: “Be comforted, my people” (Isa. 40). And shortly afterward: “Jerusalem’s iniquity has been forgiven, because she has received double from the hand of the Lord for all her sins.” And if faith should fail, punishment would make satisfaction. Consolation also occurs in various tribulations or temptations, because temptation produces patience, and patience testing, and testing hope (Rom. 5). Tears too console, by which sins are washed away. Hence it is said: “The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping” (Ps. 6). Thus, when the punishments which we endure for sins have run their course, we are certain of pardon. For in these the consolation of the Holy Spirit is not absent, provided hardness of heart is not present. “These are the just judgments of the Lord, rejoicing hearts” (Ps. 18). For *sade* is interpreted “consolation” or “justice.” Therefore we receive manifold consolation from the Lord’s passion, being justified as we are made conformed to Him in scourges and sufferings. Hence: “Son, remember that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; now he is comforted, but you are tormented” (Luke 16).

“They hunted me like a bird without cause,” that is, without reason. After so many tears [Col. 0802C] and so great a sorrow, after fear of peril and contrition, after the mockery of enemies, the consolation signified by *sade* fittingly intervenes, so that those who have been punished so severely may hope for the pardon of justice and the consolation of mercy, being washed clean of defilement by their tears. But because rest is given through Christ’s passion alone, there is lamentation for us in the voice of the Redeemer: “They hunted me,” He says, etc. By these words consolation and justice are shown from the Lord’s passion, [Note: [Col. 0801D] Supply: “pardon.”] by which we are made righteous, though the impiety of the unbelieving, like persons hunting a bird, seized Christ with swords and clubs without cause. These things, then, are plainly said of Christ, who is lamented as a bird caught. Hence Job says: “The bird does not know the path, nor has the eye of the vulture seen it” (Job 28).

[Col. 0802D] [Note: [Col. 0802D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XVIII, chapter 19.] Who is signified here by the name of bird, except Him who assumed a fleshly body and who is plainly expressed also by the designation of a vulture? For when a vulture flies and sees a corpse lying below, it descends to eat the corpse. And often it is caught in death when it comes down from on high to a dead animal. Therefore the mediator between God and men, our Redeemer, is rightly designated by the name of vulture: remaining in the height of His divinity, He saw, as from a lofty flight, the corpse of our mortality in the depths, and lowered Himself from heaven to the low places. For He deigned to become human for our sake; and while He sought a dead animal, He found death among [Col. 0803A] us, though He was immortal in Himself.

But the eye of this vulture was the very intention of our resurrection, because, dying according to His humanity, He freed us from eternal death. Therefore that faithless people of Judaea saw one who was mortal, but did not attend to the fact that by His death He would destroy our death. They saw the vulture, but did not see the eyes of the vulture. Since they refused to consider the paths of His humility, by which He lifted us to the heights, they did not know the bird’s path. For they did not take thought that His humility would raise us to heavenly things and that the purpose of His death would restore us to life. The Jewish people, therefore, did not know the path of the bird—that is, of Christ—and did not behold the eyes of the vulture; for although they saw Him whom they held in death, they refused to see what glory of life would follow from His [Col. 0803B] death. Hence they also blazed forth into the cruelty of persecution; they refused to receive the words of life and, by forbidding, raging, and striking, drove away the preachers of the kingdom of heaven. Those preachers, leaving Judaea, to which they had been sent, were scattered among the gathering of the Gentiles.

We believe that this bird, of which we have spoken until now, is the one of whom Moses said: “As an eagle provokes her young to fly” (Deut. 32), etc. Certainly the Son of God, like an eagle, calls His people—that is, the Jews—to fly, namely to do good works, hovering over them, providing good things for them in all respects and rescuing them from the enemies’ snares. When He wished to gather them beneath His wings like a hen (Matt. 23), He was weakened and seized [Col. 0803C] and handed over to death. Hence it is said: “My life has fallen into the pit” (Lam. 3). He alone trod this pit, while by dying He killed death and by rising repaired life. “And they put,” he says, “a stone upon me” (Lam. 5). What could be clearer? For a stone was placed and sealed, and after the resurrection was rolled away by an angel. Christ was reckoned among those descending into the pit, like a man without help, but was found free among the dead (Ps. 87). Waters—that is, the multitude of the people—overflowed Christ, who is our head.

It follows: “I called upon your name, Lord, from the lowest pit” (Lam. 3). This is the voice of Christ according to His humanity, crying to the Father in [Col. 0803D] His passion. As though He said: Though my life has fallen into the pit, yet I called upon you from the lowest pit, like Jonah from the belly of the whale (Jonah 2). Job says something similar: “If I descend into the depths of hell, you will deliver me from there.” Hence the head, namely Christ, confidently says: “On the day when I called upon you, Lord, you said: Do not fear.” Hence it is also said here: “You heard my voice,” etc. Without doubt, one to whom the Father is present cannot perish. He whose voice had been heard could not doubt; but because the letter *coph* is also interpreted “conclusion” or “confinement,” the one who perished rightly prays in groaning, saying: “Do not turn your ear from my sobbing,” etc.

For Jonah bore the figure of Christ, who said in the whale’s belly: “The sea covered my head; I descended to the extremities of the mountains; the bars of the earth enclosed [Col. 0804A] me” (Jonah 2). The narrative makes clear that Jonah came to the depths of the earth, by which, as by bars and pillars, the globe of the earth is sustained by God’s will. Jonah, as has been said, prefigured Christ, because Christ redeemed us through His passion. In Christ the man, therefore, the principal element and, as it were, the head was the soul, in which divinity dwelt; this descended to the lower places, where human souls were held beneath the devil’s power. These are the bars that prevent souls from departing from the lower world. The Lord breaks these bars, namely the demons, and frees those held imprisoned. For the incarnate Son of God had come to the extremities of the mountains, enclosed by the bars of earth; but He confidently knew that the Father would free His life from corruption. Pressed with us and grieving for us, He said: “I called upon your name, Lord, from the lowest pit.” Jonah, placed in the whale’s belly, had prefigured this.

Thus *coph* is rightly called “conclusion,” because God “concluded all things under sin” (Gal. 3), so that the gate of life might be opened to us through Him who came in the passibility of the flesh to the lowest places of the pit, but was heard in His prayer because of His reverence (Heb. 5). We also, enclosed by corruption and sin, believe the same concerning ourselves in the future. Therefore: “You drew near to me,” He says—that is, you caused yourself to draw near—“on the day when I called upon you; you said: Do not fear,” so that we too may confidently say and hope for the same.

But we who are thus enclosed ought to look and look about us. Hence *coph* is interpreted “look.” As though [Col. 0804C] He said: Look, because mortality and corruption have brought me to the lowest pit; look at the snare in which I am confined. Do not disregard weakness and peril. Each person is enclosed by innumerable snares. *Coph* is also called “calling,” so that, confined, we may continually call upon Him who came from heaven and bore our infirmities (Isa. 53), who said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9). You have wounds: do not delay the remedy. Look with spiritual eyes at how you are confined. Hence David says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120). And elsewhere: “Our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us” (Ps. 122).

[Col. 0804D] Hence, under the same letter, it is also said above: “Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord” (Lam. 2). Therefore under this letter the figure of our Redeemer is set forth: He calls from the lowest pit and prays confidently. He groans and cries, not with the voice but with the mind. Everywhere He perceives God as present and Himself as drawing near on the day of calling, and God saying, “Do not fear”—He who said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16). Hence it is said: “The Lord is my illumination and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Ps. 26). Such a voice of the heart and such faith is a great cry. For there is a voice of the heart, a cry, and a voice of blood which reaches God. This voice is raised by the loftiness and harmony of virtues, not by the intensity of sounds. Great is the cry of faith by which we cry: [Col. 0805A] “Abba, Father.” The Spirit also cries for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8). Great is the voice of justice and charity, by which the dead not only speak but cry out, as Abel did (Gen. 4). Great is the voice of the Apostles, because “their sound went out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). With this voice our head cries, and the members cry; Rachel cries, weeping for her children (Matt. 2), saying: “Do not turn your ear from my sobbing and cries” (Lam. 3). Moses cries, to whom it is said: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14).

But it should be known that some cry in the heart, while others speak. Hannah spoke, when she prayed for private matters—that is, for children (1 Kings 1). Moses cried, inflamed with the ardour of charity. Under this letter, then, the conclusion [Col. 0805B] of our submersion is disclosed, and calling is made known, so that we may cry more earnestly; and it is said to each person: Look how you are enclosed. Cry to Him who is present, and say: “Do not turn your ear from my sobbing and cries,” because “God has concluded all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all” (Gal. 3). Hence it is said: “Be miserable and mourn” (Jas. 4), etc. As though he said: Look at your confinement; call upon the name of the Lord from the lowest pit.

The Lord and our Redeemer alone trod the pit, because by dying on the cross He delivered us from everlasting death. Similar is what is said elsewhere: “The Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah” (Lam. 1). Historically, however, the winepress signifies vengeance and the punishments of sinners. Hence Isaiah says: “Why is your garment red?” [Col. 0805C] (Isa. 63), etc. He represents the angels in His ascension as asking the Lord this kind of question. “I have trodden the winepress alone,” He says (ibid.), etc.—namely, that winepress in which punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good are trodden out. The Lord alone trod it, because He had no helper. For neither angel nor archangel assumed a human body in order, suffering for us, to trample down and crush the strength of our adversary.

The Lord trod this winepress in His passion for the virgin daughter of Judah, so that He might pour out rewards for believers, but the punishments of perpetual captivity and eternal condemnation for unbelievers and those who crucified Him. But the prophet, seeing the hardness of the Jews, laments because the Lord had trodden the winepress of the daughter of Judah. For what the Lord suffered for her remedy, she turned upon herself into the torment of extreme captivity and perpetual condemnation. Hence what follows indicates the person of the Synagogue itself weeping: “Therefore I weep, and my eye pours forth water, because the comforter, who should restore my soul, has gone far from me” (Lam. 1). We often find this to be so if we consider Jewish unbelief and hardness.

Metaphorically it is said: “The Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah.” Metaphorically, the Lord brought His vineyard out of Egypt and planted it in the land of promise; for a long time it remained barren and fruitless. Hence the saying: “I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5). Therefore the Lord [Col. 0806A] trod the winepress, reserved wine for Himself, and crushed the swine’s grape in perpetual captivity.

Allegorically, let it again be said, that it may be understood more perfectly. The Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah when, through his Passion, he subjected the powers of the air to his Church. For she truly is the virgin daughter of Judah, because “from Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II). The Lord trod the winepress—that is, the yoke of oppression—in order that she might be free. But since, while the Lord treads, many become *amurca*, that is, dregs or refuse, the prophet therefore laments and says: “My eye pours down water.” The letter AIN is also inserted for this reason, since it is interpreted “spring” or “eye.” For when the press of the Cross crushed him, a spring flowed from Christ’s side, whence blood and water immediately came forth [Col. 0806B] (John XIX). By this spring the bride is purchased and washed, to be joined in the bridegroom’s embrace. With this she is endowed, that she may rejoice and cling to her bridegroom alone, loving him alone who so greatly loved her. And because AIN is also interpreted “eye,” not without reason does the eye, made drunk from this spring, pour forth water of tears. Hence David: “Streams of waters flowed from my eyes, because they did not keep thy law” (Ps. CXVIII).

“The comforter is far from me,” etc. As often as the Church is afflicted by tribulations, as often as she is left bereft of God’s help, so often let her have recourse to tears as to her accustomed weapons. It follows: “My children have become lost, because the enemy has prevailed.” But when, while the teacher outwardly admonishes, the Paraclete is not present to instruct and educate her inwardly, her children therefore become lost [Col. 0806C], and the enemy prevails. Whoever, therefore, among teachers sees the Church entrusted to him converted too little, should draw from the fountain of love the means of bringing forth tears, until he brings back the Paraclete who comforts and converts. Otherwise, when the enemy prevails, her children become lost—those, namely, who have not yet been weaned and have not yet been brought to mature manhood.

It follows: “The Lord has rejected his altar; he has cursed his sanctuary; he has delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of her towers” (Lam. II).

Morally. The Lord rejects his altar when the altar of the heart is profaned and the prostituted mind and conscience are defiled—the place where the sacrifice received from us is rightly offered to God—according to the saying: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; [Col. 0806D] a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. L), etc. The sanctuary is cursed when the soul is cast down under a curse, because it refused to sanctify God’s name within itself by a worthy sacrifice. The towers of the soul are faith, hope, charity, and the other virtues by which it is raised up to heaven. The walls by which it is fortified are the works of the remaining virtues. These are delivered into the hands of enemies when the soul is laid waste in its actions, inwardly or outwardly.

Again, lamenting, he says: “They raised their voice in the house of the Lord, as on a solemn day.” Enemies raise their voices in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day when unclean spirits and monstrous vices make a tumult in the corrupted temple of the Holy Spirit within the soul, where the instruments of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0807A] and the harmony of virtues used to resound.

Allegorically. “The Lord has rejected his altar,” etc. There is one altar of God in the Church, namely Christ, who is called victim and sacrifice, high priest and priest. On this altar all sacrifices are offered. But the saints are altars derived from this altar, as light from light, mountains from the mountain, shepherds from the Shepherd. That altar, namely Christ, the Father rejected in the Passion, as he prayed for the Jews: “Father,” he says, “take this cup away from me” (Mark XIV). Rejected by them through the Father’s judgment, he is transferred to the Gentiles. Hence it is said: “But thou hast rejected and despised; thou hast delayed thy Christ” (Ps. LXXXVIII). For just as those sacrifices bore the figure of Christ, so the altar of unhewn stones [Col. 0807B], which iron had not touched (Deut. XXVII), prefigured the Lord’s body, untouched by any human workmanship.

Therefore, because Christ is transferred to the Church, the vows of the faithful are offered in him as upon an altar. For these, as though for the apostles, the Church compassionately mourns—not grieving because he has been transferred from herself, but saddened with the apostles at his death, so that afterward she may rejoice with them alike at the Resurrection. Hence the custom handed down from the apostles has become established: on the day on which Christ suffered, the offering of Christ’s body and blood is not made. This is for three reasons: either because on that day he is sacrificed in truth, whereas these are the mystical sacraments of that sacrifice on other days; or because Christ himself, the most holy high priest, who rightly offers them, descended of his own accord to hell on that day; or because, with the temple destroyed [Col. 0807C] and the altar cast down, there is no place upon which the victim of the body and blood may be offered.

It follows: “He has cursed his sanctuary”—that is, Christ, who, though he had no sin (II Cor. V), was made sin and a curse for us (Gal. III). Hence Moses: “Cursed is the man who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. XXI). He is all our sanctification, who hung upon the tree for us. Thus was fulfilled: “He delivered the walls of her towers into the hand of the enemy”—namely, the apostles, who are the walls of the other faithful. He delivered them to the temptation of the enemy, who demanded to sift them as wheat (Luke XXII).

Again he adds, saying: “They raised their voice in the house of the Lord, as on a solemn day.” How great was the confusion then in [Col. 0807D] the house of the Lord, how great in the courts, how great in the streets, how great in the whole city, though it was a festival day, the Gospel declares. Hence the Lord himself says through Isaiah: “I expected it to produce judgment, and behold iniquity; and justice, and behold a cry” (Isa. V). As though the Lord said more plainly through the prophet concerning the Israelite people: “I expected it to produce grapes,” that is, judgment, “and it produced wild grapes,” that is, iniquities; “and justice,” that is, that it might faithfully believe in me, “and behold a cry,” namely: “Away, away, crucify him” (John XIX). The Jews made a cry in place of justice because they killed Christ, whose blood cries to the Lord from the earth. Hence it is said: “The voice of the blood of thy brother Abel cries [Col. 0808A] to me from the earth” (Gen. IV). A *labrusca* is a wild vine which grows at the borders of the land. Hence it is also called *labrusca*, from *labia*, “edges,” and the extremities of the earth.

It follows: “The Lord planned to destroy the walls of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out his line, and did not turn away his hand from destruction. And the outer wall mourned, and the wall was destroyed together.”

Morally. When God sees a soul falling from the citadel of contemplation to the depths below, he plans to destroy its wall; but first he stretches out the line, that he may see by what measure it ought to be punished. First, indeed, he deliberates, so that he may leave an opportunity for return and that the soul itself may reflect upon what it has sinned. Before he destroys its wall, he stretches the line over it, as though weighing how great or of what kind its offences are, so that it too may weigh them. Otherwise [Col. 0808B] let it know that he does not turn away his hand. But because it was unwilling to consider what it had sinned, and “blood touched blood”—that is, one person killed another—the wall was destroyed and the soul made subject to enemies.

Let those hear this who do not fear to judge rashly, nor weigh causes by a just examination. The Lord does nothing without measure and deliberation, but weighs all things by a just examination, he who knows all things perfectly. The outer wall is faith, which is said to mourn when the wall has been destroyed—not that faith, namely, “which works through love” (Gal. V), but that which even demons are said to believe and tremble at (Jas. II). By this faith, before the wall was destroyed—that is, before the structure of the other virtues—Christ was its wall, and its outer wall, placed in the soul through that same faith. [Col. 0808C] But because it was unwilling to have Christ as guardian and defender, the practice of virtues is destroyed, and the outer wall mourns: namely, faith, by which it believes in judgment and trembles. Thus it cannot resist enemies—not because the place for repentance is removed, but because it scorns to return.

Allegorically, however. The Lord plans to destroy the walls of the daughter of Zion when he stretches over the Church the line of our sins and the standard of strict judgment, to afflict her according to the merits of her offences. The wall is destroyed—that is, defenders and rulers—when they are either taken away by untimely death or overcome by enemies. But because this happens through God’s just judgment, he does not turn away his hand from the affliction of those being ruined. [Col. 0808D] For Zion, the city of our strength, is ravaged no less inwardly by invisible enemies than outwardly by visible ones. The wall—that is, the Savior—mourns while he causes us to mourn. In this city Christ is both outer wall and wall, and the mourning of his members is ascribed to him. This wall is destroyed when the Church is desolated by the loss of his protection.

Similar is what blessed Job says: “As though a wall had been broken through and a gate opened, they rushed upon me and rolled themselves down upon my miseries” (Job XXX).

> [Note: [Col. 0807D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XX, chapter 53.]

What is designated in this place by the name “wall” except the Redeemer of humankind? Concerning him it is said through the prophet for the building up of holy Church: “A wall and an outer wall shall be set in her” (Isa. [Col. 0809A] XXVI). For he is our wall, who prevents the course of malignant spirits from proceeding to our hearts. He also set an outer wall to our faith, because before showing himself in the flesh he sent prophets as preachers of his mystery. Prophets are rightly called by the name “outer wall,” because, while they preached the Lord who was to follow, they stood, as it were, before the wall. But the wall is, as it were, broken through when faith in our Redeemer is destroyed in the hearts of some through the persuasions of the wicked. For when power is granted to the perverse in this life, what else is opened but the gate of error? Thus, as though a wall had been broken through and a gate opened, evil persons rush upon the good when, having received temporal power, the perverse seek also to destroy in the hearts of some the fortifications [Col. 0809B] of faith.

Of them it is aptly added: “And they rolled themselves down upon my miseries,” because, plainly, they had first fallen into their own. For unless through wicked living they had first fallen into their own miseries, they would never afterward have urged others toward those same miseries. But after their own miseries, the reprobate roll themselves down also upon ours when they draw into the evils in which they themselves are already entangled certain persons from among us who have united themselves to them.

The name “wall” may also be understood as the fortification of discipline, as Solomon testifies, saying: “I passed through the field of a slothful man and through the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. XXIV). To pass through the field of a slothful person and the vineyard of a foolish person [Col. 0809C] is to inspect the life of any negligent person and consider his works. Nettles and thorns fill it because in the heart of the negligent there spring up itching earthly desires and the prickings of vices. For it is written: “Every idle person is in desires” (Prov. XIII, according to the Septuagint). “The stone wall had been destroyed,” that is, the discipline of the Fathers had been dissolved from his heart. For because he saw that the stone wall had been destroyed—that discipline had been dissolved—he immediately added there: “When I saw this, I laid it up in my heart, and by the example I learned discipline” (Prov. XXIV). Thus, as though a wall had been broken through, the enemy enters when, through the cunning persuasion either of malignant spirits or of wicked people, the defenses of discipline are destroyed in the heart.

> [Note: [Col. 0809D] The Benedictine revisers of the works of St. Gregory erred in assigning these words to Proverbs, chapter XXVIII, verse 19, both in the body of the text and in the index of scriptural passages, whereas they plainly correspond to the passage indicated by me. Nor did the editors of Jerome, who read “Every idle person is in desires” [Epistle 97, formerly 8], know to which chapter these words belonged; for they noted none. They are cited by Cassian, *Institutes*, book X, chapter 21, and *Conferences* 24, chapter 2, where his editor Alardus Gazaeus rightly observes that in their place the Vulgate has, “The sluggard wills and wills not,” which is the passage we place in the margin, as may likewise be seen in the index of the texts of the same Cassian, according to the Septuagint version, prepared by Peter Chacon. Since, therefore, these words are found in so many and such great Fathers, we are surprised that they escaped the diligence of Peter Sabatier, who assigned them a place in the Bibles which he edited.]

[Col. 0809D] Therefore, dearest brethren, take the greatest care that the norm of the Gospel and the discipline of the holy Fathers may not be dissolved in your hearts through the persuasion of malignant spirits or perverse people. For, as has been said above, whoever in the mind dissolves the rigor of the Lord’s commands through either fleshly pleasure or wicked persuasion will provide enemies an entrance into himself [Col. 0810A]. We ought, therefore, unceasingly to fulfill the Lord’s commands in deed and call to mind the saving examples of the holy Fathers, so that, strengthened by examples and instructed by the Lord’s commands, we may walk on the straight path and depart from this valley of tears to the harbor of salvation.

The examples of the holy Fathers who went before strengthen the faithful in good work, and the commands of God, as though cords, lift them up to heaven. Hence we read in Jeremiah: “Ebed-melech the Ethiopian eunuch spoke to King Zedekiah, saying: ‘My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done against Jeremiah the prophet, casting him into the pit, that he may die there of hunger; for there is no longer bread in the city.’ Therefore the king commanded Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, saying: [Col. 0810B] ‘Take with thee from here thirty men and lift Jeremiah out of the pit before he dies.’ Ebed-melech therefore took men with him and entered the king’s house, which was beneath the storeroom; and he took from there old rags and things that had rotted away, and lowered them to Jeremiah in the pit by ropes. And Ebed-melech said to Jeremiah: ‘Put the old rags, these torn and rotten things, beneath the elbows of thy hands and over the ropes.’ Jeremiah therefore did so. And they drew him out of the pit” (Jer. XXXVIII).

Now we must say what these things signify. Just as those princes who put the prophet into the pit signify those who always desire to plunge Christ’s faithful into the mud of vices and the filth of sins, so this Ethiopian eunuch, who, pierced by the fear and love [Col. 0810C] of God, rescued the prophet, signifies the preachers from among the Gentiles who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. By the prompting of true charity they strive to draw the unjustly oppressed out of the pit of destruction; and his name also bears witness to this. For Ebed-melech is interpreted “servant of the king,” namely of him of whom it is said: “The great King above all gods” (Ps. XCIV). The order of preachers serves him through the word of the Gospel, joining the Gentiles to the faith.

That, assisted by divine admonitions and the examples of the Fathers who went before, we are liberated from the depth of this life, is aptly signified through Jeremiah, to whom ropes and old rags are lowered so that he may be lifted from the pit. For the ropes signify the Lord’s commands, which, because they come upon us and seize us while we are set in sin, bind and draw us, constrain and lift us up, as it were. But lest, bound by these ropes, we be cut while we are drawn up, old rags are also to be applied: namely, so that, lest divine commands terrify us, the examples of the ancient Fathers may strengthen us, and so that by comparison with them we may presume ourselves able to do what, from our own weakness, we fear. If, therefore, [Col. 0811A] we cannot be raised from this depth, let us quickly be bound by ropes—that is, let us be constrained by the Lord’s commands. Let old rags also be present, so that the ropes may be held more securely; that is, let us be strengthened by the examples of those who went before, lest the subtle commands wound us in our weakness. Hence it is said: “Remember your leaders, who spoke to you the word of God; considering the outcome of their manner of life, imitate their faith” (Heb. XIII).

[Col. 0812A] Therefore, beloved, let us recall before the eyes of our minds the examples of the ancient Fathers, and, setting aside every delay, follow in their footsteps, so that, bound and lifted up by the cords of God’s commands, we may be able, with Christ as our guide, to attain their fellowship—he who lives and reigns as God with the same Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## EIGHTEENTH SERMON: ON PALM BRANCHES

[Col. 0811]

[Col. 0811B] Isaiah the prophet, dearest brethren, being a noble man of urban elegance, who, taught many things by the Holy Spirit, clearly foretold Christ’s Incarnation, birth, Passion, death, descent into hell, ascension into heaven, and the sending of the Holy Spirit, again speaks concerning his second coming for our instruction and exhortation—indeed, for that of the whole Church—to the holy apostles and to all the rulers of that same Church, saying: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, thy Savior comes, and his reward is with him, and his work before him” (Isa. LXII). As though he said more plainly: O holy apostles and other teachers, to whom God has entrusted his Church, to be governed by teaching and example and guarded against visible and invisible enemies, tell that same Church, the daughter of contemplation [Col. 0811C], that, not sleeping in sins but watching in God’s commands, not negligent in works but diligent in holy actions, she should await Jesus Christ, her Savior and bridegroom, coming to judgment.

Hence the Son of God says to those same persons in the Gospel: “Watch, for you do not know when the master of the house will come: in the evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning” (Mark XIII). Certainly the holy Church is the daughter of God the Father and the bride of Christ. God the Father begot her through the Gospel of his Son. Hence it is said: “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I). And again: “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John XX). For the adopted children of God are those who maintain right faith by works and adorn it with worthy conduct. Hence in the Song of Songs the bride, that is, the holy Church, says: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song I).

Spiritually, the primitive Church, which took its beginning from Judea, is the mother of the whole Church. The sons of the mother were the holy apostles, who fought against the multitude of the Gentiles with the word and, with the Lord’s cooperation, conquered them by signs and most true arguments; having conquered them, they made them subject or devoted to Christ. Alternatively: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” The Synagogue was mother of the holy Church according to the flesh; therefore the Jews, children of the Synagogue, fought against the Church. The Church shows from whom she endured the first rage of persecutors—a persecution appearing more grievous [Col. 0812B] because she suffered it at the hands of her own fellow tribesmen.

Paul, persecutor of the Church, was according to the flesh a son of the Synagogue. Let Isaiah the prophet therefore say: O holy teachers, “Say to the daughter of Zion,” that is, to the holy Church, which, rejecting evils, pursuing goods, and discerning true things from false, is a daughter of contemplation: “Behold, thy Savior comes,” namely to judgment, “with great power and majesty” (Luke XXI). “Behold, his reward is with him,” namely, for the good and the evil, “to render to each according to his works” (Matt. XVI). “And his work is before him”: namely, the power of judging justly. For he is established by God the Father as judge of the living and the dead (Acts X).

“Behold,” he says, “thy Savior comes”—not another’s, but thine; not a stranger, but one sent by God the Father in the first coming for thy redemption; for thee born and suffering, and crucified, dead, and buried not for his own sins but for thine exceedingly grave sins; raised by his own power and that of God the Father, and exalted at the right hand of that same Father. Therefore know that he is now soon to come, to examine thee—that is, all thy acts—and the world by fire.

It follows (ibid.): “And they shall call them a holy people.” The holy apostles and other teachers will call the holy Church which they have acquired a holy people, rejoicing with her and saying: “You are a holy people; you are redeemed by the Lord.” Hence blessed Peter says: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession,” etc. (I Pet. II). And Paul: “You are now no longer strangers and sojourners, [Col. 0812D] but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household,” etc. (Eph. II).

Again he adds, saying: “But thou shalt be called a Sought-Out City, and not Forsaken.” As though it were said: O Church, thou shalt be called a Sought-Out City, redeemed by God the Father with the blood of his Son; and thou shalt not be called forsaken, as Judea was once forsaken and abandoned by God because of its denial. Hence it is said: “The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke XIX). For this is the sheep, namely the holy Church, which the good shepherd came to seek, leaving the others in the wilderness (Luke XV).

It follows (Isa. LXIII): “Who is this who comes from [Col. 0813A] Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” These words are spoken in the person of angels who are ignorant of the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, birth, Passion, and Resurrection, and who inquire at his Ascension, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” How great, how mighty, how wonderful, with so great an army, in dyed garments from Bozrah! Dyed, indeed, first with blood upon the cross; or because even then, that is, on the day of judgment, his scars will appear.

Some angels, as we have said, not fully knowing the mystery of the Incarnation, Passion, and Resurrection, see the Lord ascending to heaven with a multitude of angels and holy people by his own power, not by angelic aid. They marvel at the mystery of the Ascension and at how he opened the kingdom of heaven to himself and to others. Hence they say to the angels accompanying the Lord: “Who is this who comes from Edom,” etc. And likewise in David: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII). Augustine nevertheless appears to say in his work on Genesis that all angels, from their very creation, immediately knew in contemplation of their Creator whatsoever he was to do. Jerome, however, openly declares that some angels did not fully know until the mystery of the Incarnation had been completed.

> [Note: [Col. 0813D] From the Gloss, as the remainder.]

Edom is named either from the food of the red lentil, for which Esau sold his birthright, or from its colour. For it is interpreted “earthly” or “bloody,” and signifies the world. Esau is called “oaken” or “strong”; Seir, “rough,” that is, “hairy.” Here, however [Col. 0813C], it signifies not the man himself but the world according to the interpretation; just as the city Bozrah—that is, “fortified” or “strong”—signifies here not its own actual place but hell according to the interpretation, where souls were held fast, as though under many guards. Hence it is said: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” (Ps. LIX). Or it signifies earthly Jerusalem, fortified with very strong walls, in which the Lord suffered. Jerome says: “Jerusalem is interpreted ‘fortified’ or ‘strong.’ But Bozrah is a city situated neither in the land of promise nor in Edom, but in Moab.” Christ came from the bloody world; he came from Bozrah with dyed garments—that is, with bodily members—from the fortified city, namely Jerusalem [Col. 0813D], where he suffered; or, victorious with his faithful, from hell which he despoiled.

It follows: “This one, beautiful in his robe,” that is, in the clothing of humanity, is said in admiration. As though it were said: Who is this one beautiful in his robe—that is, in the humanity taken from the Virgin—proceeding or walking above all the heavens in the multitude of his strength, that is, in the fullness of divinity, needing no help? Of him the Psalmist says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” etc. (Ps. XLIV). As though he said: Thou, the Word, thou, the King, art beautiful in form, that is, in beautiful divinity, beyond the sons of men, because thou art not merely a man like other human beings, but God and man.

[Col. 0814A] Note that he could have said, “beyond angels”; but because he wishes to show him to be a true human being, he introduces the form of the sons of men. And this is against the heretics who said that his body was phantasmal. “Beautiful in form,” because “grace has been poured out”—that is, shall be poured out—“upon thy lips,” namely in thy proclamations, or in thy presence. Let it therefore be said by the angels asking about Christ: “Who is this one beautiful in his robe, proceeding in the multitude of his strength?”

While the angels accompanying Christ are silent, he himself answers, saying: “I am he who speaks justice, and I am a champion to save.” As though he said more plainly: I am Alpha and Omega (Rev. I), namely God before all ages and man at the end of the ages, to whom judgment has been given by God the Father. I am he who speaks justice, rendering to each according to his works (Matt. XVI); and I am a champion, against demons, for the salvation of the human race.

The angels ask again and say: If, then, thou art such, why is thy garment red and thy clothing like that of those who tread in a winepress? As though they said more clearly: Why is thy garment, that is, thy body, red with thy blood, and why are thy garments, namely thy members, red as with dark reddish must, like those of winepress-treaders? Such things seem unsuitable to thee, but fitting for murderers, adulterers, and the like. The angels seem to say: We have learned that thou speakest justice and that the salvation of all lies in thy judgment; therefore we wish to know why thy garments are stained with must, or why the tunic woven from above, which cannot be torn, and which possessed from the virginal womb such whiteness as no fuller can produce on earth—why it is stained with blood. Mercy befits thee more than cruelty.

The Son of God and man answers them: Precisely because “I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the nations there was no man with me.” All the disciples also “left me and fled” (Matt. XXVI), and yet, trodden underfoot by the Jews, I rose on the third day. The winepress signifies the punishments due to sins. Hence Jeremiah: “The Lord trod the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah” (Lam. I). Sometimes, however, it signifies the gathering of new fruits; hence the psalms “For the winepresses” are titled in a favourable sense. Certainly the Son of God trod the winepress alone: namely, the cross and all the torments [Col. 0814D] of the Passion, in which, pressed as in a winepress, even the blood of his body was poured out. Samson, after his hair was cut off, is handed over to the Philistines (Judg. XVI); that is, the Son of God is handed over to visible and invisible enemies. Neither angel nor archangel nor any heavenly spirit, nor any person of the human race, Gentile or Jew, assists him; he fights alone and conquers alone.

“I have trodden the winepress alone,” he says; and adds: “I trod them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath.” Fury is sudden, wrath prolonged; hence, “Brief wrath is fury.” Let it therefore be said: Though slain, I trod them down, namely the Jews and demons, in my fury—that is, in vengeance—and trampled them in my wrath, taking from demons the rule of the world and from the Jews their place [Col. 0815A] and nation, priesthood, temple, and every dignity, through the Romans.

It follows: “And their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I have defiled all my clothing.” As though he said plainly: Their blood—that is, my own blood, shed by them—was sprinkled upon my garments, that is, upon my members; and I defiled, that is, I permitted to be defiled, all my garments in their estimation. My blood was shed by them—that is, through the persuasion of demons and the action of Jews and soldiers. Hence it is said: “The devil put it into Judas’s heart to betray him,” etc. (John XIII). It is their blood, shed by persuasion, and they themselves were conquered and slain there. Likewise Christ’s blood is called the Jews’ blood because they shed it and therefore suffered vengeance. [Col. 0815B] This is said by analogy with victor and vanquished, for the blood of the vanquished is often sprinkled upon the victor’s garments.

Again he adds when he says: “The day of vengeance is in my heart; the year of my recompense has come.” As though it were said more plainly: The day of vengeance against demons or Jews was in my heart while I hung upon the cross, because the year of my recompense—that is, the acceptable time, or the time of the redemption of humankind—had come. It follows: “I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist.” As though he said: I looked around, namely while set upon the cross. Hence: “I looked at my right hand and saw, and there was none who knew me” (Ps. CXLI). I looked around, and there was no helper whatsoever for me; I sought a helper. Hence it is said: “I looked for one to grieve with me, [Col. 0815C] and there was none; and for one to comfort me, and I found none” (Ps. LXVIII).

Again he says: “And my arm saved for me, and my indignation itself assisted me.” As though he said: My arm saved for me—it brought about salvation for me, namely by rising again—and my indignation, that is, vengeance against demons or Jews, itself assisted me. Alternatively: My arm, that is, the Word united to flesh, or my strength, saved for me all those predestined to life.

It follows: “And I trod down the peoples,” namely the Jews, “in my fury, and made them drunk”—that is, filled them with affliction and misery through the Romans—“in my indignation, and brought down to the earth,” that is, reduced to nothing, their power: namely the power of demons and Jews. The prophet, speaking in the person of the Jewish people repenting and recognizing the Lord’s mercy toward itself, says: “I will remember the mercies of the Lord,” oppressed by the weight of evils; “the praise of the Lord,” proclaiming signs and miracles, “above all”—whether good or evil—“that he rendered to us for our sins, because the Lord is just in all his ways and holy in all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

Jeremiah the prophet, speaking as though concerning himself, plainly signifies Christ’s Passion when he says: “I am the man who sees my poverty, under the rod of his indignation” (Lam. III). It is evident to the diligent reader that almost all lamentations over events are marked in the fifth place of inquiry: [Col. 0816A] for individual misfortunes are mourned, so arranged before the eyes of the judge that they seem to see and truly move him to mercy. “I,” he says, “am the man who sees my poverty,” etc. Although this seems applicable to all, it is understood more excellently of Christ, in whom, as all things excel, so does this vision.

For what wonder is it if anyone sees his own poverty, under which nearly everyone oppressed labours? But just as Christ’s poverty is more glorious and more wonderful than all the riches of the world—he “did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II)—so this vision of poverty is more profound and must therefore be considered with the whole attention of mind and heart. Hence the Psalmist: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” [Col. 0816B] (Ps. XL). If this poverty were common, it could be discerned by sense and would not lie open to understanding alone. But now blessed is proclaimed the one who understands concerning the needy and poor. Christ’s poverty, then, is rightly to be marvelled at and investigated.

Since, according to the Apostle, the poverty of the saints is most profound (II Cor. VIII), and understood by few, how much more so that poverty which angels imitate and from the understanding of which blessedness arises. “Blessed indeed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V), but in that spirit by which this poverty is understood, which is disclosed by the Holy Spirit. Therefore the beginnings of three verses are marked by the Hebrew alphabet [Note: [Col. 0815D] Aleph.], which is interpreted “doctrine.” For this sense, concerning which the supreme author glories, needs much instruction; and, as though he alone sees [Col. 0816C] and understands, he says: “I am the man who sees my poverty.” As though the Son of God said: I, in whom are present all treasures of wisdom and knowledge, see my poverty, which I willingly undertook for others; but wretched people refuse to understand it, since they are unwilling even to give heed to their own utter misery.

“I am the man who sees my poverty.” This may be the voice of all the saints, insofar as they are united in Christ’s body, insofar as they have imitated the same poverty, and insofar as they have been gathered into a perfect man by faith and works. Hence follows: “Under the rod of his indignation.” One rod is for guidance, another for kingship; there is also an iron rod, by which earthen vessels are shattered in the wrath of fury, and another by which the saints are governed in equity, [Col. 0816D] so that they may be directed toward the prize of the heavenly calling. There is a rod of indignation, concerning which it is said to Jerusalem: “In my indignation I struck you, and in my reconciliation I had mercy on you” (Isa. X). For by this rod he strikes in order to show mercy; by this rod Christ was struck, not because he deserved indignation, but because “he was struck for the crime of the people” (Isa. LIII). This is what he says: “Under the rod of his indignation.” Because of God’s indignation at our crimes, the Son of God and man endured the poverty of the Passion, so that “by his wound we might be healed” (ibid.). Either none of the saints, or only a few, fully perceive the mystery of this poverty. How great is God’s goodness, and how great his love toward [Col. 0817A] the children of wrath! How great his mercy toward the children of reconciliation! Therefore, as though he alone perceived it, he says: “I am the man who sees my poverty,” etc. He sees his wondrous [Note: [Col. 0817D] Another manuscript: “wretched.”] and ineffable poverty; he sees the poverty of his members, by which they are united to him, knowing that “the patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Ps. IX). Thus it is rightly the voice of head and body—that is, of Christ and the Church—because “God chastises every son whom he receives” (Prov. III). Prolepsis here denotes the anticipation of matters to be stated. He puts “his” first, although he has not yet said to what it refers, because he does not doubt that it is known that the Father struck the Son with the rod of the Passion. It is therefore no wonder if his members are struck by the rod of indignation for correction, so that there may be one voice, one groaning, one lamentation in the valley of tears.

[Col. 0817B] It may also be expounded morally: “I am the man who sees my poverty.” “The spirit of man alone knows the things of man” (I Cor. II); whenever it is touched by the divine Spirit, it is moved to tears as it understands its poverty, saying: “I am the man who sees my poverty,” etc. For when it is scourged by God’s indignation and stirred by tears, it knows itself to be nothing, since it possesses no work of virtue by which it could presume upon itself. For no one can rightly boast that he has a chaste heart (Prov. XX). Therefore the humble and tearful person confesses: “I am the man who sees my poverty,” etc. For one struck by the rod of indignation does not presume upon himself; hence he added: “He threatened me and led me into darkness,” etc. For every soul, [Col. 0817C] when it recalls God’s wrath, considers the terror of judgment, and places its deeds before its eyes as though at the point of death, sees itself, infected by sorrows, dwelling in darkness, while it recognizes the poverty of its merits beneath the rod of God’s indignation. Hence it rightly says: “He threatened me and led me into darkness,” etc. When it feels nothing in itself except weakness, it laments that it has been led, as it were, into darkness. Such a soul, while contemplating the rod of God’s examination and his threats, and searching out its evils on every side, rightly believes itself led into darkness and not into light, lest, presuming upon itself, it lose humility and incur pride; for “blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V). The spirit of man, seeing its poverty, rightly trembles, since it does not doubt that it is under the rod of indignation and understands that it has been threatened and led thereto. This is the instruction signified by *aleph*: that the soul should always examine itself, uncover all that is its own, and mourn until the Dayspring from on high enlightens it, he “who came to give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death” (Luke I).

“He threatened me,” he says, “and led me into darkness and not into light,” namely when the Father willed to crush the Son in weakness, and he was “reckoned as a leper, struck by God, and humbled” (Isa. LIII); he was led, as it were, into darkness and not into light. Yet “the darkness did not comprehend him” (John I). The Church also, which he subjects to threats and terrors, he leads into the darkness of affliction and not into the light of present prosperity.

Hence follows (Lam. III): “Only against me he turned and turned his hand.” God, with a motherly affection, exposes the soul to temptations and casts it down; then at times he receives it, weeping and grieving, into his bosom, offers it the milk of teaching, and consoles it. This is what he says: “Only against me he turned and turned his hand all day long.” This too refers equally to the members and the head: “All who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus suffer persecutions” (II Tim. III); theirs is the voice: “Only against me he turned and turned his hand.” For he does not correct some, but allows them to wander freely; whereas he afflicts the Church, both from Jews and from Gentiles, with many pains of discipline. He turns his hand [Col. 0818B] to chastise, because “he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. III); and he mercifully turns it back in order to show mercy. For we turn back our hand when we withdraw it from striking. Thus he turns back his hand by sparing and helping those whom he corrects by punishing. But concerning others it is said: “They are not in the toil of men, nor are they scourged with men” (Ps. LXXII). This is aptly signified when, in the building of Solomon’s Temple, neither hammer nor sound was heard (III Kings VI): for everything was prepared and shaped outside, so that it might fit together inside in its proper places of joining. Hence it says: “He turned his hand,” namely, by filing, shaping, and smoothing the walls [Note: [Col. 0818D] “all,” i.e. “all the walls.”] so that they might fit in the building. “And he turned back his hand,” namely [Col. 0818C] by ceasing, when he assigns the justified to their proper dwellings and ranks. Therefore those whose structure is one and whose bodily joining is one have one voice and one lamentation; and the voice of Christ and of the Church is so united that the whole Christ is found.

Again he adds, saying: “He made my skin and my flesh old; he crushed my bones.” Christ is not afflicted by the oldness of sin, but his members, grown old in vices, are corrupted; and this both head and body lament together. Hence David says: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI). This man who sees his poverty has an old skin and flesh; he has ram skins dyed red for covering the tabernacle, and violet skins for adornment (Exod. XXXVI). Poor in those things which are affected by oldness; [Col. 0818D] rich in those which, for the adornment of his name, are reddened by his own blood—that is, the bodies of the saints are crowned by martyrdom. Hence it is said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII). The violet skins are those whom virginity raises to heaven, where “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as angels in heaven” (Matt. XXII). Thus in the tabernacle they are nearer heaven; likewise the skins of Solomon—that is, of Christ—whose skins are all the saints who have put themselves to death with Christ, by whom the vital members of the body are covered, so that they may imitate Christ’s Passion. Whoever is his skin will contain the divine [Col. 0819A] mysteries in the recesses of the soul, as if in the Holy of Holies. But because the use of a skin is varied, in some its beauty is praised, in others the depth of mysteries is covered, and in others the Church is defended. Hence the saying: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job II). For it is certain that the saints are handed over to sufferings, so that their own souls and those of others may be saved through instruction and example. Satan speaks as though saying: Why do you delay to give this man to me, when you hand over all the saints to sufferings for the salvation of souls? Since therefore such is the glory of skins, Christ, or the Church, groans because some are affected by the stain of sin, as by old skin. Sin belongs to oldness, virtue to newness. Hence it is said: “Putting off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new” [Col. 0819B] (Col. III), who “was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IV). The Church is worn out by this oldness, since in the present life it cannot be without spot and wrinkle. By “flesh” is signified the whole people in Christ’s body, as something soft and tender. Hence it is said: “When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh” (Ps. XXVI). For unless flesh were the oldnesses of sin, it would not be food for enemies. “He crushed my bones,” he says—that is, the stronger persons, because in Christ’s Passion even the apostles were crushed and scattered in fear. He says that God did this because in his just judgment he permitted it.

“He made my skin and my flesh old; he crushed my bones.” Morally understood: the soul laments the oldness of its sin; and it does not mourn skins, but its skin, [Col. 0819C] infected by oldness, with which the first human beings, expelled from paradise, were clothed. This is the one skin of many, darkened by oldness, which through the transgression of the first man clothed all with mortality and the horror of sin. Hence: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI). The soul therefore groans when its conscience outwardly grows old like a skin, while inwardly its beauty, like flesh, is consumed by the corruption of sin. “To eat my flesh,” he says (Ps. XXVI), that is, its fleshly affections, to which the devil first draws near, so that he may draw those in whom they are into his own body as flesh. When this flesh is consumed, we shall be spirit, and the enemy will find nothing to harm. “He crushed my bones,” that is, the virtues of the soul. For bones [Col. 0819D] are the support of the body, and the virtues are the support of the mind; when they are broken by pleasures, torments, or the deceits of the ancient enemy, the soul rightly laments its broken bones.

It follows: “He built around me and surrounded me with gall and labor.” This is the voice of the Church groaning—indeed, of Christ in his members—who, seized in the Passion, says: “I was handed over and could not go out” (Ps. XXXVII), because the Father had built an encircling siege against him, when they surrounded him with weapons and torches and led him bound before the governor (Matt. XXVII). Thus hemmed in, Christ’s humanity was afflicted as though by the gall of bitterness and the labor of tribulation. So too, surrounded by a rampart, he was led to the Passion, and there fed with gall and labor. Hence the Psalmist says in [Col. 0820A] his person: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). In the gall, the bitterness of the Passion in the mind is signified; in the labor, tribulation in the flesh, so that Christ’s whole Passion may be understood. The Church suffers these same passions daily; it is “of his flesh and of his bones” (Eph. V), in order that it may complete what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings (Col. I). Thus it says: “He built around me and surrounded me with gall and labor.” For the Church, besieged by every evil, dwells among scorpions, where Satan’s throne is (Apoc. II); it is surrounded by an army of heretics; it drinks, as it were, gall and labor from false brothers; it is oppressed on every side by the torments of persecutors. On this side worldly pleasures and desires of the flesh flatter it; on that side the ancient enemy [Col. 0820B] spreads snares everywhere. Therefore it rightly cries: “He built around me and surrounded me with gall and labor.” Hence elsewhere: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. LIV). By these and similar things it is embittered in the mind as with gall, while in the flesh it is wearied by labor.

“He built around me and surrounded me with gall and labor.” Morally, every soul likewise grieves, shut up in the gall of malice and wearied by labor, especially when it sees itself pressed on every side and filled with its own iniquities. For this is what unclean spirits attempt: whether and how they may entangle the wretched soul in depraved pleasures and fill it with most evil desires, whose final consequences become more bitter than any gall.

[Col. 0820C] Again he adds, saying: “He placed me in darkness, as the everlasting dead.” Here Christ is likened to the prophets. Hence it is said: “I was likened in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. XII). And again: “At many times and in many ways,” etc. (Heb. I). These words plainly suggest Christ’s Passion. Let it therefore be said: “He placed me in darkness,” etc. This seems especially to pertain to the head, that is, to Christ. For Christ died for us, not like the dead of the world, who receive death as the reward of wickedness and from the propagation of sin; hence, “as the everlasting dead.” For although he was truly dead, God did not cast him away forever. Yet he was placed in darkness—whether that of hell, the tomb, [Col. 0820D] or the Passion—but not as one everlasting dead, because he was “free among the dead,” being without sin. Therefore he also rose quickly.

These three verses complete the letter *beth*, which is also interpreted “confusion.” For whoever falls into oldness, with strength broken, is surrounded by the siege of the ancient enemy, filled with the gall of bitterness, and placed in darkness—that is, in confusion. But because the confusion of the human race is lamented, he rightly laments under this letter the ruin of the whole house and the stain of oldness. For *beth* is interpreted “house,” and the house says because of its confusion: “He made my skin old,” etc. The oldness of skin can indeed be referred to Christ according to the mortality of the flesh which he assumed. The remaining matters under this letter are more suitably applied to him.

[Col. 0821A] “He placed me in darkness, like the everlasting dead.” Morally: the soul placed in confusion laments in stages. First, because it lies decayed by the oldness of sin; then because, surrounded by the enemy’s deceit, it cannot go out to freedom, encompassed by the gall of desires and the labor of sins; finally, having lost light and been placed in darkness, it cannot see itself—how miserable and unhappy it is, by what evils it is oppressed, or of what goods it is stripped. For this is what the enemy especially strives for: that the soul should lose the light and not recover what it has lost. Thus the Philistines gouge out Samson’s eyes, then send him to the mill, so that, walking in a circle, he may never find the way of life. Thus Nebuchadnezzar puts out Zedekiah’s eyes, then carries him in chains to Babylon in a cage, so that, shut up in confusion, [Col. 0821B] he may see light no more. Yet while such a soul, still bound in flesh, weeps, it is not truly dead; but while it is granted a place for repentance, it lives by hope, before “the pit presses its mouth upon it” (Ps. LXVIII). But because, through God’s mercy, it returns from the depth of iniquity to life, the letter *gimel* follows, interpreted “retribution” or “fulness.”

“He built a wall against me, so that I may not go out; he made my fetter heavy.” As though Christ said: The Father stirred up the hearts of the Jews against me and surrounded me with cohorts, so that I might not escape from their hands until the prophecies of the prophets were fulfilled. He shut out this prayer, namely: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI).

[Col. 0821C] The Church likewise is shut in by the doctrines of heretics and surrounded by the punishments of persecutors; lamenting this, it attributes everything to God, by whose judgment it happens. “He made my fetter heavy,” that is, the severity of torments or deceptions, as no one doubts has frequently happened. It also groans that its prayer is shut out, when divine help is delayed for its testing, but not removed. Yet it has its anchor—that is, its hope—fixed in heaven, lest it be submerged by waves of this sort. It follows: “He shut up my ways with squared stones,” that is, the paths of the holy Scriptures with the squared utterances of philosophers, lest citizens may reach their desired homeland by the straight path of faith. “He overthrew my paths,” that is, he permitted the most subtle understandings of divine matters [Col. 0821D] to be overthrown by worldly doctrine.

“He built a wall against me, so that I may not go out; he made my fetter heavy.” Morally: the soul, for which the retribution signified by *gimel* now threatens because of its crimes, cries out: “He built a wall against me,” etc. As though it said: “The sorrows of death surrounded me, and the perils of hell found me” (Ps. CXIV). Weighed down by these fetters, lest it be unable to escape, the soul fears; its own act was to fall, but it belongs to the merciful God to rescue it. Miserable for it is this: shut up in the prison of most evil captivity, it cannot go forth into the freedom of good action. It is burdened by the fetters of offenses and carnal pleasures; it is burdened [Col. 0822A] by the enemy’s deceits, so that, bound by these snares, it cannot hasten freely toward the things unseen. Fetters are made heavier whenever we add iniquity to iniquity—iniquity which is aptly described as sitting upon lead.

Again he adds, saying: “He shut out my prayer.” Tears and prayers obtain the mercy of the judge. Therefore one may be greatly grieved when one feels that the judge is so offended that prayer cannot pass to the fountain of mercy. This happens whenever God permits us to sin in such a way that our crimes stop the ears of the merciful judge. Hence it is said: “He who shuts his ears lest he hear the law, his prayer too shall be abominable” (Prov. XXVIII). Again he says: “He shut up my ways with squared stones,” etc. Sins have their own squareness. Hence Boethius says [Note: [Col. 0821D] Vergil, *Aeneid* VI, v. 733.]:

> “Hence they fear, desire, rejoice, and grieve.”

By these the paths of our sins are made square, so that at last the unhappy soul, infected by oldness, besieged by enemies, encompassed by the gall of iniquity and misery, and wearied by vain labors, may return to itself; against it enemies rage both inwardly and outwardly. Burdened by these fetters, let it pray to the merciful Judge and cry without ceasing, that at least because of its importunity it may receive what it asks; for “the Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. CXLIV). Otherwise it cannot pass to its homeland if “the lust of the eyes, the pleasure of the flesh, and the pride of life” (I John II) obstruct its way. But if it turns to the holy Scriptures as to the pastures of life, in which it finds the straight way, [Col. 0822C] immediately the squared stones of heretics confront it, by which the way of faith is blocked and the paths are overthrown. Therefore let the soul say with the Prophet: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. LIV); and with the Apostle: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. VII). Divine grace alone delivers from all these things.

It follows: “He became to me a bear lying in wait, a lion in a hiding-place.” Historically: what could be more terrible than that the author of our salvation should become a bear and a lion to us? The bear is a deceitful beast, very strong in its forearms and loins. In Nebuchadnezzar, and in Vespasian and Titus—who elsewhere are called “the boar” and “the solitary one” [Note: [Col. 0822D] The Gloss: “wild beasts.”] (Ps. LXXIX)—the Lord is called bear and lion, in whom God’s power takes vengeance on enemies. It is therefore rightly lamented that the pious and merciful God, because sins demand it, becomes a lion or bear, so that his power may besiege and afflict his enemies. Jerusalem is made, as it were, a target for the arrow, because it is besieged on every side by surrounding enemies, so that, frequently wounded as by arrows, it may return to the physician, if only by compulsion. These arrows—that is, these nations—he sent against Jerusalem as though from a drawn bow, by measured judgment, that it might at least learn to fear God, lest, wounded by its enemies’ arrows, it should perish. Its paths are overthrown by enemies, and it itself is broken. “He became to me a bear lying in wait, a lion in a hiding-place.” Morally: [Col. 0823A] under the letter *daleth*, which signifies fear, the Church, struck with fear, laments: “He became to me a bear lying in wait, a lion,” etc. For it laments, as though desolate, that it has experienced both the force of arrows in the open and snares in secret. “He stretched his bow,” that is, his judgment, which nevertheless he delays, because he would rather find persons to reward than persons to condemn. Hence it is said: “You gave a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. LIX). The bow may also be understood as Scripture, in which the string of the New Testament bends the hardness of the Old. From it arrows are sent out by which hardness of heart is pierced. From the bow of judgment arrows are sent out to destroy vices and other things that wound charity. But the soul is like a target, so that on one side it may receive the wounds of charity and on the other repel the enemy’s darts.

[Col. 0823B] “He became to me a bear lying in wait, a lion in a hiding-place.” Allegorically: it is the common voice of head and body that he who is eternal and unchangeable has become a bear lying in wait—not because he is changed from his nature of piety and goodness, but because of his effects. For he permitted one to rise against his Son who, like a bear lying in wait, attempted by deceit and strength to kill and deceive him, just as he attempted the same against his body from the beginning to the end. “A lion in hiding-places.” By these two beasts the whole savagery of the devil is shown: by the lion, the devil himself; by the bear, his members, namely heretics and false brethren. For although the bear is very strong in forearms and loins, its head is weak, just as all evil persons have a weak head, namely the devil, [Col. 0823C] who goes about either openly as a lion or secretly as a bear, “seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V). Clearly, he trusts in his own strength, going about roaring and snarling; of his snares the Psalmist says: “He lies in wait in secret, like a lion in his den” (Ps. IX). With these weapons he fights against the head and the members. Thus the Prophet groans—or rather, Christ and the Church: “He became to me a bear lying in wait, a lion,” etc. (I Kings XVII). These are the beasts that come against David, shepherd of the sheep, because they desire to devour the flock; but David rescues the sheep from the lion’s mouth and the bear’s jaws, and tears off their forearms. This is Christ, who leads his sheep to the pastures of life, rescues them from the lion’s mouth, and breaks the forearms of bears. But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture (Ps. XCIX). They also carry off the ram [Col. 0823D] from the midst of the flock, as we know David himself said; unless the Lord had rescued it, it would not have escaped from their hand. These beasts rise against David, that is, against Christ himself; David killed the bear and lion, which occurred in Christ’s death, when he set the sheep free.

“He overthrew my paths,” he says, “and broke me; he made me desolate.” He repeats this in lament: “He made me desolate.” Jerusalem, namely, which the prophet had previously lamented, perhaps now returned to herself; indeed, Christ’s bride, endowed with his blood, groans that she is desolate and, like an adulteress, abandoned by her bridegroom. “Like a target for the arrow,” he says. For Christ and the Church are raised as a target and a banner against all aerial powers and deceits. Hence it is said: [Col. 0824A] “We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men” (I Cor. IV). Christ, in himself and in all his members, is opposed to the enemy’s darts.

It follows: “He sent into my loins the daughters of his quiver.” Historically: the Lord, by just judgment, as though from a bow long drawn, at last sends arrows—the daughters of the quiver—into their loins, to punish the lust of those of whom it is said: “Every one lusted after his neighbor’s wife” (Jer. V). By the quiver is signified God’s hidden judgment, by which Nebuchadnezzar and other ravagers are directed as arrows against Jerusalem, that it, exposed like a target, may be wounded. When the prophet rebuked it as already besieged, he mocked it as frivolous. Hence it is said: “I became a mockery to all my people, their song all day long. He filled me with bitter things; [Col. 0824B] he made me drunk with wormwood.” He laments that in himself and in his people the Lord’s threatened judgment was fulfilled. “I shall feed this people,” he says, “with wormwood, and give them gall-water to drink” (Jer. IX). Hence it is now said: “He made me drunk with wormwood.” For Jerusalem was filled and given wormwood to drink both in the first captivity and in the second, namely with distresses and necessities. By gall-water is signified the greatness of evils and the everlasting yoke of captivity, or ignorance of the Law, because, filled with the bitterness of gall, they are to receive Antichrist in place of Christ. “He sent into my loins the daughters of his quiver.” Morally also the soul is daily made drunk with these and similar bitterness, so that nothing in the present appears sweet to it while it is ceaselessly [Col. 0824C] afflicted by so many evils. “He sent,” he says, “into my loins the daughters of his quiver.” Again let this be read allegorically, so that the truth of Christ’s Passion may be understood more subtly. The letter *he* is interpreted “living” or “is”; for from the beginning of this alphabet Christ’s self-emptying is displayed, according to: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” etc. (Phil. II), on account of which he endured reproaches, sufferings, and death. It is as though he said: Although I have suffered many things, yet I truly am, and truly live, and I will the life of the sinner, because life does not will death. This is the shared voice of bridegroom and bride: she confesses that she is and lives, and he answers, “I am and I live,” according to: “I rose again, and I am still with you” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Therefore he who is and lives, and weeps for us and for them, “sent into [Col. 0824D] my loins the daughters of his quiver,” etc. The Father’s quiver is Scripture, from which, by God’s judgment as from a bow, Christ’s body received arrows, which he himself bore first. At times he makes these arrows burning, so that cold hearts may be wounded by the heat of charity. Heretics likewise bring poisoned arrows of unbelief from this quiver and strike the hearts of the innocent. From this quiver come the arrows by which the outer person is pierced by fear and the inner person moved by love. Hence it is said: “Pierce my flesh with your fear,” etc. (Ps. CXVIII). When he says, “He sent into my loins the daughters of his quiver,” that is, the affections of divine love or fear, the loins signify carnal propagation and faith the spiritual begetting of virtues. From these loins Christ begets spiritual children in the womb of the chaste Mother, [Col. 0825A] namely the Church. He sends into the loins the daughters of the quiver—that is, arrows—by which persons may be wounded unto love or fear, so that vices may be slain and virtues propagated. Hence David says: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. XXV); and elsewhere: “Your arrows are fixed in me,” etc. (Ps. XXXVII). Holy preachers likewise are directed as arrows from this quiver; hence it is said: “He hid me in his quiver” (Isa. XLIX). Christ speaks as though saying: God the Father hid me, like a chosen arrow, in his quiver, so that, hidden in the recesses of the Scriptures, I might finally be shot from the bow and test the loins and hearts of all.

It follows: “I became a mockery to all my people, their song all day long.” Similar is: “I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men [Col. 0825B] and the outcast of the people” (Ps. XXI), which was displayed in the Passion. “He filled me with the bitterness of suffering; he made me drunk with the wormwood of myrrhed wine.” Hence it is said: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LVIII). When he says that he was made drunk with wormwood, he shows that both inwardly and outwardly he was affected by the bitterness of the Passion. By these and similar pains the whole body of Christ will be tormented until the consummation. I mean the whole body of Christ, his universal Church redeemed by precious blood, which, formed by the example of its teacher and Lord, devoutly performs good works and patiently endures adversities.

Therefore, dearest brethren, recognizing God’s great benefits toward [Col. 0825C] us and venerating his Son’s Passion with spiritual love and contrition of heart, it is fitting that we should continually render him thanksgivings with tears.
