For this reason he suffered for us: that he might gain us for God the Father; cleanse our heart from every impiety; teach our tongue, which formerly praised idols, to praise the one true God in Trinity; and show that our souls must be cleansed from the filth of vices by daily tears.

For Elijah prefigured this (III Kings XVIII), where, against the false prophets and priests, he proposed a sacrifice of a bull without fire, concerning whether Baal or the God of Israel was to be worshipped. Once his prayer was completed, heavenly fire immediately consumed it; and so, before King Ahab [Col. 0825D] and the people of Israel, he conquered them and slew them at the torrent Kishon. Elijah said to all the people: “Come to me”; and when the people came to him, he repaired the altar of the Lord which had been destroyed. He took twelve stones according to the number of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel, and built an altar from the stones in the Lord’s name. Thus our Redeemer, fighting and conquering through his Passion and cross against the ruler of this world and his attendants, cleansed the Lord’s altar which had been destroyed—[Col. 0826A] that is, cleansed believers’ hearts from the stain of iniquity—and dedicated an altar to God. It is said to be built of twelve stones because the altar most pleasing to God is constructed from those who follow prophetic and apostolic faith or teaching; on it the sacrifice of praise is offered as a sweet savor.

It follows: “And he made a trench, as it were, for two furrows around the altar,” producing streams of tears from a contrite heart and humble spirit, for the benefits of Christ’s Passion and resurrection bestowed upon him by God, through fear of Gehenna and desire for eternal life. There Elijah arranged the wood, because the Son of God established the sayings and deeds of the holy Fathers as an example for believers. “And he divided the bull into its parts and placed it on the wood,” when [Col. 0826B] he taught the faithful to shape all their actions after the example of the holy Fathers. And he commanded water to be poured once, twice, and three times over the holocaust and over the wood, because at all times it is necessary to cleanse our words, thoughts, and all our works in pure prayer and the tearful compunction of heart, and not to cease until the trenches of the watercourse are filled—that is, until the future joy which succeeds sorrow is perfectly fulfilled. And so it shall be according to what follows: “The fire of the Lord fell and devoured the holocaust, the wood, and the stones.” When the discerning heavenly Judge, perfectly examining our words, deeds, and whole life, places us, after testing us as silver and gold are tested by fire (Zech. XIII), immortal and blessed in an everlasting dwelling, then, after the example of the Israelites, [Col. 0826C] we shall sing forever in rejoicing: “The Lord himself is God” (Ps. XCIV). Without doubt, the Lord himself is God: one in Godhead and three in persons; apart from him there never was, is not, nor shall be another, who mercifully deigned to set us free from the eternal fires of Gehenna by the most precious blood of his Son.

Therefore, beloved, as we have already said above, let us melt the hardness of our hearts in tears, giving thanks to God the Father, “who did not spare his only Son, but delivered him up to suffering and death for us all” (Rom. VIII). It is fitting, therefore, dearest brethren, that, as he suffered for us, we too should crucify our flesh with its vices and desires for love of him; that we should follow his footsteps as far as [Col. 0826D] possible; and that, despising this world’s enticements, we should die with him. Then, where he ascended—namely, to the right hand of the Father—we too, aided according to our measure by his grace and advancing from virtue to virtue, may ascend; and with all the saints may praise without ceasing him who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, is the one true God, through his own granting, he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through endless ages of ages. Amen.

## Nineteenth Sermon: On the Branches

[Col. 0827]

[Col. 0827A] “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, meek, sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke” (Zech. IX).

The King of heaven commands and announces to you, dearest brethren, through the prophet Zechariah, the joy of his coming. The Lord comes for reconciliation; because of the sin of the first parent, he had been, as it were, a stranger and alien to humankind. Therefore, before he came, he sent ambassadors ahead—namely, the patriarchs and prophets—commanding them and saying: “Say to the daughter of Zion,” that is, announce it to my Church, which is called the daughter of Zion because *Zion* is interpreted “watching” or “contemplation.” For the holy Church ought to be a daughter of watchfulness and discernment, choosing what is good and pleasing to God, rejecting evils and what is contrary to God, and, by watching in the holy Scriptures, guarding itself against enemies. [Col. 0827B] Hence the Lord says to the prophet: “If you separate the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. XV). Therefore the holy Church, or any holy soul, becomes as the Lord’s mouth, because through it the Lord’s will is carried out by distinguishing good things from evil.

And he adds what the messengers of this almighty King are to say: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle.” Because of the sin of the first man, the Lord had withdrawn from the human race, though he had formerly been near to it while it lived rationally. For the Lord is seen to have been angry with Adam when, after Adam’s sin, he is read to have walked in Paradise in the breeze after midday. By this act God showed that he wished to help [Col. 0827C] wretched man: he who had first been close to him through creation now walked at a distance from him because of the transgression of sin, though nevertheless, as if grieving with him, he said: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III). As though he said: “In what great misery have you been placed?” The Lord walked among them and did not stand, because they had not stood firm in his commandments. And fittingly the Lord walked in the breeze after midday, because that more ardent light of charity was already being taken away from them, while the darkness of vices drew near. For they hid themselves amid the tree, because, forgetting the commandments of their Creator, they had turned themselves over to error and to the choice of their own will; and the breeze in which the Lord walked signified the cooling of charity in the human mind. [Col. 0827D]

But the Lord, who had withdrawn from man in justice, came to man in mercy. “Through the bowels of mercy the Dayspring from on high visited us” (Luke I). Hence the Prophet says in the Psalm: “He bowed the heavens and came down; and darkness was under his feet” (Ps. XVII). He bowed the heavens—that is, he humbled heavenly things: he joined divinity to humanity, [Col. 0828A] united heavenly things with earthly, and joined the highest to the lowest; he even recalled the angels to peace with man. “And he came down,” that is, by taking the form of a servant in this manner, he made himself low out of compassion for the restoration of the human race. The angels were bowed when, coming to the Lord, they ministered to him (Matt. IV).

But although our Lord Jesus Christ was made humble for us, although he shared our frailty, nevertheless “darkness was under his feet”—that is, the devil, who is darkness and blindness to worldly people, was beneath his feet: he was completely subject to Christ and conquered by him. When the strong warrior, namely Christ, came to battle, “he placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII). Christ’s tabernacle [Col. 0828B] was his body, in which he fought for God the Father. He placed—that is, established—it in the sun, that is, in the Virgin, who was “fair as the moon and chosen as the sun” (Cant. VI). She was fair as the moon because she illumined the darkness of night, namely of this age. She shone as chosen like the sun because, alone among women, she burned with the heat of the Holy Spirit and conceived. Truly he placed his tabernacle in the sun, that is, in the manifestation of good works: for he healed the sick, raised the dead, and justified sinners. Therefore, by union with flesh, having become the bridegroom of the Church, he went forth from his bridal chamber—that is, from the Virgin’s womb. He “rejoiced as a giant,” namely as a strong man, to run the course of his warfare (Ps. XVIII), and came [Col. 0828C] to battle against the prince of this world, saying: “Now the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John XII), namely from human minds, in which he had formerly reigned. Then he chose a few poor disciples, as the Apostle says: “God chose the foolish things of this world and the contemptible, that he might confound the wise; and the weak things, that he might confound the strong” (I Cor. I). Thus, when he hastened to Jerusalem, he did not seek the mount of a powerful horse, but of a humble and despised little ass.

It is therefore necessary, beloved, that we return to what we have set forth. “Behold,” he says, “your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke.” This coming of Christ is the redemption and salvation of both peoples. It is as though he said: The King of heaven, not [Col. 0828D] a stranger but yours, comes through assumed humanity, and comes to you—that is, certainly for your salvation, not for his own, who has no need of a servant, but for yours, since you were poor, exiled, and in need of the Lord. He comes “raising the needy from the earth and lifting up the poor from the dung-hill” (Ps. CXII): raising those filthy in sins from earth, that is, from earthly pleasures, needy of heavenly [Col. 0829A] riches; and lifting from the dung-hill of vices those poor in virtues. Hence it is written: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I), that is, fools in the dung of vices. This King of heaven and earth comes not angry or terrifying, but gentle and humble; for “he humbled himself unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. II). Indeed, he was so humbled for our salvation that, in the very passion, he seemed to be forsaken by God the Father. Hence, already placed upon the cross, he said to God the Father: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. XXVII). And again he had foretold through the Psalmist: “I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. XXI); and again: “My God, I shall cry by day, and you will not hear; and by night, and it is not folly to me” [Col. 0829B] (ibid.).

But we must see how, at the very point of his passion, the Son of God, who is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father, says that he is forsaken by God the Father. God granted the ancient Fathers only temporal goods: abundance of grain, wine, and oil, and victory over their enemies. But God and the Son of God, coming into the world, preached and promised other goods, which the human race lost from the beginning through its sin. Therefore he chose to be poor in this world, in order to show by word and example that temporal goods ought not to be sought by the faithful, but rather despised. Thus, that he might bestow upon us the riches of his goodness, he endured such poverty that at his birth his mother laid him in a manger [Col. 0829C] (Luke II); that, weary from his journey, he sat beside a spring and asked water from a woman (John IV); and that he had nowhere to lay his head (Luke IX). Behold, this Son of God and man seemed, according to his humanity, to be forsaken by God, who allowed him to suffer want and affliction; and therefore he says: “My God, look upon me” (Ps. XXI), that is, strengthen me, and do not allow me to fail in this passion, in which I seem to be forsaken by you. Therefore look upon me, because you have forsaken me—that is, you have seemed to forsake me. “And why have you forsaken me?” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Others do not know, but I know; others are ignorant why you permit me to undergo this sentence of suffering, but I shall explain it. Namely, you have forsaken me amid temporal [Col. 0829D] adversities in order that you may glorify me amid eternal spiritual things. For this reason you permit me to suffer adversity in this present life: that after death you may exalt me in your glory. I know most certainly that you willed me at this time to be subject to suffering, in order that after the resurrection you might set me in your eternity “over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII); so that the humanity which, at your command, I received from the substance of my Virgin mother might have in your right hand the glory by grace which I had with you by nature before the world was made. Therefore, sweetest Father, you forsook me because the sins of my people, whom I came to redeem, required this. This is also the meaning of: “The words of my transgressions”—namely, of my people—“are far from my salvation” [Col. 0830A] (Ps. XXI), because their sins require that I be slain for them, and thus that your will be fulfilled. “I,” he says, “am a worm and not a man.” For this reason our Lord Jesus Christ is compared to a worm: because, like a worm, he is generated without intercourse. As moist earth, warmed by the rays of the sun, produces a worm, so the Virgin Mother of God, ever Mary, overshadowed by God’s power alone and inflamed by the fervour of the Holy Spirit, gave birth to Christ.

Let it therefore be said: “I am a worm,” that is, trodden underfoot and lowly like a worm; I was not reckoned as a man but as a worm, because I am “a reproach of men and the outcast of the people. My God, I shall cry to you by day, and you will not hear,” and so forth. These words are to be understood in this way: As the person of Christ consists of two [Col. 0830B] substances, namely divinity and humanity, so there were in him two wills, one natural and the other spiritual. It belongs to the natural will to love this present life, to shrink from and avoid death as far as it can, and to love prosperity. Yet this will is not sin if, in accordance with reason, it wills to consent to the spiritual will. It belongs to the spiritual will to love heavenly things, not to fear death, indeed to love it as an entrance into the kingdom, and willingly and patiently to endure adversities for the love of God. Christ therefore indicated that he possessed both wills, in order to teach how both ought to be possessed by the faithful. From the nature of the flesh he shows that he fears, when he says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. XXVI). But through the spiritual will [Col. 0830C] he always overcame the natural will. For when he prayed for prosperity of the flesh, he was not heard; but when he prayed for adversity, namely the redemption of the world, he was heard.

This, then, is: “My God, I shall cry by day,” that is, in prosperity, “and you will not hear.” He cried in the day, that is, in prosperity, when he fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fishes, and the people therefore wished to make him king (John VI). This was what the will of the flesh would have wanted, but the spiritual will overcame everything; for, when he learned the people’s intention, he withdrew from them and fled alone to the mountain (ibid.). Therefore this human will wanted these things, but was not heard. Again: “I shall cry [Col. 0830D] in the night, and you will not hear.” He cried in the night, that is, in the adversity of the passion, when he said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI), that is, this passion. The flesh prayed this, but was not heard, because such a prayer was contrary to human salvation. But what did the spiritual will pray? “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” See how the flesh struggled with the spirit; nevertheless, God’s will was preferred to the carnal will and was heard, because it was necessary for human redemption. The head, that is, Christ, feared so that the members, namely the martyrs, might not despair when they feared sufferings through the frailty of the flesh. For unless the head had feared, perhaps the members would say: “I am not of the head, [Col. 0831A] because my head did not fear the adversities of suffering.”

But now let us see what follows. As the Lord approached his passion and came to Jerusalem, he sent two disciples into the village, where an ass was tied with her colt before a door at the crossroads outside; and he said to them: “Untie them and bring them to me” (Matt. XXI). The ass under the yoke signifies the Jews, who were bound under the yoke of the Law by many transgressions and many sins. The ass’s colt is the newly formed Gentile people, because it has newly been converted to the faith. The people of the Gentiles are rightly signified by the ass’s colt, because they were converted to the Lord through the primitive Church, which took its origin from Judaea. The two, namely Jews and Gentiles, were before the door at the crossroads, [Col. 0831B] because Christ is the door, as he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the door” (John X). Both were outside this door while both remained bound by sins. They were held bound at the crossroads because they followed many paths of error. Two disciples were sent because there were two kinds of preachers directed to the two peoples. Hence Paul says: “He who worked in Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked in me among the Gentiles” (Gal. II). The Lord sat upon them when they were untied, because he found rest in their hearts.

Likewise, most beloved brethren, the Lord comes to Jerusalem sitting on the ass whenever, governing the soul of each believer as his own beast of burden, he leads it to the vision of inward peace. [Col. 0831C] The Lord also sits upon the beast of burden when he presides over the holy universal Church and carries it onward in desire toward heavenly peace.

Let us therefore go out to meet him, beloved, with palms—that is, with victories won over the devil and his temptations—and with the flowers of virtues and good works. Charity is the root of all virtues; for as many branches of a tree come forth from one root, so many virtues are generated from one charity. It is fitting, therefore, beloved brethren, that we take branches from the tree of charity and go out with them to meet Christ as he comes to our hearts, offering them before his sight with the highest devotion. Let one person first offer [Col. 0831D] the flower of virginity, which is acceptable to God, greatly loved by angels, and exceedingly praiseworthy to all saints. This virtue is held so much the more acceptable before God as it is found more rarely among human beings. Let another offer the lily of chastity, which is purity of mind and body. Certainly, without chastity no one can be holy, worthy, or perfect in a good work—especially since those who preserve purity of heart and body have been promised that they shall see the face of God (Matt. V). Let another take from the root of charity a branch of humility and go out with it to meet Jesus Christ, who said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). Let another spread flowers of mercy in Christ’s way, so that he may be numbered among the blessed and obtain mercy from him: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V). Let another, holding the branch of patience, imitate Christ, who promised the kingdom of heaven to those suffering persecution for [Col. 0832B] righteousness’ sake (ibid.). Let another refresh Christ in the poor by his alms, remembering that Gospel saying: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. XXV). Let another burn incense of prayers in his heart, saying: “Let my prayer, O Lord, be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. CXL).

But amid these things, beloved, you must return inwardly to yourselves; and if, in the days of this holy Lent, you find that you have been diligent in God’s service, give thanks to God, the giver of all good things. But if any one of you sees that he lacks something—for example, if he has not kept chastity, if he has not hastened to church at a suitable time to hear God’s word, if he has not refreshed the poor [Col. 0832C] with his alms, if he has not restored peace among those in discord, or has not performed other worthy works pleasing to God—then by tears and pure prayers, and by more generous alms according to his Master’s counsel, let him strive to amend his life for the better, so that on the holy day of Easter he may be able worthily to receive the most holy body of Christ with a pure conscience and love of God and neighbour. May the grace of the Holy Spirit accomplish this in us, so that none of us may appear empty in the sight of the Lord (Exod. XXXIV); but may we all cry out with devout mind and unfeigned faith: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXI). Therefore let us beseech the very Son of God with all devotion that [Col. 0832D] after this life he may deign to lead us with himself into the heavenly Jerusalem—he who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit and in the perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TWENTIETH SERMON: ON PALM SUNDAY

[Col. 0831]

[Col. 0831D] “When Jesus had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives,” etc. (Matt. XXI). Not only the works and virtues which the Lord performed [Col. 0832D] are full of mysteries; even the places in which he taught or walked must sometimes be believed not to be devoid of mysteries. This is demonstrated at the beginning of this [Col. 0833A] reading, when the Lord, drawing near to Jerusalem, is said first to have come to the Mount of Olives. The Mount of Olives is not far from Jerusalem: a very fertile and beautiful mountain, planted with trees, especially olive trees, from which it has taken the name “of Olives.” On its side is Bethphage, once a village of priests, where they prepared the offerings which they were to present in the temple of the Lord. Spiritually, however, the Mount of Olives signifies the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the mountain of abundance and mercy, because he came mercifully to redeem the human race; for Greek *eleos* is translated into Latin as *misericordia*, “mercy.” For this is that mountain concerning which Isaiah says: “In the last days, the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be raised above [Col. 0833B] the hills [Note: [Col. 0833D] The words ‘and it shall be exceedingly lofty’ do not belong to this passage, but to chapter LII, verse 13, unless perhaps chapters II and LII were joined in the Bibles consulted by our author. We note this again in vol. III.], and it shall be exceedingly lofty” (Isa. II). And Daniel says: “I saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth” (Dan. II). Bethphage, moreover, which is interpreted “house of the mouth” or “of the jaws,” signifies the Church, which without interruption keeps open its mouth—commonly called *bucca*—in confession of the Lord, saying with the Psalmist: “Let us come before his face in confession, and make a joyful noise to him in psalms” (Ps. XCIV). Bethphage is thus rightly said to be situated on the side of the Mount of Olives, because the Church was formed from the side of Christ hanging on the cross, when one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance and immediately blood of redemption and water of baptism came forth (John XIX). Jerusalem, [Col. 0833C] which is interpreted “vision of peace,” signifies the heavenly homeland, where the highest and true peace comes from the vision of the Creator. Therefore, when the Lord tends toward Jerusalem, he is beautifully described as having come to Bethphage at the Mount of Olives, because everyone who desires to attain the vision of heavenly peace must first both believe in the Lord Jesus Christ in his heart and confess him with his mouth (Rom. X); and just as the priests at Bethphage prepared and cleansed the offerings that they were to present in the Lord’s temple, so each believer in the present Church must purify himself from every vice and sin by good works, so that he may become an acceptable offering, according to the Apostle’s exhortation: “I beseech you through the mercy of God to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, your reasonable service” (Rom. XII). [Col. 0833D]

The two disciples whom the Lord sent before him signify understanding and action, because one who undertakes ecclesiastical governance must be perfect in word and deed. Hence is that saying of David: “Good understanding to all who do it; his praise endures for ever and ever” (Ps. CX). The village to which they are sent is understood as Jerusalem, because it is the practice of Scripture sometimes to call a village a city, and a city a village. Spiritually, however, the village to which they are sent signifies the world, which is said to have been hostile to them because, at the beginning of the preaching, the whole world resisted them with all its effort. [Col. 0834A] The words that follow, “And immediately you will find an ass tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me,” are spoken according to the custom of that region. For in those regions it was customary for each city, village, or town to have prepared an ass or some other animal fit for riding; and if any of its citizens needed support from such a means of transport, he would ride it for the journey of one day. Those who lived in the city jointly provided the animal’s upkeep. This custom was accordingly observed at Jerusalem when the Lord sent his disciples there, saying to them: “You will find an ass tied, and a colt with her; untie them and bring them to me.” Spiritually, by the ass, which was tamed, is figured the Synagogue, which was made gentle—or worn down—under the yoke of the Law and trained in observing the ceremonies of the Law. By the frolicking, untamed colt, which ran here and there without reins, is signified the Gentile people, who, bound by no instruction of the Law and furnished with no knowledge of God, uncertain and wandering, ran after the idols made by their own hands. Concerning it, the Evangelist fittingly says: “Upon which no man had sat” (Mark XI), because upon the Gentile people no patriarch had yet imposed his instruction, and no prophet had ever exercised his preaching. Not only is the ass said to have been found tied, but also the colt, because not only the Gentile people but also the Jewish people were bound by the chains of sins. Hence the Apostle says: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. [Col. 0834C] III). As though to untie the ass, the Lord sent the apostles when he directed them specifically to preach to the Synagogue, saying: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles,” etc. (Matt. X). Again, as though to untie the colt, he sent them when, after the resurrection, he commanded them: “Going into all the world, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). What follows is: “And if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them; and he will immediately let them go.” Spiritually, it is related that the ass and colt whom the apostles untied had many masters, because the peoples of Jews and Gentiles were devoted not to one error but to many. The many masters [Col. 0834D] who opposed their release are to be understood as unclean spirits, because after sin they claimed the human race for themselves by a kind of tyranny and were therefore enemies of human salvation. But after the disciples said, “The Lord has need of them,” they immediately let them go, because after they displayed Christ’s signs—namely, raised the dead, healed the sick, expelled unclean spirits from possessed bodies, and performed other miracles in the Lord’s name—they at once abandoned them, that is, the human race, because they failed in their attempt.

All this happened in order that what had been spoken [Col. 0835A] through Zechariah the prophet might be fulfilled: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon an ass and a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke.” Spiritually, he calls Jerusalem the daughter of Zion, which was placed in its height not only for defence but also for contemplation. Let it therefore be said: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle,” etc. It is as though he said: O Jews, to whom that Lord is to come in the flesh, recognize your king by these signs. When you see him coming gentle [Note: [Col. 0835D] Here perhaps supply: “not angry.”], not proud but humble; not terrible in the splendour of arms, as Nebuchadnezzar and Antiochus once came for your destruction, but for restoration; not sitting upon a foaming horse that loves discord, that paws the ground with its hoof and scents battle from afar, but upon an ass, a friend of peace, or upon the ass’s colt. Your gentle King comes to you, not to take away your temporal kingdom but to bestow an everlasting one. He comes, I say, not to lead you captive into a foreign land, but to restore you free to your own land. The King comes, not a stranger but yours, born from you, nourished among you, and sent for your salvation. Spiritually, moreover, the daughter of Zion, interpreted “contemplation,” signifies the Church, which daily contemplates with a pure heart him who said: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John VIII). “Behold,” he says, “your king comes to you, gentle,” that is, inhabiting not the minds of the proud but of the humble. The ass or colt, because they are brought for the Lord to sit upon, represent a simple and innocent soul. For the Lord, as it were, sitting upon the little ass tends toward Jerusalem when, inhabiting a simple mind, he makes it hasten eagerly toward the vision of inward peace. [Col. 0835C]

It follows: “The disciples went and did as Jesus commanded them, and brought the ass and the colt.” Then the disciples brought the ass to Christ when they called many from the Synagogue of the Jews to faith in Christ, as we read that, when Peter preached, three thousand believed in one day (Acts X). As it were, they brought the colt when, since the Jews were for the most part unbelieving, the disciples went out and preached everywhere, the Lord cooperating and confirming the word through the signs that followed (Mark XVI). It is further added: “And they laid their garments upon them, and made him sit above them.” The apostles’ garments signify doctrine. Therefore the apostles, as it were, laid garments upon the ass and colt, so that Jesus might sit more softly, when through their doctrine they instructed human hearts so that they might have God as their indwelling inhabitant. But it is asked how Christ is said to have sat upon both animals in so short a journey. For if he sat on the ass, the colt had no rider; but if he sat on the colt—which is more fitting—the ass remained free of a rider. Yet it is possible that he first sat upon the ass and then, as he approached Jerusalem [Col. 0836A] with crowds coming out to meet him, chose to sit upon the little ass, as John the Evangelist says: “Jesus found a little ass and sat upon it” (John XII).

A very great crowd spread their garments in the way; others cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way. The holy apostles laid their garments upon the ass when, through their doctrine, they prepared human minds to be God’s dwelling-place. Those who spread their garments in the way showed the simpler people a path by which they might reach heaven. Those who cut branches from the trees and spread them in the way are the holy martyrs and teachers who, while they set forth the manifold judgments of the preceding Fathers, necessary [Col. 0836B] for our instruction, adorn the way as though cutting branches from spiritual trees.

The crowds going before and following signify the faithful of both Testaments, namely the Old and the New. We believe that Christ has already come and redeemed the world; the Fathers of the Old Testament believed that he would come and redeem the world. We believe that Christ was born of a Virgin and once suffered, died, was buried, rose again for human salvation, and was glorified by the same Father in the Father’s glory above all that was created; and that at the end of the world he will come to judge the living and the dead. Similarly, the ancient saints believed that he would be born of an undefiled Virgin, [Col. 0836C] suffer for the salvation of the whole world, die, rise again, ascend to heaven, and judge the world.

There is therefore one faith of all who believe in Christ in the Old and New Testaments, because he whom we believe has already come, they believed would come. All, therefore, who went before Christ in this procession signified the faithful of the Old Testament—namely the patriarchs and prophets and all others predestined to eternal life; those who followed represented the saints of the New Testament, namely the apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and every people rightly believing in Christ. For with one voice all who went before and all who followed cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who [Col. 0836D] comes in the name of the Lord,” because the faith of those who preceded and those who followed Christ’s coming is one, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Through the grace of Christ we believe that we shall be saved, even as they” (Acts XV).

Let us hear what they cried: “Hosanna to the Son of David,” etc. *Hosanna* is properly Hebrew. *Osi* is interpreted “saving,” and *anna* is an interjection signifying a movement of the mind in the feeling of one who entreats. *Hosanna*, therefore, is rendered in our language as “Save,” or “Save us,” or “save the whole world.” *Hosanna* is indeed the cry of those both exulting and praising. As I suppose, this verse is taken from the one hundred and seventeenth Psalm: “O Lord, save me; O Lord, prosper [Col. 0837A] me; blessed is he who is to come in the name of the Lord.” The crowds acknowledge as Son of David him who, our Saviour, came down to us from David’s stock. Therefore, when the crowds cried “Save” or “Save us,” they surely believed him to be the Saviour; and they declared that the Blessed One was to come in the name of the Lord, because Christ came not in his own name but in the Father’s name, and sought not his own glory but the Father’s.

Therefore, beloved brethren, if it is true that the Mount of Olives, a most fertile and beautiful mountain planted with trees, especially olive trees, from which it has its name, spiritually signifies Christ, it is necessary that from that same mountain—namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who is truly the mountain of mercy, the mountain of the Lord’s house, the rich, most fertile, beautiful mountain, planted with the trees and flowers of every virtue, and raised on the summit of the mountains above all hills, that is, above all saints—we take branches of good works and flowers of virtues, and joyfully and devoutly go out with them to meet him as he comes to our hearts, offering them in his sight with the highest reverence. Therefore from him and in him let us take such spiritual branches, namely [Col. 0838A] robust faith, sure hope, true charity, courage, prudence, temperance, justice, patience, humility, and kindness. These are spiritual branches that never wither; the flowers of these spiritual branches are chastity, continence, long-suffering, mercy, prayers, vigils, fasts, goodwill, generosity in alms, and other good works which flourish with devoted mind through his love and help. These are the branches of good works that never wither; these are the flowers of virtues that flourish unfadingly in summer and winter; these are the fruits of eternity, which do not fail but always increase. With these branches, then, beloved, let us go out to meet Christ; let us spread them before him as he comes in the way, and with all the faithful of the Old and New Testaments let us cry in the highest glory and joy of mind: “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” so that after this life, with him as our guide, we may be able to enter the heavenly Jerusalem with him, who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in the perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TWENTY-FIRST SERMON: ON THE LORD’S SUPPER

[Col. 0837]

[Col. 0837C] “Our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread; and giving thanks, he blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat, for this is my body, which shall be given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new testament in my blood. Do this as often as you drink it in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (I Cor. 11 and the Gospel).

As the moment of the Lord’s passion drew near, beloved brethren, when he was already almost at the point of betrayal, the Lord—who had previously observed the legal rites and sacrifices, all of which were figures of his Incarnation and [Col. 0837D] passion—wished, when the truth came, to destroy the shadow. For the lamb sacrificed under the old Law prefigured the true Lamb to be sacrificed on the cross. He therefore wished to eat and sacrifice the prefigured lamb and to preserve the shadow of the future reality until the sacrifice of the true Lamb should occur. Thus before the time of his passion he wished to celebrate the old Passover with his disciples and eat the lamb, putting an end to the figurative signs. Therefore, after the lamb’s supper, he instituted the new Passover when the old was ended; and he gave his body and blood to his disciples. [Col. 0838C] For if he had first given his body and then afterward eaten the lamb, the old Passover would not seem to have received its end through the new. He therefore took bread, blessed it, and gave it to them, and afterward the cup.

It must be known that the whole of human nature was corrupted in soul and body. It was therefore fitting that God, who came to free both, should unite both to himself: namely, so that soul might fittingly be freed through soul and body through body. For this reason we place bread and wine upon the altar, to represent both: so that, through bread made into his body and worthily received by us, we may believe our body is to be conformed to Christ’s body in immortality and impassibility; and likewise, through wine changed into true blood and likewise received by us, [Col. 0838D] we may believe our souls will be made conformed to Christ’s soul in all purity while we live, and in glory when we rise again. But since Christ’s soul had to be represented by some bodily thing, as his body is represented by bread, nothing was found among all creatures by which it might be represented more closely than blood, in which the soul itself is said to have its seat. But because it seemed horrible to human nature to receive blood, wine was put in place of blood to signify the soul. Yet it must not be understood that in receiving the blood we receive the soul only and not the body, or that in receiving the body we receive the body only and not the soul; rather, in receiving the blood we receive the whole true Christ, God and man, and likewise in receiving the body we receive the whole. And although the body is received separately and the blood separately, they are received not twice but once.

But this custom of receiving separately became established in the Church because Christ at the supper gave separately to the disciples, so that by this they might understand that they ought to be conformed to the soul and body of Christ. Water, moreover, is placed with wine in the sacrament so that the water together with the blood that flowed from Christ’s side may be represented; this water signifies the people, or baptism, in which the people are cleansed by the shedding of Christ’s blood [Col. 0839B]. There can be no doubt that, through the sacred words of the celebrating priest, the bread is transubstantiated into Christ’s true body, so that the substance of bread does not remain; yet He willed only the colour and taste of bread to remain, and the true substance of Christ’s body to lie concealed beneath that appearance, lest, if it appeared in the identity in which it truly exists, the human mind should recoil from receiving a living man. Hence, when the Lord said, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man, you will have no share in me” (John 6), some who heard this turned back, recoiling and supposing that they were commanded to eat him in the form in which he appeared to them. And a Christian must necessarily believe that, by the authoritative words of blessing, the Lord’s body can equally be consecrated by the hands of any priest who has only the order of priesthood, whether good or bad [Col. 0839C], and that the Holy Spirit is then present in that consecration.

This offering of Christ’s body, as Augustine says, is repeated daily, although Christ suffered once, because daily we fall into sins, without which, burdened by bodily weakness, we cannot live. Christ willed, moreover, to show his body under the form of bread because he himself is the living bread that came down from heaven (ibid.); and he willed under the form of bread to signify the union of the body with its head, as the Apostle says: “We, though many, are one bread, one body in Christ, who partake of the one bread” (1 Cor. 10). For just as one bread is made from different grains, so from different members we are made one body of Christ by the union of faith, hope, and charity [Col. 0839D]. Therefore, whoever wishes to be joined to Christ’s body as a member should partake with others of the heavenly bread. For the Lord broke the bread and gave it, because he willed that what is one should be partaken of by all, when he says: “Receive through conformity, and eat this sacrament itself. Do this in remembrance of me,” so that, in receiving the body and blood, we may remember his passion: that, as he suffered for us, so we also may die for him, if necessary. Likewise concerning the cup, which he called the New Testament—that is, the new promise—because by that blood he promised not temporal things but eternal ones. And this commemoration must be made until he comes [Col. 0840A], namely, to the end of the age, when he will come for judgment.

But observe what follows: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup.” Unworthy is one entangled in a grievous sin, or remaining willing to commit grievous sins. Let a person examine himself, not by comparison with others, but considering by himself alone what manner of person he is; for one who eats and drinks unworthily eats judgment—that is, condemnation—upon himself. Therefore many among you are weak, whom God punishes in this life with many infirmities because they have received his body unworthily; and, what is worse, many sleep in death [Col. 0840B], just as we still see that mortality frequently follows after Easter.

Therefore, dearest brethren, since the Lord willed that his body should be received and shared by us in order to preserve unity, if anyone departs from unity through anger, hatred, or discord, he will not worthily receive the Lord’s body, nor can he be united with Christ through participation in it. For just as the bond of charity gathers many together, so discord and hatred, which are one thing, divide them. See to it, then, brethren, that the poison of discord does not produce hatred among you, corrupting and annihilating within you the sweetness of charity. Look to your Head; consider the cause of your redemption. For Christ saved us solely out of his love, as the Apostle says: “God [Col. 0840C], who is rich in all things, because of his exceeding charity by which he loved us, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with him; by whose grace we are saved” (Eph. 2). Thus, when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son (Rom. 5). “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15). Yet Christ had a greater love than this, because he suffered not for friends but for enemies: that is, while we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God through his death. For he died, the just for the unjust (1 Pet. 3); for who would dare to die for a good person? (Rom. 5). No one. Therefore, before he preached love, he displayed love; and when [Col. 0840D] he frequently invited them to love, in his final discourse he established love more firmly in the hearts of the disciples by word and example.

For John says, as you have just heard from the Gospel: “Before the feast-day of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end” (John 13). Since he was about to depart for a time, lest the disciples who were in the world should be troubled or divided from unity, at the end he showed them a sign of his love, so that they might not abandon him through fear. He invited and strengthened them in one concord, lest discord separate them. Behold the sign of love: “He rises from supper and lays aside his garments; and [Col. 0841A], having taken a linen cloth, girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded.” When Peter recoiled in awe at this humility, he said to him: “What I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward.” He preached by his deeds and also preached by words; and what he willed to be understood in his deeds, he afterward explained. For after he had washed their feet, he took his garments, reclined again, and said to them: “Do you know what I have done to you? You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If therefore I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you should do also.” Behold: by his deeds the Lord invites the faithful to humility and love [Col. 0841B], lest anyone should thereafter blush to do what the Lord himself did. It seems very lowly for a person of power to wash another’s feet; but it is now fitting and honourable to do what was done by the Creator. Therefore, having strengthened them by this example, and seeing their coming sorrow over his passion, he began to comfort them in these words and exhort them to the bond of love: “Where I go, you cannot come now. I give you a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you.” And again: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” As though he said: “I am about to depart from you for a time and go to my Father; where, until the way is prepared, until I destroy the wall that stands between God and men, you cannot come [Col. 0841C].” As though he said openly: “I am going to another country; for the present I leave my household, and therefore I warn you that meanwhile there be no dissension among you. Nor do I merely warn you: I make it a commandment, so that no one may dare transgress it. And I call new what nevertheless is old [Note: [Col. 0841D] Old.], lest it grow old within you, but may always be renewed in your mind. Therefore I lay this commandment upon you especially, because by this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” Other virtues may be shared by good and evil alike; but true love is granted only to true Christians. It is as if he said: “I have set a mark upon my sheep by which they may be distinguished from others. By this mark all shall know that you are my disciples [Col. 0841D], if you have love for one another.”

Accordingly, the same bridegroom of the Church—namely Christ—commands that same Church in the Song of Songs, saying: “Set me as a seal upon your heart and upon your arm” (Song 8). Thoughts are in the heart and works in the arm. Therefore the holy Church sets the sign of Christ’s love upon her heart and upon her arm [Col. 0842A] when, for love of him, she diligently devotes herself to good works. For holy Church bears Christ like a sign inwardly and outwardly: while she labours continually in meditating upon him; while she does not cease to imitate him by doing good; while she loves friends in God and patiently and lovingly endures enemies for God’s sake; and while she keeps the most vigilant watch that she may deserve to be his beloved, she displays within herself, as it were, the sign of Christ’s love. He himself explains what love they ought to have, by which God’s servants may be distinguished from other people, when he says: “As I have loved you”—not, certainly, with that love by which people love one another unto wrongdoing, nor for the advantage of passing things, but with that by which God loved us [Col. 0842B], namely, because of his own kindness. This, then, is true and ordered love: that we love God in all things and above all things; that we love our neighbour in God—that is, in what is good; and that we endure an enemy with love, not for his own sake but for God’s.

Therefore, dearest brethren, carefully heed the words of our Lord Jesus Christ; and if you desire to be his disciples, show love to one another. If you desire truly to be counted among Christ’s disciples, show in all your conduct the sign of that love. If you love Christ with your whole heart, let your mind meditate upon the holy Scriptures and your hands be exercised in good works. By Christ’s command, love your neighbours as yourselves, and for his love persevere in holy [Col. 0842C] actions. Let your heart be kindled with the fire of Christ’s charity, and for love of him let your neighbour be loved without pretence. Let your mind be pure in Christ’s love and generous in your neighbour’s need. Love Christ, the King of kings, with all devotion; and aid your neighbour according to your means in necessities. Let Christ’s love in you not be empty but full of every goodness. Let Christ’s love in you not appear idle, but let it be active and diligent in good works. Therefore let us jointly beseech Jesus Christ himself, who for the salvation of us all deigned on this night to be handed over into the hands of sinners, and on the morrow voluntarily to be crucified by the hands of soldiers; who, after the third day, presented himself alive to his disciples [Col. 0842D], and on the fortieth day ascended into heaven and came to the session of God the Father, that after this life he may also deign to bring us to the fellowship of his elect. He who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TWENTY-SECOND SERMON: ON THE LORD’S SUPPER, II

[Col. 0843]

[Col. 0843A] Jeremiah the prophet, instructed by the Holy Spirit from his very conception, so to speak, foreseeing for the salvation of the human race that the Word coeternal with God the Father, from the stock of David, through whom all things were made from nothing, would be born, and that he would suffer from that same Jewish people reproaches, mockery, scourges, spitting, the lance, the cross, and finally death of his own will—among the many things he foretold concerning that same Redeemer’s most merciful passion, he also said: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, engraved with an adamantine point upon the broad surface of their hearts” (Jer. 17) [Note: [Col. 0843D] Isidore, *Against the Jews*, book I, chapter 21]. This applies not unfittingly either to Judas or to the Jews, who sinned against Christ: their sin is not written in ink, which perhaps could be erased, but engraved with an iron stylus upon an adamantine point [Col. 0843B], so that the transgression of their hearts cannot be erased unless they believe in the Lord Jesus Christ. Thus Judah’s sin is indelible, as though written with an iron stylus upon an adamantine point, which in Hebrew is called *samir*—not because any point is called *samir*. But the diamond, which receives its name because it is untamed and unbreakable, possesses such brilliance and smoothness that it can be written upon without any impediment by an iron stylus, so that the hard material of iron writes upon a harder tablet and the writing remains forever, according to the saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). Elsewhere this prophet also says in Christ’s person: “Attend, O Lord, to me, and hear the voices of my adversaries [Col. 0843C]” (Jer. 18)—namely, of the Jews saying, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23). Jeremiah, in a type of the Saviour, suffered all things at the hands of the Jews; afterward they were devastated when the Babylonian king came. But these things were more fully accomplished in Christ, when the city was overthrown by the Roman sword—not through idolatry, which then did not exist, but because they clamoured for death to the Son of God, saying: “Take away, take away [Note: [Col. 0843D] Or, “Take away, take him away,” as the Gloss, which the author here transcribes, reads; or, “Take away such a one. We have no …”] such a one. We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). And their imprecation is fulfilled forever: “His blood, namely, be upon us and upon our children.”

Again he says: “Is evil rendered for good? For they dug a pit—that is, a deceit—to take away my life. Remember that I stood in your presence to speak good for them,” etc. (Jer. 18). This is as though Christ spoke to God the Father, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23).

“Therefore give their children over to famine, and deliver them into the hands of the sword; let their wives become childless and widows, and let their men be slain by death” (Jer. 18). [Col. 0844A] We pass quickly over what is plain, so that we may dwell upon what is obscure—not following the absurdities of some who interpret this as the captivity of the heavenly Jerusalem, but pursuing the clear history and most manifest prophecy with full confidence in every word and meaning. “Let a cry be heard,” he says, “from their houses,” namely of weeping and wailing; “you will suddenly bring a robber upon them,” Nebuchadnezzar or the Roman army—deservedly, because “they dug a pit to capture me and hid snares for my feet.” He openly explains what they did against the Son of God and what they suffered. “But you, O Lord, know all their counsel against me unto death. Therefore do not forgive their iniquity, and let not their sin be blotted out from before your face” (ibid.). This does not conflict with the preceding sentence, in which he prays for the people; [Col. 0844B] but because the period for repentance had passed, and they remained in their malice, they are punished not so much for themselves as for others, lest their great sin become an example. “Let them fall before your sight in the time of your wrath.” As though it were said more openly: Let them stumble against the stone of offence and rock of scandal, of which it is said: “The stone which the builders rejected,” etc. (Ps. 117). And shortly afterward: “I heard the reproaches of many, ‘having condemnation because they have made void their first faith’” (1 Tim. 5), “and terror on every side. Pursue him, and let us pursue him,” from all the men who had been at peace with me and guarded my side: “perhaps he may somehow be deceived, and we may prevail against [Col. 0844C] him” (Jer. 20). The Lord alone tests righteousness; he alone sees the conscience of the heart. Hence it is said: “Jesus, knowing their thoughts” (Luke 6). He is God, certainly not by advancement, as some suppose, but by nature; of him it is said similarly in the Psalms: “No living being shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142), namely in virtues—much less, then, one dead in sins. “The Lord is with me,” by grace or free choice, “as a mighty warrior”: in our own sufferings let us also say the same. “Therefore those who persecute me shall fall and be weak. They shall be utterly confounded, because they did not understand the everlasting reproach which shall never—that is, by no forgetfulness—be erased” (Jer. 20). As though he said: Because the Jews persecute me, [Col. 0844D] enemies shall persecute them, and they could not understand the prophet; hence their confusion. “And you, O Lord,” he says, “of hosts, tester of the righteous,” or “you who test righteous things, who see the reins and heart, let me, I pray, behold your vengeance upon them” (ibid.). Although he knows that he has God as his champion, nevertheless, in the patience of human frailty [Col. 0845A], he desires already now to see what he knows is to come. “For to you, O Lord,” he says, “I have revealed my cause” (ibid.), you who say: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32).

In the person of the same Son of God the prophet adds, saying: “He has broken my teeth by number; he has fed me with ashes” (Lam. 3). Allegorically, Christ’s teeth—the apostles and other disciples—were broken and scattered in the passion; through them as though through teeth Christ transfers believers into his body. “He has fed me with ashes,” he says, according to the saying: “I ate ashes as bread [Note: [Col. 0845D] Note that the manuscripts here read *meum* (“my”), though it is commonly interpreted thus; but because both the Gloss transcribed by Blessed Martin and all the others read *manducabam* (“I ate”), or something similar, we have adapted it to this reading, which elsewhere does not reject it by [uncertain: *senon*].],” etc. (Ps. 101). By these evils his soul was cast down: namely, those whom he loved most and for whom he came persecuted him with every hatred. Hence it is said: “Jesus began to be afraid and distressed” (Mark 14) [Col. 0845B]. Under the letter VAU, therefore, these things are intensified, and by it harsh utterances are moderated; it means, “not so was he,” or “and not he.” For although he said, “My end and my hope from the Lord have perished” (Lam. 3), he did not think it so, nor did he forget the good things that he always had with the Father or received according to his humanity, of which it is said: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26). Therefore, although his soul was cast down by the Jews’ hardness, he did not think so; but he indicates the exceeding pain of his soul and death, as though intoxicated by the bitterness of the passion, unable to remember blessings, and, embittered, saying: “My end has perished.” Yet among men he seemed to have perished [Col. 0845C], who said: “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. 27). Thus the Church, cast down by the evils of heretics and persecutors, forgets former blessings and, oppressed by pains, says to us: “My end has perished,” etc. Hence it is said: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out” (Ps. 72):—“He has broken my teeth by number,” etc. Morally, the soul afflicted by distaste for holy Scripture laments the breaking of the teeth with which it ought to have ground and chewed the word of God. For an animal that does not chew the cud is forbidden by the Law. To chew and grind the word of God with the faculties as though with teeth is health and nourishment. Hence it is proclaimed that Moses’ teeth were not moved (Deut. 34), because he always chewed the Word of God with mouth and heart and ceaselessly ate the bread of angels [Col. 0845D]. But when the teeth are broken, it is rightly fed with ashes, in which sorrow of heart and repentance are signified. Thus Job, when he had seen and heard the Lord, said:

“I condemn myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42), because, having seen God’s loftiness, he recognized himself as dust and ashes. For the less anyone sees himself, the less he is displeased with himself; and the more light of greater grace he receives, the more fully he recognizes himself as blameworthy. [Col. 0846A] For when he is inwardly raised, he strives in all that he is to conform to the standard which he beholds above himself. And because human frailty still hinders him, he sees that he departs from it in no small respect, and all in him that does not accord with the inward standard burdens him. Blessed Job, after the scourges, beholds this standard more fully as he advances, and differs from himself in his human self-reproof, saying: “Therefore I condemn myself.” But since no recognition of rebuke exists unless the lamentations of repentance follow, it is rightly added after the rebuke: “I repent in dust and ashes.” For to repent in dust and ashes is, upon beholding the supreme essence, to recognize oneself as nothing other than dust and ashes. Hence the Lord says to the reprobate city in the Gospel: “If the mighty works that were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11) [Col. 0846B]. In sackcloth, indeed, harshness and the cleansing of sins are shown; in ashes, the dust of the dead. Therefore both are customarily employed in repentance, so that in the cleansing of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through fault, and in the ash-dust we may consider what we have become through judgment. Let the piercing vices be considered in sackcloth; let the just punishment of vices that follows through the sentence of death be considered in ashes. Since after the sin of the flesh dishonours arose, let a person see in the harshness of sackcloth what he did by being proud, and see in ashes how far he came through sinning [Col. 0846C]. Sackcloth may also signify the very remembrance, in repentance, of piercings and pains; for in saying, “I condemn myself,” blessed Job is, as it were, pricked by a certain sackcloth, while in his mind he is pierced by the harsh goads of rebuke. But he repents in ashes because he attentively considers what has resulted from the first sin through just judgment, saying: “I repent in dust and ashes.” As though he said openly: “I do not pride myself on any gift of my Creator, because, taken from dust, I know that by the sentence of imposed death I shall return to dust.”

Therefore let the holy soul say: “He fed me with ashes.” As though it said: “Because I delayed to chew the word of God, I groan, fed with the ashes of mortality and afflicted by the piercing of vices. My soul has been cast down; I have forgotten good things” [Col. 0846D]. It grieves that it has been cast away by God and exposed to temptations, nor can it freely return to the good things it perceives; oppressed by the bitterness of grief, it cannot remember blessings. Therefore it added: “My end and my hope from the Lord have perished.” This is well signified by the letter VAU, which means “he is not”: for its end has perished and is not in the Lord, who is the true end and consummation. Therefore it laments that its hope from the Lord has perished, because it is unable to raise itself to him. Hence ZAIN follows fittingly [Note: [Col. 0846D] Manuscripts: ZAI.], interpreted as “lead yourself” or “hither.” It is as though the teacher’s voice says: “Do not be long [Col. 0847A] entangled in these evils, but lead yourself”; and, as though it asks where it should go, it answers demonstratively: “Hither,” namely, into the way of prayer. And it then adds what and how it ought to pray.

“Remember my poverty and transgression, wormwood and gall.” Historically: from the beginning of this alphabet he describes the miseries of the wretched city and the sufferings of Christ and of the suffering Church, so that, almost in despair, he has said: “My end has perished,” etc. But when, as though heard from God, he is told, “Lead yourself hither,” immediately lifted by new hope, he turns to the Lord, sends prayers, and promises thereafter to hope for better things, forgetting past offences. Hence it should be noted that these letters were marked out with great mystery, in which the Holy Spirit has, as it were, composed metrical play with the sacraments of great understanding in the prophet [Col. 0847B]. And thus God’s hidden speech is nevertheless shadowed by mysteries which, once opened, become manifest to human understandings. The Holy Spirit excellently introduced these and similar things in order to remove readers’ weariness and refresh the minds of those who understand amid tears.

“Remember my poverty and transgression, wormwood and gall.” Morally also: the soul is made alive and born again in this word addressed to it: “Lead yourself hither.” As though it were said: “Take up your bed and walk” (Mark 2). Therefore it says in supplication: “Remember my poverty and transgression,” etc. For in Adam, as in its first blossom, it transgressed and was stripped by poverty; but when it is commanded under this letter to lead itself away, it is recalled by remembrance, and, like the daughter of Abraham, [Col. 0847C] is raised from hope against hope and comes to the letter HETH [Note: [Col. 0847D] Manuscripts corruptly: BET.], which is interpreted “life” or “fear,” so that after the tears of complaint it may conceive the fear of God, of which it is said: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110). It likewise tastes the word of God and says in the voice of confession: “It is by the Lord’s mercies that we are not consumed” (Lam. 3). Having individually set out its misfortunes, it seeks the judge’s favour from the person of itself, of the judge, and of the adversary, each of which is marked in its proper place.

“Remember my poverty and transgression, wormwood and gall.” Allegorically: these are the words of Christ, and also of the participating Church, to which it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0847D] (Matt. 5). Yet Christ neither transgressed nor does anyone bring his transgression before the judge; rather he modestly utters: “Turn away your face from my sins” (Ps. 50). Nevertheless, Christ was made transgression of the law for us, as also curse and sin; hence it is said: “Cursed is the man who hangs upon a tree” (Gal. 3; Deut. 21). And he who knew no sin was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5), that he might erase both our sin, curse, and transgression. Great, then, is the saying: “Remember my poverty and transgression,” because he became poor for us so that he might make us rich. And he joins the body to the head, so that the body may be cleansed by the prayer of the head [Col. 0848A]. But because the body does not live without transgression in the present life, it is filled with many miseries and with the bitterness of wormwood and gall.

“I will remember with remembrance, and my soul shall waste away within me.” Namely, through remembrance of eternal life; and therefore my soul shall immediately waste away, longing for it, according to the saying: “My soul has failed for your salvation,” etc. (Ps. 118). Hence he adds: “Recalling this in my heart, I shall hope in God.” For when the Church directs herself to contemplation of him, she groans as though fainting and, as explicitly as possible, says: “I will remember with remembrance”—that is, from that remembrance of eternal life, inwardly breathed which gives life—so that Christ’s members may learn to remember, think of, or love nothing else than to be reformed unto newness. And the Church’s sudden progress should be noted [Col. 0848B]: she had first come to despondency, but when she heard the saving voice, “Lead yourself,” she immediately wasted away in remembrance; and recalling what she endured, brought far onward in that word, she says, “I shall hope in God.” As though she said: “At your word I will let down the net” (Luke 5). Thus she grew strong in hope against hope, refreshed by remembrance of eternal life.

Again he adds, saying: “You have judged, O Lord, the cause of my soul, redeemer of my life.” *RES* is interpreted “head,” “of the head,” or “primacy.” He is our head, or the form of a head, so that we may consider the author of life, who is our head, nourishing and governing all things and filling them with perception. For the understanding of the wise is in the head. Once the head is removed, the body is not recognized, nor does a reason for living remain. Let us hear, then, what the head thinks concerning itself: “You have judged,” it says, “O Lord, the cause of my soul, redeemer of my life.” This voice belongs equally to head and body, so that neither body is without head nor head without body. The cause of the soul is righteousness, which is fitted to the head; the redemption is that of the body. For one who is sold under sin is redeemed. The body does not trust in its own strength unless the head’s righteousness aids it. Therefore Christ’s righteousness is the Father’s judgment and humanity’s redemption. In rhetorical fashion, then, it seeks favour from the judge’s person, praises the heavenly judge, then presents the cause of the soul, and finally shows why he came, namely redemption. For he is the redemption of our life, which he declares to be his own because of charity, so that we may live in him and he in us. Yet [Col. 0848D] it recalls the adversaries’ iniquity and fury in indignation, in order to make the judge merciful toward itself but angry toward the adversaries. As though it said: Although you have tested the cause of my soul, you have seen their fury against me; therefore judge my judgment. In this it is clear that he punishes iniquity by rejecting it, loves equity, and examines each person’s thoughts—he who governs and gives life to the members like a head, and orders all things justly. This is the voice of the elect, that is, of Christ’s body, who have obtained the primacy of blessing. For *RES* signifies primacy. One people is that which, in Esau, sold the birthright; another is that which bought it. Thus the individual [Col. 0849A] members of the body partake of the head’s grace and claim the primacy of grace, so that the head’s vigour may reach every member. In the head are the vigour of life and the primacy of our inheritance. We must guard this, as explained throughout, at all times, just as a serpent guards its head and exposes its body, as though it knows that life is in the head. Without this head—that is, without Christ—we do not live. Thus in these three verses the elect are commended to the Father through the head, which is Christ; they are justified by his judgment; redemption is offered; the adversaries’ iniquity, fury, and thoughts are condemned; and the unalloyed unity of head and body is declared. “Redeemer of my life”; others read, “defender.” Redemption belongs to the members, but defence to head and body. Therefore redemption and defence of our whole salvation are offered through Christ to the Father, so that through his single death a twofold redemption may be granted to us [Col. 0849B]. It remains, then, for us to preserve the primacy in the head, which cannot be taken away unless Christ is taken away. Let care for the head therefore be the summit of our endeavour and work, the summit of hope and truth, so that we may be in the unity of Christ’s body, by which, being united [Note: [Col. 0849D] Gloss and other manuscripts: “joined.”], we belong to our head. Hence Isaiah says: “I shall remove from Judah head and tail” (Isa. 9), that is, beginning and end. Judah lost the head when it did not receive Christ, who is the beginning of the Church, the primacy, and the firstborn from the dead (Col. 1). He is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes. Through him iniquity is condemned, equity crowned, and the fury and thoughts of adversaries rejected.

Now let us see what the letter SIN brings against them. “You have heard their reproaches, O Lord, all their thoughts against me” (Lam. 3) [Col. 0849C]. SIN is interpreted “of teeth” or “upon a wound.” The reproaches of teeth against Christ are lamented, of which it is said: “Their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). Their lips rise against the truth, like deceitful lips speaking in heart and heart (Ps. 11). Under this same letter David says: “Princes persecuted me without cause,” etc. (Ps. 118). Elsewhere, as though explaining the interpretation of this letter, he says: “They added to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. 63). It is as though the Jews took death from medicine. Hence the saying: “Add iniquity to their iniquity, and let them not enter into your righteousness” (ibid.). For, as we have said, this letter is interpreted “upon a wound.” Therefore the Prophet laments that, though wounds are healed by this medicine, those who repaid evil for good added to them, reaping perfidy from the prophets’ faith and adding murders to perfidy. The just Judge presents these accomplished evils to the Father’s just judgment to be punished: their unbelief, wound upon wound, was the Lord’s killing. Medicine is rightly applied upon a wound, that the wound’s sharpness may be eased; oil is poured upon a wound, that it may be softened. But these people, rejecting the medicine, added perfidy and death upon the wound of unbelief [Col. 0850A]. So all reprobate persons, from God’s patience—which leads us to repentance—store up wrath for themselves according to their hardness of heart (Rom. 2). “All their thoughts,” he says, “are against me.” He indicates God, present everywhere, before whom thoughts and hearts stand ready. It follows: “You have heard their reproaches, O Lord,” etc. For him, hearing is seeing, and seeing is knowing: nothing is hidden from him, and all things lie open before him. But the reprobate store up wrath for themselves, as it were, upon the wound of sin. Hence he added: “Their sitting and their rising,” etc. For by deriding and mocking they rage no less against the head than against the body, like judges and teachers sitting in the chair of pestilence (Ps. 1); none of them is soothed by medicine, because “the whole head is sick and the whole heart sorrowful: from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no health in it” (Isa. 1) [Col. 0850B]. And where the whole is in peril and the entire body is consumed, it is no longer time to apply a poultice.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IV, chapter 9.] *Collyria* is a Latin term, so called because it cleanses defects of the eyes; *epithema*, because it is laid on over other preceding remedies; *cataplasma*, because it is merely an application; *emplastrum*, because it is spread upon something; *malagma*, because it is softened without fire and applied to a wound. These things have been said briefly concerning bodily medicines; now let us add something concerning spiritual medicines.

There is also a wound of the mind, which is soothed by the oil of the Holy Spirit and by peaceful words through which the poison of wickedness is expelled. For there are fomentations and medicines of words [Col. 0850C]; there are bonds of the law, by which those who are bound are released and those who are broken are made whole. Under these verses, therefore, the incurable madness of the wicked is lamented: they reject every remedy which Christ brought, as it were, upon the wound—Christ who poured wine and oil into the wounds of the man left half-dead, bound them up, and entrusted him to the innkeeper to care for him, when he was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10). Let us beware, then, lest we descend from Jerusalem by sinning; rather, let us ascend by doing good. Yet if we have sinned, let us not despair, because we have a physician who applies to the wound the bandage of heavenly words, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3). This medicine—namely repentance—heals wounds and makes what is broken whole. Therefore the desperate are lamented: those who continually rage against Christ and the Church, mocking and deriding, and who will be judged according to their works.

Whence it follows: “You will repay them, O Lord, according to the work of their hands.” THAU is interpreted “he erred” or “he brought to completion.” For the things said here are signs of future events. Hence the Psalmist: “You have shown your people hard things,” etc. And again: “You have given those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from before the bow” (ibid.). But because they would not heed it: “You will repay them, O Lord, according to the work of their hands.” He first repaid this to the Jews [Col. 0851A], who, hardened in heart and blinded by faithlessness, were driven still farther from faith and truth, and cannot enter into the righteousness of God and the way of salvation. For those who took life away deserved death. They erred, indeed, according as the letter THAU is interpreted “he erred.” And every reprobate errs who is hardened by an unrepentant heart. Therefore the Lord also brought His righteousness to completion; this is signified by the letter THAU, which denotes righteousness. Hence it follows: “You will give them a shield of the heart—your toil”; because, plainly, when they mocked the toil of His Passion, they thereby covered their own hearts and did not permit themselves to be pierced by the arrows of preaching.

Thus also the reprobate, whom God’s patience invites to repentance, set that same patience before themselves as a shield of the heart, so that they may not see that He who endures suffers [Col. 0851B]; and so they store up wrath for themselves. The bow of judgment is drawn while God’s patience endures; but they set up hardness of heart and excuses, lest they receive the words of life. Hence the Son of God says through the prophet: “I have labored in enduring” (Jer. 6). He endured laboriously then, when in His Passion He mercifully awaited their repentance. Therefore, because they despised the sign given so that they might flee from before the bow, it rightly follows: “You will pursue them in wrath and crush them beneath the heavens, O Lord”; so that, because they were hardened, sitting in the seat of pestilence and rising up against the Lord, they may be crushed beneath the heavens like dust from the face of the earth, since they were unwilling either to be heaven or to cleave to heavenly disciplines. For those who persecuted Christ and His members were justly crushed by the persecution of wrath, so that they may hear: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire,” etc. (Matt. 25).

For these are the signs that went beforehand, that they might flee from before the bow; and they would not. Hence, earlier, under this letter, it was said in the voice of the Church: “Let all their evil come before you; and deal with them as you dealt with me because of my iniquities” (Lam. 1). And in another alphabet: “There was none in the day of the Lord’s wrath who escaped and was left,” etc. (Lam. 2). THAU, therefore, rightly denotes completion, because under it righteousness—which is Christ—received the faith and completion of consummation; while impiety received the completion and end of condemnation, so that it might no longer be able to exalt itself. In both cases the preceding signs display the force of their meaning.
