[Col. 0851D] For the Lord showed His people hard things in the sign of the cross, so that the elect might be delivered; but those who refused to be marked with the sign of the cross consequently receive the truth of the signs and the crushing of eternal punishment, since they opposed the shield of faithlessness to teachings and miracles. The elect, however, possess the shield of good will by which they are crowned, because God crowns in reward those whom He helps by protecting.

Of the shield of the reprobate it is said: “His body is like molten shields” (Job 41). For the body of the devil—that is, the reprobate—is like molten shields: fragile and weak. Molten shields are indeed strong against arrows, but fragile when they fall. So also the reprobate are hard through obstinacy, frail through their manner of life, and are pierced by no arrow of preaching [Col. 0852A], because they are protected by the shield of perverse defense.

> [Note: Col. 0851D. Gregory, *Morals*, book 33, chapter 24.] Sacred Scripture is accustomed sometimes to use the name “shield” in a favorable sense, and sometimes in an adverse sense. For the defense of a shield is used for divine protection, but is sometimes mentioned for human resistance. It is used for divine protection when the Psalmist says: “You have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5). The Lord is said to crown us with a shield because those whom He helps by protecting, He crowns by rewarding. Again, the same prophet uses “shield” for human resistance, saying: “There he broke the powers: namely horn, bow, shield, sword, and battle” (Ps. 75). In the horn, indeed, is signified the pride of the arrogant; in the bow, the snares of those who strike from afar; [Col. 0852B] in the shield, the obstinate hardness of defenses; in the sword, a blow struck at close range; and in battle, the very movement of the mind against the Lord. All this is surely broken in the holy Church when the minds of those resisting God are subdued beneath the imposed yoke of humility.

Hence again the same Psalmist says: “He will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (Ps. 45). For the Lord breaks the bow when He destroys the hidden contrivances of plotters. He shatters the weapons when He crushes the human supports raised against Him. He burns the shields with fire when He kindles, with the heat of the Holy Spirit, toward repentance and the fervor of confession the minds of sinners who defend themselves with obstinate hardness. [Col. 0852C] But the fact that in this passage the body of this Leviathan is compared to molten shields suggests that we should consider that every vessel which is molten is indeed hard, but is nevertheless ordinarily breakable when it falls. Shields, then, if they are molten, are strong in receiving the blows of arrows, but breakable when they fall. They are not penetrated by the stroke of those who strike them, but by their own fall they are broken into fragments. The body of this Leviathan, that is, all the wicked, is compared to molten shields because they are hard through obstinacy but frail through life. For when they hear the words of preaching, they permit no arrow of correction to pierce them, because with every sin they commit they oppose a shield of proud defense.

For when anyone is rebuked concerning the guilt of such wickedness, he does not immediately consider [Col. 0852D] how he may correct his fault, but what he may set up in aid of his own defense. Thus no arrow of truth pierces him, because he receives the words of holy correction upon the shield of proud defense. Hence Jeremiah rightly says of the Jews who protected themselves with proud defense against the Lord’s commandments: “Repay them, O Lord, according to the work of their hands” (Lam. 3). And immediately he set forth that same repayment more explicitly, saying: “You will give them a shield of the heart—your toil.” For the toil of the Lord, apparent among human beings, was His passible humanity. When the Jews, puffed up with pride in their supposed wisdom, saw it, they despised it; and they disdained to believe Him immortal whom they saw to be passible by nature and [Col. 0853A] mortal. When they beheld His humility, hardened by the pride of arrogance, they took the greatest care that the words of holy preachers should not pierce their minds.

Therefore, when the Lord repaid them for their evil works, He gave them His own toil as a shield of the heart, because by a just judgment He displayed against Himself their proud obstinacy precisely through that by which He labored for us in weakness. For they rejected the words of preachers because they disdained in the Lord the weaknesses of His sufferings. Thus they had the Lord’s toil as a shield of the heart against the Lord Himself, because to those puffed up in pride it appeared contemptible in Him that He was humble for their sake. This shield, as we have already said above, was held by that first sinner, who, when the Lord asked him why he had touched the forbidden tree, did not attribute the fault to himself, but replied that he had received it from the woman whom the Lord had given him (Gen. 3), as though he might indirectly strike back his own guilt against the Creator who had given the woman to persuade him to such things.

The woman too, when questioned, held this same shield, when she did not attribute the fault to herself but referred it back to the serpent’s persuasions, saying: “The serpent deceived me, and I ate” (ibid.); so that she too might indirectly turn her guilt back upon the Creator, because He had allowed the serpent to enter there to persuade her to such things. The serpent, however, is no longer questioned, because his repentance was not sought. But those whose repentance was sought brought forth the shield of most wicked defense or corruption. Hence this practice has continued among sinners even now: when guilt is at issue, it is defended; and that from which guilt ought to have received pardon becomes the means by which it is increased. [Col. 0853C] Therefore it is well said: “His body is like molten shields” (Job 41), because all the wicked, lest the words of those who rebuke them reach them, prepare shields of defense, as though against the arrows of those who correct them.

Of such people, therefore, it is rightly lamented: “You will give them a shield of the heart—your toil.” For, abusing God’s patience, they imagine that God does not care for such things, or does not see them, or that the Creator is at fault—as Adam said: “The woman whom you gave me persuaded me, and I ate”; and the woman, throwing the fault back upon the serpent, indirectly turns it back upon the Creator. Protected by this shield, Cain said proudly and insultingly: “I do not know, Lord; am I my brother’s keeper?” (Gen. 4). “I do not know, Lord”: deceitful humility and false denial. “Am I [Col. 0853D] my brother’s keeper?”: a defiant reproach against God.

So everyone who abuses God’s patience, disdains to fear the signs of judgment, is not fortified by the sign of this letter, and is punished by the just retribution of condemnation: he has not merely erred, but has also brought to completion and filled up the measure of his sins. Hence it is said: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. 15); once they were complete, the promise and vengeance came at once. This too is shown here through the letter that is interpreted “he brought to completion.” “Sin, when completed, brings forth death” (Jas. 1), and a hard and unrepentant heart brings completion. Therefore let us pray with groaning and tears that the Lord may soften our heart, that we may fear His signs and, made to drink of the wine of compunction, flee from before the bow (Ps. 59).

Again he adds, saying: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven; they pursued us upon the mountains, they lay in wait for us in the wilderness” (Lam. 4). Allegorically, because the prophet transforms into himself all the laments, persons, and characteristics of all people, becoming all things to all, he laments the persecutions of the Church, whose persecutors are swifter than eagles. For unclean spirits are swifter, in wickedness, deceit, and agility of nature, to tear and devour than the eagles of heaven—that is, preachers—are to rescue. Of these it is said: “Where the body is, there [Col. 0854B] the eagles also will be gathered” (Matt. 24), because the memorial of Christ’s Passion is celebrated, and bread and wine are transubstantiated through the mystery of holy prayer into the body and blood of the same our Lord Jesus Christ. The eagles of heaven fly there as if to food, that they may receive life from His death.

But the aerial powers are swifter, because “there is no power upon earth which may be compared to them,” as the Lord says to blessed Job concerning Leviathan (Job 41).

> [Note: Col. 0853D. Gregory, *Morals*, book 34, chapter 17.] His power is declared to be higher than all things on earth, because although by the merit of his actions he falls below all, nevertheless by the condition of angelic nature he surpasses the whole human race. For though he lost the blessedness of inward felicity, he did not lose the greatness of his nature. Its powers still surpass all human things, although he lies beneath holy people because of the abasement of his merits. Hence the merit of their reward increases for those saints who fight against him, because he is conquered by those whom, through the power of his nature, he boasts that he has as though by right surpassed.

This Leviathan, therefore, and his attendants roar and seek whom they may devour. “They pursued us upon the mountains,” he says, etc., because when they are raised to the governments of the Church, they excite them more fiercely to persecution. Nor are they secure even in the watchtower of the apostolic see, because those whom they see raised upon mountains so that, by diligently watching over the rest, they may preserve them and summon them to the heights of virtue, they attack all the more ardently and boldly. “They lay in wait for us in the wilderness.” By the wilderness [Col. 0854D] is signified the monastic or eremitic life, lived in deserts and solitudes. Against its adherents the invisible enemies rage as against stronger athletes. But because, free from worldly cares, they are concerned only with their enemies and are watchful, the enemies lay snares for them more secretly, seeing that they withdraw into hidden places. But those who stand eminent, exalted upon mountains, they attack with visible forces and frequent assaults.

> [Note: Col. 0854D. “Assaults” (*insultibus*).]

These enemies are often swifter in deceiving than the eagles of heaven are in guarding against them. They are suitably called eagles of heaven because, despising earthly things, they range through heavenly ones. It should be noted, however, that they are not said to be swifter than sheep, oxen, horses, vultures, or any other birds, but than the eagles of heaven. Hence elsewhere: “My people have become a lost flock; their shepherds led them astray and made them wander upon the mountains,” namely, those who “passed from mountain to hill, forgetting their resting place” (Jer. 50).

It follows: “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, was taken in our sins. Of whom we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations.’” The Jews think that this was said of Josiah [Note: Col. 0855D. Said of Josiah (4 Kgs. 23:29)], because a righteous king was killed not for his own sins but for the sins of the people, in whom they placed their hope and whose wings they set before the nations everywhere. But Christ is most truly understood here: He was taken and slain by the Jews for the sins of the human race, not for His own sins. His divinity is indicated when it is said: [Col. 0855B] “The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord,” etc. For the Son is called Spirit, according to: “Renew a right spirit within my inward parts” (Ps. 50). His humanity is intimated when it is said: “Christ the Lord was taken in our sins.” Since man and God are one person, where Christ is taken, God too is said to be taken.

Christ is fittingly called “the breath of our mouth,” because we believe in Him with the heart and confess Him with the mouth, according to: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). Moreover, the mouth breathes in and breathes out: by breathing in we receive the infusion of grace, and by breathing out we make confession. But this is properly the voice of those who have the word of truth, which is Christ, in their mouths as in their hearts, because “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12). [Col. 0855C] “Christ was taken in our sins,” that is, in order to blot out our sins, not for His own, because He paid what He did not seize (Ps. 68).

“Of whom we said: ‘In your shadow we shall live among the nations,’” because He is the expectation of the nations (Gen. 49), and the seed of Abraham in whom all nations will be blessed (Gen. 12). The prophet believed in this Christ with his heart and proclaimed with his mouth: “In your shadow we shall live among the nations.” For Christ was to come so that He might save the nations together with the Jews. Hence he said in the future tense, “we shall live,” though we were dead in sins. “In your shadow,” he says, “we shall live,” concerning which it is said: “Protect me under the shadow of your wings” (Ps. 16). Christ was taken and crucified; beneath the shadow of His Passion He protected us, as though with wings extended upon the cross. His flesh was a shadow for us, cooling the heat of our mind [Col. 0855D] and tempering its various burning passions; for through His grace the shadow of the apostles also healed the sick (Acts 5).

His flesh was like a shadow, because “we saw Him without form or beauty” (Isa. 53). Of it it is said: “The Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt,” that is, the world (Isa. 19). This is the bright cloud over the apostles, lest the heat of wickedness burn them up. The prophet already foretold this, namely: “In His shadow we live among the nations.” For the prophet also saw Him in shadow, who, illuminated by the divine Spirit as in a mirror of the mind, foresaw the future. But now He illuminates the whole [Col. 0856A] world, although we still see Him through the shadow of His body—that is, the Church—and not yet face to face. Refreshed in this shadow, we live in hope.

It should be noted that the intention of all lamentation tends toward this end, in which every affliction comes to an end. Afterwards, as it were, a fork in the road is shown: the elect portion keeps to the right, while the reprobate portion, defiled by sins, embraces the left. Thus for the one there is eternal condemnation, for the other everlasting life, when the Lord has wiped every tear from the eyes of all the saints (Rev. 21). This the cross of the Lord foreshadowed as a judge’s tribunal, where, by faith, one of those hanging on either side was received, while the other was condemned through blasphemy (Luke 23), because he despised the way set before [Note: Col. 0856D. “Hanging.”] his eyes.

[Col. 0856B] “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven,” etc. Heretics are often swifter in disputation than the eagles of heaven—that is, the teachers of the people—whom they persecute upon the mountains: namely, upon the mountains of the Scriptures and of the teaching of the apostles and holy Fathers. They lay snares for hermits through deceit and honey-sweet words. Observe how many evils press upon us. In secret, snares are urgent; openly, persecution rages upon the mountains, in order to cast down the shepherds and strike down the sheep, according to: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. 13).

“The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord.” As from this air we draw breath, return it to it, and live from it, so the inward person draws in the Spirit of God by faith and lives from Him. And again, whatever he lives, prays, does well, [Col. 0856C] or thinks—[Note: Col. 0856D. The Gloss reads more correctly, “indeed.”]—he returns to Him, attributing all his good things to Him.

How long, then, Jews, will you remain unbelieving and refuse to believe in the Son of God, who was announced to you by the most manifest proclamations of the prophets and shown beforehand by most certain proofs and figures? Was not that most holy prophet Elijah—whose tongue, because your sins, as is true, demanded it, shut heaven by prayer and, when God showed mercy, opened it again at the fitting time—a figure in his works of the Son of God, who was to come and die for our salvation and that of the whole Church, when he raised the widow’s son?

For thus it is read in the history of that prophet: “The son of the woman, the mistress of the household, fell sick,” etc. (ibid.). [Col. 0856D] This widow, with whom Elijah lodged and whose flour and oil he blessed, is the synagogue of the Jews, widowed by the death of Moses, which was nourishing a little son—that is, the carnal people. At Elijah’s coming, that is, at the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, this son was weakened by the fever of unbelief, because he did not believe in Him, but in pride despised Him and, hating Him, fastened Him to the cross without cause. Hence his mother, the Synagogue, complains of His coming and preaching—namely, Christ’s—as though He were the cause of the people’s death, saying: “What is there between me and you, man of God? Have you entered to me so that my iniquities might be remembered and [Col. 0857A] my son put to death?” (ibid.).

This is why Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11). As the prophet was not angered by the widow’s words but instead pitied her, so our Redeemer was not angered by the wickedness of the Jews, but, taking pity on His people, took him from his mother’s bosom when He removed him from the carnal observance of the law. He placed him upon His own bed—that is, He showed him that he had life in His death. The Son of God stretched Himself over the boy three times when He taught the Jewish people the faith of the holy Trinity. Elijah took the boy and restored him to his mother when our Lord, saving the believing people, showed signs and miracles to the unbelieving, so that they might know that the one who believes in His [Col. 0857B] name truly lives. And thus it will happen toward the end of the world: the Jewish people, overcome by truth, will cry out to Christ and say: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God,” that is, the true Son of God and man, “and that the word of the Lord”—that is, the word of God the Father—“in your mouth is true.”

I wonder, Jews, why you are not ashamed. You find in your law and nation so many figures and such completely true testimonies concerning Christ, and yet you refuse to believe that He is God and true man, though He so often delivered you from the harshest yoke of slavery and from every evil.

Naboth also, of your own stock, when he was killed for his vineyard, foreshadowed in his death the same Son of God, who was to suffer for human salvation (3 Kgs. 21). [Col. 0857C] Naboth, indeed, is interpreted “conspicuous” or “possession.” Jezreel means “God’s honor” or “seed of God.” All this accords with the Son of God, who is the splendor of glory and whom God the Father appointed heir of all things (Heb. 1). This Naboth, namely Christ, had a vineyard, of which it is said: “You transplanted a vineyard from Egypt,” etc. (Ps. 79). Ahab desired this vineyard—Ahab being interpreted “brother of the Father,” that is, the Jewish people. From that vineyard, that is, from that people according to the flesh, Ahab wished to make a vegetable garden, so that where spiritual wine ought to have sprung up, he might transplant the fragile doctrines of the Pharisees.

When Naboth refused to give his vineyard—that is, when Christ would not consent to the superstitions of the Pharisees—the impious Jezebel, that is, the Synagogue, plotted His death. Jezebel is interpreted “cohabitant” or “vain flux,” because the Synagogue seemed to dwell in the house of the Lord but flowed away through various desires. Therefore Naboth’s vineyard is the Church gathered from the nations. After Christ was killed, the evil tenants sought to seize this vineyard, when they strove to extinguish the faith which is through Him, to prefer their own righteousness derived from the law, and to implant it among the nations they were teaching. Naboth, accused by false witnesses, was stoned; but Christ, against whom the Jews made false assertions, was crucified. Naboth was stoned for the vineyard of his fathers; Christ was crucified for His vineyard—that is, for the Church from [Col. 0858A] both Jews and nations—in order to gain it for God the Father, rescue it from the hand of the ancient enemy, and raise it with Himself to the joys of eternal life. Naboth was stoned outside the walls of the city of Samaria; Christ was crucified outside the gate of Jerusalem at the place called Calvary.

O unhappy—indeed, most unhappy—Jews, how long will you remain in unbelief and refuse to give faith to such manifest signs and figures, found in your law and nation, concerning Christ’s birth, Passion, and resurrection? What more open or clearer thing do you wish to hear? You can hear nothing truer, firmer, or more beneficial beneath heaven. But if you do not know this most true truth, or doubt it, you are surely deprived of every good.

[Col. 0858B] Elisha also, the disciple of that same Elijah, foreshadowed Christ in his works. Elisha is indeed interpreted “salvation of God.” Even in the fact that hair flowed down from his head, he foreshadowed Christ, abandoned by His disciples in the Passion. For Christ is the head of the whole Church, and the hairs of this head are all the apostles and the other faithful made perfect in His love and teaching. Hence it is said: “My teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 7). Thus Christ was bald in the Passion, because He was abandoned by all the disciples. As we have said, Elisha is interpreted “salvation of the Lord,” because he foreshadowed the one who was to be sent by God the Father for the salvation of the world.

> [Note: Col. 0857D. Isidore, *Questions on 4 Kings*, chapter 3.]

When Elisha was going up the mountain, boys mocked him, saying: “Go up, bald one; go up, bald one” [Col. 0858C] (4 Kgs. 2), because our Elisha, namely Christ, was to go up to the place of Calvary, where the Jews mocked Him, shouting to Pilate: “Crucify, crucify Him” (Luke 23). Elisha, going up to Bethel, that is, the house of the Lord, cursed the boys who mocked him; and two bears came out from the wood and tore forty-two of them. Likewise Christ, after He ascended to heaven, in the forty-second year sent two bears from the forests of the nations, namely Vespasian and Titus, who overthrew the Jews with great cruelty; and their blood was shed there where they hanged the Lord.

The Shunammite woman had a son, whom, because she had no other, she brought up delicately. One day [Col. 0858D] he left the house and was going into the field to his father and the harvesters. As I think, struck by the heat, he died that same day in his mother’s lap (4 Kgs. 4). This boy represented the children of Israel, whom God delivered from Egypt through Moses. As the boy went out to go to his father and the laborers and died that same day, so the Israelite people went out from Egypt to go to God the Father and to the laborers of the harvest—that is, Moses, Aaron, and the other teachers of their salvation—and died on the way, that is, in the wilderness, in the lap of their mother the Synagogue. In this passage the Shunammite signifies the Synagogue.

Why did the Israelite people die in the wilderness? Because, plainly, after they had multiplied in Egypt and had been led through Moses into the wilderness, they heard the Lord’s voice. When they ought to have been enlightened by the light of knowledge, they immediately turned in mind to idolatry and died. Therefore, as it were, the Shunammite asks Elisha concerning the boy, that he may be raised from death, when Moses, Aaron, Hur, Joshua, and the other fathers beseech God not to cast them down in the wilderness on account of their sins but mercifully and powerfully to lead them into the land of promise. Hence Moses: “Let your anger rest, Lord, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people,” etc. (Exod. 32).

Elisha, who in this passage bears the figure of the Lord, sends his staff by a boy to raise the dead man; yet the same dead man did not rise.

> [Note: Col. 0859D. Gregory, *Morals*, book 9, chapter 22.]

Therefore [Col. 0859B], when the Lord gave the law through Moses, He sent the staff as it were through the boy. But the boy, namely Moses, was unable by the staff—that is, by the terror of the law—to raise the dead man, because “the law brought no one to perfection” (Heb. 7). Therefore the Son of God Himself came in person and stretched Himself over the corpse, because, though He was in the form of God, He emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2). He walked back and forth in the house because He called both Jews and nations through faith to the heavenly kingdom. Elisha breathed upon the dead man, while the boy yawned seven times, because the grace of the divine gift breathes the sevenfold Spirit into those lying in the death of sin. At once the boy whom the staff of terror could not raise returned to life through the spirit of love. Therefore he calls the Israelite people a boy because it was little in the knowledge of God.

[Col. 0859C] How long then, Jews, will you remain unbelieving, with ears stopped and faithless hearts, though you see such great and glorious benefits of Christ displayed toward you, and yet do not believe that He is the true Son of God? Like a most loving Father, He encouraged, soothed, and nourished you; delivered you from visible and invisible enemies; gave temporal goods; promised everlasting ones; and summoned you to His love and affection through examples, most true figures, and the preaching of holy prophets. But you were not merely always ungrateful for His benefits and unbelieving toward the proclamations of the prophets: you even provoked Him by wicked works. You refused to hear His words [Col. 0859D] and those of the holy apostles; you preferred to serve foreign gods rather than Him; finally, because of envy, you fastened Him to the cross, and after He was taken down from the cross and buried, you caused Him to be guarded with all diligence.

But He, having been buried and leaving His flesh in the tomb, descended in soul to free the elect who were held captive in hell. On the third day, after despoiling hell, He returned to the tomb and raised the same body which He had laid down. On the fortieth day, ascending into heaven, He placed in eternal blessedness that same captivity which He had mercifully and powerfully led with Him from hell, and received Himself at the Father’s right hand, from which He had never departed [Col. 0860A], although He had mercifully descended to us. His divinity too, although it descended with the soul into hell, nevertheless did not leave the body in the tomb.

Now therefore, Jews—a faithless nation, who, as Moses says, are without counsel and without spiritual prudence (Deut. 32)—if you wish to have the same Son of God and man as a favorable judge, and to escape His wrath, faithfully worship with us Him who reigns at the Father’s right hand. Perhaps you will say to me: “Even though late, if we are converted to Him, shall we share in that resurrection?” But if you say this, you can prove by the examples of the ancients that what I have said is true.

You know that Elisha, of whose miracles we have said something above, was a truthful prophet established by God among your people [Col. 0860B]. When he began to be ill and Joash king of Israel came down to visit him, wept before him, shot an arrow through the eastern window at his command, and struck the ground three times with an arrow, the man of God foretold to him how many times he would strike Syria. Elisha therefore died in that same illness and was honourably buried by the aforesaid king and his people. But in that year raiders from Moab came into the land. Some men who were burying a man saw the raiders and threw the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came to life and stood upon his feet (4 Kings XIII).

Elisha, therefore, as we said above, means “the Lord’s salvation”; he thus bore the figure of Christ, who came to save the world [Col. 0860C]. In arming the king of Israel against Syria, he also prefigured Christ, who clothes the rulers of the Church with spiritual weapons and commands them to fight against the ancient enemy. They too are commanded to strike the earth—that is, carnal persons—with the arrow of preaching. To strike the earth three times with the arrow is to instil, by teaching, faith in the Trinity into carnal persons. The arrows are the words uttered by teachers, because they reach as far as the hearers’ hearts. The raiders signify demons, who snatch souls away to destruction. The raiders may also signify heretics, who, by wicked persuasions, turn the faithful away from the path of truth so that they may not believe rightly in Christ, and miserably and damnably drag them with themselves to perdition [Col. 0860D]. The corpse of the dead man signifies the whole human race. The resurrection of the corpse through touching Elisha’s bones therefore signifies that whoever touch Christ’s death with steadfast faith and truly place their hope in him will without doubt share in his resurrection. The corpse would by no means have risen unless it had touched Elisha’s bones; for the human race would in no way have risen through the righteousness which is Christ, but, as its sins deserved, would have slept in eternal death, unless it had faithfully believed in Christ dead, buried, truly raised again, and reigning at the Father’s right hand. Christ, then, is the cause of resurrection [Col. 0861A], and, together with the Father, of all our blessedness. Thus those who truly believe in him are rescued from eternal death and live eternally in him. Hence he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Why then, Jews, do you remain unbelieving even now, when in your Law and among your people you find so many witnesses to the truth and such manifest signs concerning Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection? Why, through your folly and unbelief, do you not only lose the blessedness of eternal life but also appoint yourselves for the flames of eternal fire? If you deny that Christ is the Son of God, you are deprived of every good. Repent, then, that you have denied him until now, and henceforth show him true faith. Believe that he was ineffably begotten of God the Father before all ages [Col. 0861B], and that at the end of time he assumed from his virgin mother true human substance for the salvation of the human race. From the Father he naturally possesses true, eternal, and unchangeable divinity; at the end of time he naturally received true humanity from his mother. We know that if you had recognized him as the King of glory, you would never have crucified him (1 Cor. II). Therefore, with his divinity unimpaired and untouched, he suffered for our salvation in the humanity he assumed. If, then, you seek to obtain full pardon from him, delay no longer in believing in him. But if perhaps you do not wish to believe me, a Christian urging true faith upon you, at least believe King David and prophet, who commands you the same thing.

[Col. 0861C] Hear, then, with a receptive ear what he commands you: “Draw near to him,” he says, “and be enlightened; and your faces shall not be confounded” (Ps. XXXIII). As we indicated above, our Lord Jesus Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God. Draw near to him, therefore, by faithful belief, because through him God the Father created all things out of nothing. He never drives away from himself those whom he sees faithfully believing in him, but mercifully receives them. From the beginning he has been accustomed to drive away from himself only those whose minds he knows remain obstinate against him. By a just judgment he rejects those exalted against him, and with wondrous love binds to himself those devoted to him; because from the beginning he resists the proud and gathers the humble (James IV). Hence Abigail said to David:

[Col. 0861D] “The soul of my lord shall be kept, as in a bundle of the living, with the Lord. But the soul of your enemies shall be whirled about as by the force and circling of a sling” (1 Kings XXV). By a most beautiful comparison she distinguishes the state of the righteous and the reprobate. She calls the souls of the former living, but those of the latter overtaken by spiritual death: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII). She likened these to a bundle, those to a sling-stone. For a bundle is bound together in order to be preserved; a stone is placed in a sling in order to be thrown away. Thus the elect are bound tight by the pressures of tribulations, so that, admonished by them, they may be more closely joined to one another by mutual love and, united, may be preserved for ever by the hand of the Redeemer. The more freely the reprobate are given over to their own pleasure, the farther [Col. 0862A] they are cast from the glory of the divine vision. For they have been driven from the hand of God (Ps. LXXXVII). He wonderfully describes the providence of the almighty heavenly protector when he says that the soul of the holy man is kept with him as in a bundle of the living. For just as it is easy for anyone to preserve in his hand a bundle of grass or hay that he holds, so the power of our Saviour preserves the elect from beginning to end. Of them he himself says: “No one shall snatch them from my hand” (John X). And just as a bundle is tied together, so the company of saints is bound by a single love and surrounded by divine protection.

I return to speak to you, Jews, because I grieve deeply over your unhappiness when I see you insufficiently devoted to faith in Christ. If, therefore, as has been said [Col. 0862B], you wish to be kept and bound together in the bundle of the living, draw near faithfully to Christ, who is the true light and will enlighten you, because he enlightens every person coming into this world (John I). For he is the sun and refreshment of angels, whom God the Father begot from himself before all ages. Hasten, then, while you can, to believe in him; for if you do not have the Son, you cannot have the Father at all. While he patiently awaits your repentance, seek pardon from him with tears, lest perhaps, if you refuse, he condemn you in the examination of his strict judgment as sacrilegious persons and guilty of so great a murder. Although you crucified him without cause and delivered him to death through envy, nevertheless, if with contrite mind you do penance before him, do not doubt that you will obtain full forgiveness from him [Col. 0862C]. For he is naturally merciful and kind toward penitents. Set before his sight the tears of true compunction, and, like the most compassionate father, he will blot out your iniquities like a cloud and as though they were mist. Hasten to draw near to him and trust in his mercy. Delay not in believing in him, and doubt his goodness no longer.

Meanwhile, I ask you, dearest brothers, to pour out continual prayers to the Lord for the blindness of that same faithless people, that he may deign to soften their hearts with the dew of his grace and mercifully turn them to himself; for he is able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones (Matt. III). Let the persistence of your prayer drive from their hearts the darkness of unbelief [Col. 0862D]. Let the earnestness of your prayers join them to the crowds of the faithful. If it can be done with God’s help, bring them back by prayer to the bosom of holy Church. Although they are not worthy to obtain mercy, yet when you pray for them you acquire eternal rewards for yourselves. Yet, beloved, I want you to know that Christ was promised to them but given to us. He himself says: “I was not sent except to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Therefore, he was given to us by God the Father and taken from them. He was rejected by them with disgrace, but received by us with honour. God took from them for ever their nation and place, but gave him to us as an eternal possession. Finally he also delivered them to all the nations [Col. 0863A] under heaven into captivity, but led us to freedom. What, then, dearest brothers, do you observe amid these things? Did God grant us such great benefits for our merits? Did we do anything good for which we deserved to receive such great goods from the Lord’s hand? Not at all. For we were redeemed by him, not through our merits, but by his grace alone.

For, as blessed Gregory says:

> Grace from above does not find a person’s merit in order that it may come, but makes it after it has come.

[Note: [Col. 0863D] Book XVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 22, at the end.]

Thus, coming to an unworthy mind, God renders it worthy of himself by coming; and he creates in it merit which he may reward, whereas he had found only that which he might punish. In the midst of these matters, it is pleasing to direct the eyes of the mind to that thief who ascended the cross from the sickle [Note: [Col. 0863D] Read: “from the jaws” (*fauce*).], and from the cross to paradise [Col. 0863B]; and we shall plainly recognize that we have been redeemed, not by our merits but by God’s grace alone. Let us observe what he was when he came to the gibbet and what he was when he departed from the gibbet. He came guilty and stained with a brother’s blood, but upon the cross he was changed by inward grace. Yet he who had inflicted death upon his brother proclaimed the life of the dying Lord, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII). On the cross nails had fastened his hands and feet, and nothing in him remained free except heart and tongue; but, God inspiring him, he offered God all that he found free in himself, so that, according to what is written, he might believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. X). The Apostle bears witness that three virtues especially remain in the hearts of the faithful [Col. 0863C], saying: “But now remain faith, hope, and love” (1 Cor. XIII). Filled suddenly with divine grace, the thief both received and preserved these upon the cross. For he had faith, because he believed that the Lord would reign, whom he saw dying beside him. He had hope, because he asked for entry into his kingdom, saying: “Remember me when you come into your kingdom.” He also held love vigorously in his death, because he both rebuked for wickedness and proclaimed the life he had come to know to his brother and fellow-thief, dying for a similar crime, saying: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive things worthy of our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong” (Luke XXIII). He who came to the cross such a man through guilt, behold what a man he leaves the cross through grace. He confessed the Lord, whom [Col. 0863D] he saw with himself in human weakness [Note: [Col. 0864D] Supplement: “dying.”], at the time when the apostles denied him whom they had seen working miracles by divine power. But those who maintain that a human being is saved by his own powers suppose that this same human confession comes from the human being’s own power. If that were so, the Psalmist would not say in praise of God: “Confession and magnificence are his work” (Ps. CX). Therefore we receive from him the power to make right confession, from whom we are also given the power to do great things. Since, therefore, we have offered no good work for which we have received such great goods from the Lord’s hand, we must give him thanks without ceasing.

Therefore, as has already been said above, the Son of God had been promised to the Jews but was given to us. He was cruelly handed over to death by them [Col. 0864A], but devoutly received by us. Long before, indeed, Isaiah had said of them: “I have nourished and exalted sons, but they, despising me, have rejected me” (Isa. I). But of us the Psalmist says: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). Therefore, beloved, although we have not deserved to see him with bodily eyes, it is fitting that we obey him by hearing of the ear, because blessed are those who did not see him and yet faithfully believed in him (John XX). Let us therefore love him with sincere minds and serve him with all our strength. According to the Apostle, let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach (Heb. XIII). What is it to go out to Christ outside the camp, except, having renounced all the delights [Col. 0864B] of this age and the enticements of secular life, to bear the cross for love of him and—what is more glorious—if necessity requires it, to shed our own blood as he shed his for us? We go out to him outside the camp if we strive to serve him devoutly beyond father, mother, children, all relatives, and our own wills. “Bearing his reproach,” he says. To bear Christ’s reproach is not to be ashamed of his cross, passion, scourges, the piercing of the nails, the wound in his side, the drinking of vinegar, the blow of the reed, slaps, insults, mockery, spitting, crown of thorns, death, and burial; rather, it is to preach them devoutly and openly to all nations. Hence the Apostle warned Timothy [Col. 0864C], saying: “Do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Tim. I). It is as though he said more openly: Do not be ashamed to preach Christ crucified by the Jews; for although he endured passion—scourges, the cross, death, and reproaches—yet, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he was given by God the Father all power over everything that has been created. We too bear his reproach when, following his example, we think humbly of ourselves, curse pride, maintain humility, reject temporal glory, choose to be lowly in the house of God, despise riches, willingly endure poverty, patiently bear injuries inflicted upon us by neighbours, and strive to serve him in cold and nakedness, in many vigils, hunger and thirst, and many fasts [Col. 0864D]; when, at the recitation of his venerable passion, we shed tears; cut the hair of our heads in the likeness of his crown of thorns; bear the banner of his life-giving cross upon our foreheads; and moreover are called Christians in his name. For when pagans persecute or kill us out of hatred for his name, heretics assail us, and Jews blaspheme us: if we endure these things freely for love of him, we undoubtedly bear his reproach. Therefore let his reproach be our glory, his death our life, his cross our triumph, and his resurrection our blessedness.

Let us, then, beloved, give thanks together [Col. 0865A] to God the Father, to his Son our Lord Jesus Christ, and to the Holy Spirit, for so great and incomparable a benefit bestowed by him upon us unworthy persons. By the will of God the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, Christ, in assuming our humanity, emptied himself and willingly gave up his own soul; and from his death he prepared for us a medicine by which he mercifully healed our wounds. Therefore, dearest brothers, let us show ourselves such in his service that, through the prevenient gift of his grace, his passion may be remission of our sins; his wounds, remedies for our infirmity; the bitterness of his passion [Col. 0866A], our consolation; his crown of thorns, our honour; and his resurrection, through the favour of the same Lord Jesus Christ, a happy passage from the theatre to the palace, from prison to the court, from earth to heaven, from perpetual death to eternal life, and from the mire of vices to fellowship with the angels. On this night, for the salvation of the whole world, he permitted himself to be seized by the wicked and brought before the chief priests and the judge. He lives and reigns with God the Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Twenty-Third Sermon. On the Lord’s Supper III

[Col. 0865]

[Col. 0865B] God the Father, before all ages, begot a Son equal to himself, through whom he created all things visible and invisible; and through whom he also determined, in his eternity, to deliver the human race, which he foresaw would fall from the state of uprightness through the deceit of the devil. From the beginning of the world, therefore, he made known the birth, passion, and resurrection of this same Jesus Christ his Son through figures: he foreshadowed them by the examples of the patriarchs, foretold them through the prophets, and openly showed them through the apostles.

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 30.]

Did not Joseph prefigure the Son of God, who was to suffer for our salvation, when he was sold by his envious brothers, brought into Egypt, and there exalted? (Gen. XXXVII.) Joseph, one of Jacob’s twelve sons, whom his father loved above his other sons, prefigured Christ the Lord [Col. 0865C], whom God the Father preferred, as born according to the flesh, above his other brethren descended from Abraham’s stock. Hence it is also said there that Jacob begot him in old age (*ibid.*). For when the world was growing old, the dawning Son of God came late through the birth of Mary, the most holy and most glorious virgin, as a son of old age according to the mystery of the humanity he assumed—he who was with the Father before the ages. The many-coloured tunic which his father made for him signified the diversity of peoples from all nations gathered into the body of Christ.

Joseph’s sheaf is that which was fulfilled in Christ: “All kings of the earth shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. LXXI), namely, bringing forth the fruit of good works. He is the one whom sun, moon, and stars worship; concerning that sun it was said: “Praise him, sun and moon, and all stars and light” (Ps. CXLVIII). For the excellence of the saints, under the name of the sun and the image of love, and the Church and the multitude of all peoples in the figure of the stars, worship him. Hence Joseph’s father rebukes him, saying: [Col. 0866B] “Shall I, and your mother, and your brothers worship you upon the earth?” (Gen. XXXVII.) This rebuke of the father signifies the folly or pride of the people of Israel, who, because they know Christ to have been born from themselves, disdain to worship him. Jacob sent his son Joseph to take concern for his brothers; and God the Father sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race weakened by sins. He is sent by that Father, of whom it is written: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. VIII), that he might see whether the sheep were sound. And the Lord says in the Gospel: “I came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). Joseph therefore found his brothers in Dothan, which means “defection.” Truly they were in great defection, since they were contemplating fratricide [Col. 0866C]. When Joseph’s brothers saw him from afar, they planned to kill him; and when the Jews saw the true Joseph, the Lord Jesus Christ, they all resolved upon one plan, that they might crucify him, saying to Pilate: “Let him be crucified” (Matt. XXVII).

It follows: “A most wicked beast devoured him”—that is, the Jewish beast killed Christ. Of it the Lord says in the Gospel: “Behold, I send you as sheep in the midst of wolves” (Matt. X). Thus Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his many-coloured and long tunic; and the Jews stripped Christ, by the death of the cross, of the tunic of his body, many-coloured—that is, adorned with the diversity of all virtues. They sprinkled the tunic with a goat’s blood [Col. 0866D], because they accused him with false charges—that is, testimonies. Joseph is then sent into the cistern; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell. He too is raised out of the cistern and sold to the Ishmaelites—that is, to the Gentiles; and Christ, after coming forth from hell, is purchased by all nations through the commerce of faith. Joseph is sold by Judah’s counsel [Col. 0867A]; and Christ is sold, through the counsel of Judas Iscariot, for thirty pieces of silver. Then Jacob, lamenting the loss of his offspring, mourned as a father for his lost son and wept as a prophet over the destruction of the Jews. Finally he tore his garments, as we read that the chief priests did at the Lord’s passion. The veil of the Temple also was torn (Luke XXIII), so that the patriarch might show his own people laid bare and the kingdoms divided. Joseph therefore went down into Egypt, and Christ into the world. A eunuch bought him—that is, a people chaste in evangelical disciplines. Joseph was handsome in appearance (Gen. XXXIX); so David also says of Christ: “You are fairer in beauty than the children of men; grace has been poured upon your lips,” etc. (Ps. XLIV). “And the woman,” he says, “cast her eyes upon him” [Col. 0867B], to commit adultery with him (Gen. XXXIX). This woman was a figure of the Synagogue, which often, as Scripture says, committed adultery after foreign gods (Jer. III). Likewise, she wanted to hold Christ in adulteries by her wickedness, so that he might deny himself to be God and observe the commands of Pharisees and scribes rather than those of the Law, though he was her husband. But Christ, refusing the unlawful doctrine—that is, the adultery—of the adulterous Synagogue, was seized by the hand with the garment of his body; he put off the flesh and ascended, free from death, into heaven. The woman—that is, the Synagogue—slandered him when she could not hold him, saying that he blasphemed the Temple of God and was said to be contrary to the Law or a transgressor of it. But prison did not frighten him [Col. 0867C], nor did the lower regions hold him; for even when he had gone down as though to be punished, he freed others from there. Finally, Joseph found two eunuchs of the king’s household bound in prison, signifying the figure of the two peoples, namely believers and unbelievers, who were held shut up under Adam’s sin and liable to transgression. They are called eunuchs because they had received the chaste rule of discipline. Hence the saying: “The words of the Lord are chaste” (Ps. XI). Finally, after the Lord’s resurrection from the dead on the third day, and after he revealed the obscure things of the Law, like Joseph revealing dreams, the people of believers was freed from sins and delivered from hell’s prison, and returns to service in the divine Law. But the unbelieving and impious people of the Jews, because it did not believe in the wood of salvation, is hung upon the wood of transgression [Col. 0867D], as happened to the other eunuch, who represented the Jews.

Moreover, Pharaoh tells a dream, and Joseph interprets it. But what was signified by the seven full ears of grain, or what was shown by the seven fat cows, except the gifts of the seven spiritual charisms, in which abundance overflows with generous mercy? Conversely, the seven barren and lean ones signified the famine of truth and righteousness in the last times. Joseph gathered, during seven years, all the abundance of crops—that is, he stored the grain of faith belonging to the saints in granaries through those seven charisms, as through seven years—so that when the seven years of scarcity should come, that is, when that iniquity under Antichrist should arise, consisting in the seven capital sins [Col. 0868A], when there should be famine of faith and salvation, then saints and faithful alike might possess the abundant harvest of righteousness and their faith might not fail, weakened by scarcity of the word. Accordingly Joseph, who had assumed the type of Christ, received a chariot; and with a herald preceding him, the king set him over all the land of Egypt. Our Lord too, after being sold away from Judaea, like Joseph by his brothers, and rising from the prison of hell, ascended the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, of which it is said: “The chariots of God are ten thousands” (Ps. LXVII). He also received from God the Father authority to preach and judge, as Paul says: “And he gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). He also received a ring—the high priesthood [Col. 0868B] of faith—by which the souls of believers are marked with the sign of salvation, and by the sign of the cross the grace of the eternal king, that is, the light of his countenance, is impressed upon our foreheads and hearts. He is clothed with a linen robe—that is, holy flesh brighter than linen—and a robe of immortality. He also received a golden collar—that is, good understanding. A herald goes before him, and John the Baptist, preceding Christ, proclaimed: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Matt. III). He will also have another herald, namely the trumpet of an angel, because he himself, speaking as if of another, said of his coming to judgment: “He will come with the trumpet of an angel” (Matt. XXIV). Joseph, indeed, is called in the Egyptian language “saviour of the world” [Col. 0868C], which is said more clearly of Christ, because under the figure of Joseph the Saviour is shown not only as saviour of the one land of Egypt, but also of the whole world. Joseph was thirty years old (Luke III) when he stood before King Pharaoh, and Christ is likewise read to have been thirty years old when, under Pharaoh’s type, he appeared revealed before the world. He therefore received a wife from the Gentiles—that is, the Church—from whom he begot two sons, that is, the two peoples gathered from Jews and Gentiles.

Therefore, after the years of abundance, famine prevailed over the whole world. Rightly so, because there was none who did good. Afterwards Joseph, by abundance of grain, saves Egypt, and Christ, by the abundance of God’s word, frees the world. For Christ opened his granaries throughout the world and subdued everything by the distribution of his grain [Col. 0868D]. Had Joseph’s brothers not sold him, Egypt would have perished; and had the Jews not crucified Christ, the world would have perished. Joseph also means “increase” or “enlargement”; but in that Joseph enlargement belonged only to Egypt. In our Joseph, however, the whole world deserved to have increase. He distributed wheat; Christ, the word of God. “For his sound has gone out into all the earth, and his words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). Jacob says to his sons: “There is grain in Egypt” (Gen. XXII). God the Father also says: “Out of Egypt I called my son,” etc. (Hos. XI). The ten leaders therefore go down—that is, the Jews, established in the Decalogue of the Law—whom Joseph recognized, though he was not recognized by them. The Hebrews are recognized by Christ, but they themselves do not recognize Christ [Col. 0869A]. They gave him money indeed, but Joseph gave grain and returned the silver, because Christ is not bought with money but with grace.

Joseph saw Benjamin, his little brother. Mystically too, the Lord Jesus saw Paul when a light from heaven shone round him (Acts IX). Paul [Note: [Col. 0869D] Because Jacob’s blessing upon Benjamin was fulfilled in a spiritual sense in the Apostle Paul, as the Fathers commonly affirm, Isidore therefore inserts here matters which Luke relates concerning the Apostle. But Martin’s manuscript reads *Paulus* (“Paul”) where the printed editions read *parvulus* (“little”); yet, to state what we think, we trust neither reading sufficiently.] was so called because he did not yet possess mature age of faith in the flesh. Hence he is also called a young man, because he kept the garments of those stoning Stephen (Acts VII). Joseph wept, and Paul’s blindness was Christ’s weeping. Christ washes his face when Paul is baptized, through whom the Lord Jesus himself might be seen by many. Then the silver cup is put into the sack of the younger alone (Gen. XLIV). But what does it mean [Col. 0869B] that the cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, except that in Paul’s heart the eloquence of heavenly doctrine already shone, while he was trained in the Law? But because he was not subject to Christ, doctrine did not shine perfectly in him. The cup within the sack was doctrine within the Law, a lamp under a bushel. Yet Ananias was sent and laid his hand on him; he untied the purse, and, when it was untied, the silver shone. As the scales fell, like certain bonds of the sack, the sack was opened; that is, with the veil of the Law put away, Paul gained the grace of freedom and, with the face of the word unveiled, preached the Gospel (Acts IX).

Benjamin was given thirty [Note: [Col. 0869D] According to the Vulgate the reading here should be “three hundred”; [Col. 0870D] but Isidore is following another version, whereas Ambrose, from whom he derived these matters, retains the Vulgate in chapter 13 of *On Joseph*.] pieces of silver with five excellent robes (Gen. XLV). Whoever preaches the Trinity or Christ’s cross receives thirty pieces of silver from Christ. [Col. 0869C] Hence Paul also says: “For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. II). Paul received five robes, that is, wisdom and the manifold disciplines of all the senses.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Correct this passage as follows: “Paul received five robes, that is, the manifold disciplines of all the senses.” *Praecessit* [printed edition: *Praecellit*].]

Paul therefore went ahead, and his share of merits surpasses that of the others; yet the brothers—that is, the other preachers—also have their own grace, namely two robes: that they may confess Christ both God and man, as is read in Proverbs: “All her household are clothed in double garments” (Prov. XXXI), that is, in mystical or moral understanding. Gifts are also sent to the father: the son honours the father; Christ honours his people with gifts promised in life. The asses—that is, Gentiles—carry these gifts: they carry gifts in Christ’s type, and in the Gospel they carry the giver of gifts. Joseph dismissed his brothers, who announced to their father: “Joseph your son lives, and he rules over all the land of Egypt” (Gen. XLV). Jacob was astonished—that is, the cruel people—but after it has learned Christ’s deeds at the end, its spirit will revive; and the one who seemed dead will be made alive by faith in Christ’s resurrection [Col. 0870A]. Jacob, that is, the Jewish people, is called by his sons—namely Peter, Paul, John, and the other apostles—and invited to grace. Judah, whose name means “confession,” meets him: confession now goes before those whom faithlessness previously possessed; and thus the true Joseph, that is, Christ, meets him. For who will receive in the last times the Jewish people, not according to its merits but according to the election of his grace, and lay his hand upon its eyes to remove its blindness, except Christ? He delayed its blindness so that he who previously did not think it should be believed might believe last. Hence the Apostle says: “Blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel might be saved” (Rom. XI). After this Joseph gave his parents and brothers the best land, Goshen, providing them food because famine had oppressed the land [Col. 0870B]. So too the Lord chose the best land for his parents—that is, the patriarchs and prophets, from whom he deigned to be born according to the flesh—or for all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel: “These are my brothers, who do my will” (Matt. XII). To these, therefore, he gives the land, namely the land of the promised kingdom of God, of which the prophet says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. XXVI).

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Isidore, as above, chapter 31.]

Then Joseph, hastening to receive his father’s blessing, presented his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim (Gen. XLVIII). In them happened what had occurred with Esau and Jacob. For the elder, Manasseh, whose name means “forgetfulness,” bore the type of the Jews, who forgot their God who made them. The younger bore the type of Christians; his name signifies fruitfulness, which belongs properly to the younger people, made fruitful across the breadth of the world [Col. 0870C]. When Jacob wished to bless them, Joseph placed Ephraim at his left hand and set Manasseh at his grandfather’s right. But Jacob, crossing his hands and prefiguring the mystery of the cross, transferred his right hand to the younger and laid his left upon the elder. Thus, with the likeness of the cross marked over their heads, he foreshadowed the cross as a scandal to Jews and future glory to Christians. We also see the elder, Manasseh, through the mystery of the cross, made left from right; and the younger, Ephraim, right from left, because as the Jews fall away at our left hand, we have obtained their glory [Col. 0870D]. By such a sacrament, then, the younger people of the Gentiles was set above the elder people of the Jews. Hence the same patriarch says: “He indeed shall become a people, but the other shall be exalted” (*ibid.*).

From the beginning, therefore, the Son of God did not remain silent; rather, through the patriarchs and prophets he foretold his coming, [Col. 0871A] so that the faithless Jewish nation might be able to find absolutely no excuse for its unbelief. Although God foresaw that they would not believe, nevertheless through the heralds of law and truth he never ceased to warn them faithfully to meet him at his coming. Thus Jeremiah, speaking in the person of the Lord, foretold: “The house of Judah has dealt treacherously against me, says the Lord: they have denied me and said, ‘He is not he’” (Jer. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Isidore, Book I Against the Jews, ch. 18.]

Even now, to this very day, the Jews say this of Christ: “He is not he,” awaiting another with whom they may perish—namely, Antichrist. And Isaiah says: “He had neither form nor beauty; and we saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him: despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and knowing how to bear infirmity; and as though his face were hidden [Col. 0871B] and despised, so that we did not esteem him” (Isa. 53). By these words the unbelief of the Jews is indicated: they considered Christ to have neither form nor beauty. Therefore he was not esteemed by them as God. That they would neither recognize nor receive him, the same Isaiah confirms when he says: “I have nourished and exalted children, says the Lord; but they, scorning, have despised me” (Isa. 1). And again: “The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; Israel has not known me, my people has not understood” (Isa. 6). He adds further: “You shall hear a hearing and not understand; seeing, you shall see and not know. The heart of this people has grown gross.” Hence Ezekiel: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, you dwell in the midst [Col. 0871C] of a provoking house, which has eyes to see and does not see, and ears to hear and does not hear” (Ezek. 12). For they were so blinded that they neither recognized nor received the Savior. The day of him whom Abraham saw and rejoiced over (John 8), the Jews saw with grief and, crying aloud, said: “He is deserving of death” (Matt. 26). The prophets awaited Christ’s coming with great longing; but these unhappy men both saw him and did not recognize him, and moreover, blaspheming, said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). Why? “Their malice blinded them” (Wis. 2). The hardness of this people is no more changed than the Ethiopian’s color or the leopard’s spots, as Jeremiah testifies: “If the Ethiopian [Col. 0871D] can change his skin and the leopard its spots, this nation has changed the perversity and hardness of its heart” (Jer. 13).

[Note: [Col. 0871D] Isidore, cited above, ch. 19.]

That Jews and Gentiles were to assemble to kill the Son of God and man is read as follows: because the Jews, not recognizing him, gathered to crucify him, giving universal assent to his passion: “Why have the nations raged, and the peoples devised vain things? The kings of the earth stood,” that is, Herod and Pilate, “and the rulers assembled as one”—namely, the chief priests and elders of the Jews—“against the Lord and against his Christ” (Ps. 2). Again, in the person of the Lord: “Many dogs surrounded me; the council of evildoers besieged me” (Ps. 21). Isaiah writes thus: “His watchmen are blind; mute dogs unable to bark” (Isa. 56). As though he said: “His watchmen did not know; all are blind” (ibid.). That is, the scribes and Pharisees, priests, kings, and rulers, not possessing Christ the true light, or faith and the other virtues, are all mute dogs, unable to bark against enemies with the voice of preaching, because, bound by vices, they are ashamed to preach. So also today in the Church, “if a blind man leads a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15). Thus the Jews, following the blind rulers and teachers of their law, crucified Christ and fell with them into the pit of eternal damnation. “For,” as blessed Hilary says, “[Col. 0872B] it is the habit of dogs to play about their shepherd, recognize the flock, and pursue beasts lying in ambush.” But the Jews, blind dogs, neither seeing their shepherd nor understanding their office, turned their barking not against beasts but against the flock, not against thieves but against the Lord. Therefore the Lord himself says through another prophet: “They have become to me a returning arrow,” because Christ was to be sold by Judas for thirty pieces of silver.

Now that he was valued and sold for thirty pieces of silver, he himself foretold through Zechariah, saying: “If it is good in your sight, give me my wage: thirty pieces of silver. And the Lord said to me: Throw them to the statuary, the handsome price at which I was valued by them” (Zech. 11).

[Note: [Col. 0872D] Isidore, ibid., ch. 20.]

For it is well known to everyone that Judas, moved by repentance, brought back the money [Col. 0872C] and threw it in the Temple, then went away and hanged himself with a noose, so that what Isaiah says might be fulfilled: “A false witness shall not go unpunished, because he sold the righteous man for silver.” Let it therefore be said: “If it is good in your sight,” that is, if you please, freely bring me my wage, because I chose you, a few, and rejected the nations; therefore keep my commandments. But if you do not wish to render my wage or to be named after me, be still; openly refuse; do what you wish. “And they took my wage, thirty pieces of silver” (ibid.), they who had said: “All that God has commanded we will do” (Exod. 24). Afterwards they gave thirty pieces of silver to Judas the traitor for my blood. The Jews maliciously interpret the thirty pieces of silver as thirty commandments of the Law which they are commanded to perform, and again thirty-seven others which are forbidden. “And the Lord said to me”—the Father, that is, to the Son, or to the prophet—“Throw them to the statuary,” that is, the refiner: “the handsome price at which I was valued by them.” As though it were said more plainly: You shall tell them to render the silver of God’s commandments to God, their maker and creator; and because they refused to do this, they were cast away. He does not say, “Lay it down,” but “Throw it,” so that by the judgment of the maker—that is, the refiner—the Lord’s wage might be exposed. “To the statuary,” he says, that is, to the caster of statues, whom others call a *plastes*, that is, a maker—

[Note: [Col. 0872D] “Finctorem” [maker].]

—or a potter, so that [Col. 0873A] the Creator of all might judge concerning the price, which he calls “handsome” ironically. It is as though he said: The people whom I chose as a son judged that I should be bought and sold for so cheap a price.

Again he adds, saying: “And I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord, to the statuary” (Zech. 11). Hence it is said: “And, having thrown down the pieces of silver in the Temple, he went away and hanged himself with a noose” (Matt. 27). A *status* or *statamus* is a weight; hence *statuarius*, that is, a weigher. For the Son of God had performed many good works among the Jews: restoring life to the dead, sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and walking to the lame (Matt. 11). For all these things the Jews, in their wicked valuation of thirty pieces of silver, gave him death as his wage.

[Col. 0873B]

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Isidore, ch. 21.]

That the Lord pointed out the traitor to the disciples by the bread extended to him, David shows in the Psalms to have been fulfilled, saying: “He who ate my breads has multiplied treachery against me” (Ps. 40). And again: “But you, a man of one mind with me, my guide and my acquaintance, who together with me took sweet food; in the house of God we walked in agreement” (Ps. 54).

That the Son of God willingly died for us, Isaiah openly shows, saying: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and thus he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53). And again: “Because he delivered his soul unto death, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall be directed in his hand” (ibid.). The Father’s will was indeed directed in Christ’s hand, because God the Father deigned to send him for the redemption of the human race. [Col. 0873C] He himself speaks through Jeremiah, saying: “I have forsaken my house and my inheritance; I have delivered my beloved soul into the hands of enemies” (Jer. 12), namely, the Jews who killed me.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Isidore, ch. 23.]

That the Son of God and man was to be seized by the Jews, the prophet Jeremiah foretold long beforehand when he said: “The Lord Christ was taken in our sins” (Lam. 4). By this prophecy he plainly showed both that he is Christ the Lord and that he was delivered up for our sins. Likewise, the Book of Wisdom says: “The wicked said among themselves: Let us seize the righteous man, because he is useless to us and contrary to our works. He promises that he has the knowledge of God and calls himself the Son of God. And if he is the true Son of God, he will receive [Col. 0873D] him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries” (Wis. 2). And below: “Let us test his reverence and know his patience; let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (ibid.), that is, fastening to the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Isidore, ch. 24.]

That the Son of God and man was to be judged by the Jews, David cries out in the person of the people sinning against God: “Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you, that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50). For Christ, coming in the flesh, presented himself as though guilty, in order to justify us from sins; and the judge of all offered himself to human beings to be judged. Thus, gentle and patient, [Col. 0874A] when he was judged he prevailed, because the persecuting people found in him nothing for which he might rightly be judged. Hence the prophet Micah, foretelling his judgment, thus threatens that same impious people, setting forth the Lord’s benefits toward his people and, conversely, their evils against the Lord: “Hear what the Lord says to me: Arise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice” (Mic. 6).

The mountains are the ministering spirits to whom the administration of human affairs has been entrusted.

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Isidore, from the Gloss.]

The prophet is commanded to contend in judgment against these, so that, if those mountains or hills are found not to have cared well for the people, it may be seen whether the fault lies with God, who did not appoint suitable overseers; or with the angels themselves, if they did not do what belonged to their office; or with the people, who disdained to obey good prelates. Since fault can be found neither in God nor in the angels, it remains that it is found in the people, and that they are justly punished. Yet God does not immediately wish to inflict punishments upon sinners by sheer power; rather, in order to appear just, he summons sinners to judgment, so that under the testimony of angels and the whole creation they may answer whether they can bring any charge against God. Some call Abraham and the patriarchs mountains; when they have been summoned to judgment, the people’s case is to be examined. Again the prophet speaks to the mountains as he had been commanded: “Let the mountains hear,” he says, “the judgment of the Lord, and the strong foundations of the earth,” namely, those under whose guardianship human beings are founded in virtues; “for [Col. 0874C] the Lord has a judgment with his people, and I will dispute with Israel.” The Lord grants his people leave to argue against him. It is as though the prophet said more plainly: Therefore I compel you to listen, because the Lord wishes to proceed against you not by power but by judgment. “My people, what have I done to you that I ought not to have done? In what have I troubled you, or by what labor have I oppressed you? Answer me.” Perhaps you long for the flesh-pots of the Egyptians, grieved that you have been freed from slavery so that you might serve Pharaoh and the devil in mud and brick. “Because I led you out of the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery.” As though he said: Perhaps I troubled you in this—that I freed you from the land of Egypt, where enemies afflicted you—and “sent before your face leaders,” namely [Col. 0874D] Moses, my friend; Aaron, the priest; and Miriam, the prophetess? And if these seem small things, remember that time when Balak hired against you Balaam the diviner, whom I compelled to bless you against his will.

He who once served Pharaoh and the Egyptians in mud and brick, if his redeemer ever disputes with him, ought not to neglect the voice of the reprover. Rather, he should know that God sent before him Moses, that is, the spiritual Law; Aaron, namely Christ the high priest; and Miriam, that is, the prophecy of the prophets. He also delivers him from the hand of Balak, whose name means “destroying,” that is, from the devil who desires to destroy, the king of those who abuse the Law. Balaam means “vain people”; Beor is interpreted “from skin.” But when the devil, through the vain people of the Gentiles, which sprang from skin—that is, devoted to works of the flesh—wishes to curse a human being, God on the contrary compels him to bless. For the people, though vain, sees the devil as never stable but always wavering, until he comes and brings others into Gilgal, which is interpreted “a rolling-place.” If, therefore, we see some people rising against us who thirst for our blood, let us say: “Balaam came from Shittim as far as Gilgal, that the righteousness of the delivering God might be known” (Mic. 6). In Mount Sinai grow shittim trees like white thorn. In this passage, then, as we said above, he shows God’s benefits [Col. 0875B] toward his people and, conversely, their evils against the Lord Christ. He adds also what is to come upon that people: “Hear, tribe: Who has approved it? There is still fire in the house of the wicked and a treasury of iniquity” (Mic. 6).

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Isidore, ch. 26.]

That the Son of God was to be accused by false witnesses, the same Lord says through the prophet Hosea: “Woe to them, because they have departed from me”—namely, by worshiping idols—“they shall be laid waste by enemies and shall be miserable, because they have dealt treacherously against me,” by worshiping calves and transgressing my commandments, to whom I said: “You shall not make for yourselves foreign gods” (Exod. 20). All alike, from king to beggar, shall be laid waste, just as idols were fashioned by common counsel. [Col. 0875C] These words can be referred to Christ’s passion: just as they plotted his death by common counsel, so during the Paschal feast they were cut down by enemies. Again he says: “I instructed them and strengthened their arms; but they devised evil against me. They turned back so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow” (Hos. 7). And Malachi: “Your words have prevailed against me, says the Lord, and you have said: ‘What have we spoken against you?’” (Mal. 2). By these words he openly shows Christ’s passion, just as the Evangelist says of these same Jews: “Their voices prevailed as they unanimously said: ‘Away, away, crucify him’” (John 19). And David in the Psalms, in the person of Christ: “Do not deliver me to the souls of those who afflict me, because unjust witnesses rose up against me, and iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. 26). It is as though Christ said to God the Father: Do not deliver me to the souls of those who afflict me—not, I say, into their hands, but into their souls; that is, do not permit them to be filled with my evils, so that I consent to them, even if you deliver my flesh into their hands. Hence Job says: “The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the face of its judges” (Job 9).

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Gregory, *Morals*, Book IX, ch. 15.]

For what is expressed by the name “earth” but flesh? Who is meant by the designation “wicked” but the devil? The hands of this wicked one were those who raged in the death of our Redeemer. Thus the earth was given into the hand of the wicked, because the ancient enemy could not corrupt the Redeemer’s mind by tempting him directly, [Col. 0876A] but destroyed his flesh through his own servants; and, without knowing it, served the dispensation of heavenly mercy through this very permission. For though assaulting our Redeemer with three temptations, he could not violate the heart of God; but when he stirred up the minds of the Jews to the death of his flesh, and delivered him to the cohort, the chief priests, and the servants of the Pharisees, that wicked one indeed stretched his hands out against the earth. The judges of this earth were the priests and rulers, Pilate, and the soldiers who mocked him. Therefore this wicked one covered the face of its judges, because he veiled the hearts of the persecutors in a cloud of malice so that they might not recognize their maker. Hence Paul says: “To this day, when Moses is read, his veil is placed over [Col. 0876B] their heart” (2 Cor. 3). And again: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). The face of the judges was therefore covered because the minds of the persecutors did not recognize, even through miracles, that he whom they could hold in the flesh was God.

Therefore, on the day of his betrayal, let Jesus Christ say to God the Father: “Do not deliver me to the souls of those who afflict me,” and so forth. As though he said more plainly: Deliver, if you please, my flesh into the hands of those who afflict me, O most just Father; but do not deliver my soul into their hands. Let flesh devour flesh, earth earth; but let my soul be kept unharmed for you.
