And as though someone asked, “Why do you say this?” he answers: Behold why: “Because unjust witnesses have risen against me,” speaking falsely to me about me, so as to move me and turn me back from you, as though I sought glory from [Col. 0876C] human beings. But I would thus be delivered to their souls if I were false with them and pursued human glory. “And iniquity lied to itself,” not to me—that is, it delighted in its own lie, but did not move me; hence my glory is greater in heaven. Or “iniquity lied to itself,” that is, to its own ruin. For every sin returns upon its own author.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Isidore, ch. 27.]

That the Jews cried out to Pilate for the Son of God and man to be crucified, the same Lord had already foretold through Jeremiah concerning the Synagogue: “I have forsaken my house; my inheritance has become to me like a lion in the forest. It uttered its voice against me” (Jer. 12), namely, blaspheming and saying: “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23). Elsewhere he says: “Against whom [Col. 0876D] have you opened your mouth, and against whom have you let loose your tongues?” (Isa. 57). And Isaiah: “Jerusalem has fallen,” he says, “and Judah has collapsed, because their tongues are against the Lord” (Isa. 3). Their tongues were against their Lord when they cried to Pilate: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). And again: “Take this man away, and release Barabbas to us” (Luke 23). Therefore, because the tongues of the Jews were against the Lord, Jerusalem fell and Judah collapsed, and the Roman people devastated it from its foundations. Concerning that same most impious nation, through the same prophet, the Lord again complains: “I expected it to produce judgment, and behold iniquity; and justice, and behold a cry” (Isa. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Isidore, ch. 28.]

That the Jews, by crucifying Christ, condemned their offspring when they said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27), Isaiah had long before foretold with rebuke: “Most evil seed, prepare your children for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers” (Isa. 14). For when the Romans came to Jerusalem, the children were slaughtered in their fathers’ iniquities.

Because the Son of God was scourged and struck on the cheek in his passion, blessed Job says thus of him: “They struck my cheek; they were satisfied with my punishments” (Job 16). Gregory: “The cheeks of the Church are indeed the holy preachers, as it is said under the figure of Judah through [Col. 0877B] Jeremiah: ‘She wept, weeping in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks’ (Lam. 1). In the Church’s adversity, those grieve more deeply who had known how to break the life of carnal persons by preaching. Through them, indeed, holy Church crushes the wicked away from vices and, as it were swallowing, turns them into her own members. Hence it is said to the first preacher himself, as though to the Church’s cheek: ‘Kill and eat’ (Acts 10). This is also why Samson took the jawbone of an ass and slew his enemies: our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of his preachers, slew carnal persons in their vices. And the jawbone, thrown down on the ground, afterwards poured forth waters, because the bodies of preachers given to death displayed great miracles to the peoples. Therefore the perverse strike the cheek when they persecute the Church’s good [Col. 0877C] preachers. And because the reprobate then think they have done something great when they kill the lives of preachers, after the striking of the cheek it is fittingly added: ‘They were satisfied with my punishments.’ For he satisfies them with punishment who temporally chastises holy Church through them.”

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Here already Isidore, ch. 29, and the Gloss.]

In the Psalms also, the Son of God and man says of himself: “I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is always before me” (Ps. 37). As though he said: I am ready for scourges, which the Jews did not suppose, but they thought me forced into scourges. If they understood that my being scourged was an act of obedience—because “no one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down” (John 10)—they would not have spoken great things against me [Col. 0877D] (Ps. 54). I am therefore ready for scourges, so that I might suffer the things which they would have suffered had I not been willing to suffer for them. Otherwise: This is why I became like one mute and not hearing: because I am ready for scourges, that is, I voluntarily underwent death, not by compulsion. For I am ready for scourges; I am troubled; I suffer. But my enemies and those of my servants live—that is, flourish in this life—and therefore have been strengthened against me, that is, they have prevailed in the cause against me and mine, outwardly speaking. For in my passion the Jews prevailed against me, beating and killing me. Augustine: “‘Ready for scourges’: I was born for this very purpose, that I might bear scourges [Col. 0878A] for the sins of the people.” And again: “They rejoiced against me and gathered together; scourges were gathered against me, and I did not know” (Ps. 34). Augustine: Here Christ speaks, explaining how impiously the Jews acted against him. It is as though the same Redeemer of the human race said: I was sorrowful over their destruction, and they rejoiced against me. As though they are glad and I am sad. For while I grieve piously, the Jews rejoice impiously. They assembled in a council, and scourges were gathered against me, that is, they prepared tortures; and I did not know, according to their opinion. Otherwise: “They rejoiced against me and gathered together,” that is, they became united in this, not to follow after me but to be against me; and—what is worse—they did it not under compulsion or with any fear, but “rejoiced,” that is, did it gladly. And while they thus assembled, scourges were gathered against me. These were without any fault of mine, because I did not know not the punishment but the cause of punishment, since there was no fault in me. Or the scourges of the whole world were gathered upon me because throughout all lands I suffer in my members. Likewise the Lord himself says through Isaiah: “I am not rebellious and do not contradict. I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn away my face from those reproaching and spitting upon me” (Isa. 50). And through Jeremiah he says: “I set my shoulders to scourges and my cheeks to blows” (ibid., according to the Septuagint). Again Jeremiah says of him: “He shall give his cheek to one who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches” (Lam. 3).

[Col. 0878C]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Isidore, ch. 30.]

That the head of the Son of God and man was struck with a reed and that he endured it patiently, Isaiah had thus foretold: “He shall not break a bruised reed” (Isa. 42). Matthew the Evangelist also testifies to this, saying: “And stripping him, they put around him a scarlet cloak in place of the purple which kings wore; and, plaiting a crown of thorns in place of a diadem, they placed it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand in place of a scepter. And, kneeling before him, they mocked him, saying: ‘Hail, King of the Jews’” (Matt. 27). Kneeling, they worshiped him as king, not knowing that he was King of kings and Lord of lords, through whom kings reign (Prov. 8), and who grants to his soldiers not only earthly kingdoms but also heavenly ones. [Col. 0878D] It follows: “And spitting on him, they took the reed and struck his head.”

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Isidore, ch. 31.]

That a crown of thorns was placed upon the head of the Son of God and man is said in the Song of Songs, in the person of the Father announcing the Son’s insults and Jerusalem’s iniquity: “Go forth, daughters of Jerusalem, and see King Solomon” (Song 3), that is, Christ the peaceful king, “in the diadem”—that is, the crown—with which his mother crowned him: namely, the crown of thorns which the Synagogue placed upon his head. To all who mourned for him in his passion, the same Son of God and man says: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but [Col. 0879A] weep over yourselves and over your children” (Luke 23). He also says through Jeremiah: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of their sins.” Again Isaiah says: “I planted my chosen vineyard and expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes” (Isa. 5). Certainly, because it had degenerated from the fruit of the patriarchs, it brought to its maker not the fruit of righteousness but the thorns of death and the cross.

That the Son of God and man was to be clothed in a scarlet garment in his passion—and that the soldiers in mockery clothed Christ in scarlet—Isaiah foretold, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63). And again: “Why is your clothing red, and your garments like those of one treading in a winepress?” To this he replies: “I have trodden the winepress alone” (ibid.). He said that he had trodden the winepress alone because he alone endured the passion for the sin of the world. Alone, because he washed human sins in his blood. And Matthew the Evangelist: “Stripping him,” he says, “of the purple, they put around him a scarlet cloak” (Matt. 27).

That the Son of God and man was silent while he suffered is attested by the voices of the prophets. Isaiah says of him: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before one shearing him he shall be dumb, and thus he shall not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away,” etc. (Isa. 53). And again: “He did not cry out, nor shall anyone hear his voice in the streets” (Isa. 42). [Col. 0879C] The same Son of God and man also says through that prophet: “The Lord God opened my ear, but I do not contradict; I did not turn backward. I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them” (Isa. 50). Elsewhere he says: “I was silent and kept still; shall I always be silent?” (Isa. 42). For at first he was silent in order to be judged, when like a lamb before one shearing him he was without voice and did not open his mouth, restraining his power. But concerning the last time it is written thus: “God shall come openly; our God, and he shall not be silent” (Ps. 49). For he was silent in order to be judged when he came hidden; but he will by no means be silent when he comes openly to judge.

That he was suspended on the wood of the cross, Jeremiah, speaking in the person of the same Son of God and man, had said long before: “I was like a gentle lamb being led to sacrifice, and I did not know that they devised plans against me, saying: ‘Let us put wood into his bread and erase him from the land of the living’” (Jer. 11). The prophet sets forth as though done to himself those things which the Lord was to suffer from the Jews. For what is wood put into bread except the fastening of Christ’s flesh to the wood? We recognize his body as bread. Our faith recognizes the wood in his bread as the cross in his body, because the life of that body is bread. Hence Moses speaks typologically to the Jewish people: “And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear by day and by night, and you shall not believe your life” (Deut. 28). As though he said more plainly: Your life—that is, the Son of God—shall hang on the cross before your eyes. He is the true life of angels and all saints, in whom even you, though unworthy, live and move; and you will not believe him when he proclaims eternal salvation to you. “And you shall fear,” he says, “by day and by night,” namely on account of Christ crucified by you, lest you incur God’s wrath and lose kingdom, priesthood, place, and nation through Roman rulers.

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Again, Isidore.]

But David also says in the Psalms that the Son of God and man stretched out his hands on the cross: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140). Whether because he laid down his soul on the cross as the evening of the world approached, or because the sun was already declining toward evening, the Lord, raising his hands upon the wood of the cross, [Col. 0880B] offered himself to God the Father as a sacrifice for us, so that through that sacrifice—so great, of such a kind, and most pure—our sins, or rather those of the whole world, might be blotted out. Isaiah likewise writes of the preaching of his cross: “Authority shall be upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9), that is, the banner of his cross, which he bore upon his shoulders, in accordance with David’s prophecy: “The Lord reigned from the wood” (Ps. 95). Habakkuk also says of his cross, upon which he was lifted up and drew all things to himself: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. 3). What else is this but the trophy of the cross? The same prophet also says of his ascent upon the cross: “The Lord my strength shall set my feet in the consummation; he shall place me upon high places, that I may conquer in his glory” (ibid.). “His brightness,” he says, [Col. 0880C] “shall be as light; horns are in his hands.” Truly the Son of God shone forth like the sun of righteousness, because he illuminated the whole world with signs, miracles, and the teaching of the Gospel. Horns often stand for kings; but here they are understood not as kings but as the arms of Christ’s cross. For after Christ’s miracles increased, his hands were fixed upon the horns of the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Isidore, ch. 36, and the Gloss.]

That the hands and feet of the Son of God and man were fastened with nails upon the cross, he himself speaks through David, saying: “They dug my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21). Behold the Gospel narrative, for these things are read as having happened in the Gospel. Gentile soldiers dug my hands [Col. 0880D] and feet with nails. Cassiodorus: “Observe that he does not say ‘pierced’ or ‘wounded,’ but ‘dug’; for just as dug earth produces fruit, so Christ, wounded, gave the fruit of life.” It follows: “And they counted all my bones,” that is, they made them countable. Here the punishment of the cross is precisely described. Augustine: “The extension of the body upon the wood could not have been described better than by saying: ‘They counted all my bones.’” Cassiodorus: “Although these words are rightly taken literally, the digging of the hands nevertheless suggests that the Jews did not believe his works; the digging of the feet, that they harassed the apostles. So they also counted the bones, that is, the apostles: seeking to destroy them lest they grow to a greater [Col. 0881A] number, namely, so that they might be few and countable.”

Otherwise: “They dug my hands and my feet,” that is, they deceitfully planned to overthrow my works and my affections—that is, the miracles and my will to lay down and take up my soul. Hence this: “Lord, we have remembered that while still alive that deceiver said: ‘After three days I shall rise again.’ Therefore command that the tomb be guarded until the third day, lest perhaps his disciples come and steal him and say to the people, ‘He has risen from the dead’” (Matt. 27). And when they corrupted the guards with bribes, so that they might say: “His disciples came and stole him from us by night while we were asleep” (Matt. 28). “They counted all my bones,” as though he said: They sought my preachers so carefully to harm them, as though they knew their certain number. By these words he surely signified the body stretched on the cross, hands and feet fastened and pierced through by the nails; because the Jews, as has been said, did not believe his works, drove the apostles out of the province, and cruelly shed the blood of holy martyrs because of hatred of that very name. Finally, David is not said to have had either hands or feet dug through; we read that he rested in peace without any bodily injury. Therefore this was plainly said of Christ’s passion: he was fastened with nails to the wood by the Jews. Again in the Song of Songs: “My hands dripped myrrh” (Song 5). This was said especially because of the marks of the nails. Again the Son of God and the Virgin speaks through the prophet Malachi to those same Jews, who repaid him evil for good: “Will a man fasten God, because you have fastened me? And you have said: ‘In what have we fastened you?’ And the Lord said to them: ‘You have fastened me, the whole nation’” (Mal. 3). As though he said more plainly: I redeemed you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the power of all enemies, and gave you a land flowing with milk and honey; but you fastened me to the cross, though I raised your dead and healed the sick. “You have fastened me, the whole nation,” that is, all together. The Lord himself testifies to this through Zechariah: “They shall look upon me whom they fastened, and they shall mourn for him” (Zech. 12)—understand, for me—“with mourning as for an only-begotten son, and they shall grieve over him as is customary [Col. 0881D] at the death of a firstborn.” He speaks of himself as though of another. This mourning, therefore, will be then, when the Jews see Christ reigning in his glory; they will grieve for him whom they crucified and, understanding that he was God’s Only-Begotten, the firstborn of all creation.

Again the prophet continues, saying: “On that day,” that is, on the day of judgment, “there shall be great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo. And the land shall mourn,” that is, the sinners who said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27); “and the families shall mourn, each family separately,” that is, tribe by tribe, each distinct from the other. When? On the day of judgment, namely, when all titles of rank shall be laid aside, and what is written, “Behold the man” (John 19)—namely, the man and his works—shall be fulfilled; and the chaff shall have been separated from the wheat. Then there shall be great mourning, not in another place, but in Jerusalem. For punishment and judgment shall begin with the holy ones; and kings, priests, prophets, and teachers shall beat their breasts with their hands when they see him whom they crucified reigning in the majesty of his Father and of himself.

It follows: “The families of the house of Nathan shall mourn separately, and their women separately; the families of the house of David separately, and their women separately; the families of the house of Levi separately, and their women separately; the families of Shimei separately, and their women separately; all the remaining families, family by family, separately.” The fact that men and women mourn separately signifies that in a time of tribulation we ought not to devote ourselves to marriage and the work of weddings. Therefore now the tribe of the house of David and the other tribes are separated from their wives, that they may mourn the Lord Jesus, of whom they had said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). In David the royal tribe is understood; in Nathan the prophetic order is signified; in Levi, the priests; in Shimei, the teachers. For from this tribe the ranks of masters sprang forth. The remaining tribes are passed over, because they possess no special privilege of dignity.

That the Son of God and of the Virgin was crucified between two thieves for the salvation of the world was foretold long before in these words: “And he was counted among the wicked” (Isa. 53). And Habakkuk says: “O Lord, I have heard thy report, and was afraid,” etc. (Hab. 3). As though he said: Lord, I have heard thy report, that God has become man; and I was afraid, because it is exceedingly wonderful. It follows: “Lord, I considered thy works and was amazed.” Why? “Because thou shalt be known in the midst of two living creatures.”

As though he said: I heard thy word in the Scriptures with the inner ear, and I contemplated thy works, so that from created things I might understand the Creator; and through them I was amazed, having lost human understanding: I was turned to holy madness, or, troubled by wonder, burst forth into thy praises, saying: “Thou shalt be known in the midst of two living creatures,” that is, the Father is understood through the Son and the Holy Spirit; or through the two cherubim, which look toward one another and have the oracle between them; or through the two seraphim, one of which cries to the other the mystery of the Trinity, one of whom cleanses the prophet’s lips, saying: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will but that it should burn?” (Luke 12).

But, in the plain sense, Christ was recognized between two thieves; or between the Jews and Gentiles surrounding him on either side; or between the two Testaments, which breathe life. “In the midst of the years,” he says, “thou shalt make known thy work”; namely, when the time of fulfilment comes, thou shalt show the truth of what thou hast promised—namely this: that in the midst of two living creatures, that is, two thieves, thou shalt be recognized as hanging for human salvation. Hence a certain faithful and wise man, not only commemorating the names of these thieves but also deeply discerning the difference of their merits, and likewise keenly considering the divine omnipotence of the Son of God, who hung on the cross between them for the salvation of the whole world, says:

> Three bodies hang upon the branches, unequal in their merits:  
> Dismas and Gestas; in the middle, divine power.  
> Dismas seeks the heights; unhappy Gestas, the depths.

Appropriately indeed he said that they hung from branches and declared that they were unequal in merits, because, as a discerning man, he understood that each person’s works were different. But let us, with devout minds, add something concerning their works individually to the verses cited above, as the Holy Spirit may dictate. Let us therefore begin from the lowest point, so that we may fittingly be able to reach the highest, namely Christ, who with the Father is the supreme Good.

Thus unhappy Gestas, who hung at Christ’s left, persisted in his malice until death. He was greedy and cruel in the world, hateful and obstinate upon the gibbet. While he lived, he willingly seized what belonged to others; and hanging on the wood he was abusive. Having free use of himself, “his feet were swift to shed blood” (Ps. 13); and even fastened with nails, insults came forth from his mouth. He perpetrated whatever evils he could; and, at the point of death, he blasphemed Christ. Therefore, as was said above, after death this unhappy Gestas did not ascend to the heights, but, as a reprobate and blasphemer, sought the depths.

But Dismas, who hung at Christ’s right, inflamed by the fires of greed and avarice, did not seek his daily livelihood, as he ought, by the labor of his hands; but contrary to God’s command, who said, “Thou shalt not steal” (Exod. 20), he strove to covet, steal, and seize what belonged to others. This mother of all other evils led him—acting not under compulsion but voluntarily—to shed his brother’s blood. Defiled by it, he was seized by the people and suspended on a gibbet at Christ’s right.

Thus Dismas, suspended on the wood, was afflicted with nails; but, prevented—that is, anticipated—by divine grace, he was suddenly changed. Made a sheep from a wolf, he devoutly turned to God. Set upon the cross, he received from the Father of lights, from whom is every good gift and every perfect gift (Jas. 1), three virtues: faith, hope, and charity. He had faith, because he believed Christ, whom he saw dying with him, to be true God, when he said: “Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom” (Luke 23). Without doubt he had firm faith, for he saw Christ dying and did not doubt that he would reign after death. Dismas confessed Christ while hanging on the wood, when the apostles did not dare to draw nearer for fear of the Jews. Dismas had never seen Christ working miracles, and yet, though the disciples had withdrawn, he believed him to be true God and man.

Moreover, Dismas possessed certain hope, since he entreated Christ to deign to remember him, saying: “Remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” He also truly possessed charity, because he rebuked his fellow thief for wickedness and proclaimed the Christ whom he had recognized, saying: “Dost thou not fear God, seeing that thou art in the same condemnation? And we indeed receive the due reward of our deeds; but this man hath done nothing evil.” He also had humility, because he acknowledged himself guilty and judged that he suffered what he deserved, saying: “We receive the due reward of our deeds,” etc.

Therefore Dismas, because, divine grace having gone before, he humbly declared himself guilty; because he not only recognized the Redeemer of all but also proclaimed his innocence; because he rebuked his brother and fellow thief for blasphemy; and because he humbly prayed to Christ that he might deserve to enter the threshold of the heavenly kingdom—sought not the depths but the heights, as has already been said. And therefore he at once deserved to hear from Christ: “Amen I say to thee, today thou shalt be with me in paradise.”

What, then, shall we say of the Son of God and of the Virgin, who was crucified between these thieves for the salvation of humankind? Though consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father, yet by the Father’s will he mercifully assumed our humanity. In it he endured scourging, ascended the cross, tasted and destroyed death; leaving his body in the tomb, he descended in soul to hell. Having despoiled it and conquered the devil, on the third day he rose victoriously from the dead, confirmed the disciples in faith, and on the fortieth day ascended into heaven while those same disciples watched. The very flesh which he had assumed from his inviolate Virgin Mother he placed with himself at the Father’s right hand.

Because, therefore, obedient to God the Father, he humbled himself even unto death (Phil. 2), the Father crowned him with glory and honor and exalted him in his glory above all the works of his hands. To this Jesus Christ, the supreme priest, the Father gave all power in heaven and on earth (Matt. 28), according to the assumption of manhood; power which he possessed eternally with God the Father according to the substance of divinity. Therefore let it be said:

> Three bodies hang upon the branches, unequal in their merits.

How beautifully and how truly he said that they were unequal in merits! For as far as heaven is from earth, and east from west, so far their merits are distant from one another. Unhappy and blasphemous Gestas, according to his malice and obstinacy, was plunged into hell. But Dismas, humbly acknowledging himself guilty and praising divine justice, entered paradise with Christ as his guide. God and man, after victory, was exalted above the heavens of heavens and made supreme priest forever.

[Col. 0884D] That Christ’s garments were allotted by lot after the sentence of the cross, the Lord himself testifies through the Psalmist, saying: “They considered and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and upon my vesture they cast lots” (Ps. 21). Jesus Christ speaks these things in his own person. Hence blessed Augustine, the outstanding teacher, says: “Those Jews, unchanged from their malice, considered what was taking place, but did not understand; and they merely looked upon me. With bodily eyes they saw as far as the flesh, and with the eyes of the heart as far as the Word.”

Cassiodorus: Or, “they considered and looked upon me,” that is, they looked attentively and with pleasure upon me as I bore such things, though people normally turn their eyes away from a cruel spectacle. Behold how obstinate the Jews were. Nothing happened by chance, nor was their heart softened by so many miracles. “And they divided my garments among themselves.” Literally, into four parts, as John the Evangelist says. “And upon my vesture they cast lots.” This was seamless, woven throughout from above.

These things may also be understood mystically. By Christ’s garments are understood the Scriptures or the sacraments of the Church. By the seamless tunic, over which lots were cast, is understood charity, or the unity of the Church. By those who divided the garments are understood corrupters of the Scriptures. Cassiodorus: Therefore, just as those men actually divided Christ’s garments, so those who do not strive for unity have divided the garments for themselves—that is, the spiritual sacraments—and have corrupted the Holy Scriptures.

Augustine: Christ’s sacraments and Scriptures can be divided through heresies, but not the tunic woven from above, that is, by God: this is charity and the unity of the Catholic Church, which no one can divide. For ecclesiastical charity is not torn apart; rather, through the lot and gift of God it comes to certain persons. Augustine: Whoever possesses this ecclesiastical charity is secure, and no one moves him from the Catholic Church. Even if he begins to possess it outside, he is admitted, as the olive branch was brought by the dove to the ark. Rightly, therefore, it is said in Christ’s person through the Prophet: “They divided my garments among themselves, and upon my vesture they cast lots.”

[Note: [Col. 0885D] Isidore, Book I against the Jews, ch. 38.] The Gospel narrative relates how this prophecy was fulfilled. For when the other garments had been divided by the soldiers, they said concerning the Lord’s tunic: “Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it, whose it shall be.” It was woven throughout in every part (John 19).

[Col. 0885C] That they gave him vinegar mixed with gall while he hung on the cross had already been foretold in the Psalms by the same Son of God and of the Virgin: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68). Cassiodorus: This is the completion of the Passion. For when he said, “I thirst” (John 19), they offered him gall with vinegar, thereby displaying their own most bitter dispositions.

Or it may be understood of the disciples and women, who, although they were grieved, were not grieved together, but in the same manner; and this is: “There was none to grieve together with me” (Ps. 68). Augustine: For the disciples and the women who wept over him were grieved, but not together. They grieved carnally over the mortal life which was to be transformed by death, whereas they ought to have grieved piously for the blind Jews who were killing the physician; and no one then did this. It follows: “And I found none to comfort me,” namely, by advancing spiritually. Since I found none both grieving with me and steadfast, this was gall to me—that is, bitter because of sorrow—and vinegar—that is, sour because of their oldness. And this is: “They gave me bitter gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink.”

Literally, the Gospel says that gall was offered him, but as a drink, not as food. Augustine: This is said mystically. It is therefore fitting that he did not say, “They gave gall for food,” but “They gave gall for my food,” because the Lord had already received food when he ate the Passover with the disciples, where he showed the sacrament of his body. This is sweet food, pleasant food, the food of Christ’s unity, which the Apostle commends when he says: “We, though many, are one bread and one body in Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Into this food, therefore—that is, upon the pleasant food which is the food of Christ’s unity—they cast gall, that is, bitterness, by resisting truth and contradicting the Gospel. This the despiser of him who sits in heaven still does today, and sins more grievously than the man who crucified him while he walked on earth. As the Jews then did, so they also today give him a bitter drink when, by drinking wickedly, they bring scandal upon the Church and become embittered heretics. The Lord tasted it, teaching us to taste—that is, endure—such persons, but he did not drink, because such persons cannot be received into his body.

Thus this is mystically foretold, just as it was mystically done in the Passion. “And in my thirst,” in which I desired their faith, “they gave me vinegar to drink,” that is, old sourness, because I found nothing in them but oldness.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] Isidore, as above, ch. 39.] Thus he also elsewhere cries out to Jerusalem, saying: “I planted thee, my chosen vineyard; how hast thou turned into the bitterness of an alien vine?” (Jer. 2). For God planted a good vineyard, that is, the Jewish people; but it, corrupted by its own fault, gave its Creator bitterness to drink. Hence Moses says: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter” (Deut. 32). And above, rebuking them, he says: “Thus, foolish and unwise people, hast thou rendered this to the Lord?” As though he said more plainly: Perverse and crooked generation, is this what you render to the Lord, foolish and senseless people? (ibid.)

[Note: [Col. 0885D] Isidore, ch. 40.] That they fastened a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop had already been foretold in the Psalms: “Thou shalt sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). Hence in the Law, those who wished to be cleansed were sprinkled with the blood of the lamb by means of a bundle of hyssop (Exod. 12). By this it was signified that through the Lord’s Passion the sins of the world are washed away.

[Note: [Col. 0885D] Isidore, ch. 41.] That the inscription of Christ’s cross was not altered—concerning which inscription the Jews said to Pilate: “Do not write, King of the Jews”; and Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19)—had already been prophesied in the fiftieth Psalm thus: “Do not corrupt the writing of the inscription” (Ps. 56, in the title).

[Note: Another reading after the word *fuerat* (“had been prophesied”) says: “For this reason the fifty-eighth Psalm, which speaks of the Lord’s Passion, and the two preceding Psalms are entitled ‘Do not corrupt,’ etc.” But the highly learned Juan de Mariana rightly observes on this chapter of Isidore that these words occur in only one Spanish Psalter, namely that which the old edition of the Mozarabic Breviary gives in the title of Psalm 56, as we note here in the margin; they occur by no means in the titles of Psalms 50, 57, and 58, as the manuscripts of our Martin allege.]

Therefore David warned the faithless Jewish people, or Pilate, not to corrupt Christ’s title, though he foresaw in the Spirit that Christ would suffer for the salvation of the world, and had openly said much above concerning him. Pilate is thus urged by the Jews to erase the inscription of truth; but the divine dispensation, which had ordered it to be written thus, prevailed more strongly. Therefore Pontius Pilate, although a Gentile, was divinely warned not to erase the written title, which declared him King of all; because what had been confirmed by divine command could not be rendered void.

Who could abolish the title of that King, our Lord Jesus Christ, whom it is certain is the Creator of heaven and earth? It is repeated frequently in order that excuse may be taken away from those who contradict it. The Jews say to Pilate: “Do not write, King of the Jews, but that he himself said, ‘I am King of the Jews.’” But he said: “What I have written, I have written.” Repetition is confirmation.

That the Son of God and of the Virgin, hanging upon the cross, prayed to the Father for his enemies, Isaiah foretold: “He bore the sins of many, and prayed for transgressors” (Isa. 53). And the Psalm says: “In return for my love, they slandered me; but I prayed” (Ps. 108). As though Christ said more plainly: In return for my love—that is, because they ought to have loved me—they slandered me, denying that I was the Son of God and saying: “By Beelzebub I cast out demons” (Matt. 9).

Or, according to another reading: “In return for my love, they killed me and slandered me.” For they killed him because they slandered him. Those who slander Christ in his members, killing the souls of believers, do more harm than those who killed his flesh, which was soon to rise again. And the sense is: They rendered evil for good; worse still, they slandered him; but I, on the contrary, prayed for them—not only for the faith of the disciples.

Again Habakkuk, after saying, “Thou shalt be known in the midst of two living creatures,” added: “When my soul shall have been troubled, O Lord, in wrath thou wilt remember mercy” (Hab. 3).

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Isidore, ch. 42.] For under this statement the prophet prefigured in himself the person of the Jews, who, stirred by wrath, crucified Christ. Yet the Son of God, set upon the cross by them, remembered mercy and said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23).

That the Lord was crucified not for his own sins but for ours, Isaiah the prophet declares, saying: “For the iniquities of his people he was led to death” (Isa. 53). And again: “He will give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death” (ibid.). And again: “He was wounded for our iniquities and bruised for our crimes, and by his bruise we have been healed” (ibid.). Again he says: “All we like sheep have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way; the Lord has placed upon him the iniquities of us all” (ibid.), in accordance with the Apostle, who says: “Though he knew no sin, he was made sin for us” (2 Cor. 5).

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Isidore, ch. 44.] That the Son of God and of the Virgin died after the scourges and cross, and after drinking gall and vinegar, the Law itself did not pass over in Genesis, saying: “Reclining, he lay down,” that is, slept, “as a lion and as a lion’s cub; and who raised him up?” (Gen. 49). Jacob the patriarch also prophesied concerning him when blessing his son Judah, saying: “Thy hand shall be upon the necks of thine enemies” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VII, ch. 7.] Judah is interpreted “confession,” because when Leah bore him, she gave praise to the Lord, saying: “Now for this I shall confess the Lord” (Gen. 29); and for this reason he was called Judah. His name is therefore derived from confession, which is thanksgiving.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] Id., *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31.] Through this Judah, therefore, Christ the true confessor is represented, who according to the flesh arose from his tribe. Rightly, then, it is said concerning Christ: “Thy hand shall be upon the necks of thine enemies,” because with those same hands and by the same trophy of the cross he both sheltered his own and bent down his enemies, according to the Father’s promise to him: “Sit thou at my right hand until I make thine enemies the footstool of thy feet” (Ps. 109).

The lion’s cub is the Son of God and of the Virgin, because in being born he became little. Hence it is said: “A little one has been born to us” (Isa. 9). Again he continues, saying: “Thou hast gone up for prey, my son,” that is, thou hast gone up upon the cross for the salvation of the world, and through it hast redeemed captive peoples; and those whom that opposing lion, namely the malignant enemy, had seized, thou hast rescued by dying. “Resting,” he says, “thou hast lain down as a lion.” It is evident that Christ lay down in his Passion when, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit; or when in the tomb he rested securely, as it were in a bodily sleep.

But why “as a lion,” and “as a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion, because he fulfilled this not by necessity but by power. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I have power to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me; but I lay it down and take it again” (John 10). But the addition, “and as a lion’s cub,” is because he died in the same nature in which he was born.

The Greek word *leōn* is interpreted in Latin as “king,” because it is the chief of all beasts. Its species, as Isidore, the teacher of the Spaniards, says, is threefold.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] *Etymologies*, Book XII, ch. 2.] Of these, the short lions with curly manes are timid; but the long ones with straight manes are fierce. Their spirit is indicated by their brow and tail. Their strength is in their breast, their firmness in their head.

[Note: [Col. 0887D] I have corrected this passage from the printed editions, for in the manuscripts it was strangely corrupted, namely: “But long, and with a straight mane, fierce spirits; their brow and their tail indicate their strength. In their head and breast is firmness.” If we corrected it thus: “Long . . . and with a straight mane, of fierce spirit; their brow . . . indicates their strength; in their head,” etc., we should extract a complete sense; but we preferred to restore the passage to the sense of Isidore rather than emend at will.]

Surrounded by hunters, they look at the ground, lest they be frightened at the sight of hunting spears. They fear the noise of wheels, but fire still more. When they sleep, their eyes remain awake; when they walk, they cover their tracks with their tails, lest the hunter find them. When a lioness has borne a cub, the cub is said to sleep for three days and three nights; then at last, as though the place of its den were shaken by its father’s growl or roar, the sleeping cub is said to be raised. Lions have such a nature toward humans that, unless injured, they cannot become angry. Their mercy toward humans is clear from frequent examples: they spare those who have fallen, allow captives whom they meet to return home, and kill a human only in great hunger.

These things, therefore, are very fittingly applied to Christ’s death of the Passion and life of the Resurrection. For he lay three days and three nights in the bed of the tomb, fulfilling the sleep of death. Rightly, therefore, Christ rested as a lion: he not only did not fear death’s bitterness, but even in death itself conquered death’s dominion. Again, rightly, he was as a lion’s cub, because he rose on the third day. Therefore this is added concerning his resurrection: “Who shall raise him up?” That is, no human being, but he himself, according to what he said of his own body: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

[Note: [Col. 0889D] Again from the book *Against the Jews*, cited above.] The sixty-seventh Psalm also proclaims this same death, saying: “Our God is the God of saving; and of the Lord, the Lord, are the issues of death” (Ps. 67). What could be said more plainly? For the Lord Jesus, whose name means Savior, our God, will save us. Because it was necessary that he should be born and depart this life through death, the following was added: “The Lord’s death, and the Lord’s departure” (Isa. 53).

[Note: [Col. 0889D] Isidore said this correctly, since he had read the passage above in this form. But Martin, who followed the Vulgate version, translated this exposition less correctly. Juan de Mariana is mistaken here in believing that Isidore did not read “the Lord’s death, and the Lord’s departure,” but perhaps “the departure of the Lord God from death.” For, apart from the fact that in this chapter he gives twice the reading which the annotator confused by adding the word *mortis* (“of death”) from the Tarragona manuscript, the same words occur in the exceptional Psalter printed in the most recent edition of the Gothic Breviary.]

Again Isaiah: “He shall be led as a sheep to the slaughter; and as a lamb before the one who shears it, without a voice he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth. For the sins of his people he was led to death” (ibid.).

[Note: The word “he shall be silent” is lacking in the printed edition, while it remains here.]

But the Jews expect that the Christ for whom they hope will not die; and therefore this prophecy pertains to Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, who truly redeemed us by his own blood.

Again, in Jeremiah he says concerning himself: “I have filled the weary soul with drink, and satisfied every hungry soul; and therefore I was raised as though from sleep; and I saw, and my sleep was sweet to me” (Jer. 31). Truly Christ’s sleep, that is, the death which he endured for the salvation of humankind, was sweet to him. Through it he reconciled the whole world to God the Father, shattered the powers of the devil, despoiled hell, and, rising again, bore its spoils with him into heaven in great glory.

To Daniel also the angel says thus concerning Christ’s slaying and death: “Daniel, attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks have been shortened upon thy people and upon thy holy city, that transgression may be brought to completion, sin receive an end, iniquity be blotted out, everlasting justice be brought in, and vision and prophecy be sealed” (Dan. 9). Therefore, if we wish to count these seventy weeks from Daniel’s time, we prove with complete certainty that they were completed before Christ was born according to the flesh.

Since, therefore, the seventy weeks were completed before Christ’s birth, eternal justice, as the angel says, was manifested; and the Holy of holies, that is, Christ, was anointed; vision and prophecy were sealed; and sins were forgiven, through faith in Christ’s name, to all who rightly believe in him. What does it mean that vision and prophecy are sealed, except that all the prophets announced concerning Christ that he would come and redeem humankind? Since prophecy was fulfilled through his coming, the angel said that vision and prophecy were to be sealed, because he is the seal of the prophets, fulfilling all that they had formerly foretold concerning him. After his coming and Passion, we no longer need vision and prophecy announcing that Christ will come.

As though the angel spoke more plainly to Daniel: Daniel, know that from this day on, when I now speak to thee, these things will happen to thy people in stages. First, God, whom thou art now earnestly beseeching, will be reconciled to thee; sin will be blotted out, and transgression will receive an end. Now, therefore, the city having been destroyed and the temple destroyed to its foundations, the people are in mourning; but it shall be rebuilt after no long time. After these seventy weeks of years Christ shall be born, who is everlasting justice; vision and prophecy shall be sealed, so that a prophet shall no longer be found in Israel; and the Holy of holies shall be anointed, namely the Son of God and of the Virgin, concerning whom the Psalter reads: “Therefore God, thy God, hath anointed thee with the oil of gladness above thy companions” (Ps. 44). And elsewhere he says concerning himself: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 11).

And after these things Christ himself shall be slain, and he shall not have a people, because they will deny him. Then the Roman people, under their leader Vespasian, shall again destroy the city of Jerusalem, deprived of God’s help, and also the sanctuary; sacrifice and offering shall utterly fail, and desolation shall endure until the end of the world. Because they delivered the Son of God and of the Virgin to death without cause, they consequently lost city, sanctuary, and sacrifice without restoration.

Wretched and unhappy Jews preferred to hand over to death their Savior—who had delivered their fathers from Egyptian bondage, fed them in the desert with heavenly bread, and by wondrous power given them drink from water drawn out of the hardest rock—rather than faithfully believe in him; and therefore their desolation endures without recovery. By the just judgment of God, indeed, they who rendered evil for good to their Creator are handed over as slaves to all nations under heaven. Again, in Solomon it is thus written concerning his death, insults, and torments: “Let us question him, that we may know his reverence; and let us test his patience; let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. 2).

### On the darkening of the sun in the Passion of the Son of God and of the Virgin

[Note: [Col. 0891D] Isidore, ch. 45.]

That at the Lord’s Passion darkness came over the whole earth from the sixth hour until the ninth, and the sun itself was darkened, the prophet Amos shows, saying: “It shall come to pass on that day, saith the Lord: I shall make the sun set for you at noon, and I shall darken the earth in the day of light” (Amos 8). On that day, that is, on the day of Christ’s Passion, the sun set for the unbelieving Jews, because they preferred to kill the Son of God, who is the true Sun of justice, rather than be enlightened by him through faith. Of him it is said: “For you who fear God, the Sun of justice shall arise” (Mal. 4).

For the sun set for them at noon because, when they could have been illuminated by the rays of that true light, they handed themselves over to eternal darkness. But when he says, “At noon the sun shall set for you,” it is as though he said: While they still had time to repent and do good works, darkened by the hardness of most wicked obstinacy, they lost the light of the true sun, namely the face of God. Hence the faithful say: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us,” etc. (Ps. 4).

“I shall darken the earth,” he says, “in the day of light.” By darkness sinners are signified, but by day the faithful. Thus, in the day of light—that is, in Christ, who is the true day and true light—when he illumined the hearts of those believing in him by the rays of faith and his love, he permitted the reprobate, obstinate against him, to be blinded by the darkness of unbelief.

[Col. 0891C] The prophet Amos foresaw that the day of Christ’s exaltation on the cross would be darkened, when he exhorted that same utterly impious and unbelieving people faithfully to seek Christ, saying: “Seek the Lord and live”: I mean the Lord “who makes Arcturus,” that is, Boötes, “and Orion, and turns darkness into morning and changes day into night; who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name” (Amos 5).

By Arcturus, which consists of seven stars, is signified the Church redeemed by Christ’s blood, filled with the sevenfold Spirit, and enriched with heavenly gifts through the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension into heaven of that same Son of God and of the Virgin. But by Orion, which rises in winter and by its rising stirs up storms, are signified the imitators of Christ’s Passion, namely the apostles and holy martyrs, who preach to unbelievers in a time of unbelief and stir up against themselves the storms of persecution.

In speaking of Arcturus and Orion, the prophet preferred to call them by names invented by the Gentiles rather than by Hebrew names, lest they should seem barbarous to us; in this he indicates that this prophecy is also to be read by Gentiles.

It follows: “And turning darkness into morning, and changing day into night.” Truly the Son of God ought to be loved by human beings with all devotion and sought with a pure mind. Through him God the Father changes the darkness of ignorance or tribulation into the clear light and prosperity of his chosen ones; and he changes the day of temporal happiness into the night of everlasting condemnation for the ungodly. The Jews, by crucifying Christ, who were thought to be day, are changed into the night of sins. From the sixth hour onward, as a figure of Jewish blindness, day was turned into night while they crucified Christ (Matt. 27). The light also which shone in the Law and the Prophets was changed for them into darkness. Of them it is written: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their backs forever” (Ps. 68). Wickedness darkened the Jews’ eyes, and God bent their backs when he handed them over to the slavery of all nations.

[Col. 0892B] It follows: “Who calls the waters of the sea and pours them out upon the face of the earth: the Lord is his name.” The Son of God suspends bitter waters by heavenly heat and, transformed into the sweet flavor of rain, spreads them abroad for the watering of the earth, when, taking disciples from their carnal way of life and instructing them spiritually, he sends them like clouds, with the rain of heavenly teaching, to water human hearts that are carnal.

The bitter waters are sinners, whom he pours out so that, changed into sweetness, they may preach to others, while whatever earthliness and bitterness was in them is burned away by the heat of the true sun. “The Lord is his name,” he says. The Son of God and man is indeed Lord and is called Lord, before whom every knee bends—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2).

And Jeremiah says: “She who bears children is exhausted,” namely Jerusalem, “and her soul is afflicted. Her sun has set while the day was still at noon; she is confounded and accursed; I shall give her remnant to the sword” (Jer. 15). This happened through Vespasian and Titus.

### That the legs of the Son of God and man were not broken on the cross  
[Note: [Col. 0891D] Isidore, ch. 46.]

Moreover, that they did not break his legs, but only those of the robbers (John 19), had already been foretold in the Law. “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12). For they had been commanded to celebrate the Passover in the likeness of [Note: [Col. 0892D] Supplement: a sheep.] a sheep, in which the shadow of the Lord’s Passion had gone before: he who “was led as a sheep to the slaughter” (Isa. 53). That figure of the lamb signified Christ’s Passion.

### That the side of the Son of God and of the Virgin was struck with a spear on the cross

That his side was struck by a spear (John 19) was thus foretold by Job speaking of him: “He has broken me and set me up as a target; he has surrounded me with his spears; he has wounded my loins. Heaped wound upon wound”—that is, the wounds of the nails upon the wound of the spear (Job 16). Hence David says: “They added to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. 68).

It is as though he said: Upon the pain of my mortality they added the pain of my wounds, because they hastened my death. Or: They added to the pain of my wounds—that is, to the blows of the spear [Col. 0893A] and the nails they added wounds; or, they added to my death, because they bribed the guards to deny that I had risen. Or: They added to the pain of my wounds my pain, understand, because it was not enough for them to kill my servants sent to the vineyard unless they also killed me, the heir (Matt. 21). Or: They added to the pain of my wounds, because, after killing me, they raged against the apostles and my other members, killing them.

Hence he himself also speaks through Jeremiah concerning God the Father: “He stretched out his bow and made me a target for the arrow” (Lam. 3). And again: “He sent into my loins the daughters of his quiver.” Again, concerning those unbelieving Jews, he says through the prophet: “They became to me a returning arrow.” And Zechariah says: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12), namely, the man whom they crucified. By this testimony Christ was also promised as one who would come in the flesh in which he was crucified.

[Note: [Col. 0893D] Isidore, ch. 48.] That blood and water flowed from the side of the Son of God and of the Virgin as he hung on the cross had thus been foretold by the prophet Zechariah. Addressing that same Jesus Christ, whom he knew in the Spirit would be born and would suffer for human salvation, he said: “You also, in the blood of your covenant, have sent forth your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water” (Zech. 9).

It is as though he said: O Christ, Son of the living God, by the blood of your covenant—that is, of your Passion—you mercifully freed those who were held bound in the prisons of hell, where there is no refreshing mercy, which the rich man sought but was not worthy to find (Luke [Col. 0893C] 16). At Christ’s resurrection, the righteous, who had been held bound in hell because of Adam’s sin, rose and appeared to many in Jerusalem (Matt. 27).

In the figure of this pit, Joseph was sent by his brothers into a pit—that is, a cistern—in which there was no water (Gen. 37); Daniel by the Chaldeans (Dan. 6); Jeremiah by the Jews (Jer. 38); and Benaiah also, in a time of snow and cold, descended into a pit in order to kill a lion there (1 Chron. 11). So Christ descended from heaven into this world, and from the cross into hell, in order to seize the roaring lion seeking to devour humankind, strip away his weapons, break his strength, and hand him over to eternal fire.

And again: “When the man went out from the east, behold, waters overflowing from the right side,” namely, of Christ (Ezek. 47). Likewise, another prophet spoke thus of the same water which flowed from his side: “Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7): namely, the waters of baptism, which give life to believers and are bestowed upon those who thirst, when that which is written is fulfilled: “Wash yourselves; be clean,” etc. (Isa. 1). And the Psalmist says: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50).

### On the burial of Christ’s body  
[Note: [Col. 0893D] Isidore, ch. 46.]

That Christ’s body was buried, he himself says thus of himself in the Psalms: “He placed me in darkness, as those dead from of old,” etc. (Ps. 142). It is plainly evident that the Jews [Col. 0894A] placed Christ in darkness—that is, in the tomb—like those dead from of old, and assigned guards lest the disciples should steal him.

Likewise Isaiah says: “The Lord shall be called an everlasting sign, which shall not be removed” (Isa. 55); and “his sepulchre shall be glorious” (Isa. 11). Elsewhere: “He shall give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death” (Isa. 53).

[Note: [Col. 0894D] Isidore, ch. 50.] That, after the Son of God and of the Virgin was buried, a stone was placed at the door of his tomb. Hence he says through Jeremiah: “My life has fallen into the pit” (Lam. 3). And again: “They placed a stone against me” (ibid.). Again he says: “He shut up my ways with squared stones; he built around me, so that I might not go out” (ibid.).

### On the descent of the Son of God and of the Virgin, in his soul, into hell

[Col. 0894B] That he descended into hell, the same Lord says thus in Ecclesiasticus: “I shall penetrate all the lower parts of the earth; I shall behold all who sleep, and I shall enlighten those who hope in God” (Ecclus. 24). Likewise, in the Psalms: “My life drew near to hell” (Ps. 87). And again: “I was reckoned among those descending into the pit; I became as a man without help, free among the dead” (ibid.). For he descended into hell as a man; but he alone was free among the dead, because death could not hold him.

### That the Son of God and of the Virgin mercifully freed from hell those whom the devil had unjustly taken captive

Likewise, because, descending into hell, he rescued those captured by the devil and thus returned again to the heavenly realm, he himself declares through Hosea: “I, I shall take hold, and there is none to rescue. I shall go and return to my place,” that is, to my heavenly throne (Hos. 5). And below: “From the hand,” he says, [Col. 0894C] “of death I shall free them” (Hos. 13).

It is as though he said more plainly: From the hand of death—that is, from the work of sin which draws one to death—I shall free them. Hence it is said: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18). Or the hand of death is the devil’s power. It follows: “And from death I shall redeem them” (Hos. 13). It is as though he said: From the hand of hell I shall redeem them with the price of my blood.

Christ speaks to those whom he deigned to free by his grace: namely, Jews and Gentiles who believe in him, or even heretics who come to their senses. Therefore it is added: “I shall be your death, O death”; that is, by dying I shall destroy you. “I shall be your bite, [Col. 0894D] O hell” (ibid.), by bringing forth my elect while leaving the reprobate in you. Or death and hell are the devil, whom Christ bit so that he should lose his power, not so that he should utterly cease to exist.

Because of the crimes of the Jews and their insults against Christ, the prophet Isaiah, foreseeing that Jerusalem would be laid waste by the Gentiles, said: “Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their devices are against the Lord” (Isa. 3). It is as though he said: The city of Jerusalem itself has fallen without God’s help; and Judah—that is, the province of Judah—has collapsed, because their tongue and their devices were against the meek Lord, provoking [Col. 0895A] the eyes of his majesty—that is, the look of his mercy—to anger.

Certainly their tongue was against the Lord when they unanimously cried to Pilate: “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23); “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). Thus they also fell without God’s help, and there was no one to help them, because their devices rose against the Lord when, blaspheming, they said: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John 8).

For this reason the Lord threatens the same faithless Jews through the prophet Amos, saying: “I shall turn your feasts into mourning and all your songs into lamentation” (Amos 8). These words aptly apply to the time of Christ’s Passion, when, at the sixth hour, the sun, [Col. 0895B] unable to endure the sight of the Lord dying upon the cross, withdrew its rays; when, the Jews’ hearts being blinded, the true sun set in the day of light, and, when the Romans came, their feasts and songs were changed into mourning.

From that day, certainly, all things were filled with tears, penitence, and sackcloth; and they were made bald because they do not possess Christ, who is the covering of all the elect. Then the people of Israel, formerly God’s firstborn (Exod. 4), was handed over to everlasting mourning. The men of Keilah, ungrateful for David’s benefits, whom he delivered from the hands of the Philistines (1 Sam. 23), signify the Jews’ unbelief and instability, for they ungratefully plot against their Redeemer before the powers of this world.

[Col. 0895C] [Note: [Col. 0895D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31. See vol. I, p. 256.] The patriarch Jacob also, already foreseeing in the Spirit that the Son of God would suffer for the salvation of the whole world, when blessing Simeon and Levi among his other sons, said: “Simeon and Levi, instruments of the iniquity of warriors” (Gen. 49).

[Note: [Col. 0895D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 31. See vol. I, p. 256.] By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes and priests of the Jewish people. From Simeon came the Jewish scribes; from the tribe of Levi came the leaders of the priests, of whom it is written: “They took counsel to deliver Jesus to death” (Matt. 27). Concerning this counsel, the patriarch, who already beheld God in his mind, says: “Let not my soul enter into their counsel,” etc. (Gen. 49). For even at that time this holy patriarch shuddered to see such great crimes as the Jews would commit in the last times.

[Col. 0895D] It follows: “For in their fury they killed a man,” namely Christ. Hence [Note: [Col. 0895D] It was customary for Isidore to make one passage out of two and to attribute to one source alone what belongs to both, as John de Mariana often observed in books of the Blessed Father against the Jews, and as other annotators ought to have noticed in his remaining works. For, if García de Loaysa alone is excepted, the others seem to have neglected this task of great importance. [Col. 0896D] In this place the holy bishop gives the words of Isaiah, ch. 3, v. 9, “Woe to their soul,” and the words of Wisdom, ch. 2, vv. 1 and 12, “because they devised,” etc.; nevertheless he attributes both passages to Isaiah. Blessed Martin translates him here too tersely, as we have often said, although in vol. I, p. 257, he cited this passage somewhat differently.] Isaiah says: “Woe to their soul, because they devised an unjust counsel against themselves, saying: Let us seize the just man, for he is useless to us!”

Again Jacob adds concerning them: “In their pain”—namely, Simeon’s and Levi’s—“they undermined a wall.” This truly happened when [Col. 0896A] the priests and scribes, descended from their stock, pierced with a spear that spiritual and most strong bulwark which guards Israel, namely Christ. Again he says: “Cursed be their fury, because it is stubborn.” Certainly the Jews were stubborn, who perpetrated so great a crime against their Lord, the Son of God. They persisted stubbornly when, inflamed with fury and wrath, they presented Christ to Pontius Pilate, saying: “Crucify, crucify him; for if you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend” (John 19).

He adds also: “And cursed be their indignation, because it is harsh,” while they asked for Barabbas the robber and crucified the Prince of Life, that is, Christ. It follows: “I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel.” These two terms, division [Col. 0896B] and scattering, are used because some of them believed in the Lord while others remained in unbelief. Those who are separated from the Jews and come to faith are called a division; but those who, their temple having been overthrown, are scattered from their native land—the unbelieving people being dispersed throughout the world—[Note: [Col. 0896D] Supplement: scattering.] are, by God’s just judgment, scattered through the whole world because they refuse to believe in one God in three Persons.

The prophet Isaiah likewise foresaw that the same city Jerusalem would be devastated, and that its utterly impious people would long ago be scattered, when he said: “I shall sing to my beloved a song of my cousin concerning his vineyard” (Isa. 5). A song is sometimes made in joy, but sometimes in sorrow, as was this one, composed by him [Col. 0896C] who, seeing the city, wept and said: “If you too had known” (Luke 19).

Let the prophet Isaiah therefore say: “I shall sing to my beloved”—that is, to God the Father—“a song,” namely a mournful poem, “of my cousin,” that is, Christ, born from the same people as I; this song he composed concerning his vineyard. A *patruelis* is the son of one’s paternal uncle. It follows: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.”

Everything said concerning the vineyard may be referred to the condition of the soul. Planted by God, it brought forth not grapes but wild grapes, and was handed over to beasts to be trampled. Nor does it receive the rain of doctrine, because it despised previous gifts. Isaiah says: “A vineyard was made for my beloved” (Isa. 5), that is, for Christ, of whom it is said: “You are my beloved Son,” etc. (Luke 3), “upon a horn, the son of oil,” that is, in the power and strength of him [Col. 0896D] of whom the Psalmist says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44).

The same Son of God fenced this vineyard about with the protection of angels; he selected stones out of it—that is, he cast away from it its stone idols and everything obstructing divine worship—and planted a choice vineyard drawn from all nations, not from any ordinary stock. But [Col. 0897A] according to another edition: “a vineyard of Sorek,” which is a kind of most excellent and fruitful vine, bearing continual fruit. He built a tower in its midst, namely a temple from which they might watch the fruits and the beasts lying in wait. He also constructed a winepress in it, so that grapes might be pressed in that same place—that is, so that the blood of sacrificial victims might be poured out there.

And he expected it to produce grapes, namely the fruits of good works; but it produced wild grapes, namely the bitterness of vices. They are called *labruscae* [wild grapes] because they grow on the edges (*labra*) of vineyards. “Now therefore, since I have done what I ought, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, having heard my case—which the vineyard does not contradict—judge between me and my vineyard. What more ought I to have done for my aforesaid vineyard that I have not done? Was it that I expected it to produce grapes”—as though this perhaps appears to be beyond my duty—“and it produced wild grapes,” as though uncultivated?

According to some, he said this above, privately to himself; here he puts to others what he had thought. It is as though he said more plainly: Since you do not wish to answer, I shall answer for you. Now I shall show you—not another, but I myself—what I shall do to my vineyard. As though he said: Since it returned evil for good, it shall undergo this judgment. “I shall remove its hedge,” namely the aid of angels, “and it shall be plundered by the nations,” so that those who did not know God through benefits may know him through punishments. He threatens punishment in order to turn them to repentance: “I shall tear down its wall, and it shall be trampled; and I shall make it desolate.” Repetition confirms the statement. Hence: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23).

[Col. 0897C] It follows: “It shall not be pruned,” namely by the sickle of God’s word—that is, when it sins, it shall not be corrected; “nor dug about,” namely it shall not be humbled by the admonition of the fear of God. “And briars and thorns shall grow over it,” namely a multitude of vices; “and I shall command the clouds”—namely the preachers, who rain words, flash with miracles, and shine with virtues—“not to rain rain upon it,” namely drops of doctrine.

This occurred after the Lord’s ascension, when they had no prophets and rejected the apostles, concerning whom it is said: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60). “And I shall command the clouds,” he says, “not to rain rain upon it”: as under Elijah, because all were idolaters, it did not rain for three years and six months [Col. 0897D] (1 Kings 17), lest they bring forth thorns instead of grapes, but might ask him, because of their dryness, who gives the rains of virtues. Hence it is said: “I shall make your heaven iron and your earth bronze” (Lev. 26). And Moses says: “The heaven above your head shall be bronze, and the earth beneath you iron” (Deut. 28).

For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, namely the ten tribes, or the whole people. And the men of Judah, namely the two tribes, are his delightful planting by comparison, because after the other tribes that worshipped idols had been separated, it afterwards sprang up. When the kingdom was divided, ten tribes were called Israel, while two were called Judah, in which kings from Judah reigned. [Col. 0898A] The men of those tribes, the men of Judah, were a delightful planting to God because priests and Levites, religious men, were among them when Isaiah spoke these words; or because Christ was to be born from them.

Again he adds: “And I expected it to produce grapes,” that is, judgment; “and behold iniquity,” that is, wild grapes; “and righteousness,” namely, that they should devoutly receive Christ; “and behold a cry,” that is, “Away, away, crucify him” (John 19).

O unbelieving nation, stripped and bereft of almost every good, which preferred to fasten Christ, the medicine of the whole human race, to the cross rather than believe in him! O perverse generation, abandoned by God! Did not that bronze serpent, which Moses lifted up in the wilderness before your fathers, prefigure him, the Son of God, whom your tongues suspended upon the cross?

[Col. 0898B] [Note: [Col. 0897D] Isidore, *On Numbers*.] The thirty-fifth station of the children of Israel is at Selmona; the thirty-sixth at Phion. Although these two stations are not found in the order of the historical narrative, nevertheless at them, after Aaron’s death, the children of Israel murmured against the Lord and Moses; despising manna, they were wounded by serpents (Num. 21).

But what does this signify—that they were healed from the deadly bite of serpents by the lifting up of the bronze serpent—except that now, in the type of the Saviour, who conquered the fierce and ancient serpent upon the gibbet, the devil’s poisons are overcome? Thus, whoever faithfully beholds the true image of the Son of God, his Passion and his cross, does not perish but is preserved forever.

For this is also signified by the Lord’s own words: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3). Rightly it is a bronze serpent suspended on wood. For bronze is customarily more enduring among metals; thus the bronze serpent was suspended on wood, so that the Lord might be signified as dead in the serpent and eternal in the bronze: namely, that he should be shown to have died according to his humanity and yet to be eternal according to his divinity.

Moreover, the first station, Selmona, is aptly interpreted as “bonds of the image” [Note: [Col. 0898D] Edition: “a little image.”], because there the image of the Saviour was undoubtedly expressed through the bronze serpent hanging upon the wood. The second, Phion, is also rightly called “mouth,” because, after we know the Passion of the Son of God, we pronounce with [Col. 0898D] the mouth what we believe in the heart, reading that apostolic saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). For we believe in the heart and confess with the mouth that Jesus Christ suffered by the will of God the Father, in order to free his people from the hand of the ancient enemy.

That God the Father handed over this same most beloved Son, coeternal with himself, to the Passion, the prophet Zechariah shows by speaking in his person: “Awake, sword, against my shepherd, against the man who cleaves to me, says the Lord” (Zech. 13). It is as though it were said more plainly: Sword—that is, the anguish of death—which kills the servants, kill also the heir. [Col. 0899A] “Awake against the shepherd,” that is, against my Son, whom I have appointed heir of all things: “the man who cleaves to me,” who is one and the same with me, and who says: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). Hence it is said: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14).

It is not strange if a father, forgetting natural affection, pronounces a sentence of death against a sinful son, when, by the will of God the Father, his only Son, though free from evil, was handed over to death for the sins of humankind. Again he adds: “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.” It is as though he said: O sword, rise up in such a way that you strike and kill the shepherd, namely Christ, and the sheep—that is, the disciples—are scattered. It is clear that, in the Passion, all the disciples abandoned Christ and fled (Matt. 26).

[Col. 0899B] It follows: “And I shall turn my hand toward the little ones. And in all the land there shall be two parts, says the Lord; and they shall be scattered and shall perish, and a third part shall remain in it. And I shall bring the third part through fire, and I shall burn them as silver is burned; and I shall test them as gold is tested.”

It is as though the Son of God said: “I shall turn my hand toward the little ones.” Leaving the proud Jews, I, the humble teacher, shall gather humble disciples. And then throughout all the earth there shall be two parts, namely Jews and Gentiles, and these two parts, Jews and Gentiles, shall be scattered and perish together in Christ’s Passion; but a third part shall remain in the land. The unbelieving Jews and Gentiles perishing, the third people, that of Christians, [Col. 0899C] shall grow up and alone shall be reserved for the life of virtues and the dwelling-place of the Church.

And lest this third part of Christians be delicate and secure, “I shall lead them through the fire of tribulation, and I shall burn them as silver is burned, and test them as gold is tested.” Of this fire it is said: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and I desire that it should burn” (Luke 12). And the apostles are said to be baptized in the Spirit of God and fire (Acts 1).

Again he says: “He shall call upon my name, and I shall hear him; and I shall say: You are my people; and he shall say: You are my God.” When the little ones—that is, the holy apostles, toward whom God will turn his hand—and through them the multitude of nations, that is, Christians, have so been tested, then the faithful people shall call Jesus Christ by his name; and when he says, “You are [Col. 0899D] my people,” the Christian people shall answer, “You are my God.”

A *framea*, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0899D] *Etymologies*, book 18, ch. 6.], is a sword sharpened on both sides, which the common people call a *spatha*. It is also a *romphaea*. It is called a *framea* because it is made of iron: for, just as *ferramentum* [an iron implement] is named from *ferrum* [iron], so *framea* is named from iron; consequently every sword is a *framea*. *Spatha* is said to derive from a Greek word concerning suffering, because *patim* in Greek is said to mean “to suffer.” Others maintain that *spatha* is called so in Latin because it is broad (*spatiosa*), that is, wide and ample. Hence also *spatula* in cattle [Note: [Col. 0899D] Edition: “in breasts.”].

Again, the same prophet, as though in the person of angels marveling at Christ’s ascension, asks the Son of God himself, [Col. 0900A] saying: “What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?” (Zech. 13). He answers: “I was wounded with these wounds in the house of those who loved me,” that is, in the house of the children of Israel, who ought to have loved me as their duty required. Hence it is said: “They repaid me evil for good, and hatred for my love” (Ps. 108).

The Jews, therefore, because they repaid their Creator, Jesus Christ, hatred for love and evil for good, lost the fruits of righteousness, forfeited their former dignity, and became utterly barren of all good works.

King and prophet David, who, although he could have returned evil to his persecutors, did not do so, but grieved over their death and, grieving, shed abundant tears, signified this stubborn barrenness of the Jews when [Col. 0900B] he cursed the mountains of Gilboa, saying: “Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you,” etc. (2 Sam. 1). [Note: [Col. 0900D] Paterius, *On this book*, ch. 1.]

What offense had the mountains committed? But because Gilboa is interpreted “descent,” and because by Saul, the anointed king who died, the death of our Redeemer is expressed, the proud hearts of the Jews are rightly signified by Gilboa. While they pour themselves out in desires of this kind, they associated themselves with the death of the anointed king, that is, Christ. And because the anointed king died bodily among them, they are dried up from every dew of grace, so that they cannot be fields of firstfruits.

For the proud minds of the Hebrews do not bear the first fruits, because at the Redeemer’s coming, remaining for the most part in faithlessness, they refused to follow the beginnings of faith. The holy Church, indeed, made fruitful in her firstfruits by the multitude of the Gentiles, will scarcely receive, at the end of the world, those Jews whom she finds; and, gathering what is last, she places them as it were the gleanings of the harvest.

Although the unbelieving and barren Jewish nation proudly rejected Christ’s preaching, he nevertheless testifies through the prophet Isaiah that he was sent by God the Father for the instruction of humankind, saying: “The Lord gave me a learned tongue, that I might know how to sustain one who has fallen” (Isa. 50).
