It is as though he said more plainly: The Lord, namely the Father, gave to me, a man born of the Virgin, a tongue instructed in knowledge and wisdom, so that I might sustain by the word of preaching the human race which had fallen through sin into death. “He raises [Col. 0900D] my ear of the mind in the morning,” as a teacher raises it, from my birth, from the beginning of my preaching, so that I may hear him as a teacher; for I do not speak from myself. The Lord God, namely the Father, opened for me the ear of understanding; but I do not resist his will, nor have I gone backward, departing from him.

Again he says: “I freely gave my body to the Jews or Roman soldiers who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled them,” who slapped me. “I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked me and spat upon me.” All these things were fulfilled in the Lord’s Passion. “The Lord God is my helper, and therefore I am not confounded.” It is as though he said: Since God the Father was my helper in the Passion, [Col. 0901A] I am not confounded in my hope of resurrection. “Therefore I set my face like the hardest stone,” before those mocking and striking me, “and I know that I shall not be confounded. He who justifies me is near,” ready to help me, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). “Who shall contradict me,” as though I were not just? “Let us stand together,” namely in judgment. “Who is my adversary,” saying that I was rightly crucified? “Let him come near to me,” so that we may be judged together by comparison, not by authority, according to the saying: “Sodom [Note: [Col. 0901D] Other manuscripts add after ‘Sodom’: ‘your sister.’] has been justified by you” (Ezek. 16).

Who then shall condemn me? No one. For behold, all adversaries in hell “shall be worn out like a garment,” and none of them can be justified in my presence: [Col. 0901B] “The moth shall eat them,” namely the consciousness of sins, or the envy of the Gentiles. A garment is corrupted and consumed by age and moths.

Likewise, in the forty-second year after Christ’s Passion, the Jews, called to repentance but at last, through their neglect, crushed, were devoured by the moth of an evil conscience when the Romans came. Again he says: “For who among you,” namely among the unbelieving Jews, “fears the Lord” as a son fears a father, “hearing in his heart the voice of his servant,” that is, of his Son, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4)?

It is as though he said: You scourged me and spat upon me; yet I call you to repentance, for “I do not desire the death of the sinner” (Ezek. 18). “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” but perfect love casts out fear. “He who fears is not perfect in love” (1 John 4). But here fear is used in the sense of timidity. Hence it is said: “Blessed is he who fears everything” (Prov. 28), that is, who is reverently fearful in God’s religion. Of this fear it is written: “The fear of the Lord surpasses all things” (Ecclus. 25). Elsewhere: “There is no want for those who fear God” (Ps. 33). And again: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 18). This fear keeps the souls of the saints whole, chaste, and pure. Hence: “Fear the Lord and give him glory” (Rev. 14).

[Col. 0901C] It follows: “Who has walked in darkness, and has no light?” Namely Christ, rejected, of whom it is said: “Neither did we esteem him”; and “he has no light” (Isa. 53), that is, no glory among his own people, as he himself says: “A prophet is not without honour, except in his own country” (Matt. 13).

The Gentile people too walked in the darkness of unbelief and had no light except Christ, who said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8). Henceforth let him hope not in idols but in the name of the Lord, and lean upon his God, so that human frailty may be sustained by divine majesty; thus the light of joy and gladness shall come to him.

Certainly the Son of God walked among the Jews as though in darkness, because they did not receive him with glory, but mocked him, suspended on the cross as a deceiver. David fittingly signified this when he transferred the ark of the Lord’s covenant from the house of Amminadab to Jerusalem, and Michal despised and mocked him as he danced among the maidservants of his servants [Col. 0902A] (2 Sam. 6).

So too, when Christ transferred the new covenant into his Church, he was a laughing-stock to the Synagogue upon the cross. He appeared naked when, concealing the power of his divinity from the Jews, he displayed the weakness of the flesh as though it were a linen ephod. The maidservants of the servants signify the souls of the saints, among whom he was made more glorious through the triumph of the cross. While Michal—that is, the Synagogue—mocks him, he appears glorious to the maidservants. She, in the type of the Synagogue, remains barren to this day, concerning whom it is said: “She who had many children has become weak” (1 Sam. 2). It is no wonder that he appeared naked among the maidservants of his servants, because, in order to redeem us, he took the form of a servant (Phil. 2).

[Col. 0902B] Concerning him God the Father says through the prophet: “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be exceedingly high” (Isa. 52). It is as though he said more plainly: My servant, namely the Son, God’s Word and God’s Wisdom, obedient to the Father unto death, shall understand the will of his Father; and therefore he shall be exalted through the preaching of the apostles, lifted up above all heavens, and made exceedingly high at the right hand of the Father.

So that there may be no doubt who said, “I who spoke, behold I am present,” and what is the arm of the Lord, the Father teaches plainly. According to his humanity Christ is the Father’s servant; according to his divinity he is equal to God the Father. “As many were astonished at him,” namely admiring his miracles [Col. 0902C] before the Passion, “so shall his appearance be dishonoured among men”; his miracles in the Passion being so much greater, because he was spat upon, scourged, and crucified; and “his form,” namely his appearance, “without honour among the sons of men.”

Yet he was truly “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44), because he was not a mere human being but God and man. “He shall sprinkle,” that is, wash in baptism, or rather by his own blood, far better than under the Law by the blood of a lamb, many nations predestined to eternal life. Over him—that is, over his wisdom—the kings, namely philosophers, shall shut their mouths while the apostles preach, because their wisdom was overthrown by the preaching of the cross. For the nations to whom nothing concerning him had been told by the prophets saw; and those who had not heard—namely from the Lord himself preaching in [Col. 0902D] the flesh—understood by faith. Of these it is said: “Blessed are those who have not seen,” etc. (John 20).

In saying, “Those to whom it was not told concerning him have seen,” he reproves the hardness of the Jews by comparison with the Gentiles. The Gentiles had not heard through the prophets and yet believed through the preaching of the apostles alone. To the Jews themselves it is said: “You shall hear indeed, and not understand” (Isa. 6). Therefore the choir of prophets complains concerning the same Jews: “Lord, who has believed our report?” As though they said: How few Jews believe what they hear from us! “And to whom has the arm of the Lord”—that is, the Son, through whom God the Father made all things—“been revealed?” so that he might believe, [Col. 0903A] even though he heard from us.

God the Father announced through the prophets that his Son would come into the world and, before the scandal of the cross, promised the glory of his resurrection, saying: “He shall be exalted and lifted up,” etc. (Isa. 52). Therefore the choir of prophets replies that it fulfilled the office of preaching and proclaimed the arm of the Lord, but few among the Jews believed what they heard from them concerning the coming of the Son.

Again the prophet adds: “And he shall rise up like a shrub,” the same Son of God and of the Virgin, rising, ascending, and filling the world with faith before him; “and like a root from a thirsty land,” that is, from the Virgin’s womb, pure from sexual intercourse. Hence it is said: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root,” etc. (Isa. 11).

Symmachus here calls him a branch, thereby signifying the man who came forth from the Virgin’s womb. Aquila says that he rises “like a root from an untrodden land,” where the privilege of virginity is shown, because he was created without male seed from land formerly untrodden.

It follows: “He has no beauty,” that is, in the judgment of the wicked; “nor comeliness”: his divinity, hidden in the flesh, does not appear. “And we saw him”—we prophets, with the eyes of the heart—“and there was no appearance” in his passion; “and we desired him,” having long before desired to see him: despised by the Jews as he hung upon the cross and was made a curse for us; “the last of men,” that is, held to be the most worthless; “a man of sorrows,” because, being truly human, he truly suffered, though he overcame suffering by his divinity; “and acquainted with infirmity,” assumed for our sake; “and as it were his face hidden,” [Col. 0903C] and despised by the Jews: that is, his divinity hidden in a human body. Therefore “we did not esteem him,” namely, many of us who would later believe. Hence it is said: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know you” (Isa. 45).

Again the prophet speaks of him in the person of the human race, saying: “Truly he bore our infirmities,” that is, our sins—he himself, and no other, took them from us—“and carried our sorrows in his body upon the wood” (1 Pet. 2); not in appearance, but truly crucified and truly suffering. Hence those words: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26). Isaiah speaks in the person of the Gentile people, saying: “We thought him as it were a leper, stricken by God and humbled.” [Col. 0903D] As if he said more plainly: We, who sinned in ignorance but now believe in repentance, thought him to be as it were a leper—that is, a sinner—stricken by God for his own sins and humbled, namely cast down for our sake, because he was crucified with thieves. But he, the true Son of God and man, was wounded not for his own iniquities but for ours, so that by his wound he might heal our wounds. He was crushed for our crimes—by scourges and blows—and made a curse for us. Hence the Psalmist says in his person: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they numbered all my bones” (Ps. 21).

It follows: “The chastisement of our peace was upon him,” namely the scourging through which we were reconciled to God and the angels; “and by the stripes of his rods we were healed” from sin. [Col. 0904A] It is clear that, just as his body was scourged and torn, so his soul suffered for us, lest Christ be believed true in one respect and false in another.

“All we like sheep went astray,” and therefore we all need God’s mercy. For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. In handing over the Son of God to death, we went astray like the sheep which perished (Ps. 118), which was carried back to the flock upon the shoulders of the loving shepherd (Luke 15). Each turned aside into his own crooked way from Christ, who is the true way, by worshipping idols and crucifying Christ. Very many also turn aside into their own error by holding differing opinions concerning the crucified Christ. Again he says: “The Lord laid upon him the iniquities of us all,” namely the punishment of all our sins, which we could not endure; God-man endured it. [Col. 0904B] He was offered upon the altar of the cross as a sacrifice for us, and no one compelled him, because he himself willed it. Hence it is said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” (John 10). “And he did not open his mouth,” namely to curse, lest the salvation of the human race be delayed; but like an innocent sheep he was meekly led to slaughter. Hence the Apostle: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). The Son of God, who takes away the sins of the world (John 1), like a lamb not resisting before its shearer, “will be silent and will not open his mouth,” not even against the soldiers striking him. Indeed, like a lamb he was led to the passion, in whose figure the people Israel ate a lamb in Egypt (Exod. 12): the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world, who feeds us with [Col. 0904C] his flesh and blood and clothes us with the fleece of protection.

Therefore he was taken up from the distress of the passion and from unjust judgment in the resurrection, when all power in heaven and on earth was given to him (Matt. 28). The Judge of all found no truth in the judgment, but was condemned without cause. Therefore the prophet marvels that the God of all gave himself over to suffering. “Who shall declare his generation,” divine or human? No one comprehends or explains it by human reasoning, even if by God’s inspiration he comes to know it. “For he was cut off,” namely by the Jews, “from the land of the living,” that is, from human society, in order to live in heaven. Hence it is said: “Let us root him out from the land of the living” (Jer. 11). God the Father also speaks of him, saying: “For the crime of my people I struck him.” [Col. 0904D] As if it were said more plainly: For the blotting out of the crime of my peculiar people, I struck him by permission. Hence those words: “I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered” (Matt. 26).

It follows: “And he will give the wicked”—that is, the Jews—“to the Romans for his burial”; for they persecuted him even unto death and fortified his tomb, sealing the stone and setting guards (Matt. 27). “And he will give the rich for his death,” namely the scribes and Pharisees, who gloried in the riches of their knowledge of the Law, because they delivered him to death. Alternatively: “He will give the wicked for his death,” namely the Gentiles, who were without piety toward God the Father, because by dying and being buried he acquired them; “and the rich,” namely the Jews who gloried in the riches of the Law and prophets. [Col. 0905A] Why? “Because he did no iniquity, neither was deceit found in his mouth”: this can be said of no one else, since no one is clean from defilements. But he, the Son of God and the Virgin, was righteous in deed and true in word. Therefore he suffered because God the Father, by grace alone, willed to crush him in the weakness of the flesh for human salvation.

“If the same Son sets his soul for our sin,” that is, his life, “he shall see a long-lived seed,” namely believers reigning forever; or the word of the Gospel, which will not grow old like the Old Testament. Hence it is said: “The sower went out to sow his seed” (Luke 8). “And the will of the Lord,” namely of the Father, “shall prosper in his hand”: that is, the redemption of the human race shall be accomplished in work, so that whatever God the Father willed may be fulfilled through his powers. [Col. 0905B] Hence those words: “Father, I have kept in your name those whom you gave me” (John 17).

Again the prophet says: “Because his soul laboured in vain, he shall see and be satisfied.” His soul laboured as though in vain, because the Jews refused to be converted. In preaching to the Jews, performing miracles, and enduring scourges, the Son of God found no rest among them. Hence it is said: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8). And elsewhere: “I have laboured in enduring” (Jer. 6). “He shall see,” he says, “and be satisfied.” As though he said: He shall see churches from among the Gentiles throughout the world, and shall be satisfied by the faith of the Gentiles, as he is today. Thus, when hungry and thirsty above Jacob’s well, [Col. 0905C] he refused the food brought to him, because he was already satisfied by the faith of the Samaritan woman and of those who were coming out of the city to him.

“In his knowledge,” that is, in his teaching, “my righteous servant”—namely the Son, who took the form of a servant—“shall justify many.” He did not commit sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2); not himself justified, but justifying—not all, but many, because “many are called, but few chosen” (Matt. 20). “And he bore their iniquities,” that is, the punishment for sin, “in his body upon the wood” (1 Pet. 2), because they could not bear it.

Again God the Father speaks of him, saying: “I shall allot him many, and he shall divide the spoils of the strong.” As if he said: Because he became obedient even unto death (Phil. 2), I shall allot him many—namely faithful Gentiles in place of negligent Jews. [Col. 0905D] Hence it is said: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance” (Ps. 2), etc. And he shall divide the spoils of the strong, namely the demons: that is, the human race snatched away from the devil. He shall divide the spoils among the apostles, so that one may preside over believing Jews and another over the Gentiles. Hence those words: “When the heavenly one distinguishes kings” (Ps. 67), or nations, etc. And again: “The king of the powers of the beloved, of the beloved, is for dividing the spoils of the beauty of the house” (ibid.). And, as is written of blessed Paul: “In the morning he shall devour, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. 49). Why will this happen? Because the Son of God willingly delivered his soul, that is, his life, unto death, and was reckoned by the Jews among criminal thieves. He was reckoned with criminals in order to redeem criminals from sin, becoming all things to all. [Col. 0906A] Hence he himself says through the Psalmist: “I was reckoned with those who go down into the pit; I became as a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87). For he bore our sins in his body; and Paul, his imitator, says: “I became all things to all, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9).

It follows: “And he bore the sins of many,” namely of the predestined: he washed them in his own blood. And “he prayed for transgressors,” that is, the persecuting Jews, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23). At this utterance, according to the Gospel of the Nazarenes, many thousands of Jews standing around the cross believed.

Again the prophet adds, saying: “The righteous man perishes” [Col. 0906B] (Isa. 57)—namely Christ, in the judgment of unbelievers or through the immensity of his torments. Hence it is said to Pilate in the Gospel: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man.” And Pilate: “What shall I do with Jesus, who is called righteous?” (Matt. 27). The righteous man perishes because of blind watchmen and mute dogs, because, blind and mute, ignorant of wisdom, they do not consider the things of God. “The righteous man perishes,” he says, “and there is no one”—namely among the reprobate Jews—“who considers and reflects in his heart that he suffers for us, not for himself.” “And men of mercy are gathered,” namely the apostles sent to us by God’s mercy, because through torments they pass from the world to God; and there is no one who understands that they suffer unjustly and are therefore justly crowned. “For from the face of wickedness,” that is, from the presence of sin, [Col. 0906C] “the righteous man has been gathered”: namely Christ, to the right hand of the Father; because he himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness; “by whose stripe you were healed” (1 Pet. 2). Christ was doubtless gathered away from the face of wickedness in order that he might not see the evils of the age, and might reign forever over all the works of his Father’s hands.

It follows: “Let peace come,” namely Christ to the Gentiles through the apostles, to whom it was said: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you” (John 12). Again the prophet adds, saying: “Let him rest in his bed,” namely Christ in the glory of the Father, who “walked in his uprightness,” returning to the Father by a straight path. The prophet prays that Christ may come and, having risen from the dead, rest in his bed, namely in the glory [Col. 0906D] of the Father’s majesty; or in the Church, in which he walked uprightly, because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (1 Pet. 2).

In Christ’s passion the Jews preferred to cry to Pilate, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19), rather than receive Christ, the true king, the Son of God and the Virgin. This, indeed, the elders of Israel prefigured when, despising Samuel, they demanded a king for themselves. The Jews, having rejected Samuel, asked for a king; and the scribes and Pharisees, having rejected Christ, the true king and priest, chose a Roman ruler. Hence Samuel’s name is interpreted “God.” Saul means “asked for” or “request,” because he was sought by the people; and he is understood as Barabbas. Kish means “hard” or “vomiting”; Abiel, “My Father is God.” Thus the Jews, hard and vomiting, confess God the Father but deny the Son; yet whoever denies the Son denies also the Father who sent him (1 John 2). Unless God the Father had sent him for the redemption of the world, the human race could by no means have been delivered from the most harsh slavery of the ancient enemy. For no patriarch or prophet, however justly and devoutly he lived, was able by his merits to conquer him. Indeed, the enemy proved invincible to all the saints before Christ’s coming, and no one could be rescued from his hand by his own power.

That wicked enemy was prefigured by Goliath the Philistine, against whom none of the children of Israel dared to fight. Allegorically, the Philistines signify demons, and Goliath their head, who could not be overcome before the coming of the true David, namely Christ. [Col. 0907B] Gath, Goliath’s city, is interpreted “winepress” and signifies the world or hell, in which the ancient enemy, as in a winepress, trampled those enslaved to sins. Having abandoned the heavenly rest, as it were the seventh day, he fell into this world made in six days. The height of Goliath signifies the pride of the devil [Note: [Col. 0907D] “Pride.”], by which he gained dominion over the children of pride, as though raising a palm. Goliath’s weapons signify the devil’s snares or cunning devices for doing harm.

David was sent by his father to visit his brothers, and Christ by God the Father to the sheep which were lost of the house of Israel (Matt. 15). David carried an ephah of parched grain—that is, a measure of three modii—to his brothers; and Christ entrusted to believers the mystery of the Holy Trinity. David brought ten small cheeses to the commander, and [Col. 0907C] Christ gave the Decalogue to the Jews. A modius is a measure of forty-four pounds. Eliab is interpreted “My God, Father”; and the Jews falsely claiming God the Father as their God, because they envied Christ, lost their birthright. David’s staff signifies Christ’s cross. Goliath, struck in the forehead, fell and was subjected to David; and the devil is struck upon the forehead of his own people when the sign of the cross is impressed in that place, and he is subjected in his members to Christ. David carried Goliath’s sword to Jerusalem; and Christ transferred to that same Jerusalem, for the defense of the Church, those whom he snatched from the devil’s power. Saul inquires about David as though he were unknown, although David had long been attending him; and the Jews knew that Christ was to come, yet, although they could recognize by his miracles in his bodily presence that he was the Son of God, they say as though ignorant: “Who are you?” (John 8), and “Where is your Father?” (ibid.). [Col. 0907D] Thereafter Saul persecutes innocent David and drives him beyond the province; the impious Jewish people persecutes innocent Christ and casts him out of the Synagogue. Hence it is said: “Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away to a city called Ephraim, and there remained with his disciples” (John 11). And again: “They took stones to throw at him; but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8). Yet this alone did not suffice them: they also condemned him, crying out to Pilate [Col. 0908A] and declaring him guilty of death (Matt. 26).

But he, as the hour of his passion drew near, returned to Jerusalem in order to beget for himself a holy people. For that city he willingly tasted death, lifted up on the cross; swallowing up and mightily conquering death, he destroyed the power of the ancient enemy and finally most graciously commended to God the Father the people whom he had acquired. Hence a certain wise and Catholic man, devoted in conduct and life to the same almighty Jesus Christ, spoke thus in Christ’s person, for the strengthening of the Catholic faith:

> Hanging on the wood, I restore to the Father those whom I have sought.
>
> Hanging on the wood, I beget for myself a holy people.
>
> Hanging on the wood, I break the head of the wicked enemy.
>
> Hanging on the wood, I am slain by a people worthy of death.

[Col. 0908B] In these four short verses he briefly establishes the faith of the entire ecclesiastical religion. He also shows that the Redeemer of the human race himself assumed true humanity from his Virgin mother in time, and possessed true divinity from God the Father before all ages. In these words he proclaims him weak and strong, true God and man, eternal and mortal, visible and invisible, the most loving acquirer of lost sheep, their good and most merciful shepherd and keeper, the most valiant conqueror of the ancient enemy, and in all things obedient to God the Father even unto death.

Moreover, our Lord Jesus Christ, as we find written, bestowed innumerable benefits upon the unworthy, from whom he endured unworthy treatment: [Col. 0908C] he gave life, endured death; preached saving things, endured reproaches; offered prayer to God the Father for them, but heard curses from them; and finally, strengthening his own in the faith, ascended into heaven. Therefore, that we may understand more fully the verses of this most devout abbot, it is fitting, as the grace of divine love goes before us, to discuss them more subtly, so that the minds of listeners, sprinkled as with spices by the fragrance of their sweetest scent, may be refreshed by spiritual sweetness. He says therefore:

> Hanging on the wood, I restore to the Father those whom I have sought.

As if he said more plainly: Sent from heaven by God the Father, I came into this world; I visited the sheep which had perished, the house of Israel (Matt. 15); and I made known to them the name of him [Col. 0908D] who sent me and showed them the straight way by which they might reach ever-green pastures. But because they did not give credence to my warnings—indeed, repaying me evil for good—I endured from them scourges, reproaches, mockery, and many adversities. Now also, hanging upon the wood, I restore to the same Father who sent me those whom I have sought: namely those whom I acquired, that is, those whom I predestined with him for eternal life; I entrust them to his protection. Hence it is said: “I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours” (John 17). And again: “Holy Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one as we are” (ibid.).

In the Son’s saying to the Father concerning us, [Col. 0909A] “May they be one, as we are,” we understand the one essence of Father and Son. But in what he said before—“Father, keep in your name those whom you have given me”—we recognize the distinct persons of Begetter and Begotten. Here, dearest brethren, a great and incomparable benefit of our Redeemer toward us is shown, and we recognize a great token of his love. It did not suffice him mercifully to rescue us from the devil’s power unless he also most graciously commended us to God the Father. He redeemed us with his most precious blood and prayed to God as Father for us, that he might preserve us from evil. By suffering in the flesh he acquired us for God the Father, and, hanging on the wood, restored us to him. He was not content to promise, “Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28), unless he also commended us to God the Father with the affection of love.

[Col. 0909B] It should be noted that, in praying to God the Father for us, he revealed to us the riches of his love. Thus he says: “The Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and believed” (John 16). And again: “As he loved me, I also loved you. Remain in my love” (John 15). He prayed for us, I say. Who prayed for whom? The shepherd for the sheep, the teacher for the disciples, the Lord for servants, the righteous for the unrighteous, he who was free from every stain of sin for those given over to every criminal vice. For what did he pray for us? That the heavenly husbandman, namely the Father, [Col. 0909C] cleansing us as branches from sins and vices and preserving us from evil, namely eternal damnation, might open for us the gate of the heavenly kingdom and lead us to that true and supreme high priest, our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence it is said: “Father, I desire that where I am, those also may be with me, that they may see the glory which you have given me” (John 17).

It follows:

> Hanging on the wood, I beget for myself a holy people.

Truly the Son of God and the Virgin, hanging upon the cross, begot for himself a holy people. For just as Eve was formed from the side of sleeping Adam, so the Church, redeemed by Christ’s blood, grew from the side of Christ sleeping upon the cross. By the word of preaching he adopted her as his bride; by the blood of his passion he redeemed her from the slavery of the ancient enemy and washed her from sins, and consecrated her with the water of baptism. [Col. 0909D] Of him it is indeed written: “He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. 1). And again: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death” (Rom. 6).

By dying on the cross he also begot her as a young heifer having neither spot nor wrinkle: “Having neither spot nor wrinkle,” he says (Eph. 5)—the spot, namely, of heretical perversity, and the wrinkle of perverse conduct. He adopted her as a young heifer in the world’s old age because he begot her by the preaching of the new Gospel. “Hanging,” he says, “on the wood, I beget for myself a holy people.” He purposed to beget this holy people for himself when, in the Old Testament, he himself said: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 19). As if it were said more plainly: Make your ways and your pursuits good, because from you a holy nation is to arise. Be holy, because I am holy—I who, at the end of the world, desire to beget from you yourselves a holy people for myself. [Col. 0910A] For the primitive Church was a daughter of the Synagogue. Thus from that nation the Lord begot for himself a holy people, because he sent its holy children, namely the apostles, to baptize all nations. Therefore, hanging upon the wood, he begot for himself a holy people, as he said of himself in the Gospel: “Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12).

For the harvest of believers could never arise unless he had died upon the cross. But because that grain of wheat—the [Col. 0910B] Word consubstantial and coeternal with God the Father—willed to fall into the earth through the mystery of the most sacred Incarnation, he raised up with himself through faith a great harvest of believers throughout the whole world. He remained as though alone eternally in the bosom of the Father when he had not yet been sent into the world for the redemption of the human race. The Apostle says thus concerning God the Father: “He delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1). And again: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). [Col. 0910C] God the Father surely transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love when, through the Gospel of that same most beloved Son, he called us to eternal joys and permitted him to die for our redemption. He did not spare him, but gave him over for us who were unworthy; for while he permitted him, guiltless, to die solely through love, he mercifully rescued us from eternal death. God the Father mercifully gave him over for us into the hands of the ungodly—him who truly is the life of angels. He gave over his innocent and most holy Son in order to redeem a guilty and unworthy servant.

Let it therefore be said: “If the grain dies, it bears much fruit.” The Son of God rightly compared himself in this place to a grain of wheat, since he is indeed the nourishment of the citizens above. Because, therefore, he did not refuse to die for us according to the flesh, he carried back with himself to the Father who sent him a harvest of many souls. For the salvation of our souls he willingly [Col. 0910D] offered his own soul into the hands of the Father, that he might lead us back with himself to the heavenly homeland. Thus he did what he had foretold: he gave himself over to death and bore much fruit. The grain of wheat died according to the flesh, and the harvest of many believers grew.

Again he says:

> Hanging on the wood, I break the head of the wicked enemy.

This devout abbot appropriately calls the devil here “the wicked enemy,” because from his very creation he doubtless persisted in his wickedness. As soon as he was created, he wished to exalt his throne in the north above the height of the clouds and make himself equal to his Creator (Isa. 14); but constrained by divine justice and omnipotence, he immediately fell to earth with his followers. Of him it is said: [Col. 0911A] “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10). Cast down from heaven, irrecoverably falling to earth, and persisting in his wickedness, he infected with the poison of his wickedness the man whose mind God had created in his image. He turned him away from the state of uprightness, stripped him of the garments of honour and innocence, deprived him of the delights of paradise, and at last miserably cast him and his descendants into this valley of tears. He alienated him from love of the Creator through the worship of idols, and tyrannically held dominion over this world for nearly five thousand years. Of him it is said: “While the strong man armed guards his courtyard, what he possesses is in peace” (Luke 11).

Nor did this suffice the same wicked enemy: he even presumed to tempt the Son of God, [Col. 0911B] sent from heaven by God the Father for human salvation. Defeated by him, he fell and departed in confusion. Of this the mightiest warrior himself says in the Gospel: “The ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

Seeing, therefore, that he could not conquer our Redeemer by tempting him, that same wicked enemy and insatiable murderer stirred up the people against him without cause. The Lord, then, hanging upon the wood through the tongues of the Jews and the hands of the soldiers, immediately—this is true—broke the head of that wicked enemy. Thus was completely fulfilled what the Lord had threatened him at the beginning of the world: “I shall put enmities between you and the woman; she shall crush your head, and you shall lie in wait for her heel” [Col. 0911C] (Gen. 3). This is understood of the fruit of the most glorious Virgin Mary, namely Christ. As if it were said more plainly: You shall always trip up the son of the Virgin Mary so that he may die upon the cross; but he, having conquered death, shall rise again and crush your head, which is death or pride.

Thus the prophet David also said to God in exultation in the psalm:

> “You broke the heads of the dragon; you gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians” (Ps. 37).

As if he said: You broke the heads of the dragon—that is, the pride of the prince of dragons—which was prefigured by the calf’s head broken by Moses (Exod. 32). You gave him—that is, the dragon himself in his body—as food, namely nourishment, to the peoples of the Ethiopians: that is, to those [Col. 0911D] to whom it was said, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). They were once Ethiopians, that is, darkened; but now they are most radiant because made like God, as are the apostles. The dragon’s members were nourishment to them because, according to faith, they incorporated those members into themselves. Hence it was said to Peter: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10).

Such food was prefigured when Moses reduced to powder the calf which the people of Israel worshipped, scattered it in water, and gave it to them to drink. That calf reduced to powder signifies unbelievers who, confessing humbly, burn their self-exaltations and pride in the fire of divine love and are thus sprinkled with the water of baptism and incorporated among believers. Or otherwise: “You gave him as food to the peoples of the Ethiopians,” [Col. 0912A] because the persecutions of unbelievers were like food and refreshment to believers. Therefore the Son of God and the Virgin, hanging upon the wood, as was foretold from the beginning of the world, shattered the wicked enemy’s head and weapons, plundered his spoils, recaptured the captivity which he had taken captive, and led it with himself to the heavenly kingdom.

Again, this same devout and wise abbot, considering the innocence of the Son of God and the Virgin, and the obstinacy and unbelief of the Jews, speaks in the person of Christ hanging upon the cross, saying:

> Hanging on the wood, I am slain by a people worthy of death.

O blind, cruel, and impious nation! Why were you not ashamed to hand over without cause to death him who powerfully and mercifully raised your dead, gave sight to the blind, restored hearing to the deaf, opened the mouths of the mute [Col. 0912B] for speech, restored walking to the lame, cleansed lepers, expelled demons from possessed bodies, healed the sick, rebuked your perversities with fatherly affection, and showed you the way of salvation? Why did you not receive with reverence and due honour him who had been prefigured for you by the patriarchs, figures, and enigmas; promised in the Law; foretold by the oracles of the prophets; sent by God the Father in the sixth age of the world; born true God and true man from the incorrupt Virgin of David’s stock; and presented to your sight, as you cannot altogether deny?

For this reason Moses sternly rebukes you in the Law, because he knew that you had always acted contentiously against the Lord and had by no means obeyed his commands. Let him therefore say:

> [Col. 0912C] “I know that after my death you will act wickedly and quickly turn aside from the way which I showed you” (Deut. 31).

What else does “you will act wickedly” mean but openly to say: You will find no cause of death in Christ, the Son of God and the Virgin, sent by God the Father for your salvation, and yet you will nail him to the cross? Again, denouncing and abhorring the wicked works of your pursuits, he says: “O crooked and perverse generation! Is this how you repay the Lord, foolish and senseless people?” (Deut. 32). As if he said: Foolish and senseless people, why, repaying evil for good, do you crucify your Creator so cruelly and offer gall and vinegar so irreverently to his honey-sweet mouth? “Is he not your Father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” O blind [Col. 0912D] and unbelieving nation! What could be said more plainly or demonstrated more surely about Christ? Is not the Son of God and the Virgin, whom you unjustly hanged upon the wood, your Father—the one who created you from nothing, redeemed you from Egypt, led you across the Red Sea on dry ground, fed you with manna in the wilderness, rescued you from the deadly bite of serpents, delivered you from the greater and stronger people of the Amorites who opposed you on your way, brought you into the promised land after you crossed the Jordan, and destroyed the inhabitants of the land, hanging their kings on gibbets?

Why, then, did you neglect to call so many benefits to mind, receive your God and Lord himself with honour, and devoutly obey his commands? Why did you cruelly kill as an enemy him whom you ought to have loved and honoured as your sweetest Father? Why did you prefer to deliver him to death rather than reign with him forever? Is it not written in your Law that whoever curses father or mother shall die (Lev. 20)? Yet you not only cursed the same Father, your God and Lord Jesus Christ, but also injured him with unclean and most foul spittle, struck him with fists, scourged him, did not blush to bind his most glorious hands—which shortly before had bestowed countless benefits upon the sick—and moreover nailed those hands and feet to the cross. You pierced with a spear that most holy side—indeed, the temple in which are all the treasures of the wisdom [Col. 0913A] of God (Col. 2). You presumed to offer vinegar mingled with gall to his honey-sweet mouth; you did not fear to strike with a reed that venerable head, dreadful to angels [Col. 0913B] and all the powers of heaven; you were not ashamed to kneel and worship him, not truly, but in mockery; as you passed by, shaking your heads, you blasphemed him (Matt. 27); and you even delivered him unjustly to death.

Therefore, because it did not suffice you to curse him, but you also resolved to hand him over to death, you are nevertheless worthy of death according to the judgment of the Law. And if the gate of the heavenly kingdom does not admit cursers, it will doubtless not admit you either, guilty as you are of so great a murder, unless you produce fruits worthy of repentance. Let it therefore be said:

> Hanging on the wood, I am slain by a people worthy of death.

Who is slain, and by whom? The Creator by creatures; the Father by sons; the king by ministers; the lord by servants; [Col. 0913C] the merciful one by the impious; the righteous by sinners; the good by the wicked; the lion by worms; the mighty by the weak; the rich by the poor: he who redeemed with the price of his blood a world already destined for eternal death. Therefore, O wretched and unhappy Jews, because you presumed to kill the Author of life (Acts 3), and demanded that his innocent blood be upon you and your children, you made yourselves sacrilegious and murderous, and rendered yourselves worthy of eternal death—unless, before he comes for judgment, you devoutly and faithfully submit yourselves to that Son of God and the Virgin, whom you killed but who rose again and sits at the Father’s right hand, and produce fruits worthy of repentance in accordance with the discipline of ecclesiastical religion.

For he is merciful and devout, kind toward those who repent; nor, as he himself says, did he come to destroy souls but to save them (Luke 9). Therefore implore him with tears, your faces cast down to the ground, that he may remove the veil of Moses from your hearts, drive away unbelief, soften the hardness of your breast with the dew of his grace, fill the dwelling-place of your mind with the sweetness of his love, open your inward eyes to contemplate the brightness of his countenance, free your tongues from the bonds of evil habit for the praise of his name, and join you to the children of the holy Church by the bond of love. [Col. 0913D] If, therefore, you do all these things, as I have said, you will be able to obtain forgiveness from that same supreme and most merciful shepherd, not by your merits but by his abundant goodness.

[Col. 0914A] Meanwhile, dearest brethren, it is fitting that we render the thanks due to almighty God, who has deigned to reveal to us, though unworthy, the riches of his goodness and glory. For he has revealed to us—not by our merits, but solely through the condescension of his mercy—the secret of his eternal counsel, which has remained hidden from the Jews to this day because of their malice. The little boy of Jonathan aptly represented their ignorance: gathering the arrows which his master had shot, he carried them into the city, wholly unaware of their purpose.

For Jonathan, as the history relates, wishing to save David while he was concealed in a field beside a stone, shot two arrows as a sign. The little boy, not knowing what he was doing, gathered them and carried them into the city (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 20). What, then, did this signify,

[Col. 0914B] except that the Father had hidden in the letter of the Law—unknown to the Jews—his only-begotten Son, whom he intended to send for the salvation of humankind? David, therefore, was hidden in the field, and Christ in this world. Hence it is said: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1). The Son of God sat in the world beside the stone, because he was written by the Father’s finger on the stone tablets of the Law. Hence it is said: “The Lord your God is one” (Deut. 6); and again: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.”

Saul judged David to be a son of death amid the feast; and Jewish unbelief deliberated upon the Lord’s death amid the Paschal feast. When morning had dawned, Jonathan came into the field at the place agreed with David, and the little boy was with him. He shot one arrow; he shot

[Col. 0914C] another. Thus God the Father, at the dawning of faith, first brought forth the testimony of the Law concerning Christ, and then sent the prophets. Jonathan’s boy gathered the arrows and, unaware of what he was doing, carried them back to his master. So the Jewish people, carrying the books of the Law and the Prophets, honoured them as divinely written, but did not know Christ, whom Moses and the prophets had foretold. Without doubt, they would not have crucified him had they known that he was the Lord of glory (1 Cor. 2). But because blindness of mind had taken hold of them, they preferred unjustly to drive him from their kingdom, as they persecuted David—that is, to fasten him to the cross—rather than faithfully believe in him.

David alone fled from Saul’s face, and Christ in his Passion alone endured the indignities inflicted upon him by the Jews. Abimelech [Note: Achimelech, Col. 0913D] is the same person as Achias, grandson of

[Col. 0914D] Eli. Abimelech, whose name means “my brother is king,” signifies the apostles, whom Christ, the King of kings, calls his brothers. David said: “I have appointed such and such a place for my young men” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21); and Christ said to his disciples: “After I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee” (Matt. 26). David came by a defiled way; and Christ, himself undefiled, passed through the impure actions of the Jews. David said: “This way is defiled, but today it shall be sanctified in my vessels” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21); and the vessels of the Lord—that is, the holy apostles—were sanctified by faith from the contagion of the Jews.

Truly the holy apostles proved to be sanctified vessels, because, filled with the new wine of the Holy Spirit, they watered the whole world with spiritual teaching

[Col. 0915A] (Acts 2). Abimelech said to David: “I have no common loaves” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21). *Laos* is Greek for “people”; hence “common loaves,” that is, loaves for the populace. Accordingly the glorious confessor of the Lord, Isidore, our patron, says [Note: *Questions on 1 Kings [1 Samuel]*, ch. 15, Col. 0915D]:

> So far as prophecy is concerned, this was fulfilled in Christ, who, having been placed in the flesh, passed to the apostles while avoiding the Jews’ savagery, and with them took the desired meal. Hence he himself said: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22).

David took Goliath’s sword (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 21), and Christ, stronger than the most powerful devil, broke the weapons in which he trusted and seized his spoils. Saul killed the priests who had received David (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 22); and the devil inflicted

[Col. 0915B] many evils upon those who received Christ—namely tribulations and deaths. “For all who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Hence it is said: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15).

David fled into the cave of Odollam [Note: Odollam, Col. 0916D]; and when his brothers and all his father’s household heard this, they went down to him there (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 22). This signifies that our Redeemer, after accomplishing his Passion and the redemption of humankind, first established the Church in Judaea from the Israelite people, from whom he also took flesh. There his brothers, namely the apostles, and his father’s household—that is, those Jews who believed—came to him. And all came together to him who were in distress: that is, those placed amid sins, who did not possess the breadth

[Col. 0915C] of charity; those oppressed by debt, namely the tribute of sins which they pay to the devil; and those bitter in spirit, while they give over their members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity. And he became their leader. The nations must repent in bitterness of spirit and come to David—that is, to Christ, desired by all nations—that he may become their leader. For he is the judge of the living and the dead, the prince of the kings of the earth and of peace, whose kingdom shall have no end. Hence the saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11).

These words of our Redeemer, dearly beloved, are sweet and must by no means be passed over with a deaf ear. Rather, they must be stored more attentively

[Col. 0915D] in the mind, meditated day and night upon, and carried out in good deeds. In this passage our Redeemer commands not the idle and wandering, but those exercised in good works for love of him, to come to him; and he promises them the refreshment of eternal sweetness. He also calls those unable to bear the burdens of the Law, that they may submit their necks to his light and sweet yoke, when he says: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” Let none of you, therefore, grow sluggish in his service; let none love idleness; let none contrive delays in doing good. Rather, while it is day, let each exercise himself in good work for love of him. Yet care must be taken that understanding does not grow sluggish through idleness,

[Col. 0916A] nor vanish through the fault of pride amid the exercise of good works.

Without doubt, this is signified by the axe-head which fell from its handle into the depths of the water while Elisha’s disciple was cutting timber—that is, unfruitful wood (4 Kings [2 Kings] 6). The iron in the handle is understanding in the heart; these timbers are cut when wrongdoers are rebuked. But when this is done carelessly, when the fall into vain glory is not avoided, the iron is lost in the water, because understanding is made foolish through undisciplined action. It is given for this purpose: that it may be restored before the eyes of the giver, namely God, through good action. “This very thing,” he says, “I had borrowed” (ibid.). But when the elect stumble, they return quickly to their hearts and pursue their fault with tears. Hence it is said: “Alas,

[Col. 0916B] alas, my lord” (ibid.). Those who examine themselves carefully in tears consider not only what evil they have committed, but also what good they ought to have rendered from the gift received. Hence it is said: “This very thing I had borrowed.” As though he said: “Through careless laxity I lost that which I received from the Redeemer’s grace in order to repay it through good works.” Yet God never abandons the mind that truly acknowledges itself to be in sins.

Therefore Elisha cast down a piece of wood and drew the iron to the surface, because our Redeemer humbles the sinner’s heart and restores the understanding it had lost. Hence another translation says: “Elisha broke the wood, cast it into the water, and thus retrieved the iron.” To break the wood is to crush the heart’s pride;

[Col. 0916C] to cast it into the depths is to humble thought by awareness of one’s own weakness. Immediately the iron returns, because understanding resumes its former usefulness in action. The more pride lifts the mind upward, the more dangerously it hurls it down; but the more humility presses it down, the more it advances it upward.

For pride joined with desire had seized Absalom’s mind; he wished to kill his father and reign in his place. Absalom indeed prefigured Judas the betrayer, who sold his Lord and master to the Jews. David endured Absalom as his persecutor and nevertheless earnestly commanded the leaders of his army not to kill him. But Christ endured Judas as though unaware of his thoughts, shared a meal with him—in which he entrusted the sacrament of his body and blood to the disciples—and moreover, in this present betrayal, offered him a kiss. Absalom conspired with Israel’s elders to kill his father; Judas conferred with the chief priests and Pharisees in order to hand Christ over to death. Absalom, with the Jews consenting and assisting, drove David without cause from his kingdom; and Judas, having received the price, sold innocent Christ to the chief priests for crucifixion. Absalom, riding a mule while pursuing his father—thus serving the flow of lustful flesh—was caught by his hair in an ancient oak

[Col. 0917A] and, pierced by Joab’s spears, died. After Judas sold his master and father, namely the Son of God and the Virgin, he was moved by repentance and returned the price. Having cast it down in the Temple before the Jews, and driven by the devil’s counsel, stripped of charity and every good, he went away and hanged himself with a noose. A great heap of stones was cast upon Absalom, remaining until the present day [Note: No one will readily believe that, at the end of the twelfth century, when this author was writing, a great heap of stones still remained over Absalom’s tomb. We therefore suspect that these words have fallen in here through error, since the sacred writer of the Book of Kings also omitted them, Cols. 0917D, 0918D]. But upon the unhappy Judas fell the sin of enormous weight which will never be blotted out.

After Absalom’s destruction, David regained his kingdom in great glory, as the leaders of all Israel’s tribes came to meet him. So the Son of God and the Virgin, after Judas’s utterly unhappy death, received from God the Father glory and

[Col. 0917B] honour, kingdom, and everlasting authority in heaven and on earth—authority which he possessed without beginning according to his divinity. All the leaders of the heavenly host came to meet him and rejoiced beyond expression; indeed, as we believe, they reverently adored him with bowed faces. He ascended and sits at the right hand of the Father’s majesty. The heavens shall reveal Judas’s iniquity, and the earth shall rise against him; and his sin shall be manifest on the day of the Lord’s wrath, together with those who said to the Lord God: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job 21). He shall be brought to judgment to receive the full measure of torments—that is, to be punished in body and soul.

But to Jesus Christ, the supreme priest, all judgment has been given by God the Father, so that all may honour him as they honour the Father; and on the last day he shall judge the living and the dead,

[Col. 0917C] and the world by fire. He shall assign the devil and his companions, and likewise all the impious, to everlasting fire; but he shall admit the righteous with himself to the eternal banquet. Then he shall hand over to God the Father the entire kingdom which he acquired for him forever at the price of his blood.

It must indeed be known, dearest brethren, that many abhor Judas’s crime yet do not guard against it. Many detest Judas because he sold his Lord and master, yet do not cease to do similar things. Anselm says:

> For those who live in adultery, fornication, and other disgraceful acts; who sell or buy ecclesiastical honours; and who kill God’s people by their evil examples, betray and at the same time crucify the Lord Jesus Christ. Likewise, whoever sets a price upon Masses, as Judas did, sins grievously against Christ. For those who receive payment for Christ’s sacrifice undoubtedly sell Christ’s body.

The priests of the Church ought to celebrate Masses solely for God’s sake, for their own salvation, and for that of the whole Church. But—grievous though it is to say—those who celebrate them not in order to obtain Christ’s grace, but to be honoured by people and enriched with temporal goods, are beyond number. Therefore those who,

[Col. 0918A] as stated, sell the mystery of Christ’s Passion for human favour or temporal profit, what else do they do but betray the very Son of God and the Virgin? And when they presume with filthy hands and a defiled conscience to handle that most holy body, in whose presence angels stand and before whose sight not even the heavens are clean, what else do they do but crucify the Lord?

Sometimes too—and this is more grievous—the people incur guilt through priests who unworthily handle Christ’s body, as we read in the Old Testament. For when Eli’s sons defiled the Lord’s sacrifice, the ark of God was captured by the Philistines, and nearly all the people perished with them. Hence it is clear that whoever follows blind priests into the pit and shares with them, although unwittingly,

[Col. 0918B] also shares their punishments. Why? “Whoever touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13). So also those who communicate with unworthy priests, although unknowingly, are nevertheless defiled by them.

Though such men act unworthily, live perversely, and spend their lives in crimes, they nevertheless change the substance of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood. For it is not they, but Christ, who consecrates and who works salvation for his children even through unworthy ministers. Thus Christ’s body is not darkened by the unworthy, nor made better by the good, just as the sun’s ray is not dirtied by sewer-filth nor made brighter by a sanctuary.

But perhaps someone says: “If what is accomplished through unworthy priests is good, and if it is consecrated and given to those receiving it not by the priests, but by Christ, the supreme priest,

[Col. 0918C] why is this good thing turned to the recipient’s destruction?”

But it must be fully understood that the good not only does not benefit its recipient but even harms him, if, contrary to the prohibition, he receives it from one from whom he ought not to receive it. In Paradise no fruit was evil, since God made all things very good; yet man turned a good thing into evil for himself when he did not refuse to receive it from the serpent—indeed, from the devil. Therefore, if a faithful person, detesting the unworthy conduct of priests but reverencing Christ’s good body, simply receives communion from them, I believe that person is saved by this faith; for Joseph also received Christ’s body from Pilate.

Therefore such priests, who serve their own enticements, cannot appease God for themselves or for the people; rather, they offend him all the more. Moreover, by their entrance they pollute holy places and defile with their touch sacred vestments and vessels dedicated to divine worship.

[Col. 0918D] The assembly of angels abhors such men; the Lord himself flees and detests them. Of them it is said: “His sons provoked him—indeed, not sons, but men in filth” (Deut. 32) [Note: All here read: “They sinned,” Col. 0918D]. The Lord says to them through Moses: “I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their latter end” (ibid.). He called them sons because of their priesthood; he immediately added “not sons” because of their filth.

The Lord does not receive their sacrifice but abhors it. Hence it is said: “My soul hates your sacrifice, says the Lord, because you have offered me polluted bread.” Although the Lord’s body cannot be polluted, so far as they are concerned it is polluted when it is received indiscriminately as though it were ordinary bread. Their prayer is not received, but becomes sin, because God does not hear it. Their blessing is turned into a curse, as it is said: “I will turn your blessing into a curse, says the Lord.” Such men do not receive the Lord’s body, because they do not fear to handle it without reverence and worthy conduct. Only God’s children, who are to be incorporated into Christ and see the Father’s face, receive Christ’s body unto salvation;

[Col. 0919A] but those who do not remain in Christ, though they seem to put Christ’s body to their mouths, do not receive it; rather, they eat and drink judgment.

Christ’s body, as we believe, is carried to heaven by the hands of holy angels; but into their mouths a demon casts a coal, as the most glorious martyr Cyprian testifies. And because they receive Christ’s blood as though it were another wine, it is changed in them into dragons’ gall and the incurable poison of asps.

One may ask whether Judas received at the supper from the Lord’s hand the same thing that Peter received. The answer is that, as their intentions differed, so too did their reception of Christ’s body. Because Peter loved the Lord, he received the sacrament given by the Lord with its power. But Judas, because he hated the Lord, received the outward appearance of bread and wine, while the power of the sacrament remained in Christ. Again, so that Christ might show his betrayer more plainly, he gave Judas only a morsel of dipped bread—that is, unconsecrated—and immediately after it the devil entered into him and put into his heart the purpose of betraying the Son of God and the Virgin.

[Col. 0919C] Thus Judas harmed himself and benefited us by approaching a good thing evilly, because Jesus turned Judas’s evil into good for us. He harmed himself because, deceived by greed and avarice, he sold his Lord and master for thirty pieces of silver and nevertheless incurred eternal condemnation. He benefited us because through his betrayal our Redeemer was led to be crucified, we were freed from the devil’s power, and we were brought to the fellowship of the citizens above. He harmed himself because, proudly lifting his heel against his Creator, whose bread he ate, and deceitfully offering him a kiss, he consigned himself to eternal flames. He benefited us, I say, because the supreme shepherd patiently endured his manifold malice; suffered mercifully for us; willingly and with sovereign power laid down his life in death; and sought the sheep for which he had descended from the Father’s bosom. When he found it, he humbly placed it upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock of the heavenly fold.

[Col. 0920A] In this we surely recognize that all things are subject to God, so that even those who appear to oppose his providence unwillingly accomplish his will.

Therefore, beloved, as was stated above, many abhor Judas’s sin yet do not guard against it. For those who today, within the holy Church, repay evil for good to their prelates; stir up assemblies of foolish—indeed, mad—brethren to insult them; provoke lawsuits; multiply quarrels and scandals; willingly inflict losses; insolently hurl reproaches; intensify insults; slander secretly; publicly and irreverently bring forward false charges, sometimes even unheard-of ones; and strive more to resist their commands than to obey them—what else do they do

[Col. 0920B] but follow the perverse example of Judas the betrayer?

Those also who hate their superiors and, prompted by the devil, do not cease to criticize their actions with venomous tongues; who, spurred by envy, boldly contradict them; who with hearts inflamed by rage resist with all their strength even just actions; who strive to cast a stain upon their virtues; who seek to defame their good life in Christ; and who day and night do not cease to search—not in order to learn from them the discipline of heavenly life, but in order to find something by which they may accuse them—occupy the place of Judas Iscariot within the holy Church. So too, those placed in charge of ecclesiastical property, if from avarice they make private property out of common goods or secretly conceal anything, are imitators of most unhappy Judas.

[Note: Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 7, ch. 9, Col. 0919D.] This Judas Iscariot took his name either from the village in which he was born or from the tribe of Issachar, by a certain presaging of his future condemnation. For *Issachar* means “payment,” signifying the betrayer’s price by which he sold the Lord, as it is written: “And they received my payment, thirty pieces of silver—the price at which I was valued by them” (Zech. 11).

Therefore, dearest brethren, it is fitting that you who shudder at his detestable crime should also strive to avoid his evil works. Do not presume to sell or buy ecclesiastical offices, lest you suffer eternal punishments in hell with that same betrayer of the Lord. Prepare yourselves, in heart and body alike, with purity to consecrate the body and blood

[Col. 0920D] of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you may deserve to be satisfied by it at the banquet of eternal life. For he is the unfailing bread of angels and the sweet refreshment of all the saints. Do not receive temporal reward for celebrating Masses, lest you incur the condemnation of Judas the betrayer. Do not seek to sell for corruptible metals—gold or silver—the body of the Lord, dreadful to all the heights of heaven, venerable to the Powers, and adored by angelic spirits, lest you suffer in Gehenna torments worthy of so great a crime.

It is not beneficial but indeed condemnable to sell again for money the body of the immaculate and undefiled Lamb, Jesus Christ,

[Col. 0921A] who of his own will once offered himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross for us all (1 Pet. 3). Do not sell for a price the gifts of the Holy Spirit which you received freely.

Therefore, dearest brethren, strive to celebrate Masses solely for God’s honour, your salvation, and that of the entire Church. If anyone asks you, because of some need pressing upon him, to offer sacrifice before almighty God, whether for his own salvation or for the release of the dead, accomplish charitably what he asks, demanding nothing from him. Whatever he offers voluntarily, receive not as a price but as God’s gift. It is lawful for ecclesiastical persons to receive what the faithful voluntarily offer to God and to pour out prayers to God without ceasing for all the faithful, both living and dead. Hence the saying: “Those who serve at the altar share with the altar” (1 Cor. 9).

Therefore offer to God the Father the sacrifice of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for the living and for the faithful departed; and, making no demand and entering into no agreement, receive whatever the children of the Church devoutly offer to God.

[Col. 0921B] Perhaps one of you says: “I do not wish to receive their offerings, nor to pour out prayers to the Lord for them.” You who say this sin in two ways. You despise receiving what has voluntarily been offered to you for God’s sake, and make yourself proud; and by scorning to pray for the faithful, you show yourself avaricious, useless, and alien from the Church’s members. “If one member suffers, all members suffer with it” (1 Cor. 12). But perhaps you do not suffer with them because you have been cut off from the Church’s members.

Another says: “I have despised the world and entered a monastery; therefore I am not bound to pray for the dead or receive their offerings.” The answer is that precisely because one has especially despised this world’s riches for love of God, he ought especially to offer the sacrifice of Christ’s body for the salvation of the living and the repose of the dead, and to be sustained by the offerings and benefactions of the faithful. Only let him seek payment for this from no one, but receive what is voluntarily offered to God. For offerings are made not merely to the priest but also to Jesus Christ, the supreme priest.

Meanwhile, dearest brethren, it is fitting that we render due thanks with the utmost devotion to almighty God the Father, who did not spare his beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, but on this day delivered him into the hands of the impious for us all—indeed, for the salvation of the whole Church (Rom. 8).

[Col. 0922B] Let us therefore together beseech him with devout minds and abundant tears, that his most merciful Passion may be the forgiveness of our sins and his most glorious blood the price of our salvation, through him who lives and reigns as God with the same Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Twenty-Fourth Sermon: On the Resurrection of the Lord

[Col. 0921]

[Col. 0921C] The apostle Paul, dearest brethren, desiring by warning, exhorting, and correcting us to lead us with himself to the kingdom of God, says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3). It is as though he said: “If you have risen with Christ, despise earthly things for Christ’s love; love heavenly things; disdain transitory things; desire eternal things; put aside vain things; long for everlasting things; leave perishable and fleeting things; seek what always remains; despise carnal and visible things; pursue spiritual things; and finally strive to reach the heavenly homeland where Christ sits at God’s right hand.”

But amid these things it must be known that no one can rise with Christ unless he has first died to earthly vices for love of Christ. Without doubt, no one can rise with Christ unless he has first put himself to death in this world for love of Christ.

[Col. 0921D] We must die to the world in the flesh, lest we die to Christ in the soul. Christ is the life of the soul.

Therefore, dearest brethren, if we desire to rise with Christ to

[Col. 0922C] eternal glory, it is fitting that, as he deigned to die for us, so we too should strive in this life to die to sins and vices for love of him. “You are dead,” says the apostle, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” And again: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (ibid.). A person puts his members to death when he disciplines his eyes, lest they see unlawful things. The eyes are the first cause of desire and deception; for the mind is ensnared through the eyes, since through the eyes the arrow of wrongful love enters the depths of the heart [Note: Isidore, *Sentences*, book 2, ch. 39, Col. 0921D]. The eyes are the first weapons of fornication; unlawful words, the second.

Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). The apostle also says elsewhere: “Let not sin reign

[Col. 0922D] in your mortal body” (Rom. 6). If the uncleanness of fornication delights the mind more than the love of chastity, sin reigns in the person; but if love of most beautiful chastity delights the mind more than the foulness of fornication, sin no longer reigns

[Col. 0923A] in the person, but righteousness reigns.

Therefore every religious man should restrain his sight, lest his eye carelessly behold what his mind unlawfully desires. For as lust hurls the soul into hell, so chastity raises the soul to heaven. Whoever wishes to rise with Christ and reach the heavenly homeland must also close his ears so that he does not hear slander. Hence Scripture says: “Fence your ears about with thorns, lest you hear evil” (Ecclus. 28). Not only one who slanders his brother but also one who willingly listens to slander is guilty before God. Not only the person who bears false witness against an innocent person shall be condemned before God, but also the person who believes those speaking it. Nor is only the person guilty before God who utters a falsehood about another, but also the one who quickly lends an ear to those who speak evil.

For as a worm gnaws wood, and as a moth corrupts clothing, so slander corrupts the minds of its hearers. Hence the apostle James says: “Do not slander one another, brethren; for whoever slanders a brother slanders the Law and judges the Law” (James 6). Solomon also warns against presuming to slander one’s brother: “Remove from yourself,” he says, “a perverse mouth, and let slandering lips be far from you” (Prov. 4).

Blessed Isidore, our patron, says [Note: *Sentences*, book 3, ch. 32; but somewhat differently, namely: “Woe, however, to the man who refuses to correct his own life and does not cease to disparage the good,” Cols. 0923D, 0924D]:

> Woe to those who neglect to correct their own life and never cease to slander the good.

Accordingly, he also gives this counsel [Note: *Synonyms*, book 2, “On avoiding slander,” Col. 0924D]:

> Do not slander the sinner, but grieve with him. What you slander in another, fear rather in yourself. When you slander another, examine yourself; when you bite another, rebuke your own sins; look not at another’s offences, but at your own. You will never slander another if you examine yourself well. Do not defile your mouth with another’s evil.

[Col. 0923C] Therefore the servant of God must keep his ears apart from slanderers as from serpents, because, just as serpents infect the bodies of those whom they strike with poison, so slanderers pour deadly poison into the ears of those who hear them.

Truly, those who slander their brethren carry the devil’s poison on their tongues, because they do not cease to eat the raw flesh of their brethren. Hence blessed James also says: “The tongue is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3). The prophet David, detesting slander, also says: “The one who secretly slandered his neighbour, him I persecuted” (Ps. 100). It is as though he said: “If I knew someone slandering in my house, I never allowed him to approach me, but drove him far from me.”

One who desires to rise with Christ must also restrain his tongue from idle speech. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I tell you that for every idle word which people speak, they shall render account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12). Vain words ought not to be in the mouth of God’s servant. The servant of God’s words ought to be marked by gravity and teaching. Why? Because, as evil conversations corrupt good

[Col. 0924A] morals (1 Cor. 15), so good conversations correct bad morals. Let the servant of God’s words, therefore, be weighty and useful to hearers, as Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. 12). By his sweet words, God’s servant ought to strengthen the good in God’s service; urge the negligent to do good; call the discordant back to harmony; reconcile those in conflict; strengthen the weak; raise the despairing to God’s mercy; and do other things pleasing to God. For it is pleasing to the Lord (Ps. 149) that every ecclesiastical man should admonish his neighbours not to do evil and to persevere in goodness, and should recall to them the fear and love of God.

Hence in the Song of Songs the bridegroom, namely Christ, urges the bride—that is, the holy soul—to speak for the edification and exhortation of neighbours, saying: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening; make me hear your voice” (Song 8).

[Col. 0924B] It is called a garden because fruit grows in it. Other land bears fruit once a year, but a garden continually brings forth fruit. Thus Christ’s bride is rightly said to dwell in gardens, because the holy soul does not dwell in streets or public places but in gardens—that is, in cloisters and enclosed places. *Claustra* means enclosed places. There the soul that loves God encloses itself, hides from the tumult of earthly affairs, separates itself from the society of secular people, refreshes itself in the delights of holy Scripture, and, as far as possible, comes to know by tasting the sweetness and delightfulness of Jesus Christ, its bridegroom.

Let it therefore be said: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening; make me hear your voice.” It is as though he said: “O my bride, my friend, you who dwell in gardens—that is, who dwell in mind amid the delights of holy Scriptures; who meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord (Ps. 1); who devote yourself with utmost zeal to the fruitfulness of virtues—make me hear your voice, that is, the voice of your preaching, because friends are listening.”

[Col. 0924C] It is as though the bridegroom, namely Christ, were speaking more openly to the bride, that is, the holy soul, saying: “O my bride, my dearest one, I greatly desire that your sweet voice should sound in my ears, and that my friends who are listening should hear that same voice: namely your brethren and neighbours, who are my friends through the performance of good works. Thus may the sweetness and delight of my love bear fruit and give forth fragrance in their hearts through your preaching.”

The bridegroom, Christ, desires to hear the bride’s voice, because this is especially pleasing to Christ: that every religious man should strengthen the infirm and weak in God’s service and urge the negligent to do good.

“Friends are listening,” because the faithful in the Church eagerly await the friend of the bridegroom as he speaks. “Friends are listening,” because God’s servants in the holy Church,

[Col. 0925A] the more they love God, the more they desire to hear God’s words; for those who do not love God cannot hear God’s words. Hence the saying: “Whoever is of God hears the words of God” (John 8).

Therefore, dearest brethren, as has already been said, if you desire to rise with Christ, despise with your whole mind all things that are in this world, and with every desire pant after heavenly things; and, as though buried in a tomb, let there now be no concern for the world in you. As one dead in the tomb speaks evil of no one, is angry with no one, envies no one, injures no one, slanders no one, murmurs about no one, whispers about no one; takes no pleasure in seeing beautiful things, no delight in tasting pleasant things, no exultation in touching what is soft, no cheer in hearing laughter and jokes, nor is moved by hearing lyres and citharas: so neither should temporal things deceive you, most beloved brethren; let transient things not seduce you, vain things not flatter you, nor worldly things hinder you. Finally, despise while living those things which you cannot possess after death, so that, cleansed from all sins, you may be able to rise with Christ and may merit to attain the heavenly homeland, where Christ sits at the right hand of God: by the help of him who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in the Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TWENTY-FIFTH SERMON. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

[Note: [Col. 0925D] Sermon 160, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. V.]

[Col. 0925]

[Col. 0925B] Although all the books of the Old Testament foretold long beforehand the Passion or Resurrection of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, nevertheless the Holy Spirit also clearly showed it through the mouth of the prophet David, saying: “The God of vengeances, the Lord; the God of vengeances has acted freely” (Ps. 93). For he alone acted freely who today showed us what he did.
