[For even if, according to his humanity, he died for us, yet he was free in the very depths of hell. Hence in another psalm he says: “I became as a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87). And he was rightly free, since he was able to raise himself, as he had elsewhere said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall rebuild it” (John 2). Now our Lord Jesus [Col. 0925C] Christ became as a man, formed not merely in appearance but in truth, because he is both man—and who knows him? For, “being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2), so that through that obedience we might see his glory, “glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1). Thus the pattern of Scripture is maintained: both the glory of the Only-Begotten and the nature of the perfect man are preserved in Christ. Therefore he became as a man without help (Ps. 87), because, just as he did not need anyone’s help when he made the world, so he did not need a helper when he redeemed it.

[Note: [Col. 0925D] What we enclose in brackets the author interweaves from St. Ambrose, *On Faith in the Resurrection*, book II, no. [Col. 0926D] 102 and following.]]

Therefore the God of vengeances, the Lord, acted freely, because he was free among the dead, as a man without help.

[Col. 0925D] Yet do you wish to know what he did? Hear what he accomplished. Under no necessity, but by his own will, he permitted himself to be suspended on the wood; he did not refuse to have his body pierced by nails; by laying down his soul he endured death; he placed his flesh in the tomb; and, with his soul accompanying him, he descended to hell. He bound the prince of darkness and death, threw his legions into confusion, shattered the iron bars of the gates of hell, released all the righteous who were held bound by original sin, recalled captives to their former freedom, and himself illuminated with his splendid light those blinded by the darkness of sins.

Behold, you have heard how the defender of our vengeance is described as having acted freely. For after he was exalted—that is, suspended on the cross by the Jews—to summarize everything briefly, as soon as he gave up his spirit, that is, his soul united to his divinity descended to the depths of hell. And when he, like some splendid and terrible plunderer, had reached the boundary of darkness, the princes of hell and Tartarean legions, seeing him, were terrified and trembling.

([Note: [Col. 0926D] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the printed editions.] As though stupefied, and not recognizing that king, they fled from his presence, fastening the gates of hell; and immediately the prophetic or angelic utterance addresses them terribly, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be raised up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23). But the princes of hell, with excessive fear and great astonishment, began to ask and say: “Who is this King of glory,” so strong, so splendid, so illustrious, and so terrible? That world which was subject to us and always paid the tribute of death for our use has never sent us such a dead man; it has never allotted such gifts to hell. Who, then, is this man who has entered our borders so fearlessly, and not only does not fear our punishments but even releases others from [Col. 0927A] our bonds? Could he perhaps be the one of whom our prince said a little while ago that by his death he would obtain power over the whole world? But if this is he, the pronouncement of our prince has been turned to the opposite result: while our warrior seemed to himself to conquer, he himself has rather been conquered and overthrown.

[[Note: [Col. 0927D] Here too the entire material enclosed in brackets is absent from the edition.] The answer of the divine utterance: “This is the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” As though it said: the Lord strong in his Passion, mighty in his Resurrection; strong in flesh, mighty in divinity; strong because he conquered the strong one, that is, the devil; mighty because he despoiled hell: the Lord mighty in this battle. Therefore lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter: namely, he who came into the world without sin, against whom your prince unjustly stirred up the people [Col. 0927B] and handed him over to death without cause, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). At this voice the ministers of punishments, suddenly terrified and as though grieving inconsolably, reproached their prince, saying: “O our prince, why did you will to do this, to lay your hands upon a man in whom you found no sin?”]]

Is this not he whose future death you always celebrated? Is this he in whose cross you believed the whole world would be subjected to you? Is this he at whose departure you promised us such great spoils? What have you done? What did you intend to do? Behold, now he himself has driven away all darkness with his splendor, broken all prisons, cast out captives, loosed those in chains, and changed their mourning into joy. Behold, those who used to sigh beneath our torments now mock us because they have received salvation; and not only do they no longer fear anything, but they even threaten us. Never have the dead here been so proud; never could captives be so joyful. Why did you wish to bring this man to us, when at his coming all have been restored to joy who had formerly been subject to sorrow? No more of their bellowing is heard here; no groaning resounds. O our prince! You have lost through the cross those riches which you acquired by deceiving the first man. All your joy has perished; your gladness has been turned into mourning. While you suspend Christ upon the wood, do you not know how great losses you suffer in hell? [Col. 0927D] Why did you not foresee that you were bringing the destroyer of your kingdom to death without any guilt? You should have considered the cause; you should have sought for a fault. Why were you bringing into our country one in whom you had found no evil? You brought in one who was free, and lost all those who were liable.

After these utterances of the cruel infernal beings, without any delay all the iron bars were broken at the command of our Lord and Savior. Behold, suddenly innumerable multitudes of saints, who were held captive in death, fell at the knees of Jesus Christ their liberator and begged him with tearful supplication, saying: “You have come, Redeemer of the world; you have come, whom we daily hoped for in longing; you have come, Christ, whose coming the Law and Prophets had announced to us. You have come, granting in the flesh, while living, forgiveness to the sinners of the world, and to free the dead captives of hell. You descended to hell for us; do not abandon us when you return to the heights. You have set up the banner of glory in the world; set up the sign of victory in hell.”

Without delay, once the petition and dispute of the innumerable captives had been heard, at once, by the Lord’s command, all the ancient righteous receive the rights of authority and immediately turn punishments upon their own tormentors, crying to the Lord in humble supplication with ineffable joy and saying: “Ascend, Lord Jesus: despoil hell, bind the author [Col. 0928B] of death in his own chains, and now restore joy to the world. Let your faithful rejoice at your ascent as they behold the scars of your body.”

This Christ did, as was said above. Having made prey in hell, he came alive out of the tomb. By his own power he raised himself and again clothed himself with immaculate flesh. To remove doubt from unbelievers, he appeared to his disciples; to leave no ground for suspicion to the Manichaeans, he showed the wounds of the nails, ate and drank. Afterwards he appeared in the sight of many, ascended through a cloud into heaven, and returned to his seat at the Father’s right hand, from which the Word had never departed. Therefore let the Christian peoples rejoice, for whom Christ’s blood [Col. 0928C] was shed. Let us all rejoice in the Lord, who solemnly celebrate the resurrection of the flesh in Christ. Let the whole Catholic Church throughout the world rejoice, because Christ the Lord diminished nothing of his divinity and freed from the enemy’s power the human being whom he had made.

“[Note: [Col. 0928D] These are Ambrose’s words in the passage cited.] In him the world rose, in him heaven rose, and in him earth also rose.” In Christ the whole world rose, because through his death the faithful are rescued from eternal death, and through his resurrection are daily brought to eternal life. In him heaven rose, because through his resurrection he restored the losses of the heavenly kingdom. For he left ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness—that is, in heaven—and sought on earth the one that was lost, that is, the human being cast out of paradise through the devil’s envy; having found it and placed it on his shoulders, he brought it back to the flock (Luke 15). That is, he assumed our humanity from the virginal womb without sin and, having redeemed it from the enemy’s power through the triumph of the cross and resurrection, he took it up into heaven and placed it at the Father’s right hand.

Hence the Apostle said that all things in heaven and on earth are restored in Christ (Eph. 1), because Christ redeemed the human race, from which comes the restoration of the angelic ruin. Therefore Isidore, our teacher of Spain and our patron, says:

[Note: [Col. 0928D] Book I of the *Sentences*, ch. 10.]

“The number of good angels, diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be made up from the number of elect [Col. 0929A] human beings; and this number is known to God alone.”

Blessed Gregory likewise says:

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Homily 34 on the Gospels.]

“That heavenly city consists of angels and human beings; and we believe that as many elect human beings ascend to it as angels remained there.”

Hence it is written: “He set the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the sons [Note: [Col. 0929D] He persists in the distinctive reading, ‘sons of God,’ concerning which we have spoken elsewhere.] of God,” that is, of the angels.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] *Sentences* II, distinction 9: “It should be noted.”]

But since there are nine orders of angels, and there would have been no more even if the evil angels who fell had remained in their stability, it is asked how Scripture can say that a tenth order is to be completed from human beings. The answer is that a tenth order is not to be formed from human beings, as though there were nine orders of angels and a tenth of humans; rather, humans are to be assigned, according to the quality of their merits, [Col. 0929B] within the individual orders of angels.

Therefore, as has been said above, heaven rose in Christ because Christ then perfectly restored the losses of heaven, when, at the end of the world, he enters with his bride—that is, with all the saints—into the city of his Father, Jerusalem, in triumphal glory. As he himself says in the Gospel, speaking of servants who wait: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, will minister to them” (Luke 12). That is, having laid aside the form of a servant, he will show himself to the elect in the Father’s glory as he is, as he elsewhere promised his friends: “I shall manifest myself to them” (John 14). Hence it is also written: “We shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). “He will make them recline,” that is, rest eternally in the Father’s kingdom. “[Col. 0929C] Passing by, he will minister to them”: that is, on the last day, once that terrible judgment has been completed, passing by—that is, ascending to heaven and showing himself to them in his divinity—he will minister to them; that is, as he promised, he will prepare for them a place according to the quality of their merits, so that each in his own order, rank, and measure may receive a dwelling in which he may rejoice eternally in the vision of Christ himself and of his Father.

Alternatively: in Christ heaven, earth, sea, and the things in them rose, because, just as they experienced losses through the sin of the first human being, so through the triumph of Christ’s resurrection they will be restored to a better state. For when God has made a new heaven and a new earth after judgment, then heaven, sun, moon, stars, and waters—which now hasten in an unceasing and unretarded course, as though desiring to be changed into a better condition—will remain fixed in an immovable state. For then heaven will put on the glory of the sun, and the sun will shine sevenfold more brightly than it now shines, as Isaiah testifies. “On that day,” he says, “the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold,” that is, “as the light of seven days” (Isa. 30); because as brightly as the sun shone in the first creation before [Col. 0930A] the sin of the first human being, so brightly it will shine after judgment.

Hence the eminent teacher Isidore says:

[Note: [Col. 0929D] See the note in vol. I, p. 26, where we said that these statements are drawn from the *Master of the Sentences*, distinction 48, book IV, [Col. 0930D] and are not found in Isidore; rather, they have been compiled from the book circulating under his name, *On the Order of Creatures*, although in the cited chapter nothing more akin to this appears than what we there quoted.]

“On that day the sun will not set, nor the moon, but they will stand in the order in which they were created, lest the wicked, placed beneath the earth in torments, enjoy their light.” Hence Habakkuk says: “The sun and moon stood in their habitation” (Hab. 3), that is, in their order.

There will then be no alternation of day and night; rather, continual day and light will shine for the saints. Nor will the assembly of saints on that day need the light of sun or moon, because God will be their everlasting light. The stars also will shine with the splendor of ineffable beauty. But the water which merited to bathe Christ’s body and has washed the saints in baptism is said on that day to surpass all the beauty of crystal. The earth, indeed, which cherished the Lord’s body in [Col. 0930B] its bosom, will be wholly renewed like paradise; and because it has been watered by the blood of the saints, it will forever be adorned, unfadingly, with fragrant flowers—namely lilies, roses, and violets. And this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76). Therefore, as has already been said above, through the triumph of Christ’s Passion and Resurrection God will restore all things in heaven and on earth that experienced losses through the sin of the first human being.

It is therefore fitting, beloved, that we give thanks to almighty God the Father, who through the Passion, cross, and Resurrection of his beloved Son has deigned to redeem us from the enemy’s power and open to us the gates of the heavenly kingdom. Therefore, if God [Col. 0930C] the Father has raised us from eternal death in Christ and opened for us through his ascension the gate of the eternal kingdom, we ought, as far as possible, to walk as Christ walked. Let us therefore follow his footsteps as far as we can—not with bodily steps but with good conduct. Let us put to death sins and vices in our members; let us hasten through his grace to acquire the virtues of the soul.

For it is a virtue of our soul to love God above all things; to love a friend in God, that is, in goodness; to bear an enemy patiently and diligently for God’s sake. It is a virtue of our soul to pursue patience and avoid every impatience. It is a virtue of our soul to preserve chastity of both body and mind. It is a virtue of our soul to despise the vain glory of this world, [Col. 0930D] to scorn all perishable things, and, for love of him who redeemed us, to labor while we live in the body. It is a virtue of our soul to strive for humility and restrain pride. It is a virtue of our soul to repress anger and rage and show goodwill to our neighbors. It is a virtue of our soul to turn away from every folly and seek divine wisdom by every means. It is a virtue of our soul to reject every pleasure of the flesh and raise our mind toward Christ.

Through these virtues, dearest brethren, let us strive to die to sins and vices and rise with Christ; to be rescued from the hand of hell and hasten to the heavenly homeland, through the granting of the same our Lord Jesus Christ, who by being born, dying, [Col. 0932A] rising again, and ascending to heaven, deigned to win us for God the Father; with whom he lives and reigns as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## TWENTY-SIXTH SERMON. ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

[Col. 0931]

[Col. 0931A] John the apostle and evangelist says in his Apocalypse, for the instruction of the Church, among other things: “I saw another angel descending from heaven, having [Col. 0931B] the key of the abyss and a great chain in his hand. And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years; and cast him into the abyss, shut it, and sealed it over him, so that he should deceive the nations no longer, until the thousand years should be completed. After these things he must be released for a short time” (Rev. 20).

Thus blessed Isidore says concerning the nature of the dragon:

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Book XII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 4.]

“The dragon is greater than all serpents and than all animals upon the earth. The Greeks call it *drakōn*, whence the Latin *draco*, ‘dragon,’ is derived. It is often said to be drawn out from caves into the air, and because of it the air is stirred up. It is crested, has a small mouth and narrow passages through which it draws breath, and it [Col. 0931C] puts forth its tongue.”

[Note: [Col. 0931D] The edition reads: “and puts forth its tongue.”]

“It has its power not in its teeth but in its tail, and harms more by its lash than by its jaws. It is harmless in respect of venom; but therefore [Note: [Col. 0931D] Edition: ‘for this one . . . If it binds anyone, it kills him; from it not even an elephant is safe,’ etc. The words ‘tail,’ ‘immediately,’ and ‘even’ appear to be missing: [Col. 0932D]] it does not need venoms to cause death, because if it binds anyone with its tail, it kills him immediately. Not even an elephant is safe from it because of the size of its body: for, lying hidden by the paths through which elephants usually [Note: [Col. 0932D] Edition: ‘elephants customarily.’] pass, it binds their legs in knotted [Note: [Col. 0932D] Edition: ‘in various.’] bonds and kills them by suffocation. The dragon is produced in Ethiopia and India, amid the very blaze of perpetual heat.”

These statements about the dragon’s nature are fittingly applied figuratively to the devil. The dragon is called greater than all serpents and all animals upon the earth because, as the Lord says to Job among other things, “There is no power on earth that can be compared with the devil” (Job 41), whom the dragon represents. It is often drawn out from caves, because the same malicious enemy is frequently expelled from possessed bodies by divine invocation. The air is stirred because of it when he incites gatherings of the faithful to disputes and quarrels. The dragon’s crest signifies the pride of the ancient enemy. Hence he himself said: “I shall set my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). It is crested, has a small mouth, and narrow passages through which it draws breath and puts forth its tongue, [Col. 0932A] because, plainly, it suggests unlawful things not openly but secretly. “Narrow passages,” he says, “through which it draws breath,” but the breath of error, blasphemy, contention, [Col. 0932B]

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Other manuscripts: “detraction.”]

whispering, murmuring, and every kind of malice (2 Cor. 12). The dragon is said to have its power not in its teeth but in its tail, because the devil lies in wait for the heel. It harms more by its lash than by its jaws because in the present life it stirs against the elect temptations, sicknesses, tribulations, temporal adversities, and hardships; yet, guarded by divine grace, it cannot swallow them—that is, absorb them into its own body. Therefore, if it binds anyone with its tail, it kills him, because whomever it deceives on the day of death it draws with itself into destruction.

Therefore let blessed John say: “I saw an angel descending from heaven, having the key of the abyss and a great [Col. 0932C] chain in his hand; and he seized the dragon and the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan,” and so forth. *Anguis* is the name for every serpent, something that can be twisted and coiled. Therefore it is called *anguis* because it is angular and never straight. Thus that insatiable dragon, that is, the devil, is called *anguis*, because it never proceeds by a straight path but always by a crooked one.

*Diabolus* is a Hebrew word which in Latin means “flowing downward,” because it scorned to stand at rest in heaven and, weighed down by pride, fell downward. In Greek, however, *diabolus* is called “accuser,” because either it reports to God the crimes into which it itself entices human beings, or because it accuses the innocence of the elect with false charges. Hence in the Apocalypse it is said in an angelic voice: “The accuser of our brethren has been cast down, who accused them before our God day and night” (Rev. 12). In Greek it is called *Satanas*; in Latin it means “adversary” or “transgressor.” For it is the adversary, the enemy of truth, who always strives to oppose the virtues of the saints. It is the transgressor because, having become a prevaricator, it did not remain in the truth in which it was created. It is also the tempter, who asks to test the innocence of the elect.

Let it therefore be said: “I saw an angel descending from [Col. 0933A] heaven, having the key of the abyss,” and so forth. The angel whom he saw descending from heaven is the Lord Jesus Christ, who at his first coming came humbly for the redemption of the human race. Truly, the Most High and coeternal with God the Father descended from heaven when he humbly inclined himself to assume our humanity. The Son of God is fittingly understood here as this angel, who is called by the prophet Isaiah the “angel of great counsel.” The Son of God was indeed the angel of great counsel, because, sent by God the Father, he announced to human beings the counsel of eternal salvation.

“I saw,” he says, “the angel,” namely the Son of God, “descending from heaven,” that is, humbling himself in the flesh, “having the key of the abyss,” that is, eternal power, “and a great chain in his hand,” namely an incomparable binding in the working of his Passion and Resurrection. In this passage blessed John openly reveals the condemnation of the devil; he sets forth the reason why it is condemned, the time when it will be condemned, and who can overcome it—namely, the angel of great counsel.

Before Christ’s incarnation, that most savage dragon possessed his court—that is, this world—in peace, as a strong armed man; but one stronger than he, namely the Son of God, came upon him and bound him. He plundered his vessels, namely the hearts of human beings in which he dwelt, and broke his weapons, namely the pride and power by which he ruled the human race through tyranny. The Son of God and man, who in his first coming came humbly and was able to bind that dragon, the ancient [Col. 0933C] enemy, through his Passion and Resurrection whenever and however he willed, will undoubtedly be able altogether to destroy him when he comes in his majesty at the second coming.

Therefore Christ, God and man, at his first coming held in his hand the chain—that is, the unchangeable power which binds all things—by which he bound the dragon, that is, the devil, restraining it from harming as much as it wished. The dark abyss signifies the hearts of the wicked or the devil himself. Thus the Son of God, as it were, carries the key—that is, eternal power—in his hand when he restrains the devil so that even among the reprobate it may rage no more than is permitted it. The Lord himself speaks at the beginning of the book of the Apocalypse, saying: “I am the first and the last, and living; and I was dead, and I have the keys of death and hell” (Rev. 1), so that you may understand that he himself is this key, which is the one we read of at the beginning of the book. Christ has the keys of death and hell, because the key of life and death is one. For he casts down to hell those who live wickedly, and raises to heaven those who live well.

He adds again, saying: “And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years, and cast him into the abyss.” “He seized,” he says, “the ancient dragon,” namely, he hooked with a fishhook the one who harmed [Col. 0934A] human beings from the beginning of the world. “And bound him for a thousand years,” that is, deprived him of his former power, from the time of his Passion until Antichrist, during which time human beings can be made perfect through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Concerning this the Lord says to Job: “Behold Behemoth, whom I made with you; he eats grass like an ox!” (Job 40). *Behemoth* in Hebrew is interpreted in Latin as “animal.” It is also called an animal because, unwilling to remain humbly in heaven, driven out by divine power it fell into the world, in which, as was said above, it eats grass like an ox—that is, it continually absorbs into its body those who are weak and lax in God’s service.

Concerning it, God the Father, figuratively commending the Passion and Resurrection of his only-begotten Son, the Redeemer of the world, and indicating the order of Behemoth’s condemnation, at once speaks to blessed Job, saying: “In his eyes he shall catch him as with a hook” (ibid.).

Gregory says:

[Note: [Col. 0933D] *Morals*, book XXXIII, ch. 7.]

“For in a hook bait appears, but the barb pricks. Thus our Lord, coming for the redemption of the human race, made of himself, as it were, a hook for the devil’s destruction. For he assumed a body, so that while this Behemoth unjustly desired in it, as though it were its bait, namely death, it might lose us whom it held as though justly. Therefore it was captured by the hook of the Incarnation, because while it desired in him the bait of the body, it was pierced by the hook of divinity. For where there was humanity to draw the devourer toward itself, there was divinity to pierce it; where there was manifest weakness to provoke it, there was hidden power to wound the ravisher. Therefore Behemoth was caught by the hook because it perished from the very thing it devoured. This Behemoth indeed knew the incarnate Son of God but did not know the manner of our redemption. For it knew that the Son of God had been incarnate for our redemption, but it did not know at all that our Redeemer would pierce it by dying. Hence it is rightly said: ‘In his eyes he shall catch him as with a hook,’ for we say that we have in our eyes what we see placed before us.”

For the ancient enemy of the human race saw before him the Redeemer, whom it recognized and confessed, and, confessing, feared, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to destroy [Note: [Col. 0933D] Although the author transcribes all this from Gregory the Great, nevertheless, where the holy doctor reads ‘torment,’ Martin has written ‘destroy,’ with Augustine and others.] us?” (Matt. 8). Thus it was caught with a hook in its own eyes, [Col. 0934D] because it both knew and bit, and was ignorant before it feared; yet afterward it did not fear when it desired in him, as its own bait, the death of the flesh.

Therefore the Son of God and of the Virgin, through the victory of his Passion and Resurrection, seized this dragon, as was said above—that is, he showed it to have acted proudly—when it killed him who was free from sin. Therefore that malicious enemy was cast out from the hearts of the faithful through the cross and Resurrection of Christ, and began to rule more harshly over evil people. Hence it is also read in the Gospel that it entered into the swine (Matt. 8; Mark 5; Luke 8). “He bound him,” he says, “for a thousand years.” The number one thousand is used for the perfection of a thing. Hence it is said: “Of the word which he commanded for a thousand generations” (Ps. 104). Therefore, because of its perfection, this number signifies the entire time from the Lord’s Passion until the end of the age.

Moreover, it should be known that the devil was bound in the same way in Abraham and the other faithful as in those of the present time; but in them the hope of the future Christ bound him, whereas in these Christ himself, having come, bound him. For in Greek letters a thousand is marked by alpha: in alpha, which is the beginning, Christ is signified; and in the mark above it the cross is understood, which is our victory and the apprehension of opposing malice. Therefore in his cross and authority Christ bound the enemy of righteousness, who tempted the inhabitants of the earth. For no time comes upon that eternity, and his eternity is not to be enclosed by any end nor ended by a number of years.

It follows: “He shut and sealed over him, so that he should deceive the nations no longer, until the thousand years are completed.” “He shut,” that is, he forbade permission to go out. “And he sealed over him,” that is, he placed a seal, namely the sign of his holy cross, by which he so overcomes him that he repels him from the hearts of the faithful. It follows: “So that he should deceive the nations no longer,” namely to the point that those who are to be saved in God’s predestination should perish eternally; and thus a part is understood from the whole. “Until the thousand years are completed,” that is, until Antichrist comes. Therefore Christ set the bolt of the cross against him, so that he should no longer prevail or deceive the nations, which indeed he restored [Col. 0935C] through the Resurrection to a better state.

But the phrase “he sealed over him” means that it is hidden who belongs to the devil’s party and who to Christ’s. For even of those who appear to stand, we do not know whether they will fall; and of those who lie down, whether they will rise. He says again: “After these things he must be released for a short time.” Why? Because God so ordained that he should receive the power which he had before Christ’s coming; for then he will, as it were, go out to deceive the nations, because in comparison with that deception, the deception now at work is denied to be deception. Therefore the devil is not to be feared by God’s servants, because he is to be released for a short time.

Hence blessed Ambrose says: “The devil is allowed to be released for a short time so that the power of God and the weakness and impotence of that same devil may be revealed. God’s power makes his faithful strong and powerful; the devil’s weakness is overcome by girls and the tenderest little children.” I saw, during the time of this binding, the Church so released for good works, and in that same time I saw those who die for Christ enter immediately into glory and never descend to hell, as Abraham and the other prophets descended, although they were righteous.

Therefore God the Father granted his faithful a great gift through the Resurrection of his Son Jesus Christ: namely, that if they live perfectly, he at once places them through the ministry of holy angels in heavenly seats, [Col. 0936A] which was not granted before, however justly they lived. Through Christ, who died and rose for the salvation of the whole world, in this sixth age God the Father restores in his faithful—or rather, what is true, reforms into a better condition—whatever had perished through Adam’s transgression when the devil deceived him. Christ died for our sins and raised us with himself to eternal life. For this was prefigured by Moses’ rod: cast upon the ground, it was changed into a serpent; and when its tail was again grasped, it was changed back into a rod at the Lord’s command.

Let us, if you please—indeed, since it pleases us—review the history of that time more fully, so that we may more completely recognize what that sign foreshadowed. When Moses was sent to deliver the people of Israel, he is said to have questioned the Lord thus: “What sign have I, that they may believe that you have sent me?” And the Lord said to him: “Throw to the ground the staff which you carry in your hand.” He threw it down, and it was changed into a serpent. Moses was afraid and fled. And the Lord said to him: “Take hold of its tail; do not be afraid.” He took hold of it, and it became a staff again (Exod. 4).

What does this signify? For the serpent persuaded man to death; therefore death came forth from the serpent. Thus the staff in the serpent is Christ in death; and yet Moses was afraid and fled. What is Moses’ fleeing from that serpent, except what is recorded as having happened in the Gospel? Christ died, and the disciples were afraid; they withdrew from the hope in which they had been. But what is written? “Take hold,” he says, “of its tail.” What is the tail [Col. 0936C] except the latter parts? This signifies: “You shall see my back parts” (Exod. 33). For first it became a serpent; but, when the tail was grasped, it became a staff, because he was killed; afterward, however, when all things had been accomplished, by rising again he returned to what he had been, and there, through the restoration of life and the destruction of death, nothing serpentine appeared in him.

The serpent’s tail also signifies the end of the age, since thus the mortality of the Church rolls onward through slippery times. Some go and others come through death, as through a serpent. Death is the pathway; but at the last end, as at the tail of the age, we return to the hand of God. When it has grasped us, we shall be restored; and, with death—the last enemy—destroyed, we shall rise again and be the staff of the kingdom in God’s right hand.

[Col. 0936D] Now, since the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 0935] These are the words of Isidore, Book I Against the Jews, chapter 53.] did not see corruption in the tomb, but, having immediately conquered death, rose and returned from hell, he himself foretold this through the Prophet in the Psalms: “I kept the Lord always before my sight, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved” (Ps. 15).

As though saying more plainly: “I kept before my sight,” that is, even from that tribulation I saw from afar the Lord as rewarder; “before my sight,” that is, inwardly, where true sight is; and this not for an hour but always, or in all my works. Nor is this surprising: “Because he is at my right hand,” that is, at my better part, or as my helper and one favourable to me. Did he not help sufficiently when he caused me to rise again? And this was “so that I may not be moved” [Col. 0937A], that is, so that I may not seem to desist from my purpose because of any tribulation or persecution.

And because the Lord was at my right hand, therefore my heart—that is, my inward mind—rejoiced in the Passion, certain of recompense; “and my tongue exulted” (ibid.), that is, it uttered exultant words when he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me; rather weep over yourselves and over your children” (Luke 23). And elsewhere: “Amen, I say to you: today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid.). And similar things.

It follows: “Moreover, my flesh also shall rest in hope,” that is, not only did my heart rejoice, not only did my tongue exult, but further, my body received death as though it were rest, because of the hope of resurrection.

Otherwise, according to the same connection: “My flesh,” that is, the Church, “shall rest in hope.” Hence the Apostle says: “And the two shall be one flesh” (1 Cor. 6). Placed amid persecution and tribulation, it reckoned itself as being, as it were, at rest because of the hope of the second resurrection, which it conceived from my resurrection. Truly, “my flesh shall rest in hope,” because it will rise, as he says next: “For you will not leave my soul in hell.” These are the words of the Son crying to the Father. As though saying more plainly: “Father, you will not leave my soul in hell, but rather through it you will break the gates of death and snatch away your spoils through it,” as in that saying: “O death, I shall be your death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13).

Again he adds, saying: “Nor will you give your Holy One, who has been sanctified by you, to see [Col. 0937C] corruption” (Acts 2). As though saying: You will not only not leave my soul in hell, but neither will you allow my flesh to rot in the tomb. And rightly so, because “you have made known to me the ways of life,” that is, you have made known to me humility and obedience, which are the ways to life. For as we fell through the pride and disobedience of the first parent, so we rose through Christ’s humility and obedience.

Otherwise: Therefore you will not give “your Holy One,” that is, me, your only Son, to see corruption, because you have already made known to me the ways of life, that is, the resurrection by which one goes to salvation. And because I rose, or because I was humble and obedient unto death (Phil. 2), “you will fill”—that is, fill and refresh exceedingly—[Col. 0937D] me with joy in your countenance; that is, when I enjoy your glorious presence, delights and joys will be mine at your right hand, namely in the ascent to your better part.

Hence comes the saying: “He ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of God the Father” (Apostles’ Creed). This is not because there is a right or left hand in the Father, but is said solely by analogy with power: that is, among the Father’s highest goods.

Otherwise: “At your right hand,” that is, in your favour and graciousness, “there will be delights for me unto,” that is, continually, tending toward an end and never arriving at it; or tending toward the end in such a way that they are after all other delights. Certainly, at the Father’s right hand Christ’s delights are perfect and eternal; for although he received our humanity in time from his Virgin mother, nevertheless from God the Father he possesses true and unchangeable eternity. According to our humanity, indeed, he suffered for us and rose from the dead; but according to his divinity he lives and reigns eternally at the right hand of God the Father.

Of him the bride, that is, the holy Church, replying among other things in the Song of Love to the daughters of Jerusalem who questioned her, said: “His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires” (Song 5). What is signified by the belly except mortality, and by ivory except incorruption? For ivory is regarded as a very durable bone and is used for royal ornaments. Therefore Christ’s belly is rightly called ivory, because his mortality is brought to immortality when, through the resurrection, he is placed in eternal life in the glory and honour of his Father, namely the eternal [Col. 0938B] King. Of him it is said: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6), etc.

He is truly used as an ornament of kings who is shown to be king and lord of his own flesh. Likewise, through Christ’s mortality and resurrection, one is adorned with the love of kinship and the hope of immortality when he governs his deeds according to the rule of Gospel teaching. Hence it is said: “Let him who glories glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1), etc.

But his belly is said to be set with sapphires because, in the corruption which he bore for us, he interwove heavenly works with our sufferings through the miracles which he performed. For the sapphire, which bears an airy colour, aptly signifies the heavenly deeds shown in miracles. Therefore Christ’s belly is set with sapphires [Col. 0938C], because while he worked divine miracles amid the sufferings of the flesh, incorruption was, as it were, variegated within corruption. By this dispensation the apostles were trained in faith and made strong to endure sufferings.

Because the same Son of God and of the Virgin suffered for the salvation of humankind and rose from hell on the third day, the prophet Hosea foretold thus: “Come, and let us return to the Lord; for he has seized us, and he will heal us; he will strike and cure us” (Hos. 6). In this passage the faithful exhort one another to return to the Lord by doing good, having departed from him by doing evil. Thus this is the voice of the faithful. As though they said: “Come, let us return to the Lord, whom we abandon by sinning, [Col. 0938D] because he has seized us through becoming incarnate for us, since he took hold not of angels but of Abraham’s seed; and he will heal us,” namely by recalling our captivity to freedom through his Passion and resurrection. “He will strike,” like a loving father by chastising, “and he will cure” us from the wounds of sins through repentance.

It follows: “He will give us life after two days.” All these things were fulfilled in Christ; for he was betrayed on Thursday, suffered on the Preparation Day, and, rising from hell about dawn on the Lord’s Day, returned from there. Again he says: “On the third day he will raise us, and we shall live before him.” By these words it is shown that Israel and Judah will have one shepherd and king, namely David—that is, Christ—who according to the flesh was born from David’s line, when they have believed in the same risen Lord.

“He will give us life,” he says, “after two days,” namely those during which he lay in the tomb; and, rising from the dead on the third day, he will raise us with himself, and we shall live, healed, made alive, and raised, both in the present and in the future, before him—apart from whom we lay dead. We shall know him, namely in the majesty of his Godhead, either now by imitating him or by ascending to heaven, so that we may know the Lord face to face. Hence it is said: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). Full of the Holy Spirit, the prophet spoke these things concerning the future, which we now truly know to have been fulfilled through Christ.

The Hebrews dream for themselves at this point of salvation after a cycle [Col. 0939B] of a thousand years; but salvation is promised on the third day, on which Christ rose. They, however, refer the second day to the coming of their Christ, and the third day to the judgment by which they are to be saved. But let them answer: what is the first day, that is, the first coming of the Saviour? Since they cannot answer, let us say that the first day is the humble coming of the Saviour; the second, when he will be seen by men in glory; the third, when, judgment having been completed, he will show the elect a fuller glory of his brightness.

The Jews who accept the second and third day acknowledge that they have lost the first, because the second and third cannot be called such except in relation to the first. Or the first day is the first time of the age; [Col. 0939C] the second, Christ’s first coming, by which we are made alive through faith, or already confidently hope to rejoice with Christ in heaven; the third day is that of the resurrection, in which, through the same Christ rising again, we shall rise with him.

Otherwise: For us the first day is when we are reborn through baptism; the second, when we enter the rest of souls; the third, at the general resurrection. Moreover, when the prophet says, “We shall rise and live before him,” this may also be referred to those who were held captive in hell and rose with him on the third day.

Again the prophet adds when he says: “His going forth is prepared like the dawn.” Dawn is the beginning of light, by which darkness is driven away. As though saying more plainly: “Come, let us return to Christ; for as the darkness of night is driven away when dawn rises, so, when Christ went forth from the bridal chamber of the virginal womb [Col. 0939D], the darkness of sins is dispersed and the light of truth appears.”

Concerning Christ’s birth he adds further: “And he will come to us like the early and latter rain upon the earth.” According to the literal sense, the early rain causes scattered seeds to take root; the latter brings the fruits to ripeness. Hence the prophet says: “I shall give you rain in its seasons.” In the land of promise, indeed, rain is given from heaven once a year, as is said (Lev. 26). Spiritually, therefore, Christ is the early rain for us when he inspires faith, and the latter rain when after good works he leads us to the granaries; and he is always ready for those who rise in the morning [Col. 0940A].

Therefore the Jews who do not receive the early rain wait in vain for the latter. Swollen with human wisdom, they attempted to resist the divine dispensation; but immediately God’s wisdom caught them in their very cunning. For precisely where they unwillingly carry out God’s will, they strive to alter it; and while they attempt to resist the counsel of almighty God, they serve it. Hence it is said in Job: “He catches the wise in their own cunning, and scatters the counsels of the wicked” (Job 5).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0939D] Moral Discourses, Book VI, chapter 12]: “For it is certain that what frivolously resists the dispensation of God through human effort often openly serves that dispensation.” Therefore the Lord catches the wise in their cunning when he turns to the use of his will even that by which human will opposes him.

Let us consider further the wisdom of the Hebrews, and see what it forbade by foreseeing it, and what it provoked by forbidding it. Certainly, when a crowd of believers flocked to the miracles of our Redeemer, and the people’s priests, kindled with the torches of envy, proclaimed that the world was going after him, saying, “You see that we accomplish nothing. Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12), they attempted by his death to end his power, so as to cut off from him the force of such a great conversion, saying: “It is expedient that one man die for the people, and that the whole nation not perish” (John 11).

But the Redeemer’s death availed for the joining together of his body, that is, the Church, rather than for its separation. Hence, too, the Law commands that the throat of a turtledove [Col. 0940C] or dove, as a figure of our sacrifice, be cut (Lev. 5), but not entirely severed, so that even after death the head remains attached to the body. For the mediator between God and men, that is, the head of us all, and the true sacrifice of cleansing, by that through which he suffered death for us, adhered to us more truly. Therefore after the cutting the turtledove’s head remains attached to its body, because even intervening death does not divide Christ from the Church.

Thus the persecutors accomplished what they perniciously devised. They inflicted death in order to cut off from him the devotion of the faithful; but faith grew from the very source from which the cruelty of the unbelieving thought to extinguish it. And although they supposed that by persecuting him they were cutting off his miracles, they were, without knowing it, compelled to spread them abroad. Therefore the Son of God and man [Col. 0940D], when he allowed himself to be killed by the Jews, joined the Church to himself inseparably by rising again. Thus the Lord catches the wise in their cunning when he turns to the service of his mercy even what human cruelty kindled against him.

Crucified by the Jews and placed in the tomb, on the third day—after hell had been despoiled—his soul returned to his body; raising it from the tomb to live forever victorious, he appeared openly to almost all his disciples. Elisha fittingly prefigured him when he brought the iron up from the depths of the river to its handle (4 Kings 6). For when one of the sons of the prophets had cut down wood for himself, the iron of the axe happened to fall into the water. Thus the Son of God and of the Virgin, being in the flesh, was cutting materials: that is, he rebuked the Jews for unbelief. Hence it is said: “Now the axe is laid to the roots of the trees” (Matt. 3).

Therefore when Christ was fastened to the cross by the Jews and placed in the tomb, his divinity, descending in the soul to hell, left the body in the tomb as the iron of the axe leaves its handle. When the soul returned to the body, he rose on the third day as iron returns to its handle, and strengthened the disciples in faith.

But Elisha not only restored the iron to its handle, but also repaired it for cutting wood better than before. This signifies that God the Father not only raised from the dead the Son who is coeternal with himself [Col. 0941B], but also placed him at his right hand; and, for the lifting up of the humble, the destruction of the proud, and the building up of his Church, made him live more gloriously after the resurrection than before the Passion, subjecting all things beneath his feet. As though God the Father said to that same most beloved Son: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to scatter, to build, and to plant” (Jer. 1). Materials are unfruitful pieces of wood, and they signify people without the fruit of good works.

Before Christ’s Passion, errors and diverse doctrines, like contrary winds, disturbed the little ship of the Church and the whole human race. But after his Passion and resurrection, the tranquillity of faith was restored, peace was granted to the Church, the creature acknowledges the Creator, the thing made its Maker, sinners are converted to God in repentance, the lame leaps like a deer, the tongue of the dumb speaks, and the ears of the deaf are opened.

The prophet Jonah had already prefigured this, when he boarded a ship at the harbour of Joppa and fled to Tarshish from the face of the Lord, lest he preach to the Ninevites. But what does Scripture say? “The Lord sent a strong wind upon the sea, and there was a great storm on the sea, and the ship was endangered” (Jonah 1). The sailors cast lots among themselves; the lot fell upon Jonah, and immediately they threw him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. Therefore, as the sea ceased from its raging after Jonah was cast down, so after Christ’s descent into hell, his resurrection, and his ascension [Col. 0941D] into heaven, the errors of this world, the diverse doctrines of philosophers, and the superstitions of idols were quieted.

It follows: “And the men feared the Lord with great fear; and they offered sacrifices to him and made vows.” These men were not Hebrews but Gentiles; therefore their little ship bore the type of the holy Church. Before the Lord’s Passion they cried out in fear to their Gentile gods; but after his resurrection they fear God by revering and worshipping him, and offer sacrifices to him—not sacrifices which, according to the literal sense, they did not have amid the waves, but the sacrifice of a contrite spirit. And they make vows, namely that they will no longer depart from the Lord, seeing from the flight of the storm that the prophet’s words had been true.

Thus the holy virgin Church vowed [Col. 0942A] to cleave to Christ, her heavenly bridegroom, so that she might not depart from him under any sufferings or persecutions. Hence it is said: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or dangers, or the sword?” (Rom. 8), etc. Therefore, to God and man, her bridegroom, the holy Church hastens from all parts of the world with the highest devotion and approaches faithfully, because she knows that she has been redeemed by his most precious blood.

Accordingly the prophet Micah had foretold this long before, when, taught by the Holy Spirit, he figuratively cried: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains” (Mic. 4), etc. The mountain of the house of the Lord, that is, the Son of God, will come in the last days—that is, at the last hour—to hire workers [Col. 0942B], namely the holy apostles and ecclesiastical men, into his vineyard. Indeed, at the end of the ages, that is, in the time of grace, Christ has been raised not merely among the mountains but above the mountain-tops: above the patriarchs Moses, Aaron, Joshua, Samuel, and David, and above all the prophets who foretold him. That is, through the mystery of his most victorious Passion and resurrection, he was placed and glorified at the right hand of God the Father.

It follows: “And he shall be exalted above the hills.” He who appeared humble in the form of a servant shall be exalted above everything created. “And peoples shall flow to him”: great crowds of Jews and Gentiles shall gather in the manner of rivers, and nations from every people under heaven shall hasten to believe in him. This occurred after his resurrection. All the writings of the prophets are low by comparison with the prophecy concerning the Saviour’s coming and do not reach to the summit of the mountains. Compared with Christ’s manner of life, every human life is called a plain and a valley.

“And many nations,” he says, “shall hasten and say: ‘Come, let us ascend the mountain of the Lord,’” that is, to Christ, encouraging one another toward the banner of his holy cross; “‘and to the house of the God of Jacob,’” that is, the Church of the Saviour. Therefore ascent is necessary if anyone is to be able to reach Christ by the steps of good works. For the Son of God mercifully descended to us as if by certain steps of compassion, and again, after his resurrection, as the true [Col. 0942D] Sun of righteousness, he received himself into the Father’s right hand.

The prophet Isaiah figuratively showed beforehand this most humble descent of Christ and his most glorious ascension into heaven. For the consolation of King Hezekiah he caused the sun to descend ten steps on the sundial and then, by the Lord’s command, to ascend again through those same steps (4 Kings 20). Therefore the ten steps of the lines seem fitting for Christ’s mystery, so that they may interpret, without violating the rule of faith, the shadows of figures in the descent of this same our Saviour; through these same steps the same Sun of righteousness, Christ, ascended to heaven after his resurrection.

The first step of Christ’s descent from God was in the angels, because he was the angel of great counsel; the second in the patriarchs [Col. 0943A], because, as the Apostle says, “he worked in all things” (1 Cor. 12); the third in the giving of the Law, because it was he who spoke in the Law; the fourth in Joshua son of Nun, when he led the people into the land of promise; the fifth in the judges, because through them he judged and ruled that same people; the sixth in the kings of the Jews, because in them he reigned; the seventh in the prophets, because in them he was foretold; the eighth in the high priests, because he is the high priest and priest of his supreme Father; the ninth in man, because in order to redeem us he assumed the flesh of our mortality; the tenth in the Passion which he humbly and mercifully endured for us.

Through these ten steps, as through the shadow of the ancient Law, Christ descended to us from the Father’s bosom; and again, after his resurrection, the same Sun of righteousness ascended to heaven through them and illumined all that shadow of the Law with the rays of truth. For he is the light of those who believe in him, the life of those who trust in him, the way of those who desire to reach heaven; he is the fountain of spiritual gifts, the mountain of all virtues, the guardian of those who live well, the restorer of those who perish, the most merciful physician of the sick, and the most powerful raiser of the dead. He puts to death those living amid this world’s pleasures, lest they consume life uselessly; he gives life to those persisting in sins, lest they perish altogether.

Therefore blessed Anna, Samuel’s mother, exulting and praising God with her whole mind, says: “The Lord kills and gives life; he brings down to hell and brings back” (1 Sam. 2). [Col. 0943C] Undoubtedly the Lord kills with respect to vices and gives life with respect to virtues to those whom, through the Passion and resurrection of his most beloved Son, he predestined to eternal life.

When she repeats and adds, “he brings down to hell and brings back,” she looks to what the Apostle says. For he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things which are above” (Col. 3). For those to whom it is said, “Seek the things which are above, not those which are upon the earth,” are beneficially put to death, so that they may be those who passed over the earth while hungry. “You are dead,” he says—beneficially, that is—and “your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Rom. 4). Therefore we must both die to the world and live to God, because Christ died for our sins and rose for our justification.

“The Lord,” she says, “kills and gives life; he brings down to hell and brings back.” This may also be referred to Christ, because God the Father permitted him to die in the flesh for his people, brought him down to hell, raised him from the dead, and placed him at his right hand. Hence it is said: “You will not leave my soul in hell” (Acts 2). Concerning him she adds again, saying: “The Lord makes poor and makes rich; he humbles and lifts up” (Ps. 15). For us God the Father made Jesus Christ poor when he gave him to become incarnate for us, and enriched that same one with the surpassing glory of the resurrection.

“He raises,” she says, “the needy from the dust and lifts up the poor from the dung-heap.” As though saying more plainly: God swiftly raised needy Christ, who became poor for us, so that his flesh [Col. 0944A] might not see corruption. He raised him from the dust because he rescued him from corruption. Hence it is said: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption.”

It follows: “And he lifts up the poor from the dung-heap,” that is, from the sinful mass, namely from the Jewish people. Among that people, when the Apostle had said that he had persecuted the Church, he added: “The things that were gain to me, for Christ I considered dung” (Phil. 3). Again he adds: “That he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.” These words are plainly spoken of Christ: “That he may sit,” he says, “with the princes,” namely those to whom it is said, “You also shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19); “and hold the throne of glory,” namely by sitting in equality with the Father, because the Father has given all [Col. 0944B] judgment to the Son (John 5), and because his kingdom shall have no end (Luke 1).

Indeed, the kingdom of Jesus Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, shall have no end, because God the Father appointed him over all the works of his hands (Ps. 8). Of him the archangel Gabriel said to his most glorious Virgin mother: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever; and his kingdom shall have no end” (Luke 1). He is undoubtedly the most mighty lion from the tribe of Judah, who conquered Goliath—that is, the devil, the head of all wickedness—overcame the Philistines, that is, the demons, and delivered his Church from their hand.

Therefore the battle of the Philistines against Israel may be understood as the battle of demons against the holy Church. [Col. 0944C] Goliath signifies the devil’s pride, which David—that is, Christ—overthrew in single combat, namely through his cross and resurrection, and rescued God’s people. He also killed the lion and the bear, namely the devil and Antichrist: the one now lying in ambush secretly, the other later raging openly.

Thus pride challenged humility to combat, malice goodness, avarice charity, the creature its Creator, the devil Christ. David took up weapons of war which, because of his age and small stature, he could not carry, and laid them aside. He took five stones from the river and put them in a shepherd’s vessel; armed with these he conquered.

Thus Christ, at the time of the revelation of the New Testament, namely when grace was being set forth and commended, laid aside the bodily sacraments of the Law, which were not imposed upon the Gentiles: those, namely, which we read in the old Law and do not observe carnally, but understand as established for some signification already set forth. Christ laid these aside as burdens of the Law and took up the Law itself. For the five stones signify the five books of Moses. Christ took the five stones from the river, that is, from the age; for the mortal age flows away like water. The five books were in the river, like stones, for the first people. There they lay idle and did no good. The river passed over them; but David, that is, Christ, received grace so that the Law might be useful, which could not be fulfilled without grace. “For the fulfilment of the Law is charity” (Rom. 13).

Therefore, because grace makes the Law effective, grace is signified by milk [Col. 0945A]; for this is what is freely given in the flesh, when a mother does not seek to receive but to give. She gives freely and is saddened if no one is available to receive. David showed that the Law cannot operate without grace when, wishing to unite those five stones—by which the Law in five books is signified—to grace, he put them in the shepherd’s vessel in which milk was usually drawn. Armed with these, he went forth against the proud man.

He took one stone and threw it; he struck him in the forehead, and he fell at that part of his body where he did not have Christ’s sign. He took five stones, but sent one. Five books were chosen, but unity conquered. Therefore, as the Apostle says, the fulfilment of the Law is charity: “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4).

When Goliath had been cast down, David took his sword and cut off [Col. 0945B] his head. Thus Christ killed the devil with what belonged to him when the Magi believed—the very men whom he held in his hand and through whom he slaughtered others—and turned their tongues against the devil. Thus Goliath’s head is cut off with his own sword. The devil, as it were, killed himself with his own sword when he put it into Judas’ heart to hand over the Son of God to the Jews. That evil enemy was slain as if by his own sword and despoiled of the weapons in which he trusted when he delivered the Son of God to death by Jewish hands.

That most true Son of God and of the Virgin then conquered that same ancient serpent, that is, the devil, bound him with fiery chains in the depths of hell, and plundered his vessels, when, hanging upon the cross through the members of that evil enemy, he commended his soul into the Father’s hands. In that soul also, descending into hell, he drew out his own who were held captive there; and, rising from the dead on the third day, lifted them with himself to heaven on the fortieth day. For he endured the Passion not for his own sins but for our sins; and therefore he carried with himself to heaven those whom he rescued from the enemy’s power.

Hence blessed Peter says: “Christ died for our sins, the just for the unjust, that he might offer us to God” (1 Pet. 3), etc. In Christ’s person, blessed Job, bearing the type of the holy Church, speaks thus: “I have suffered this without iniquity in my hand, while I had pure prayers to God” (Job 16).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0945D] Moral Discourses, Book XIII, chapters 8 and 9]: “For the Son of God and man endured the Passion without iniquity in his hand, because ‘he committed no sin, [Col. 0945D] nor was deceit found in his mouth’ (1 Pet. 2); and yet he bore the pains of the cross for our redemption. He alone above all had pure prayers to God, because even in the pain of the Passion he prayed for his persecutors, saying: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23). For what could be said or thought more pure in prayer than that the mercy of intercession is granted even to those from whom the pain of the Passion is endured?”

Hence it came about that the persecutors who had furiously shed the Redeemer’s blood afterward drank it as believers and proclaimed him to be the Son of God. Concerning this blood he fittingly adds: “Earth, do not cover my blood, and let not my cry find within you a place of hiding” (Job 16). The sinful human being was told: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). That earth, namely, did not conceal the blood of our Redeemer, because every sinner who receives the price of his redemption confesses and praises it, and makes it known, insofar as he can, to his neighbours. The earth also did not cover Christ’s blood because the holy Church has now proclaimed the mystery of its redemption in every part of the world.

It should be noted what follows: “And let not my cry find in you a place of hiding.” For that very blood of redemption which is received is the cry of our Redeemer. Hence Paul also says: “And the sprinkling of blood speaking better things than Abel” (Heb. 13). Of Abel’s blood it had been said: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries to me from the earth” (Gen. 4). But Christ’s blood speaks better than Abel’s, because Abel’s blood demanded the death of his fratricidal brother, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors.

Therefore, lest the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection be idle in us, we ought to imitate what we receive and proclaim to others what we venerate. His cry finds in us a place of concealment if the tongue is silent about what the mind believes concerning his Passion and Resurrection. Therefore, lest his cry be hidden in us, but that each person, according to his capacity, may make known to his neighbours the mystery of his own quickening, it is fitting to turn the eyes of the mind back to the hour of the Lord’s Passion [Col. 0946C], when the Jews raged in persecution and the disciples fled in fear. For he who seemed to die in the flesh was by no means believed to be God. Hence it is aptly added here: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is in the heights.”

For when faith was shaken on earth, there was nevertheless a witness in heaven. The Father is indeed the Son’s witness, of whom he himself says in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me himself bears witness concerning me” (John 5). He is rightly also called one who knows him, because the Father always works with the Son in one will and one counsel. He is also his witness because “no one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11). Thus Jesus Christ had a witness in heaven and one who knew him in the heights when those who saw him dying in the flesh did not know how to consider the power of his divinity [Col. 0946D]. And although human beings were ignorant at his death, the mediator between God and men knew what the Father was working with him.

This may perhaps also be referred to the voice of his body, that is, the Church. For holy Church endures the adversities of this present life so that heavenly grace may bring her to eternal rewards. She despises the death of her flesh because she fixes her gaze upon the glory of resurrection; transient are the things she suffers, everlasting those for which she waits. She has no uncertainty concerning these everlasting goods, because she already holds the faithful testimony—namely, the glory of her Redeemer. In her mind she beholds the resurrection of his flesh and is strongly established in hope [Col. 0947A], because she hopes that what she already sees accomplished in her Head will wholly be accomplished in his body.

Beholding this holy Church as destined to abide in perpetual perfection, the Psalmist describes her under the name of the moon, saying: “The moon is perfect for ever” (Ps. 88). And because the Lord’s Resurrection strengthens her in the hope of resurrection, he rightly adds: “And a faithful witness in heaven.” Therefore, that she may not tremble concerning her own resurrection, she has in heaven as witness him who rose from the dead. Thus, when the faithful people suffer adversity, let them raise their minds to the hope of the glory to come and, trusting in their Redeemer’s Resurrection, say: “For behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who knows me is in the heights.” He is rightly called one who knows, because he knows our nature not only by creating it, but also by assuming it; for his knowing it is his having taken ours upon himself [Col. 0947B]. Hence it is said also through the Psalmist: “He knows our fashioning” (Ps. 102). For what wonder is it that he is said particularly to know our fashioning, since it is clear that there is nothing he does not know? Yet his knowing our fashioning is his mercifully assuming it into himself.

Nevertheless, this utterance can also agree with each one of us along with blessed Job. Every person who seeks human praise from what he does seeks a witness on earth; but one who hastens to please almighty God by his deeds considers that he has a witness in heaven. It often happens that even the good works within us are reproved by heedless people. But because a person has a witness in heaven, he ought not to fear human reproach.

[Col. 0947C] Truly God the Father is witness of the Son, because he himself sent him from heaven to show the way of salvation to the human race. Therefore, coming into this world as sent by the Father, he preached eternal salvation to Jews and Gentiles. Jonah, sent to preach to the Ninevites, indeed prefigures in his actions this same Son of God, to whom the Lord says: “Arise, and go to Nineveh, the great city, and preach in it the proclamation which I speak to you” (Jonah 3). As though God the Father were saying to Christ: “Arise and go to Nineveh,” that is, into the world, “and preach in it the proclamation which I speak to you”—my only-begotten Son, whom I begot before the ages. Christ’s preaching, then, is the Father’s. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I do not speak from myself” [Col. 0947D] (John 14). And again: “My teaching is not mine, but that of the Father who sent me” (John 7).

It follows: “And Jonah rose,” that is, Christ rose from the death which he endured and destroyed, by the Father’s will, for the redemption of humankind; “and he went to Nineveh,” that is, into the whole world through the apostles, in whom he was indeed speaking; “and he went according to the word of the Lord,” that is, according to the Father’s command. Allegorically, after Christ returns victorious from the lower world, he is properly said to rise; and he is said to preach when he sends the apostles to preach to human beings in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This is a journey of three days. Yet this sacrament of human salvation is accomplished by a journey of one day, that is, by confession of the one God, with Jonah—that is, Christ—preaching in the apostles [Col. 0948A], who said: “I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Nineveh was so vast a city that it could scarcely be traversed in a journey of three days.

Thus the Son of God, sent by the Father, came into this world and sought the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 10); and, that they might return to ever-green pastures, he admonished them gently and mercifully. This, indeed, was prefigured in Saul when he was sent by his father to seek the she-asses (1 Sam. 9). Saul, seeking his father’s she-asses, was assumed into the kingdom; and the Saviour, sent by the Father from heaven to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, and suffering for the salvation of those same sheep, was assumed as king over all the people. For the she-asses signify the same thing as the sheep. Saul receives a shoulder from Samuel [Col. 0948B], and Christ, after his Passion and remission, receives pre-eminence from God the Father. Saul was anointed by Samuel, and Christ was anointed by God the Father with a spiritual anointing. Saul towered above the people from the shoulder upward, because our Head, namely Christ, is raised above all things at the Father’s right hand.

Therefore through his Passion and Resurrection all things are subject to him, as the prophet Zechariah, long before in providing for human salvation, says: “Let all flesh be silent before the Lord, because he has risen together from his holy dwelling” (Zech. 2). He does not simply say, “He has risen,” but “He has risen together,” because he drew many with himself from eternal death to the Father, who is the highest good. “He has risen together,” he says, “from his holy tabernacle” [Col. 0948C]. For he rose, as it were, from his holy dwelling when, for the liberation of the human race, he descended from the bosom of the Father—from which he never departed. Christ therefore rose together when, for the redemption of his people, he spoke from his dwelling-place through patriarchs and prophets, apostles and evangelists, in whom and through whom he called back all nations to eternal life.

Again the prophet adds, saying: “The Lord showed me Jesus the great priest, standing before the angel of the Lord; and Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. 3). Allegorically, the Lord Jesus Christ is a great priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek. Though he cannot himself be seen, he is shown by the Lord through the assumption of flesh [Col. 0948D], standing before the angel, through whom is understood the Angel of Great Counsel. This does not mean that we receive two persons in the Son; rather, one and the same person is shown as a human being stained with filth, and is said to appear as the angel, the mediator between God and men. He stands because he remains in an unshaken station.

It follows: “And Satan stood at his right hand to oppose him,” because the Lord was tempted in every respect without sin (Heb. 4), and the tempter stands at the right hand because he strives to oppose Christ’s powers. “And the Lord said to Satan: May the Lord rebuke you”—namely, the Father; not because Christ cannot rebuke him, but because, in the unity of nature, when one rebukes, he who speaks also rebukes, for Father and Son are one Lord. Hence it is said: “He who sees me sees the Father” [Col. 0949A] (John 15). Therefore let Christ the great priest say: “May the Lord rebuke you, Satan; and may the Lord rebuke you, who chose Jerusalem.” God speaks in this passage in the third person. It is as though he said more plainly: “May the rebuke of God deprive your evil will of its effect, so that you may not harm as much as you desire.” This Son of God and of the Virgin chose Jerusalem, that is, the Church, which contemplates God’s peace.

“He is a brand plucked from the fire,” because he was in the world and was not touched by its blaze; for “the bush burns and is not consumed” (Exod. 3). He is also “clothed in filthy garments,” because he who committed no sin was made sin for us. But this filthy garment was removed from him when, by suffering on the cross, he blotted out our sins; so that, because he was clothed in filthy garments, we, rising in him, may always have white garments [Col. 0949B]. The changes of clothing are flesh now immortal and incapable of suffering. The turban upon his head indicates the splendour of divine majesty, so that he may be understood as the same God and man.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0949D] *Morals*, Book XX, ch. 18.]: “Satan stood at his right hand because he seized that people also which had formerly been beloved. The Gentiles, who had been regarded as the left hand, believed; and the Jewish people, who had been regarded as the right, turned aside into unbelief. But because a remnant is to be saved at the end [Note: [Col. 0949D] Isa. 10:22, according to the Old Latin version [Col. 0950D] followed by the Apostle in Rom. 9:27.], the Lord removes Satan from his right hand, saying: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan’; he also indicates the deliverance of that same people, who chose Jerusalem.”

Again he adds, saying: “Thus says the Lord [Col. 0949C] God of hosts: If you walk in my ways and keep my charge, you also shall judge my house, and keep my courts; and I will give you those who walk among these who now stand here.” God’s speech is directed to Christ, who for our sake was made poor in the flesh; whatever is said concerning his members is referred to him as their head, because our advancement is his victory. For he mercifully assumed our humanity, in which he conquered the devil, despoiled hell, and raised us with himself to eternal life.

Therefore, when we come “to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fulness of Christ,” that same Christ will judge God’s house—namely, us, who are the Church—according to each person’s merits, appointing in the churches prophets, apostles, teachers, and persons of this sort [Col. 0949D], as he is recorded to have done already in the primitive Church. Hence: “God stood in the assembly of gods; but in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81), distributing to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12). Then angels will also be given to the same Son of God and of the Virgin to minister to him: that is, human beings still established in the flesh who will lead an angelic life. They will not waver, but will stand before him, standing with him in steadfastness.

It follows: “Hear, Jesus, great priest, you and your friends who dwell before you, because they are men of portent.” He had first promised that he would judge his house, keep the courts, and have ministering angels—that is, persons of angelic dignity. But now he says to him and to his friends [Col. 0950A], that is, his disciples and prophets, that they are “men of portent,” set as signs of things to come, because they will possess complete felicity and perfect blessedness when he comes whose name is “THE EAST” or “THE RISING” (*Oriens*) (Zech. 6). He is also called the cornerstone, joining two walls into one (Eph. 2), and upon this stone are seven eyes, concerning which Isaiah says: “Upon him shall rest the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. 11).

Again he says: “For behold, I will bring my servant THE RISING. For behold, the stone which I have set before Jesus: upon the one stone are seven eyes.” Allegorically, Jesus the great priest is the Lord and Saviour, and his friends are the apostles [Col. 0950B], who are men of portent—that is, who behold his deeds mystically and know future things from present ones, and who interpreted the man born blind as signifying the Gentile people. According to another figure, he is called THE RISING because of the light, and the stone which, according to Daniel, was cut from the mountain (Dan. 2), because of the strength by which he shatters all kingdoms.
