Let God the Father therefore say to Christ the Saviour: “You and your apostles, hear the promises which I have made and which are to be fulfilled in you.” Then the speech at once turns toward the hearers, speaking of Jesus Christ: “For behold, I will bring my servant the Rising,” namely the Lord Christ, who is also the stone that crushes his enemies, “which I set before Jesus son of Jozadak”; because he came after him and was set before his face, since he understood that he himself was prefigured in him [Col. 0950C], in whom alone are seven eyes, because in him is the fulness of all spiritual grace.

Again he says: “Behold, I will engrave its engraving, says the Lord of hosts; and I will remove the iniquity of that land in one day.” He maintains the metaphor of the stone. It is as though he said: “I will cause this stone, namely Christ, to be wounded by the nails of the cross and the soldier’s lance; and in his Passion the iniquity of the earth will be blotted out in one day,” that is, the present day, of which it is said: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it” (Ps. 117).

It follows: “In that day, says the Lord of hosts, each man shall call his friend beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree.” It is as though he said more plainly: “On the day of Christ’s Resurrection, the man—that is, the person made perfect in Christ—shall call his friend, namely those who believe in Christ [Col. 0950D], whether from Jews or Gentiles, so that they may be beneath the vine, whose fruit gladdens the human heart, which says, ‘I am the vine’ (John 15), and beneath the fig tree,” that is, the most sweet refreshment of the Holy Spirit.

Again the angel asks the prophet Zechariah, saying: “What do you see?” And he answered: “Behold, I see a lampstand, wholly of gold, with its lamp upon its head; and seven lamps upon it, and seven pouring-vessels; and two olive trees above its head, one at the right, namely of the lamp, and the other at its left” (Zech. 4). Allegorically, the golden lampstand is the Church because of the spiritual understanding of the Scriptures; the lamp signifies Christ, who shines in the Church [Col. 0951A]; the seven lamps and their pouring-vessels signify the grace of the Holy Spirit, through which the Church receives the oil of God’s mercy; the two olive trees are Moses and Elijah, that is, the Law and the Prophets, who preached Christ’s Passion; or they signify the Gospel, which is at the right, and the Law, which is at the left, which prefigured it.

Again he adds, saying: “Who are you, great mountain, before Zerubbabel? And he shall bring forth the chief stone, and he made grace equal to grace.” In this passage the mountain is the devil and Antichrist, who dares to raise himself against Christ, saying: “All these things I will give you if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4). The Lord treads him down and says: “Go away, Satan; for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (ibid.). The chief stone is the Word, who was in the beginning with the Father [Col. 0951B] and descended from the Father’s bosom into the womb of the most chaste Virgin. He makes the grace of the Law equal to the grace of the Gospel, so that believers from Israel and the Gentile people may receive an equal gift.

Some interpret allegorically the two branches of olive trees, or ears of grain, and the sons of oil—that is, of richness or brightness—as the priesthood and the Law, which bring joy to the whole earth. Others understand Enoch and Elijah, one of whom pleased God in uncircumcision and the other in circumcision, and was taken bodily into heaven. The chief stone, therefore, signifies Christ, whom the Jewish priests sought to kill lest faith in him should increase further among the Gentiles.

For Saul’s sending his attendants at night to David’s house [Col. 0951C] to watch him likewise foreshadowed Christ’s burial and Resurrection. Saul here signifies the kingdom of the Jews. Thus it may be said: “Saul sent his attendants at night to David’s house, to watch him, that he might be killed in the morning” (1 Sam. 19). The Jewish people sent chief priests and soldiers to guard Christ in the tomb, that he might be killed in the morning—that is, that his remembrance and faith might be removed from human hearts. For Christ, having been crucified, died and was buried. His burial was like a house, to guard which the kingdom—that is, the Jewish people and the chief priests—sent men, when guards were stationed at the Lord’s tomb.

That the house was guarded in order that David might be killed refers to Christ’s body, which was guarded in the tomb [Col. 0951D]. For to take away Christ’s name is to kill Christ; for Christ would not have been believed in if the guards’ falsehood had prevailed, who said: “While we slept, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. 28). But neither could Saul kill David nor could the kingdom of the Jews remove Christ’s remembrance. Those, however, who presumed upon Saul’s power, that is, upon the kingdom of the Jews, stumbled against Christ, the stone of stumbling, as though against a statue of a kid; and the kid appeared to them to be a lamb, because they killed as a sinner him in whom they found no sin. He himself permitted them to crucify him—not because they prevailed, but because he willed it. He suffered for the salvation of the whole world, not under compulsion, but of his own accord.

Therefore in the third psalm he himself says: “I slept and was overcome with sleep, because the Lord upheld me” [Col. 0952A] (Ps. 3). And again: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me” (ibid.), etc.

Here the end of the matter, that is, of the Passion, is shown; hence he states that there is nothing to fear. Why? Because the Lord upheld and heard me. In what respect? Namely, in this: that I rose from death, and that the Father received me into the kingdom, from which, having sent the Spirit, he strengthens the preachers. And rightly so, because he voluntarily accepted death. This is what he means when he says, “I slept,” that is, I voluntarily allowed my Passion, “and was overcome with sleep.” Or, according to another reading, “and I began to sleep,” that is, death followed, as one passes from drowsiness to sleep.

Otherwise, according to the sequence of the text: “Because the Lord upheld me” [Col. 0952B]. The Jews rage against me, but I would not sleep unless I willed it; and this is “I slept.” It must therefore be pronounced with emphasis: I, who am so great, slept—that is, I was subjected to injuries. “And I was overcome with sleep,” namely, buried in the heart of the earth. “And afterward I rose,” because the Father upheld me.

It follows: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me.” It is as though he said: “Because the Lord upheld me, I am therefore now delivered, and I shall no longer fear thousands of people surrounding me as I hang upon the cross.” Augustine: “How great was the multitude that stood around the crucified one, yet after the Resurrection it could do him no harm.”

Otherwise: “I slept and was overcome with sleep,” etc. As though the Son of God and the Virgin said: “Truly the Lord heard me, because I slept—that is, endured tribulations—not under compulsion but led by voluntary will. And I not only slept, but was overcome with sleep,” that is, I endured death, “and rose.” Lest this should seem to have been possessed by himself, he adds: “Because the Lord upheld me,” that is, took me up again. For the Lord took me up from the womb and took me up from the tomb.

It follows: “I shall not fear thousands of people surrounding me,” etc. It is as though he said more plainly: “Because the Lord upheld me, I shall not fear; and, that I may not fear in my disciples: O Lord, arise”—that is, make me arise—“so that those who now lie in fear may be eminent in persecution; and make them arise so greatly that you save me in my own,” that is, make them persevere; “for he who perseveres to the end shall be saved” [Col. 0952C] (Matt. 10). “You, Father and my God,” that is, the God of my faithful people; for they worship no other God but you alone, Creator of all.

What else does prophecy indicate by these words—that Christ slept and rose—unless death is sleep and resurrection awakening? This is shown more plainly also in the fortieth psalm, where he himself speaks concerning himself.

“But you, Lord, have mercy on me and raise me up, and I shall repay them” (Ps. 40). Above he had said: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” (ibid.); and in this passage he cries to the Father, saying: “Have mercy on me and raise me up.” It is as though he said more plainly: “Have mercy on me, because I am needy and poor.”

Note that Christ petitions as man what he accomplishes as God. “Have mercy on me,” he says, “and in this way raise me up [Col. 0953A], so that I may repay them: in the present, by scattering them; and in the future, by condemning them.” Augustine: “That the Jews are now scattered throughout the whole world is for their warning, not yet for their condemnation; that will truly be at the last.”

Again he adds, saying: “By this I knew that you willed me, because my enemy shall not rejoice over me.” It is as though he said: “By this—that you willed me, that is, that I have always pleased you—I knew that my enemy shall not rejoice over me,” namely because you will raise me, and consequently they will not rejoice. For they rejoiced at his death but were confounded by his Resurrection. Or thus: “By this I knew that my enemy shall not rejoice over me”—namely, because you raise me—“I knew that you willed me,” that is, love me [Col. 0953B]. For in raising him, the Father’s love also appears.

Otherwise: “But you, Lord, whom I obey in this matter, have mercy on me,” that is, show mercy to my own by raising me. “Have mercy” in this way, that is, raise me up, “and I shall repay them,” either by converting them to good or by judging them for evil, having been appointed judge after their judgment. Or I shall repay them here also temporally, because what they thought they would retain—both place and nation—by my death, will rather become the reason why they lose both place and nation; for after forty-two years they were captured and slain by Titus and Vespasian.

And indeed, Father, you will raise me, because my enemy, who rejoiced over me dead, shall not rejoice over me raised. And in this, namely that you will raise me, I knew that you willed me, that is, that my obedience and sacrifice pleased you. As though my enemy will not rejoice, but I shall rejoice; and this is what he says: “But you received me from the tomb,” or, “you made your received one,” because of innocence, since, “free among the dead” (Ps. 87), I paid what I did not seize. And you not only raised me, but also established me [Col. 0953C], that is, made me immortal and incapable of suffering before you for ever.

For God the Father established Jesus Christ his Son as immortal in glory, because he is the true life of angels and of all saints, of whom it is said: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no more dominion over him. For in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6).

[Col. 0953D] And concerning him blessed Job says: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth” (Job 19).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0953D] *Morals*, Book XIV, no. 67.]: “For in not saying, ‘My Creator lives,’ but ‘My Redeemer lives,’ he openly declares him who, after creating all things, appeared incarnate among us in order to redeem us from captivity, and by his Passion delivered us from everlasting death.”

And it should be noted with how great a faith blessed Job binds himself to the power of the divinity, concerning whom Paul says: “Although he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13). For he says: “I know that my Redeemer lives.” It is as though he said in plain words [Col. 0954A]: “Every unbeliever knows him as scourged, mocked, struck with palms, crowned with thorns, insulted with spittle, crucified, and dead. But I believe with certain faith, and confess with free voice, that he lives after death: my Redeemer lives, who perished among the hands of sinners.”

“But what,” blessed Job, “do you confidently expect through the Resurrection? We ask you, confess it in plain speech.” It follows: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” For the Resurrection which he showed in himself will also take place in us. The Resurrection which he himself displayed he promised to us, because the members followed the glory of their Head. Our Redeemer therefore accepted death so that we might not fear to die. He showed the Resurrection so that we might trust that we can rise. Thus he did not will that the same death should last more than three days [Col. 0954B], because if his Resurrection had been delayed, we would utterly despair concerning ours.

This is fittingly said concerning him through the Prophet: “He shall drink from the torrent in the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109). For he deigned to drink, as it were, from a certain stream of our Passion, not in a permanent abode but on the way; because [Note: [Col. 0954D] The edition more correctly reads “because.”] he underwent death only temporarily, that is, for three days, and did not remain in that death, as we do, until the end of the world, but rose immediately after three days to live for ever.

He shows what follows in his body, that is, the Church: for by his example he showed what he promised as a reward, so that, as the faithful recognized that he himself had risen, they might likewise hope in themselves for the rewards of resurrection at the end of the world [Col. 0954C]. Behold, through the death of the flesh we remain in the dust until the end of the world; but on the third day he blossomed from the barrenness of death and, by the renewal of his own flesh, showed us the power of his divinity.

This is well demonstrated through Moses by the twelve rods placed in the tabernacle. For when Aaron’s priesthood, he being of the tribe of Levi, was despised, twelve rods corresponding to the twelve tribes were commanded to be placed in the tabernacle. And behold, the rod of Levi blossomed and showed what power Aaron’s gifts possessed (Num. 17). What, indeed, is signified by this sign except that all of us who lie in death until the end of the world remain, like the other rods, in barrenness? But while all the rods remained barren, the rod of Levi returned to flower, because the body of the Lord, namely of our true priest, placed in the barrenness of death, burst forth into the flower of Resurrection. By this flower Aaron is rightly recognized as priest, because through this glory of Resurrection our Redeemer, who sprang from the tribe of Judah and Levi, is shown to be our intercessor [Col. 0954D].

Therefore this rod of Aaron now flowers after barrenness, but the rods of the twelve tribes remain in barrenness, because the Lord’s body indeed now lives after death, but our bodies are still delayed from the glory of resurrection until the end of the world. Hence he cautiously introduced this very delay, saying: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” Thus, in considering the glory of our Head, we possess hope of our resurrection.

But perhaps someone may say in silent reflection that he rose from death because he, one and the same, was God and man, and by his divinity overcame the death which he endured through his humanity. But we, because we are mere human beings, cannot rise from death by ourselves. Rightly, at the time of his Resurrection, “the bodies of many saints who had fallen asleep rose” (Matt. 27), so that he might both show us an example in himself and strengthen us by the resurrection of others who were like us in mere humanity; so that, when a human being despaired of receiving in himself what God-man had shown in himself, he might presume that what he knew had been accomplished in those whom he did not doubt were merely human could also take place in himself [Col. 0955A].

There are, however, some who, considering that the spirit is separated from the flesh, the flesh turned to decay, decay reduced to dust, and dust dissolved into the elements before it is seen by human eyes, despair that resurrection can occur. As they look on dry bones, they doubt that these can be clothed with flesh and grow green again into life. Even if they do not hold faith in the resurrection from obedience, they ought surely to hold it from reason. For what does the world daily imitate in its elements but our resurrection?

At every daily moment, temporal light itself, as it were, dies when, as the darkness of night comes on, that which was seen is withdrawn; and it rises, as it were, each day when the light removed from our eyes is restored once the night has been suppressed. In the passing moments of the seasons, too, we see trees lose the green of their leaves and cease from bearing fruit; and behold, suddenly, as though a resurrection were coming from drying wood, we see leaves burst forth, fruits swell, and the whole tree clothed in renewed beauty [Col. 0955B].

We continually see the small seeds of trees entrusted to the moisture of the earth; not long afterward we see great trees rise from them and put forth leaves and fruits. Let us consider, then, the small seed of any tree cast into the earth so that a tree may grow from it, and let us grasp, if we can, where in such a tiny seed the immense tree lay hidden which proceeded from it: where the wood, where the bark, where the greenness of the leaves, where the abundance of fruit. Was anything of this kind visible in the seed when it lay in the earth? Yet, with the Maker of all hidden things wonderfully ordering everything, both the roughness of bark lay hidden in the softness of the seed, and the strength of timber was concealed in its tenderness, and the abundance of fruit in its dryness.

What wonder, then, if he reforms into a human being the finest dust, reduced beyond our sight into the elements, when he restores immense trees from the tiniest seeds? Therefore, because we were made rational, we ought to derive hope of our resurrection from the very appearance and contemplation of created things. But because the faculty of reason has grown numb within us, the grace of the Redeemer was added as an example. For our Creator came, accepted death, and showed the Resurrection, so that we who refused to hold the hope of resurrection by reason might hold it by the aid of his example [Col. 0956A].

Therefore let blessed Job say: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” Whoever despairs that the power of resurrection can be accomplished in himself should be ashamed before the words of a faithful man placed among the Gentiles. Let him consider again how heavily he ought to be struck with punishment if he still does not believe [Note: [Col. 0955] We have corrected this from the edition, since our manuscripts, owing to the omission of the word *credit* (“believes”), yield an incomplete sense.] in his own resurrection, though he already knows the Lord’s Resurrection to have taken place—if Job, that is, believed in his own resurrection, though he still hoped that the Lord’s Resurrection was to be accomplished.

But behold, I hear of resurrection; yet I seek the effect of this same resurrection. For I believe that I shall rise, but I wish to hear what I shall be like.

It must indeed be known by me whether I shall rise again in some other body, perhaps subtle or aerial, or in that body in which I die. But if I rise in an aerial body, I shall no longer be the one who rises. For how can there be a true resurrection if the flesh cannot be real? Clear reasoning therefore suggests that, if there is no real flesh, there will undoubtedly be no true resurrection. Nor can that rightly be called a true resurrection in which that which fell does not rise. But, blessed Job, remove these clouds of uncertainty for us. And since, through the grace of the Holy Spirit which you have received, you have begun to speak to us of the hope of our resurrection, state openly whether our flesh truly rises. It follows: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin.” Since skin is plainly named, every doubt concerning the true resurrection is removed.

Gregory: For, contrary to what Eutychius of the city of Constantinople wrote, our body in that glory of the resurrection will not be impalpable, subtler than winds and air. In that glory of the resurrection [Col. 0956C] our body will indeed be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, but palpable through the reality of its nature. Hence our Redeemer also, when his disciples doubted his resurrection, showed them his hands and side, and offered his bones and flesh to be touched, saying: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24).

When I had cited this testimony of Gospel truth to this same Eutychius, while he was in the city of Constantinople, he said: “The Lord did this in order to remove from the hearts of the disciples their doubt concerning his resurrection.” I replied: “The claim you advance is exceedingly strange: from that by which the doubting hearts of the disciples were healed, doubt arises for us. For what could be said that is worse than that we should become doubtful of the reality of his flesh precisely through that by which his disciples were cleansed of every doubt and brought to faith? For if he is asserted not to have possessed what he showed, then what confirmed the disciples’ faith destroys ours.”

The same Eutychius further added, saying: “Christ had a palpable body when he showed it. But after the hearts of those touching him had been confirmed, everything in the Lord that could be touched was reduced into some subtle state.” To this I answered: “It is written: ‘Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death shall have no further dominion over him’ (Rom. 6). If, therefore, anything in his body could be changed after the resurrection, then, contrary to the truthful judgment of Paul, after the resurrection [Col. 0957A] the Lord returned to death. What fool would dare to say this, unless one who denies the true resurrection of his flesh?”

Then this same Eutychius objected to me, saying: “Since it is written, ‘Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 15), on what grounds must it be believed that flesh truly rises?” I replied: “In sacred speech, flesh is spoken of in one way according to nature and in another way according to fault. According to nature it is said: ‘This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh’ (Gen. 2); and again: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1). But flesh according to fault is meant in the saying: ‘My spirit shall not remain in man forever, because he is flesh’ (Gen. 6); and as the Psalmist says: ‘He remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return’ [Col. 0957B] (Ps. 77). Thus Paul also said to the disciples: ‘But you are not in the flesh, but in the spirit’ (Rom. 8). They were not without flesh, to whom he was sending letters; rather, because they had overcome the passions of fleshly desires, they were now free through the strength of the Spirit and were not in the flesh.

“Therefore, when the apostle Paul says that ‘flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God’ (1 Cor. 15), he wishes flesh to be understood according to fault, not according to nature. He immediately shows that he means flesh according to fault by adding: ‘Neither shall corruption possess incorruption’ (ibid.). Therefore, in that glory of the heavenly kingdom, flesh according to nature will be present, but flesh according to the desires of passion will not be present; for, with the sting of death conquered, it shall reign in eternal incorruption.”

Having heard this, Eutychius immediately replied that he agreed; nevertheless, he still denied that a palpable body could rise. In the little book which he had written on the resurrection, he had also inserted the testimony of the apostle Paul: “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies; and what you sow is not the body that shall be, but a bare grain” (ibid.). He was evidently eager to show that flesh either would be impalpable, [Note: [Col. 0957] Correctly, “impalpable” (*impalpabilis*); *impalpabile* here is a copyist’s error: “not palpable,” as it is read in all editions except the Maurist edition.] or would not exist at all. Yet when the holy apostle, speaking of the glory of the resurrection, says, “You do not sow the body that shall be, but a bare grain,” he indicates what we see: grain grows with stalk and leaves, though it is sown without stalk and leaves. Thus, in arguing for the glory of the resurrection, he did not say that the seed-grain would lack what it had, but that it would possess what it had not.

Then, after we had been drawn into a long dispute on this matter, we began to withdraw from the bitter controversy with great restraint, when the emperor Tiberius Constantine of pious memory summoned both him and me privately, learned what disagreement existed between us, and, having examined the arguments of both sides, decided that the same book which Eutychius had written on the resurrection—its own arguments also refuting his claims—ought to be burned in the flames. When we left him, a severe illness immediately followed me; illness and death immediately followed Eutychius. After his death, because there was almost no one who followed his opinions, I neglected to pursue what I had begun, [Col. 0958A] lest I seem to be hurling words at ashes.

Yet while he was still alive and I was suffering from very severe fevers, all my acquaintances who went to him to pay their respects, as I learned from their reports, saw him hold the skin of his hand before their eyes and say: “I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh.” As they themselves testified, he had previously been accustomed wholly to deny this.

But setting these matters aside, let us inquire carefully in the words of blessed Job whether the resurrection and the body in the resurrection will be real. For we can no longer doubt the hope of resurrection, since he says: “And on the last day I shall rise from the earth.” He also removed doubt concerning the resurrection of the real body when he said: “And again I shall be clothed with my skin.” And, further to remove the ambiguities of our thought, he adds: “And in my flesh I shall see God my Saviour.” Behold, he openly confesses the resurrection, the skin, and the flesh. What, then, remains for our mind to doubt?

If, therefore, this holy man believed, before the accomplishment of the Lord’s resurrection, that flesh would be restored in its whole condition, how great will be the guilt of our doubt if the true resurrection of the flesh is not believed even after the Redeemer’s example? For if after the resurrection the body will not be palpable, then certainly one rises other than the one who dies; and, dreadful as it is to say, I die and another rises. Therefore, blessed Job, I beg you: add what you think, and remove for us the scruple of this question.

It follows: “Whom I myself shall see, and [Col. 0958C] my eyes shall behold, and not another.” For if, as certain followers of error suppose, after the resurrection the body will not be palpable, but the subtlety of an invisible body will be called flesh although it is not the substance of flesh, then certainly one dies and another rises. But blessed Job destroys their opinion by his truthful utterance: “Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another.”

Following the faith of blessed Job, and truly believing that the body of our Redeemer after the resurrection was palpable, we confess that after the resurrection our flesh will be the same and different: the same in nature, different in glory; the same in reality, different in power. It will indeed be subtle, because incorruptible. [Col. 0958D] It will also be palpable, because it will not lose the essence of its real nature. But let the holy man add with what hope he holds this confidence in the resurrection and with what certainty he awaits it: “This hope,” he says, “is laid up in my bosom.” We believe that we possess nothing more certainly than what we hold in our bosom. Therefore he held hope laid up in his bosom who confidently relied on the true certainty of resurrection.

Thus the Son of God and of the Virgin suffered for us wretched sinners, truly rose from the dead, and at the end of the world we too shall rise in this same flesh in which we now live.

The Jews thought that they could completely put him to death upon the gibbet of the cross; but he, possessing power, escaped from their hands on the third day—that is, he rose from the dead. The priest Abiathar prefigured him, for he alone escaped from the hand of Doeg (1 Sam. 22). Doeg the Idumaean, Saul’s chief shepherd, who was keeper of the camels—that is, of the unfruitful and crooked flock (1 Sam. 21)—is interpreted “moved” or “anxious.” He also struck the high priest Abimelech, [Note: [Col. 0959D] Ahimelech.] whose name is interpreted “my brother is king.” By name and deed he signifies Judas, through whom the devil worked deceit against Christ the true king, so that the king of glory himself might suffer and his disciples and priests might be put to death for his name.

But Abiathar alone, chief of the priests, escaped from the house of Abimelech, because, although the Jews handed Christ, the chief of priests, over to death according to the humanity which he assumed from the Virgin, [Col. 0959B] none could harm him. After his passion, however, rising victoriously from the dead, he ascended into heaven and carried with him red garments, that is, the marks of his passion. Concerning him Zechariah the prophet speaks figuratively:

“I saw by night, and behold, a man riding upon a red horse; and he stood among the myrtle trees which were in the deep” (Zech. 1).

By the night in which the vision is seen, the obscurity of mysteries is allegorically signified. The man upon the red horse is the Saviour, whose garments—that is, whose flesh—are red with the blood of his passion. He is shown on a red horse to the captive people, that is, the human race enslaved under the devil’s dominion. [Col. 0959C] Before his coming the Lord appeared to the patriarchs and prophets upon a high and exalted throne; but after the passion and resurrection he is shown in red garments and on a red horse, that he might plainly show that he endured scourges and wounds in his flesh for our redemption. In the Apocalypse of John, after his ascension and the liberation of the people from the hand of the ancient enemy, he is shown in white (Rev. 6). Here he stands among the myrtle trees, that is, among angelic powers, which ministered to him even while he was in the deep, namely, in the flesh.

It follows: “And after him horses red, dappled, and white”: namely, the apostles and apostolic men, sent by Christ after his resurrection, who travelled throughout the whole world. Some of them are red by martyrdom; others are dappled by works, teaching, and the diversity of signs; others are white through virginity, integrity of teaching—because they do what they teach—and purity of heart.

When the prophet questioned the Saviour concerning the revelation of the hidden prophetic sense, he promised that he would show what he saw. Yet while he promised, not he himself but the one standing among the myrtle trees replied, saying: “These are those whom the Lord has sent to walk through the earth.” As though he said: “These are the apostles, sent by the Lord to fill the whole world with his teaching.” Having again fulfilled the office of preaching, they return to the Angel of Great Counsel with thanksgiving, saying: “We have fulfilled the work entrusted to us, and the earth [Col. 0960A] formerly desolate is inhabited by God and rests from the conflicts of vices.”

The petition full of mercy, “How long, Lord, will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and on the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry?” refers to this: neither Jerusalem—that is, the Church—nor the cities of Judah—that is, souls confessing God—will receive true freedom and perfect consolation until the seventy years of this age have passed, true peace comes, and the sabbatical rest is fulfilled. Finally, the Lord answered with good words, consoling words, because “we know in part and prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13). But when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away; and, freed from the Babylon of this age, we shall cry: “When the Lord turned again the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted” (Ps. 125).

It follows: “And he shall pass through the strait of the sea”—namely, the Lord—“and shall strike the waves in the sea, and all the depths of the river shall be confounded; the pride of Assyria shall be brought low, and the sceptre of Egypt shall depart” (Zech. 10). With the Lord going before, we pass through the strait of this age. The apostles descended into this sea, where the elect are hemmed in, and the Lord himself first descended, that he might free us from its most bitter waves; and, when the strait had been trodden down, all the depths of the river might be confounded, so that, preaching amid the waves of the world, they might pass over on foot. With the devil humbled, his dominion shall depart from the saints; and the faithful, freed, shall be strengthened and glory in the Lord, saying: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6), etc.

Isidore [Note: [Col. 0959D] *Etymologies*, Book XIII, chapter 18.]: “*Aestus* pertains to the Ocean; *fretum* to either sea. For *aestus* is the advance or retreat of the sea. Hence there are changing conditions through which the sea now advances and now retreats. But *fretum* is so called because the sea there is always boiling: for a *fretum* is a narrow and, as it were, boiling sea, named from the boiling of its waves, such as the sea of Gades or the Sicilian sea. Varro says that *freta* are called as though *fervida*, that is, boiling, and possessing the movement of boiling.”

Therefore, as stated above, with the Lord going before we pass through the strait of this age; that is, by his resurrection we are freed from the dangers of this world. For our salvation he was born of the Virgin and lived among men, visible in body and invisible in majesty. He suffered at the hands of the Jews, and yet was not recognized [Col. 0960D] by them. David unquestionably prefigured him when he feared the face of King Achish and altered his mouth before him and his servants. Hence Scripture says: “David altered his mouth before them, and he was falling down between their hands” (1 Sam. 21).

Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain [Note: [Col. 0960D] *Questions on 1 Samuel*, XVI.]: “Achish is interpreted, ‘Why is he not?’ and thereby ignorance is signified; for it is an expression of one who is astonished and does not recognize.” This was fulfilled in the Jews, who saw Christ but did not recognize that he was the Son of God. Before the Jews Christ altered his mouth and departed, that is, made himself absent. There were then carnal commandments and sacrifices, and a priest according to Aaron; but he himself instituted from [Col. 0961A] his body and blood a sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek. Christ altered his mouth in priesthood and commandments, giving another testament and rendering the carnal observance void. He fell down in their hands when they seized and crucified him.

David fell before the entrance of the gate, and Christ humbled himself at the beginning of our faith. The Church begins from faith and comes to hope. That saliva, as of a madman, ran down his beard, the Apostle explains in saying: “We preach Christ crucified: to Jews indeed a stumbling block, but to Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). Saliva signified weakness; but because “the weakness of God is stronger than men” (ibid.), saliva flows over the beard. For as weakness is shown in saliva, so strength is shown in the beard. Therefore the Son of God concealed his strength beneath bodily weakness: what was weak outwardly appeared like saliva; divine power lay hidden within, like a beard. He suffered from our weakness, but rose by the divine power hidden within him. Placed upon the cross, he washed us from our sins in his blood; and, laid in the tomb, he penetrated the depths of hell and, by rising, carried with him to heaven his own who had long been held captive there.

Hence he himself said to blessed Job, in the form of a question: “Have you entered the depths of the sea, and walked in the lowest places of the abyss?” (Job 38). As though Jesus Christ, always coeternal with God the Father, said more plainly of himself: “Have you entered [Col. 0961C] the depths of the sea?”—understand, as I have: I not only sought the sea, that is, the world, through the assumed flesh and soul, but also, through that soul willingly laid down in death, descended even to the furthest depths of hell, as though to the depths of the sea.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0961D] *Morals*, Book XXIX, §23.]: “For if, according to the manner of divine speech, the sea ought to be understood as the world, nothing prevents us from understanding that the Lord sought the depths of the sea when he entered the furthest regions of hell in order to rescue the souls of his elect. Hence it is said to him through the prophet: ‘You made a way in the depths of the sea, that the redeemed might pass over’ (Isa. 51). Before the coming of our Redeemer, this depth of the sea was not a way but a prison, because it enclosed even the souls of the good, although not in places of punishment. Yet the Lord made that depth a way, because he permitted those whom he had freed from punishments and the prison-bars of hell to pass from there to the heavenly places. Hence it is openly added: ‘That the redeemed might pass over.’

“What he had called the depths of the sea, repeating it in other words, he calls the lowest part of the abyss; for just as the abyss of waters is not comprehended by our sight, so the hidden things of hell are not penetrated by any faculty of our knowledge. We see those who are taken away from here, but we do not see what recompense of punishments awaits them according to their merits. Yet it must be thoughtfully considered that he declares that he has walked in the lowest places of the abyss. For walking belongs not to one bound, but to one free. The steps of one held fast by chains are necessarily impeded. Since, therefore, the Lord endured no bonds of sin, he walked in hell. The free one came to those bound. Hence it is written: ‘I became as a man without help, free among the dead’ [Col. 0962A] (Ps. 87).

“Therefore, for the Lord to walk in the lowest places of the abyss is to find nothing that could detain him in the places of damnation, as Peter testifies when he says: ‘Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it’ (Acts 2). Or certainly, just as, while walking, we are led from place to place and are found present here and there, so the Lord is said to walk in hell in order to show that by the power of his divinity he was present to the souls of the elect in each place. Hence the spirit of wisdom is described as mobile (Wis. 7), so that by this it may be signified that, since it is absent nowhere, it meets us everywhere.”

The more marvellous the Lord regards this descent of his, the more frequently he impresses it upon redeemed humanity; for, repeating it again, he adds:

“Have the gates of death been opened to you, and have you seen the dark doors?” The gates of death are the hostile powers. Destroying them, the Lord opened them, because by dying he overcame them in strength. By another designation they are also called dark doors, because through the snares of their hiddenness, unseen as they are, they open the way of death to deceived minds. The Lord sees and crushes these dark doors because he perceives the fraudulent malice of unclean spirits. Unless he himself prevented them by his command while we remain unaware, our mind would know nothing of their snares and, captured by those same snares, would perish. We too see these dark doors when we are illumined by the rays of the light above. Hence it is said through the Prophet: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall look upon my enemies” [Col. 0962C] (Ps. 117). Therefore he himself sees our enemies who makes them visible to us.

Or, certainly, the Lord saw the dark doors when, penetrating the prison-bars of hell, he struck down the cruel spirits and condemned by his death those set over death. This is said here not yet in the future but in the past, because what he was going to accomplish in deed he had already accomplished in predestination. Since after his death and resurrection the Church grew and spread among all nations, it fittingly follows: “Have you considered the breadth of the earth?” For, while he sought the narrow places of death, he spread his faith among the nations and extended the holy Church into innumerable hearts of believers.

To her it is said through the prophet: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; spare not; lengthen your cords and strengthen your stakes. For you shall spread abroad to the right hand and to the left, and your seed shall inherit the nations” (Isa. 54). This breadth of the earth certainly would not come about unless he had first shown by rising the life which we did not know. For in his death he opened the eyes of our death and showed what life we ought to follow.

Hence in the Gospel: “Cursed is the deceitful man who has in his flock a male, and, making a vow, sacrifices a weak thing to the Lord; for I am a great king, says the Lord, and my name is terrible among the nations” [Col. 0963A] (Mal. 1). By the cursed and deceitful man is signified the Jewish people, who possessed in the flock of their nation the male lamb who takes away the sins of the world, and had made a vow concerning him: that they would humbly receive him when he came and reverently worship him. But when they saw him caught by the horns among the thorns (Gen. 22), that is, clothed in our humanity, they would not sacrifice him—that is, devoutly receive him and have him as advocate with the Father—but offered a weak thing, choosing Barabbas, by whom the devil is signified. But because Christ was the great king over all things, the nations venerate his name with fear and reverence, honourably worship his cross, and do not at all doubt—but confess and proclaim—that he rose from the dead on the third day, ascended to heaven, and sits at the Father’s right hand.

From the bosom of the Father he descended into the womb of Mary, ever Virgin; he illumined the whole world by the teaching of his Gospel; and he ascended again to the heavens from which he had descended. Of him John says: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). And concerning him the Father says to Job: “Can you bring forth the morning star in its time, and cause the evening star to rise over the children of the earth?” (Job 38).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0963D] *Morals*, Book XXIX, chapter 17.]: “God the Father brought forth the morning star in its time, because, as it is written: ‘When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of [Col. 0963C] a woman, made under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption as sons’ (Eph. 4). Born of the Virgin, he appeared like the morning star in the darkness of humanity’s night, because, having driven away the darkness of sin, he announced to us the eternal light of morning. He made himself known as the morning star because he rose from death at dawn and, by the radiance of his light, illumined the dark gloom of our mortality. Hence John fittingly says of him: ‘The bright and morning star’ (Rev. 22). Appearing alive after death, he became a morning star to us, because, by giving us in himself an example of resurrection, he indicated what light would follow.

“But the Lord causes the evening star to rise over the children of the earth because, as their merits demand, he permits Antichrist to rule over the unbelieving hearts of the Jews. They are justly subjected by the Lord to this evening star, that is, Antichrist, because they themselves willingly chose to be children of the earth. Seeking earthly rather than heavenly things, they were blinded to behold the brightness of our morning star, that is, Christ; and, while desiring the evening star to rule over them, they are submerged in the eternal night of the punishment that follows. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘I have come in the name of my Father, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive’ (John 5). Hence Paul says: ‘Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, that they may believe a lie, and that all may be judged who did not believe the truth [Col. 0964A] but consented to iniquity’ (2 Thess. 2). The evening star would by no means rise over them if they had wished to be children of heaven. But when they desire visible things, they lose the light of the heart and grow dark under the leader of night.

“Yet, if we consider this morally, we find how it occurs daily: for the morning star rises for the elect, while, by God’s permission, the evening star rules over the reprobate. For one and the same word of God is in the preacher’s mouth; when the former hear it with joy and the latter with envy, they turn for themselves the brightness of the morning star into the darkness of evening.”

Isidore [Note: [Col. 0964D] *Etymologies*, Book III, chapter 71.]: “Lucifer is so called because he bears more light than all the stars; he is one of the five planets. He is properly called *iubar* [radiance], because he pours forth the radiance of light. The splendour of the sun, moon, and stars is likewise called *iubar*, because their rays stretch forth in the manner of a mane (*iuba*). Hesperus is the western star, said to have been named after Hesperus, king of Spain. It too is one of the five planets, leading the night and following the sun. It is said that this star, when rising, makes Lucifer, and, when setting, makes the evening star. Concerning it Statius says:

> One planet is suspended in alternate rising.

“Planets are stars not fixed in heaven like the rest, but carried through the air. They are called planets from Greek ἀπὸ τῆς πλάνης, that is, ‘from wandering’ or ‘error’; for they are sometimes carried southward, sometimes northward, most often contrary to the heavens’ motion, and sometimes with it. Their Greek names are Phaethon, Phaethonta, Phironia, Hesperus, and Stilbon. The Romans, deceived themselves and wishing to deceive others, consecrated these stars under the names of their gods: Jupiter and Saturn, Mars, Venus, and Mercury.”

But the Son of God and of the Virgin, coming from the bosom of the Father, condemned idols through the preaching of his Gospel and the power of his resurrection; in the members of his Church he cut away vices and built up virtues by which the joys of the heavenly kingdom might be deserved. Of these it is said: “They have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5). Hence Jeremiah: “All destroyers have come upon all the ways of the desert, because the sword of the Lord shall devour from one end of the earth even to the other end” (Jer. 12). As though it were said more plainly: “Upon all the ways of the desert,” that is, upon all the nations, “all destroyers have come,” namely the holy apostles, because “the sword of the Lord,” that is, the preaching of his Gospel, shall devour vices and carnal observances from one end of the earth to the other.

Therefore, O human being, consider the earth that is within you and how it has been laid waste; and you will see that, after Christ’s resurrection, what was said has been fulfilled: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3), since the earth no longer works its works and there are no longer found in the righteous person those things by which the flesh was formerly nourished—namely fornication, impurity, lust, and so forth. Hence it is said: “I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). Before that Son of God and of the Virgin came, there was no sword upon the earth. [Col. 0965A] Holding [something unspecified], he says to his disciples: “Thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer, to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations” (Luke 24). For few from the people of Israel believed while he himself preached, but innumerable peoples of the nations followed the way of life when he died. While still passible and living, he endured the proud; but, having died to the passible life, he overthrew them.

Samson long ago fittingly expressed this figuratively in himself: while still alive he killed only a few, but after the temple was destroyed, he killed innumerable enemies when he died. Thus the Lord extinguished a few from the arrogance of pride while he lived, but many more when the temple of his body was destroyed; and those proud people from the nations whom he endured while living, he overthrew all together by dying. By rising, however, he recalled his elect to eternal joys.

For this purpose he himself was chosen by God the Father from the entire sinful mass before the foundation of the world: that he might powerfully and mercifully redeem the human race. Concerning him God the Father speaks through the prophet Isaiah: “Behold my servant: I will uphold him; my chosen one, in whom my soul has been well pleased” (Isa. 42). Christ is called servant because, according to his assumption of humanity, he was the son of Mary ever Virgin. Therefore Christ is servant in the form of a servant, and in the form of a servant, according to divinity, he is Lord of all. Thus let it be said by God the Father: “Behold [Col. 0965C] my servant, my chosen one; my soul has been well pleased in him.” Since God the Father says that he was well pleased in him, he shows that all other people displeased him: “For all have sinned and need the grace of God” (Rom. 3). Therefore God the Father chose him before and above all, through whom he decreed to defeat the devil and redeem the human race.

Of his praises the bride, that is, the holy Church, answers the daughters of Jerusalem when they ask, saying: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from among thousands” (Song 5). White, namely, in the Transfiguration; ruddy in the Passion. Hence it is said: “His face shone like the sun, but his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17). He was also ruddy with the blood of the Passion, as the prophet testifies in saying: “Why is your garment—that is, your body—red, and your garments—that is, your members—like those of one treading in the winepress?” (Isa. 63).

Thus he is called white and ruddy because, having absolutely no sin, he retained in full the beauty of righteousness, and yet approached the passion of death as though he were a sinner. He is “chosen from among thousands,” because, as was said above, among the whole mass of the human race no one besides him is found without sin. Yet he not only was without sin, but also redeemed sinners by his righteousness and blood.

“Chosen,” it says, “from among thousands,” because he was assumed from among many and for the salvation of many. He is fittingly called chosen from among thousands because after many thousands of years—that is, at the end of the ages—he deigned to become human and ascend the cross for the restoration of angels and human beings. The holy Church follows her sweetest bridegroom and Lord without hesitation, devoutly imitates him by enduring the manifold adversities of this world, willingly receives the cross for love of him, [Col. 0966B] and hastens unceasingly after him toward the heavenly homeland.

Therefore, in the Song of spiritual love the most noble Bridegroom himself addresses her in congratulation and praise, saying: “O dearest bride, how beautiful and lovely you are in delights! Your stature is compared to a palm tree, and your breasts to clusters” (Song 7). By the palm tree, Christ’s cross is understood. For the palm, rising very high, bears sweetest fruits; and Christ’s cross has prepared for us heavenly food, namely Christ, who truly is the bread of life for angels and human beings. Of him it is said: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77 [78]). The bride’s stature is likened to this palm—that is, to the cross—[Col. 0966C] because, through perfectly loving Christ, she willingly endures not only death but every adversity for his sake. Concerning this palm—that is, the cross—the same most glorious Bridegroom continues: “I said, I will climb the palm tree; I will grasp its fruits.” The most merciful Bridegroom of the Church, namely Christ, truly spoke and ascended; for, just as God the Father had ordained before the ages that he should die in order to rescue us from death, so at the end of the world he graciously and faithfully fulfilled it. Therefore he ascended the palm—that is, the cross—and grasped its fruits, because, hanging upon the cross, he found the fruit, took hold of it, and graciously bestowed it upon us. Hence what follows was fulfilled: “And your breasts shall be like clusters of the vine.” Truly, through the cross the breasts of the bride—that is, of the Church—are like clusters of a vine, because [Col. 0966D] in the death of Jesus Christ, her Bridegroom, the faculties of the soul received the two commandments of love. Nourished by these, the soul may be made drunk; made drunk, it may forget what lies behind and stretch forth to what lies before, so that, dying perfectly to the world and rising with that same Bridegroom, it may deserve, with him as guide, to attain the Father of all. For this reason he deigned to suffer for us and to rise again, and to make us rejoice with him forever in the sight of his Father and the holy angels. He hung suffering upon the cross for us, not because the Jews had power to do this, but because he himself willed it.

The prophet Malachi foresaw that this same Son of God and the Virgin would suffer for the salvation of the whole world, when he openly cursed in the word of the Lord those same Jews who crucified him, saying: “Cursed is the deceitful one,” [Col. 0967A] neither did the flesh desire against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh (Gal. 5). But after his passion and resurrection we were taught what belongs to flesh and what to spirit; and his teaching, like a sword thrust in, divided the earth—that is, the flesh—from the spirit, and destroyed it, because we carry about the mortification of Jesus in our hearts and live not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. But the spirit lives in us, and we sow not in the flesh but in the spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh, but eternal life from the spirit (Gal. 6).

Therefore, if we truly wish to celebrate Passover, we must by no means have bare but shod feet. Thus Jeremiah says: “Keep your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst” (Jer. 2). And in the Old Testament those about to celebrate Passover are commanded to have footwear on their feet (Exod. 12). The Apostle also proclaims the feet of those who are prepared in the Gospel to be shod (Eph. 6), lest, while they walk through the wilderness of this world, they be exposed to venomous creatures, which ought to be trodden down and crushed by the Gospel-foot. “Keep,” he says, “your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst” (Jer. 2). Hence it is said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink; and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). And again: “He who drew near to your feet shall receive of your teaching” (Deut. 33). Truly the Son of God and the Virgin abundantly pours the teaching of heavenly life into those who draw near to him, because in mercy he slept in death for his elect and rose again, as he says of himself through the Psalmist: [Col. 0967C] “In peace, in the selfsame, I will sleep and rest” (Ps. 4).

Exulting in spiritual delight and the hope of resurrection, he says this. It is as though he said to God the Father: “You have given me gladness” (ibid.), namely because in peace, which is “in the selfsame”—that is, immutability—I shall sleep, far from every tumult of the world, when this mortal has put on immortality; and I shall rest, that is, enjoy blessed life. And this will truly be so, because hope already exists which does not confound. This is what he says: “For you, O Lord, have established me singularly in hope” (ibid.). Cassiodorus.

Or thus: “In peace, in the selfsame”: “Those multiplied by temporal things labor, but I shall sleep in peace of mind, forgetful of this world, striving toward the selfsame—that is, toward that good which is in the selfsame, namely that which is changed by no variation but remains itself, abiding in unchangeable permanence—and I shall rest in the future. And this, Lord Father, will truly be, because you have already established me, or made me dwell, singularly in hope—that is, in the one hope in which the one and true good is singularly hoped for.” For God the Father established Jesus Christ our Lord singularly in hope, because he alone so rested that, immediately after death, he rose again, as indeed he did. For what is hoped for even by God’s saints will not be in multiplicity and the possession of temporal things, but in hope of heavenly goods. Augustine: “And he rightly says, ‘singularly.’” [Col. 0968A] This may also be understood in contrast to those lovers of the world who are multiplied by the season of their grain, wine, and oil. For this multiplicity perishes, while singularity is retained among the saints, of whom it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul in God” (Acts 4). Separated from all things born and dying, lovers of eternity and unity ought to cleave to the one God, who through the resurrection of his most beloved and almighty Son destroyed the devil’s powers and rescued his servants from his dominion.

Therefore the prophet Jeremiah says in amazement: “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and shattered!” (Jer. 50). The devil is the hammer of the whole earth. But there is one who does not care for the hammer of the whole earth: namely, the man [Col. 0968B] standing upon adamantine walls, with an adamant in his hand. History relates that adamant is stronger than every hammer that strikes it, remaining unbroken and invincible. Adamant, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0967D] *Etymologies*, book 16, chapter 13], is an Indian stone, small and unattractive, having an iron-rust color and the brightness of crystal. It is never found larger than a hazelnut kernel. It yields to no substance—not even iron or fire—and is never heated. Hence, in the Greek interpretation, it received the name “untamed force.” But although it resists iron and scorns fire, it is broken by fresh, warm goat’s blood; thus, softened by many blows of iron, it is shattered. Engravers [Note: [Col. 0968D] Editions: “engravers” (*scalptores*).] use its fragments for marking and perforating gems. [Col. 0968C] Moreover, it resists the magnet stone, so greatly that, when placed near iron, it does not allow the magnet to draw it away; or, if the magnet when brought near has seized it, it snatches it away and carries it off. Having briefly said these things concerning the nature of adamant, let us return to what we omitted above.

Thus the man who does not care for the hammer of the whole earth is the Son of God, standing upon adamantine walls—that is, above every treasury of virtues—because “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Col. 2). And the adamant in his hand is the righteous person. That is to say more plainly: the Son of God, who is true strength, does not care for the hammer of the whole earth—that is, the devil—and all his temptations. Nor is the adamant, that is, any righteous person [Col. 0968D] in Christ’s hand, trusting in his power, conquered by the assaults of that same ancient enemy. Although the hammer—that is, the devil—stands over him, and the anvil is placed beneath, namely the dragon, as an unconquerable coldness, nevertheless the adamant standing in the Lord’s hand and before his face—that is, the holy person—suffers nothing.

There are, therefore, two things contrary to the righteous adamant: the hammer and the anvil. Hence the proverb concerning those oppressed by anxieties: “They are between the hammer and the anvil.” Yet the righteous person does not care for hammer and anvil, because the more he is struck, the more brightly his virtue shines. Moses could not break the hammer of the whole earth, nor Abraham before him, nor Joshua after him, nor any of the prophets. But Christ powerfully shattered it, as the amazed prophet says: “How the hammer of the whole earth has been broken and shattered!” (Jer. 50). The hammer, that is, the devil, was first broken when he said to the Redeemer: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4), etc. Afterwards he was crushed through the triumph of the holy cross and condemned forever in his own cunning. He is also broken through each one of us when we are brought into the Church and perfected in faith. He is crushed and ground down when we attain perfection. Therefore the Son of God and the Virgin crushed the hammer of the whole earth through the triumph of the cross, when, in his passion, his disciples left him, [Col. 0969B] the Jews fastened him to the cross, all who knew him stood at a distance, while the women drew nearer—indeed, they persevered even to the burial.

To this may fittingly be applied, in a typological sense, what blessed Job says in his affliction: “My bone clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed, and only my lips were left around my teeth” (Job 19). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0969D] *Morals*, book 14, chapter 23]: “Strength is signified by bone, but bodily weakness by flesh. Since the holy Church is joined to Christ her head, what is signified by bone but the Lord himself? And what by flesh but the disciples, who in the time of his passion had weak understanding? And by the skin, which remains outside the flesh upon the body, [Col. 0969C] what is signified but those holy women, who served the Lord in outward ministries, preparing what was needed for his body? For while his disciples, though not yet firm, preached to the people the faith of truth, the flesh clung to its bone. And while the holy women prepared the outward necessities, they remained like skin outside the body. But when the hour of the cross came, a heavy fear arising from the Jews’ persecution overcame his disciples: all fled, but the women stood by. Thus, with the flesh consumed, the Lord’s bone clung to his skin, because at the time of his passion, when the disciples fled, his strength found the women near him.

“Peter indeed stood for a time, yet, frightened, he afterwards denied him. John also stood by, to whom at the very time of the cross it was said: ‘Behold your mother’ [Col. 0969D] (John 19). But he could not persevere in the least, because it is also written of him that ‘a certain young man followed him, clothed with a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he cast off the linen cloth and fled from them naked’ (Mark 14). Although afterwards he returned at the hour of the cross to hear the words of his Redeemer, he nevertheless fled in fear first. But the women are remembered not merely as neither fearing nor fleeing, but also as standing even to the tomb.

“Therefore let this same Son of God and the Virgin say: ‘My bone clung to my skin, my flesh being consumed, and only my lips were left around my teeth.’ That is: those who ought to have clung more closely to strength were consumed by fear at the time of my passion; but those whom I had appointed to outward ministries I found faithfully adhering to me in my passion without fear. Here it is aptly added that these words are spoken mystically, when it follows: ‘And only my lips were left around my teeth.’ What have we around the teeth but lips, even if we suffer no scourges? But what is signified by lips except speech, and what by teeth except the holy apostles? They were placed in the body of the Church for this purpose: to bite the carnal by correction and break them from their stubborn hardness. Hence the same first of the apostles, like a tooth placed in his body, is told: ‘Kill and eat’ (Acts 10).

“But these teeth, which in the time of his passion had lost through fear of death the bite of correction, lost also [Col. 0970B] confidence of strength and the efficacy of every kind of action, so that two of them, walking after his death and resurrection, spoke on the road and said: ‘We hoped that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel’ (Luke 24). It is rightly said now: ‘Only my lips were left around my teeth.’ They were still talking about him, but no longer believed in him. Only lips had remained around his teeth, because they had lost the power of good action; and while they uttered only words of conversation about him, they still had the bite of correction and the movement of speech. Thus only lips remained around the teeth, because they still knew how to talk about him, but feared now to preach him or to bite the vices of unbelievers.”

But he, as teacher of truth and source of all goodness, rebuked their hardness, strengthened them in faith, made them burn in love for himself, opened to them the meaning of the Scriptures, and made known the truth of his resurrection, saying: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer, and r. a. d. t. [Note: [Col. 0969D] Since in both manuscripts this text appears only in initial letters, as may be seen, it may be read: “rise again on the third day.”], and thus enter into his glory?” (ibid.). [Col. 0970C] By these words our Lord Jesus Christ produced the ardor of love in the disciples’ hearts and proclaimed to all his people the joy of eternal salvation, as God the Father had long before foretold through the prophet Jeremiah.

“I,” he says, “will lay upon them a scar and healing, and I will heal them; and I will reveal to them the prayer of peace and [Col. 0970D] truth, and I will restore the restoration of Judah and Jerusalem” (Jer. 33). It is as though God the Father more plainly set forth to the nations the mercy of the advent, the remedy of the passion, and the glory of his most beloved Son’s resurrection. “Behold, I,” he says, “and no other, will lay upon them a scar and healing”: that is, upon the nations wounded by the devil through the serpent, I shall bestow the medicine of the passion and the healing of the resurrection of Christ, my only Son. “And I will heal them,” namely through baptism and repentance from the infirmities of sins. “And through the apostles I will reveal to them the prayer of peace and truth,” namely my spiritual praises. “And I will restore the restoration of Judah and Jerusalem,” namely true Christians confessing Christ, to the bosom of the holy Church. It follows: “And I will be merciful to all their iniquities, in which they sinned and despised me.” It is as though he said: Through Christ’s passion and resurrection I shall be merciful to all their iniquities, while the apostles impart baptism and repentance to them. “I shall be merciful,” he says, “to their iniquities by which they despised me, because, despising me, they worshipped idols.”

Again he says: “And this name shall be to me for praise and joy and exultation among all nations of the earth, which shall hear all the good things that I will do for them.” Mystically, this passage prophesies the restoration through faith in Christ of the Church of the nations, which had been deserted by the Lord because of idolatry and the greatness of its crimes, and its filling with a multitude of believers from diverse [Col. 0971B] nations. To it Isaiah says: “The desert and trackless land shall rejoice, and the wilderness shall exult” (Isa. 35), etc. And elsewhere: “Praise, barren woman who does not bear; sing praise and cry out, you who did not give birth; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54).

Again the Lord, continuing to speak of the praises of the Church, which are today devoutly offered to him by the faithful in great glory, says: “There shall again be heard in this place,” that is, in the Church, “the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride, the voice of those who say: ‘Give thanks to the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good, for his mercy is forever’; and of those bearing vows into the house of the Lord.” What could be said more beautifully, sweetly, [Col. 0971C] or plainly concerning Christ and the Church? These words clearly announce the gathering of the Church, the rejection of the Synagogue, and the glorification of Christ. It is as though he said: There shall again be in the Church a voice of joy and gladness—that is, Alleluia; the voice of the bridegroom, namely the preaching of the Gospel of Jesus Christ; and the voice of the bride, that is, of the Church; the voice of those saying, “Give thanks to the Lord of hosts, for the Lord is good”—namely the choirs of religious men, monks, canons, consecrated women, and the rest who serve God, praising him day and night and saying, “For he is good, for his mercy is eternal.” There shall also be heard the voice of those bearing their vows, that is, offering themselves to God, into the house of the Lord not made by hands.

Indeed, within the holy Church the tabernacles of converted believers of both sexes are rebuilt—namely, monasteries endowed with an abundance of every good thing for the praise of God—so that from them the Lord’s glory may be proclaimed and praise and joy may arise among all nations. These things seem to refer to the time of Christ’s resurrection and ascension, in which the Lord, through the grace of the Holy Spirit and through the holy apostles preaching throughout the world, bestowed every good thing—namely gifts of grace—upon his faithful, that they might live in all peace and concord. Hence it is said: “Peace I leave to you; my peace I give to you” (John 14). And elsewhere: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

Again the Lord speaks of the stability of the holy Church, [Col. 0972A] which he redeemed by the blood of his only Son, saying: “There shall again be in this place, and in all the cities of Jerusalem, flocks of shepherds lying down; and in the towns of the plain, and in the towns toward the south, and in the land of Benjamin, and around Jerusalem, and in the towns of Judah.” It is as though he said: There shall again be in Jerusalem and its environs—that is, in the holy Church—and in every part of the world, flocks of faithful peoples, belonging to shepherds, namely apostles, evangelists, and doctors of the New Testament, lying down—that is, resting in hope of eternal goods. It follows: “The flocks shall again pass under the hand of the one who counts them, says the Lord.” It is as though he said more plainly: The flocks of faithful Christians shall pass justly and devoutly along the way of this life beneath the hand [Col. 0972B] of the one who counts them, namely him who “counts the multitude of the stars” (Ps. 146 [147]). They shall pass through the way of this life according to the ordinance of the true living shepherd, who says: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10).

Under the hand of Jesus Christ, the supreme Shepherd, pass the flocks of the Church gathered from the nations: they are fixed on the heights of virtue and yet do not abandon humility, but through the fervor of the Holy Spirit practice works of goodness and keep the laws of love, by which the flocks are joined together. They dwell in the land of Benjamin, around Jerusalem, and in the towns of Judah, because many of that former people come to faith in Christ and abandon the number of their sheep destined to perish, concerning whom it is said: “My sheep shall hear my voice. And I know them, and they follow me” (John 10). For the sufferings of these same sheep the Son of God and the Virgin deigned to suffer, to die, and to rise from the dead on the third day according to the Scriptures, the pains of hell having been loosed.

Therefore God the Father also speaks through the Psalmist, saying: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor, now I will arise, says the Lord” (Ps. 11 [12]). Cassiodorus: “Christ is said to be sent by the Father against the evils of this age; his utterances are true, whereas those of the ungodly are false, as though they preach these things and perform evil deeds. But God the Father says against these things: ‘I will arise,’ that is, I will appear in the Son, ‘now,’ that is, in this time of grace, which I did not do among the former people; [Col. 0972D] and this is in order to remove the misery and groaning of the needy, namely the Gentiles, and of the poor, namely the Jews.”

Augustine: “The Gentiles are rightly called needy because they had neither law nor prophets; the Jews are called poor because they did not understand the law spiritually.” And the sense is: Because of the want and poverty of spiritual goods suffered by Jews and Gentiles, I shall send my Son; or, by “needy” and “poor” he means the same persons: I shall send my Son to remove the misery of the needy, namely mortality and susceptibility to suffering; and I shall do this because of the groaning of the poor, who groan over evils and are contrite for their sins, for otherwise they would not be worthy of help. What God the Father will do when he arises, he adds, saying: “I will place [him] in salvation,” that is, in Jesus, not in servants. He does not state what he will place there; but it should be understood to concern the consolation of the poor. Cassiodorus: It is as though God the Father said: “I will place in Jesus the consolation of the poor, and I will act confidently”—that is, powerfully—“in him, because nothing will resist him.” Augustine: The same Savior will also teach, not like the scribes and Pharisees, but, as one having authority, will add to the law and change certain things according to his most just will, as author of the law. Therefore God the Father says: “I will act confidently in him,” which he did not say of servants.

Otherwise: Above, the faithful, seeing that they cannot be saved through fleshly observances, persevere and ask God the Father to send him whom he is to send, namely Christ, so that, saved and freed through him, they may attain the inheritance which they lost through the first parent. [Col. 0973B] For the Prophet says in their person: “Save me, O Lord, because the holy one has failed,” namely the first human being, who was made holy and unstained by you. In answer to this, God the Father, mercifully hearing their prayers, says: “Because of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor,” who descended from his stock, “now I will arise”: that is, by helping the fallen, in relation to whom I seem to lie down, I shall arise. I, who acted more leniently when I sent servants to the vineyard, shall act more attentively when I send the Son to it. Of these it was said: “The husbandmen seized his servants; they beat one, killed another, and stoned another” (Matt. 21). And I shall do this to take away the misery of the needy and console the groaning of the poor.

The Gentiles are called needy because they had no help for rising again either in themselves or in anyone else, since they lacked the law and prophets. But the poor are those who, reckoning themselves insufficient for salvation, namely the faithful from the Jewish people, understood already that they could not be saved by the shadowy law and, groaning, implored the help of the spiritual law through the advent of the new man Jesus Christ. Hence comes the saying: “While all things kept deep silence and night was in the midst of its course, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from the royal thrones” (Wis. 18). “I will place,” says God the Father, “the removal of their misery and consolation of their groaning in salvation”—that is, I shall give it to them through my Son, who will be salvation for all laid low. Hence blessed Simeon’s words: “For my eyes have seen your salvation, which you have prepared before the face of all peoples” (Luke 2). For God the Father placed confidently—that is, powerfully—the consolation of the needy and miserable, indeed of all the predestined, in salvation, that is, in Christ, because through him he mercifully redeemed the human race. Among all human beings the Son of God was free from sin; therefore he alone sufficed for the redemption of the world. Concerning him, God the Father speaks to Job in a certain question:

“Who let the wild ass go free, and who loosed its bonds?” (Job 30). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Morals*, book 30, chapter 15]: “The wild ass may certainly signify God incarnate. For the wild ass is an animal of the field; and because the incarnate Lord benefited the Gentile world more than Judaea, by assuming an animal body he came, as it were, not into a house but rather into a field. Of this field of the Gentiles it is said through the Psalmist: ‘The beauty of the field is with me’ (Ps. 40 [41]). Thus the incarnate Lord, in the form of God, is equal to the Father; and in the form of a servant, less than the Father. Therefore let it be said by God the Father of the Son according to the form of a servant: ‘Who let the wild ass go free, and who loosed its bonds?’—‘Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin’ (John 8). And because the incarnate Lord became a participant in our nature but not in our guilt, he is called ‘let go free’ because he is not held under the lordship of sin. Elsewhere it is said of him: ‘Free among the dead’ (Ps. 87 [88]). Therefore he is said to have been let go because, coming to our flesh, [Col. 0974B] he is held under no yoke of iniquity.

“Although no stain of our guilt touched that flesh, the passion of our mortality nevertheless bound it. Thus, after he is called ‘let go free,’ it is fittingly added of him: ‘And who loosed his bonds?’ His bonds were loosed when the weaknesses of his passion were changed into the glory of resurrection. The Lord had, as it were, certain bonds: the weaknesses of our mortality which we suffer because of our wickedness, by which he willed to bind himself even unto death and which he wonderfully loosed through resurrection. That he hungered, grew weary, was seized, scourged, and crucified: these were bonds of our mortality. But when death was completed, the veil of the Temple was torn, rocks were split, tombs were opened, and the barriers of hell were thrown open: what else was shown by so many proofs and such great wonders but that those bonds of our weakness were being loosed? Thus he who had come to assume the form of a servant, released from the bonds of hell in that very servant-form, might return freely even to heaven with his members.”
