Concerning these bonds the apostle Peter testifies, saying: “Whom God raised up, having loosed the pains of hell, because it was impossible for him to be held by it” (Acts 2). Isidore [Note: [Col. 0974D] *Etymologies*, book 12, chapter 1]: “*Onager* means ‘wild ass.’ For the Greeks call an ass ὄνος (*onos*). Individual males preside over herds of females. When males are born, they hide them and bite off their testicles; the mothers, guarding against this, conceal them in hidden places. Arcadian asses are so called because they were first brought from Arcadia; they are large and tall.”

Therefore the Son of God, who came down from heaven for the salvation of the whole human race, endured many insults and reproaches in our flesh, as has been said above, in order to bring us to freedom, as he himself says through the Psalmist: “They devised a wicked word against me: will not one who sleeps add that he may rise again?” (Ps. 40 [41]). “They devised a wicked word against me,” namely, “It is expedient that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11). Augustine: “The wicked word is, namely, ‘If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend’” (John 19). These Jews are the evil tenants who, after killing the servants, deliberate about killing [Col. 0975A] the son of the householder, saying: “Let us kill him, and we shall have his inheritance” (Matt. 21). So the Jews say; but does not one who sleeps have power to lay down his soul? Does he not also have power to take it again? And this is the meaning: “Will not one who sleeps”—not, as you suppose, dead by necessity or unwillingly, but sleeping voluntarily and soon to awaken—“add that he may rise again?”

And observe that he says “sleeps.” For just as from the side of sleeping Adam, who was a type of the one to come, namely Christ, a rib was taken, from which Eve was formed (Gen. 2), so Christ slept the sleep of death, so that from the side of the sleeper, from which blood and water flowed—the sacraments of our redemption—the bride, the Church, might be formed for him. Alternatively: “They devised a wicked word against me,” namely, an unjust sentence, saying: “He is guilty of death” (Matt. 26). They themselves condemned me to death. But what concern is that? Shall I not rise again? Certainly I shall rise. And show this by a comparison: Does not one who sleeps add that he may rise again? Certainly he does. What they thought death was my sleep, because it was voluntary, not forced. The first Adam slept so that Eve might be fashioned; the second Adam slept so that the Church might be fashioned.

Or thus: They truly devised a wicked word against me, because even “the man of my peace,” that is, the one who showed peace to me by giving a kiss, “in whom I hoped”—not with regard to myself, for I knew what was in a human being, but as regards the common grace, namely the one in whom I ought to have hoped—“I hungered” (Matt. 25), etc., because I hoped that my food was in him. “He who ate *panes meos* (‘my breads’),” that is, he who was refreshed by the same teaching as those who ate with me; or, “he who ate *panes meas* (‘my breads’),” that is, the one to whom I gave the first Eucharist at supper among the others, “magnified treachery against me,” that is, betrayed me more than the others. For he said: “He is the one; seize him and lead him away carefully” (Mark 14). It is as though he said: Guard him diligently lest you lose him, for I know his deeds and deep designs. But I, for the salvation of my own, shall willingly sleep—that is, lay down my soul in death—because I have power to rise again quickly.

Therefore we give thanks to you, highest and sweetest Father, [Col. 0975D] because you did not spare your same beloved Son Jesus Christ, but mercifully delivered him up for us all, that he might redeem us from the power of the ancient enemy. For unless he, by your will, had piously poured out his blood upon the cross, the human race would have utterly perished. We also bless you, best Shepherd, with the Father and the Holy Spirit: obedient for us wretches to God the Father even unto death, by your resurrection you raised us from everlasting death; moreover, by your ascension you opened the gate of the heavenly kingdom to us, though unworthy.

Therefore I also exhort you, dearest brothers, always to call such great benefits of his to mind and devoutly to persevere at every time in his praises. He offered himself as medicine to us in our weakness, by which he mercifully healed our maladies [Col. 0976A] and enlightened the eyes of our mind to know the truth, which he himself is, as a certain wise man says:

> Our flesh is clay; the Father’s Wisdom is spittle.  
> By this medicine the human race is restored to health.

This wise man fittingly called the Wisdom of God “spittle” and our flesh “clay,” because unless God the Father had mercifully united that same Wisdom to human nature, humanity could never have opened the eyes of its heart to contemplate God’s brightness. Therefore the Wisdom of God the Father is Christ, of whom it is said: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9), that is, the holy Church. Again, Wisdom herself says of herself: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Sir. 24). [Col. 0976B] Our flesh too is clay, as God says to the sinning human being: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3).

Jesus Christ saw a man blind from birth—that is, the human race—and had mercy on him. For his seeing is his having mercy. This blindness came upon the first human being because of sin, from whom we all derive our origin—not only of death but also of iniquity. For if blindness is unbelief, then illumination is faith. The one born blind went to the pool of Siloam—which is interpreted “Sent”—washed, and saw; and the human race, blind from its first creation, came to Christ, who was sent by God the Father. Baptized in him, it received knowledge of the Creator and the light of true faith. For unless he had been sent, no one would have been released from iniquity. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1).

Therefore it is rightly said:

> Our flesh is clay; the Father’s Wisdom is spittle,

because he made it like clay when he mercifully united our same flesh to himself. And he anointed the eyes of the one born blind—that is, of the human race—when, by preaching, he showed it the faith of truth, that is, made it a catechumen. He enlightened it when through the apostles he baptized it in the name of the whole Trinity. It follows: “By this medicine the human race is restored to health.” The devil, suggesting what was unlawful at the first creation, wounded the human race; and Christ, of his own will hanging on the cross, healed our wounds. The apostle Peter testifies to this, saying: “He himself bore [Col. 0976D] our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness; by whose stripe we have been healed” (1 Pet. 2).

We devoutly behold Him exalted on the cross with the eyes of the heart, and by His power are freed from the bite of the ancient serpent. For He is the Samaritan—that is, the most powerful guardian and most kindly physician of the human race—who healed with poured-in oil and wine the wounds inflicted upon His neighbour by robbers, that is, demons; set him upon His beast, brought him to an inn, and entrusted him to the innkeeper to care for him (Luke 10). Therefore the wisdom of God is the medicine for our weakness, and, as has been said, the whole human race is restored to health by this remedy. He Himself, then, is the medicine and the fountain opened for the washing away of sins [Col. 0977A], through whom God the Father healed His elect from spiritual maladies and cleansed them from the vices of harmful conduct.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us continually pray to Him with faithful mind and pure devotion, our faces bowed down, that He who deigned by being born, dying, and rising again to redeem us from the hand of the ancient enemy [Col. 0978A], may also deign, after this life, to lead us through Himself to that same His Father. He, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity for all ages of ages. Amen.

## TWENTY-SEVENTH SERMON. FOR THE SECOND SUNDAY AFTER EASTER.

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977B] You must know, dearest brethren, that just as there were two cities, namely Jerusalem and Babylon, of which one afflicted and took the other captive, so now there are two cities: one of the good and the other of the evil, mingled in body but separated in heart—namely Jerusalem and Babylon. Jerusalem, therefore, is held captive in Babylon, but not wholly. For its citizens include angels, free from every misery; but it is held captive in respect of those human beings predestined to glory, who through sin are captives and exiles from their homeland. Thus it is of this captive city that the present passage speaks; above, however, it spoke of repayment [Note: [Col. 0977D] “Of repayment,” as in the Gloss.] in that Psalm, namely: “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion” (Ps. 64).

There it says, “Praise is fitting for you, O God, in Zion”; but here: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat [Col. 0977C] and wept when we remembered” (Ps. 136)—that is, because in this Babylon, the confusion of this age, we dwell not as citizens but are held captive; and we sit humbled in repentance and confession of sins. There are also others who will be citizens of Jerusalem: they already belong to it by predestination, but in body and heart are still citizens of Babylon and serve it. For Babylon has its lovers, who seek temporal peace, hope for nothing beyond it, and place all their joy there; and we see them labour greatly for the commonwealth and for earthly things.

Yet whoever live in it not proudly but faithfully, so that, insofar as they understand, they show such faith as they can and to whom they can—God does not allow them to perish in Babylon, because He has predestined them as citizens of Jerusalem. For He understands their love [Note: [Col. 0977D] Augustine says “captivity,” but blessed Martin adheres to the Gloss, from which, and from the aforesaid Father, he expounds. He stitched all these matters together in this Psalm.], that is, their earnest striving; and He shows them another city for which they may labour, to which they may sigh, and to which they may exhort others. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who is faithful in a little thing is faithful also in a great thing” (Luke 16). And again: “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?” (ibid.).

Yet this Psalm does not speak of such people’s sighing [Col. 0978B] [Note: [Col. 0977D] This word is absent from the Gloss and is wholly superfluous.], but of those who are citizens of Jerusalem in mind and desire. Its arrangement has two parts. This Psalm [Note: [Col. 0978D] A corrupt passage, which the Gloss has thus: “First, it introduces those who were to be carried captive long afterward by Nebuchadnezzar—whom Jeremiah bewailed—lamenting their evils here, yet not forgetting Jerusalem even amid evils, etc.”] first introduces Jerusalem, as a figure of ourselves, to those whom Nebuchadnezzar would carry captive long afterward and whom Jeremiah bewailed, to lament their evils here; nor does it counsel them to forget evils. Secondly, there is an address to God against the enemies, where it says: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom” (Ps. 136).

Therefore prophecy, in the person of the captive people—stirred, as it were, by the praises of those standing in the house—poured forth this lament out of longing for its homeland, saying:

“By the rivers of Babylon”: that is, in so noble a place, we sat humbled—not raised up by pride, not lying down through ruin. The rivers of Babylon are all things loved here which pass away. Observing them, the saints [Col. 0978C] do not mingle themselves with them in love, but sit above them by despising them; and they weep for those who are swept away and for themselves, who are held captive there. Hence follows: “and we wept,” namely, over our sojourn. We sat, I say, and wept when we remembered Zion, where nothing flows away. It is not that we weep for anything other than Zion, as righteous persons do. For many weep with Babylonian weeping and rejoice with Babylonian joy, because they rejoice in profit and lament temporal losses. Both belong to Babylon. Certainly everyone ought to weep, but by remembering Zion.

Again it says: “Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments.” For in an enemy’s land the remembrance of one’s homeland is sweet. “Upon the willows,” that is, upon the evils [Col. 0978D] which are in its midst—namely, those watered by the rivers of Babylon, barren in good work, and in the midst of Babylon, that is, exceedingly evil: the covetous and avaricious. For some are in Babylon’s outer regions, not so overwhelmed by desires. Upon those willows, I say, which are in the midst of Babylon—that is, because of those exceedingly evil people—we hung up, that is, deferred and withheld, our instruments: namely the Scriptures and the promises of God.

[Col. 0979A] Augustine: “For we turn the Scriptures away from these swine and dogs; we do not tie them to such persons, but hang them up by deferring them.” And it should be said that the force of grief is heightened when the delight by which they were accustomed to console themselves is suspended.

It follows: “For there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs.” And why did we hang up our instruments? Augustine: Because there—that is, in Babylon—those who led us captive asked us, tempting rather than seeking fulfillment: namely the devil and his angels, who are said to ask when they question through those in whom they work. What did they ask? Namely, words of songs or canticles—that is, the prayers of our thanksgiving and confession—when such questions are put:

“What profit is Christ? Or what is this other life? Since Christ came, have not worldly affairs been worse than they were before? Were not human affairs happier then than now? Let Christians tell us what good Christ has brought. Why do you command me to believe concerning Christ and another life which I do not see?”

“And those who carried us away”—namely from the fellowship of angels—“and brought us to these miseries,” understand, asked us there, saying: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion.” But to those who ask us such things we reply: Babylon carries you, Babylon holds you, Babylon nourishes you; and you cannot grasp anything except what flows away in time. You do not know how to meditate on eternal things; you are full of evil desires. But to those who are filled with evils we should not strike the instrument [Col. 0979C], but hang it up. For the devil cunningly seeks through his own people to mock.

Therefore we must answer them: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” We must beware lest anyone, fearing to displease such people, desire their friendship and begin to take delight in Babylon. Augustine: “But this people, surrounded by questioners, flatterers, mockers, and reprovers, and as if endangered among them, raised its mind to the remembrance of Zion and bound itself by an oath, saying: ‘If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be forgotten.’”

Augustine: As though he said: “I did not sing to them; but if amid their words ‘I forget you, Jerusalem,’ because I desire to please them, ‘let my right hand be forgotten,’ or let my right hand forget me”—that is, eternal life, which is my right hand. Hence elsewhere: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). My left hand is temporal life. Whatever you do for eternal life, your right hand performs. But if you aim at something else, the left hand has intruded; and if you take delight in it as though it were the right, you lose eternal things.

Cassiodorus: Note that he sets down a condition which must necessarily come to pass: if he has forgotten Jerusalem, he must be given over to forgetfulness. Again he says: “Let my tongue cleave to my jaws, if I do not remember you.” Augustine: As if the people of Israel, placed in captivity, said: “May I become speechless and mute in the praises of God, if I do not remember you”—you who are the consolation of weeping and miseries. And it came about as he declares. For one who does not remember God becomes mute; [Col. 0980A] for what sound does he make, what does he say, who does not sound the song of Zion? The song of Jerusalem is our tongue, namely the tongue of believers. The song of delight in this age is a barbarous tongue. Therefore he who has forgotten Jerusalem is dead to God. Hence he rightly says: “If I do not remember you,” namely with love.

Therefore he adds: “If I do not set you, Jerusalem, at the beginning of my joy”—that is, if my chief joy is not in you and concerning you, O Jerusalem. For there is supreme joy, where we shall enjoy God, where we shall be secure in the fellowship of those joined together, because nothing but good will delight there. Every necessity will die there, and every happiness will arise.

Again he continues, saying: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem.” This is the second part, in which there is an address to God against enemies. As if he said: I stand thus; but, O Lord, remember the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem. Edom is the same as Esau. He was called Edom, Esau, and Seir. The children of Edom, that is, the Idumeans, hindered the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem after their return from Babylon; or they joined the Babylonians in Jerusalem’s destruction. Therefore it says afterward: “O wretched daughter of Babylon.” The sense is: Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom—that is, punish them for what they did on the day of Jerusalem’s restoration, which they hindered, or on the day when they overthrew it in union with the Babylonians.

Behold what those do who say: “Lay it bare, lay it bare,” and so forth. As if they said more plainly: Remove everything in it down to its foundation; let not one stone or one citizen remain [Col. 0980C] in Jerusalem. It follows: “O wretched daughter of Babylon. Blessed is he who repays you the repayment which you repaid to us.” As though they said: But, O daughter of Babylon, you too are wretched in your exultation and presumption. And he calls Idumea the daughter of Babylon because it allied itself with the Babylonians. “But blessed,” he says, “is he who will repay you the repayment which you repaid to us.” Namely, God will repay it. What repayment? “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock.” God did this literally through the very people who struck the Jews.

Or it may be understood mystically. Augustine: Esau signifies all carnal people, and Jacob spiritual people. Esau was called Edom from a certain red lentil dish [Col. 0980D], for which he sold his birthright to his younger brother, Jacob (Gen. 25). The latter granted food for pleasure and took the honour of dignity; and thus the one who was younger in time became greater in dignity. Therefore the carnal person is greater, the spiritual lesser, because “what is animal comes first, and afterward what is spiritual” (1 Cor. 15). For everyone who is born is carnal and begins as an animal person. But if one turns from captivity, he is renewed in the return to Jerusalem; and a kind of renewal occurs in respect of the inner person. And as the elder brother Esau was Jacob’s enemy, so all carnal people are enemies of spiritual people. Hence he says: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom.”

Cassiodorus: “‘Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom’—that is, carnal people, who are enemies of the saints: deliver us from them on the day of Jerusalem’s separation,” namely when they shall be separated from Jerusalem, so that the evil themselves may be punished and the good crowned. It follows: “Who say, ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation in her’”—namely Jerusalem, the Church. This is said by comparison with a cistern: if water is drawn from it, one reaches down to its foundation. Yet it benefits even such people to take away life, when eternal life is in their foundation, which is Christ. While the evil think that they harm them, they give crowns to the good.

Then, turning his address toward their city, he says: But, O daughter of Babylon, you are wretched in your very exultation, in your very presumption, and in relation to your enemies.

Note that the city of the evil is called Babylon and the daughter of Babylon, just as the Church is called Zion and daughter of Zion [Col. 0981B]. Babylon has become Babylon’s daughter through succession and imitation, just as the Church has become Zion’s daughter through succession. Again he adds: “Blessed is he who repays you the repayment which you repaid to us”—namely, spiritual dashing in return for the carnal dashing which you repaid to us; that is, hatred in return for our love.

Augustine: What repayment? “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock,” that is, Christ: namely, who will lead your captives back to the way of truth. While they are little, they can be led back, not yet wholly hardened in wickedness.

Or the whole may be understood in a moral sense. Edom, which means “earthly” or “bloody,” is carnality, which deceives us through unlawful impulses as through its children. The sense is: “Remember, O Lord, the children of Edom,” that is, the unlawful impulses of the flesh, that you may dash them on the day of Jerusalem—that is, in the good things which are the days of the Church. Hence it is said: “Day pours forth a good word to day” (Ps. 18). “Who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, down to its foundation in her.’” For through an accumulation of vices distrust creeps in; but wretched is the daughter of Babylon.

Cassiodorus: The daughter of Babylon is the flesh, which brings in the confusion of sins. A fitting recompense is given to it: just as it incites to vices, so, when restrained, it is subjected to virtues.

Hence it is added: “Blessed is he who repays you the repayment which you repaid to us.” Cassiodorus: To repay the flesh is the work of the blessed, who also restrain the little ones [Col. 0981D] born from the flesh—that is, great impulses before they grow—lest they become free; and dash them against Christ the rock, so that, shattered, they may perish. Hence follows: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash her little ones against the rock.” Behold the fitting repayment.

Augustine: Just as Babylon stifles those born into the world while little by the errors of parents and of this age, so those who are already mature, having been granted knowledge of God, dash Babylon’s little ones—that is, impulses being born—before they gain strength. Just as they are more easily conquered while small, so the larger ones too must be killed against the rock.

Therefore, dearest brethren, we must depart from Babylon—that is, from carnal conduct—and dash against the rock, which is Christ, the vices of seductive flesh [Col. 0982A], which are called little ones, so that, with God’s help, freed from encumbrance, we may be able to reach the heavenly Jerusalem, in which we have been appointed to be citizens, according to Jeremiah’s counsel.

“Flee from the midst of Babylon,” he says, “that each may save his own soul” (Jer. 51). Mystically, the prophet directs these words as an exhortation to the faithful, that they may flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, from the multitude of confusion. As if he said: Do not go sluggishly or step by step, but leave swiftly. The discourse is directed to you, whoever have a soul confused by the passion of various vices. It may happen that someone is in Babylon but, being at its outermost boundaries, appears in some manner to be outside Babylon. But it is one thing to be in the midst of Babylon, where the distance is equal on every side [Col. 0982B], dwelling at its navel, as it were, in the middle of an animal’s heart.

For just as the heart is the middle of an animal, and Luke [Note: [Col. 0981] Rather Matthew (12:40), for he alone says: “The Son of Man shall be in the heart of the earth.”] calls the heart of the earth the middle of the earth, so Tyre in Ezekiel seems to be described as placed in the heart of the sea (Ezek. 27). Now sinners also ought to flee from the midst of Babylon, that is, from its heart. Thus let it be said: “Flee from the midst of Babylon,” so that, abandoning its middle, you may begin to be at its borders, not in its midst.

For whoever is deeply immersed in vices is an inhabitant of the midst of Babylon. Whoever gradually abandons vices, turns his nature toward better things, and begins not so much to possess virtues as to desire them, flees from the midst of Babylon, though he has not yet departed from it wholly. Interpreting in this way, we should believe that the sacred Scriptures do not have even one jot empty of God’s wisdom. For He who says, “He shall not appear before me empty” (Exod. 23), speaks far more certainly not in vain Himself. Those who were prophets, receiving from His fullness, sang from the fullness they had received. Therefore the volumes that were made breathe a spirit of fullness, and there is nothing that does not descend from the fullness of divine majesty.

They breathe, however, to those who have eyes for seeing heavenly things, ears for hearing divine things, and nostrils for perceiving things belonging to fullness. First, then, one must flee from the midst of Babylon; next, each soul must be saved again. He did not merely say “save,” but, according to another edition, “save again.” For some, having tasted salvation and then fallen from it through sin, come into Babylon [Col. 0982D]. Therefore each person must save his own soul again, so that he may begin to recover what he has lost.

Hence we read that the blessed apostle Peter said: “We shall receive the end of our souls’ faith” (1 Pet. 1:9; perhaps the word “salvation” is missing), and so forth. But it lies with us to flee from Babylon and, if we will, it lies in our power to raise up what has fallen. What has fallen in us we undoubtedly raise up if, amid the evils which we suffer, we humbly call our faults to mind and praise God’s justice; if in adversities, as in prosperity, we give thanks to almighty God. By these weapons the ancient enemy is more sternly assailed by us, and his weapons are broken, if we patiently endure adversities [Col. 0983A], correct the sins for which they are brought upon us by God’s just judgment, and amid these things not only do not murmur against God, but unceasingly bless His name—as we read that blessed Job did amid his scourges.

For when his wife said to him, “Do you still remain in your simplicity? Bless God, and die” (Job 2), he immediately replied: “You have spoken like one of the foolish women.” And he added: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?”

Gregory [Note: [Col. 0983D] *Morals*, Book III, no. 15.]: Behold, everywhere the enemy is broken; everywhere he is overcome. He was defeated by every device of temptations, he who even lost that familiar solace of his from his wife. Amid these events it is pleasant to behold the holy man outwardly empty, inwardly [Col. 0983B] full of God. When Paul saw in himself the riches of inward wisdom and saw himself outwardly as a corruptible body, he said: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4).

Behold, in blessed Job the earthen vessel outwardly felt the rupture of wounds, yet this treasure remained inwardly whole. For outwardly he burst forth through wounds, but the treasure of wisdom, arising inwardly without failing, flowed out through words of instruction, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” By “good things” he means God’s gifts, whether temporal or eternal; by “evil things,” present scourges, concerning which the Lord says through the prophet: “I am the Lord, and there is no other; forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil” [Col. 0983C] (Isa. 45).

For evils which possess no subsisting nature of their own are not created by the Lord. But the Lord declares that He creates evils when He fashions things well created into scourges for us who act wickedly, so that the same things may be evils to sinners through the pain by which they strike, and good through the nature by which they exist. Thus poison is death to a human being, yet life to a serpent.

For through love of present things we withdrew from the love of our Maker; and the perverse mind, when it subjected itself to delight in the creature, separated itself from fellowship with the Creator. Therefore it had to be struck by the Creator through those things which, in its error, it had preferred to its Maker—so that where, in pride, a human being did not fear to admit guilt, there he might find punishment by which to be corrected; and so that he might look back more swiftly toward what he had lost, the more he saw that the things he sought were a punishment of pain [Note: [Col. 0984D] Gregory: “full.”].

[Col. 0983D] Hence it is rightly said: “Forming light and creating darkness,” because when outward darkness is created through scourges of pain, inwardly the light of the mind is kindled through instruction. “Making peace and creating evil”: because peace with God is then restored to us when those things which were well created but not well desired are turned into scourges which are evil for us. Through guilt, indeed, we became at odds with God; and therefore it is fitting that we return to His peace through scourges, so that when each thing well created is turned into pain for us, the corrected human mind may humbly be restored to peace with its Maker.

Blessed Job therefore calls these scourges evils because he weighs the good of salvation and tranquillity by the disturbance which they inflict [Col. 0984A]. But this must be carefully observed in his words: how great an art of reflection he uses to collect himself against his wife’s persuasion, saying, “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” For it is a great consolation in tribulation if, when we suffer adversities, we recall the gifts of our Maker. What confronts us from pain does not break us, if what raises us through His gift comes more swiftly to mind.

Hence it is written: “On the day of good things do not forget evil things; and on the day of evil things do not forget good things” (Ecclus. 11). Whoever receives God’s gifts, if he does not fear scourges even amid the reception of gifts, falls through joy into pride. But whoever is crushed by scourges, if at the time of chastisement he does not console himself from the gifts which have fallen to his lot to receive, is destroyed from steadfastness of mind by utter despair. Thus both must be joined, so that each is always supported by the other: the memory of gifts may temper the pain of the scourge, while the expectation and dread of the scourge may sting the memory of gifts.

Therefore, that the holy man may soothe his oppressed mind amid wounds, he considers the comforts of gifts amid the pains of scourges, saying: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” And rightly he first says: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women.” For the fault belongs to the perverse woman, not to the sex; therefore he does not say, “You have spoken as one of the women,” but “as one of the foolish women,” in order to show [Col. 0984C] that what has a perverse taste belongs to an accidental folly, not to created nature.

It follows: “In all these things Job did not sin with his lips.” We sin with our lips in two ways: when we either say unjust things or keep silent about just things. For if silence were never a fault, the prophet would not say: “Woe is me, because I have kept silent” (Isa. 6). Thus blessed Job did not sin at all with his lips in all that he did: he neither spoke proudly against Him who struck him, nor kept silent about what was right against the one who gave evil advice. Therefore he did not sin either in speaking or in silence, because he gave thanks to the Father who scourged him and offered wisdom’s teaching to his ill-advising wife. For he knew what he owed to God and what to his neighbour: patience to his Creator, wisdom to his wife. Therefore he both taught her by rebuking her and praised Him by giving thanks [Col. 0984D].

Which of us, if he received even one wound from such a blow, would not immediately lie prostrate, crushed in his inmost being? Behold, laid low outwardly by wounds of the flesh, he remains inwardly raised up by the fortification of his mind; and beneath himself he sees every dart fly past which the raging enemy himself fixes outwardly with a strict hand. Vigilantly he detects the darts: now wounds hurled against him in the face, now words twisted, as it were, from the side. Our warrior, caught amid the fervour of battles surrounding him, everywhere sets before them the shield of his patience, meets the missiles coming from every direction, and turns his watchful mind through every side of virtue against the wounds that rush upon him.

But [Col. 0985A] the more ardently the ancient enemy is defeated, the more ardently he is stirred up still to lay snares. For he grieves at the progress of the whole Church, rejoices in its losses, envies its goods, exults over its evils, suggests vices, and without ceasing provokes not only the little ones of the Church but even its rulers to do unlawful things and commit deeds contrary to God.

The prophet Zephaniah, seeing this in the Spirit and, as it were, rebuking the crimes of these same ministers of the Church, spoke figuratively under the image of the city Nineveh:

“This is the glorious city, dwelling in confidence, which said in her heart: ‘I am, and besides me there is no other.’ The pelican,” he says, “and the hedgehog, or chameleons, shall lodge upon her thresholds. The voice of one singing in the window, a raven upon the lintel, because her strength shall be brought low” (ibid.).

Let us, if you please, hear the kinds and natures of these birds and beasts as blessed Isidore describes them [Note: [Col. 0985D] *Etymologies*, Book II, chapter 7.]. The onocrotalus, as it is called in Greek, is a bird having a long and strong beak. There are two kinds of it: one aquatic and the other of the wilderness. The raven, or *corax*, has its name from the sound of its throat, because its voice sounds *cor*. It is said that this bird, after producing its young, does not fully provide them food until it recognizes in them, through the blackness of their feathers, a likeness to its own colour. But once it sees them clothed in dark feathers, recognizing them wholly, it feeds them more abundantly. This bird first seeks the eye in corpses.

The chameleon has no single colour, but is sprinkled with varied diversity, like a leopard. It is said that this little creature’s body changes with the greatest ease into the colours which it sees—whereas the bodies of other animals are not so readily changed. It is called the chameleon-leopard because, although like a leopard, being sprinkled with white spots, with a horse-like neck, ox-like feet, and a head like a camel, it is especially produced in Ethiopia.

The hedgehog is an animal covered with spines. It is called *ericius* because it raises itself up when it closes itself within its spines, by which it is protected on every side against snares. For as soon as it senses anything, it first raises itself and, turned into a ball, gathers itself back into its own weapons. Such is its cleverness: after it has cut grapes from the vine, it rolls itself upon them on its back and thus presents them to its young [Col. 0985D].

Having briefly set forth these matters from blessed Isidore, we must again call to mind what Zephaniah had said above: “This is the city dwelling in confidence, which said in her heart: ‘I am, and besides me there is no other.’ The pelican and the hedgehog, or chameleons, shall lodge on her thresholds. The voice of one singing in the window, a raven upon the lintel, because her strength shall be brought low.”

Under the image of the city Nineveh, the prophet speaks figuratively of the holy Church—things which we cannot say without fear and deep groaning. For today some boast vainly that the Church is beautiful, but deny it by their deeds. Within them dwell herds of vices, animals serving the belly, and beasts that devour their hearts; and the pelican or chameleons, having varied colours—that is, clinging to diverse vices—and the hedgehog, a spiny animal, dwell in their hearts [Col. 0986A]. The raven also, an unclean bird, is in the window—that is, in the bodily senses—so that they may always hear or speak evil things.

They suffer all these things because, though devoted to evil works, they promise themselves blessedness, despise others, and become proud. Therefore they become the lodging place of beasts, so that where the Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit, and ministering angels formerly dwelt, demons may now have a place. And the holy angels, who formerly remained in them but now merely pass by, will marvel [Col. 0986B] and be astonished; they will not uphold those who fall, but will raise their hands, withdrawing their support from them.

Again he adds, saying: “How has she become a desert, a lodging place of beasts! Everyone who passes through her shall hiss and wave his hand.” These words may be understood of the devil and his angels, who devastated the vine which had been transplanted from Egypt. Demons also pass through a soul which had been the temple of God and has ceased to be so; and the serpent, hissing, vomits into it the poisons of his malice and moves his hands—that is, his works. Hence Solomon says: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18), that is, in its works.

It follows: “Woe to the provoking and redeemed city; the dove did not hear the voice, nor did she receive discipline” [Col. 0986C] (Zeph. 3). As though he said: Woe to the provoking city, which turns God, who is sweet and willing to show mercy, into bitterness toward itself and compels Him to punish. And the redeemed city—that is, the Church, redeemed by the Lord—is called a dove because it was once simple; it did not hear the voice of God’s command, and did not receive correction when it was reproved.

Again it says: “She has not trusted in the Lord, nor drawn near to her God.” As if he said: Even when evils pressed upon her, she did not trust in the Lord; she did not draw near to her God, although He says, “I am God who draws near”; she did not follow after Him. “Her princes,” namely the Church’s princes, “are roaring lions in her midst.” After the general rebuke, he also describes the vices of the princes, who are always engaged in prey and the blood of those subject to them.

Again he adds, saying: “Her judges are evening wolves; they did not leave anything until morning.” As though he said: Her judges are ravening wolves, who left nothing for others in the morning that they themselves could seize.

Therefore the Church, as was said above, is allegorically the city redeemed by Christ’s blood and a dove because of the simplicity and multitude of believers. A threat is made against it because it behaved insolently toward God, would not hear God’s law or receive correction, and did not trust in the Lord, because it would not draw near to God through good works, believing it could serve both God and the world. Its rulers, when they rage cruelly against those subject to them, ought to be called lions rather than shepherds [Col. 0987A].

Its judges too are like killing wolves: always remaining in the evening of darkness, not looking toward the sunrise, they plunder the Church’s possessions as though in a night in which no one sees, so that the poor may have nothing to eat in the morning of true light, since not even a small amount of food was left for the needy. The prophets—that is, the teachers who ought to teach others from the Scriptures—are not faithful but, as it were, faithless, since they destroy by their deeds the faith which they build up in words. The priests also, who distribute the Lord’s blood to the people, are imperfect in Christ’s law if they think that the life of priests is not required in the administration of the Eucharist, but only a solemn prayer. Of them it is said: “A priest in whom there is a blemish shall not approach to offer an oblation to the Lord” (Lev. [Col. 0987B] 21).

When these evils are in the Church, the Lord is merciful in that He does not depart from the Church, and just in that He renders to each according to merits. When the morning comes after the night of this age, He will bring judgment into the light; neither He nor His judgment will be hidden. And when He exacts from each person the money entrusted to him, He will not act unjustly, but will destroy proud princes and cast them down from their seats. The corners—that is, twisted thoughts in which the Pharisees pray, while despising the cornerstone—will be scattered. Their roads will also become desolate, according to the saying, “The way of the ungodly shall perish” (Ps. 1), so that they may not walk in pride and perversity. Their ill-built cities will be destroyed, so that they may not have evil builders.

As though God were speaking to His Church in these words, saying: “I have threatened all these things, O Church, so that by casting away vices and receiving correction, you may not perish utterly.” In commanding it to receive correction and cast away vices, He desires, as a most merciful Father, to lead it to spiritual life. God always advances the holy Church toward better things through His servants; the ancient enemy always strives to tear it apart, trouble it, and hinder it from good works through the ministers of his malice. But God powerfully restrains his forces, lest he inflict upon the children of that Church as many evils as he desires. For “where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5).

Whence it is read in Job: “The roaring of lions, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of lion-cubs are broken” (Job 4). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0987D] *Morals*, Book V, ch. 17]: Because the nature of every thing is composed of diversity, different things may rightly be represented in sacred speech by any one thing. For the lion possesses strength, but also savagery. Its strength therefore signifies the Lord; its savagery denotes the devil. Thus it is said of the Lord: “The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered” (Rev. 5). Thus Peter says of the devil: “Your adversary the devil prowls about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5).

By the name “lioness,” moreover, the holy Church is sometimes designated, and Babylon at other times. Because she is bold against adversities, the Church is called a lioness, as is confirmed by the words of blessed Job himself, who indignantly says of Judaea, abandoned by the [Col. 0988A] Church: “The sons of merchants have not trodden it, nor has the lioness passed through it” (Job 28). At other times the city of this world—that is, Babylon—is truly expressed by the name of lioness: it rages against the life of the innocent with unrestrained cruelty. Allied to the ancient enemy as to a most savage lion, it conceives the seeds of his perverse persuasion and brings forth from itself reprobate children, like cruel cubs in his likeness.

The lion-cubs are certain reprobates, begotten for an iniquitous life through the error of malignant spirits; and together they make up the whole city of the world which we have called Babylon. Yet each of these children of Babylon is called, not a lioness, but a lioness’s cub. For just as the whole body together is called Zion, while the children of [Col. 0988B] Zion are each individually numbered among the saints, so each child of Babylon is numbered among the reprobate, while Babylon itself denotes all the reprobate together.

But so long as holy men live in this life, they guard themselves with vigilant circumspection: lest the prowling lion creep in by ambush—that is, lest the ancient enemy kill under some appearance of virtue; lest the lioness’s voice ring in their ears—that is, lest Babylon’s glory turn their minds away from love of the heavenly homeland; lest the cubs’ teeth bite—that is, lest the persuasion of the reprobate gain strength in their hearts. Heretics, on the contrary, are now as though secure in their holiness, because they suppose that they have overcome all things by the merits of their lives. Hence it is now said: “The roaring of lions, the voice of the lioness, and the teeth of lion-cubs are broken.” It is as though heretics and all the enemies of the Church were openly saying: [Col. 0988C] “We are not worn down by any scourges because, overcoming by the merits of our lives the power of the ancient enemy, the desire for earthly glory, and the persuasions of all reprobates, we trample them underfoot.”

And it is further added: “The tiger has perished because it had no prey, and the lion-cubs are scattered.” By the term “tiger” he repeats the one whom he denoted by the designation “lion.” Satan is called a lion because of his cruelty, and is not inappropriately called a tiger because of the variety of his manifold cunning. At one time he presents himself to human senses as the lost being that he is; at another he shows himself as an angel of light; at one time he persuades the minds of fools by flattery; at another he drags them into sin by terror; now he openly strives to recommend vices; now he disguises himself in his suggestions under the appearance of virtues.

[Col. 0988D] This beast, then, which is marked by such diversity, is rightly called a tiger; among the Septuagint translators it is called *formicoleon* [Note: [Col. 0988D] Rather: *myrmicoleon*, as in Gregory.]. This creature, hidden in dust, kills ants carrying grain: for the apostate angel, cast down from heaven to earth, ensnares the minds of the righteous, who are preparing for themselves the refreshment of good works, in the very course of their action. When he overcomes them through ambush, he unexpectedly kills them like ants carrying grain.

It is rightly called *formicoleon*, that is, “lion and ant.” As we have said, it is a lion to ants, but an ant to flying creatures: for the ancient enemy is strong against those who consent, but weak against those who resist. [Col. 0989A] If assent is given to his suggestions, he cannot be endured, like a lion. But if he is resisted, he is crushed like an ant. Thus he is a lion to some and an ant to others: carnal minds can scarcely endure his cruelty, while spiritual persons trample his weakness beneath the foot of virtue. Therefore, as stated above, God always leads his Church to better things and crushes beneath her feet the ancient enemy and all his adversaries.

But, grievous to say, what is often read in the psalm is almost fulfilled in the holy Church today: “All,” he says, “have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good” (Ps. 13). And Jeremiah says: “Babylon is a golden cup in the hand of the Lord, making the whole earth drunk” (Jer. 51). It is as though he said: Babylon is a golden [Col. 0989B] cup—that is, ornamented speech—in the hand, that is, in the power, of the Lord, making the whole earth drunk with vice, namely all who are earth. See that nearly all people are drunk. We are made drunk by anger and sorrow; and we lose our minds through love, lust, and vain glory. Observe that the entire earth is full of sins, and you will not ask how Babylon has made the whole earth drunk.

For the righteous person is not on earth but above the earth, having his citizenship in heaven. It does not suit him to be told, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3), but rather, “You are heaven, and into heaven you shall go.” For he bears the image, not of the earthly man, but of the heavenly one. The golden cup therefore makes the whole earth drunk. Nearly all of us, as stated above, are intoxicated by it while we are on earth. Again the prophet adds, [Col. 0989C] saying: “Wail over Babylon, and bring resin for her pain, if perhaps she may be healed.”

It must be known, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 0989D] *Etymologies*, Book XVIII, ch. 7], that there are very many kinds of resin. One resin is called cedar resin, produced by the cedar tree; it is so useful in preserving books that books coated with it suffer neither moths nor decay with age. It is found in Crete, Syria, and Africa. Of the poplar tree, one kind is white and another black. The white poplar produces resin, near the river Eridanus, resembling alum. There is another resin produced by the mastic tree, called *mastix*; the greatest quantity and best quality of it is found on the island of Chios. Turpentine resin is superior to all the others. It is brought [Col. 0989D] from Arabia [Note: [Col. 0989D] Isidore: Arabia Petraea], Judaea, Syria, Africa, Cyprus, and also from the Cycladic islands. [The Cycladic islands were anciently Greek islands.] [Note: [Col. 0989D] The words enclosed in brackets are also from Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XIV, ch. 6, but seem rather inappropriately inserted here.] There are besides pine resins: one is called *pitines*, another *peucine*, and another dry resin; they are brought from Tyrrhenian Colophonia, from which Colophonian resin also took its name.

Let the prophet therefore say to the ministers of the Church concerning Babylon: “Wail over Babylon, and bring resin for her pain, if perhaps she may be healed.” It is as though the prophet were speaking more plainly to the angels—that is, the prelates of the Church—saying: “O you angels, that is, physicians of souls, [Col. 0990A] wail, that is, lament, over Babylon, that is, over a soul wrapped in vices, because no soul is beyond God’s healing. And bring resin for her pain, if perhaps she may be healed”—as though she can be healed if she is willing.

The prophet here gives counsel to the teachers of the Church, who can bear witness to the migration into the heavenly Jerusalem: they should take resin to make medicines and plasters, and with whatever zeal they can restore to health Babylon—that is, the soul devoted to the confusion of sins. Let us therefore ask the Lord to give us the rational remedy of which the monogamous man—that is, the husband of one Church, namely Christ—applies a poultice, oil, and bandages; and, applying them, let us bind the wounds of Babylon—that is, of the sinful soul—[Col. 0990B] so that it may be healed and, once cured, cease to be what it was. [Note: [Col. 0990D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book IV, ch. 9.] A *cataplasm* is so called because it is merely an application. An *emplastrum* is so called because it is spread on. A *malagma* is that which is softened and kneaded without fire. *Enema* is Greek; in Latin it is called *relaxatio*, “a loosening.”

Let the prophet therefore say: “Bring resin for her pain, if in any way she may be healed.” Where are the heretics who, introducing certain natures, assert that there is a hopeless material which is utterly incapable of receiving salvation? But God does not despise Babylon—that is, the sinful soul—but commands the physicians to take resin, if in any way it may be healed.

Again the prophet, speaking in the person of teachers answering the Lord, says: “We have treated Babylon, and she has not been healed; let us leave her and let each go [Col. 0990C] into his own land, for her judgment has reached up to heaven and has been raised up to the clouds.” This is the voice of spiritual physicians. It is as though they said more plainly: “We have treated Babylon, that is, the sinful soul, through repentance, and she has not been healed. Yet the fault is not in the art or in the resin, but she refuses to obey us. Let us therefore leave her, hopeless in her weakness, because the work and the expense are being lost; and let each of us go to his own land, that is, to his own occupation. For her judgment has reached to heaven and has been raised to the clouds, because as guilt grows, condemnation also grows.”

See, therefore, lest at some time God command the angels—that is, the teachers of the Church—to prepare remedies for your sick [Col. 0990D] soul, if somehow it may be healed, and they answer him: “We have treated Babylon,” displaying the soul confused by passion, “and she has not been healed.” They do not blame either their medical knowledge or the power of the resin, but you, who refused to obey them.

There are physicians under the great physician God, namely God’s angels and the prelates of the Church, who desire by God’s command to heal our souls from vices. We ourselves repel them when we do not assent to their counsel. Seeing therefore that their efforts are being lost, they say to one another: “Let us leave her,” and so forth. It is as though they said: “The medicine was entrusted to us by God, that we might treat the human soul; we employed assistance and remedies, but she herself is stubborn and refuses to keep what we say. Our effort is not followed by success. Let each of us depart to his own land,” that is, to his domestic and personal occupation.

Take heed, therefore, whatever soul you are, lest at some time the physician, or God’s angel, or the one entrusted with the care of preaching remedies for salvation, abandon you. If they abandon you and say, “Let each of us depart to his own land, because her judgment has drawn near to heaven,” it is clear that the physician’s departure is your condemnation, as one incurable and unwilling to be healed. What happens to those whom physicians despair of then happens to you: by indulging the will of the disease, they thereafter suffer more severely and more dangerously.

Often a prudent physician kills a sick person, [Col. 0991B] though medical art and diligence have done all they can. But if the illness is so great that it resists treatment, or if the patient, through impatience with pain, acts contrary to what is prescribed, the physician leaves him in despair, lest he expire in his hands and the physician seem responsible for his death. Therefore, lest we die in the hands of the holy angels, they will leave us in despair, saying: “There is no poultice to apply, nor oil, nor bandage, because her judgment has drawn near to heaven and has risen to the stars.”

One who has a small sin does not raise his judgment to heaven and the stars, for it is small and lowly. But one who grows in crime grows also in judgment, and will be reproved together with his vices and his punishment. Because he has sinned so greatly that his judgment is lifted up to heaven [Col. 0991C] and, resisting God in his impiety, rises toward higher things, God brings forth his judgment to humble what has been exalted. For a human being who, at the devil’s persuasion, despises God’s commands, is often lifted up and exalted like a cedar of Lebanon (Ps. 36); then, illuminated again by divine grace so as to know the misery of his own frailty, he humbly returns into himself.

The same ancient enemy never ceases to devise snares against faithful people, to trouble them through innumerable temptations, and to lead them, if possible, even to despair. For unless the dwelling-place of our mind is supported by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the ancient enemy violently drives it toward ruin by the assaults of vices and, once discernment is overcome, casts it down from its state of uprightness. Hence it is said of blessed Job:

“While your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their eldest brother, suddenly a violent wind came from the region of the desert, shook the four corners of the house, and, when it fell, it crushed your children; and they are dead, and I alone escaped to tell you” (Job 1). Gregory [Note: [Col. 0991D] *Morals*, Book II, ch. 26]: The region of the desert is the forsaken multitude of unclean spirits. Because it abandoned the blessedness of its Creator, it has, as it were, lost the hand of its cultivator. From it comes a violent wind and overthrows the house, because a strong temptation creeps in from unclean spirits and overturns the conscience from its state of tranquility.

[Col. 0992A] This house stands upon four corners because the structure of our mind is upheld by prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The house subsists upon four corners because in these four virtues the entire structure of good work is raised. Thus four rivers water the earth, because when the heart is filled with these four virtues, it is moderated from every heat of carnal desires.

But sometimes, when sloth creeps into the mind, prudence grows cold. For when the mind lies numb with weariness, it does not foresee what is coming. Sometimes, when pleasure creeps into the mind, temperance languishes; for to the degree that we are led into enjoyment of present things, to that degree we are less restrained from what is unlawful. Sometimes fear insinuates itself into the heart and disturbs the powers [Col. 0992B] of our fortitude; we are less able to withstand adversity because we immoderately fear losing certain things we love. Sometimes self-love enters the mind and, by a hidden movement, turns it aside from the uprightness of justice; and because it neglects to render itself wholly to its Maker, it resists the claim of justice within itself.

Thus the violent wind shakes the four corners of the house when strong temptation attacks the four virtues by hidden movements. Once the corners are shaken, the house falls: when the virtues are assailed, the conscience is troubled. But within these four corners of the house the children feast, because within the hidden places of the mind—which is raised to the summit of highest uprightness principally in these four virtues—the other virtues, like certain offspring of the heart, nourish one another.

The gift [Col. 0992C] of the Holy Spirit, which first forms prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice in the subject mind, then endows that same mind with seven virtues so that it may be trained against each temptation: against foolishness, wisdom; against dullness, understanding; against rashness, counsel; against fear, fortitude; against ignorance, knowledge; against hardness, piety; against pride, fear.

Yet sometimes, when our mind is supported by the abundance and richness of so great a gift, if it enjoys continual security in these things, it forgets from whom they come and thinks it possesses from itself what it never sees absent from itself. Therefore grace sometimes profitably withdraws these gifts and shows the presumptuous person how weak he is in himself. We truly know whence our goods come when we feel them as though by losing them, because they cannot be kept by us.

For the instruction of this inward benefit, it often happens, when a moment of temptation bursts in, that such foolishness strikes our wisdom that the troubled mind does not know how to confront the evils threatening it or how to prepare itself against temptation. Yet the heart is wisely instructed by this very foolishness, because from the point at which it is deceived [Note: [Col. 0992D] Gregory: “becomes foolish,” instead of “is deceived.”] for a moment, it afterward thinks more truly and more humbly; and wisdom, from the point at which it seems to be lost, [Col. 0993A] is more certainly possessed.

Sometimes, while the mind exalts itself through understanding sublime things, it becomes sluggish with grave dullness in lowly and insignificant matters, so that one who was quick to penetrate the highest things suddenly finds even lowly things closed to him. [Note: [Col. 0993D] Thus the manuscripts.] Yet this very dullness preserves understanding for us while it withdraws it; for, by humbling the heart for a moment, it strengthens the heart more truly to understand sublime things.

Sometimes, while we rejoice to do everything with the gravity of counsel, when an urgent occasion arises we are carried away by sudden rashness; and we who thought that we had always lived in an orderly manner are suddenly devastated by inward confusion. Yet through the instruction of this same confusion we learn not to attribute our counsels to our own powers; and we are restrained toward gravity all the more maturely when we return to it as though it had been lost. [Col. 0993B]

Sometimes, while the mind bravely despises adversities, when adverse events arise it is struck by violent fear. Yet, shaken through this, it learns to whom it should attribute the fact that it stood firm against certain things; and it retains fortitude afterward with greater strength, in proportion as it sees that, when fear suddenly burst in, this fortitude had as it were escaped from it.

Sometimes, while we rejoice that we know great things, we grow numb through the blindness of sudden ignorance. Yet because the mind’s eye is closed for a moment by ignorance, it is afterward opened more truly to the things that should be known, [Note: [Col. 0993D] “knowledge.”] so that, instructed by the scourge of its blindness, it may know the very one from whom it has knowledge.

Sometimes, while we order everything religiously and rejoice that we fully possess the bowels of compassion, we are struck by a certain hardness of mind. But [Col. 0993C] being, as it were, hardened, we recognize to whom we should attribute the goods of the piety we have possessed; and piety is received more truly as though restored from extinction when, seeming to have been lost, it is loved more abundantly.

Sometimes, while the mind rejoices that it is subject to the fear of God, it suddenly stiffens under the temptation of pride. Yet, immediately fearing greatly what it did not fear, it hastens to bend itself once more toward humility; and it receives humility all the more firmly because it has weighed the worth of that virtue by seemingly losing it.

When, therefore, the house is overthrown, the children die, because the virtues born in the heart are suddenly and momentarily overwhelmed, when the purpose of the conscience is disturbed in temptation, for the benefit of self-knowledge. [Note: [Col. 0994D] Gregory: “when the conscience is disturbed in temptation.”] These children truly live inwardly through the spirit while they die outwardly in the flesh, because our virtues, during temptation, though they fail for a moment from the soundness of their state when disturbed, nevertheless remain whole in the root of the mind through perseverance of intention.

With them the three sisters also fall, because charity in the heart is sometimes troubled by scourges, hope shaken by fear, and faith assailed by questions. For we often grow numb as though toward love of the Creator when we are wearied by chastisement beyond what we think fitting for us. Often, when the mind fears more than is necessary, it weakens its confidence in hope. Often, when the mind is struck by immeasurable questions, faith, disturbed and as though about to fail, is wearied. Yet the daughters who die when the house is shaken live, because although the disturbance itself declares that hope, faith, and charity within the conscience have almost perished, perseverance in right intention keeps them living before God’s eyes.

Thus the servant who reports these things escapes alone, because the mind’s discernment remains sound even amid temptations. The servant enables Job to receive back his children through weeping when, through the report of discernment, the grieving mind preserves by repentance the powers it had begun, as it were, to lose.

This is done with us by a wonderful dispensation: our mind is sometimes struck by the assault of sin. For a person would think himself possessed of great strength if he never felt any failure of those very powers within the hidden places [Col. 0994B] of the mind. But when temptation bursts in, shakes him, and wearies him as though beyond endurance, the defense of humility is shown to him against the snares of his enemy; and from the very source in which he fears, even weakly, to fall, he receives strength to stand firmly.

The tempted person learns not only from whom he receives strength, but also with how great vigilance he must preserve it. Often one whom the contest of temptation could not overcome is more grievously overthrown by his own security. For when someone relaxes in leisure after becoming weary, he offers his unguarded mind to the corrupter. But if, through the dispensation of heavenly mercy, temptation knocks in a moderating and instructive approach rather than suddenly bursting in with violence, the person is indeed awakened to foresee ambushes, so that he may cautiously arm himself against the enemy in battle. [Col. 0994C]

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us pray more earnestly to God that he will not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can endure (1 Cor. 10), and that through the grace of the Holy Spirit he may mercifully grant us strength to resist the ancient enemy. Let us acknowledge that we are sinners and frail; defended by his protection, let us resist the tempter manfully. “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Yet even because of grave sins we must not despair of God’s goodness, for, though unworthy, we have in heaven a most kind—indeed, a most merciful—Father, God, who wills not the condemnation but the conversion [Col. 0994D] of sinners (Ezek. 18). Whoever subjects himself to sins and vices departs far from God and from the Church. Hence it is said: “Some of them came from afar” (Mark 8). As soon as a person falls away from the Church by sinning and is separated from God, he is made a slave to the devil’s dominion.

Therefore blessed Isidore, the eminent teacher and our patron, says [Note: [Col. 0994D] *Sentences*, Book II, ch. 15]: “Whom God abandons, demons receive.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). Let us therefore approach that most merciful Father, as stated above, seeking with tears forgiveness of sins, because he is accustomed in his kindness to receive through repentance those who return to him.

It also gives us great confidence in obtaining pardon that Jeremiah once said, in the word of the Lord, to the Jews living in Babylonian exile: “Thus says the Lord God of hosts, the God of Israel”—that is, the God of the Christian people who see God in the spirit—“Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruits; take wives and beget sons and daughters; give wives to your sons and your daughters to husbands; multiply there, and do not become few in number. Seek the peace of the city to which I caused you to migrate, and pray to God for it; for in its peace shall be your peace” (Jer. 29).

O how you ought to be glorified, praised, and proclaimed, almighty God, in your works and in your great mercies: you do not repel even those who sin against you from your mercy. The Jews, despising you, had served idols; yet you, most merciful Father, do not cease to show them the way of salvation.

Therefore, dearly beloved, having confidence in God’s great mercy, as has been said, if—God forbid—we have departed through sin from Jerusalem, that is, from the Church, and have been handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, of whom the Apostle says, “I have judged such a person to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved on the day of Christ” (1 Cor. 5), and elsewhere, “I have handed them over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1), we ought not, then, to be secure in [Col. 0995C] idleness or lethargy, nor to despair utterly.

Rather, first, according to the Lord’s command, let us build houses—not upon sand but upon rock (Matt. 7)—such as the midwives built in Exodus because they feared the Lord (Exod. 1). Next, let us plant gardens, such as the paradise the Lord planted, placing in it the tree of life (Gen. 2), that is, of wisdom; concerning it Scripture says: “It is a tree of life to those who lay hold of it, and blessed is he who holds it fast” (Prov. 3). Third, let us take wives, one of whom is wisdom, concerning whom Solomon says: “Love her and she will keep you” (Prov. 4). And again: “I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride” (Wis. 8), and so forth.

Nor is one wife enough, since we must have several: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. Let us also give our daughters—that is, good works—to men, namely, let us join them to faith and truth, that we may beget many sons and daughters. Thus, putting away what belongs to children and growing into the perfect man, we may hear from the Evangelist the words of consolation: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John 2); and say with the Apostle: “Through the Gospel I have begotten you” (1 Cor. 4).

Let us further seek the peace of the Church, our city and land, that we may deserve to return to it—that is, to paradise—from which we were removed by the Lord’s judgment, to dwell in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of error. The Lord’s mercy must also be considered most carefully: he commands us to pray for enemies and to do good to those who hate us (Matt. 5).

Again God mercifully speaks to the Jews dwelling in Babylon—and indeed to us living in this world. For he says: “When seventy years begin to be completed in Babylon, I will visit you, raise up over you my good word, and bring you back to this place” (Jer. 29). In the anagogical sense, we remain in the course of this world until we deserve to receive the rest of the number seven; and, having received repentance, God will fulfill what he promised and bring us back to our place, that is, to the Church and then to the heavenly homeland. He wounds in order to heal; he will give us an end to labor, affliction, and patience. We shall call upon and pray to him, and we shall be heard; we shall seek him with our whole heart and find him.

Some understand the seventy years according to the words: “The days of our years in them are seventy years” (Ps. 89). In this present life, therefore, we are held captive in Babylon, that is, in the confusion of sins, as though for seventy years. For the human lifespan is seventy years. But if it exceeds eighty, it will endure labors and pains in Babylon, that is, in the present life, which scarcely any mortal can pass through without sin.

Therefore let it be said: “Our years shall be meditated upon like a spider; the days of our years in them are seventy years.” It is as though he said: [Col. 0996C] “Our years shall meditate like a spider,” that is, we labor at deceitful and empty thoughts; we work in corruptible things and weave emptiness. Thus he aptly says that the years “shall meditate,” not “shall work,” because they pass without the fruit and usefulness of good work, as though in empty reflection.

Or it may be understood passively: “shall be meditated upon,” that is, our years shall be reckoned as a spider—that is, as empty and useless; the days of our years shall be completed in them, seventy years. Or, the days of our years are so short that within them there are seventy years. [Note: [Col. 0995D] Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XII, ch. 5.] A spider is an air-worm, so named from its nourishment of air; from its tiny body it draws out long threads, is always intent upon its webs, never ceases from labor, and suffers a perpetual suspension in its craft. Our years are rightly compared to its empty work.

Another reading [Note: [Col. 0995D] Add here from the Gloss: “or years”; for it indicates that some editions read *anni* (“years”), as does the Vulgate, while others read *annis* (“in years”), as does the Old Latin.]: by this span of time people are called long-lived who seem to retain some strength even up to eighty years. Hence it adds: “If people live more than seventy years, or live very long, which is rare, they may be in powers,” that is, they may retain some strength and power up to eighty years; and if they live beyond that, theirs is labor and pain—that is, if one lives beyond eighty years, labor and pain increase. Old age itself is an illness.

[Col. 0997A] Isidore [Note: [Col. 0997D] Ibid., Book XI, ch. 2]: Some think that old men (*senes*) are so called from the diminishing of their senses, because through age they are now becoming foolish. For physicians say that foolish people have colder blood and prudent persons warmer blood. Hence old men, in whom warmth is already cooling, and children, in whom it has not yet grown warm, are less wise. This is also why the age of children and old people resembles each other. Old men rave because of excessive age; children, through playfulness and infancy, do not know what they say.

But *senes* is exclusively masculine, just as *anus* is feminine. For *anus* is used only of a woman. She is called *anus* from many years, as though *annosa*, “full of years.” [Note: [Col. 0997D] Here is lacking a passage which Peter Chacon, and Grialius with him, judged foreign to Isidore, namely: [Col. 0998D] “For if the name were common to both sexes, why would Terence say ‘an old woman’?” By a sufficiently strong argument, those great men seem not to have conjectured badly.] Hence also *vetula*, because she is old (*vetusta*). As *senectus*, “old age,” is named from *senex*, so *anilitas*, “old-womanhood,” is named from *anus*. Grey hair (*canities*) is named from whiteness (*candor*), as though *candities*. Hence the line:

[Col. 0997B] “Flowering youth, milky-grey old age”—that is, white old age.

Old age brings with it many goods and evils. Its goods are that it frees us from most imperious masters, places a limit on pleasures, breaks the impulses of lust, increases wisdom, and gives more mature counsel. Its evils are that advanced age is most miserable through weakness and contempt. For diseases come upon it, and sorrowful old age. There are two things by which bodily strength is diminished: old age and illness.

Having briefly stated these things concerning the misery of old people from blessed Isidore, we must return to what we omitted above. It was said above that if one lives beyond eighty years, labor and pain are multiplied for the old person. These words can be understood literally; but because some are sick and old even before eighty, while some beyond that age remain vigorous in their powers, it is better to understand them mystically.

Seventy and eighty make one hundred and fifty. One hundred and fifty has the same significance as fifteen, a number composed of seven and eight. Seven signifies the Old Testament because of the Sabbath which it commanded to be observed. For the fathers of the Old Testament observed the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh month, and the seventh year of the seventh decade, which is called the jubilee. Eight signifies the New Testament because of the Lord’s resurrection celebrated on the eighth day, which is observed in the New Testament, so that the eighth age of the future resurrection may be awaited.

Hence there are fifteen [Col. 0997D] steps in Solomon’s Temple; hence the fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms; hence the waters of the Flood rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains.

Note carefully, therefore, what he says: “In them are seventy years, and in powers.” The meaning is: Such are the meditations of our years, and thus the days of our years—that is, our life—are in those seventy years. Or, “in them which are seventy years,” that is, in the temporal things promised in the Old Testament, which are signified by seventy. Thus he said “seventy” because temporal things were promised in the Old Testament, in which our life pertaining to the Old Testament consists.

But if our life is not in those years, but “in powers”—that is, if it is not in temporal things but in eternal and spiritual ones—then the days of our years will be eighty years. That is, our life will belong to the New Testament, which is signified by eighty, or by eight, because the New Testament is in hope of the resurrection of the future eighth age. “And beyond them is labor and pain”: that is, whoever goes beyond this faith and seeks something further finds labor and pain.

Or it may be understood thus: it is as though he said that life which is in powers belongs to the New Testament. And although people are in the New Testament, yet beyond this there is labor and pain for them: that is, although we are in the New [Col. 0998B] Testament, our life still has labor and pain while we groan within ourselves awaiting the redemption of our body.

Or by seventy years may be understood the desire for earthly things, which are done in seven days, because eternity is signified by eighty. Thus the days of our years—that is, our life—are in those seventy years, that is, in the appetite and desire for temporal things. But if our life is “in powers,” that is, in virtues, then there are eighty years, that is, eternity and blessedness.

Therefore, in Babylon—as was said before—that is, in the present life confused by sins and vices, we sit as though at the age of seventy years, weeping and sighing, not desiring temporal goods but awaiting entry into the heavenly Jerusalem, that is, into the peace above.

The Lord mercifully brought the children of Israel out of the captivity of Babylon, and the Gentiles out of the sacrilegious worship and superstition of idols. He brought the former back from Babylon to Jerusalem after seventy years; the latter, after the long deception of demons, back to the holy Church. Thus the prophet Jeremiah, foreseeing in the Spirit this time of revealed grace, rejoiced in the word of the Lord concerning the Jewish unbelievers and the children of the holy Church, though far removed, saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when they shall no longer say: ‘The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt’; but: ‘The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of the north and from all the lands [Col. 0998D] to which I had driven them’; and I will bring them back to their own land, which I gave to their fathers” (Jer. 16).

In this passage the restoration of the Christian people is plainly proclaimed. It is as though he said more openly: Behold, days are coming in which they will no longer say: “The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel—the carnal people, the child of the Synagogue—out of Egypt through Moses and Aaron”; but: “The Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel—the spiritual people, the child of the Church, who sees God through faith and devotion—out of the northern land,” in which, by worshipping idols, they had been subjected to the devil; “and from all the lands under heaven to which, because their sins demanded it, they had been driven [Col. 0999A]; and I will bring them back to their own land,” flowing with milk and honey—that is, the teaching of the apostles and prophets—which I gave to their fathers, namely the apostles, evangelists, and ecclesiastical men. Hence it is said: “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 11).

We may also say this of the persecutions which befell God’s people from the days of Nero until the time of Maximian.
