At last, taking pity on his people, the Lord brought them back from every land into their own land—that is, into the Church which he gave to their fathers, namely the apostles and apostolic men. Again the Lord adds concerning the gathering of the Gentiles: “Behold, I will send many fishermen,” namely apostles and teachers, “and they shall fish for them.” Hence: “Come after me, and I will make you [Col. 0999B] fishers of men” (Matt. 4). It follows: “And after this I will send them many hunters,” namely ecclesiastical men or angels, who, when the consummation of the age has come, will hunt them from every mountain of spiritual doctrines, every hill of good works, and the caverns of rocks—that is, of the apostles, who are called rocks from Christ, who is called the Rock (1 Cor. 10). Hence he also granted Peter that he should be called a rock (Matt. 16); and those resting in his understanding are rightly said to have been transferred from the rock.

Likewise, in the sacred Scripture’s account of the captivity of Zedekiah (Jer. 39), it announces the order of our captivity. Gregory [Note: [Col. 0999D] *Morals*, book 7, chapter 13]:

> The king of Babylon is the ancient enemy, possessor of inward confusion. He first slew the sons before the eyes of the beholder, because he often [Col. 0999C] destroys good works in such a way that the captive mind itself, grieving, sees that it is losing them. For often the mind groans, yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, loses the good things that it loves while grieving for them; it considers the losses it suffers, and yet does not lift the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon—that is, against the malignant enemy—by resisting vices. But while it is struck by the sight of its own wickedness, the mind is sometimes brought by habitual sin to such a point that it is deprived even of the light of humanity itself. Thus the king of Babylon, after first extinguishing the sons, put out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the malignant spirit, after removing good works, also takes away the light of understanding. Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah, which means “these many things.” For the light [Col. 0999D] of reason is sometimes shut off when it is weighed down by evil habit and the multitude of its iniquity. The king of Babylon brought Zedekiah into his own house and put him in the prison-house until the day of his death, because the soul, bound in confusion by the fetters of vices, is led by malignant spirits into the prison-house until the day of death: it is shut up in mental distress, awaiting the sentence of death.

The prophet Ezekiel likewise foretold, in his vision, both that return of the Israelite people from Babylon and the future general resurrection of us all, when he said: “The Lord showed me very many dry bones, and said to me: ‘Son [Col. 1000A] of man, do you think these bones will live?’ And I said: ‘Lord God, you know’” (Ezek. 37). Jerome:

> By this parable of resurrection, the resurrection—that is, the return of the people Israel from Babylon—is treated. For just as it seems unbelievable that dry bones, worn away by great age, should rise again, so too does the resurrection—that is, the return—of the people Israel led into captivity. But this certainly appears doubtful to those who do not know the power of almighty God. Yet the Lord says that their resurrection will come, because “I have spoken, and I will do according to my word.” Indeed, the earlier prophecy in which the ancient condition is promised to the mountains of Israel—when it is said to them, “I will turn to you, and you shall be tilled” (Ezek. 36)—and all the related matters now spoken [Col. 1000B] under the parable of the dry bones, are fulfilled by what the Lord says in the Gospel: “What is impossible with men is possible with God” (Matt. 19).

The Jews, then, were brought out through both the power and mercy of God from the graves of captivity and the bonds by which they had been held fast in Babylonian slavery. The Jews falsely maintain that these things were fulfilled under Zerubbabel, when a great upheaval occurred and the kingdom of the Chaldeans was transferred to the Medes and Persians; or that they will be fulfilled at the coming of their Christ, whom they await. But we understand them spiritually after the Savior’s cross, and as occurring daily in those who, like Lazarus (John 11), are bound in the wrappings of their sins and raised at the Lord’s voice. And truly they are the house of Israel, once dry and [Col. 1000C] without any hope of salvation; but when the spirit of grace enters them and the Lord stretches out his hand, they are delivered from the depths of hell. Those who previously had said through Ezekiel concerning dry bones, “Lord God, you know” whether they could be raised, will now, once set free, hear: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14).

Thus, as Ezekiel prophesied in the Lord’s word, the spirit entered the dry bones; they lived and stood upon their feet. Some refer this to the general resurrection: just as in the first creation of man God breathed into his face and man became a living soul, so in the second resurrection of the dead they will be made alive when the Spirit breathes upon them. Hence it is said: “Send forth your Spirit [Col. 1000D], and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103). But those who read this chapter concerning the general resurrection refer it to the resurrection of the saints, of which it is said: “Blessed is he who has a part in the first resurrection” (Rev. 20).

Therefore, dearest brethren, if we seek to escape Babylonian captivity—that is, the misery of this world or the confusion of sins—and to rise among the ranks of the elect, we must diligently consider our frailty and, through continual repentance, wipe away with tears the stains of sin, as we read that blessed Job did in his affliction. For Scripture testifies that he “sat [Col. 1001A] upon a dungheap, scraping his discharge” (Job 2). Gregory [Note: [Col. 1001D] *Morals*, book 3, no. 9]:

> Of what is a potsherd made, except clay? And what is bodily discharge except clay? Thus he is said to scrape the discharge with a potsherd. It is as if one said plainly: “He wiped clay with clay.” For the holy man considered the source of that which he bore, and with a fragment of a broken earthen vessel scraped the broken earthen vessel—that is, his weak flesh. By this deed he clearly showed how healthily he had subjected his body to himself: even when stricken, he treated it with such contempt. What indulgence, indeed, did he grant his flesh, when he applied to his wounds neither clothing nor fingers, but a potsherd? He scraped the discharge with a potsherd so that, considering himself even in the fragment, he might also take care of his mind while cleansing the wound. Yet because the mind is often inflamed [Note: [Col. 1001D] Edition: “inflated,” rather than “inflamed.”] by things surrounding the body, and because what is done to us removes our bodily frailty from the eyes of the heart, some worldly persons [Col. 1001B], when supported by temporal dignities—when they preside in higher offices and see the services of many readily available to their desire—neglect to consider their frailty. Forgetting that the vessel they bear is earthen, they take no thought at all how swiftly it must be broken.

> But blessed Job, so that he might draw the consideration of his frailty even from his circumstances and increase before his eyes the force of his self-contempt, is described as sitting not upon any ground whatsoever, which is found nearly everywhere clean, but upon a dungheap. [Note: [Col. 1001D] Edition: “But blessed . . . Job, in order that he might draw the consideration of frailty . . . and increase before his eyes the force of his self-contempt, sat not upon any ground whatsoever,” etc.] He placed his body on the dungheap so that even from the stench of the place he might understand that the body would soon return to stench.

> But behold: while blessed Job endures the loss of so many possessions, grieves, struck by so many deaths of his children, bears so many wounds, scrapes his running discharge with a potsherd, melts away through decay, and remains seated on a dungheap, it is fitting to ask why almighty God so severely afflicts, in apparent contempt, those whom he sees as so dear to himself for eternity. When I consider the wounds and sufferings of blessed Job, I suddenly turn my mind’s eyes to John. With profound astonishment I reflect that he who was filled with the spirit of prophecy in his mother’s womb and, so to speak, sanctified before his birth (Luke 1); he who was the bridegroom’s friend; he than whom none greater arose among those born of women (Matt. 11); he who was a prophet and more than a prophet—was sent to prison and beheaded for a girl’s dancing (Mark 6). A man of such sanctity dies [Col. 1001D] for the amusement of the shameless.

> Do we suppose that there was anything in his life which that death, so despised, was to wipe away? For when did he sin even in food, who ate only locusts and wild honey? (Matt. 3). What offense did he commit against God concerning the quality of his clothing, who covered his body with camel’s hair? What could he have done to offend in his way of life, who did not leave the wilderness? What charge of talkativeness could have defiled him, who lived far apart from people? When did the fault of silence touch him, who so sternly rebuked those coming to him, saying: “You brood of vipers, who showed you to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3).

> [Col. 1002A] Why, too, is Job preferred to his friends by God’s testimony, yet struck down by wounds upon a dungheap? Why is John praised by God’s voice, yet dies, as the reward for a dance, because of drunken words? Why does almighty God so severely humble in this world those whom he chose before the ages for exaltation, unless it is what is clear to the devotion of the faithful: that he presses them down in lowly places because he sees how he will reward them in the heights; and casts them outward into contempt because he leads them inward to incomprehensible things? From this, then, let each person infer what those whom he rejects will suffer there, if here he so torments those whom he loves. Or how will those who are to be accused in judgment be struck, if the life of those whom the Judge himself praises by his testimony is so oppressed? [Col. 1002B]

But that we may more perfectly wipe away the discharge of vices by the severity of spiritual discipline, it is necessary, dearest brethren, that we again hear the words of stricken Job, morally expounded by blessed Gregory. The words are repeated precisely in order that they may be impressed more firmly upon the hearts of hearers. Let it again be said of blessed Job [Note: [Col. 1001D] Same book, no. 58]: “He scraped his discharge with a potsherd, sitting on a dungheap.”

> What is signified by the potsherd except the vigor of severity, and what by the discharge except the flow of unlawful thought? Therefore, when stricken, we scrape the discharge with a potsherd when, after the defilements of unlawful thought, we cleanse ourselves by harshly judging ourselves. A potsherd may also signify the frailty of mortality: to cleanse discharge with a potsherd is to consider the course and frailty of mortality and wipe away the decay [Col. 1002C] of wretched pleasure. [Note: [Col. 1002D] Edition: “A potsherd may also be understood as the frailty of mortality. Thus to cleanse discharge with a potsherd is to consider the course and frailty of mortality,” etc.] For when anyone considers how swiftly the flesh will return to decay, he quickly overcomes that which inwardly assails him shamefully through the flesh.

> Thus when an evil thought flows into the mind from temptation, discharge runs as though from a wound. But the discharge is wiped away more quickly if, in our reflection, frailty is held as a potsherd in the hand. Things which, though they do not proceed to outward effect, still move unlawfully in the mind, must not be treated lightly. Hence the Redeemer came, as it were, to scrape discharge from wounds, when he said: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” [Col. 1002D] (Matt. 5). Discharge is therefore wiped away when guilt is cut off not only from deed but also from thought.

> Hence also Jerobaal [Note: [Col. 1002D] Some older editions read “Gideon,” as do the Vatican manuscripts; the Maurist edition reads “Jerobaal.”], while threshing grain from the chaff, saw an angel. At his command he immediately cooked a kid, placed it upon a rock, and poured the broth of the meat over it. The angel touched these things with his rod, and fire coming forth from the rock consumed them (Judg. 6). What is it to strike the grain with a rod except to separate by the uprightness of judgment the grains of virtues from the chaff of vices? But to those doing this the angel appears, because the more diligently people cleanse themselves from exterior things, the more the Lord reveals inward things [Col. 1003A] to them. He commands the kid to be killed—that is, every appetite of our flesh to be sacrificed; and the flesh to be set upon the rock and the broth of the flesh poured over it.

> Whom else does the rock signify except him of whom Paul says: “The Rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10)? We place the flesh upon the rock when we afflict our body in imitation of Christ. He also poured the broth of the flesh upon it who, in the manner of life of Christ, emptied himself even of carnal thoughts. For the broth is poured as liquid upon the rock when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts. Yet the angel immediately touches these things with the rod, because the power of divine assistance never abandons our intention. [Col. 1003B] Fire came from the rock, consuming the broth and the flesh, because the Spirit, breathed forth by the Redeemer, burns our heart with so great a flame of compunction that it burns away every unlawful thing in it, whether of deed or thought. Thus, what it means there to pour broth upon the rock is here to cleanse discharge with a potsherd.

> For the perfected mind diligently watches so as not only to refuse to do perverse things, but also to wipe away everything that shamefully melts within it through thoughts. Yet the very victory in the struggle often gives rise to another conflict: when an impure thought is overcome, the victor’s mind may be struck by pride. Thus the mind must necessarily be raised through purity, yet carefully laid low in humility. Therefore, after it was said of the holy man, “He scraped his discharge with a potsherd,” it is fittingly added at once: “sitting on a dungheap.” To sit on a dungheap is to think lowly and contemptible things about oneself. For us to sit on a dungheap is to bring back the eyes of the mind in repentance to the things we have done unlawfully, so that, when we see before us the dung of our sins, we may bend down everything which rises in the mind through pride.

> [Col. 1003C] He sits upon a dungheap who carefully considers his own weakness and is not puffed up by the good things received through grace. Was not Abraham sitting upon a dungheap within himself when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes”? (Gen. 18). We plainly see the position in which he placed himself within himself, since even while speaking with God he judged himself to be dust and ashes. If, then, one who ascended to the honor of divine conversation so despises himself, we must carefully consider with what punishment those are to be struck who do not advance to the heights and yet are exalted over trifles. For there are some who, when they do little, think great things of themselves and believe that they surpass others in the merits of virtues. Such persons abandon inwardly the dungheap of humility and climb the heights of pride, imitating him who was not satisfied with the dignity of his created condition, saying: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will exalt my throne” (Isa. 14).

> Hence Babylon joined to him in reprobation—that is, the confused multitude of sinners—says: “I sit as a queen, and am no widow” (Isa. 47, according to the Septuagint). Whoever swells inwardly sets himself high in his own estimation. But he presses himself down into the depths all the more grievously inasmuch as he scorns to recognize truthfully that he is lowly [Col. 1004A].

> There are some who do not indeed strive to perform any virtue, but when they see others sin, suppose themselves righteous by comparison with them. Not one and the same fault, or a similar one, pierces everyone’s heart. Pride entraps one; anger perhaps trips another; avarice torments one; lust inflames another. It frequently happens that someone pressed down by pride observes how anger inflames another; and because anger does not so readily incite him, he already considers himself better than the angry person and grows proud within himself, as though by righteousness, because he neglects to weigh the vice by which he is held more grievously. It frequently happens that one wounded by avarice sees another plunged into the gulf of lust; and because he sees himself free from carnal defilement, he does not attend to the inward filth of the spiritual vice in himself [Col. 1004B]. While he weighs in another an evil that he does not possess, he neglects to consider what he does possess. Thus he becomes more confidently proud over another’s failings in proportion as he more carelessly fails to know his own.

> On the contrary, those who truly desire to rise to the heights of virtue, when they hear of another’s faults, immediately turn their hearts back to their own; and they judge the former more rightly in proportion as they grieve more truly over the latter. Therefore, because every elect person restrains himself by considering his own weakness, it is rightly said that the holy man sits grieving upon a dungheap. For one who truly humbles himself, as he progresses, weighs with the eye of continual consideration the filth of the sins by which he is surrounded.

Therefore, as has been said, we ought through the harshness of repentance to wipe away the very wounds of pleasures, and, if any flow issues in thought, cleanse it by the judgment of rigorous severity. No one who neglects to cleanse himself from sins and vices will be able at all to see the face of God. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Therefore, whoever desires to attain the fellowship of God’s elect and behold the essence of the divine majesty must strive with all earnestness to preserve purity of mind and body and manfully resist the temptations of the ancient enemy, who never ceases to defile the good conduct of the elect.

For the devil himself pursues our good works in three ways, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1003D] *Morals*, book 1, no. 50], [Col. 1004D] so that what is done uprightly before people may be spoiled in the sight of the inward Judge. Sometimes he defiles the intention, so that the action which follows may be impure from its origin. If he does not prevail in this, he opposes us in the action itself, as it were on the road: so that, while someone proceeds more confidently in his purpose of mind, he may be destroyed by a vice secretly added, as though from an ambush. At other times he neither corrupts the intention nor trips us on the way, but ensnares the good work at the end of the action. Hence it is said: “In this way in which I walked, they hid a snare for me” (Ps. 141). It is as though he said: “In this way in which I walked,” that is, in Christ; for this is what they conceal: that I belong to Christ. They place a snare in this way, not according to the truth of the matter but so far as concerns themselves—that is, according to their own opinion [Col. 1005A]—because they intend to place it there, but place it outside the way. Thus heretics too do not place the snare in the way, but hide it outside it. Hence elsewhere: “They set a stumbling-block beside the path for me” (Ps. 139).

Augustine:

> Thus according to their intention the snare is placed in the way, but according to truth it is beside the way. For Christ is the Way, and he does not permit them to place a snare in the way so that there may be no way for us to go; yet he permits them to place it beside the way, so that we may not turn aside. Not only unclean spirits place snares beside the way, but wicked people do so as well. For he too believes that he places a stumbling-block in the way who says: “Do you worship a crucified God?” [Note: [Col. 1005D] Augustine, *On Psalm 93*, 12: “This is the very humility displeasing to pagans, because of which they insult us: ‘What kind of God do you worship, who was born? What kind of God do you worship, who was crucified?’”] He reproaches the cross of Christ, which he does not understand. But for one who understands it, this is not a stumbling-block but glory.

Or “way” in this passage means charity.

[Col. 1005B] Note that elsewhere he said “my paths” in the plural, but here “way” in the singular, because there are many ways and one way. There are many ways because there are many commandments. There is one way because all are reduced to one thing, namely charity. Thus: “In this way,” that is, in charity, which bears all things, in which I walked by suffering for you, “the persecutors, according to their own opinion, hid a snare for me.” [Note: [Col. 1005D] Indeed, Psalm 141 itself also has “paths”; elsewhere too Scripture frequently mentions paths.]

Thus the devil pursues our course in the above-mentioned ways, so that our good deeds may be accounted reprobate in the sight of God, as Jeremiah shows figuratively, saying:

“Eighty [Note: [Col. 1005D] The manuscripts formerly read “seventy.”] men came from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria, with their beards shaved, their garments torn, and grieving; they had offerings and incense in their hands, to offer [Col. 1005C] in the house of the Lord” (Jer. 41). [Note: [Col. 1005D] Gregory, *Morals*, book 1, no. 52.]

> They shave their beards who withdraw confidence in their own strength from themselves. They tear their garments who do not spare themselves by inwardly rending the beauty of their souls. Those who come to offer incense and gifts in the house of the Lord are those who promise to offer themselves in sacrifice to God through prayer joined to works. Yet if they perceive themselves cautiously returning on the way of holy devotion, Ishmael son of Nethaniah comes in their course; because every malignant spirit, born into the error of pride after the example of its former master Satan, sets itself in opposition in order to deceive. It is well said of him that “he went on, weeping,” because, in order to prevail in killing devout minds as he passes by [Note: [Col. 1006D] Thus other manuscripts; ours reads “on the way.” The edition: “in killing them by striking.”], he hides himself beneath a covering of virtue; and while he pretends to agree with those who truly mourn, he is more safely admitted into the heart’s depths and more quickly kills inwardly, where he is hidden [Col. 1005D], because he often promises to raise them to higher things. [Note: [Col. 1006D] Edition: “He kills what is hidden inwardly by virtue. He often promises to advance them to higher things.”]

> Hence he is reported to have said: “Come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.” While promising greater things, he even removes lesser ones. Hence it is said: “When they came to the middle of the city, he killed them.” He kills in the middle of the city men coming to offer gifts to God because minds devoted to divine things, unless they guard themselves with great circumspection, lose their life at the very point of their journey while carrying the sacrifice of devotion, when the enemy [Col. 1006A] steals in.

> Hence it is fittingly added: “Ten men were found among them who said to Ishmael, ‘Do not kill us, for we have treasures in the field: wheat, barley, oil, and honey.’ And he stopped and did not kill them with their brothers” (Jer. 41). Hope in repentance is a treasure in a field. Because it is not seen, it is held buried, as it were, in the soil of the heart. Those who had treasures [Note: [Col. 1006D] Edition: “Those who had . . . treasures . . . were saved, because those who afterward . . .”] in the field were preserved. For those who, after falling into the fault opposed to their watchfulness, return to mourning, do not die as captives.

> When the ancient enemy neither strikes at the beginning of intention nor intercepts along the course of action, he stretches harder snares toward the end, besieging one all the more wickedly because he sees that only the end remains for him to deceive. [Note: [Col. 1006D] We have added “the end” from another manuscript; it is absent even in Gregory.] The Prophet had seen snares placed at their end when he said: “They shall watch my heel” (Ps. 55). For by the heel, which is the end of the body, the termination of an action is signified.

As has been written above, the ancient enemy always strives to deceive us, so that our works may be reprobate before God’s eyes. He frequently suggests that we should do evil; and whatever good may exist, he strives by every means to corrupt. He hinders us with all his effort from tending toward the heights and gladly drives us so that we may more readily plunge into the depths. Created in heaven, he fell miserably through his wickedness into hell, and out of envy desires to bring us with himself into eternal condemnation. We have done him no evil; but because, through God’s mercy, we have been called to the heavenly homeland [Col. 1006C] from which he himself was cast out, he labors enviously with all his might to hurl us into hell. It is not enough for him that, having stripped us of virtues, he cast us from the pleasantness of paradise into the misery of this world; rather, what is more grievous, he does not cease by countless devices to bring us to eternal destruction—God forbid.

That ancient enemy is called Nebuchadnezzar because he has led us captive from Jerusalem, that is, from the vision of peace, into Babylon, that is, into the confusion of vices, and has subjected us to the most grievous yoke of his cruelty. Of this it is said: “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Sir. 40).

What then, dearest brethren? Must we yield to the persuasions [Col. 1006D] of this most cruel tyrant or give our assent? By no means. Rather, what is more beneficial, we must resist with all our strength, aided by God. Hence blessed James, speaking to the twelve tribes, says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you; draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Jas. 4). Therefore let us resist, beloved, with God’s help, the devil and his most evil persuasions; and let us follow Christ, by whose precious blood we have been redeemed by the Lord from the same ancient enemy [Col. 1007A]. We ought rather—and more blessedly—to follow the most loving shepherd who redeemed us than the most wicked robber who made us captives.

The devil cast us from the state of uprightness into this valley of tears through pride and envy; Christ recalled us to the heavenly homeland through charity and humility. So great was the devil’s pride and envy that he offered us death; but Christ’s charity and humility prevailed so greatly that he mercifully restored us to our first rank and dignity. The pestilential pride of the devil harmed us unto death; the saving humility of Christ rescued us from death. The devil, to give us an example of perversity, says through pride: “I will ascend into heaven” [Col. 1007B] (Isa. 14); Christ, for our instruction, says through humility: “My life has been humbled to the earth” (Ps. 43). The devil says through pride: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14); Christ, through humility, “though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, becoming obedient to God the Father unto death” (Phil. 2). The proud and covetous devil says: “I will ascend above the stars of God, and on the mountain of God’s covenant, on the sides of the north, I will exalt my throne” (Isa. 14); the humble and gracious Christ says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11).

The proud and covetous devil says through Pharaoh: “I do not know God, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5); the humble and gracious Christ says: “If I said that I did not know my Father, I would be a liar like you. But I know him, and [Col. 1007C] I keep his commandments” (John 8). The proud and covetous devil says: “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. 29); the humble and gracious Christ says: “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5). “But my Father, dwelling in me, he has done the works” (John 14). The covetous devil says: “All the kingdoms of the world and their glory are mine; and I will give them to whom I will” (Luke 4). Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake, so that through his poverty we might become rich (2 Cor. 8). The proud and covetous devil says: “As abandoned grapes or eggs are gathered, so I gathered all the earth; and there was none to move foot or wing, to open the mouth and chirp” (Isa. 10); the humble and meek Christ says: “I became like a pelican” [Col. 1007D] (Ps. 101). And again: “I kept watch and became like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (ibid.). The proud and covetous devil says: “By the tread of my feet I dried up all the streams of embankments” (Isa. [Col. 1008A] 37); the humble and meek Christ says: “I do not seek my own glory, but I honor my Father” (John 8). The devil, proud and envious alike, exalts himself proudly to heaven. And, to conclude at last: the devil through pride is hurled down with great ruin into hell; Christ through humility is lifted up to heaven.

Therefore, dearest brethren, I have set forth for you a few snares of diabolical deceit and degrees of holy humility from the sayings of blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 1007D] Rather, of Paulinus of Aquileia, whose work is *On Saving Precepts*, from which Martin took these things. [Col. 1008D] Gregory the Great, *Morals*, book 34, final chapter, gives very similar material.], so that you may more easily understand how to escape these snares and attain through humility the heavenly kingdom. Therefore, beloved, if we truly wish to complete the course of our contest and attain eternal blessedness, let us first beware harmful covetousness [Col. 1008B] and diabolical pride, and with all humility endeavor to follow Christ’s footsteps. Since it has often been said already that the devil captured us through pride and Christ redeemed us through humility, we must therefore renounce the devil in every way and follow Christ with all strength and diligence of soul. Let us give thanks to him and joyfully say with all the saints: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted” (Ps. 125).

This is the seventh degree, in the figure of the Old Testament, signified by the number seven; through the coming Christ it prophesies the return of the faithful from the captivity of vices, as though from Babylon. Hence, for that return there is now consolation and sowing in good works and mercy, so that there may be a greater harvest. [Col. 1008C] The Prophet speaks here of that return as though it had already occurred, although it was still future, with prophetic certainty, in the person of those redeemed by Christ’s blood and converted from spiritual captivity—that is, in mind—because they serve the law of God. They sing these things while they are pilgrims, mourning upon the way and awaiting the redemption of the body. They are therefore already redeemed, yet in part still to be redeemed. Thus, in the person of the redeemed, as though returning from Babylon, he says: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those comforted.”

Let us therefore give thanks to this same Lord Jesus Christ, who by being born, dying, rising, and ascending delivered us from the devil’s captivity and, by the will of the Father, called us to the fellowship of the citizens above [Col. 1008D], to great consolation. May he deign to bring us there—he who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Twenty-Eighth Sermon: On the Litanies

[Col. 1009]

[Col. 1009A] Many Latin-speakers use the name *litanies*, yet do not know the interpretation of this name. It is fitting, therefore, that those who devoutly observe these days for love of God and for the salvation alike of their souls and bodies should know the meaning of the name. These days must be observed by the faithful people in fasting and prayer, and they ought not to be ignorant why or by whom they were instituted.

Litanies, then, as Isidore, teacher of the Spains, says [Note: [Col. 1009D] *Etymologies*, book 6, chapter 19], are called by a Greek name; in Latin they are called *Rogations* or “supplications.” The difference between litanies and *exomologesis* (“confession”) is this: *exomologesis* is performed solely for the confession of sins, whereas litanies are appointed to be made for the purpose of praying to God and obtaining his mercy in some matter. Yet although both terms fall under one designation, common usage no longer distinguishes whether they are called litanies or *exomologesis*.

The name *supplication*, however, is in some sense retained from paganism. For among the Romans, festival-days were either established by law or proclaimed. The proclaimed days were so called because the ancient poverty of the Romans led them to sacrifice from a public collection, or at least from the property of condemned persons. Hence sacrifices made from the property of the condemned were also called *supplications*. Thus *supplication* was named from *punishment* (*supplicium*), for sacred offerings were made from the possessions of those accursed.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we desire to celebrate the Rogation Days for the welfare of temporal life and for the salvation of souls, it is fitting, for the simpler among us, briefly to recall how they originated. For they are not to be thought to have come into customary observance without evangelical and apostolic authority. Indeed, when the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, having frequently promised His apostles that He would send them the Holy Spirit, He said among other things: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24). After they saw Him ascend into heaven, they returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and, as Luke the Evangelist records, “they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God” (ibid.). In order that they might deserve to receive the Holy Spirit, they prepared themselves by persisting in fasts and prayers, as the same Luke recalls in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “All these were persevering unanimously in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and His brethren” (Acts 1). But after they received the Holy Spirit, sent from heaven by the Father and the Son, and were scattered throughout the whole world to preach the Gospel to the nations, they handed down these days, as we believe, for observance by their successors; and thereafter Christian devotion began to celebrate them yearly with religious observance, that believers might deserve to share in the gift of that same Holy Spirit.

That these days are now observed by the Church not after, but before, the Ascension of the Lord, has the following cause. [Note: [Col. 1009D] Amalarius, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, ch. 37.] Saint Mamertus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, endured many calamities, by God’s hidden judgment, together with all his people. During his episcopate, therefore, a very great earthquake occurred, which overthrew many churches and also the shaken houses of many persons; and many beasts—wolves, namely, and others of the same ferocity—entered the city and devoured people, and did this throughout the whole year. When holy Easter came and the same bishop had celebrated the solemnities of Mass, on that very vigil—that is, at the first dawn of the Lord’s Resurrection—the royal palace, which stood in that city, was divinely set ablaze. And while these perverse disasters of destructive evils occurred daily, as the day of the Lord’s Ascension approached, the holy man appointed a three-day fast for all the people, in mourning and a spirit of contrition; and shortly afterward this tribulation and devastation itself ceased. [Note: [Col. 1010D] These matters are from Alcuin, or from the author of *On the Divine Offices*, ch. 33, “On the Rogation Days.”] Thereafter the bishops of Gaul assembled at that same Vienne, namely the chief city of Gaul, and jointly decreed that in each Church a three-day observance of fasting should be celebrated with due veneration before the day of the Lord’s Ascension, even unto the present. This custom is observed among us—indeed, throughout the universal Church of the faithful—most devoutly to this day, for various calamities: for the remission of sins, for peace, against pestilence, for the preservation of crops, and for other necessities.

Since, therefore, we ought to celebrate the Rogation Days—that is, the days of supplication—we have thought it fitting, beloved brothers, to say something for your strengthening upon the Lord’s words, as they have long ago been expounded by the holy Fathers. Knowing that prayer is exceedingly necessary for the human race amid adversities and continual needs, the Lord teaches us by a certain comparison that no weapons are so useful, none so victorious, as persevering prayer. Therefore, in speaking to human beings, the Lord sets before them things more familiar to them, so that, being Himself at once their instructor and helper, they may more readily reach the unknown through what is known. He thus offers them the comparison of a friend praying importunately and, through importunity, obtaining what he had requested.

That most glorious—indeed, most wise—Master, namely the Son of God and of the Virgin, seeing that after the loss of free will we are unable to possess any good from ourselves, exhorts and admonishes us not only to pray devoutly but also persistently, so that through prayer there may be supplied by Him who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), whatever the power of nature in us lacks. For while He was engaged in prayer, as the preceding Gospel passage related, His disciples came to Him and asked Him, saying: “Lord, teach us to pray, as John the Baptist also taught his disciples” (Luke 11). That most gracious Master said to them: “Thus pray: Our Father, who art in heaven; hallowed be Thy name; Thy kingdom come; Thy will be done, [Col. 1011B] as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil. Amen” (Matt. 6). In these words He briefly comprehends what we ought chiefly to ask for.

Meanwhile, it must be known that some gifts are natural and others are not. Natural gifts are, for example, the five bodily senses; non-natural gifts are faith, hope, charity, and other such things. Hence it is read in the Catholic Epistles: “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1). He calls the natural gift a *datum*, but the non-natural gift a *donum*. Among those things which are not natural, some are such that no one can be saved without them, such as faith, hope, and charity; while others are such that a person can be saved without them, such as the gift of prophecy, the gift of tongues, and the like.

It should further be noted that there are four things which follow one another: petitions, gifts, virtues, and rewards. First we ask something of God; then it is given; afterward virtues follow; and finally rewards. It must therefore be understood that in this Lord’s Prayer there are seven petitions; that there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, found in Isaiah (Isa. 11); seven virtues; and seven gifts or beatitudes—namely, the virtues and rewards which the Lord sets forth in the Gospel (Matt. 5).

[Col. 1011D] Now it must be seen what the petitions, gifts, virtues, and rewards are, and how they correspond to one another. The first petition is that we be delivered from evil, which is placed last in the *Our Father*; the second petition, that we not be led into temptation; the third, that our sins be forgiven; the fourth, that our daily bread be given us; the fifth, that God’s will be done in us; the sixth, that God’s kingdom may come; the seventh, that God’s name may be hallowed.

The first gift is the spirit of the fear of the Lord; the second, the spirit of piety; the third, the spirit of wisdom; the fourth, the spirit of fortitude; the fifth, the spirit of counsel; the sixth, the spirit of understanding; the seventh, the spirit of knowledge. The first virtue is poverty; the second, meekness; the third, mourning one’s own sins and those of others; [Col. 1012A] the fourth, hungering and thirsting after righteousness; the fifth, having mercy; the sixth, having a pure heart; the seventh, being peaceable. The first beatitude is possessing the kingdom of heaven; the second, possessing the earth; the third, consolation; the fourth, satiety; the fifth, obtaining mercy; the sixth, seeing God; the seventh, being called a son of God.

Now the first petition, namely to be delivered from evils, is nothing other than casting off every concupiscence, which is the first thing we ought to do. And because we cannot do this except in the spirit of the fear of the Lord, that gift rightly corresponds with this petition; and from this follows the first virtue, namely poverty; and from virtue, the first beatitude, which is to possess the kingdom of heaven, and this is common to [Col. 1012B] all the good. And because, when we wish to cast off earthly desires, temptations usually rise up, we ought to make the second petition, namely that we not be led into temptation. This means forgiving insults, even to those who inflict them; and this cannot be done without the spirit of piety, which therefore corresponds to this petition. Because this is done through meekness, meekness follows; and from this virtue follows the second beatitude, namely to possess the earth. By “earth” he here means the same thing as the kingdom of heaven; and “to possess” is more than “to have.”

The third petition is that our sins be forgiven us, as we forgive our debtors. Since this cannot be done without the spirit of knowledge, it rightly corresponds with this petition; and from this follows the third virtue, [Col. 1012C] namely mourning one’s own sins and those of others; and from this follows the third beatitude, namely consolation, because we shall be comforted in the future. The fourth petition is that our daily bread be given us. By bread he means the body and blood of the Lord, which strengthens us in this age and will make us glad in the future. This cannot be done without the spirit of fortitude, which therefore corresponds to this petition; and from this follows the fourth virtue, namely to hunger and thirst after righteousness, because we cannot fully possess it at present. From this follows the fourth beatitude, namely satiety, because we shall be filled in eternal blessedness.

And it should be noted that the first three petitions can be fulfilled in this age; three only in the future; [Col. 1012D] while the middle petition can be fulfilled both in this life and in the future, because in this life the body of the Lord strengthens us, and in the future it will make us glad. The fifth petition is that God’s will be done in us, which is nothing other than never resisting God’s will; and no one can fulfill this in the present age. The spirit of counsel rightly corresponds with this petition, as do mercy, which is the fifth virtue, and the fifth beatitude, which is the obtaining of mercy. The sixth petition is that the kingdom of God may come, that is, that we may attain to the vision of God. Here he calls the vision of God “the kingdom”; and we ought to ask that the kingdom may come, that is, that we may come to the vision of God. This rightly corresponds to the spirit of understanding, which is the sixth gift; to the sixth virtue, which is purity of heart; and to the sixth beatitude, [Col. 1013A] which is the vision of God. The seventh petition is that God’s name may be hallowed, which is nothing other than delighting in His name. To this rightly correspond the spirit of wisdom, being peaceable, which is the seventh virtue, and being called a son of God, which is the seventh beatitude.

And note that there is a difference between being peaceable and being pure of heart, and between the spirit of wisdom and the spirit of understanding. A peaceable person is one who feels no stirring in the flesh; a person pure of heart is one who, although he feels a stirring, nevertheless resists it. A person is said to possess the spirit of understanding when he understands the things of God with great desire. But one is said to possess the spirit of wisdom when, after understanding the things of God, he delights in them.

[Col. 1013B] We have said that there are seven petitions, seven gifts, seven virtues, and seven beatitudes. He gives seven beatitudes because the kingdom of heaven belongs both to those who are poor in spirit and to those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, and it is one and the same beatitude.

But it should be noted that Isaiah begins with the higher gift, whereas Christ begins with the lower virtue: because Isaiah showed God’s descent to human beings, whereas Christ indicated humanity’s ascent to God. Therefore, as stated above, when His disciples asked Him—and indeed, through them, we also asked Him—the Son of God commanded us to pray thus: that is, to ask for these seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer. Then He showed, by adding a comparison, how persistently we ought to persevere in asking, saying: “Which of you will have a friend and go to him at midnight?” (Luke 11). Spiritually and truly, this friend is understood to be God Almighty, who, though He is God and Creator of all creation, has deigned to call faithful servants His friends, saying: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15). And again: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things whatsoever I heard from my Father” (ibid.).

O most wise Maker of heaven and earth and of all creatures! O most merciful Restorer of the human race! O most gracious Governor of the whole world! You do not disdain to call friends Your little servants, whom You created from nothing! “We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17); we have an earthly foundation; we bear the frailty of the flesh; we sit upon the dung-heap of vices; we cannot perfectly avoid sins; we dwell in dust; we inhabit a house of clay. Yet You, most high King, eternally abiding without beginning, reigning without end, embracing all things, governing all things, loving good, not willing iniquity—You in whom and through whom all elements subsist, without whom the whole is nothing—You who measured the heavens with Your palm, suspended the mass of the earth upon three fingers, set a boundary to the sea, mightily penetrated the depths below, touch the mountains and they smoke (Ps. 143), look upon the earth and make it tremble: You whose face the angels and spirits of the righteous [Col. 1014A] always desire to see; seeing whom, they are satisfied without weariness, desire to see without toil, and desire to be satisfied without necessity; in whose sight the heavens are not clean; whose beauty the sun and moon marvel at—indeed, in comparison with whose brightness they seem not to shine but to be darkened; whose will is omnipotence; whose work is mercy; at whose command the dead return to life; by whose help the weak are strengthened; whose grace all saints desire; whose wrath the ungodly fear; who reign everywhere and thunder in the clouds; whose praise no one can fully express; whose wisdom no one can wholly know; whose greatness the world cannot contain; whose essence cannot be perfectly seen by anyone; whose peace surpasses all understanding; whose majesty neither begins [Col. 1014B] nor ends. And although You are supremely good and wonderful, immeasurable, incomprehensible, beyond estimation, beyond narration, and unchangeable, nevertheless by Your grace You cleanse from sins and vices those who serve You faithfully, illuminate them with virtues, and, because of Your exceeding charity, make them sharers in Your ineffable friendship.

O most merciful Father, what thanks worthy of You can we render for such innumerable and immeasurable benefits as You have deigned to grant us, though unworthy? Or with what praises can the frailty of the human race worthily honor You, who have most graciously opened to it the bosom of Your grace? By what merits can we obtain Your incomparable friendship, unless we are always obedient to Your commands? Therefore, O supreme ruler of kings, illuminate our hearts with the light of Your countenance, so that, ever fulfilling Your commandments in all things, we may be able to remain without end in Your sweetest friendship.

[Col. 1014C] Meanwhile, dearest brothers, it must be noted that no one who neglects to fulfill God’s commandments can be counted among God’s friends. But whoever endeavors without deceit to observe them, namely for love of God, is rightly called God’s friend. Hence it is said: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John 15).

Let us again recall the Gospel comparison which the Son of God proposed to stir the minds of the faithful to persist in prayer, so that, when examined more closely, it may be understood more clearly. “Which of you,” He says, “will have a friend?” (Luke 11), and so forth. As has already been said above, this friend is understood spiritually as God Almighty. Night, however, everywhere signifies tribulation. For as day belongs to joy, so night belongs to sorrow. We must therefore come to the friend at midnight, because under the pressure of tribulation we ought neither to prepare for vengeance nor to break ourselves, but humbly to entreat His help, who said: “In the world you shall have tribulation; but take courage, for I have conquered the world” (John 16). Although God must always be asked, yet especially when persecution rages or a storm arises, we ought to seek His aid lest we fail in tribulation, as the Psalmist did, [Col. 1015A] saying: “In my tribulation I cried unto the Lord, and He heard me” (Ps. 119).

Nevertheless, it must be understood that, as blessed Isidore says, prayer is prevented in two ways from obtaining what anyone asks. [Note: [Col. 1015D] Book III of the *Sentences*, ch. 7.] This happens if someone still commits evil, or if he does not forgive debts to one who has sinned against him. Once anyone has wiped this twofold evil away from himself, he immediately applies himself securely to prayer and freely directs his mind to those things which he desires to obtain by petitions. For if we do what God commands, we undoubtedly obtain what we ask. But whoever turns away from God’s commandments does not deserve what he asks in prayer, nor does he obtain from Him the good he requests, whose law he does not obey. Hence it is written: “He who turns away his ear lest he hear the law, his prayer [Col. 1015B] shall be abominable” (Prov. 28).

He also spreads out his hands culpably in prayer who boastfully displays his deeds while praying, just as the Pharisee prayed boastfully in the temple and wished himself, rather than God, to be praised for righteous works (Luke 18). Again, the prayer of some is turned into sin, as is written concerning Judas the traitor: “And let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108). For one who prays boastfully, seeking human praise, not only does not have his sin erased by his prayer, but prayer itself becomes sin. Thus Jews or heretics, although they may appear to fast, do not profit by their prayer toward the merit of purification; rather, it is changed into sin. Therefore the prayer of the elect is sometimes delayed amid their afflictions, so that the perversity of the wicked may increase. But when the righteous are heard in temporal matters, this occurs for the salvation of those who afflict them, so that, when temporal help is given to the former, the eyes of the wicked may be opened from their confusion. Thus the fire was cool for the three youths, [Note: [Col. 1015D] Compare here the note of the very learned García de Loaysa.] so that Nebuchadnezzar might acknowledge the true God, as the Prophet says in the Psalms: “Because of my enemies, deliver me” (Ps. 68).

Accordingly, the prayers of some are heard more slowly so that, being delayed and thereby stirred up more strongly, they may be enriched with greater rewards—after the example of frosts and the checking of crops, in which the later the sown seeds emerge, the more abundantly they grow to fruit. Whenever we pray and are not quickly heard, let us set our deeds before our own eyes, so that the very delay may be attributed to divine justice and to our own fault. Sometimes our not being heard quickly, though we pray persistently, is for [Col. 1015D] our benefit, not our adversity. For God often does not hear many according to their wish, in order to hear them according to their salvation. Many who pray are also not heard because God provides for them things better than what they themselves ask. This often happens to little children who entreat God not to be beaten at school; but because such an answer would hinder their progress, the result of their petition is not granted them. The same happens to certain elect persons who beseech God concerning some advantages or adversities of this life. Yet divine providence does not at once comply with their temporal desire, because it promises them better things eternally.

[Col. 1016A] What we ought to ask in prayer, however, the Son of God declares when He adds: “Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has come to me from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him” (Luke 11). For this is what we should seek and ask in prayer: that the friend, namely God, may pour into our hearts knowledge and love of the Holy Trinity. Or certainly, in prayer we should ask for three loaves—that is, faith, hope, and charity—without which it is difficult [Note: [Col. 1016D] Rather, impossible, as he said elsewhere.] for anyone to be saved.

The friend who is said to come from the road is our mind, which withdraws from us as often as it disperses itself in thought through the broad desires of this world. But it returns to us from the road when, setting our mind before itself, it begins to despise transient things and to hold fast and desire those things [Col. 1016B] which are eternal and enduring. But lest it perish from hunger, the friend must be asked to lend us three loaves, because the Lord’s mercy must be implored to grant our hearts, as was said, love of the Holy Trinity. And because God sometimes lengthens our desires, not to lessen the reward but to increase merit, it is fittingly added: “And he from within shall answer and say: Do not trouble me; my door is already shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give you.” The friend’s door is the understanding of the divine mystery, which Paul desired to be opened for him so that he might speak the word of God boldly (Eph. 6). This door, therefore, remains shut to us until it is opened to us by divine grace for knowing the divine mysteries.

By the children of the householder we should understand the apostles or their successors. They are rightly said to be with him in bed, because they have now been received into eternal rest. Concerning them it is said through the Prophet: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their beds” (Ps. 149). Those who are said to be in bed are aptly called children, because those who are children and innocent will attain eternal rest, such as those to whom the Lord says: “Children, have you any food?” (John 21). And again: “Allow the little children to come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). Peter the Apostle exhorts his hearers to become such persons, saying: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2). [Col. 1016D] It follows:

“And if he persists in knocking, I tell you, even if he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needs.” The comparison here is from the lesser: understand that even if a human being gives what he previously denied, not for friendship’s sake but overcome by weariness, God will much more give to those who ask Him, since He Himself urges us to ask. For unless He wished to grant these things, He would by no means invite us to ask. For when elsewhere He said that “one ought always to pray” (Luke [Col. 1017A] 18), He gave the comparison of the unjust judge whom a certain widow approached daily, saying, “Vindicate me against my adversary.” And for a long time he was unwilling. Afterward, overcome by weariness, he said to himself: “Although I do not fear God nor respect man, yet because this widow troubles me, I will vindicate her” (ibid.).

God wishes us to be importunate petitioners, [Note: [Col. 1017D] Saint Pope Celestine I was the first to state these words—“that His gratuitous gifts may also be our merits”—in Epistle 21 to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 12, saying: “So great … is God’s goodness toward all human beings that He wills His own gifts to be our merits.” Finally, the holy Council of Trent confirmed these words verbatim as a matter of faith (*Session* VI, *On Justification*, ch. 16), and afterward anathematized those who said that the good works of a justified person are God’s gifts in such a way that they are not also good merits of that justified person (ibid., canon 32).] so that His gratuitous gifts may also be our merits. For the ears of divine mercy are always open to our prayers, provided that we do not cease from petitions and do not waver in faith, as the Apostle James testifies, saying: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach. But let him ask in faith, wavering in nothing” (James 1).

Accordingly, when the Lord expounded the comparison [Col. 1017B] which He had proposed, He added: “And I say to you: Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives; and he who seeks finds; and to him who knocks it shall be opened.” Therefore eternal life must be requested through prayer, sought through good living, and knocked for through perseverance in good works. For there are two things which we must carefully consider in prayer. First, that we ask for those things which God wills; second, that our life not disagree with our prayers. For he applies himself to prayer in vain who either asks for things displeasing to God, or, if the things he requests are good, shows himself unworthy by living perversely.

Hence Eliphaz says to blessed Job: “Call, if there is one who will answer you” (Job 5). [Note: [Col. 1018D] Gregory, *Morals*, book V, ch. 30.] Almighty [Col. 1017C] God often disregards in distress the prayer of one who despises His commandments in tranquility. Our calling is to beseech God with humble prayer; God’s answering is to grant effect to prayers. He says therefore: “Call, if there is one who will answer you.” As though he plainly said: Though you cry out in affliction as much as you please, you have no God to answer you, because a voice in tribulation does not find Him whom the mind despised in tranquility.

Therefore, one who despises God’s commandments by living wickedly turns away from himself the hearing of divine goodness. Hence the Apostle James says: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly” (James 4). What things ought chiefly to be asked in prayer, however, the Lord elsewhere makes manifest, saying: “Seek first the kingdom of God [Col. 1017D] and His righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matt. 6). And again: “Ask, and you shall receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16). And lest we despair in prayer of receiving what we ask, the Lord further added another comparison, saying: “Which of you, when he asks his father for bread, will he give him a stone? Or for a fish, will he give him a serpent instead of a fish? Or if he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?”

Bread in this place signifies charity, and fittingly so. For just as bread is the chief article among human foods, so charity holds primacy among the other virtues. The Lord showed this when a learned scribe asked Him which was the greatest commandment in the law, and He answered: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with all your strength; and your neighbor as yourself. This is the great and first commandment” (Matt. 22). Or, indeed, charity is denoted by bread because, just as a table, even if it is filled with various foods, nevertheless seems poor without bread, so the other virtues are proved to be nothing without charity, as the Lord says in the Gospel: [Col. 1018B] “To everyone who has shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even what he has shall be taken away” (Matt. 13). Hence blessed Isidore, that outstanding teacher, says: [Note: [Col. 1018D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 3.] “Although some appear to share in faith and holy works, yet because they lack the charity of brotherly love, they possess no increase in virtue. For, as the Apostle says, ‘If I deliver my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing’” (1 Cor. 13). Without the love of charity, even if one believes rightly, one nevertheless cannot attain blessedness; for charity has such power that prophecy and martyrdom themselves are believed to be nothing without it. No reward can equal charity, because charity holds primacy over all virtues. Hence charity is called by the Apostle “the bond of perfection,” [Col. 1018C] because all virtues are bound together by its bond (Col. 3).

The opposite of this virtue, namely charity, is the stone—that is, hardness of heart without mercy. Fish, however, signifies faith, and very fittingly, because as a fish is nourished by water, so faith is strengthened by baptism, as the Lord says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16). Or faith is understood in another way through the fish: as a fish is hidden in the waters, so faith concerns those things which are not seen, as the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, [Note: [Col. 1018D] Supplement: ‘the evidence.’] of things not apparent” (Heb. 11). Or again, faith is signified by the fish because, just as a fish is beaten by rippling waves and grows all the more thereby, so faith advances all the more the more it suffers persecutions. Of this the Lord says: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Pass from here,’ and it will pass” (Matt. 17).

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Isidore, ibid., ch. 25.] The serpent is contrary to faith, namely unbelief or poisonous thoughts which kill the soul. For we sin not only in deeds but also in thoughts, if we take delight in them when they arise unlawfully. [Col. 1019A] For, as blessed Isidore says: [Note: [Col. 1019D] The same author, *Etymologies*, book XII, ch. 4.] “As the viper is torn apart and killed by the young placed in its womb, so our thoughts, nourished within us, kill us; conceived inwardly, they consume us with viperous poison and destroy our soul with a cruel wound.” The viper is called so because it perishes by force (*vi pereat*). [Note: [Col. 1019D] Read: *pariat*, “it gives birth.”] For when its belly comes to birth and groans, the young, not waiting for nature’s mature delivery, gnaw through its sides and burst out by force, at the cost of their mother’s life. Hence Lucan:

> “The viper’s knots unite, their bodies broken apart.”

[Note: [Col. 1019D] Manuscripts: “Vipers … with the knot of the body broken.”]

It is also reported that the male inserts his mouth into that of the viper and spits out semen; she, then, driven from the pleasure of lust into frenzy, bites off the male’s head when it has entered her mouth. Thus each parent dies: the male during copulation, the female during parturition. From the viper, moreover, are made lozenges which are called *Tyriaci* by the Greeks. It follows:

“If he asks for an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” In the egg hope is signified, because, just as the offspring in an egg is not yet seen but is believed to be future, so hope is not seen by the eyes but hoped for by the mind, as the Apostle says: “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience” (Rom. 8). Every righteous person, indeed, as blessed Isidore says, [Note: [Col. 1019D] Book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 4.] rests upon hope and fear: for now hope raises him toward joy, now the terror of Gehenna subjects him to fear.

Thus, as stated above, the offspring in an egg is not yet seen because all kinds of birds are born twice. First they are produced as eggs; then they are formed and animated by the warmth of the mother’s body. [Note: [Col. 1019D] The same author, *Etymologies*, book XII, ch. 7.] Eggs (*ova*) are called so because they are moist within (*uvida*). Hence a grape is called *uva* because within it is full of moisture. For *humidum* means what has moisture externally; *uvidum*, what has it internally. Some, however, think that *ovum* has a Greek origin for its name. They call them ὦα (“eggs”), with the letter V removed. Certain eggs are conceived from an empty wind, but they are not capable of generation unless they are conceived through male intercourse and penetrated by seminal spirit. [Note: [Col. 1020D] Perhaps: “have been.”] They say that eggs have such power that wood soaked with them does not burn, while a garment, by contrast, is scorched. Mixed with lime, they are also said to glue together fragments of glass.

Therefore, as has already been said, just as the offspring in an egg is not yet seen but is believed to be future, so hope is not seen with the eyes but is hoped for by the mind. The contrary of this virtue, namely hope, is the scorpion bearing its sting in its tail—that is, despair, which attempts to draw us back from all everlasting things. The scorpion, as blessed Isidore says, is an earthly worm [Note: [Col. 1020D] Ibid., ch. 5.] which is counted rather among worms than serpents: an animal, namely, armed with a sting. It is so called in Greek because it fixes its tail and pours out poison through its curved wound. It is characteristic of the scorpion that it does not strike the palm of the hand.

[Col. 1020A] By these comparisons, therefore—bread, stone, fish, serpent, egg, and scorpion—the Lord shows that, being himself gracious and merciful, he grants no evil things to one who asks for good things. For he does not give a stone in place of bread, because he does not grant to one who loves charity a hard and merciless disposition. Nor does he give a serpent in place of a fish, because he by no means compels one who sincerely seeks faith into unbelief. Nor does he offer a scorpion in place of an egg, because he does not force one who has hope within himself to fall into despair. It is characteristic of boundless goodness sometimes to make evil people good, but never to compel good people to become evil. Therefore he further concludes his statement, saying: “If you, then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give a good spirit to those who ask him?” Here our name is plainly made known, when it is said: “Though you are evil.” For, created good by God, we have become evil through sin. But if our goodness is compared with his goodness, it is not even called goodness. Thus, made evil through evil intention, we have a Father in heaven by virtue of our creation. It is as though the Lord said: If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children—that is, bread, fish, eggs, and the other things which human custom is accustomed to reckon among the goods of this present life—how much more will your Father from heaven give a good spirit to those who ask him: those, namely, who, enlightened by his Spirit, learn not only to ask for faith, hope, and charity, but are also worthy to receive them. Therefore, when he says, “He will give a good spirit to those who ask him,” [Col. 1020B] he includes all virtues of the soul; for the good things granted to human beings by God are administered through the Holy Spirit, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “The charity of God has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances, to another discernment of spirits” (1 Cor. 12).

Let us therefore ask without ceasing, dearest brethren, since assuredly our heavenly Father wishes to grant us good things, he who frequently admonishes us to ask. Let us cleanse our hearts of unlawful thoughts and our hands of wicked deeds, so that we may be found worthy of heavenly gifts and may offer prayers before almighty [Col. 1020D] God in our dangers and necessities. Hence we read that Zophar the Naamathite said to blessed Job: “If you remove from yourself the iniquity that is in your hand, and injustice does not remain in your tent, then you shall be able to lift up your face without stain, and you shall be steadfast and shall not fear” (Job 11). Gregory [Note: [Col. 1020D] *Morals*, Book 10, ch. 15. *Patrologia*, vol. 75, col. 935. We omit this excessively long passage for the sake of brevity.]: “Every sin is committed either by thought alone,” etc., down to: “Hence it is written: ‘It shall be well with one who fears God at the end’” (Ecclus. 1).

Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, children are the inheritance of the Lord, the reward is the fruit of the womb” (Ps. 126). Cassiodorus: “When he gives sleep,” that is, temporal death, in which there is secure rest—he gives it, I say, to his beloved. Augustine: After death the beloved shall rise [Note: [Col. 1021D] “All … shall rise” (Augustine continues, lest we suppose that he means only the beloved will rise), “but not as the beloved … Those others”—the reprobate—“shall rise for punishments; we shall rise as the Lord rose … He has risen, no longer to die … Hope for such a resurrection; and for this reason be a Christian, not for the happiness of this earth.], because the Lord was exalted after death. Therefore hope also for your own exaltation after death. Sit down first, then you shall rise. Cassiodorus: “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord.” Secondly, he states what the inheritance is and how it is gathered. It is as though he said: The beloved shall rise after sleep, that is, after death. And who are the beloved? Namely, the children. Which children? Those, indeed, who are the fruit of the womb. And what shall be theirs? Behold, theirs then shall be the inheritance of the Lord. What is that inheritance? Behold, the reward—that is, eternal life. Augustine: Observe that he says, [Col. 1021B] “the fruit of the womb.” Not all the children of the Church, which like a certain woman gives birth in pain, are the fruit of the womb, but only the good. For the womb of the Church, like Eve, gives birth in pain to good and evil children; as Rebekah bore in her womb twins at variance with one another, whom, when the birth had appeared, she distinguished, and loved Jacob (Gen. 25). So too the Church, in whose figure it was said to Eve, “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3), gives birth to good and evil. Hence the Apostle: “My little children, whom I am again in labor to bring forth until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4). Therefore the good are the fruit of the womb, like Jacob, beloved by his mother. The reward of these is to rise through suffering and to rejoice after the bread of sorrow. Thus for the present pain and groaning are theirs, but in the [Col. 1021C] resurrection, inheritance; because then the Church’s offspring shall appear, then it shall be seen who they are. But through what were these children acquired? Namely, through arrows: for “as arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of those who have been cast out.”

Or thus: “Behold, the inheritance.” Cassiodorus: Who are the beloved? “Behold, the inheritance of the Lord”: namely, children reborn from water and the Holy Spirit. These are the inheritance, because such persons are “the reward, the fruit of the womb”; that is, they are the reward rendered to the man Christ, who is the fruit of the virginal womb, and who acquired them through the obedience of his Passion.

If therefore, dearest brethren, as was said above, we seek to receive those things which we ask from God in necessities and distresses, we must with the utmost diligence remove iniquity from our hands and injustice from the tent—that is, from the heart. Then without doubt we shall be able to obtain from our heavenly Father what we ask in prayer, if we strive to lift innocent hands and a clean heart to him. One fittingly lifts his face—that is, his mind—to God in prayer if he takes care to wipe iniquity from his hands and injustice from his heart. We ought to show ourselves such persons by living well, so that by prayer we may be able to turn away from ourselves and from the whole Church the scourges of God which we suffer for [Col. 1022A] our sins. For God scourges those whom he loves (Heb. 12) in this life, lest he condemn them in the life to come. God often mercifully chastises his people by scourges in this world, but not all accept discipline. Of them Jeremiah speaks to the Lord, saying: “Lord, you struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jer. 5). Gregory [Note: [Col. 1021D] *Morals*, Book 23, ch. 13.]: “Every divine blow is either a purification for us in this present life or the beginning of the punishment to follow. On account of those who make progress it was said to God through the Psalmist: ‘You who devise pain in the commandment’ (Ps. 93); because, when the wicked man is scourged and corrected, who refused to hear the commandment, he has heard pain [Note: [Col. 1022D] After the word *pain*, Gregory begins another sentence, saying: “Pain … is devised for him in the commandment who is restrained from evil deeds by pain, as though pain were a commandment.” Martin copies the marginal gloss at the passage in Jeremiah.], and is restrained from evil as though by a commandment, namely pain. But concerning those whom scourges condemn and do not amend, it is said: ‘You struck them, and they did not grieve.’ These scourges begin in this life and endure eternally. Hence it is said: ‘A fire [Note: [Col. 1022D] Gregory and the Gloss: “A fire has blazed from my wrath, and it shall burn down to the lowest hell.”] has been kindled in my fury, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell’ (Deut. 32).” There is one scourge which begins temporally and is completed in eternal punishments.

The Prophet therefore fittingly speaks to the Lord concerning those who are corrected and amended: “Can a throne of iniquity cling to you, you who devise pain in the commandment?” (Ps. 93). It is as though he said: No wicked person sits with you, because there is no fellowship of light with darkness. Or the throne of iniquity is possession of the world joined with its love, which does not cling to God. It is as though he said more plainly: No wicked person clings to you, you who did not spare even us from the scourge. And this [Col. 1022C] means: you are the one who “devises,” that is, makes and fashions, labor and pain. Another reading: “You devise pain even for your children in the commandment.” Hence Peter says: “Judgment now begins with the house of God” (1 Pet. 4), that is, with the faithful. And if children are scourged, what ought most wicked servants to expect? And again: “If it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel?” (ibid.). Again: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall the ungodly and sinner appear?” (ibid.). How then shall the wicked be with you, when you do not spare even your faithful from the scourge?

It follows: “You devise pain in the commandment.” It is as though he said: You make pain, and that labor or pain is “in the commandment,” that is, it serves in the place of a commandment. For just as a commandment corrects, so the pain of a scourge amends children. He therefore fittingly used “you devise,” that is, you make and fashion. For one kind of pain is formed, another is unformed. Formed pain is that which instructs and corrects, and that pain is a commandment; otherwise it is unformed. Or thus: “You devise pain or labor in the commandment,” that is, labor and pain make a commandment for us, so that pain or labor itself may be a commandment to us. For the commandment includes: “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5), and: “those who suffer persecution for [Col. 1023A] righteousness’ sake” (ibid.). He commands these things with good reason, because labor is the price of the kingdom of God, by which that kingdom is loved as something purchasable. Therefore God commands labor and pain, so that a human being may not be without fear and may not love something else, having forgotten the true good. For Christ sleeps in calm weather, and then a wave arises in which he is awakened. So in some people faith in Christ grows lukewarm through the calm of ease, and the wave of temptation rises. But when a person is mercifully chastised by God and aided by his grace, he begins to overcome temptations, despise vices, love virtues, cling to God, and desire eternal goods.

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Gregory, *Morals*, Book 10, ch. 13.] “He who is still placed in the struggle of this life also, when he shall think himself consumed, as Zophar the Naamathite says, shall rise like the morning star” (Job 11); because, while falling outwardly, he is renewed inwardly; and the more [Col. 1023B] he endures adversities outwardly, the more abundantly he shines inwardly with the light of virtues. Paul bears witness when he says: “Though our outer human being is corrupted, yet our inner human being is renewed day by day according to God. For that which is present, momentary and light, of our tribulation works in us beyond measure, in sublimity, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4).

And it should be observed that he says not, “when you have been consumed,” but “when you think yourself consumed,” because what we do not see is uncertain, whereas what we hope for is certain.
