Thus Paul himself did not know himself to be consumed, but thought so; because, even as he fell amid adverse tribulations, he shone like the morning star, [Col. 1023C] saying: “As dying, and behold we live; as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as needy, yet enriching many” (2 Cor. 6). It must indeed be known that the mind of the good person, which endures harsher things for truth’s sake, hopes more certainly for the rewards of eternity. And again, the joy of eternal recompense is never reaped unless it has first been piously sown here through tribulation.

For this reason it is said through the Psalmist: “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. 125). Cassiodorus: “Going, they went,” by progress into a better life. [Note: [Col. 1023D] Here the name “Augustine” is missing; what follows down to “the sick” is his.] “And they wept,” who [Note: [Col. 1024D] “Because.”] were miserable among the miserable. For it is better that no one should be miserable than that you should perform mercy. Those who, in order to perform mercy, desire that others be miserable possess a cruel mercy. [Col. 1023D] So too a physician is cruel who, in order to practise his art, desires many sick people. “They went and wept, casting their seeds,” as though sending ahead of themselves into that future age seeds—namely, mercy and good works. By these they ascend: their own seeds, that is, works not produced by robbery but by their own labor. Let it therefore be said: “Going, they went and wept,” amid the miseries of this age, casting the seeds of good works. Although we are placed amid God’s scourges and the dangers of this world, we should nevertheless never cease from good work. God often scourges his elect in this present life so that he may spare [Col. 1024A] them in the life to come; and he afflicts them with various blows so that they may be corrected from wicked deeds.

Jeremiah, grieving and lamenting, declares this, saying: “The Lord has bent his bow like an enemy; he has strengthened his right hand like a foe; and he has slain everything that was beautiful to the sight in the tent of the daughter of Zion, and he has poured out his indignation like fire” (Lam. 2).

Allegorically. The Lord bends his bow against the Church as though he were an enemy, because she, like an enemy, is unwilling to hear the Lord crying out that she should repent and return to him. By the bow is understood judgment, by which each person is now struck in order to be corrected from evil. Either he is punished initially, or the bow is drawn for a long time, so that, when sins have reached their completion, it may be loosed for a graver punishment. In God’s bow are diverse arrows, of which some are sent to destroy the old human being with his deeds; others to afflict the whole people with various calamities, whether for a crown, correction, or punishment. Jeremiah laments, in the person of the Church, those whom the Lord strikes like an enemy—whether through the devil or through heretics, of whom it is said:

“The sinners have bent their bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, that they may shoot the upright in heart in darkness” (Ps. 10). Jerome: Since, behold, it is almost evident that sinners—that is, heretics—have bent the bow, that is, they have twisted Holy Scripture toward themselves, namely against its own intent, in order to wound the souls of the simple. Cassiodorus: Or they have bent the bow, that is, in the Scriptures [Col. 1024C] they possess a subtle understanding, as it seems to them, and suppose that others possess a lax one. “They have prepared their arrows in the quiver,” that is, they have poisonous words ready in their heart. For what purpose? “That they may shoot the upright in heart in darkness,” that is, those living with a simple understanding. Or, “that they may shoot the upright in heart in darkness,” that is, amid their own ambiguous and obscure opinions. They do this by means of the bow, not because Scripture has force for this purpose—that is, not through a defect in Scripture—but because they have “destroyed” through evil living or interpretation; that is, they have perverted the things which you made in the Scriptures, which you published perfectly, or perfected by fulfilling them in yourself.

Or according to another reading: “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the dark moon” [Note: [Col. 1024D] *Expositions on Psalm* 10.]. The moon fittingly signifies [Col. 1024D] the Church. Augustine: There are two opinions about the moon, and which is truer can either not be known at all, or can be known only with difficulty. Some say that it has its own light, but that one half of its globe is luminous and the other dark. As it gradually turns the part which shines toward the earth so that it may be seen, it appears horned and thus grows until that whole part is visible. When it turns again, the dark part begins to appear, until its whole body is again offered to our sight. This is the Church, which shines in part through spiritual persons and is dark in part through carnal persons. Its spiritual part at one time appears to human beings through good works, and at another lies hidden [Col. 1025A] in a conscience known to God alone, being seen only in the body; as happens when we pray in the heart and seem to be doing nothing, although we direct our hearts not to the earth but upward to the Lord.

Others say that the moon has no light except from the sun; but when it is with the sun, it has turned toward us the part which is not seen by the sun, and therefore it does not shine upon us. But when it withdraws from the sun, it is illuminated on the side it turns toward us, until, as the sun sets, it rises full in the east. But when it begins to draw near to the sun from the other side, its upper part is illuminated and the lower part is darkened. This too fittingly agrees with the Church, which has no light except from the sun of righteousness—that is, Christ—who in many places of Scripture is allegorically called the sun. Whichever of these two opinions mentioned above may be true, the Church is aptly understood allegorically by the moon. But if anyone avoids these obscurities because he either does not wish, does not have leisure, or does not have the intellectual strength to exercise his mind upon matters more troublesome than fruitful amid such obscurities, it is enough for him, leaving obscure causes aside, to observe with ordinary eyes the increase and decrease of the moon: it wanes in such a way that it is renewed. It signifies the Church, in which the resurrection of the dead is believed to be future. Behold how the moon signifies the Church. We must now see how the moon’s darkness signifies the darkness of the Church.

The moon is darkened in three ways: either when it comes to the end of its monthly course, or when a cloud is set against its brightness, or in an eclipse, when it appears blood-red. Similarly, the Church was dark when, at the beginning [Col. 1025C] of faith, still new, she had not yet shone greatly over the earth; or when, covered by clouds of blasphemies, she is reviled; or when she is bloodied by the slaughter of martyrs. In these terrors and obscurities of the Church, the wicked shoot deceitful words in order to pervert the upright, because they know that these times are suitable for deceiving the weak. Let it therefore be said: “That they may shoot the upright in heart in the dark moon,” that is, in the darkness of the Church, which is darkened in three ways, as was stated above. Augustine: The Church is called dark when many of her children, both unlearned and carnal, abound in her; then wicked heretics, taking occasion from the dark moon, heap reproaches on Catholics because they dwell with such persons and receive sacraments from such persons. Therefore the sinners, as was already said, have bent [Col. 1025D] their bow, prepared their arrows in the quiver, in order to shoot the upright in heart in darkness; for arrows of this kind come from the bow of the Lord, that is, from divine judgment.

Hence blessed Job says: “The arrows of the Lord are in me” (Job 6). But the Lord does not strike some persons in order that they may be corrected, because the bow is drawn in wrath so that those hardened in heart may be struck more severely. Hence it is said: “You gave a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the bow” (Ps. 59). Augustine: O Lord, by present tribulations you have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they may flee from the face of the bow—namely, from the assault of future vengeance, that is, future judgment. This bow, as though already drawn, threatens but does not yet strike; for judgment terrifies us but does not yet condemn us. Its signification is given to us [Col. 1026A] through present things, because if God punishes us so harshly here, what will he do at the future judgment? Judgment is aptly called a bow, because the farther a bow is drawn backward, the more forcefully the arrow is carried forward. So too, the longer judgment is delayed, the more grievously it will come.

Or the sign is understood as the banner of the cross, which is given as the sign of the cross so that we may follow Christ’s sufferings and thereby escape from the face of the bow; for if we are companions in his sufferings, we shall also be companions in his resurrection (2 Cor. 1). “You gave a sign to those who fear you,” that is, the banner of the cross to imitate, so that through it they may flee from the face of the bow—that is, judgment. Or: “You gave a sign to those who fear you,” namely the holy Scriptures, so that through them they may flee from the face of the bow—that is, judgment.

[Col. 1026B] The Psalmist saw himself wounded by these arrows when he groaningly said to God: “Your arrows have been fixed in me, and you have strengthened your hand over me” (Ps. 37). Augustine: Here the penitent, in the person of those afflicted, enumerates the adversities he suffers, so that because they are many, they may be enough—that is, sufficient—for God, lest he suffer worse things. It is as though he said: Do not rebuke me in fury, because the things I suffer may suffice you. And this is: “For your arrows have been fixed in me.” The arrows are God’s acts of vengeance, namely pains of soul and body; for just as arrows are drawn and fixed, so God’s acts of vengeance were drawn in Adam through the threat by which God warned him, saying: “On whatever day you eat of the forbidden tree, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). And because he ate, the arrows were fixed [Col. 1026C] also in us through punishment and guilt. For he was the origin of this misery, and we his offspring. They were fixed, and not for an hour; rather, “you have strengthened” them, namely for a long time, so that they may remain until the end of the age; and in many things, namely in body and soul; and in those same things in many ways, as is shown below. “You have strengthened,” I say, “your hand over me,” that is, your vengeance.

Hence Jeremiah says: “The Lord strengthened his hand like an enemy and slew everything beautiful to the sight in the tent of the daughter of Zion” (Lam. 2). The Lord strengthens his hand as an enemy against the Church when he afflicts her without ceasing, so that, corrected, she may return, or, hardened, may pay the penalties. He slays what is beautiful to the sight when he permits her precious members to perish. He pours out [Col. 1026D] his indignation like fire. This no longer needs exposition, but tears and sighs, because we plainly see all things consumed by the fires of discord, the flames of desire, and the afflictions of the air. We read these things more certainly in ourselves than we recall them from Scripture.

Morally. The Lord bends his bow against the sinful soul as though an enemy when, though it sins, he does not soften it to repentance, but permits it, with his hand stretched out, to go after carnal desires and does not turn it back. Thus everything beautiful to the sight is slain: namely, the decency of morals in its conscience. The Lord is said to destroy when he permits destruction, and hands it over to shameful passions and the flames of lust, so that, inflamed by its desires, it may follow its lovers—the demons [Col. 1027A]—to perdition. But he acts mercifully when, visiting sinners by scourging, he does not allow them to perish in their crimes. He, the most just Judge, leaves no sin unpunished, but ordering all things carefully, grants to each according to his merit, as he says through Ezekiel in a certain interrogative form:

“What is this proverb that you repeat among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’?” (Ezek. 18). This proverb is what is stated more openly in Exodus: “I am he who repays the sins of fathers upon their children, unto the third and fourth generation, to those who hate me” (Exod. 20). And elsewhere: “I am God, repaying iniquity upon children and children’s children, unto the third and fourth generation” (Deut. 5). For this has one sound in its words and another meaning in its sense. Up to now we have thought that the two testimonies set out above were not a proverb but expressed a straightforward proposition; and although we do not dare to say anything—as neither does a clay vessel against its potter (Isa. 45)—we nevertheless suffer a hidden stumbling-block: that it should seem unjust for one person [Note: [Col. 1027D] “Another.”] to sin and another [Note: [Col. 1027D] “Another.”] to pay for the sins. For if God repays sins unto the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one person should sin and another be punished. But he adds: “To those who hate me.” For children are not punished because their fathers sinned, but because, like them, through a kind of inherited evil, they hate God. As was stated above, therefore, the Lord says in Exodus: “I am he who repays the sins of fathers upon children unto the third and fourth generation.” But here the heretics who do not accept the Old Testament say: How great is the cruelty of the law of God and the prophets, which extends its wrath unto the third and fourth generation! But they must be answered that even in this God the Creator’s mercy is shown. For it is mercy not to punish at once, but to withhold the sentence and defer vengeance.

There are some who explain it thus: they say that the father within us is the slight impulse [Note: [Col. 1027D] Perhaps *impulse*; the reading below has the same word.] of carnal sensations and the incitements of vices; the son, when thought has conceived sin; the grandson, when you have fulfilled in action what you thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, [Col. 1027D] when you have not only committed the sin but also gloried in it, according to the saying: “When the wicked man has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). God therefore does not punish the first and second stirrings of thoughts, which the Greeks call *propatheiai* (προπάθειαι, “pre-passions”), without which no human being can exist, [Note: [Col. 1027D] Supply “not”: otherwise the statement neither agrees with the truth nor with what is said on the following page, [Col. 1028D].] but he does punish if anyone resolves to carry out what has been conceived in thought and refuses to correct by repentance the things he has done. Hence it is said: “No human being is without sin, not even if his life on earth has been but one day” (Job 14). And elsewhere: “Who shall boast that he has a clean heart?” (Prov. 20). And: [Col. 1028A] “Even the stars are not clean in the sight of God” (Job 15); and [Note: [Col. 1028D] The marginal gloss, to which all these words belong, reads: “And against his angels God found something perverse.”] “God finds perversity in his angels” (Job 4). But if that exalted nature, before it was confirmed by God, was not free from sin, how much more so human beings, who say with the Apostle: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Even when he has done every good thing, he ought to say: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126).

Cassiodorus: The Lord Christ builds; unless he works inwardly, no one can make progress in virtues. At his admonition we desire good things; with his help we begin; with his continued support we complete them. By his aid we persevere in good works; when he abandons us, we immediately fall away from the good things we have begun. Thus what he says of himself in the Gospel is true: “Without me, you can do nothing” (John 15). Alternatively: Unless the Lord Jesus Christ builds the house—that is, the Church—those who build it labor in vain: namely, preachers, speaking outwardly as ministers of building, and guardians of those built. The house is the people of God, the temple of God, the city of God. Everyone who makes progress ascends to it; everyone who falls away falls from it. By loving God you ascend; by loving the world you fall. For these are words of those who love and burn with a certain holy desire. Unless therefore the Lord builds this house, those who build it labor in vain, because “neither he who plants is anything nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

[Col. 1028C] Augustine: All who preach the word of God in the Church labor in this building, namely, the ministers of God’s sacraments. Therefore, to prove that the first impulse of thought—indeed, the small prompting of the mind—is not punished by God, but rather that a person is punished if he carries out in action what he has conceived in his mind, one must cite the passage in Genesis where it is said: Ham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, but the sentence of cursing was received not by him but by his son Canaan, in the words: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant of servants to his brothers” (Gen. 9). For what justice is there in a son’s being punished when his father sinned? The Apostle, indeed, sets against this the statement that a woman is saved if her children remain in faith, holiness, and chastity (1 Tim. 2). It seems not to be just that parents should be saved if their children and grandchildren are good. For many holy parents have evil children, and many sinners have holy children. Therefore, according to the sense we have stated, the sins of fathers must be understood as punished in the branches, not in the root. Let this suffice concerning the proverb or parable: namely, that the Law and the Prophets—that is, Exodus and Ezekiel, indeed God himself, who spoke both here and there—may not seem to differ in their judgments.

That a righteous son is not punished for an unrighteous father, nor a righteous father condemned for the unrighteousness of his son, [Col. 1029A] the Lord declares through Ezekiel, saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18). That is, just as the sins of children do not harm fathers, so the sins of fathers do not pass on to children; but the soul that sins shall die. That soul alone which sins shall die—not through annihilation of its substance, however, but by being separated from God, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). And elsewhere: “Everyone who lives and believes in me shall not die for ever” (John 11). And again: “If anyone keeps my word, he shall not see death for ever” (John 8). But Balaam’s saying, “Let my soul die the death of the righteous” (Num. 23), must be understood thus: Let it die to the world and to sin, and live with the souls of the righteous, whose life [Col. 1029B] is Christ. Hence the prophet, trusting in God’s mercy, said: “I shall be pleasing to the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114). Explaining this, blessed Augustine says: “I shall be perfectly pleasing to the Lord, because there shall be no fall of walking feet, no slipping of weak flesh; and this in the land of the living, who live eternally—something I shall not do while I live in mortal flesh.”

It should be observed that he did not say “I am pleasing,” but “I shall be pleasing.” It is as though he said: I shall be pleasing then, which I cannot be now. Balaam is also interpreted as “vain people,” that is, the nations which desire to have fellowship with animals. Balaam therefore does not wish that his soul should die with beasts, but with the righteous—that is, with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who are called upright and righteous. [Col. 1029C] Hence the book of Genesis received its name from their designation.

Therefore, beloved, it is not surprising if, by divine judgment, we are continually afflicted by scourges, since we continually provoke against ourselves the wrath of God’s indignation not only by unlawful thoughts but also by wicked deeds. For in this present time we are not crushed for the sins of our fathers, but for our own offenses, by which we daily provoke God and kindle against ourselves the fire of his wrath. For this reason the Lord pours out his fury upon the Church, as Jeremiah the prophet declares: “The Lord has completed his fury and poured out the wrath of his indignation; he has kindled a fire in Zion, and it shall devour its foundations” (Lam. 4).

Allegorically. The Lord’s fury has been completed upon the Church because she has filled up the measure of her sins. Hence it is said: “Contempt has been poured out upon princes, and he makes them wander in a trackless place, not on a way” (Ps. 104). It is as though he said: Lifted up in pride, they strove with one another to act unjustly and to live contrary to God’s commandments and will. They are called princes because they are ruled not by the Lord’s command but by the desire of their own pleasures. The Lord made them wander—that is, he permitted it. Of them it is said: “He dismissed them according to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own inventions” (Ps. 80). And again: “He dismissed them into the hand of their iniquity, that they might do things which are unfitting” (Job 8).

[Col. 1030A] Alternatively. Contention has been poured out upon the princes of heretics, because proud heresiarchs contend against Catholics; and the Lord made those princes wander by leaving them to themselves. Hence it is said: “He gave them up to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1). Thus he led them astray, because he abandoned them to themselves. For, if you inquire properly, they lead themselves astray. “For whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6). Therefore he made them wander by leaving them in a trackless place and not on the way. The Lord thus poured out the wrath of his indignation because through sinning we have been poured out. He kindled a fire in Zion—not that which descended from heaven upon the apostles (Acts 2), but that which consumed Job’s children (Job 1). For God has various fires, which he sends forth from his treasuries; “whose fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). Some he sets ablaze in order to instruct, and others in order to burn them up. Once these fires are kindled, he permits every foundation—that is, sound and true faith—to be utterly overthrown. Thus we ought to lament our miseries rather than those of the Jews: in us the fire of desire has been kindled, the devouring flame of other vices has seized all, “the pot kindled from the face of the north” boils (Jer. 1), and the furnace of the Babylonian king—that is, of the devil—burns up whatever Chaldeans it finds (Dan. 3).

Let us therefore, dearest brethren, entreat the almighty Lord with every affection of devotion that he may not permit us to walk according to our iniquities, but that, as a most gracious Father, by scourging and correcting us, he may make us fulfil his will in all things. For it is far better, for our salvation, to be scourged temporarily by God our most merciful Father than to be condemned eternally for our crimes.

Therefore Eliphaz the Temanite, as though consoling blessed Job, says: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects” (Job 5). Gregory [Note: [Col. 1029D] *Morals*, Book VI, ch. 23, near the end.]: The first virtue is that vices which must be avoided should not be committed; the second is, at least, to correct them once committed. But often we not only fail to avoid faults when they are impending, but do not even acknowledge those we have committed. And the sinner’s mind is darkened all the more deeply because it does not understand the harm of its own blindness. Thus it often happens, through the abundance of the divine gift, that punishment follows fault, and scourges open the eyes of the offender [Col. 1030D], which security amid vices had blinded. For the torpid mind is touched by a blow in order that it may be awakened, so that one who, secure, has lost the condition of his uprightness may, when afflicted, consider how far he has fallen. Thus the very severity of correction becomes for him the source of light. Hence Paul also says: “Everything which is reproved is made manifest by the light” (Eph. 5). Therefore the strength of pain is an argument for salvation. Hence Solomon says: “A remedy will cause the greatest sins to cease” (Ecclus. 10). Again he says: “Whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3). Hence the Lord speaks to John in an angelic voice, saying: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3). Hence Paul says: “All discipline indeed for the present [Col. 1031A] seems not to be a matter of joy but of sorrow; yet afterwards it will yield to those trained by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness” (Heb. 12). Although pain and blessedness cannot coexist, it is nevertheless rightly said here: “Blessed is the man whom the Lord corrects,” because by being weighed down with the pain of correction, the sinner is at some time instructed toward that blessedness which is without the intervention of pain.

It follows: “Therefore do not reject the Lord’s rebuke.” Whoever is struck on account of a fault, but rises up in complaint about his own beating, rejects the Lord’s rebuke, because he charges that he suffers it unjustly. But those who are struck not for the cleansing of sin but for the testing of their strength, when they investigate the causes of their affliction, are by no means to be said to reject the Lord’s rebuke, because they strive to discover in themselves what they do not know. Thus blessed Job too, bursting forth into words of freedom amid the blows of his affliction, questions the judgments of the One striking him all the more rightly because he more truly does not know within himself the causes of his suffering. Eliphaz, therefore, who judged blessed Job—bearing the type of holy Church—to have been struck not by a test of proving but for purification, thought that, in speaking freely amid the scourges, Job had rejected God’s rebuke. Therefore, while still proclaiming the ordinances of the heavenly dispensation, he adds:

“It is God himself who wounds and heals; he strikes, and his hands will heal.” Almighty God wounds in two ways those whom he intends to bring back to salvation. Sometimes [Col. 1031C] he strikes the flesh and melts the hardness of the mind by his fear. Thus, by wounding, he calls back to salvation when he outwardly afflicts his elect so that they may live inwardly. Hence he also speaks through Moses, saying: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I myself will heal” (Deut. 32). For he kills in order to give life; he strikes in order to heal, because he permits outward blows precisely in order to cure inward wounds of sins.

But sometimes, even though outward scourges seem to cease, he inflicts inward wounds, because he strikes the hardness of our minds with his desire; but in striking he heals, because, pierced by the dart of his fear, he calls us back to a sense of uprightness. For our hearts are badly healthy when they are wounded by no love of God, when they do not feel the misery of their exile, when they do not languish with even the slightest feeling for a neighbor’s infirmity [Col. 1031D]. Therefore they are wounded in order to be healed, because God makes unfeeling minds ardent through the fire of charity by the shafts of his love. Hence the bride in the Song of Songs says: “I am wounded by love” (Song 5).

For the soul, badly healthy and cast down in the blind security of this exile, neither saw the Lord nor sought to see him. But, struck by the shafts of his charity, it is wounded in its inmost parts by an affection of compassion; it burns with desire for contemplation, and in a wondrous manner is brought to life by a wound—it having previously lain dead in health. It grows hot, pants, and now desires to see him whom it had fled. Thus it is brought back to salvation by a blow, when it is recalled from the security of inward repose by the disturbance of his love. But when the wounded mind has begun to pant after God, when, despising all the allurements of this world [Col. 1032A], it tends by desire toward the eternal homeland, whatever had formerly seemed pleasant and friendly in the world immediately becomes a temptation to it. For those who had been accustomed to love it while it sinned cruelly attack it when it lives uprightly; and the mind upright in God endures the wars of its flesh, in which it had formerly lain pleasantly while serving vices. Former pleasures return to memory and rise against the mind that is casting them off in a grievous conflict. But because, while we are worn down by temporary labor, we are freed from everlasting pain, he aptly adds:

“In six tribulations he will deliver you, and in the seventh evil will not touch you.” For what is signified by the number six, followed by the seventh, except the activity and course of the present life? For on the sixth day, after completing all things, God created humankind [Col. 1032B]; on the seventh he rested. This seventh day has no evening, because no boundary thereafter encloses the rest which follows. Therefore, when all things are completed, rest follows; for after the good works of the present life comes the recompense of eternal rest. Thus in six tribulations the Lord delivers us, so that evil may not touch us in the seventh; because through the training of paternal mercy he wears us down by the labor of the present life, but at the coming of judgment hides us from the scourge. Thus he will then present us to salvation with all the greater certainty, insofar as his scourges now cut us more harshly.

Adding again, he says:

“In famine he will rescue you from death, and in war from the hand of the sword.” As famine of the flesh is the withdrawal of bodily support, so famine of the mind is the silence of divine speech. Hence it is rightly said through the prophet: “I will send [Col. 1032C] famine upon the land: not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God” (Amos 8). And because when divine speech abandons the human mind the temptation of the flesh prevails against it, it is aptly added: “And in war from the hand of the sword.” For we suffer war when we are attacked by the temptations of our flesh. Concerning this war the Psalmist says:

“Shade my head in the day of battle” (Ps. 139).

It is as though he said: O truest Lord! You are not as human masters, who purchase from a little purse; rather, you purchased me with your blood. Men purchase from a little purse, that is, with the money of a very small bag. For all money is nothing in comparison with the blood of Christ. It is as though he said: Hear me, you who are the strength [Col. 1032D] of my salvation, that is, who give strength to my salvation—namely, the perseverance by which I may be saved. He says this because he saw dangers; he saw an abundance of evils, through which charity grows cold and iniquity abounds; and he saw the consolation, namely, that whoever perseveres in bearing sufferings, temptations of the flesh, and the adversities of this world, will be saved (Matt. 10). Perseverance, therefore, belongs to strength. Since it is difficult to persevere on a long road, he says: “You are the strength of my salvation” (Ps. 139), that is, you give the strength to persevere in good things, so that by persevering I may be saved; and I hope in you, who are strength, because on the day of battle—that is, while I fight outwardly against false believers and inwardly against the law of the members—you have shaded my head through the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore almighty God shades our head [Col. 1033A] through the grace of the Holy Spirit when, mercifully protecting us, he frees us outwardly from the attacks of ungodly people and inwardly from the temptations of vices.

[Note: [Col. 1033D] Gregory again.] Therefore, since the reprobate, while they fail through famine of the word, are also pierced by the sword of war, the Lord both rescues his elect from death in famine and hides them from the sword in war, because, while refreshing their minds with the food of his word, he makes them strong against bodily temptations. But there are some who, although they refresh themselves from inward famine through divine speech, and although they are already supported against the battles of temptations by the power of continence, nevertheless still fear to be struck by human detractions; and while they dread the darts of tongues, they often strangle themselves in the snare of sin.

Thus it is plainly added: “You will be hidden from the scourge of the tongue.” [Col. 1033B] The scourge of the tongue is the reproach of an inflicted insult. Those strike the good with the scourge of the tongue who persecute their works by mocking them. For the tongue often calls one back from a good work while it censures, and puts itself forth like a scourge, because it beats the back of the timid mind. The Prophet had perceived this scourge of the tongue lying in wait for the mind of the elect person when he said: “He himself will deliver me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word” (Ps. 90). For hunters seek nothing other than flesh. But we are delivered from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word when, by despising them, we overcome both the snares of fleshly persons and the insults of mockery. Their harsh words, indeed, are those that oppose our good paths. But to escape the harshness of speech is to tread down, by disregarding them, the mockeries of detractors. Thus the holy soul is hidden from the scourge [Col. 1033C] of the tongue because, while it does not seek the honor of praise in this world, it does not feel the insults of detraction.

But there are some who now despise the words of detractors and regard mockeries as nothing, yet still fear bodily punishments and torments. For the ancient adversary attacks in many forms in order to draw us back from right intention; he assaults our temptation now through famine of the word, now through conflict with the flesh, now through the scourge of speech, now through the calamity of persecution.

But since every perfect person, once he has conquered vices within himself, at once arms himself also against the vices of suffering, it is aptly added: “And you will not fear calamity when it comes.” For holy men, because they see themselves fighting against a many-formed [Col. 1033D] adversary, prepare themselves in many ways for the contest. Against famine, they have the nourishment of the divine word; against the sword of war, the shield of continence; against the scourge of the tongue, the protection of patience; against the loss of outward calamity, the aid of inward love. Thus it wonderfully comes about that, the more numerous the temptations with which the zealous enemy assails them, the richer in virtues the watchful soldiers of God become.

Therefore, beloved brethren, following the footsteps of Christ’s soldiers, let us willingly endure the adversities of this present world, so that, cleansed from sins, we may be able to attain the riches of the heavenly kingdom. For this reason we are mercifully scourged by God in this life for our iniquities, so that we may be found cleansed at his judgment [Col. 1034A]. For this reason, by the ordering of divine grace, adversities are brought upon us, so that we may not be condemned with this world (1 Cor. 11). We are struck on every side and filled here and there with bitterness; yet this is not for condemnation, but so that, purified from vices, we may deserve heavenly gifts. For God does not cruelly ulcerate us as an enemy, but kindly chastises us as a most loving father. Nor does he strike us in hatred as enemies, but corrects us in love as sons. Therefore we ought not murmur under God’s scourges, but give thanks, since he scourges us precisely in order to rescue us from eternal death. “For what son is there whom his father does not correct?” (Heb. 12). Whoever, therefore, is made alien to a father’s discipline is plainly proved foolish.

Hence Solomon speaks in correction: “My son, do not [Col. 1034B] neglect the discipline of the Lord, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him; for whom the Lord loves he corrects, and, like a father, delights in his son” (Prov. 3). Whoever murmurs against God under scourges accuses the justice of the Judge and provokes him to greater wrath. For what is done by a just judge cannot be unjust. We know, therefore, that we suffer justly because he scourges us who always judges with justice. Let us not, then, murmur, but give thanks to God, because he mercifully wearies us now with adversities in order to rescue us hereafter from eternal punishments.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us also observe these days of the litanies according to the measure of our smallness, with the greatest reverence and devotion of mind, with abstinence [Col. 1034C] of the flesh and humility of spirit; not only that we may escape the rage of visible wolves, but, what is better, that we may be able to overcome the temptations of invisible wolves—that is, unclean spirits. For fasting is a most powerful weapon against the temptations of demons, as the Lord says: “This kind is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Matt. 17). Fasts not only help against temptations, but also raise the mind to understand divine mysteries. Thus Moses, in order to deserve to receive the Law, fasted for forty days and forty nights (Exod. 24). Daniel, moreover, in order that he might understand secret mysteries, was not only remarkably abstinent in the court of Babylon, but for the days of three weeks flesh [Col. 1034D] and wine did not enter his mouth; nor was he anointed with ointment until the days of three weeks were completed (Dan. 1).

We likewise, in order to deserve to share in the gift of the Holy Spirit, ought to celebrate these days with purity of mind and body, abstinence from food, distribution of alms, love of God and of humankind, hatred of vices, confession of sins, compunction of tears, and zealous practice of the other virtues; so that where our flesh feels affliction, there the hunger of the poor may feel consolation. Nor should we pray only for our own needs, but also for the needs of the whole Church: namely, for the peace of the Church, [Col. 1035A] the tranquility of the times, the abundance of crops, and temperateness of the air; for kings and the other governors of the faithful people, as the Apostle exhorts when he says: “I urge, first of all, that prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for kings and for those established in high position, and for all people, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity; for this is acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of truth” (1 Tim. 2).

Since these days, as has been said above, are days of abstinence, not of rejoicing, let no one wear costly garments on them; rather, we ought to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Let feasting, drunkenness, fornication, quarrels, disputes about temporal things [Col. 1035B], and absolutely all fleshly pleasures be forbidden. Let no one presume to ride in the procession; let no one utter idle or shameful words; let no one dare to absent himself because of worldly business or gain; let no one wear shoes, but let all proceed barefoot. Let men by no means go through the streets singing vain and worldly songs, nor let women lead dances in the manner of girls [Col. 1036A]; but let all come devoutly to the general procession, men separately and women separately.

It should further be noted that this litany is called the *minor* litany, in distinction from that litany which Roman custom devoutly performs on the day of Saint Mark the Evangelist with great earnestness in prayer. It is called the *major* litany because of Roman authority. For that one [Note: [Col. 1035B] Thus the manuscript, but read: “this one.”] was established by Pope Saint Gregory for two reasons: namely, because of the threat of war, which at that season is easily aroused because of the new grass; and because it is necessary for the preservation of crops. But this one [Note: [Col. 1036B] “That one.”] was instituted by Saint Mamertus, bishop, as by a lesser author. Therefore, beloved brethren, following the footsteps of the holy Fathers and obeying their sacred ordinances, let us observe these days with [Col. 1036B] all veneration, so that in this present life we may be delivered from all adversities, and, after the consummation of this age, aided by their prayers, may deserve to enjoy eternal joys—through him who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON TWENTY-NINE: ON THE ROGATION DAYS

[Note: [Col. 1035D] In the manuscript index: “Another sermon on the litanies.”]

[Col. 1035]

[Col. 1035C] First we must consider, dearest brethren, what a litany is; second, since there are two litanies, why one is called major and the other minor; third, why they were instituted; fourth, how one ought to fast and dress during them, and what the people ought to sing in the litany. A litany, therefore, means a supplication or a rogation. It is called a supplication because then we entreat God that almighty God may deliver us from sudden death and other adversities. It is called a rogation because then we ask the saints to intercede for us with God. There are two litanies, namely the major and the minor. The major is held on the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist. It is called major both because of the authority of its founder—for Pope Gregory, who is also called the Great, instituted it—and because of the authority of the place. For it was instituted [Col. 1035D] in Rome, and it was decreed that it should be celebrated everywhere. This litany, namely that before the Ascension of the Lord, is called minor because it was instituted by a lesser person, that is, Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne.

Saint Gregory relates the time when the first litany, which is celebrated on the feast of Saint Mark, was instituted, saying [Note: [Col. 1035D] *Dialogues*, Book III, ch. 19.]:

“Five years before this, when the Tiber overflowed its bed in this city of Rome, swelling so greatly that its water flowed over the walls of the city and occupied very extensive districts within it [Col. 1036C], the river Adige, overflowing at the city of Verona, came to the church of blessed Zeno, martyr and bishop. While the doors of that church stood open, the water did not enter it at all; but, rising somewhat, it reached the windows of the church which were near the roof. Thus the standing water closed the door of the church, as though that liquid element had been changed into the solidity of a wall. Since many were found inside who, with the church entirely surrounded by the great waters, had no way by which they could leave, and feared that they would perish there from hunger and thirst, they came to the church door and drew water to drink, which, as we have said, had risen as high as the windows; yet it did not flow down into the church in any way. It could be drawn as water [Col. 1036D], but it could not flow as water. Standing before the door in order to show everyone the merit of the martyr, it was both water for assistance and, as it were, not water for invading the place.”

Paul, monk of Monte Cassino and historian of the Lombards, also speaks of the institution of this litany, saying [Note: [Col. 1035D] The blessed author conflates the two accounts [Col. 1036D] of Gregory of Tours and Paul the Deacon, as may be seen: the latter in Book III of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, ch. 23; the former in *History of the Franks*, Book X, ch. 1.]:

“In the time of Pope Pelagius there was such a flood of waters throughout Italy that the waters rose to the upper windows of the church of Saint Zeno at Verona, and yet the waters did not enter the church. They swelled so greatly that the flood occupied very extensive districts and cast down many ancient walls. The violence of these waters also overthrew the granaries of the Church, in which many thousands of measures of wheat perished. Then a multitude of serpents, with a great dragon like a stout beam, descended through the bed of the Tiber into the sea. But the beasts were suffocated amid the salty waves of the troubled sea and, without delay, were cast up on the shores. There had not been so great a flood in Rome since the time of Deucalion, or even since the time of Noah.

“But the air was corrupted by the breath of these serpents; consequently a plague of the groin arose, by which people died everywhere, either immediately, or after two days had passed, or three. Such a plague is a swelling [Col. 1037B] which is in the groin, though sometimes in the throat. Likewise, whoever drank from the water through which the dragon had passed died. Then Pope Pelagius proclaimed a fast for all and commanded them to make a procession; and this was done. But in accordance with what is read in Ezekiel, ‘Begin from my sanctuary’ (Ezek. 9), the same disaster immediately struck down and destroyed Pope Pelagius and seventy others in that procession. After they had died, such slaughter of the people occurred that, inhabitants having everywhere been taken away, very many houses in the city remained empty. After Pope Pelagius died, Gregory the Great, son of the most illustrious man Gordian and of blessed Silvia, was appointed in his place. At the beginning of his elevation, when the crisis of the same disaster pressed on, he commanded that this sort of litany be observed everywhere in the world on the day of Saint Mark the Evangelist.”

Concerning the litany which is celebrated for three days before the Ascension of the Lord, Gregory of Tours, archbishop, writes [Note: [Col. 1037D] None of what follows is said by Gregory of Tours; rather, it was wrongly ascribed to him by Amalarius in Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 37, from which Blessed Martin perhaps drew it.] that, in the time of Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, earthquakes occurred at Vienne so great that large houses and churches fell. On the Saturday of Easter, while Saint Mamertus himself was celebrating the divine office, the king’s palace, which was in that city, was burned by fire sent from heaven; and this tempest continued throughout the year. Moreover, beasts—namely wolves and boars—came out of the woods and, entering the city, devoured people. Because of these plagues, blessed [Col. 1037D] Mamertus proclaimed a three-day fast in imitation of the Ninevites, when Jonah preached their destruction: all put on sackcloth and abstained from food, even infants from the breast, and God had mercy on them because of their fasting (Jonah 3). He commanded them to hold processions for three days, so that, as those people escaped the destruction of their city, these likewise might be delivered from the adversities which they suffered. And so it happened. Saint Mamertus therefore instituted that this litany should be celebrated every year for three days [Col. 1038A] before the Ascension of the Lord in the church of Vienne; it was also canonically established at Rome.

Pope Liberius [Note: [Col. 1037D] This decree, falsely attributed to Liberius, is capitulary [Col. 1038D] 112, Book I. In his notes Baluze says that the author of this false attribution was Burchard, who omitted mention of the edict . . . lest any traces of the capitularies should remain in this place. See also the very learned Constantius at the end of the notice concerning the letter of Liberius.] [corruptly “Tiberius” in the manuscript] also commanded that, because of famine, war, pestilence, disaster, and similar imminent adversities, they should always hold litanies, and thus escape them through supplications, prayers, and fasts. These processions are called *litanies*, a Greek term, because of the authority of the Greek language, like *Pascha* and *Pentecost*. In these litanies one must fast with Lenten food and wear penitential clothing; all, both male and female servants, must cease from worldly work on those days until the procession has been celebrated, and must attend the procession, so that, just as all have sinned, all may likewise plead for pardon [Col. 1038B].

In the great churches they proceed in seven ranks in these processions. In the first rank are the clerics; in the second, those of the cloister, namely monks and canons; in the third, women religious; in the fourth, boys; in the fifth, laypeople and those advanced in age; in the sixth, widows; in the seventh, married women. But what we cannot accomplish in the number of persons, we make up in the number of litanies, because we must say the litany seven times. We hold these litanies at this time because wars are especially accustomed to arise then, and the fruits of the earth, which are still tender or in bloom, are accustomed to be spoiled by the harmfulness of mists or in many other ways. Therefore, that God may avert all these things and defend us [Col. 1038C] and rescue us from unseasonable weather, from wars, and from enemies of the Christian religion, we hold these litanies. For this reason also we join this litany to the Ascension, so that through fasting and prayers we may deserve to follow Christ and ascend to heaven.

In certain churches, during those three days of litanies, an image of a dragon is carried, now before the cross, now after it. The dragon, therefore, which is carried during those three days with a long, inflated tail, and which goes before the cross and banners on the first two days but behind them on the last day, signifies the devil, who deceived humankind in three periods—before the Law, under the Law, and in the time of grace, signified by the three days—and still desires to deceive them. During the first two days, that is, periods, the devil was, as it were [Col. 1038D], lord of the world; concerning him Christ says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12). But in the time of grace he was conquered by Christ, and he does not dare to rule as openly as before; rather, through suggestions he secretly seduces those whom he sees sluggish in good works and negligent, and not following the way of life—as, in the desert, enemies coming up from behind killed weak and feeble Israelites, and those who remained last, as though straying. Hence on the first two days the dragon goes before, and on the last [Col. 1039A] he follows.

He is dragon and lion alike. He is now a dragon because he deceives people not openly but secretly, looking behind to see whether anyone falls from the uprightness of faith, so that he may incorporate that person into himself. He will be a lion in the time of Antichrist, because then he will rage openly in Christ’s name. He was a dragon when, on the pinnacle of the temple—that is, the first walkway, where he had formerly seduced many through vainglory—he secretly wished to deceive and tempt Christ, saying: “If you are the Son of God, cast yourself down” (Matt. 4). And so that he might safely do this, he added: “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, and they will bear you in their hands, lest perhaps you strike your foot against a stone” (ibid.). For the devil understood the Scriptures, and therefore he kept silent about what was against him, namely this: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90).

But he was a lion in the Lord’s Passion, because he caused him to be crucified. John says concerning him in the Apocalypse: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning, and he drew with him the third part of the stars” (Rev. 12). By the stars, therefore, are signified people, who are divided into three parts: the perfect, the imperfect, and the reprobate. The devil, then, draws with him the third part of the stars—that is, the reprobate—and these are his tail. Elsewhere Christ calls him Satan, saying: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 4). But where he himself says to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 8), it must not be understood that he calls him the devil, but *adversary*, which is the meaning of *Satan*. The sense is: “Get behind me, Satan,” that is [Col. 1039C], follow me by imitating my Passion, and do not hinder my Passion. Or otherwise: for Christ, as Saint Hilary says, saw the demon whispering into Peter’s ear to disrupt his Passion, and said to him: “Begone, Satan.” It is as though he said: “You labor in vain.” Then, turning to Peter, he said: “Get behind me,” that is, follow me by imitating my Passion.

Note that the office of the litanies accords with the reasons why litanies were instituted. Prayer is offered that God may avert plagues. The Epistle is read concerning prayer, where it says: “The constant prayer of a righteous person is of great power” (Jas. 5). And lest a person think little of himself, it treats there of another and says: “Elijah was a passible man; and [Col. 1039D] he prayed to the Lord, and it did not rain for three years” (ibid.). Note that the constant prayer both of the righteous and of the unrighteous is of great power: that of the unrighteous, namely, on account of prayer itself, because it comes from the Holy Spirit. For what it speaks, it speaks from the Holy Spirit. But the constant prayer of the righteous is of great power both on account of the person and on account of the prayer itself.

In the Gospel, moreover, prayer is commended where it is said that, if a friend is unwilling to give to a friend because he is his friend, he will nevertheless give to him because of his importunity—that is, his persistence (Luke 11). It then adds again concerning the egg, the bread, and the fish. By bread are understood all things necessary for human sustenance, such as food and drink. By the egg are understood every kind [Col. 1040A] of offspring, such as animals and fruits, and so forth. By the fish are understood all kinds of natural things. Again, by the egg hope is understood, because, just as it is possible to have a chick from an egg, so if we possess God by hope, it is possible to possess him in reality. Again, by the fish faith is understood, because faith is nourished in waters, that is, in tribulations. By bread, too, charity is understood. Therefore, in the Mass of the litanies, prayer is made that God may deliver us from plagues affecting crops and offspring, and grant us hope, faith, and charity. Care must be taken that no one ride in the procession during these three days; care must also be taken that women do not dance or sing a song other than *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy.” These are called black processions because of the black garments and because they signify human death.

[Col. 1040B] Therefore, dearest brethren, since your fraternity ought always to be invited and admonished to confession and repentance, especially during the holy fasts which the holy Fathers devised and established for the forgiveness of sins, the health of bodies, the abundance of crops, serenity of the air, tranquility of the times, and peace of kings, it ought to confess its faults and attend devoutly to prayer, according to the counsel of the blessed Apostle James, who says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5).

Yet discernment must be applied in confession, so that we may know which sins ought to be confessed, and to whom. For we ought not confess sins to just anyone, except in great necessity, because the power to forgive sins has not been given to everyone, but has been given only to those [Col. 1040C] to whom it is said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20)—that is, to the holy apostles and to those who hold their office, namely bishops and priests. [Note: [Col. 1039D] *Sentences*, distinction 18.]

These keys are not bodily but spiritual: namely, the knowledge of discernment and the power of judging, that is, of binding and loosing, by which the ecclesiastical judge ought to admit the worthy and exclude the unworthy from the kingdom; for as he has the right to bind, so also to loose. Hence Saint Ambrose: “The Lord willed that there should equally [Note: [Col. 1040D] “Equal right.”] be a right both to bind and to loose, because he promised each upon equal condition. Therefore whoever does not have the right to loose does not have the right to bind either. It is certain that the Church has the right to both, [Col. 1040D] whereas heresy has neither. For this right was promised to priests alone. The Church rightly claims it, therefore, because it has true priests; heresy cannot claim it, because it does not have true priests.”

Yet it must be known that there are certain light sins which we commit daily, which we can confess reciprocally to those equal to us, and which are cleansed by the prayers of our neighbors. Thus daily in the Church clerics say among themselves, “I confess to God”; and blessed James speaks here of this confession when he says: “Confess your sins to one another,” that is, confess your daily and light sins to equals, namely presbyters; but the uncleanness of a graver leprosy to a priest, that is, to an abbot or bishop. According to their judgment, these are to be redeemed and cleansed by fasts and alms [Col. 1041A]. For in the ancient Law these greater sins are signified by leprosy, which was commanded to be shown to the priests. Hence in the Gospel the Lord commands the lepers, saying: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17).

Moreover, it should be noted that there are four things which hinder confession: shame, fear, hope, and despair. Some are hindered by shame: that is, merely because of embarrassment they blush to confess their sins. Hence it is said through Solomon: “There is a shame that brings sin” (Ecclus. 4). Concerning those who confess, however, he again says: “And there is a shame that brings glory” (ibid.). The Prophet also commends them, saying: “You have put on confession and beauty; clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103). And elsewhere: “Confession and magnificence are his work, and his righteousness endures for ever and ever” (Ps. 110).

Cassiodorus: “Confession” here means public proclamation, that is, confession of praise and of sin; “magnificence” means good work, and this is his work. Or, as blessed Jerome says: “Glory and beauty are his work,” because the things he does are praiseworthy and beautiful; and his righteousness, by which he will judge, remains unchangeable for ever and ever, when he says to some, “Depart into eternal fire,” and to others, “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25), etc.

Or it may be understood thus from the passage, “Great are the works of the Lord” (Ps. 110). Here he speaks generally of all God’s works. As though he said: Therefore I shall confess, because the works of the Lord are great. Indeed, every work of God is great, if it be “sought out in all his wills,” that is, if in it the purpose and will of God who performs it may be seen—if it be understood with what purpose God willed to do it. Then he discloses what God’s purpose and will are in his works, adding: Confession, namely of sins, and the magnificence of good works, are his work; that is, the reward which is justly given endures for ever and ever. As though he said: This is his will: that from his works there should be in man confession of sins, magnificence of good works, and righteousness—that is, the reward which is justly given.

There is therefore, as was said above, a shame that brings glory, because true confession of sins leads a person to eternal glory. Since we have said above how shame hinders the confession of some, let us again see how fear hinders others. They fear that, if they confess, a severe penance will be imposed upon them. Job rebukes such persons, saying: “Upon him who fears frost, snow will fall” (Job 6).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1041D] *Morals*, Book VII, ch. 11]: Frost freezes below, whereas snow falls from above. Often, while certain people fear temporal adversities, they expose themselves to the retribution of eternal strictness. Of them the psalmist rightly says: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. 13).

Augustine: “There they trembled with fear,” that is, they fear earthly things which were not to be feared; and they do not fear what ought to be feared—eternal punishments. Such were the Jews who killed Christ lest they lose their place and nation (John 11).

Gregory, by way of example: One man already desires freely to defend the truth, but in that very desire he trembles in fear of the displeasure of human authority. And while on earth he fears a man against the truth, he endures from heaven the anger of that same truth. Another, conscious of his sins, now desires to distribute what he possesses to the needy; but he fears that, after giving away his goods, he himself may lack necessities. While he anxiously preserves provisions for the flesh, he kills his soul by withholding the sustenance of mercy. And while he fears suffering want on earth, he cuts himself off from the eternal abundance of heavenly regard.

Some also resolve within themselves to confess their sins, but they tremble lest abstinence from food or harshness of clothing be imposed upon them. Because, therefore, they desire bodily pleasures and refuse to suffer adversity for the salvation of the soul, they hand themselves over to eternal punishments. Thus it is rightly said: “Upon those who fear frost, snow will fall.” For those who fear things to be trampled underfoot below suffer things to be feared from above. When they will not pass through what they could have trodden down, they receive judgment from on high, which they cannot possibly endure.

Yet those who do these things obtain the glory of the world for a time. But what will they do at the time of their summons, who will then fearfully leave all at once the things which they preserved here with grievous fear? Hence it aptly adds: “At the time when they are scattered, they shall perish.” Those whom the anxiety of this present life adorns are scattered by neglect; and then they perish outwardly also, who long ago perished inwardly by neglecting eternal things. Of them it is rightly added: “And when they grow warm, they shall be removed from their place.” Every wicked person, when he grows warm, is removed from his place, because, approaching the judgment of inward discernment, when he has begun almost to burn through knowledge, he is separated from that flesh to which he had long clung.

Hence it is said through the prophet against the reprobate: “Vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. 28), because they do not understand eternal realities except when, for temporal things, they are punished without amendment. Then the mind burns and inflames itself with the fires of fruitless repentance. It fears to be led to punishments and clings through desire to its present life; but it is removed from its place, because, abandoning the pleasures of the flesh, its hardness is melted by punishment.

Therefore, as has been said, he who fears frost will have snow fall upon him: for he who, through fear of severe penance, fears to confess his sins, will have eternal condemnation fall upon him. There are also some who still desire something in this world and think that they will not obtain what they desire if, through confession, people come to know what they are like. Their confession is hindered by hope—that is, by the covetous desire of attaining their wishes. To such the Lord threatens in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in those days” (Matt. 24).

[Col. 1043A] There are likewise others who fear none of these things, but fear only that after confessing their sins they would be altogether unable to abstain from them. They are hindered by despair. To them may fittingly be applied the saying: “When the sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). It sometimes happens that all these things which we have mentioned above hinder confession together. But one who is held back from confessing his sins by these four evils—shame, fear, hope for earthly desires, and despair—already lies rightly in the tomb and, according to the Gospel, already stinks after four days (John 11).

For it is written: “From one dead, as though he were not, confession perishes” (Ecclus. 17). But if he who does not confess is dead, then certainly he who confesses returns to life. Let Jesus therefore come and say: “Come forth” (John 11); and at his voice the dead man will immediately be raised. Let then our dead man receive the awakening and not delay confession. Let it be said to him whom shame afflicts: Why are you ashamed to speak of your sin, when you were not ashamed to commit it? Or why do you blush to confess to God, from whose eyes you cannot be hidden? But if you are ashamed to confess or disclose your sin to one man, perhaps himself a sinner, what will you do on the day of judgment, when your conscience will lie exposed before all?

Three considerations, therefore, must be set against shame: the consideration of reason, reverence for God who sees, and comparison with the greater shame. Likewise, three things must be opposed to fear: how long, how grievous, and how fruitless the punishment of hell is. Against hope for earthly things, likewise, three things are set: the goods of the future age are greater, more certain, and more lasting than the goods of this present life. Compared with them, whatever can be desired in this world is slight, uncertain, and, so to speak, momentary.

Likewise there are three remedies against despair. The first is one’s own strength, which one gains from confession. The second is the grace of God, which one merits by humility. The third is the help one receives from the compassion of the person to whom one confesses. This also is a great consolation in repentance, which the Lord says in the Gospel: “There is joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” (Luke 15).

For through repentance—that is, through fruits worthy of repentance—the holy Church is daily renewed in her members, while she still sighs for God as a pilgrim upon earth. For this utterance is also that of the heavenly Jerusalem, namely of the holy angels who rejoice together with this Church which is a pilgrim on earth.

“Your offshoots,” he says, “are a paradise of pomegranates” (Cant. 4). Now there are three offshoots of the Church. The first is that of married people doing penance in the world; the second, of converted continent persons in the cloister; the third, of prelates preaching and praying for God’s people.

Of the first offshoot—that is, repentance—the angels speak, who have joy over one sinner doing penance: “Who is this that ascends through the wilderness like a column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer?” (Cant. 3). The repentant soul is said to ascend through the wilderness, that is, through an impassable and waterless land, by remembering her sins. She ascends like a column of smoke by humbly confessing those same sins. This confession is rightly said to be made like a column of smoke, because through many kinds of sin it is diffused like smoke from a censer through very many openings.

And it should be noted that smoke never has brightness, though sometimes it may have fragrance. That this smoke of confession has a certain prayer of devotion is suggested by what follows: “From spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powder of the perfumer.” Confession ought always to be accompanied by myrrh and frankincense—that is, mortification of the flesh and prayer of the heart. For either without the other profits little or nothing. If anyone mortifies the flesh but ceases to pray, he is proud, and the Lord says to him:

“Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Ps. 49).

As though he said: I desire these things not in sacrifices, but in the poor. Above he had said: “All the beasts of the forests are mine, the cattle on the mountains, and the oxen. I know all the birds of heaven, and the beauty of the field is with me” (ibid.). Here, then, he mystically signifies the holy Church by these comparisons. The beasts of the forests are the Gentiles; the cattle upon the mountains are the simple who stand on the height of faith; the oxen are the apostles and prophets; the birds of heaven are the heavenly powers of angels; the beauty of the field is the converted Gentiles, who are the adornment of the earth. God hungers for the salvation of all human beings and rejoices in the progress of all; but he does not desire the flesh of bulls in sacrifices, but among the poor. God prefers that the poor be fed from the flesh of animals rather than that it be offered to him in a burnt offering.

Therefore, as has been said above, one who mortifies his flesh but neglects to pray is proud. Again, if he prays but neglects to mortify his flesh, he will hear: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do the things that I say?” (Luke 6). And this: “He who turns away his ear lest he hear the law, his prayer shall be abominable” (Prov. 28). Therefore each supports the altar, since it is certain that either is rejected without the other.

It follows: “And every powder of the perfumer.” After remembrance and confession, after mortification and prayer, the fruit of almsgiving must be offered. Alms are aptly called powder because they are made from earthly substance; they are of the perfumer because they give forth a most sweet fragrance. Hence the angel rightly said to Cornelius, who was doing good: “Your prayers and alms have ascended into the sight of God” (Acts 10). Unless alms together with prayers exhaled some sweet fragrance, they could by no means rise into God’s sight. Or “every powder of the perfumer” is said because not only great sins but even every least sin must be crushed through confession.

[Col. 1045A] These things concerning the three offshoots, signifying the three kinds of persons whom holy Church contains in this life—also represented in Ezekiel by Noah, Job, and Daniel (Ezek. 14)—have been said, although they may not inappropriately be assigned to individual perfect persons. In these also the first offshoot is repentance; the second, righteousness; the third, teaching. First they are converted by repenting; second, by living well they practise righteousness; third, if they have made good progress, they teach by word the very righteousness which they hold in their life.

But because vices lie in wait for virtues and are placed so near them that whoever fails to take care falls into them [Note: [Col. 1045D] *Incurrat*: “falls into them”], repentance must be without shame, lest one blush to confess sins committed. Let righteousness beware of pretence; let prelacy banish self-exaltation. For where greatness of graces is found, there too is greatness of danger.

Therefore, most beloved, in these holy days beneficially established by the holy Fathers for the peace and salvation of the whole Church, while doing penance for our sins, we find nothing worthy in ourselves or in any earthly things which we may offer to God for our expiation or reconciliation. This cannot be comprehended in burnt offerings, even if we were all burned in sacrifice; nor, as was said above, in yearling calves, so that, leaving milk behind, we may be worthy of solid food in the acceptable year of the Lord, of which the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6).

Therefore, even if, understanding all the Levitical victims spiritually, I present them in myself; even if I offer the firstborn—that is, what is first in me—I nevertheless offer nothing worthy of his greatness. The blood of Christ alone suffices to blot out all my evils. Hence, when God had summoned the Jewish people to judgment, and that people, conscious of sin, did not dare to contend but to plead, yet did not trust in its prayers, it said: “What worthy thing shall I offer to God? Shall I bend my knee from on high? Shall I offer him burnt offerings and calves? Can God be appeased by thousands of rams or by many thousands of fat goats?” (Mic. 6). You understand: so that souls may be washed from sins.

The answer of Micah the prophet is: O people of God, because you do not know, I shall tell you what is good and what God requires of you: namely, to do judgment and righteousness, to love mercy, and to walk attentively with your God (ibid.). As though he said: I shall tell you what is good, not that it may profit me who command it, but you who do it. Or, more plainly: You seek and do not find in yourself anything that can worthily be offered to God for the washing away of sins; but I shall find a sufficient victim and teach you afterward what good you ought to do: that you may do nothing without reason and counsel; that you may perform works of mercy not under compulsion but out of love; and that in these you may seek no other reward than to please God and walk with him, as Enoch did (Gen. 5), and through him be transferred from earth to heaven, as Elijah was (4 Kings 2).

Not only is the person saved who does judgment and loves mercy; this utterance is also addressed to the whole Church, so that all who fear God, even though they stand in a lower rank, may have salvation of their souls through the mercy and teaching of Christ.

Therefore, dearest brethren, we must maintain this worthy repentance for the remission of our sins: namely, let us do judgment, righteousness, and mercy, and let us walk continually, attentive and devout, with God our maker, that we may attain him who is truly the highest good. Let us pour out without ceasing the tears of true humility, that we may deserve to wipe away the stains of sins and obtain forgiveness. For no one can wash away sins perfectly day by day in this present life; nevertheless, tears, if poured out from a humble and simple heart, greatly help in obtaining forgiveness.

Hence blessed Job, observing his own imperfection and considering the subtle divine examination, said: “If I am washed as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though most clean, yet you will plunge me in filth, and my garments will abhor me” (Job 9).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1045D] *Morals*, Book IX, ch. 19]: The waters of snow are the lamentations of humility, because before the eyes of the strict Judge, when it surpasses other virtues, it gleams as though by the whiteness of great merit. There are indeed some who have lamentations but do not have humility: distressed, they mourn, yet even in their weeping either are proud against the life of their neighbours or rise up against the ordering of their Creator. These certainly have water, but they do not have waters of snow, and cannot be clean because they are not washed by tears of humility. He had washed his fault with waters of snow who said: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50).

Jerome: The sacrifice of sinners that pleases God is a bruised spirit, in which hope of conversion is given if they are willing to repent.

Cassiodorus: A joyful and wanton spirit binds one to sin, but a contrite spirit is the sacrifice by which sins are loosed. The promise concerning this sacrifice follows: “O God, you will not despise a contrite heart in repentance.”

Augustine: God rejects a bull, a goat, and the other things which had their time when they promised something to come. I mean a heart contrite and humbled by confessing to God, not puffed up by excusing sins.

Cassiodorus: He says first “contrite” and afterward “humbled,” because it cannot be humbled unless it is contrite. Therefore, as has been said above, one washes away guilt with waters of snow who humbly pours out tears in God’s sight.

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Gregory, ibid.] Those also who are afflicted by lamentations but rebelliously murmur do indeed break their mind, but disdain to be humbled. Yet the waters of snow can be understood in another way. Water from a spring or river rises from the earth, but snow-water falls from the air. There are many who afflict themselves by works and lamentations but who, through all the labour of their lamentation, sweat only for earthly desires. They are pierced in prayer, but seek the joys of passing prosperity. Snow-water does not wash them, because their tears come from below. They are, as it were, drenched with earthly water who are pierced in prayer for earthly goods. But those who weep because they desire heavenly rewards are washed by snow-water, because heavenly compunction is poured into them. For when through lamentations they seek their enduring homeland and, kindled by its desires, mourn, they receive from above that by which they are cleansed.

But what is signified by hands except works? Hence it is said to some through the prophet: “Your hands are full of blood” (Isa. 1), that is, full of works of cruelty. It should be noted, however, that the holy man did not say, “My hands shone most clean,” but, “My hands shone as though most clean”; for so long as we are bound by the punishment of our corruption, although we perform upright works, we by no means attain true cleanness but only imitate it.

Hence he plainly adds: “Yet you will plunge me in filth.” God is said to plunge us in filth—that is, to show us immersed in filth—because the more truly we rise toward him through good works, the more subtly we recognize the filth of our life, by which we differ from his purity. Therefore he says: “If I am washed as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though most clean, yet you will plunge me in filth.” As though he more plainly said: Although I am drenched with the lamentations of heavenly compunction, although I am exercised by the practice of right action, yet in your purity I see that I am not clean.

For the corruptible flesh still strikes the mind intent upon God and defiles the beauty of his love with shameful and illicit movements of thought. Hence it is added: “And my garments will abhor me.” For what is expressed by the name of garment except this earthly body, with which the clothed soul is covered, lest it appear naked in the instability of its substance? Hence Solomon says: “Let your garments be white at all times” (Eccles. 9), that is, clean from filthy actions. Hence Isaiah says: “A garment mixed with blood shall be for burning” (Isa. 9). To mix a garment with blood is to defile the body with carnal desires. The psalmist feared being polluted by these when he said: “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation” (Ps. 50).

Augustine: We all know that in Latin one does not say *sanguines* (“bloods”), but *sanguinem* (“blood”).
