But although the plural may be less idiomatic in Latin than the singular, he nevertheless used the plural more properly, suggesting that many sins are drawn from the origin of sinful flesh—that is, from flesh corrupted by original sin. Hence is the saying: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15), that is, the sins which come from the corruption of flesh and blood. Therefore this means: “Deliver me from bloods, O God,” that is, from carnal sins, which are many, so that I may now cease from them.

Cassiodorus: “Deliver me from bloods,” that is, from every corruption of punishment and guilt, and give me incorruption; this will be fulfilled in the future. Hence follows: “O God, God of my salvation.”

Augustine: This salvation will be in incorruption, when this mortal has put on immortality; but now it already exists in hope. It follows: “My tongue shall rejoice in your righteousness,” that is, when I have been cleansed from sins, it shall proclaim your righteousness with rejoicing. Therefore, as was said above, the prophet desired to be delivered from the contaminations of corruptible flesh when he said: “Deliver me from bloods, O God, God of my salvation.”

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Gregory, as above.] Hence it is said by an angel to John: “You have a few names in Sardis who have not defiled their garments” (Rev. 3). In the manner of sacred speech, however, our garments are said to abhor us because they make us abominable, just as it is also said through Peter concerning Judas: “This man acquired a field with the reward of iniquity” (Acts 1). Judas could not have acquired the potter’s field with the price of blood; but after returning the thirty pieces of silver for the betrayal, he immediately punished within himself an even more guilty mind. Yet he is said to have “acquired” it when he caused it to be acquired.

Thus here “my garments will abhor me” means: they make me abominable. For while the members rise up against the mind, while they interrupt the pursuits of holy desire with the disturbances of their temptations, the soul, placed in this very struggle, recognizes how far it is still despised by God. Though it longs fully to pass beyond its corruption, it cannot do so and is defiled by the foul dust of thought.

He had experienced this abhorrence of garments who said: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind and leading me captive in the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7). He also hastened eagerly to put off these garments, in which he could not perfectly please God, in order to take them up again in a better form at some future time, saying: “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (ibid.).

Let the holy man therefore say: “If I am washed as with waters of snow, and my hands shine as though most clean, yet you will plunge me in filth, and my garments will abhor me”; for however much he may ascend to the heights through the compunction of contemplation, however much he may gird himself for work through the exercise of labour, he still feels something unworthy from the body of death and considers himself abominable in many things which he bears from the weight of corruption. This is made more grievous for him because he often does not even understand the source of his fault. He receives scourges, but does not know what in him displeases the strict Judge more or less. Hence it adds:

“For he is not a man like me, that I should answer him, nor one who can be heard with me as an equal in judgment” (Job 9).

When we contend in judgment with anyone as an equal, we both know what is said against us and are heard in what we say; and in proportion as we clearly apprehend the objections, we answer the matter before us boldly. Since the invisible Judge sees what we do, he is, as it were, hearing what we say. But since we do not fully know what displeases him, we are, as it were, ignorant of what he says. Therefore the holy man, considering the abhorrence of his garments, fears all the more because he cannot be heard as an equal in judgment. So long as he is weighed down by the burden of his corruption, he suffers this as the graver part of his punishment: he does not know the mind of his reprover. As though he plainly said: In this I am not heard as an equal: all that I do lies open, yet I myself do not know for what I am reproved.

Therefore, beloved, we must always be watchful and fearful even in the things that we do rightly, lest in anything we offend the eyes of the divine majesty. For although we are drenched with the lamentations of heavenly compunction and exercised by the practice of right action, in his purity we nevertheless see that we are not clean. Yet he himself is the fountain of all goodness, forgiveness, and mercy; and he has power to wash from sins us who turn to him through repentance, as he elsewhere says through Moses: “I will kill, and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32). As though he said more plainly: I will kill the old person and make the new person alive.

Hence also through the prophet Zephaniah [Note: [Col. 1049D] The manuscript wrongly reads “Malachi.”], he beneficially threatens sinners, as though Ethiopians, so that through repentance they may turn from vices to virtues, saying:

[Col. 1049C] “O Ethiopians, you shall be slain by my sword” (Zeph. 2).

As though he plainly said, as the most merciful Father: By the sword of my word I shall slay in you the old person and make the new person alive. The prophetic word again adds: “And the Lord will stretch out his hand over the north, and destroy Assyria; and he will make the beautiful city—that is, Nineveh—a solitude, a trackless place, and like a wilderness; and all the beasts of the nations shall lie down in its midst; and the pelican and the hedgehog shall dwell upon its thresholds.” All these are judgments of desolation and solitude.

Those are called Ethiopians who are plunged into vices, though they can also be converted to better things, so that no one who is willing to repent may despair of salvation. Hence Moses also took an Ethiopian woman as wife (Exod. 2). But God threatens those who persist in vices and refuse to wash away the colour of darkness through repentance, that they will be slain by that sword which he uses to guard the way to the tree of life. This threat is therefore made so that, fearing it, they may repent and not suffer what is threatened.

Hence the Lord says elsewhere through the same prophet concerning future believers: “Beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, from there my suppliants shall bring me an offering” (Zeph. 3). God will also stretch out his hand to inflict punishments, so that the north—that is, the cold and hard-hearted—may feel punishments. The Lord will also strike Assyria—that is, the devil who accuses and convicts. For he suggests sins and afterward rebukes sinners; he is the prince of the Assyrians and has Nineveh as his metropolis. But once the prince of this world has been destroyed—that is, condemned—Nineveh also, namely the world, will be reduced to solitude; none will pity it, but all will hiss at its ruin and shake their hands (Zeph. 2).

It is therefore fitting, beloved, that we should put off the Ethiopian colour—that is, the blackness of vices—through pure confession and worthy repentance, so that before the sight of our Creator we may stand not black with sins, but whitened above snow with virtues. For our Creator himself urges us to wash away our sins through repentance and to shake from our necks the yoke of diabolical slavery, because “he who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8).

The Lord, as a most merciful Father, seeks to free us from the captivity of this most wretched slavery when he says through the prophet: “Depart from the midst of Babylon, go out from the land of the Chaldeans, and be like kids before the flock” (Jer. 50). As though he said: Depart, you captives in sins, from Babylon—that is, confusion—by repenting; depart from the land of the Chaldeans, namely the demons who have made you captive; and, having heard the voice of the Gospels, return to Jerusalem—that is, to the holy Church, the place of vision and peace—and be like kids, that is, penitents, before the flock, namely the people of the Catholic Church.

Origen [Note: [Col. 1049D] The manuscript wrongly reads “Horace.”]: As our body occupies some place on earth, so the soul, according to its condition, is said to be in some place on earth [Note: [Col. 1050D] *Nuncupative*—“by naming it thus”]. Our body, then, is in Egypt, Babylon, Syria, Palestine, or wherever it may be. Similarly, the soul too is distinguished by diversity of places according to the character of its life. It is in Babylon when it is confused, troubled, and, peace being abandoned, endures the wars of passions. To such souls it is said: “Flee from the midst of Babylon, and let each one save his soul” (Jer. 51). For one who is in Babylon cannot be saved.

But whoever remembers Jerusalem while there groans and says: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136). For it is impossible for one established in Babylon to sing to God with instruments. The instruments of God’s hymns are idle there. Hence it is said: “On the willows in its midst, we hung up our instruments” (ibid.). For in a hostile land the remembrance of one’s homeland is sweet. On the willows—that is, among the wicked who are in its midst, namely those watered by the rivers of Babylon yet barren in good works, and who are in the midst of Babylon—that is, very wicked: the covetous and avaricious.

For there are some in the outer regions of Babylon, that is, not so overwhelmed by desires. Upon those willows which are in the midst of Babylon—that is, upon those who are very wicked—we have hung up, that is, postponed and withdrawn, our instruments, namely the Scriptures and promises of God.

Augustine: We turn the Scriptures away from such swine and dogs, lest we bind them to these people; but by deferring them we hang them up. And it must be said that the force of sorrow is heightened when they have hung up the pleasure by which they were accustomed to console themselves. Therefore our instruments are hung up while we are in Babylon, upon the willows by the rivers of Babylon.

But if we come to Jerusalem, the place of vision and peace, we shall play instruments, sing psalms, play the lyre, and always praise God. As the sinner’s soul is in Babylon, so the just person’s soul is in Judaea; but according to the quality of life and faith, in this very life souls are separated from one another in various places. One is in Dan, which is the outermost part of Judaea; another in somewhat better places higher up; another in the middle regions of Judaea; another around Jerusalem. But the entirely blessed soul is that which stands in the middle of Jerusalem.

But the sinner oppressed by excessive crimes is in Babylon. One who has not yet committed many crimes dwells in the regions of Egypt. Certainly, whoever lives well approaches God, but whoever lives badly removes himself from God. Therefore, when we do things pleasing to God, we follow him by the steps of good works; but if we despise his commands, we undoubtedly withdraw far from him.

The prophet foresaw in the Spirit those who had long withdrawn from God by sinning and subjected themselves to the dominion of the ancient enemy, but now, converted to God through fruits worthy of repentance, worthily serve God in the Church. Rejoicing, he said:

“The children of Israel shall come, they and Judah together; walking and weeping, they shall hasten, seeking the Lord their God in Zion. Their faces shall come here, and they shall be joined to God by an everlasting covenant which no forgetfulness shall erase” (Jer. 50).

As though he said more plainly: The children of Israel—namely Christians who see God through faith—will come to the Church; they and Judah, namely true confessors of Christ, walking from virtue to virtue, weeping for their sins, and doing penance, will hasten. Seeking the Lord their God in Zion—that is, in the Church—they will inquire into the way of truth, as happens today.

It follows: “Their faces shall come here,” that is, the intentions of their hearts; “and they shall be joined to God by an everlasting covenant which no forgetfulness shall erase,” because neither death nor life can separate them from the love of Christ (Rom. 8). This promise signifies the return of God’s people from the captivity which they suffered from the devil, when they assembled from diverse nations into the Catholic Church. There they sought their God, seeking and learning the way of righteousness—that is, evangelical teaching—and turned the countenance of their heart toward doing God’s will, that they might be joined to him by an everlasting covenant, as a bride is joined to her bridegroom by the bond of love.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us hasten with all the effort of our mind to set the will of God before our own wills, so that we may please him in all things and be joined to him by an everlasting covenant. Let us also confess ourselves sinners in his sight and transgressors of his commandments, so that through true confession and the most abundant compunction of tears we may deserve to obtain from him forgiveness of our offences. For humble confession justifies the sinner, and compunction of tears washes away the stains of sin.

For blessed Job believed that he would be justified through confession and hastened to wash away offences with tears, when, placed amid scourges, he said groaning:

“ I will not spare my mouth” (Job 7). Gregory [Note: [Col. 1051D] *Morals*, Book VIII, ch. 10]: He does not spare his mouth who is not ashamed to confess the evil he has done. For to put one’s mouth to labor is to employ it in confession of the iniquity one has committed. But the righteous person does not spare his mouth, because, forestalling the wrath of the strict Judge, he fiercely assails himself with the words of his own confession. Hence the Psalmist says: “Let us go before his face with confession, and rejoice before him in psalms” (Ps. 94 [Vulgate; 95 Hebrew]).

[Col. 1052B] It is as if he said: Let us go before his face, because he is to come, lest the enemy forestall us by accusation, and lest there then be anything in us requiring examination. This is “in confession”: that is, praising him and accusing ourselves—distinct vows, concerning which it is elsewhere said: “I will render to you my vows, which my lips have distinguished” (Ps. 65 [Vulgate; 66 Hebrew]). Therefore he distinguishes vows who praises God and accuses himself. For confession is twofold: confession of praise and confession of sin. Indeed, confession of sin belongs to the praise of the God who forgives; concerning this praise he adds, saying: “And let us rejoice before him in psalms”; that is, let us inwardly rejoice in what we say in psalms or do in a good work. Rightly, therefore, it is said: “Let us go before his face with confession,” lest we be condemned in the examination of the strict Judge.

[Col. 1052C] [Note: [Col. 1052D] Gregory, ibid.] Hence Solomon says: “He who conceals his crimes shall not prosper; but he who confesses and forsakes them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. 28). Hence again it is written: “The righteous man is the accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18). Yet the mouth is never opened for confession unless the spirit, through consideration of the strict judgment, is constrained by fear. Thus he appropriately adds at once: “I will speak in the tribulation of my spirit.” For tribulation of spirit moves the tongue, so that the voice of confession may attack the guilt of an evil deed.

It should also be known that the reprobate often confess their sins, yet scorn to lament them. The elect, however, pursue with tears of strict self-correction the faults which they disclose in words of confession. [Col. 1052D] Therefore blessed Job, after promising that he would not spare his mouth, immediately added the tribulation of his spirit. It is as though he openly confessed, saying: Thus my tongue speaks its guilt, so that my spirit may not wander elsewhere untouched by the stimulus of sorrow; but, considering my fault for its correction, I seek the healing of my wound from the medicine of salvation. For one who reveals the evils he has committed, but refuses to weep over what he has revealed, is like one who removes a garment and exposes his wound, yet in mental sluggishness applies no medicine to it. Thus sorrow must shake out the voice of confession, lest the disclosed but neglected wound, now touched more freely through human knowledge, fester all the worse.

By contrast, the Psalmist [Col. 1053A] had not merely uncovered the wound of his heart but also applied to it, once uncovered, the medicine of sorrow, saying: “I will declare my iniquity, and I will be anxious because of my sin” (Ps. 37 [Vulgate; 38 Hebrew]).

Augustine: This penitent speaks as though saying: Whence comes the pain in my heart? Surely not from the scourge, which is medicine, but from the wound of sin. For unless he were in pain, he would not accuse himself in this manner; and this is what “I will declare my iniquity” means—that is, I will confess it. And since confession is not enough, he adds, “and I will be anxious”: that is, I shall be solicitous and diligently act for the healing of my sin.

Cassiodorus: There are two modes of perfect repentance: confession and amendment, the latter effected through tears, alms, and such things.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] Again Gregory.] Therefore, in declaring it, he uncovers the hidden wound; [Col. 1053B] and in reflecting upon it, what else does he do but apply medicine to the wound? But for the afflicted mind, anxiously considering its own losses, a quarrel arises on its own behalf against itself. For when it urges itself to the laments of repentance, it tears itself with hidden reproach. Hence blessed Job appropriately adds at once: “I will converse with the bitterness of my soul.”

For those afflicted by fear of the divine judgment, while lamenting certain evil deeds, are awakened by the very force of their bitterness to examine themselves more vigilantly; and they find in themselves further matters over which to weep. For what lay hidden when they were sluggish often becomes more subtly known when they weep; and the afflicted mind more surely finds an evil which it had done without knowing it, while its own inner quarrel more truly reveals to it how far it has departed from the peace of truth. For, stirred within itself, it discovers guilt which it did not remember while secure.

The growing bitterness of repentance importunately places before the ashamed heart the unlawful acts it committed; it shows it the strict Judge opposed to these deeds; it instills threats of punishments; fear strikes the mind, shame confounds it, reproves unlawful impulses, and disturbs the repose of harmful security. It enumerates the good things its Creator bestowed upon it, and the evil things it itself returned for his benefits: that it was wonderfully created by him; freely nourished; enriched with the substance of reason in speech [Note: [Col. 1053D] The editions read “in [his] creation”]; called by the grace of its Creator; unwilling, though called, to follow him; that his mercy [Note: [Col. 1054D] “Mercy.”] did not despise it though deaf and resistant; that, illuminated by gifts, it nevertheless through its own choice was blinded by wicked acts even after such gifts; [Col. 1053D] that it was cleansed from the errors of its blindness by the scourges of paternal care; that it was brought back from the pains of scourging to the joys of salvation by the medicine of mercy; that, although subject only to certain faults which are not grave, it nevertheless does not cease to sin even amid scourges; and that heavenly grace does not abandon the sinner even when it has been scorned.

Therefore, when it rebukes the afflicted mind with such severity, now by recounting God’s gifts, now by recalling the depravity of its own conduct, the bitterness of soul in the hearts of the righteous has its own language—a language that speaks to it all the more subtly because it is heard more inwardly. Hence it is not said, “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul,” but, “I will converse with [Col. 1054A] the bitterness of my soul”; for the force of sorrow, recounting each sin and arousing the sluggish mind to lamentation, as it were forms words of conversation addressed to it, by which it may find itself rebuked and rise more watchfully to guard itself.

Therefore let the righteous man, who in his own voice bears the type of holy Church, say in our voice: “I will converse with the bitterness of my soul.” It is as though he said more plainly: Within, I speak against myself with the grief of my heart, and outwardly I hide myself from the Judge’s scourge. But the mind pressed by the pains of repentance is also constrained within itself and, by vigorous reflection, separated from every pleasure of the flesh. It longs to advance to things on high, yet still feels the resistance arising from the corruption of the body. Thus he appropriately adds at once: “Am I a sea, or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?” [Col. 1054B]

A human being is surrounded with a prison because he often strives, by progress in virtue, to rise to lofty things, yet is hindered by the corruption of the flesh. The Psalmist fittingly prays for deliverance from this corruption, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name” (Ps. 141 [Vulgate; 142 Hebrew]).

This prison may be called the world, where all things are vain, because “all is vanity under the sun” (Eccl. 1); hence he asks that his soul be brought out, because it suffers many things there.

Augustine: The human body is called a prison. But to leave the body is no great matter, since the wicked also do so; nor is it charity if the righteous person is excessively eager to leave it. For he ought to wish to remain in the flesh if this is necessary for his brothers. Or rather, [Col. 1054C] the body is a prison not in respect of that which God made good (Eccl. 7), but in respect of that whereby it is corrupted and weighs down the soul (Wis. 9): that is, its corruption, which came from sin, is the prison. From this corruption he wishes to be brought out, so that he may become incorruptible and the soul may rest in incorruptible flesh, whereas now it groans and is distressed in corruptible flesh. Thus the body is now the soul’s prison because of corruption; in the future it will be its house because of incorruption and freedom. For merits make the prison. Just as one dwelling is a prison to its inmate but a house to its keeper, so freedom makes a house and servitude a prison. Therefore it is not the flesh which God makes, but corruption and temptation, that is the prison [Col. 1054D] from which he prays to be brought out, saying: “Bring my soul out of prison,” that is, out of the body’s corruption; for in corruption, which is the body’s punishment, it is distressed.

Let blessed Job therefore say: “Am I a sea, or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?” Thus, as has been said, the human being is surrounded with a prison when the soul is enclosed and weighed down by corruptible flesh.

But what is denoted by the name of the sea-monster except the ancient enemy, who, by possessing the minds of worldly people, as it were swims in their slippery thoughts? Yet the sea-monster is bound in prison because the malignant spirit, cast down to the lower regions, is restrained by the weight of his punishment so that he cannot prevail in soaring to heavenly things. Peter testifies to this, [Col. 1055A] saying: “God did not spare the angels who sinned, but, having cast them down into the roaring hells, delivered them to Tartarus, to be kept for torments at the judgment” (2 Pet. 2).

Therefore the sea-monster—that is, the ancient enemy—is bound in prison because he is forbidden to tempt the good as much as he desires. The sea also is surrounded by a prison, because the swelling and mad desires of carnal minds are burdened by the constraint of their own inability to commit the evils they desire. They often long to rule over their betters, but, by the divine judgment wonderfully ordering all things, they remain subject to them. In their pride they desire to harm the good, and yet, being subject, hope for help from them. To fulfill the pleasures of the flesh they desire a long life in this present world, yet are swiftly carried away from it. Concerning them the Psalmist rightly says: [Col. 1055B] “He set the waters as in a bottle” (Ps. 77 [Vulgate; 78 Hebrew]).

Mystically [Note: [Col. 1055D] This is from the gloss.]: He who then made the waters stand still and brought the children of Israel across now restrains the unstable flow of desires when the world is renounced and all sins, as enemies, are destroyed. The faithful people are brought through baptism; and afterward he led them on before placing them in their homeland, in the cloud by day.

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Again Gregory.] Therefore waters are in a bottle when the slippery hearts or desires of carnal people, because they find no effect in action, are pressed down beneath the carnal heart. Thus the sea-monster and the sea are pressed by the enclosing [Note: [Col. 1055D] “Enclosing.”] prison, because the malignant spirit, and those who follow him, gathers himself in the minds of the wicked and rolls within them the waves of swelling thoughts; and because they cannot carry out the evils they desire, heavenly severity constrains them.

[Col. 1055C] But holy men, the more purely they contemplate the secrets of heaven, the more daily they pant after them with increasing ardor; and they long to be fully satisfied there, where as yet they taste only a little through the mouth of contemplation. They perfectly desire to subdue the stimulus of the flesh and to endure nothing unlawful in thought from its corruption. But because it is written: “The body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9), they already rise in intention above themselves, yet, still subject to the uncertain movements of their infirmity, grieve that they are shut up in the prison of corruption.

He therefore says: “Am I a sea, [Col. 1055D] or a sea-monster, that you have surrounded me with a prison?” It is as though he plainly said: The sea and the sea-monster—that is, the wicked and the malignant spirit who acts in them—because, unrestrained, they seek only liberty to commit iniquity, are rightly bound in the prison of their punishment. But why am I, who now long for the freedom of your eternity, still oppressed by the prison of corruption?

Yet this is not arrogantly demanded by the righteous. Inflamed by love of truth, they perfectly desire to pass beyond the constraints of infirmity; nor is it unjustly ordered by the author of righteousness. For, delaying the wishes of his elect, he purifies them through affliction, so that they may sometime grow stronger in love and more worthily receive what they desire. [Note: [Col. 1056D] “Who.”]

But so long as the elect are delayed from inward rest, [Col. 1056A] they return to their hearts and, hidden there from the tumults of their flesh, seek a most pleasant retreat as it were. Yet there they often feel the stings of temptation, endure the incitements of the flesh, and find their heaviest labors where they sought great repose from labor. Therefore, because blessed Job believed that through confession of sins he could obtain pardon, he rightly said in his suffering: “I will not spare my mouth.” For even while he conversed with the bitterness of his soul, he poured forth tears of compunction in confession.

It is fitting also, dearest brothers, that we, who are enclosed and burdened in a prison—that is, in corruptible flesh—should humbly pour out tears before God in remembrance of our sins, without which we cannot be perfectly cleansed at all. [Col. 1056B] For this purpose we have been established in God’s Church and are supported by the alms of the faithful: that we may devoutly pour out prayers to the Lord not only for our own peace and salvation but also for that of the whole faithful people, and for the remission of all sins, as we read that Jeremiah did in the person of the Church.

“She wept, weeping in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks,” he says (Lam. 1).

Allegorically: Christ’s Church weeps in the night, that is, amid the adversities of this life. For although predestined for glory, while it moves amid the darkness of ignorance and the perils of blindness, it inwardly laments the miseries of its infirmity. But it weeps, weeping, because it is first inwardly pierced by remembrance of sins and thus outwardly baptized in its own tears, which flow from [Col. 1056C] the fountain of the heart. Indicating their abundance, the prophet says: “She wept, weeping in the night,” and so forth. In this manner the outward person no less than the inward is washed and renewed from sins. Hence follows: “Her tears are on her cheeks.”

The cheeks of the Church are those who know how to bewail both their own sins and those of others, rather than wipe them away. Of these it is said in the Song of Songs: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from [Note: [Col. 1056D] Here the gloss reads, as does the Vulgate, “apart from that which lies hidden within you.”] your hidden things” (Song 4). In them the beauty of the Church is displayed, and through their preaching we are brought into the body of the Church. Since they labor more than others in Christ’s body, they groan and weep more for those whom they see living in the night of sins and held in the blindness of error.

The Church—that is, the congregation [Col. 1056D] of the faithful—weeps in the night, because it does not ignore the darkness of its sins. It bears tears on its cheeks, by which it daily renews its beauty. Mary benefits Martha as she labors, when, praying, she weeps at the Lord’s feet (Luke 10). The bride, separated from the embrace of her bridegroom and placed in the valley—that is, in the night of this ignorance—weeps, weeping for longing for the heavenly homeland and for her own sins and those of others in this age. She weeps in those who have died to the world. She weeps in virgins and widows; she weeps in all who confess that they are strangers and pilgrims upon the earth.

It follows: “There is no one [Col. 1057A] to comfort her among all her beloved”—that is, the saints or angels—unless she receives consolation from Jesus Christ, her bridegroom. Therefore it is said: “All her friends,” namely all angels and saints, “have despised her,” whom God despises; “and have become her enemies,” with whom God is offended, when they withdraw help. Therefore we who offend God by sinning must implore his mercy through confession and tears.

Morally: The soul weeps in the night, namely in the blindness of sins, concerning which it is said: “Let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise” (Job 3).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1057D] *Morals*, Book IV, ch. 19]: There are some who not only do not bewail the evil they do, but do not cease even to praise and defend it. And indeed, when a fault is defended, it is doubled. Hence [Col. 1057B] it is said: “Have you sinned? Be still” (Sir. 21). For he adds sin upon sin who even defends evil deeds. Nor does he leave the night solitary who adds the supports of self-defense to the darkness of his fault.

Thus it was that the first man, questioned about the night of his error, refused to leave that night solitary. For when he was summoned by questioning to repentance, he added the aids of excuse, saying: “The woman whom you gave me gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3), secretly directing the blame of his transgression against his Maker. It was as if he said: You supplied me with the occasion of sinning, because you gave me the woman. Hence a branch of this error extends in the human race from that root down to the present: what is wrongly done is still defended.

Therefore let him say: “Let that night [Col. 1057C] be solitary and not worthy of praise.” It is as though he openly prayed: Let the fault we committed remain alone, lest, while it is praised and defended, it bind us more grievously in the sight of the Judge. We certainly ought not to have sinned; but would that, without adding anything else, we might at least abandon alone the deeds we have done.

Otherwise: “Let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise.” The ancient enemy is called a solitary night because the blindness of his accomplished pride so weighs him down that he shall never return to those lofty ranks of inward brightness. He is no longer joined to the standing dignities of the citizens above, because by the desert of his darkness he is always pressed down to the depths. And because that same malignant enemy remains forever excluded from the multitude of the heavenly homeland, it is rightly said of him: “Let that night be solitary and not worthy of praise.” That night becomes solitary because, by everlasting strict judgment, it is separated from the multitude of the heavenly homeland.

Yet this may also be understood otherwise: namely, that he may lose the human being whom he had made his companion in perdition, and that the enemy may perish alone with his own body, while the Redeemer’s grace restores many whom he had destroyed. Thus the night becomes solitary when, those who are elect having been taken away, the ancient enemy alone is consigned to the eternal fires of Gehenna.

It is well said, moreover, “not worthy of praise.” For when the human race, oppressed by the darkness of error, believed in gods of stone, by serving idols what else did it do but praise the deeds of its seducer? Hence Paul rightly says: “We know that an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. 8), but “the things which the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons” (1 Cor. 10). Therefore those subjected to the worship of idols do nothing but praise the darkness of night. But now we see that this night is known not to be worthy of praise, since idol-worship is rejected by the redeemed human race. And the night is left solitary, because people do not go to torments with the condemned apostate spirit.

Morally, then, as has been said, the soul weeps while placed in the blindness of sins. But the soul does not weep by its own choice, but by the Lord’s mercy. Thus the lamenting prophet says in the person of the Lord: “How does the city sit solitary?” [Col. 1058B] (Lam. 1)—that is, the soul, which, full of virtues, ought to have been God’s dwelling-place, has become as a widow and despised, deprived of love for her heavenly bridegroom. For unless the Lord, moved by mercy, had seen it sitting alone, it would never have bewailed itself. “The Lord looked upon Peter, and he wept bitterly” (Luke 22).

“Her tears,” he says, “are on her cheeks” (Lam. 1). The soul’s cheek is conscience. The face is formed in the cheeks; but the character of each person is shown in conscience. A conscience which knows its own sins ought always to be watered by the fountain of tears. Hence David: “I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. 50 [Vulgate; 51 Hebrew]).

Cassiodorus: He seeks the mercy of him whom he knows to be just in punishing sins, that he may acknowledge [his sin] [Note: [Col. 1058D] For. reads “forgive”]. “For [Col. 1058C] I know my iniquity.” For one might say to the person asking pardon: Do you seek mercy—that your sins may be wiped away?

Augustine: What then will happen? Will justice perish through mercy, so that this sin goes unpunished? No, because I punish it. It is as though he said more plainly: You, God, need not punish, because I know my iniquity. It is as if he said: Forgive, because I acknowledge it; I do not conceal it.

It follows: “And my sin is always against me.” This sinner has done to himself what God will do at the judgment. Hence it is said above: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49 [Vulgate; 50 Hebrew]). Or according to another reading: “And my sin is always before me.” He does not have his sin behind his back, as he had it previously when he neglected it.

[Col. 1058C] Augustine: David had his sin behind his back when, forgetting himself, he pronounced judgment upon the rich man who stole the poor man’s ewe-lamb (2 Sam. 12).

Therefore the soul which recognizes itself to be sinful diligently pours out tears, that it may obtain consolation from God concerning its sin. Thus the prophet appropriately continues:

“There is no one,” he says, “to comfort her,” because the true Comforter has been lost, namely the Holy Spirit; especially since all her friends—that is, the affections of perverse love—become her enemies when, on the day of judgment, thoughts arise, according to the Apostle, accusing or defending the wretched conscience (Rom. [Col. 1059A] 2), along with the most wicked demons, persuaders who now flatter while deceiving. Again he says: “All her friends have despised him and become his enemies,” when he is afflicted and despised for his sins, both by outward and inward enemies.

Therefore, beloved, it is fitting that we be pierced with compunction in tears for our sins, lest, by living luxuriously for a long time, we—God forbid!—be despised by the heavenly bridegroom and mocked by enemies. Let us therefore devoutly fast during these Rogation days; and let us join sackcloth and ashes to our fasting so that, by God’s favor, the city of Nineveh—that is, the body of sin—may be overthrown, and the walls of Jerusalem—that is, the virtues of the soul, which is the dwelling-place of the supreme King—may be built up. Thus Jonah, counselling the Ninevites, says: “Yet forty [Col. 1059B] days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3).

The number forty is appropriate to sinners for repentance, so that through fasting, prayer, sackcloth, tears, and perseverance in supplication, they may be delivered from present and future adversities and obtain forgiveness of sins from almighty God. Moses (Exod. 24), Elijah (2 Kings 19), and the Son of God (Matt. 4) fasted for this number of days. This number is prescribed for us, to prepare our hearts and souls for the food of Christ’s body.

“Yet forty days,” he says, “and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

Augustine: Nineveh was overthrown, which had been evil; and that which had not existed, namely a good Nineveh, was built. While its walls and houses remained standing, the city was overthrown because the habits [Col. 1059C] of its wicked way of life were destroyed. And although what those people feared would come, as Jonah preached, did not happen, nevertheless what had been foretold with foreknowledge did happen.

It follows: “And the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord; and they proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least.” Sackcloth and fasting are the weapons of penitents. From the greatest to the least they put on sackcloth, because no one is without sin—not even an infant whose life upon earth is only one day (Job 14).

A fine order: God commands the prophet; the prophet preaches to the city; first the men believe, as being readier for good, as it is written: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 30 [Vulgate; 31 Hebrew]).

Augustine: “Act manfully,” lest love be idle, but let it work good without ceasing; so that, persevering without failure in good works, you may reap eternal things without failure, even if grievous things happen. Therefore let your heart be strengthened in the Lord; be earnest in doing good, in patiently bearing evils, and in stirring others by preaching to work well.

Thus, in the fact that the men of Nineveh believed in the Lord and proclaimed a fast to others, namely to the lesser persons, they held the pattern of teachers in the Church: for they first did themselves what they afterward preached to others. When the men proclaim fasting, every age is clothed in sackcloth. The men preach not sackcloth but fasting only. [Col. 1060A] But those upon whom repentance is enjoined add sackcloth to fasting, so that an empty stomach and mourning attire may more powerfully entreat God. Those who had offended God through luxury and ambition appease their condemnation by the things through which they had previously offended. First fasting is offered to God in secret; then sackcloth is displayed outwardly to human beings.

Again it is said: “Who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and turn back from the fury of his anger, so that we do not perish?” These words are spoken in uncertainty, so that people, being doubtful of their safety, may perform repentance more vigorously and provoke God more strongly to mercy. It is as if the king and his nobles said more openly: Who knows whether, if we turn, God will turn toward us, forgive our crimes, and turn back [Col. 1060B] from the fury of his anger, which he has almost begun to pour out, and thus, once it has turned back, we shall not perish?

It follows: “And God saw their works, that they had turned from their evil way; and God had mercy on them.” God did not hear words such as Israel often promised, saying: “We will do all that God has said to us” (Exod. 24); rather, he saw the affliction of the Ninevites crying to him in truth, because “the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144 [Vulgate; 145 Hebrew]). Nor does the prophet say that God heard their voices, but that he saw their works; because it is not everyone who says, “Lord, Lord,” but the one who does the Father’s will who can have God favorable to him (Matt. 7).

The Lord therefore had mercy upon his people, because, as he himself testifies through the prophet Ezekiel, he desires the amendment and life of the wicked more than their death (Ezek. 18). For as soon as he sees works changed for the better, he willingly changes his sentence. Or rather, let us say that God perseveres in his purpose, having wished to show mercy from the beginning. For he did not wish to punish, nor was he going to punish, though he threatened. As he threatened the Ninevites then, so God threatens the peoples of the world every day, that they may repent. If they turn, he too turns his sentence and is changed by the conversion of the people, though by nature he is unchangeable.

Therefore, because almighty God is abundant in forgiveness (Isa. 55), it is fitting, dearest brothers, that, departing from wicked actions, we turn to him with all devotion. If we truly repent for past sins [Col. 1060D] and henceforth withdraw from unlawful works, we shall be able to obtain pardon from him. Let no one silently say to himself: “I have committed no grave sins, because I have lived innocently from childhood, and therefore have no need for forgiveness of sins.” Whoever says this should carefully attend to what the blessed evangelist John wrote in his Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1). And blessed Job says: “What is man, that he should be without stain?” (Job 15).

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1059D] *Morals*, Book XII, ch. 16]: For in the very fact that he is called *homo* (“man”), he is described as earthly and infirm. For *homo* is named from *humus* (“ground”). [Col. 1061A] And how can one be without stain who, made from earth, has fallen by his own will into infirmity? To this is added: “And how can a man born of woman appear righteous?” For it was a woman who first administered injustice to man in paradise. How then can one appear righteous who is born of her who proved to be the minister of injustice?

It follows: “Behold, among God’s saints none is immutable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight” [Note: [Col. 1061D] Ch. 17]. By the name “heavens” he repeats what he had earlier signified by the designation “saints.” For it is written of these same saints: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18 [Vulgate; 19 Hebrew]).

Cassiodorus: The heavens are the apostles, in whom God dwells as in heavens.

Augustine: “The heavens declare the glory of God”: that is, they expound Christ’s glory, in which he is equal to the Father; both that he is God and that he freely forgives sins. Or “the glory of God” is the glory by which the Son himself glorified the Father upon earth; and “the firmament” means these same apostles, made steadfast by the Holy Spirit and made heaven, though they had formerly been earth through fear. They proclaim the works of his hands: that is, the Lord’s deeds of power which he performed according to his humanity—namely, his birth, passion, death, resurrection, and such things.

Cassiodorus: They are rightly first called “heavens,” that is, lofty, because they proclaim lofty things. They are also called in Christ the “firmament,” that is, those made steadfast, because it is necessary to suffer for him. For they did not suffer because they preached that the Word was in the beginning with the Father (John 1), but because they proclaimed that the same Son of God had become man, suffered, died, and risen again. Hence the Apostle says: “I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Rom. 1). And elsewhere: “We preach Jesus crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1).

Therefore the heavens, as has been said, are not clean in God’s sight: that is, holy people, so long as they live in this little mortal body, cannot be perfectly justified from fault, because by nature all possess in themselves their own mutability. Yet while they always earnestly desire to cling to immutable truth, by clinging they act so as to become clean and immutable. And while they hold to it with their whole affection, they sometimes receive the grace that, carried above themselves, they conquer what they had found mutable in themselves. [Col. 1061D]

For what is mutability except a kind of death? When it changes any thing into another, it as though kills what it was, so that it begins to be what it was not. For it is said of God: “Who alone possesses immortality” (1 Tim. 6). God alone is immortal because he alone is immutable. James says of him: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 1). For mutability itself is a shadow which would, as it were, darken light if it cast it into shadow through changes. But because mutability does not befall God, no shadow of change interrupts his light.

It is well said, [Col. 1062A] “the heavens are not clean in his sight,” because in themselves, before God’s strict judgment, even those who become preachers of purity cannot be perfectly clean. If, therefore, among God’s saints no one is immutable, and the heavens are not clean in his sight, who may presume upon the work of righteousness within himself?

Hence it adds: “How much more abominable and useless is the man who drinks iniquity like water?” The one who previously denied that a person could be spotless and righteous through himself now calls him [Note: [Col. 1062D] “This” in the editions.] abominable and useless: abominable, indeed, on account of the impurity of his stain; useless on account of the unrighteousness of his imperfect life.

Yet “abominable and useless” may be understood differently. Sometimes a perverse person seems to do certain things rightly; but, through the things that are wicked, even the things that are right in him are destroyed. And since the evils greatly displease God, even the things which seem good do not please him. Thus a person is abominable to God in his evils and useless in his goods, because, while he presents himself to God as detestable through wicked works, even that which seems right does not please God.

It is well said, “who drinks iniquity like water.” For what is eaten is swallowed slowly, because it is chewed in order to be swallowed. But what is drunk has no such delay in being swallowed, because it requires no chewing. Thus the fault committed by a foolish person without any restraint is like iniquity drunk. Whoever does unlawful things without fear swallows the drink of injustice without impediment.

[Col. 1062C] Therefore, dearest brothers, if, as has already been said, one born of woman cannot appear righteous before God or be spotless through himself without divine cleansing grace, no one ought to presume upon righteousness or holiness, or pride himself as though he possessed these from himself. Rather, he should appear humble before God at all times. Let us therefore recognize that we are sinners and unworthy; and amid the adversities of this world which, for our sins, we suffer by God’s just judgment, let us humbly give thanks to that most just Dispenser. For by the ordering of the just Judge we endure adversities, because we who could have done good freely committed unlawful acts.

We therefore, who by living well and preaching what is good ought to have shown God’s people the light of truth and the way of salvation, [Col. 1062D] have provoked God against ourselves by acting wickedly; and for this reason we suffer countless afflictions of body and atmosphere together with all the people. For through the fault of ecclesiastical persons, the simple people of God often suffer scourges. Hence David bore the person of the Church’s preachers when he said to the smiting angel: “It is I who have sinned; I who have acted wickedly. But these, who are the sheep—what have they done?” (2 Sam. 24.)

Jeremiah, foreseeing in the spirit and lamenting those same rulers of the Church who live wickedly, said: “The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn feast” (Lam. 1).

Allegorically. The ways mourn whenever the Church—that is, the faithful people—is inwardly or outwardly filled, because of its sins, with the bitterness of God’s wrath. The ways rightly mourn; the gates lie destroyed; the priests groan; the virgins are squalid, so that the whole structure of the house, marked by the number four, seems shaken. Hence elsewhere the same Jeremiah says: “Stand in the ways, and see, and ask for the ways of the Lord” (Jer. 6), etc. The ways are the patriarchs, prophets, and others through whom one comes to Christ, who is the true way. For just as holy men are called light by Christ, so they may not incongruously be called ways by him. Thus Abraham is called the first way of faith. These are the ways of Zion, that is, of the heavenly city. They mourn and groan because there are none who come to the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Why? Because the gates are destroyed [Col. 1063B]: for those who hold office neither enter themselves nor allow others to enter. The priests groan because the ways mourn; the virgins are squalid because the gates are destroyed. Priests are rightly joined to virgins, because the priesthood is distinguished by virginity, and virginity requires the governance of priests. When these ranks are violated, the multitude that follows dies with them. Hence it follows generally: “And she herself,” namely the holy Church, “is oppressed with bitterness,” because, when the head is sick—that is, when the order of prelates acts perversely—all the members, namely the people subject to them, are infected, that is, suffer, being afflicted by various disasters. When the rulers of the people do not walk in the straight way, those who follow fall grievously.

Hence it often happens that frost burns the fruits of the earth; drought dries them up [Col. 1063C]; hail strikes them; the scorching wind leaves the crops empty; excessive rains destroy them and do not permit them to reach maturity; storms of the air crush and scatter them. Therefore the Church is oppressed with bitterness as the sins both of rulers and subjects deserve: for famine often presses upon her; a pagan people invades her borders; the fury of wolves presumes to tear human limbs; the perversity of heretics seeks to seduce her children and infect them with the poison of its error.

Morally. “The ways of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the solemn feast”: that is, the virtues leading to the heavenly Jerusalem mourn because none come to the feast of the soul whose bridegroom has been taken away, when the soul slips from the height of heavenly intention [Col. 1063D] into outward actions. Its solemn feast is the inward contemplation of heavenly life. But there are none who come to the solemnity: that is, the effects of the former life do not come to the solemn observance of divine contemplation, because the gates of the senses have been destroyed.

For there are gates of death and also gates of righteousness, concerning which it is said: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered through them, I shall confess the Lord” (Ps. 117), etc. For the third time the faithful soul desires for itself the gates of Jerusalem. It should be noted that three things are here distinguished: the gate by which one enters, what is done within, and who enter it. As though he said: “That this inheritance may be known, O prophets and apostles who bear the keys of the kingdom of heaven, open to me the gates of righteousness,” that is, the teaching [Col. 1064A] of sacred Scripture, which teaches righteousness.

Augustine: Here it is shown through what gate one enters; and as if someone asked, “What will you do within?” he answers: “Having entered through them, I shall confess the Lord,” that is, I shall praise him.

Cassiodorus: For those who enter through these gates of teaching truly praise God. Outside the Catholic Church, however, there is no praise of God. Therefore through the gate of spiritual teaching, which is governed by spiritual senses, the kingdom of heaven is entered by perfected human beings. But all these gates lead to one gate, which is Christ; and this is the gate of the Lord—that is, this gate is the Lord—to whom those gates lead. Hence he himself says: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10). And elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).

Cassiodorus: [Col. 1064B] This is the gate through which the righteous enter. Hence he adds: “The righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 117), that is, through it they shall enter heaven, where good and evil will no longer be mixed together.

Therefore, as has already been said above, there are gates of death and gates of righteousness, of which Isaiah also says: “Open the gates, and a holy, or righteous, nation shall enter” (Isa. 26). But because “death entered through our windows” (Jer. 9), the soul’s virginity is squalid, as has been said above, and the royal priesthood groans, while in place of virtues we are filled with the bitterness of vices. Let us therefore leave the gates of death and rebuild the gates of life, asking which is the Lord’s gate, so that we may walk in it.

The gate of the Lord, then, is the Lord; because through himself he deigned to call us to faith, and causes [Col. 1064C] us to seek himself, find him, love him when found, hope in him, enter the heavenly kingdom through himself, and rejoice without end in himself. This gate, therefore, is the goodness of the Lord; for, as holy David says: “The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, and in those who hope in his mercy” (Ps. 146). And again: “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33). Jeremiah too, speaking of God’s goodness, says: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him” (Lam. 3).

For who truly waits upon the Lord except one who, through zeal for charity, is shut off from every stain of vice? Who hopes except one who truly loves and desires? For what we hope for, we await through patience. Thus the one who hopes waits; and the one who waits excludes carnal affections through patience. Therefore it is rightly said: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him,” because those who wait for him in charity, aided by his grace, are delivered in this life from imminent dangers and in the life to come from eternal punishments. For those who hope do not sin. Hence David, acknowledging God’s benefits toward himself and humbly and devoutly praising him, said:

“You have dealt kindly with your servant, O Lord, according to your word” (Ps. 118).

In this ninth letter, Teth, the prophet, speaking in the person of the Church, gives thanks to God for his humiliation and patience, through which he came to righteousness, and because it is good to be humbled. For patience removes sadness and grants joy even amid [Col. 1065A] tribulations. Accordingly the letter Teth, which is interpreted “good” or “exclusion,” is fittingly prefixed to this octonary, because it treats here of repentance, which excludes sadness arising from adversities and makes suffering good and joyful. For martyrs who truly serve Christ, fearing neither persecutions, swords, nor fires, offered themselves even to hostile kings and conquered them through their patience.

As though he said: “Teach me your ordinances, because you have already shown, O Lord, goodness, or pleasantness, or sweetness, to your servant.” You have made goodness delightful by making a son out of one who was a servant. It is a great gift of God that a good work be done not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness—not slavishly but freely. For the servant, what he formerly was, does not remain in the house forever; the son remains, which he now is. For from a servant he has been made a son. Or it may also be understood thus: “servant” now means humble, not proud.

Great, therefore, as we have said, is the gift of God by which we patiently endure adversities, humbly give thanks to God for benefits bestowed, repent of sins committed, and prudently discipline ourselves so that we may not sin again. For one who truly knows and loves God understands that he is kind and merciful. The Psalmist had experienced God’s kindness in many things when he said devoutly and with a kind of amazement: “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart!” (Ps. 72).

Augustine: The faithful servant, remembering his error [Col. 1065C], repenting of it, and chastising himself, says with amazement: “How good—that is, how pleasant—is the God of Israel!” This had not always seemed so to me. But to whom is he good and pleasant? Namely, to those who are upright in heart. To the perverse, however, he appears perverse. It follows: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps were almost poured out.” As though he said: “Now I confess that God is good; but formerly, when my heart was not upright, my feet were almost moved into error, my steps were almost poured out into a fall.” The feet were not altogether moved, nor were the steps poured out, but almost; because I had begun to go astray, but had not gone astray; I had begun to fall, but had not fallen. Feet and steps are the same thing, namely, the affections of the mind.

Cassiodorus: Or he understands feet as the choice of the mind, which departed from truth [Col. 1065D] when it did not perfectly know God to be good. Therefore he does not perish, because he quickly returned when he believed that God is supremely good to the upright in heart.

It is therefore rightly said: “The Lord is good to those who hope in him” (Lam. 3). And lest hope be idle, he immediately adds: “To the soul that seeks him”; for the one who hopes does not yet possess, but enjoys in hope what he will possess in reality. Hence it is said: “Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3). There four things necessary to everyone who seeks are indicated: that one should first consider within oneself what one seeks; and where, and when, and how long—namely, until one finds. For anyone who seeks God in the bed of repose and in the night of blindness plainly cannot find him. Therefore one who desires to find the bridegroom of the soul, that is, Christ, should leave the bed, come into the day, and seek until he finds.

But Moses indicates where God must be sought when he says: “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. 30). David also says of him: “His place is made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75). As though he said more plainly: His place—that is, God’s place—is made in peace among those who have made peace within themselves, having harmony with holy conduct and conflict with vices. For so long as a person groans in this tabernacle, it cannot be that the tinder of sin does not trouble him; but he ought not consent to it. If anger arises, he should make himself such that it finds in him no weapons for iniquity by which it may stretch out its hand against a neighbor. Or if other unlawful motions arise, let them find no instruments of iniquity. Hence Paul says: “Sin is in your mortal body, but let it not reign” (Rom. 6).

For whoever is in Judea—that is, receives remission through confession—must be such that he may deserve to see God: now through faith, later face to face. Once Israel is seeing, it remains for him to be a Jerusalemite and thus have peace with God. For as long as anyone disdains to confess, he quarrels, as it were, with God through pride; as long as what displeases God pleases us, we quarrel with him. Drunkenness displeases him, but pleases us; theft displeases him, but we praise the thief; novelty displeases him, but antiquity pleases us; and thus we banish ourselves from his [Col. 1066C] image, in which we were created. But if at some point what pleases him also pleases us, we cease from quarrels and make peace with him by reforming ourselves to his image. Hence it is now said: “His place is made in peace,” and finally “his dwelling shall be in Zion,” that is, in true contemplatives, who contemplate not the things seen but the things unseen (2 Cor. 4).

Therefore, as has been said, “The Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him,” but in the place of peace. For his dwelling is in peace—that is, in the hearts of those who love God and neighbor, love peace and concord, and hate disputes and quarrels. For he himself speaks peace to his people and to those who turn to him (Ps. 4). [Col. 1066D] Since God is immeasurable, he must always be sought and awaited, and devoutly invoked amid the scourges of the present time; for he is indeed the salvation of the wretched and the most merciful deliverer of the afflicted who truly cry out to him.

Therefore, beloved brothers, amid the adversities justly inflicted upon us for our sins, we must call to mind the evils that we have done, give thanks to that most just Judge, and praise his justice, so that by his mercy we may at once be cleansed from the filth of vices and delivered from impending evils.

Hence Isidore, teacher of Spain [Note: [Col. 1065D] *Sentences*, Book III, ch. 4, but somewhat differently.]: “If you wish to be cleansed from guilt amid scourges, accuse yourself [Col. 1067A] and praise God’s justice.” And again: “Whoever murmurs amid God’s scourges accuses the justice of the Judge and provokes him all the more to anger.” For blessed Job too did not murmur at God’s scourges, but bore them with equanimity, saying: “I shall not contradict the words of the Holy One” (Job 6). One who calls his striker holy even amid blows does not murmur against the justice of the one who strikes.

Gregory [Note: [Col. 1067D] *Morals*, Book VII, ch. 7.]: It must be known that sometimes the adversary crushes us, and sometimes God crushes us. By the crushing inflicted by the adversary, we fall away from virtue; but, broken by the Lord’s crushing, we are strengthened in virtue against vices. The Prophet had perceived this crushing when he said: “You shall rule them with a rod of iron, and break them like a potter’s vessel” (Ps. 2).

[Col. 1067B] As though he said: “I shall give you the nations,” and deservedly so: because you will be no tyrant, ruling with an iron rod—that is, with inflexible justice or royal power—but will rule in mercy.

Augustine: “And you shall break them,” unto life, “like a potter’s vessel”: that is, insofar as they are a potter’s vessel—namely clay—you shall crush in them whatever they have contracted from the mire of the sinner [Note: [Col. 1067D] Interlinear Gloss: “of sin.”]. Or the passage may be understood partly in a good and partly in an evil sense, according to Simeon’s words: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and the rising again of many” (Luke 2); “let the one who is righteous still be made righteous, and let the one who is filthy [Note: [Col. 1068D] Marginal note: “in filth.”] become still more filthy” (Rev. 22).

Cassiodorus: “You shall rule them with an iron rod,” he says, chastising the good in mercy. This is Christ’s royal power. “And you shall break [Col. 1067C] them,” namely sinners, by permitting them to become still more filthy; they are like a potter’s vessel, which is both made of clay and easily broken.

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Again, Gregory.] Therefore, as has been said, the Lord rules and breaks us with the rod, because by the strong rectitude of his dispensation, while he inwardly restores us, he outwardly afflicts us. For by the same governance through which he humbles the strength of the flesh, he exalts the purpose of the spirit. Hence this same breaking is compared to a potter’s vessel, as Paul says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4), that is, in bodies. Expressing at once both breaking and governance, he says: “Although our outward person is decaying, yet our inward person is renewed day by day” (ibid.).

Therefore the holy man who desires to draw near to God even through scourges should say in a spirit of humility: “May he who began himself break me” (Job 6). For the Lord often begins to work the crushing of vices in us; but when the mind is lifted up by its progress from the very beginning, and already raises itself up as though because of its virtues, it opens an entrance to the adversary raging against it. Penetrating the inner recesses of the heart, he breaks everything he finds there arising from the zeal of a good beginning; and he displays himself all the more violently in that breaking, the more grievously he is distressed because he had been cast down, even if only a little. Hence, as the Gospel testifies in the voice of Truth, the spirit that went out alone returns to the neglected house of conscience with seven spirits (Luke 11).

Therefore, lest after the beginnings of divine [Col. 1068A] correction the ancient enemy creep in and lead one into the breaking of virtues, the holy man fittingly prays, saying: “May he who began himself break me.” As though he plainly said: “May he not cease to complete by striking what he began in me, nor abandon me to the adversary for crushing.” Hence it is well added: “Let him loose his hand and cut me down.”

For we are often puffed up with confidence in long prosperity and rise into a certain state of pride. When the Creator sees us lifting ourselves up, if he does not exercise his love toward us through blows, he keeps, as it were, his hand bound from striking our vices. Had he not bound his hand in the affection of his love when he said to the sinning people: “I shall no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you” (Isa. 54; Ezek. 16)? Therefore he is said to loose his hand and exercise his love.

And it is rightly added: “And cut me down.” For when some sudden pain of scourging or trial of sickness strikes us while we are secure and puffed up with an abundance of virtues, immediately the pride of our mind is cut down from the summit of its condition, so that it presumes nothing from itself but, cast down by the blow of weakness, seeks the hand that raises it. Hence holy men, when they are uncertain of the hidden disposition toward them, fear prosperity itself more greatly. They desire to be tested; they long to be scourged, so that pain and fear may train the incautious mind and, on this path of pilgrimage, when the enemy bursts forth from ambush, its own security may not overthrow it more grievously. Hence the Psalmist says: “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart” (Ps. 25).

[Col. 1068C] As though he said: Since no one understands his sins, lest any of my hidden things remain concealed from me, test me, O Lord, and try me—that is, test me by temptations; that is, judge me proven, or make me known as such, not to yourself, for you know all things, but to me and to other people, lest any sin remain. Therefore, he says, try me, because if he did not try us, we would be negligent.

Cassiodorus:

Note that God tests, man tests, and the devil tests; but God does so in one way, man in another, and the devil in another. God tests in order to instruct; man tests in order to learn what he does not know; the devil tests in order to deceive. Therefore God’s testing is proving, as God tested Abraham (Gen. 22). Observe that here the perfect man, in the person of the perfect, prays for tribulations, lest anyone murmur against them. Hence he adds: “And with the fire of tribulation, namely, burn my reins and my heart.”

Augustine: “Burn my reins and my heart,” that is, apply the medicinal purgatory of tribulation to my pleasures, lest anything evil delight me, and to my thoughts, lest I think anything evil. For he used heart for thoughts and reins for pleasures. Since, then, we are cleansed from sins by God’s scourges, we must not murmur against God in them, lest we grow sluggish through negligence. For it contributes to our benefit when divine goodness crushes us with blows. Indeed, we were born into this world in order to endure the sentence imposed for transgression. Holy David understood this—indeed knew it with certainty—and weeping said: “I am prepared for scourges, and my pain is always before me” (Ps. 37).

Cassiodorus: “I am prepared for scourges,” knowing that I have sinned.

Augustine: “Prepared for scourges,” that is, I was born for this, to bear scourges, because God scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12).

For the holy man rightly says, “I am prepared for scourges,” because, when the minds of good people consider that the wound of their corruption [Note: [Col. 1069D] Again, Gregory.] cannot be without putrefaction, they willingly prepare themselves under the physician’s hand for incisions, so that, once the wound is opened, the poison of sin may flow out which was killing within under sound skin. Hence he further adds: “Let this be my consolation: that, while afflicting me with pain, he does not spare me.”

Whenever the elect know that they have committed unlawful deeds, but upon close examination find that they have suffered no adversity for them, they waste away through immense fear, burn with dread, and suffer while tossed by ominous suspicions: lest God’s grace may have abandoned them forever because no recompense for their evil corrects them in this present life. They fear lest the vengeance delayed be reserved in a more severe form for the end. They desire to be struck by paternal correction and consider the pain of the wound a medicine of salvation. Therefore it is rightly said: “Let this be my consolation, that while afflicting me he does not spare me.” As though he plainly said: Because he spares some here in order to strike them forever, and strikes others in order to spare them forever, I am consoled by affliction; because, knowing the putrefaction of human corruption, I am made certain of hope for salvation from the wound.

And because he uttered this with a humble rather than an inflated mind, he made it clear by adding, as we have said: “I shall not contradict the words of the Holy One.” Often God’s words to us are not sounds of speech, but effects of actions. For he speaks to us in what he silently works toward us. Blessed Job, therefore, would contradict God’s words if he murmured at his blows. But he indicates what he thinks of his striker, since, as we have already said, he calls holy the one whose blows he endures. And because Job himself praises God amid his scourges, he indicates what we ought to do amid our own blows. For he bears the type of the holy Church and therefore teaches the whole Church in his words and deeds.

It follows: “For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should be patient?” [Col. 1069D] It should nevertheless be known that the strength of the righteous is one thing and that of the reprobate another. The strength of the righteous is to conquer the flesh, oppose their own pleasures, extinguish delight in the present life, love this world’s hardships for the sake of eternal rewards, despise the blandishments of prosperity, and extinguish in their hearts the fear of adversity. But the strength of the reprobate is to love transient things without ceasing, endure insensibly against the scourges of their Creator, refuse to desist from love of temporal things even through adversity, attain vain glory even at the cost of life, seek increases in wickedness, assault the life of the good not only with words and depraved conduct but even with swords, place hope in themselves, and commit iniquity daily with no diminution of desire.

Hence the elect are told through the Psalmist: “Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, all you who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 30). As though he said: “Act manfully,” that is, do not fail in your labors; and let your heart be strengthened in hope of so great a reward, even if the flesh is weak—all you who hope in the Lord rather than in the world, namely, who hope for the reward of your labor in the Lord and in no other thing except the Lord himself.

Of the strength of the reprobate Isaiah the prophet likewise says to those same reprobate persons: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5). Hence Solomon says, because all the saints contemplate inward repose with no weakness of desire: “Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty strong men surround it, of the strongest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled in war” (Song 3). Hence the Psalmist, setting forth the voice of the Redeemer in the Passion against the reprobate, says: “Behold, they seized my soul; strong men rushed upon me” (Ps. 58).

How well Isaiah encompassed both strengths when he said: “Those who trust in the Lord shall change their strength” (Isa. 40). Since he did not say “shall take” but “shall change,” he plainly made known that one strength is laid aside and another begun. Are not the reprobate also strong—those who run after the desire of the present life through so many labors, boldly expose themselves to dangers, willingly endure insults for gain, are driven back from the lust of their appetite by no opposition, become hardened by blows, and bear the world’s evils for the world; and, seeking its joys, so to speak, lose them, yet are not wearied by considering these things?

Hence it is said through Jeremiah in the voice of humankind: “He has made me drunk with wormwood” (Lam. 3). For the drunk person does not know what he suffers. Therefore one is drunk with wormwood who, through love of the present age, is estranged from God’s commandments and from rational sense: while he considers light whatever he suffers for the world and does not recognize the bitterness of the labor he endures, because he is delightfully drawn into everything by which he is painfully wearied.

On the contrary, the righteous man strives to be weak with respect to enduring the world’s dangers for the world; he sees his end; he considers how transient the present life is; and he refuses to suffer outward labors for that life whose inward delight he conquers. Therefore, pressed by the adversities of the present life, blessed Job speaks from his own person, and also from the voice of all the faithful: “For what is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should be patient?” As though he plainly intimated: “I cannot bear the world’s evils for the world, because I am no longer strong in its desire. Since I see the end of the present life, why should I bear the burden of that whose appetite I trample down?” And because, as we have said, the unjust bear its labors all the more strongly the more greedily they are fed by its delight, he immediately adds the same strength of the reprobate, saying:

[Col. 1071A] “My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze.” What is signified here by bronze or stones except the hearts of insensible people, which often receive heavenly blows and yet are not softened by any stroke of correction? In contrast, the Lord promises the elect through the prophet: “I shall take away from you the heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11). Paul likewise says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13).

We know that struck stones cannot give forth a clear sound; bronze, however, when struck, produces a very melodious sound from the blow. But because, like stones, it is without life, it has no understanding in its sound. There are some who, like stones, have become so hardened against the precepts of piety that, when the blow of heavenly judgment examines them, they do not render the sound of humble confession. Others, differing in no way from bronze, when they receive the scourges of heavenly chastisement, emit the sound of devout confession; but because they do not utter voices of humility from the heart, being restored to a state of salvation, they do not know what they have promised.

Those, therefore, struck after the manner of stones, have no voices; while these do not flee the likeness of bronze at all, for, under blows, they speak good things that they do not feel. The former deny even words to the reverence due to the one who strikes them; the latter cry out without life, promising what they do not fulfill. Therefore the holy man, fleeing the hardness of the reprobate amid blows, says in the person of the elect: “My strength is not the strength of stones, nor is my flesh bronze.” As though he openly confessed: “I flee the likeness of the reprobate under the lash of correction. I have not become so hardened like stones that, under the stimulus of blows, I fall silent concerning the mystery of confession; nor, again, do I resound with a voice of confession like bronze while failing to understand the meaning of that voice.”

Therefore, beloved brothers, following the example of blessed Job, amid God’s scourges we must flee both the strength of stones and the insensibility of bronze: that is, we must beware hardness of mind and the voices of unfruitful confession. Our minds must neither become hardened against recalling God’s benefits, nor must our understanding grow sluggish in uttering words of humble confession and praise; rather, amid blows, humbly confessing, we should recognize our sins and praise God’s justice.

Hence Jeremiah [Col. 1071D], foreseeing in the spirit the holy Church set amid the dangers of the present world, and compassionately sharing her miseries as a pious man, speaks in counsel, saying: “Arise, praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches; and pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord. Lift your hands to him for the lives of your little ones, who have failed from hunger and perish at the head of every crossroads” (Lam. 2).

The prophet says, “Arise, and praise in the night,” and so forth.
