One rises in the night who, lifted above the tribulation or distress of the present life by hope of heavenly goods, shakes off the torpor of negligence and tirelessly arms himself manfully against every adversity. “Praise,” he says, “at the beginning of the watches,” because the cunning enemy, when he brings scourges, intends that God should be blasphemed. Hence blessed Job says: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

We must praise at the beginning of the watches so that we may refer everything we do or suffer to his praise and glory, lest, being sluggish at the beginning of the work, we be overcome by the sleep of deception. Hence the Apostle says: “Do everything for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10), “giving thanks to God the Father through Christ” (Col. 3). We ought to praise God with voice and heart and exalt Christ’s name not only in words but also in deeds. As though he said: Do all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, not for your own glory but for his, giving thanks not to the Law but to God the Father through Christ himself, through whom he gave all things [Col. 1072B]. As though he said: all things—not only whatever you do in deed or word, but also in thought and whatever else there may be. Or: whatever you do, do it wholly—that is, perfectly—attributing it to God; and this is to do it in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, at the beginning of the watches, as has been said, we must praise God: that is, we must refer every good thing we do and every adversity we suffer to God’s praise. Yet it should be known that there are many watches in which God must be praised; and one must especially beware lest the work be condemned from the outset by its intention. But when a work has begun well, watches still remain in which it must be brought, until the end, to the glory of God.

“Pour out your heart like water,” he says. One pours out his heart like water before the Lord who brings forth tears of compunction from the innermost affection of the heart, because “a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50). Yet if such a great rain of tears is not present, one must not despair. Hence it is said: “I stretched out my hands to you; my soul is before you like land without water” (Ps. 142).

Cassiodorus: “I stretched out my hands to you in prayer,” signifying the form of the cross, which is also salvation. Or: “I stretched out my hands to you,” that is, I enlarged my affections or works that were formerly constricted; “and my soul,” which of itself is like earth without water, “clings to you, not to me, because I cannot water it.”

Augustine: You, O God, rain upon my soul, that it may yield more fruit, because it is dry. The penitent heart spreads out its parched soul like land without water before the Lord so that he may water it [Col. 1072D] with his rains—he who brought waters from the rock for the thirsty people (Exod. 17). The heart too is poured out like water, because, melted by love of God and neighbor, it is dissolved like ice by the warmth of charity.

Hence follows: “Lift your hands to God for the lives of your little ones.” One lifts a hand to God for little ones who raises works of mercy for Christ’s humble members, who perish from hunger and thirst because they have clung to earthly things. This, however, is perfect charity: that the heart should be poured out like water to God and hands should be raised mercifully toward one’s neighbor. Just as Moses is recorded to have raised his hands so that the people of God might not be defeated (ibid.), so the little ones of the Church—or the tender thoughts of the soul—are overcome unless they are preserved by the protection of those greater than themselves or by divine help.

Hence in the Song of spiritual love it is said: “My soul melted when he spoke” (Song 5), namely Christ. For the heart or soul is not dissolved from the cold of unbelief except by the warmth of divine inspiration. Therefore one must always pray that the north wind may rise, the south wind may come, and the spices of charity may flow (Song 4). For then the spices of prayers flow, when the mind is breathed upon by the divine Spirit.

But lest love of God alone seem sufficient, hands must be raised for the little ones who perish from hunger for the word of God at the head of every crossroads. For unless they were in the roads and at the head of crossroads, they would not have suffered from hunger or thirst for God’s word and from the adversities of this world. A crossroads is called that road at which several ways meet, like a three-way intersection. [Col. 1073B] Therefore the faithful peoples—that is, the Church’s little ones—must be called back from three-way intersections, streets, and the head of every crossroads, so that they may come to the Lord’s banquet and not perish forever from hunger for God’s word.

The hands of Moses—that is, of the Church’s rulers—must be raised, so that Amalek may be conquered, that is, so that the devil may be overcome; that God may be merciful to the wretched; that sins and vices may be avoided; that God’s scourges may be mitigated; that a favorable or temperate condition of the air may be restored; and that God’s wrath may be turned away. But undoubtedly only those who truly love God and neighbor can obtain what they ask.

Therefore the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Though Moses and Samuel should stand before me, my heart is not turned toward this people” (Jer. 15). Gregory [Note: [Col. 1073D] From the Gloss: for Gregory has it somewhat differently.]: “The many Fathers are passed over, and [Col. 1073C] Moses and Samuel alone are brought forward: their remarkable power of obtaining requests is shown, since even they are said unable to intercede. It is as though he said: ‘I do not heed even those whom, because of the great merit of their petition, I by no means despise.’ What then is the reason why Moses and Samuel are preferred above the other Fathers in petition, unless it is that these two alone, throughout the whole course of the Old Testament, are recorded as having prayed even for their enemies? One is assailed by stones from the people, and yet prays for those who stone him; the other is expelled from office, and yet answers kindly, saying: ‘Far be it from me to sin in ceasing to pray for you.’ ‘Though Moses and Samuel,’ he says, ‘should stand before me, my heart is not turned toward this people’ (1 Sam. 12). It is as though he said: ‘Even now I do not heed those whom I know, by the merit of their great virtue, to pray even for enemies.’ The power of true prayer, therefore, is the height of charity; for each person obtains what he rightly asks when his mind is not darkened, even in petition, by hatred of an enemy.”

Therefore, dearest brethren, if you desire happily to obtain from God what you ask, show one another true charity. If you seek to escape impending pestilences, offer pure prayers before God. Yet God must be prayed to with the greatest earnestness that he may not strike his faithful [Col. 1074A] people for condemnation, but may mercifully correct them by chastisement. For whenever he teaches sinners by striking them, he sends scourges in order to spare them. But when, by striking, he ends the life of one persisting in sin, he sends a scourge but does not spare. He who sent the scourge in order to spare will sometimes send it so as not to spare. For in this life the Lord is so much the more intent upon sparing as he chastises more by waiting. Hence the saying: “Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3). But of the scourge of condemnation it is written: “The sinner has been caught in the works of his own hands” (Ps. 9). It is as though he said: The punishment of the wicked does not proceed from God, but from himself, because sins themselves are his pains and torments. Concerning the scourge of condemnation [Col. 1074B] the Lord also says through Jeremiah: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jer. 30). Again, through the same Jeremiah the Lord says to Israel: “I will make an end among all the nations among whom I have scattered you; but of you I will not make an end. Rather, I will chastise you in judgment, so that you may not seem innocent to yourself” (ibid.). It is as though he said: I have not handed you over to punishment but to instruction, that I might judge you as my own rather than destroy you as strangers.

If, therefore, as has been said above, we seek to obtain from almighty God what we ask, it is necessary that we show one another true charity. But how we should pray, and what we should ask in prayer, is shown by that supremely wise teacher himself, who said to his disciples in the Gospel:

[Col. 1074C] “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth. Give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil. Amen” (Matt. 6).

This [Note: [Col. 1073D] Martin took this explanation—or rather transcribed it—from chapter 40, “On the celebration of the Mass and its meaning,” in the book *On the Divine Offices*, which circulates under Alcuin’s name. The distinguished Mabillon believes, in vol. V of the *Acta*, in his encomium of Alcuin, that the author of this chapter was Remigius, monk of Auxerre.] prayer is called the Lord’s Prayer because the Lord taught it to his disciples, and therefore it is called “the Lord’s” from the Lord. This, then, was the occasion of the prayer. The disciples asked the Lord to teach them how they ought to pray. That most gracious teacher said to them: “You need not say much in prayer, for the almighty Lord knows what is needed before you ask him. Therefore, when you pray, say: ‘Our Father’” (ibid.).

“Father” is said from *patrare*, “to accomplish,” that is, “to bring to completion.” Therefore one who calls the Lord Father ought to prepare himself so as to be worthy to be called his son. If he calls him so unjustly, he will receive punishment for that very unjust invocation. For as a good son imitates a good father—as Isaac imitated Abraham, and Jacob Isaac—so we, who call God Father, ought as good sons to imitate his holiness, that we may be holy and unstained in his sight (Eph. 1), according as he himself says: “Be holy, because I, [Col. 1075A] the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 19).

At first almighty God was the Father of the Hebrews and of the ancient saints, according as he says through the prophet: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4). And again: “I have nourished and exalted sons” (Isa. 1), etc. But what happened? He ceased to be their Father because of their unbelief. Yet through his mercy he became our Father through faith and love; and daily we entreat him, saying: “Our Father, who art in heaven.”

Almighty God is called Father in two ways: either because he made us—that is, wondrously fashioned both flesh and soul in our mothers’ wombs when we did not yet exist—or because he caused us to be born again from water and the Holy Spirit when we had been lost. The first birth made us children of transgression; [Col. 1075B] the second, children of reconciliation, forgiving us all our original and actual sins.

“Who art in heaven.” The Psalmist says to God: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there; if I descend into hell, thou art present” (Ps. 138). It is as though he said: “Where shall I flee from thee when thou art angry? Nowhere, surely. For if I ascend into heaven, thou art there”—that is, if I exalt myself through pride, I find thee restraining me; if I become proud of righteousness, thou art there to strike me, whose righteousness thou truly art. Again, “if I descend into hell,” that is, if by sinning I come into the depth of evils, and, unwilling to confess, say, “Who sees me?”—even there thou art present to exact vengeance. Where, then, shall I go so as to flee thy face—that is, not to feel thee angry?

[Col. 1075C] Rightly, then, it is said: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” because he is wholly everywhere. Hence he himself says through the prophet: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Likewise it is written of him in the book of Job: “He is higher than heaven, deeper than the abyss, broader than the earth, longer than the sea” (Job 11). Thus he is everywhere through the fullness of his divinity, not by spatial extension. Why, then, does he say in a special way that he is in heaven? Because by “heavens” angels and righteous human beings are understood, in whom God chiefly dwells, according to what is written [Note: [Col. 1075D] Learned persons have hitherto not discovered in what place Holy Scripture contains these words. Although they are frequently adduced by the Fathers as belonging to Scripture—namely by Augustine on Psalm 46, v. 9, and sermon 200, formerly 30, *On the Seasons*; Fulgentius, *To Trasimund*, book I, ch. 18; Gregory, book XXIX of the *Morals* and homily 38 on the Gospels; Anselm, *Book of Meditations*, meditation 3; Bernard, sermon 1 *On the Purification*, no. 4; sermon 5 *On the Words of Isaiah*, no. 5; sermons 25 and 27 on the Song of Songs, nos. 6 and 8—none of the very learned men who published more recent editions of these Fathers has firmly identified the sacred book from which they came. Some refer them to Wisdom 7:7 or 7:27; others to Proverbs 12:13, according to the Septuagint and the Syriac version. Alcuin or Remigius differs here alone from all the others in reading “the seat of God,” whereas they consistently read “the seat of wisdom.” Now in vol. I, fol. 477, Blessed Martin translated this more common reading; and in the sermon *On the Trinity* he reads the same place differently, namely: “The soul of the righteous person is the throne of wisdom,” following the Master of the Sentences. This reading strongly supports the conjectures of the Benedictine Fathers who edited Gregory: namely, that these are the words of Proverbs 12:13 according to the Septuagint: “A prudent man is the throne of understanding”; or, in the Syriac version: “A cautious man is the seat of knowledge.”]: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of God.” Let us therefore say: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” that is, who dwellest in angels and righteous people, whose dwellings are heavens. It follows:

“Hallowed be thy name.” God’s name is holy and hallowed in itself. Why, then, do we say, “Hallowed be thy name”? Clearly because, when we were born again from water and the Holy Spirit at the time of baptism, we were hallowed in the name of almighty God, when the priest said: “I baptize thee in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Therefore we pray that the holiness accomplished in us at baptism through invocation of God’s name may remain with us eternally, so that we may not defile it but always be holy—that is, so that, just as we were made holy, we may remain holy forever.

Or otherwise: “Hallowed be thy name,” that is, may we understand how great is the holiness of thy name; may it be held holy in us and in our works, that we may worship thy holiness and fear to sin. Or again, suppose that a Christian performs good works. A pagan or Jew sees this and says: “Blessed is the God who has such a servant.” Then the Lord’s name is blessed [Col. 1076B] for ever—that is, Christ is praised because of that good person. Conversely, suppose there is a bad Christian whom a pagan sees doing evil and says: “This is a bad Christian; we pagans are better.” Thus God’s name is blasphemed because of him. Hence Paul says to certain unworthy Christians: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. 2). But we pray that God’s name may be hallowed—that is, praised and glorified in our work. Whatever good we do is referred to his praise, but whatever evil we do, to his dishonour.

Again he adds: “Thy kingdom come.” Almighty God reigns in heaven and on earth, and we do not now know how he reigns; therefore we pray that his kingdom may come. What is this kingdom? [Col. 1076C] Namely, the eternal blessedness concerning which he will say to the elect: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25), etc. We pray for that kingdom to come, namely the day of judgment, for which everyone ought to be very well prepared. Or otherwise: Almighty God reigns in his elect through faith, hope, charity, and other good things. Conversely, the devil reigns through lust, drunkenness, hatred, and other evils. Therefore we pray to God that he himself may reign in us through righteousness, where the devil reigned through sin. It follows:

“Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth,” that is, in angels, who have not sinned: as their service is held acceptable, so may thy will be done in all people upon earth, so that their service may likewise please thee. Or otherwise: By heaven our Lord Jesus Christ is understood, and by earth the holy Church. We know that, as a woman receives seed from a man, so the earth receives all [Col. 1077A] fruitfulness from heaven. So too the holy Church receives from Christ, her husband, whatever good it has, according as it is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). It is as though he said: As thy will is in heaven, that is, in Christ, so may it be done on earth, that is, in the Church, which is his body. Or: As thy will is in heaven, that is, in righteous people, so may it be done on earth, that is, in sinful people, so that through repentance they may be able to please thee. Or: “Thy will be done as in heaven,” that is, in our minds, “so on earth,” that is, in our bodies. It follows:

“Give us this day our daily bread,” that is, grant us today—that is, at every time—everything necessary for food and clothing. Or otherwise: By bread here we may understand the Lord’s body and blood, of which he himself elsewhere says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you” (John 6). Therefore we pray that he may give us his flesh and blood to eat, so that through what we visibly receive we may be able to receive within ourselves what we do not see, namely almighty God, according as he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (ibid.).

The word “today” cannot be referred generally to the Lord’s body and blood, because some cannot communicate daily: either they are defiled by some discord [Col. 1077C] against a neighbour, or contaminated by nocturnal pollution, and so cannot always be prepared. Whoever is defiled by a nocturnal illusion, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 1077D] Book III of the *Sentences*, ch. 6.], although he feels himself defiled apart from any remembrance of shameful illusions, should nevertheless attribute to his own fault the fact that he was tempted, and immediately wipe away his uncleanness with tears.

Conversely, for those who can communicate daily, the Lord’s words to Zacchaeus are fitting: “Today I must remain in thy house.” And he received him gladly (Luke 19). For such persons ought with joy to receive the Lord’s body and blood. But those who cannot receive the Lord’s body daily may say with the centurion: “Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof” (Matt. 8) today; but thou wilt enter, if it please thee, on another day. There are also those who, unwilling to withdraw from their wickedness, abstain from the Lord’s body and blood for humility’s sake. To them blessed Augustine says: “Brothers, your humility pleases me, because you fear to approach the Lord’s body and blood; but it would be better for you to withdraw from your wickedness, be made clean through repentance, and receive the Lord’s body and blood.”

Or otherwise: By bread we may understand the divine utterances—that is, the knowledge of the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the Gospels. “Give us this day our daily bread,” that is, refresh us throughout every time of our life with the food of the holy Scriptures. For as the body is refreshed by bodily food, so the soul is refreshed by spiritual food unto love and knowledge of him. It follows:

“And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” We become debtors to God in two ways by sinning: namely, by doing what he forbade to be done, or by not doing what he commanded to be done. He says in the Gospel: “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Matt. 22). And again: “Honour thy father and thy mother” (Mark 7). If, therefore, we do not do this, we are debtors—that is, sinners. The Lord commanded the foregoing things to be done. Again he says: “Thou shalt not kill; thou shalt not commit adultery; thou shalt not steal; thou shalt not swear” (Exod. 20). If we do these things and things like them, which the Lord forbade to be done, we are debtors—that is, sinners. Since, therefore, we commit such great offences against [Col. 1078B] God’s commands, it is necessary, if we wish them to be forgiven us by the Lord, that we forgive from the heart a brother who sins against us.

We are also sinners against our neighbour in two ways: namely, if we strike him, or if we do not love him and do not forgive him what he has committed against us. For the Lord commanded us to love our neighbour and to pardon him. If, therefore, we pardon him, we can truly say: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” And the meaning is: May almighty God forgive us our debts, as we forgive those who have sinned against us, namely our debtors. Hence the Lord says: “If you do not forgive, neither will your sins [Col. 1078C] be forgiven you” (Mark 11).

“And lead us not into temptation.” One kind of temptation pertains to testing, of which Moses says to the people of Israel: “The Lord tempts”—that is, tests—“you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13). And the Psalmist says: “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my reins and my heart” (Ps. 25). Thus God tested Abraham, and he was found faithful (Gen. 22). Another kind of temptation pertains to deception, concerning which James says: “God tempts no one” (Jas. 1). But the devil tempts in order to destroy, and from this temptation we pray the Lord not to permit us to be tempted beyond what our frailty can endure. Our God leads us into temptation when he does not free us from it. We read something of this sort [Col. 1078D] concerning Pharaoh: “The Lord says: Pharaoh’s heart was hardened” (Exod. 7). This means nothing other than that he did not soften his heart, which was hardened.

“But deliver us from evil,” that is, from the devil, from the punishments of hell, and from every adversity of this age. Amen. “Amen” means “truly” or “faithfully,” and this too, like “Alleluia,” is Hebrew. These two words, “Amen” and “Alleluia,” as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 1078D] Book VI of the *Etymologies*, ch. 19.], may not at all be translated completely into the language of Greeks, Latins, or barbarians, nor proclaimed in another language. For although they can be interpreted, their ancient form in their own language was retained by the apostles because of its more sacred authority. For the names are so sacred that John too reports in the Apocalypse that, by revelation of the Spirit, he saw and heard the voice of the heavenly host, like the voice of many waters and great thunder, saying: “Amen” and “Alleluia” (Rev. 19). Therefore both ought to be spoken on earth as they resound in heaven.

“Amen,” then, as stated above, is the seal of this Lord’s Prayer, just as a seal is the confirmation of some decree. It is as though the one who chants this prayer says to God: Certainly what I have said thus far is true; for if I forgive one who sins against me, thou, O God, wilt forgive what I have sinned against thee. If, therefore, I do not forgive him, neither wilt thou forgive me.

[Col. 1079B] It should be noted that there are seven petitions in this Lord’s Prayer. The first three pertain to the soul and eternal life; the following four to the body and the present time. “Hallowed be thy name,” “thy kingdom come,” and “thy will be done” pertain to the future life. “Give us this day our daily bread,” “forgive us our debts,” “lead us not into temptation,” and “deliver us from evil” are necessary for us in the present, because in the future there will be no hunger, but eternal satisfaction for the elect through contemplation of almighty God. In this life, however, bread and forgiveness of sins are necessary; for here we sin, and here it is necessary that we be freed from the devil’s temptation and the dangers of this age. But in the future neither will the devil harm the good, nor will there be any adversity for them.

But whoever delights in banquets and idle tales [Col. 1079C] quickly generates from himself a most foul stench before the Lord—the stench, I mean, of depraved action and unlawful speech. So long as a person prays well and performs good works, Christ remains in him. But when he occupies himself with idle matters, Christ does not remain in his breast but the devil does. A person can know what sort of inhabitant he has within himself by hearing whether he brings forth good or evil things.

Therefore, most beloved, let us unceasingly ask almighty God for our daily bread, that is, the exposition of the holy Scriptures, so that, while we suffer so many adversities outwardly, we may feel some inward relief from its refreshment. Holy Scripture is indeed a spiritual table, at which the little ones of the Church [Col. 1079D] are refreshed with spiritual sweetness, while the great—that is, those more advanced in virtues—make progress in holiness. But, as blessed Gregory says, though there may be faithful people who gladly hear God’s word, there are nevertheless none to speak it.

Jeremiah the prophet saw with spiritual eyes that this hunger for God’s word would come in the holy Church, when he said mourning and sorrowing: “All her people groan and seek bread” (Lam. 1). Allegorically: All the groaning people seek the bread of God’s word, which descended from heaven, amid the necessity of spiritual hunger and the distress of pestilence and manifold tribulation. The Church seeks this bread—that is, the exposition of the Scriptures—from teachers, and does not find it. Why? Because the teachers themselves have given every precious thing for food: heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for [Col. 1080A] perishable, to refresh the soul but not to satisfy it. For they can refresh a soul inflamed with countless desires, but cannot satisfy it. Hence the people are said to groan and seek bread, because the wicked are afflicted and tormented when the abundance of a luxurious life is not available as they wish.

Morally: The soul gives every precious thing for food when it inclines the virtues of the mind toward transient pleasure and strives to refresh itself by contriving to satisfy diverse desires. Hence the people groan and seek bread in lamentation, because, although they have given precious things for food, the affection of concupiscence is nevertheless not satisfied by sight, taste, and the other senses. Thus, even if some virtue perhaps returns and the soul, restored by God’s Spirit, grows strong, it rightly cries out in mourning with the multitude of the elect: “See, O Lord, and consider, for I have become vile” (ibid.). It is as though it said: I have become vile and humble to myself, in my own eyes, because the hand of the Lord has touched—that is, fastened upon—me. For *caph* means “hand.” When the Lord’s hand touches the Church, whether by punishing or relieving punishments, by instructing the soul or chastising one who is negligent, it at once returns to itself and groans, saying: “See, O Lord, and consider how vile I have become.” It is as though it says to God: Consider thy handiwork, namely the soul, how vile it is: once it gloried in the pleasures of vices, but now, touched by the Lord’s hand, it declares itself vile, though it had been created in the image of its Creator.

The faithful people, therefore, as has already been said—that is, the holy Church—groaning, seek from teachers the bread [Col. 1080C] of God’s word in a time of need and distress, and do not find it, because the teachers themselves have given precious things for food: they have exchanged eternal things for temporal, spiritual things for carnal, and devote more attention to earthly gain than to winning souls. Thus the people groan under God’s scourges, and there is no one to break for them the bread of consolation. For the people themselves, by living badly, deservedly deprive themselves of the consolation of the holy Scriptures and of the preaching of teachers.

For often, because of the wickedness of the people, preachers are forbidden to proclaim God’s words. Hence the Lord says through the prophet to a sinful nation: “Because you have defiled the land by your fornications and your wickedness, [Col. 1080D] therefore the stars of the rains have been withheld—namely Orion, the Hyades, and Arcturus—and there has been no latter rain” (Jer. 3). Gregory says: “Sometimes the brightness of preachers is signified by the name of the sun, as it is said in the Apocalypse: ‘The sun became like a sackcloth of hair’ (Rev. 6). For at the end of time the sun is seen as a sackcloth of hair because the shining life of preachers is displayed as harsh and contemptible before the eyes of the reprobate. They are also figured by the brightness of stars, because, while preaching right things to sinners, they illuminate the darkness of our night. Hence it is said: ‘The stars of the rains have been withheld.’ Since the sun shines by day and the stars by night, moreover, the eternal homeland is often signified by day and the present life by night. Holy preachers become suns to us when they open the contemplation of the true light, and [Col. 1081A] stars when, through the active life, they provide for the necessities of the present life.”

Therefore, as stated above, sometimes through the negligence of teachers the people suffer hunger for God’s word; at other times, through the fault of subjects, the word of preaching is taken away from teachers. Now, then, in God’s Church we are mingled, evil and good alike, and by God’s just judgment we endure scourges. The good frequently entreat God that storms in the air and other hardships may depart from the Church; but the wicked provoke God to anger by their depraved works. Thus the wicked are mingled with the good in the Church, and cannot easily be recognized until the coming of the Lord.

For then, as Jeremiah says, the Lord will open his treasury and bring out the vessels of his wrath, because the Lord God has work to do in the land of the Chaldeans. It is as though he [Col. 1081B] said: At the last time the Lord will open the treasury—that is, his Church—and bring out the vessels of his wrath, namely sinners, because the Lord God of hosts has work to do in the land of the Chaldeans, that is, of those who ascribe events on earth to the stars and assert that they occur at the stars’ prompting.

Another edition reads: “Open his storehouses, search her as a cave, and scatter her; let there be no remnant of her. Dry up her fruits, and let them go down to slaughter. Woe to them, for their days will come, the time of their vengeance.” Hence the Apostle says: “God endured with much patience the vessels of his wrath prepared for destruction, over the vessels of Christ’s mercy” (Rom. 9), etc. Thus some are vessels of mercy and others vessels of wrath. Pharaoh and the Egyptians were vessels of wrath; Paul, who “first obtained mercy” (1 Tim. 1), and the other apostles, together with believers from Jews and Gentiles, were vessels of mercy.

Therefore there are vessels of wrath in the Lord’s treasury, as it is written: “The Lord opened his treasury and brought forth the vessels of his wrath” (Jer. 50). The Lord’s treasury is the Church, in which evil people often lie hidden, who are vessels of wrath. The time of wrath will come, then, when the Lord opens the treasury of the Church. For now the Church is closed, and vessels of wrath dwell together with vessels of mercy, chaff with grain, and bad fish with good fish which have fallen into the net. When he opens it in judgment and brings out the vessel of wrath, the vessels of mercy may perhaps say of those departing: “The vessels of wrath went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

[Col. 1081D] There are vessels of wrath in God’s treasury, but outside the treasury are sinful vessels that are not vessels of wrath, but lesser vessels. For they are servants who do not know the Lord’s will and do not do it (Luke 12). But one who enters the Church is either a vessel of wrath or of mercy. One who is outside is neither of wrath nor of mercy. Therefore I seek another name for this: “The prophet says, ‘The Lord God has work to do in the land of the Chaldeans.’” According to diverse senses, an earthly place receives many names. And as Christ has many names by different rationales, though in his underlying subject he is one and manifold in powers, so earthly affairs, though one in their underlying subject, have many names through the diversity of their meanings because of the wickedness of the human race.

For Christ is one underlying subject, but in one sense [Col. 1082A] he is physician. Hence it is said: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick do” (Mark 2). In another sense he is called shepherd, because he presides over irrational creatures; in another, king, because he rules rational creatures; in another, the true vine, because people grafted into him bear abundant fruit; and similarly in other respects. Therefore, just as in Christ there are many meanings of diverse names though the underlying subject is one, and just as earthly affairs are one in their underlying subject but many in meaning, so in allegory we have often said that Babylon is earthly affairs, which are always confused and afflict Egypt with vices. Chaldaea is so called because many people dedicate to the stars what they do on earth, asserting that it occurs at their nod.

Therefore anyone who thinks that stars make people lustful, adulterous, chaste, [Col. 1082B] or the like, is in the land of the Chaldeans. God therefore threatens those who are spiritually in the land of the Chaldeans. But when God was leading Abraham out of the land of the Chaldeans, he said by way of admonition: “I am he who brought thee out of the land of the Chaldeans” (Gen. 15). God is also able to lead us out of the land of the Chaldeans, so that we may believe that no one but he dispenses our life according to the quality of our merits. Thus the Lord of hosts has work to do in the land of the Chaldeans.

“Since her times have come, open her storehouses,” that is, the doctrines of nativities. “Search her as a cave, and scatter her.” Whoever rejects their calculations of nativities; whoever employs the word of truth against them; whoever shows that what astrologers say is false; whoever teaches that God’s judgments are unsearchable [Col. 1082C] and cannot be comprehended by human beings; whoever maintains that the stars are not causes of events occurring on earth, especially of what happens to Christians—such a person carries out the Lord’s command. *Mathematica* is called in Latin “doctrinal science”; its four branches are arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. Those skilled in these arts are called *mathematici*.

Thus, as we said before, the wicked are mingled with the good within the net of faith. But by living wickedly, the evil provoke God to anger, whereas the good unceasingly appease God by prayers. It is the aim of the wicked to cast down the Church of the saints by committing unlawful deeds; but the good strive, by entreating God, to rescue it both from the perils of the present [Col. 1082D] age and from the fires of Gehenna. Therefore, through the depravity of the wicked, the holy Church is worn down by diverse scourges under God’s governance; but through the diligence and prayers of the good, it is often delivered by God’s mercy, as we read in the prophet Jonah concerning the wise and devout king of the Ninevites and his princes: “Yet forty days,” he says, “and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3).

When this word reached the king, immediately terrified by the fear of God, he rose from his throne, cast off his purple garment, laid aside the diadem from his head, put on sackcloth, and sat in ashes. Having summoned his princes, he commanded them to proclaim throughout the entire city—that is, to every age and sex—a fast and rough clothing. This king and his princes immediately resorted to the arms of prayer and the remedies of fasting, to implore God’s mercy. Then, so that they might obtain divine clemency, they rejected an abundance of food, subjected themselves to continuous fasts, laid aside precious and gilded clothes, and devoutly clothed themselves with the garments of poverty and humility.

Appropriately indeed, they are said to have rejected the ambitions of this world and the delights of the flesh, through which they had incurred God’s wrath against themselves, and to have sought their remedy from that through which they had deserved destruction. Certainly, when danger threatened them, they observed the teaching of ecclesiastical rule: they strove to mitigate by abstinence the indignation of God which they had incurred by excess of food and abundance of pleasures, and to cast off through the garb of poverty and humility the pride which they had contracted [Col. 1083B] through abundance of riches. That king and his princes had never heard Gregory preaching, yet in their preaching they were already imitators of Gregory. For that eminent teacher says [Note: [Col. 1083D] Homily 20 on the Gospels.]: “Those who have not committed unlawful deeds should use lawful things. But those who have committed unlawful deeds should abstain from lawful things.” Rightly, then, because they had committed unlawful deeds, they abstained from lawful things.

[Note: [Col. 1083D] Maximus of Turin, *Homily on the Litany and on the Fast of the Ninevites*, which Martin here inserts in scattered portions down to the end [Col. 1084D].] For the king of that same city, as has already been written above, upon hearing the Lord’s judgment threatening the city with overthrow, immediately laid aside his diadem and purple, covered the limbs of his body with haircloth, sat in sackcloth and ashes, persevered in prayer by day and night, proclaimed a fast to every age and sex, and thus stirred the whole city to repentance [Col. 1083C] by his own example.

This king was certainly wise, for he took up different weapons suited to the character of the time. Against enemies he used weapons of iron, and to obtain God’s clemency he took up the weapons of humility. The wise and discerning king defeated enemies with material weapons; he turned away God’s wrath with tears and prayers. He conquered enemies by courage; he overcame God’s indignation by humility.

He had once delivered the city by arms; now he delivers it by prayers and fasts. This king was indeed exceedingly wise and compassionate, for the deliverance of his citizens he did not refuse to endure fasting, the harshness of sackcloth, and the lowliness of ashes. He was truly a wise king, who, after hearing through the prophet of the power and indignation of the heavenly king, regarded himself not as a king but as a sinner. For when he feared the judgment of almighty God, remembering more the weakness of his flesh than the dignity of his kingdom, he devoutly hastened to repentance, and so deserved to be a king of righteousness.

Moreover, in wisely calling the people subject to him to repentance, he showed himself in every respect an imitator of a ruler of the Church. First he did what he afterwards commanded others to do. First he afflicted himself with fasts, prayers, and vigils; he wrapped his own body in sackcloth and ashes; and thus he lawfully imposed repentance on all subject to him. [Col. 1084A] This king did what we know Paul said of himself: “I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore he first chastised his body by hunger, thirst, and harshness, and afterward preached fasting to others. Surely he was a devout ruler who, in order to rescue from danger the people entrusted to him, diligently fasted, rolled himself in ashes, covered his tender limbs with sackcloth, and persevered in prayer.

What then? Did he lose his kingdom for this reason? By no means. For he did not lose his kingdom, but transformed it—that is, made it nobler—when he showed it subject and devoted to the heavenly King. [Note: [Col. 1084D] “it,” as below.] No, I say, he did not lose his kingdom, but gained it, when, through God’s mercy, he rescued it from destruction. Without doubt he would have lost it if he had not humbled himself before God with the utmost devotion. In him, indeed, we see fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 23). Therefore, because he humbled himself before God, he deserved to be exalted by God not only before all the nobles of his whole kingdom, but also before the Catholic Church. Formerly, by fighting against enemies, he had been a leader of soldiers; but by preaching repentance, he became a leader among the Church’s teachers. By that same preaching through which he then rescued the city of Nineveh from the danger of overthrow, he now rescues the whole Church from the ruin of eternal condemnation. And he who then justly ruled a pagan nation now devoutly instructs the Christian people. O happy king, who, while devoutly humbling himself before God, frees his people from temporal and eternal death! For the Ninevites, according to the Lord’s judgment, will rise at the judgment and condemn the generation of the Jews, because at Jonah’s preaching they repented of their sins (Matt. 12). Happy, I say, is the king who, although he had not heard evangelical instruction, nevertheless did not depart, either in practice or preaching, from the teaching office of the Church’s doctrine. Rightly, then, he is to be called not merely a king of righteousness, but also one to be imitated by all churchmen, since, according to John the Baptist, he produced fruits worthy of repentance (Matt. 3). Therefore, as we said, he did not lose his kingdom, but changed it for the better: formerly he held the chief command of worldly soldiery; now, by preaching, he holds the teaching office of heavenly discipline. He is also rightly said to have held the teaching office of heavenly discipline, since at the Lord’s urgent command he made not only old men and young men fast, but compelled even little children and beasts to abstain from food for the salvation of their elders. It did not seem to him that the abstinence of the adults could suffice to appease God unless the innocence of children, the cries of beasts, the lowing of herds, and the bleating of flocks assisted them in obtaining God’s mercy. There, indeed, the tears of the innocent washed away the sins of the elders and of all the citizens.

What, dearest brethren, do you observe amid these things? Is so perfect a repentance of the ancient Gentiles to be consigned to oblivion by the rulers of the Church? On the contrary, it must be laid up more attentively in the mind and imitated in every way. Certainly, if we carefully and wisely weigh what was written in the Old Testament, we must not doubt that it was written for our instruction. The repentance of the Ninevites is set before us to be read precisely so that, whenever we are afflicted by God’s scourges on account of our sins, we may have recourse to similar weapons—namely, fasting, prayers, and tears—by which, through God’s mercy, we shall undoubtedly be able to overcome every adversity. Let us therefore approach him with a pure heart and a devout mind, because all our salvation rests in him. For the Prophet says of him: “The Lord is near to all who call upon him, to all who call upon him in truth” (Ps. 144). Let us therefore diligently implore mercy from him, and before him bewail our sins, for which we justly endure continual and most grievous pestilences. We send fitting messengers to appease God when, by fasting, praying, keeping vigils, giving alms, persisting in good works, and humbly pouring out tears before him in our tribulation, we do so. Let messengers therefore go forth from our very depths, that they may devoutly intercede with God for our reconciliation. Or where shall we find messengers able to entreat divine mercy for us more devoutly?

Let us therefore, beloved, approach God with a contrite heart; for the nearer we are to him by good works, the nearer he, the most merciful Father, will make himself to us, graciously accepting our satisfaction and mightily delivering us from the impending storms of the world. For this purpose he invites us through the prophet, saying: “Return to me, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1). Conversely, concerning those who depart from God by evil living, it is said to God through the Psalmist: “Behold, those who remove themselves from you shall perish” (Ps. 72). If those who withdraw from God perish, then without doubt those who draw near to him shall be saved. Let us therefore draw near to him, so that in him we may be saved from all temporal evils and eternal punishments, lest, by departing from him, we perish without him. Perhaps one of you silently says within himself: “How shall I draw near to God? By the steps of my body?” By no means. You cannot draw near to God by bodily steps, but by good works: namely, fasts, prayers, alms, and humility of mind, without the admixture of any evil work. For then we shall truly be able to obtain from almighty God the worthy things for which we ask, if we strive to persevere in good works and to withdraw from unlawful deeds. Surely, earnest persistence in prayer drives away every adversity.

Therefore, beloved brethren, let us earnestly persevere before God—with the multitude of both sexes, that is, men and women, youths and children—in fasting, prayers, vigils, alms, and other good works; so that, as he spared the Ninevites, mercifully accepted their repentance and satisfaction, and delivered them from the danger of overthrow, he may likewise deign mercifully to look upon the holy Church, drive famine and sudden death away from her, restrain her visible and invisible enemies, curb the savagery of beasts, soak the dry face of the earth with the gentle waters of clouds, grant a favorable or temperate atmosphere, bestow every good thing upon her, and deliver her from all evils. Thus may he lead her through temporal goods so that, after the end of this world, she may be able to attain the fellowship of the citizens above and reign eternally with Jesus Christ, her bridegroom, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON THIRTY. ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD.

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085D] Habakkuk the prophet, dearest brethren, descended from the tribe of Simeon and inspired by the divine Spirit, marvelling in astonishment at the great works of the Lord—namely, the Incarnation, birth, passion, resurrection, and Ascension into heaven of the Son of God—and figuratively praising the same Son who is both God and man, speaks among other things for the instruction of the faithful, saying: “The sun was lifted up into heaven, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. 3).

Christ is compared to the sun for a threefold reason. The sun illuminates, warms, and gives increase to things. Likewise, Christ illuminates, warms, and gives increases of virtues to people predestined for eternal life. Of him John the Evangelist says, among other things: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). For no one is enlightened except through him. He warms, that is, with the ardor of true charity; he kindles the minds of his own to act well. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). The disciples also felt themselves kindled by this same fire at Emmaus, when they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24). Christ gives increase to things. Hence blessed Paul says: “I planted”—that is, by preaching to the Church—“Apollos watered,” by baptizing, “but God gave the increase” (1 Cor. 3): that is, he bestowed the first grace by supplying virtues.

Christ is also compared to the sun for four reasons: on account of the prerogative of beauty, the intensity of heat, the greatness of brightness, and the composition of its body. For, as the sun has a spherical—that is, round—body, having neither beginning nor end, so Christ, who is Alpha and Omega (Rev. 1), lacks beginning and end. On account of the prerogative of beauty: because, as the sun holds a prerogative among the other planets in beauty, so Christ is truly “fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44). On account of the intensity of heat: because, as God placed the sun in the midst of the source of all heat, so “our God is a consuming fire,” burning up vices (Deut. 4). On account of the greatness of brightness: as the sun illumines the whole world, so whoever is enlightened is enlightened through Christ, because he enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). Christ, therefore, as has been said, is compared to the sun, because he illumines the hearts of the predestined, strengthens them with the sweetness of his love, and grants them increases of virtues for acting well.

“The sun,” says the prophet, “was lifted up into heaven.” The Psalmist, seeing and marvelling at this from afar in the Spirit, speaks to God the Father, saying: “O Lord, our Lord, how admirable is your name in all the earth!” (Ps. 8). As if he openly said: O Lord of all by nature, but our Lord by grace, how admirable I see your name—that is, your future glory or praise—to be, not only in Judaea, but throughout all the earth. Why? Because “your magnificence has been raised above the heavens” (ibid.); that is, Jesus Christ your Son has been assumed by you—that is, lifted up—above all heavens, or above the apostles, who are called heavens because they pour spiritual rain upon the rational earth. Therefore the sun was lifted up: that is, Jesus Christ our Lord was assumed into heaven, as far as the very session of God the Father.

[Col. 1087D] Three heavens are said to exist: the aerial, the ethereal, and the empyrean, that is, fiery. “Heaven” is also understood to mean God the Father, as the Prophet testifies in the psalm: “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18). That is, he descended from the Father’s bosom in order to free the human race. Again, heaven is also understood to mean the Son. Hence it is said: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 113). Heaven is also said of angels or apostles, as is read in the psalms: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18), and so forth. It is also used of Scripture, as the Psalmist says: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8).

“Heaven” is understood of God the Father, as is read in the psalm: “He rejoiced as a giant”—that is, the Son of God—“to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18). He came forth from the virginal bridal chamber, and in coming forth rejoiced, because he did not unwillingly undertake the labor of running the course—not of dwelling in it, because he did not remain on the course of this world. “He rejoiced as a giant,” that is, as the strongest one, surpassing all people by incomparable power. He is rightly compared to a giant because, untroubled, unchangeable, and unconquerable, he surpasses human nature in power. And what course did he run? “His going forth,” he says, “is from the highest heaven; and his meeting is even unto its height.” Behold, he who eternally came forth from the Father came into the world made man; again, leaving the world, he ascended to the Father. This therefore is what he says: “His going forth is from the highest heaven,” that is, from the Father—namely, from equality with the Father. His going forth, by which he was born of the Father, was not temporal but eternal; understand: in time he was made man. And the meeting of that same man who was made is “unto its height,” namely, the Father’s: that is, the very man in whom “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2) meets the Father. “Meeting,” therefore, belongs to Christ according to his humanity, when, ascending to the Father’s seat, he meets him. He ascended according to his humanity. But in saying “unto its height,” note that, insofar as he is God, he is equal to the Father. The same thing which the Prophet says here, Christ says of himself in the Gospel: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16).

It follows: “And there is none who can hide himself from his heat,” namely, after the incarnation of the Word. For the Word made flesh, taking on our mortality, did not permit any mortal to excuse himself on account of the shadow of death—that is, sins—because the heat of the Word, that is, Christ’s love or grace, penetrated and dissolved even the shadow itself, when “a light arose” for those sitting “in the region of the shadow of death” (Isa. 9). Or the Holy Spirit is the heat whom the Son of God, returning to heaven, sent to the apostles after the Ascension; from him no one is hidden, because, as God, he knows all hearts, so that he may convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16). In these words the Trinity, unity, and both natures of Christ are shown. Where he says “from the highest heaven,” the Father is understood; where he says “going forth,” the Son’s eternal generation is understood; when he says “meeting,” the same Son is understood according to his humanity; when he says “unto its height,” he is understood as equal to God the Father; when he says “from his heat,” the Holy Spirit is understood; but by saying “his,” he denotes the unity of the Trinity. Therefore “his going forth is from the highest heaven”: that is, the Word proceeded from the Father, who is called the highest heaven—not in the essence of majesty, which is one in the three persons, but in the order in which he willed to make himself known to human beings. The first and highest heaven, then, is the Father, because from him proceeds the Son—that is, the will through which he works all things—which is not other in essence than the Father himself, because in God there is no diversity and no accident.

[Col. 1089A] The second heaven is the Word proceeding from the Father. The third heaven is charity—that is, the love and harmony of the will of God the Father—because his will is never changed, nor departs from him, nor, better stated, dissents from him. Heaven is also said of angels or apostles, as is read in the psalms: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). The heavens—that is, the angels—declared God’s glory when angels announced Christ’s birth to the shepherds (Luke 2), and when, at his Ascension, they stood beside the apostles and said to them: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will so come as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1). The heavens—that is, the apostles—also preached God’s glory. What glory? Namely, that “not by works of righteousness which we ourselves have done, but according to his mercy he saved us” (Titus 3). And again: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3). “The heavens,” he says, “declare the glory of God,” that is, the mercy shown to the human race through the Son, in which God the Father is to be glorified; “and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18). What above is “glory,” here is “works”; what there is “heavens,” here is “firmament”: under different imagery, the same preachers of the New Testament, strengthened in heart by the Holy Spirit and made a firmament against the attacks of the raging enemies who reject this glory of God, proclaim—that is, announce with great confidence—the works of his hands, that is, God’s own works: such as no one could perform except God alone.

Heaven is also used of Holy Scripture, as the Psalmist says: “For I shall behold your heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. 8). In this way sacred Scripture is called heaven. Heaven is a kind of instrument compared to God’s finger. As sculptors carve with that instrument, so writers work by the finger of the Holy Spirit. And as the works engraved upon heaven contain diverse images within themselves, so the Scriptures appear to possess diverse senses among themselves: namely, the historical, typological, and moral senses. Thus we read that Moses said in Genesis: “God made the firmament, heaven, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above the firmament” (Gen. 1). But what Moses said historically, we must understand spiritually. [Note: [Col. 1089D] Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, ch. 1.] Therefore God made the firmament of heaven, that is, the solidity of the holy Scriptures in the Church. For the divine Scriptures are understood as the firmament in the Church, because “the heaven shall be folded up like a book” (Isa. 34). And over this firmament God divided the waters, that is, the heavenly peoples of angels, who have no need to contemplate [the text reads *suscipere*, but *suspicere*, “contemplate,” is evidently intended] this firmament in order that, by reading, they may hear God’s word; for they always see and love him. But beneath this firmament of his Scripture he placed the weakness of the lower peoples, so that by looking there they may know how to distinguish between carnal and spiritual things, as between the upper and lower waters.

[Col. 1090A] Therefore the sun was lifted up: that is, Christ, who is the true Sun of righteousness, was lifted up into heaven, that is, to the right hand of God the Father, as he himself said to his disciples: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20).

Moreover, it should be noted that there were five exaltations of Christ. The first was on the cross. Hence he himself says: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). And elsewhere: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3), and so forth. The second exaltation was in the Resurrection, as the apostle Paul says to the Philippians: “Therefore”—namely, because of his obedience—“God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). The third was in the Ascension, as the Psalmist testifies: “Your magnificence has been lifted up above the heavens” (Ps. 8). The fourth was in the sending of the Holy Spirit, as the same Son of God says: “He shall glorify me,” that is, exalt me, “because he shall receive of mine” (John 16). The fifth exaltation was in the preaching among the nations, as he himself says through the Psalmist: “I shall be exalted among the nations, and I shall be exalted in the earth” (Ps. 45). Therefore the sun, namely the Lord Jesus Christ, was lifted up, as has been said—indeed, more nobly and gloriously than human speech can think or express—into heaven, “and the moon stood in its order.” The Church is compared to the moon because it undergoes waxing and waning. Since sacred reading has brought the sun and moon to our attention, let us, if it pleases you, hear what blessed Isidore, our patron, says concerning their size, height, nature, and variation.

“Interlunium,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1090D] Book III of the *Etymologies*, ch. 55 and following.] “is that period of the moon between its waning and its new birth. On the thirtieth day the moon does not shine; and it cannot then be seen because, joined to the sun, it is obscured. But, being renewed at that very moment, it gradually becomes visible by withdrawing from it. Some say that the moon has no light of its own but is illuminated by the sun’s rays; hence it undergoes eclipse if the earth’s shadow interposes between it and the sun. The moon is governed in a monthly period by the alternations of lost and regained light. For this reason it moves in an oblique, not straight, course like the sun: namely, lest it enter the earth’s center and suffer eclipse frequently. For its orbit is near the earth. When waxing, it turns its horns eastward; when waning, westward, rightly so, because it is going to set and lose its light. Because the moon is nearer to the earth than the sun, it completes its course more quickly in a smaller orbit. For the course which the sun completes in three hundred and sixty [Note: [Col. 1090D] The edition has ‘three hundred and sixty-five,’ correctly.] days the moon traverses in thirty days; hence the ancients reckoned months by the moon, but years by the sun’s course.

“An eclipse of the sun occurs when the moon, on its thirtieth day, reaches the same line along which the sun travels and, interposing itself, obscures the sun. For the sun appears to fail us when the disk of the moon is set before it. An eclipse of the moon occurs whenever the moon enters the earth’s shadow. For it is thought not to possess light of its own but to be illuminated by the sun; hence it undergoes eclipse if the earth’s shadow interposes between it and the sun. It undergoes this on the fifteenth day of the moon, until it leaves the center and shadow of the interposed earth, sees the sun, and is seen by the sun. The size of the moon is also reported to be less than the size of the sun. For although the sun is higher than the moon and yet appears to us larger than the moon, if it came near us it would appear much larger than the moon. The size of the sun is greater than that of the earth. Hence at the very moment when it rises, it appears equally both to east and west. But although it appears to us to measure a cubit, we must consider how far it is from the earth; that distance makes it appear small to us. As the sun is greater than the earth, so the earth is greater than the moon by some measure. Although the sun is fiery, it grows still hotter because of the excessive motion of its revolution. Philosophers say that its fire is nourished by water and receives the power of light and heat from the contrary element; thus we see it often moist and dewy. We say that the sun moves by itself and is not turned with the world. For if it remained fixed in heaven, all days and nights would be equal. But since we see it set tomorrow in one place and to have set yesterday in another, it is evident that it moves by itself and is not turned with the world. By unequal intervals it completes its yearly circuits because of the changes of seasons. (‘The east makes the day; the west brings on the night.’) [Note: [Col. 1091D] The words enclosed in parentheses are from the following chapter, 51, and have here fallen out through error.]

“For by going farther from the south it makes winter and enriches the earth with wintry moisture and frost. By drawing nearer to the north, it brings summer, so that crops may harden by ripeness and things which are unripe in moist conditions may soften when heated. Day is the sun above the earth; night is the sun beneath the earth. From it come the hours; from it comes the day when it rises; from it also comes the night when it sets; by it months and years are counted, and by it the alternations of the seasons occur. But when it runs through the south—that is, in winter—it is nearer the earth; when it is near the north, it is raised higher.” [Note: [Col. 1091D] The remaining material found after this in the editions was drawn from the book *On the Nature of Things*, as Grialius noted.]

“The rising sun has its course through the south; after it comes to the west and plunges into Ocean, it travels by unknown paths beneath the earth and returns again to the east.” Having briefly heard these matters concerning the natures of the sun and moon, as blessed Isidore teaches, we must return to what we had proposed.

“The moon,” says the prophet, “stood in its order.” The Church is compared to the moon because of the two properties which the moon has: it undergoes waxing and waning, and it shines by borrowed light. Likewise, because people sometimes come to faith, the Church grows; sometimes, because some apostatize from the faith, it suffers diminution, and yet remains whole, because, as the moon is illuminated by the sun, so the Church is illuminated by Christ. Indeed, the holy Church is compared not only to the moon but also—more happily—to the sun, as the most wise Solomon testifies in the Song of spiritual love: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army drawn up in battle-array?” (Song 6). [Note: [Col. 1092D] Gregory, on this passage.] The holy Church will come forth like the rising dawn at the last judgment, because, leaving behind the darkness of corruption, it will be renewed in the brightness of incorruption. It is rightly called chosen as the sun, because it will be brought to the same glory to which its head, Christ, ascended, who is declared to be the Sun of righteousness. Hence the true Sun of righteousness himself prays according to his humanity, saying: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which you have given me” (John 17); and again: “Where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John 12).

Yet this can also be understood of the members of that same Church who still live in the flesh. There are some who, with great earnestness, consider what the torments of the reprobate are and strive to examine their own deeds without flattery. When they recognize that they have sinned and therefore fear that they are going to the torments of the reprobate, they suddenly abandon the darkness of iniquity and desire to be kindled by the light of righteousness. Immediately they rise to holy action and, by the good they do, begin to shine before their neighbors. These without doubt go forth like the rising dawn, because, suddenly dispelling the night of sin, they expand more and more toward the light. Thus the soul which was formerly in darkness now appears radiant; and the soul that was darkened even in itself now shines upon others with the light of holy action. Concerning it he fittingly adds:

“Fair as the moon, chosen as the sun.” When the moon illumines the night, it shows darkened eyes the path by which a person may walk. So every holy soul which abandons darkness and gives itself to holy action, when it furnishes its neighbors an example of right conduct, as it were sheds light upon darkening eyes. For when sinners see a good work and turn themselves to do the same, they return to the path like those wandering by night through the moon’s light. Therefore, when this soul offers sinners examples of right conduct, it shines like the moon at night; but when it grows more and more, and through the habit of good works day by day receives the light of righteousness in perfection, so as to furnish even the good with examples for imitation—though it had formerly seemed fit to be imitated only by sinners—it surely becomes from moon a sun. For the soul which formerly shone in the night upon those who wandered now displays the light of truth to those who walk in the day. Hence follows: “Chosen as the sun,” concerning which he fittingly adds:

“Terrible as an army drawn up in battle-array.” Those who have experienced it know that when soldiers go out in marching order against enemies, if they march closely and in concord, they are feared by the enemies advancing against them. For, because the enemies see no opening through a breach, they cannot find, in their uncertainty, how to penetrate them; and what makes them an impenetrable defense is that, arranged in concord, they protect themselves by one another. For while they make a rampart for themselves from themselves, they leave no entrance for enemies to come among them; and, though attacked in order to be killed, they themselves kill more readily. So it is in the holy Church, that is, in the multitude of believers, which, since it does not cease to fight against wicked spirits, must be bound together in the peace of charity if it is to remain safe. For if it maintains peace, it appears terrible to its enemies; but if it is divided by discord, it is easily penetrated by enemies on every side. Therefore let the holy Church fortify herself with peace, bind herself with unity, unite herself with charity, so that, while she suffers no harm from a breach in herself, she may always follow her leader rejoicing without confusion. Let her stand in her order, lest she be conquered by the devil. Through love of God and neighbor let her devote herself to good works, and let her carefully beware lest enemies break her ranks. Let her persist in good works as an ordered battle-line, and without ceasing shoot the darts of pure prayer against her enemies. Let her gird herself manfully for spiritual battle and love all the faithful as her own members. Let her never lay aside spiritual arms, and let her bind all who believe in Christ with the bond of charity. Hence blessed Paul said to faithful disciples: “Above all, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” (Col. 3 [printed: “LIII”]). Therefore let the holy Church receive all Christ’s faithful into the bosom of charity, and carefully keep watch lest any one of them perish.

Thus Solomon too, praising the same Church as Christ’s bride, says in the Song of spiritual love: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet” (Song 4). The preachers of the faithful are called the lips of the Church because through them she speaks the precepts of life to the peoples. They are rightly called like a ribbon, because, by their preaching, they restrain the loose thoughts in human hearts, as though checking scattered hair lest it flow down without restraint. But why are they compared not merely to ribbons, but to scarlet ribbons, unless because the scarlet dye signifies the flame of charity by which they burn and through which others are kindled? Through them the speech of the holy Church is made sweet, because, while doing the good things that they say, they set their preaching before people like sweet foods.

It follows: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of a pomegranate, apart from your hidden things.” [Note: [Col. 1093] Gregory follows the Vulgate: “apart from that which lies hidden within.” But Martin retains the distinctive reading which he also gave above.] What do we understand by the Church’s cheeks except these same preachers, who, as they diligently labor for the people’s advancement, appear openly as it were on the Church’s face? The pomegranate signifies the Church itself, because, while nourishing many peoples in the unity of faith, it binds many seeds together beneath one rind. But the fragment of pomegranate represents the holy preachers, because, while they afflict themselves more vigorously than others in God’s service, despise all worldly things, renounce their pleasures, and completely mortify their vices, they surpass others; and, while nourishing others by their examples, they offer themselves as food, as though broken open and laid bare.

Thus the moon—that is, the holy Church—stands in her order when those subject to teachers imitate them in good works, when sheep follow good shepherds, and when all the Church’s children together strive to follow in the footsteps of their head, Jesus Christ, going into heaven. Hence she herself rejoicing speaks through Solomon: “The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered charity within me” (Song 2). What is signified by the wine-cellar except the teaching of evangelical instruction, in which is the wine of preaching? For through this charity is ordered in the bride of the highest King, Jesus Christ—that is, in the holy Church—because in its teaching one learns clearly how God and neighbor are to be loved in due order. Therefore the holy Church refreshes all the faithful with the bread of the heavenly word and, like a mother, binds them in the unity of faith within the bosom of charity.

Of this same immaculate and perfect holy Church, constituted in the number twelve, John the Evangelist speaks figuratively when he says in his Apocalypse: “I saw around the throne twenty-four seats, and upon the twenty-four seats twenty-four elders sitting, clothed in white garments, with golden crowns upon their heads” (Rev. IV). Behold, he plainly shows by the twenty-four elders [Col. 1094C] all the holy teachers of the New and Old Testaments. By these twenty-four elders, therefore, we understand the patriarchs and prophets, the apostles and evangelists, and their successors, through whom God formerly instructed the Jewish people and now governs the holy Church. The number of the twelve prophets and the twelve apostles consists of the numbers three and four, and therefore signifies all the preachers of the Holy Trinity in the New and Old Testaments, who preached through the four regions of the world. These are the living stones—namely, the patriarchs and prophets, the apostles and evangelists, and their successors—founded in the foundation of the Church, that is, in Christ, who is the most steadfast foundation, besides which no one can lay another (I Cor. III).

[Col. 1094D] Upon these living stones the Church is founded from the beginning of this world and grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Upon this foundation blessed Peter raised a building when he said to the disciples: “And you also, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses” (I Pet. II). For Paul also, the teacher of the Gentiles, built upon this foundation when, rejoicing, he said to the children of the Church: “Now you are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II). This, therefore, is Jerusalem—that is, the holy Church—which “is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI). For since that vision of supreme peace [Col. 1095A] is constructed from the gathering of holy citizens, the heavenly Jerusalem is built as a city.

Yet, while she is in this land of pilgrimage, while she is lashed with scourges and beaten by tribulations, her stones are squared every day. And she is the city—the holy Church—which, though destined to reign in heaven, still labours on earth. Blessed Paul says to her citizens: “You are God’s field; you are God’s building” (I Cor. III). This holy city plainly has here, in the conduct of the saints, its great building. In a building one stone bears another, because stone is laid upon stone. He who bears another is borne by another. Thus, in the holy Church, each bears another and is borne by another, so that through them the building of charity may rise. Hence Paul admonishes us, saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. VI). Declaring the power of this law, he says: “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XIII).

Therefore blessed Gregory says: “If I neglect to bear you in your conduct, and you disdain to tolerate me in mine, the building of charity does not rise among us. Those whom mutual love joins through patience have a work that advances toward the heavenly building. But in a building, as we have said, stone bears stone: for just as I now tolerate the conduct of those who are still untrained in the practice of good works, so I too am tolerated by those who preceded me in the fear of the Lord and bore me, so that I might learn to bear others; and they themselves [Col. 1095C] were likewise borne by their elders. But the stones placed at the height and extremity of the structure are indeed borne by others, yet bear no others; for those who are to be born at the end of the Church—that is, at the end of the world—will be tolerated by their elders, so that their conduct may be shaped toward good merits; but since none follow them who might advance through them, they bear above themselves no stones of the faithful structure.”

Ezekiel likewise prefigured these holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments upon whom the Church is built, when, describing what he had seen in a vision, he said among other things: “I saw four tables prepared for the burnt offering, constructed of squared stones” (Ezek. XL). Let wise Gregory, if you please, come forward and expound for us who desire to hear what the aforesaid tables signify.

“What,” he says [Note: [Col. 1095D] Homily 21 on Ezekiel], “do we understand in this place by squared stones, except any holy persons whose life knows how to stand firmly in prosperity and adversity alike? A squared stone stands equally firm, whichever side it is turned upon. Therefore whoever is not exalted in prosperity and is not broken in adversity, is not drawn by persuasion into evil deeds, and is not recalled by reproaches from the good that he has begun—such a person is a squared stone, and, as it were, stands on every side, because he does not fall in any change of circumstance. Certainly, when the prophet knew that the Jewish people would perish from the faith, and foresaw that the holy apostles would arise in the Church, through whom many from the Gentiles would be made firm in faith and strength of life, he spoke in great consolation for that same Church, saying: ‘The bricks have fallen, but we shall build with squared stones’ (Isa. IX).”

[Col. 1096A] For the prophet, seeing apostles, martyrs, and teachers arise in the holy Church, grieved less over the fall of the bricks—that is, over the destruction of the Jews—because he perceived that the building of almighty God, namely the holy Church, was being built of squared stones. This, then, is the virgin and mother Church, built upon squared stones—that is, founded upon the twenty-four elders, or rather upon all the teachers of the Old and New Testaments. Of her David the prophet says: “Her foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). That is as if he said: She is founded upon the teaching of the holy prophets and apostles. “He gave some indeed as apostles, some as prophets, others as evangelists, and others as pastors and teachers, for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of ministry, for the building up of Christ’s body, until we all meet in the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

This is the litter which the peaceful King Solomon—namely, our Lord Jesus Christ—made for himself. Hence the bride, praising him, says in the Song of spiritual love: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon; its pillars he made of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Cant. III).
