[Col. 1096C] For it is not to be believed, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1096D] Homily 15 on Ezekiel, and *Paterium on the Song of Songs*, ch. 24], that Solomon, a king of such greatness, who so abounded in immeasurable riches that the weight of his gold could not be estimated and silver had no value in his days, made himself a litter from the wood of Lebanon. Rather, this King Solomon is our Lord Jesus Christ, who is truly the peaceful king, whom God the Father sent into this world to reconcile the human race to himself, and who made himself a litter from holy persons. For the cedar wood of Lebanon is very resistant to decay. Therefore the litter of our King is the holy Church, constructed from the strong Fathers of the Old and New Testaments—that is, from minds resistant to decay. It is rightly called a litter, because every day it bears souls to the eternal banquet of its Creator.

[Col. 1096D] Silver pillars were made for this litter, because the Church’s preachers shine with the light of speech. With the silver pillars there is a golden reclining-place, because through what is clearly spoken by holy preachers, the minds of the hearers find the splendour of inward brightness in which they may recline. For through what they hear lucidly and openly, they rest in that which shines in the heart. Thus silver pillars and a golden reclining-place were made, because through the light of speech repose of brightness is found in the mind. For that eternal splendour now irradiates the mind, so that through its intention it may rest there where the grace of preaching is not sought.

Of this same holy Church it is written: “The wings of the dove are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. LXVII). The mind which is here filled with the spirit of gentleness has, like a dove, silvered wings and bears the appearance of gold upon the hinder parts of its back; because it clothes its preachers with the light of speech, while in the age to come it displays within itself the brilliance of splendour. But, in order to show what kind of ascent leads to that brightness displayed within, he immediately adds concerning the same litter: “An ascent of purple.”

True purple, indeed, dyed in the blood of the murex, is fittingly seen in the colour of blood. The murex, as blessed Isidore says [Note: [Col. 1097D] Book XII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 6], is a sea-shell (*conclea* or *cochlea*), so called from its point and roughness. (And *conclea* is said as a diminutive, like *conchula*, “little shell.”)

[Note: The material enclosed here in brackets survives: it is an etymology of the word *conclea*, or *cochlea*, which Isidore explains as follows: “Shellfish and snails are called so because, when the moon wanes, they are hollowed out—that is, emptied …; *conchae* is a primary form, but *cochleae* is a diminutive, as though *conchulae*, ‘little shells.’”]

It is also called *conchilium*, [Col. 1097B] because, when cut around with iron, it emits tears of purple colour, from which purple dye is produced. It is also called *ostrum*, because this dye is drawn from the moisture of the shell [Note: [Col. 1098D] Gregory again]. Therefore true purple, which is dyed from blood, appears in the colour of blood. And because a very great multitude of the faithful, at the beginning of the Church’s birth, came to the kingdom through the blood of martyrdom, our King made a purple ascent in his litter; for one comes to that brightness hidden within through the tribulation of blood.

What, then, shall we wretched people, bereft of every strength, do? Behold, we cannot be pillars in this litter, because in us there shines neither strength of work nor the light of preaching. We do not possess a golden reclining-place, because we do not yet, as we ought, behold through spiritual understanding the repose of inward [Col. 1097C] brightness. We are not a purple ascent, because we are unable to shed blood for our Redeemer. What is to be done concerning us? What hope will there be if no one reaches the kingdom except one endowed with the highest virtues? But our consolation is also present. Let us love God insofar as we can; let us love our neighbour; and then we too belong to God’s litter, because, as it is written there: “He paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.” Therefore have charity, dearest brothers, and without doubt you will arrive where both the silver pillar is raised and the purple ascent is held.

For it is plainly shown that this is said on account of our weakness when it is immediately added there: “For the daughters [Col. 1097D] of Jerusalem.” For the word of God, which says not “sons” but “daughters,” signifies by the female sex nothing other than the weakness of minds. This, therefore, as has been said, is the litter of Solomon, the peaceful king, our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, the holy Church, constructed from holy souls resistant to decay. The Fathers of the Old Testament, therefore, were placed in the foundation of the holy Church, while the teachers of the New Testament are built at the top. The former stood, as it were, on the outside in the Church’s building; modern teachers stand within.

The two thresholds which Ezekiel saw in the doorway of the house of the Lord signified these Fathers of the New and Old Testaments, as blessed Gregory testifies when he says [Note: [Col. 1098D] The same Homily 15]: “What are these thresholds of the house of the Lord, except the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments? Not only those from whom the Lord deigned to be incarnate, but all the Fathers of the Old Testament were thresholds of this gate, because, by meriting to foretell him and to hope in him, they opened the entrance of faith to all who came to him, so that everyone who believed that the Lord was to come might enter, as it were, through the gate of this threshold. But why is one called the outer threshold and the other afterward the inner threshold, except because the Fathers of the Old Testament came first, and afterward [Col. 1098B] the teachers of the New Testament?

“The outer threshold rightly signifies the Fathers of the Old Testament, because through their preaching perverse deeds were punished. But through the sayings of the New Fathers the inner mind of each person is also restrained from unlawful thoughts, since guilt is shown to be complete even in the heart’s deliberation. For those Fathers of the Old Testament took care to forbid their hearers acts of shame, cruelty, and plunder; but these Fathers of the New Testament, by cutting off not only perverse deeds but also unlawful thoughts, have become for us nothing other than an inner threshold. Hence Truth itself speaks, saying: ‘You have heard that it was said to the ancients, “You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.” But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment’” (Matt. V).

[Col. 1098C] “The outer threshold also rightly signifies those Fathers who existed at intervals of time before the Incarnation itself of our Redeemer. Indeed, from the blood of Abel the Church’s suffering had already begun, and the Church of the elect who precede and those who follow is one. Yet because it is said to the disciples, ‘Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it’ (Luke X), to have stood, as it were, outside was for the ancient Fathers not to have seen the presence of our Redeemer. They were, therefore, outside, yet not separated from the holy Church, because in mind, deed, and preaching they already held by faith these sacraments. They beheld that height of the holy Church [Col. 1098D] which we behold not by still awaiting it, but by now possessing it.”

[Note: The same homily, and *Paterium on Exodus*, ch. 45.] Therefore, in the construction of the tabernacle, bronze pegs [Note: *aenei*, “bronze”] were commanded to be driven into the ground all around on the outside, so that the tabernacle might be held fast by cords tied to them, while silver pillars stood within. Silver pillars stand within, but bronze pegs [Note: *aenei*, “bronze”] are driven around the outside, and cords are tied to them so that the tabernacle may remain fixed. This signifies that, in order that the holy apostles [Col. 1099A] might stand firm in the light of their preaching, and that the secure tabernacle—that is, the holy Church—might remain in the integrity of faith, the Fathers and prophets of the Old Testament were fixed outside like bronze pegs [Note: *aenei*, “bronze”]. By the cords of their words they bound the minds of preachers in steadfastness and fastened this dwelling of God in the state of faith.

The pegs are outside, therefore, because they existed before the time of this holy Church; yet they bind those who are within it, because, by foretelling heavenly mysteries still to come, they made them credible to all once they had been revealed. Thus, in order that the pillars may stand unmoved within, the pegs outside hold the cords; for the preaching of those who were able, before it happened, both to see in the Spirit and to proclaim it, brought it about that the holy apostles might perfectly believe the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation. Hence the first of the apostles himself, namely a great pillar of the true tabernacle, rightly says: “We have the more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp burning in a dark place” (II Pet. I). By these words he indicates upon what fastening it may remain in faith, though it has risen to lofty heights. This lamp of prophetic speech now indeed shines for those who understand, but remains covered for those who do not yet understand by the obscurities of allegory.

Therefore the Psalmist also says: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. XVII). It is as if he plainly said: Teaching is obscure in the clouds—that is, in the prophets and ancient teachers—who, raised above earthly things, rain the word of God upon those below. “Dark water,” he says, “is in the clouds.” These clouds—that is, the preachers of the divine word—have passed to the Gentiles and are no longer in Judaea. For the clouds, that is, the holy apostles, passed to the Gentiles, explaining the hidden knowledge of the prophets and preaching the manifest teaching of Christ. Of them Isaiah says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX).

[Col. 1099C] It is therefore not without reason that silver pillars and bronze pegs were made, because what the apostles now preach clearly, the prophets spoke obscurely under mystical understanding. They were rightly represented by the metal bronze, because they were not clear in their preaching. But the holy apostles, because they possessed the light of preaching through the mystery of our Redeemer, were represented by silver pillars. It should be noted that silver sounds and shines, whereas bronze sounds but does not shine, because the preachers of the New Testament spoke openly of things which they were also able to show to many. But the preachers of the Old Testament, because they uttered obscure sayings concerning the heavenly mystery through shadows of allegory, produced sound, as it were, without light. What is therefore signified by pegs and pillars is also signified by the outer threshold and inner threshold.

We have inserted these things, dearest brothers, from the sayings of holy men into this reading so that your charity may more readily understand that there is one catholic holy mother Church, constructed from living and elect stones—[Col. 1100A] that is, from the holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments. In praise of her, the heavenly bridegroom of that same Church says: “My dove is one, my perfect one; she is the only one of her mother, chosen by her who bore her” (Cant. VI).

[Note: Gregory, on this passage.] The mother of the Church is regenerating grace, with whom one dove is chosen, because she gathers only those who remain in simplicity and are not divided from unity. For many believers, while they pursue the same end, nourish one another with the single desire of Christ, and, having one heart and one soul (Acts IV), bind themselves together in charity, make one body out of many members; and all who live in the simplicity of unity are one dove. She alone is called chosen by her mother, that is, by divine grace, because outside this Church, which we call constructed from the holy Fathers of the New and Old Testaments, no one can attain perfection or eternal life. From the diverse merits and virtues of all the saints, therefore, the holy Church is joined together and grows in the knowledge of her Creator. Standing in her proper order, as we have stated above, the holy Church is built by the preaching of the holy Fathers, instructed by their examples, and happily raised to heavenly things through their prayers.

These holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, who truly build the one holy Church, were signified by the ten curtains which, joined by hyacinth-blue loops and suspended from golden rings, [Col. 1100C] made and adorned the one tabernacle of God (Exod. XXVI). Therefore, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1100D] Homily 19 on Ezekiel], the curtains of the tabernacle signify all the saints, who, through various colours of virtues, advance in the adornment of the holy Church. They veil the inner parts and in every way adorn the outer parts. For their life, insofar as it is seen, is an ornament; while their understanding is hidden within, because the heavenly things they preserve in the mind and cannot express are in some manner veiled in them.

There are rightly ten curtains, because the hearts of the saints advanced through the keeping of the Decalogue. Fifty hyacinth-blue loops were commanded to be made for the curtains. Hyacinth has the appearance of heaven. Therefore the loops of the curtains are heavenly commandments, in which souls are bound so that, lifted from lower things, they may hang above. These loops plainly also have golden rings: that is, understanding and true, shining wisdom. Since this understanding must in every respect be circumspect and fortified by the watchfulness of prudent care, it is rightly signified by golden rings. It should be observed that the loops or rings are commanded to be made on the side and at the top of the curtains, because heavenly commandments and spiritual understanding ought not only to suspend us upward in love of God, but also join us to our neighbour in charity. In loving our Creator, we hang, as it were, by the upper loops. But in loving our neighbours as ourselves, we have loops and rings at the side, so that the curtains of the tabernacle—[Col. 1101A] that is, the souls of the faithful—may be joined through charity and not divided through discord.

This, therefore, is the virgin and mother Church, prefigured in the number of the twenty-four elders, firmly founded upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, wisely prepared to endure the adversities of the present world, and “terrible as an army drawn up in battle array” to overcome the temptations of the devil (Cant. VI). “I saw,” says the Evangelist, “twenty-four elders clothed in white garments and crowned with golden crowns” (Rev. IV). These twenty-four elders signify all the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, preachers of faith in the Holy Trinity, who are dispersed by divine providence through the four regions of the world: elders, I say, clothed in white garments—namely, clothed in righteousness and purity.

[Col. 1101B] The holy Church is covered on every side with white garments; that is, she is adorned with blessed immortality, impassibility, and the other virtues which she received in baptism through the grace of the Holy Spirit. And she received golden crowns upon their heads: having conquered the devil and his temptations, the Church received from the Lord’s hand, in her members, golden crowns—that is, victories in diverse contests, bright with charity and divine wisdom. Concerning these crowns Paul, the chosen vessel, rejoicing in the Lord, said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day; and not to me only, but also to all who love his coming” (II Tim. IV).

The holy Church, constituted in the number of the twenty-four elders, is one day with her head, Jesus Christ. A day is bounded by the spans of the twenty-four hours of night and day, and is called one day. Thus, before the Lord’s coming, the law shone only in the patriarchs and prophets; in the rest there was night. But the New Testament, which Christ revealed when he came in the flesh, was called his manifestation’s light and day, as John the Evangelist testifies in his Epistle: “The darkness has passed, and the true light now shines” (I John II). Therefore Paul also said to the children of the Church: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” [Col. 1101D] (Eph. V). And the glorious king and prophet David says in the psalm: “Light has arisen for the righteous, and gladness for the upright in heart” (Ps. XCVI). That is as if he plainly said: Light—that is, Christ—has risen for the righteous people, namely those predestined to eternal life; and for the upright in heart there is joy at the reconciliation of the human race, the devil having been conquered. Isaiah also says: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. IX). Therefore Christ, who is truly the head of the Church, is called the sun, as the prophet testifies: “For you who fear God the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV).

This true day, namely Christ, chose twelve apostles, through whose preaching he illuminated the whole world. He taught them in person, poured the gift of the Holy Spirit into their minds, [Col. 1102A] and strengthened them to endure the fury of human wickedness. Therefore the Psalmist, intoxicated with the Holy Spirit, says: “Day utters speech to day” (Ps. XVIII). That is as if he plainly said: Christ, who is the true day, utters speech—namely, he manifests himself, who is the Word of God the Father, to day, that is, to the apostles, who are the twelve hours of the day; indeed, he continually inspires all the children of the Church with the word of evangelical instruction. The Son of God himself also says of himself: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII); and he testifies of his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V). Twelve hours make a day. Therefore the apostles are day from day, light from light, proclaiming throughout the world the word of eternal salvation.

It should further be noted that in these twelve apostles [Col. 1102B] the Son of God established the entire body of bishops, and in the body of bishops he joined together all the faithful people by the word of evangelical preaching and the bond of charity. On the sixth day God made Adam and subjected to him a woman as a helper (Gen. I). The woman, therefore, subjected to the man, signified the whole Christian people; but Adam bore the figure of all bishops. As the woman is subject to the man, so the faithful people ought to be subject to their bishop. Women are subject to the commands of their husbands; Christian peoples should be subject to the priests of the Church. Yet priests must labour for those who are less perfect, so that, advancing through the milk of preaching to solid food, they may know [Col. 1102C] the one true God, three in persons: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

For the Apostle shows that all members of the faithful are joined to God when he says: “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” (II Cor. IV). Thus all members of the faithful are not separated from one another, but are inseparably joined, in the unity of true faith, through Catholic priests, to Jesus Christ their head.

For he is the true light of the Church, concerning whom the Psalmist speaks to God the Father, saying: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. XXXV). That is as if he said: O God the Father, with you is the fountain of life, namely Christ, from whose breast flow streams of living water—that is, spiritual teaching, which truly is the word of life. And in your light, that is, in Christ, we shall see the light by which you illuminate the eyes of the mind through faith, hope, and charity. We shall see light—namely you, God the Father; after this life we shall have full knowledge of you, concerning which knowledge it is said: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI).

[Col. 1102D] Hence the Sun of righteousness himself says of himself in the Gospel: “No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter”—namely, the holy Church—“may see the light” (Luke XI). Therefore the Church is Christ’s body, and Christ is the Church’s head; his humanity is the lampstand, his divinity the lamp, which “enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I).

[Col. 1103A] The beaten-work lampstand which the Lord commanded to be made in the tabernacle of Moses prefigured this lampstand—namely, the Son of God who was to illumine his Church. “You shall make,” he says, “a lampstand of purest gold, beaten work: its shaft and branches, bowls, knobs, and lilies proceeding from it” (Exod. XXV). Explaining this, blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1103D] Homily 6 on Ezekiel, and *Paterium on Exodus*, ch. 40]:

“Who is signified by the lampstand except the Redeemer of the human race, who in the nature of his humanity shone with the light of divinity, so that he might become the lampstand of the world and, in his light, every sinner might see in what darkness he lay? Since he assumed our nature without fault, the lampstand of the tabernacle is commanded to be made of purest gold. But beaten work is shaped by hammering, because [Col. 1103B] our Redeemer, who from conception and birth was perfect God and perfect man, endured the pains of sufferings and thus came to the glory of the resurrection. Therefore he was a lampstand of purest gold, wrought by beating, because he had no sin and yet his body, through the indignities of the Passion, advanced to mortality. Indeed, as regards the virtues of his soul, he had absolutely nothing in which he might advance through blows. But in his members, which we are, he advances daily through blows, because while we are struck and made worthy to be his body, he advances.

“Concerning this body it is written: ‘From whom the whole body, supplied and built up through joints and bonds, grows with the increase of God’ (Col. II). For we all are Christ’s body; and through joints and connections the body is bound together. As the breast is joined to the head, the arms to the breast, the hands to the arms, and the fingers to the hands, these limbs and the rest adhere to their respective limbs, and the whole body is completed. Thus the holy apostles, because they stood close to our Redeemer, adhered to the head like the breast. Because martyrs followed them, they were like arms joined to the breast. When pastors and teachers were joined to these through good works, hands adhered to the arms. This entire body of our Redeemer is daily supplied through joints and connections in heaven, because when elect souls are led there to him, his members are added to him. Therefore it is well said of him: ‘Supplied and built up, it grows [Col. 1103D] with the increase of God,’ because almighty God, our Redeemer, who has nothing in himself by which he may advance, nevertheless daily receives increase through his members. Hence it is again written: ‘Until we all meet in a perfect man, in the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ’ (Eph. IV).

“The shaft of this lampstand should be understood as the Church herself, which is his body, because she stands free amid so many adversities. The branches proceeding from the shaft are preachers, who gave forth a sweet sound in the world, namely a new song. Bowls are accustomed to be filled with wine. What, then, are the minds of hearers but bowls, which [Note: [Col. 1103D] Another manuscript: ‘whenever.’] are filled with the wine of knowledge when holy preachers preach? But what is a small sphere [Col. 1104A] except the mobility of preaching? A sphere rolls on every side. And preaching which is neither cast down by adversity nor raised up by prosperity is a sphere, because it is strong amid adversity and humble amid prosperity, and has neither the angle of fear nor that of self-exaltation. Thus it cannot be bent from its course, because it moves itself nimbly through all things.

“But, to pursue the example we have offered: lilies are fittingly described upon the lampstand after the branches, bowls, and knobs, because after the grace and mobility of preaching of which we have spoken, there follows that verdant homeland which blossoms with holy living beings—that is, eternal flowers. The small spheres, therefore, belong to labour; the lilies to recompense.”

Christ, then, is the true Sun of righteousness, enlightening those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death; he is the sufficient sacrifice, offering himself to God the Father for the redemption of the human race; he is the priest ever pleading with the Father for his bride, the holy Church. “He entered not into holy places made by hands, but into heaven itself, to appear now before the face of God for us” (Heb. IX). Nor did he enter with another’s blood but with his own, nor into a movable or shadowy tabernacle but into the highest heaven. Many hear the name of the tabernacle yet do not know how God commanded it to be made through Moses. Let us therefore ask blessed Paul, most diligent in the law of God, and listen carefully to whatever he tells us concerning the arrangement of the tabernacle.

“Now the first tabernacle,” he says, “was made, in which were the lampstands, the table, and the setting forth of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place.” [Note: All these matters concerning the tabernacle are taken from the Ordinary Gloss.] In this tabernacle was a golden lampstand; but the Apostle says “lampstands,” because, though it was one, it nevertheless had seven branches. For in the middle was a shaft, from which three branches extended on the right and three on the left, having at three points cups, little spheres, and lilies. There was also in it a certain table, like an altar, with four feet, after the entrance of the tabernacle. It was made of shittim wood and overlaid with the purest gold; it had a golden rim all round, and above it an openwork golden crown, four fingers high, and above that another small golden crown. It also had, at each [Col. 1104D] corner, golden rings into which poles were inserted so that it could be carried; these were of shittim wood and covered with gold. Upon the table were twelve loaves set before God, made of fine flour, and all were changed every Sabbath. But if one of them was needed before the Sabbath, it could not be taken unless another were immediately put in its place. Above the loaves were a golden dish and a handful of the brightest incense. In the same tabernacle there was also the altar of incense, where incense was burned upon glowing ashes; for the ashes were carried there from the altar of sacrifices, which stood outside the tabernacle in the open court and was square, [Col. 1105A] five cubits broad and as many long. The first tabernacle is therefore called the Holy Place because of the reverence then paid to it, and because it signifies the present Church, which is holy. The second is called the Holy of Holies because it was held in greater reverence, and because it signifies the heavenly Church, where there is no sin. In that tabernacle was a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, made of shittim wood, covered within and without with gold, two and a half cubits in length, and with a golden ring at each [Note: “At each and every.”] corner—two on the right and two on the left—in which there were continually fixed, for carrying it, poles of shittim wood overlaid with the purest gold. In the ark were three things: namely, a golden jar containing manna, Aaron’s rod that had budded, and the tablets [Col. 1105B] on which the Law had been written. Over the ark was the mercy-seat: that is, a slab of the same length and breadth as the ark, made of the purest gold, called the mercy-seat or oracle, because there the angel of God appeared to Moses and spoke when God was about to be propitiated toward the children of Israel. Above the mercy-seat were two cherubim, most gloriously adorned, looking at one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy-seat. No one was permitted to enter this Holy of Holies with blood except the high priest, once a year, and then only if necessity perhaps required it because of the sin of the priest or of the whole synagogue. Into the first tabernacle, however, the priests entered daily to perform the rites of sacrifices (Exod. XXXVII).

[Col. 1105C] All this is a parable and shadow of heavenly goods. For the first tabernacle is the present Church, rightly called a tabernacle because in it service is rendered to God before one arrives in heaven. A tabernacle properly belongs to those at war. In it is the golden lampstand: that is, Christ shining with power and wisdom among the faithful, who themselves are also golden lampstands because they shine with wisdom. Gold signifies wisdom. Christ himself is the stem bearing three branches on the right and three on the left, because he is the true vine (John XV), in which are founded three orders of branches—that is, of the faithful. Those who belong to the time of grace are on the right, that is, more worthy; those before grace were, as it were, on the left. These three orders of the faithful are signified by the [Col. 1105D] three men whom Ezekiel saw would be saved: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. XIV), namely rulers, the continent, and married persons. These are also those who, according to the Gospel, are said to be in the field, in bed, and at the mill. For it is thus read there: [Note: The Gospel passage is cited specially here; see Peter Sabatier on Matthew XXIV after verse 41, and others cited by him.] “Two shall be in the field: one shall be taken and the other left. Two shall be in bed: one shall be taken and the other left. And two women grinding at the mill: one shall be taken and the other left” (Matt. XXIV). Those in the field signify rulers, as does Noah; those in bed, the continent, as does Daniel; while those [Col. 1106A] at the mill signify married persons, as does Job.

The first part of the shafts was like golden reeds. Then came cups, then little golden spheres, and finally lilies. The reeds are saints nourished in the moistness of the divine fountain, hollow so as to receive and pour out to others the liquid of grace. They are likewise cups when they offer to others to drink what they themselves have drunk—namely, wisdom and the knowledge of God. The same are little spheres: that is, rounded, perfect, and mobile amid prosperity and adversity, held back by nothing until they arrive at the lilies of eternal joy; having, as was said above, neither the corner of fear nor the brow of pride. Seven lamps were placed upon these: that is, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which remain most fully in Christ and are distributed to the faithful [Col. 1106B] according to his will. The table at the entrance is Holy Scripture: it remains; it is set before those who enter; it shows eternal joys and the way in which they are reached; and it supplies the food of life. On it were twelve loaves of the world: that is, the twelve apostles and their successors, who offer to God the incense of prayer. If one of them dies, another is immediately substituted in his place; but in the seventh age all shall be removed.

The second tabernacle beyond the veil is the heavenly Church, which remains veiled while we live here. The censer signifies Christ, full of the fire of charity, always interceding with the Father for us (Rom. VIII). The ark is Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Col. II). It is [Col. 1106C] golden in every part because in his thought, speech, and action nothing but pure truth is found. Its length signifies the perseverance of teaching, denoted by one cubit, and of action, denoted by the other cubit; the half-cubit signifies that human understanding is imperfect in relation to the perfection of these. Its breadth signifies the perfection of charity; its height, the perfection of hope, to which we are but halves—that is, imperfect. The four rings are the four perfect Evangelists, through whom the ark, that is, Christ, is carried through the four parts of the world. To them are always attached the golden poles: that is, preachers shining with wisdom and always ready against enemies. For in the ark was the jar containing manna: that is, Christ’s soul containing the fullness of wisdom, by which even [Col. 1106D] angels are refreshed. The rod signifies Christ’s priestly power; the tablets, that he is the giver of the Law; the mercy-seat, Christ who makes propitiation for us; the two cherubim, all the orders of heaven, which rest in him and are joined together by mutual love, because, though wise, they overshadow him as far as lies in them. Priests entered the first tabernacle daily to complete the rites of sacrifice, because in the present Church the faithful ought daily to offer themselves, mortifying their flesh with its vices and desires (Gal. V). But the high priest entered the second tabernacle with blood once [Col. 1107A] in the year, because Christ, the true and supreme priest, once in the year of graciousness—that is, of restoration—having shed his blood for the remission of sins, entered the inner places of heaven and on this day opened to the faithful the previously closed gate of paradise. A great mystery lies here. Gold signifies wisdom, and the ark the secret counsel of God. The Law, manna, and Aaron’s rod were commanded to be placed in the ark. The Law contains commandments; the rod signifies power; manna, grace, because without grace there is no power to fulfil the commandments. But because the Law is not fulfilled in every respect by anyone making progress, the mercy-seat is above it. God must therefore be propitious, and for that reason it is placed above, because mercy exalts above judgment—that is, it exalts the human being above judgment [Col. 1107B] (Jas. II).

Therefore Jesus did not enter holy places made by hands, copies of the true ones, but heaven itself, now to appear before the face of God for us. Why did Jesus not enter holy places made by hands? Because they are copies of the true ones; and the true priest ought to enter not shadowy but true holy places. [Note: This corrupt passage should be restored from the Gloss as follows: “Consider how great the differences are between old and new. In place of the copy—that is, the temple which was there—here there is heaven. The high priest also differs,” etc.] What a difference! In place of the copy—that is, the temple—there is heaven. The high priest also differs: he stands before the face of God, ever living to intercede for us (Heb. VII). There, often [Note: Supply: “he offered.”]; here, once; there, with another’s blood; here, with his own. He is therefore both priest and victim. Thus Jesus did not enter holy places made by hands, which are copies of the true ones, but [Col. 1107C] heaven itself, signified by those places, in order to appear before the face of God for us: that is, to intercede with the Father for us and, after the consummation of the present age, draw us after himself.

Therefore many priests were made under the Law because death prevented them from remaining; but Jesus Christ, because he remains for ever, has an everlasting priesthood (ibid.). Having shown that the old priesthood is destroyed through Christ’s priesthood, the Apostle commends Christ’s action—namely, the abolishing of the old priestly office—by contrast. Since Jesus Christ therefore remains for ever, he has an everlasting priesthood. Hence he is able to save perpetually, approaching God through himself, ever living to intercede for us. Because [Col. 1107D] he, the Son of God and of the Virgin, approaches God not through other victims but through himself as a living victim, he is able to save the people subject to him. Thus he approaches God not through another high priest but through himself, ever living to intercede for us by presenting himself. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). In that nature by which he is high priest—that is, his human nature, which in ascending he raised to heaven—he intercedes with the Father for us. Such, then, it was fitting for us to have as high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens [Col. 1108A]. As if he said: It was fitting that such a priest, approaching by himself, should be ours who are sons; for servants—that is, those placed under the Law—had other high priests. He is holy in the possession of virtues; innocent toward his neighbour; undefiled through the removal of vices—not merely now undefiled, but always without sin; separated from sinners, that is, from the former priests of the Old Testament; and made higher than the heavens, namely higher than every heavenly nature, which all angels adore. For he is holy in every respect: innocent in hands, undefiled in body, separated from sinners, that is, free from every sin. He has no daily necessity, as the Levitical priests did—who were only his figure—to offer victims first for their own offences and then for those of the people. As if he [Col. 1108B] plainly said: He has no need to offer daily—not that he ever has such need, but in order to remove from him what happens to others. For the Lord Jesus Christ did this once, by offering himself. So great is this sacrifice that, although it is one and offered once, it nevertheless suffices for eternal salvation. As if he said: He offered this sacrifice, namely himself, not for his own offences but for those of the people; once, because it sufficed for all, and therefore need not be repeated. For the Law appoints as priests human beings who have weakness. As if he plainly said: Those priests must daily offer sacrifice for themselves because they have the weakness of sinning and dying; but this one offering suffices once, because he is perfect God and perfect man. The Law, therefore, appoints as priests human beings having weakness; but the word of the oath, which came after the Law, appoints the Son of God an eternally perfect priest [Col. 1108C]. Thus the word of the oath, spoken after the Law through David, appoints the Son of God and man as a perfect priest who shall remain for ever, saying: “The Lord has sworn and will not repent: You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX).

It follows: “We have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the majesty of God in heaven, minister of the holy things and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man” (Heb. VIII). As if he said: We have such a high priest, who long ago sat down in the equality of the deity seated—that is, of power—[Col. 1108D] at the right hand of the throne of majesty, that is, of the Father, because he is true God and true man, who rests and judges. For God the Father gave all judgment to the Son, that all may honour the Son as they honour the Father (John V). He is also minister of the saints, namely of mercy here and in the future, and of the tabernacle—not the shadowy tabernacle but the true one, which God pitched and not man: that is, the souls of the saints, to whom he ministers eternal joys. Similar is what he says elsewhere concerning himself as though concerning another: “Amen I say to you, that he shall gird himself, make them recline, and, passing by, shall minister to them” (Luke IX). [Col. 1109A] Hence the Son of God and of the Virgin, about to ascend into heaven, said to his disciples: “I go to prepare a place for you. In my Father’s house are many dwelling places. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I shall come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John XIV).

Did he not, when he spoke these things, minister eternal joys to his disciples—indeed, to all who believe in him? Christ, therefore, according to the Apostle, is minister of the saints, because every high priest is appointed to minister. We thus have such a high priest, who sits in heaven at the right hand of God the Father, whether above the material heavens or above thrones and dominions. There he is minister of the saints, because, as has been said, he ministers eternal life to the saints; or he ministers in heaven [Col. 1109B] the glory figured by the Holy of Holies. The same Son of God, ascending into heaven, is minister of the true tabernacle—that is, of the truth which the old tabernacle prefigured: namely, righteousness in the present Church and glory in the future. God, not man, pitched this true tabernacle, that it might remain for ever; but the shadowy tabernacle was not fixed but portable, because God established the old tabernacle, yet through human ministry.

“But Christ, having come as high priest of future good things, through a greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made by hands—that is, not of this creation” (Heb. IX). As if he said: Christ, high priest of future good things—namely, present righteousness and eternal blessedness, which were future in the time of the Law—through the flesh [Col. 1109C] conceived without male seed, stands before the Father to intercede, or before the faithful to help, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, namely heaven. It is not made by hands—the name of the signifying thing indicates the thing signified—that is, it is not of this creation, like that in the wilderness which man, namely Moses, pitched, but is established by God in a wholly different way. It follows: “Neither through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, he entered once into the holy places, having found eternal redemption.” As if he said: Neither through the blood of goats or calves, shed under the Old Testament, but through his own blood, he entered once—because it is perfect and ought not to be repeated—into the holy places, that is, into the heavenly tabernacle, [Col. 1109D] having found eternal redemption: namely, through this entrance into the Holy of Holies, because we are redeemed eternally. The goat signifies Christ because of the likeness of sinful flesh. Christ therefore entered the tabernacle, that is, heaven, through one greater because it contains more than that earthly tabernacle, and more perfect because blessedness is perfect there. For this purpose he deigned to be born, suffer, die, and rise again: to raise our humanity to heaven and in it forever supplicate the Father for us.

For he is the Angel of great counsel, who mercifully bore our sins on the cross and always intervenes for us before the justice of the Father. Blessed Job desired this Angel to plead for the salvation of humankind when he said:

[Col. 1110A] “If there shall be for him an angel speaking one of the like things, that he may declare righteousness” (Job XXXIII). Explaining this verse, blessed Gregory says: “For who is this angel, except he of whom it is said through the prophet, ‘the Angel of great counsel’?” (Isa. IX, according to the Septuagint.) Because in Greek *evangelizare* means “to announce,” the Lord, announcing himself to us, is called an angel. And he rightly says, “if there shall be for him an angel speaking,” because, as the Apostle says, he also intercedes with the Father for us (Rom. VIII). But let us hear what he speaks for us: “One of the like things.” It is the practice of medicine sometimes to cure like with like and sometimes opposites with opposites. For it often cures hot things with hot, but also cold things with hot and hot things with cold. Therefore our physician, coming down to us from above [Col. 1110B] and finding us oppressed with such great ailments, applied to us something like us and something contrary. He came to human beings as a human being, but to sinners as a righteous man. He agreed with us in the truth of nature, but differed from us in the strength of righteousness. For sinful humanity could not be corrected except by God. Yet the one who corrected it had to be seen, so that, by providing a pattern for imitation, he might change a life of former wickedness. But because God could not be seen by human beings, he became human so that he might be seen. Therefore the righteous and invisible God appeared as a visible human being like us, so that, while seen through likeness, he might heal through righteousness; and while agreeing with our condition in the truth of kind, he might oppose disease by the power of his art. Therefore, because the Lord, coming in the flesh, did not take our guilt from vice nor our punishment from necessity [Col. 1110C] (for, stained by no blemish of sin, he could not be held under the condition of our guilt, and therefore, having trampled down every necessity, he voluntarily accepted our death when he willed), it is rightly said that this Angel speaks one of the like things for the tempted human being. For he neither died, nor rose again, nor was taken up into heaven in the same manner. He was conceived not through cooperating intercourse, but through the coming of the Holy Spirit; and when born, his mother’s womb both showed itself fruitful and remained incorrupt. Again, all of us die unwillingly, because we are constrained by the condition of our guilt to pay the debt of punishment. But he, because he had no share in any guilt, submitted to no punishment by necessity; rather, because he subjected our guilt by his dominion, he mercifully took up our punishment, as he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it again” (John X). And he had already said: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down myself” (ibid.). Again, he was not raised as the rest are, because our resurrection is delayed until the end of the age, while his was accomplished on the third day. We indeed shall rise through him, but he through himself; for he who was God had no need to be raised by another as we are. Therefore his resurrection differs from ours in this: we shall not rise through ourselves, as he rose through himself. Because we are simply human beings, we need higher assistance in order to be able to rise. But he, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, displayed as God the power of that resurrection [Col. 1111A] which he alone received in his humanity. Likewise, ascending into heaven this day in great glory while his disciples looked on, he did not need another’s help, as Elijah did, who was carried up in a fiery chariot (IV Kings II). Nor is it surprising that Enoch and Elijah needed the aid of angels to carry them up (Gen. V), since they were merely human beings. But the Lord Jesus Christ, because he was true God and true man, did not need another’s aid to penetrate the heavens. By being born, he enriched his mother with the gift of virginity; by ascending, he placed human nature at the Father’s right hand.

Since the Lord was truly born, truly died, truly rose again, and was truly exalted at the right hand of God the Father, [Col. 1111B] yet in all these things differs from us by the greatness of his power, while agreeing with us only in the truth of nature, it is rightly said that this Angel speaks one of the like things for us. For though in all his works he surpasses us by immeasurable power, in one thing he does not differ from us: namely, in the truth of his form. By this he speaks to the Father for us: by showing himself like us. For his speaking, or interceding with the Father for us, is his showing himself as a human being for human beings. And after saying, “he speaks one of the like things,” he immediately added, “that he may declare to human beings truth,” because unless he became like human beings, a righteous human being would not appear before God. From that very fact he declares our righteousness [Col. 1111C] that he deigned to take upon himself our weakness. That hostile persuasion had polluted all of us with the infection of guilt from the very root; and no one who could speak for sinners before God appeared free from sin, because equal guilt found all alike born from the same mass. Therefore the only-begotten Son of the Father came to us, taking from us our nature without committing guilt. He certainly had to be without sin in order to intervene for sinners, because he would not wipe away the contagion of another’s pollution if he bore his own. It is therefore rightly said that, in appearing like us, he declared humanity’s righteousness. For while interceding in heaven with the Father for sinners, he displayed himself as the righteous human being who might merit pardon for others. It follows:

[Col. 1111D] “He will have mercy on him and say: Deliver him, that he may not go down into corruption; I have found one in whom I may be propitious to him.” Christ Jesus, the human mediator between God and humankind, has mercy on humanity in that he assumed human form. By this mercy he says to the Father concerning redeemed humanity: “Deliver him, that he may not go down into corruption.” As we have already said, his saying to God the Father, “Deliver humanity,” consists in demonstrating humanity free by assuming human nature. For in that flesh which he assumed, he also showed free the flesh which he redeemed. That redeemed flesh is we ourselves, who are bound by the thought of our guilt but freed by the righteousness of so great a mediator, as he himself says: “If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free” (John VIII). And [Col. 1112A] it is well said concerning redeemed humanity: “Let him not go down into corruption.” For above it had been said: “His soul drew near to corruption” (Job XXXIII); afterward it is said, “let him not go down into corruption.” As if he said: Because by recognizing his own weakness he does not fail to know that he is near corruption, therefore let him not descend to the destruction of corruption. For he would rightly descend to corruption if he judged himself far from corruption by his own strength. But because he humbly drew near to corruption, he ought mercifully to be delivered from it, so that he may be strong against attacking vices precisely because he knows himself weak in his own merits. Whoever exalts himself above himself is weighed down by the very weight of his pride; and he plunges himself the more into the depths the more, falling into the vice of pride, he departs from him who is truly exalted. Thus he seeks the depths more intensely precisely from where he imagined himself joined to higher things, as the Lord says through the prophet to the self-exalting soul: “The more beautiful you are, descend and sleep with the uncircumcised” (Ezek. XXXII). For everyone who neglects to consider the ugliness of his own weakness, but in arrogant pride attends to the glory of his own virtue, descends from the very point at which he is more beautiful, because by exalting himself on account of his own merits he falls into the destruction of his soul from that point at which he judged himself glorious. Descending, he sleeps with the uncircumcised because he fails into eternal death with the other sinners. Since, then, this person has humbly recognized himself to be near corruption, it is well said of him: “Deliver him, that he may not go down into corruption,” so that he may escape punishment all the more [Col. 1112C] because he does not turn his eyes away from his guilt. But because there was no one by whose merits the Lord ought to be propitiated toward us, the only-begotten Son of the Father, assuming the form of our weakness, alone appeared righteous, interceding for sinners. And this speaking Angel rightly says concerning redeemed humanity: “I have found one in whom I may be propitious to him.” As if the mediator between God and humankind plainly said: Because there was no human being who appeared before God as a righteous intercessor for human beings, I made myself human in order to make propitiation for human beings; and, by showing myself human, I found in what righteous human being I might be propitious to humanity. And because the Lord, taking our weakness upon himself, endured our punishment by dying, changed our corruption for the better by rising, and glorified it by ascending into heaven, this Angel—that is, the Son of God—rightly adds the scourges of our mortality and, having mercy on them, says:

“His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let it return to the days of its youth.” For in that first human being, having departed from the Lord and been driven from the joys of paradise, we fell into the misery of this mortal life; and the grievous sin we committed at the serpent’s persuasion we feel in the vengeance of our punishment. Having fallen here, we found nothing outside God except that by which we might be afflicted; and because we followed the flesh through the sight of the eyes, we are scourged in that very flesh which we preferred to God’s commandments. In it we daily endure groaning, torment, and death, so that, by a wondrous dispensation, the Lord might turn into punishment for us that through which we committed guilt. [Col. 1113A] Nor would the present judgment of punishment arise from any other source than the cause of sin, so that by the bitterness of that flesh a human being might be trained for life through whose delight of pride he came to death. Since therefore the human race was oppressed by innumerable sufferings of carnal life, but with the coming of our Redeemer both the vices of our corruption and its torments were destroyed, let it be said of this redeemed person: “His flesh has been consumed by sufferings; let it return to the days of its youth.” As if he said: Cast down by the punishment of mortality into the old age of his antiquity, let him return to the days of his youth—that is, let him be renewed by the integrity of his former life—so that he may not remain in the condition into which he fell, but, redeemed, may return to that for which he was created to receive. Sacred Scripture often uses youth to mean newness of life. Hence the Bridegroom is told in the Song of spiritual love: “The young maidens [Note: “Young maidens.”] loved you” (Song I): that is, the souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism, who do not decay in the practice of the old life but are adorned with the conduct of the new human being. He lamented the old age of the old human being, wasting away amid vices, who said: “I have grown old among all my enemies” (Ps. VI).

As if he said: I have grown old among all; I was free from none; I consented to all. Or it may be read thus: For this reason I labour in groaning and tears, because I have grown old, having become a member of the old human being. He speaks by the comparison of an old garment, which is fit neither for use nor adornment. “I have grown old,” he says, “among all my enemies,” visible and invisible, to whom [Col. 1113C] I consented by sinning. He says this lest anyone despair because of the multitude of sins. But whence is this? Because my eye has been disturbed by wrath experienced by the first parent—that is, by the punishment inflicted upon the first human being, through whom it has been transmitted to all posterity. For he is the first parent, the origin; we are the offshoot of punishment.

Blessed David wrote these things in the person of penitents. Conversely, another wise man, encouraging rejoicing in virtues, says: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Ecclus. XI). As if he said: Let the strong person [Note: Perhaps: “let the strong person.”] rejoice in his renewal; that is, let him establish his joy not in the pleasure of the old life but in the conduct of the new life. But because we are recalled to this strength of newness not by our own powers but through the Redeemer’s intervention, let the Angel, pleading for this scourged person, say: “Let him return to the days of his youth.” And because, while our Redeemer intercedes with the Father for us in heaven, we too, shaking off the torpor of our former life, are inflamed with zeal for prayer, it is plainly added concerning this redeemed person: “He shall pray to God, and God shall be gracious to him; and he shall see his face with joy.” The Angel is first said to ask, and afterward the human being; because unless the Lord himself had first, through his Incarnation, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, interceded with the Father and sought our life, our insensibility would never stir itself to seek [Col. 1114A] the things that are eternal. But the prayer of his Incarnation, resurrection, and ascension came first, in order that the awakening from our torpor might follow where the same Redeemer of the human race had gone before. Jacob the patriarch indeed prefigured this Son of God and of the Virgin, returning to God the Father after the triumph of his passion and resurrection, when he blessed his son Joseph and said with highest reverence:

“Joseph is a growing son” (Gen. XLIX), etc. This prophecy, after the Lord’s passion and resurrection, bore the image of the Father’s voice by which God the Father addresses Christ returning to heaven after victory, saying: “Joseph is a growing son.” The Son of God is growing among the Gentiles, because, after leaving the people of the Jewish synagogue because of unbelief, he enlarged the innumerable multitude of the Gentiles—that is, the holy Church gathered from all nations. The patriarch David also sang this, saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord” (Ps. XXI). As if he plainly said: Not Jews only, but Gentiles also, who had previously forgotten the Lord, shall remember him; and those formerly turned away shall turn to the Lord, giving to creatures the honour which they ought to give to the Creator—all the ends of the earth, that is, people from all the earth. And, once converted, they shall worship in his sight: that is, in a pure heart, where he alone sees; or in his sight and not in the sight of human beings, so that he alone may see and reward. “All the families of the Gentiles,” he says: that is, persons from every family of the nations. It follows: “A growing son, and beautiful in appearance.” [Col. 1114C] For Christ’s beauty surpasses all, as is read concerning him in the psalm: “Beautiful in form beyond the children of human beings” (Ps. XLIV), etc. As if he said: You, the Father’s Word; you, the immortal king; you, beautiful in form—that is, in beautiful divinity—beyond the children of human beings.

Note that he could have said “beyond angels”; but because he wishes to show him to be truly human, he introduced the form of the children of human beings. This is against the heretics who said that his body was phantom-like.

Again he adds: “The daughters run along the wall”: that is, the nations of the Church, which believed in Christ and, kindled by love of Christ’s beauty, run along the firmness of faith as upon a wall, [Col. 1114D] so that by contemplation they may behold the true bridegroom and be united and cling to him by the kiss of charity. Of this love or kiss, the same Bridegroom is told in the Song of spiritual love: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine, fragrant [Note: “Fragrant.”] with the finest ointments” (Song I). Joseph’s brothers wronged him, and the Jews reviled Christ when, falsely accusing that same Nazarene—that is, the Holy One of the Lord and Son of God—they tried to oppress him through false witnesses. It follows:

“And those having arrows envied him.” No one in fact shot arrows or any missile of wounding at Joseph; but this applies specially to Christ. Again it says: “His bow rested in strength.” For Christ placed his bow and the spiritual weapons of battle in God, who is a strong defender. He sits at his right hand; by his power all the wickedness of the faithless is broken. “And the bonds of his arms were loosed”: those bonds by which his brothers brought him bound to Pilate. For they were cut off by the hand of Almighty God the Father, from whose mouth the Lord himself came forth, the good shepherd, the stone and strength of believers in Israel. It follows: “The God of your father shall be your helper.” Who aided the Son except God the Father alone, who said: “Behold my servant; I will uphold him” (Isa. XLII)? He shall be exalted, namely above all heavens, and raised above every order [Col. 1115B] of heavenly powers, and [Note: Here again the author seems to ascribe the words “and he shall be very high” to Isaiah chapter two, [Col. 1116D] thus appearing to confirm our suspicion.] “shall be very high” (Isa. LII). “For my soul has been pleased in him” (Isa. I).

Again he adds, saying: “Almighty God will bless you with the blessings of heaven above, with the blessings of the deep lying below,” so that, seated in heaven, he may rule over all angels and human beings. It follows: “With the blessings of the breasts,” namely of the two Testaments, by the one of which he was foretold and by the other revealed; or with the blessings of Mary’s breasts, which were truly blessed, because that most holy ever-Virgin herself gave the same Lord milk to drink. Hence in the Gospel a certain woman says to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked” (Luke 11).

Again he says: “With the blessings of the breasts and womb.” [Col. 1115C] Here too the womb of that same mother is blessed, namely that virginal womb which brought forth Christ the Lord for us, concerning which it is said through Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1), etc. It follows: “The blessings of your father have been strengthened by the blessings of your fathers.” As though he said: The blessings of your heavenly Father, given to you by the Most High of heaven and of the deep, have been strengthened—that is, have prevailed—above the blessings of your fathers. For the Father’s blessing in the Son has prevailed beyond the merit of all the holy patriarchs and prophets, so that none of the saints can be equalled with him. “Until the desire of the everlasting hills should come,” he says. The hills are the fathers [Col. 1115D] of the Old Testament, who, foretelling Christ’s coming, awaited his incarnation with great longing. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Many righteous kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Luke 10). As though he said: Blessed are the eyes—not, I say, the outward eyes of the Pharisees, which see my body, but the blessed inward eyes that see what you see: that is, which know those mysteries revealed to little ones, to whom I have revealed myself and the Father. The prophets and righteous persons saw from afar the Lord’s glory through a mirror and in an enigma; but the apostles, having the Lord present with them [Col. 1116A] and asking him whatever they wished, were not taught through angels or various kinds of visions. Thus the holy fathers of the Old Testament are called hills because of their excellence in holiness; they are also called everlasting because they attain eternal life and do not perish with the world, but are believed to be everlasting.

“May they be upon the head of Joseph”: that is, all these blessings are placed upon the head of Christ, which he received when incarnate; and upon the crown of the Nazirite, concerning whom it is written, “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matt. 2), that is, the holy one of God among his brethren. For he is the head, pre-eminent in heaven and on earth over all the saints, because all things are subjected beneath his feet. Coming from the bosom of the Father, he mercifully assumed our humanity; rising from the tomb on the third day, he glorified it; ascending into heaven on the fortieth day while his disciples watched, he placed it at the right hand of God the Father. He whose divinity is of one substance with God the Father chose, for our salvation, to assume from the Virgin the frailty of our mortality. From God the Father he possesses true and unchangeable eternity; in time he received from the Virgin Mother true passible flesh, [Col. 1116B] which, by the triumph of his resurrection and the glory of his ascension, he restored to incorruption.

The prophet Ezekiel indeed typologically foreshadowed this Son of God and man—weak and strong, temporal and eternal—when he spoke of the man standing in the gate of the city that faced south [Col. 1116C]:

“And behold, there was a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, and a linen cord was in his hand; he stood in the gate” (Ezek. 40). Explaining this passage—most useful and necessary for Christ’s Church—blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1116D] Homily 13 on Ezekiel]:

For he is signified in the man who is portrayed in the gate. This man is said to measure the building. Rightly is the Lord signified both by the man and by the gate, because he himself orders all things within holy Church by judgment; and he himself bears that same holy Church and, bearing it, raises it with himself to the heavenly homeland where he is. Thus in the holy Gospel too our same Redeemer says: “He who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep” (John 10). And a little later: “I am the door.” Again, shortly afterwards, he adds: “I [Col. 1116D] am the good shepherd.” Since, therefore, he himself is the shepherd, he himself the door, and the shepherd enters through the door, he is rightly signified in this passage by the aforesaid man standing in the gate.

But we must ask why it is said of this man: “Whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze.” We all know that bronze is an exceedingly durable metal and wholly resonant. What, then, is meant by the appearance of the Mediator of God and humankind being likened to the appearance of bronze, except what we plainly know: that the only-begotten Son of God, taking the form of a servant, transformed the frailty of human flesh into eternity by the victory of his resurrection and the glory of his ascension? Since, therefore, flesh in him was made immortal, it is now durable without end. [Col. 1117A] For, “rising from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6). But why is his Incarnation itself said to have sounded forth to all humanity the glory of his majesty? [Note: [Col. 1117D] The passage, shortened here, should be completed as follows: “But why is his Incarnation itself compared with resonant metal, except because through that same assumption of our humanity the glory of his majesty sounded forth to all?”] And he has, as it were, the appearance of bronze in his body, because God became known to the world through flesh. Hence John says: “He had written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19). For what is his garment, except the body which he received from the Virgin? Yet his garment is not one thing and he another. For our flesh too is called our garment; nevertheless, we ourselves are the flesh with which we are clothed. Isaiah, seeing long beforehand this garment of his bloodied through the cross of his passion, said: “Why is your clothing red [Col. 1117B] and your garments like those of one treading the winepress?” (Isa. 63). He himself answered: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and there was no man with me from among the nations” (ibid.). For he alone trod the winepress in which he was trodden, because by his own power he conquered the passion he endured. He who suffered the cross even unto death rose victoriously from death and ascended gloriously into heaven.

And it is well said: “There was no man with me from among the nations,” because those for whom he had come to suffer ought to have been participants in his passion; because, since they did not yet believe at that time, those whose life was being sought by that passion are sought among them in the passion. “He had,” he says, “written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords.” [Col. 1117C] By the thigh is understood the propagation of flesh. Since therefore, as Matthew and Luke recount, he was born in this world from a Virgin through the succession of the human race as set out in the genealogies, he made known through the mystery of his Incarnation that he was king and lord to all nations everywhere. Thus he had written upon his garment and upon his thigh: “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

Therefore the appearance of this king and lord was like the appearance of bronze, because the mystery of that Incarnation sounded forth to the whole world through the truest heralds, and because he brought the same body, which he assumed without sin from the Virgin, into eternity through the glory of his resurrection and ascension. For he sits at the right hand of God the Father and, through himself—who truly is the door [Col. 1117D] of the sheep—causes those who believe in him to attain the brightness of perpetual light. For this purpose the eternal high priest deigned to descend from the bosom of the Father: that by his sweet preaching he might teach us to desire that same light of eternal brightness and to strive most earnestly to attain it. Thus we know that blessed Job said:

“He declares concerning his friend that it is his possession, and that he may ascend to it” (Job 36). As though he plainly said: The Son of God, coming from the bosom of the Father, declares to the faithful people, or to any Christian predestined to eternal life, concerning the heavenly light, that it is his possession, if he lives well and piously; and that he may ascend to that same light of the heavenly homeland through love of God and neighbour, working good deeds. Explaining this, the great teacher Gregory says: A friend of truth is one who loves right action. Hence Truth itself says to the disciples: “You are my friends, if you do the things that I command you” (John 15). For a friend is called the guardian of one’s mind. Therefore, not without reason, one who strives to keep God’s will in his commandments is called his friend. Hence Truth again says to those same disciples: “I have called you friends, because all things whatsoever I heard from my Father I have made known to you” (ibid.). Therefore God declares to his friend concerning the light of the eternal homeland that it is his possession, so that he may not despair in the frailty of his weakness; so that he may consider, not what he is created, but that for which he was created; [Col. 1118B] and so that he may know all the more certainly that he will possess the brightness of that light, the more truly he now tramples the darkness of the vices that assail him. And it is fittingly added in the promise: “And that he may ascend to it.”

For what is more difficult than for a human being born on earth, bearing earthly and frail limbs, to climb the heights of heaven and penetrate the hidden things of the heavenly spirits? But the Creator of those very spirits came to us and showed himself as a human being even beneath them, as the Prophet says to the Father concerning him: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8).

As though he said: You made him lower in relation to yourself; and not only in relation to yourself, but you also made him [Col. 1118C] lower than the angels—yet only a little, namely only in the capacity for suffering of the flesh. But what wonder is this? For you crowned him with the glory of resurrection and the honour of ascension, and set him over the works of your hands—that is, over the heavenly, earthly, and rational creation, which by excellence is called the work of your hands. “Hand” signifies the power of God’s operation, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit. As a hand is divided into many parts, so the Holy Spirit, who is wholly present everywhere, is divided into many gifts.

Or otherwise: You crowned him with glory because, when his soul descended into hell, where there had been everlasting darkness, a great light shone forth; and with honour because, when, returning from the lower regions with a multitude of angels, [Col. 1118D] you caused many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep to rise, in testimony to the true resurrection, and to appear to many in the holy city Jerusalem (Matt. 27); and you set him—that is, you caused him to sit at your right hand, O God the Father. Therefore our Redeemer deigned to be made a little lower than the angels according to his humanity, that he might bring us to the fellowship of those same blessed spirits.

And because he found between us and those spirits the scandal of a discordant manner of life, by marvellous power and yet more marvellous mercy, creating the highest things and assuming the lowest, he joined the lowest to the highest. Thus, when that same king was born, the choirs of angels came forth at his announcement, sang a hymn to God, and, once the discord of their evil way of life had been defeated, recognized as fellow citizens those whom they had formerly despised, proclaiming with one harmonious voice: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). [Col. 1119A] As though they plainly said: Let the goodness now born upon earth unite those whom wickedness had separated from us.

Thus it is that before his Incarnation, in the Old Testament, an angel is recorded as having been worshipped by a human being, yet is not forbidden to be worshipped. But after the Mediator’s coming, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, when John prostrated himself to worship an angel, he immediately heard from that angel: “See that you do not do this; for I am your fellow servant and of your brethren” (Rev. 19). For why is it that the angels formerly permitted themselves to be worshipped calmly, but afterwards refuse worship from a human being, except because they formerly despised human beings, given over to fleshly corruptions and not redeemed from those same corruptions, all the more justly as they knew them to be more abject; whereas afterwards they could not regard human nature as beneath them, since they saw it exalted in its Author even above themselves? For that which deserved to be revered as set above in the very head of the members ought no longer to be despised as subject in the members. Therefore he who for our sake was made a little lower than the angels made us equal to angels through the power of his becoming lower. Hence, by dying, he taught us not to fear death; by rising, to have confidence in life; by ascending, to glory in the inheritance of the heavenly homeland, so that, wherever they see the head has gone before, [Col. 1119C] the members may rejoice to follow there.

Thus our same head rightly says: “Wherever the body shall be, there also the eagles shall be gathered” (Matt. 24). Blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, likewise says: “Unto an incorruptible and undefiled and unfading inheritance reserved in heaven” (1 Pet. 1). Blessed Paul also says: “We know that, if our earthly house of this habitation be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in heaven” (2 Cor. 5). But if we too, who are born on earth, ascend into heaven, how is it that Truth again says: “No one ascends into heaven except he who descends from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven?” (John 3). This saying is at once confronted by what the same Truth says: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17). These statements are not inconsistent with one another; rather, they kindle the zeal of our minds to investigate what seem to be contradictions. For because all of us have been born in his faith, we are beyond doubt his body. Therefore, because by the marvellous dispensation of mercy the Lord became the head of his members, and because the multitude of the reprobate has been cast away, he alone is also with us. Thus no one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven; because, since we have now become one with him, he alone returned in us to the place from which he alone came in himself. And he who always is in [Col. 1120A] heaven ascends daily to heaven, because he who remains above all things in his divinity daily draws himself to heaven in the union of his humanity.

Therefore let human frailty not despair. Let it consider the blood of the Only-Begotten and see in its price how great is that which is worth so much. Let it carefully consider where the head, namely Christ, has gone before; and let that which is bound by commandments for living be strengthened by his example for hoping. Let it have confidence that it will ascend to heaven; let it hope to possess the heavenly homeland; let it know that it is the companion of angels; let it rejoice that in Christ, its head, it is even set above angels. Therefore it is rightly said of this light of the inward homeland: “He declares concerning it to his friend that it is his possession.” These things are exceedingly wonderful, exceedingly awe-inspiring: that a human being born on earth and, because of deserving sins, condemned far from the heavenly homeland, is not only restored to the state of his creation but exalted still more gloriously. One who lost paradise receives heaven; not only does the guilt of his debt no longer bind him, but after sin the gifts bestowed upon him increase more abundantly. The one who despised God, the imitator of the devil, if he returns to the fruit of repentance, ascends to the height of beholding the divine majesty. Whose heart, then, does not leap at the wonder of such mercy? Whose numbness does not shudder when raised by so great a reflection?

Undoubtedly this was a great price, by which so grave a sin could be wiped away. Great too is this priest, who so mercifully restored to heaven human beings born on earth and entangled in diverse sins. For he was without fault; his body, once offered to God the Father upon the altar [Col. 1120C] of the cross, sufficiently removed the guilt of the human race. He came forth from God the Father and came into this world, and no deceit was found in his mouth.

What the Lord said to Moses in the Law, among other things, can indeed be understood typologically of this supreme high priest: “The high priest, that is, the great priest among his brethren, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, and whose hands have been consecrated in the priesthood, and who is clothed in sacred garments, shall not uncover his head, shall not rend his garments, and shall not enter at all near any dead person. He shall not be defiled even over his father or mother. Nor shall he go out from the holy things, lest he defile the sanctuary of the Lord, because the oil [Col. 1120D] of God’s holy anointing is upon his head. He shall take a virgin as wife; he shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a harlot, but a maiden of his own people; nor shall he defile his seed” (Lev. 21).
