[Note: [Col. 1119D] Isidore, Questions on Leviticus, chapter 12.]

The great priest among his brethren is he who mercifully deigned to be born, suffer, die, and rise again for the salvation of the human race, and who, early at dawn on the day of his resurrection, said among other things to Mary Magdalene: “Go to my brethren and say to them: I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20). The oil of anointing was poured upon his head, as the Psalmist says: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Hence the Son of God and of the Virgin himself says of himself through the prophet Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim to the meek,” etc. (Isa. 61).

It follows: “Whose hands have been consecrated.” This eternal high priest has consecrated hands when he stretches them out upon the cross for the expiation of the whole age. His garment is not rent: that is, he does not allow his Church, which by adhering to him is his own garment, to be divided into heresies and schisms. The figure of this garment was that seamless tunic, woven throughout as one piece (John 19), which was not rent in the Passion but remained undivided with the one who possessed it. [Col. 1121B] He shall not approach a dead person because he committed no sin. For death is understood through sin, as it is written: “The soul that sins shall die.”

“He shall not be defiled,” he says, “in father and mother” (Ezek. 18). Christ was not defiled in his mother when, before the ages, he was born from the Father. Likewise, neither was he defiled in the Father when, in the world, he was born from the Virgin Mother. For he alone was born pure, proceeding from a virginal womb without male contamination. Indeed, all of us are defiled in the father from whom we are created when we sin [Note: [Col. 1121D] The manuscripts corruptly read: “in God the Father, from whom we are created,” etc.], if we lapse into heresy. Likewise, we are defiled in the mother if, believing in God, we injure the Church in any respect or disgrace the freedom of our heavenly mother by an unworthy slavery to sin. “He shall not depart,” he says, “from the holy things” [Col. 1121C], because Christ so descended into the world by assuming flesh that he never abandoned heaven.

“He shall not take as wife a widow, a divorced woman, or a harlot, but a virgin.” The widow and divorced woman is the Synagogue, of which the Lord speaks through Isaiah, saying: “What is this bill of divorce of your mother by which I sent her away?” (Isa. 50). Heresy is the harlot, open to the lust of many errors. Such women are not joined to Christ, but only the virgin Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle (Eph. 5), of which the Apostle says: “I have espoused you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). The soul is also called Christ’s bride, but only that soul which is proved incorrupt and virginal by simplicity of faith and purity of actions. The soul is a widow when, departing from the yoke of the Law, it does not keep the Gospel’s commandments. It is divorced when by sinning it is separated from Christ’s body, even if it is not expelled from the Church. It is also a harlot when it receives lovers—that is, the opposing powers of demons—which seek eagerly to capture its beauty. For the soul is created beautiful and sufficiently fair by God, having his image and likeness.

It follows:

This great priest takes a wife from his own stock [Note: [Col. 1121D] “He shall take,” as above and below.], namely the soul joined to him in faith. And he does not defile his seed—that is, his word. Hence he himself [Col. 1122A] says in the Gospel: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8). In order that the seed of his word may not be defiled by heretics or wicked people but remain preserved in its purity, he says to his disciples: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them beneath their feet” (Matt. 7).

Thus far, the things which [Note: [Col. 1122D] “Which.”] are said in the Law concerning a mortal and changeable priest pertain to Christ, the Son of God and the Virgin, the supreme and eternal high priest who penetrated the heavens. Thereafter these same matters are interpreted in the members of that same supreme high priest, seated at the right hand of God the Father, and especially in the priests to whom spiritual sacraments have been entrusted. It must also be briefly explained how great are their privileges. “He shall not uncover his head,” that is, he is to honour the mystery of Christ, who is his head, with the veil of mysteries. “He shall not rend his garments,” lest he fall into heresy or schisms. “He shall not enter near any soul that is dead,” that is, he shall not approach any sin that pertains to death. “He shall not be defiled over his father and mother,” namely, he must not indulge the love of his parents with such excessive affection that he offends his Lord and Creator; nor must he show such pity for his relatives that he appears guilty before God. For how many monks, canons, and other religious men, while giving immoderate care to their own parents, have lost their souls. Therefore, in the third book of Sentences [Col. 1122C], our blessed patron Isidore says [Note: [Col. 1122D] Chapter 21]:

Many monks, through love of their parents, become entangled not only in worldly cares but also in legal disputes, and, for the temporal welfare of their own relatives, lose their souls.

What is said of monks is consequently to be understood of all religious men.

It follows: “The high priest shall not go out from the holy things,” namely, that he may always dwell in holy work and thought. One who speaks what is idle and deserving of rebuke goes out from the holy things and defiles God’s sanctification, because he does not walk as Christ’s servant. Therefore the Son of God and the Virgin himself says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, that for every idle word whatsoever that people speak, they shall render an account on the day of judgment” [Col. 1122D] (Matt. 12).

“He shall not take as wife a widow, a divorced woman, or a harlot, but a virgin”: that is, he shall embrace nothing of the old human being or of former pleasure, but possess a life flourishing in every purity. “He shall take a wife from his own stock”: namely, he is to embrace the life of the saints, to whom he is near through faith, so that he does not depart from their footsteps. Besides these things, it is commanded that the same priest, ministering in the Temple, should not drink wine or strong drink, lest he be weighed down by drunkenness, gluttony (Lev. 10), and the cares of this life. Nor should he have a portion in the land (Num. 18), save God alone, lest, while contemplating earthly things, he forget the commandments of heaven. From the meal of such an ecclesiastical priest, the neighbour and the hired servant are commanded to be excluded (Lev. 22), and only the remnants of food are to be given to servants. The neighbour is the heretic, who claims to be near by the title of the Christian name. The hired servant signifies the Jew, who seeks the observance of the Law carnally. Thus God’s priest does not share the nourishment of the Gospel, which serves the salvation of souls, with these persons, but only with Christ’s servants.

Moreover, from the things offered on the altar (Lev. 7), the priest receives the breast and the right arm: namely, that in his breast he may have pure thoughts and knowledge of evangelical teaching; in his right arm, good works, combat against the devil, and an armed hand, so that what he has conceived in his heart he may accomplish [Col. 1123B] by good works. He is also given the jaw from the private offerings, that he may possess speech that is both sweet and discerning. From the victims he is also given the belly, by whose indication he may learn to extinguish lust and restrain in himself the appetite of gluttony. These things, therefore, as has been said, pertain typologically to Jesus Christ the supreme high priest; and they pertain morally, when expounded, to his members, namely the priests of the Church.

Moreover, it should be known with what garments this eternal high priest, who has entered once into the holy places—that is, into heaven—now appears before the face of God for us (Heb. 9). For Aaron the priest, wearing his sacred garments, prefigured this eternal and supreme high priest shining in virtues. For in Leviticus we read: “And Moses did as the Lord commanded him. [Col. 1123C] And he brought near Aaron his brother and clothed him with a tunic” (Lev. 8). Among them it is worn as a garment of byssus; among us, as linen. Byssus is a kind of very white flax, brought to the highest whiteness through much labour and many washings. This garment is called in Greek *poderis*, that is, a garment reaching to the ankles, because it extends from the neck to the ankles. That garment was varied by four colours—byssus, purple, hyacinth, and scarlet—by which colours are signified the four elements, from whose mixture human nature consists and from whose imbalance or corruption the flux of the flesh is generated, unless it is restrained by medicinal continence. Those who connect, or conjecture concerning, the natures wished the earth to be signified by byssus, because it comes from the earth; water by purple, [Col. 1123D] because it is made from the blood of sea-shellfish; air by hyacinth, because it is of a clear-sky colour; and fire by scarlet, because it gleams with a flame-like colour.

In the high priest’s adornment there is also placed upon his head a mitre, otherwise called a *cidaris* or tiara, because it signifies the sovereignty of the five senses, in which the high priest ought to excel. For the use of all bodily senses is found in the head. A golden plate is also placed above it, inscribed with the name of God which the Hebrews call ineffable. It is called ineffable not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot in any way be comprehended or delimited by human sense and understanding. Priestly breeches are necessary because priests ought to govern and cover their private parts with due modesty. Clothed in these and various other ornaments, the high priests of the Old Testament entered, according to the Law, the man-made holy places in order to offer gifts to God for themselves and for the people subject to them.

Let us also see with what garments the Son of God and the Virgin, adorned as an eternal high priest, enters heaven. Let us, if it please us, compare his vestments with those of the ancient priesthood, and we shall plainly recognize that, by as much as the Creator differs from creatures, the lord from servants, salvation from the sick, the king from the wretched, deliverance from the lost, redemption from captives, mercy from the condemned, heaven from earth, and light from darkness, by so much does the dignity of this eternal priest differ from the dignity of the priests of the Old Testament.

[Col. 1124B] Therefore the priestly garment of Jesus Christ, the supreme high priest, is the Church, of which the Apostle says: “For this reason the Son of God suffered, that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5). That the holy Church—that is, all the saints—are Christ’s garments is attested by the prophet Isaiah, who says: “With all these,” that is, with all the saints, “you shall be clothed as with a garment” (Isa. 49). As though he spoke more plainly to Jesus Christ himself, the supreme priest, saying: All the saints whom you are to redeem from eternal damnation by the passion of the cross will adhere to you inseparably, as members to a body, through faith and charity; and without end they will praise you in great glory with God the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The four colours from which the garment of this [Col. 1124C] eternal high priest is woven are the diversity of merits that shines within holy Church, the body of Christ. By that *poderis*, that is, priestly linen garment, we understand Christ’s Incarnation; and it is signified in the feet, because the garment extends to the feet. The feet of the Son of God signify the Incarnation, which is subject to the divinity. For as his divinity is expressed by the head, so his humanity is expressed by the feet. Of this humanity we read in Exodus: “They saw the Lord”—namely Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of the people—“and beneath his feet was as it were a sapphire stone, and as the sky when it is clear” (Exod. 24). As by the sapphire stone he wished figuratively to signify heavenly creatures or the holy angels, so by the clear sky he wished to signify the holy Church gathered from chosen human beings; over these two creatures the assumed human being, namely the Son of God and the Virgin, reigns for ever. Hence we read in the Psalm: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8), etc. Thus by the *poderis*, that is, the priestly linen garment, we understand Christ’s Incarnation. For flax, from which linen is woven, springs from the earth. [Note: [Col. 1123] Isidore, Questions on Exodus, chapter 59. The same material is in volume I, folio 375.]

By the *cidaris* upon the head of this same eternal high priest and by the golden plate, we understand the splendour of divinity, so that the one and same Son of God and the Virgin is adorned with the *poderis* according to his humanity and with the *cidaris* according to his divinity. The breeches with which he is clothed signify the chastity and integrity of Christ’s body. [Col. 1125A] The girdle that binds the priestly breast signifies the choir of saints, or their harmony, who embrace Christ in the unity of faith. That ankle-length tunic, falling from head to foot, is the same Church, which shall remain until the end of time. This whole garment is made hyacinth-coloured. Hyacinth gleams with the colour of the sky, so that the whole Church may set its mind on things above and rise wholly to the love of heavenly things. The pomegranates placed below declare the unity of that same Church. For as many seeds are protected within one outer rind of a pomegranate, so the unity of faith covers the peoples within the number of the holy Church, while a diversity of merits is contained within them.

The sounding bells among the pomegranates signify prophecies [Note: [Col. 1125D] “Prophets.”] and holy teachers placed in the midst of the Church. Their tongue, resounding with the teaching of knowledge, strikes both sides of the bell—that is, the parts of the Law and the Gospel. These bells are placed at the edge of the garment so that, discussing the end of the world and the future life, they may never be silent. The ephod, that is, the Saviour’s mantle, signifies power and kingship, as it is written: “Government has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9). The two emerald stones [Note: [Col. 1126D] “Also.”] placed on the ephod at the right and left are the two peoples: the Gentile people on the right and the Jewish people on the left, bearing on themselves the carved names of the twelve patriarchs, namely to imitate the pattern of life of the holy apostles. Other teachers have said that these same two stones are the two Testaments, or the letter and the spirit, in which all the mysteries of the Law are contained: the spirit on the right, the letter on the left. [Col. 1125C] The breastplate placed upon the chest and arranged in four rows of stones signifies the Gospel message, which in a fourfold order has set forth for us the truth of faith and the doctrine of the Trinity. The apostolic message corresponds to it both in power and in number, in its jewels. This breastplate is double, because the knowledge of evangelical teaching is open and hidden, plain and mystical.

Likewise, the supreme priest Jesus Christ is fittingly interpreted in his members, and especially in the priest, who dwells among the saints and, with sacred mouth, prepares and offers for the people the flesh of the immaculate Lamb. [Col. 1125D] For first, the breastplate of judgment, fastened by binding bands upon Aaron’s breast, signifies that the priestly heart should by no means be occupied by wandering thoughts, but should be restrained by reason alone. And it is fittingly added concerning this breastplate that the names of the twelve patriarchs should be inscribed upon it. For the priest ought always to bear the holy Fathers thus inscribed upon his breast, never ceasing to imitate their examples.

Accordingly, the priest is bound on each shoulder by the covering of the ephod, so that he may always be armed with the ornaments of virtues against adversity and prosperity alike. And in that the ephod is commanded to be made of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, it is shown how great a diversity of virtues the priest ought to display in life. For in the priest’s dress gold gleams when the understanding of wisdom shines forth. To this is joined blue, which glistens with the colour of the air, namely so that in everything he undertakes he may rise to the love of heavenly things. Royal purple is mixed with it, so that he may repress the suggestions of demons as though by royal power. Twice-dyed scarlet is also joined to the ephod, so that before the eyes of the inward Judge every good work of virtue may be adorned by charity. And this charity, because it depends upon understanding in the love of God and neighbour, shines as though from a double dye. To the twice-dyed scarlet is joined twisted fine linen. For fine linen springs from the earth in a green appearance, by which is signified the bright adornment of purity and bodily chastity. This fine linen [Col. 1126B] is woven into the beauty of the ephod because chastity is then brought to the perfect brightness of purity when the flesh is afflicted through abstinence.

Likewise, the high priest is girded with a belt, by which the impulses of the loins and the desires of lust are restrained. When the priest enters the tabernacle, he is surrounded by bells on his tunic, so that he may have the voice of preaching, lest he offend the judgment of the heavenly Inspector by silence. Pomegranates are also joined with the bells, so that through his teaching the unity of faith may be signified. And because the priest entered daily into the first part of the tabernacle to offer victims, we are commanded to be constant every day, so that we may never depart from this place where the people of God are nourished by heavenly utterances; but daily we may offer to God confession and [Col. 1126C] praise—that is, the humility of our souls—which are true victims and a spiritual sacrifice, as the Psalmist says: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50).

But the fact that once a year the high priest, leaving the people behind, entered into the Holy of Holies, where the propitiatory was, signifies our high priest, the Lord Jesus Christ. While he was in the flesh, he was with the people throughout the whole year—that is, the year concerning which he himself says through Isaiah the prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me. He has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor, and to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of propitiation” (Isa. 61). Therefore this eternal high priest once in this year, namely on the day of propitiation, entered into the Holy of Holies: that is, when the dispensation of the Incarnation, nativity, passion, and resurrection had been completed, he penetrated the heavens, entering to God the Father through his humanity, from whom he never departed in his divinity, in order to make him propitious toward humankind and to intercede through his humanity for all who believe in him.

Thus far we have spoken of the spiritual garments of the supreme priest Jesus Christ, clothed in which he entered heaven. Now again, if it please you, let us briefly show from the sayings of the holy Fathers how the sacrifices of the Old Testament prefigured him. [Col. 1127A]

[Note: [Col. 1127D] Isidore, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 1. The same material in the first part, fol. 495.]

The book of Leviticus enumerates various kinds of victims, whose type bore the image of Christ’s Passion. For after he had been offered to God the Father, all those victims ceased which had gone before in type or shadow of him, prefiguring that [Note: [Col. 1127D] “That.”] sacrifice which the one true priest—namely, the mediator between God and human beings—offered. It was necessary beforehand to celebrate in animal victims the promissory figures of his sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1127D] “Of the sacrifice.”] for the future cleansing of flesh and blood: through that one victim there would be remission of sins of flesh and blood, in contrast to the goats, who shall not possess the kingdom of God, because this same bodily substance will be changed into a heavenly [Col. 1127B] condition.

For he himself was offered in the calf because of the power of the cross; in the lamb because of innocence; in the ram because of sovereignty; in the he-goat because of the likeness of sinful flesh, so that “through sin he might condemn sin” (Rom. 8). In the turtledove and the dove he was offered because of God, since Christ Jesus, mediator of God and man, was shown in the conjunction of two substances. Further, in the mixture of fine flour he clearly demonstrated the Church, gathered from believers through the water of baptism, which is the body of Christ. But we, dearest brothers, morally offer God a calf when we conquer the pride of the flesh; a lamb, when we restrain irrational and foolish impulses; a kid, when we overcome wantonness; [Col. 1127C] a dove, when we preserve simplicity of mind; a turtledove, when we guard chastity; unleavened bread, when we walk not “in the old leaven,” but “in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

[Note: [Col. 1127D] Isidore, ibid., ch. 6. The same material in the first part, [Col. 1128D] fol. 536.]

At the beginning of the book of Leviticus, four principal kinds of offerings are described, which are commanded to be offered to the Lord as a sweet savour; by them that eternal high priest is especially prefigured. First, from the herd, an unblemished calf; second, a lamb from the sheep; third, a turtledove and a dove; fourth, unleavened fine flour, anointed with oil and baked in an oven. The remaining sacrifices were offered, according to the nature of the cases, in the person of the people.

Thus the first sacrifice, namely the calf from the herd, signifies Christ descending from the lineage of the patriarchs. [Col. 1127D] With the plough of his cross he subdued the earth of our flesh and enriched it with the fruitful seed of virtues by the Holy Spirit. This calf is without blemish, because he is led to the Passion without sin. He is offered not in the tabernacle but at the door of the tabernacle, because that great high priest suffered outside the camp (Heb. 13). His blood is offered by the sons of Aaron the priest; this is understood of Annas and Caiaphas, who, having held a council, shed his innocent blood.

The second victim, the unblemished lamb offered from the sheep, figures Christ because of [Col. 1128A] innocence. This is the Lamb who, through Isaiah the prophet, is said to be put to death for the crimes of the people: “Like a sheep,” he says, “he shall be led to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer shall be silent, so he shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53), etc. What that truthful prophet foretold would happen, we now believe without hesitation to have been done. Indeed, the eyes of the apostles, who saw in the flesh this same unblemished Lamb of God and were present at his Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, were beyond doubt our own eyes. This is that Lamb first shown to mortals through John the Baptist: “Behold,” he says, “the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). Thus the lamb was fittingly offered in sacrifices, so that the figure of Christ’s innocence and Passion [Col. 1128B] might be shown. And fittingly also the he-goat, because through his death the devil, author of sin, is known to have been conquered, bound, and held captive in hell.

The third sacrifice is called the turtledove and the dove. In this place the turtledove signifies Christ’s most chaste flesh; John the Evangelist declares that the dove bears the figure of the Holy Spirit, saying: “He upon whom you shall see the Holy Spirit descending as a dove—he it is who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). And therefore the turtledove and the dove [Note: [Col. 1128D] “Turtledove . . . dove . . . the flesh of Christ . . . united.”]—that is, the flesh of Christ united to the Holy Spirit through the mystery of the Passion—are a sacrifice to God as a sweet savour.

Christ Jesus offers these three sacrifices to God the Father according to his humanity, through which he also intercedes [Col. 1128C] for us with the Father; according to his divinity, he is one God with that same Father and the Holy Spirit. He now appears through his humanity before the face of God, interceding for us; through his divinity he reigns everywhere with that same Father and Holy Spirit, bestowing every good upon us.

Therefore Jesus Christ offers the aforesaid three sacrifices to God the Father insofar as he is man; but the fourth sacrifice, of fine flour, prefigures the soul of the Catholic Church, which, like fine flour, is gathered from fitting members, from the many grains of believers. It is restored by the mill of the Law and the Gospels in letter and spirit [Note: [Col. 1128D] “Separated,” as in Isidore.], united also through the water of baptism, anointed with the oil of chrism, strengthened by the fire of the Holy [Col. 1128D] Spirit, and made a sacrifice pleasing to God through humility of spirit.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us give thanks to God the Father, “who has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1). For he delivered us from the power of darkness—that is, from the ministers of hell and from ignorance of sin—because they truly ruled over us; and he transferred us into the kingdom, that is, into heaven, so that we might be the kingdom of the Son of his love, namely of the eternal high priest Jesus Christ: [Col. 1129A] “In whom we have redemption and forgiveness of sins; who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.”

Redemption is the capacity for freedom after the power of the devil has been destroyed. The Son of God himself is the image of the Father; but an image of a king on a coin is one thing, and an image in a Son another. We are a coin in which there is the image of God, namely Christ the Son. No image of God ought to be worshipped except that one which is what he is; nor should it be worshipped in place of him, but with him. For he himself is the image of the invisible Father, that is, wholly like the Father. He is coeternal with God the Father, himself alone first begotten before every creature. “In him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers.” “All things,” he says, “were created in him”—understand, even the elements—[Col. 1129B] from which all things were made. Thus through him what they were before was life in him. [Note: [Col. 1129D] The interlinear gloss, more clearly: “Thus through him, beforehand, that which they were was life in him.”] Or: all things are in him, because they do not exceed him in magnitude, breadth, or height, because he is immeasurable.

He was truly begotten before every creature, because through him all things were created which are in heaven and which are on earth: visible things, namely the sun and moon, and invisible things, namely angels and souls; even those highest beings, namely thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers. As he was born before all things from God the Father so that he might create all things, so, having become man, he first rose from death so that he might restore all things, and might always be first and chief. Hence John the Evangelist says in his Apocalypse to the seven churches—that is, to the sevenfold Church: “Grace to you and peace from him who is, and who was, and who is to come, [Col. 1129C] and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and ruler of the kings of the earth” (Rev. 1).

Other human beings have the Word of God in themselves, but of none of them is it said, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1). Therefore Christ Jesus, God and man, being assumed more excellently, bears as it were the person of the wisdom of God, just as the head, in which all the senses are located, manifests the person of the soul, which gives life to the whole body. For the Son, according to divinity, is in no respect less than the Father. Therefore all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things—that is, because none is equal to him even insofar as he is man; and all things subsist in him, because as he created all things with the Father, so he sustains and governs all things with him. And he is [Col. 1129D] the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, in order that he himself may hold primacy in all things.

He is the head of the Church—that is, of the body—because he stands in relation to the Church as a head does to a body. But since the Church began with righteous Abel, how is he its head? Certainly because he is the beginning of the Church, that is, its founder. Truly he is the beginning of the Church—namely, its head, ruler, and founder—because he is the firstborn from the dead, in order that he himself may hold primacy, that is dominion, over all things, both those before and those after: “For in him it pleased all the fullness of divinity to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether things in heaven or things on earth.”

[Col. 1130A] Christ, Son of God and man, fittingly holds primacy, not only because he is the firstborn, but also because it pleased the Trinity that in him all fullness of wisdom should not merely be present, but should dwell; and that he should reconcile all things, namely Jews and Gentiles, not through another victim, but through the blood of the cross, which is a more shameful death than other deaths. “All things,” I say, “in heaven and on earth”: namely, all heavenly powers and all the elect predestined to eternal life. It pleased God the Father to reconcile all things through Christ, and he himself freely brought heavenly and earthly things into peace through his blood, because through him the way into heaven is open to humankind. For “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” [Col. 1130B] (Col. 2), and therefore he is able to do all things through himself.

He also, remaining in his divinity, could have broken the forces of the ancient enemy and delivered us from his power; but rather, by the eternal counsel of the whole Trinity, in which he is the third [Note: [Col. 1130D] “Second.”] person, he chose humbly to assume the form of a servant and in it to defeat the enemy of humankind. He humbled himself, becoming a participant in our death, in order to redeem us from the devil’s slavery. Though he is the Most High, he showed himself humble in order to free humankind from everlasting condemnation. Therefore, dearest brothers, since our Lord Jesus Christ deigned humbly to be born, suffer, die, and rise again for us, we too ought, following his example, to show humility to one another. For he suffered for us, [Col. 1130C] leaving us an example of compassion and humility, that we might follow in his footsteps (1 Pet. 2). Hence the apostle Paul, exhorting us to patience and humility, says:

“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 2).

It is as though he said: As Christ sought not his own interests but ours, so we ought through charity to bear one another’s burdens. Therefore let it be known by experience that what was in Christ is in you also: “Who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” The Apostle first sets forth lofty matters concerning Christ, so that those in whom there is room for lowliness may not disdain to be humbled: “He did not regard equality with God as robbery.” It is as though he said: He knew himself to be equal with God, committing no robbery—that is, not usurping what was not his own, as the devil and the first human did. Or: according to his humanity, he did not consider himself equal to God, since that would have been robbery—that is, presumptuously taking what was not his own—but he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.

To empty oneself is to show oneself visible from the greatness of one’s invisibility. Or, more plainly: he who was in the form of God, that is, in the full essence of God the Father, did not regard equality with God as robbery, because he was truly equal by nature, but emptied himself. Although remaining what he was in the form of God, [Col. 1131A] nevertheless, by taking the form of a servant, he as it were laid aside dignity when he united the form of a servant to the form of God. And lest you should suppose that the form of a servant thereby became immortal, he adds: “Made in the likeness of human beings,” that is, passible and mortal, “and found in habit as a man.” Habit is the assumption of a human being as though of a garment, which does not change that which it clothes. “Made in the likeness of human beings,” he says—though he had not been made—and also found, in his outward manner, that is, his conduct, by those wishing to test him. As a man, he ate, drank, slept, and so forth.

“He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” It is as though he said: He so high humbled himself, becoming obedient to God the Father, not only by enduring insults and reproaches, but unto death—not just any death, but [Col. 1131B] death on a cross, which is more shameful than other deaths. “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.”

Or, more plainly: God exalted him according to his human nature above everything created; in this sense his divine nature too may be said to have been exalted according to manifestation, because what it was began to be known—just as it is said to have been emptied in the assumption of flesh. God the Father gave him the name that is above every name. He possessed this before the resurrection, but after the resurrection and ascension what he was had been made manifest, so that demons and human beings might know it.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] *Sentences*, Distinction 17, chapter “On Merit.”]

The Apostle plainly says that Christ was exalted through the glory of passibility, resurrection, and ascension because [Col. 1131C] he was humbled through the obedience of the Passion. Thus the humility of the Passion was the merit of exaltation, and exaltation the reward of humility. Blessed Augustine, explaining the foregoing chapter, says: “In order that Christ might be glorified by resurrection and ascension, he was first humbled by the Passion. Humility, then, is the merit of glory, while glory is the reward of humility; but all this took place in the form of a servant. For glory always was and will be in the form of God.” [Note: [Col. 1131D] Ibid., ch. “And Not Only.”]

God the Father also gave Christ the name above every name, namely the honour by which he is called God. For the Son of God possessed this name, insofar as he is God, eternally by nature; but insofar as he became man, he possessed it in time by grace. Nevertheless, blessed Augustine says that this name was given to the man, not to God, because he possessed it when he existed only in the form of God. But when it is said, “Therefore he exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name,” it is sufficiently clear why he exalted him, namely because of obedience, and in which form he was exalted. For in the form in which he was crucified, in that form he was exalted; and in it the name was given him, so that together with the form of a servant he might be called the only-begotten Son of God. This was given to the man which God himself already possessed in the form of God. Therefore he received this by grace: that, being human [Col. 1132A] or subsisting in the form of a servant—that is, in soul and flesh—he should be named and be God, and that at his name every knee should bend: those of heaven, earth, and hell, namely angels, human beings, and the ministers of hell. And at last every tongue, both of good and evil persons, should confess, willingly or unwillingly, that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father, namely equal to the Father according to divinity, at whose right hand he sits.

For by dying he became the victim of our deliverance; by rising again he received from God the Father the glory of impassibility and immortality; and by ascending to heaven he opened for us the gate of the heavenly kingdom.

For God had decreed in a mystery, by his lofty and just counsel, as blessed Ambrose says [Note: [Col. 1132D] Ibid., ch. “Why Then?”], that because of [Col. 1132B] the sin of the first human being, no human being should be admitted into paradise—that is, admitted to the contemplation of God—unless there should be found in one human being such humility as could suffice for all who were his, just as in the first human being there was such pride as harmed all who were his. But no one among human beings was found through whom this could be fulfilled, except the Lion from the tribe of Judah, “who opened the book and loosed its seals” (Rev. 5), fulfilling in himself all righteousness, that is, humility most complete, beyond which none can exist. For other human beings were debtors, and scarcely did each person’s own virtue and humility suffice for that person. Therefore none of them could offer a victim sufficient for our reconciliation. But Christ, God and man, was a sufficient and perfect victim, who humbled himself far more by tasting the bitterness of death than Adam had exalted himself in pride by enjoying with harmful delight the eating of the forbidden tree.

If, therefore, Adam’s pride was the ruin of all his descendants, sending him out of paradise and closing its gate against others, much more was Christ’s humility, by which he tasted death, able to open to all who are his the entrance of the heavenly kingdom, once God’s decree was fulfilled, and to erase the bond of the decree. Thus the entrance to the heavenly kingdom could not be opened, nor salvation accomplished, through another victim, but only through the death, resurrection, and ascension of him whose humility and patience, as has been said, were so great that by his merit the entrance of the heavenly kingdom might stand open to those who believe in him. Great benefits, therefore, were bestowed upon us in the death of the only-begotten Son of God and of the Virgin, so that we may be allowed to return to our heavenly [Col. 1132D] homeland; just as formerly, at the death of the high priest, those who had fled to cities of refuge were permitted safely to return to their own homes (Num. 35).

Therefore, as has been said, none was found able to redeem humankind from the power of darkness except the Lion from the tribe of Judah, who opened the book and loosed its seals. For he is above all, because he is not mere man but true God and true man. Of him blessed John the Baptist says: “He who is of the earth speaks from the earth; but he who comes from heaven is above all” (John 3). It is as though he said: He who is of the earth, that is, born of earthly parents, is earthly and speaks from the earth; namely, from himself [Col. 1133A] he thinks and says earthly things. But he who comes from heaven—namely Christ, from God the Father into the world—is above all, that is, above human beings and angels. For Christ Jesus, the human mediator between God and human beings, is above all holy people because he was conceived and born from the Virgin without sin. He is also above all angels, because, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he has been exalted above all heavenly orders—that is, at the right hand of God the Father.

Hence the prophet Ezekiel says concerning the winged creatures shown to him: “Over the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of a firmament, like the appearance of terrible crystal, stretched out above their heads” (Ezek. 1). Let us carefully hear what blessed Gregory says concerning this verse. “By the Lord’s gift,” he says [Note: [Col. 1133D] Homily 7 on Ezekiel.], “we explain these things in two ways, leaving it to the reader’s judgment to decide what should be chosen. For by the name ‘firmament’ the heavenly powers may be understood. This firmament is rightly said to be like the appearance of crystal, because crystal is indeed exceedingly hard, yet is formed from water. And when angelic nature was created, it received free will, so that it might choose whether to remain in humility and abide in the sight of almighty God, or slip [Note: [Col. 1133D] “Slip.”] into pride and fall from blessedness, departing from the likeness in which it had been made. But since, when others fell, the holy angels remained in their blessedness and received the gift that they could not fall at all, their nature, because it can no longer be led into changeability, has been hardened as it were in the hardness of crystal.

“Now this terrible crystal is said to be stretched above the heads of the living creatures [Col. 1133C] because those angelic powers which stand before the presence of almighty God are terrifying and dreadful to us, who are still placed in this corruption. Their joys, because they surpass the capacity of our minds, are said to be above the heads of the living creatures. For who, placed in corruptible flesh, can comprehend what that ineffable and endless joy of angels is: that blessedness which without failure sees the face of the Creator and remains unchangeably in his delight?

“By the name ‘firmament,’ our Redeemer himself may also be understood figuratively: true God above all things, and made man among all things, namely perfect man, in whom our nature has been established before the Father. Of him too it is prophetically said through the Psalmist to God [Col. 1133D] the Father: ‘Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you have strengthened for yourself’” (Ps. 80).

Certainly the Prophet here foreshows both natures of our Redeemer, divine and human, when he asks that the hand of God be upon the man of God’s right hand and upon the son of man. For the right hand of God is the Son of God; the finger of God is the Holy Spirit; and the son of man is the son of the Virgin. Who then is the man of God’s right hand, except the Son of the Virgin, assumed by the only-begotten Word of God the Father and made one person with him? Let David the prophet, therefore, speak in prayer and desire to God the Father concerning the strengthening of our Redeemer: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, and upon the son of man whom you have strengthened for yourself.” It is as though he said plainly: Give him power over all flesh, because he is the son of man; and you strengthened him for yourself when your paternal voice was heard over him, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3).

Here the Prophet uses words of future time. It is as though he said: When the fullness of time comes, let your hand—that is, the working of the Incarnation—be upon the man of your right hand, that is, upon Christ; as you have firmly determined with yourself in predestination, bring it to effect in its proper time.

Human nature, therefore, as has been said, before it was assumed by [Col. 1134B] the Creator of all things, was earth; for it was not a firmament. For the human being who sinned was told: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3). But after it was assumed by the author of all things, raised into heaven, and exalted above angels, it became a firmament which had formerly been earth. But the likeness of the firmament seen over the heads of the living creatures is further explained when it is said: “Like the appearance of terrible crystal.”

Let us hear what blessed Isidore says about the nature of crystal. “Crystal,” he says [Note: [Col. 1133D] Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, ch. 13.], “is called a shining stone, watery in colour, because it is snow hardened into ice over many years; hence the Greeks gave it its name. It is produced in Asia and Cyprus, especially in the northern Alps, where the sun, even in summer, is never found intensely hot. Thus this long-lasting hardness, enduring over years, produces the form called crystal. Set opposite the rays of the sun, it catches flame to such an extent that it supplies fire to dry tinder or leaves. Tinder [Note: [Col. 1134D] Isidore says nothing here about tinder, but in Book XVII of the *Etymologies*, ch. 10.] is found on trees; it is boiled in water and dried in the sun, and so is readily kindled by fire struck from a stone; it is also commonly called *esca*. The use of crystal is also intended for cups, and it can endure nothing but cold.”

Accordingly, we must return to the matters omitted above.

“The likeness,” he says [Note: [Col. 1134D] Gregory again.], “of the firmament over the heads of the living creatures was like terrible crystal.” Crystal, as has been said, freezes from water and becomes hard. But we know how great is the mobility of water. The body [Col. 1134D] of our Redeemer, because it was subject to suffering up to death, was in one respect like water; for through birth, growth, weariness, hunger, thirst, and death, it moved through the moments of time up to his Passion. Beholding this course, the Prophet says: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course,” etc. (Ps. 19). But because through the glory of resurrection and ascension it gained strength out of its own corruption in the power of incorruption, it hardened like crystal out of water, so that in him the same nature remained, but the changeability of corruption which it had possessed [Col. 1135A] no longer remained. Thus water was turned into crystal when the weakness of its corruption was changed by his resurrection into the firmness of incorruption.

But it should be noted that this crystal is called terrible, that is, dreadful. Yet who does not know what beauty crystal possesses? It is remarkable how beauty and dread can coincide in this crystal. But all who know the truth agree that the Redeemer of humankind will be beautiful to the righteous and terrible to the unrighteous.

Again, a little later he adds: “And above the firmament which was over their heads was the likeness of a throne, like the appearance of a sapphire stone; and above the likeness of the throne was a likeness as though of the appearance [Col. 1135B] of a man above” (Ezek. 1). [Note: [Col. 1135D] Now from the homily.] What is signified by the throne but those angelic powers which surpass even angels themselves in the dignity of a higher place? For although angels are called messengers and angels often come to announce certain things to human beings, thrones are never read to have been sent as ministers or messengers, because the Creator of all things presides over them at a far more exalted level. Hence the apostle Paul, describing the order of heavenly hosts which he had seen in the third heaven, says: “Whether thrones, dominions, principalities, or powers: all things were created through him and in him” (Col. 1). Therefore he named thrones before those orders of angels over which he knew them to be set.

The throne is aptly compared with a sapphire stone, because sapphire has the colour of the air. [Col. 1135C] Thus the powers of the heavenly orders are signified by the sapphire stone, because those spirits over whom almighty God presides more highly [Note: [Col. 1135D] “Presides.”] hold the dignity of a higher place in heaven. But above the throne is the likeness of a man, because above those powers too which surpass our angels is the glory of our Redeemer.

The order maintained must therefore be observed. Above the living creatures is the firmament; above the firmament, the throne; and above the throne, the man. For above holy human beings, still living amid this bodily corruption, are angels; and above angels are the higher angelic powers nearest to God; but above the powers nearest to God has been exalted the human mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus. [Col. 1135D]

But if, as we said above, the firmament must be understood to mean the mediator between God and human beings by reason of his assumed humanity—because under the designation of one name prophecies often signify many things—then the voice was made above the firmament which sounded from heaven above the baptized Lord, saying: “You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased” (Luke 3). Or, as another Evangelist says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). Let us therefore ask how the living creatures hear this voice and lower their wings. Let the prophet Habakkuk, when questioned, answer: “Lord, I heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and was dismayed” (Hab. 3). By being afraid, he lowered his wings. For everyone who by repentance corrects the evils he has done thereby shows that he is displeased with himself because he repents, since he amends what he has done wrongly. Whoever, therefore, pierced by repentance, corrects the evil he has committed, humbly lowers the wings of pride and swelling.

But what is it that the Father says of the Son, declaring: “In whom I am well pleased”? Almighty God the Father, insofar as human beings could understand, spoke in human fashion concerning sinners, saying: “I repent that I made man upon the earth” (Gen. 6). For in sinners whom he had created he was, as it were, displeased with himself. But in his only-begotten Lord Jesus Christ alone [Col. 1136B] he was well pleased, because he did not repent of having created among human beings the one human being in whom he found absolutely no sin, as the Psalmist says of him: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110).

[Note: [Col. 1135D] Augustine, or the author, *On the Essence of the Divinity*, in the Appendix, vol. VIII, p. 67.] God is said to “repent,” not, however, in the sense that he repents of past actions in our human manner. For he who knows all things before they happen (Dan. XIII) cannot repent of his completed acts. God’s repentance, therefore, is the changing of what has been decreed: what had first been begun in one way is, as sins require and with his permission, altered into something else. Thus we read concerning Saul that God repented of having made him king (1 Sam. XV). We see the same thing now in the Jewish people [Col. 1136C]: although it had been the people of God (Hos. II), because of its impiety it became the synagogue of Satan. There is likewise a change from evil to good, as happened among the Gentile people, who formerly were not a people but now, through Christ’s grace, have become God’s people. In the same manner, by God’s hidden judgment, Judas fell from the rank of the apostleship and was plunged into the abyss of hell (Acts I); whereas the thief, after the crime of robbery, was led from the cross into paradise (Luke XXIII). We therefore call this change from good to evil, or from evil to good—effected by the hidden and righteous judgment of God, either through the severity of his justice or through his mercy—his repentance.

[Note: [Col. 1136D] Again, from Gregory.] Therefore, as has been said, the Father was well pleased in our Redeemer alone [Col. 1136D], because in him alone he found no fault for which he might reproach himself, as it were, by repentance. The holy living creatures thus hear the voice above the firmament and are greatly afraid, because he alone, the Son both of God and of the Virgin, is without sin; and in his innocence they see how greatly they themselves sin daily, sins which they must unceasingly lament. The holy living creatures—that is, holy people—also consider that even the Author of life did not depart this life without the labor of suffering. Thus this voice was uttered above the firmament, because the decree of God the almighty Father extended even to the death and resurrection of the Only-begotten Son [Col. 1137A]. But when the voice is uttered above the firmament, the living creatures stand still and lower their wings, because all the saints, when they behold even the Only-begotten One scourged in this world, lay aside whatever confidence they place in their own merits. For if he who came without sin did not leave this world without the scourge, how shall those who came into the world with sin not deserve scourges? The firmament itself, which is above the heads of the living creatures—that is, which surpasses the minds of the righteous—has a voice above it, because our Redeemer endured in the flesh the decree which, in his divinity, he had ordained together with the Father. Hearing it, the righteous are afraid and lay aside every presumption in their own strength. However powerful they may be in virtues, what sort of life can be worthy for sinners, when even his life [Col. 1137B], which was subject to no sin, underwent the scourge for us?

But see, a grave question arises for us when it is said that “above the firmament, which was stretched out over their heads, was something like the appearance of a sapphire stone, the likeness of a throne.” For if the Lord is signified by the firmament, while the sapphire stone and likeness of the throne signify those highest angelic powers, how can they be believed to be above the firmament—that is, above the Lord—when it is immediately added: “And above the likeness of the throne was a likeness, like the appearance of a man above it”? For if, as has been said, the Lord is represented by the firmament, and again the Lord is understood as the man, on what grounds can he be understood as both above [Col. 1137C] the throne and beneath the throne? But while we speak, the Holy Spirit by his breath loosens and opens the tightly bound knots of this question, which had been closed. For the incarnate Only-begotten Son of the Father, in that he became man, was beneath the angels, as the Prophet says of him: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. VIII).

It is as though the Prophet were speaking to God the Father and saying: Not only in other people has human nature been humbled, but also in Christ; for you humbled, beneath the angels, him who is the head of all believers, since he was capable of suffering and mortal—yet only a little, because in many respects he surpasses the angels over whom he rules. And he plainly says: You made him a little lower, but afterward you crowned him with glory—that is, with the splendor of an incorruptible body—and with honor, namely, so that he might be venerated by all. He rightly says, “You crowned,” because the circle of the world, which is somewhat like a crown, came to his faith. It follows: “And set him,” that is, established him over the works of your hands. Since the angels are works of God’s hands, and the Only-begotten Son of God has been set over them, it consequently follows: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet,” that is, beneath the dominion of his power. “All sheep and oxen,” he says, “and moreover the beasts of the field.” Why, leaving aside the higher things—namely, the hosts of angels and human beings themselves—does he enumerate these lowly things: sheep, oxen, and beasts of the field? But these must be understood mystically. By sheep he means innocent people; by oxen [Col. 1138A], those who till the earth and make us fruitful. This is also said of angels and people, in order to show that all are subject to Christ. “You have subjected sheep,” he says—that is, innocent angels as well as people—and oxen, namely teachers who plough and thresh, who in the Lord’s vineyard with the spiritual ploughshare cut down the thickets of sins. “All oxen”: he uses the feminine gender, evidently to indicate those who bear fruit, who by the seed of God’s word cause human hearts to bear fruit; and these are both people and angels. It follows: “And moreover the beasts of the field.” By saying, “and moreover the beasts of the field,” he distinguishes them from the holy ones mentioned above. For these beasts are dregs, just as the saints mentioned above are wine: beasts of the field, that is, carnal people living amid the expanse of pleasures [Col. 1138B].

Thus the Son of God and of the Virgin, in that he became man, is beneath the throne, because he was made a little lower than the angels. But in that he is coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father, he is above the throne—that is, exalted above all the powers of the heavenly orders, because all things are subject beneath his feet. Rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he sits at the right hand of God the Father and presides over all angelic powers. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). Therefore the firmament is beneath the throne and the man is above the throne, because by assuming human nature he was both born beneath the angels and exalted above the angels [Col. 1138C]. Even before he was exalted through the glory of the resurrection, he was above the angels in his divinity; yet, as was said, he was made lower than the angels in his humanity, through which he was also subject to death. But after he trampled death by rising again, he set his humanity even above the powers of the archangels. Accordingly, first thrones are described as seen above the firmament, and afterward a man above the throne, because the Redeemer of humankind exalted above the angels, by ascending, the humanity which he had assumed beneath the angels by descending. We say that he was made beneath the angels in the same sense in which, as the Apostle proclaimed, we have heard that he was made under the law (Gal. IV). We understand the assumed humanity as beneath the angels on account of that abasement in which he deigned to appear. For as soon as the Word became flesh [Col. 1138D], God-made-man immediately possessed power above the angels. For the Evangelist says of him: “Behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV). Yet, in order that the weakness of his humanity might be shown, it is again written concerning him: “An angel from heaven appeared to him, strengthening him” (Luke XXII). Thus, as evidence of both natures, angels are described as ministering to him, and an angel as strengthening him. For he is one in both natures: he who existed as God before the ages became man at the end of the ages. Before his Passion, angels both ministered to him and an angel strengthened him; but after his Passion, resurrection, and ascension, angels can minister to him, but can no longer strengthen him. For, as has been stated, even though the firmament first appeared beneath the throne [Col. 1139A], the man is now above the throne. In his person, in order to show that he had seen the union of the two natures, divine and human, the holy prophet immediately added: “And I saw something like the appearance of electrum” (Ezek. I). What does it mean that the appearance of a man on the throne is seen as something like electrum, except that in electrum, as we said far above, gold and silver are mingled so that one thing is produced from two metals? In this mixture the brightness of gold is moderated by silver, and the appearance of silver shines through the brightness of gold. In our Redeemer, however, the two natures, divinity and humanity, are united to one another without confusion and without separation: through his humanity, the brightness of his divinity could be tempered for our eyes; and through his divinity, the human nature in him might shine [Col. 1139B] and, exalted in heaven, possess a splendor beyond that which it had as created. Mercifully, therefore, as has been said, he assumed our humanity, and powerfully exalted it above all the heavenly orders of blessed spirits.

In his descent, he was likened to a vulture descending upon a corpse; in his ascent, to an eagle carrying prey upward—that is, to heaven. Descending from heaven upon the corpse of the human race, as a vulture descends for food, he recalled it from death to life; and again, flying to heaven as an eagle, he placed that corpse—our humanity—at the right hand of the Father, carrying it with himself. [Note: [Col. 1139D] Gregory, *Morals*, book XVIII, chapter 19, near the end.] The Son of God and of the Virgin is also rightly designated by the name of a vulture [Col. 1139C]. For when a vulture flies and sees a corpse lying below, it descends to feed upon the corpse. And it is often caught to its death when it comes down from above to a dead animal. Thus Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings, is rightly figured by the designation of a vulture: remaining in the height of his divinity, he beheld from a kind of lofty flight the corpse of our mortality in the depths, and lowered himself from heaven to the lowest places. He also deigned to become man for our sake; and while he sought the dead animal—that is, the human race, dead in sins—he who was immortal in himself found death among us. Hence blessed Job, speaking of the rejection of the Jewish people, says: “The bird does not know the path, nor has the eye of the vulture seen it” (Job [Col. 1139D] XXVIII). The eye of this vulture was the very intention of our resurrection, because after three days he, though dead, delivered us from eternal death. That faithless people of Judea saw him as mortal, but paid no attention to the fact that by his death he would destroy our death. They indeed saw the vulture, but did not see the vulture’s eyes; for, unwilling to consider the paths of his humility by which he raised us to the heights, they did not know the bird’s path. They did not strive to weigh how his humility would lift us to heavenly things, and the purpose of his death restore us to life. Thus the Jewish people did not know the bird’s path and did not behold the vulture’s eyes, because although they saw him whom they held in [Col. 1140A] death, they were unwilling to see what great glory for our life would follow from his death.

The Son of God and of the Virgin is also rightly designated by the name of the eagle, because the body which he assumed from the Virgin without sin he raised from the tomb and lifted above all the heavens. As blessed Isidore says, the eagle is named from the keenness of its eyes. For it is said to possess sight so powerful that, when borne above the seas on motionless wings and invisible to human gaze, it sees little fish swimming from so great a height; then, descending like a missile, it snatches its prey and draws it to shore with its wings. It is also said not to turn aside its gaze before the sun’s rays. Therefore it exposes its young, suspended from its claws, to the rays of the sun; those whose eyes it sees holding their gaze steady it preserves as worthy of their lineage, while those whom it observes turning away their sight it rejects as degenerate. Having briefly stated what blessed Isidore says concerning the eagle’s nature, we must return to what we omitted above [Col. 1140B].

Therefore, as was said, the Son of God and of the Virgin is rightly designated by the name of the eagle, because, abiding in the bosom of the Father, he saw the human race held captive by the devil upon the earth and mercifully lowered himself from heaven to the depths, as an eagle to seize its prey. But, when the mystery of his coming had been accomplished [Note: [Col. 1140D] “mystery.”], namely his Nativity, Passion, and Resurrection, on the fortieth day he carried back to heaven with himself, captive like an eagle’s prey, that same human nature which he had rescued from the devil’s hand. Concerning him the Psalmist, taught by the Holy Spirit, speaks of the future as though it were past; rejoicing with utmost devotion over the restoration of humankind, he says [Col. 1140C]: “You ascended on high; you took captivity captive; you received gifts among men” (Ps. LXVII). It is as though he plainly said: You ascended, O Christ, on high in place and dignity. You who descended to instruct us ascended on high—that is, above all the heavens, to the right hand of God the Father—and before ascending you took captive those who were held captive in the lower world. These are the spoils, and this is the likeness of a triumph. The Apostle expounds this concerning Christ in his Epistle, where he says: “What does Christ’s ascension into heaven mean except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” [Col. 1140D] (Eph. IV).

It follows: “You took captivity captive,” that is, after sin, you seized and happily made captive the people who were captives under the devil. They are called captives because they were caught in Peter’s nets. Hence Peter too is told: “From now on you will catch people” (Luke V). They were placed beneath the Redeemer’s light and pleasant yoke. Hence in this chariot—that is, in the holy Church—there are many thousands rejoicing rather than mourning. Continuing, he says: “You received,” namely from the Father, “gifts among people to be received”; that is, by receiving people, you received gifts in people; or, you received from the Father gifts among people, namely gifts to be given [Col. 1141A] to the people whom you had received—that is, gifts which you would give to those whom you had received. Paul, with apostolic authority, says that Jesus gave gifts to people (Eph. IV). Insofar as the Son is God, he gave gifts together with the Father, sending the Holy Spirit to the apostles, who is of the Father and the Son. But insofar as that same Son is in the Church, he received gifts in his members, when the members themselves receive them, with whom he is one, according to the saying: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. XXV). Thus after the resurrection the Son of God ascended on high like an eagle, and he brought captive with himself to the right hand of God the Father, as has been said, the prey—that is, the captivity which he had wrested from the devil’s hand. Solomon, speaking typologically in Proverbs, is believed to have spoken of the unknown paths of this exceedingly swift eagle.

[Col. 1141B] “There are three things impossible to know, and a fourth which I do not recognize: the tracks of a flying eagle, the path of a serpent upon a rock, the course of a sailing ship, and the way of a man in youth” (Prov. XXX). The tracks of a flying eagle—that is, the tracks of Christ descending to earth and returning to heaven—cannot be comprehended or described. The serpent is the devil; the rock is Christ himself, who said: “The ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV), and concerning whom blessed Peter said: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. II). The ship is understood to be the holy Church: although it daily suffers in this age the tribulations of storms like a ship at sea, it is never dashed against a rock or submerged in the depths. “The way of a man,” he says, “in youth.” This man is understood as Christ, concerning whom Paul says: “Until we all meet in the unity of faith and knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV). And again: “I have betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (1 Cor. XI). No one can comprehend the paths of his virtues [Col. 1141C].

That the Redeemer of humankind is designated by the name of the eagle is also plainly shown in Ezekiel, where the face of the eagle is described as appearing above the four beings (Ezek. I). [Note: [Col. 1141D] Gregory, Homily 4 on Ezekiel.] The four winged living creatures also signify the four Evangelists, as the beginnings of their respective Gospel books attest. Since Matthew [Col. 1141D] began with Christ’s human birth, he is fittingly signified by the man; since Mark began with the cry in the wilderness, rightly by the lion; since Luke began with sacrifice, aptly by the calf; and since John began with the divinity of the Word, he is worthily signified by the eagle, for he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). As he fixed his attention on the very substance of divinity, he fixed his eyes upon the sun, as an eagle does. But because, as blessed Gregory says, all the elect are members of our Redeemer, while our Redeemer himself is the head of all the elect, there is no obstacle to his also being signified in all these figures by which his members are represented. For the Only-begotten Son of God [Col. 1142A] truly became man; in the sacrifice of our redemption he deigned to die as a calf; through the power of his strength he rose as a lion. The lion too is said to sleep with its eyes open, because in the very death in which our Redeemer could sleep according to his humanity, he remained wakeful by abiding immortal in his divinity. He also ascended to heaven after his resurrection and was raised to the heights as an eagle. Thus he is all these things together for us: by being born, man; by dying, calf; by rising, lion; and by ascending into heaven, eagle.

But because we have already said above that the four Evangelists, and at the same time all the perfect under their figure, are signified by these living creatures, it remains to show how each of the elect is represented by these visions of animals [Col. 1142B]. Every elect person who is perfect in the way of the Lord is a man, a calf, a lion, and an eagle. A human being is a rational animal. A calf is customarily slain in sacrifice. A lion is a strong beast, as it is written: “The lion, strongest among beasts, will fear no encounter” (Prov. XXX). An eagle flies to the heights and gazes with undazzled eyes upon the sun’s rays. Everyone, then, who is perfect in reason is a man. Because he mortifies himself from the pleasure of this world, he is a calf. Because, through this voluntary mortification of himself, he has the strength of confidence against every adversity, he is a lion. Hence it is written: “The righteous will be confident like a lion, without fear” (Prov. XXVIII). And because [Col. 1142C] he contemplates on high the things that are heavenly and eternal, he is an eagle. Therefore, since every righteous person becomes a man by reason, a calf by the sacrifice of self-mortification, a lion by the strength of confidence, and an eagle by contemplation, every perfect person may rightly be signified by these holy living creatures. We say this in order to show that what has been said concerning the four living creatures also pertains to each of the perfect.

But a great question arises for us concerning these Evangelists and holy preachers: why are the man and the lion said to be at the right of all four, while the calf is said to be at the left of all four? It is not without cause for wonder that those two are said to be on the right and this one on the left. Again, we must ask why the eagle is recorded as being not at the right [Col. 1142D] or at the left, but above all four. We therefore raise two questions which, as the Lord opens the way, must be resolved. The man and the lion are said to be at the right, and the calf at the left. For we associate joyful things with the right and sad things with the left. Thus we call “sinister” whatever we judge to be adverse. And, as we said above, the man signifies the Incarnation, the calf the Passion, and the lion the resurrection of our Creator. All the elect rejoiced at the incarnation of the Only-begotten Son of God and of the Virgin, by which we were redeemed. Yet the first of the elect, namely the holy apostles, were saddened by his death, and again rejoiced at his resurrection [Col. 1143A]. Therefore, because his birth and resurrection gave joy to the disciples, whereas his Passion saddened them, the man and lion are described as having been at his right and the calf at his left. The holy Evangelists themselves rejoiced in his humanity; they were strengthened by his resurrection after having been saddened by his Passion. Thus the man and lion are at their right, because the Incarnation of our Redeemer made them glad. But the calf was on the left, because his death cast them down for a brief time into unbelief. The eagle’s position is rightly described as not beside them, but above them: whether because it signifies his ascension, or because John declares that the Word of the Father is God with the Father, John surpassed the other Evangelists in the power of contemplation. Along with them he speaks of Christ’s divinity, but he contemplates it more subtly than all. Yet, if the eagle is numbered with the other three as one of four living creatures, it is remarkable how it is described as above all four, unless John, in seeing the Word in the beginning, also rose above himself. For unless he had transcended himself, he would not have seen the Word in the beginning. Therefore he who went beyond even himself was above not merely the other three, but, including himself, above all four [Col. 1143B].

Thus, as was said above, the Word who was in the beginning, who was with God and was God, descended from the bosom of the Father into the depths like a vulture, to redeem and raise up the corpse of humankind. Then, like an eagle carrying prey, he carried back to heaven with himself the captivity—that is, the same human nature which the devil had taken captive and which he recaptured [Col. 1143C]. He therefore ascended because he had first descended into the lower parts of the earth. Accordingly, as blessed Paul says: “He who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. IV), that is, that he might repair the losses of the heavenly country.

It is therefore true what the Psalmist foretold about him long before. [Note: [Col. 1143D] Another manuscript: “What the Psalmist foretold concerning Christ’s ascension.”] “He ascended upon the cherubim and flew; he flew upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. XVII). It is as though he said: He ascended above the cherubim, that is, into heaven above the fullness of knowledge, which is charity, so that no one might come to God except through charity. And he flew, because he showed himself incomprehensible to those who love him, lest they seek to comprehend him by bodily images. He flew, I say, above the wings of the winds, because his incomprehensibility surpasses the powers of souls, by which, as though by wings, they raise themselves from earthly perils and fears into the air of freedom [Col. 1143D].

The most wise Solomon, by the prophetic Spirit, foresaw that the same Son of God and of the Virgin, coeternal with God the Father according to his divinity, would come to unite the holy Church to himself. Speaking figuratively of him, he said: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song II). [Note: [Col. 1143D] Gregory, on this passage.] Christ, intending to come from the bosom of the Father to the embraces of his bride, graciously assumed our humanity. To accomplish this mystery he came, as it were, leaping upon mountains, because among human beings he displayed certain works so exalted and beyond humanity that the human race could marvel at them but could not attain them. That he was born of a Virgin; that an angel instructed shepherds to go and visit him while he was crying; that a star led the Magi to worship him lying in a manger; that while hanging on the cross he gave up his spirit at the hour he chose; that though dead, on the third day he raised himself; that ascending into heaven he gave the Holy Spirit to those people whom he pleased; that through fishermen [Col. 1144B] and unlearned men he subjected the world to his faith—in doing these things he made, as it were, certain leaps upon the mountains which no creature could follow. In these works, surely, he skipped over the hills, because by the power of his action he surpassed all saints, however greatly they had advanced.

The Prophet, taught by the Holy Spirit, declared that these leaps or steps of Jesus Christ, Lord and King, had been seen; representing what was future as already past, he joyfully said in the Psalm: “They have seen your goings, O God, the goings of my God, my King, who is in the sanctuary” (Ps. LXVII). Or according to another reading: “Your steps were seen, O God,” namely, the steps by which you came into the world. This grace was formerly hidden in the Old Testament; now it is manifest when the Son, sent from God [Col. 1144C] the Father from heaven, is proclaimed among the Gentiles. Whose steps did they see? “The goings,” I say, “of my God,” namely by creation, [Word—Note: [Col. 1143D] The name *Word* is an interlinear gloss by a glossator on the name *God*. Removed from its proper place here, it disturbs the sense.] “of my King,” by governance, who is God in the holy temple—that is, in heaven, or in angels and holy people, or in the holy body born of the Virgin—although unbelievers do not see him insofar as that body suffered. It is as though he plainly said: “They have seen your goings, O God,” that is, they will recognize how you became known to the world through human nature. Nor will they recognize only your steps in this way, but also your “goings,” that is, the apostles, who are the goings of my God, who created me in the first creation; of my King, who regenerated me in holy baptism; who is in the Holy One—that is, in each person sanctified by him [Col. 1144D], or in the virginal body born of the Virgin.

The virginal flesh of Jesus Christ, taken from his Virgin Mother and offered to God the Father as an odor of sweetness, was typologically prefigured by the virgin daughter of Jephthah the leader, whom her father, returning victorious from battle, offered to God. Thus we read in the book of Judges [Note: [Col. 1144D] Isidore, *Questions on Judges*, chapter 7]: Jephthah, a Gileadite fleeing from the face of his brothers, was made leader for the battle against the children of Ammon. Returning after his triumph, he offered his own virgin daughter, who after the victory was the first to come out from his house to meet him. For he had made a vow that whatever first met him on his return he would offer to the Lord (Judg. XI). Who, then, was foretold by Jephthah except our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, fleeing from the face of his brothers—that is, the Jews—received dominion among the Gentiles? Thus the Evangelist says concerning him: “Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (John VIII).
