And again: “Jesus no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the wilderness near the city called Ephraim, and there remained with his disciples” (John XI). Thus fleeing from the face of the Jews, his brothers according to the flesh, he received dominion among the Gentiles. He also fulfilled, as though under oath, all the mysteries of human salvation and, as it were, offered his own flesh as a daughter to the Lord for the salvation of his people [Col. 1145B]. For, as the Psalmist testifies, we read that the Only-begotten One swore to God the Father: “As he swore to the Lord, he made a vow to the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI). Taken literally, that king David, son of Jesse, was very meek, so much so that he would not repay Saul evil for evil. For David showed such humility toward Saul that he acknowledged him as king and himself as a dog or a flea. Yet this passage does not speak of David, but rather of what he signifies—that is, Christ. For David typologically signifies the one man whose voice is often heard in the Psalms: namely, the whole Christ, head and body; whose humility and meekness are commended here. “He swore,” it says, “to the Lord; he made a vow to the God of Jacob.” “He swore,” that is, as though under the pledge of an oath; “he made a vow,” that is, he firmly determined by the vow of his will to build for God the Father a house through the Passion of the cross—that is, to acquire the holy Church and redeem it from the hand of the ancient enemy through the shedding of his own blood [Col. 1145C]. Therefore Jephthah the leader, in order to free his people from the servitude of the children of Ammon, offered to God what first came to meet him from his house, namely his daughter. But the Son of God, prince of the angels, in order to rescue humankind from the devil’s captivity, offered upon the altar of the cross to God the Father, by the vow of his will, his own virginal flesh, taken from a Virgin without sin; and he exalted it above all the heavens. Therefore the Prophet urges all nations to praise Christ, foretelling that same ascension in these words [Col. 1145D]:

“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord” (Ps. LXVII). And again: “Sing praises to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east” (*ibid.*). Sing praises, I say; sing praises to God—that is, to Christ—who ascends insofar as he is man. [Note: [Col. 1145] Isidore, book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 56, and the Gloss.] For insofar as he is God, he is equal to the Father. “He ascends,” it says, “above the heaven of heaven,” that is, above all the heavens, at the right hand of the Father—namely, above all higher creatures—so that he has nothing above himself except God the Father. Where did he ascend? Toward the east. And from where did he ascend? Namely, from the east. It identifies the place where he rose and from which he ascended, because Jerusalem, where he rose and from which he ascended, lies in the east [Col. 1146A]. Or he ascended toward the east of our illumination—that is, in order to make the light of grace rise for us. Or “east” is understood as the Word begotten from the Father, by whose power that man ascended. “He ascended toward the east,” that is, by the power of the Word he ascended to the right hand of the Father. Hence the prophet Amos also says: “The Lord has built his ascent in heaven, and established his promise upon the earth” (Amos IX). God builds his ascent in heaven daily when he draws his saints from lowly things to heavenly ones, over whom he presides and in whom he ascends. For what the Lord cries through Isaiah also declares the resurrection and ascension of Jesus Christ: “Now I shall arise, says the Lord; now I shall be exalted, and now I shall be lifted up” (Isa. XXXIII). For he did not rise alone, but raised many with himself. It is as though he plainly said: Now I shall rise, namely from the dead; now I shall be exalted in heaven; now [Col. 1146B] I shall be lifted up in the kingdom. Hence Isaiah again says: “Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted and lifted up exceedingly” (Isa. LII). This certainly pertains to Christ’s ascension and to the glory of his kingdom. David the prophet, beholding in the Spirit this heavenly exaltation of Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, and speaking of the future as though it were past, says in the Psalms:

“ The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Psalm 109).

The prophet, first revealing the nature of the Godhead, says: “The Lord said to my Lord.” The Prophet speaks in our manner when he says “said,” namely, so that a human being might be instructed, because he did not utter it with our mouth but said it in deed—that is, by effect—or rather in deed, that is, by generation. Or, “said” means that he eternally appointed it for my Lord, that is, for his Son, who is my Lord even according to the fact that he is human—that is, he himself is man, though not by virtue of being man.

By saying “the Lord to my Lord,” therefore, and repeating the same name, he distinguishes the persons and clearly reveals the one nature and power of the persons. Likewise, when he says “my Lord,” this indicates divinity. But when he says “sit,” and “the Lord will send forth the rod of your power,” this indicates humility.

What did God the Father say to the Son? Clearly: “Sit,” that is, rest after the labor of the Passion. It is as though God the Father openly said: “According to the fact that you are human, sit—not only on high, so that you may rule over all creatures as their superior, but also in concealment, so that you may be believed to be hidden and concealed.” For there is no reward of faith unless what we believe remains hidden.

Those who live here below, namely in this world, are subjected to him; they do not yet look upward, and they believe what they do not see. This is the righteousness of faith of which the Son of God and the Virgin himself speaks in the Gospel: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 14), “he will convict the world concerning sin, because they did not believe in me; and concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me; and concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has already been judged” (John 16).

“I go to the Father,” he says, “and you will no longer see me.” It is as though he were saying: “This is your righteousness: that you believe in him whom you do not see.” For “the righteous person lives by faith” (Galatians 3), if he believes what he does not see.

When God the Father therefore says to the Son—that is, to our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ—“Sit,” he marks two things: namely, that after the labor of the Passion he rests and reigns with the Father, and that until the day of judgment he is, as it were, in concealment.

“Sit,” I say, “at my right hand,” that is, among my more excellent goods. Or: “Sit at my right hand,” that is, reign with me in my glory and eternity [Note: Isidore, at the place cited above, chapter 57].

Let the Jews therefore inquire to whom God the Father said, “Sit at my right hand.” Was it said to an angel, or an archangel, or to one of the prophets? Certainly not. For none of them possesses that glory. The one whom the invisible God the Father considers worthy of sitting with him therefore sits at his right hand. And just as he is worthy of his seat, so is he worthy by nature and by name.

The prophet David foresaw that he would reign over all nations when, taught by the Holy Spirit, he joyfully said:

> “God will reign over the nations; God sits upon his holy throne” (Psalm 46).

It is as though he were saying: “Let those who despise the humble Christ at least submit to his power.” “God will reign,” I say: the Son of God and the Virgin, after his Passion, will reign over all nations, whereas formerly he reigned over the one nation of the Jews. This prophecy has now been fulfilled in Christ and in the Church.

“God sits,” he says, “upon his holy throne,” that is, over all the heavens, reigning at the right hand of God the Father throughout the ages. Or the holy thrones are the thrones, dominions, and powers of heaven, together with all the saints. He therefore sits upon his holy throne, that is, over all the heavenly powers and over holy souls.

Hence it is said: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of God” [Note: Martin persists in this distinctive reading, “the soul of the righteous is the throne of God,” although Bede here and the marginal Gloss retain the more common “the throne of wisdom,” following Augustine on this psalm.]

How did he reign over the nations? Because the princes of the peoples, namely the holy apostles, the teachers of the Church, and their followers, were gathered together—that is, they came together by believing with the God of Abraham, namely with Christ, who is the God of Abraham.

For he is the true God who powerfully raised up children for Abraham from stones (Matthew 3). Certainly God raised up children for Abraham from stones when he converted to the love and faith of himself the stony hearts of the Jews, who were already almost dead in unbelief. Whoever rightly believes in Christ exists by faith as a son of Abraham. Truly, whoever places his faith in Christ, who is true life, rises from death to life.

Thus, as though the Jews had been expelled, the nations coming from east and west take their place as children of Abraham, possessing the promises.

The prophetess Deborah [Note: It will certainly seem incredible unless we attest it as eyewitnesses: there was a man of such utter ignorance that he corrected the manuscript here and throughout this entire chapter, substituting *Delbora* for *Debbora*, as we restore it, for no other reason than to make it conform to another copy.] typologically prefigured this rejection of the Jews and calling of the nations when she foretold that Sisera, the enemy of the Jews, would be handed over not into the hand of a man but into the hand of a woman.

For thus it is read in the Book of Judges: “Deborah the prophetess judged the people at that time, and she sat beneath a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, on Mount Ephraim. And the children of Israel went up to her for every judgment” (Judges 5) [Note: Isidore, *Questions on Judges*, chapter 2.]

Deborah, whose name is interpreted as “bee,” or “speech,” is to be understood in prophecy and as a figure. Of her it is written: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Psalm 118).

Let us therefore consider where the place of prophecy is said to be. “Beneath a palm tree,” he says. Prophecy has its seat beneath a palm tree because it leads those whom it teaches by its instructions to the palm of the heavenly calling.

Prophecy is also said to sit between Ramah and Bethel. Ramah is interpreted as “lofty,” while Bethel means “house of God.” This is because it teaches us, placed within the house of God, to seek not the things that are on earth but those that are in heaven.

This Deborah, then, who signifies prophecy, sent for Barak and summoned him to her. For Barak is interpreted as “lightning.” Lightning possesses light, but not permanently: it shines for a brief time and then fades.

Barak therefore represents the former people, namely the Jewish people. First of all, through prophecy, they were called and invited to hear the words of God; they shone forth in the splendor of the Law and flashed for a short time, but did not endure long.

When Deborah—that is, prophecy—said to Barak, namely to the Jewish people: “The Lord God of Israel commands you to ascend Mount Tabor and take with you ten thousand men,” Barak answered prophecy in the person of the Jewish people: “I will not ascend,” he said, “unless you ascend with me.”

Deborah said to him: “I will go with you, but victory will not be credited to you on the road on which you are traveling, because the Lord will hand Sisera over into the hand of a woman” (Judges 4). This plainly shows that primacy is not with that people, nor does victory remain with it, but with Jael, a foreign woman, namely the holy Church.

For Jael, this foreign woman into whose hand victory was given, represents the Church gathered from the nations. Jael is interpreted as “ascent,” because through the Church one ascends to heaven.

She killed Sisera, the enemy, by driving a tent peg into his temple—that is, she destroyed the devil by the point and power of the cross—which Barak, namely the Jewish people, could not do.

For Jael alone, the foreign woman, namely the holy Church, through the wood of the cross, in which the salvation of believers lies through spiritual mysteries, strikes down the enemy of faith. Then, after he has died, she covers him with skins, that is, leaves him enclosed within the hearts of carnal people.

For the ancient enemy is hidden only among those who live in the corruption of life and commit mortal sins. When such people live wickedly and are separated from the body of Christ, they become members of the devil.

The Jews, certainly, who deny Christ are members of the devil. Among other things, the evangelist John says in the Apocalypse, speaking in the person of God and of the man Jesus Christ to the angel of the Church of Smyrna:

> “Thus says the First and the Last, who was dead and lives: I know your works, your poverty and tribulation, but you are rich; and you are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan” (Revelation 2).

It is as though he were saying plainly: “The one who according to divinity is the First and the Last, and who according to humanity was dead, giving us an example that we ought to die for him, now lives, raised up eternally immortal and impassible, and says this: ‘O bishop of the Church of Smyrna, I know the tribulation that you willingly endure with your subjects for me, and I see your poverty, because outwardly you have been stripped by persecutors; yet inwardly you are rich in virtues. You are blasphemed by those who say that they are Jews and are not, but are instead the synagogue, that is, the congregation of Satan.’”

Thus they are no longer Jews through the faith of Abraham, that is, confessors of Christ; through blasphemy and obstinate unbelief they are the dwelling and lair of the devil.

“The kingdom of God has been taken from them and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21). For this reason the Son of God descended from the bosom of the Father into the womb of the undefiled Virgin: to uproot every plant that God the Father had not planted—that is, the works of the devil which had grown strong in human hearts (Matthew 15)—and through the apostles’ preaching to gather into one the children of God who had been scattered (John 11).

After he had completed the mystery of his most victorious Passion, burial, and resurrection, and had clearly manifested himself alive and true to his disciples by many proofs over forty days, “finally,” as the evangelist Mark says—that is, on this very day—he appeared to the same eleven disciples as they reclined, reproached their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen (Mark 16).

Rightly did the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, after his resurrection, rebuke the disciples for unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him risen.

For when the holy women who had come with spices to his tomb saw two angels in white garments, one at the head and one at the feet, where his body had been placed (John 20), and heard from them that he was already alive, and reported all this to the disciples, they did not immediately believe them. Rather, before them these words appeared to be like delirium (Luke 24).

Those two men also, one of whom was Cleopas, were going to Emmaus. When they recognized him in the breaking of bread, rose at that same hour, and returned to Jerusalem, and reported what had happened on the road and how they had seen the Lord, nevertheless, as the evangelist Mark says, they did not believe them (Mark 16).

Nor is it surprising that the apostles did not give credence to the words of the women or of their fellow disciples, since they did not perfectly believe even the Son of God and the Virgin, their teacher, with whom they had previously lived for so long. He stood among them, offered them peace (Luke 24), showed them his feet and hands, displayed the wounds of the nails and the lance, invited them to touch him, and testified with his own mouth that he was the one whom they had seen before his Passion raising the dead, cleansing lepers, enlightening the blind, preaching to the crowds, and performing the other miracles that no one else had performed; the one who, after his betrayal, hung upon the cross, rested for three days in the tomb wrapped in linen cloths, and was raised from the dead on the third day. He himself declared:

> “I am he; do not be afraid” (Matthew 28).

Yet they still did not perfectly believe that it was he, as the evangelist Luke testifies:

> “While they still did not believe, and were marveling for joy, he said to them: ‘Have you anything here to eat?’ But they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, he took the remnants and gave them to them. And he said to them: ‘These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you’” (Luke 24).

What do you observe amid these things, dearest brethren? Why did the holy apostles, who had been instructed by such evident proofs, doubt Christ’s resurrection? Why did Jesus Christ, God and man, permit the disciples whom he had chosen before the foundation of the world, through whom he had determined with the Father and the Holy Spirit to teach his Church, to remain in doubt concerning the faith for so long?

For “their eyes were held, so that they would not recognize him” (Luke 24). Was this for their rejection or condemnation? Certainly not, but for our instruction. For, as blessed Gregory says, they doubted so that we would not doubt. While they are led back to faith through prolonged looking, touching, and handling, we are strengthened by their doubt.

For this reason another appearance was shown to the disciples going to Emmaus and doubting Christ’s resurrection, so that they would not recognize him except in the breaking of bread, so that all might understand that they do not recognize Christ unless they have become partakers of his body, that is, of the Church. The Apostle commends the Church’s unity in the fragment of bread, saying: “One bread, one body, we, the many, are in Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

For the bread that we break in the Lord’s name, that is, in commemoration of his Passion, is his body; and the cup that we drink is his blood.

When therefore the Son of God and the Virgin, rising from the dead, hands the blessed bread to the disciples, their eyes are opened so that they may recognize him. The obstacle that Satan had placed before their eyes, so that Jesus would not be recognized, is removed.

The one who takes the word of salvation from the hearts of hearers, so that those who believe may not be saved (Luke 8), himself obstructs the disciples’ eyes so that they do not recognize Christ. The Lord therefore permits this obstacle to remain in their eyes until they come to the sacrament of the bread.

But once they have partaken of the unity of Christ’s body, the enemy’s obstacle is removed, so that Christ can be recognized after the resurrection. Meanwhile, the appearance of weakness is withdrawn from bodily eyes, so that the glory of the resurrection may begin to appear to their minds.

Hence it follows:

> “And they said to one another: ‘Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?’” (Luke 24.)

They did not recognize him in the exposition of the Scriptures, but they recognize him in the breaking of bread, because “it is not the hearers of the Law who will be justified, but the doers” (Romans 2). Truth is better understood by doing good than by hearing.

After the sermon had been heard, the heart, previously cold with the sluggishness of unbelief and fear, was kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit, so that it now burns with heavenly desire and reaches out to believe the truth. By the commandments [Note: *Quot.*], a person is instructed and, as it were, inflamed by so many torches.

After his resurrection the Lord displayed two different things in his body: namely, his body both tangible and of the same nature, so that he might form believers for faith, and incorruptible and possessed of another glory, so that he might invite them to the reward.

The apostles knew that Christ was true God and true man; but after he died, they did not believe that true flesh could rise from the tomb on the third day. They therefore thought that they were seeing the spirit which he had released in his Passion.

But the Lord removes this error, saying:

> “See my hands and my feet, because I myself am he” (Luke 24).

By many proofs he persuades them of his resurrection, presenting himself to be seen by their eyes and touched by their hands. When he displays his bones and flesh to their touch, he signifies the condition of his resurrection and ours: in it our body will be subtle through the effect of spiritual power, yet tangible through the reality of its nature.

To make the truth of his resurrection known, he wished not only to be touched but also to eat with them—not because either we or he will need food after the resurrection, but to show that he possessed a true body. He ate, therefore, by power, not by necessity.

For thirsty earth absorbs water in one way, while a hot ray of the sun absorbs it in another: the former through need, the latter through power.

“The evangelist says that they offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb.” The broiled fish is the mediator between God and human beings, who suffered without sin for the salvation of humanity. He was found in the waters of the human race, caught in the snare of persecutors, and broiled at the time of his Passion.

In the resurrection he became for us a honeycomb. Honey in wax is divinity in human nature.

“And when he had eaten before them, he took the remnants and gave them to them.” The eating of this honey signifies that in his body he received into eternal rest those who, while suffering tribulations for God, do not depart from the love of inward sweetness. Those who are broiled here by tribulations for righteousness will there be satisfied with true sweetness.

When he displayed the scars of his wounds, therefore, he healed the wound of unbelief. He preserved those scars then, and he will display them at the judgment.

Why? First, to establish faith in the resurrection; second, so that, interceding with the Father for us, he may always show what kind of death he endured for human beings; third, to indicate to those redeemed by his death how mercifully they were helped, by setting before them the signs of that death; finally, to announce at the judgment how justly the wicked are condemned, by displaying the wounds that he received from them.

Thus he preserved the scars not from inability to heal them, but in order to bear forever the triumph of his victory.

He therefore removes every uncertainty concerning his resurrection. He was seen and touched by the disciples; after the resurrection he ate and drank before them; and, lest he should seem in any respect to have deceived human senses, he brings forward the Scriptures and opens the disciples’ understanding of them, saying:

> “It was necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

This was so that, even if he might seem to have accomplished what he wished by magical arts, as the pagans say, he might not seem able to have been prophesied before he was born.

We have joined these matters, dearest brethren, concerning Christ’s most true resurrection and the disciples’ necessary and providential doubt to this sermon, so that your charity may more readily understand how reasonably Jesus Christ, God and man, when about to ascend into heaven, reproved them for unbelief and hardness of heart.

Why? Namely, so that a heart of stone might be removed from their hearts and a heart of flesh take its place, filled with love of God and neighbor.

It follows:

> “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16).

Let us hear what blessed Jerome says about this verse, full of spiritual sweetness:

> “Before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the apostles were like vessels of clay, that is, formed from mud; but now, made firm through the fire of the Holy Spirit, they are told: ‘Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature,’ that is, to every nation of the gentiles, which has something in common with every creature—namely, with angels, sinners, wood, stones, fire and water, heat and cold, moisture and dryness—because the human being is called a lesser world.

> “For previously it had been said: ‘Do not go into the way of the gentiles’ (Matthew 10), so that the preaching of the apostles, first rejected by Judaea, might then assist the gentiles when that proud land had rejected it as a testimony to its own condemnation.”

In this passage one may fittingly apply in a figurative sense what the Lord, after enumerating some works of his power, says to blessed Job in a manner of rebuke:

> “Who prepares its food for the raven, when its young cry to God, wandering because they have no food?” (Job 38.)

[Note: This passage was corrected by that utterly blind man whom we have often mentioned, although the manuscript plainly read *vagantes* (“wandering”), as do all the witnesses and blessed Gregory himself, who is copied here and repeated below, here and in the other manuscript—except in the text, where it corruptly printed *vagientes* (“crying”).]

Let blessed Gregory approach in reverence to the great Church of Christ and, according to the wisdom granted him by God, expound this verse for us.

For what else is signified by the young of ravens but the Jewish people, black through the fault of unbelief? Their young are said to cry to God so that food may be prepared for that raven by the Lord, because the holy apostles, born in the flesh from the Israelite people, while pouring out prayers to God for their nation, fed the people from whom they had been carnally born, as it were the parent raven, with spiritual understanding.

The young also—that is, the holy apostles—do not presume upon themselves, but upon the strength of their Redeemer. Hence it is well said: “When its young cry to God.” For they know that they can do nothing by their own power; and though with devout desires they hunger for the gain of souls, they nevertheless desire that this be accomplished by him who inwardly works all things through them.

For they grasp by true faith that “neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3). Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

Therefore, while its young cry, food is prepared for the raven; because while the holy apostles pray, the people formerly faithless are brought to the knowledge of faith and are satisfied by the preaching of their children, as though by the voices of their young.

Yet we must diligently observe in this verse that food is said to be prepared for this raven first while its young cry and afterward while they wander.

Food was prepared for the raven while its young cried when, as the apostles preached, Judaea heard the word of God and was fed with spiritual understanding, now in three thousand people (Acts 2), now in five thousand (Acts 4).

But when the multitude of the reprobate—namely, the scribes, Pharisees, and priests—exercised their cruelty against the preachers and, as it were, killed the lives of the young, the same young, that is, the holy apostles, were scattered through all parts of the world.

Hence the apostles say to those same carnal fathers, namely the Jews:

> “It was fitting that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but because you have rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the gentiles” (Acts 13).

Undoubtedly, the apostles, children of the Synagogue according to the flesh, knew that after the gentiles had believed, Judaea too would come to faith, as it is written:

> “Until the fullness of the gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved” (Romans 11).

Therefore, since the holy apostles first labored intensely to preach to those who listened, and afterward to show to those who resisted examples of the converted gentiles, like hungry young they sought food for this black raven, that is, faithless Judaea, first by crying and afterward by wandering.

For where the young wander throughout the whole world, there the raven finds its food: because when the Jewish people looks upon the gentiles converted to God through the apostles’ labor, at last it will one day be ashamed of the folly of its unbelief.

Then it understands the sayings of Holy Scripture, when it recognizes that they had become known to the gentiles before they became known to itself. When the wandering of the young has been completed, it opens the mouth of its heart to receive the sacred words, because, after the apostles’ journeys through the world have been accomplished, it receives spiritually, though late, those things from which it long fasted while unbelief bound it.

Since the power of divine might alone accomplishes all these things, it is rightly said:

> “Who prepares its food for the raven, when its young cry to God, wandering because they have no food?”

You are to understand: except I, who endure the faithless people while its children pray, feed it while they preach, and await its eventual conversion at the end while they wander elsewhere?

There is another moral interpretation of the raven. After producing its young, it is reported to feign withholding food from them in full measure. Before they darken as they put forth feathers, it allows them to suffer hunger, until its own likeness appears in them through the blackness of their plumage.

They wander to and fro in the nest and seek the aid of food with open mouths. But when they begin to turn black, it seeks food for them all the more eagerly, the longer it had delayed feeding them.

Certainly, the raven is every learned preacher, who cries aloud while bearing, as a kind of blackness of color, remembrance of his sins and awareness of his own weakness.

When disciples are born in faith but perhaps do not yet know how to consider their own weakness, perhaps turn their remembrance away from past sins, and thereby do not display the blackness of humility which they ought to assume against this world’s glory, they open their mouths, as it were, to receive food when they seek instruction concerning lofty mysteries.

But their teacher gives them the food of elevated preaching in proportion as he sees that they are less worthily grieving for their past sins.

He waits and admonishes them first to grow black from the brightness of present life through the lamentations of repentance, and only then to receive the fitting, most subtle nourishment of preaching.

The raven sees the gaping mouths of its young, but first seeks that their bodies be clothed in blackness of feathers; and the discerning teacher does not minister inward mysteries to minds which he sees have not yet cast themselves away from this world.

Therefore, the less black the disciples are outwardly through the adornment of present life, the less they are inwardly filled with the food of the word. And the less they empty themselves of bodily glory, the more they fast from spiritual refreshment.

But if, in confession of their former life, they put forth the groans of their lament as blackening feathers, the teacher immediately flies in contemplation, like a raven considering refreshment for its young by bringing down food from on high; and, while they gape, he brings food again to their mouths, supplying by speech the nourishment of life to hungry disciples from the understanding which he has begun to receive.

He refreshes them from heavenly things all the more eagerly as he knows more truly that they are becoming black from the world’s brightness through the lamentation of repentance.

Moreover, while the young clothe themselves in the black color of feathers, they promise flight from themselves; for the more disciples think lowly of themselves and afflict themselves by despising themselves, the more abundantly they promise hope of their progress toward higher things.

Hence the teacher takes greater care to feed quickly those whom he already foresees, by certain signs, may benefit others also. Thus Paul admonishes Timothy to nourish more attentively those young which are putting forth feathers, saying:

> “What you have heard from me before many witnesses, entrust to faithful people who will be capable of teaching others also” (2 Timothy 2).

[Note: This most ignorant man made an even cruder mistake here when he corrected *commenda* (“entrust”) to *commendas* (“you entrust”), because the other manuscript had read it most corruptly. But a wiser hand has already erased the letter *s* in it, and we too have expunged it here.]

When this discernment in teaching is cautiously preserved by a preacher, a more abundant supply of preaching is granted him by God. For when through charity he knows how to suffer with afflicted disciples, and through discernment understands the fitting time for instruction, he receives greater gifts of understanding not only for himself but also for those upon whom he expends the efforts of his labor.

It is fitting, therefore, dearest brethren, that we give thanks to almighty God, who, while he prepared food for the raven—that is, for the Jewish people, black through the fault of unbelief and destined to come to faith at the end of the world—by the young crying to him, namely the apostles preaching, brought us to the knowledge of his faith through their wandering, by which they were scattered throughout the whole world.

Persecuted by the Jews, they were driven from their own places, as has been said, and wandered far and wide for our instruction.

But let us hear what our Redeemer, when about to ascend into heaven, says to the young of this raven—the holy apostles, sons of Judaea according to the flesh:

> “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16),

that is, to every nation.

And he added:

> “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.”

As if to say: “He who believes with that faith which works through love shall be saved” [Note: Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 2.]

Undoubtedly, the person who joins works worthy of right faith will be saved. “But he who does not believe shall be condemned.”

God looks upon faith in the heart, where people cannot excuse themselves when they feign truth with their mouths while retaining in their hearts the impiety of error.

Hence blessed Isidore, our patron, says [Note: *Ibid.*]:

> “Faith without works is empty, and in vain does he flatter himself on the basis of faith alone who is not adorned with good works. Some are Christians only in faith, but in deed depart from Christian teaching.”

It follows:

> “And these signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak with new tongues; they shall take up serpents.”

Are we therefore not believers if we do not perform these bodily signs? These signs were necessary at the beginning of the Church’s birth, so that faith might be nourished by miracles. Now that the Church has been established in faith, signs are not necessary [Note: Repeat here: “They shall cast out demons”; and below: “They shall speak with new tongues.”]

Yet even today the Church spiritually performs these signs, when through the grace of exorcism it lays hands upon believers and expels evil spirits.

This happens when believers leave behind the worldly words of their former life, proclaim holy mysteries, and extol God’s praises and power as far as they are able.

They take up serpents when by good exhortations they remove malice from others’ hearts.

“And if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them.” Those drink something deadly, as it were, who hear destructive persuasions; but these will not harm them if they do not break forth into the practice of wicked deeds.

“They shall lay hands upon the sick, and they shall be well.” Through God’s grace, ministers of the Church frequently do this when they strengthen their neighbors in good work and fortify them by the example of good conduct.

These miracles are greater in proportion as they are spiritual, because through them souls, not bodies, are raised.

Let us also question Luke the Evangelist, dearest brethren, and most gladly hear what the Son of God and the Virgin said to his disciples when about to ascend into heaven.

> “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).

After he had perfectly instructed the disciples in the power of prayer, although he could, if he wished, have strengthened them at once, he delayed, saying: “But remain in the city,” and so forth.

Why did he not immediately strengthen them to endure the adversities of human wickedness? Namely, in order to give an example to those who followed, lest the imperfect presume to preach before the proper time.

Moreover, one remains in the city who confines himself within the enclosure of his own mind, lest he wander abroad in vain speech, so that, when he has been perfectly imbued with divine power, he may then go out from himself, as it were, to instruct others.

It follows:

> “And he led them out as far as Bethany, outside the city, and lifting up his hands he blessed them.”

Beautifully did the Son of God, about to bless his disciples, lead them out into Bethany, which is called “the house of obedience,” because he who descended from heaven on account of the disobedience of the perverse—namely, the first human beings—ascended on account of the obedience of those converted.

This village, Bethany, is situated on the side of the Mount of Olives, because the house of the obedient Church, worthy of apostolic hospitality, has laid the foundations of faith, hope, and love nowhere but on the side of the highest mountain, that is, Christ.

From this side it rejoices that the sacrament of blood and water, by which it is born and nourished, flowed forth. From his power, that is, his divinity, it desires the gifts of spiritual anointing and awaits the promises of light and peace.

Further, because Bethany was near Jerusalem, about fifteen stadia away—a number suited to the mysteries of Scripture because it consists of seven and eight—it contains either the life which now is and that which is to come; or the Old and New Testaments; or the future sabbath-rest of souls and the resurrection of the flesh.

Therefore, those to whom he opened the knowledge of both Testaments, those whom he taught every rule for living and hoping, he led forth fifteen stadia, namely to the place where he would bless them and entrust to them the commands for teaching.

Rightly he separated the place of ascension from the place of the Passion by fifteen stadia, in order to strengthen equally in desire and love all who wish either to live or to die for him: first, by the desire of rest after death, and finally by the desire of resurrection from the dead.

Then follows: “And it came to pass, while he was blessing them, that he withdrew from them and was borne up into heaven. And they, worshipping him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy.” He withdrew in body, but was present in majesty. He departed in bodily presence, but through his divinity he was with them all days, even to the consummation of the age. “They returned,” he says, “to Jerusalem with great joy.” For there they were commanded to await the promise of the Father: namely, the Holy Spirit, the Comforter, the wisest Teacher, and against every adversity the strongest guardian and defender. Nor without reason did those who saw the Redeemer of all ascending to God the Father after the triumph of the resurrection return with great joy to the holy city. [Col. 1157B] “And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God.” Fittingly indeed they stood in the house of God, praising and blessing God, since they had seen their master, true God and true man, penetrate the heavens.

This, surely, is that lioness—that is, the primitive Church, at first constituted in the small number of disciples; and these are the hungry cubs of that lioness, of whom the blessed Job speaks when he says:

“Will you take prey for the lioness, or fill the soul of her cubs?” (Job 38). [Note: [Col. 1157D] Gregory, *Morals*, book 30, ch. 7.]

This surely is that lioness of whom blessed Job had earlier spoken, when he saw proud Judaea passed over while the Church preached: “The sons of merchants have not trodden it, nor has the lioness passed through it” (Job 28). [Col. 1157C] [Note: [Col. 1157D] “While the Church preached.”] Therefore the Lord takes prey for this lioness, that he may fill the soul of her cubs, because for the increase of this Church he seized innumerable peoples from the Gentile world, and by the gain of souls satisfied the hungry desires of the apostles.

For they were called cubs because of the tenderness of their minds and the weakness of their fear, since, after the Lord’s suffering, they sat with the doors shut, as it is written: “When it was evening on that day, the first of the Sabbaths, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst and said to them: Peace be with you” (John 20). Hence concerning these same cubs [Col. 1157D] it is aptly added: “When they lie in their dens and lurk in caves.” [Note: [Col. 1158D] “Also.”]

For when the holy apostles did not yet rise up against the members of the devil—that is, against the priests and Pharisees—with the voice of free preaching, and, not yet strengthened after the Lord’s passion by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, did not preach their Redeemer with firm authority, they still lay in wait against their adversaries as though in dens. With the doors shut, the cubs who were to seize the world lay as it were in certain dens, or hidden away in their caves, and afterward would carry off the prey of souls. At that time it is certain that, by hiding even from themselves, they feared the assault of the world. With those doors shut, these cubs sought by ambush the death of our death, in order to kill our guilt and put to death in us every life of sin. [Col. 1158A]

To the first of these hungry cubs, now already strong, when the Gentile world was shown in a sheet, as though prey had been displayed, it is said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). To these cubs, still weak as it were and therefore required to lie in dens, the Lord says: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).

Are they not rightly called the lioness’s cubs—that is, the Church’s children—who, born in the Church, seized the hostile world with their mouth? We know that these things were done by the holy apostles, and we see them now also done by upright teachers. For although they are fathers of the peoples who follow them, they are nevertheless children of those who went before them. [Col. 1158B] Hence they are not without reason called cubs. Or certainly, although they are teachers of some believers, they glory in being disciples of the universal Church.

Thus the Lord takes prey for the lioness, because by the power of his inspiration he snatches the life of sinners from error, and fills the souls of her cubs, because through the conversion of many he first satisfies the desires of teachers. Of these cubs it is rightly added: “When they lie in dens and lurk in caves.”

For not every time is suitable for teaching. Often a teacher’s strength is lost if a word is uttered out of season. Often, too, what is said more gently is given force by the fitting concurrence of time. He, therefore, knows how to teach rightly who knows how to keep silence in due order. For what advantage is there in rebuking an angry person at the very time when, with his mind unhinged, he can scarcely bear even himself, much less take in another’s words? [Col. 1158C] Whoever rebukes a raging person by invective is like one who inflicts blows on a drunkard who feels nothing.

Therefore, in order that teaching may reach the hearer’s heart, it must weigh the moments of time that are suitable to it. Thus it is well said of these same cubs: “When they lie in dens and lurk in caves.” For holy teachers sometimes perceive matters requiring rebuke; yet, while they restrain themselves in thought through silence, they lie hidden as though in caves and cover themselves as though in dens, because they conceal themselves within their own hearts. But when they find the opportune moment, they suddenly leap forth. They keep silent about none of the things that ought to be said, and immediately terrify the neck of the proud by rebuke. [Col. 1158D]

Whether through the apostles, therefore, or through the teachers whom he has appointed in the apostles’ place, the Lord daily takes prey for this lioness, that is, the holy Church; and through those whom he has captured, he does not cease to capture others also. For the righteous seize sinners from this world in order that, through those converted, others too may be seized from the world. Hence the Gentile world itself, captured by the devout mouth of the apostles, now hungers for others with as great a hunger as it recognizes that it itself had been desired by the apostles. [Note: [Col. 1158D] “Desired.”]

Then follows: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand [Col. 1159A] of God.” Note that we sometimes find “heavens” in the plural and sometimes “heaven” in the singular; but by a certain loose manner of speech we use singular things in the plural and plural things for the singular. Let it therefore be said more plainly: the Lord Jesus, who descended from heaven, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven—namely, whence he had come—and sits at the right hand of God; and now judges all things with the Father, and at the end of all things will come as judge.

But Stephen, when he was being stoned, saw him standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7), because, being engaged in combat, he had him as his helper. “But they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by the signs that followed.” [Note: [Col. 1159D] “The word.”] The command is accompanied by obedience, and obedience by signs.

[Col. 1159B] Meanwhile, let us hear what Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles. “After Christ’s ascension,” he says, “the apostles returned to Jerusalem from the mountain called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath-day’s journey away; and they persevered in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers” (Acts 1).

Their prayer was pure indeed, since it merited heavenly gifts; beyond doubt it was clean from every evil, since it obtained from God such abundant spiritual gifts. This pure prayer of the holy apostles and most holy prayer of the other faithful was prefigured by that incense which, at the Lord’s command through Moses, was compounded from four most fragrant substances ground to the finest powder: stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense [Col. 1159C] (Exod. 30).

Blessed John also shows in the Apocalypse that these were prepared as figures of the prayers of the faithful, saying: “The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each having harps and golden bowls full of fragrances, which are the prayers of the saints” (Rev. 5).

Although the natures and kinds of these four fragrances also seem to signify the four elements: frankincense, by its brightness, corresponds to air; stacte to waters; galbanum and onycha to earth and fire. Thus prayer, the incense of praise offered to God by this creation, comes from all things that are in heaven, beneath heaven, on earth, and in the waters. [Col. 1159D]

Let Matthew also, the wise and discerning evangelist, enriched with the gift of the Holy Spirit, come forward and tell us, who desire to hear, what the Son of God and of the Virgin commanded his disciples as he was about to ascend into heaven: “Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28).

This order is entirely fitting. The hearer must first be taught, then imbued with the sacraments, and then trained to keep the commandments; for before the soul receives faith, baptism is not to be given. Nor can anyone be cleansed by baptism unless he has endeavoured to do good works.

It follows: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” namely, in confession of the holy Trinity, because unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, one cannot enter the kingdom of God (John 3). “Teaching them,” he says, “to keep all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28), because faith without works is insufficient for attaining eternal blessedness.

Therefore I tell you and solemnly charge you, O Jews: unless you believe in Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, and faithfully receive his baptism in the name of the holy Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as said above—you cannot be saved.

But even if you do not believe me because of envy or hatred, question the Apostle Paul: born of your own people, educated at the feet of Gamaliel your teacher, instructed in the law of God, mercifully enlightened by Jesus Christ, the Son of God and man, and caught up even to the third heaven. Ask him diligently whether circumcision or baptism avails for salvation; hold firmly what he judged ought rather to be maintained, and hasten zealously to fulfil it.

He too grieves deeply over your blindness and unbelief, as he often reports in the Acts of the Apostles. “I wished,” he says, “to be anathema from Christ for my brothers, who are of the race of Israel” (Rom. 9). And again: “Brothers, the desire and prayer of my heart for them is made to God for salvation” (Rom. 10).

Therefore answer your fellow-tribesmen and kinsmen, O holy Paul, and offer them counsel as to what will most profit them for eternal salvation. If, as you assert, you became debtor to all—to the wise and the foolish, Greeks and barbarians alike (Rom. 1)—yet you must first announce Christ’s commands to the Jews.

“If you are circumcised,” he says, “O Jews, Christ will profit you nothing. For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5).

But if perhaps, O Jews, because of hatred for Christ’s name, you are unwilling to receive the wholly true testimony of the Apostle Paul, surely you cannot deny the sayings of your prophets, which agree with Paul’s testimony. Rather, you ought beyond doubt to yield faith to their words as heralds of truth.

Did not the prophet Zechariah, one of the Twelve and taught by the Holy Spirit, when he said, “On that day”—that is, at Christ’s advent—“there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and Jerusalem” (Zech. 13), foretell that Christ’s baptism would exist in the Church? [Col. 1160D]

For the house of David and Jerusalem are Christ’s Church, in which the fountain of baptism remains for the remission of sins. “On that day,” he says, “there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman.”

Tell me, unhappy and faithless Jews, who, following to this day the blindness of your fathers, observe bodily circumcision without cause and deny the Son of God to your own condemnation: tell me, who is this open fountain, if not he in whom all Christians are baptized in the name of the holy Trinity—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—through whom the bonds of sins are loosed and the defilements of the menstruous woman, that is, of the unclean soul, are washed away? [Col. 1161A]

Of the waters of this fountain the same prophet testifies elsewhere, saying: “On that day living waters shall go out from Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and half of them toward the western sea” (Zech. 14).

What then are these living waters but the waters of baptism, which make a human being alive through the infusion of the heavenly Spirit? But why are they announced as going out from Jerusalem, except because the Lord, dwelling among that people, said to his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit”?

But one half of them goes to the eastern sea, that is, to the people of the circumcision, [Col. 1161B] and one half to the western sea, that is, to the people of the Gentiles, last in faith; so that he may grant remission of sins through baptism to all peoples, Jews and Gentiles alike.

Of these waters it is further said through the same prophet that they go out from the house of the Lord, increase into a river, and proceed to the Dead Sea or to the wildernesses, and that all things to which they come are made alive and healed (Ezek. 47). For he says:

“I returned to the gate of the house of the Lord, and behold, water went out from beneath the threshold of the house toward the east; for the front of the house faced eastward. And the waters descended along the side of the temple, at its extremity, namely south of the altar. And I returned by the way outside the outer gate, the way which faced eastward; and behold, waters overflowing from the right side” (ibid.), [Col. 1161C] that is, from Christ’s side.

“On that day,” he says, “the Lord shall be one, and his name one” (Zech. 14), with all idols, namely, destroyed. Truly there is one God, besides whom there is no other: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and his name is one, in which all the faithful ought to be baptized, washed from sins, and renewed in the knowledge and love of that one God.

To him Solomon says in the Song of Spiritual Love: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you” (Song 1). [Note: [Col. 1161D] Gregory, on this passage.]

For what are signified by the young women except holy souls, regenerated by the water of baptism through the Holy Spirit and transferred into Christ’s new creation through the New Testament? [Col. 1161D] They love Christ because of the pouring out of oil, because, called to grace, they find in him the sweetness of everlasting life; and for love of that sweetness they reject all the pomp and riches of the world.

For your salvation also, O Jews, I exhort you to drive from your hearts the oldness of the ancient law and hasten to be renewed by Christ’s baptism, so that you may be counted among God’s elect. Do you think that you can reach the homeland of paradise without baptismal purification? By no means. For no one can be saved unless born again of water and the Holy Spirit (John 3).

But if you do not believe me, a Christian man bearing the banner of Christ’s cross on my forehead, read the prophet Isaiah, and you will find that baptism was foretold by him. Thus he himself sang beforehand of the future for Jews and Gentiles desiring to be saved in Jesus Christ.

“You shall draw waters with joy,” he says, “from the fountains of the Saviour” (Isa. 12). By these words he also indicates the Saviour himself, from whose fountains he proclaims that waters of purification are to be drawn—that is, from Jesus. For *Jesus* is interpreted in the Hebrew language as “Saviour.”

Hence he himself cries out, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.” “This,” however, “he said of the Spirit, whom those believing in him receive,” namely in baptism (John 7). John baptized with water, but Jesus baptizes in the Holy Spirit: to this sacrament of baptism Isaiah likewise summons Jews and Gentiles, [Col. 1162B] saying: “All who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55), namely, the waters of baptism and the reception of the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit also announces these waters and this fountain through the prophet Joel, saying: “The mountains shall drip sweetness, the hills shall flow with milk and honey, waters shall go through all the streams of Judah, and a fountain shall go out from the house of the Lord and water the torrent of thorns” (Joel 3), that is, it shall purify the whole body of the Gentiles in baptism.

Let the prophet Micah also come forward, O unbelieving and obstinate Jews, and show you the sacraments of baptism under the figure of the crossing of the sea. If you do not believe me, at least believe him, whom you cannot contradict at all. O Micah, prophet of truth, show Jews and Gentiles the fountain of their salvation! [Col. 1162C]

“According to the days of your coming out of the land of Egypt, O Israel, I will show them”—namely, the Gentiles—“wonders. The nations shall see and be confounded; they shall put their hand over their mouth. They shall glorify and fear your God” (Mic. 7).

And he added: “What god is like you, who takes away iniquities,” namely through baptism, “and removes the sin of the remnant,” that is, of the Gentiles, namely those who are to be born about the ninth hour? “He will cast down all our iniquities and cast all our sins into the depth of the sea” (ibid.).

In this statement the reader should observe that the mystery of baptism is revealed most plainly to Jews and Gentiles. “According to the days of your coming out of Egypt,” he says, “I will show them,” namely the Gentiles, “wonders.” [Col. 1162D] What testimony could be clearer or more explicit?

Israel—that is, the Christian people, seeing God through faith—goes out from Egypt when it renounces the world. It enters the Red Sea, that is, baptism, marked by Christ’s blood. Then the pursuing enemies perish, because sins immediately die—that is, are wiped out—and the souls of those regenerated rise again.

Moreover, when he turns back to himself in saying, “He will cast down all our iniquities and cast our sins into the depth of the sea,” he shows that the Jews too will someday come to faith and obtain remission of sins through Christ’s baptism.

O Jewish people, crooked and perverse people, people without counsel and without spiritual understanding! Why do you not faithfully receive—indeed, what is more serious, why do you pass by with deaf ear—the testimonies of so many truth-speaking prophets from your own law, testimonies consistent with one another? [Col. 1163A]

O miserable people! You have the law constantly before your hands, yet do not understand its sacraments at all. Therefore you depart empty from its reading, because you do not seek its spiritual understanding. But although you are ungrateful for God’s benefits and for my warnings, I shall nevertheless willingly explain to you the figures of the law.

When, at the Lord’s command, Moses washed Aaron and his sons with water, did he not prefigure Christ’s baptism? You cannot deny, even if you wished, that Aaron was washed with water before he entered the Holy of Holies. His sons also, sharers in their father’s priesthood, are purified at the Lord’s command by the sanctification of water (Exod. 29). [Col. 1163B]

Even then that sanctification bore the form of baptism, by the sacrament of whose washing the entire people of the Church—indeed, the body of the great and true priest Jesus Christ—is now washed for remission of sins; and, its filth cleansed, it is consecrated in sanctification to divine worship.

Thus, even at that time Aaron and his sons prefigured the cleansing of the Christian people, the holiness of all things belonging to ecclesiastical religion, and the sacraments of baptism. They do not receive their garments until their filth has first been washed away; nor are they adorned for sacred rites unless they are reborn as new persons in Christ.

That Moses washes the priests indicates the law. For we must be washed by God’s commands, so that, when made fit for Christ’s clothing and having put off the tunics of skin of our first parents, we may then put on the linen garment that has nothing of death in it, but is wholly white; so that, rising from baptism, we may gird our loins in truth and all the shamefulness of former sins may be hidden. [Col. 1163C]

Know therefore, O Jews, that unless you receive Christ’s baptism in devout faith, you cannot be saved at all (John 3). But if perhaps, as faithless and rebellious people, you still do not believe me, I shall bring forward to overcome your unbelief the judgment of almighty God, uttered through the mouth of the prophet Isaiah.

Certainly, if until now you have refused to receive the testimonies of the holy prophets, at least now you ought joyfully to receive, for your salvation, the command of God, who gives the law and governs all things, and whom you are altogether unable to resist or contradict.

For when the Lord, rejecting your sacrifices, feasts, and new moons, had said through the prophet mentioned above:

“What is the multitude of your victims to me? I am full of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fatlings; I have not desired the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. Offer sacrifice no more in vain; incense is an abomination to me. New moons, Sabbath, and other feasts I will not endure, for they have become burdensome to me” (Isa. 1),

he immediately, approving—or rather already foretelling—baptism, added shortly afterward: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (ibid.). [Col. 1163D]

Therefore, in place of all the victims he had mentioned, and of all new moons, Sabbaths, and solemnities, he commands baptismal purification alone. Likewise, in place of every defilement of sins, he sets forth the washing of regeneration alone, by which sins are washed away.

Because this man rejects it, O Jews, hear Ezekiel threatening you: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, make Jerusalem know her abominations, and say to them: Thus says the Lord: Jerusalem, your root and your generation are from the land of Canaan; your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. And when you were born, on the day of your birth, your navel was not cut, and you were not washed with water for salvation” (Ezek. 16).

This shows that Jerusalem is in great sins, and will therefore perish if it is not washed with water for salvation—which is assuredly the full sanctification of baptism. [Col. 1164B] But to those who are converted and baptized, the word of the Lord there says: “I entered into my covenant with you, says the Lord, and I washed you with water, cleansed your blood from you, and anointed you with oil” (ibid.), signifying by the covenant the New Testament, and by water and oil baptism and chrism.

The Holy Spirit promises through the same prophet that the purification of this baptism shall come upon them, saying: “I shall take you from the nations, gather you from all lands, and bring you into your own land. And I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36), namely, through the sacrament of baptism.

[Col. 1164C] Since, therefore, I grieve for your miseries, O Jews, I return so often to address you. If you listen to me patiently and receive my warnings with a simple and faithful mind, I shall give you counsel for eternal salvation: namely, that by gradually withdrawing from your former manner of life—that is, from ancestral error—you may be renewed among the children of the Church, understand the Scriptures of the Old Testament spiritually, and advance day by day in the knowledge of God.

This, then, is my counsel: set aside every doubt and receive the New Testament. For a new man came into the world, namely the Son of God and of the Virgin, and gave new commandments to the world—to all human beings.

Know assuredly that unless you faithfully and firmly believe in Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, conceived by the Holy Spirit, you will by no means be able to understand spiritually the Scriptures of the Old Testament, as Isaiah declares to you in these words: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand, nor shall you remain” (Isa. 7). [Col. 1164D]

Truly, because neither you nor your fathers believed in Christ the Son of God, you have been blinded with respect to understanding the Scriptures. Nor have you remained: neither in God’s commandments nor in the land of promise; but by God’s just judgment, as sacrilegious murderers and reprobates, you have been scattered through all parts of the world and oppressed in servitude under all peoples beneath heaven.

Therefore, O most miserable Jews, because you did not believe, neither have you remained. Has this not happened to you just as you read in the prophet Hosea? For, foreseeing your captivity by the prophetic Spirit, he speaks in great sadness and grief, saying:

“The children of Israel shall sit without king, without priest, without altar, and without sacrifice” (Hos. 3).

That this is so, as is written, is plain to all. Do you not understand, O Jews, why such great evils have happened to you? By no means. I know well that you do not understand, precisely because you do not believe.

But I, because I firmly and faithfully believe in one true God—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—understand why such great evils have come upon you; and for your salvation I wish briefly to explain it to your ears. The severe and cruel judgment of your fathers bound you to such evils even before you came forth from your mother’s womb. [Col. 1165B]

Desiring without cause cruelly to shed the blood of Jesus Christ himself, God and man, they shouted insolently to Pilate: “His blood be upon us and upon our children!” (Matt. 27).

This imprecation—that is, curse—once expelled you from Judaea, grievously afflicts you today, subjects you to servitude beneath all the nations under heaven, and at the final judgment will without doubt condemn you unless you faithfully believe in Christ and devoutly receive his baptism.

What then, O most miserable people, are you doing? Why do you moreover spend time in vain? You do not observe the law; you have no king; you do not honour priests; you do not build an altar; you do not offer sacrifice; you do not keep the Old Testament; you do not receive the New; you observe without cause circumcision, which long ago came to its end in Christ; and you reject Christ’s baptism, prefigured by patriarchs and prophets in your law, in which remission of sins is found. [Col. 1165C]

O unhappy—indeed, most unhappy—people! You are not Jews, you refuse to be Christians: what good, then, do you do? Since you live irrationally—that is, without law and without Gospel—and squander God’s benefits ungratefully, you are undoubtedly heading toward eternal damnation.

What then? Do you fear that, if you receive the New Testament, you will offend God? By no means. God himself, author of the Old and New Testaments, commanded you to forget the carnal observances of the old law and to receive the sacraments of the Gospel, where he says through the prophet Isaiah:

“Do not remember former things, and do not look upon ancient things. Behold, I shall make new things, which shall now spring forth, and you shall know them” (Isa. 43). [Col. 1165D]

And, to show what these would be, he added: “I shall make a way in the wilderness and rivers in a waterless place, to give drink to my chosen people and my people whom I have acquired” (ibid.).

What did he signify by these words except the future purification of baptism? In it no one is now marked by the old bodily circumcision, but by the grace of baptism alone, through which one is also washed by faith.

Know also, O Jews, that although you possess the law and the prophets, you cannot be saved at all, as Jeremiah testifies in the voice of the Lord:

“Even if Moses and Samuel should stand before me, my soul is not toward this people. Cast them out from before my face, and let them go forth” (Jer. 15).

For Moses signifies the law and Samuel the prophecies. Although you have them, O Jews, you are nevertheless cast away because of the impiety of your error. For your works and your righteousness will not profit you without faith in Christ, as the Lord testifies through the same prophet: “Because you have forgotten me, behold, I shall proclaim your righteousness, and your works shall not profit you” (Isa. 57). [Col. 1166A]

What profit is it to you, then, O miserable people, to exist unhappily in this age and perish in the future? Your works are useless and hateful to God. You labour in vain, therefore; you spend in emptiness the days granted to you in this present life, and you tend toward non-being while you deny the Son of God and of the Virgin and refuse to receive his Gospel.

It is better to die than to live badly; better not to be than to be unhappy. It would have been far better for you not to have been brought into being in this world than to suffer the eternal punishments of unbelief in hell.

In this present life, as the Psalmist says, because of unbelief you have been rejected from the hand of God (Ps. 87); and in the life to come you are to be condemned unless you have been born again of water and the Holy Spirit, as we have already testified many times.

Therefore return inwardly to yourselves, and cleanse by the hand of discernment the eyes of your mind, now bleared by the long-standing blindness of unbelief, so that you may receive with devout mind and pure heart the new commandments of Jesus Christ, God and man. [Col. 1166C]

Moses the lawgiver undoubtedly prefigured this deadly blindness of your mind when, after a fast of forty days, he descended from the mountain with a horned—that is, glorified—face from communion with God’s speech; and, when it was seen, he covered it with a veil lest the children of Israel be terrified (Exod. 34). [Note: [Col. 1165D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 43.]

Thus Moses’ descending again from the mountain, his face being seen as horned—that is, glorified—yet covered with a veil, signified that the same law is covered and concealed by a mystical veil for unbelieving people, as the prophet Isaiah testifies:

“The words of this book,” he says, “shall be like the words of a sealed book; if anyone gives it to one who does not know letters and says, ‘Read,’ he will answer, ‘I do not know letters.’ And again, if it is given to another who knows letters and one says, ‘Read,’ he will answer, ‘I cannot, for the book is sealed’” (Isa. 29). [Col. 1166D]

These, O foolish Jews, are the seals of the Old Testament, which your obstinacy of mind has closed to you, but the Son of God and of the Virgin has opened to us who believe.

For the law is bound up only among the faithful, as the Lord testifies through the prophet Isaiah: “Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples” (Isa. 8). Why? Namely, lest Jews, pagans, or heretics find it, because they are not Christ’s disciples.

The word of the law, therefore, as has been said, possesses the hidden glory of knowledge; it also possesses the horns of the two Testaments, by which it advances armed against doctrines of falsehood.

When, therefore, O Jews, Moses is read, a veil lies over your heart; and clearly, while you read the Scriptures of the prophets and, through the excessive dullness of your heart, understand them carnally, the whole face of Moses is covered by a kind of veil, so that you cannot endure the glory of the law that speaks.

But unless you believe in Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin, and faithfully receive his Gospel—that is, the New Testament—the veil will not at all be taken from your hearts. Thus Isaiah’s sentence is entirely true: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand, nor shall you remain” (Isa. 7). [Col. 1167A]

[Note: [Col. 1167D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 55.]

This obscurity of the prophets too was certainly prefigured by the veil that hung in the middle of the temple and concealed the Holy of Holies within, lest it be seen by people (Exod. 40). [Col. 1167B]

But after Christ came, at the time of his passion that veil was torn from top to bottom; all those things which had been hidden were revealed through his passion, resurrection, and ascension, for the strengthening of our faith, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “God has revealed them to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep and lofty things of God” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore the mysteries of the law have been laid open to believers through Christ; but to you, O foolish and malicious Jews, they are shut, just as the angel says to Daniel among other things: “The words are closed and sealed until the time of consummation” (Dan. 12), that is, until Christ’s incarnation, until many may learn and the vision be fulfilled; and then those who are instructed shall understand all these things. [Col. 1167C]

Why then, O Jews, do you remain unbelieving so long and neglect the salvation of your souls with such obstinacy? You know from the Scriptures that the fullness of the time appointed by God came long ago; you see that the figures and enigmas of the patriarchs, as well as the sayings of the prophets, have manifestly been fulfilled in Christ; you read in so many attestations of the holy Scriptures that the New Testament was commanded by the Lord; you plainly see that Christ’s baptism was prefigured in your law.

What further do you await, O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken? Does any scruple of unbelief still remain in your mind? Certainly, if because of the hardness of your stony heart you refuse to believe the other teachers of your law, you ought at least to give faith to the sayings of Solomon, the wisest king. [Col. 1167D]

Listen then with a tranquil ear to what he says in the Song of Spiritual Love concerning the two Testaments, in the person of the bride—that is, the holy Church—to Jesus Christ, the heavenly bridegroom:

“All manner of fruits, new and old, my brother, I have kept for you” (Song 7). [Note: [Col. 1167D] Gregory, on this passage.] Here, by “all fruits” [Note: [Col. 1168D] Fruits.] are understood the senses of the holy Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments. As these reach us from the holy Fathers—namely, the patriarchs and prophets, the apostles, and the other doctors of the Church—and are believed, they are like fruits growing from trees, by which souls are delighted. Therefore the bride keeps all fruits, new and old, for her beloved Jesus Christ, because the Catholic Church receives the New Testament without rejecting the Old; and venerates the Old in such a way that she always understands the New spiritually, even within the old and carnal sacrifices: rejoicing that Christ has come in the New, while in the Old always awaiting his coming. Therefore, just as grain is nourished and stored in the ear, so the New Testament is contained and veiled in the Old. I therefore urge you, O Jews, to hold the Old Testament in such a way that you understand the New spiritually within it; and to strive to fulfil not the carnal works of the Old Testament but the spiritual works of the New. Do you fear that, if you receive the New Testament, you will act against God’s command? By no means. For while you remain unbelieving, the veil of Moses is still laid over your hearts. Hear therefore, O rebels and unbelievers, more full of deceit and fraud than all other people, how mercifully God promises to all believers the gifts of the two Testaments: “I will give you,” he says, “the early and the latter rain,” that is, the Old and New Testament, “and with both showers I will water you” (Deut. 11). For the rain of each Testament is understood as doctrine. Hence it is said: “Let my utterance be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew, like a shower upon the grass, and like drops upon the herbage” (Deut. 32). Therefore, O Jews, since you are convicted by so many suitable witnesses drawn from your own law and nation, and sufficiently instructed by an abundance of most true reasoning, you ought no longer to be prepared to resist the truth, but to receive the New Testament and believe that the Son of God and of the Virgin came into the world for human salvation. Indeed, we have produced so many testimonies of truth from the Law and the Prophets in order that, once Moses’ veil has been removed from your hearts and Christ’s baptism received, we may be able to have you as fellow sharers in eternal blessedness.

Your Law has long shown, through many authorities which you read, that Christ’s baptism—without which no one can be saved—was prefigured for you. Therefore it is necessary also to show you how the holy chrism, by which the heads of all Christians are anointed in baptism in the name of the Holy Trinity, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, was foreshadowed by God in that same Law: both to confirm our faith and to remove your uncertainty, so that, being perfectly instructed in all things and devoted to the Catholic faith, you may be counted among the children of the holy Church. For all believers who believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit ought to be anointed with sacred chrism, as the Lord speaks figuratively to Moses, saying:

“Take for yourself the finest spices and olive oil, and make [Col. 1169A] a holy oil of anointing, namely a compounded ointment; and with it anoint the tabernacle of testimony, the ark of the covenant, the table with its vessels, the lampstand and all its implements, the altars, namely of incense and of burnt offering, and everything belonging to their service. You shall sanctify all these things, and they shall be Holy of Holies; and whoever touches them shall be sanctified. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and sanctify them, that they may exercise the priesthood for me. You shall also say to the children of Israel: This oil of holy anointing shall be yours throughout your generations” (Exod. 30). [Note: [Col. 1169D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 57.]

The figure of this former tabernacle is applied as a type of the Church. Moreover, the ointment by which the tabernacle is anointed is the chrism by which the faithful people are anointed, among whom the Divinity dwells as in a tabernacle. [Col. 1169B] The entire diversity of its peoples is anointed as a testimony of holiness, which was figured through that diversity of works, so that all, anointed with the anointing of sacred chrism, may be sanctified and, once sanctified, prepared for the glory of God. This ointment may also be understood as the virtues of the saints, or as the fragrance of righteousness spread far and wide, of which the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us in every place the fragrance of his righteousness” (2 Cor. 2).

Therefore, O Jews, receive Christ’s baptism with the utmost devotion, so that through his gift you may be renewed in his fear and love, as he himself promises you through the prophet: “I will give you,” he says, “a new heart, and I will put my Spirit in your midst, and [Col. 1169C] I will cause you to walk in my commandments,” namely evangelical commandments, “and to keep and perform my ordinances” (Ezek. 36).
