That is, that you may reciprocally possess the love of God and neighbour, which is the fulfilment of the Law (Rom. 13). If, therefore, you are truly Jews—that is, confessors—you ought not to be last among the other nations in confessing God, but altogether first. Just as the word of God ought first to have been preached to you, so you ought to have been readier than all nations to obey the faith. Depart, therefore, from the devil, whom you have long served, and he will flee from you; and, according to the counsel of the blessed Apostle, draw near to God and he will draw near to you (Jas. 4).

Hear also David, king and prophet, namely [Col. 1169D] wise in speech and mighty in battle, and willingly do whatever he tells you for your salvation. “Draw near,” he says, “to God and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be confounded” (Ps. 33), namely at the examination of his final judgment. With the same Prophet pour out prayers to the Lord, that he may mercifully deign to drive away the darkness of ignorance from the eyes of your minds. Let each of you, then, say to God with the Psalmist, in a suppliant mind and pure devotion: “Unveil my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your Law” (Ps. 118). Therefore preserve the faith whole and inviolate, and fulfil it in worthy conduct, for it is truly the gate of the Church. For no one [Col. 1170A] can enter the holy Church unless he has first held the Catholic faith. “For without faith no one can please God” (Heb. 11). Therefore, as Scripture says, “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2), because, as the body is dead without the soul, so the soul is dead without faith (Jas. 2).

Therefore, O Jews, the more grievous the bondage under which you are oppressed in the present age, the more ardently you ought to strive toward true liberty. In the patriarchs and prophets, on account of God’s goodness, you were dearer to God than all the nations under heaven; but now, on account of the faithlessness of your unbelief, you have become more contemptible. For according to Moses’ pronouncement, you have always provoked the Lord by the works of your hands (Deut. 31), and therefore you have become a reproach to all [Col. 1170B] people. You too have filled up the measure of your fathers (Matt. 23): you fastened to the cross the Son of God, especially promised to you by God the Father in order to call you back to the pastures of eternal life. His apostles, who showed you the way of salvation, you not only refused to hear, but, after inflicting many beatings and wounds upon them, you stubbornly and cruelly drove them out of your borders. Therefore, unless you repent in accordance with the standard of ecclesiastical rule, you are worthy not of life but of death. Repent, therefore, according to the counsel of the blessed apostle Peter, and let each of you be baptized for the remission of sins (Acts 2), so that by humbly making satisfaction you may recover the grace of God which you lost by sinning. [Note: [Col. 1169D] From Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, ch. 31.] Appropriately, indeed, [Col. 1170C] blessed Peter, when about to command baptism, first set forth the tears of repentance, so that they might first wash themselves in the water of their affliction and afterward be washed by the sacrament of baptism. With what disposition, then, can those who neglect to mourn their past faults live secure concerning forgiveness of sins, when the chief shepherd of the Church himself judged that repentance should be added even to this sacrament which principally extinguishes sins? Therefore, whoever desires to be secure at death concerning pardon should never, throughout his whole life, be without repentance.

For this reason, O Jews, I admonish you so often for your salvation, because I desire all of you to be within the bowels of Jesus Christ. Receive, then, Christ’s baptism with a devout mind, and as true Christians produce worthy [Col. 1170D] fruits of repentance (Luke 3), so that you may worthily deserve to be counted among the members of the Church. Certainly, as has been said above, no one can obtain forgiveness of sins or reach the heavenly homeland except through the holy Catholic Church. Therefore, you who are prudent in secular affairs, why do you neglect for so long the salvation of your souls? Love the holy Church, then; honour her priests. For she is accustomed to pour out devout prayers to the Lord [Note: [Col. 1170D] Friday in Parasceve.] that he may mercifully deign to remove the veil of error from your hearts. May Almighty God deign to associate you, cleansed by the water of baptism from every stain of sins and aided by the prayers of that same holy Church, [Col. 1171A] with the citizens of the heavenly homeland. Amen. “I commend you to God and to his Word” (Acts 20).

Moreover, dearest brothers, we ought to desire the salvation of the souls of all people. Accordingly, after introducing authorities from the Old and New Testaments, we have exhorted the Jewish people to receive the Catholic faith, as the Holy Spirit dictated. But now, with God’s help, we must return to the narrative proposed, which we briefly interrupted above for their admonition. Let us all together hear what the most blessed Luke further reports in the Acts of the Apostles about Christ’s Ascension.

“While they watched, he was lifted up; and a cloud received [Col. 1171B] him from their eyes” (Acts 1). The vision of the prophet Daniel agrees with the words of this holy Evangelist. “I was watching,” he says, “in a vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven, and came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, kingdom, and honour, and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him” (Dan. 7). And he adds: “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be corrupted” (ibid.). By saying that he saw the vision in the night, he plainly shows that amid the pressures and distresses of this present time we walk by faith and not by sight: we do not contemplate God face to face, but as though in a mirror and in an enigma (1 Cor. 13). But when he adds, [Col. 1171C] “the Son of Man was coming in the clouds of heaven,” he indicates Christ’s virginal flesh, conceived from his Virgin Mother without male seed, solely through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit. It is of this cloud that the noble and wise prophet Isaiah speaks figuratively: “The Lord ascends upon a light cloud, and will enter Egypt” (Isa. 19). The Lord indeed ascends upon a light cloud [Note: [Col. 1171D] Perhaps “indeed”.], because the only-begotten Son of God assumed human nature without sin; clothed with it, he entered this world, which signifies Egypt, to defeat the ancient enemy. Thus the Lord ascended in a cloud, because in that same flesh which he assumed he penetrated the heavens.

Daniel again adds: “And he came even to [Col. 1171D] the Ancient of Days.” By the Ancient of Days he means God the Father, to whom the Psalmist says: “You, Lord, endure for ever, and your memorial from generation to generation” (Ps. 101). And again: “You, Lord, are the same, and your years shall not fail” (ibid.). It follows: “And they presented him before him”: namely, the angels who had ministered to him from the beginning of his human birth, as we believe, conducted him with supreme honour and reverence to the throne of paternal glory. Again he adds: “And there was given to him,” namely by God the Father, “dominion, honour, and kingdom; and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him. His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away; [Col. 1172A] and his kingdom one which shall not be corrupted.” By this testimony he shows that Christ so received dominion and kingdom from Almighty God the Father that his power is eternal and his kingdom remains for ever without an end of corruption.

That Son of God and of the Virgin, who suffered, died, and was buried for human salvation, rose again on the third day, was raised to heaven on the fortieth day, and glorified at the right hand of God the Father, was prefigured by Samson, that most mighty man, who fought against the Philistines and delivered God’s people. When one day he had entered the city of Gaza, the Philistines at once stationed guards in order that they might seize him. [Note: [Col. 1172D] From Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 12.] But he arose in the middle of the night, carried away the city gates, and [Col. 1172B] climbed to the top of the mountain (Judg. 16). Whom did Samson typify in this action except the Son of God and of the Virgin, who redeemed us by his death? What does the city of Gaza signify except hell? What is indicated by the Philistines except the faithlessness of the Jews? When they saw the Lord dead and his most holy body already laid in the tomb, they immediately appointed guards (Matt. 27), rejoicing as if they had caught and held within the prison of hell, like Samson in Gaza, him who had shone forth as the author of life. But Samson not only went out at midnight; he also carried away the gates. For our Redeemer, rising before dawn, not only went freely out of hell, but also destroyed the very barriers of hell. He carried away the gates and climbed the summit of the mountain because, by rising, [Col. 1172C] he removed the barriers of hell, and, by ascending, penetrated the kingdoms of heaven. Therefore the angels who, as stated above, ministered to him while he was in the flesh, descended with him, as we believe, when he descended to the lower world; and ascended with him when he returned to heaven. In their person, the prophet David, instructed by the Holy Spirit, says:

“Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, O eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23).

The Prophet says this in the assumed person of the angels, who went before Christ as he descended into hell or ascended into heaven. Thus the angels going before Christ to hell say to the powers of Tartarus: “O princes of hell, lift up [Col. 1172D] your gates”—that is, remove the power by which until now you have held everyone in hell. The same angels, going before Christ at his Ascension, say: “O eternal gates, which until now have been closed—the approach to heaven, the entrance into paradise—be lifted up,” that is, opened; “and the King of glory,” that is, Christ, “shall enter into heaven.” The demons, then, marvel when they hear, “Lift up your gates, O princes,” and say: “Who is this King of glory?” As though they said: We have our own king, namely the devil. Who then is this King of glory? The angels going before Christ into hell reply: “He is the strong and mighty Lord,” who conquered death and overcame the devil; [Col. 1173A] “the Lord mighty in battle” against the devil, namely your prince, because he has bound the strong one and now comes to overthrow his house and plunder his vessels—that is, to break the infernal barriers and lead captivity captive (Eph. 4). Again, the angels accompanying Christ as he returns from hell and going before him in his Ascension address the heavenly powers, that they may prepare the way for the Lord who is coming and meet him, saying: “O princes, lift up the gates,” that is, unbar the heavenly approaches for the Lord who is coming; and, “O eternal gates, be lifted up,” that is, let the approach to heaven and eternal entrance lie open. Let the ethereal gates—that is, the everlasting doors—be opened, and the King of glory shall enter into heaven, where at the Father’s right hand he will intercede for us. But these very angelic powers, astonished at the new mystery of the King clothed in flesh, [Col. 1173B] ask in wonder: “Who is this King of glory?” Other angelic powers answer them: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory.”

Therefore our Redeemer, coming for our deliverance, defeating the prince of this world, casting him out of the hearts of the faithful, and again ascending to heaven with supreme victory, through the humanity which he assumed sinlessly from the Virgin, asks God the Father, saying:

“Deliver me, and set me beside me [Note: [Col. 1173D] You.]; and let any man’s hand fight against me” (Job 17).

Almighty God the Father delivered his own Son to suffering, but delivered him by resurrection and set him beside himself by Ascension, because having gone into heaven he sits at his right hand. [Note: [Col. 1173D] From Gregory, *Morals*, Book XIII, ch. 10.] Since, after the glory [Col. 1173C] of his Ascension, Judaea was stirred up in persecution of his disciples, it is rightly now said: “And let any man’s hand fight against me.” For then the fury of persecutors raged in his members; then the flame of cruelty blazed against the lives of the faithful. But where could the wicked Jews go, or what could they do, when he whom they persecuted on earth was already seated in heaven? Of their reprobation blessed Job says: “You have removed their heart far from discipline” (ibid.). For if they had known the observance of discipline, they would never have despised our Redeemer in his preaching or driven his disciples out from their borders so that they migrated to the peoples of the Gentiles.

Let Luke the Evangelist, physician not only of bodies but also of souls, come again and add something after what has been said concerning Christ’s Ascension, which we desire with the greatest eagerness to hear. “And as they gazed into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood beside them in white garments” (Acts 1). Let us hear what blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1174D] *Homilies on the Gospels*, Homily 29.] on this verse. “We must ask,” he says, “why, when the Lord was born, angels appeared, yet are not recorded as having appeared in white garments. For white garments signify joy and festivity of mind. Why, then, when the Lord was born, do angels not appear in white garments, except because a great festival came to the angels when God-man [Col. 1174A] penetrated heaven? For at the Lord’s birth the divinity appeared humbled, but in his Ascension humanity was exalted. White garments are more fitting to exaltation than to humiliation. Therefore, at his assumption the angels ought to be seen in white garments, because he who at his birth appeared as God humbled was at his Ascension shown as man exalted.”

It should further be noted that for two reasons two men, that is, two angels, appeared to the disciples at the Lord’s Ascension: namely, that they might comfort them in their grief at the Lord’s absence and demonstrate that the Lord had truly ascended. Then the apostles and the other disciples returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which has a Sabbath-day’s journey because of its abundance of olives; that is, it was distant from Jerusalem by a Sabbath-day’s journey, [Col. 1174B] namely the space of a mile, because Jews were not permitted to proceed a greater distance from the city or village where they were, but could walk about for a thousand paces. The old edition reads: “from the mountain of three lights.” Mount Olivet was so called because at night it was illuminated from the western side by the fire of the Temple. For the fire upon the altar was continually maintained with the greatest care. In the morning it received the first rays of the sun from the east before they illuminated the city; it also possessed an abundance of oil, which is the fuel of light. When the apostles had returned to Jerusalem, all the other disciples and citizens of the city escorted them unanimously and honourably as far as their lodging, and afterward returned to their own homes. We represent this procession of the disciples, who went out unanimously [Col. 1174C] with the Crucified One going before them, when we leave the church carrying the cross before us. And although the Crucified One did not return with them, we nevertheless carry the cross as we return, because, although he was not with them in bodily presence, he was without doubt with them in spiritual presence, as he himself says: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). Thus, when we go out in procession carrying the Lord’s cross before us, we represent their going out with the Crucified One going before them. But when we carry the Lord’s cross back with us to the church, we represent his saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age.” But let us hear what the two angels clothed in white say to the apostles: “Men [Col. 1174D] of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts 1).

They are rightly called Galileans, because they had already passed from vices to virtues in resolve and desire, had already migrated from earth to heaven, and had raised the eyes both of mind and body to contemplate the glory of their Lord and Master. Since Christ fought in them, as blessed Jerome says, their citizenship was no longer on earth but in heaven (Phil. 3). Therefore the apostles and other disciples transferred their desire and love to him whom they saw penetrating heaven by his own power. We read in the Old Testament that Enoch was translated [Col. 1175A] (Gen. 5), and Elijah lifted up to the aerial heaven, which is nearest the earth (4 Kings 2). Enoch was translated not by his own power but by divine power; Elijah was caught up in a fiery chariot, because a mere human being required another’s help. He could not ascend the aerial heaven by himself, being weighed down by the weakness of his nature. Therefore both were borne up with angelic assistance, since they could not at all be lifted up by their own power. But our Redeemer is not recorded as being raised by a chariot or angelic assistance, because he was not a mere human being but true God and true man. He therefore rightly ascended by his own power above all created things, because through him God the Father made all things from nothing. For through his humanity he ascended to the place where through his divinity he always was; and he returned bodily from the place [Col. 1175B] where he remained in divinity, because with the Father and Holy Spirit he likewise contained heaven and earth.

It should further be noted that Mark says, “Jesus was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16), but Stephen says, “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God’s power” (Acts 7). Why, then, does Mark testify that he saw him sitting, but Stephen standing, except because sitting belongs to one judging, while standing belongs to one fighting or helping? Therefore, because the Son of God and of the Virgin, after his Resurrection, was taken up into heaven and now judges all things, and at the end will come as judge of all, Mark describes him as sitting after his Ascension; for after the glory [Col. 1175C] of his Ascension he will be seen as judge at the end. But Stephen, placed in the struggle of his labour, saw him standing, whom he had as helper; for in order that he might overcome on earth the unbelief of persecutors, that one’s grace fought for him from heaven. In that same flesh in which he ascended, he is believed and awaited by the faithful as coming to judge the living and the dead, as the aforesaid two men clothed in white testify concerning him. For as the holy apostles watched him going into heaven, they said:

“This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1); that is, he will come to judge in the same form and substance of flesh in which he had come to be judged. Hence the faithful witness John the Evangelist says [Col. 1175D] in his Apocalypse: “Behold, he comes with the clouds, and every eye shall see him, even those who pierced him” (Rev. 1). He first came hidden in the humanity which he assumed; shortly he will come manifest in majesty and glory for judgment. Thus the Catholic Church throughout the world also sings: “Behold, in the clouds of heaven the Son of Man will come with great power and majesty.” Therefore he will come in or with the clouds for judgment, that is, with the saints, through whom and with whom he will judge the human race; for in this world they were clouds, showering upon others the rain of heavenly doctrine. Or he will come in clouds because, just as a cloud received him when he ascended to heaven, so he will come in [Col. 1176A] a cloud for judgment. “And every eye,” he says, “shall see him, even those who pierced him.” As though he said: Every eye, of righteous and wicked alike, shall see—that is, know—him coming to judgment with great power and majesty, so great, mighty, terrible, and glorious. Nor will other wicked people alone see him, but also those who pierced him, that is, those who crucified him. “And they shall mourn over him,” they themselves and all the tribes of the earth, namely Jews, pagans, and evil Christians who despised his commandments. Why will they mourn over him? On seeing the glory of the saints in the clouds coming to meet Christ, and in view of punishments and torments that never end, they will grieve inconsolably. The prophet Zechariah unquestionably testifies that this will be so: [Col. 1176B] “They shall see him whom they pierced, and shall mourn him with mourning as for an only-begotten son, and shall grieve over him as one is accustomed to grieve at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. 12; John 19). Those will rightly mourn and grieve on that day who crucified the Creator of heaven and earth by their own hands, counsel, permission, or consent, when they behold him coming in the seat of his majesty to judge the living and the dead. For authority to judge all nations was given to him by God the Father, as John the Evangelist speaks figuratively of him in the Apocalypse, saying:

“I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one sitting [Col. 1176C] like the Son of Man, having a golden crown on his head and a sharp sickle in his hand” (Rev. 14).

As though he said plainly: I saw a white cloud, that is, Christ’s humanity made immortal and impassible; and upon this cloud I saw God, namely the Word equal and coeternal with God the Father, resting and judging. I call Christ God and man, “like the Son of Man,” that is, no longer mortal or passible; having upon his head a golden crown, that is, victory over the devil obtained through divine wisdom, in the divinity united to him; and he had a sharp sickle, that is, the divine judicial sentence separating all good and evil, and this in his hand, that is, in his power. For the power of divine judgment, as blessed Gregory says [Col. 1176D] [Note: [Col. 1175D] *Morals*, Book XXXIII, ch. 10.], is called a circle because it encloses on every side; and it is denoted by the name of a sickle because it includes everything within itself by cutting. For whatever is cut by a sickle, in whichever direction it bends, falls inward. And because the power of the heavenly judgment cannot be escaped—for we are all within it, however we may try to flee—it is rightly said that the coming Judge holds a sickle. Being powerful, he meets all things and encircles them by cutting. The prophet David knew that he was within the Judge’s sickle when, considering divine omnipotence, he said: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell in the farthest parts [Col. 1177A] of the sea, even there your hand will lead me and your right hand will hold me” (Ps. 137). He saw himself to be within a certain sickle when he knew that no place afforded him an avenue of escape, saying: “Neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the desert mountains”—understand: “is the way of escape open.” Why? “For God is judge” (Ps. 74). As though he said plainly: The way of escape is absent on every side, because he judges who is present everywhere.

Truly God is a most just judge, who humbles one person and exalts another. He humbles the Jewish people, who exalt themselves and presume upon themselves; but exalts the Gentile people, who humble themselves. This was signified by the Pharisee and the Publican, because the Pharisee exalted himself and was humbled, but the Publican humbled himself and deserved to be exalted by God (Luke 18). Therefore God humbles one and exalts another by his just judgment, because he casts down the proud and raises up the humble. And why is this? Because “a cup in the hand of the Lord is full of pure wine mixed” (Ps. 74), after the example of a powerful cupbearer, who offers sweet wine from the cup to his friends and sour wine to his enemies; for the cup, that is, recompense, is in the Lord’s hand. I call it a cup full of pure wine, that is, just recompense, because he judges no one unjustly, but gives to each according to the quality of merits. Therefore he encloses all heavenly and earthly things within the sweep of his sickle, because the power of his judgment comprehends all things.

[Col. 1177C] It should further be noted that from the time when the Son of God and of the Virgin ascended into heaven, his bride, that is, the holy Church, has most earnestly desired that he should come for judgment. Thus, wearied by desire for him, she urgently entreats him through Solomon in the Song of spiritual love to come, saying: “Return, my beloved; be like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song 2). [Note: [Col. 1177D] Gregory, on this passage.] The Beloved departed bodily from the Church when, after his Resurrection, he ascended into heaven. But he will return when, at the end of the world, the bodies of all people having risen again, he is manifested in judgment. He will truly appear like a roe and a young hart, because, coming in our flesh to judgment, he will show himself to all. By the roe, [Col. 1177D] which is a clean animal, the Church is signified; for while she dwells in heavenly things in her mind, she feeds, as it were, upon mountains. But by stags what else are signified except the ancient Fathers, from whose flesh Christ was born and presented to the world as a young hart. Bethel is interpreted “house of God.” It is rightly called the Church, because God dwells in it when our hearts are cleansed through faith. Therefore he will appear upon the mountains of Bethel like a roe and a young hart, because he will come in judgment in the same form of humanity which he took from the Church, when he was born lowly in this world from the lineage of the Fathers, like a young hart from stags. [Col. 1178A] He will truly appear both like a roe and upon the mountains of Bethel, because in the form of his humanity he will be like the Church, yet will stand higher than those supreme Fathers, who excel like mountains in the Church.

Hence also, in the Apocalypse, the angel coming out of the Temple and bearing the person of the Church cries with a loud voice to the angel—that is, the Son of God and of the Virgin, resting in the humanity assumed from the Virgin, that is, reigning at the right hand of God the Father and holding a sharp sickle in his hand—saying: “Send your sickle into the earth and reap, because the hour of reaping has come, since the harvest of the earth has become ripe” (Rev. 14). The angel crying out from the Temple typifies the order of prelates and of others who live perfectly, who, coming from the Temple—that is, from the Church—[Col. 1178B] excel others in contemplation of the divine essence and dwell in heaven in spirit with the Lord. He cries with a loud voice, that is, with great desire, directing his cry to Christ and saying: O Lord, send your sickle, that is, execute judgment; and reap, that is, gather your faithful, because the hour has come and it is fitting that the harvest be reaped—that is, that your faithful be gathered into the heavenly granary. The harvest of the earth has withered: the multitude of unbelievers, succumbing to earthly actions, has become wholly dry, possessing scarcely any charity, faith, hope, or any other virtue, receiving no spiritual watering, and thus has altogether failed. For the more fully [Col. 1178C] the iniquity of the wicked is completed, the more perfect are the righteousness and goodness of your servants. Come, then, and send your sickle into the earth: by judgment separate the good from the evil, the elect from the reprobate, the wheat from the chaff; place the wheat in the granary of the heavenly kingdom, but burn the chaff with unquenchable fire.

Moreover, it must be known, as Isidore, the doctor of Spain, says [Note: [Col. 1177D] *Sentences*, Book I, chap. 27], that divine judgment is twofold: one by which certain persons are judged in this life through various tribulations; the other by which they will be judged in the future by the Lord’s public sentence. Thus, for some, temporal punishment serves to cleanse sins; while for others condemnation begins here, and everlasting destruction awaits them there. There is likewise [Col. 1178D] a twofold judgment: namely, hidden and manifest. The Lord’s hidden judgment, then, as blessed Augustine says, is understood as the punishment by which each person is moved toward cleansing or conversion, or, if he despises it, is blinded unto condemnation [Note: [Col. 1178D] In the exposition of the heading of Psalm IX in the *Master*; *Sentences*, Book IV, dist. 46, chap. “Quod ergo”]. Thus God’s hidden judgment is called the punishment by which he judges by cleansing, converting, or blinding.

He whose mind’s eyes God has not enlightened in the present life for good works can by no means be delivered from everlasting death. Hence blessed Job, considering God’s hidden and just judgments, says among other things which he recalls lamentingly in his affliction: “My eye shall not return to see good things” (Job 7).

[Col. 1179A] Let us hear what the great doctor Gregory says in explaining this verse. “The eye of a man who has died,” he says, “does not return to see good things, because the soul, once stripped of the flesh, does not return to perform righteous works. Hence it is that the rich man, whom the flames of hell were tormenting, when he realized that he could not restore himself by doing good works, strove to benefit, not himself, but the brothers whom he had left behind, saying: ‘I beg you, Father Abraham, send Lazarus to my father’s house; for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments’” (Luke 16).

“For hope is accustomed to revive a sorrowful or weary mind; but, in order that the reprobate may feel their punishment more grievously, they also lose hope of pardon” [Note: [Col. 1179D] “May lose.”]. Therefore, handed over to avenging flames, he desired, as we have said, to help not himself but [Col. 1179B] his brothers; for he knew that he would never lack the torments of fire, with the added punishment of despair. Hence Solomon says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it earnestly; for there shall be neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in hell, whither you are hastening” (Eccles. 9).

“Therefore the eye does not return to see good things, because, once the mind has found its recompense, it is in no way recalled to the exercise of work. Since, then, everything visible passes away, while those things which follow will remain, blessed Job aptly embraced both in one verse, saying: ‘Remember that my life is wind, and my eye shall not return to see good things.’ Considering the course of present things, he says: ‘Remember that my life is wind.’ [Col. 1179C] But considering the eternity of what follows, he adds: ‘And my eye shall not return to see good things.’

“It follows: ‘Nor shall the sight of man behold me.’ The sight of man is the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of our insensibility when it looks upon it. Hence, as the Gospel also testifies, it is said: ‘The Lord looked upon Peter. And Peter remembered the word which Jesus had spoken; and, going out, he wept bitterly’ (Luke 22). But the soul stripped of flesh is no longer beheld by the sight of man, because after death grace does not deliver the person whom it did not reform unto pardon before death. For this reason Paul says: ‘Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation’ (2 Cor. 6). Hence the Psalmist says: ‘For his mercy is for ever’ (Ps. 105).

“For assuredly [Col. 1179D] the person whom the mercy of the Lord does not now rescue from condemnation, justice alone condemns after the present age. Hence Solomon says: ‘In whatever place a tree falls, whether toward the south or toward the north, there it shall remain’ (Eccles. 11). For when, at the time of human falling, either a holy or an evil spirit receives the soul departing from the enclosure of the flesh, it will retain it with itself eternally and without any alteration: so that neither, when exalted, may it plunge into punishment, nor, when sunk in eternal punishments, may it thereafter ascend to the remedy of deliverance.

“Therefore let the holy man consider the losses of the human race—what is taken from the present age without knowledge of the Redeemer and irreparably buried in eternal fires—[Col. 1180A] and, taking its voice upon himself, say: ‘Nor shall the sight of man behold me.’ For the grace of the Redeemer does not then look upon a person to hide him from destruction whom it does not now behold in order to correct him. Indeed, when the Lord comes for judgment, he sees the sinner in order to strike him, but does not see him so as to acknowledge him by bestowing the grace of salvation. He examines sins and does not recognize the life of those who perish.”

[Note: [Col. 1179D] *Sentences*, Book IV, as above.] Thus God’s hidden judgment is called the punishment by which he judges by cleansing, converting, or blinding. God’s judgments are sometimes also called his dispositions concerning all things. Hence a certain wise man says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). Hence the Psalmist says: “The judgments of the Lord are a great deep” (Ps. 35).

But the manifest judgment [Col. 1180B] by which he will judge in the future is understood as the sentence by which the threshing-floor will be winnowed; that is, the good will be locally separated from the evil by the ministry of angels, the righteous led to eternal life, and the wicked sent into eternal punishment—those who are now mingled together.

It is commonly asked [Note: [Col. 1180D] *Sentences*, Book IV, dist. 48, chap. “Solet quaeri”] in what form Christ will judge the world. But, as Catholic doctors affirm, he will judge in the form of a servant, which will appear to all at the judgment, so that they may see him whom they pierced (Zech. 12); but wicked people will not see his divinity. Hence Isaiah says: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). Therefore they will see Christ’s humanity in order that they may fear; but not his divinity, lest they rejoice. For divinity cannot be seen without joy.

But since [Note: [Col. 1180D] Chap. “Sed cum”] it is certain that he will appear at the judgment in human form, it is asked whether he will appear in a glorious form, as he truly is now, or in the form in which he was in his Passion. Some think that he will be seen by the wicked as they saw him when they crucified him, because Scripture says: “They shall see him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12). But blessed Augustine expressly says that the glorified form of the servant will then be seen by the good and the wicked alike. For when good and wicked see the Judge in the glorified form of a servant, the wicked man will be taken away lest he see the brightness of God as God, which only the pure in heart shall see (Matt. 5), and which will be eternal life to them.

Thus Christ’s glorified human form will be seen in judgment by good and wicked alike. Hence [Col. 1180D] Christ is said to be about to judge because he is the Son of Man. For thus we read in John’s Gospel: “And he”—namely, God the Father—“gave him power to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5). This does not mean that he will judge by the power of his humanity, or that he alone, without the Father and the Holy Spirit, will perform the judgment; but that he alone, judging in the form of a servant, will be seen by good and wicked alike.

Therefore, when it is said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (ibid.), this must not be understood as though the Son judges alone and the Father does not. Rather, the Son’s human form will appear to all at the judgment—not infirm, however, but glorified. He will judge [Col. 1181A] by the power of divinity, not without the Father and the Holy Spirit; and he will appear terrible to the wicked and gentle to the righteous. He will be terror to the wicked and light to the good. According to the diversity of consciences, as blessed Isidore says, Christ will appear gentle in judgment to the elect and terrible to the reprobate. For whatever conscience each has borne, such a judge he will have: Christ remaining in his own tranquillity, he will appear terrible only to those whom conscience accuses of evil.

Therefore, just as Christ is said to judge according to the form of a servant because he is the Son [Note: [Col. 1181D] Supply: “of man.”] of Man, so also according to his humanity he is said to raise the bodies of the dead—although he will raise them by the power of divinity, not by that of humanity. Yet this is said for the reason that in his humanity he underwent that which is the cause of [Col. 1181B] our resurrection, namely, the Passion and Resurrection. Accordingly, for the reasons stated above, the resurrection of the dead is ascribed to him according to his human nature.

Hence blessed Augustine says: “By the Word, the Son of God, the resurrection of souls takes place; by the Word made flesh, the Son of Man, the resurrection of bodies takes place.” Again: “He judges and raises bodies—not the Father, but the Son—according to the dispensation of humanity, in which he is less than the Father.” Christ, insofar as he is the Son of God, is life, which gives life to souls; but insofar as he is the Son of Man, he is judge. Thus, according to the form of humanity, he is said to be about to raise bodies and to judge.

[Note: [Col. 1181D] *Sentences*, Book IV, dist. 47, chap. “Non autem.”] It should also be noted that Christ will not judge alone, [Col. 1181C] but the saints too will judge the nations with him. For he himself says to his disciples: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). Nor should it be thought that Christ promised this only to the twelve apostles. For Paul, who “laboured more than all” (1 Cor. 15), would have nowhere to sit for judgment if no more than twelve persons were to sit there.

By the twelve thrones, therefore, as was said far above, is understood the completeness of the tribunal—that is, the whole body of those judging: the holy apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, hermits, monks, regular canons, and all the perfect who have truly followed Christ. But by the twelve tribes of Israel is signified the whole body of those being judged [Note: [Col. 1181D] “Of those to be judged.”]. All the saints will judge all people on the day of judgment, not only by comparison but also by authority and power. Hence it is written: “Two-edged swords are in their hands” (Ps. 149), that is, the sentence separating good from evil is in their power.

[Note: [Col. 1182D] Chap. “Cum autem.”] Therefore, when the Lord comes for judgment, fire will go before him, by which the face of this world will be burned up; and it will pass through heaven and earth (Matt. 24), not in substance but in appearance, which will be changed for the better. I mean the aerial heaven, [Col. 1182A] not the ethereal heaven. For, as holy doctors affirm, the fire at the judgment will rise as high as the waters rose in the Flood.

For, as blessed Augustine says: “This conflagration of the world will be for the saints what the furnace was for the three youths.” But for the wicked who are found alive that fire will be destruction, while for the good it will be purification. Those in whom anything must be purified will be purified through that fire; but it will cause no distress to others. Once the world has been purified by fire and the Lord comes for judgment, that voice will be uttered at which all the dead shall rise. Then the threshing-floor will be winnowed by the ministry of angels: the good will be gathered from the four quarters of the world by angels, who will also snatch them up into the air to meet Christ; while the reprobate remain upon the earth which they loved, [Col. 1182B] and immediately after the judgment hell will swallow them up.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals” (Matt. 13). And again: “The angels will go forth and separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid.).

[Note: [Col. 1182D] Chap. “Erunt autem.”] There are, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1182D] *Morals*, Book XXVI, chap. 20], two parties—namely, the elect and the reprobate—who will be publicly dealt with at the judgment; but each party contains two orders. Some are judged and perish; others are not judged and perish; others are judged and reign; and others are not judged and reign.

Those are judged and perish to whom this divine proclamation is addressed: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; naked, and you did not clothe me; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me” (Matt. 25). To them is prefaced: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

Others are not judged and perish; concerning them the Lord says through the Prophet: “The wicked shall not rise in the judgment, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous” (Ps. 1). And concerning them the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). Paul also says of them: “Those who have sinned without the law shall perish without the law” (Rom. 2). All unbelievers will indeed rise, but for torments, not for judgment. For their [Col. 1182D] case will not then be examined, because they will come before the sight of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. They are also said not to be judged because their condemnation is known and evident to all.

But those who retain the profession of faith in words while lacking the works of confession will be rebuked so that they may perish. Those, however, who have not even retained the sacraments of faith will not hear the Judge’s rebuke in the final examination; for, already condemned by the darkness of their unbelief, they do not deserve to be rebuked by the accusation of him whom they despised. At least those will hear the Judge’s words who have at least held his faith in word. But these, in their condemnation by the eternal Judge, do not even receive his words, because they were unwilling to preserve even verbally [Col. 1183A] reverence for him. Those perish according to the law who sinned while placed under the law. To these, in their destruction, nothing is said concerning the law, because they made no effort to possess anything of the law.

For example: a ruler governing an earthly commonwealth punishes differently a citizen who sins within it and an enemy who rebels from without. In the former case, he consults his laws and condemns him under words of fitting accusation or rebuke. Against the enemy, however, he wages war, employs instruments of destruction or [uncertain: imperfection], and inflicts the punishments due in war; but he does not inquire what the law provides concerning the enemy’s evil. Nor need one be put to death by a law by which he could never be bound. Thus, at the final judgment, [Col. 1183B] the legal accusation strikes that person because he departed in action from what he held by profession; but this person is punished without the accusation of judgment because he is not bound by the law of faith.

From the party of the elect, however, some are judged and reign: namely, those who wipe away the stains of life with tears, who redeem earlier evils by good works, and who cover before the Judge’s eyes whatever unlawful thing they have committed by adding almsdeeds over it. When the Judge comes, he says to those standing at his right hand: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” and so forth (Matt. 25).

Others are not judged and reign: those who even surpass the precepts of the law by the power of perfection. They are not content merely to fulfil everything commanded by the divine law; rather, in a more excellent desire, [Col. 1183C] they seek to offer more than they have heard in the general precepts. To them the Lord’s voice says: “You who have left all things and followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). Of them the prophet Isaiah says: “The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3). And Solomon, speaking of the Spouse of holy Church, says: “Her husband is renowned in the gates, when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31).

Hence blessed Job aptly says: “The Lord grants judgment to the poor” (Job 36). Therefore, these are rightly not held under the general judgment but come as judges, because by living they have surpassed the general precepts [Col. 1183D] and, leaving all things, have followed Christ. Well, then, does he grant judgment to the poor; for the more they are now despised by this world in great humility, the more they will then rise to the summit of greater power. For the Son of God and of the Virgin says of such persons in the Apocalypse:

> “To him who conquers I will grant to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sit with my Father on his throne” (Rev. 3).

The conquering Lord sat with the Father on the throne, because after the struggle of the Passion, the palm of the Resurrection, and the glory of the Ascension, it was made manifest to all that he was equal to the Father. “To him who conquers,” he says, “I will grant to sit with me on my throne,” and so forth. This is as though he plainly said: “To him who conquers”—namely, sins, [Col. 1184A] temptations, and the adversities of the present age for my name’s sake—“as I conquered, I will grant to sit,” that is, to rest and judge with me on my throne, that is, on my seat, just as I sit, that is, rest and judge with my Father on his throne.

For us, to sit on the Son’s throne is to judge by the power of that same Son [Note: [Col. 1183D] From Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXVI, chap. 21]. Since we receive the primacy of judging through his power, we sit, as it were, on his throne [Note: [Col. 1183D] Again, from chap. 20]. These are not judged and reign at the final judgment, because they come as judges with their Creator. For, leaving all things, in eager devotion they fulfilled more than they had heard generally commanded.

For by a special command, addressed to a few and more perfect persons—not generally to all—is said what the rich young man heard from Christ: “Go,” he says, [Col. 1184B] “sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19). For if a general command bound everyone under this precept, it would certainly be sinful to possess anything in this world. But one thing is commanded generally to all through sacred Scripture; another is enjoined specially upon the more perfect. These, therefore, are rightly not held under the general judgment, because by living they have surpassed the general precepts.

For just as those who, at the persuasion of unbelief, disdain to be bound by the law are not judged and perish, so those who, at the persuasion of godliness, accomplish even beyond the general precepts of the divine law are not judged and reign. Hence Paul, surpassing even the special precepts, offered more in deed [Col. 1184C] than he had received in the constitution of permission. For although he had received the right that, while preaching the Gospel, he might live by the Gospel (1 Cor. 9), he proclaimed the Gospel to his hearers and nevertheless refused to be supported at the Gospel’s expense. Why, then, should this Apostle be judged in order to reign, who received a lesser rule to observe but found a greater rule by which to live?

[Note: [Col. 1184D] *Sentences*, Book IV, dist. 43, chap. “Postremo.”] Therefore a Christian ought in no way to doubt, but firmly to believe, that the flesh of all who have been born or will be born, who have died or will die, will rise again, as was said above. Hence the prophet Isaiah says: “The dead shall rise, and those who are in the tombs shall rise” (Isa. 26). The Apostle likewise says: “We do not wish you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve as the rest do, [Col. 1184D] who have no hope”—namely, of resurrection. “For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who live, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in clouds to meet Christ in the air; and thus we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

By these words both the truth of the resurrection and the cause and order of those rising are most clearly indicated. The cause [Note: [Col. 1184D] Chap. “Causae.”] of the resurrection of the dead will be the trumpet’s voice, which all will hear at the Judge’s coming; by its power the dead will be awakened and rise from their tombs. Hence David, king and prophet, says in the Psalm: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power; give glory to God over Israel; his magnificence and his power are in the clouds” (Ps. 67).

[Col. 1185A] This is as though he plainly said: Behold, at the judgment the Son of God will give to his voice—or rather, his own voice—a voice of power, that is, the efficacy of raising all the dead. Formerly, “like a lamb without voice before one shearing it, he was silent” (Isa. 53), but at the end of the world he will come with the voice of a trumpet. Therefore sing and give glory to God. “He will give,” he says, “his voice,” and then over Israel—that is, over all the faithful—God’s magnificence will be manifest, because there will no longer be a mingling of evil persons with good. And his power will be in the clouds, because he will not come alone to judgment but “with the elders of his people” (Isa. 3), who are clouds pouring down the rain of spiritual teaching.

This is expressly attested by blessed John the Evangelist, who says: “The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who have done good [Col. 1185B] shall go forth unto the resurrection of life, but those who have done evil unto the resurrection of judgment” (John 5). The Apostle says that this voice will be that of the archangel (1 Thess. 4), that is, of Christ himself, who is truly the prince of archangels. It is also called the last trumpet (1 Cor. 15), because after it there shall be no other. This trumpet, as blessed Augustine says, is the cry of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “At midnight there was a cry: Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. 25).

By the name “trumpet” is also understood some evident and glorious sign. It is called by the Apostle the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, and in the Gospel it is called the voice of the Son of God and a cry: the voice that the dead will hear and rise.

[Col. 1185C] But the Judge of all will come at midnight, as blessed Augustine says, not with reference to an hour of time, but because he will come when he is not expected. Hence [Note: [Col. 1185D] The *Master* lacks: “Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel.” Nor are the following words found in the Gospel, but in Paul. Martin, however, also printed them in vol. I, fol. 284 as though they referred to the Gospel.] the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thess. 5).

Yet it may not incongruously be understood that he will come at the time of midnight, because, as Cassiodorus says, at this time the firstborn of Egypt were struck, and at this time too the bridegroom will come. Master Anselm, a man wholly wise and discerning, agrees with this opinion. “At midnight,” he says, “at the hour when the angel devastated Egypt and the Lord despoiled hell, at that hour he will deliver his elect from this world.” In many places authors also attest that Christ’s coming is called the day of the Lord, not because of the character of the time but [Col. 1185D] because of events; for then the thoughts and counsels of hearts will be laid open. Hence we read in Daniel: “The Ancient of Days sat down, and books were opened before him” (Dan. 7). The books are the consciences of individuals, because they will then be opened to others. For then will be fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and nothing hidden that shall not be known” (Matt. 10).

[Note: [Col. 1186D] Dist. 47, chap. “Cum autem.”] Finally, that judicial sentence is pronounced upon both groups, namely, upon the elect and the reprobate: [Col. 1186A] “Come, you blessed of my Father,” and so forth (Matt. 25) [Note: [Col. 1186D] Supply: “and ‘Go, you cursed,’ and so forth.”], whether by an audible voice or in some other manner.

Some ask [Note: [Col. 1186D] Chap. “Solet etiam.”] how that sentence of judgment will be delivered, but it is not clear how to explain it. For Scripture has not determined whether those words are spoken aloud [Note: [Col. 1186D] Supply: “‘Come, you blessed’; and ‘Go, you cursed.’”], or whether the Judge’s power works in such a way, with the consciences of individuals bearing witness, that what is future is said now because the effect of the Judge’s power is signified by his utterance.

Many also think that the words, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25), will be expressed in consciences rather than in words, because the Apostle teaches that the mystery will be completed “in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Cor. 15). But others refer that only to the state of resurrection, not to the judgment, since they maintain that the sentence of judgment, the rebukes of the wicked, [Col. 1186B] and the praises of the good will be expressed in words [Note: [Col. 1186D] Dist. 49, chap. “Post resurrectionem.”].

When the judgment has been completed, two cities will remain forever with their citizens: one, Christ’s; the other, the devil’s; one of the good, the other of the evil; yet both consist of angels and human beings. For the former, there can be neither a will nor an ability to sin, nor any condition of dying; while the latter endure unhappily in eternal death, without the power to die. For both are without end; but the righteous [Note: [Col. 1186D] More correctly, “the former,” as in the edition.] will remain in blessedness, one more excellently than another, while the others remain in misery, one more intolerably than another.

From this it is clear that, just as the good will be glorified differently in eternal blessedness, so the evil will be punished differently in hell. [Col. 1186C] For as there are many dwelling-places in the house of God the Father (John 14), that is, differences of rewards, so there are diverse dwelling-places in Gehenna, that is, differences of punishments. Yet all will suffer eternal punishment, just as all the elect will have the same denarius, which the householder gave to all who worked in the vineyard (Matt. 20).

By the name “denarius,” therefore, is understood something common to all the elect: namely, eternal life, which is God himself, whom all will enjoy, though not equally. For just as the glorification of bodies will differ, so too will the glory of souls differ. “Star differs from star” (1 Cor. 15), that is, one elect person differs from another in brightness of mind and body. Some will contemplate God’s form more nearly and more clearly than others, and this very difference in contemplation is called diversity of dwelling-places.

Thus the house is one and the denarius is one; but there is diversity of dwelling-places within it, that is, difference of brightness, because the supreme good, the blessedness and life of all, is one—namely, God himself. All the elect will enjoy this good, but some more fully than others. They will enjoy it by seeing face to face, not “through a glass darkly” (1 Cor. 13). To possess life, therefore, is to see life—that is, to know God [Col. 1187A] face to face. Hence Truth, speaking to God the Father in the Gospel, says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, to be the only true God” (John 17).

It is also commonly asked whether they are unequal in joy, just as they differ in the brightness of knowledge [Note: [Col. 1187D] Chap. “Solet etiam quaeri an in gaudio.”]. Blessed Augustine says this concerning the matter: “There will be many dwelling-places in the one life, but varied degrees of reward. Yet because God will be all in all, there will be equal joy amid unequal brightness; so that what each possesses will be common to all, because the glory of the Head will belong to all through the bond of charity.”

From this, therefore, it is understood that all will have equal joy, although they have unequal brightness of knowledge. For through charity, which will be perfect in each person, each will rejoice in another’s good as much as he would rejoice if he himself possessed it.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Chap. “Post hoc.”] It is also commonly asked whether the blessedness of the saints will be greater after the judgment than before it. But it must without any doubt be believed that they will have greater glory than before, because their joy will be greater, as Augustine has testified above, and their knowledge more ample. Hence blessed Jerome, greatly useful and necessary to Christ’s Church, says: “Once the judgment has been completed, God will show the elect a fuller glory of his brightness.”

It may also be asked [Note: [Col. 1187D] Dist. 50, chap. “Hic quaer.”] why the darkness in which the wicked will be enveloped in Gehenna is called outer darkness. For although the reprobate suffer darkness in the blindness of the mind, they are nevertheless not altogether outside God’s light, nor are they deprived of bodily light. Hence blessed Augustine, the eminent doctor of the Catholic Church, says: [Col. 1187C] “The wrath of God will exist also at the judgment; and it exists here in blindness of mind, when the wicked are given over to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1). But there, that is, after the judgment, there will be outer darkness, because sinners will then be altogether outside God. For what is it to be altogether outside God except to be in the utmost blindness? For God dwells in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6).

This darkness already begins here in the sinner when he is shut out from God’s inward light, but not altogether while he remains in this life. Behold why the sinner is said to suffer outer darkness there, and not here: because there he is wholly shut out from God’s light, which is not the case here.

Moreover [Note: [Col. 1187D] Chap. “Praeterea.”], it is commonly asked whether the souls of the reprobate, [Col. 1187D] now tormented in hell, know what happens in this life to their own people, and whether they grieve in any way over the misfortunes of their loved ones. Blessed Augustine partly resolves this question, saying: “Concerning this question it may briefly be said that the dead do have concern for their loved ones, as is read of the rich man who, while suffering torments in hell, raised his eyes to Abraham and said among other things: ‘I beg you, Father Abraham, send Lazarus to my father’s house (for I have five brothers), that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments’ [Col. 1188A] (Luke 16).” Thus the dead, even when placed in places of punishment, have concern for their friends, as that rich man had for his brothers. Yet it does not follow that they know everything, whether joyful or sorrowful, that happens here to their loved ones.

It is also commonly asked [Note: [Col. 1188D] Chap. “Solet.”] whether those who are in hell and those who are in glory see one another in turn. But, as holy doctors teach, both good see the evil and evil see the good until the judgment. After the judgment, however, the good will see the evil, but the evil will not see the good. Hence blessed Gregory, the magnificent defender of Christ’s Church, says: “The unbelievers placed below, that is, in hell, before the day of judgment will see above them the faithful at rest, whose joys they will not be able to behold after the judgment.”

But [Note: [Col. 1188D] Chap. “Sed.”] when the saints see the wicked [Col. 1188B] in torments, will they not be moved by some compassion for them? Will they not wish them delivered from their torments? Recall that Gospel saying which Abraham gave in answer to the rich man: “Between us and you a great chasm has been fixed, so that those who wish to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us” (ibid.). What is that chasm between good and evil except justice on this side and iniquity on that, which cannot be joined together in any way?

For the saints will be so devoted to God’s justice that they cannot cross over to the reprobate through any compassion, nor offer prayers to God for them. How, then, are some said to wish to cross over from there if they cannot? Namely because, if God’s justice permitted it, their deliverance would not be burdensome to them. Or they are said to will and not to be able, not because they do will and cannot [Col. 1188C] do so, but because, even if they willed it, they could not help them at all.

On this matter the great doctor Gregory says: “Just as the reprobate wish to pass from punishments to the glory of the saints and cannot, so the righteous, through mercy of mind, wish to go to those placed in torments in order to deliver them, but cannot; because, although the souls of the righteous possess mercy in the goodness of their nature, yet then, joined to the justice of their Creator, they are bound by such uprightness that they are no longer moved by any compassion for the reprobate.”

Hence it is read in blessed Job: “You shall laugh at devastation and famine” (Job 5). The reprobate, as blessed Gregory explains [Note: [Col. 1188D] *Morals*, Book VI, chap. 16], will then suffer devastation and famine, when, condemned at the final judgment, they are separated from the vision of the eternal bread. Hence the Lord says of himself: “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6). Thus devastation and famine will torment them together, because they will not only feel torments outwardly, but inwardly also perish from the plague of hunger. Gehenna will lay them waste because it will burn them; hunger will kill them because the Redeemer will hide his face from them.

For they will receive the recompense of punishment inwardly and outwardly, because they sinned both in thought and in deed. Hence the Psalmist fittingly says: “You shall make them as a furnace of fire in the time of your countenance,” and so forth (Ps. 20). For what is devoured [Col. 1189A] by fire is set ablaze from within, while a furnace burns inwardly. Therefore, at the time of the Lord’s countenance, all the unjust will be made like a furnace and will be devoured by fire: because, when the Judge appears and their multitude has been driven away from his sight, their conscience will burn within through the desire to see God, while Gehenna will torment the flesh without.

Therefore the righteous person will laugh amid devastation and famine, because when final vengeance has struck all the wicked, he will rejoice in the glory of his deserved recompense. Nor will he then, out of human feeling, pity the condemned, because, cleaving by direct vision to divine justice, he will be established in the unshaken strength of inward strictness. No misery will affect the minds of the elect, raised in the brightness of heavenly rectitude, because the height of blessedness will render them strangers to miseries.

Hence [Col. 1189B] the Psalmist also fittingly says: “The righteous shall see and fear; they shall laugh at him and say: ‘Behold the man who did not make God his helper’” (Ps. 51). The righteous now see the wicked and fear; then they will see and laugh. Because they can now lapse into imitation of them, they have fear here; but because then they will be unable to help the condemned, they will have no compassion there. They read, in the very justice by which they are blessed, that those delivered to everlasting punishment are not to be pitied; for—an opinion it is not lawful to entertain—they would diminish the quality of the happiness commanded for them if, established in the kingdom, they willed what they could in no way accomplish.

[Note: [Col. 1189D] C. Finally.] The question is raised whether even the sight of the punishment of the reprobate diminishes the glory of the blessed, or contributes to their beatitude. [Col. 1189C] On this subject blessed Gregory says: “The punishment of the reprobate, when seen, does not darken the blessedness of the righteous; for where compassion of mercy will no longer exist, it cannot lessen the joy of the blessed. And although their own joys suffice for the righteous, yet, for their greater glory, they behold the punishments of the wicked which they escaped through God’s grace; because those who see God’s brightness have nothing in creation which they cannot see. Nor is it surprising if the saints, now immortal, see the reprobate by the understanding of their minds, since prophets still mortal deserved to see all these things. Therefore the hammer of heretics, namely blessed Jerome, says on Isaiah: ‘The elect shall go forth, not in place but by understanding, or by manifest vision, to see the torments of the wicked; and, seeing them, they shall not be affected with sorrow, but shall be filled with joy, giving thanks to God for their own deliverance when they have seen the ineffable damnation of the impious.’ Therefore Isaiah, describing in the Lord’s voice the torments of the wicked and expressing the joy of the good at their sight, says: ‘The elect shall go forth and shall see the corpses of the men who have transgressed against me.’ And again: ‘Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished; and they shall be unto satiety for all flesh,’ that is, for all the elect. Their worm shall gnaw their conscience within, [Col. 1190A] while fire shall burn their body without.”

Moreover, the question is raised [Note: [Col. 1189D] Distinction 43, chapter “Here it is asked.”] whether the elect will then have [Note: [Col. 1189D] “Will be present.”] a memory of sins or torments, just as they will of good things. But it may be answered that the memory of past evils will neither sadden the saints nor darken their blessedness, but will make them more grateful to God. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88). Let us willingly hear what blessed Gregory says on this verse [Note: [Col. 1189D] Book IV of the *Morals*, chapter 31.]: “If, in eternal blessedness, a man is touched by no memory of his sin, from what will he glory that he has been delivered? Or how will he give thanks to the Giver for the pardon he has received, if, through forgetfulness of his past wickedness, he does not know that he was [Col. 1190B] liable to punishment? How will he sing for ever of the mercies of the Lord if he does not know that he was miserable, if he is forgetful of his former misery, and if he does not render praises to the Giver of mercy?”

Again indeed [Note: [Col. 1189D] Here another manuscript improperly begins a different discourse, whereas the author continues by transcribing the same passage of Gregory [Col. 1190D]; and an even more improperly—indeed, more ignorantly—corrector deleted in our manuscript the two words *Iterum vero* (“Again indeed”), in order to conform it to the other, which began absolutely: “We must inquire,” etc.] it must be asked how the mind of the elect can be perfect in blessedness if, amid its joys, it is touched by remembrance of its own guilt. But it must be understood that, just as in times of health we often gladly remember past illnesses and thereby become more cheerful and grateful, so then we shall remember past wickedness without harm to our blessedness. Thus in that blessedness there will be a memory of sin—not one that defiles the mind or afflicts it with grief, but one that makes us more devoted in rendering thanks to the Deliverer and Giver of every good.

[Col. 1190C] It is also commonly asked [Note: [Col. 1190D] Same chapter, “Here it is asked.”] whether the sins committed by the elect while they were still living will then become known to all, just as the evils of those to be condemned will be known to all. Hence it may not unreasonably be believed that sins covered and erased here through repentance will also there be concealed from others. But those which were not confessed here will there be manifest to all.

Again it is commonly asked [Note: [Col. 1190D] C. “It is asked.”] whether those whom Christ finds alive at his coming will never die at all, or whether, in the very instant in which they are caught up to meet him in the air, they will pass with miraculous swiftness into immortality. For it must not be said to be impossible that they may be borne upward through the air and, in that interval, die and return to life. The Apostle seems to urge us toward this interpretation—that we should judge them, within a brief interval, both to suffer death and to receive immortality—when he says: “We shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15). And elsewhere he says: “O foolish man, what you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (ibid.). Why, then, should it seem incredible to us that this multitude of bodies should in some manner be sown in the air and immediately there revive immortal and incorruptible, when we believe that the resurrection will occur in the twinkling of an eye, and that the dust of ancient corpses will return with such swiftness into limbs that shall live without end? [Col. 1191A] “We shall all rise,” says the Apostle, namely both good and evil; “but we shall not all be changed” (ibid.), that is, in the glory of the resurrection. Hence blessed Ambrose, the most zealous persecutor of heretics, says: “In the very rapture of those who are caught up alive there will be death and resurrection, so that the soul, as though departing from the body in sleep, may in a moment be restored to that same body.”

[Note: [Col. 1191D] C. “But these matters.”] Christ is also said in two ways to judge the living and the dead. Either “the living” means those found alive at his coming, though they die in their rapture, and “the dead” those who departed earlier; or the living and the dead mean the righteous and the unrighteous. Some also commonly inquire [Note: [Col. 1191D] Distinction 44, chapter “They commonly.”] whether [Col. 1191B] all will rise in the same age and bodily stature. Some have thought that all will rise according to the bodily age of Christ, because the Apostle says: “Until we all come unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4). But by these words not the same stature, but the same age, is assigned to those rising again. For all shall rise at the same age at which Christ died and rose, whatever age they may have been when they died. He used “man,” moreover, not to distinguish sex, but to signify the perfection of virtues which they will then possess; yet not all will have the same bodily stature. Hence blessed Augustine, the most faithful defender of ecclesiastical teaching, says: “The Apostle did not say, ‘unto the measure of the body’ [Col. 1191C] or ‘of stature,’ but ‘of age’; for each person shall receive his own measure—either that which he had in youth, even if he died old, or that which he would have had if he had died before reaching it. But the age will be that which Christ attained, namely youthful age, about thirty years.” For Christ was thirty-two years and three months old when he died and rose again [Note: [Col. 1191D] C. “But this.”]. Therefore the bodies of the saints shall rise without any defect, without any deformity, just as they shall be without any burden or difficulty of corruption; and in them capacity shall be as great as blessedness. For this reason the Apostle called them spiritual, although they will undoubtedly be bodies and not spirits (1 Cor. 15). From this it is apparent that all the risen will have one age, namely youth; but their stature will differ, namely that which each had in youth, or would have had if he died before reaching it. Nothing of the substance from which human flesh is made shall perish; rather, by the gathering together of all its particles the natural substance of the saints’ bodies shall be restored. Those bodies shall rise shining like the sun, without any defect (Matt. 13), with the deformities they had here abolished and cut away.

With regard to the reprobate [Note: [Col. 1191D] C. “Concerning the reprobate.”], too, it is commonly asked whether they rise with the deformities they had here. But [Col. 1192A] blessed Augustine does not affirm this; he leaves it doubtful, saying: “What need is there to labor in inquiry whether the impious shall rise with the defects and deformities of their bodies, whatever they had in them? For their uncertain deformity or beauty should not weary us, whose damnation will be certain and everlasting.” But if [Note: [Col. 1192D] C. “But if.”] it is asked concerning the bodies of the wicked how they burn in fire and are not consumed, Augustine establishes by various examples that they burn in everlasting fires and are not consumed by any burning. For example: just as the mind, by whose presence the body lives, can suffer pain and cannot die, so also the bodies of the impious can be burned but cannot be consumed. For what we know now to exist [Col. 1192B] in the souls of all will then exist in the bodies of the condemned. How do you understand “mind” (*animus*)? Understand *animus* to be the same thing as “soul” (*anima*), although the soul receives different names according to the functions of its causes. [Note: [Col. 1192D] This is from Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XI, chapter 1.] For while it gives life to the body, it is *anima* (“soul”); while it wills, it is *animus* (“mind”); while it knows, it is *mens* (“intellect”); while it recollects, it is *memoria* (“memory”); while it judges what is right, it is *ratio* (“reason”); while it breathes, it is *spiritus* (“spirit”); while it perceives anything, it is *sensus* (“sense”). Indeed, *animus* is called *sensus* on account of those things which it perceives; from this also *sententia* (“judgment”) has received its name.

It is also commonly asked [Note: [Col. 1192D] Again from Mag., chapter “It is asked.”] whether demons burn in bodily fire. Blessed Augustine answers: “That Gehenna, which is called the lake of fire and sulphur (Rev. 10), will be bodily fire, and it will torment the bodies of condemned human beings and demons: the solid bodies of human beings, the airy bodies of demons.” [Col. 1192C]

Certainly, dearest brothers, it has sufficiently been shown to you above, from the authorities of the holy Fathers, that Jesus Christ, God and man, will come for judgment just as he was taken up into heaven; and also what he will be like when he comes, why he will come, with whom he will come, and what he will do at his coming. Nevertheless, while we live in this present age, as the Apostle says, “We know in part and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come,” namely eternal blessedness, “that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore, while you have time, persist in good works, so that you may be delivered from the fires of Gehenna and attain to the brightness of the heavenly homeland. Abandon the superfluous [Col. 1192D] cares of this life, so that by the narrow way you may deserve to arrive at the spaciousness of the eternal kingdom. Of this spaciousness the prophet Ezekiel speaks figuratively, saying:

“The man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze measured the vestibule of the gate: eight cubits, and its front, two cubits; but the vestibule of the gate was inward” (Ezek. 40). Let blessed Gregory, of great holiness and wisdom in Christ’s Church, come forward and graciously expound to us the depth of this verse [Note: [Col. 1192D] Homily 16 on Ezekiel.]. “What,” he says, “is signified by the inward vestibule except the spaciousness [Col. 1193A] of eternal life? Of this the Psalmist says: ‘Enter into his gates with confession, into his courts with hymns’ (Ps. 99). For when we confess our sins through tears, we enter the gate of narrowness. But when after this we are brought to eternal life, we enter the courts of our gate in the praises of confessions; because there will then be no narrowness when the joy of the eternal solemnity has received us. Because of the narrowness of our confession, Truth says in the Gospel: ‘Strive to enter through the narrow gate’ (Luke 13). And when the Psalmist presumed that he would be received into the spaciousness of eternal joy, he said to God: ‘You have set my feet in a spacious place’ (Ps. 30). Thus one proceeds to the court through the gate, because one reaches the spaciousness of eternal solemnity through the narrowness of confession. Therefore those joys are called ‘courts’ by David, but ‘the inward vestibule’ by Ezekiel. Hence this vestibule itself is said to be measured at eight cubits. For all present time unfolds through seven days. The eternal day which follows the completed cycle of seven days is the eighth. Hence also, when the Psalmist considered the day of resurrection, because he was about to speak of the strictness of the final judgment, he prefixed the title: ‘For the end: a Psalm of David, for the eighth.’ And, in order to show more clearly what eighth he meant, he added: ‘O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, neither chasten [Col. 1193C] me in your anger’ (Ps. 6). For now whoever is corrected by the scourges of discipline is corrected not in anger but in gentleness. But in that strict examination every reproof and correction will be fury and anger, because after the correction there will be no pardon.

“The reason for this number eight is that the Lord willed to rise from death after the Sabbath. For the Lord’s Day, which is the third from the Lord’s death, is counted as the eighth from creation in the cycle of days, because it follows the seventh. Hence also the true passion and true resurrection of our Redeemer prefigured something concerning his body in the days of his compassion. For he suffered on the sixth day, rested in the tomb on the Sabbath, and rose from the dead on the Lord’s Day. For our present life is still the sixth day, because it is spent in pains [Col. 1193D] and afflicted by hardships. But on the Sabbath we rest, as it were, in a tomb, because after the body we find rest for the soul.
