But on the Lord’s Day—that is, the third from the Passion and, as we have said, the eighth from creation—we shall now rise from bodily death, and in the glory of the soul shall rejoice also with the flesh. What our Savior wonderfully did in himself, therefore, he truly signified in us: so that pain may receive us on the sixth day, rest on the seventh, and glory on the eighth. Hence it is said through Solomon: ‘Give a portion to seven and also to eight, because you do not know what evil shall come upon the earth’ (Eccl. 11). For we give a portion to seven and eight when we so order the things which revolve through seven days that through them we may come to eternal goods, provided that, by God’s grace, we act prudently and [Col. 1194A] afterward avoid the wrath of the coming dreadful judgment. Thus the inward vestibule is measured at eight cubits, because through the light that follows seven days the spaciousness of eternity is opened to us.”

Therefore, sweetest brothers, trusting in Christ’s goodness and help and following his footsteps insofar as possible, we must strive to advance from virtue to virtue for the better, and hasten to ascend to that same spaciousness of eternity. For through the humanity which he received from the Virgin without sin, he ascended first to the right hand of God the Father so that the ascent to heaven might not seem difficult to any believer. Let us therefore consider the ascents of this same Lord Jesus Christ, that by them we may be able to imitate him—that is, to follow him to the heavenly homeland. [Col. 1194B]

We have also learned from the testimony of the Gospel that there were seven ascents of the Lord. By the number seven universality is likewise signified. Accordingly, by these seven numbers all his ascents may be understood. For he ascended: first, from the Jordan into the wilderness; secondly, onto Mount Tabor, and was transfigured upon it; thirdly, alone onto a mountain to pray; fourthly, onto a mountain when he chose the apostles and delivered to them the law of the Gospel in his discourse; fifthly, upon the she-ass on which he came to Jerusalem; sixthly, the cross in his Passion; and seventhly, into heaven on the present day—that is, on such a day after the resurrection. We do not give much attention to whether he ascended in this order; rather, we order our own ascent.

[Col. 1194C] Therefore he first ascended into the wilderness in order to be tempted by the devil (Matt. 4); secondly, onto Mount Tabor in order to be transfigured (Matt. 17); thirdly, while praying, in order to be glorified by the Father (John 16); fourthly, in order to be understood by those to whom he preached; fifthly, in order to be acknowledged by the crowds as a gentle king. Hence comes the saying: “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle,” etc. (Matt. 21); sixthly, in order to be lifted up upon the cross. Hence he himself says: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12); seventhly, in order to be raised into heaven. Hence it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “While they saw, he was lifted up, and a cloud received him from their eyes” (Acts 1).

Thus in the first ascent he conquered the devil’s temptations; in the second his face shone like the sun; in the third, praying to [Col. 1194D] the Father, he offered us an example of prayer; in the fourth he taught the disciples; in the fifth, approaching Jerusalem, he wonderfully arranged the procession of those going before and following him in praises of himself and of God the Father; in the sixth he redeemed us from the devil’s power and moreover despoiled hell; in the seventh, while the disciples watched, he penetrated the heavens and, interceding, continually shows God the Father the wounds which he bore in his body for our redemption. The Son of God and of the Virgin did all these things for us. And that he endured such things for us was required not by his necessity, but by ours.

His first ascent, then, was for our comfort, when he ascended from the water of the Jordan into the wilderness and conquered the devil, the tempter. The second [Col. 1195A] was for consolation, manifesting the hidden treasure of his divinity in human nature. For in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2). His third ascent was for our refuge, when, according to his humanity, he prayed alone upon a mountain and gave us an example of praying in secret. For his solitary prayer is our refuge, since it is poured out for the remission of our sins. The fourth was for our instruction, because ascending a mountain and there giving a discourse, he taught the disciples, through whose preaching he reconciled the world to himself. The fifth was for our help: for his supreme humility aided our faith, when, coming on an ass, he willed that he should be divinely praised by the crowds, called king, and [Col. 1195B] glorified. His sixth ascent was for our ransom, because, in order to redeem us from the devil’s power, he gave the price of his own blood. The seventh was for our reward, because, having conquered death, he ascended above all the heavens on this day and, sitting at the right hand of God the Father, made that same Father propitious toward us. For God is our blessedness and eternal reward, the unfailing light of the citizens above. He is the way for those running to him; he is the joy of those arriving at him.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since we have thus far spoken of the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ as the Holy Spirit dictated, it is most necessary that, adorned with good conduct, we present ourselves as fit and devout for so splendid a solemnity. For just as [Col. 1195C] the holy apostles and the other disciples, in the place of prayer amid words of praise and blessing, waited for the promised coming of the Holy Spirit with hearts and bodies prepared in every respect, so after celebrating in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—the solemnities of the Passion and Resurrection, let us, with Christ as our guide, seek Bethany, so that with a tranquil mind we may be refreshed and instructed by the sacraments of his body and blood. Let us take care to be a house of obedience, because thus we are daily raised by his blessing, if, daily mindful of his triumphant ascension, we rest in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of hoped-for peace—praising and blessing God, like people awaiting their lord, namely Jesus [Col. 1195D] Christ, when he returns from the wedding (Luke 12), that is, from heaven into this world for judgment. The evangelist Luke fittingly says that Christ’s apostles, who were to become ministers of the New Testament, stood in the Temple not amid the blood of victims but in the praise and blessing of God. For among other things he says: “He”—namely the Son of God and of the Virgin—“led them outside the city to Bethany; and lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he departed from them and was borne up into heaven. And they, worshipping, returned to Jerusalem with great joy; and they were continually in the Temple, praising and blessing God” (Luke 24).

Therefore on this day the sun, namely the Redeemer of the human race, was lifted up into heaven, to the throne [Col. 1196A] of paternal glory, and the moon stood in its order, as the prophet Habakkuk says at the beginning of this discourse (Hab. 3). Of this John the Evangelist speaks figuratively, saying: “I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain, having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth” (Rev. 5). As though he said openly: I saw in the midst of the throne, that is, in the shared benefit of the Church; and of the four living creatures, that is, the preachers of the New Testament; and in the midst of the elders, namely the apostles and prophets; the Lamb standing as though slain, that is, simple and innocent, helping those who strive, because though he died through weakness, he nevertheless lives through the power of God (2 Cor. 13). [Col. 1196B] Or he is as though slain among his own, in whom he is daily put to death. Having seven horns, namely holy people—that is, saints in the seven ages of the world. The horns and eyes signify the Holy Spirit, who gives the kingdom signified in the horns; the eyes, because they enlighten those called to eternal life. Or the horns are the more eminent saints, established in Christ the head and surpassing the carnal life. Thus the holy Church stands in its own order: it is possessed by Christ as a throne, fed as the living creatures, honored as the elders by the judgment of authority; built upon Christ, it is exalted in the kingdom by the seven horns of strength and enlightened by the seven eyes, signs and powers.

It follows: “And he came and received the book from the right hand [Col. 1196C] of him who sat upon the throne.” As though he said: He came to human knowledge by being born a man of the Virgin, and received the book from the right hand of the Word, namely the Word bound to himself—the Word, I say, of God the Father sitting upon the throne. Christ, the Redeemer of the human race, received the book when he fulfilled in deed what had been foretold of him through the prophets. For this reason the Old and New Testaments are called one book, because neither can the New be separated from the Old nor the Old from the New. He opened the book when he opened the understanding of the disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures. The opening of the seal is the revelation of the mystery hidden from ages and generations. But by the seven seals, as was said above, is signified the fullness of the hidden mysteries [Col. 1196D] that lay concealed before Christ’s coming. And these seven seals, which were loosed in Christ—that is, made manifest throughout the whole world—are these: first, embodiment; second, birth; third, passion; fourth, death; fifth, resurrection; sixth, glory, namely of the ascension and of sitting at the right hand of God the Father; seventh, kingdom, namely the subjection of all creatures after the Day of Judgment. The holy Church has these seven seals loosed, and these are the acts of that same Church from the Incarnation until the Lord’s second coming. Therefore from this day onward, Jesus Christ, ascending into heaven, especially opened to his Church his own will and that of God the Father, as he himself subsequently says to his faithful servant John: “Come, I shall show you what [Col. 1197A] must quickly take place after these things” (Rev. 4), namely the mysteries of heavenly secrets which had not yet been revealed.

Now, beloved brothers, if it please you, let the length of this discourse be restrained, lest it seem to produce weariness in readers and hearers alike. Therefore Jesus Christ, God and man, will come for judgment, but not as rain upon fleece; rather, as a ruin drawing an inescapable weight. Coming, I say, like one [Col. 1198A] exhilarated with wine (Ps. 77), he will make glad those who are at his right hand, but will thunder terribly against those at his left, with an evil hearing [Note: [Col. 1197A] *auditionem* …] and a harsh word [Note: [Col. 1197A] *malam*—“evil.”]. May that same Son of God and man deign to deliver us from this evil hearing and harsh word—he who, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

# THIRTY-FIRST SERMON: ON THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD, II

[Col. 1197]

[Col. 1197B] [Note: [Col. 1197D] Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 40.] Daniel, born of noble family from the tribe of Judah, was carried to Babylon as a very young boy after the destruction of Jerusalem, together with the three youths. He became chief of the Chaldeans: a glorious man, handsome in appearance, humble in mind, chaste in body, perfect in faith, outstanding in deed, illustrious in virtue, foreknowing future things, and conscious of heavenly secrets. From these he spoke thus for our instruction: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven, and came even unto the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and a kingdom; and every people, tribe, and language shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away; and his kingdom, which shall not be corrupted” (Dan. 7). Daniel [Col. 1197C] the prophet, dearest brothers, understanding through persistence in fasting and prayers the mysteries of the heavenly sacraments, speaks of Christ’s ascension, saying: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, the Son of Man came in the clouds of heaven,” namely our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true Son of God, whom God the Father begot from himself before all ages, as he says of him through the Psalmist: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2), that is, in my eternity. He is fittingly also called Son of Man, because at the end of time Mary, ever virgin, bore him from her own substance. Of him we read written: “A man was born in Zion, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86). The Son of Man is rightly said to come in [Col. 1197D] the clouds of heaven because, as Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles, while the disciples watched, a cloud received him from their sight (Acts 1).

It follows: “And he came unto the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him,” namely the choir of angels. For from the day of his incarnation holy angels always ministered to him with all devotion; accompanying him with supreme reverence on the day of the Ascension, they presented him, in the same flesh which he assumed, before the Father’s presence. [Col. 1198B] Thus by the Ancient of Days is understood God the Father, to whom the Prophet speaks in the Psalm: “Lord, they shall all grow old as a garment; and as a covering you shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101). For he is eternal and without beginning, because he created all things from nothing. For from him, and through him, and in him are all things that have been created in heaven, on earth, and in the sea. Divine eternity precedes all times, because past and future are present to him.

Thus the Son of Man came unto the Ancient of Days when our Lord Jesus Christ, true Son of God and man, conquered death, rose again, and on the fortieth day ascended into heaven while his disciples stood by, raising himself to the throne of paternal glory [Col. 1198C] from which he had descended. Jacob the patriarch prophesied much earlier of this when he blessed his son Judah, from whose seed Christ himself came forth.

“You have gone up for the prey, my son” (Gen. 49), that is, you have gone up onto the cross, because by dying you rescued those whom that hostile lion—the devil—had seized. Then, returning from hell, you ascended on high, that is, into heaven, and led captivity captive: you powerfully and mercifully liberated the elect who were being held captive in hell. And he added: “Resting, you have lain down like a lion.” It is altogether evident that Christ lay down in his Passion when, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit; or when he rested securely in the tomb, as in a kind of bodily sleep. The Psalmist, beholding this ascension in the Spirit as though already accomplished, says to Christ: “You ascended on high; you took captivity; you received gifts in men” (Ps. 67). He speaks of the future as though it were past. As if he said: You shall ascend into heaven and shall take captivity, because you shall recapture the human race, formerly held captive by the devil. “You received gifts in men,” that is, you shall receive as your gifts from God the Father those very human beings [Col. 1199A] whom you are about to redeem from the enemy’s hand. Again Daniel adds: “Every people, tribe, and language shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away; and his kingdom, which shall not be corrupted.” This is what the same Lord says in the Gospel: “All things have been delivered to me by my Father” (Luke 10). And again: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

Again, the Psalmist speaks of him to God the Father, saying: “You have crowned him with glory and honor, and have set him over the works of your hands” (Ps. 8). Truly God the Father crowned the Son with the glory of the resurrection and the honor of the ascension, and set him over the works of his hands—that is, over the rational creature in heaven and on earth, which, because of its excellence, is called the work of his hands. God the Father also crowned Christ with glory because, when his soul descended into hell, where darkness had been everlasting, a great light shone forth. He crowned him also with honor when, returning from hell with a multitude of angels, he caused many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep to rise, in testimony to the true resurrection, and to appear to many in the holy city Jerusalem (Matt. 27); and he exalted him at his right hand above everything created. [Col. 1199B]

Nor did God the Father set the Son over the good alone; he also subjected beneath his feet all sheep and oxen, as well as the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fishes of the sea which pass through the paths of the sea (Ps. 8). We understand the sheep to be the heavenly orders of angels and the souls of saints, because of their innocence and simple life. Hence the Lord said in the Gospel: “Does he not leave the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness,” that is, in heaven, “and come to seek the one which had perished?” (Luke 15). By oxen we understand the preachers cultivating the Lord’s vineyard, that is, the holy Church, with the plough of their preaching. For as oxen, when threshing, separate the grains from the chaff, so good preachers, by preaching, raise human minds from earth to heaven. “And also the beasts of the field”: the beasts of the field are those who live luxuriously and pursue the gluttony of the belly. “The birds of heaven, and the fishes of the sea, which pass through the paths of the sea”: the birds signify the proud, that is, heretics, who utter falsehoods against heavenly things [Col. 1199C] and by deception cause others to adhere to them. By the fishes of the sea we understand those who eagerly desire things which, like the paths of the sea, are vain and transitory. Thus both good and evil have been committed to the dominion of Jesus Christ and subjected beneath his feet, that he may reward the good and condemn the evil. This, then, is what follows: “All peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him,” that is, the heavenly city Jerusalem, gathered from every tribe, people, language, and nation, will with supreme devotion render him praise for ever. Thus John testifies in the Apocalypse that he heard it from angels: “I saw,” he says, “and heard the voices of many angels round about the throne, and the four living creatures, and the elders; and their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a [Col. 1200A] great voice: ‘Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.’ And every creature that is in heaven, and on earth, and under the earth, and in the sea, and the things which are therein, I heard saying: ‘To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb: blessing, and brightness, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, honor and power and strength be to our God for ever and ever. Amen’” (Rev. 5). The Psalmist indicates his ascension into heaven as follows:

He, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced as a giant to run his course. His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his return unto its height (Ps. 18). For, coming from heaven, he descended as far as the lower world; and on returning he resumed his dwelling-place, ascending to the seat of the Father, from which he had previously gone forth alone [Col. 1200B]. But the angels, who ministered to him while he was clothed in flesh and accompanied him as he ascended, said: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter in” (Ps. 23). For when the powers of heaven saw Christ’s flesh ascending in the clouds, and did not know the mystery of his incarnation, they asked in great wonder, saying: “Who is this King of glory?” As though they said: “We always behold the Son reigning together with the Father, and have never seen him depart from him; who then is this King of glory?” The angels accompanying the Lord reply: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory,” that is, the Lord of angels, whose gifts are powers, is himself the King of glory, and no other [Col. 1200C]. And he is rightly the Lord of powers, because, having become man for us, delivered over to death, and consigned to the infernal darkness, he mercifully undertook this, patiently endured it, bravely conquered it, and wondrously accomplished it. Trampling down hell with power, he returned in triumph to the heights, ascended gloriously into heaven, and now, seated at the Father’s right hand, intercedes for us, he with whom he eternally governs all things.

Isaiah likewise says, in the person of the angels marveling at the magnificence of Christ as he ascends: “Who is this that comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63). Esau, the son of Isaac, is Edom itself. Bozrah, however, is a city in the land of Moab, and its name is interpreted “firm,” or Jerusalem, which was built with most solid walls. Edom [Col. 1200D], indeed, is interpreted “blood-stained,” and signifies the people of the Jews, who were defiled by the blood of Christ and of the prophets. For to that people it was said: “You shall live by the sword” (Gen. 27), because that people, devoted to bloodshed, exercised killing against the prophets and against Christ. Therefore this is the Son of God who comes from Bozrah and from Edom—that is, from the persecution of this world—with dyed garments: namely, with his body wounded and made purple by the blood of his passion and the water of redemption.

That too which, in the Old Testament, the high priest alone did once a year—leaving the people behind and entering into the Holy of Holies, where the mercy-seat was (Exod. 30; Lev. 16)—signified our high priest, the Lord Jesus Christ. When the dispensation of his passion and resurrection had been completed, he entered once into the Holy of Holies [Col. 1201A], that is, he penetrated the heavens in entering to the Father, in order to make him propitious to humankind and to plead for the sins of all who believe in him. Hence the Apostle Paul said to the Hebrews:

“Christ, appearing as High Priest of the good things to come, through the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—nor through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9). Hence he is also able to save forever those who approach God through himself, ever living to intercede for us. Every high priest, certainly, must first offer sacrifices to God for his own sins, and then for those of the people (Heb. 7). But the Lord Jesus Christ has no need to offer [Col. 1201B] sacrifices for himself, because, as the Apostle Peter says, “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2). Such, therefore, beloved, it was fitting that we should have as high priest: namely, holy, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens (Heb. 7). Truly our Lord Jesus Christ has been made higher than the heavens, of whom blessed Paul says: “For Jesus did not enter holy places made with hands, copies of the true ones, but heaven itself, that he may now appear before the face of God for us” (Heb. 9).

Therefore the prophet, inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, urges us to sing psalms with all devotion to this same supreme king, Jesus Christ.

“Sing psalms,” he says, “to God, who ascended above the heaven of heaven, toward the east” [Col. 1201C] (Ps. 67). Therefore the Lord Jesus, who descended from heaven to deliver our weakness from the hand of the enemy, also ascended above the heavens of heavens and sits at the Father’s right hand. But when he says “toward the east,” he plainly indicates Jerusalem in the literal sense, whence the Lord ascended into heaven in the disciples’ sight. That land is found full of many miracles, in which the faith of believers is instructed more by sights than by readings.

For he ascended above the heaven of heaven, that is, above every rational heavenly creature, which is the heaven of heaven, and as far as the east—that is, as far as equality with the Father, from whom he always springs, because his origin had no beginning and will have no end. Hence: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” [Col. 1201D] (John 3). And again: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us” (Luke 1). And elsewhere: “Dayspring and Splendor is his name” (Zech. 6). For he alone ascended into heaven by himself; but all others who ascend to heaven can ascend only through him. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).

He, therefore, now exalted at the Father’s right hand, “will give to his voice the voice of power” (Ps. 67). While still present in this world, the Son of God gave the voice of humility when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26); then he gave the voice of power when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead [Col. 1202A] (John 11). That too was a voice of power when he said to the paralytic: “Rise and walk” (Matt. 9). Appropriately, our Lord Jesus Christ, when he came to be judged, gave the voice of humility; but when he comes to judge, he will give the voice of power. His magnificence and power will then be in the clouds (Ps. 67), when he comes in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty, to render to each according to his work.

When will Christ give the voice of his power? Namely, when the dead rise at his voice. For he himself says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear shall live” (John 5). Again the Son of God will give the voice of his power when he says to the righteous: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared [Col. 1202B] for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25). Then too his magnificence and his power will be in the clouds, when he says to the wicked: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid.).

For this reason, dearest brothers, I exhort you: while you still live in this mortal body, give glory to God in psalms and hymns, presuming nothing of yourselves in good works. But if, in those things which you do rightly, you ascribe glory not to yourselves but to God, you will by no means fear that voice of power and rebuke which the wicked will hear. Yet I want you to know that those sing to God who persevere in good works. Those truly sing a psalm to his name [Col. 1202C] who keep his commandments with their whole mind.

What is it to praise God? It is, plainly, to live well. Whoever lives well praises God; whoever lives badly blasphemes God. Hence Paul said to certain disciples: “Let not the good name be blasphemed among the Gentiles through you” (Rom. 2). In saying that the good name must not be blasphemed, he commands them to lead a good life. As though he said more plainly: “Your good conduct pertains to God’s glory, but bad conduct to blasphemy.” Hence blessed Augustine, the outstanding teacher, says:

[Note: [Col. 1201D] *Expositions on Psalm 148.*] “You cease to praise God when you depart from righteousness and from that which pleases him. For if you never turn aside from a good life, your tongue is silent, but your life cries out; and God’s ears are directed toward your heart.”

Therefore those worthily offer praises to God who always direct themselves to his contemplation with a pure and faithful mind [Col. 1202D]. On the contrary, those who devote themselves from morning until evening to murmuring and detraction can in no way worthily praise God. Nor do those appear to praise God who gladly speak vain and idle words. How can one suppose that he worthily praises God who does not cease all day long to stir up quarrels, hatreds, and scandals against his brothers? Or how does one think he praises God who constantly, by whispering and slandering, provokes God’s servants to scandal? Nor does he worthily praise God in choir who, by sowing discord, disturbs his brothers in the cloister.

Therefore, beloved, if you desire to please God in psalms and hymns [Col. 1203A], first show one another charity and concord; flee vain and useless tales; drive curses and insults far away from yourselves; hate whispering and detraction; abhor quarrels and disputes; set aside envy and harmful desire; love peace and affection. Sing to God from the depths of your hearts; sing to him with a voice of jubilation. Let a clear voice praise God; let a good life praise him also. Let the mind within the breast be devout and gracious, and let there be in the mouth a voice of exultation and praise. Let the love of true charity burn within, and let sweet melody resound without. Let the eye of the mind remain pure for contemplating God; let a loud and harmonious voice proceed from the mouth in his praise. Let there be the work of charity in the hands and the speech of truth on the tongue. Let the tongue be exercised in God’s praise, and the hands in works of mercy [Col. 1204A]. Let the tongue be loosed to bless God, and let the hands be stretched out in the needs of neighbors.

Therefore, beloved, continually raise the desire of your devotion toward the heavenly homeland, and lift the gaze of your pure mind as far as the very Son of God, who sits at the Father’s right hand. With all urgency of prayers and perseverance in good works, entreat him, so that through himself, who is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), he may cause you also to reach that same Father—his by nature and yours by grace—and that you may forever be able to return thanks and praise to him, together with all the saints, for benefits bestowed. May he grant this, who with the same Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Thirty-Second Sermon: On the Feast of the Holy Spirit

[Col. 1203]

[Col. 1203B] [Note: [Col. 1203D] Isidore, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 34.] Your charity ought to know, dearest brothers, that the day of Pentecost first began when, in the Old Testament, the voice of God thundered from above on Mount Sinai and the law was given to Moses (Exod. 19). But in the New Testament Pentecost began when he sent the Holy Spirit whom he had promised to the apostles; and the Spirit could by no means come upon them unless Christ himself had ascended into heaven (John 16). Finally, when Christ had entered the gate of heaven, after ten days had intervened, the place in which the apostles were gathered in prayer suddenly shook; and as the Holy Spirit descended upon them, they were inflamed, so that they spoke the mighty deeds of God in the languages of all nations (Acts 2).

Thus the coming of the Holy Spirit from heaven upon the apostles, poured out in the diversity of languages, transmitted the feast to posterity; and for that reason Pentecost is celebrated and the day itself is accordingly held to be illustrious. This feast of the Gospel agrees with the feast of the Law. In the Old Testament, after the lamb had been sacrificed, the law written by the finger of God was given to Moses after fifty days had intervened. But in the New Testament, after Christ, who “was led like a sheep to slaughter” (Isa. 53), had been killed, the true Passover is celebrated; and after fifty days have intervened, the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, is given to the one hundred and twenty disciples, a number corresponding to Moses’ age. Moses was one hundred and twenty years old when he died (Deut. 34); Solomon’s temple was one hundred and twenty cubits [Col. 1203D] high (2 Chron. 3); and the Holy Spirit descended upon the one hundred and twenty disciples in the upper room [Col. 1204B] (Acts 1). This number signifies the perfection of both Testaments.

[Note: [Col. 1203D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 28.] Therefore, just as, as stated above, the law was given to Moses on the fiftieth day after the old Passover had been completed, so also, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s passion—by which that Passover was prefigured—the promised Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, descended upon the apostles and those who were with them in the city of Jerusalem; and, as the tongues of believers were divided, the whole world was filled with Gospel preaching.

There the law is said to have been written by the finger of God, who overcame the magicians and cast out demons. Then all the people look there upon voices and lamps, the smoking mountain, thunderings and lightnings, and the resounding blast of the trumpet. In the voices and thunderings, indeed, the cry of the preaching apostles is understood [Col. 1204C]; in the lamps, the splendor of miracles; in the trumpet’s sound, the powerful preaching of the saints. All these things were fulfilled at the coming of the Holy Spirit, when all Christ’s disciples thundered forth commandments and signs in a diversity of languages.

Sinai, moreover, is interpreted “bush,” which signifies the Church, in which the Lord speaks to Moses. That the Lord descended in fire and smoke when about to give the law signifies that he illuminates believers by the brightness of his manifestation and darkens the eyes of unbelievers through the smoke of error. That he is seen in darkness signifies that the wicked, who savor earthly things, did not recognize him when he descended in the darkness of malice—

[Note: [Col. 1204D] “Him descending . . . being born.”]

—that is, when he was born in humanity. Therefore, being seen in darkness [Col. 1204D], he gave the law, because those who do not follow the truth of his law—that is, unbelievers—walk in the darkness of ignorance [Col. 1205A]. To them the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who see may not see, and those who hear may not understand” (John 19).

[Note: [Col. 1205D] Isidore, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, as cited above.] Indeed, this feast, Pentecost, has another mystery as well. It consists of a week of weeks. Seven weeks of days produce that same Pentecost in which forgiveness of sins takes place through the Holy Spirit. But weeks of years make the fiftieth year, which among the Hebrews is called the Jubilee, in which likewise there is remission for the land, freedom for slaves, and restoration of possessions that had been purchased for a price (Lev. 25). For seven, as has been said, multiplied seven times produces the number fifty when the monad—that is, unity—is added. The authority of the fathers has taught that this unity is assumed from the figure of the age to come. For it is itself always both the eighth and the first; indeed, it is always the one day, which is every day.

Therefore the Sabbath-rest [Note: [Col. 1205D] “Sabbath-rest.”] of souls must meet the people of God there and be completed there, where the eighth portion is given; as blessed Gregory, wisely expounding Solomon’s words, says:

[Note: [Col. 1206D] Homily 16 on Ezekiel.] “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight; for you do not know what evil shall be upon the earth” (Eccles. 11).

For we give a portion to seven and eight together when we arrange the things that pass through the seven days in such a way that through them we may come to eternal goods. For this reason, during the forty days after the Lord’s resurrection abstinence is relaxed and the time is celebrated in joy alone, because of the figure of the future resurrection, where there will no longer be toil but rest and eternal joy. For this reason too, during these days the knees are not bent in prayer, because, as a certain wise man says, bending the knee is a sign of penitence and mourning. Pentecost, therefore, in which forgiveness of sins takes place through the Holy Spirit, signifies, as has been said, the eternal rest for which the entire Church yearns with utmost devotion.

The spacious place extending as far as the front of the vestibule of the inner gate, which in Ezekiel measured fifty cubits (Ezek. 40), likewise signifies that same eternal and most blessed rest. Hence that place too is said to have been measured at fifty cubits. The number seven has its perfection, because on that day the number of days is completed and, through the Law, the Sabbath is given as rest to God’s people. But this number seven, multiplied by itself, reaches forty-nine. If the monad, that is, one, is added to it, the number fifty is attained, because all our perfection will be in the contemplation of that One, in whose vision there will no longer be anything lacking to our salvation and joy. Hence too the Jubilee, as stated above—that is, the fiftieth year—was given for rest, because whoever reaches the eternal joys of almighty God will thereafter have neither toil nor groaning.

[Col. 1206A] It should be noted that the place which is described as extending fifty cubits is said to reach the front of the vestibule of the inner gate. Therefore, in this passage the prophet does not describe the vestibule itself of the inner gate, but the inner place which extends toward the vestibule of the inner gate. Through this place, certainly, as we have said, our hope is signified; for while it seeks eternal rest, it directs the mind inward toward the vestibule. For in the very fact that we desire heavenly things, yearn for the promised joys, and seek the rest of eternal life, we already draw near to the front of the inner vestibule.

Let faith, therefore, be signified by the gate; charity by the court; and hope be figured by the place which drew near to the front of the vestibule of the inner gate. Without these three virtues, whoever is now able to use reason cannot enter the heavenly building [Col. 1206B]. Faith, then, is found in the gate, because it introduces us to understanding; charity in the court, because it enlarges the mind into love of God and neighbor; hope in the place described as fifty cubits, because through desires and sighs it introduces the soul to the hidden joys of eternal rest.

The ten curtains which, at the Lord’s command through Moses, were joined to one another by fifty golden rings (Exod. 26), prefigured all the faithful of the Church, who are united by the gift of the Holy Spirit and the bond of charity. Let us therefore pursue this history more fully and examine more closely how the ten curtains signify the children of the Church.

Thus the coverings [Col. 1206C], sewn with loops, suspended by rings, and fastened with cords like curtains, extending twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth, prefigured the entire multitude of believers, who cling and hang upon the cords of faith. For “a threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccles. 4): this is faith in the holy Trinity, from which the whole Church hangs and through which it is sustained.

That curtains of one measure extend twenty-eight cubits in length and four in breadth signifies the law of the Gospel.

[Note: [Col. 1206D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 53.]

For the number seven commonly signifies the law, on account of the many sevenfold mysteries joined to the four Gospels. Four times seven makes the number twenty-eight [Col. 1206D]. There are ten curtains, however, so that they may make up the complete number of perfection and signify the Decalogue of the Law. Yet they are joined to one another by fifty golden rings, because all believers are united by the gift of the Holy Spirit in the bond of faith and charity. For the number fifty, as has often been said, belongs to the Holy Spirit. Hence on the fiftieth day after Passover—that is, today—the Paraclete Spirit, namely the Consoler, descended upon the apostles.

Truly the Son of God and of the Virgin illumines his Church, that is, his faithful people, by the gift of the Holy Spirit; gathers it into the unity of true faith; cleanses it from original sin by the water of baptism; and unceasingly invites it, through himself and through his preachers, to the prize [Col. 1207A] of heavenly blessedness.

Hence, in the Song of spiritual love, he addresses her in a sweet-sounding voice, saying: “Come from Lebanon, my bride; come from Lebanon, come: you shall be crowned” (Song 4).

[Note: [Col. 1207D] Gregory, on this passage.]

Lebanon, indeed, is interpreted “whitening.” What then is understood by Lebanon except baptism, in which the holy Church is washed with sanctified water and made white from the blackness of sins through the Holy Spirit, whom she receives, and through faith in Christ? Hence it is written: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. 50). Therefore the holy Church comes from Lebanon to the crown, because in Christ’s baptism it receives faith; through that faith, with Christ’s grace, it merits to be able to receive the heavenly reward.

But what does the threefold repetition, “Come,” mean, except that whatever she does is established in faith, hope, and charity [Col. 1207B]? Fortified by these three virtues, she has the strength by which she does not grow weary on the way. Of faith it is said: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts 15). And again: “Without faith it is impossible for anyone to please God” (Heb. 11). Of hope it is said: “None who hope in you, Lord, shall be confounded” (Ps. 24). And again it is said to him: “For who has hoped in you and been forsaken?” (Ecclus. 2). Of charity it is said: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (Prov. 10). And again: “If I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I deliver my body so that I may be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). And the Apostle John says: “God is charity” [Col. 1207C] (1 John 4).

Yet the threefold “Come” may also be understood differently. The bride—that is, the Church or the holy soul—comes to Christ when, living in this world, she does whatever good she can; she comes when, at the hour of death, she is stripped of the flesh; she comes a third time when, on the day of judgment, she resumes the flesh and enters the heavenly bridal chamber with Christ. There she will receive the rewards of all her labors; there, with her enemies wholly overthrown and excluded, she will be gloriously crowned.

Hence she is next promised: “You shall be crowned from the summit of Amana, from the top of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards” (Song 4). What is meant by Amana, Sanir, and Hermon—the names, namely, of mountains—except the powerful of this age, who seem to the lowly to be all the higher and stronger in proportion as they are richer? But from these mountains the holy Church is crowned, because, while it preaches the eternal kingdom and demonstrates by its example that all worldly things are worthless, it also inclines the powerful themselves to repentance and prepares for itself a crown in heaven through their conversion. Thus the humble children of the Church overthrow the proud of the world, and the lowly bend down the lofty. Hence it is written: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (Isa. 40).

But why is the Church said to be crowned not only from mountains but also from the summits of mountains [Col. 1208A], except because we see this fulfilled: even the loftiest persons, namely kings and emperors, now believe in Christ and obey his commandments through the preaching of that same Church? For kings and emperors, as has been said, serve Christ; laying down their crowns by humbly repenting, they seek forgiveness for their sins in the Church and attain it through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

If, then, by the heads of mountains we understand the highest persons, rightly by the dens of lions and mountains of leopards are signified secular rulers and officials who serve cruelty and deceive by their wiles those whom they cannot injure by force.

[Note: [Col. 1207D] Add “not.”]

For leopards always bear spots on their skin; and what else do these signify but hypocrites or the discordant? In those who pursue cruelty demons lie as lions; in those as leopards they build mountains, when they consent to mingle certain virtues with their vices and desire the glory of praise for all their good deeds [Col. 1208B]. These are truly changed by the variegation of leopards, because, while they pursue vices along with virtues, they are divided, as it were, by the difference of colors in a mottled hide.

But the Church is crowned from the dens of lions and from the mountains of leopards, because, when the cruel are converted to mercy and hypocrites to humility of life through its preaching, instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, it will receive the reward which it deserves for all of them.

We see, therefore, that what the prophet Isaiah promised is already fulfilled in the Church through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, when he says: “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid” (Isa. 11).

[Note: [Col. 1208D] The same Gregory, Homily 16 on Ezekiel.]

For the wolf dwells with the lamb within the bosom of holy charity, because those who were plunderers in the world rest in peace within the bosom of the Church together with the gentle and meek. And the leopard lies down with the kid, because one who was mottled with the stains of his sins consents to humble himself in the holy Church together with one who despises himself and confesses that he is a sinner. Then it adds: “The calf, the lion, and the sheep shall dwell together” (ibid.), because the one who, through a contrite heart, prepares himself as a daily sacrifice to God; another who raged with cruelty like a lion; and another who endures in the simplicity of his innocence like a sheep, have gathered together in the folds of the holy Church.

Behold what great and mighty power belongs to the charity poured out in the hearts of believers by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven by God: it kindles, burns together, fuses, and reforms diversities of minds as though into one form of gold [Col. 1208D]. But because the elect love one another thus in divine charity, they must hasten toward God by doing good works, so that they may deserve to see him in heaven.

For one is our Lord and Redeemer, with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Here he illumines the hearts of his elect by the Holy Spirit, binds them to humanity, and continually stirs them through inward desires toward heavenly love. Hence it is further added there: “And a little child shall lead them” [Col. 1209A]. Who is this little child except he of whom it is written: “A little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9)? He leads his faithful who dwell together in the Church, because, lest our hearts cling to earthly things, he daily sets us aflame through inward desire and the fire of the Holy Spirit.

And this very leading of his is to kindle us incessantly toward his love, lest, when we love one another in return, we remain in mind in this exile; lest the rest of this life so please us that we are brought to forgetfulness of our heavenly homeland. Hence he mixes chastisements with his gifts, so that everything which formerly delighted us in the world may become bitter to us; and so that that fire of the Holy Spirit may rise in the mind which disturbs and awakens us toward heavenly desire and, if I may put it so, bites delightfully, torments sweetly, and makes us sorrowful cheerfully [Col. 1209B]. Therefore the little child leads us, because he who “was made a little lower than the angels” (Ps. 8), through the charity which he grants us in the Holy Spirit, does not permit our minds to settle in this world.

Hence, when Moses expressed the life of the elect through the colors of garments, he commanded that twice-dyed scarlet be used in the high priest’s ornament (Exod. 28).

[Note: [Col. 1209D] From Gregory, cited above.]

For what is signified by scarlet except charity, which is always kindled by the flame of love? But scarlet is dyed twice when our charity is inflamed not only by love of God but also by love of neighbor. For when someone loves God in such a way that he neglects care for the neighbor entrusted to him, scarlet in him is still dyed only once [Col. 1209C]. And when someone loves a neighbor in such a way that he diminishes the desire with which he ought to burn toward God, the color of double dyeing is not in him.

Therefore we ought to love those with whom we live and to pant with all our desires after him in whom we truly live. Scarlet is therefore twice-dyed in us if we both love our neighbors here as ourselves and, together with those whom we love, hasten toward the Author of all things. He sent his most beloved Son from heaven for the redemption of humankind; he chose and instructed the apostles; and, lest they should fear the adversities of the present world or the rage of persecutors, he strengthened them by the Holy Spirit and sent them throughout the whole world to gather his Church from the four quarters of the world [Col. 1209D].

Speaking among other things of their powers, blessed Job says: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job 26). Explaining this, Gregory, the great teacher of the Church, says: “Whom did God adorn as heavens, except those of whom it is written, ‘The heavens declare the glory of God’ (Ps. 18)?” Without doubt, the Spirit then adorned those whom he filled. We have learned this from Luke’s account, who says: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in various languages, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” [Col. 1210A] (Acts 2).

From this, therefore, the holy apostles received the adornments of power, though previously they had been possessed by an immense ugliness of fear. We know, certainly, that the foremost of those heavens—that is, of the apostles—before receiving the grace of this Holy Spirit, denied life as often as he feared dying. He was cast down not by punishments, not by afflictions, not by anyone’s terrifying authority, but by the question of a single servant. Indeed, lest a stronger sex should appear formidable, he was tested by a maidservant questioning him. Again, so that the weakness of the other sex might be rendered even more contemptible by the lowliness of her office, he was questioned not merely by a maidservant but by a maidservant who was a doorkeeper. Behold how contemptible was the person who questioned him in order to test him! Thus it might be openly shown how great [Col. 1210B] was the weakness of fear which possessed him, since he could not stand even before the voice of a serving-girl who kept the door.

But now let us hear what sort of man he, who shortly before was fearful, became after the coming of the Holy Spirit. Certainly, Luke’s testimony teaches us with what authority he preached the Lord against priests and rulers. For when a question had arisen after a miracle was performed, and the chief priests, elders, and scribes had assembled to persecute the apostles, they set them in their midst and sought to ask by what power they had performed the miracle. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter said to them: “Rulers of the people and elders, if today we are judged concerning the good deed done to an infirm man, by which this man has been made whole, let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified and whom God raised from the dead, this man stands before you whole” (Acts 4).

When the fury of the persecutors grew against these words, and the priests and rulers forbade them to preach Jesus, the authority with which Peter rose against the anger of the rulers is shown by what is immediately added there: “Peter and the apostles said: ‘We must obey God rather than men’” [Col. 1210C] (Acts 5). But when the commands of the resisting priests did not suppress the authority of the preaching apostles, they proceeded to scourging. For it follows: “Then the chief priests, having beaten them, commanded them not to speak at all in the name of Jesus, and released them.” But that scourges could not suppress the apostles’ strength is plainly shown by what is immediately added: “And they indeed went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were judged worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.”

Immediately afterward it is also shown what they did after rejoicing in their scourges: “Every day in the temple and from house to house they did not cease teaching and preaching Jesus Christ.” Behold, he who shortly before was fearful now speaks in languages, shines with miracles, rebukes the unbelief of priests and rulers with a free voice, provides the others an example of authority in preaching Jesus, and is forbidden by beatings to speak in Jesus’ name, yet is not restrained [Col. 1210D]. He despises the scourges of those who beat him, though shortly before he had feared the words of those who questioned him. He who, when questioned by a maidservant, had been afraid of her strength, when beaten subdues the strength of rulers.

For the holy apostle, now strengthened by the charity of the Holy Spirit, trampled down with the foot of freedom the heights of this world, so that he might see as lowly whatever swelled high against the grace of the Creator. These are the adornments of the heavens, as stated above, with which God adorned the heavens. These are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are customarily manifested in diverse powers. Paul enumerates these gifts, divided by the grant of hidden dispensation, saying:

“To one, indeed, through the Spirit is given the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, the grace of healings in one Spirit; to another, the working of powers; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of languages; to another, interpretation of utterances.” Immediately concluding with a general definition [Col. 1211A], he says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Of these heavens too it is said in the Psalm: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32). And concerning these adornments of the Spirit it adds: “And by the Spirit of his mouth, all their power” (ibid.) [Col. 1211B].

As if he said more plainly: “The heavens were made firm, not by themselves, but by the word of the Lord,” that is, by the Son of the Father; “and by the spirit of his mouth,” namely the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son—who is the Father’s mouth—their strength was made firm. And not merely a part, but all their strength was made firm, because they possessed nothing of themselves, as though supplementation came to them from God. Observe that the work of the Word, that is, the Son, and of the Holy Spirit is one. For “all their strength” is the same thing as their having been made firm. Therefore [Col. 1211C] the Son and the Holy Spirit do this; but do they do so without the Father? Certainly not. Rather, the Father works through his Word and the Holy Spirit, who teaches and strengthens the pillars of heaven, that is, the preachers of the Church. Thus it is rightly said: “His Spirit adorned the heavens,” because holy preachers, unless they received the promised gifts of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, would have shone with no beauty of strength.

Therefore “the heavens were made firm by the word of the Lord”: that is, by the teaching and operation of the Son of God. The heavens—that is, the apostles, raining doctrine, thundering threats, and flashing with miracles—were made firm by hope and charity. The Son of God is called the Word because he interprets for us the will of God the Father. And “by the Spirit of his mouth,” that is, by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1211D], sent from heaven by his mouth, namely Christ, who is the mouth of the Father, through whom God the Father spoke to us. Here it is shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son. For the Son of God and of the Virgin himself said to his disciples: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete, that is, the consoling Spirit, will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16). The Holy Spirit therefore proceeds from the Father, and proceeds also from the Son; he is sent by the Father, and is sent also by the Son, because the same Holy Spirit is of one will and operation with the Father and the Son. From that Spirit comes all the strength of the apostles: namely, their thundering with threats, flashing with miracles [Col. 1212A], and constancy in suffering. Thus, descending upon them in the appearance of fire, the Holy Spirit made them strong to endure the rage of persecutors; and, in order to instruct the Church, he taught them inwardly all truth perfectly.

Concerning this spiritual fire, the prophet Jeremiah, setting forth the future as though it were already past, speaks figuratively in the person of the Church, saying: “From on high he sent fire into my bones, and instructed me” (Lam. 1). As if he said openly: God the Father, from himself and from on high—from his Son Jesus Christ, through whom he works all things—sent the fire of the Holy Spirit into my bones, that is, into the apostles. In the Church, by enduring adversities for love of God and neighbour and by doing good works, they are stronger than the rest; and thus he instructed me by spiritual teaching.

[Col. 1212B] Allegorically. Those who believed from among the Jews or the Gentiles and became one Church rightly say: “From on high he sent fire into my bones,” that is, the Holy Spirit, by whom every strong virtue might be strengthened; and the Church herself is divinely instructed, so that she may serve idols no longer or seek worldly delights. This is aptly signified by the letter MEM, which is interpreted from the very gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which the rejoicing Church declares that she has been instructed, so that she may chastely love and cherish the same Son of God together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. The Church also blushes in repentance for the very vices to which she had formerly been enslaved.

It follows: “He spread a net for my feet; he turned me back.” As if he said plainly: He spread the net of spiritual teaching for my feet, that is, for the pleasures [Col. 1212C] of my flesh; and he turned me back, from vices to virtues, from unhappiness [Note: [Col. 1211D] Variant: “from unbelief.”] to faith, so that I might hear the voice of one warning behind my back. As if he said more plainly: He spread before my feet the net of preaching, lest I should follow the vanity of errors and the carnal desires of concupiscence. Hence: “From every evil way I have restrained my feet, that I may keep your words” (Ps. 118). As though he said: He turned me back so that I might go after him, not run before him. This net was entrusted to the holy apostles, that they might draw rational fish out of the sea of this age.

Again the prophet adds in the person of the Church: “He made me desolate.” As if he said: He made me bereft of earthly consolation, consumed all day by sorrow [Col. 1212D], that is, throughout the whole time of this present life, by pain and longing for future blessedness. Long burning—indeed, exhausted—by this longing, the Psalmist said: “My tears became my bread by day and by night” (Ps. 41). “He made me,” he says, “desolate” of present goods, which had formerly been a consolation to me; “consumed all day by sorrow,” namely, by the pain of present tribulations and the sorrowful longing for future goods. Let this statement of the prophet Jeremiah be repeated, so that it may be more firmly impressed upon the mind for the soul’s benefit.

“From on high he sent fire into my bones,” etc.

Morally. When the soul is rebuked by the Lord for its sins, it returns to itself and is beneficially pierced with compunction; and in its bones [Col. 1213A], that is, in the marrow of its thoughts, it declares that fire has come from the Lord. Hence it is chastised and instructed by God. And because it senses the nets of God’s teaching spread before its feet, it turns back, abstains from unlawful things, changes the extravagance of pleasure and concupiscence into tears, and, set ablaze inwardly by the fire of the Holy Spirit and wounded by the arrow of divine love, it weeps all the more strongly, consumed by sorrow, and accepts no consolation from the present life, the more truly it recognizes that it had wandered through various desires.

Thus Ezekiel, when in a vision a building was shown to him upon a mountain, speaking figuratively said: “A man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze measured the chamber, one reed in length and one reed in [Col. 1213B] breadth” (Ezek. 40). Let blessed Gregory, most subtle investigator of the Scriptures, come forward and explain to us the profundity of this little verse. “Let us consider,” he says, “what is customarily done in a bridal chamber, and from that infer what is done in the holy Church. For in the bridal chamber bridegroom and bride enter into covenant and are joined to one another in love. What, then, are bridal chambers in the holy Church except the hearts of those in which souls are joined to the invisible Bridegroom by spiritual love? They burn with longing for him and desire none of the things that are in the world any longer; they reckon the length of the present life a punishment; they hasten to leave the body and swiftly reach their heavenly homeland; and they long to rest in the vision of the heavenly Bridegroom, in the embrace of love.”

Thus a mind [Col. 1213C] that has become such accepts no consolation from the present life, but sighs, burns, pants, and is distressed from its inmost depths for him whom it loves. Even the health of its own body becomes cheap to it, because it has been pierced by love’s wound. Hence the holy soul itself, the bride of Christ, says in the Song of spiritual love: “I am wounded by charity” (Song 2). But the heart’s health which knows no pain from this wound is unhealthy. When, however, the soul begins to pant with heavenly longing and to feel love’s wound, it becomes healthier through the wound, whereas before it was sick through health.

Yet for a mind strongly loving Christ its Bridegroom, delay in the present life is wont to be no small or vain consolation, if, through its delay from his vision, the souls of others may profit by its word and be set aflame with the torches of love for the heavenly Bridegroom. [Col. 1213D] It grieves because it sees itself delayed. Everything it sees is sad to it, because it does not yet see him whom it longs to see. But, as I have said, it is no small consolation if, while the soul is delayed from seeing him, many other souls are gathered into the kingdom through it: so that, though late, it may see with many the one whom alone it had wished to see sooner.

Hence again in the same Songs, the holy soul herself, the bride of Christ, says: “Support me with flowers; surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (ibid.). For what are flowers but souls now beginning good work and fragrant with heavenly desire? What are apples arising from flowers but minds already perfect in goodness, which come to the fruit of good work from the beginning of a holy purpose? [Col. 1214A] Therefore she who languishes with love seeks to be supported with flowers and surrounded with apples, because, if she is not yet permitted to see him whom she desires, it is nevertheless a great consolation for her to rejoice in the progress of others. Thus let the soul languishing with holy love be supported by flowers and apples, so that it may rest in its neighbour’s good work while it is not yet able to contemplate the face of God.

Let us consider what a bridal chamber Paul’s mind had been, when he said: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1). With how great a love had he joined himself to almighty God, who reckoned Christ alone to be life for himself and death to be gain! Hence he says again: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.” But behold, holy Paul: you desire to be dissolved; show us with what love you languish. Since you see that you are meanwhile delayed, why, I ask, do you not seek to be supported [Col. 1214B] with flowers? “I do seek it,” he says, plainly. For he continues: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake.” As if he said openly: So far as I am concerned, I would now wish to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but for your sake it is necessary that I remain in the flesh, so that, supported—indeed, crowned—by your progress, I may be able to come with you to Christ. Hence he says to his disciples as they make progress: “For what is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Is it not you before our Lord Jesus Christ?” (1 Thess. 2).

Hence the aforesaid bridal chamber is said to have been measured one reed in length and one reed in breadth. Length pertains to the long-suffering of waiting, and breadth to the expansiveness of charity. Therefore each bridal chamber possesses as much length [Col. 1214C] as it is able to possess breadth; because the mind aflame with heavenly desire displays as much long-suffering in waiting for God as it has love for gathering its neighbour to God. It patiently bears the delays of length because the expansiveness of charity stretches it out toward the progress of its neighbour. This same length may also signify the patient long-suffering shown toward one’s neighbour. And because breadth signifies charity, which reveals the mind’s disposition and receives friends and enemies alike into love, the chamber’s length is as great as its breadth: for as broad as the mind is through love, so patient it will be through long-suffering. If you cease to love, you cease to endure. For we endure less readily those whom we love less, [Col. 1214D] because, when charity’s wing no longer lightens them, the deeds of our neighbour are more quickly made burdensome by a benumbing weariness.

Therefore God sent the fire of the Holy Spirit from on high into the bones, that is, into the stronger men of the holy Church—namely, the prophets and apostles. With the same fire of the Holy Spirit he enlightened and strengthened them, so that they might endure with equanimity the threats of persecutors and the torments of suffering for love of God and desire of the heavenly homeland, and might preach with complete confidence throughout the whole world the faith of the holy Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 1213] Gregory, *Morals*, book 28, ch. 6; and “Pater.” on Exodus, ch. 43.]

These most holy and valiant preachers—the prophets, apostles, and their successors [Col. 1215A], upon whom the holy Church is built at the Lord’s command—were prefigured by the silver, cast bases and the gilded boards which the Lord commanded Moses to set up in the tabernacle of the covenant (Exod. 26). What else do we understand by the gilded boards except the holy apostles and, after them, the other teachers of the Church, who, preaching Christ’s Gospel, are spread throughout the entire world? And what do the silver bases signify except, as has been said, the prophets, who strongly and firmly support the boards placed above them? For the life of the apostles and other preachers of the Church, while it is instructed by the preaching of the prophets, is founded upon their authority. Hence two joined bases are placed beneath each board, because when the holy prophets agree in their words concerning the incarnation of the Mediator [Col. 1215B], subsequent preachers build up the Church without hesitation; and since the prophets do not disagree among themselves, they fix those preachers more strongly within.

Nor without reason is it commanded that the bases signifying the prophets should be made of silver. Silver’s brightness is preserved by use; without use, it turns black. Likewise, the sayings of the prophets before the coming of the Mediator, because they were not in use for spiritual understanding, remained, as it were, black. But after the Mediator of God and men came and wiped them before our eyes with the hand of his incarnation, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth, and he made the understanding of the preceding Fathers available for use, because he expounded words by realities. And in making silver bases and gilded boards, he showed that the precepts of the apostles are far brighter than those of the prophets [Col. 1215C].

We therefore rightly place the apostles of Jesus Christ above all teachers of the Old Testament, because by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which they received abundantly and visibly at this feast, they preached to us more subtly and openly the salvation of souls and the will of God.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] Gregory, Homily 18 on Ezekiel.]

But why do we marvel at the life of the holy apostles, when even the ancient Fathers, considering their life, greatly marvelled? Did not the Psalmist marvel at the virtues of the Church’s teachers when he said: “But to me your friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their dominion has been exceedingly strengthened” (Ps. 138)? The Truth himself shows in the Gospel of which friends he speaks, saying: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15). Isaiah too, beholding their life in the Spirit, says: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). Holy preachers are rightly called clouds because they rain with words and flash with miracles. They are also said to fly like clouds because, though living on earth, everything they do is done beyond the earth. Hence it is said through a certain cloud: “Though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 10). The earlier Fathers used marriage, begot children, possessed property [Col. 1216A], and attended to the concerns of household affairs. But foreseeing by the spirit of prophecy that these men would abandon possessions, seek no marriage, beget no children, seek nothing on earth, and possess nothing, he calls them not men walking upon the earth but clouds flying. For they fly who do not, as it were, touch the earth, because they desire nothing in it; and they are like doves at their windows, because through the spirit of their gentleness they covet nothing with their eyes.

Allegorically. These are the seven sons born to most blessed Job (Job 1), that is, to Jesus Christ, Son of God and man. In his deeds, Job, wounded and scourged, bore the type of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1215D] Gregory, *Morals*, book 1, ch. 5.]

For *Job* is interpreted “sorrowing.” Whom else, then, does that weak and stricken Job signify by his name except him [Col. 1216B] of whom the prophet speaks, saying: “He himself bore our sorrows” (Isa. 53)? In the number seven, as blessed Gregory says, the fullness of perfection is expressed.

[Note: [Col. 1216D] Ibid., ch. 6.]

Therefore seven sons were born to Jesus Christ through faith: namely, the apostles, proceeding courageously to preach. By carrying out the precepts of perfection, they maintained in their manner of life the strength, as it were, of the superior sex. Hence, being filled in the perfection of grace with the sevenfold Spirit, twelve were chosen. For from the number seven one rises to twelve. The number seven, multiplied in its component parts, reaches twelve: whether four are multiplied by three or three by four, seven is transformed into twelve. Hence the holy apostles were chosen as twelve because they were sent to preach the Trinity in the four quarters of the world, so that by their number also they might show the perfection which they preached by life and speech [Col. 1216C].

“And three daughters were also born to him.” What do we understand by the daughters except the weaker multitudes of believers? Though they do not remain in the perfection of works with vigorous strength, they nevertheless hold firmly to their known faith in the most holy Trinity. Thus, in the seven sons the order of preachers is signified; in the three daughters, the multitude of hearers. The three daughters may also signify the three orders of the faithful. For daughters are named after sons because, after the strength of the apostles had been seen, three distinctions among the faithful arose in the life of the Church: namely, pastors, the continent, and the married [Col. 1216D]. Hence the prophet Ezekiel states that he heard of three men delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14). What is signified by Noah, who guided the ark amid the waves, except the order of rulers, who, while presiding over peoples as an example of life, govern the holy Church amid the waves of temptations?

[Note: [Col. 1216D] “Of temptations.”]

What is figured by Daniel, whose remarkable abstinence is recorded (Dan. 1), except the life of the continent, who, abandoning everything that belongs to the world, rule with lofty mind over despised Babylon? What is signified by Job except the life of good married persons, who, while doing pious works with the worldly things they possess, make their way as if by an earthly road toward the heavenly homeland? Therefore, because these three distinctions of the faithful followed after the holy apostles [Col. 1217A], three daughters are rightly shown to have been born after the sons.

It follows: “And his sons went and held a feast in their houses, each on his own day.” The sons went to hold feasts in their houses when the apostolic preachers, in diverse regions of the world, supplied banquets of virtues to their hearers, as though to those eating. Hence it is said to these same sons concerning the hungry crowds: “Give them something to eat yourselves” (Matt. 14); and again: “If I send them away fasting, they will fail on the way” (Mark 8). As if that most merciful Father, grieving for our misery, said to the apostles: Let them receive in your preaching the word of consolation, lest, remaining hungry for the food of truth, they also succumb to the labour of this life.

How those feasts were offered is added when it immediately continues: “Each on his own day” [Col. 1217B]. If the darkness of ignorance is undoubtedly the night of the heart, understanding is not undeservedly called day. Hence Paul says: “One judges one day above another; another judges every day” (Rom. 14). As if he said openly: One understands certain things while omitting some others; but another knows all things to be lived [Note: [Col. 1217D] Variant: “to be seen.”] as they are. Therefore each son offers a feast on his own day, because every holy preacher feeds the minds of hearers with the banquets of truth in proportion to his enlightened understanding. Blessed Paul had made a feast on his own day when he said: “They will be happier if they remain thus”—namely, in virginity—“according to my counsel” (1 Cor. 7). He urged each person to consider his own day when he said: “Let each be fully convinced in his own mind” (Rom. 14) [Col. 1217C].

It follows: “And they sent and called their three sisters, that they might eat and drink with them.” The sons call their sisters to the feast because the holy apostles preach the joys of heavenly refreshment to weak hearers; and, seeing their minds hungry for the food of truth, they feed them with the riches of divine speech. It is well said, “that they might eat and drink with them.” For sacred Scripture is sometimes food to us and sometimes drink. It is food in its more obscure passages, because it is, as it were, broken by exposition and swallowed by eating. But it is drink in more open passages, because it is drunk as it is found. The prophet saw sacred Scripture as food, because it would be broken by exposition, when he said: “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4) [Col. 1217D]. He saw sacred Scripture as drink when he said: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55). If open commandments were not drink, Truth himself would not cry out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come and drink” (John 7).

Again he adds: “And when the days of the feast had gone round, Job sent to them and sanctified them. And rising early, he offered holocausts for each one.” The days of the feast go round [Col. 1218A] when ministries of preaching are carried out. When the feasts have been completed, Job offered a holocaust for his sons, because Jesus Christ prayed to God the Father for the apostles returning from preaching.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] Variant: “from preaching.”]

He is aptly said to sanctify by sending, because, when he poured the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, who proceeds from the Father and from himself, into the hearts of the disciples, he cleansed away whatever guilt could have been present. And he is rightly said to rise early to offer holocausts because, by offering for us the voice of his intercession, he dispels the night of error and illumines the darkness of unbelief [Note: [Col. 1217D] “The phrase ‘of unbelief’ is absent from the edition and seems superfluous.”] in our minds.

“For he said: ‘Perhaps my sons have sinned and blessed God in their hearts.’” To bless God means, in fact, to curse him: to claim glory for oneself from his gift. Hence the Lord rightly washed the feet of the holy apostles after preaching (John 13), in order openly to show that even in good work the dust of sin is often acquired, and that the steps of speakers are defiled from the very source through which the hearts of hearers are cleansed. For often, while some people speak words of exhortation, they inwardly exalt themselves, however slightly, because through them the grace of cleansing is conveyed. And while they wash away others’ wicked works by their speech, they take, as it were, the dust of evil thought from a good journey. What, then, was it to wash the disciples’ feet after preaching [Col. 1218B], except to wipe away the dust of thoughts after the glory of preaching and cleanse the steps of the heart from inward self-exaltation?

Nor does the saying, “Perhaps my sons have sinned,” conflict with the Mediator’s complete knowledge. For, though knowing all things, he assumes our ignorance in himself and, by assuming it, teaches us; at times he speaks as if from our own uncertainty, as when elsewhere he says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith on earth?”

“Thus Job did every day.” Job does not cease to offer sacrifice every day, because our Redeemer unceasingly offers a holocaust for us: without ceasing he presents to God the Father his Incarnation on our behalf. For his Incarnation itself is the offering for our cleansing.
