When he shows himself to be man, intervening, he washes away human sins; and he offers the mystery of his humanity as a perpetual sacrifice [Col. 1218D], because what cleanses is eternal.

Therefore God cleansed the hearts of the holy apostles by faith, taught them by the Holy Spirit, and strengthened them against all adversities.

[Note: [Col. 1217D] Another manuscript places a full stop after “strengthened” [Col. 1218D] and, under the heading “Second Sermon of the Holy Neume,” begins thus: “The immeasurable God entrusted to his apostles his one vineyard,” etc.]

He entrusted to them his vineyard—that is, the holy Church—to cultivate after the wicked labourers had been destroyed; and he commanded them to render its fruit in its seasons.

Concerning this vineyard Solomon says in the Songs of spiritual love: “A vineyard belonged to the peaceful one in the place that has peoples; he entrusted it to keepers” (Song 8).

[Note: [Col. 1218D] Gregory, on this passage.]

Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, is rightly called [Col. 1219A] “the peaceful one,” because through him the whole human race is reconciled to God. Thus this peaceful one had a vineyard, because amid the labour of carnal commandments he planted the Synagogue. Of it it is said: “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5). This vineyard was “in the place that has peoples,” because it was situated in the law, which gathered many peoples under itself. Of them it is said: “The peoples devised vain things” (Ps. 2). He entrusted this vineyard to keepers because he committed the Synagogue to Moses and the other Fathers of the Old Testament to guard. It aptly continues: “A man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” This vineyard bore fruit, because from the Synagogue came forth through human birth that great cluster brought from the land of promise—Christ Jesus [Col. 1219B].

Let us therefore, if you please, survey the history of the Old Testament more fully, so that we may understand more completely how that cluster, pressed in the winepress of the cross, refreshes the children of the Church with the abundance of spiritual wine. Moses accordingly sent twelve scouts into the holy land to inspect it and bring back fruits from it.

[Note: [Col. 1219D] Isidore, *Questions on Numbers*, 15.]

These scouts, sent to explore the fertile land, who frightened the people lest they believe that they could receive the land promised by the Lord, represented the scribes and Pharisees. For just as those men were sent by Moses to examine carefully the land’s fertility, so these men were commanded through the Law and the prophets to contemplate, through the testimony of Scripture, the coming of the Lord [Col. 1219C]. In him was the land, that is, our humanity, which he assumed from the Virgin without sin; and in him they could obtain also the kingdom of God, the abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life. But just as the scouts terrified the people through despair lest they trust in God’s promise, so the scribes and Pharisees persuaded the Jewish people not to believe in Christ. They longed to return to Egypt, that is, to the pleasures of this world; they rejected the manna of faith; they sought the black pots of sins, the rotten onions of blasphemies, melons of vices, and the decaying corruption of lusts.

But that cluster, which two bearers carried upon a piece of wood from the land of promise, certainly prefigured Christ: born according to the flesh from the earthly stock of Mary, the ever-Virgin, promised to the Gentiles, and suspended upon the wood of the cross. The two bearers walking under the burden of that cluster signify the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile. The former, Jewish people, cut off and turned away, ignorant of present grace and pressed beneath the burden of the one hanging above them, to whom it is subject for judgment. Hence it is said: “Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see; and bend their back always” (Ps. 68). The latter bearer represented the peoples of the Gentiles, who, believing in Christ [Col. 1220A], holding him before their eyes, always see him as they carry him, and follow him as a servant follows his lord and a disciple his master, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16).

[Note: [Col. 1219D] Edition: “This is . . . the cluster which, poured out for our salvation, [became] wine,” etc. And below, less confusedly: “This is . . . the cluster which our mother Church, a pomegranate, followed by the grace accompanying the gift; having within herself, through the number of seeds, a multitude of peoples, shining through the redness of Christ’s blood in its seal,” etc.]

This, then, is the cluster which, by the crushing of the cross, poured forth for our salvation the wine of his blood and gave the Church the cup pressed out by his passion to drink. This is the cluster which the pomegranate, our companion—namely, mother Church, aided by divine grace—followed. Within herself, by the likeness of seeds, she contains a multitude of peoples; through the redness of Christ’s sacred blood, shining with its seal; and she also has distinct seeds within, as the Apostle says: the diverse gifts of charisms [Col. 1220B] distributed by the grace of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12). Judging themselves unworthy of all these things, the unbelieving did not deserve to receive the land of Christ’s flesh, flowing with milk and honey, which his servants—that is, Christian peoples—obtained through faith. Of his teaching the Church says daily: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. 118).

The fig, however, which they brought from the land of promise with the cluster, is shown by Gospel examples to have had the image of the Law [Note: [Col. 1220D] Supply here: “of the Law.”], just as the cluster is plainly a figure of the Saviour, as the Church says of Christ in the Song of Songs: “My brother is like a cluster of cypress” (Song 1). For Christ cannot exist without the Law, nor the Law without Christ [Col. 1220C].

[Note: [Col. 1220D] Again from Gregory, on the previously cited passage in the Song.]

This vineyard, then—as was said above—which God transplanted from Egypt, bore fruit because the Synagogue generated Christ according to the flesh. Concerning this fruit God the Father said to David: “Of the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131). Hence the Apostle also writes: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ came according to the flesh” (Rom. 9). Therefore a man brings a thousand gold pieces for this fruit, because, for love of Christ, every servant of God willingly despises everything he possesses. By the thousand silver pieces in this passage we understand all earthly property, concerning which the blessed apostle Peter says: “Silver and gold I do not have” (Acts 3). Therefore for the vineyard’s fruit a man brings a thousand silver pieces, because whoever behaves manfully in the faith he has received willingly leaves all earthly things completely, that he may truly possess Christ in whom he believes [Col. 1220D]. For a thousand is a perfect number; therefore by it the perfection of any matter is shown. In the primitive Church these silver pieces were offered by those of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “All who possessed fields or houses sold them; and bringing the prices of what they sold, they laid them at the feet of the apostles. It was distributed to each as anyone had need” (Acts 4) [Col. 1221A].

These gathered persons—the holy apostles and the other disciples—built another vineyard, namely the holy Church, with Christ’s help and the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit. As good cultivators, they propagated it with their blood and extended it by their preaching to the ends of the earth, so that now it fills almost the whole world and, leased to holy cultivators, yields fruit in its seasons. Thus, in the Gospel, when the Lord asked, the chief priests and Pharisees replied: “He will utterly destroy the wicked men, and lease his vineyard to other cultivators, who will render him fruit in its seasons” (Matt. 12). Concerning this vineyard now leased to good cultivators, the peaceful one himself—the Son of God and of the Virgin—subsequently says in the same Songs: “My vineyard is before me” (Song 8) [Col. 1221B].

Truly his vineyard stands before him, because, after evil cultivators have been destroyed, he instructs the holy Church with a gracious regard through good teachers enlightened by the Holy Spirit. Again, rejoicing over her, he says: “A thousand are for you, O peaceful one, and two hundred for those who keep its fruit” (ibid.). Who are these peaceful ones, said to number a thousand, and the two hundred, except those aforesaid silver pieces? For when we completely relinquish them for Christ, we acquire peace for ourselves through their distribution with the holy apostles, who despised everything for Christ. Hence the Lord commands in the Gospel: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16) [Col. 1221C]. But what do we understand by the two hundred except the twofold reward, of soul and body, which [Note: [Col. 1221D] “Which.”] we acquire when in this world we completely despise for Christ those things—that is, earthly possessions?

Thus the thousand and two hundred silver pieces belong to the Church, because when each of the faithful completely leaves all that he possesses and makes peace with the saints, he receives the reward of the present life together with the heavenly reward. He certainly makes peace with the saints who becomes their imitator. And this is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever leaves house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or children, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and possess eternal life” (Matt. 19). But to whom is this reward thus doubled, except to those who keep its fruit? And who are those who keep the vineyard’s fruit except those who persevere in the holy work they have begun? For a work begun from holy desire, if steadfastness of mind is not retained to the end, is reckoned fruitless, because it prematurely collapses back into that from which it proceeded. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10) [Col. 1221D].

Thus this vineyard—that is, the holy Church—then began to extend its branches from sea to sea and from the river to the ends [Col. 1222A] of the world (Ps. 71), when the Synagogue, inflamed with hatred of Christ’s name, burned in persecution of the apostles. Driven on by malice, it expelled the heralds of truth from its borders, and remained cold and abandoned in the unbelief of its perversity.

Therefore the prophet Ezekiel, speaking figuratively in his vision, says: “I looked, and behold, a whirlwind came from the north, and a great cloud, and enfolding fire” (Ezek. 1). Blessed Gregory, expounding this according to the wisdom given him by God, says [Note: [Col. 1221D] *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 2. The author brings forward much from it which, in the interests of brevity, we omit. [Col. 1222D] See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 799.]: Because the north wind constricts with cold, etc., down to: “Her husband is noble in the gates,” namely Christ, “when he sits with the elders of the land” (Prov. 31), that is, with the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, and the other teachers of the Church.

But we miserable people, placed in [Col. 1222B] this valley of tears, are in no way able to turn our minds from lowly delights and raise them to desire heavenly things, unless we have first been touched by heavenly inspiration. Thus the human mind can neither despise earthly things nor perfectly fear God’s judgment unless it has first been anticipated by the light of divine love.

Therefore it is said in the book of blessed Job: “He shall hear the hearing in the terror of his voice, and the sound going forth from his mouth” (Job 37). Blessed Gregory, expounding this, says [Note: [Col. 1222D] *Morals on Job*, book XXVII, chapter 17. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 418, line 14.]: “God’s voice is not in joy,” etc., down to: “struck by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he may pursue it with daily tears.”

Thus the holy Church of God heard the voice in terror; because, when in the apostles and the other disciples [Col. 1222C] she received the grace of the Holy Spirit, she withdrew from the devil’s bondage through apostolic preaching, turned herself to the fear and love of God, and raised herself to contemplate the true God and man, Jesus Christ, now reigning at the right hand of God the Father. For rightly, when the human mind, lifted up in contemplation, hears or beholds something through heavenly inspiration, it is immediately terrified; for a fragile vessel cannot endure the great weight of heavenly light. Hence Abraham, when he heard God speaking, said: “I will speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). For when he called himself dust and ashes, he undoubtedly humbled himself in God’s sight. And Daniel too, after seeing a certain terrible vision, [Col. 1222D] said: “But I languished and was sick for many days” (Dan. 8).

Elijah likewise, after hearing, beyond all circumscription, the sound of the divine substance, stood at the entrance of the cave and covered his face with his cloak. Hence the same prophet subsequently says: “Behold, the Lord passes by; a great and strong wind overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks before the Lord; the Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, fire; the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings [Col. 1223A] 19). [Note: [Col. 1223D] Gregory, *Morals*, book V, chapter 26, and Paterius, *On 3 Kings*, chapter 10.]

The wind before the Lord overthrows mountains and breaks rocks, because the dread that rushes upon us at his coming both casts down the height of our heart and melts its hardness. But the Lord is said not to be in the wind, earthquake, and fire, while his presence in the whisper of a gentle breeze is not denied; because surely, while the mind is suspended in the sublimity of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to behold is not God. But when it perceives something subtle, this is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. For we perceive, as it were, the whisper of a gentle breeze when, by sudden contemplation, we delicately taste the savor of unbounded truth. Therefore what we know of God is true when we feel that we cannot fully know anything of him.

Hence it is well added there [Col. 1223B]: “When Elijah heard it, he covered his face with his cloak and went out and stood at the entrance of his cave.” After the whisper of the gentle breeze, the prophet covered his face with his cloak, because in that most subtle contemplation of truth one recognizes how great is the ignorance with which a human being is veiled. To cover the face with a cloak is to veil the mind with consideration of its own weakness, lest it dare seek loftier things; so that it may not rashly open the eyes of understanding beyond itself, but may reverently close them before that which it cannot grasp. Because he did this, he is described as standing at the entrance of the cave. For what is our cave but this dwelling of corruption, in which we are still held through the old nature? And when we begin to perceive something of the knowledge [Col. 1223C] of divinity, we stand, as it were, already at the cave’s entrance. Since we cannot advance perfectly, yet while longing for knowledge of the truth we already catch something of the breeze of freedom. To stand at the cave’s entrance is to begin, once the impediment of our corruption has been restrained, to go forth toward knowledge of the truth. Hence, when the cloud descended upon the tabernacle, the Israelites, seeing it from afar, are said to have stood at the entrances of their tents (Exod. 33), because those who in some measure behold the advent of divinity—that is, heavenly inspiration—already, as it were, go out from the dwelling-place of the flesh.

Thus, as has been said, the holy Church heard the hearing—that is, the coming of the Holy Spirit—in terror; because, as soon as through the preaching of the apostles she learned God’s [Col. 1223D] will, she most devoutly offered herself for contemplation of the blessedness of heavenly goods. Therefore the preachers of the Church, perfectly instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit and strengthened to endure the adversities of this present world, preach in harmony God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the holy and indivisible Trinity—and lift the eyes of the mind to behold his glory. Ezekiel fittingly shows figuratively this harmony of the Church’s preachers when, speaking of the likeness of the four living creatures, he says:

[Col. 1224A] “The likeness of the four living creatures: each had four faces, and each had four wings.” What is signified by a face, as blessed Gregory says [Note: [Col. 1223D] *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 3. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 806.], except knowledge, etc., down to: “When this is given by some to others, and faith is maintained by the hearers, the rescued [Note: [Col. 1224D] Sarepta edition.] woman—that is, the holy Church—is no longer held under the debt of her creditor.”

Concerning this spiritual oil, the bride—that is, the holy Church—praising the bridegroom, namely Christ, says thus in the Song of love: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young maidens loved you” (Cant. 1). [Note: [Col. 1224D] Gregory, on this passage.] The bridegroom’s name is Christ; but the bridegroom’s name is poured out like oil, because all who are truly called by the Christian name are filled with holy charity. By it they are softened, and by that same charity they are continually refreshed so as to send forth the flames of a good reputation. By this charity [Col. 1224B] they are more vehemently kindled in love for Christ himself; and from him they receive that by which they may cling to him more fully—the very charity with which they are anointed.

Hence follows: “Therefore the young maidens loved you.” For what is signified by the young maidens except holy souls, regenerated by the Holy Spirit through the water of baptism and transferred into Christ’s new life through the New Testament? Because of the infusion of oil they love Christ, for, called to grace, they find in him the sweetness of everlasting life; and for love of that sweetness they reject all the pomp and riches of the world. There are some who so love God that they despise themselves: they draw themselves inward in order to find God. And because God does not lie upon the surface, they examine their thoughts most carefully, devote themselves to reading, labor in meditation, and never cease by every means to seek how God may be found. Such persons truly smell the fragrance of the ointments and anoint themselves with the outpouring of spiritual oil; for, while they cast away every rottenness of vices, they find flowers for themselves, from whose combination, by God’s favor, they prepare sweet-smelling ointments. By these they also lead others with them to the knowledge and love of God.

Indeed, the gifts which the Israelite people, at the Lord’s command, offered of their own free will for the building of the tabernacle prefigured those manifold virtues of the faithful by which, with the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit, they build God’s Church. [Note: [Col. 1224D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 56.] Various gifts are offered with one purpose for the building of the tabernacle, as is written: gold, namely, silver, and precious stones (Exod. 25). Moreover, fine linen, scarlet, violet-blue, and purple; also red-dyed rams’ skins and violet-blue skins; incorruptible wood; and goats’ hair for the construction of the tabernacle. Men together with women supplied also whatever was necessary for worship and sacred vestments: bracelets and earrings, rings and ornaments for the right hand; every golden vessel was set apart as an offering to God. Thus the figure of the former tabernacle is a type of the Church. [Col. 1225A] By these gifts of the former tabernacle are signified, as has been said, the virtues of the faithful and the gifts of merits with which holy Mother Church is adorned.

Thus the faith of the holy Church is compared to gold, and the word of preaching to silver. The fact that men together with women offered what was necessary for adornment or for the tabernacle signifies that, within the holy Church, both the virtues of the perfect, represented by men, and the slight works of the weak—that is, of those subject to others, indicated by women—find their proper place, are received for holy edification, and are acceptable to God. The contribution itself is made not from necessity but freely, because faith is voluntary. For by bracelets, which bind the upper arms, are shown the works of rulers who labor mightily; by earrings is expressed the obedience of subjects; and by rings is shown the seal of hidden mysteries. Hence teachers of the Church conceal certain things from the less understanding, storing them away, as it were, beneath a seal, lest God’s sacraments be revealed to the unworthy.

Let the humble and discerning churchman therefore rejoice and say: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (Ps. 118). Further, by ornaments for the right hand are signified those good works which are granted to the faithful through the Holy Spirit and indicated by the right hand. A golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord is understood as the knowledge of divinity, which is separated from the custom and understanding of lower things in proportion as it is joined to those who love only eternal things. Further, violet-blue [Col. 1225C] signifies hope in heavenly goods; purple signifies the blood or sufferings by which holy martyrs are crowned in the heavenly homeland. By twice-dyed scarlet is shown charity, with whose perfection each person is dyed twice, because he is adorned by love of God and of neighbor. By fine linen are signified those immaculate in flesh and incorrupt in mind, and the most splendid brightness of holiness is displayed. By goats’ hair, from which the roughness of haircloth is woven, is understood the hard affliction of penitents.

Therefore, while some perhaps exercise mystery through bracelets and rings; others possess through a golden vessel a splendid and subtler understanding of God; others, through violet-blue, purple, and scarlet, are shown to hope, believe, and love the heavenly things they have heard; others offer through fine linen flesh that is incorrupt; others through goats’ hair bitterly lament what they have willingly lost—behold, through so great a diversity of works one tabernacle is made, just as one globe of earth is compacted from diverse dust when watered by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, by the incorruptible shittim wood are understood all the saints, incorrupt in mind and body, perishing neither in the present nor in the future age but remaining forever. Precious stones are the apostles, martyrs, confessors, and priests, and all the saints, whom the blessed apostle Peter also calls living stones, saying: “You yourselves also, as living stones, are built up into spiritual houses” [Col. 1226A] (1 Pet. 2), etc. All these things are offered in God’s tabernacle—that is, in the Church—so that no one may despair of salvation.

Beyond this, one offers gold, that is, wisdom; another silver, namely divine speech; another bronze, that is, the voice of preaching. Moreover, many things are made in the tabernacle: namely, a table, lampstand, altar, columns, bases, boards, chair, cups, censers, bowls, mortars, snuffers, pegs, tents. By these diverse things the whole beauty of that tabernacle—that is, of the Church—is distinguished. For, as we have said, the tabernacle is the Church, in which is the table, that is, unity of faith, or certainly Holy Scripture, from which all the faithful are fed with spiritual food. The lampstand with seven lamps signifies Christ [Col. 1226B] with the seven Churches; its snuffers signify the twofold Testament, namely the Old and the New. The columns are holy teachers, made firm by the solidity of faith; and the bases likewise are the prophets, supporting the Church’s structure by their foundation. There too are the boards, namely the apostles, broadened by the expansiveness of preaching. There are also tents, namely rulers and preachers, who labor against the storms of this age. There too are chairs, namely the distributions of gifts. Hence the Apostle says: “All these things are wrought by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). There are also pegs, that is, the leaders of the Church, upon whom all kinds of peoples hang as though they were vessels. The cups are utterances or sounds of teaching; and the censers [Col. 1226C] are the virtues of good works, or the prayers of the saints, by which a sweet fragrance rises to the Lord. The bowls are the apostles and teachers, full of life-giving and spiritual waters. There are lilies, that is, the brightness of virginity; there are mortars, namely endurance of labors and sufferings, by which the members of penitents are mortified. These forms and administrations of gifts are distributed to the faithful through the Holy Spirit, so that in the individual distributions the perfect tabernacle of Christ—that is, the perfect Church in which he dwells—may be built in the midst of the faithful.

Without doubt the Son of God and of the Virgin dwells in the midst of the Church, because he himself illumines her with gifts of the Holy Spirit and, having rescued her from carnal conduct, summons her to transform herself into him. Hence he himself said in the Gospel: “Whoever serves me, let him follow me” (John 12). To follow, indeed, is to imitate. Therefore Jesus Christ dwells in the midst of the faithful, because he truly is the example of every virtue. It is necessary, then, most beloved brethren, that we take from him the example of living well—from him “who committed no sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found” (Isa. 53). Concerning him, when the prophet Ezekiel described the likeness of the four living creatures, he spoke figuratively, saying:

“Behold, a great cloud and enfolding fire, and in its midst the likeness of four living creatures, and in them the appearance of a man” (Ezek. 1). Blessed Gregory, expounding this, [Col. 1227A] says [Note: [Col. 1227D] Homily 2 on Ezekiel.]: “Who is described here as a man except he of whom it is written: ‘Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized; but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man’” (Phil. 2)? “And what is understood by the four living creatures except the number of all the perfect? These living creatures, then—that is, all the children of the Church—strive toward the likeness of this man, namely Christ, so that they may be able to rise to the virtue of holiness. For the living creatures would not be holy if they did not have the likeness of this man. Whatever is in them of the bowels of compassion, whatever of gentleness of spirit, whatever of zeal for uprightness, whatever of guarding humility, whatever of the fervor of charity—[Col. 1227B] this they have drawn from the very fountain of mercy, the very root of gentleness, the very power of justice, the very mediator of God and men, God and Lord.

“The outstanding preacher shows that he has the likeness of this man, saying: ‘Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ’ (1 Cor. 11). He also admonishes us to rise to his likeness, saying: ‘The first man is from the earth, earthly; the second is from heaven, heavenly. As we have borne the image of the earthly man, let us bear also the image of him who descended from heaven’ (1 Cor. 15). Each saint is led to the likeness of this man to the extent that he imitates the life of this same Redeemer. For to differ from his commands and deeds—what else is it but to depart far from his likeness?

“Holy preachers mourn the lives of sinners, as it is written of our own head: ‘The Lord wept over Jerusalem’ (Luke 19). They rejoice in the good acts of their subjects and love those who act rightly, as is written of our Redeemer: when a certain young man said, ‘I have kept all these things from my youth,’ he loved him more and said, ‘Sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’ (Mark 10). Holy preachers endure insults brought against them and return no insult, just as our Redeemer, when he was told, ‘You have a demon,’ did not return abuse but gently answered: ‘I do not have a demon’ (John 8). Holy preachers burn with zeal for uprightness, [Col. 1227D] as our Redeemer, having made a whip of cords, drove sellers and buyers from the temple, overturned the seats of those selling doves, and poured out the coinage of the money-changers (John 2). In everything they do courageously, they guard humility with their whole intent, as our Redeemer says: ‘Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart’ (Matt. 11). Holy preachers also love their persecutors, as the very author and Redeemer of all, while undergoing his passion, prayed for his persecutors, saying: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ (Luke 23). They lay down their bodies in suffering for [Col. 1228A] their brethren, as the author of life gave himself up even to death for the life of the elect.

“Let it therefore be said of the holy living creatures that the likeness of a man is in them, because whatever is holy and wonderful in them comes from the character of that likeness, that is, from the power of imitating him. For our Redeemer is the head of us all. Thus it is said through Solomon: ‘The eyes of the wise are in his head’ (Eccl. 2). We have eyes in our head when we behold the life of the Redeemer in silent meditation. When all our intent rises in his imitation, whoever neglects to behold the ways of light with the eyes of the mind at once falls, blinded, into the darkness of error. The Prophet was hastening to rise to the likeness of this man when he said: ‘I will exercise myself in your commandments, and I will consider your ways’” (Ps. 118).

[Col. 1228B] [Note: [Col. 1227D] These too are Gregory’s words, but in *Morals*, book XVII, chapter 5.] What did he disdain to see by these ways except the paths of human conduct? It is as though he openly answers, saying: “I now refuse to look upon what is mine, because I burn to proceed by the steps of conduct along the way of your imitation.” For whoever now resists love of the present world, through continual exercise directs the eyes of his heart to the ways of his Redeemer, so that the mind may flee prosperity and prepare itself for adversity; may desire nothing that soothes the mind, and fear nothing believed to cause terror. Let it count sorrow as joy, reckon the joys of the present life as losses of sorrow, not fear the injuries of abasement, but through these seek the place of abiding glory. Truth showed these ways to the eyes of those following him when [Col. 1228C] he said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me” (John 12). He called back to these ways the swollen hearts of the disciples when they were already seeking a place of glory but did not know the way to that glory, saying: “Can you drink the cup that I am to drink?” (Matt. 20). For they had sought the exalted seat at his right and left, but did not know how narrow was the way by which they would ascend there. Thus the cup of the passion to be imitated was immediately set before their eyes, so that, if they wished to attain the joys of exaltation, they must first keep the way of humility.

[Note: [Col. 1228D] Again from the homily on Ezekiel.] Therefore, whoever, as stated above [Note: [Col. 1228D] None of these things stated above remains.], silently considers the Lord’s ways in his mind and hastens to exercise himself in his commandments—what else does he do in himself except reform the image of the new man? Because this is continually done in the hearts of the saints, it is rightly now said of the living creatures: “The likeness of a man is in them” (Ezek. 1). We must further know that after this likeness, which is now maintained in conduct, one will someday attain the likeness of glory. For John says: “Now we are children of God, but what we shall be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears,” namely Jesus Christ, “we shall be like him” (1 John 3), namely immortal and incapable of suffering. He immediately adds the reason why this can be so: “Because we shall see him as he is” (ibid.).

For God’s being is to remain eternal and immortal. [Col. 1229A] Everything that changes ceases to be what it was and begins to be what it was not. But God’s being is never to be otherwise. Hence it is said to Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3); and, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (ibid.). Blessed James also says of him: “With whom there is no change or shadow of turning” (Jas. 1). Therefore it is rightly said: “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is,” because by beholding the essence of his nature, freed from our mutability, we shall be fixed and established in his eternity. We shall indeed be changed in Christ, whom we shall see; because in seeing life, we shall be free from death. We shall transcend our mutability by seeing immutability, namely God. We shall be held by no corruption [Col. 1229B] by seeing incorruption.

Then the likeness of the man will also be in our bodies. Thus Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven, whence we also await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who transformed the body of our lowliness, making it conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3). Then the bodies of the elect will be conformed to the brightness of the Lord’s body. Although by nature they will not possess equality with his glory, by grace they will nevertheless possess the likeness of his conformation. Therefore, because the likeness of the life of God and man, Jesus Christ, is now impressed upon the conduct of the elect, and in the resurrection likeness to eternity will follow in the mind, “because we shall see him as he is”; and because our bodies too will receive his likeness in conformation, it is rightly said of the holy living creatures—that is, of all the holy preachers of the Church—that “the likeness of the man,” namely Jesus Christ, “is in them.” He himself, therefore, as has been said, is the example of every virtue; he is the head of the whole Church and the true light. He illumines his Church by the Holy Spirit proceeding from himself and the Father; he bears and governs her.

For the seven-branched lampstand, as has already been said, which God commanded Moses to make of purest gold in the tabernacle, prefigured the true God and man, Jesus Christ, illuminating the sevenfold Church by evangelical teaching. [Note: [Col. 1229D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 49.] Thus by the seven-branched lampstand [Col. 1229D] we understand the Son of God and of the Virgin, bearing the seven Churches, which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit illumines with its shining splendor. We speak of seven Churches although there is one holy catholic—that is, universal—Church, in order to indicate that she is filled with the sevenfold Spirit. Snuffers, called pincers in the Law, are made for this lampstand. These snuffers signify the two Testaments, by which sins are cleansed and which are joined to one another in the unity of the Holy Spirit. The lampstand is commanded to burn outside the veil of testimony which has been spread over it, because the truth of the Holy Spirit now shines without any veil of the Old Testament. [Col. 1230A] The oil from olive trees, which the Lord commanded to be supplied for the lighting of the lamps, signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit, containing in itself peace and mercy through the Savior’s advent; from it the light of truth is kindled in our hearts. For in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily, as the Apostle says (Col. 2). And from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace (John 1).

Therefore the grace of the Holy Spirit descends from God the Father through him, who is the head of all the faithful, gradually upon the whole Church, like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard, and from the beard to the hem of his garment (Ps. 132). All these things must nonetheless be understood spiritually. [Col. 1230B] Aaron the priest signifies Christ, who offered himself to God the Father as a fragrant offering for the redemption of humankind; who once entered the Holy of Holies by his own blood; who was both victim and priest; who, finding in the world nothing clean that he could offer, offered himself; who is head and judge of the whole Church.

Thus in the head of the Church—that is, in Christ—is the ointment of the Holy Spirit, because in him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily (Col. 2), and to him the Spirit is not given by measure (John 3). Therefore, after Christ the head ascended to heaven, the Holy Spirit came into his beard—that is, into the strong and vigorous men devoted to good works, namely the apostles and the others who were with them, whom the beard signifies [Col. 1230C] because it is a mark of the male sex. Hence, when we describe someone as strong, we call him bearded. Thus the ointment, that is, the Holy Spirit, descended after the Lord’s ascension, first from the head to the beard—that is, to the apostles and others who endured the first assaults of persecutors but could not be conquered by the power of that same Holy Spirit—and from them it descended to the hem of his garment.

Christ’s garment is the Church, which is without spot or wrinkle. The hem of the garment is its end, where the garment is completed. These are the perfect persons in the Church, who live in unanimity and harmony and fulfill Christ’s law. Hence the saying: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6). Or the hem to which the ointment of the Holy Spirit descends is not understood as the one [Col. 1230D] at the sides of the garment, but as that which is the opening of the garment. Such are those who dwell in unanimity and harmony in the house of God. For just as a person’s head enters through these upper openings of a garment in order to be clothed, so Christ enters through fraternal and spiritual harmony in order to be clothed by the Church. Hence Isaiah speaks to the same God and man, Jesus Christ, saying: “You shall be clothed with all these,” that is, with all the faithful, “as with an ornament” (Isa. 49).

Or, by the hem which is the end of the garment are understood the saints who will be in the Church in the last times, upon whom God will pour out his help and mercy lest they be conquered by [Col. 1231A] Antichrist. Therefore from the fullness of divinity that dwells bodily in Christ we have all received; and in the light of him who is truly the Church’s lampstand, we see the light by which, with his help, we believe that we shall attain the heavenly homeland. Nor can anyone attain the Father, or perfection of spiritual life, except through him, because he truly is the door of the heavenly homeland.

Hence the prophet Ezekiel, speaking figuratively in his vision, says: “The ascent of the gate had seven steps, and a vestibule before it” (Ezek. 40). Blessed Gregory, expounding this verse, says [Note: [Col. 1231D] Homily 19 on Ezekiel.]: “The gate is ascended by seven steps, because Isaiah, enumerating the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit in our very head, Jesus Christ, or in his body, which we are, [Col. 1231B] says: ‘The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him; the spirit of counsel and fortitude; the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him’” (Isa. 11).

“He enumerated these steps, when speaking of heavenly things, in descending rather than ascending order: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear. And since it is written, ‘The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom’ (Ps. 110), it is undoubtedly evident that people ascend from fear to wisdom, rather than return from wisdom to fear; for charity possesses perfect wisdom, as it is written: ‘Perfect charity casts out fear’ (1 John 4). The prophet, therefore, because he spoke from heavenly things down to lowly things, begins [Col. 1231C] with wisdom and descends to fear. But we, who strive from earthly things to heavenly, number these same steps in ascending order, so that we may be able to arrive from fear at wisdom.

“The first step of ascent in our mind is fear of the Lord; the second, piety; the third, knowledge; the fourth, fortitude; the fifth, counsel; the sixth, understanding; the seventh, wisdom. Fear of the Lord may be in the mind; but what kind of fear is it if piety is not with it? Whoever does not know how to have mercy on a neighbor, whoever pretends not to share in that neighbor’s tribulation—such a person’s fear is nothing in the sight of almighty God, because it is not raised to piety. But piety often errs through disordered mercy, if it perhaps spares things that should not be spared. For sins that may be struck by the fires of Gehenna [Col. 1231D] must be corrected by the rod of discipline, because disordered piety, while sparing temporarily, draws a person to eternal punishment. Therefore, for piety to be true and ordered, it must be raised to another step, namely knowledge, so that it may know what to punish from justice and what to remit from piety.

“But what if someone knows what should be done yet lacks the power to do it? Our knowledge, then, must increase into fortitude, so that, when it sees what ought to be done, it may be able to do it through strength of mind; lest it tremble in fear and, collapsing in terror, be unable to defend the good which it recognizes. But fortitude, if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices, often rushes forward vainly through its own presumption. [Col. 1232A] Therefore let it rise to counsel, so that by foresight it may prepare in advance everything which it can courageously do. But counsel cannot exist where understanding is lacking; for one who does not understand the evil that weighs upon the doer, how can he establish the good that helps? Let us then ascend from counsel to understanding.

“But what if understanding is wakeful with great acuteness yet does not know how to govern itself through charity? Therefore from understanding let there be ascent to wisdom, so that wisdom may maturely order what understanding has discovered acutely. Thus, because through fear we rise to piety, through piety we are led to knowledge, through knowledge strengthened to fortitude, through fortitude we strive toward counsel, through counsel advance in understanding, and through understanding arrive at the maturity of wisdom, by seven steps [Col. 1232B] we ascend to the gate through which the entrance of spiritual life is opened to us.”

It is fittingly said that there was a vestibule before the gate, because unless a person first possesses humility, he does not ascend to these steps of spiritual life, as it is written: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). Of this the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83). The more holy people cast themselves down outwardly by despising themselves, the more abundantly they are inwardly nourished by the contemplation of revelations. Those whom the valley of humility holds outwardly in weeping are raised inwardly by the ascent of contemplation. A valley, indeed, is a low place. And whenever a sinner humbly afflicts himself in tears in deed, he advances in his heart by the ascent of virtues. The Psalmist again says: “He sends forth springs in the valleys” (Ps. 103), because almighty God grants the gifts of spiritual grace to the humble.

Faith may also be understood by the vestibule. For faith itself is the corner and the gate, because we first come to faith and afterward enter the approach to heavenly life by the steps of spiritual gifts. One does not come to faith by virtues; rather, one reaches virtues by faith. For Cornelius the centurion, whose alms before baptism were praised by the testimony of an angel, did not come to faith by works, but came to works by faith. For the angel says to him: “Your prayers and your alms [Col. 1232D] have ascended before God” (Acts 10). If he had not believed in the true God before baptism, whom did he pray to? Or how had almighty God heard him, if he had not asked God himself to make him advance in good things? He knew God, the Creator of all things; but he did not know that his almighty Son had become incarnate. For he could not do good unless he had first believed. For it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). He therefore had faith, since his works and alms could please God. But through good action he merited to know God perfectly and to believe the mystery of his Incarnation, so that he might attain the sacraments of baptism.

[Col. 1233A] While Peter was still speaking, and proclaiming to Cornelius himself and to all who were with him the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word (Acts 10), and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. Rightly, in this passage, Cornelius—a devout man and one who feared God—can say, both for himself and for all whom he himself had summoned to hear God’s word, indeed even in the person of all Gentiles, what the bride in the Song of spiritual love says to Christ: “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

For, as has been said, he prayed and laboured in good works, yet lay benumbed under the darkness of ignorance, because he did not know the true light, which is Christ. But after God, “who wills that no one should perish, but that all men should come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2), had enlightened his mind by the Holy Spirit, He drew him after Himself by the bond of charity. Therefore He anointed his mind with the unction of the Holy Spirit and, driving out the darkness, enlightened the eyes of his heart to contemplate Himself. [Note: [Col. 1233D] Gregory, on this passage of the Song.] Thus no one runs unless he is drawn, because the person whom divine grace does not help is weighed down by the burden of ignorance or corruption. “We shall run,” she says, “after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1). Divine grace also goes before us; showing us the sweetness of inward goods, it pierces us with compunction concerning outward things. Then the mind, passing into those spiritual realities, despises all temporal things because of their sweetness and loveliness. Thus this man, because he is drawn, runs: gladly following the bond [Col. 1233C] of love, strengthened by love for divine grace, he passes every obstacle without heaviness. Nor is it strange that he runs while following the fragrance of the ointments: for when the sweetness of spiritual gifts is perceived, what is there in this temporal life whose desire can hold back the holy soul, Christ’s bride, from hastening there? For there she rejoices in the gentleness of the ointments; and, as she breathes through the nostrils of discernment, charity smells sweetly to her.

This is why she passes from the singular to the plural when she says: “We shall run after the fragrance of your ointments.” The whole Church also runs after Christ’s fragrance, because it follows His teaching and longs with the highest desire to attain Him.

Moreover, most beloved brethren, we should note that blessed Peter the Apostle maintained, at the beginning of the holy Church, the pattern [Col. 1233D] of preaching which God showed to the prophet Jeremiah. For the Lord says to Jeremiah: “I have appointed you over nations and over kingdoms, that you may uproot, destroy, ruin, and scatter, and build and plant” (Jer. 1). [Note: [Col. 1233D] Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chap. 35.] Unless he first destroyed what was perverse, he could not usefully build what was right. Unless he first uprooted from the hearts of his hearers the thorns of a wrongful will, he would plainly plant the words of holy preaching in them in vain.

Hence blessed Peter first uproots in order afterwards to build. He did not immediately instruct the Jews what they should do [Col. 1234A], but rebuked them for what they had done wickedly, saying: “Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God among you by mighty works, wonders, and signs, which God did through Him in your midst, as you yourselves know—this man, delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God the Father, you afflicted and killed by the hands of wicked men; but God raised Him up, having loosed the pains of hell” (Acts 2). He rebuked them sharply, therefore, so that, broken by awareness of their cruelty, they might seek the edification of holy preaching more anxiously and hear it more profitably. Hence they at once replied: “What then shall we do, brethren?” To them it is immediately said: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.).

Certainly they would have despised these words of edification unless they had first heard, for their healing, of the ruin brought by their destruction. Thus he uprooted both cruelty and unbelief from their hearts in order to plant in them faith in the holy Trinity. When he was about to speak of baptism, he first put forward the tears of repentance, so that they might first be drenched with the water of their compunction and afterwards be washed in the sacrament of baptism. As Peter preached, the grace of the Holy Spirit enlightened their hearts, so that they might repent of past sins and receive with devout minds faith in the holy Trinity.

Hence Ezekiel the prophet, speaking figuratively, says: “The appearance of the four living creatures was like burning coals of fire and like the appearance of lamps” (Ezek. 1). By the four living creatures, as has often been said, are understood all the holy preachers [Col. 1234C] of the New and Old Testaments. [Note: [Col. 1234D] Gregory, Homily 5 on Ezekiel.] Therefore, because holy men set beside them some persons whom they kindle, as it were by touching them, to love for the heavenly country, they are coals; but when they shine for others who are far away, becoming lamps for their journey so that they may not fall into the darkness of their sin, they are lamps. One who lives well in secret, if he does not benefit another’s progress, is a coal; but one placed before others as an example of holiness, who displays to many the light of righteousness from himself, is a lamp, because he burns for himself and shines for others.

It follows: “And this was the vision moving to and fro in the midst of the living creatures: namely, the brightness of fire, and lightning coming forth from the fire.” The brightness of fire and lightning issuing from fire are seen to move to and fro among the living creatures, because unless those winged creatures—that is, the holy preachers—received heat from the fire of truth, they themselves would not burn in the likeness of coals and lamps. For the Holy Spirit is commonly signified by the name of fire, as Luke the Evangelist bears witness in this solemnity: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and one sat upon each of them” (Acts 2).

When the carnal mind receives the Holy Spirit, it is set ablaze with spiritual love and laments the evil it has done. The earth burns when, with conscience accusing itself, the sinner’s heart is burned and consumed in the sorrow of repentance. Hence it is again written: “Your God, O Israel, is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4). Therefore our Creator is called a consuming fire, because He makes clean from the rust of sins the mind which He has filled. Thus the Holy Spirit is said to move to and fro among the living creatures as the brightness of fire and lightning coming forth from fire, because, filling the whole Church, He sends forth from Himself flames of love in the hearts of the elect, so that He may strike the heart with fear through terror and kindle torpid hearts to His love.

But since the Holy Spirit, God, is coeternal before the ages with the Father and the Son, we must ask why He is said to move to and fro. Everyone who moves to and fro comes to a place where he was not and leaves a place where he was. In what sense, then, can we say that the Spirit moves to and fro, when all things are within Him and there is nowhere where He is not? As it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” [Col. 1235B] (Wisdom 1). Yet, when wisdom’s praise was described, it was added: “For in her is a spirit of understanding, manifold, subtle, mobile” (Wisdom 7); and shortly afterwards: “human, steadfast” (ibid.). Again a great question arises from these words: why is this Spirit, who fills all things, called at once mobile and steadfast?

But if we turn to ordinary human usage, we find the speaker’s meaning more readily. A man who runs about everywhere in the region where he is, beyond doubt encounters people everywhere and is suddenly found where he is not expected. Thus, in order that His presence everywhere might be signified, the omnipotent Spirit is called both steadfast and mobile. He is steadfast because by nature He encompasses all things; mobile because He comes upon people everywhere, even without their knowing it. Therefore, containing all things, He is called steadfast; displaying Himself present to all, He is called mobile.

Thus the brightness of fire and lightning issuing from fire move to and fro among the winged living creatures, because the Holy Spirit is specially present at once to every one and to all the elect—especially to the Apostles and Evangelists and to all the teachers of the Church. He kindles those whom He touches and enlightens those whom He has kindled, so that, fired after their former coldness, they may burn and, through the fire of love which they have received, give forth the flames of good examples. For lightning coming forth from this fire strikes torpid minds, and by striking awakens and inflames them, so that, burning and shining alike after love for Him, they may run to do good works.

[Col. 1235D] The brightness of this fire and lightning coming forth from the fire, moving to and fro among the winged living creatures—that is, among the holy Apostles—made them at once burning and shining, and rendered them strong for preaching. Burning and shining with that fire, the great winged living creature, Peter the Apostle, sharply rebuked the Jews for their committed sacrilege, namely Christ’s Passion, and terrified them like lightning. Burning with the fire of charity, he summoned them to repentance and, as stated above, promised them hope of pardon through God’s goodness, saying: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts 3). But they, set ablaze by the fire and struck by the lightning of that same Holy Spirit—all who had been predestined to eternal life—repented [Col. 1236A] and received the faith with devout minds.

This passage may also be understood from what is written elsewhere: “His throne was flames of fire; His wheels burning fire” (Dan. 7). Those who are guardians of souls and have undertaken the care of feeding the flock are not permitted to change their places. But those who remain in one place, bear within themselves the presence of divinity, and burn, are called God’s throne and flame of fire: they are, that is, God’s throne, kindled with love of God and neighbour. But those who run to and fro in preaching through love of the Lord are His wheels and burning fire, because, as they go through various places in longing for Him, they themselves burn and kindle others.

Yet the movement to and fro and mobility of the Spirit may be understood according to another consideration. In the hearts of the saints He always remains in respect of certain virtues; but in respect of others, He comes in order to depart and departs in order to come. In faith, hope, and charity, and in other goods without which one cannot attain the heavenly country—such as humility, charity, justice, and mercy—He does not abandon the hearts of the perfect. But in the gift of prophecy, eloquence, and the working of miracles, the Holy Spirit is sometimes present to His elect and sometimes withdraws Himself. He is present so that they may be lifted up, and withdraws Himself so that they may be humbled. He is present so that the displayed power may glorify them; He departs so that, when His power is withdrawn, they may know themselves. He is present to show what they are through Him; He departs to reveal what and how they remain without Him.

Therefore, in those virtues without which life cannot be attained, the Holy Spirit remains in the hearts of His elect; but in those through which the power of holiness is displayed, He is sometimes mercifully present and sometimes mercifully withdraws. Thus the Spirit is called moving to and fro and mobile, because He is not continually possessed in signs and powers according to each person’s wish. He is rightly said to move to and fro among the holy living creatures. For movement to and fro belongs to swiftness. The Holy Spirit moves to and fro among the perfect because, even if He should withdraw from their hearts for a little while, He returns swiftly. Thus the brightness of fire and lightning coming forth from fire move to and fro in the midst of the living creatures, because the Holy Spirit, descending upon the Apostles [Col. 1236D] in the form of fire, kindled them, as has been said, with spiritual love and enlightened them both with the power of action and with the teaching of truth. Filled with the Holy Spirit, they kindled those near them by preaching, that they might rise to love for the heavenly country; and they shone for those far away through the examples of good works.

Therefore the Holy Spirit appeared above them in fiery tongues and gave them knowledge of every language. What, then, is signified by this miracle except that the holy Church, filled with the same Spirit, was to speak in the voices of all nations? Those who attempted to build Babel’s tower against God lost the fellowship of one language. But to those who humbly feared God all languages were united. Thus the humility of the latter obtained power, while the pride of the former obtained confusion.

[Note: [Col. 1237D] Gregory, Homily 30 on the Gospels.] But we must ask why the Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and the Son, appeared in fire; why in both fire and tongues; why He is sometimes shown in a dove and sometimes in fire; and why He appeared over the only-begotten Son of God in the form of a dove, but over the disciples in fire—so that He came neither upon the Lord in fire nor was shown over the disciples as a dove. By God’s help, we must resolve these four questions which we have proposed.

The Holy Spirit, coeternal with the Father and Son, is shown in fire because God is incorporeal, ineffable, and invisible fire, as Paul testifies when he says: “Our God is a consuming fire” [Col. 1237B] (Heb. 12). God is rightly called a consuming fire because through Him the rust of sins is consumed. Of this fire Truth says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what will I, but that it should burn?” (Luke 12). By “earth” are meant the hearts not of spiritual but of earthly people, which, as they continually heap up thoughts of the lowest things, are trampled by evil spirits. But the Lord sends fire upon the earth when He kindles the hearts of carnal people by the breath of the Holy Spirit. And the earth burns when the carnal heart, formerly cold in its own pleasures, abandons the desires of the present age and enters into love for God. Rightly, therefore, did the Holy Spirit appear in fire, because from every heart which He fills He shakes off the numbness of coldness and kindles it in longing for His eternity.

Moreover, He was shown in fiery tongues because that same Holy Spirit is coeternal with the Father and has the closest affinity [Note: [Col. 1237D] “Affinity” (*cognationem*).] of tongue with the Word. For the Word of the Father is the Son. Since the Spirit and the Word are of one substance, the Spirit ought to have been shown in a tongue. Or certainly, since the word proceeds through the tongue, the Spirit appeared in tongues because whoever is touched by the Holy Spirit confesses God’s Word, the same only-begotten Son. Nor can one deny God’s Word who now possesses the tongue of the Holy Spirit. Or again, the Holy Spirit appeared in fiery tongues because He makes all whom He fills both burning and speaking. Teachers possess fiery tongues because, while preaching through love for God, they inflame the hearts of their hearers. For a teacher’s discourse is idle if it cannot impart the fire of love.

They had received this fire of teaching from the very mouth of Truth, when they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while Jesus spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24). The soul is set ablaze by the word heard, and the coldness of numbness departs. The mind becomes anxious in heavenly desire and estranged from earthly desires. The true love which fills it torments it in tears; and while it is tormented by such burning, it is nourished by its very torments. It delights to hear heavenly commandments; and through what it is taught by the commandments it is, as it were, inflamed by so many torches. What was formerly numb through carnal desires subsequently burns through the words of holy preaching.

Hence it is said through Moses: “A fiery law in His right hand” [Col. 1238A] (Deut. 33). The reprobate, who are to be set on the left, are called the left hand; but God’s right hand denotes the elect. In God’s right hand is a fiery law, because the elect do not hear heavenly commandments with cold hearts, but burn at them with the torches of inward love. The word is brought to the ear, and their mind, angry with itself, is consumed by the flame of inward love.

The Holy Spirit was shown both in a dove and in fire because He makes all whom He fills simple and burning: simple in purity, burning in zeal for virtues. For neither simplicity without zeal for righteousness nor zeal without simplicity pleases God. Hence Truth Himself says: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” (Matt. 10). In this matter it should be noted that the Lord did not wish to admonish His disciples about the dove without the serpent, nor about the serpent without the dove, so that He might kindle the simplicity of the dove with the shrewdness of the serpent and temper the shrewdness of the serpent with the simplicity of the dove. Hence Paul says: “Do not become children in understanding” (1 Cor. 14). We have heard the serpent’s shrewdness; now let us again be admonished about the dove’s simplicity by the same Apostle: “But in malice be little children” (ibid.). Hence it is said of blessed Job:

“He was a simple and upright man” (Job 1). [Note: [Col. 1238D] Now from Book I of the *Moralia*, chap. 5.] Uprightness signifies justice, but simplicity gentleness. Often, when we practice the uprightness of justice, we abandon gentleness; and when we wish to preserve gentleness, we turn aside from the uprightness of justice. But the Lord, coming in the flesh, maintained simplicity together with uprightness: neither in gentleness did He lose the strictness of justice, nor again in the strictness of justice did He lose the virtue of gentleness.

Thus, when certain persons wished to test Him by bringing before Him an adulterous woman, so that He might fall into the fault either of harshness or injustice, He answered both points, saying: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone upon her” (John 8). He gives the simplicity of gentleness in saying, “Let him who is without sin among you”; He gives zeal for justice in saying, “be the first to cast a stone upon her.” [Col. 1238D] Therefore it is said to Him through the Prophet: “Proceed prosperously, advance and reign, because of truth, gentleness, and justice” (Ps. 44), so that He might neither lose zeal for uprightness under the weight of gentleness nor disturb the weight of gentleness through zeal for uprightness. [Note: [Col. 1238D] Again from Homily 30.] What, then, is uprightness without simplicity, or simplicity without uprightness? Plainly, something inadequate and imperfect.

Therefore, since the Son of God and of the Virgin, dwelling among men, perfectly maintained simplicity and uprightness, and instructed His disciples to be gentle and simple, the Holy Spirit rightly had to be shown both in fire and in a dove, so that [Col. 1239A] every heart touched by His grace might become both tranquil through the gentleness of meekness and aflame with zeal for justice.

Finally, we must ask why the Holy Spirit appeared in a dove upon our Redeemer Himself, but in fire upon the disciples. Certainly the only-begotten Son of God is judge of the human race. But who could have borne His justice if, before gathering us by gentleness, He had wished to examine our sins with the zeal of uprightness? Therefore, having become man for men, He showed Himself gentle to men. He did not wish sternly to strike sinners, but mercifully to gather them. He first wished gently to gather them, so that He might have those whom He would afterwards save in judgment.

Thus the Holy Spirit ought to have appeared in a dove over the Son of God and the Virgin, since He came not to strike sins already with zeal, but still to bear with them through gentleness. On the contrary, the Holy Spirit ought to have been shown in fire over the disciples, so that, since they were merely human and therefore sinners, spiritual fervour might inflame them against themselves, and they might punish in themselves through repentance the sins which God spared through gentleness. For even they, though cleaving to heavenly teaching, could not be without sin, as John testifies when he says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Therefore He came in fire into men and descended in a dove upon the Lord, because we must carefully behold with zeal for uprightness and burn with the ardour of repentance the sins which the Lord mercifully bears through gentleness. Thus the Holy Spirit was shown by a dove in the Redeemer, but by fire in men, because the more the severity of our Judge has been tempered for us, the more our weakness ought to be inflamed against itself.

Therefore, beloved brethren, let us call to mind alike the lives and teaching of the holy Fathers, so that, following their footsteps, we may be able to attain eternal joys. Let us wipe away with tears the stains of our past life, and receive their precepts with devout minds, so that we may be fit for the gifts of heavenly grace. For to those holy teachers—to the Apostles and Evangelists and their successors—was given the possession of “a heavenly treasure in earthen vessels” [Col. 1239D] (2 Cor. 4), and the opening of the mysteries of the Gospel to their hearers.

Hence Ezekiel the prophet, speaking figuratively in the vision which he saw in the spirit, says among other things: “I saw at each chamber a doorway in the fronts of the gates, where they washed the burnt offering” (Ezek. 40). Explaining this verse, blessed Gregory, whose holiness God enriched with a great gift of wisdom, says: [Note: [Col. 1239D] *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Book II, Homily 8. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 1036.] “The chambers are the hearts of holy teachers,” etc., down to: “Let us consider how grievously we sin daily, and, that we may appear clean after our sins, let us wash the burnt offering with tears.”

[Col. 1240A] For this purpose the very fountain of all mercy, namely Jesus Christ, God and man, mercifully descended from the bosom of the Father into this world: that He might raise us, who lay dead in sins, and carry us with Himself to the brightness of the heavenly country. Through compassion, indeed, He received our flesh together with its mortality and made us sharers in His life. To raise up the human race sunk in sins, He first sent prophets and teachers of the Law, then Apostles; at last, coming Himself, He raised it from death to life.

Elisha fittingly prefigured Him when, to raise the son of the Shunammite, he first sent his staff through a servant and then came himself (4 Kings 4). [Note: [Col. 1240D] Father, above, on this book, chap. 3.] The servant sent by Elisha with the staff did not raise the dead boy. But Elisha, coming himself, stretched himself upon the dead child, conformed himself to his limbs, walked to and fro, and breathed seven times into the dead child’s mouth; and immediately, through the mystery of compassion, restored him to the light of life.

Thus God, the author of the human race, grieved for us as for a dead child when He looked mercifully upon us, extinguished by the sting of iniquity. Since through Moses He issued the terror of the Law, He sent, as it were through a servant, a rod. For God wielded a rod through the Law when He said: “If anyone does this or that, he shall surely die.” Therefore fear of the Law could not raise us from the death of sin; but the grace of breathed gentleness raised us to the state of life. The servant with the rod could not raise the dead child, because, as Paul testifies, “the Law brought nothing to perfection” [Col. 1240C] (Heb. 7).

But the Son of God and the Virgin, coming Himself and humbly stretching Himself upon the corpse, made Himself one with the dead man’s limbs, to enact them in Himself; because, “though He was in the form of God, He did not deem equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2). He walked to and fro because He called both nearby Judea and the Gentiles far away. He breathed seven times upon the dead because, through the opening of the divine gift, He breathes the grace of the sevenfold Spirit into those lying in the death of sin. Immediately the living child rises, because the child whom the rod of terror could not raise returned to life through the spirit of love.

Therefore He is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), who mercifully rescued the human race from everlasting death. Through Him God the Father enlightened the world by the Holy Spirit and reconciled to Himself, by apostolic preaching, the children of wrath. Hence the Lord speaks to blessed Job in a question, saying:

“Tell me, if you know all things, by what way is light scattered?” (Job 38). For He Himself is the Way, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” [Note: [Col. 1240D] Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXIX, chap. 12.] Therefore light is scattered by this Way, because through His presence the whole Gentile world is enlightened. He fittingly said “scattered,” because through the teaching of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1241A] and the voices of the Apostles, the light of preaching shone forth broadly—not narrowed or confined.

But because, after the light of conversion has been received, the power of love burns inwardly, so that past evils are anxiously lamented and future goods most ardently sought, it is fittingly added: “Heat is divided over the earth.” For once light has been scattered, heat is divided over the earth because, when justice is openly preached, the heart’s anxiety in seeking God is expanded through the exercise of virtues: so that one may shine in the word of wisdom, another in the word of knowledge; this person may be strong in the grace of healings, that one in the working of powers. And while individuals receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit differently, all, necessarily joined together, are kindled in one accord.

But after light is said to be scattered, it may fittingly be understood that persecution is denoted by heat. Once the light of preaching shone brightly, the ardour of persecution immediately blazed from the hearts of the faithless. The Lord’s own saying testifies that persecution is expressed by heat, concerning seed scattered on stony ground: “When the sun rose, all things were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered” (Matt. 13). When He explained this shortly afterwards, He called the heat persecution. Therefore, once light was scattered, heat was divided over the earth because, as the lives of the faithful became bright, the cruelty of the faithless was kindled. The heat was divided when persecution raged now at Jerusalem, now at Damascus, now in other regions far away. For it is written: “On that day a great persecution arose against the Church which was at Jerusalem, [Col. 1241C] and all were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria” (Acts 8). And again it is written: “Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, approached the chief priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any men or women of this Way, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem” (Acts 9).

Thus, because persecution had increased now here, now there, those who had recognized the light of truth gasped, as it were, beneath the burning of divided heat. But since we have heard blessed Job questioned concerning hidden judgments, we ought to examine more subtly what has been said of scattered light and divided heat. For he is still questioned by a lofty interrogation, that at least he may be taught when he does not know; and it is said to him:

[Col. 1241D] “By what way is light scattered, and heat divided over the earth?” What is denoted by the name of light except justice? Of this it is written: “The people who walked in darkness saw a great light” (Isa. 9). But everything that is scattered is cast forth not continuously, but with a certain interval. Therefore light is said to be scattered because, although we now perceive some things as they are, we do not see other things as they ought to be seen. Peter’s heart possessed scattered light: he shone with such faith and such splendour of miracles, yet, when the Gentiles were converted and he imposed the burden of circumcision, he did not know what was right to say.

Thus in this life light is scattered, because it is not possessed continuously for the understanding of every matter. While we grasp one thing as it is but do not know another, we see, as it were, scattered light in part and remain in darkness in part. But scattered light will no longer be ours when our mind, wholly caught up to the Lord, shines. [Note: [Col. 1241D] “Will shine” (*fulgescet*).] Since the ways in which this same light is imparted to the human heart are unknown, it is rightly asked: “By what way is light scattered?” This is as though it were openly said: Tell by what order I pour My justice into the hidden recesses of the heart, when I am not seen in My approach and yet invisibly alter the visible deeds of men; when I illuminate one and the same mind now with this virtue, now with that, and yet through scattered light still permit it to remain in some degree in the darkness of temptation.

Therefore let man, who does not know, be asked by what way light is scattered—as though it were plainly said to him: When I soften hard hearts, bend rigid ones, make rough ones gentle, kindle cold ones, strengthen weak ones, make wandering ones steadfast, and confirm those that waver, consider, if you can, by what paths I, coming incorporeally and invisibly, enlighten them. We see all these things accomplished, but we do not know how they are brought about inwardly. Truth shows in the Gospel that this way of light is invisible to us, saying: “The Spirit breathes where He wills; you hear His voice, but do not know whence He comes or whither He goes” (John 3).

But because, when light is scattered, temptations immediately increase from the hidden adversary against the shining [Col. 1242C] mind, it is rightly added: “Heat is divided over the earth.”

For the crafty enemy strives to inflame with unlawful desires the minds of those whom he sees shining with the light of justice, so that they often feel themselves more pressed by temptations than when [Note: [Col. 1242D] Supply: “when.”] they did not see the rays of inward light. Hence, after the Israelites were called, they complain to Moses about their increased labour, saying: “May the Lord see and judge, because you have made our odour stink before Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in his hand to kill us” (Exod. 5). For when they wished to depart from Egypt, Pharaoh had taken away their straw but still demanded works in the same quantity. Thus the mind, as it were, murmurs against the Law after attaining knowledge of it, because it bears sharper stings of temptations. When it sees its labours increase, it grieves that, in what displeases the adversary, it seems to stink in Pharaoh’s eyes. Heat follows light because, after illumination by the divine gift, the struggle of temptation increases.

Thus heat is rightly said to be divided, because individuals are not afflicted by all vices, but by certain ones close and adjacent to them. For the ancient adversary first observes the particular mixture of each person’s disposition and then sets the snares of temptation. One person has a cheerful temperament, another a sad one, another a fearful one, another a proud one. Therefore the hidden adversary prepares deceptions suited to nearby dispositions, by which he may easily take them captive. Since the pleasure of joy is near at hand, he offers lust to cheerful dispositions; and since sadness easily slips into anger, he gives the sorrowful the cup of discord. Because fearful people dread punishments, he threatens terrors to the frightened. Since he sees the proud exalted by praise, he draws them wherever he wishes by flattering favour.

Therefore he lies in wait for individual persons through various vices. For he would not easily capture them if he offered battles to the lustful or prostitutes to the avaricious; if he assailed the gluttonous with the glory of abstinence or the abstinent with the weakness of gluttony; if he sought to capture the gentle through zeal for conflict or the wrathful through fearfulness. Therefore, since in the heat of temptation he craftily lies in wait for each person and hides snares near to his disposition [Col. 1243B], it is rightly said: “Heat is divided over the earth.”

But when it is first said, “By what way is light scattered?” and immediately added, “Heat is divided over the earth,” it is indicated that heat too is divided by the same way through which light is scattered.
