For the lofty and incomprehensible grace of the Holy Spirit, while illuminating our minds with its light, also regulates and moderates the adversary’s temptations: so that many do not come upon us at once; so that only those which can be borne touch a soul now enlightened by God; and so that, while they torment us with the heat of their touch, they do not consume us with the fire of perfection. Paul testifies to this when he says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will also make with the temptation a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” [Col. 1243C] (1 Cor. 10).

The crafty deceiver divides this heat of vices in one way, and the merciful Creator in another. The former divides it in order to destroy more swiftly through it; the latter, in order to make it bearable. And because, when we are wearied by temptation, we are instructed not only by God’s inward Spirit but also aided by the outward words of preachers, it is rightly added after the divided heat: “Who has given a course to the most violent rain?” (Job 38).

If, however, as we said above, the persecution in that region of Judaea is denoted by the name of the divided heat, then, because the very harshness of the persecution did not restrain the holy preachers—helped by a gift from above—from the mystery of their preaching through any fear, it suitably adds:

[Col. 1243D] “Who gave the course to the most violent rain?” As though he said: “Who but I?” For to give a course to the most violent rain when the heat has been divided is to strengthen the force of preaching amid the very straits of persecutions, so that the power of the preachers might grow all the more as the cruelty of persecutions opposed them more fiercely; so that they might pour drops of rain into the parched hearts of their hearers and more abundantly water the dryness of unbelief, and so that, although the heat of rage blazed against them, nevertheless through them the voice of grace might not fall silent. Paul endured this heat of persecution and yet watered the hearts of his hearers when he said: “I labor even to chains, as an evildoer; but the word of God is not bound” (2 Tim. 2). Of this rain it is elsewhere said: “I will command my clouds not to rain rain upon her” (Isa. 5). Of this course of rain, which is set in motion in the hearts of the elect, the Psalmist testifies, saying: “His word runs swiftly” (Ps. 147).

Yet often there is rain without a course, because preaching reaches the ears but, when the inward grace of the Holy Spirit is absent, does not pass into the hearts of the hearers. Concerning the words of this preaching, on account of the elect, it is said: “For your arrows pass through; the voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. 76). For God’s arrows pass through when the words of his preaching descend from the ears into the heart. And because this is accomplished solely by the divine gift, the Lord testifies that he has given a course to the rain.

But I observe that he calls this same rain not “violent” but “most violent.” Violent rain is great power; most violent rain is the immeasurable power of preaching. The rain was violent when holy preachers urged people to believe in eternal joys. But it became most violent when, on account of hope, they urged that all things be forsaken, all visible things despised for the sake of invisible things, and present penalties and torments endured for the grace that had been heard. Yet when faith had been recognized, and the heat of persecution raged, so many elect persons left their possessions, forgot fleshly affections, and, for the joy of souls, surrendered their bodies amid diverse tortures—what else did the Lord do but give a course even to the most violent rain? By the grace of the Holy Spirit and the words of preaching, he watered the hidden recesses of the heart even unto the carrying out of the highest commandments.

Hence it is suitably added: “And a way for the sounding thunder.” For what is understood by thunder except the preaching of heavenly terror? When we receive that terror, our hearts are shaken. Sometimes, however, the incarnate Lord himself is figured by thunder, because, through the converging prophecy of the ancient Fathers, he was brought to our knowledge as though from the shaking of clouds; and, visibly appearing among us, he sounded forth terribly those things which were above us. Therefore the holy apostles themselves, begotten from his grace and strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, were called Boanerges, that is, “sons of thunder,” on account, namely, of their steadfastness and greatness of faith.

At other times, as has been said, thunder signifies his preaching itself, [Col. 1244D] through which the terror of heavenly judgments is heard. But any preacher may give words to the ears; he cannot open hearts. Unless almighty God alone, through the inward grace of the Holy Spirit, invisibly grants the words of preachers an entrance into the hearts of hearers, preaching is received in vain by the hearing ear, since it is prevented from reaching the depths by a deaf heart. Yet the Lord declares that he gives a way to the sounding thunder, for when he grants words of preaching, he pierces hearts through fear.

Paul, the outstanding preacher, recognized that he could not give this way from himself; and, while he sounded forth heavenly mysteries with awe, he urged his disciples, saying: “Pray at the same time for all and for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery [Col. 1245A] of Christ” (Col. 4). Therefore, although he spoke mysteries, he prayed that the Lord would open a door for those same mysteries into the hearts of his hearers. He indeed already possessed thunder, but he sought that a way might be given to it from above. John also knew that he could by no means give this way, when he said: “You have no need that anyone should teach you; but, as his anointing—that is, the Holy Spirit—teaches you concerning all things” (1 John 2). Again Paul indicated who gives this way when he said: “Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters; but God who gives the increase” (1 Cor. 3).

Having received the way, then, let us hear what this rain and thunder say: “That it might rain upon a land without people, in the desert where no mortal dwells” [Col. 1245B] (Job 38). To rain upon a land without people in the desert is to preach the word of God to the Gentile world. Since it possessed no worship of divinity and displayed in itself no appearance of good work, it was plainly a desert; and since there was no lawgiver there, nor anyone who sought God rationally, there was, as it were, no human being in it. It remained empty of lovers, as though occupied only by wild beasts. Of this desert land it is elsewhere said: “He placed a way in the desert” (Isa. 43). Of this preaching granted to the Gentiles the Psalmist testifies, saying: “He made rivers into a desert, and springs of water into thirst” (Ps. 106).

It should indeed be noted that, after the heat was divided over the land, the most violent rain received a course so that it might rain in the desert. For after the harshness of persecution became known in Judaea—so that it not only utterly refused to receive the faith, but even attacked it with swords—every preacher sent from Israel turned aside to summon the Gentiles. Hence the holy apostles say to the Hebrews who persecuted them, and whom they leave behind: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

Therefore, once the heat has been divided, the deserted land without people is drenched with rain; because, after persecution was scattered through the regions of Judaea, the Gentile world—long abandoned and as though estranged from rational infusion—is moistened with drops of preaching. What this Gentile world was like when it was still found by the preachers is shown when he adds:

[Col. 1245D] “That it might fill the trackless and desolate land.” What it made drenched with rain is shown when it is immediately joined: “That it might bring forth green plants.” For the Gentile world was formerly trackless, because no way was opened to it by the word of God. When our Redeemer came, the Gentile world received the calling of grace in such a way that the way of prophecy had not previously existed within it. It was also rightly called desolate, being deprived of rational counsel and of the fruit of good work. Thus the Lord gave a course to the most violent rain and a way to the sounding thunder, in order that it might rain in the desert, fill the trackless and desolate land, and bring forth green plants: that is, he joined to outward preaching the inward inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that the parched hearts of the Gentiles might become green, the trackless places be drenched, the barren germinate, and the closed be opened.

For in sacred Scripture “plant” or “greenness” sometimes signifies the bloom of temporal glory; sometimes the devil’s refreshment; sometimes the support of preachers; sometimes good action; sometimes knowledge and teaching of eternal life. The bloom of temporal glory is understood, as the Prophet says: “In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it flourish and pass away” (Ps. 89). To flourish and pass away like grass in the morning is, amid the prosperity of this world, swiftly to wither through the splendor of temporal glory.

Grass signifies the devil’s refreshment, as the Lord says of him: “The mountains bear herbs for him” (Job 40). As though he said: “The proud and puffed-up, when they exalt themselves through unlawful thoughts [Col. 1246B] and deeds, feed him with their iniquities.” Grass denotes the support of preachers when it is said: “He brings forth hay on the mountains, and grass for the service of men” (Ps. 146). For hay is produced on the mountains, and grass for the service of men, when the exalted persons of this world, called to the knowledge of faith, bestow temporary provisions upon holy preachers on the journey of this life.

Grass stands for good action, as it is written: “Let the earth bring forth green grass, making seed” (Gen. 1). Although we hold that this was historically done in the creation of the world, we may fittingly understand the earth to have figured the Church, which brought forth green grass when it produced fruitful works of mercy in response to the word [Col. 1246C] of faith.

At times we understand grass as knowledge and teaching of eternal greenness, as it is said through Jeremiah: “The wild asses stood upon the rocks; they drew in winds like dragons; their eyes failed because there was no grass” (Jer. 14). By this saying the proud and utterly wicked persecution of the Jews is prophesied. They are called wild asses because of the exaltation of their minds; they are called dragons because of their venomous thought. They stood upon rocks because they trusted not in God but in the highest powers of this world, saying: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). They drew in winds like dragons because, inflated by the spirit of pride, they swelled maliciously with arrogance. Their eyes failed because their hope fell away from that at which it aimed: loving temporal things, it neglected to await eternal things; and it lost earthly things because it placed them before God. For they said: “If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him; and the Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). They feared that, unless the Lord were killed, they would lose their place; yet, having killed him, they lost it.

But why these things befell the wretched is then added: “Because there was no grass”; that is, because the knowledge of eternity was absent from their hearts and no verdure of inward teaching refreshed them with nourishment. Therefore what else do we understand here by “green plants” except the knowledge of holy teaching or fitting works? Thus the deserted land is drenched, that it may bring forth green plants, because when the Gentile world receives the rain of holy preaching, [Col. 1247A] it produces both works of life and words of doctrine.

This greenness is promised by the prophetic voice to the deserted land, when it is said: “In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, there shall arise the green growth of reed and rush” (Isa. 35). What does the reed signify except writers?

[Note: [Col. 1247D] Another manuscript, with the edition: “preachers.”]

And what does the rush signify, which always grows in moisture beside water, except the small and tender hearers of sacred speech? Therefore, in the dens of dragons, the green growth of reed and rush arises, because among those peoples whom the malice of the ancient enemy possessed, both the knowledge of teachers and the obedience of hearers are amassed through the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

Yet these things said generally concerning the Gentile world, if we look carefully, we see taking place individually within the bosom of holy Church. For very many people are utterly insensitive to the words of God. They are indeed counted by the name of faith and hear with their ears the words of life, but they do not allow them to pass into the inward parts of the heart. What else are these but a deserted land, a land without a human being because their mind lacks rational perception? No mortal dwells in this land because, even if thoughts of rational understanding sometimes enter their conscience, they do not remain. Perverse desires find a seat in their hearts, but right thoughts, whenever they come, are cast down as though driven away.

But when the merciful God deigns to grant the course of his rain and the way of sounding thunder, pierced inwardly by the grace [Col. 1247C] of the Holy Spirit, they open the ears of the heart to the words of life. Then the trackless land is filled because, as it gives hearing to the word, it is filled with mystery. And it brings forth green plants, because it not only gladly receives the words of preaching poured in through the grace of compunction, but also yields them abundantly. What it formerly could not hear, it now thereafter desires to speak; and, though it had inwardly withered even by not hearing, it now nourishes any who hunger by speaking holy things through its own greenness. Hence it is well said by the Prophet: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created; and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103). Thus the face of the earth is changed by the power of renewal: the mind, formerly dry, is drenched when grace comes, and after its former aridity is clothed, as it were, in the greenness of knowledge through the production of plants.

The grace of our Creator is commended to us still more profoundly when it is added: “Who is the father of the rain? Or who begot the drops of dew?” As though he said: “Who but I, who freely sprinkle the dry land of the human heart with drops of knowledge?” Of this rain the Psalmist again says: “You will set apart a willing rain, O God, for your inheritance” (Ps. 67). For the Lord sets apart a willing rain for his inheritance because he grants it to us not for our merits but through the gift of his goodness. Therefore in this place he is called the father of rain, because heavenly preaching is generated for us not from our [Col. 1248A] merit but from his grace.

The drops of dew are the holy preachers themselves, who pour the grace of heavenly bounty upon the fields of our breast—parched amid the evils of this present life, as amid the darkness of a dry night. Concerning these drops it is said to stubborn Judaea: “Therefore the drops of rain have been withheld, and there was no latter rain” (Jer. 3). These are indeed sparks of dew, and also sparks of rain. For when they moderate their preaching by some arrangement of dispensation, they sprinkle tender dew; but when they speak with such strength as they have concerning what they perceive of heavenly things, they pour forth abundant flowing rain.

Paul sprinkled dew when he said to the Corinthians: “For I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” [Col. 1248B] (1 Cor. 2). And again he poured rain when he said: “My mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; my heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6). Hence Moses, knowing that he would speak both strong things to the strong and tender things to the weak, said: “Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deut. 32).

Therefore the trackless land—that is, as was said above, the dry hearts—through the infusion of the Holy Spirit and the preaching of teachers brings forth green plants. For they not only gladly receive the words of teaching, but also gladly instruct their neighbors from those things which they hear from holy preachers. Hearts formerly parched and barren in good works now, through words of preaching, yield abundant fruit like a well-watered garden [Col. 1248C] and make others fruitful.

Therefore the Bridegroom, namely Christ, praising the bride—that is, holy Church—in the Song of spiritual love, says: “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of apples” (Song 4).

[Note: [Col. 1248D] Gregory, on this passage.]

What does holy Church send forth except holy words together with holy works, by which she begets and nourishes children? Since she brings some to martyrdom and trains others in holy conduct; since she sends the former, red with the blood of martyrdom, to their eternal homeland, and sets the latter, living in holy works, before their neighbors as examples of holiness—what else does she send forth but pomegranates and fruits of apples? Pomegranates contain a multitude of seeds beneath their red rind; fruits of apples possess within themselves the sweetness of refreshment. Thus martyrs, while they labor beneath the fire of tribulation and do not hesitate outwardly to pour out their blood for Christ, inwardly gather within their minds a multitude of virtues. Likewise, all holy persons who live in the peace of the Church bear the fruits of apples, because, while accomplishing holy works, they provide their neighbors with useful examples, by the presentation of which those who wish may refresh themselves.

For all the saints in the Church—whether they burn in the fire of suffering or grow in peace while resting in the Church—do not cease, while they live, to build within themselves the fragrance of holy virtues as a paradise of sweetness and delights. Scripture displays the abundance of this paradise when, in the voice of Jesus Christ, the heavenly Bridegroom, it designates the several virtues by the names of shrubs, saying:

[Col. 1249A] “Henna with nard; nard and saffron; cane and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes, with all the chief ointments.” What is designated by these diverse kinds of aromatic trees except the honor and growth of holy virtues possessed in the saints? From these kinds royal perfumes are made, and from them remedies for bodies are found. Thus they fittingly signify the virtues of souls: when these are gathered and prepared, a good fragrance of reputation goes forth, and fitting health is restored to sick souls through the working of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1249B] Yet the Bridegroom’s praise of the Church continues, when it adds: “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, flowing with force from Lebanon.” A fountain of gardens and a well of living waters are rightly described among the shoots of the Church. For what do the fountain and well signify except holy Scripture, which so produces the water of wisdom that it continually refreshes those who drink, yet never ceases to flow? It is rightly said to belong to gardens because holy Scripture belongs particularly to those in whose minds the seeds of virtues arise.

But we must ask why Scripture is called both fountain and well at once, since a fountain appears at the surface, whereas a well lies hidden in the depths and exercises all who seek it with greater labor. We should know that divine Scripture is clear in some places but presents itself as obscure in others. At times it is drunk lightly, as it is found, like a fountain; at times it needs great investigation in order to be found and received. That the understanding of holy Scripture is signified by water is shown elsewhere, when the divine voice says of the reprobate:

[Note: [Col. 1249D] The edition supplies here: “I will send them thirst for water and hunger for bread” (Amos 8).]

Therefore Isaiah says: “The Lord removes from Jerusalem and Judah every support of bread and every support of water” (Isa. 3). Here it should be noted that the support of bread is removed first, and then the support of water. For when the difficult utterances of Scripture are not investigated as commanded, the mind gradually falls away from knowledge, until at last it cannot even grasp light matters by understanding.

These waters are rightly said to flow with force from Lebanon. “Lebanon” is interpreted “whitening.” For in baptism we are whitened, when, having lost the blackness of sins, we are refashioned into the purity of new life. Thus the waters of the well flow from Lebanon because in baptism all the elect receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which, being enlightened, they understand the sense of holy Scripture. This knowledge of Scripture flows with such force that, when it touches the elect, it removes them from the love of this life and carries all who cleave to it in the force of its current toward eternal joys.

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “The force of the river makes glad the city [Col. 1250A] of God” (Ps. 45). For the force of the river makes glad the city of God when, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, the wisdom of Scripture strongly overflowing makes holy Church, or the mind of anyone who receives it, joyful by its infusion. The wisdom of the holy Scriptures makes glad the city of God—that is, holy Church—when it enlightens the hearts of hearers through the mouths of preachers, urges them to act well, corrects and reforms transgressors of God’s commandments, and raises the peoples of the Old and New Testament to the knowledge and love of the Creator.

For when we speak of holy Scripture, we understand the Old and New Testament. Hence the prophet Ezekiel, speaking of the living creatures shown to him, says among other things:

[Col. 1250B] “When I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth” (Ezek. 1). But what does the wheel signify, as blessed Gregory says,

[Note: [Col. 1249D] Homilies on Ezekiel, book 1, homily 6. See *Patrologia*, vol. 76, col. 829.]

except holy Scripture, etc., as far as: “Let Ezekiel the prophet therefore speak concerning the living creatures shown to him: ‘When I looked at the living creatures, one wheel appeared upon the earth.’”

Let blessed Gregory, the most subtle interpreter of the holy Scriptures, come forward and explain to us this verse of such profound depth. “We must ask,” he says,

[Note: [Col. 1250D] The same homily, ibid., col. 833.]

etc., as far as: “because holy Scripture in both Testaments is right in admonishing, lofty in promising, and terrible in threatening.”

The wheel, that is, holy Scripture, is also rightly described, as stated, as having four faces: because it first recognized the sins in humankind that needed correction through the Law; then through the Prophets; more perfectly through the Gospel; and finally through the apostles sent to preach universally to all nations. Whatever the Old Testament prefigured concerning Christ and his bride, that is, holy Church, the New Testament openly manifested in the four quarters of the world through apostolic preaching. Thus through apostolic teachings the Law became known to the whole world, because it agreed with the Gospel. Hence the Lord, speaking figuratively to Moses, said:

“Make for yourself two beaten silver trumpets” (Num. 10). And shortly afterward: “When the broken blast has sounded, the camps shall move.”

[Note: [Col. 1250D] From Gregory, *Morals*, book 30, chapter 4, and Pater, on Numbers, chapter 6.]

For the army is led by two trumpets because, through the two Testaments and the two commandments of charity, God’s people are summoned to the battle-line of faith. These trumpets are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of preachers may shine with the brightness of eloquence and confuse the minds of hearers with none of their own obscurity. They are beaten because those who preach the life to come must grow through the blows of present tribulations. It is rightly said: “When the broken blast has sounded, the camps shall move,” because, surely, when the discourse of preaching is treated more subtly and minutely, the minds of hearers are more ardently aroused against the combats of temptations.

Thus the sound of the trumpets resounded terribly throughout the whole world, because through apostolic teaching the spiritual understanding of the New and Old Testament became clearly known everywhere. For this purpose the Son of God and of the Virgin—as has already been said—sent throughout the whole world heralds made fit for his incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven; fully instructed by the teaching of the Holy Spirit and strong to endure the wickedness of unbelievers who persecuted them. They were sent to call those predestined to eternal life, from whom he might build for himself a temple, that is, holy Church, as from living stones; and in it he, the true Sun of righteousness, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, might dwell not only in this present age but also forever.

[Col. 1251B] Hence Solomon, speaking figuratively, says: “Wisdom has built herself a house; she has hewn out seven pillars. She has sacrificed victims, mixed wine, set her table, and sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and the walls of the city.”

[Note: [Col. 1251D] From *Morals*, book 33, chapter 15, and Pater, on Proverbs, chapter 16.]

For Wisdom built herself a house when the only-begotten Son of God created a body for himself within the Virgin’s womb through the mediation of a soul. Thus the body of the Only-Begotten is called the house of God and is also called the temple of God. So too the one and same Son of God and man is both he who dwells and he who is dwelt in.

Yet this may rightly be understood otherwise. The Church is called the house of Wisdom; it has hewn out for itself seven pillars because it raises up the minds of preachers, separated from the love of this present world, to bear the structure of that Church. Because they are supported by the power of perfection, they are signified by the number seven. The Lord sacrificed victims by offering himself to God the Father for us; or he sacrificed victims because he allowed the life of preachers to be slain in persecution. He mixed wine, that is, he blended the cup of his commandments from historical narration and spiritual understanding. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: “A cup of pure wine is in the Lord’s hand; it is full of mixture.”

[Note: [Col. 1251D] These matters are not from Gregory.]

The cup is called one of pure wine with respect to spiritual understanding; it is full of mixture—that is, of the dregs of bodily sacraments. These sacraments settle and remain among the Jews; from them all spiritual understanding is poured out and strained into the humble Gentiles. But among the Jews the dregs of the figure remain, from which all unbelievers have drunk.

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Again from the same author.]

In another sense, Wisdom—that is, the Son of God—mixed wine because he preached to us together the mysteries of his divinity and humanity. “She set a table,” that is, holy Scripture, which refreshes us with the bread of the heavenly word when we come weary from the labor of this world, and strengthens us by its refreshment against adversaries.

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Again, not from the same author.]

Hence holy Church sings in joyful thanksgiving to Jesus Christ, her Bridegroom: “You have prepared before me a table against those who afflict me” (Ps. 22).

[Col. 1252A] The table of the Lord and the blessed banquet are heavenly food for those satisfied with faith, concerning which the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats judgment for himself” (1 Cor. 11). “You have prepared before me a table,” he says: namely, communion in your body, O Christ, who are truly the Wisdom of God the Father; by this I understand that I ought to imitate the footsteps of your passion. Hence Proverbs says: “You have sat at a great table,” that is, Christ’s; “know that you ought to prepare such things,” (Prov. 23), that is, to suffer as he did. Therefore elsewhere the Psalmist says: “I will take up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115).

We read of three tables: the first in the Law, the second in the Gospel, the third in heaven. Moses wrote of the first in Exodus, where it is read that it was placed in the tabernacle [Col. 1252B] by the entrance. Upon it were twelve loaves of presentation made of fine flour, and over each one a golden dish with a handful of incense (Exod. 25). Of the second the Apostle says: “You cannot partake of the table of Christ and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. 10). Of the third the Lord says to his disciples: “I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22). The first table, therefore, did not prepare refreshment but showed it; the second satisfies; the third glorifies. The first is in the letter, the second in the Spirit, the third in hope. The first teaches, the second helps, the third brings to completion.

[Note: [Col. 1252D] Again from Gregory.]

Again he adds, saying: “She sent her maidservants to call to the citadel and walls of the city,” because he chose to have weak and lowly preachers who might gather the faithful peoples to the lofty buildings of the spiritual homeland. Hence in the Gospel the Lord praises Nathanael (John 1), yet does not number him among the lot of preachers; for those who came to preach needed to be such as had nothing from their own praise, so that what they accomplished might be recognized all the more as belonging to Truth alone, since it might be openly seen that they themselves had not been fit to do it. Therefore, in order that wondrous power might shine forth through the tongues of preachers, something still more wondrous was first done: the preachers themselves possessed no merit.

For this purpose Wisdom, that is, the Son of God, sent his maidservants—namely, his disciples, first weak, lowly, and unlearned, but afterwards made strong and subtly instructed by the Holy Spirit teaching inwardly—to call to the citadel and walls of the city. For while they proclaim eternal life, they raise us to the lofty walls of the heavenly city; and only the humble ascend those walls. Hence Wisdom itself immediately adds: “If anyone is little, let him come to me” (Prov. 9). As though it said openly: “Whoever thinks himself great narrows for himself the entrance and ascent; for one reaches higher insofar as each person’s mind is more truly humbled within itself.”

But however greatly anyone may advance in virtue or grow in knowledge, he is not sufficient to penetrate how greatly our Creator governs us by moderation. He has prepared invisible goods for us in the heavenly Jerusalem, and through his preachers he does not cease mercifully to call us to them. The things he has granted us, though unworthy, in the present age are innumerable; but he promises far greater things in heaven. “For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5). He bestows visible goods on us in this mortal life, but through the utterances of his preachers he urges us to desire invisible things.

This weakness or ignorance of the human mind—by which, while we are in the present life, we are prevented from contemplating eternal joys perfectly—was without doubt prefigured by the veil which, by the Lord’s command, hung in the middle of the tabernacle and separated the inner parts from the outer so that they could not be seen (Exod. 26). For the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 55.]

Therefore, as long as we are in this world, we see the truth of the heavenly kingdom as through a mirror, placed as it were in the sanctuary and not yet attaining the Holy of Holies. “Holy things” may be those who can maintain holy conduct in the present age; but the Holy of Holies, into which one enters only once, is the passage to heaven.

[Note: [Col. 1253D] Supplied from the edition: “is the passage.”]

There are the propitiatory and the cherubim; there God appears also to those pure in heart. Yet while we are established in this manner of life—that is, in the present Church—we do not stand without the help of the Holy Spirit. For from the one fountain of the Holy Spirit we have seven lamps that illuminate the people of the Church: that is, the sevenfold grace of the Lord sent throughout the whole world, which enlightens the peoples of the Church by the brilliance of the Holy Spirit in the diverse radiance of gifts.

The stretched-out veil—

[Note: [Col. 1253D] “Oppansum”: “oppassum,” i.e. stretched over.]

—which hid the inner portion of the tabernacle from view may indeed prefigure that former time under the Law, because the things sung by the Law and Prophets were hidden and could not be fully understood through the veil set between. But when Christ came, at the time of his passion he tore that veil from top to bottom (Matt. 27), and through his passion revealed all those things that had been hidden, to strengthen our faith, as the Apostle says: “God has revealed them to us through his Spirit” (1 Cor. 2).

Truly, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, the holy apostles and other disciples were few in number, weak to endure the adversities of unbelievers, and untaught to preach the mysteries of the Bridegroom and bride—namely, Christ and the Church. For when holy Church existed only in the apostles, it was not able to nourish either itself or others with the milk of preaching.

Solomon says of it in the Song of spiritual love: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts” [Col. 1254A] (Song 8). What could Peter and the other disciples preach to others when, shut within one house, they did not dare to appear outside? Thus at that time the Church was little and had no breasts, for after the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, terrified by fear of the Jews, it feared not merely to preach but even to be seen.

[Note: [Col. 1253D] From Gregory on this passage and *Morals*, book 10, chapter 9.]

The age of holy Church is described as is that of each individual person. Thus it was little then, when, newly born, it could not preach the Word of life; it had no breasts because, before it had advanced through growth in virtue, it could not offer the words of preaching to weak hearers. But the Church is called adult when, united to the Word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, it is made fruitful in conceiving children through the ministry of preaching—children whom it brings forth by exhorting and bears by converting.

Of this stage of its life it is said to the Lord in the Song of love: “The young women loved you” (Song 1). For all the Churches, as blessed Gregory says in the *Morals*, are called young women because they make one catholic Church: no longer old through sin, but new through grace;

[Note: [Col. 1254D] This is from the same author, on Song 1.]

not barren through old age, but at an age of mind suitable for spiritual fruitfulness. Or by “young women” are signified holy souls, regenerated through the water of baptism by the Holy Spirit and transferred into Christ’s new life through the New Testament.

But when this holy catholic Church, in the times of Antichrist, weakened as if by a certain old age, with wickedness abounding and the love of many growing cold, has at times ceased to bear children through preaching, remembering its former fruitfulness it may speak, as if making lament, with blessed Job:

Just as I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tent” (Job 29). [Note: [Col. 1254D] This is from the *Moralia*, cited above.] As though he said more plainly: “Who will grant me to be as I was in the days of my youth?” Yet after those same days, in which she will be grievously oppressed by persecutors, she will nevertheless, near the very end of time, be strengthened by the great power of preaching. For, when the Gentiles have been received in full, she will draw into the bosom of her faith the whole Israelite people that shall then be found. For it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel [Col. 1254D] should be saved” (Rom. 11).

At that time, as we believe, when the Synagogue sees the holy Church persevering in Christ’s love, preserving an uncorrupted faith, willingly enduring adversities for righteousness’ sake, preaching that Christ, true God and true man, is one God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and calling all nations to the faith, she will awaken from the sleep of ignorance and say: “Alas, unhappy me [Note: [Col. 1254D] “Unhappy, deceived.”] and long deceived! What profit was it to me that I remained unbelieving for so long a time? I did not believe when the prophets proclaimed Christ’s incarnation; I did not receive Christ, sent from heaven by God the Father [Col. 1255A] for my salvation. But, what is more grievous, after inflicting many injuries upon him, I fastened him to the cross and delivered him to death; I drove far from my province, after scourging them, his apostles who preached to me the word of salvation. And thus, down to the present time, I have walked in the darkness of ignorance and have wholly failed to know the light of truth.”

Therefore, when, as has been said, the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in near the end of the world, the Synagogue, enlightened by God, repenting of its past sacrileges and other sins, will faithfully enter the bosom of the holy mother Church. In her person Solomon speaks figuratively in the Song of spiritual love, saying:

“I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab” (Song 6). [Note: [Col. 1255D] Gregory, on this passage.] As though she said: “Seeing so many virtues performed [Col. 1255B] in the holy Church, why did I wander unlawfully for so long? Why did I persist in unbelief? Why did I remain so long in the darkness of ignorance through my unbelief?” But the Synagogue is troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab, who will at some time be stirred by Christ’s Gospel to receive the faith. For *Aminadab* is interpreted “the willing one of my people.” And Christ Jesus, sent by the Father, is rightly and without doubt called “the willing one of my people,” because in truly willing love he descended to save his people, and, to raise us from death, willingly and by gracious kindness underwent death on the cross. Hence the good shepherd himself says to the Father: “I will sacrifice to thee willingly, and I will confess thy name, O Lord, [Col. 1255C] because it is good” (Ps. 53).

Hence also the Psalmist speaks in the person of the Church, saying: “Hear me, O Lord, because thy mercy is gracious; according to the multitude of thy compassions look upon me” (Ps. 68). Therefore the Synagogue is troubled because of the chariots of Aminadab: for when at last she beholds, in faith, the four Gospels of Christ running through the world and burning in human hearts, she will immediately be ashamed of the darkness of her unbelief; and, as saving shame arises, she will be moved to repentance. The kindly Church speaks to her, saying:

“Return, return, Sunamite; return, that we may behold thee” (Song 6). For *Sunamite* is interpreted “captive.” Thus the Sunamite is called to return, [Col. 1255D] because, at the end of the world, the faith of the Synagogue will be offered to God through the holy catholic Church, so that she may recover her former dignity—the dignity she lost while she was held captive by demons under the yoke of unbelief. And she is well instructed to return four times, because the Jews are now dispersed into the four parts of the world; wherever they shall then be, they will, as has been said, be converted at the end, as was foretold through the prophet: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. 10).

Let the Sunamite therefore return, that we may behold her—that is, let the Synagogue be converted to the faith and, in her repentance, show the whole Church how great an evil she committed and what detestable sacrilege she perpetrated [Col. 1256A] when she suspended Jesus Christ, God and man, upon the cross. But as soon as the Church desires to behold the end of the Synagogue, the bridegroom, namely Christ, asks in rejoicing:

“What will you see in the Sunamite, unless the choirs of camps?” (Song 7).

For camps belong to those engaged in warfare. Thus camps will be seen in the Shulamite, because for the faith which she now attacks, she will then fight vigorously against the faithless. Therefore, as was said, the holy Church was small and timid before the coming of the Holy Spirit; for that reason she did not dare to preach, and she had no breasts, because she could not nourish her hearers with the milk of preaching. But after she received the gifts of the Holy Spirit, she immediately shone with miracles, advanced in virtues, and through the ministry of preaching [Col. 1256B] begot many in the faith. She despised the threats of kings and princes and, protected by divine grace, extended herself to the ends of the earth. For the Son of God and of the Virgin, who redeemed her with his own blood by the Father’s will, continually anoints her with the anointing of the Holy Spirit, refreshes her with the sweetness of his most holy preaching, and ever kindles her with the fire of love to emulate the greater gifts.

Hence Ezekiel the prophet, speaking typologically, says: “Above the likeness of the throne was a likeness as of the appearance of a man above it; and as the appearance of fire within it round about, from his loins upward. And from his loins downward, I saw as it were the appearance of shining fire round about” (Ezek. 1). Blessed [Col. 1256C] Gregory, expounding this, says [Note: [Col. 1255] Homilies on Ezekiel, book I, homily 8. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 865.]: “What is it that the Mediator between God and men,” etc., as far as “that he may now be seen by us in eternal and infinite brightness.”

Hence also in the Song of Songs the bride says to the same Son of God and of the Virgin: “Flee, my beloved” (Song 8). The beloved flees because, ascending into heaven and sitting at the right hand of God the Father, he has withdrawn himself, so that he may not be perfectly seen by mortals still placed in this present life. Therefore, dearest brothers, it is necessary that we direct the eyes of our minds toward him, love him with the Father and Holy Spirit in all things and above all things, and strive, insofar as we can, to fulfil his commandments. We are truly his disciples if we keep his commandments without complaint.

Hence he himself, admonishing his disciples—indeed, all of us—says: [Col. 1256D] “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14). The performance of a work is evidence of love. “And I,” he says, “will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever” (ibid.). He asks the Father according to his humanity, he who gives with the Father according to his divinity. “And he will give you another Paraclete,” that is, a comforter, “to remain with you,” just as I am present with you in the flesh: namely, that he may teach and enlighten you, do other such things, and afterward bring you to behold eternally the essence of the divine majesty.

How does he command them to love and keep the commandments, so that they may receive the Holy Spirit, whom, unless they have him, they cannot love or keep the commandments? They had him less openly, and they were to receive him more manifestly, so that they might come to know what they had. Lovers of the world do not have spiritual eyes by which they may see the Holy Spirit; nor can they see him with bodily eyes, because the Holy Spirit did not appear clothed in humanity. “The Father,” he says, “will give you the Spirit of truth,” namely the Holy Spirit, who is consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and Son; whom the world—that is, the people who love worldly things—cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him, having no spiritual eyes by which the Holy Spirit is invisibly seen. “But you will know him, because he will remain with you and will be in you.” As though he plainly said: “He will be in you, so as to remain; he will not remain, so as to come into being.” For to be somewhere comes before remaining there, as a visible guest with another; but he is already in them, and therefore can be known by them, though not by lovers of the world.

It follows: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” As though he said: “I shall not leave you as strangers, but, like a loving Father, I shall come to you after the resurrection in the flesh, while in the presence of my divinity I am always with you. The Holy Spirit will not be given in my place in such a way that I myself am no longer with you.”

As Isidore says in the *Etymologies*, [Note: [Col. 1257D] Supplement of the doctor.] “pupils” are so called not on account of their condition, but because of their childhood. [Note: [Col. 1258D] *Etymologies*, book XI, chapter 2.] *Pupilli* are said to be, as it were, “without eyes,” that is, bereft of parents. Those are properly called *pupilli* whose fathers died before they received a name from them; the rest are called bereaved. Orphans are the same as *pupilli*, but [Col. 1257C] the former name is Greek and the latter Latin. Thus in the psalm, where it is read, “Thou wilt be a helper to the fatherless” (Ps. 9), the Greek has “to the orphan.” Therefore those called *orphanoi* in Greek are called *pupilli* in Latin.

Again Jesus Christ, God and man, adds for the consolation of his disciples: “Yet a little while, and the world sees me no longer.” As though he said: “The world, which now sees me with bodily eyes, will shortly no longer see me; for after I rise again, I shall be removed from the ungodly, lest they see the glory of the resurrection, which is granted to the righteous alone to behold. But you, my little children, see me, because I, who am the true life, live, and you shall live in me. On that day, when you live, you shall know what you now believe, [Col. 1257D] namely, that, as a ray is in the sun, I am in my Father—one with him—and you are in me as branches in the vine, and I am in you as a father in his children.”

It follows: “He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me.” As though he plainly said: “Not only you, O apostles, will see and know these things mentioned above, but also everyone who has my commandments in memory and keeps them in life, or has them by doing and keeps them by persevering—he is the one who loves me.” But he who loves me, what fruit does he have in this? “He will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” As though he said: “I will love him for this purpose, that I may manifest myself to him, because even now I love him.”

[Col. 1258A] “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” Love is the cause, proved by keeping the words; “and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” God comes to a human being when the human being comes to God. A human being comes by believing, obeying, beholding, and receiving; but God comes to a human being by helping, enlightening, and filling. “I and the Father,” he says, “will come, and we shall make our dwelling with him who loves me.” That dwelling, vision, and love will without doubt not be passing but eternal. Love makes one dwell for ever in the house in which the Father, with the Son and Holy Spirit, makes his dwelling.

It follows:

“He who does not love me does not keep my words.” Whoever does not love Christ, God and man, [Col. 1258B] and does not keep his words, will never see the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the form of God, though they will see, to their own condemnation, the form of a servant—that is, Christ’s humanity. Again he adds: “And the word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me.” Because the word is not his own but the Father’s, and because he wished himself to be understood as one, he said: “The word which you have heard is not mine,” though previously he had said in the plural: “He does not keep my words.”

It follows: “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you,” namely in bodily presence. If this presence is now being taken away, do not be afraid, because “the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and bring all things to your remembrance”—that is, secretly [Col. 1258C], not because he is inferior; or, “will make you mindful of all things whatsoever I have said to you.” “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you; not as the world gives do I give to you.”

About to ascend to the right hand of God the Father, he says to his disciples—indeed, to all the children of the Church: “Peace I leave with you”; and, repeating the same thing, “My peace I give to you.” Peace exists in this world: by remaining in it we overcome the enemy, if we love one another and do not judge one another concerning hidden matters. Peace will exist in the future, when we shall reign without fear of an enemy, where one cannot disagree with another, where all things will be naked and open, and where each one’s praise will come from God. Both kinds of peace are in Christ and from Christ. For he is our peace, [Col. 1258D] “who made both one” (Eph. 2); we believe him because he is, and we shall see him as he is (1 John 3). Hence, from what follows, “my peace” must also be understood in what came before. Or, in this world there is our peace, which is partial and incomplete; but in the future there is his peace, where nothing is opposed.

It follows: “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.” As though he said: “I give you one steadfast heart, so that you may always keep it lifted up.” Since therefore I leave you in peace, let not your heart be troubled because I said, “I go to the Father,” as though, in the shepherd’s absence, the wolf might attack the flock; for if I go as man, I am present as God. You heard that I [Col. 1259A] said to you: “I go, and I come to you.” I go in body and remain in you in divinity; or, I now depart from you in the flesh, but at the time of judgment I shall come to you in bodily presence.

“If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice because I go to the Father; because the Father is greater than I.” As though he plainly said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because the human nature which I assumed must be congratulated for being raised to the Father’s right hand, where the same heaven is hoped for; for the Father, according to the humanity which I assumed, is greater than I.”

“And now I have told you before it happens, that, when it has happened, you may believe.” He did not say, “when you see it has happened,” because there is neither praise nor merit of faith—indeed, not even faith—in what is seen, but in what is not seen. Rather, he says: “that, when it has happened, you may believe,” namely that I am the Son of God: not with a new [Col. 1259B] faith, since you believed before, but then your faith will be increased and perfected. For when the Son of God and of the Virgin, after he had supped—namely, before he was betrayed by a disciple—said these things to the apostles and the others who were with them, their faith was then small and imperfect. When that loving teacher afterward died on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, it was almost nonexistent, because, as was said, faith is not concerned with things seen. Thus they advanced in faith and virtues through Christ’s resurrection, his ascension into heaven, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, though previously they had been doubtful and weak.

It follows: “I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” As though he said: “The prince of this world is coming,” [Col. 1259C] namely the devil, who is truly prince of ungodly human beings, as the Lord testifies when he says to blessed Job: “He is king over all the children of pride” (Job 41); “and he has nothing in me,” namely no sin whatever that belongs to him. “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father has commanded me, so I do.”

One might say: “Why then do you die, O Christ, who have no sin?” Namely for this reason: “As the Father has commanded me, so I do.” I proceeded from him before heaven and earth were made; being sent by him, I came for the redemption of humankind; and without interruption I do those things which please him. Therefore let not your heart be troubled, my little children, nor let it be afraid; for although [Col. 1259D] I depart from you in body, I am nevertheless present in divinity until the consummation of the world. For God the Father will also send in my name the Paraclete Spirit for your consolation; he will instruct you perfectly in all things and preserve you powerfully and wisely amid the adversities of this world.

For the Holy Spirit himself, as blessed Isidore says, [Note: [Col. 1259D] *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 3.] is preached as God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son and is of the same substance. For nothing other than what the Father himself is could proceed from the Father. [Col. 1260A] [Note: [Col. 1259D] A different sense seems to be intended here than in the edition, as will be evident to every reader.] The Holy Spirit is called, in relation to something else, “breathing”; certainly, he is one who inspires by spirit, and from this he is called Spirit. But in a certain proper sense he is called the Holy Spirit, namely in so far as he is related to the Father and Son, whose Spirit he is. For even the name “Spirit” is not always used in relation to something else, but in so far as it signifies a certain nature.

Therefore the Spirit of God is called holy because he is the holiness of the Father and Son. For although the Father is Spirit and the Son, according to divinity, is Spirit; and though the Father is holy and the Son is holy, yet he himself is properly called the Holy Spirit, as the coessential and consubstantial holiness [Col. 1260B] of both. The Holy Spirit, as blessed Isidore says, is not called begotten, lest two Sons be supposed in the Trinity. Nor is he proclaimed unbegotten, lest two Fathers be believed in the Trinity itself. He is called proceeding, on the testimony [Note: [Col. 1259D] Isidore presents this testimony differently, namely: “I still have many things which I shall say to you, but you cannot hear them now. But the Spirit [Col. 1260D] of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father and will receive from what is mine; he will declare all things to you.” Martin likewise adduces it more consistently with this in the following sermon; for in this sermon he transcribes the Vulgate, which in this place says nothing about the procession of the Holy Spirit, which Isidore here proves.] of the Lord saying: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16). And a little later: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and declare it to you” (ibid.).

But he proceeds not only in nature, but continually and without ceasing proceeds to accomplish the works of the Trinity. This is the difference between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds: the Son is born from one, while the Holy Spirit [Col. 1260C] proceeds from both. Hence the Apostle says: “But anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). The Holy Spirit is also understood as an angel by reason of his work. For it is written of him: “He will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16). *Angel* in Greek is translated *messenger* in Latin. Hence two angels appeared to Lot (Gen. 19), through whom we understand the Son and the Holy Spirit; for the Father is never read of as having been sent.

The Holy Spirit, called Paraclete, derives his name from consolation. For *paraklēsis* in Greek is called *consolatio*, “consolation,” in Latin. Christ sent him to the mourning apostles after he himself ascended to heaven from their sight. For the Comforter is sent to the sorrowful, according to the saying of the same Lord: “Blessed [Col. 1260D] are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5). He also said: “Then the children of the bridegroom shall mourn, when the bridegroom has been taken away from them” (Matt. 9). Again, he is called Paraclete because he provides consolation to souls that lose temporal joy. Others translate *Paraclete* into Latin as “pleader” or “advocate.” For the Holy Spirit himself speaks; he himself teaches; through him the word of wisdom is given; by him Holy Scripture was inspired. Hence: “It is not you [Col. 1261A] who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaks in you” (Matt. 10).

The Holy Spirit is called sevenfold on account of the gifts which each person, according as they are worthy, deserves to receive in part from his single fullness. For he is the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord. The “principal Spirit” is read of in Psalm 50; because “Spirit” is repeated there three times, some have understood the Trinity—namely because, as it is written, “God is Spirit” (John 4). For what is not body and yet is, seems to remain Spirit. Thus some understand that the Trinity is signified there (Ps. 50): the Father in the principal Spirit, [Col. 1261B] the Son in the right Spirit, and the Holy Spirit in the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is called a gift because he is given; for *donum*, “gift,” is named from giving. It is well known that, after the Lord Jesus Christ had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, he gave the Holy Spirit, by whom believers, filled with him, spoke the languages of all nations (Acts 2). He is God’s gift to the extent that he is given to those who love God through him. For he is with God in himself, but with us he is a gift. The Holy Spirit is eternally a gift, distributing gifts of graces to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12). He grants prophecies to whom he wills, and forgives sins to whom he wills. For sins are not pardoned without the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit is properly called love, [Col. 1261C] either because he naturally joins those from whom he proceeds and shows himself to be one with them, or because he effects in us that we may remain in God and he in us. Hence among God’s gifts there is nothing greater than love, and no gift of God greater than the Holy Spirit. He is also grace, which, because it is freely given not by our merits but by the divine will, is therefore called grace. Just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name Wisdom, though the Holy Spirit universally is wisdom and the Father himself is wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name Love, though both Father and Son universally are love.

The Holy Spirit is most plainly declared in the books of the Gospels [Col. 1261D] to be the finger of God. For when one evangelist said, “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke 11), another said the same thing thus: “By the Spirit of God I cast out demons” (Matt. 12). Hence the Law was written by the finger of God and given on the fiftieth day after the slaughter of the lamb (Exod. 31), and on the fiftieth day after the Passion of our Lord, that is, Christ, the Holy Spirit came. He is called the finger of God in order that his active power with the Father and Son may be signified. Hence Paul says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). And just as through baptism we die and are reborn in Christ, so we are sealed by the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God and the spiritual seal.

[Col. 1262A] The Holy Spirit is written to have come in the form of a dove so that his nature might be declared through the bird of simplicity and innocence. Hence among other things the Lord says in the Gospel: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. 10). For this bird is bodily without gall, possessing only innocence and love. The Holy Spirit is called by the name of fire because in the Acts of the Apostles he appeared in divided tongues as of fire, and rested upon each one of them (Acts 2). He gave the apostles the grace of diverse languages so that they might be made fit to instruct the peoples of believers. That he is said to have rested upon individuals has this purpose: that it may be understood that he was not divided among many, but remained whole in each of them, as is almost customary with fires.

[Col. 1262B] For fire, once kindled, has this nature: however many look upon it, however many upon the lock of its purple brightness, to so many it grants the sight of its light, to so many it affords the service of its gift, while it nevertheless remains in its own integrity.

The Holy Spirit is called water in the Gospel, where the Lord cries out and says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink, and rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). But the Evangelist explained of whom he spoke, for he continued: “This he said of the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.” But the water of the sacrament is one thing, and the water signifying the Spirit of God another. The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what takes place in the soul. Through that [Col. 1262C] Holy Spirit the soul itself is cleansed and sealed.

The Holy Spirit is called an anointing, as John the apostle testifies (1 John 2), because, just as oil by its natural weight rises above every liquid, so in the beginning the Spirit moved above the waters. Hence the Lord is read to have been anointed with “the oil of gladness” (Ps. 44), that is, with the Holy Spirit. John the apostle also calls the Holy Spirit an anointing, saying: “And let the anointing which you received from him remain in you. And you have no need that anyone should teach you, but as his anointing teaches you concerning all things” (1 John 2). For the Holy Spirit himself is the invisible anointing.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let us pray more earnestly to God that he may send us the anointing of his most holy love, [Col. 1262D] which may teach us concerning all things: that it may make known how we should believe in him, what we should think and say concerning him, and in what manner we ought to fear and love him; or may show us, by inward illumination, how, setting aside earthly pleasures, we may be able to please him; and may supply strength to accomplish the good which it has inspired.

Therefore, sweetest brothers, because God is love, show true love to one another, without which no one can see the essence of the divine majesty. Although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are universally love, the Holy Spirit is nevertheless properly called by the name of love, as was stated above. As blessed Fulgentius says, one who walks in love can neither err nor fear, because love itself protects, love itself guides, [Col. 1263A] love itself leads a human being to the heavenly homeland. Therefore love is the way by which one goes to God. For thus Jerome, one of the strongest pillars of the catholic faith, says: “Just as no one can reach the place toward which he tends without a way, so without love no one is able to attain God.”

This way has fifteen steps, which the Apostle Paul enumerates in order, saying: “Love is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own; is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with truth; bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13). Whoever, aided by divine help, devoutly ascends [Col. 1263B] these fifteen steps may indeed attain perfection. Therefore we must ascend by them step by step, as if from virtue to virtue, in good works; and, for the benefit of hearers, briefly expound them, since we must live justly and religiously and break spiritual bread for little ones.

Love, therefore, as we have said, is patient, because it willingly suffers adversity for the love of Christ and neighbour and does not return evil for evil, even when it can. It is kind because it freely gives what is its own, compassionately shares the sufferings of the afflicted, feeds enemies, and gladly prays for them. It does not envy, because it is not envious but rather rejoices in another’s good. It does not act perversely, because it thinks nothing wicked and does nothing deceitfully; [Col. 1263C] for it has a simple heart, open to every good work and full of loving affection. It is not puffed up because it glories in its good works not in itself but in the Lord. It is not ambitious because one who desires to see God does not pursue ambition—that is, does not covet worldly honours, but rather despises them and chooses to be lowly in the house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Ps. 83).

It does not seek its own because it does not set private things before common things, but common things before private things; nor does it demand back what is its own according to the Gospel commandment (Luke 6), but rather patiently suffers wrong. It is not provoked because it is not stirred to anger but always avoids disputes and occasions of dispute. It thinks no evil because it has a secure and unsuspecting [Col. 1263D] conscience and does not keep its ears open to rumours or slanders. It does not rejoice over iniquity; rather, it grieves for the tribulations and distresses of the wretched and shares the sufferings of the oppressed innocent. But it rejoices together with truth because it praises the judgment of divine justice in the recompense of both the good and the evil. It bears all things because, though it sees the wicked prosper and the good oppressed, it is not thereby disturbed. It believes all things that agree with faith and truth. It hopes all things because it is certain that God’s promises will be fulfilled. It endures all things because, though the promises are delayed, it is long-suffering in hope and cannot thereby be moved, having already conquered the world and been established in that portion of future blessedness.

[Col. 1264A] Truly and deservedly, one who has ascended to this fifteenth step is called long-suffering, because such a one has a long soul: though placed upon earth, he already holds heaven and knocks at God’s throne. Whoever has ascended to this fifteenth step will never descend. The Apostle had ascended to this step when he said: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8), etc. Few now attain this step. God knows whether any of us is now even on the first step; for how shall we endure enemies when we do not even endure our fathers? On the first step love is patient. Therefore one who does not possess this first step in conduct cannot attain the summit.

But after God’s servant has ascended these fifteen steps, [Col. 1264B] he will attain that perfection which the same Apostle points out when he says: “Love never fails” (1 Cor. 13). These are the fifteen steps of the Temple by which one ascended from the outer part into the Holy of Holies. This love is that ladder of Jacob which he saw in a dream while his head rested upon a stone, because angels ascended to heaven (Gen. 28). Love, on the path of this life, shuts a person’s eyes against the desire for earthly pleasures and sets the mind upon Christ.

It should be noted that to love God is nothing other than that a person’s own spirit is joined to the Holy Spirit by a certain loving presence, the Holy Spirit himself touching the lover’s heart. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6), namely with him. I speak as one without experience. Only the souls of devout persons feel and understand those most joyful, sweet, and solitary approaches by which the human mind is joined to the Holy Spirit—that is, to divine love. They can show us how great a sweetness, how delightful a pleasure, soothes their hearts while, in that sweet contemplation, they attend with the spirit alone and with the joy of tears.

Two handmaids most closely attached to love walk daily upon this way of divine love—namely humility and carefulness—and diligently show the path to those who wish to ascend to God, teaching most rightly how they should ascend. Carefulness cries out through the Apostle Paul, saying: “See [Col. 1264D] how carefully you walk, not as unwise but as wise” (Eph. 5), and admonishes through Solomon, saying: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Prov. 4). And again: “He paved its midst with love” (Song 3). As though he said: “Whoever preserve unfailing love in their conduct will likewise be able to attain with God’s elect the brightness of eternal blessedness.” It also cries out through a certain philosopher, saying: “Hold the middle with steadfast strength.” And it is said through the poet [Note: [Col. 1263D] Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.136.]:

> . . . . . . in the middle you will go most safely.

Humility also cries out, teaching how we may ascend to the fifteenth step of love, where it says: “When you have done well all these things which are commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17). And again: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to thy name” (Ps. 113). Many have attempted to ascend, but because they walked without love, they were unable to ascend at all. But because it is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. [Col. 1266A] 9), it is fitting, dearest brothers, that we pray more earnestly to almighty God that he may make us attain himself by the way of love, and rejoice for ever with his elect—he who lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON THIRTY-THREE. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY SPIRIT, II

[Col. 1265]

[Col. 1265B] King Solomon, beloved and dear to God, wise in judgment, just in sentence, glorious and peaceful in his kingdom, and enlightened by God’s grace, says: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (Wisdom 1). [Note: [Col. 1265D] From Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, as above.] The Spirit of God is called holy because he is the holiness of the Father and of the Son. For although the Father is Spirit, and the Son according to his divinity is Spirit, and although the Father is holy and the Son is holy, yet he himself is properly called the Holy Spirit, as the coessential and consubstantial holiness of both.

Therefore the Holy Spirit is not said to be begotten by the Father, but to proceed, lest two sons be supposed in the Trinity. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is not called unbegotten within the Trinity, lest two Fathers be believed to exist in [Col. 1265C] the Trinity. The Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father on the testimony of the Lord, who says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But the Spirit of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father, and he will receive from what is mine and announce all things to you” (John 16, 26). This is the difference between the Son who is begotten and the Holy Spirit who proceeds: the Son is born from one, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ is not his” (Rom. 8).

The Holy Spirit is also understood from his activity to be an angel; for it is said of him: “And he will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16). And certainly *angel* in Greek is translated *messenger* in Latin. [Col. 1265D] Hence two angels appeared to Lot (Gen. 19), in whom the Lord is named in the singular; through them we understand the Son and the Holy Spirit. But the Father is never read to have been sent. The Holy Spirit, who is called the Paraclete, is so called from consolation. For *paraclisis* in Greek is called *consolation* in Latin. Christ sent him to the apostles as they mourned, after he himself had ascended into heaven from their sight.

The Holy Spirit is called sevenfold because, from his single fullness, each person merits to receive portions according as they are worthy. For he is [Col. 1266B] “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11). (The gift of the Holy Spirit is distributed individually among the members of the Church, and particular gifts are allotted to particular persons. Christ, however, possessed every fullness of graces; of him it is thus written: “Full of grace and truth” [John 1]. Therefore in Christ is every fullness of graces, whereas particular gifts are distributed among individual elect persons.) [Note: [Col. 1265D] What we enclose in brackets has been inserted from book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 15.]

Hence Paul also says: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (1 Cor. 12). And as through baptism we die and are reborn in Christ, so also we are sealed through the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God and the spiritual seal. The Holy Spirit is written to have descended upon Christ at his baptism in the form of a dove [Col. 1266C] in order that his nature might be declared through the bird of simplicity and innocence. For the dove lacks gall, possessing only innocence and love. The Holy Spirit is called by the name of fire because, at this feast, he appeared over the apostles in divided tongues as fire (Acts 2). [Note: [Col. 1266D] These things are from the cited chapter in book I of the *Sentences*.]

Before the coming of the Lord, only the patriarchs and prophets [Note: [Col. 1266D] The edition reads better: “And a few righteous persons from the whole people.”]—the righteous from among the whole people—merited the gift of the Holy Spirit; but after the coming of the Lord it was bestowed upon all believers, in accordance with what the Lord says through the prophet Joel: “And it shall be in the last days: I shall pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” [Col. 1266D] (Joel 2). For the grace of the Holy Spirit has now been granted to all nations. It abides not among a small number and a few persons, as among the Jewish people, but throughout the whole multitude of believers.

It is therefore rightly said: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world,” because not only the holy prophets of the Jewish people awaited Christ’s coming, but there were also among the nations many holy men possessing the gift of prophecy, to whom Christ was revealed through the Holy Spirit and by whom his coming was awaited: such as Job, Balaam, [Col. 1267A] and the Sibyl, who indeed proclaimed Christ’s coming.

But amid these matters it must be known that, in the division of gifts, different persons receive different gifts of God. All gifts are not granted to one person; rather, through the pursuit of humility, this is so arranged that one may have something to admire in another. Through the grace of the Holy Spirit, one receives the gift of charity, another humility, another patience and sobriety. From the gifts of the Holy Spirit, some are given power in prayer, some in keeping vigil, and others in fasting. One, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, is generous in almsgiving; another is ready to visit the sick and bury the dead; and another is willing to teach his neighbours. This person wonders how that one can [Col. 1267B] endure all adversities so patiently; that person wonders how this one is able so perfectly to despise the world.

Therefore all the gifts of the Holy Spirit are not given to one person in this age, so that one may have something to admire in another. Thus, when anyone receives some gift through the grace of the Holy Spirit, let him not, perhaps by desiring to seize another’s gift, lose that which he has merited. For he who, not content with his own office, usurps another’s, throws the whole order of the body into confusion. Therefore let each person remain, according to the Apostle’s command, in that calling in which he has been called through the grace of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 7). Let him persevere in the same measure and rank in which he has been chosen. Let him not seek what belongs to another; let him not look for what is not his; let him not covet what does not concern [Col. 1267C] him.

Meanwhile, dearest brothers, let us hear what Luke the Evangelist relates. “After the Lord’s ascension,” he says, “the apostles returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem with great joy, and they persevered unanimously in prayer with Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers” (Acts 1). They are rightly said to have persevered in prayer, because perseverance is the strength of a good work. A good work is performed in vain if it is abandoned before its completion. Therefore they persevered unanimously in prayer and fasting, because the time had now come of which the Lord, when the Jews were accusing him, said: “The sons of the bridegroom cannot mourn or fast while the bridegroom is with them; but the day will come [Col. 1267D] when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast” (Matt. 9).

A bridegroom is so called from *spondere*, that is, from promising. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is rightly called, and is, the bridegroom of the Church, because on this day he sent the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and himself, whom he had promised to his disciples. The bridal chamber of Christ was the Virgin’s power; the Word of the Father became the bridegroom. The bride, moreover, was human flesh. The holy apostles are the sons of this bridegroom, because each person is called the son of the one whose teaching he follows.

Therefore the sons of the bridegroom, namely the holy apostles, who previously could not mourn or fast, when the bridegroom—that is, Christ—ascended into heaven, were kindled with his love [Col. 1268A] and longing. Persevering unanimously in prayer and fasting, they devoutly awaited the gifts of the Holy Spirit promised them by Christ. Already, for Christ’s love, they despised earthly things and desired heavenly things. Already, for Christ’s love, they scorned visible things and laboured most earnestly to become worthy of heavenly gifts. And they showed the sign of love for that same Jesus Christ, their bridegroom, not only in their hearts but also in good works.
