Concerning this sign, the same bridegroom—our Lord Jesus Christ—commanded the bride, that is, the holy Church, in the Song of Songs, saying: “Set me as a seal upon your heart, and as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8). [Note: [Col. 1267D] Gregory, on this passage.] In [Col. 1268B] the heart are thoughts, and in the arm are deeds. Then the bride, that is, the holy Church, truly places Christ as a seal upon her heart and arm when, for Christ’s love, she performs a good work in will and in action. The holy Church bears Christ as a sign inwardly and outwardly, because she labours daily in meditating upon him and does not cease to imitate him in outward action by doing good works.

Concerning this sign the bridegroom himself said to these same disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14). As if to say: This will show that you love me: if you keep my commandments. For the performance of a work is evidence of love. Thus they had already placed Christ as a sign upon heart and arm, because for Christ’s love they did not cease to think, speak, [Col. 1268C] and do things worthy of him.

It follows: “And when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, all the disciples were together in one place” (Acts 2). *Pentecost* in Greek is translated into Latin as “five times ten.” Consider more attentively, beloved brothers, what is said: “All the disciples,” he says, “were together in one place.” They were together in body, together in mind, and together in devotion; with equal charity, equal affection, and equal love they were in one place, in one position, and in one upper room, persevering in prayer. Therefore they merited to receive from Christ the Holy Spirit promised to them.

You therefore, dearest brothers, taught by the example of the holy apostles and instructed by their [Col. 1268D] teaching, as you await the coming of the Holy Spirit, be together in one place—that is, in the monastery. Yet among these things you must know that those separated from one another by hatred are not together in one place; nor are those whom discord divides from one another together in one house. Certainly, if the distances of lands do not separate those whom charity unites, neither does one house contain those whom discord divides. Nor are they together in the cloister whose minds wander outside in the world, seeking superfluous and vain things. Nor are those together in one place who stand bodily in choir but in thought are occupied in the marketplace.

Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart” [Col. 1269A] (Matt. 6). As if to say: Where your desire is, there also is your heart; where your delight is, there also is your thought; where thought is, there is the dwelling-place of the inner person. For each person is said to dwell according to the inner person where he is occupied in thought. Thus those who place their heart’s delight in the vanity of this world, though they seem to be bodily in one place, are nevertheless scattered and divided outwardly in mind. But their minds are scattered abroad amid worldly vanities because they are not bound by the chain of God’s charity. Therefore their spirits are carried outward into superfluous cares because they are not gathered inwardly into the love of their Creator. It is most unfitting for a servant of God to remain within the walls of the cloister while running in spirit through the streets of the city [Col. 1269B]. Therefore, while the body is in church, let the mind not be in the street.

Therefore, beloved, if you truly prepare in your hearts a dwelling for the Holy Spirit, let hatred not separate you from one another. If you truly desire to celebrate the coming of the Holy Spirit, drive hatred and offence from your hearts; show charity and love toward one another. Let pride not cast you down; let discord not divide you; let envy not consume you; let anger not inflame you; let hatred not make you murderers; let offence not make you enemies; let vainglory not deceive you; let boasting not lift you up; let greed not inflame you; let love of the world not trouble you. And according to the Apostle’s command: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption; but let all bitterness, wrath, indignation, [Col. 1270A] shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Eph. 4). And: “Be kind to one another, merciful, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (ibid.).

The dwelling-place of our heart is sanctified by God’s grace and by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit when charity, peace, goodness, kindness, humility, patience, concord, gentleness, and other such things are within it (Gal. 5). These are our inner riches: good morals and virtues. If, therefore, you desire the Holy Spirit to dwell in your hearts, drive away offences and quarrels, disputes and strife, for these are works of the flesh; and, as the Apostle says, “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (ibid.).

[Col. 1270B] Also, beloved, let the dwelling-place of your heart be closed to the devil and opened to the Holy Spirit; and cleanse your hearts of every unclean thought, because the Holy Spirit is kind and withdraws himself from thoughts that lack discernment and understanding (Wisdom 1). Therefore, dearest brothers, if you love Christ, keep Christ’s commandments, and he will ask the Father and give you another Paraclete, that is, Comforter (John 14), who will guard you amid the dangers and temptations of this present life, show you the straight path by which you may reach heaven, lead you—purified from vices—to behold the face of God the Father, and make you reign eternally with his elect: he who proceeds from the same Father and Son and remains in them essentially through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## THIRTY-FOURTH SERMON. ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY TRINITY

[Col. 1269]

[Col. 1269C] [Note: [Col. 1269D] *Sentences*, I, distinction 2, chapter “Hoc quoque.”] It must be known, dearest brothers, and stored more attentively in the mind, that it must be held by true and devout faith that the Trinity is the one and only true God, as blessed Augustine says in the first book of *On the Trinity*: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This Trinity is said, believed, and understood to be of one and the same substance. It is the highest good, perceived by minds that are most purified. For the gaze of the human mind cannot be fixed in so surpassing a light unless it is cleansed through the righteousness of faith.

Therefore this highest and most excellent matter must be treated with modesty and fear, and heard with attentive and devout ears, when the unity of the Trinity is investigated—namely, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—for nowhere is error more dangerous, nothing is sought with greater labour, and nothing is found more fruitfully. Accordingly, everyone who hears or reads what is said concerning the ineffable and inaccessible light of the Godhead should endeavour to imitate and observe what the venerable [Col. 1270C] teacher Augustine says of himself in the first book of *On the Trinity*: “I shall not be reluctant, wherever I hesitate, to inquire; nor ashamed, wherever I err, to learn. Therefore whoever hears or reads this, where he is equally certain, let him proceed with me; where he equally hesitates, let him inquire with me; where he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back. Thus let us enter together upon the way of charity, tending toward him of whom it is said: ‘Seek his face always’” (Ps. 104).

But all [Note: [Col. 1270D] Chapter “Omnes.”] Catholic writers, as blessed Augustine says in the same book, who have written concerning the Trinity which is God, have intended to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of one substance and, in inseparable [Col. 1270D] equality, are one God: so that there is unity in essence and plurality in persons. That is, there are not three gods, but one God; although the Father has begotten the Son and therefore the Son is not the Father, because he is the Father; although the Son has been begotten by the Father and therefore the Father is not the Son, because he is the Son; and although the Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but only the Spirit of Father and Son, coequal with both and belonging to the unity of the Trinity.

Let us therefore hold that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God, as Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*. Yet let us not hold that the Father is the same person as the Son, nor that the Son is the same person as the Father, nor that the Holy Spirit is the same person as the Father or the Son. For there is one essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, which the Greeks call *homoousion* (“of the same substance”); in it the Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

[Col. 1271B] Moreover, [Note: [Col. 1271D] Chapter “Caeterum.”] as Augustine teaches in the first book of *On the Trinity*, it must first be demonstrated from the authorities of the holy Scriptures whether the faith is thus constituted. Then against verbose reasoners, more arrogant than capable, Catholic arguments and suitable analogies must be employed in defence and affirmation of the true faith, so that by answering their inquiries we may instruct the gentle more fully, while those who cannot discover what they seek may complain of their own minds rather than of truth itself or of our exposition.

Let us [Note: [Col. 1271D] Chapter “Proponamus.”] therefore set forth the authorities of the Old and New Testaments by which the truth of the divine unity and Trinity is demonstrated. First let the very beginnings of the Law come forward, where Moses says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” [Col. 1271C] (Deut. 6). Likewise: “I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt; you shall have no other gods besides me” (Exod. 20). Behold how he signified the unity of the divine nature when he said “God” and “Lord.” For, as blessed Ambrose says in his book *On the Trinity*, the name of nature is the name of power.

Again, elsewhere God, speaking to Moses, says: “I am who I am. And if they ask my name, tell them: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3). For by saying “I am,” not “we are,” and “he who is,” not “we who are,” he declared most plainly that there is one God alone. In the Song of Exodus, moreover, we read: “God Almighty is his name” (Exod. 15). [Note: [Col. 1271D] The edition here reads “of the Lord,” and below likewise “of the Lord”; but since our author read “God,” he ought afterwards to have said “gods”; and perhaps “God” is a copyist’s error.] He did not say “God” in the accusative [*Deum*], but “God” in the nominative [*Deus*], wishing to signify unity.

He also shows simultaneously the plurality of persons and unity of nature when, in Genesis, he says: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). By saying “let us make” and “our,” he shows plurality of persons; by saying “image,” he demonstrates unity of essence. For, as Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*: “If there were only one person in that nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it would not be said: ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness.’” When he says “in [Col. 1272A] the image,” he shows the one nature of the essence in whose image man was to be made; but when he says “our,” he shows that the same God is not one person but several persons.

Now [Note: [Col. 1272D] Chapter “Nunc vero.”] let us bring forward other holy authorities to show the plurality of persons and the unity of the divine essence. Moses says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). By “God” he signifies the Father; by “beginning,” the Son. And where we say “God,” the Hebrew Truth has *Heloim*, which is the plural of the singular *Hell*. Thus, because it was not said *Hell*, meaning “God,” but *Heloim*, which can be translated “gods” or “judges,” this relates to the plurality of persons. To this also seems to belong what the devil said through the serpent: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. [Col. 1272B] 3), for which the Hebrew has *Heloim*. As if he said: “You shall be like divine persons.”

David too, that greatest of prophets and kings, who declares his understanding superior to that of others by saying, “I have understood beyond the elders” (Ps. 118), showing the unity and eternity of the divine nature, says: “The Lord is his name” (Ps. 67). He did not say “of the Lord,” but “the Lord.” Elsewhere, also showing both the same unity and eternity, he says in God’s person: “Israel, if you will hear me, there shall not be in you a recent god, nor shall you worship a foreign god” (Ps. 80). One of these expressions, as blessed Ambrose says in his book *On the Trinity*, signifies eternity; the other, the undivided unity of substance, so that we may not believe the Son or Holy Spirit to be later than the Father or of another divinity. For if the Son is later than the Father, or the Holy Spirit is recent, and if he is not of one divinity, he is foreign. But he is neither later, because he is not recent, nor foreign, because the Son is born from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Elsewhere, also intimating the distinction of persons, he says: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32). Elsewhere he says: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66). The threefold confession of God expresses the Trinity of persons; but he discloses unity of essence when he adds in the singular: “May all the ends of the earth fear him.” Isaiah also says that he heard the seraphim crying: [Col. 1272D] “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Hosts [Sabaoth]” (Isa. 6). By saying “holy” three times, he signifies the Trinity; by adding “Lord God,” he indicates unity of essence.

David likewise clearly intimates the eternal generation of the Son, speaking in the person of the Son: “The Lord said to me: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Ps. 2). Isaiah also says of this ineffable generation: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53). In the book of Wisdom, too, the Son’s eternity with the Father is shown, where Wisdom speaks thus: “The Lord possessed [Col. 1273A] me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. I was ordered from eternity, before the earth was made; the depths did not yet exist, and I had already been conceived; the springs had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet been established in their massive weight; before the hills I was brought forth. He had not yet made the earth or the regions of the world. When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he suspended the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things, and I delighted day after day, playing before him” (Prov. 8).

Behold a plain testimony concerning eternal generation, in which Wisdom itself declares that it was conceived before the world, brought forth in birth, and exists eternally with the Father. It also says elsewhere: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature” (Ecclus. 24). The prophet Micah likewise intimates at once the eternal generation of the Word and his temporal birth from Mary, saying: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are small among the thousands of Judah. From you shall come forth one who shall be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5).

We also have explicit testimonies concerning the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1273D] Chapter “De Spiritu.”] [Col. 1273B] in the Old Testament. For in Genesis we read: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). David says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 38). Likewise, in the book of Wisdom we read: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw himself from thoughts devoid of understanding. For the Spirit of wisdom is kind” (Wisdom 1). Isaiah too says: “The Spirit [Col. 1273C] of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61).

Now [Note: [Col. 1273D] Chapter “Nunc vero.”] after the testimonies of the Old Testament concerning faith in the Trinity and unity, let us proceed to the authorities of the New Testament, so that truth may be known “in the midst of two living creatures,” and a coal may be taken with tongs from the altar to touch the mouths of the faithful. Thus the Lord clearly intimates unity of divine essence and Trinity of persons when he says to the apostles: “Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). He said “in the name,” as blessed Ambrose says in the first book of *On the Trinity*, not “in the names,” in order to show unity of essence. Through the three names which he added, he declared that there are three persons.

He himself also says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). He said “one,” as Ambrose says in the same book, lest a distinction of power or nature be made. He also added “are,” so that you may know Father and Son: namely, so that it may be believed that the perfect Father begot a perfect Son, and that Father and Son are one not by confusion but by unity of nature. Blessed John likewise says in the Catholic Epistle: “There are three who bear testimony in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one” (1 John 5). He also says at the beginning of his Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1). Here he plainly shows that the Son always and eternally [Col. 1274A] existed with the Father, one with another.

The Apostle also plainly shows the Trinity, saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4). And elsewhere: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwells in you” (Rom. 8), etc. Again, elsewhere he most clearly commends eternity and unity, saying: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ages of ages. Amen” (Rom. 11). “From him,” Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, is said with reference to the Father; “through him,” with reference to the Son; “in him,” with reference to the Holy Spirit. But by not saying “from them, through them, and in them,” nor “to them be glory,” but “to him,” he intimated that this Trinity is one God.

But because nearly every individual writing of the New Testament harmoniously intimates this truth of the ineffable Trinity and unity, let us refrain from producing further testimonies on this matter and show, as far as our weakness permits, through arguments and fitting analogies that it is so.

[Note: [Col. 1273D] Distinction 3.] For the Apostle says: “The invisible things of God are discerned and beheld through those things which have been made, from the creation of the world; likewise his eternal power and divinity” (Rom. 1): they are understood through the creation of the world. Therefore, because of the excellence by which humanity surpasses other creatures, or because of its affinity with every creature, a human being could, or even did, behold the invisible things of God with the understanding of the mind through things that have been made—that is, through visible or invisible creatures. For he was aided by two things: by his nature, through which he was rational; and by works made by God, so that truth might be made manifest to him. Therefore the Apostle says: “Because God revealed it to them” (1 Cor. 2), namely, when he made works in which some indication of the maker shines forth.

For, [Note: [Col. 1274D] Chapter “Nam.”] as blessed Ambrose says, so that God, invisible by nature, might be known from visible things, he made a work which, through its own visibility, made its maker manifest; so that the uncertain might be known through the certain, and that he might be believed to be God of all things who made what would be impossible for a human being to make. They therefore could know, or did know, that he who made those things which no creature can make or destroy is above every creature. Let whatever power of creaturely nature come forward and make such a heaven and such an earth, and I shall say that it is God. But because no creature can make such things, it is evident that he who made them is above every creature; and through this the human mind could know that he is God.

In another [Note: [Col. 1274D] Chapter “Alio.”] way [Col. 1274D] also, they could, or even did, know the truth of God by the guidance of reason. For, as Augustine says in *The City of God*, the greatest philosophers saw that no body is God, and therefore transcended all bodies in seeking God. They also saw that whatever is mutable is not the supreme God and the principle of all things; [Col. 1275A] and therefore they transcended every soul and mutable form. Then they saw that everything mutable can exist only from him who exists immutably and simply. Thus they understood both that he had made all these things and that he could have been made by no one.

They also considered [Note: [Col. 1275D] Chapter “Consideraverunt.”] that whatever exists among substances is either body or spirit, and that some spirit is better than body, but far better is he who makes both spirit and body. They understood also that bodily form is sensible and spiritual form intelligible, and they preferred intelligible form to sensible form. By sensible things we mean those which can be perceived by sight and touch of the body; by intelligible things, those which can be understood by the vision of the mind. Since, therefore, in their sight both body and mind were more or less beautiful, and would be nothing at all if they could lack every form, [Col. 1275B] they saw that there is something by which those things were made beautiful, in which is the first and immutable form, and therefore an incomparable one. They most rightly believed this to be the principle of things: that which was not made, and from which all things were made.

Behold, by so many ways the truth of God can be, or could be, known. Therefore, since God is one and simple essence, composed of no diversity of parts or accidents, the Apostle nevertheless speaks in the plural, “the invisible things of God,” because the truth of God is known in several ways through the things that have been made (Rom. 1). For from the enduring continuance of creatures the eternal Creator is understood; from the magnitude of creatures, the omnipotent Father; from their order and arrangement, the wise one; and from their governance, the good one.

But all these things pertain to demonstrating the eternity of the Godhead. It remains [Note: [Col. 1275D] Chapter “Nunc restat.”] now to show whether, through things that have been made, any indication, however slight, of the Trinity could be had. On this Augustine says in book VI of *On the Trinity*: “We must understand the Trinity by beholding the Creator intellectually through the things which have been made.” A trace of this Trinity appears in creatures. For the things made by divine art show in themselves a certain unity, form, and order. Whatever among created things is some one thing—as are the natures of bodies and souls—is also formed by some form—as are the figures or qualities of bodies, [Col. 1275D] and the doctrines or arts of souls—and seeks or maintains some order—as do the weights or relations of bodies, and the loves or delights of souls. Thus in creatures a trace of the Trinity shines forth.

For in that Trinity are the highest origin of all things, most perfect beauty, and most blessed delight. The highest origin, as Augustine shows in *On True Religion*, is understood as God the Father, from whom are all things, from whom are the Son and the Holy Spirit. The most perfect beauty is understood as the Son, namely the Truth of the Father, in no respect unlike him; him we venerate with the Father and in the Father. He is the form of all things which are made from one [Col. 1276A] and referred to one. Yet all these things would neither be made by the Father through the Son nor remain preserved within their own bounds unless God were supremely good: he neither begrudged to any nature what it received from that Good, nor failed to give, in order that it might remain in that Good itself, to some as much as he willed and to others as much as they could receive. This goodness is understood as the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of the Father and Son. It is fitting that we worship and hold this gift of God, equally immutable with the Father and Son.

Therefore, by consideration of creatures, we understand the Trinity of one substance: namely, one God—the Father from whom we are; the Son through whom we are; and the Holy Spirit in whom we are. That is, the source to which we return, the form which we follow, and the grace [Col. 1276B] by which we are reconciled: the one by whose authorship we were created; his likeness, through whom we are restored to unity; and the peace by which we cling to unity. Namely, God who said, “Let it be” (Gen. 1); the Word through whom everything was made which exists substantially and naturally; and the gift, namely his goodness, by which it pleased him that what was made through the Word should be reconciled to its Maker and not perish.

Behold, under the instruction of blessed Augustine, it has been shown in what manner an image of the Trinity is in some measure indicated in creatures. Yet sufficient knowledge of the Trinity cannot be obtained, nor could it have been obtained, through contemplation of creatures without a teacher or revelation by inward inspiration. Hence those ancient philosophers saw truth as though through [Col. 1276C] a shadow and from afar, failing in the direct contemplation of the most holy truth of the Trinity, like Pharaoh’s magicians at the third sign. Yet through the things that have been made we are assisted in faith concerning invisible things.

Now let us proceed [Note: [Col. 1276D] C. “Now let us proceed.”] to the discussion in which we are to find the image of the Trinity in the human mind, which knows God, or is able to know him. For, as blessed Augustine says in Book XIV of *On the Trinity*, although the human mind is not of the same nature as God, nevertheless the image of him—than whom nothing is better—must be sought and found in that in which our nature has nothing better, namely, in the mind. For in the mind itself, even before it becomes a participant in God, his image is found. For although it is made deformed by the loss of participation in God, the image of God nevertheless remains. [Col. 1276D] For the mind is the image of God precisely in that it is capable of him and can participate in him. Let us therefore seek in it the Trinity which is God.

Behold, then: the mind remembers itself, understands itself, and loves itself. If we discern these things, we discern a Trinity—not God, but the image of God. For here there appears a certain trinity: that of memory, understanding, and love. These three, therefore, as blessed Augustine says in Book X of *On the Trinity*, are not three lives but one life; not three minds but one mind, one essence. Memory, however, is spoken of in relation to something; and understanding and will, or love, are likewise spoken of in relation to something. But life is spoken of in relation to itself, as are [Col. 1277A] mind and essence. Therefore these three are one inasmuch as they are one life, one mind, one essence; and whatever else each of them is called in relation to itself is also called of them together, not in the plural but in the singular. Yet they are three inasmuch as they are referred to one another.

They are equal [Note: [Col. 1277D] C. “Equal.”] also, not merely each to each, but each to all; otherwise they would not contain one another. But they do contain one another. For each contains each of the others, and each contains all. For I remember that I have memory, understanding, and will; and I understand that I understand, will, and remember; and I will that I will, remember, and understand; and I remember all my memory, understanding, and will together. For whatever of my memory I do not remember is not in my memory. [Col. 1277B] But nothing is so much in memory as memory itself. Therefore I remember it wholly. Likewise, whatever I understand, I know that I understand; and I know that I will whatever I will. But whatever I know, I remember. Therefore I remember my whole understanding and my whole will. Similarly, when I understand these three, I understand them all together.

For there is nothing to be understood that I do not understand, except what I do not know; and what I do not know, I neither remember nor will. Therefore, whatever intelligible things I do not understand, I consequently neither remember nor will. Whatever intelligible things, therefore, I remember and will, I consequently understand. My will also comprehends my whole understanding and my whole memory, while I make use of all that I understand and remember. Since, therefore, each contains each other whole and each contains all of them whole, they are equal: each whole to each whole, and each whole together to all the wholes. And these three are one: one life, one mind, one essence. Behold, the human mind, though unequal to it, is an image of that supreme unity and Trinity, in which there is one essence and three persons.

Here “mind” is taken for the soul itself, in which the image of the Trinity exists. More properly, however, “mind,” as blessed Augustine says, is not the soul itself but what is more excellent within it. It must also be known that memory is not only of absent and past things, but also of present things, as blessed Augustine says in Book XIV of *On the Trinity*; otherwise it would not comprehend itself.

[Col. 1277D] Here it must be carefully noted [Note: [Col. 1277D] C. “Here it must be noted.”] in what sense we are to understand the statement above that those three—memory, understanding, and will—are one, one mind, one essence. This plainly does not seem true according to the strict sense of the terms. For mind—that is, rational spirit—is a spiritual and incorporeal essence; but those three are natural properties or powers of the mind itself, and differ from one another, because memory is not understanding, nor is it will or love. These three are also referred to themselves, as blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity*. For the mind cannot love itself or remember itself [Col. 1278A] unless it also knows itself. For how does it love or remember what it does not know? Thus, in a wonderful manner, these three are inseparable from one another; and yet each of them and all together are one essence, although they are also spoken of relatively to one another.

But we must now see [Note: [Col. 1277D] C. “But now.”] how these three are said to be one substance. Namely, because they exist substantially in the soul or mind itself, not as accidents which can be present and absent. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity*: “We are admonished, if anywhere we are unable to see it, that these exist substantially in the mind, not as in a subject, as colour in a body; for although they are spoken of relatively to one another, each nevertheless exists substantially in its own substance.” Behold in what sense those three are said [Col. 1278B] to be one, or one substance. Whoever, as blessed Augustine says in Book XI of *On the Trinity*, keenly considers these three, naturally and divinely established in the mind, and considers how great it is that in it the eternal and mutable nature can also be remembered, perceived, and desired—such a person remembers through memory, beholds through understanding, and embraces through love; and assuredly finds in it an image of that supreme Trinity.

Nevertheless, let him beware [Note: [Col. 1278D] C. “Nevertheless.”] of so comparing this image, made by the same Trinity, with that Trinity as to think it altogether similar; rather, in whatever similarity there may be, let him also perceive a great dissimilarity. This may be shown briefly. One human being, indeed, remembers, understands, and loves through those three, while he [Col. 1278C] is neither memory, nor understanding, nor love, but has these three. Therefore one human being has these three, yet is not himself these three. But in the simplicity of that supreme nature which is God, although there is one God, there are nevertheless three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and these three are one God. Thus the Trinity itself is one thing, and the image of the Trinity in another thing is another. On account of this image, both that in which these three occur and the image itself are called an image: namely, a human being as the image of God, and a tablet and the painting upon it; yet the tablet is called an image because of the painting upon it.

Again, this image [Note: [Col. 1278D] C. “Again.”] which is the human being possessing those three, is one person; but that Trinity is not one [Col. 1278D] person, but three persons: the Father of the Son, the Son of the Father, and the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Thus in this image of the Trinity, these three are not one human being, but belong to one human being. But in that supreme Trinity, of which this is an image, those three do not belong to one God, but are one God; and they are three persons, not one person. For those three are not a human being, but belong to a human being, or are in a human being. But can we say that the Trinity is in God in such a way that it is something belonging to God and is not itself God? Far be it from us to believe this.

Therefore let us say that there is in our mind an image of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 1278D] “Images of the Trinity.”], but a slight and whatever-kind-of image, which bears such a likeness to the supreme Trinity [Col. 1279A] that for the greater part it is unlike it. It must indeed be known that this trinity of the mind, as blessed Augustine says in Book XIV of *On the Trinity*, is not the image of God merely because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, but because it can also remember, understand, and love him by whom it was made.

[Note: [Col. 1279D] C. “It can.”] The Trinity in the soul, which is the image of that supreme and ineffable Trinity, can also be distinguished in another manner and by other names. For, as Augustine says in Book XI of *On the Trinity*, mind, knowledge, and love are three things. For the mind knows and loves itself, nor can it love itself unless it also knows itself. The mind and its knowledge are two things. Likewise, [Col. 1279B] the mind and its love are two things. When the mind knows and loves itself, there remains a trinity: mind, love, and knowledge. Here “mind” is not taken for the soul, but for that which is more excellent in the soul; and although these three are distinct from one another, they are nevertheless said to be one because they exist substantially in the soul.

And the mind itself [Note: [Col. 1279D] C. “And it is.”] is, as it were, a parent, and its knowledge is, as it were, its offspring. For when the mind knows itself, it begets knowledge, and it alone is the parent of its knowledge. The third here is love, which proceeds from the mind itself and its knowledge, while the mind, knowing itself, loves itself. For it could not love itself unless it knew itself. It also loves its pleasing offspring, that is, knowledge; [Col. 1279C] and thus love is indeed the embrace of parent and offspring. Nor is the offspring less than the parent, since the mind knows itself as fully as it is. Nor is love less than parent and offspring—that is, than mind and knowledge—since the mind loves itself as much as it knows itself and as much as it is.

These individual things [Note: [Col. 1279D] C. “They are.”] are also in themselves: for the mind that loves is in love, love is in the knowledge of the one loving, and knowledge is in the mind that knows. Behold, in these three there appears some trace of the Trinity.

The rational mind [Note: [Col. 1279D] C. “Mind.”], therefore, considering these three and the one essence in which they exist, extends itself to contemplation of the Creator and sees unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity. For it understands [Col. 1279D] that God is one, essence one, principle one. It also understands that, if there were two, either both would be insufficient or one would be superfluous. For if one lacked something which the other possessed, supreme perfection would not be there; but if one lacked nothing possessed by the other, since all things were in one, the other would be superfluous. Therefore the mind understood that God is one, the one author of all things; and it saw that he is not without wisdom, as though he were a foolish thing. It therefore understood that he has wisdom, begotten from himself; and [Col. 1280A] because he loves his wisdom, it understood that love also exists there.

Accordingly, on the basis of this consideration [Note: [Col. 1280D] C. “Accordingly.”], as blessed Augustine says in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, let us believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, creator and ruler of the whole creation; and that the Father is not the Son, nor is the Holy Spirit either the Father or the Son, but that the persons of the Trinity are mutually distinct. For, as blessed Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*, the nature or essence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, but the person is not one. For if the person were one in the same way as the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, it would not truly be called a Trinity. Again, the Trinity itself would not be one God if, just as [Col. 1280B] Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinguished from one another by the property of their persons, so they were also separated by diversity of natures.

But the faith of the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles proclaims that the Trinity is one God. Therefore in that holy Trinity there is one God the Father, who alone essentially begot from himself one Son; one Son, who alone was essentially born from the one Father; and one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son. But all this cannot belong to one person—that is, to beget itself, be born from itself, and proceed from itself. For, as blessed Augustine says in Book I of *On the Trinity*, there is no thing which begets itself in order to exist.

[Col. 1280C] Here [Note: [Col. 1280D] Distinction 4.] a necessary question arises. It is certain, indeed, and incontrovertibly true, that God the Father begot the Son. Therefore it is asked whether one ought to concede that God begot God. For if God begot God, it seems that he begot either himself as God or another God. But if he begot another, there is not only one God; while if he begot himself as God, some thing begot itself.

—Solution of this question.—In reply we say that it is sound and catholic to concede that one begot one, because God the Father begot God the Son. It is also written in the Creed: “Light from Light, true God from true God.” But when it is added, “therefore he begot himself as God, or another God,” we say that neither alternative should be conceded. That he did not beget another God is clear, because there is only one [Col. 1280D] God. That he did not beget himself is shown by blessed Augustine in Book I of *On the Trinity*, who says: “Those who think God to be of such power that he himself begot himself err the more because they think this. For neither bodily nor spiritual nature can beget itself. There is no thing that begets itself in order to exist.” Therefore it must neither be believed nor said that God begot himself.

[Note: [Col. 1280D] Distinction 5.] After this it is asked whether one ought to concede that God the Father begot the divine essence, or that the essence begot the Son, or that [Col. 1281A] essence begot essence; or whether the divine essence neither begot nor was begotten at all. Agreeing with catholic writers, we say that neither the Father begot the divine essence, nor did the divine essence beget essence. Here, however, by “essence” we understand the divine nature, which is common to the three persons and whole in each. Therefore it must not be said that the Father begot the divine essence; for if the Father were said to have begotten the divine essence, then the divine essence would be spoken of relatively to the Father, or would be used as a relative term. But if it were spoken of relatively or used as a relative, it would not signify essence. For, as Augustine says in Book V of *On the Trinity*, what is said relatively does not indicate substance.

Likewise, since [Col. 1281B] God the Father is the divine essence, if he were its begetter, he would certainly be begetter of that thing which he himself is; and thus the same thing would have begotten itself, which Augustine denies, as we have shown above. God the Father [Note: [Col. 1281D] The Master lacks this passage here, and it is strangely also corrupted by Martin; please consult Augustine in that book, chapter 3.] is wisdom, as blessed Augustine says in Book VII of *On the Trinity*; and the Son is called the wisdom of the Father, just as he is called the light of the Father. And just as “light from light” and each—namely, Father and Son—is one light, so “wisdom from wisdom” is to be understood, and each is one wisdom and one essence.

[Note: [Col. 1281D] C. “Likewise.”] Augustine likewise proves in Book VII of *On the Trinity* that the Father is not wise by the wisdom which he begot; because if he is wise by it, he is it. For in God, to be is to be wise. “But if [Col. 1281C] for you to be is to be wise, the Father is not wise through that wisdom which he begot. For what else do we say when we say, ‘For him to be is to be wise,’ except, ‘He is by that by which he is wise’? Therefore, whatever is the cause for him to be wise is also the cause for him to be. If, then, the wisdom which he begot is the cause for him to be wise, it is also the cause for him to be. What could be more absurd?” Thus, if the Father had begotten the essence by which he is, the essence which he begot would be the cause of his existence. Therefore he did not beget the essence which he is. For in that simplicity, says blessed Augustine, because there is no difference between being wise and being, the wisdom there is the same as the essence. Therefore what we say concerning wisdom we also say concerning essence. Thus, just as God the Father did not beget the wisdom by which he is wise, neither [Col. 1281D] did he beget the essence which he is. For just as he is wise by wisdom and powerful by power, so he is essence; and wisdom and power are the same as essence. It is therefore clear from what has been said that the Father did not beget the divine essence.

It is also said [Note: [Col. 1281D] “It is said.”] and frequently read in Sacred Scripture that the Father [Note: [Col. 1282D] “The Father.”] begot the Son from his own substance. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On Faith to Peter*: “God the Father, begotten by no one, once begot from his own nature, without beginning, the Son who is God, [Col. 1282A] equal to himself and coeternal in the same divinity by which he himself is naturally eternal.” Behold, this eminent teacher Augustine says here that the Son was begotten from the Father’s nature, and that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one nature. Therefore, if the Son was begotten from the Father’s nature, the Holy Spirit proceeds [Note: [Col. 1282D] Better in the edition: “begotten from the nature of the Son and the Holy Spirit.”] from the nature of the Son and the Holy Spirit—indeed, from the nature of the three persons.

The same blessed Augustine also says in Book XV of *On the Trinity* that Christ is the Son of the Father’s substance and begotten from the Father’s substance, in treating the Apostle’s words concerning God the Father: “Who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1). “By ‘the Son of his love,’” he says, “we should understand nothing other than his beloved Son, that is, the Son of his substance. [Col. 1282B] For the Father’s love, because his nature is ineffably simple, is nothing other than his nature itself, as we have often said before and do not tire of repeating. Thus the Son of his love is none other than he who was begotten from his substance.” Behold, blessed Augustine says openly here that the Son was begotten from the Father’s substance and is the Son of the Father’s substance.

For this reason, the same blessed Augustine in Book V *Against Maximinus the Heretic* maintains that the substance of God begot the Son and that the Son was begotten from the Father’s substance, saying: “Filled with carnal thoughts, you do not think that the substance of God begets the Son from itself unless it undergoes what the substance of flesh undergoes when it begets. You err, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matt. [Col. 1282C] 22). “For you in no way conceive the true Son of God if you deny that he was born from the substance of the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 1282D] Distinction 8.] We must now discuss the truth, or propriety, immutability, and simplicity of the divine nature, whether it be called substance or essence. Therefore God is, as wise Augustine says in Book V of *On the Trinity*, without doubt substance—or, if that name is better, essence, which the Greeks call *ousia* (*οὐσία*). For just as wisdom is named from being wise, and knowledge from knowing, so essence is named from being. And who more truly is than he who said to his servant Moses: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3)? And again: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent [Col. 1282D] me to you’” (ibid.). He alone is truly and properly called essence, whose essence knows neither past nor future.

Hence blessed Jerome, writing to Marcella [Note: [Col. 1282D] “Damasus.”], says: “God alone, who has no beginning, truly possesses the name of essence; because in comparison with him who truly is and is immutable, mutable things are as though they were not. For that of which it is said, ‘was,’ is not; and that of which it is said, ‘will be,’ is not yet. But God alone is, who knows neither having been nor being future.” Therefore God alone truly is, [Col. 1283A] compared with whose essence our being is not.

Here we must carefully observe how the words of Saint Jerome are to be understood—namely, “God alone is and knows not having been”—as though one could not say of God “was” or “will be,” but only “is,” when we frequently find it written of God: “He was from eternity,” “He was always,” “and he will be for ages,” and the like. Hence it seems that one must not say of God only “was,” or “is,” or “will be.” For if only “was” were said, it might be thought that being had failed him; if only “is” were said, it might be thought that he had not always been but had begun to be; if only “will be” were said, it might be thought that he does not exist now. Let it therefore be said that he always was, is, and will be, so that it may be understood that he neither began, nor ceased, nor ceases, nor will cease to be.

Saint Augustine says concerning this in his commentary on John: “Although, strictly speaking, ‘is’ is said of an eternal thing, in relation to us ‘was,’ ‘is,’ and ‘will be’ are rightly said: ‘was,’ because he never ceased; ‘will be,’ because he will never fail; ‘is,’ because he always is. He has not passed away, as something that does not remain; nor will he arise, as something that was not. Therefore, although our speech changes through times, verbs of every time are truly said of him who has not ceased, does not fail, and will not fail at any time.” Therefore it is not surprising if Truth, speaking of the Spirit of truth, used the future tense: “Whatever he hears, he will speak” (John 16). That is, he will hear from him from whom he proceeds. His hearing is the same as his knowing, and also as his being from him from whom he is. Therefore, from whom he has essence, from him he also has hearing—that is, knowledge—which is nothing other than essence. Therefore he said “will hear” [Col. 1283C] in respect of what he heard and hears; that is, what he always knew, always knows, and will know. Behold, blessed Augustine says here that words of every tense are said of God, although “is” is proper.

Therefore what blessed Jerome says must be understood thus: “He knows not having been or being future, but only is”; that is, when God is said to have been or to be future, it must not be understood that he has passed away or will come to be, but that he exists simply, without any temporal motion. For although substantive verbs of different tenses are said of God—such as “was,” “will be,” “is,” and “was”—they do not then distinguish temporal movements, namely past or future, imperfect past, perfect past, or pluperfect past; rather, they also signify the existence of the Godhead simply. Therefore God alone is properly called essence, or being. Hence Saint Hilary says in Book VII of *On the Trinity*: “Being is not an accident to God, but subsisting Truth, abiding cause, and a property of his natural kind.”

The essence of God alone [Note: [Col. 1283D] C. “Of God.”] is also properly called immutable, for it neither changes nor can change. Hence wise Augustine says in Book V of *On the Trinity*: “Other essences or substances admit accidents, by which a great or any change is present in them. [Col. 1284A] But nothing of this sort can happen to God; and therefore the only immutable substance or essence is that which is God, to which being belongs most especially and most truly. For what changes does not preserve the same being; and what can change, even if it does not change, can cease to be what it was. Therefore only that which not only does not change, but absolutely cannot change, is most truly said to be: namely, the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

For this reason the Apostle, speaking of God, says: “Who alone has immortality” (1 Tim. 6). For, as blessed Augustine says in Book I of *On the Trinity*: “Although the soul is in a certain sense called—and is—immortal, it would not be said, ‘He alone has immortality,’ unless true immortality were immutability, which no creature can possess, because it belongs to the Creator alone.” Hence the Apostle James says: “With whom there is no change” (James 1). David likewise says: “You shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same” (Ps. 101).

For this reason Augustine says in his commentary on Genesis that God is moved neither through places nor through times, whereas the creature is moved through times and places. To be moved through times is to be changed through affections; but God can be changed neither in place nor in affection, he who says through the prophet: “I am God and I do not change” (Mal. 3). Hence he alone is rightly said to possess immortality. For in every mutable nature, as Saint Augustine says against Maximinus, bishop of the heretics, change itself is a kind of death, because it makes something in it cease to be what it was.

Thus even the human soul, which is called [Col. 1284C] immortal because in its own manner it never ceases to live, nevertheless has a kind of death of its own. For if it lived righteously and sins, it dies to righteousness; if it was sinful and is justified, it dies to sin—not to mention its other changes, of which it would take too long to speak now. Even the nature of heavenly creatures could die, because it could sin. For angels sinned and became demons, whose prince is the devil; and those who did not sin could have sinned. That any rational creature is granted not to be able to sin belongs not to its own nature but to God’s grace. Therefore God alone, as the Apostle says, has immortality (1 Tim. 6), because not by anyone’s grace but by his own nature he neither could nor can be changed in any way [Note: [Col. 1284D] “Conversion.”]—that is, he neither could nor will be able to sin through any change.

Accordingly, as Doctor Augustine says in Book I of *On the Trinity*, we ought to contemplate and know the substance of God, which makes mutable things without any change in itself and creates temporal things without any temporal motion in itself, although this is difficult. Therefore the essence of the Godhead alone is truly and properly immutable, since without changing itself it created all natures.

And it alone [Note: [Col. 1284D] C. “And the same.”] is properly and truly simple, where there is no diversity, variation, or multiplicity at all of parts, accidents, or forms of any kind. But in order that you may know how that substance is simple, attend first, as blessed Augustine teaches in Book VI of *On the Trinity*, to why every creature is composite and in no way truly simple; first concerning bodily, then concerning spiritual creatures. Bodily creation is certainly composed of parts, such that one part is smaller and another greater, and the whole is greater than any part. In every body, moreover, magnitude is one thing, colour another, and shape another. For the same colour and shape can remain while magnitude changes; the same shape and magnitude can remain when the colour changes. Thus the nature of a body is proved composite, and in no way simple.

Spiritual creation [Note: [Col. 1285D] C. “Spiritual creation.”] too, such as the soul, is simple in comparison with the body; but without comparison with [Col. 1285B] the body it is composite and not simple. It is called simple in relation to the body because it is not extended by bulk through spatial location; rather, in every body it is wholly present in the whole and wholly present in every part of it. Thus, when something occurs in even the smallest part of a body which the soul perceives, although it does not occur in the whole body, the whole soul nevertheless perceives it, because nothing escapes the whole soul.

Yet even in the soul itself there is no true simplicity. For since one can find in the nature of the soul being skilful, being dull, being keen, being retentive, desire, fear, joy, sorrow, and innumerable other such things, and since some can occur without others and some in greater or lesser degree, it is clear that its nature is composite, not simple. For nothing simple is mutable; but every creature is mutable. Therefore no creature is truly simple.

God, however, although described in many ways, is truly and supremely simple. For he is called great, good, wise, blessed, true, and whatever else may fittingly be said; but his greatness is the same as his wisdom. For he is great not by bodily bulk but by power; and his goodness is the same as his wisdom, greatness, and truth. Nor is blessedness one thing in him and being great, wise, true, good, or simply being another.

That in the nature of the Godhead [Note: [Col. 1285D] C. “But that.”] there is no diversity of accidents and absolutely no mutability, but perfect simplicity, blessed Augustine shows in Book V of *On the Trinity*, saying: “Let us understand God, so far as we can, as good without quality, great without quantity, Creator without need, presiding without position, containing all things without habit, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet wholly discover what he is, nevertheless devoutly takes care, so far as possible, not to think anything of him that he is not.” Behold, if you attend carefully, these words and those previously stated show that the categories [Col. 1286A] of dialectical art do not at all apply to God’s nature, which is subject to no accidents.

Hence [Note: [Col. 1285D] C. “Hence.”] he is not properly called substance, as blessed Augustine shows in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, saying: “Just as essence is named from being, so we call substance from subsisting—if it is fitting that God be said to subsist. For this is rightly understood of those things in which are subjects the things said to be in a subject, such as colour or shape in a body. For a body subsists and is therefore a substance.” Thus mutable and non-simple things are properly called substances. For it is impious to say that God subsists and underlies his goodness, and that goodness is not substance—or rather essence—and that God himself is not his goodness, but goodness is in him as in a subject. Hence it is clear that God is called substance improperly, so that by this more familiar name essence may be understood, which is truly and properly said, so that perhaps God alone ought to be called essence. For he alone truly is, because he is immutable.

The simplicity and purity of this essence [Note: [Col. 1286D] C. “Of this.”] are such that nothing is in it which is not itself; rather, that which has and that which is had are the same. Hence Saint Hilary says in Book VII of *On the Trinity*: “God, who is life, does not subsist from compounded things; he who is power is not held together from weak things; he who is light is not joined together from dark things; he who is spirit is not formed from unlike things: all that is in him is one.” The same writer says in Book VIII of *On the Trinity*: “God is not composed after the human fashion, so that one thing in him is what he has and another he who has it; rather, all is life—namely, perfect and infinite nature—and he is not constituted from unlike things, but is life itself throughout.”

Augustine likewise says in *On Faith to Peter*: “In God’s substance there is nothing which is not substance, as though substance were one thing there and something occurring to substance another; rather, whatever can be understood there is substance.” These things may indeed be easily said and believed, but cannot at all be seen except by a pure heart. The same writer says in Book XV of *On the Trinity*: “It is so possessed in the nature of each of the three persons that he who possesses is that which he possesses, as in the [Col. 1286D] immutable and simple substance.” Hence Isidore, the teacher of Spain, says: “God is called simple, both because he does not lose what he has and because he himself is not one thing while that which is in him is another.”

And although the divine nature is of such simplicity and holiness, there is nevertheless a Trinity of persons in it. Hence Augustine says in *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 1286D] Book XI of *The City of God*, chapter 10.]: “We do not call the nature of the supreme good simple because the Father alone is in it, or the Son alone is in it, or the Holy Spirit alone is in it; nor because this Trinity is merely a trinity of names, or a single substance of persons, as the Sabellians thought. Rather, it is called simple because it is what it has, except where a person is also said relatively to another and is not that other. For certainly the Father has the Son, to whom he is referred relatively, yet is not the Son; and the Son has the Father, yet is not the Father. But where he is said in relation to himself to be living by having life, that same life is himself.”

For this reason, then, this nature is called simple: because that which has is not one thing and that which it has another, as is the case in other things. For that which has liquid is not liquid; a body is not colour; and a soul is not wisdom. Behold how great the identity of the divine substance is, set forth according to the capacity of our weakness.

[Note: [Col. 1287D] Distinction 9.] Let us now approach the distinction of the persons. Therefore let us hold, as wise Augustine teaches [Col. 1287B] in *On Faith to Peter*, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are naturally one God; yet the Father is not the one who is the Son, nor is the Son the one who is the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit the one who is the Father or Son. For the essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, in which Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not different things, although personally the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

For the Son was begotten [Note: [Col. 1287D] C. “Begotten.”] by the Father and therefore is another; yet the Father did not exist before the Son. For the three persons are coeternal with one another. But [Note: [Col. 1287D] C. “But.”] the heretic says against this, as Saint Ambrose reports in Book I of *On the Trinity* [Note: [Col. 1287D] The Master often cites Saint Ambrose’s books *On Faith to Gratian* under the title *On the Trinity*; but here he cites them under their proper title, *On Faith*. The manuscript examined by B. Martin perhaps had *On the Trinity*.]: “Everything [Col. 1287C] that is born has a beginning; therefore, because the Son is Son, he has a beginning and began to be.” Thus it was said through the mouths of heretics. For Arius himself, as Augustine recalls in Book VI of *On the Trinity*, is reported to have said: “If he is Son, he was born; if he was born, there was a time when the Son was not.” Whoever says this does not understand that, in God, being born is being eternal, so that the Son is coeternal with the Father, just as the radiance generated and emitted from fire is coeval with it; and it would be coeternal if the fire were eternal.

[Note: [Col. 1288D] C. Likewise.] Saint Augustine’s reply against the heretics: “If,” he says, “the Son of God is the power and wisdom of God, God was never without power and wisdom; therefore the Son is coeternal with God the Father.” The Apostle says that Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God [Col. 1287D] (1 Cor. 1). Therefore either the Father did not exist when the Son did, or at some time God did not possess power and wisdom—which is madness to say. It is therefore established that He always possessed wisdom; consequently, He always possessed the Son. Ambrose likewise answered this Arian question as follows: “I confess that the Son was born of God the Father. For it is written thus in the Old Testament: ‘Before me no other God was formed, nor shall there be after me’” (Isa. [Col. 1288A] 43). Who says this—the Father or the Son? If the Son: “Before me,” he says, “there was no other God.” If the Father: “After me,” he says, “there shall not be.” This one—that is, the Son—has no predecessor; that one—that is, the Father—has no successor. For the Father is known reciprocally in the Son, and the Son in the Father. When you have named the Father, you have indicated His Son, since no one is his own father. When you name the Son, you also confess the Father, since no one is his own son. Thus neither can the Son exist without the Father, nor the Father without the Son. Therefore the Father always was, and the Son always was.”

But perhaps you ask me, [Note: [Col. 1288D] C. But you ask.] O heretic, Ambrose says, how, if the Son exists, He does not have the Father as one prior to Him. I in turn ask you: how do you suppose that the Son was begotten? For it is impossible for me to know the secret of that generation. [Col. 1288B] Mind fails; speech is silent—not mine alone, but even that of angels. It is above the powers and above the angels, above the cherubim and above the seraphim, and above every understanding, because it is written: “The peace of God surpasses every understanding” (Phil. 4). And if the peace of God is above every understanding, so great a generation exceeds every understanding. Therefore put your hand over your mouth, for it is not permitted to search out the heavenly mysteries. It is permitted to know that He was born, but it is not permitted to investigate how He was born. I may not deny the former, and it is fearful to inquire into the latter. For that generation is ineffable. Hence Isaiah says: “Who shall declare His generation?” (Isa. 53).

Here one may ask [Note: [Col. 1288D] C. Here one may ask.], since the generation of the Son from the Father [Col. 1288C] has neither beginning nor end, because it is eternal, whether one ought to say: “The Son is always being begotten,” or “He has always been begotten,” or “He will always be begotten.” On this point Pope Gregory says in his commentary on Job: “The Lord Jesus, in that He is the power and wisdom of God, was born of the Father before time; or rather, since He neither began to be born nor ceased, let us say more truly that He is always born. Yet we cannot say, ‘He is always being born,’ lest He seem imperfect. But, in order that He may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both ‘always’ and ‘born’: so that ‘born’ may pertain to perfection, and ‘always’ to eternity. Although, by the very fact that we call Him perfect, we depart far from an adequate expression of that truth, because what has not been made cannot properly be called perfect. Let us therefore say that the Son was born of the Father before time and is always born from the Father; but more fittingly, that He has always been born. And we confess that He is from eternity and coeternal with the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 1288D] Distinction 10.] Now, after the eternity of the Son, let us, insofar as God grants us, discuss the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is the love, or affection, of the Father and the Son. Hence blessed Augustine says in the fifth [Note: [Col. 1288D] Fifteenth.] book *On the Trinity*: “The Holy Spirit belongs neither to the Father alone nor to the Son alone, but to both; and therefore [Col. 1289A] He signifies to us the mutual charity by which the Father and Son love one another.” John, however, says in the Catholic Epistle: “God is charity” (1 John 4). He did not say, “The Holy Spirit is charity.” Had he said this, the wording would have been more explicit and no small part of the question would have been settled. But because he said, “God is charity,” it is uncertain and therefore must be asked whether God the Father is charity, or the Son, or the Holy Spirit, or God the Trinity itself—for the Trinity also is not three gods but one God.

Augustine speaks thus on this matter in the same book: “I do not know why, [Note: [Col. 1289D] Supply: just as.] just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are called wisdom, and all together are not three wisdoms but one wisdom, charity should not likewise be called the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, while all together are one Trinity [Note: [Col. 1289D] Charity.].” Yet no one should consider it inappropriate for us to call the Holy Spirit charity, because God the Father and God the Son may also be called charity; just as the Word of God is properly called the Wisdom of God, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are wisdom.

If, therefore, [Note: [Col. 1289D] C. Therefore.] one of these three must properly be called charity, who more fittingly than the Holy Spirit? That is, in that simple and highest nature, substance may not be one thing and charity another; rather, substance itself is charity and charity itself is substance, whether in the Father, in the Son, or in the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, the Holy Spirit is properly called charity. By these words blessed Augustine plainly shows [Col. 1289C] that in the Trinity charity is sometimes referred to the substance, which is common to the three persons and wholly in each of them, and sometimes specifically to the person of the Holy Spirit; just as the Wisdom of God is sometimes understood as the divine substance and sometimes as the Son. This is found in many places [Note: [Col. 1289D] C. More fully.]. Therefore, just as we properly call the one Word of God by the name Wisdom, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are universally that very wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name charity, although the Father and the Son are universally charity.

But the Word of God, [Note: [Col. 1289D] C. But the Word of God.] the only-begotten Son of God, is expressly called the Wisdom of God by the Apostle, who says: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1). [Col. 1289D] We find where the Holy Spirit is called charity if we carefully examine John’s words. After saying, “Let us love one another, because charity is from God,” he adds: “Everyone who loves has been born of God, because [Note: [Col. 1289D] Editions: ‘Because love is God’; likewise, apparently [Col. 1290D] B. Martin.] God is charity” (1 John 4). Here he made clear that he had called that love God which he said was from God. Therefore love is from God. But since the Son also was born from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, it is rightly asked which of them ought here to be understood as having been called love. For the Father alone is God in such a way as not to be from God; therefore the love which is God in such a way as to be from God is not the Father Himself, but either the Son or the Holy Spirit.

But later, when blessed John had mentioned the love by which God loved us and had thereby exhorted us also to love one another, so that God might thus remain in us—because he had indeed called God love—he immediately, wishing to speak more plainly on this subject, says: “By this we know that we remain in Him and He in us: because He has given us of His Spirit” (ibid.). Thus the Holy Spirit, of whom He has given us, makes us remain in God and Him in us; that is, He is love. Therefore He Himself is God-love. Thus God the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1290B] who proceeds from God, is signified where it is read: “God is love, and love is from God.” By these words blessed Augustine plainly says that the Holy Spirit is the charity of the Father and the Son.

Now indeed [Note: [Col. 1290D] C. Now indeed.] let us endeavor to demonstrate what we began to show: namely, that the Holy Spirit is the affection or love of the Father and Son, by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father. Saint Jerome says in his commentary on the fourteenth [Note: [Col. 1290D] Seventeenth.] Psalm: “The Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but is the love which the Father has toward the Son and the Son toward the Father.” Blessed Augustine also says in the sixth book *On the Trinity*: “In all things the Son is equal to the Father and is of one and the same substance. Therefore the Holy Spirit also abides in the same unity [Col. 1290C] and equality, whether [Note: [Col. 1290D] C. Whether.] He is the unity of both, or holiness, or charity. It is manifest that He is not one of the two by whom each is joined to the other, by whom the Begotten is loved by the Begetter and loves His Begetter, so that they keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4), not by participation but by their own essence, nor by a gift of some superior being but by their own proper gift.”

Here you have that the Holy Spirit is that by which the Son is loved by the Father and the Father by the Son, and by which those two maintain the unity of peace. Therefore the Holy Spirit, as the teacher Augustine says in the same book, is something common to the Father and Son, whatever that may be: “But this communion itself is consubstantial and coeternal. If it can suitably be called friendship, let it be so called; but more fittingly it is called charity. And this too is substance, because God is substance and God is charity. Therefore there are three, and no more: one loving Him who is from Him, one loving Him from whom He is, and love itself. If it is nothing, how is God charity? And if it is not substance, how is God substance?”

It should be noted here [Note: [Col. 1290D] C. It should be noted.] that, just as the Holy Spirit [Col. 1291A] in the Trinity is specifically called charity, which belongs to the Father and Son, so He also properly bears a name which in some fashion belongs jointly to the Father and Son. Thus the wise Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “If the charity by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably manifests the communion of both, what is more fitting than that He who is the Holy Spirit, common to both, should properly be called charity? For it is more soundly believed and understood that not only is the Holy Spirit charity in that Trinity, but that He is not called charity without cause, for the reasons stated above; just as He is not the only Spirit or the only holy one in that Trinity, since the Father is Spirit, the Son is Spirit, the Father is holy, and the Son is holy; and yet [Col. 1291B] He is not called the Holy Spirit without cause. For because He is common to both, He is therefore properly called what both are jointly—namely, the Holy Spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 1291D] Distinction 11.] Here it must be said that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, and proceeds from the Father and the Son—a point denied by many heretics. That He proceeds from both is proved by many testimonies of the divine utterances. For the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts,” etc. (Gal. 4). Here He is called the Spirit of the Son; and again: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him” (Rom. 8). The Son Himself says in the Gospel concerning the Holy Spirit: “Whom I shall send to you from the Father” (John 15). He is called the Spirit of the Father where it is written: “If the Spirit of Him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you,” etc. (Rom. 8). Christ Himself says: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father” (Matt. 10). And elsewhere: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, He will teach you all things” (John 14). By these and many other authorities it is shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Greeks, however, [Note: [Col. 1291D] Greeks.] say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and not from the Son. They say this because Truth, speaking in the Gospel—which wholly contains the faith—of the procession of the Spirit, mentions the Father alone: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John [Col. 1291D] 15). They also say it because, in the principal councils held among them, their creeds were established with accompanying anathemas so that no one might teach or preach otherwise concerning the faith of the Trinity than what is contained there. In those creeds the Spirit is said to proceed from the Father and not from the Son. “Whoever,” they say, “adds that He proceeds from the Son incurs anathema.”

But we [Note: [Col. 1291D] C. But we.] interpret those words [Note: [Col. 1291D] The following words, ‘Whoever teaches otherwise,’ etc., are found in the Master, as may be seen [Col. 1292D] in B. Martin; not the preceding words, ‘Whoever . . . from the Son,’ etc.] thus: “Whoever teaches otherwise or preaches differently”—that is, teaches what is contrary or preaches in a contrary way—“let him be anathema.” Thus he uses “something else” (*aliud*) for “what is opposite,” just as the Apostle does in the Epistle to the Galatians (ch. 1): “If anyone,” he says, “proclaims something else to you”—that is, what is contrary—“let him be anathema.” He did not say, “If anyone adds,” because if he had said that, as blessed Augustine says, he would have prejudiced his own case; for he wished to come to some to whom he wrote, as to the Thessalonians (1 Thess. 3), in order to supply what was lacking in their faith. But one who supplies what was lacking adds; he does not take away what was there. Yet one who transgresses the rule of faith does not approach the way but withdraws from it.

To the objection which the Greeks draw from the Gospel, we answer thus: because Truth says there that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, He does not deny this of the Son; but He names the Father alone because even what belongs to the Son is customarily referred to the Father, since the Son has it from Him. Yet it must be known [Note: [Col. 1292D] C. It must be known.] that the Greeks confess that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Son as to the Father, because the Apostle calls Him “the Spirit of the Son” (Gal. 4), and Truth in the Gospel calls Him “the Spirit of truth” (John 14, 15, 16). But since for the Holy Spirit to belong to the Father or Son is nothing other than to be from the Father or Son, they seem in this respect to agree with us in the same doctrine of faith, although they differ in words.

Hence [Note: [Col. 1292D] C. Hence.] some of their Catholic teachers, understanding that the foregoing expressions—that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and that He belongs to the Son—have one and the same meaning, professed that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son. Thus their teacher Athanasius says in the Creed [Col. 1292C] of faith: “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, neither made nor created nor begotten, but proceeding.” See: he plainly says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Didymus also, their greatest teacher, says in his book *On the Holy Spirit* that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: “The Savior, who is also Truth, ‘will not speak from Himself’” (John 16), “that is, not without me and without the will of me and the Father, because He is inseparable from me and from the Father’s will; namely, because He is not from Himself, but is from the Father and from me. For His very subsistence and speech are from the Father and from me.” Again: “The Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot hear from the speaking Son what He does not know, [Col. 1292D] since He is Himself that which is brought forth from the Son—that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from Truth, the Consoler abiding from consolation.”

Likewise Bishop Cyril, in an epistle addressed to Nestorius, says: “The Spirit is understood in Himself, insofar as He is Spirit, and is not the Son; nevertheless, He is not alien from Him. For He is called the Spirit of truth and proceeds from the Son, as from God the Father.” John Chrysostom also says in a homily *On the Exposition of the Creed*: “This is the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, who distributes His own gifts as He wills.” In another homily he says: “It must be believed that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son. We declare this Holy Spirit equal to the Father and Son and proceeding from the Father and the Son. Believe these things, lest evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Thus we have plain testimonies of this kind from the teachers of the Greeks, showing that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore let every tongue confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Now [Note: [Col. 1293D] Distinction 12, ch. “Now.”] it seems necessary to examine whether the Holy Spirit proceeds more fully or more greatly from the Father than from the Son. We answer that just as He does not proceed from the Father before He proceeds from the Son, so He does not proceed more greatly or more fully from the Father than from the Son. Yet Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity* that [Col. 1293B] the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father: “Not without reason in this Trinity is none called the Word of God except the Son, none the gift of God except the Holy Spirit, and none He from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally, except God the Father” [Note: [Col. 1293D] Supplied: “except God the Father.”]. You have heard that the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father.
