But lest this trouble you, he immediately explains in what sense he said it: “I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is found to proceed also from the Son. But this the Father gave Him not as one already existing and not yet possessing it; rather, whatever He gave to the only-begotten Word, He gave by begetting. Thus He begot Him so that the common gift might also proceed from Him, and the Holy Spirit might be the Spirit of both.” He himself has explained how the Holy Spirit [Col. 1293C] proceeds principally from the Father: not because He proceeds from the Father earlier or more fully than from the Son, but because, although He proceeds from the Son, the Son Himself has this from the Father.

[Note: [Col. 1293D] Distinction 13.] After this it must be considered: since the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is of the Father’s substance, why is He not said to be born, but rather to proceed; or why is He not called Son? Blessed Augustine shows why the Holy Spirit is not called or is not born, and therefore is not the Son, in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*, saying: “If the Holy Spirit were called Son, He would certainly be called the Son of both, which would be most absurd. For no one is the child of two except of a father and mother. Far be it from us to imagine anything such between God the Father and God the Son! Therefore He would most absurdly be called Son of both.”

But since [Note: [Col. 1293D] C. But since.] the Holy Spirit is not called begotten, but only proceeding, it is commonly asked why the Son is not called only begotten but also proceeding, as He Himself says in John’s Gospel: “I came forth from [Col. 1294A] God,” or “I proceeded, and came into the world” (John 16). Therefore not only the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, but the Son also. We answer that, although each proceeds from the Father, they do so differently. For the Holy Spirit, as blessed Augustine says in the fifth book *On the Trinity*, proceeds from the Father not as born but as given [Note: [Col. 1293D] Supply: “or as a gift.”]—as gift; whereas the Son proceeds by being born, as begotten. The Holy Spirit is not called Son because He was neither born as the Only-Begotten was, nor made so as to be born in adoption through God’s grace, as we are.

But while we live here, we are unable adequately to distinguish [Note: [Col. 1293D] C. Between.] between the generation of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, let us hear what blessed Augustine says concerning this: “The Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from the Father. But the former is begotten; the latter proceeds. The former is the Son of the Father from whom He is begotten; the latter is the Spirit of both, because He proceeds from both. For unless He also proceeded from the Son, He would not say to the disciples: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20), and give Him by breathing upon them; for by breathing He plainly showed what He gave secretly, signifying that He proceeded also from Himself.”

[Note: [Col. 1293D] Distinction 14.] Furthermore, it must carefully be observed that the procession of the Holy Spirit is twofold: namely, the eternal procession, which is ineffable, by which He proceeds from the Father and Son [Note: [Col. 1293D] Supplied here from the edition: “He proceeded eternally and without time”; and the temporal procession, by which He proceeds from the Father and Son.] in order to sanctify the creature. And just as from eternity He proceeds jointly and simultaneously from the Father and Son, so also in time He proceeds jointly and simultaneously from both to the creature—not divided [Note: [Col. 1294D] Separately.] from the Father into [Col. 1294C] the Son, and from the Son into the creature. Hence the wise Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “The Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son to sanctify the creature; rather, He proceeds from both simultaneously, although the Father gave the Son this, that as He proceeds from Himself, so He should also proceed from the Son.”

Bede speaks thus concerning the temporal [Note: [Col. 1294D] C. On the temporal.] procession in his homily for the first Sunday after the Ascension: “When the grace of the Holy Spirit is given to human beings, the Holy Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and sent also by the Son; He proceeds from the Father and proceeds also from the Son.” By these words he plainly shows that the gift of grace is called the procession or mission of the Holy Spirit. But since the giving of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than His [Col. 1294D] procession, it is evident [Note: [Col. 1294D] Another edition: “But since giving or bestowal is only temporal, it is evident,” etc.] that this procession or mission is temporal.

Augustine also indicates this temporal procession of the Holy Spirit in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*, saying that the Holy Spirit proceeded from Christ [Note: [Col. 1294D] More properly here than in the printed editions: “The Holy Spirit proceeded from Christ.” Augustine does not cite those words there; rather, the Master does so in order subsequently to introduce the Father’s testimony, beginning with the words “When He had risen.”] when, after the resurrection, He breathed upon the disciples in [Col. 1295A] these words: “When Christ had risen from the dead and appeared to the disciples, He breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20), in order to show that He proceeds also from Himself. And He is the power which went out from Him, as is read in the Gospel, and healed all (Luke 6). To show that this procession of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the gift of that Spirit, he adds: “After His resurrection the Lord Jesus Christ gave the Spirit twice: once on earth, for love of neighbor, and again from heaven, for love of God; because through this gift—that is, through the Holy Spirit—charity is poured out into our hearts” (Rom. 5), by which we love God and neighbor.

There are, however, [Note: [Col. 1295D] C. There are.] some who say that God the Holy Spirit Himself is not given, but His gifts, which are not the Spirit Himself. They say that the Holy Spirit is said to be given when His grace, which nevertheless is not Himself, is given to human beings [Note: [Col. 1295D] Slightly differently in the editions: “The Holy Spirit is said to be given when His grace, which nevertheless is not He who is given to human beings, is given.”]. But blessed Augustine plainly shows in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity* that the Holy Spirit Himself, who is God and the third person in the Trinity, is given: “We ought not to doubt that it was this same Holy Spirit whom Jesus gave when He breathed upon them, and of whom He immediately says: ‘Go, baptize all nations in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 28). “He is also the One who was given from heaven on the day of Pentecost. How, then, is He not God who gives the Holy Spirit? Indeed, how great is the God who gives God?” By these words he plainly says [Col. 1295C] that the Holy Spirit Himself—that is, God—is given to human beings by the Father and Son; and that the Holy Spirit, who is God and the third person in the Trinity, is given to us, poured into and entering our minds.

Saint Ambrose also plainly shows this in the first book *On the Holy Spirit*, saying: “Although many are called spirits, because it is written: ‘He makes His angels spirits’” (Ps. 103), “yet there is one God, Spirit. The apostles and prophets received this one Spirit. Thus also the Vessel of Election says that we drank one Spirit [Note: [Col. 1295D] The Benedictine editors of Augustine, in book XV of *On the Trinity*, ch. 19, appear to have thought that this passage of Paul was the other statement of the same Apostle, ‘all drank the same spiritual drink,’ when they noted 1 Cor. 10:4 in the margin. But, besides the fact that the great Father himself, in book XXI *Against Faustus*, ch. 7, gives almost the whole twelfth chapter of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, where he also follows this reading of Ambrose, Peter Sabbatier adduces others who support the same reading, although he omitted to mention Augustine in the aforesaid book *On the Trinity*.] (1 Cor. 12), as though He could not be divided, but is poured into souls and enters the faculties, so as to restrain the burning heat of worldly thirst. This Holy Spirit is neither of the substance of bodily things nor of the substance [Col. 1295D] of invisible creatures.” By these words he plainly says that the Holy Spirit Himself, who is not a creature, is poured into our minds.

Again, in the same work: “Every creature is changeable, but the Holy Spirit is not changeable. Why then should I hesitate to say that the Holy Spirit has been given, when it is written: ‘The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit [Col. 1296A] who was given to us’?” (Rom. 5). “Though inaccessible in nature, yet by His goodness He can be received by us, filling all things with power; though shared only by the righteous, He is a simple substance, present to each person with abundant powers, distributing to each from His own, and wholly present everywhere.” Here too blessed Ambrose plainly says that the Holy Spirit, who is simple substance and one, is given to many.

Here it is asked [Note: [Col. 1296D] C. Here it is asked.] whether holy men also give, or can give, the Holy Spirit to others. If they give Him to others, then, since His giving has been described above as procession, the Holy Spirit seems to proceed from them or to be sent by them. But the Creator neither proceeds from nor is sent by a creature. It remains, therefore, that they do not give the Holy Spirit and cannot give Him. Thus the outstanding teacher Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “No disciple of Christ gave the Holy Spirit. Rather, they prayed that He might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they themselves did not give Him. The Church still observes this custom in her presiding ministers. Finally, when Simon Magus offered money to the apostles, he did not say: ‘Give me this power, that I may give the Holy Spirit’; but: ‘Let anyone on whom I lay hands receive the Holy Spirit’” (Acts 8). “For Scripture had not said above: ‘But when Simon saw that the apostles gave the Holy Spirit’; rather, it had said: ‘But when Simon saw that the Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands’” (ibid.). By these words blessed Augustine shows [Col. 1296C] that neither the apostles nor other prelates gave the Holy Spirit. Moreover, [Note: [Col. 1296D] C. And what is more.] he says in the same book that they cannot give Him, adding: “It is written of Christ that He received from God the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit and poured Him out upon the disciples” (Acts 2), “in which both natures, namely divine and human, are manifested. For He received as man and poured out as God. We, however, can receive this gift according to our measure, but certainly cannot pour it out upon others; rather, that this may happen, we call upon God over them, He by whom it is accomplished.” By these words he expressly says that we cannot pour the Holy Spirit upon others.

[Note: [Col. 1296D] Distinction 15.] Here it must be considered: since the Holy Spirit [Col. 1296D] is given to human beings by the Father and Son—which is His proceeding or being sent temporally from both—is He also given by Himself? If He is given by Himself, He proceeds and is sent by Himself. We answer: because the Spirit is both God and gift, or given gift, He gives and is given. He gives insofar as He is God, and is given insofar as He is gift. But the giving or bestowal [Col. 1297A] of the Spirit is an operation of God; and the operation of the three persons is common and undivided. Therefore the Holy Spirit is given not only by the Father and Son, but also by Himself.

Hence blessed Augustine says in the fifteenth [the text has “fifteenth fifteenth”] book *On the Trinity* that the Holy Spirit gives Himself: “Just as a body of flesh is nothing other than flesh, so the gift of the Holy Spirit is nothing other than the Holy Spirit. Therefore He is the gift of God insofar as He is given to those to whom He is given; but in Himself He is God, even if He is given to no one, because He was God, coeternal with the Father and Son, before He was given. Nor is He less than them because they give and He is given; for He is given as God’s gift in such a way that, as God, He also gives Himself. For He cannot be said not to be master of His own power, of whom it was said: ‘The Spirit [Col. 1297B] breathes where He wills’” (John 3). See: he plainly says that the Holy Spirit gives Himself. For if the Spirit cannot give Himself, while the Father and Son can give Him, the Father and Son can do something which the Holy Spirit cannot. Again, if the Father and Son give the Holy Spirit, but He Himself does not give, [Note: [Col. 1297D] More clearly: “nor does He Himself give.” The word *etiam*, “also,” is lacking in the editions, although it remains in the text.] then the Father and Son perform something which the Holy Spirit does not perform. Therefore the Holy Spirit gives Himself. But if He gives Himself, then He proceeds and is sent from Himself—which is certainly true. For the temporal procession or mission of the Holy Spirit is His own bestowal, and this is an operation of God. Therefore the Holy Spirit proceeds temporally from Himself and is sent by Himself, because He is given by Himself.

[Col. 1297C] But lest you wonder [Note: [Col. 1297D] C. But lest you wonder.] that the Holy Spirit is said to be sent or to proceed from Himself: Augustine says likewise in the second book *On the Trinity* concerning the Son of God that He was sent not only by the Father, but also by Himself and by the Holy Spirit. He asks how the Son or the Holy Spirit can be sent, since each is everywhere as God; for, Augustine says, each is read to have been sent. Of the Holy Spirit it is written: “Whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14); and again: “If I go away, I shall send Him to you” (John 16). The Son says of Himself: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world.” And the Apostle says: “God sent His Son” (Gal. 4). But it is written in the prophet in the person of God: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Therefore God is everywhere; hence the Son is everywhere and [Col. 1297D] the Holy Spirit is everywhere also. Therefore the Son and Holy Spirit were sent to the place where They already were.

Accordingly [Note: [Col. 1297D] C. Accordingly.] it must be asked how the mission of the Son or Holy Spirit is to be understood. “The Father alone,” blessed Augustine says in the same book, “is nowhere read to have been sent, but the Son and the Holy Spirit are.” Let us first see how the Son is sent. The Apostle says: “God sent His Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4). In this he sufficiently shows that God sent the Son precisely by making Him of a woman. [Col. 1298A] Consequently, He could not be sent by the Father without the Holy Spirit, because the Father is understood to have sent Him when He made Him from a woman; and He certainly did not do this without the Holy Spirit. Here he says that the Son was sent by the Father and by the Holy Spirit.

And that [Note: [Col. 1297D] C. And that.] He was also sent by the Holy Spirit is, as blessed Augustine says in the same book, confirmed by authorities. Christ Himself says through Isaiah: “Now the Lord and His Spirit have sent me” (Isa. 48). Saint Ambrose says of this in the second book *On the Holy Spirit*: “Who is it who says, ‘The Lord and His Spirit have sent me,’ except He who came from the Father to save sinners? Therefore the Father sent the Son, and the Holy Spirit also.” Again, in the same book, he says: “As Isaiah says, He was given by the Father: ‘A child is born to us, and a Son [Col. 1298B] is given to us’” (Isa. 9). “I dare to say that He was given also by the Holy Spirit, because He was sent also by the Holy Spirit. For the Son of God Himself says: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He has anointed me; He has sent me to preach good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives,’ etc.” (Isa. 61). “When He read this in the book of Isaiah, He said in the Gospel: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing’” (Luke 4), “thereby signifying that it had been said of Him. But He said briefly, ‘upon me,’ because as the Son of Man He was both anointed and sent to preach; for according to His divinity the Spirit is not upon Christ, but in Christ.” By these words blessed Ambrose shows that the Son was sent and given to us not only by the Father but [Col. 1298C] also by the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1298D] C. Moreover.] The Son was also sent by Himself, because the Father and Son have one will and an inseparable operation. Therefore understand that birth from the Virgin, in which the Son is understood to have been sent, was accomplished inseparably by one and the same operation of the Father and Son, without the Holy Spirit being separated from it. Therefore the same Son was sent by the Father and the Son, because it was brought about by the Father and the Word that He should be sent—that is, that, having been incarnate, He should appear to human beings. From the foregoing [Note: [Col. 1298D] C. From the foregoing.] it is plainly shown that the Son was sent by the Father, the Holy Spirit, and Himself; and what this mission is, namely the incarnation: that He was made man, whereby He appeared visibly. This is the common work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But to this [Note: [Col. 1298D] C. But to this.] an objection is made: [Col. 1298D] If the Son was sent by Himself, why then does He say, “I did not come of myself” (John 8)? Blessed Augustine answers this in the second book *On the Trinity*, saying that this was said according to the form of a servant, according to which He did not bring it about that He was sent—that is, He did not effect the incarnation—but according to the form of God.

[Note: Col. 1298D, “To which.”] Moreover, it should be known that the Son is said to be sent in two ways: either when he visibly appeared to the world clothed in flesh, or when he so enters devout souls that he is perceived and known by them. Blessed Augustine plainly distinguishes these two modes of mission in the fourth book *On the Trinity*, saying: “The Son is not said to be sent merely because he was born of the Father, but either because he appeared to this world—the Word was made flesh [Note: Col. 1299D, supplied *de*, “from.”; the word *est* remains]—whence he says: ‘I came forth from the Father and came into the world’” (John 16); “or because he is perceived in someone’s mind in time.” Behold, the two modes of the mission of the Son of God are distinguished: according to one, he was sent only once; according to the other, he has often been sent and is sent daily.

Here it is asked [Note: Col. 1299D, “Here it is asked.”] why the Father is not said to be sent, although he is perceived in time by someone, as is the Son. To this we say: because in him is the authority of the principle, since he has no one from whom he is, whereas the Son [Col. 1299B] and the Holy Spirit are from him.

[Note: Col. 1299D, Distinction 16; Col. 1300D, “Besides.”] We must now consider, with regard to that ineffable and eternal procession by which the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and not from himself, what his temporal procession is, which is called mission or gift. We answer: just as the Son is said to be sent in two ways—one in which he visibly appeared, the other in which he is invisibly perceived by pure minds—so too the Holy Spirit is said to proceed, or to be sent, or to be given, by the Father and Son and by himself in two ways: one visibly, the other invisibly. For he was given through the manifestation of a visible creature, as on the day of Pentecost and on other occasions; and he is given daily, invisibly entering into the minds of believers.

[Col. 1299C] First, therefore [Note: Col. 1300D, “And first.”], let us treat of that mode of mission which occurred in a visible appearance. Blessed Augustine says thus concerning it in the second book *On the Trinity*: “It is easy to understand why the Holy Spirit too is said to be sent. For at a particular time a form of creature was made, in which the Holy Spirit might be visibly shown: either when he descended upon the Lord himself in the bodily form of a dove” (Matt. 3), “or when, on the day of Pentecost, there suddenly came from heaven a sound as though a mighty wind were rushing, and those divided tongues, as of fire, were seen, and it settled upon each one of them” (Acts 2). “This operation, visibly expressed and presented to mortal eyes, was called the mission of the Holy Spirit: not that his own substance might appear—for he too is invisible and immutable, like the Father and the Son—but so that, stirred by external sights, human hearts might be turned from the temporal manifestation of him who comes to the hidden eternity of him who is ever present.”

By these words the eminent teacher Augustine makes clear that mode of mission which is visibly displayed, although the Holy Spirit is not seen in his own nature, and was no more present in those creatures than in others. For through the temporal motion of the creature, the spiritual and invisible infusion of the Holy Spirit was signified. And, to state it more plainly [Col. 1300A], by that bodily displayed mode of the Holy Spirit’s mission was shown the spiritual and inward mission, or gift, of the Holy Spirit, of which we must speak.

But first [Note: Col. 1300D, “But first.”] it must be asked: since the Son is said to be less than the Father according to the mission in which he appeared in a creaturely form, why is the Holy Spirit not likewise said to be less than the Father, since he appeared in a creaturely form? For Blessed Augustine plainly shows in the fourth book *On the Trinity* that the Son is less than the Father according to the form in which he appeared when sent, saying: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, so very small as to be made; therefore he was sent in that respect in which he was made. We therefore confess him made less; and again, less insofar as made; and again, made insofar as sent.” You see, then, that the Son, insofar as he is sent—that is, made—is less than the Father.

Why, then, is the Holy Spirit not called less than the Father, when he too assumed a creature in which he appeared? Because the Holy Spirit assumed the creature in which he appeared in one way, and the Son of God in another. The Son assumed it by union; the Spirit did not. For the Son assumed humanity so as to become man; but the Holy Spirit did not so assume the dove as to become a dove. On this Blessed Augustine says in the second book *On the Trinity*: “Therefore nowhere is it written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, or that the Holy Spirit is less, because the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed as the Son of Man was assumed [Col. 1300C], in which form the very Word of God was presented—not as possessing the Word of God, as other holy wise persons do, but because he himself was the Word. For the word in flesh is one thing, the Word made flesh another; that is, a word in a human being is one thing, the Word as man another. For ‘flesh’ is used for ‘human being’ in the saying, ‘The Word was made flesh’” (John 1).

Therefore the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed as that flesh and human form from the Virgin Mary was assumed. For he did not bless the dove or that fire and join it to himself in unity of person forever. From the foregoing it has plainly been shown in what respect the Son is called less than the Father, and why the Son, but not the Holy Spirit, is so called [Col. 1300D].

It should be noted [Note: Col. 1300D, “It should be noted.”], however, that the Son, insofar as he was made man, is called less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit and even than himself. Augustine shows in the first book *On the Trinity* that he is called less even than himself according to the form of a servant: “People erred by transferring to Christ’s everlasting substance things said of him according to his humanity. Such is what the Lord says: ‘The Father is greater than I’” (John 14), “which Truth says on account of the form of a servant, according to which the Son is also less than himself. How was he not made less even than himself, who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant?” (Phil. 2). “For he did not so take the form of a servant as to lose the form of God, in which he was equal to the Father. Thus, in the form of God the only-begotten Son of the Father is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant he is less even than himself. Scripture therefore rightly says both: that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son. The former is understood with respect to the form of God, the latter with respect to the form of a servant.”

On the same matter Blessed Augustine says in the second book *On the Trinity*: “The Son of God is equal to the Father according to the form of God, in which he is [Note: Col. 1301D, editions: *qua*, ‘in which’]; and less than the Father according to the form of a servant, which he received. In that form he is found less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit [Col. 1301B], and not only this, but even than himself.” On this account, as Augustine himself says against Maximinus, bishop of the heretics, he was made less not only than the Father but also than himself and the Holy Spirit, and was “made a little lower than the angels” (Heb. 2). Therefore, as the same Blessed Augustine says in the first book *On the Trinity*, the Son of God is equal to God the Father in nature, less in condition—that is, in the form of a servant which he assumed. These authorities plainly show that the Son, according to the form of a servant, is less than the Father, himself, and the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Col. 1301D, Distinction 17.] Let us now proceed to set forth the mission of the Holy Spirit, by which he is invisibly sent into the hearts of believers. For the Holy Spirit himself—who is God and the third person in the Trinity, as shown above—proceeds temporally from the Father, the Son, and himself; that is, he is sent and given to believers. But we must consider what this mission or gift is, and how it occurs.

For this purpose [Note: Col. 1301D, “For this purpose.”], so that it may be taught more intelligibly and perceived more fully, something very necessary must first be set forth. It has indeed been said above, and demonstrated by sacred authorities, that the Holy Spirit is the love of the Father and Son, by which they love one another and us. To this must be added that this same Holy Spirit is the love or charity by which we love God and neighbor. When this charity is in us in such a way as to make us love God and neighbor, then the Holy Spirit is said to be sent or given to us; and one who loves that very love by which he loves his neighbor thereby loves God, because that love itself is God.

But lest [Note: Col. 1301D, “But lest.”] we seem to introduce anything of our own into so great a matter, let us confirm what has been said by sacred authorities. Blessed Augustine says in the thirteenth book *On the Trinity*: “Whoever loves his neighbor, it follows that he especially loves love itself. But God is love [Col. 1302A]; therefore it follows that he especially loves God.” Again, in the same work: “God is love, as John the Evangelist says” (1 John 4). “Why, then, do we go and run to the heights of heaven and the depths of earth, seeking him who is with us, if we are willing to be with him? Let no one say, ‘I do not know what I should love.’ Let him love his brother, and let him love that same love. For he knows love better than the brother whom he loves [Note: Col. 1301D, editions: *qua*, ‘by which’]. Behold, he can now have love as better known than his brother [Note: Col. 1301D, Master: *potes*, ‘you can’; Master and Augustine: ‘can have God as better known’]—plainly better known, because more present, more inward, more certain. Embrace the love of the Lord, and by love embrace God. Love itself is that which joins all good angels and all servants of God in the bond of holiness [Col. 1302B]. Therefore, the sounder we are from the swelling of pride, the fuller we are of love; and who is full of love if not one who is full of God?”

By these words wise Augustine sufficiently shows that the very love by which we love God and neighbor is God. But he adds more plainly in the same book: “Let us consider how John the Evangelist commends brotherly love [Note: Augustine: ‘Let us consider how greatly John the Apostle commends brotherly love.’ Master: ‘Let us consider how he commends love, as Augustine does.’]. ‘He who loves his brother,’ he says, ‘abides in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him’” (1 John 2). “It is clear that he has placed the perfection of righteousness in love of one’s brother. For one in whom there is no stumbling-block is certainly perfect; and yet he seems to have said nothing of love of God—which he would never do unless he intended God to be understood in that very brotherly love [Col. 1302C]. For a little later in the same Epistle he says most plainly: ‘Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God. And everyone who loves has been born of God and has known [Note: Augustine: *knows*, with the Vulgate] God; whoever does not love has not known God, because God is love’” (1 John 4).

“This connection [Note: editions: *contextio*, ‘connection’] quite plainly declares that this same brotherly love—for brotherly love is that by which we love one another—is proclaimed on John’s great authority not only to be from God but also to be God. Therefore, when through love we love our brother, through God we love our brother; nor can it happen that we do not especially love that same love by which we love our brother, since God is love.” Again: “Whoever does not love his brother is not in love; and whoever is not in love is not in God, because God is love.” Behold, he plainly says that brotherly love is God [Col. 1302D].

Since, however [Note: Col. 1302D, “Since, however.”], brotherly love is God, it is neither the Father nor the Son, but only the Holy Spirit, who in the Trinity is properly called love or charity. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “If among God’s gifts there is none greater than charity, and there is no gift of God greater than the Holy Spirit, what is more consequent [Col. 1303A] than that he himself should be the charity which is called both God and from God? For John the Evangelist says: ‘Love is from God’” (1 John 4). “And a little later: ‘God is love’” (ibid.). “There he makes clear that he called that love God which he had called from God. Therefore love is God from God.” Again in the same work: “John, wishing to speak more plainly of this matter, says: ‘By this we know that we abide in him and he in us: because he has given us of the Holy Spirit’” (ibid.). “Therefore the Holy Spirit, of whom he has given us, causes us to abide in God and him in us. But this is caused by love. Therefore God himself is love.” From these things it is evident that the Holy Spirit is charity.

But lest [Note: Col. 1303D, “But lest.”] someone perhaps say that “God is charity” (1 John 4) is said by expression of cause—namely, because charity is from God and is not God himself—just as God is called “our patience” and “hope,” not because he himself is these things but because they are from him, Augustine meets this objection. In the fifteenth book *On the Trinity* he shows that this was not said as a statement of cause, as were those expressions: “We shall not say that charity is called God merely because it is God’s gift, rather than because charity itself is that substance worthy of the name God, as it is said of him: ‘You are my patience’” (Ps. 70). “Certainly this was not said because our patience is the substance of God, but because it is from him; whence elsewhere: ‘My patience is from him’” (Ps. 61). “The very reading of Scripture easily refutes this interpretation [Col. 1303C]. For ‘You are my patience’ is like ‘O Lord, my hope,’ and ‘My God, my mercy’” (Ps. 90, 58), “and many similar expressions. But it is not said, ‘O Lord, my charity,’ or ‘You are my charity,’ or ‘God is my charity’; rather it is said, ‘God is charity,’ just as it is said, ‘God is spirit’” (1 John 4). “Whoever cannot discern this should seek understanding [Note: ‘understanding’] from the Lord, not an exposition from us; for we can say nothing more plainly.” Therefore God is charity.

From what has been said, it is clear that the Holy Spirit is the charity by which we love God and neighbor. Hence we can more easily show how the Holy Spirit is sent or given to us.

For then [Note: Col. 1303D, “For then.”] he is said to be sent or given to us when he is in us in such a way [Col. 1303D] as to make us love God and neighbor, through which we abide in God and God in us. Hence Blessed Augustine, indicating the mode of this mission, says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “God is the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from God; and when he has been given to a human being, he kindles that person to love God and neighbor, and he himself is love. For a human being has no source from which to love God except God.” Behold how the Holy Spirit is given or sent to us, inasmuch as he is called given or gift. Blessed Augustine commends this gift, explaining more clearly how it is given in the same book:

“The love of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts, as the Apostle says, through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5). “There is no gift of God more excellent than this. It alone distinguishes between children of the kingdom and children of perdition. Other gifts also are given through the Holy Spirit, but without charity they are of no benefit. Unless, therefore, the Holy Spirit is imparted to someone so as to make that person a lover of God and neighbor, that person is not transferred from the left to the right. Nor is the Holy Spirit properly called a gift except because of love. Whoever lacks it, even if speaking with all tongues, having prophecy, all knowledge, and all faith, distributing all possessions, and delivering up the body to be burned, gains nothing thereby” (1 Cor. 13). “How great, then [Col. 1304B], is that good without which such great goods bring no one to eternal life! Love or charity itself—for both names denote one thing—does bring one to the kingdom. Therefore the love which is from God and is God is properly also the Holy Spirit, through whom it is poured into our hearts. God, therefore, is charity, through which the whole Trinity dwells in us. For this reason the Holy Spirit, although God, is most rightly also called God’s gift. And what is this gift properly to be understood as, except charity, which leads to God, and without which no other gift leads to God?”

Here it is made clear what was said above: namely [Note: editions: *scilicet*, ‘namely’], in what sense charity is the Holy Spirit and the most excellent gift, and how [Col. 1304C] this gift, namely the Holy Spirit, is given to us. It is imparted to someone in such a way—that is, it exists in someone in such a way—as to make that person a lover of God and neighbor. When it does this, it is said to be given or sent to that person; and then that person is properly said to have the Holy Spirit.

Here it is asked [Note: Col. 1304D, “Here it is asked.”]: if charity is the Holy Spirit, and charity itself increases and decreases in a human being and is possessed more or less at different times, must it be conceded that the Holy Spirit increases in a human being and is possessed more or less? For if he increases in a human being and is given or possessed more or less, he seems mutable. But God is altogether immutable. It therefore seems that either the Holy Spirit is not charity, or charity [Col. 1304D] does not increase or decrease in a human being. Again: charity is given to one who does not have it, so that the person may have it; and to one who has it, so that the person may have it more fully. Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is charity and is given to one who does not have it so that the person may have it, and to one who has it so that the person may have it more fully, how is he given to one who does not have him, since, as God, he is wholly everywhere and in all creatures? And how is he given or possessed more fully without undergoing change in himself?

To this [Note: Col. 1304D, “To this.”] we answer that the Holy Spirit, or charity, is wholly immutable: he neither increases nor decreases in himself, nor admits in himself a greater or lesser degree; but he is increased in a human being—or rather, for a human being [Col. 1305A]—and is given or possessed more or less. For our God can be magnified and exalted in us, though he is neither magnified, diminished, nor exalted in himself. Thus the prophet says: “Let a person approach the deep heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 18). A marginal gloss on this verse says: “God becomes great not in himself but in the human heart.” Thus the Holy Spirit is given to a human being, and, once given, is given more—that is, increased—and is possessed more or less; yet he remains immutable.

And although [Note: Col. 1305D, “And although.”] he is everywhere and wholly in every creature, there are nevertheless many who do not possess him. For not all in whom the Holy Spirit is have the Holy Spirit; otherwise irrational creatures too would have the Holy Spirit, which the piety of faith does not allow.

[Col. 1305B] [Note: Col. 1305D, “That I may think.”] To make what we have said more certain, let us confirm it by authority. Blessed Augustine shows, in his commentary on John, that the Holy Spirit is perceived more or less, increased for a human being, given to one who does not have him, and given to one who has him so that he may be had more fully: “Without the Holy Spirit, it is certain that we cannot love Christ and keep his commandments; and we can do and perform this so much the less as we perceive him less. But so much the more as we perceive him more. Therefore he is not promised in vain, not only to one who does not have him—indeed, to one who does not have him, that he may be had—but to one who has him, that he may be had more fully. For if he were not possessed less by one person and more by another, holy Elisha would not have said to holy Elijah: ‘Let the spirit which is in [Col. 1305C] you be double in me’” (4 Kings 2).

“But to Christ, who is the Son of God, the Spirit was given without measure” (John 3). “For the man Christ Jesus, mediator between God and humankind, is not without the grace of the Holy Spirit” (1 Tim. 2). “That he is the only-begotten Son equal to the Father belongs not to grace but to nature. But that a human being was assumed into the unity of the person of the only-begotten belongs to grace, not to nature. To others, however, he is given by measure, and what is given is added, until each one’s proper measure is filled according to the measure of his perfection.”

Here you have the explicit statement that the Holy Spirit is given or received more and less; that he is given to a human being and increased; and that he is given both to one who has him and to one who does not have him [Note: Correct the passage: “And, once given to a human being, he is increased, and is given both to one who has him and to one who does not have him.”], because the Holy Spirit is charity, which is given to one who does not have it and grows and advances in one who has it. Indeed, to speak more truly [Col. 1305D] and properly, the human being advances in it and at times declines; then charity itself is said to advance or decline, though it neither advances nor declines in itself, because it is God. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the ninth homily on the Epistle of John: “Let each person test how far charity has advanced in that person, or rather how far that person has advanced in charity. For if charity is God, it neither advances nor declines. Thus charity is said to advance in you because you advance by it.” This explains how the Holy Spirit is said to increase in us: namely, because we advance in him [Col. 1306A]; and similarly in other such expressions.

Here it is asked [Note: Col. 1306D, “Here it is asked.”], since the Holy Spirit, through whom gifts are distributed, is himself a gift, whether it should be conceded that gifts are distributed and given through a gift. We answer that through the gift which is the Holy Spirit, particular gifts are distributed to individuals, while all the good have the gift itself in common. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*: “Through the gift which is the Holy Spirit, many gifts, which are proper to particular members of Christ, are distributed in common. For not every individual has all gifts, but one has some and another others, although all have the gift itself through which each person’s proper gifts are distributed—that is, the Holy Spirit.” He also plainly says that gifts are given through the gift [Col. 1306B].

[Note: Col. 1306D, Distinction 18.] Moreover, it must be carefully considered, since the Holy Spirit is called “gift” (*donum*) and “given” (*datum*), whether both names belong to him on the same ground; and this indeed might seem so. Since for the Holy Spirit “to be given” and “to be bestowed” are the same thing, the Holy Spirit seems to be called both “given” and “gift” on the same ground. Augustine seems to signify this in the fifteenth book *On the Trinity*, when he says: “The Spirit is God’s gift insofar as he is given to those to whom he is given; but in himself he is God, even if he is given to no one.” Behold, he plainly says that the Holy Spirit is called a gift because he is given. But if he is called a gift only because he is given, he was not a gift from eternity, because he is given only in time [Col. 1306C].

To this [Note: Col. 1306D, “To this.”] Master Peter says that the Holy Spirit is called both gift and given, or bestowed. But he is called “given” or “bestowed” only because he is given or bestowed, and this belongs to him only in time. He is called “gift,” however, not merely because he is bestowed, but because of the property which he possessed from eternity. Hence he was a gift from eternity. For he was eternally a gift, not because he was given, but because he proceeded from the Father and the Son. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the fourth book *On the Trinity*: “As for the Son, to be born is to be from the Father; so for the Holy Spirit, to be God’s gift is to proceed from the Father and from the Son.” Here it is plainly shown that the Holy Spirit is a gift because he proceeds from the Father and the Son, just as the Son is from the Father because he is born from him.

[Col. 1306D] From the foregoing [Note: Col. 1306D, “From the foregoing.”] it is clear that the Holy Spirit is eternally a gift and temporally given or bestowed. From this appears the twofold distinction of procession discussed above: according to one procession he is called bestowed or given; according to the other [Note: Col. 1306D, “And according to.”] he is called a gift. Insofar as he is eternally a gift, he is related to the Father and the Son; insofar as he is called given or bestowed, he is related both to the one who gave and to those to whom he is given.

[Col. 1307A] [Note: Col. 1307D, Distinction 19.] Now that we have indicated, according to the measure of our capacity, the coeternity of the three persons, it remains to say something about their equality. For the Catholic faith asserts that the three persons are coequal, just as they are coeternal. The Son is equal to the Father in all things, and the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son. For, as Blessed Augustine teaches in the book *On Faith to Peter*, briefly explaining how equality is to be understood [Note: the word *ait*, “says,” remains]: “None of these either precedes another in eternity, exceeds another in greatness, or surpasses another in power. For the Father is neither earlier nor greater than the Son or the Holy Spirit, as regards the unity of the divine nature; nor is the Son greater than the Holy Spirit. For it is eternal and without beginning that the Son exists from the nature of the Father; and it is eternal and without beginning that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the nature of the Father and the Son [Col. 1307B]. Therefore we rightly believe and say that the three are one God, because the divinity of the three persons is altogether one eternity, one immensity, one natural divinity.”

Here wise Augustine has briefly set forth wherein the equality of the three persons consists: namely, that none surpasses another in eternity, power, or greatness. Although these are enumerated as though distinct in God, they are nevertheless one and the same thing: the simple and immutable divine essence. Hence Blessed Augustine says in the seventh book *On the Trinity*: “A human being is great in one respect and God in another; but God is great by being God, because for him being great is not one thing and being God another” [Note: editions read, “not great in one respect and God in another, but …”; our manuscript is corrupt here]. “For his greatness is the same as his power, and his power the same as his greatness. Thus Father and Son together are one essence, and there is one greatness.”

Likewise, God’s power is the divine essence. Thus Blessed Augustine says in the seventh book of the *Confessions*: “God’s will and power are God himself.” God’s eternity is also the divine essence. Augustine demonstrates this in his exposition of the Psalm verse, “Your years are in generation upon generation” (Ps. 101), saying: “And the generation of generations which does not pass away, gathered from all generations—that is, the saints. In it shall be the years of God, which shall not pass away: that is, the eternity of God. For God’s years are not one thing and he another; rather, God’s years are God’s eternity, and God’s eternity is God’s own substance, possessing nothing mutable.” Let us therefore hold firmly [Col. 1307D] that divine essence, eternity, power, and greatness are one and the same thing. Yet Scripture customarily presents these and similar things as distinct. Thus he has briefly embraced in these words the equality of the three persons, whereby none surpasses another in eternity, greatness, or power. That none of the three persons exceeds another in eternity has been shown above, where their coeternity was set forth.

It remains now [Note: Col. 1308D, “It remains now.”] to show that none exceeds another in greatness [Col. 1308A] or power; and first let us consider greatness. It should be known, therefore, that the Father is not greater than the Son; neither the Father nor the Son is greater than the Holy Spirit; two persons together are not something greater than one; nor are three together something greater than two; nor is the essence greater in three than in two, or in two than in one, because it is whole in each. Hence John of Damascus says: “We confess that the whole nature of the Godhead is perfectly present in each of its hypostases—that is, persons: wholly in the Father, wholly in the Son, wholly in the Holy Spirit. Therefore God the Father is perfect, God the Son perfect, and God the Holy Spirit perfect.” Hence the Father is said to be in the Son, and the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both, and each [Col. 1308B] in each.

Thus Saint Augustine says in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “Because of natural unity, the whole Father is in the Son and the Holy Spirit; the whole Son is in the Father and the Holy Spirit; and the whole Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son. None of these is outside any of the others because of the unity of the divine nature. Therefore we confess the same likeness of power and fullness of deity in both, because Truth says in the Gospel: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’” (John 14).

[Note: Col. 1308D, Distinction 20.] It remains to show how none of these persons surpasses another in power, so that, just as the greatness of the three is one and undifferentiated, their power too may be shown to be one and undifferentiated. It should therefore be known that the Father is not more powerful than the Son, nor is the Son or the Father more powerful than the Holy Spirit. Augustine establishes this convincingly by arguments and authorities in his work *Against Maximinus the Heretic*, who taught that the Father was more powerful than, or greater than, the Son: “He who says, ‘All that the Father has is mine’” (John 16), “has nothing less than the Father. For if he has less in power than the Father in any respect, all that the Father has is not his. Therefore he has as great a power as the Father, because in divinity he is equal to the Father” [Col. 1308C].

[Note: Col. 1308D, “Again.”] In another way Blessed Augustine proves against Maximinus the heretic that the Son is equal to the Father: “You say that the Father begot a Son less than himself, and in this you disparage the Father as well. For if he begot his only Son as less, he either could not or would not beget one equal to himself. If you say that he did not will it, you have said that he is envious; if he could not, where is the omnipotence of God the Father? The matter is wholly reduced [Note: *colligitur*, ‘is reduced’] to this alternative: God the Father either could not or would not beget a Son equal to himself. If he could not, he is found weak; if he would not, envious. But both are false. Therefore the Son is truly equal to the Father. The Father, then, begot a Son equal to himself, and from both proceeds the Holy Spirit, equal to both. For if, as Blessed Augustine says against that same Maximinus, bishop of the Arians, God the Father could beget in his only Son his own full form, yet did not beget it in fullness but as lesser, you are compelled to call the Father envious. Therefore God the Father begot a Son who is fully God and equal to himself.”

The venerable Augustine further demonstrates this by a human analogy, saying: “A human father, if he could, would beget a son equal to himself. Who, then, dares say that almighty God could not do this? I add that, if a human being could, he would beget a son greater and better than himself; but nothing can be greater or better than God. Why, then, did God not beget an equal Son, as you say [Note: *ais*, ‘you say’], when he needed no years through which equality might be attained [Col. 1309B], and lacked no omnipotence? Let us therefore believe that the Son is equal to God the Father.”

[Note: Col. 1309D, Distinction 22, chapter “These.”] To this must be added that, as Blessed Augustine says in the fifth book *On the Trinity*, certain names belong to God in time and are said relatively to the creature. Some of these are said of all the persons, such as Lord, Creator, and refuge; others are not said of all, such as bestowed, given, and sent. Moreover [Note: Col. 1309D, “Moreover.”], there is one name which is not said separately of any person, but of all the persons together: Trinity. This is not said according to substance, but, as it were collectively, signifies the plurality of persons. There are also [Note: Col. 1309D, “There are also.”] certain names that belong to God in time and are not said relatively, such as incarnate, made human, and the like. Behold, we have set forth six distinctions of names used when speaking of God [Col. 1309C].

[Note: Col. 1309D, Distinction 23, chapter “Therefore there arises.”] Here there arises a difficult but not useless question: why are these three not called one person, as they are one essence and one God? Augustine carefully treats and fittingly explains this question in the seventh book *On the Trinity*, saying: “Why do we not call these three together one person, as we call them one substance and one God, but say three persons, although we do not say three gods or three essences? It is because we wish to preserve some one term for the signification [Col. 1309D] by which the Trinity is understood, lest we be wholly silent when asked, ‘What three?’ since we confess that there are three persons.”

[Note: Col. 1310D, “By what necessity.”] “Therefore, when it is asked, ‘What three?’ or ‘What are the three?’, we set ourselves to find some name that will embrace these three; but none occurs to the mind, because the eminence of the Godhead surpasses the capacity of ordinary speech. For God is more truly thought than spoken, and more truly exists than thought.”

The Father [Note: Col. 1310D, “The Father.”], then, and the Son and the Holy Spirit, since they are three—what three are they? They are, namely [Col. 1310A], three persons. If, therefore, they are called three persons, that which “person” is is common to them. Certainly, because the Father is a person, the Son is a person, and the Holy Spirit is a person, they are called three persons. We therefore say three persons because that which “person” is is common to them. From the foregoing it may plainly be understood that the Latins said “three persons” out of necessity, although “person” is said according to substance; hence that which “person” is is common to all three.

[Note: [Col. 1310D] Distinction 26, ch. “Now concerning”] Let us now consider the properties of the persons, which are also commonly called notions or relations in Scripture. For in that holy Trinity (which is so often repeated by us in order that it may be more firmly impressed upon our heart [Col. 1310B]), as the venerable Augustine says in the book *On Faith to Peter*, begetting is one thing and being born another; and proceeding is one thing, while begetting or being born is another. Hence it is evident that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. It is proper to the Father alone, not merely that he himself is not born, but that he has begotten one Son; proper to the Son alone, not merely that he himself has not begotten, but that he was born from the essence of the Father; and proper to the Holy Spirit, not merely that he himself was neither born nor begot, but that he alone proceeds from the Father and the Son. Thus blessed Augustine has briefly set forth the three properties of the persons.

Here the question is raised [Note: [Col. 1310D] Ch. “Here the question is raised.”] how it can be said to be proper to God born that he is the Son of God, or begotten [Col. 1310C] from God, when human beings too are called and are sons of God, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81 [LXX]); and when the Lord said to Moses concerning the people of Israel: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4). But there is a great difference between these cases. Human beings are sons of God by creation, not by the property of birth. But God the Son is Son by the property of his origin and by the reality of his birth, not by creation or adoption. Those human beings exist before they become sons of God. For they become sons of God; they are not born sons of God.

Hilary, showing that the one God born is the Son of God by the property of his origin, distinguishes most clearly between him and human beings who are sons of God, saying in the twelfth book *On the Trinity*:

[Col. 1310D] “The Son who [Note: [Col. 1310D] Edition: “alone.”] is born from the true Father is truly a Son; and we are sons of God, but by creation. For we were once children of wrath; but we have been made sons of God by adoption rather than by being born. And because everything that comes to be did not exist before it came to be, we, who were not sons, are made sons. For previously we were not sons of God, but were made so by grace—not born, nor begotten, but acquired. For God acquired us for himself, and thus he is said not to have begotten us but to have acquired us. For we never find God said to have begotten sons [Col. 1311A] with the signification of a property. A human being becomes a Son of God by adoption, not by generation; and this is not a property belonging to him, but a designation. Accordingly, he is not truly a son, since he is said neither to have been born properly nor always to have been a son. But the only-begotten God was never at any time not Son; nor was he anything before he was Son; nor is he himself anything except Son. Thus he who is always Son by the property and reality of birth is the Son of him alone who begot him; and he alone who begot him is his Father. For as the one is Son by origin, so the other is Father by generation.”

[Note: [Col. 1311D] Ch. “Man.”] But a human being who is a son of God by creation is the son not only of the Father but also of the Son and the Holy Spirit—that is, of the whole Trinity. And the Trinity itself may be called his Father [Col. 1311B]. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity*: “The Trinity cannot be called Father, except perhaps figuratively with reference to the creature because of the adoption of sons. For what is written, ‘Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one’ (Deut. 6), must certainly not be understood as excluding the Son or the Holy Spirit. We rightly call him our one Lord God, and we rightly call him our Father, begetting us by his grace.”

Hilary likewise says in the sixth book *On the Trinity*: “God is Father to all through faith, to whom he is Father through that same faith [Note: [Col. 1311D] Supply: “by which.”] by which we confess Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” Thus it has been shown why it is said to be proper to God born that he is Son: namely, because he alone is properly said to have been born [Col. 1311C].

[Note: [Col. 1311D] Distinction 35, ch. “This must be considered.”] Here it must be considered whether knowledge or foreknowledge, disposition or predestination, could exist in God if nothing were future. To this one must reply that knowledge [Note: [Col. 1311D] Ch. “Knowledge.”] or wisdom concerns not only temporal things but eternal things also. Therefore, even if nothing were future, knowledge would nevertheless be in God—the same knowledge that is there now; it would not be less than it is now, nor is it greater than it would have been. God therefore knew the eternal from eternity, and he knew immutably everything that was to be. He knows past and future things no less than present things, and by his own eternal and immutable wisdom he knows all things that are known. For, as Saint Ambrose says, the whole principle of heavenly and earthly wisdom is in him, because his immeasurable knowledge comprehends all his wisdom and knowledge [Col. 1311D].

[Note: [Col. 1312D] Ch. “For this reason.”] For this reason all things are said to be in God and to have been from eternity. Hence the venerable Augustine says in his commentary on Genesis: “These visible things, before they were made, did not exist. How, then, were they known to God? And again: how would he make things that were not known to him? For he made nothing in ignorance. Therefore he made them known, not made [Note: [Col. 1312D] Supply: “he knew them.”]. Accordingly, before they were made, they both were and were not. They were in God’s knowledge; they were not in their own nature. I do not dare to say that they became known to God in another way when he made them than by the way in which he knew them in order to make them.” Of him Saint James says: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow due to turning” (Jas. 1).

Here you have that these visible things were in God’s knowledge before they were made. In this sense, therefore, all things are said to be in God, and everything that was made is said to be life in him—not because the creature is the Creator, or because these temporal things are essentially in God, but because they are always in the knowledge of him who is life [Col. 1312A].

Hence [Note: [Col. 1312D] Ch. “Hence.”] all things are said to be present to him: not only the things that are, but also those which have passed and those which are future, according to the saying, “Who calls the things that are not as though they were” (Rom. 4), because, as Saint Ambrose says in *On the Trinity*, he knows things that are not as he knows things that are. For this reason all things are said to be in him or with him, or present to him.

Hence the outstanding teacher Augustine, commenting on the verse of the Psalm, “And the beauty of the field is with me” (Ps. 49 [LXX]), says: “It is with me because with God nothing passes away and nothing is future. All future things are with him, and things already past are not taken away from him. All things are with him by a certain ineffable knowing of God’s wisdom.” Here wise Augustine makes plain in what sense such expressions are to be understood: “all things are present to God,” “all things are in God,” “with God,” “before God,” or “life in him”—because the ineffable knowledge of all things is in him [Col. 1312B–C].

[Note: [Col. 1312D] Distinction 36.] Here it is commonly asked: since all things are said to be in God’s knowledge or presence, or to be in God through knowledge, and since his knowledge is the divine essence, must it be granted that all things are in the divine essence, or in God through essence? We say in reply that God’s knowledge is certainly his essence, and that his presence, in which all things are, is his knowledge. Yet not everything that is in his presence or knowledge ought to be said to be in his essence. For if this were said, those things would be understood to be of the same essence as he is.

Things are said to be in God through essence when they are the divine essence and are God. Therefore God has in his presence that which he does not have in his own nature [Col. 1312D]. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On the Words of the Apostle*: “‘He chose us before the foundation of the world’ (Ps. 94 [LXX], Eph. 4). Who is sufficient to explain this? Those who do not exist are chosen, and he who chooses does not err. Yet he chooses, and he has as chosen those whom he will create in order to choose them; he has them with himself, not in his nature but in his presence. Those to whom the promise was made did not yet exist, but they themselves also were promised, to those to whom the promise was made.” Here he plainly says that God had the elect with himself before the world, not in his nature but in his presence [Col. 1313A], though his presence is nothing other than his nature, because his presence is his knowledge.

After what has been said [Note: [Col. 1313D] Ch. “After what has been said.”], the question arises: since all things are said to be in God not through the essence of nature but through the knowledge of cognition, and God knows good and evil, should it simply be granted that evils are in God, or are in God through knowledge? For God knows, and always knew, all things, good as well as evil, before they were made, and from eternity he foreknew that they would be. Therefore, when we say that all good things are in God through the foreknowledge of cognition, it seems, by the same reasoning, that all evils must be said to be in him, since he has always known them and they have been present to him through knowledge.

For God foreknew from eternity that certain persons would be evil, and, as blessed Augustine says, he foreknew their wickedness [Col. 1313B], but did not prepare it. Therefore, since he knows the sins of all, must they be understood to be included in the general statement in which the Apostle says that all things are in God? “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. 11). But who except a madman would say that evils are in God? Those things are understood to be in God which are from him and through him. Things are through him and from him when he is their author; but he is author only of good things. Therefore only good things are from him or through him. Thus only good things are in him.

Therefore evils are not in God, although he knows them; yet he does not know them altogether as he knows good things, because he knows evils as if from afar, as the Prophet says: “And he knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137 [LXX])—that is, pride. Elsewhere, speaking to God concerning the wicked, the Prophet says: “Their belly has been filled from your hidden things” (Ps. 16 [LXX]). Explaining this, blessed Augustine says: “‘Hidden things’ means sins, which are hidden from the light of your truth” [Note: [Col. 1313D] This word remains.].

But how are sins hidden from the light of divine truth when they are known by God? For if he did not know them, how would he judge concerning them and condemn the wicked for them? Elsewhere the Prophet says: “For he is absent neither from east nor from west” (Ps. 74 [LXX]). Explaining this, Cassiodorus says: “God is absent neither from the good nor from the evil, but is present to all and knows all.”

God, then, knows good and evil by knowledge; but he knows good things also by approval and good pleasure, whereas he does not know evil things in that manner. Hence [Note: [Col. 1313D] Ch. “And hence.”] only good things, not evils, are said to be in God; the former are near, the latter far away. Although certain things are said to be in God because they are present to his knowledge, and although God knows good and evil alike, he knows evils only by awareness, whereas he knows good things not merely by knowledge but also by approval and good pleasure. Because of such knowledge, things are said to be in God—namely, because he knows them in such a way as also to approve them and take pleasure in them. He knows good things in such a manner that he is their author [Col. 1313D].

[Col. 1314A] [Note: [Col. 1313D] Distinction 37, ch. “And since, at the end.”] By many authorities of the holy Fathers it is shown that God is everywhere: he is present and powerful in every creature. Hence he himself says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23). Moreover, he dwells more excellently in his saints [Note: [Col. 1313D] Ch. “In the saints.”], in whom he is by grace, and who are his temple and seat. Thus the Lord himself says through Isaiah: “Heaven is my seat, but earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66). That is, God dwells and reigns in the elect, who are heaven and who devoutly obey his will; but he tramples the wicked, who are earth, in the severity of judgment.

Hence it is also said in the Book of Wisdom: “The soul of the righteous is the throne of wisdom,” because God is more specially in the righteous than in other things, though in all things he is wholly present. As blessed Augustine says in his letter to Jerome *On the Origin of the Soul*: “The soul is wholly present at once in every part of the body; it is not less in smaller parts nor greater in greater ones. Yet it acts more intensely in some and more remissly in others, although it is essentially present in every particle of the body.” So also God, though essentially and wholly present in human beings, is nevertheless said to be more fully in those whom he inhabits—namely, those in whom he is so present as to make them his temple; and persons such as these are with him. But the wicked, although they are where he is, who is absent nowhere, are nevertheless not with him. Blessed, therefore, are those who are with him, who enjoy him and see him as he is [Col. 1314B].

But if [Note: [Col. 1314D] Ch. “But if.”] you ask: “Where did God dwell before there were saints?” [Col. 1314C] we answer: he dwelt in himself. Hence the distinguished Augustine says against Maximinus, bishop of the heretics: “God dwells in his temple [Note: [Col. 1314D] This word remains.], namely in the saints, who are now the temple of God while they walk by faith; and at some time they will be [Note: [Col. 1314D] “Will be.”] the temple of God also by sight, as the angels too are now the temple of God. But someone will say: Before God made heaven and earth, before he made saints, where did he dwell? Beyond doubt God dwelt in himself. Without doubt, O human being, God dwells in you if you fear and love him, and he is with you. The saints therefore are not God’s house in such a way that, if it were removed, God would fall; rather, God so dwells in the saints that, if he should depart, they would fall.”

From the foregoing it is clear that God is wholly everywhere through essence, and dwells in the saints through grace [Col. 1314D].

It is also commonly asked by some [Note: [Col. 1314D] Ch. “It is commonly.”] how God can be substantially present in all things and yet not be touched by the defilements of bodily filth. This is so frivolous a question that it is not even worthy of an answer, since even a created spirit cannot be defiled by the filth of a body, even a leprous body or one polluted to whatever degree. The sun likewise sheds its rays without polluting itself upon places and bodies not only clean but also unclean and foul with filth. Human beings and certain other things are contaminated by contact with such things [Col. 1315A], but the rays of the sun remain unpolluted and uncontaminated while touching them.

It is therefore no wonder if the utterly simple and immutable divine essence fills every place and is essentially present in every creature, yet is neither contaminated nor touched by the filth of any thing. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On the Nature of the Good*: “Although all the things that God has created are in God, those who sin do not defile him” [Note: [Col. 1315D] “Not.”]. Of his Wisdom, “which reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8), it is said: “It reaches all things because of its purity, and nothing defiled comes into it” (Wis. 7).

The divine essence, therefore, is wholly everywhere: it contains the whole and penetrates the whole; because of its simplicity it cannot be divided, because of its purity it cannot be stained, and because of its immensity it cannot in any way be comprehended [Col. 1315B]. Hence Father Augustine also says: “God is everywhere; we approach him not by places but by actions.”

Augustine says in *On the Christian Conflict*: “Some fear what cannot happen—namely, that the truth and substance of God may be defiled in human flesh—yet they proclaim that the visible sun scatters its rays through every kind of refuse and filth, while keeping them pure and untainted. Therefore, if visible clean things can be touched by visible unclean things and not defiled, how much more so invisible and immutable Truth?”

And since [Note: [Col. 1315D] Ch. “And since.”] the divine nature is truly and essentially in every place and at every time, it nevertheless is not moved through places or times, nor is it local or temporal. It is not local because it is not at all circumscribed [Col. 1315C] by place: it is not in one place in such a way that it is not in another; nor does it have dimensions like a body, to which are assigned according to place beginning, middle, and end; front and back; right and left; above and below—by its interposition causing the surrounding things to be separated.

For Scripture calls something local or circumscribable in two ways, and conversely [Note: [Col. 1315D] This particle remains.]: either because, possessing the dimensions of length, height, and breadth, it causes spatial separation, as a body does; or because it is bounded and determined by a place, since, being somewhere, it is not found everywhere. This applies not only to bodies but to every created spirit as well.

Every body, then, is local in every respect. A created spirit, however, is local in one sense and non-local in another [Col. 1315D]. It is called local because it is limited by determination: when it is wholly present to one thing, it is not found elsewhere. The divine essence alone, therefore, is altogether non-local and uncircumscribed. It is not moved by places in any way, either through finite determination or assumed dimensions; nor is it moved by times—namely, in effect and knowledge, as has been said. For by these two, place and time, a creature changes; and the creature is far from the Creator.

Hence Father Augustine, commenting on Genesis, says: “God Almighty, by his immutability, eternity, will, and truth, always the same, moves the spiritual creature through time; he also moves the bodily creature through time and place, so as by that motion to govern the natures which he created. When, therefore, he does something of this kind, we must not suppose that his substance, which is God, is mutable in times and places or movable through times and places. For he is inward to every thing, because all things are in him; outward to all, because he is above all; older than all, because he is before all; and newer than all, because he is the same after all”—that is, after the beginnings of all things [Col. 1316A].

Here it is plainly shown that God is neither changed nor moved by places or times. The spiritual creature, however, is moved through time, whereas the bodily creature is moved through both time and place.

[Col. 1316B] To be changed [Note: [Col. 1316D] Ch. “To be changed.”] through time is to vary in inward or outward qualities existing in the thing that is changed—for example, when it undergoes alternations of joy, sorrow, knowledge, forgetfulness, or a change of form or of some outward quality. This change that occurs through time is a variation of qualities occurring in a bodily or spiritual creature, and for this reason is called time.

Created spirits, then [Note: [Col. 1316D] Ch. “Created spirits, then.”], are in a place and pass from place to place; in a certain sense they are local and circumscribable, though not in every way in which bodily creatures are. The uncreated Spirit, however—that is, God—is indeed in a place and in every place, yet is altogether non-local.

Hence the Venerable Bede, commenting on Luke, says: “When angels come to us, they fulfill their ministry outwardly in such a way that inwardly they nevertheless stand before God in contemplation. For although an angel is a circumscribed spirit, the highest Spirit, who is God, is uncircumscribed, and within him the angel runs wherever it is sent” [Col. 1316C]. Here it is said that the angelic spirit is circumscribed, whereas the Spirit who is God is uncircumscribed.

Likewise Saint Ambrose, showing the difference between the uncreated and created spirit, says that the seraph passes from place to place. Thus he says in *On the Trinity*: “Isaiah said that one of the seraphim was sent to me” (Isa. 6). “The Holy Spirit too is said to be sent, but the seraph is sent to one person, the Spirit to all. The seraph is sent in ministry, but the Spirit works the mystery. The seraph passes from place to place [Col. 1316D], for it does not fill all things, but is itself filled by the Spirit.” Here it is plainly shown that spirits are in a certain manner local.

Let us therefore confess [Note: [Col. 1316D] Ch. “Let us confess.”] that, by its immensity, the divine nature is absent nowhere; that it alone is altogether non-local and uncircumscribable; that it is enclosed by no place, but reaches from end to end—not by spatial magnitude or local motion, but by the immensity and immutability of its essence.

Hence blessed Augustine says to Dardanus: “We should not suppose that God is spread through all things by spatial magnitude, as earth or this light is spread abroad [Col. 1317A], but rather as there is one wisdom in two wise persons, one of whom is greater in body than the other but not wiser: wisdom is not greater in the greater person, nor less in the lesser, nor less in one than in two. So God, without labor governing and containing the world, is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, and wholly in both; he is contained by no place, but is wholly everywhere in himself.”

He also says: “It belongs to the Word of God not to be in a part, but to be everywhere through itself. For this is the Wisdom of God, which ‘reaches mightily from end to end’ (Wis. 8), yet not by local motion but by its own immobility. If, for example, some stony mass fills a place, it is said to reach from one end of that place to the other, although it does not leave one end by occupying the other [Col. 1317B]. That Word, therefore, has no local motion, and that Wisdom is solid and everywhere.”

From the foregoing it is clear that God is everywhere through essence in such a way that he is neither spread abroad by spatial magnitude nor occupies one place after abandoning another, because he has no local motion. Therefore wise Augustine, wishing to exclude from God’s purity every local motion and local circumscription, says rather that all things are in him than that he is somewhere; yet he is not a place, since he is not in a place. It now seems sufficiently demonstrated how all things are said to be in God, and God in all things (1 Cor. 15).

[Note: [Col. 1317D] Distinction 39, ch. “Furthermore.”] Furthermore, it is commonly asked whether God’s knowledge can increase or diminish. To this we reply that God’s knowledge [Col. 1317C] is altogether immutable and can neither increase nor diminish.

It remains to consider what predestination is and how it differs from foreknowledge. [Note: [Col. 1317D] Distinction 40, ch. “Predestination.”] Predestination is the preparation of grace, which cannot exist without foreknowledge; but wisdom [Note: [Col. 1317D] Edition: “foreknowledge.”] can exist without predestination. For by predestination God is said to foreknow those things which he himself was going to do. But God also foreknows the things which he himself is not going to do—that is, all evils. He predestined those whom he chose; but he reprobated the rest—that is, he foreknew that they would sin unto eternal death.

No one of the predestined [Note: [Col. 1317D] Ch. “Of the predestined.”] seems able to be damned, nor any of the reprobate able to be saved. Hence the venerable Father Augustine says in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “In the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 1317D] This word remains.], it is said: ‘Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown’” (Rev. 3). “If another cannot receive it unless this man loses it, the number of the elect is fixed: it can neither increase nor diminish” [Col. 1317D].

[Note: [Col. 1318D] Distinction 42, ch. “But to this.”] God the almighty Trinity is also truly and properly called omnipotent because through himself—that is, by natural power—he can do whatever he wills. For he wills nothing to be done that he cannot do through himself or through a creature [Col. 1318A]. Nothing can resist his will. Nor is will greater than power, nor power than will, because power and will are one and the same thing—namely, God himself [Note: [Col. 1318D] Distinction 43, ch. “But to these things.”]. He would be greater than himself if will were greater than power, or power than will.

We also confess that God can do many things which he does not will, and can refrain from things which he does do. To hold this more certainly and firmly, let us establish by testimonies of Scripture that God can do more than he does. Truth itself says in the Gospel according to Matthew: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26).
