These words plainly imply both that the Son could ask what he did not ask and that the Father could provide what he did not provide. Each, therefore [Col. 1318B], could do what he did not do.

Likewise blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “The will of the Almighty can do many things which it neither wills nor does. For he could have caused twelve legions of angels to fight against those who seized Christ.” Again, in the same work: “Why were miracles not performed among some people who would have repented had they been performed (Matt. 11), while they were performed among those who would not have believed? Then what is now hidden will not be hidden; nor did God surely will or do anything unjustly. But then, as has been said, it will be seen in the clearest light what the faith of the godly now holds before seeing it by manifest knowledge: how certain, immutable, and most efficacious is the will of God, which can do many things and does not will them.”

Blessed Augustine also says in *On Nature and Grace*: “The Lord raised Lazarus in body; must it be said that he could not raise Judas in mind? He certainly could, but by his hidden and just judgment he did not will it.” By these authorities and many others it is plainly taught that God can do many things which he does not will [Col. 1318C].

We must now say something concerning the will of God, according to the weakness of our understanding. [Note: [Col. 1318D] Distinction 45.] It must therefore be known that “will,” or “willing,” is said of God according to essence. For willing and being are not different things in him; they are altogether the same. This supremely good will, therefore [Note: [Col. 1318D] Ch. “This, therefore.”], is the cause of all things that naturally occur, or have occurred, or will occur, and no cause precedes it, because it is eternal. Therefore its cause must not be sought. For whoever seeks its cause seeks something greater than it, whereas nothing is greater than it.

Hence blessed Augustine says in the book *Eighty-Three Questions*: “Whoever asks why God willed to make the world seeks a cause of God’s will. But every efficient cause is greater than that which is effected; nothing, however, is greater than God’s will. Therefore its cause must not be sought.” The same author says in his book against the Manicheans: “If someone says, ‘What pleased God in making heaven and earth?’ one must reply that those who desire to know the will [Col. 1319A] of God seek to know the causes and will of God, whereas the will of God itself is the cause of all things that are. For if God’s will has a cause, something precedes God’s will—which it is impious to believe. Whoever therefore says, ‘Why did God make heaven and earth?’ must be answered: ‘Because he willed it.’ For the will of God is the cause of heaven and earth, and therefore God’s will is greater than heaven and earth. But whoever says, ‘Why did God will to make heaven and earth?’ seeks something greater than God’s will. But nothing greater can be found. Let human rashness therefore restrain itself, and not seek what does not exist, lest it fail to find what does exist.”

These authorities plainly show that God’s will has no cause and therefore its cause must not be sought [Col. 1319B].

The will [Note: [Col. 1319D] Ch. “Will.”] of God, as blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, is the first and highest cause of all forms and motions. For nothing [Note: [Col. 1319D] Supply: “comes to pass.”] occurs which does not proceed from the inward and intelligible court of the highest Emperor, and according to ineffable justice. For where does the wisdom of almighty God not work what it wills—the wisdom which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8)? It makes [Note: [Col. 1319D] Supply: “makes.”] not only things which, through the persistence of habit, do not admit astonishment, but also things which seem marvelous because of their rarity and unusual occurrence: such as eclipses of the heavenly lights—the sun, moon, and stars—earthquakes, the births of monstrous animals, and similar things. None of these happens except by God’s will, though this is not apparent to most people.

It therefore pleased the vanity of philosophers to attribute such things also to other causes, because they could not at all see the cause higher than all others: namely, God’s will. Thus God’s will alone is the first cause of health, sickness, rewards, punishments, graces, and recompenses. It alone is the source from which comes whatever exists, and it itself has not arisen but is eternal [Col. 1319C].

This must not be omitted [Note: [Col. 1319D] “This must not be omitted.”]: Sacred Scripture customarily speaks of God’s will in various ways. God’s will is not diverse, but the mode of speaking about it is diverse, because it receives different names [Note: [Col. 1319D] Edition: “name.”] for will. For the will of God, truly and properly so called, is that which is in him and is his essence. It is one, admits neither multiplicity nor change, and cannot remain unfulfilled. Of it the Prophet says: “The Lord has done all that he willed” (Ps. 113 [LXX]). And the Apostle says: “Who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9). Elsewhere he says: “That you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Rom. 12). This will is rightly called God’s good pleasure or disposition [Col. 1319D].

At times [Note: [Col. 1320D] Ch. “At times.”], however, by a manner of figurative speech, that which is not properly his will is called God’s will: command, prohibition, counsel, as well as permission and operation. Scripture consequently sometimes speaks of God’s “wills” in the plural. Thus the Prophet says: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110 [LXX]). Although there is only one will of God, which he himself is, it nevertheless says “wills” in the plural because, as has been said, God’s will is understood in various ways and for diverse purposes.

So too the king and prophet, because of the many effects of mercy and justice, says in the plural: “I will sing forever of the mercies of the Lord” (Ps. 88 [LXX]); and elsewhere: “The justices of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts” (Ps. 18 [LXX]). Yet in God there is one mercy and one justice, and the same mercy is justice [Col. 1320A].

For this reason [Note: [Col. 1320D] Ch. “For this reason.”] command, prohibition, and counsel, though three things, are each called the will of God, because these are figures or expressions of the divine will. God’s will may be understood as his command [Note: [Col. 1320D] Ch. “For command.”] and counsel, as in: “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth” (Matt. 6); and again: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12).

Many persons oppose this will of God. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “Unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel.” Yet it must not be understood that God wills everything to happen which he commands, or not to happen which he prohibits. He commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son (Gen. 22), yet [Col. 1320C] did not will it, nor did he command it in order that it might be done, but in order that Abraham’s faith might be tested. In the Gospel (Mark 1), he commanded the man who had been healed to tell no one; but that man proclaimed it everywhere, understanding that God had not prohibited this because he did not will his work not to be proclaimed, but in order to give humanity an example of avoiding human praise.

Since we have briefly set forth the foregoing concerning the Trinity and the unity of the divine essence from the sayings of the holy Fathers, for your benefit and that of posterity [Note: [Col. 1320D] From the book *On Saving Instruction*, chap. 1, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. VI], it is necessary, dearest brethren, that we say at least something to you about the love of that same Trinity. I wish you to know—although I do not myself fully know what justice is—that most perfect and complete justice is to love God with one’s whole heart and to cleave to Him with one’s whole will, since He is the highest good. But to love the highest good, as Saint Augustine says, is the highest blessedness. Whoever loves God is good; and if good, then blessed also. The more fervently one loves Him, the better and more blessed one becomes. Therefore, that He who is this good may make you abound in this most blessed good, beloved brethren, I strive daily, though unworthy, to entreat Him with the whole desire of my heart in prayer.

Understand, therefore, that you were created by the counsel of the same holy Trinity and by the work of the divine majesty. From the very dignity of your creation, consider how much you owe your Creator, since that eternal Creator Himself immediately granted you so great a privilege in your creation, that you might love Him the more ardently in proportion as you understand that you were made more wonderful by Him. And not only were you thus excellently created by the counsel of the holy Trinity: the Creator of all things also created you in His own image and likeness, a privilege granted to no other creature but human beings alone. This is the image of the unity and Trinity of almighty God which, as stated above, our soul possesses in itself: namely, three faculties—understanding, memory, and love. The same is also indicated, though in other words, in the Gospel when it says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your will” (Matt. 22). For in these three things, as blessed Augustine says, our inner human being bears in his nature the image of our Creator in a wonderful manner. From these, as the soul’s higher faculties, we are commanded to love the Creator: that He may be loved insofar as He is understood by us, and may always be retained in the memory by which He is received. Nor is it enough merely to understand God, unless our will is directed toward love of Him. Indeed, even this is insufficient unless, together with memory and will, work is added.

Moreover, I wish you to know, dearest brethren, that human riches consist in two things: knowledge and wisdom. Wisdom is to know God; knowledge is to know oneself. “Everyone,” says blessed Isidore [Note: [Col. 1321D] *Sentences*, book II, chap. 1], “who is wise according to God is blessed. A blessed life is knowledge of the Godhead. Knowledge of the Godhead is the power of good work. The power of good work is the fruit of eternity.” The first endeavor, therefore, is to seek God, as blessed Isidore says; then, uprightness of life together with the practice of innocence. No one, however, is more guilty than the person who does not know God.

We must therefore, as was said above, know God wisely, seek Him before all things, love Him above all things, and humbly know ourselves. But whoever knows himself grieves over himself and for himself, because he has cause for grief. Hence Solomon says: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclus. 1). For the more a person knows himself, the more he finds reasons for grief, as does he who says: “I found tribulation and sorrow” (Ps. 114), that is, the misery and affliction of the flesh which I formerly endured without understanding it. And elsewhere: “My sorrow is always before me” (Ps. 37). But whoever grieves seeks consolation; and what he seeks he finds, God granting it. Hence the Paraclete Spirit is given by the Father and the Son, who consoles us amid the labors and sorrows of this present life. Such knowledge—namely, self-knowledge—is the way of salvation. To wish to go to God without this knowledge is rather to go farther away. Of this the prophet says: “My people perished because they had no knowledge” (Isa. 5). For how can one who does not know himself know God? Or how can one who does not grieve over himself and humbly lament for himself please God?

What is nearer, what is more intimate, what is more akin to a person than that person himself? Yet wretched man more anxiously seeks to know the things outside himself than the things within him. It is therefore necessary that a person love God above all things, humbly know himself, and grieve for himself, so that this fountain of love may flow forth to his neighbor. Hence it is written in the Law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19). But how can one who does not love himself love another? And when he does not grieve for himself, how will he grieve for another? “He who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” Therefore let him first drink from his own fountain, and afterward let the waters of his own well be led abroad (Prov. 5).

But people overturn this order, desiring first to know what is outside themselves rather than themselves. They become wise concerning outward things, ignorant of themselves; they search out the depths of another person’s heart, while wholly ignorant of their own. Of them the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know” (1 Cor. 8). How many labors, expenses, and outlays do they endure in order to know the courses of the sun, moon, and stars, and the circuit of heaven! Yet they are ignorant of themselves, possessing, as the Apostle says, “the form of knowledge and truth” (Rom. 2); but “knowledge is not in all” (1 Cor. 8). They labor to know what they could safely remain ignorant of, and they neglect to acquire the knowledge without which they cannot be saved.

For knowledge of outward things, upon which they so exclusively fix their attention, is fleeting and perishable: “Tongues will cease, prophecies will be abolished, knowledge will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13). Elsewhere the Lord says of this same carnal knowledge: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (Isa. 29). Why? Because “the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God” (Rom. 8). Hence blessed John the Evangelist [Note: [Col. 1322D] Rather: James the Apostle] says: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world becomes an enemy of God” (James 4). Yet though this is so, a person deceived goes out through the windows of the body, exiles himself from himself, and wanders through the form of this world, which is passing away (1 Cor. 7). In these outward things, where there is no knowledge to be learned, he seeks what is a deceptive knowledge for salvation, since it does not do what it promises.

The knowledge of this world does not make a person wise, but puffed-up and proud. Hence the Apostle: “Knowledge puffs up; love builds up” (1 Cor. 8). Some, too, through that same knowledge of outward things, imagining themselves to be wise, became foolish and vanished in their reasonings. “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1). Whoever, then, imagines that he knows anything through this outward knowledge knows almost nothing, and deceives himself. Whereas elsewhere one person is deceived and another deceives, here the same person is both deceiver and deceived. Therefore let a person at last return to himself, enter into his soul, and know himself. For once he knows himself, he cannot fail to know God, in whose image and likeness he was made.

And, to omit other matters, let him endeavor to learn of himself whether he is worthy of hatred or of love (Ecclus. 9). For who knows whether he is worthy of hatred or love? But the elect, who truly know themselves and truly grieve over and for themselves, are thereby consoled by God, because they have certain signs and testimonies through which they know that they are worthy of love; and “in the way of God’s testimonies” they delight as in all riches (Ps. 118). No rich person in his riches, no wealthy person in his money, no ambitious person in his dignities and honors, delights as much as the servants of God do in possessing already certain signs and testimonies of God’s love.

They already have testimonies indeed: namely, gifts of spiritual grace and the proclamations of the Evangelists—not for security, however, but for consolation. Thus they have true knowledge of themselves, since they already hold some pledge of love. “Those whom God the Father foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, He also called; and those whom He called, He also justified” (Rom. 8). Behold: the justification granted to a human being in the present through the grace of the Holy Spirit is both testimony concerning the past, that they were predestined, and hope concerning the future, that they will be glorified. Hence the Psalmist says: “This comforted me in my humiliation, because your word will give me life” (Ps. 118). This is that spiritual grace [Col. 1323C] which is granted and offered to the elect, although unequally. Therefore God’s servants have gifts, that is, grace, which has been given to them in different measure (Rom. 12). For the Holy Spirit distributes gifts to each person—indeed, gives even Himself to them—as He wills (1 Cor. 12).

If, therefore, O servant of God, you wish to be glorified in the future, strive to be justified in the present age and to be conformed to the image of the Son of God. Justice, godliness, and mercy are the image of God and man, Jesus Christ. Therefore you will be more like Christ to the extent that you are more just. Seek justice, then, and you will find it; you will lay hold of it, and it will meet you like an honored mother (Ecclus. 15). And after you have it, it will itself be testimony to you that you are now worthy not of hatred but of love, because those whom God justifies He undoubtedly also glorifies. Therefore, if those who truly know themselves truly grieve over and for themselves, and while grieving deserve to be consoled by the Holy Spirit through testimonies of this kind, it is certain that they are children of God, although it does not yet appear what they will be in the future (2 John 3, as cited), so long as their life, as the Apostle says (Col. 3), is hidden with Christ in God.

Now these testimonies are many: “For there are three who bear witness in heaven: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three who bear witness on earth: namely, the spirit, the water, and the blood” (John 5). We have testimony from the Holy Spirit, because “God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Gal. 4). And the Spirit Himself bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Rom. 8).

We also have testimony from water and blood. For from the side of Jesus Christ our Lord flowed these two greatest sacraments, the incomparable riches of our salvation, and the abundant redemption of the human race (John 19): water, namely, for washing, and blood for redemption. For the place in which we were held captive was an unclean and muddy prison. Hence the Psalmist said: “Deliver me from the mire, lest I sink” (Ps. 68)—from the mire, that is, of sins; from the wallowing-place of vices. Therefore, because we were defiled, water flowed from Christ’s side so that we might be washed; because we were held captive, blood came forth so that we might be redeemed. Hence in the book of Revelation it is said to the same God and man, Jesus Christ: “You redeemed—that is, acquired—us for God the Father by your blood” (Rev. 5); and thus with Him was “abundant redemption” (Ps. 129).

Water gives testimony because a person displays, in purity of conscience and newness of life, the washing away of sins which he receives in baptism. Those are proved to have been washed by water whom a holy and innocent life testifies to have been truly cleansed from sins. But he does not have testimony from water who, defiling himself with the filth of vices, retains scarcely any, or only slight, sign of the purity received in baptism. Water does not bear testimony to those in whom its effect is plainly known to have perished, and who never appear to have been washed by water, since no signs of their former washing are recognized in them. Such persons must be washed anew—not with the water of baptism, but with the tears of inward compunction. Hence King and Prophet David says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall soak my couch” (Ps. 6).

He has testimony from the blood who, by resisting vices, preserves the lordship of his redemption and freedom, and fights with the weapons of justice at the right hand and at the left for the defense of his homeland and liberty. For those are free to whom it is said: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8); and: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3). But “whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Him” (Rom. 8); rather, he is a slave of sin. For “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8), and the Holy Spirit also flees from him, because, as Solomon says: “He will not dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1).

Although one has been redeemed by Christ’s blood, whoever is held bound by the devil’s chains of vices is not Christ’s servant. For how can he boast that he has been redeemed by Christ’s blood when every injustice rules him, and sin still reigns in his mortal body? Or how can he say that he has been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity when he serves the devil more than God? Besieged by enemies, he has given them weapons for his own destruction; withdrawing from the stronghold of reason, captive beneath the dominion of evil habit and carnal pleasure, no longer his own master but another’s, he is compelled to serve as many masters as he has vices. Sold under sin, as though under Pharaoh, in mud and brick he serves uncleanness and iniquity.

But God’s elect, knowing their own sorrow, seek consolation with longing, searching with their whole heart for these and similar testimonies of God; and, as the Psalmist says, they fulfill “their desire from them” (Ps. 126). They have testimony from the Holy Spirit that they are worthy of love, because “those who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (Rom. 8)—namely, those who by God’s Spirit put to death the deeds of the flesh. Thus, as has been said, they know themselves to be worthy of love, their own conscience bearing testimony to them (Rom. 2), because “this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). By these testimonies, God of all consolation, who consoles the humble, consoles us also in all our tribulation; and as Christ’s sufferings abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds [Col. 1325B] (ibid.). Hence the Psalmist says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations made my soul glad” (Ps. 93). And thus, filled with consolation, “we abound in joy in every tribulation” (2 Cor. 7). Therefore, consoled by these testimonies mentioned above, we glory in the hope of the children of God (Rom. 5).

We must therefore, dearest brethren, as stated above, seek before all things the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—that is, the one true God; and, having found Him, faithfully believe in Him, love Him in all things and above all things. In His freely bestowed goodness He first deigned to create us from nothing, and, after the most grievous fault of the first parent’s transgression, mercifully to restore us to the first—indeed, to a better—state. We believe that no one can attain true blessedness except through true faith. Blessed is the person who both lives well by believing rightly and, by living well, keeps the right faith. “If God is believed,” says blessed Isidore, “He is rightly invoked and sought; and thereby He is perfectly praised when He is believed” [Note: [Col. 1325D] From blessed Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chap. 2].

If soldiers of this age, about to receive temporal gifts from the rulers of this world, are first bound by secular oaths and profess that they will keep faith with their masters, how much more ought those who are to serve the eternal King and receive eternal rewards to be bound by heavenly sacraments and publicly profess the faith by which they are to please Him? For the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). He who searches hearts and reins recognizes this faith in our hearts (Rom. 8); but, for preserving the unity of the Church, in this present dispensation confession with the mouth is necessary together with faith of the heart: “For with the heart one believes unto justice, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10)—not only for preachers but also for hearers.

For otherwise one brother could not rightly judge another, the peace of the Church could not be preserved, and neither teaching another nor learning from another could be necessary for salvation, unless one transmitted what he possesses in his heart to the hearts of others by the signs of words, as by its own vehicles. Faith, therefore, must be kept in the heart and expressed by the mouth. For faith is the foundation of all good things [Note: [Col. 1326D] From the book *On Faith to Peter*, in the Prologue] and the beginning of human salvation. Without it no one can come to the number or fellowship of God’s elect, because without it one receives neither the grace of justification in this age nor possesses eternal life in the age to come. And if anyone does not walk by faith, he will not attain sight.

Considering this, the holy apostles handed down a sure rule of faith, which, gathered into twelve statements corresponding to the number of the apostles, they called the Creed; by it believers might retain catholic unity and refute heretical perversity. When priests of the Church admit persons into the fellowship of the Christian religion, they ought therefore to deliver the Creed to them and thus confirm the beginning of faith by a covenant. Thus the holy apostles, binding together spiritual unity among themselves, composed this Creed.

Therefore let everyone who, professing the apostolic faith, spoke through the mouths of the godparents who bore him at baptism, when he has come to years of understanding say for himself: “I believe in God.” And what he professes with his mouth, let him meditate upon in his heart. He did not say, “I believe that God is” or “I believe God,” although these too are necessary for salvation. For it is one thing to believe that God exists; another to believe God, because He is truthful. As James the Apostle testifies: “Even the demons believe and tremble” (James 2). But they do not believe *in* God, because in believing they are not moved to go toward His will. Therefore the spirit of fear does not benefit demons, because they do not possess the spirit of love.

But we, who are children of God through the adoption of grace, should say: “I believe in God the Father almighty”—that is, we believe in Him in such a manner that we cleave to Him through love. He is called Father because before all times He begot a Son coeternal with Himself.

“Almighty Creator of heaven and earth”: that is, He who by His omnipotence is the Maker of heavenly and earthly things, that is, of visible and invisible things, so that no one may doubt that God can make these things when he has heard that He is almighty. These words were spoken against the Gentiles, who in their unbelief thought the images which they had made to be gods, abandoning the true God by whom they themselves had been made.

It follows: “And in Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord.” As one must believe in the Father, so also in the Son; and because He is equal in majesty with the Father according to His divinity, we owe Him as much honor as the Father, because by nature He is one true God with Him. Hence He Himself says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10). And again: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (John 5). For the Father is in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one true God; therefore, as the Father is honored, so must the Son be honored.

Jesus is interpreted “Savior”; Christ is named from *chrism* [anointing], because, as ancient kings were anointed with holy oil, so our Lord Jesus Christ was filled with the infusion of the Holy Spirit. These things show that He is rightly to be believed in, since besides being equal to the Father He is our Savior, redeeming us; and, as our only Lord, after conquering and despoiling His ancient enemy, He mercifully subjected us to His light and most sweet yoke.

“Who was conceived of the Holy Spirit”: the Holy Spirit, namely, was the author of this conception, though not without God the Father, because the operation of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is inseparable. For as a worm is formed from pure mud when the sun warms it, so Christ’s flesh was conceived from the virginal flesh alone of His Virgin Mother, the Holy Spirit enlightening and sanctifying the Virgin’s heart, with no seed-origin of flesh at work. Hence, comparing Himself to a worm, He says through the Psalmist: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21), that is, not conceived in the human manner.

“Born of the Virgin Mary”: that is, as in being conceived He did not open His mother’s womb, so in being born He did not corrupt it. For through the power and might of the Creator at work, “the Word was made flesh” (John 1): that is, He was made man, conceived from a Virgin and born of a Virgin, with the Father and Holy Spirit cooperating.

“Suffered under Pontius Pilate.” The mention of Pilate pertains to marking the time, not to the dignity of the person.

“Crucified, dead, and buried.” The weaknesses of the human being assumed by the Word are recalled, concerning which the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than men” (1 Cor. 1). For this reason He suffered: that He might restore us to impassibility. For this reason He was crucified: that He might free us from eternal torments. For this reason He was buried: that He might withdraw us from vices and desires and bury us with Himself. Hence the Apostle says: “We were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6)—that is, putting aside every oldness, we may be conformed to the likeness of God and man, Jesus Christ. Thus this weakness of Christ overcame all the strength of this world.

“On the third day He rose from the dead” [Note: [Col. 1327D] From Sermon 224, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. V]. The delay of the three-day burial clearly shows that, while the body lay in the tomb, that soul triumphed over the underworld [Note: [Col. 1328D] Supply here: “He ascended into heaven.”]. Therefore He placed above the heavens, at the right hand of God the Father, the condition of our nature which He assumed when born of the Virgin Mother, so that, making intercession to God the Father for us according to that nature, He may always show what manner of death He underwent. But His being said to sit does not indicate a bodily posture, but judicial authority.

“He sits at the right hand of God the Father almighty.” By the right hand we understand the highest blessedness and the glory of God the Father, just as by the left hand we understand the misery in which the goats are to be placed (Matt. 25). Therefore let every tongue confess that our Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2).

“From there He shall come to judge the living and the dead.” He shall judge the living: namely, those whom His coming finds alive, who nevertheless will die and rise again in an instant and be judged by Him. He shall judge the dead: that is, those who had long ago died He will raise up and judge according to their merits. Yet, as blessed Paul the Apostle says: “The dead who are in Christ shall rise first and shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so shall always be with Him” (1 Thess. 4). Alternatively: He shall judge the living and the dead—that is, the righteous and sinners.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit,” equal and consubstantial with the Father and the Son, proceeding from both. Therefore He must be believed in as the Father and the Son are believed in. It follows:

“The holy catholic Church”: that is, the Church of the whole world—not that church of which it is said, “Behold, here,” or “Behold, there,” that is, the one said to be in a chamber or in the wilderness—but that which is spread throughout the whole world and established in the unity of faith.

“The communion of saints”: that is, the reality of the Church’s sacraments, in which the saints who departed this life in the unity of faith shared.

“The remission of sins”: not only of those sins remitted through baptism, but also of those cleansed through humble confession and worthy satisfaction.

“The resurrection of the flesh,” which will be common to all at the Lord’s coming, though different for the good and the evil, as the Apostle says: “We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15)—that is to say, changed for the better.

“Life everlasting”: this is what the same Apostle says: “This corruptible thing must put on incorruption,” that is, immortality (ibid.).

These twelve articles, which most firmly belong to the rule of true faith, must be believed faithfully, held firmly, and defended truthfully and patiently. If we know anyone teaching doctrines contrary to them, let us flee from him as from a pestilence; let us reject him as a heretic. For these statements set forth above are so arranged and summed up in concise words, and accord so fully with the catholic faith and oppose heretical perversity, that those who cling firmly to this rule do not allow themselves to err or depart from the path of right faith. But if anyone wishes to think otherwise, let us pray that God may deign to reveal this to him. For our part, let us walk in what we have received and persevere firmly in what is certain to us.

Teach this Creed, dearest brethren, to your spiritual children, for whom you made a pledge at baptism, whom you received from the sacred font. Teach it also to your children whom you begot from your flesh; teach it to those whom you have received in order to rear them, so that through this evangelical teaching and your instruction they may avoid error, flee what is hostile to Christian faith, and accomplish with all their strength what is fitting.

Since, then, beloved, a little above we mentioned the future resurrection common to all human beings, which is to be celebrated at the end of the world, let us diligently hear what blessed Gregory says concerning it: “It is sad,” he says [Note: [Col. 1329D] Book II of the *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily 8, no. 6. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 1030], “exceedingly and very mournful,” etc., as far as: “But in miracles the only reason is the power of the doer.”

Therefore faith, dearest brethren, as stated above, must be kept in the heart and expressed by the mouth, because it is the first gate of the heavenly kingdom, the beginning of human salvation, and the strongest foundation of good works. We therefore believe that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one true God, Creator of heaven and earth, the most generous rewarder of righteous people and the most just condemner of the ungodly. He is one in essence and three in persons; abundant in mercy, almighty in works. He created from nothing all things in heaven, on earth, and in the sea, and He will raise the bodies of all people on the last day. For the Son of God will give to His voice a voice of power (Ps. 67), and all people will rise before Him with their bodies.

This is the catholic—that is, universal—faith, which the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments held in their works and left in their writings for our everlasting salvation. And because they themselves held this true faith whole and entire in word and deed, as has been said, and handed it down for us to hold, they were also gates for us through which we entered into the knowledge of God.

These were aptly prefigured by the three outer and three inner gates which Ezekiel saw on the east, north, and south, and which were ascended by seven or eight steps. Therefore, since by the name of gates we understand holy preachers [Note: [Col. 1329D] St. Gregory, book II of the *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily 8, [Col. 1330D] no. 2. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 1028], etc., as far as: “And thus the Psalm written for the eighth begins with dread of judgment when it says: ‘O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your wrath’” (Ps. 6). As though he said:

Lord, to whom I submit myself as servant, rebuke me inwardly in this world, lest You rebuke me in Your fury—that is, lest You condemn me to eternal condemnation in the future. For one who is rebuked is accused, because condemnation follows accusation. But we are outwardly rebuked when we fast, keep vigils, endure tribulations, and beseech God with tears not to condemn us for our sins before His justice. It is as though he said: Correct me inwardly in this age, that is, by inducing compunction and summoning me to repentance, lest You correct me in Your fury in the other world; lest, namely, You make me pass through that purgatorial fire through which all those pass who, having Christ as their foundation, build upon it straw, hay, and stubble.

And, lest You correct and lest You rebuke me, have mercy on me—that is, show mercy to me—“for I am weak” (ibid.), namely in good works.

For now is the time of mercy; but at that judgment there will be a day of wrath, the day on which this whole period that unfolds in seven days will end. What follows after seven days is rightly called the eighth; on that day our flesh also will rise from the dust and receive from Christ the just Judge whatever it has done, whether good or evil. Hence under the Law circumcision was commanded on the eighth day as well (Lev. 12). For by the member which is circumcised mortal generation is produced; the number of those departing and those succeeding is increased. But because in the resurrection of the dead neither propagation of the flesh will take place any longer nor will there be departure and succession, since “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22), the foreskin is commanded to be cut away on the eighth day. Where propagation of the flesh no longer has a place, there the risen flesh possesses the permanence of eternity.

Through this member the Virgin Mother came down, who conceived God in her womb without the admixture of male flesh. He first showed us, in His resurrection, the glory of the eternal homeland: He who, “rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over Him” (Rom. 6). He gave us an example that we should believe that on the last day these things will happen to our flesh which we know happened to His flesh on the day of resurrection.

Therefore, since mention of carnal circumcision has presented itself to us, I wonder, Jews, by what madness or superstition you circumcise yourselves and your children to this day, although you have long known that this same carnal circumcision came to an end in Christ. Question also blessed Paul, born from your people and educated at the feet of Gamaliel, your teacher, most thoroughly instructed in the Mosaic Law and the oracles of the prophets; and whatever he answers you concerning this same carnal circumcision, hear with a devout mind: “If you are circumcised,” he says, “Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5).

Know, O Jews, and do not doubt at all, that Christ was promised to you through the patriarchs and prophets, and was sent by God the Father in the fullness of time. Hence He Himself says in the Gospel: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). Blessed Paul says of Him: “When the fullness of time came, God sent His Son, made of a woman, made under the Law, that He might redeem those who were under the Law” (Gal. 4)—that is, you, who were oppressed under the yoke of the Law and weighed down by its burden, which, as blessed Paul says [Note: [Col. 1330D] Rather: Peter] in the Acts of the Apostles (chap. 15), neither you nor your fathers could bear.

But because, O Jews, you refused not only to receive adoption as sons, but even took up stones in the Temple in order to throw them at the Son of God and the Virgin, specially promised to you by God the Father, while He humbly and powerfully avoided your madness, hid Himself, and went out of the Temple (John 8), we therefore see fulfilled what He said in your hearing: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. 23). For He had first commanded His disciples not to go into the way of the Gentiles (Matt. 10), but rather to go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. But after you drove out Him and His disciples and persecuted them from city to city, thereby making yourselves enemies of justice, He commanded His disciples generally, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). And He added: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16).

Know therefore, O Jews, that after this decree carnal circumcision no longer has its former effect. If, then, you are circumcised, as blessed Paul said long ago, Christ will profit you nothing, because He instituted baptism for the remission of sins for all who faithfully believe in the Father, in Himself, and in the Holy Spirit. For He Himself is naturally one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. It was indeed for this purpose that He, sent by God the Father, came into the world: to give new commandments to the world. He was a new man because He was conceived without male seed in the Virgin’s womb and lived in the world without sin. Therefore, because He was sent by God the Father for your salvation and that of the whole world, O Jews, you ought to obey Him in all things.

It is commonly said: “Whoever despises a physician’s commands kills himself” [Note: He kills himself who does not wish to observe a physician’s commands. Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 12, no. 12.]. Know with certainty and do not doubt at all that, if you are disobedient to Him, you render yourselves liable to eternal condemnation. Therefore embrace that Son of God and of the Virgin with the arms of faith and love, that you may deserve to be mercifully received by Him within the bosom of the holy Church.

Receive with devout mind the baptism established by Him for the remission of your sins, so that you may obtain from Him true pardon for your ancient rebellion and unbelief. Nor do I wish you to be unaware, O Jews, that, compelled by charity, I desire you to be companions of God’s elect. [Col. 1331D] Therefore obey me, who desire the salvation of your souls and wish you to be within the bosom of holy Church, and I shall give you counsel by which you may recover the former grace of Jesus Christ, God and man, who is truly one and the true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and, after this life, attain the joys of the heavenly homeland. Have no adverse suspicion of me either, for you will find in me the fidelity of true counsel. For thus you read in the Old Testament: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI; Lev. XIX). In this respect I love you as myself, because I desire you to attain eternal joys.

[Col. 1332A] Therefore lend a patient ear to my admonitions, and I shall teach you how circumcision found its fulfilment in Jesus Christ, the Son of God and of the Virgin. For Christ was to come according to the flesh from the seed of Abraham, in whom the blessing of all nations had been promised [Note: [Col. 1332D] Isidore, *Against the Jews*, book II, ch. 16.]; and God, foreseeing that Abraham’s race might mingle with the other peoples, and that its descent might gradually become uncertain, marked the Jewish people with the sign of circumcision. Thus he commanded the Jews to be circumcised, so that, when they came among the Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, or Chaldeans, they might be distinguished by this seal from them and from other peoples and nations. Indeed, during the forty years in the wilderness no one was circumcised, for they lived alone, without intermingling with any nation. But when the Israelite people crossed the channel of the Jordan [Col. 1332B] and came into the land of promise, circumcision provided against the future error arising from mingling with the nations.

We believe that this circumcision was reasonably kept until Christ should be born, who had been promised from Abraham’s seed; he commanded that the hearts of all nations be circumcised no longer by circumcision of the flesh, but by cutting away vices.

But if you refuse, O Jews, to believe me, a Christian man bearing the standard of Christ upon my forehead, I ask you carefully to hear what Moses foretold to you concerning this same circumcision of the heart. “In the last days,” he says, “the Lord will circumcise your heart, O Israel, and the heart of your seed” (Deut. XXX). What else did he foretell by these words than the future coming of Christ, [Col. 1332C] by which the foreskins of the flesh are no longer cut with iron, but hearts are cleansed from sins by baptism? Through Moses the lawgiver, therefore, carnal circumcision was commanded in the Law; and through that same Moses, in the New Testament, the future remission of sins through baptism and contrition of heart was foretold. Since, then, he foretold the future spiritual circumcision, what else did he proclaim except that the circumcision of the flesh, practised under the Law, would be abolished at Christ’s coming?

Thus Jeremiah too, foreseeing that this time was already near, summons the Jews to the New Testament and to circumcision of the heart rather than the body, saying: “Thus says the Lord to the man of Judah and Jerusalem: Break up your fallow ground, [Col. 1332D] and do not sow among thorns; be circumcised to the Lord your God, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and Jerusalem, lest my indignation go forth like fire and burn, with none to quench it” (Jer. III). By these words Israel is urged to pass from the oldness of circumcision and the Law, which is compared to thorns, to the grace of the New Testament; and, through faith in Christ, to maintain circumcision of the heart rather than the flesh, as we read the apostle Peter saying of the Lord: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV).

Likewise, the Lord announces through Isaiah that this faith is now to be attained not through the ancient bodily signs and injury to the body, but through the new grace of the spiritual washing, [Col. 1333A] saying: “Do not remember the former things, nor look upon things of old. Behold, I shall make new things, which will now spring up, and you shall know them” (Isa. XLIII). And, to show what these were, he added: “I shall make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the waterless place, to give drink to my chosen people and the people whom I acquired” (*ibid.*). What else, then, O Jews, did he indicate by these words except the future cleansing of baptism? In it no one is now marked by the old circumcision of the flesh; rather, one is washed by the grace of the whole Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and by the water of baptism through faith in Christ Jesus.

Jeremiah the prophet foretold this deadly obstinacy of your heart, O Jews, by which you refuse to receive spiritual circumcision: “All the nations have a foreskin; but the house of Israel alone [Col. 1333B] is uncircumcised in heart” (Jer. IX). Moreover, the fact that the Hebrew people are read to have been circumcised a second time by Joshua their leader after their departure from Egypt (Josh. V) signified that, afterwards, the children of the Church, whose leader he is, would be cleansed by the Lord and Savior through circumcision of the heart. And fittingly this second circumcision was with stone knives: for “the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X), through whom believers are cleansed by spiritual circumcision from every enticement of vice.

See how the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments agree with one another and entirely nullify your carnal circumcision, O Jews. They agree in true judgments and destroy the error of your superstition. Why, then, wretches that you are, do you always wish [Col. 1333C] to observe carnally the legal commandments which, as is evident, came to an end at the coming of Jesus Christ our Redeemer? The precepts of the old Law must be understood spiritually, not obeyed carnally.

What we have said, O Jews, concerning carnal circumcision—that it long ago received fulfilment and an end in Christ, and that after the spiritual precepts of the Gospel it should no longer be observed carnally—we say also concerning the rejection of victims and sacrifices offered under the old Law [Note: [Col. 1333D] Isidore, as above, ch. 17.]. But perhaps, O rebellious and unbelieving people, you refuse to believe me. Hear the Lord himself sharply rebuking you through Isaiah the prophet and rejecting your sacrifices and solemn observances in these words:

“What use to me is the multitude of your victims? says the Lord. I am full [Col. 1333D] of the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fatlings; I have not desired the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Offer sacrifice in vain no longer. Incense is an abomination to me. New moons, Sabbaths, and other festivals I shall not endure: your assemblies are wicked. My soul has hated your calends and solemnities; they have become burdensome to me; I have grown weary of enduring them. And when you stretch out your hands, I shall turn my eyes away from you; and when you multiply prayer, I shall not hear” (Isa. V).

Again Isaiah says of the same sacrifices, now rejected [Col. 1334A] or almost nonexistent: “Their carcasses have become like dung in the midst of the streets” (Isa. V). What are these carcasses, O unhappy and miserable Jews, except your carnal sacrifices, now made void after Christ’s passion—Christ who offered himself immaculate to God the Father as an offering and sacrifice of sweetness for the redemption of the human race? And since those carnal sacrifices have now been removed from the Lord’s altar, they are reckoned by believers as dung.

Likewise Isaiah the prophet says of those sacrifices: “He who sacrifices an ox is as though he [Note: [Col. 1333D] Supply: *he who*.] killed a man; he who slaughters a beast is as though he smashed a dog’s head; he who offers an oblation is as though he offered swine’s blood; he who makes memorial of incense is as though he blessed an idol” (Isa. LXVI).

You have heard, O Jews, what the Lord has thus far said through Isaiah the prophet concerning [Col. 1334B] the rejection of carnal sacrifice. Hear also what he says through Jeremiah concerning the refusal of your victims and burnt offerings: “Why do you offer me incense from Sheba and sweet-smelling reed from a far country? Your burnt offerings and victims have not pleased me. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bring ruin upon my people, and fathers and sons alike shall fall among them; neighbor and friend together shall perish” (Jer. VI). See, therefore, O crooked and perverse Jewish people, that your sacrifices are not praised or received by almighty God in themselves as carnal acts, but only through contrition of heart and obedience of faith—things which you miserable people have lost.

Therefore the Lord adds through the same [Col. 1334C] prophet, saying: “This is the word which I commanded the children of Israel on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt: Hear my voice, and I shall be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in all the commandments which I command you, that it may be well with you. But they did not hear, nor incline their ear; instead they went after their own pleasures and the perversity of their evil heart” (Jer. VII). And after this, detesting your sacrifices, O Jews, the same prophet says [Note: [Col. 1333D] Through a lapse of memory, says John Mariana concerning this passage of [Col. 1334D] Isidore, passages from different books are cited in place of one another; for words of Hosea are attributed to Jeremiah.]:

“They shall offer victims, slaughter flesh, and eat; but the Lord will not receive them” (Hos. VIII). “They shall not pour out wine to the Lord,” he says, “nor will their sacrifices please him; they are like the bread of mourners. All who eat them shall be defiled, and they shall not enter the house of the Lord” (Hos. IX).

The words of the prophet Joel also agree, O blind people, with those of Isaiah and Jeremiah concerning the rejection of carnal sacrifices. For he says: “Sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God” (Joel I).

Undoubtedly these things are true, as you see: you build no altar, have no priests, offer no sacrifice, and observe no Law; and therefore you are no longer Jews—that is, confessors—but the synagogue of Satan. Because you crucified without cause the Son of God and of the Virgin, who fed you in the wilderness for forty years with the bread of angels and gave you drink from the rock, you lost your place and nation [Col. 1335A] and were handed over into captivity among all nations under heaven.

That your carnal sacrifices were to be driven from God’s altar, while the spiritual sacraments of Christ’s body were to remain until the end of the world, is attested by the prophet Micah [Note: [Col. 1335D] Correctly emended in another manuscript: *Malachi*.] in the voice of the Lord: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I shall not regard an offering from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place sacrifice is made and a clean offering is offered to my name; for my name is great among the nations, says the Lord” (Mal. I). By this testimony, O Jews, it is clear that your sacrifices are unclean and rejected, and that the offering of the nations alone—that is, of the children of the Church—is acceptable to God.

Therefore abandon carnal circumcision, and receive with devout mind baptism, [Col. 1335B] in which remission of sins is established, in the name of the whole Trinity—the Father, namely, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that you may deserve to share spiritual gifts with the other faithful.

You also, O wretched and pitiable Jews, keep the Sabbath carnally and yet entirely fail to know what the Sabbath is. You would keep it rightly if you understood it spiritually [Note: [Col. 1335D] From the same Isidore, *ibid.*, ch. 15.]. You therefore appropriate the name of Sabbath, since you observe it not spiritually but carnally. You delight in keeping the Law carnally, although you ought to understand it spiritually, as the Lord testifies through the Prophet: “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning” (Ps. LXXVII).

[Col. 1335C] As though he said: Incline your ear, because I shall open my mouth in parables, that is, in sayings having a likeness of things. Observe that propositions are questions containing something that must be resolved by argument. Propositions and parable differ in this: a parable expresses a resemblance, whereas propositions may be understood without a resemblance. He therefore says, “I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter propositions from the beginning,” because all that we heard promised in the Old Testament we have learned to be fulfilled in the New Testament, and this our fathers have told us (*ibid.*). Who says this? David the prophet, of course. The fathers of the Old Testament—that is, the patriarchs and prophets—therefore told us these things.

If, then, O Jews, the Law and the Prophets consist in parables and enigmas, as you cannot possibly deny, Sabbath observance must not be understood carnally but spiritually. For its carnal rest has been entirely set aside both by the Lord and by the Fathers. We read in Genesis (ch. II) that God blessed the seventh day and sanctified it, because on it he had rested from all his work which he had accomplished [Note: [Col. 1335D] *Sentences* II, distinction 15, ch. “But the question is raised.”]. Yet he is not said to have created anything new on that day, unless perhaps it be said that he completed the work on the seventh day, which he blessed and sanctified.

[Col. 1336A] For, as Master Peter says in the book *On the Creation of Things*, blessing and sanctification are works; for Solomon too did some work when he dedicated the Temple. Thus God is said to have sanctified and blessed the seventh day because he bestowed on it a mystical blessing and sanctification surpassing the rest [Note: [Col. 1335D] Chapter “That Day.”]. Hence it is said in the Law: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX) [Note: [Col. 1336D] Again Isidore.].

Again, if it is a crime, O Jews, not to observe Sabbath rest, say why Joshua, Moses’ disciple and successor, by the Lord’s command, for seven consecutive days—including, of course, the Sabbath—marched out the army and weapons, and, while the ark went round and trumpets sounded, overthrew the walls of Jericho (Josh. VI). Again, what shall I say of the Maccabees, of whom it is written: “The Jews were unwilling on the Sabbath day [Col. 1336B] to defend themselves against the foreigners; but afterwards, having adopted a plan, they fought on the Sabbath day and triumphed over their enemies” (I Macc. II)? By these testimonies we are taught that this elementary Sabbath day does not belong to faith, but another, spiritual Sabbath does.

Know, therefore, O Jews, that this carnal Sabbath was given not for purification but for testing; as the Lord says in Deuteronomy [Note: [Col. 1336D] Edition: “in the Law.”]: “I shall give them commandments, that I may test them whether they will walk in my ways or not” (Exod. XV, XVI). Hence the Lord speaks through the prophet Ezekiel, saying: “I gave them commandments that were not good, and judgments by which they would not live” (Ezek. XX). That is, O Jews, certain carnal matters were permitted you because you lived carnally; [Col. 1336C] but they ceased with the coming of the Gospel, as Ezekiel the prophet says [Note: [Col. 1336D] Edition: “as it is also said through the prophet”; for the following words of Hosea are incorrectly cited as Ezekiel’s.] “I shall cause all her joy and her Sabbaths to cease” (Hos. II)—understand, those of the Israelite people. Elsewhere, moreover, the Lord says that he hates them: “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isa. I).

I ask you, O Jews: if your Sabbaths are eternal, why did the Lord command them to cease? And if they are good, why did he hate them? But because you can offer no answer at all to so evident and subtle a pronouncement, with God’s grace preceding, accompanying, and following me, I shall briefly and carefully explain it to you.

These are the words of the apostle Paul: “That which is spiritual is not first, but that which is animal” (I Cor. XV). The first man begot us according to the flesh; the second man—namely, God and man Jesus Christ—through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit, made us spiritual children of God. Therefore, O Jews, when you were immature in knowledge and lived carnally, God first gave you carnal commandments, though not commandments that would remain forever, because he foresaw that you would sin and worship idols. “You had need of milk, not solid food” (Heb. V); for you were not yet able, nor even now are you able (I Cor. III). It was therefore not fitting, while you were still immature and [Col. 1337A] little children in the knowledge of God, to place pearls before you—that is, to impart spiritual sacraments—but rather to test or try you by legal burdens. If you had persevered in those commandments according to his good pleasure, he would have transferred you, together with the other children of the Church, to the spiritual sacraments of the Gospel and adopted you as spiritual children.

Thus the good commandments of God have become condemnatory for you because your sins demanded it, and hateful to God. God’s command saves those who obey it and condemns those who disobey it. The Sabbath, which you, O Jews, received as a gift, signifies rest of mind, so that the mind may not be wearied in this life by any craving for earthly desires. For *Sabbath* is interpreted “rest.” But you spend this idle festival of the Sabbath in feasting [Col. 1337B] and drunkenness.

[Note: [Col. 1337D] Isidore, *ibid.*] But perhaps someone says: If the Sabbath is not to be kept, why was it said among God’s commandments: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day” (Exod. XX)? And again: “For six days you shall labor and do all your work; but the seventh day is of the Lord your God: you shall do no work on it” (*ibid.*). The answer is that, in the work of the six days, the works of six thousand years are represented. For a thousand years are compared with one day before God, as the Prophet testifies: “For a thousand years in your sight are as yesterday’s day which has passed” (Ps. LXXXIX). The Sabbath of those days, therefore, is the time of the seventh thousandth year and the rest of the future kingdom and age, where there will no longer be any activity of affairs but only the rest of the saints. [Col. 1337C] For the Lord hates these temporal Sabbaths when he said: “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths” (Isa. I).

Observe, O blind and perverse people, who are without counsel and without spiritual understanding, observe the aforesaid words of God. The Lord did not say, “My new moons and Sabbaths,” but “My soul has hated your new moons and Sabbaths.” He rightly called them *your* Sabbaths, because they are no longer those which the Lord himself commanded, but those which you devised for yourselves, in which you might serve all the more abundantly feasting and drunkenness.

Perhaps you ask, O rebellious and unbelieving people, why Jeremiah said: “Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day, nor bring loads through [Col. 1337D] the gates of Jerusalem. And do not bring burdens out of your houses on the Sabbath day” (Jer. XVII). Hear me, then, you who are far from righteousness and observe circumcision and Sabbath without cause, and I shall show you how you ought to understand this sentence. He carries burdens on the Sabbath who, though believing in Christ, does not rest from sin. For Christ himself is the rest of souls, as he says in the Gospel: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI).

The question is again raised: why was the man who, as we read in the book of Numbers (ch. XV), gathered wood on the Sabbath day so cruelly slain by the people at God’s command? But this first and carnal man [Col. 1338A] who dared to violate the Sabbath prefigured the one who on the day of judgment is found with carnal work—that is, with wood, hay, or stubble fit as fuel for eternal fire. Gathering these things for his own destruction, when he is judged on the last day, he must be driven away by all the angels and immediately punished by the second death.

Again, O Jews, I return to speaking to you, because I desire you to share in all the good things which God has prepared for his elect. Therefore do not cut away the foreskin of your flesh, because after the institution of baptism, by which remission of sins is granted to all believers, it will be of no use to you. Abandon also the Sabbath which you customarily celebrate carnally. Show reverence on the eighth day—that is, the Lord’s Day—on which [Col. 1338B] our Lord Jesus Christ rose from the dead. Faithfully receive baptism; with devout mind submit yourselves to the sweet yoke of that same Lord and our Redeemer Jesus Christ, so that with the other faithful you may deserve to receive heavenly gifts.

As Isidore, doctor of Spain, says, [Note: [Col. 1337D] Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 24.] the holy apostles decreed that the Lord’s Day should be celebrated with religious solemnity because on that day our Redeemer rose from the dead. It is called the Lord’s Day so that, abstaining on it from earthly works and worldly enticements, we may serve only divine worship, giving this day honor and reverence because of the hope of our resurrection which we have in it. For, just as our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 1338C] and Savior rose from the dead on the third day, so we hope that we too shall rise on the last day. Thus on the Lord’s Day we pray standing, which is a sign of the future life. This is done by the whole Church, O Jews, which is established in this pilgrimage of mortality, awaiting at the end of the age what was prefigured in the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn of the dead.

Therefore hasten as swiftly as possible to wash away the stains of your former life in the water of the sacred font, in the name of the holy Trinity—the Father, namely, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—and gladly receive the remaining sacraments of ecclesiastical religion, without which you can by no means attain eternal joys [Note: [Col. 1338D] From the same work, *ibid.*, ch. 25.]. Furthermore, as has been said, show reverence to the Lord’s Day, [Col. 1338D] because it was revealed through the Lord’s resurrection not to Jews or pagans but to Christians alone, and from that very resurrection received its feast. It is the first day, which after the seventh is found to be the eighth. Hence Ecclesiastes says, with reference to the two Testaments: “To him seven, and to him eight” (Eccl. XI). The first Sabbath was handed down to be celebrated because it had formerly been the rest of the dead. But this was the resurrection of him who, rising from the dead, “dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. VI). Once such a resurrection had occurred in the Lord’s body—so that what the body of the Church hoped for at the end might first go before in its head—the Lord’s Day, that is, the eighth day, which is also the first, succeeded as the feast.

Moreover, O Jews, our Lord’s Day appears solemn also in the holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. It is the first day of the world: on it the elements of the world were formed and the angels created. On the same day manna was first given from heaven in the wilderness. For thus the Lord says: “For six days you shall gather manna, but on the sixth day, that is, on the Preparation, you shall gather double” (Exod. XVI). *Parasceve* means “preparation,” because then the Jews prepared their food, which they ate on the Sabbath, since they were not permitted to prepare it on the Sabbath day. The sixth day [Note: [Col. 1339D] Supply: *is*.] is the Preparation, which comes before the Sabbath. The Sabbath is the seventh day, followed by the Lord’s Day, on which manna first [Col. 1339B] came down from heaven. On it Christ also rose from the dead, and on it the Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon the apostles.

Understand, therefore, O foolish and malicious Jews, that already then, namely in the Old Testament, our Lord’s Day was preferred to your carnal Sabbath; already then it was indicated that on your Sabbath no grace of God descended from heaven, but upon our Lord’s Day, on which the Lord first rained manna.

It has been sufficiently shown to you, O unhappy Jews, by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, that the carnal commandments of the Law—namely circumcision, Sabbath, and sacrifices—have been made void [Col. 1339C] and rejected by God; and that the sacraments of the Church, instituted by the teaching of the whole Trinity—the Father, namely, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are acceptable to God and will remain until the end of the world. Yet although our Lord Jesus Christ forbade us to cast our pearls before swine (Matt. VII), nevertheless, because I deeply pity your miseries and desire you to be within the number of the elect, hear how the sacrament of the body and blood of this same Lord Jesus Christ is pleasing to God the Father and was prefigured by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 1340D] Isidore, *Against the Jews*, book II, ch. 27.].

The truth of this sacrifice, to be preferred and more necessary to the salvation of souls than can be expressed, was most plainly prefigured in Melchizedek’s offering. For this priest of God Most High, when he blessed Abraham, offered bread and wine to the Lord in sacrifice, as a mystery of the future sacrifice. Therefore the sacrifice of the nations was instituted before that of the Jews. This he first set forth as a type of the Son of God and man, Jesus Christ, to whom the Psalmist says in the person of the Father: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX), and again: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (*ibid.*). That is, according to the rite of this kind of sacrifice, which Christ fulfilled in his passion. Thus, as has been said, the Church’s sacrifice was instituted before that of the Synagogue.

Believers should therefore no longer offer Jewish victims such as Aaron the priest offered, but those which [Col. 1340A] Melchizedek, king of Salem, likewise sacrificed—that is, bread and wine—which through the words of blessing of Jesus Christ, the high priest, become the body and blood of that same Lord Jesus Christ. This is the truest sacrament of sacraments, concerning which our same Redeemer says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John VI).

Hear also, O foolish and malicious Jews, what most wise Solomon says of the same sacrament of the altar: “Wisdom built herself a house, and hewed out seven columns. She sacrificed her victims, mixed her wine, and set her table. She sent out her servants, saying: If anyone is little, let him turn aside to me. And she spoke to the foolish: Come, eat [Col. 1340B] my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you. Leave foolishness, and you shall live; and walk in the ways of prudence” (Prov. IX).

God’s Wisdom, therefore—that is, Christ—established for himself a house, namely the most holy Church, in which he sacrificed his victims, that is, the members of his body; and he mixed the wine of his blood and water in the cup of the divine sacrament. He prepared a table, namely the altar in the Church; he sent his servants, namely the apostles and teachers, to the foolish, that is, to all nations ignorant of the true God, saying to them: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you”; that is, receive the food of my holy body and partake of the cup of my sacred blood.

[Col. 1340C] Concerning this heavenly bread the Psalmist sang joyfully: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII). The angel eats it with a full mouth in the heavenly homeland. Man tastes it according to his measure, lest he fail on this road of pilgrimage. This true bread feeds the holy angels in heaven and refreshes on earth all believers from itself. For this reason the eternal bread of angels deigned to become man, so that he might nourish in himself also those who believe in him with the food of his body. How good and most glorious is this bread, which feeds the angels by vision, so that they may be satisfied with it in the heavenly homeland, and feeds those who believe in him by faith, lest they grow weary on this road of pilgrimage, tears, and tribulation.

Hence blessed Fulgentius, a man renowned for holiness, careful in expounding [Col. 1340D] the holy Scriptures and pleasing in speech, says: “That bread which gave itself to the angels for the joy of steadfastness gave itself to human beings for the remedy of health. And he who is the food of angels became medicine for us.”

You, O unhappy Jews, lost this most holy Eucharist—that is, the good grace of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—which the children of the Church received through grace, because you were always rebellious against the Lord and remained unbelieving toward his honey-sweet mouth. The lawgiver and judge himself reproaches you through Isaiah the prophet concerning this refreshment of the spiritual table, saying: “Behold, my servants shall eat, and you [Col. 1341A] shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall thirst; behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be ashamed; behold, my servants shall praise because of exultation of heart, and you shall cry because of pain of mind and howl because of contrition of spirit. And the just Lord shall kill you and call his servants by another name” (Isa. LXV), that is, Christian. For Israel is slain—that is, the Jewish people living carnally are cast off—and a people from the nations, serving God spiritually, succeeds. The Old Testament is taken from you, O rebellious and unbelieving people, and the New is given to us. As was said, the grace of saving food and the cup of the blood of Jesus Christ our Redeemer are granted to us, while you wither in hunger and thirst; and another name—that is, Christian—is given to the new people, and all things accomplished by Jesus Christ resound with newness of grace.

Hear me, then, O hard-hearted and stiff-necked people—I mean, me, a Christian man who wishes to rebuke you for your salvation on account of your long-standing unbelief. Hear what I say, listen to what I speak, heed what I warn. You hated God’s wisdom and were made guilty in your thoughts when you said to the Lord Jesus Christ: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of your ways” (Job XXI). Isaiah [Note: [Col. 1341D] Correctly in another manuscript: *Jeremiah*.] openly testifies to this, saying: “The wise have been put to shame; they are terrified and taken captive, for they rejected the word of the Lord, and there is no wisdom in them” (Jer. VIII).

For long-standing blindness has overtaken you; unbelief has turned you away from God’s worship; perversity has led you off the straight path of God’s commandments; obstinacy has hardened you against doing good; malice has made you guilty before God. Isaiah the prophet undoubtedly foresaw in the spirit this blindness of your mind when he openly said of you: “Bring forth the blind people, who have eyes, and the deaf, who have ears” (Isa. XLIII). Therefore, O unhappy people, you were driven out from God’s worship, because a people from the nations succeeded you through faith.

This blindness of yours is also noted by Isaiah the prophet, the Lord rejecting you and saying: “Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. VI). Truly, as has been said, blindness of mind has overtaken you, and unbelief has hardened you, [Col. 1341D] for you neither observe the Law, receive the New Testament, nor wish to understand the sayings of the prophets spiritually. Since, therefore, you live like beasts, you tend not toward life but toward eternal damnation [Note: [Col. 1341D] Isidore, as above, ch. 28.].

Behold: you neither accept the Savior’s coming on the authority of the Old Testament nor wish to believe that he has come. In the Law and Prophets you continually read of the conversion of the nations, yet you are not ashamed, as you ought to be, of your own rejection. You observe the Sabbath, which you know has been rejected by the testimony of Scripture. You circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, though you have lost purity of heart. But we, placed under grace, now recognize that all these acts and observances, which were signs of things to come, [Col. 1342A] have been fulfilled. For Christ has now fulfilled everything foretold by the sacraments of the Law; he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (Matt. V).

Therefore, when the truth came, the shadow ceased. Thus we are not circumcised carnally, because in the type of circumcision we are cleansed in the sacrament of the promised baptism. The Lord promises this through Ezekiel the prophet, saying: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements, and I shall give you a new spirit” (Ezek. XXXVI). We call Sabbath rest superfluous because we already hold the revealed hope of eternal rest. We do not sacrifice the sacrifices of the old Law, because through these sacrifices we recognize that Christ’s passion and the mortification of carnal vices were prefigured. We do not observe unleavened bread carnally, because, now purged of the malice of our former life, we walk in the new grace of faith. We do not observe distinctions of foods, because we discern all those things spiritually in human conduct which the diversity of unclean animals signified. We do not celebrate the eating of the paschal lamb, because “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V), and he was prefigured by that lamb; he “was led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Acts VIII). We do not observe the new moons, because in Christ the new creation has come: the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new. We do not observe the Feast of Tabernacles (*scenopegiae*), because holy people are the tabernacle of God, [Col. 1342C] in whom God dwells forever.

Again and again, O Jews, I return to you with admonition: both because I pity your manifold misfortune, and because charity constrains me to desire that you may belong to the number of God’s elect. I therefore believe that by now you have been so confounded by the many rebukes of almighty God, overwhelmed by so many testimonies of the Law, refuted by so many oracles of the prophets, and convicted by so many utterly true assertions of the holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, that you ought never again to resist or contradict such very true arguments.

Understand, therefore, the Old Testament spiritually; receive the New, not in part but wholly, [Col. 1342D] so that, renewed through baptism, you may be counted among the members of the Church. I do not wish you to remain with Moses in the land of Gilead beyond the Jordan, but, having crossed the Jordan under the leadership of Joshua son of Nun—that is, having received baptism—to enter with Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Virgin, who is truly the leader of all the faithful, into the land of promise. Certainly, if you remain with Moses in the land of Gilead beyond the Jordan—that is, if you do not receive Christ’s baptism—you will by no means be able to reach the land of promise, that is, the heavenly homeland. For, as the Apostle says, all these things happened to them figuratively (1 Cor. 10).

[Note: [Col. 1342D] Isidore, *Questions on Joshua*, ch. 14.]

This, then, was signified by the fact that Moses gave an inheritance in the land of Gilead beyond the Jordan to two tribes, namely the Reubenites and Gadites, and to the half-tribe of Manasseh [Col. 1343A] (Num. 32); while Joshua son of Nun, after the Jordan had been crossed, divided the land of promise by lot among nine tribes and the half-tribe (Josh. 13). Thus the first division of the inheritance was made through Moses; the second through Joshua son of Nun, and it is greater and better (Josh. 18). Yet Moses gave a possession beyond the Jordan only to two and a half tribes; the rest receive theirs in the land of promise after crossing the Jordan under Joshua son of Nun.
