This shows that more people were to receive the heavenly promises through the faith and baptism of our Lord Jesus Christ than obtained them through the Law. For the river Jordan signifies Christ’s baptism.

Those two tribes and [Col. 1343B] the half-tribe signified the earlier—that is, the Jewish—people. They are called two and a half tribes because those who lived under the Law had some slight knowledge of the holy Trinity—some of them, at least—but did not possess its perfect knowledge. The nine and a half tribes, however, which receive through Joshua the land of promise, as has been said, prefigured the new—that is, Christian—people, who through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and through the grace of the eternal promise received their inheritance by the washing, that is, after the crossing of the Jordan.

They are called nine and a half tribes, receiving their inheritance under Joshua, rather than a complete ten—the number called perfect and complete—because not even by the Lord’s coming or his incarnation was everything announced to us. Nor did Jesus Christ himself, God and man, explain everything in person; as he himself says to his disciples: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But the Spirit of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father; and he will take from what is mine and proclaim to you all truth” (John 16). The perfection and sum of all divine teaching, therefore, consists in the Holy Spirit. Thus no one can accomplish anything perfectly unless the Holy Spirit is present as helper.

At length, therefore, O crooked and perverse nation, which has long conducted itself in this world like beasts, without rational judgment and without spiritual prudence: lend a patient ear to my salutary admonitions, and receive with faithful minds the most true testimonies already cited [Col. 1343D] from the holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments—or rather, what is more glorious, from almighty God himself, lawgiver and judge—so that you may not be swallowed up with Dathan and Abiram in utter destruction, but, having received Christ’s baptism, may attain fellowship with God’s elect. Therefore cast out from your hearts the adamantine hardness of your breast, so that, instructed in the saving sacraments of the Church, you may deserve to be adopted into the new offspring of the children of God.

For this reason, O Jews, I return so often to speak to you: because, as I have frequently declared, I desire you to be joined to the number of the elect. I would indeed have great joy with you in the Lord [Col. 1344A] over your conversion, if I saw you, having received Christ’s baptism, united to the children of the Church. For the holy angels too will rejoice in heaven at your salvation, if, cleansed in the water of sacred baptism, you believe that Jesus Christ, redeemer of the human race, is one true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit. You also ought to rejoice with the highest gladness of heart, so that, joined to the children of the Church, your names may be written in heaven. Therefore do not contrive delays in obtaining the sacraments of heavenly grace, so that, rendered fit thereby, your names may be written in the book of life.

O foolish Jews, whose minds are estranged from the light of truth: how fortunate it is for you that the time of new grace has found you still living in this life. [Col. 1344B] Although you could not see in the flesh the Son himself of God and of the Virgin, nevertheless, if you devote yourselves to his evangelical sacraments, you will be able to obtain from him complete remission of sins. Nor do I wish you to be ignorant that you cannot recover divine grace or obtain forgiveness of your sins except through the holy catholic Church. For just as the friends of blessed Job could not make satisfaction to God by themselves unless Job had offered sacrifice for them, so you too will by no means be able to obtain forgiveness of sins unless you offer worthy satisfaction and true faith to God through the priests of the Church.

God’s manifold mercy is accustomed to assist human falls in such a way that hope of life is restored not only through baptism but also through repentance; divine provisions being so ordered, namely, that they cannot obtain pardon from him except through the prayers of priests. Therefore, O Jews, show reverence to the ministers of the Church as to fathers, and through them offer to God contrition of heart and confession from a pure mind, that you may deserve to become worthy to receive the grace of baptism.

Receive also from those same priests of the Church, with devout minds, the Creed of faith and the Lord’s Prayer, so that through them you may know briefly and by heart the rule of true faith, and avoid the wiles of heretical perversity. For “symbol,” as blessed Isidore says,

[Note: [Col. 1343D] Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 23.]

may in Greek be called an *indication*, [Col. 1344D] or a *sign*, or a *contribution*: that is, something which several persons contribute as one. For this is what the holy apostles did, each contributing into one whole, in these statements, what he believed. It is called an indication or sign because at that time, as the Apostle Paul says (2 Cor. 11; Phil. 1; Gal. 5) and as is related in the Acts of the Apostles (chs. 15, 19), many pretended to be apostles of Christ: they named Christ, indeed, but did not proclaim the tradition in its complete lines. Therefore they established this indication, by which one might recognize whoever truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules.

Finally, they say that this practice is observed also in civil wars, since the bearing of arms is alike—

[Note: [Col. 1345D] A corrupt passage, which should be corrected from the edition as follows: “since both the bearing of arms is alike, and the sound of the voice is the same, and the custom is one,” and so forth.]

—and the sound of the voice, that is, so that there may be one custom and the same methods of warfare. To prevent the stealthy intrusion of deceit, each commander gives his soldiers distinct *symbols*, that is, indications, or individual prescribed tokens, which in Latin are called *signa* (“signs”) or *indicia* (“identifications”); so that if someone is encountered concerning whom there is doubt, when questioned he may disclose the symbol—that is, the identifying sign—whether he is an enemy or an ally. For this reason the Fathers handed it down not to be written on parchment but to be retained in hearts, so that it might be certain that it had been learned not from reading, which sometimes reaches even unbelievers, but from the tradition of the apostles. Thus, when the holy apostles were about to depart, as has been said, to preach, they composed this token of their unanimity and faith.

The Creed, moreover, is the sign by which God is recognized, [Col. 1345B] and which believers accordingly receive, so that they may know how to prepare themselves for the contests of faith against the devil. In it, as blessed Isidore says, there are few words, but all the sacraments of faith are contained. For these things were gathered succinctly by the apostles from all the divine Scriptures, so that, since many believers do not know letters, or, if they know them, cannot read the Scriptures because of the preoccupations of worldly affairs, by retaining these in their hearts they may possess knowledge sufficient for salvation.

[Note: [Col. 1346D] From Isidore, Book I, *Sentences*, ch. 21.]

Therefore the Creed of faith and the Lord’s Prayer suffice, in place of the whole Law, for the little ones of the Church—that is, the simple—to attain the kingdoms of heaven. For the entire breadth of the holy Scriptures is enclosed in that same [Col. 1345C] Lord’s Prayer and the brevity of the Creed. Hence the prophet Isaiah also says: “I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a shortening over all the earth” (Isa. 28). But by this shortening is understood either what the Lord says, that the whole Law and the prophets hang upon two commandments, namely love of God and of one’s neighbor (Matt. 22), or the very brevity of the Lord’s Prayer or of the Creed, in which, as has been said, the entire breadth of the holy Scriptures is comprehended.

Therefore, O Jews, humbly request this Creed—that is, this sign of faith by which God is recognized—from the prelates of the Church; receive it with devout minds; write it with the utmost affection upon the tablets of your hearts; retain it by heart; establish it in your minds as the strongest foundation, other than which no one can lay another, [Col. 1345D] so that you may not be moved by the temptations of the devil or by the persuasions of wicked people. Though tortures compel you, though martyrdom threatens, though death is imminent, do not allow yourselves to be moved from the position of true faith. For the defense of true faith, willingly offer yourselves to the contest, so that you may attain the fellowship of Christ’s most unconquered martyrs and receive with them the palms of victory from the hand of that same eternal King, namely Jesus Christ, God and man.

Furthermore, it is necessary for you, O Jews, to know the rule of true faith [Col. 1346A] so that you may truly know how you ought to believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let blessed Isidore, therefore—

[Note: [Col. 1346D] Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, ch. 24.]

—to whom God, by a great gift of wisdom, enlarged holiness, come forward, if you please, and expound for you the norm of the catholic faith:

“This,” he says, “is the most certain faith of the Fathers after the Creed of the Apostles, which our teachers handed down: that we confess God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—one God, invisible, of one essence and the same power and eternity—such that, while the distinctive property of each person is preserved, the Trinity is neither divided substantially nor confused in any way personally. We also confess the Father as unbegotten, the Son as begotten, and the Holy Spirit as neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. The Son proceeds from the Father by being born; the Holy Spirit, however, proceeds without being born. We confess also that the Son himself took perfect humanity from the Virgin without sin, so that he might mercifully restore one who had fallen by free will, whom he had created by goodness alone. We confess that he was truly crucified, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven in that same glorified flesh, in which he is awaited as coming to judge the living and the dead.

“And although Christ, perfect in each of the divine and human substances, bore one person, he neither duplicated the person by the integrity of the two substances nor confused the two substances by the unity of the person. For one did not exclude the other, because the one preserved both in unimpaired right. The saving authority of the New and Old Testaments commended him: the one through prophecy, [Col. 1346C] the other through history truly fulfilled. Nor is anything to be thought concerning God or the creature of the world with pagans or heretics in those matters in which they dissent from truth; but only what the divine utterances testify in both Testaments is to be maintained. God created neither humanity nor all other things from any necessity; nor is there any visible or invisible substance at all except that which is God, or which is a good creature from the good God. But God is supremely and immutably good; the creature, however, is good in an inferior and mutable way. The nature of angels and souls is not a part of the divine substance, but a creature of God, made from nothing.”

This rule of true faith, as I have said above to you, O [Col. 1346D] Jews, inscribe upon the tablets of your hearts; retain it by memory; confess it with your mouths; declare it by works; show it by conduct; preserve it by life; preach it in speech. And, if necessary, contend even to the shedding of blood in its defense. Unless you keep this faith whole and inviolate, you cannot be saved. This is indeed the faith held by the Fathers of the Old Testament, namely the patriarchs and prophets; this the holy apostles and the other teachers of the New Testament preached; and in order to preserve it uncorrupted and transmit it to us whole and unstained, they willingly gave their bodies over to various [Col. 1347A] torments.

Concerning these holy Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, the prophet Ezekiel, speaking figuratively in his vision, said:

“There were chambers of the gate toward the eastern way, three on this side and three on that; the three chambers had one measure” (Ezek. 40).

Let blessed Gregory, of great reverence and usefulness in Christ’s Church, come forward—if it please you; indeed, because it pleases exceedingly—and expound this verse of such depth for us who desire to hear it. “We must inquire,” he says,

[Note: [Col. 1347D] Book II of the *Homilies on Ezekiel*, Homily 4, no. 4. See the Fathers, vol. LXXVI, col. 975.]

“what is meant by the words, ‘three on this side and three on that.’ For the chambers,” etc., as far as: “which filled the hearts of those who followed under the New Testament, as Paul also says: ‘But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written, “I believed, and therefore I spoke”; we also believe, [Col. 1347B] and therefore speak’” (2 Cor. 4).

Therefore believe, O Jews, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one true God, governor of the whole world, creator of the Old and New Testaments, and revealer of this true faith. Human wisdom did not invent this faith; rather, he who is three in persons and one true God in majesty himself showed it to his servants solely through his goodness. We must not, therefore, suppose one God of the Old Testament and another of the New, but one and the same creator of heaven and earth, lawgiver, and most just judge of all. For there is one lawgiver of the Old Testament and judge of all at the end of the world.

“For the ancient spiritual Fathers,” etc., as far as:

[Note: [Col. 1348D] See the same work, col. 977.]

“namely, of the Father, the Son, and [Col. 1347C] the Holy Spirit, is opened more generously.”

I therefore admonish you, O Jews, to offer true faith to almighty God and to love him in all things and above all things. Without that faith, as we have often said, you can by no means attain eternal salvation. Through this faith the holy Fathers of the New and Old Testaments made progress, and they handed it down to us to be held firmly. Concerning it Ezekiel, speaking figuratively of the vision shown to him, says among other things: “A man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze measured the threshold before the chambers, one cubit” (Ezek. 40). Blessed Gregory, explaining this, says:

[Note: [Col. 1348D] Same work, no. 13, col. 981.]

“What do the chambers signify,” etc., as far as: “the vision of our mediator will bring faith to its completion and perfect charity in his elect.”

[Col. 1347D] Therefore strive with all diligence, O Jews, that you may be counted among his elect, enjoy his most blessed vision, and after this life be comforted in the bosoms of the patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, namely, your fathers according to the flesh. With God’s help, I desire for this reason to advance you toward the true faith, without which you cannot be saved: so that the hardness of unbelief may be driven from your minds, and you may attain eternal joys with the children of the Church. To this end we have produced so many testimonies of truth and of the New Testament: that, putting aside the observance of carnal [Col. 1348A] ceremonies, you may receive the catholic faith with all devotion and prove yourselves worthy to receive the sacraments of ecclesiastical religion.

If you say that you are Abraham’s children, then you ought to hold Abraham’s faith. For he was a worshiper and knower of the holy Trinity—namely, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and therefore deserved to be called God’s friend. He saw three men and worshiped one, because he believed one God in Trinity and Trinity in unity. Since you boast that you are Abraham’s children, you also ought to believe what Abraham believed. What profit is it to descend from the stock of patriarchs and prophets yet to be degenerate from them through unbelief and hardness of mind? What benefit is it to be children of holy Fathers who believed in eternal life—in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and yet to be hurled with unbelievers into eternal destruction?

For the Redeemer of the human race, Jesus Christ himself, speaking to God the Father, says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). Therefore, O Jews, believe with us that the Son of God and of the Virgin is true God and true man; know without doubt that he was sent from heaven by God the Father for the redemption of the human race; firmly hold that by the triumph of his most victorious passion he destroyed death, conquered the devil, broke hell, rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven on the fortieth day [Col. 1348C] while his disciples watched, sat at the right hand of God the Father from whom he had come forth, and will come from there on the last day to judge the living and the dead, and the world through fire.

Love him, therefore, with pure and faithful minds. Through him hasten to ascend to the heavenly homeland by the steps of good works. Believe with us with all your heart that he, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, is one true God, containing all things, governing all things, reigning everywhere. Let us therefore pray together to him, who chose the patriarchs and prophets for the praise and glory of his name, that he may deign to open to you the incomparable riches of his knowledge and, raising children for Abraham from these stones—that is, changing the hardness and stubbornness of your minds into the sweetness of his love—and freeing you [Col. 1348D] from eternal death, may cause you to attain fellowship with his elect. Amen.

Meanwhile, dearest brethren, it is necessary that we who, constrained by charity, exhort the Jews to faith in and love of Christ should return to ourselves, and thoughtfully consider who we are, whence we have come, and the good things which we have received from the Lord’s most abundant kindness. Let us first consider who we are and whence we have come, who have brought forward these things from the Old and New Testaments and expounded to the Jews the judgments of the prophets and evangelists. [Col. 1349A] Certainly we have come from the Gentiles; certainly our parents worshiped wood and stones. Whence, then, have we these profound mysteries which we have thus far treated in their spiritual sense, and which even the Hebrews do not know?

Without doubt, it has been granted to us through Christ to understand spiritually the Scriptures of the Old Testament, which the Hebrews understand carnally, because they do not seek their spiritual fruit within but fix their step outside upon the letter. Let us therefore give thanks to God the Father, sweetest brethren, who through his only and most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, has deigned so nobly to instruct us in spiritual teachings and so mercifully to rescue us from the mass of the lost. Let us also give thanks to the same only Son of God the Father, [Col. 1349B] our Lord Jesus Christ, who, as blessed Gregory says, fulfilled in deed everything written concerning himself in sacred Scripture, so that things which could not be understood when heard might be disclosed when seen.

For there—in sacred Scripture—are contained the incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, and ascension. But which of us would have believed these things when heard unless we had recognized them as accomplished in the holy Scriptures? Therefore he of whom we speak, the Lion from the tribe of Judah, opened the sealed book, as is read in John’s Apocalypse (ch. 5), which no one could open and read, because in his passion, resurrection, and ascension he disclosed its mysteries to us. For by enduring the evils of our weakness he showed us the goods of his power and love. He became flesh [Col. 1349C] that he might make us spiritual; he graciously bent down that he might raise us to heaven; he went forth from the Father that he might bring us to [Col. 1350A] the Father; he appeared visible that he might show us invisible things; he endured scourges that he might heal us; he bore reproaches and mockery that he might free us from reproach; he died that he might give us life.

Let us therefore give him thanks, beloved, because he raised us with himself to eternal life. Thus Isaiah, contemplating our salvation and his passion, rightly says: “That he may do his work, his work is alien; that he may perform his work, it is foreign to him” (Isa. 28). Blessed Gregory, explaining this, says:

“The work of God is to gather the souls he created and recall them to the joys of eternal light. But to be scourged, smeared with spittle, crucified, to die and be buried—this is not in his substance the work of God, but the work of sinful man, who deserved all these things through sin. ‘Yet he bore our sins in his body on the tree’ [Col. 1350B] (1 Pet. 2); and he who remains always incomprehensible in his own nature deigned to be comprehended and scourged in our nature, because unless he had taken up the things which belonged to weakness, he would never have raised us to the power of his strength. Therefore, that he might do his own work, his work was alien; and that he might perform his own work, it was foreign to him: because God incarnate deigned to be scourged for us as a sinful human being, in order to gather us to his righteousness. And he performed an alien work so as to perform his own, because by enduring our evils in weakness he brought us, who are his creatures, to the glory of his strength; in which he lives as God with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1350C] through all ages of ages. Amen.”

## ORDER OF THE MATTERS CONTAINED IN THIS VOLUME

### ST MARTIN OF LEÓN

The printer to the reader. 9

*Life of St Martin*, written by Lucas, bishop of Tui. 9

CHAPTER I.—How Blessed Isidore miraculously gave wisdom to Blessed Martin, a canon of his monastery, by means of a little book which he compelled him to swallow. 9

CHAPTER II.—On the birth and family of Blessed Martin, canon of St Isidore, and on the names of his father and mother and the meanings of those names. 11

CHAPTER III.—On the praiseworthy life led by Blessed Martin from his childhood; and how, after the death of his wife, his father assumed the habit in the monastery of St Marcellus. 12

CHAPTER IV.—How Blessed Martin, after his father’s death, was advanced to the order of subdeacon and, in order to restrain the unlawful motions of the flesh, vigorously mortified himself through several holy pilgrimages. 12

CHAPTER V.—On Blessed Martin’s great abstinence while he was a pilgrim in Rome; and how he obtained favor in the eyes of the supreme pontiff and of those guarding the church of St Peter. 13

CHAPTER VI.—How Blessed Martin left the city of Rome for various other holy pilgrimages; and, arriving at Constantinople, bought a beautiful *planeta* [a liturgical chasuble] to carry back to his own region. 13

CHAPTER VII.—How, while Blessed Martin was returning home, he was seized in a certain city as though he had stolen the aforesaid *planeta*. 14

[Col. 1350]

CHAPTER VIII.—How, while Blessed Martin was in prison, an angel of God assigned to guard him came to him and delivered him, commanding him to return to León. 14

CHAPTER IX.—How Blessed Martin, immediately upon arriving at León, received the orders of deacon and priest, assumed the habit of Blessed Augustine in the monastery of St Marcellus, and there lived most honorably and praiseworthily. 15

CHAPTER X.—How the bishop of León removed the regular canons from the church of St Marcellus and introduced secular clerics; and how Blessed Martin transferred himself to the church of St Isidore, afterwards returned to St Marcellus, and finally went to St Isidore at Isidore’s command. 15

CHAPTER XI.—On Blessed Martin’s extreme austerity of life and abstinence, and on his holy manner of life while he lived in the aforesaid monastery of St Isidore. 16

CHAPTER XII.—How Blessed Martin, though old and infirm, began the great work of his books; how kings and magnates greatly revered him; and how, while he was alive, demons acknowledged his holiness. 16

CHAPTER XIII.—How Blessed Martin asked leave from his abbot to receive alms necessary for completing and writing his works; how he revealed to him that blessed Isidore had given him wisdom through a little book which he compelled him to swallow; and how he produced the works already mentioned and, besides them, the church of the Most Holy Trinity. 17

CHAPTER XIV.—How the smaller part of the customary portion given daily to Blessed Martin, as to the other canons, sufficed for his seven clerics, while the remainder of his portion was always left over. 18

CHAPTER XV.—How Blessed Martin cured the dean of León of quartan fever while they were disputing together over the sacred page. 18

CHAPTER XVI.—How Blessed Martin cured a noblewoman of pain in her breast. 19

CHAPTER XVII.—How Blessed Martin cured his fellow canon of a most severe toothache. 19

CHAPTER XVIII.—How Blessed Martin freed a certain boy who was in the monastery of St Isidore from quinsy. 19

CHAPTER XIX.—How Blessed Martin rescued from death itself a countess devoted to him, who was near death from the pains of childbirth. 20

CHAPTER XX.—How, by the counsel and revelation of Blessed Martin, the city of León defended itself against the kings of Castile and Aragon, who were besieging it. 20

CHAPTER XXI.—How Blessed Martin long beforehand knew the day of his death and revealed it to his brethren, to his prior, to the canons of St Isidore, and to others. 20

CHAPTER XXII.—How Blessed Martin, before departing from this world, handed over to his prior the keys and everything that he administered by the prior’s permission, and asked to be blessed by him. 21

CHAPTER XXIII.—How Blessed Martin, certain of his passage to glory, prepared himself for it with all his strength. 21

CHAPTER XXIV.—On the precious end and glorious passing of Blessed Martin, and on the notable teaching he left us concerning the most holy sacrament of viaticum. 22

Eulogies of certain persons concerning Blessed Martin. 23
